# Zig Guide Live

> A Zig tutorial and cookbook. Each build compiles and runs every snippet against current Zig master, and the snippets run in your browser as WebAssembly.

Source: https://www.ziglang.in/

Every Zig code block below was compiled and run by CI against current Zig
master before this file was generated. This guide tracks master, not a
tagged release, so anything here that contradicts a tutorial written for
0.13 or 0.14 is the current shape of the language rather than a mistake.
Unofficial and not affiliated with the Zig Software Foundation.

---

# Track: Foundations

The language and its standard library. Start here.

## Installation

*Getting Started. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/installation/*

This guide uses **Zig master**, not a tagged release. Each night, CI compiles and runs each snippet on this site against a new master build. The nightly run keeps the snippets correct. But a stable release cannot compile some of these examples.

## The full procedure

```
1. Download Zig master
        │
        ▼
2. Put zig on PATH
        │
        ▼
3. Run zig version
        │
        ▼
4. Install a matching ZLS
        │
        ▼
5. Write hello world
```

Only steps 1 and 2 are different on each platform. The other steps are the same on all platforms. Step 5 is [hello world](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/hello-world/), the next chapter.

## Get master

The easiest method is a prebuilt tarball from [ziglang.org/download](https://ziglang.org/download/). Do these steps:

1. Download the tarball under **master**, not the latest release.
2. Unpack the tarball into a directory of your choice.
3. Add that directory to your `PATH`.

<details>
<summary>Linux</summary>

```bash
curl -L https://ziglang.org/builds/zig-x86_64-linux-0.18.0-dev.xxxx+xxxxxxxxx.tar.xz -o zig.tar.xz
tar xf zig.tar.xz -C ~/.local
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/zig-x86_64-linux-0.18.0-dev.xxxx+xxxxxxxxx:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
```

The `xxxx+xxxxxxxxx` part is the name of the build, and it changes each night. Copy the current name from the download page, and put it in the two lines. If you do not change the commands, they do not work.

</details>

<details>
<summary>macOS</summary>

```bash
brew install zig --HEAD
```

Homebrew's `--HEAD` follows master. If you do not want to build from source, download the `aarch64-macos` tarball from the download page. Then add it to `PATH` in the same way as the Linux instructions above.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Windows</summary>

```powershell
winget install zig.zig
```

`winget` installs the tagged release, but this guide needs master. For master, do these steps:

1. Download the `x86_64-windows` zip from the download page.
2. Unpack the zip.
3. Add that folder to `Path` under System Properties, Environment Variables.

</details>

If you change versions frequently, a version manager does the manual step for you. A version manager works the same on all three platforms:

```bash
# zvm
zvm install master && zvm use master

# asdf
asdf install zig master && asdf global zig master
```

## Check the version

```bash
zig version
# 0.18.0-dev.xxxx+xxxxxxxxx
```

If the version does not contain `-dev`, it is a tagged release. Several chapters on this site do not build against a tagged release. If the shell cannot find `zig`, step 2 did not work.

## The version of this site

The footer shows the exact compiler that built and checked each snippet on this site. If your local `zig version` is different, expect small differences, because master changes each day.

## An editor

[ZLS](https://github.com/zigtools/zls) is the language server. The version of ZLS must be near the version of your compiler. If you use master, build ZLS from source against your Zig. A ZLS for an older release shows false errors on current syntax.

## Why master, and the cost

Zig does not have a 1.0 release yet. The language continues to change, and some changes break code. Thus a guide must select one of two targets:

- If the examples use a tagged release, they stay the same. But in less than one year, they are out of date.
- If the examples use master, they are correct today. But they can need a fix tomorrow.

This guide uses master. Each night, a build compiles and runs each snippet again against a new compiler. Thus the examples stay correct.

If an example on this site does not compile on your computer, check `zig version` first. A difference of some weeks usually causes no problem. A difference across a tagged release usually causes problems.

For software that you ship, a release is a reasonable choice. [Migrate from an older Zig](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/coming-from-older-zig/) gives a list of the differences, thus you can still use this guide.

## Keep Zig current

Master changes each day. Update one time each week. Then the changes come in small parts, and each change is easy to fix. Six months of changes at one time take much longer to fix.

```bash
zvm install master && zvm use master
```

When an update breaks your code, the error message usually tells you what changed. For example, a function has a new name, a function has a new parameter, or a namespace moved. The [what's new](https://www.ziglang.in/whats-new/) page records the changes that had an effect on this guide. Those changes are a good indication of the changes that can have an effect on your code.

## No other tools are necessary

Zig is one binary. It includes its own C compiler, and it can cross-compile to each supported target without more tools. It needs no separate build tool, because `zig build` is part of Zig. You do not need to assemble a toolchain.

You also do not install a package manager or configure a formatter. `zig fmt` is part of Zig, and it has no options. A debugger needs no special configuration. Use your current debugger on the binary.

Check your disk space. The tarball is several hundred megabytes. Most of that space is libc sources and headers for each supported target. Zig needs these files to cross-compile, and you download them one time.

## Hello World

*Getting Started. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/hello-world/*

This is the shortest Zig program that prints text. It is almost the same as the first program in each older Zig tutorial. It still compiles on current master:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// These four lines have two separate old habits: a `main` with no parameter,
// and output through `std.debug.print`. The two habits still work on current
// master, and each habit is independent of the other.
pub fn main() !void {
    std.debug.print("Hello, World!\n", .{});
}
```

*CI compiles this program against master each night, but this page does not run it. To follow the steps, save it as hello.zig. (`01-getting-started.older-main`)*

The four lines have two separate parts: the call that prints, and the signature of `main`. You can change one part and keep the other part.

A Run button on this site means that the browser sandbox can run the snippet. The Run button does not tell you which shape to prefer.

## When to use `std.debug.print`

`std.debug.print` needs no preparation and returns `void`. Thus you have no value to pass to other code and no error to handle. Use `std.debug.print` for lines that you will delete later. For example, use it to check that a loop runs, or to print a struct while you build a feature. You can use it as much as you like while you work.

Do not use `std.debug.print` for the output of a program. The first time that you use a shell, you will see the reason:

- stdout carries the data that a different program reads when you pipe this program into it.
- stderr carries the text for the person who runs the program.

The greeting above goes to **stderr**. Thus, if you redirect the program into a file, the file stays empty. To check, run `zig run hello.zig > out.txt`. The greeting prints to your terminal, and the program writes zero bytes to `out.txt`. The [standard streams](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/standard-streams/) chapter shows the two streams side by side.

There is a second reason. `std.debug.print` ends in `catch return`. If the write fails, the output is lost and the program does not know about the failure. For a temporary line, this behaviour is acceptable. For software that you ship, it is not acceptable.

Thus, use `std.debug.print` while you work. For the real output of the program, use a writer that the caller gives to your code. The other sections of this page use a writer of this type.

## Why `main` takes a parameter

The program above uses `pub fn main() !void`. On current Zig master, there is also a form that takes an argument:

```zig
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void
```

`init.io` is an **`Io`**. An `Io` is a value that gives the ability to do input and output. To write to a file, open a socket or read the clock, you give an `Io` as an argument. Thus code cannot block or start a thread unless a caller gives it an `Io`. There is no global `stdout`. Your code can write only if a caller gives it an `Io`.

The program below prints the same greeting on stdout, through the `Io` that `main` received. Press **Run**. The program runs in your browser as WebAssembly.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    try std.Io.File.stdout().writeStreamingAll(init.io, "Hello, World!\n");
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`01-getting-started.hello-world`)*

The caller selects the `Io` that it gives to `main`. The threaded implementation and the event-loop implementation are two of the choices. A later chapter, [the `Io` interface](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/io-interface/), explains them.

Zig's `Allocator` uses the same design. The `Io` applies that design to I/O: the caller supplies the mechanism, and nothing occurs without your knowledge. If you do not know `Allocator` yet, you can ignore it on this page. [Allocators](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/allocators/) is a later chapter, and nothing on this page needs it.

## Why `!void`, and when to remove the `!`

`void` means that `main` returns nothing. The `!` before `void` means that `main` can also return an error.

The greeting needs the `!` because of `try`. A write to stdout can fail. For example, the output can be a pipe that the other program closed, or a file on a full disk. In these conditions, `writeStreamingAll` returns an error.

`try` passes that error to the caller. The caller of `main` is the startup code of the program. Thus `main` must be able to return an error, and the `!` tells the compiler that it can.

When `main` returns an error, Zig prints the name of the error, for example `error: FileNotFound`. Then the program exits with status 1. A Debug build also prints the location where the error started. For a small program, this is an acceptable way to fail. Thus most examples use `!void`.

If you remove the `!` and keep the call, the program does not compile. Zig does not let you ignore an error. The compiler names the error set that the call can return. Then it tells you to use `try`, `catch` or `if`.

You can remove the `!` in two conditions:

1. Nothing in `main` can fail.
2. `main` handles each error itself, with `catch`.

For the first condition, look at `std.debug.print`. It returns plain `void`, thus the older program at the top of this page does not need `!void`. `pub fn main() void` compiles and prints the same text. Older tutorials write `!void` there because of habit.

For the second condition, look at this program:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) void {
    std.Io.File.stdout().writeStreamingAll(init.io, "Hello, World!\n") catch |err| {
        // If the return type has no `!`, handle each error here.
        std.debug.print("could not write the greeting: {t}\n", .{err});
        std.process.exit(1);
    };
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`01-getting-started.main-void`)*

The `catch` block receives the error and prints a message that a person can read. Then it exits with status 1. Nothing remains for `main` to return, thus its return type is `void`.

This form has more code than `!void`. It is useful when you want to select the message and the exit status yourself. For all other programs, `!void` with `try` is shorter, and you lose no information.

## Buffers, and the `flush` call

`writeStreamingAll` is sufficient for one fixed string. But real programs format their output. For formatted output, use a buffered writer:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    try out.print("{s} v{d}.{d}\n", .{ "zig", 0, 16 });
    for (0..3) |i| try out.print("  line {d}\n", .{i});

    // The writer writes nothing until `flush` empties the buffer.
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`01-getting-started.buffered-stdout`)*

From Zig 0.15, writers have a buffer, and the buffer is part of the **interface**, not of the implementation. People call this change *"writergate"*. You supply the memory, thus there is no hidden allocation.

There is a cost: **Zig writes nothing until you call `flush`**. If you remove the `try out.flush()` line, the program gives no output. The program formats the greeting and copies it into `buf`. When the program exits, the data in `buf` is lost. If a program must print text but prints nothing, first make sure that the program calls `flush`.

The **Edit** button opens the snippet, and the **Copy** button copies the source. To run an edited version, you need a Zig compiler in the browser. This site does not have one yet. Thus the toolbar tells you this and offers to send your version to an external playground. Each unedited snippet runs on this site.

## Run Tests

*Getting Started. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/running-tests/*

A `test` block is part of the Zig language. You do not import a test framework, register the test or add annotations to the test.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

fn add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 {
    return a + b;
}

test "a test is just a named block" {
    try expect(add(2, 2) == 4);
}

test "expectEqual reports both values on failure" {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 4), add(2, 2));
}

test "comparing slices" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("abc", "ab" ++ "c");
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u8, &[_]u8{ 1, 2 }, &[_]u8{ 1, 2 });
}

test "asserting an error is returned" {
    const failing = struct {
        fn f() error{Nope}!void {
            return error.Nope;
        }
    }.f;
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Nope, failing());
}

test "the testing allocator fails the test on a leak" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const buf = try gpa.alloc(u8, 10);
    defer gpa.free(buf); // remove this line and the test fails
    try expect(buf.len == 10);
}

test "skipping" {
    if (@import("builtin").cpu.arch != .wasm32) return error.SkipZigTest;
    try expect(true);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`01-getting-started.running-tests`)*

## Run the tests

```bash
zig test file.zig        # just this file
zig build test           # the test step of a build.zig
zig test file.zig --test-filter "name"
```

The tests in a file run only in these conditions:

- The file is the test root.
- The test root can get to the file through `@import`.

If no module imports a file, the tests in that file never run. Thus, if a test does not fail when you expect it to fail, make sure that some module imports its file.

## The assertion helpers

| Helper | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `expect(bool)` | general condition |
| `expectEqual(a, b)` | prints both values on failure |
| `expectEqualStrings` | string comparison with a readable diff |
| `expectEqualSlices(T, a, b)` | slice comparison |
| `expectError(err, expr)` | asserts a specific error |

Use `expectEqual` instead of `expect(a == b)`. When `expectEqual` fails, it tells you the actual values.

## Leak detection is on by default

`std.testing.allocator` makes the test fail if the test does not free all the memory that it allocated. You do not have to turn on this check or run a separate tool. Each test that allocates memory is also a leak test:

```zig
const buf = try std.testing.allocator.alloc(u8, 10);
defer std.testing.allocator.free(buf);   // omit this and the test fails
```

## Skip a test

`return error.SkipZigTest` marks a test as skipped, not as failed. Use it for a test that applies only to some targets.

## Where to put the tests

Put the tests in the same file as the code that they test. The standard library does this. Do the same in your code, for two reasons.

The first reason is access. Privacy in Zig applies to each file, thus a test in the same file can use private declarations. A test in a different file cannot use a helper that is not `pub`. A separate test file can make you change private declarations to public declarations without a good reason.

The second reason is that the test is also an example. A person opens the file to see how to call a function. Some lines below the definition, the person finds a call with real arguments and a checked result. People do not use documentation in a separate directory in that way.

The compiler does not put tests into your program. A `test` block exists only in a build from `zig test` or from a test step. Thus the tests cost nothing in your program, and you do not need to move them before a release.

## Give each test a name

The name is a plain string. Thus, write a sentence:

```zig
test "parseInt rejects a trailing space" { ... }
```

When a test fails, the runner prints its name. `--test-filter` also uses the name. Thus a description of the behaviour is more useful than a label. When a test fails, its name tells you what broke. You do not have to open the file.

## Read a failure

A failed assertion prints the values. Then it prints a stack trace that shows the line. The stack trace is available because the default build mode for tests is Debug, with the safety checks on. The safety checks also let a test find an out-of-bounds index. A release build does not find that error.

## These pages are the tests

CI compiles and runs each snippet in this guide. The snippets with `test` blocks report through this same runner. When you press Run, you see the real output of `zig test`. The test runs in your browser as WebAssembly.

The [testing](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/testing/) chapter has more information. It shows the assertions that report the differences. It also shows how to make sure that the error paths release their resources.

## Migrate from an Older Zig

*Getting Started. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/coming-from-older-zig/*

This guide uses **Zig master**. The version in the footer is the compiler that compiled and ran each snippet on this site. If you use a tagged release, some of this code does not build for you.

This site has no separate guide for each release. This page gives you the **delta**. For each change, the page shows what changed, the current shape, and the chapter that explains it. Usually, that is the information that you need.

If your code already builds on 0.16.0, read [What Changed in Zig 0.17](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/zig-0-17/). That page explains only the last step. It also tells you which old code still compiles and which old code does not compile.

<aside>

**Why you cannot run the old code below.** Each other snippet on this site has a Run button, because CI compiled and ran it. The "before" examples on this page show old code that *cannot* compile on current Zig. Thus this page shows them as plain code. CI checks the "after" side in the chapter that each example links to.

</aside>

## At a glance

| What | Before | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` signature | `pub fn main() !void` | `pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void` |
| Writers | unbuffered, no flush | buffered, **must** `flush` |
| File API | `std.fs.File` | `std.Io.File`, and takes an `Io` |
| Array repeat | `"-" ** 5` | `@splat` (`**` is **gone**) |
| `ArrayList` | `init(allocator)` | `.empty`, allocator per call |
| Mutex | `std.Thread.Mutex` | `std.Io.Mutex`, `lock(io)` |
| Custom `format` | four parameters, used by `{}` | one writer parameter, used by `{f}` |
| Enum reflection | `info.fields[i].name` | `info.field_names[i]` |
| `addExecutable` | source file directly | `root_module` |
| Search in `std.mem` | `indexOf`, `indexOfScalar` | `find`, `findScalar` |
| Format into memory | `std.fmt.bufPrint`, `allocPrint` | `std.mem.print`, `Allocator.print` |
| Allocator that finds leaks | `GeneralPurposeAllocator`, then `DebugAllocator` | `std.heap.SafeAllocator` |

---

## `main` takes an argument

This change breaks the first program that you write.

```zig
// before
pub fn main() !void {
    std.debug.print("Hello\n", .{});
}
```

```zig
// now
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    try std.Io.File.stdout().writeStreamingAll(init.io, "Hello\n");
}
```

`init.io` is an **`Io` instance**. It uses the same idea as `Allocator`, and applies the idea to all operations that can block. There is no global stdout. Your code writes only through an `Io` that a caller gives to it.

→ [Hello World](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/hello-world/)

## Writers have a buffer ("writergate", 0.15)

```zig
// before: appeared immediately
const stdout = std.io.getStdOut().writer();
try stdout.print("{d}\n", .{42});
```

```zig
// now: nothing is written until you flush
var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
const out = &file_writer.interface;
try out.print("{d}\n", .{42});
try out.flush();          // ← forget this and you get no output at all
```

The buffer is part of the *interface*. Thus you supply the buffer, and Zig does no hidden allocation. If you use an older tutorial, a common problem is that the code does not call `flush`.

→ [Readers and Writers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/readers-and-writers/)

## Filesystem moved onto `Io` (0.16)

```zig
// before
var file = try std.fs.cwd().openFile("data.txt", .{});
defer file.close();
```

```zig
// now
var dir = std.Io.Dir.cwd();
const file = try dir.openFile(io, "data.txt", .{});
defer file.close(io);
```

The rule is the same in all of the standard library: each operation on the disk takes the `io` instance.

→ [Filesystem](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/filesystem/)

## `**` no longer exists

```zig
// before
const dashes = "-" ** 5;
```

```zig
// now
const dashes: [5]u8 = @splat('-');
```

The error message for this change is not clear. `**` is not a token now. The compiler reports **"binary operator `*` has whitespace on one side, but not the other"**. The message does not tell you that `**` is gone. The change has no effect on `++` concatenation.

→ [Arrays](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/arrays/)

## `ArrayList` and hash maps are unmanaged

```zig
// before: the list stored your allocator
var list = std.ArrayList(u8).init(allocator);
defer list.deinit();
try list.append('a');
```

```zig
// now: you pass it to anything that can allocate
var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
defer list.deinit(gpa);
try list.append(gpa, 'a');
```

You type more code, but you can see the allocator at each call that can fail. The same change applies to `StringHashMapUnmanaged` and `AutoHashMapUnmanaged`.

→ [ArrayList](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/arraylist/) · [Hash
Maps](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/hash-maps/)

## Synchronisation moved to `Io`

```zig
// before
var mutex: std.Thread.Mutex = .{};
mutex.lock();
defer mutex.unlock();
```

```zig
// now
var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;
try mutex.lock(io);
defer mutex.unlock(io);
```

The only cause of a failure in `lock` is a *cancel* operation.

Seven declarations had the same change, and none of them has a deprecated alias. `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Semaphore`, `Condition`, `ResetEvent`, `WaitGroup` and `Pool` are not on `std.Thread` now. Each declaration that waits now takes an `Io` and is in `std.Io`. `std.Thread.spawn` did not move, and the four other calls for an OS thread also did not move. Structured concurrency with `io.async` and `Io.Group` is the better default. It also works on targets that have no threads.

→ [Migrate from `std.Thread`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/coming-from-std-thread/) ·
[Threads](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/threads/) ·
[Concurrency](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/)

## Custom `format` methods

```zig
// before
pub fn format(
    self: Point,
    comptime fmt: []const u8,
    options: std.fmt.FormatOptions,
    writer: anytype,
) !void { ... }
```

```zig
// now
pub fn format(self: Point, writer: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
    try writer.print("({d}, {d})", .{ self.x, self.y });
}
```

Also, **`{}` does not call the `format` method now**. To call it, use `{f}`. `{t}` prints the name of an enum tag or of an error.

→ [Advanced Formatting](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/advanced-formatting/)

## Enum reflection

```zig
// before
const fields = @typeInfo(Direction).@"enum".fields;
fields[2].name;
```

```zig
// now: parallel arrays
const info = @typeInfo(Direction).@"enum";
info.field_names[2];
info.field_values[2];
```

This change is recent. It came into master between `0.17.0-dev.644` and `dev.1441`. At that time, this guide had 53 snippets. Across approximately 800 commits of compiler updates, this change was the only one that broke a snippet.

→ [Enums](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/enums/)

## `build.zig`

```zig
// before
const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
    .name = "app",
    .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
    .target = target,
    .optimize = optimize,
});
```

```zig
// now: build the module first
const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
    .name = "app",
    .root_module = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    }),
});
```

→ [Zig Build](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/build-system/zig-build/)

## Renames that still compile

Each change above causes a compile error. The changes in this group do not cause an error. The old names are still in the standard library source, as aliases with the `Deprecated` mark. Code that uses the old names builds and runs exactly as before. Thus a tutorial can use an old name, and no tool reports it. This rule also applies to this tutorial.

```zig
// before
const at = std.mem.indexOf(u8, line, ": ");
const text = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "{d}", .{n});
const owned = try std.fmt.allocPrint(gpa, "{d}", .{n});
var debug: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
var seen: std.StaticBitSet(64) = .empty;
```

```zig
// now
const at = std.mem.find(u8, line, ": ");
const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d}", .{n});
const owned = try gpa.print("{d}", .{n});
var safe: std.heap.SafeAllocator = .init(std.heap.page_allocator, .{});
var seen: std.bit_set.Static(64) = .empty;
```

All of the `indexOf` functions moved to `find`. `Allocator.print` is the formatter that allocates. `SafeAllocator` also has a different shape. It takes its backing allocator as an argument, and `deinit()` returns a leak count, not `.ok` or `.leak`.

The run that compiles each snippet on this site also compares the snippet with the deprecated names in the standard library. Without that check, this guide would not find these new names.

→ [Strings](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/strings/) ·
[Formatting](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/formatting/) ·
[Allocators](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/allocators/)

---

## If you stay on a release

You do not need to upgrade quickly. For most work, a tagged release is the correct choice. This guide uses master, thus its code agrees with the current language.

Use this page to translate the code:

1. Read the chapter for the concept.
2. Change the syntax to the syntax of your release.

The *ideas* did not change: explicit allocators, errors as values, exhaustive switches, `defer` and comptime. Put your attention on these ideas.

---

## What Changed in Zig 0.17

*Getting Started. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/zig-0-17/*

The Zig team released 0.17.0 on 2 October 2026. This page gives a list of the changes between the 0.16.0 release and the 0.17.0 release. The list includes the changes that have an effect on everyday code: the language, the parts of `std` that most programs use, and `build.zig`. The list does not include compiler internals, OS ports and changes to the linker.

This guide now uses master, which calls itself `0.18.0-dev`. The changes after 0.17.0 are not on this page.

[Migrate from an Older Zig](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/coming-from-older-zig/) explains the larger changes from before 0.16, for example the buffered writers and the `Init` parameter of `main`. This page explains only the last step.

## The checks on this page

The program below runs each new shape on this page. Each night, CI compiles and runs the program against master, as it does for each other snippet on this site. The program uses only the new names, thus 0.16.0 cannot compile it.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Point = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };
const Color = enum(u8) { red = 1, green = 2, blue = 4 };

fn repeat(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    // `"-" ** 12` compiled on 0.16.0. On master `**` is gone.
    const rule: [12]u8 = @splat('-');
    try out.print("{s}\n", .{&rule});
}

fn reflection(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    // Names, types and values are parallel arrays now, not one `fields` array.
    const s = @typeInfo(Point).@"struct";
    inline for (s.field_names, s.field_types) |name, T| {
        try out.print("Point.{s}: {s}\n", .{ name, @typeName(T) });
    }

    const e = @typeInfo(Color).@"enum";
    inline for (e.field_names, e.field_values) |name, value| {
        try out.print("Color.{s} = {d}\n", .{ name, value });
    }
}

fn parse(text: []const u8) !u8 {
    return std.fmt.parseInt(u8, text, 10);
}

fn parseLogged(out: *std.Io.Writer, text: []const u8) !u8 {
    // `errdefer |err|` no longer parses. Catch, log, and return the error.
    return parse(text) catch |err| {
        try out.print("could not parse \"{s}\": {t}\n", .{ text, err });
        return err;
    };
}

fn describe(mode: std.lang.Optimize) []const u8 {
    // The build modes are lowercase: .debug, .safe, .fast, .small.
    return switch (mode) {
        .debug => "debug: every check on, no optimisation",
        .safe => "safe: optimised, checks kept",
        .fast => "fast: optimised, checks removed",
        .small => "small: optimised for size, checks removed",
    };
}

fn memory(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    // DebugAllocator is now SafeAllocator, and it takes its backing allocator.
    var safe: std.heap.SafeAllocator = .init(std.heap.page_allocator, .{});
    const gpa = safe.allocator();

    // std.fmt.allocPrint is now a method on the allocator.
    const owned = try gpa.print("{d} + {d} = {d}", .{ 2, 3, 2 + 3 });
    try out.print("gpa.print: {s}\n", .{owned});
    gpa.free(owned);

    // std.fmt.bufPrint is now std.mem.print.
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d} items", .{3});
    try out.print("mem.print: {s}\n", .{text});

    // stackFallback is gone. BufferFirstAllocator uses the buffer first.
    var stack: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var first: std.heap.BufferFirstAllocator = .init(&stack, gpa);
    const small = try first.allocator().alloc(u8, 16);
    try out.print("BufferFirstAllocator gave {d} bytes\n", .{small.len});
    first.allocator().free(small);

    // deinit returns a leak count instead of .ok or .leak.
    try out.print("leaks: {d}\n", .{safe.deinit()});
}

fn containers(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    // initEmpty() is gone. Declare the type and use .empty.
    var seen: std.bit_set.Static(64) = .empty;
    seen.set(3);
    seen.set(10);
    try out.print("bits set: {d}\n", .{seen.count()});

    // getLast() and getLastOrNull() became one method that returns an optional.
    var backing: [3]u8 = undefined;
    var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .initBuffer(&backing);
    try out.print("last of an empty list: {?d}\n", .{list.last()});
    list.appendSliceAssumeCapacity(&.{ 4, 8, 15 });
    try out.print("last: {?d}\n", .{list.last()});

    // The element now comes before the count. The old order still compiles.
    const rolls = [_]u8{ 6, 6, 1, 6 };
    try out.print("at least three sixes: {}\n", .{std.mem.containsAtLeastScalar(u8, &rolls, 6, 3)});
}

fn builtins(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    try out.print("@divCeil(7, 2) = {d}\n", .{@divCeil(@as(u32, 7), 2)});
    try out.print("@backingInt(Color.blue) = {d}\n", .{@backingInt(Color.blue)});
    const c: Color = @fromBackingInt(2);
    try out.print("@fromBackingInt(2) = {t}\n", .{c});
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    try repeat(out);
    try reflection(out);
    try repeat(out);
    _ = parseLogged(out, "300") catch {};
    try out.print("{s}\n", .{describe(.fast)});
    try repeat(out);
    try memory(out);
    try repeat(out);
    try containers(out);
    try repeat(out);
    try builtins(out);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`01-getting-started.zig-0-17`)*

The "0.16.0" blocks are different. They contain 0.16.0 code, and most of them do not compile now. Thus they cannot have a Run button.

On 2026-09-25, the author compiled each of these blocks with the two compilers, `0.16.0` and `0.17.0-dev.2056`. The error messages below come from that run.

On 2026-10-25, the author compiled the blocks again with the `0.17.0` release, and each block gave the same error. The program above also runs on `0.17.0`, and its output is the same as the output that CI checks on master.

## Summary

| What | 0.16.0 | 0.17.0 | Old code |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Array repeat | `"-" ** 5` | `@splat('-')` | fails |
| Struct and enum reflection | `info.fields[i].name` | `info.field_names[i]` | fails |
| Error capture on cleanup | `errdefer \|err\|` | `catch \|err\|` and return | fails |
| C headers | `@cImport` | `b.addTranslateC` | fails |
| Build mode | `builtin.mode == .Debug` | `builtin.optimize == .debug` | fails on `==` |
| Allocator that finds leaks | `DebugAllocator(.{})` | `SafeAllocator` | compiles, deprecated |
| Format into memory | `std.fmt.bufPrint`, `allocPrint` | `std.mem.print`, `Allocator.print` | compiles, deprecated |
| Empty bit set | `.initEmpty()` | `.empty` | fails |
| Last item of a list | `getLast()` | `last()` | compiles, deprecated |
| `containsAtLeastScalar` | count, then element | element, then count | **compiles, gives a different answer** |
| Arguments to `zig build run` | `b.args` | `run_cmd.addPassthruArgs()` | fails |
| Custom build steps | `makeFn` | a tool run with `addRunArtifact` | fails |

Read the last column first:

- "Fails" is the easy condition, because the compiler finds each of these changes for you.
- "Compiles, deprecated" continues to work for now.
- For the `containsAtLeastScalar` row, you must search your code yourself.

## `**` is gone

```zig
// 0.16.0
const rule = "-" ** 12;
```

```zig
fn repeat(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    // `"-" ** 12` compiled on 0.16.0. On master `**` is gone.
    const rule: [12]u8 = @splat('-');
    try out.print("{s}\n", .{&rule});
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `repeat` from `snippets/01-getting-started/zig-0-17.zig`.*

0.17.0 does not read `**` as one operator. It sees two `*` signs, thus the error is about a different problem:

```
error: binary operator '*' has whitespace on one side, but not the other
```

If you see that message on a line with `**`, the removal of `**` is the cause. `++` still joins two arrays.

→ [Arrays](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/arrays/)

## `@typeInfo` returns parallel arrays

In 0.16.0, the `@typeInfo` of a struct had one `fields` array. Each element had a `name`, a `type` and a default value. 0.17.0 divides that array into separate arrays. The arrays agree by index.

```zig
// 0.16.0
inline for (@typeInfo(Point).@"struct".fields) |f| {
    std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{f.name});
}
```

```zig
fn reflection(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    // Names, types and values are parallel arrays now, not one `fields` array.
    const s = @typeInfo(Point).@"struct";
    inline for (s.field_names, s.field_types) |name, T| {
        try out.print("Point.{s}: {s}\n", .{ name, @typeName(T) });
    }

    const e = @typeInfo(Color).@"enum";
    inline for (e.field_names, e.field_values) |name, value| {
        try out.print("Color.{s} = {d}\n", .{ name, value });
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `reflection` from `snippets/01-getting-started/zig-0-17.zig`.*

```
error: no field named 'fields' in struct 'lang.Type.Struct'
```

Each kind of type has the same change:

| Kind | 0.16.0 | 0.17.0 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| struct | `.fields[i].name`, `.type` | `.field_names[i]`, `.field_types[i]`, `.field_attrs[i]` |
| enum | `.fields[i].name`, `.value`, `.is_exhaustive` | `.field_names[i]`, `.field_values[i]`, `.mode == .exhaustive` |
| union | `.fields` | `.field_names`, `.field_types`, `.field_attrs` |
| declarations | `.decls[i].name` | `.decl_names[i]` |
| pointer | `.is_const`, `.alignment` | `.attrs.@"const"`, `.attrs.@"align"` |
| function | `.params[i].type` | `.param_types[i]` |
| error set | `.error_set.?[i].name` | `.error_set.error_names.?[i]` |

To read a default value now, use `field_attrs[i].defaultValue(T)`.

The helpers in `std.meta` also changed. `std.meta.fields(T)` is now a compile error with the text `deprecated in favor of @typeInfo`. `std.meta.Int` and `std.meta.Tuple` are gone. Use the `@Int` and `@Tuple` builtins. These builtins were already in 0.16.0.

→ [Enums](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/enums/) · [Inline Loops](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/inline-loops/)

## `errdefer |err|` is gone

In 0.16.0, `errdefer` could capture the error that the function returned. 0.17.0 removed that capture.

```zig
// 0.16.0
errdefer |err| std.log.err("parse failed: {t}", .{err});
```

```
error: expected block or expression, found '|'
```

Plain `errdefer` without a capture still works. When you need the error itself, do these steps where the error occurs:

1. Catch the error.
2. Do the work.
3. Return the error.

```zig
fn parseLogged(out: *std.Io.Writer, text: []const u8) !u8 {
    // `errdefer |err|` no longer parses. Catch, log, and return the error.
    return parse(text) catch |err| {
        try out.print("could not parse \"{s}\": {t}\n", .{ text, err });
        return err;
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `parseLogged` from `snippets/01-getting-started/zig-0-17.zig`.*

```
could not parse "300": Overflow
```

The function still returns the same error to its caller. The only change is the location of the code that handles the error.

→ [Errors](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/errors/) · [Defer](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/defer/)

## `@cImport` is gone

0.17.0 removed `@cImport`, `@cInclude`, `@cDefine` and `@cUndef`.

```
error: invalid builtin function: '@cImport'
```

Now the build system translates C headers. `b.addTranslateC` reads the header, and your code imports the result as it imports each other module.

→ [Import C](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/cimport/) shows the full configuration, with snippets that CI checks against master.

## Build modes are lowercase

The four modes are now `.debug`, `.safe`, `.fast` and `.small`. The type is `std.lang.Optimize`. To get the current mode, read `builtin.optimize`.

```zig
// 0.16.0
if (builtin.mode == .Debug) { ... }
```

```
error: no field named 'Debug' in enum 'lang.Optimize'
```

```zig
fn describe(mode: std.lang.Optimize) []const u8 {
    // The build modes are lowercase: .debug, .safe, .fast, .small.
    return switch (mode) {
        .debug => "debug: every check on, no optimisation",
        .safe => "safe: optimised, checks kept",
        .fast => "fast: optimised, checks removed",
        .small => "small: optimised for size, checks removed",
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `describe` from `snippets/01-getting-started/zig-0-17.zig`.*

Not all of the old names fail. These forms still compile, through aliases for the old names:

- A `switch` with `.Debug` or `.ReleaseFast` prongs.
- `const o: std.builtin.OptimizeMode = .ReleaseFast`.

A comparison with `==` does not compile. Thus you will see the error at an `if` on the build mode.

`builtin.mode` itself still works. The std source marks it for removal after 0.18.0.

`build.zig` has the same change. `if (optimize == .ReleaseFast)` fails, and `if (optimize == .fast)` works. On the command line, Zig accepts `-O fast` and `-Doptimize=fast`, and the old names also still work.

→ [Build Modes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/build-system/build-modes/)

## `std.builtin` is now `std.lang`

`std.builtin.Type` is `std.lang.Type`, `std.builtin.Endian` is `std.lang.Endian`, and the other declarations have the same change. For now, the old name is an alias. The std source marks the alias for removal after 0.17.0.

The target fields also moved. `builtin.os.tag` is `builtin.target.os.tag`. `builtin.cpu`, `builtin.abi` and `builtin.object_format` moved in the same way.

`std.gpu` has the new name `std.spirv`, and there is no alias.

## Allocators and formatting

```zig
fn memory(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    // DebugAllocator is now SafeAllocator, and it takes its backing allocator.
    var safe: std.heap.SafeAllocator = .init(std.heap.page_allocator, .{});
    const gpa = safe.allocator();

    // std.fmt.allocPrint is now a method on the allocator.
    const owned = try gpa.print("{d} + {d} = {d}", .{ 2, 3, 2 + 3 });
    try out.print("gpa.print: {s}\n", .{owned});
    gpa.free(owned);

    // std.fmt.bufPrint is now std.mem.print.
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d} items", .{3});
    try out.print("mem.print: {s}\n", .{text});

    // stackFallback is gone. BufferFirstAllocator uses the buffer first.
    var stack: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var first: std.heap.BufferFirstAllocator = .init(&stack, gpa);
    const small = try first.allocator().alloc(u8, 16);
    try out.print("BufferFirstAllocator gave {d} bytes\n", .{small.len});
    first.allocator().free(small);

    // deinit returns a leak count instead of .ok or .leak.
    try out.print("leaks: {d}\n", .{safe.deinit()});
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `memory` from `snippets/01-getting-started/zig-0-17.zig`.*

```
gpa.print: 2 + 3 = 5
mem.print: 3 items
BufferFirstAllocator gave 16 bytes
leaks: 0
```

That function shows four changes.

`DebugAllocator` is now `SafeAllocator`. It takes its backing allocator as an argument. `deinit()` returns the number of leaks, not `.ok` or `.leak`. The old name still compiles as an alias.

`std.fmt.allocPrint` is now `Allocator.print`, thus you call `gpa.print`. `std.fmt.bufPrint` is now `std.mem.print`. The two old names are aliases.

`std.heap.stackFallback` is gone, and there is no alias. `BufferFirstAllocator` does the same work. It gives memory from your buffer until the buffer is full. Then it gets memory from the backing allocator.

0.17.0 also removed some smaller declarations, with no alias:

| 0.16.0 | 0.17.0 |
| --- | --- |
| `std.fmt.bufPrintZ(&buf, fmt, args)` | `std.mem.printSentinel(&buf, fmt, args, 0)` |
| `gpa.dupeZ(u8, s)` | `gpa.dupeSentinel(u8, s, 0)` |
| `std.heap.MemoryPoolAligned` | `std.heap.memory_pool.Aligned` |

→ [Allocators](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/allocators/) · [Formatting](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/formatting/)

## Containers

```zig
fn containers(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    // initEmpty() is gone. Declare the type and use .empty.
    var seen: std.bit_set.Static(64) = .empty;
    seen.set(3);
    seen.set(10);
    try out.print("bits set: {d}\n", .{seen.count()});

    // getLast() and getLastOrNull() became one method that returns an optional.
    var backing: [3]u8 = undefined;
    var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .initBuffer(&backing);
    try out.print("last of an empty list: {?d}\n", .{list.last()});
    list.appendSliceAssumeCapacity(&.{ 4, 8, 15 });
    try out.print("last: {?d}\n", .{list.last()});

    // The element now comes before the count. The old order still compiles.
    const rolls = [_]u8{ 6, 6, 1, 6 };
    try out.print("at least three sixes: {}\n", .{std.mem.containsAtLeastScalar(u8, &rolls, 6, 3)});
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `containers` from `snippets/01-getting-started/zig-0-17.zig`.*

```
bits set: 2
last of an empty list: null
last: 15
at least three sixes: true
```

Bit sets do not have `initEmpty()` and `initFull()` now. Declare the type and write `.empty` or `.full`. These two forms also worked in 0.16.0.

```
error: struct 'bit_set.Integer(64)' has no member named 'initEmpty'
```

The error names `Integer`, not `Static`. The reason is that a small `Static` set is an `Integer` set internally.

The bit set types also have new names. `StaticBitSet` is `std.bit_set.Static`, and `DynamicBitSetUnmanaged` is `std.bit_set.Dynamic`. The old names are aliases.

`std.EnumSet` also lost `initEmpty()` and `initFull()`.

`ArrayList.getLast()` and `getLastOrNull()` are now one method, `last()`. This method returns an optional. `DoublyLinkedList.pop()` is now `popLast()`. The two old names are aliases.

`ArrayHashMap.setKey` does not allocate now. Thus it does not have an allocator argument.

→ [Set Operations on the Cheap](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/bitsets/) · [Stacks](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/stacks/)

## The change that the compiler does not find

`std.mem.containsAtLeastScalar` has its last two arguments in the opposite order now. In 0.16.0, it took the count, then the element. In 0.17.0, it takes the element, then the count.

```zig
// 0.16.0: "is there at least 1 copy of 5?"
std.mem.containsAtLeastScalar(usize, &.{ 5, 5, 1 }, 1, 5)
```

On 0.16.0, that call returns `true`. On 0.17.0, the same call asks "are there at least 5 copies of 1?" and returns `false`.

The two arguments are integers, thus the two orders are correct types. There is no error and no deprecation warning. If your code calls this function, examine each call yourself.

In 0.16.0, there was also a `containsAtLeastScalar2` with the new order. 0.17.0 removed it. Thus code that already uses `containsAtLeastScalar2` does not compile, and that is the easy condition.

## Other `std` moves

| 0.16.0 | 0.17.0 | Old code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `std.Io.File.OpenFlags` | `std.Io.Dir.OpenFileOptions` | fails |
| `std.Io.File.CreateFlags` | `std.Io.Dir.CreateFileOptions` | fails |
| `std.ascii.indexOfIgnoreCase` | `std.ascii.findIgnoreCase` | fails |
| `std.mem.writePackedIntNative(...)` | `std.mem.writePackedInt(..., .native)` | fails |
| `std.mem.byteSwapAllFields` | `std.mem.byteSwap` | compiles, deprecated |

## New builtins

```zig
fn builtins(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    try out.print("@divCeil(7, 2) = {d}\n", .{@divCeil(@as(u32, 7), 2)});
    try out.print("@backingInt(Color.blue) = {d}\n", .{@backingInt(Color.blue)});
    const c: Color = @fromBackingInt(2);
    try out.print("@fromBackingInt(2) = {t}\n", .{c});
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `builtins` from `snippets/01-getting-started/zig-0-17.zig`.*

```
@divCeil(7, 2) = 4
@backingInt(Color.blue) = 4
@fromBackingInt(2) = green
```

`@divCeil` divides and rounds up. Like `@divTrunc`, it assumes that the divisor is never zero. If you want an error instead, `std.math.divCeil` is still available.

`@backingInt` reads the integer below an enum or a packed struct. `@fromBackingInt` does the opposite operation. For those types, these builtins do the work of `@intFromEnum`, `@enumFromInt` and `@bitCast`. The old builtins still work, and the 0.17.0 language reference marks them deprecated.

`@bitCast` can now also make an enum. 0.16.0 did not accept that.

## `build.zig`

A project from `zig init` on 0.16.0 fails on 0.17.0. It fails before the compiler gets to your own code.

### `zig build run -- args`

The generated `build.zig` passed command-line arguments in this way:

```zig
// 0.16.0
if (b.args) |args| run_cmd.addArgs(args);
```

```
error: no field named 'args' in struct 'Build'
```

On 0.17.0, `zig init` writes this one line:

```zig
run_cmd.addPassthruArgs();
```

### Paths on `b`

`b.build_root`, `b.install_path`, `b.install_prefix`, `b.cache_root`, `b.pathFromRoot()` and `b.getInstallPath()` are gone.

The project root is now `b.root`. Settings such as `verbose` and `release_mode` moved to `b.graph`.

### Custom steps

In 0.16.0, you could write a step in Zig with `makeFn`, and the step ran in the build runner. That feature is gone.

Now `build.zig` only describes the build. A separate process reads that description and runs the steps.

```
error: no field named 'id' in struct 'Build.Step.StepOptions'
```

There is no direct replacement for a custom `makeFn`. Do these steps:

1. Write the work as a small Zig program.
2. Build the program with `b.addExecutable`.
3. Run the program with `b.addRunArtifact`.

### Renames that still compile

| 0.16.0 | 0.17.0 |
| --- | --- |
| `b.lazyDependency` | `b.dependencyLazy` |
| `b.runAllowFail` | `b.runFallible` |
| `run.addOutputFileArg` | `run.addOutputFileArg2` |
| `run.addDirectoryArg` | `run.addDirectoryArg2` |
| `run.addArtifactArg` | `run.addArtifactArg2` |
| `run.addFileContentArg` | `run.addFileContentArg2` |
| `run.addPrefixedFileArg` and the other `addPrefixed*` helpers | the `*2` version, with `.prefix` in its options |

### Flags

`zig build` does not accept `--global-cache-dir`, `--zig-lib-dir` or `--build-runner` now. `--zig-lib=<path>` replaces `--zig-lib-dir`. Look for these flags in your CI scripts.

### The parts that did not change

Most of a normal `build.zig` compiles without a change. `b.createModule`, `b.addExecutable` with `root_module`, `b.addTest`, `b.addRunArtifact`, `b.option`, `b.standardTargetOptions` and `b.standardOptimizeOption` all work as before.

→ [Zig Build](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/build-system/zig-build/)

## What did not change

On 2026-09-25, a comparison of the public declarations in 0.16.0 and in master (`0.17.0-dev.2056`) found no difference for each item in this list:

- `std.json`
- `std.Thread`
- `std.Io.Dir` and `std.Io.Reader`
- the reader and writer on `std.Io.File`
- `std.process.Init`

The larger changes occurred before 0.16.0. For example, `main` started to take `std.process.Init`, the writers got a buffer, the filesystem functions moved onto `Io`, and `ArrayList` became unmanaged. `std.mem.find` also replaced `indexOf` before 0.16.0.

If your code already builds on 0.16.0, those changes have no effect on your code. [Migrate from an Older Zig](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/coming-from-older-zig/) explains them.

---

## Assignment

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/assignment/*

Zig has two ways to declare a value. The default is the immutable one.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "const and var" {
    const constant: i32 = 5; // cannot get a new value
    var variable: u32 = 5000; // can get a new value
    variable += 1;

    // The compiler can infer the type from the value.
    const inferred_constant = @as(i32, 5);
    var inferred_variable = @as(u32, 5000);
    inferred_variable += 1;

    try expect(constant == 5);
    try expect(variable == 5001);
    try expect(inferred_constant == 5);
    try expect(inferred_variable == 5001);
}

test "undefined leaves memory uninitialised" {
    // `undefined` means "I will assign this before I read it". A read before
    // the assignment is illegal behaviour. The value is not always zero.
    var x: i32 = undefined;
    x = 7;
    try expect(x == 7);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.assignment`)*

## Use `const` unless you must change the value

`const` is not a hint. The compiler enforces it. A new assignment to a `const` is a compile error. A `var` that you never change is also a compile error.

If you know C, the second rule can surprise you. Because of this rule, a `var` in Zig always means *this value changes*.

This rule helps when you read code that you do not know. For each `const`, you can find its single assignment and stop. For each `var`, you must follow all of its changes. Some languages use `var` as the default and allow a `var` that never changes. In those languages, the difference gives no information, because most variables are `var` only from habit.

The same rule applies to unused declarations. They are errors, not warnings. Zig has no lint level to change here. If the code does not use a variable now, the code does not build until you remove the variable.

## `const` is about the binding, not the contents

A `const` slice or pointer prevents a new assignment to the variable. It does not prevent a write through the slice or pointer:

```zig
const items = try allocator.alloc(u8, 4);
items[0] = 1;        // fine: items still points at the same memory
items = other;       // error: cannot assign to constant
```

The element type controls the write. You cannot write through a `[]const u8`. You can write through a `[]u8`, and the `const` or `var` of the variable does not change this.

These are two separate questions. The answer to one question tells you nothing about the other question. [Pointers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/pointers/) has the same split for `*T`.

## The compiler infers types, but literals have no size

Type annotations are optional when the compiler can infer the type. `@as(i32, 5)` is an explicit cast. The snippet uses it to give a fixed type to a value that would otherwise be an untyped `comptime_int`.

This explains an error message that you will see early. A bare `5` is not an `i32`. It is a `comptime_int`, an integer of arbitrary precision that exists only during compilation. It coerces to the type that the context needs. When there is no context, it has no type to coerce to:

```zig
const a = 5;             // comptime_int, fine as long as it stays comptime
var b = 5;               // error: must be const or comptime
var c: u8 = 5;           // fine: the annotation gives the literal a size
```

A `var` must be in memory at runtime, and memory cannot hold a value of arbitrary precision. The fix is always the same: write the size that you want.

## `undefined` is a promise, not a value

```zig
var x: i32 = undefined;
```

This line means "I will write to this variable before I read it". It does **not** mean zero. If you read `x` before an assignment, the result is illegal behaviour.

In a build with safety checks, Zig fills the memory with `0xaa` bytes. Thus the mistake is easy to see. The value does not look like a normal value.

Zig selects `0xaa` on purpose:

- As a pointer, the value is very far out of range.
- As a length, the value is very large.
- As a float, the value is a signalling NaN.
- As a signed integer, the value is negative, which is easy to see.

Thus a bug that reads uninitialised memory usually gives a value that you see. It does not give a zero that looks correct and that is by chance the right answer in your test.

In ReleaseFast, Zig does not fill the memory. The memory contains the old data. Thus use `undefined` for buffers that you fill immediately. When you want zero, write `var x: i32 = 0`.

---

## Arrays

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/arrays/*

You write an array as `[N]T`. The length `N` is part of the *type*. Thus `[3]u8` and `[4]u8` are as different as `u8` and `u16`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "array literal and length" {
    const message = [5]u8{ 'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o' };
    try expect(message.len == 5);

    // `_` infers the length from the literal.
    const alt = [_]u8{ 'w', 'o', 'r', 'l', 'd' };
    try expect(alt.len == 5);
}

test "arrays are values, not pointers" {
    const a = [_]i32{ 1, 2, 3 };
    var b = a; // a full copy
    b[0] = 99;
    try expect(a[0] == 1);
    try expect(b[0] == 99);
}

test "concatenate at comptime" {
    const joined = [_]i32{ 1, 2 } ++ [_]i32{ 3, 4 };
    try expect(joined.len == 4);
    try expect(joined[3] == 4);
}

test "repeat with @splat" {
    // Older tutorials show `"-" ** 5`. The `**` repeat operator does not
    // exist on master (`**` is not even a token). Thus use `@splat`. It fills
    // an array of known length with one value.
    const dashes: [5]u8 = @splat('-');
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, &dashes, "-----"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.arrays`)*

## Arrays are values

When you assign an array, Zig copies the array. C does the opposite: in almost all expressions, a C array changes into a pointer. If you want a reference, take one explicitly with `&`. The result is a [slice](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/slices/).

`.len` is a compile-time constant. The program does not read it from a field at runtime.

An array is a value. Thus, when you give a `[4096]u8` to a function, the compiler can pass all 4096 bytes. When you give `&buffer`, the call passes a slice, which is a pointer and a length. For data that is larger than a few words, pass the slice.

## Write an array literal

With `[_]T`, the compiler counts the elements for you. Use this form, because then the length always agrees with the contents:

```zig
const a = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };        // [3]u8
const grid = [2][3]u8{             // rows of columns
    .{ 1, 2, 3 },
    .{ 4, 5, 6 },
};
```

Multidimensional arrays are arrays of arrays. Thus `grid[1][2]` is 6, and `grid.len` is 2, the number of rows. Zig has no separate matrix type, and no index syntax with commas.

## Compare and join arrays

`==` does not work on arrays:

```
error: operator == not allowed for type '[3]u8'
```

Zig does not make a silent selection between a comparison of the contents and a comparison of the addresses. To compare the contents, use `std.mem.eql(u8, &a, &b)`. This function takes slices. Thus it also compares an array with a slice of a larger buffer.

`++` joins arrays at compile time. The result is an array, and its length is the sum of the two lengths:

```zig
const joined = a ++ [_]u8{ 4 };    // [4]u8
```

The compiler must know the two operands, because the *type* of the result depends on their lengths. To join runtime data, copy the data into a buffer. No operator does this.

## `**` is gone

Older tutorials, and the current zig.guide too, show array repetition:

```zig
const dashes = "-" ** 5;   // does not compile on master
```

The `**` operator does not exist now. `**` is not even a token. Thus the compiler gives a message about whitespace around `*`, and the message is not clear. Use `@splat` instead:

```zig
const dashes: [5]u8 = @splat('-');
```

`@splat` gets its length from the type of the destination. Thus the type annotation is necessary here. The same builtin fills a [vector](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/vectors/). Read it as "each element gets this value", and the meaning is correct for the two uses.

The change does not affect `++`. It still joins arrays at comptime.

## Coercion to slices

When you take a reference to an array, the array coerces to a slice of the same element type. The slice gets the length too:

```zig
const s: []const u8 = &a;    // len 3, checked
```

The usual direction is from array to slice. Make the data with an array, where the compiler knows the size and the memory is on the stack. Then pass a slice, where the length moves with the pointer.

The other direction, from a slice to a fixed-size array, needs a length that the compiler knows. [Array recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/array-recipes/) explains this direction. That chapter also shows grids and tables that the compiler calculates at compile time.

---

## If Expressions

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/if-expressions/*

In Zig, `if` is a control-flow statement. It is also an expression that can give a value.

C, JavaScript and most other languages have truthy and falsy values. Zig does not. The condition must be a `bool`, and no other type converts to `bool`.

Zig also has no ternary `?:`. An `if` that you use as an expression does that job: `const x = if (a) 1 else 2;`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "if as a statement" {
    const a = true;
    var x: u16 = 0;
    if (a) {
        x += 1;
    } else {
        x += 2;
    }
    try expect(x == 1);
}

test "if as an expression" {
    const a = true;
    // This replaces the ternary operator. The two branches must give the
    // same type.
    const x: u16 = if (a) 1 else 2;
    try expect(x == 1);
}

test "if unwraps an optional" {
    const maybe: ?u8 = 42;
    const doubled: u16 = if (maybe) |value| value * 2 else 0;
    try expect(doubled == 84);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.if-expressions`)*

Zig has no truthiness. `if (1)` does not compile, and `if (pointer)` does not compile. The condition must be a `bool`:

```
error: expected type 'bool', found 'u8'
```

This rule removes a full family of bugs, where code uses a value as a flag by accident. Some examples from C:

- `if (strcmp(a, b))` is true when the strings are *different*.
- `if (n = 0)` is an assignment, and it is always false.
- `if (ptr)` and `if (*ptr)` have one character of difference, but their meanings are completely different.

None of these examples parse in Zig.

## `if` gives a value

Zig has no ternary operator, because it does not need one:

```zig
const x: u16 = if (a) 1 else 2;
```

The two branches must have the same type. When you use `if` as an expression, the `else` is necessary. Without the `else`, the absent branch gives `void`, and the error gives the name of that type:

```
error: expected type 'u16', found 'void'
```

An `if` with no `else` has no value when the condition is false. Thus its type is `void`. Read the message as "this expression does not always give a value".

One case gets past this rule: a condition that the compiler knows. If the compiler knows the condition at comptime, it compiles only the branch that runs. Thus `const x: u16 = if (true) 1;` builds. If you make the condition a runtime value, the build fails.

This is not a special rule for `if`. It is the same constant folding that lets the compiler remove `comptime` code fully.

## Unwrap an optional

You also use `if` to get the value inside an optional, with a payload capture:

```zig
if (maybe) |value| {
    // value is the payload, not the optional
} else {
    // maybe was null
}
```

The captured `value` is a copy. To change the value inside the optional, capture by pointer with `|*value|`, and write through the pointer. Without the `*`, the change goes to the copy, and the change is lost. Remember this, because the compiler gives no warning.

Error unions use the same shape. The error goes to the `else`:

```zig
if (parse(text)) |n| {
    use(n);
} else |err| {
    report(err);
}
```

This idea occurs again and again in Zig. The check and the unwrap are one construct, thus they always agree. No code can test for null and then read the payload through a different path that does not do the test.

## Shorter forms

`if` on an optional is the general form. Three shorter forms are for the common cases:

- `maybe orelse default`, when you only want a fallback value.
- `try f()`, when you only want to return the error to the caller.
- `f() catch |err| ...`, when you want to handle the error here.

Use `if` when the two sides do real work. Use a short form when one side is a single expression. `x orelse 0` says the same as `if (x) |v| v else 0` in a quarter of the space.

[Optionals](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/optionals/) explains optionals, and [errors](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/errors/) explains the error forms.

---

## While Loops

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/while-loops/*

The counting loop in Zig is `while (i < n) : (i += 1)`. The continue expression after the colon runs after each iteration. It also runs after an iteration that `continue` ends early.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "basic while" {
    var i: u8 = 2;
    while (i < 100) {
        i *= 2;
    }
    try expect(i == 128);
}

test "while with a continue expression" {
    // The continue expression runs after each iteration, also after one that
    // `continue` ends. Thus it is different from the last statement of the body.
    var sum: u8 = 0;
    var i: u8 = 1;
    while (i <= 10) : (i += 1) {
        sum += i;
    }
    try expect(sum == 55);
}

test "break and continue" {
    var sum: u8 = 0;
    var i: u8 = 0;
    while (i <= 3) : (i += 1) {
        if (i == 2) continue;
        sum += i;
    }
    try expect(sum == 4); // 0 + 1 + 3
}

test "while as an expression with else" {
    // `break x` gives a value. `else` runs when the loop ends normally.
    var i: u8 = 0;
    const found = while (i < 10) : (i += 1) {
        if (i * i > 20) break i;
    } else 0;
    try expect(found == 5);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.while-loops`)*

`while` takes a condition, and runs the body until the condition becomes false. Zig has no C-style `for (init; cond; step)`. A `while` with a continue expression is that loop. Zig uses `for` only for a value that has elements.

## The continue expression

```zig
while (i <= 10) : (i += 1) { ... }
```

The `: (i += 1)` part runs after **each** iteration. It also runs after an iteration that `continue` ends early. For this reason, the continue expression exists. You could put the increment at the end of the body, but when the loop uses `continue`, the two forms are not the same. The bug that results is easy to miss.

For example, this loop stops:

```zig
while (i < 10) : (i += 1) {
    if (skip(i)) continue;
    work(i);
}
```

This loop does not stop:

```zig
while (i < 10) {
    if (skip(i)) continue;   // i never advances
    work(i);
    i += 1;
}
```

The two loops look the same. But the second loop does not stop the first time that `skip` returns true. When the step is in the continue expression, the structure makes it impossible for a `continue` to skip the step.

If necessary, the continue expression can hold more than one statement, as a block: `: ({ i += 1; n += 1; })`.

## Loop until there are no more values

When the condition is an optional, the loop binds its payload. The loop ends when the optional is null. Code in the standard library uses almost all iterators in this way:

```zig
while (it.next()) |item| {
    // item is the payload, not the optional
}
```

There is no separate call that asks "is there another one". There is also no sentinel value to compare against. The same shape works with a continue expression. Thus a loop that counts the items of an iterator is one line:

```zig
while (it.next()) |_| : (n += 1) {}
```

The capture syntax is the same syntax that `if` uses. [Payload captures](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/payload-captures/) is the chapter about this syntax.

A condition that is an error union works in the same way. The error goes to an `else` capture:

```zig
while (stream.next()) |chunk| {
    consume(chunk);
} else |err| {
    return err;
}
```

The loop body runs on each success. The `else` runs one time, with the error that ended the loop.

## Loops that produce values

`break` can carry a value. A `while` can have an `else` branch, which runs when the loop ends without a `break`:

```zig
const found = while (i < 10) : (i += 1) {
    if (i * i > 20) break i;
} else 0;
```

This code is a search with a fallback, as one expression. It needs no sentinel variable, and you cannot forget the "not found" case. [Loops as expressions](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/loops-as-expressions/) gives the rules, and the error that the compiler gives when there is no `else`.

## Infinite loops

`while (true)` is the usual infinite loop, and the compiler knows that it cannot end normally. When you use it as an expression, it needs no `else`, because `break` is the only exit.

Use `while (true)` when the code decides the exit condition in the middle of the body, not at the top. This is usual for code that reads input until it sees a terminator.

## Give the loop a name

A `while` can have a label. Thus `break :outer` and `continue :outer` work on it exactly as they do on `for`. See [labelled loops](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-loops/). That chapter also explains one rule that can surprise you: a labelled `continue` still runs the continue expression of that loop.

---

## For Loops

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/for-loops/*

In Zig, `for` loops over a slice, an array or a range. To get the index, add a second sequence to the loop: `for (items, 0..) |item, index|`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "iterate values" {
    const string = [_]u8{ 'a', 'b', 'c' };
    var count: usize = 0;
    for (string) |character| {
        if (character == 'b') count += 1;
    }
    try expect(count == 1);
}

test "iterate with an index" {
    const string = [_]u8{ 'a', 'b', 'c' };
    var last_index: usize = 0;
    for (string, 0..) |_, index| {
        last_index = index;
    }
    try expect(last_index == 2);
}

test "ranges" {
    var sum: usize = 0;
    for (0..5) |i| sum += i;
    try expect(sum == 10);
}

test "iterate two sequences at once" {
    // A `for` over many sequences needs equal lengths. Zig checks the lengths.
    const names = [_][]const u8{ "a", "b" };
    const scores = [_]u8{ 1, 2 };
    var total: u8 = 0;
    for (names, scores) |name, score| {
        _ = name;
        total += score;
    }
    try expect(total == 3);
}

test "mutate through a pointer capture" {
    var numbers = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    for (&numbers) |*n| n.* *= 2;
    try expect(numbers[2] == 6);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.for-loops`)*

Zig has no `for` with three clauses, such as `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)`. Use `while` for that. The `for` loop gets its length from the sequence. Thus you never write the bound yourself, and the common case cannot have an off-by-one error.

## You get an index only when you ask

```zig
for (items, 0..) |item, index| { ... }
```

The `0..` is not special syntax. It is a second sequence, and the loop moves through the two sequences in step. You get an index only when you ask for one. The loop still cannot go past the end, because the length of `items` sets the number of iterations.

## Iterate over several sequences together

The same mechanism pairs any number of sequences:

```zig
for (names, scores) |name, score| { ... }
```

The lengths must be equal. When the compiler knows the two lengths, a difference is a compile error, and the error gives the lengths:

```
error: non-matching for loop lengths
note: length 3 here
note: length 2 here
```

When the sequences are runtime slices, a safety check finds the difference. The check panics in Debug and ReleaseSafe. In the two cases, the loop does not read past the end of the shorter sequence. A loop with an index can easily make that mistake.

A range with no upper bound can pair with each sequence. `0..` gets its length from the sequences next to it. A bare `for (0..)` with no other sequence is a compile error, because nothing tells the loop when to stop.

## Change the elements in place

A capture by value gives you a copy. To change the elements in the array, iterate over a pointer to the array, and capture by pointer:

```zig
for (&numbers) |*n| n.* *= 2;
```

The two parts are necessary:

- `&numbers` makes the loop use the original array, not a copy of the array.
- `|*n|` makes each capture a pointer into the array.

If you remove one of the two parts, the loop compiles but does nothing useful.

For a slice, the `&` is not necessary. A slice already refers to memory that it does not own. Thus `for (slice) |*item|` writes to the elements of that memory.

## Iterate backwards

Zig has no reverse range and no step. To count down, use a `while`:

```zig
var i = items.len;
while (i > 0) {
    i -= 1;
    use(items[i]);
}
```

The decrement comes first for a reason. `items.len` is a `usize`. A loop with `while (i >= 0) : (i -= 1)` never stops, because an unsigned counter cannot go below zero. In a safety build, the loop panics on the wraparound instead, thus you see the problem.

Zig accepts this cost on purpose. The forward loop cannot make this mistake. When you iterate backwards, you must control the index yourself again.

## `for` can also break and give a value

`break`, `continue`, labels and `else` work here exactly as they work on `while`. A `for` that you use as an expression gives a value with `break x`. It needs an `else` for the case where no elements remain. Thus a linear search is a single expression.

See [loops as expressions](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/loops-as-expressions/) and [labelled loops](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-loops/).

`inline for` unrolls the loop at compile time, and the compiler knows the capture at comptime. Thus a loop can visit the fields of a struct or the tags of an enum. `inline for` is a different tool with a different purpose. [Inline loops](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/inline-loops/) explains it.

---

## Functions

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/functions/*

Zig function parameters are constant. If a function returns a value that is not `void`, and you do not use the value, the result is a compile error. Thus you write a discard explicitly: `_ = addFive(1);`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

fn addFive(x: u32) u32 {
    // Parameters are const. `x += 5` here would not compile.
    return x + 5;
}

fn fibonacci(n: u16) u16 {
    if (n == 0 or n == 1) return n;
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);
}

test "calling a function" {
    const y = addFive(0);
    try expect(@TypeOf(y) == u32);
    try expect(y == 5);
}

test "recursion" {
    try expect(fibonacci(10) == 55);
}

test "values must be used" {
    // In Zig, an unused value is a compile error, not a warning. Use `_ =`
    // to discard a value explicitly.
    _ = addFive(1);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.functions`)*

## Parameters are constant

For example, this code does not compile:

```zig
fn addFive(x: u32) u32 {
    x += 5;      // error: cannot assign to constant
    return x;
}
```

If you want a mutable local, make one. The benefit is that a parameter always has the value from the call site, through all of the function body. In a long function, `x` on line 60 is the `x` that the caller gave. You do not have to read the 59 lines above to be sure.

To let the function change a value of the caller, take a pointer, and write the pointer in the type:

```zig
fn addFiveInPlace(x: *u32) void {
    x.* += 5;
}
```

Now the change is visible at the call site as `addFiveInPlace(&n)`. Zig has no reference parameters that write to the caller without a visible sign.

## The compiler decides how to pass arguments

A parameter is a value. But the compiler decides if it copies the value or passes a pointer to it. The compiler uses the type and the calling convention of the target to decide.

When you pass a large struct, the compiler does not always copy it. Parameters are immutable. Thus the code inside the function cannot see which method the compiler used, and the compiler can use either method.

## Unused values are errors

Zig has no "unused variable" *warning*, because an unused variable is an error:

```
error: value of type 'u32' ignored
note: all non-void values must be used
```

A discard is explicit:

```zig
_ = addFive(1);
```

This rule finds the case where you called a function for its result, but forgot to use the result. The rule also applies to unused locals and parameters. Thus `_ = name;` often occurs in code that is not complete. When you refactor, the compiler does not let you keep a variable that you do not use now.

A function that returns `void` is the exception. It gives no value to use, thus a bare call is correct.

## Generic functions are usual functions

The call site supplies the type of an `anytype` parameter. The compiler compiles the function one time for each set of types that the callers use:

```zig
fn maxOf(a: anytype, b: @TypeOf(a)) @TypeOf(a) {
    return if (a > b) a else b;
}
```

`maxOf(@as(u8, 3), 5)` and `maxOf(@as(f32, 1.5), 0.5)` both work, and each call gets its own machine code. Zig has no separate syntax for generics, such as a type parameter list or a constraint language.

A type is a value at compile time. Thus a function that takes types is only a function. The standard library uses this idea in many places. [comptime](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/comptime/) explains it in detail.

The cost is that errors occur when a caller uses the function with concrete types, not when you define the function. For example, a function calls `a.len` on its `anytype` parameter. The function compiles correctly until a caller passes an integer. Then the error message points inside your function, not at the call of the other person.

## Function pointers

A function is not a pointer, but you can take a pointer to a function:

```zig
const p: *const fn (u8) u8 = &addOne;
```

The type is `*const fn` and not `fn`, because the pointer can change, not the code. A callback field in a struct holds this type of pointer.

The interfaces in the standard library also use function pointers. An interface is a pointer to some state, plus a table of function pointers that know how to use that state.

## Recursion and the stack

The `fibonacci` function above is recursive. But Zig cannot always prove a limit on the use of the stack. For deep recursion, or recursion that depends on the input, an explicit stack or a loop is the safer selection. Zig does not guarantee automatic tail calls.

You cannot catch this failure. A stack overflow is a crash, not a Zig error value. How clearly the crash shows depends on the platform. When the input sets the depth of the recursion, check that depth as you check all other input.

---

## Defer

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/defer/*

In Zig, you write cleanup code with `defer`. Put the release on the line below the acquisition. When the scope exits, the deferred statements run in reverse order. `errdefer` does the same, but only when the function returns an error.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
```
