```zig
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "defer runs at scope exit" {
    var x: i16 = 5;
    {
        defer x += 2;
        try expect(x == 5); // not yet
    }
    try expect(x == 7); // now
}

test "defers run in reverse order" {
    // The last defer that you register runs first. Thus the cleanup occurs
    // in the reverse order of the acquisitions.
    var order: [3]u8 = undefined;
    var index: usize = 0;
    {
        defer {
            order[index] = 1;
            index += 1;
        }
        defer {
            order[index] = 2;
            index += 1;
        }
        defer {
            order[index] = 3;
            index += 1;
        }
    }
    try expect(order[0] == 3);
    try expect(order[2] == 1);
}

fn mightFail(fail: bool) !u8 {
    var cleaned = false;
    // `errdefer` runs only when the function returns an error.
    errdefer cleaned = true;
    if (fail) return error.Nope;
    return @intFromBool(cleaned);
}

test "errdefer only fires on the error path" {
    try expect(try mightFail(false) == 0);
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Nope, mightFail(true));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.defer`)*

The scope is the block around the `defer`, not the full function. Each path out of the block counts:

- The end of the block.
- An early `return`.
- An error that `try` returns to the caller.

## The reverse order is necessary

Deferred statements run in reverse order. The last statement that you register runs first. If you acquire A and then B, the cleanup releases B and then A. This is almost always the correct order.

Write the release directly below the acquisition. Then you can see the two lines together:

```zig
const buf = try allocator.alloc(u8, n);
defer allocator.free(buf);
```

The release is on the next line. Thus, to check an allocation for a leak, you read one line. You do not have to search for the `free` that matches it lower in the function.

## The scope is the block

A `defer` inside a loop body runs at the end of **each iteration**. It does not wait until the function returns:

```zig
var n: u32 = 0;
for (0..3) |_| {
    defer n += 1;
}
// n == 3
```

Go is different here. In Go, `defer` has function scope. Thus the deferred calls in a loop collect until the function ends, and Go gives no warning. In Zig, if you open a file inside a loop and defer its close, the file closes on each pass. Thus the loop cannot use all of the descriptors.

Because of this rule, a bare block is also a way to put a tight limit on a cleanup:

```zig
{
    const lock = mutex.acquire();
    defer lock.release();
    // held only inside these braces
}
```

## The order of `defer` and the return value

First the function calculates the return value. Then the deferred statements run. Then the function returns. Thus this function returns 0, not 1:

```zig
fn f() u8 {
    var x: u8 = 0;
    defer x += 1;
    return x;      // the 0 is already captured
}
```

Use `defer` to release resources. Do not use `defer` to change a result.

Also, you cannot `return` from inside a `defer`:

```
error: cannot return from defer expression
```

A deferred statement runs when the scope already exits. If the statement could return, it could select a different exit. Then the exit path of each function with cleanup would be hard to follow.

## `errdefer` for the failure path only

`errdefer` runs **only** when the function returns an error. Thus you can write a constructor that removes partial work on failure. On success, the constructor does not undo its own work:

```zig
const thing = try create();
errdefer destroy(thing);   // only if a later step fails
try initialise(thing);
return thing;
```

With a plain `defer`, this code would destroy the object that the function returned with success.

The selection between the two is a question about ownership:

- If this scope owns the resource for all of its life, use `defer`.
- If the resource goes to the caller, and this scope keeps it only when an error occurs, use `errdefer`.

An initialiser with many steps gets one `errdefer` for each step. Each `errdefer` undoes only its own step. Thus Zig undoes a partly built object one step at a time, in reverse order:

```zig
const a = try makeA();
errdefer freeA(a);
const b = try makeB();     // if this fails, only a is freed
errdefer freeB(b);
const c = try makeC();     // if this fails, b then a are freed
return .{ .a = a, .b = b, .c = c };
```

To see what runs on failure, read the `errdefer` lines from the bottom to the top. Each `errdefer` is next to the step that it undoes.

## If you know C++ or Rust

`defer` does the work of a destructor. But you write the pair at the place of use, and not as part of a type. Zig made this selection on purpose. No hidden code runs at the `}` that ends a block. Each action on the way out is a statement in the function that you read.

The cost is that you can forget a `defer`. For this reason, the [allocator chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/allocators/) uses an allocator that finds leaks. That allocator finds the mistakes that a code review does not find.

---

## Errors

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/errors/*

Zig has no exceptions. A function that can fail returns an **error union**. You write it as `E!T`. The value is an error from the set `E`, or a `T`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const FileOpenError = error{
    AccessDenied,
    OutOfMemory,
    FileNotFound,
};

// Error sets coerce into supersets. Thus a function that declares a wider
// set can return a narrow error.
const AllocationError = error{OutOfMemory};

test "error set coercion" {
    const err: FileOpenError = AllocationError.OutOfMemory;
    try expect(err == FileOpenError.OutOfMemory);
}

fn failingFunction() error{Oops}!void {
    return error.Oops;
}

test "catch supplies a fallback" {
    // `!u8` is a short form of "an inferred error set, or u8".
    const parsed = std.fmt.parseInt(u8, "not a number", 10) catch 0;
    try expect(parsed == 0);
}

test "try propagates" {
    // `try x` is `x catch |err| return err`.
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Oops, failingFunction());
}

test "capture the error in catch" {
    var captured: anyerror = undefined;
    failingFunction() catch |err| {
        captured = err;
    };
    try expect(captured == error.Oops);
}

fn parseOrDefault(text: []const u8) u32 {
    // `if` can also unwrap an error union, with `else |err|`.
    if (std.fmt.parseInt(u32, text, 10)) |value| {
        return value;
    } else |_| {
        return 0;
    }
}

test "if on an error union" {
    try expect(parseOrDefault("42") == 42);
    try expect(parseOrDefault("abc") == 0);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.errors`)*

## Error sets are types

```zig
const FileOpenError = error{ AccessDenied, OutOfMemory, FileNotFound };
```

A narrow set coerces into a wider set. Thus a function that returns `FileOpenError` can call a function that returns `error{OutOfMemory}`, and it needs no extra code.

`anyerror` is the set of all errors. It is convenient, but it removes the list of possible errors. That list is the reason that error sets are useful.

You combine sets with `||`. A function that calls two subsystems uses `||` to declare that it can fail in the two ways:

```zig
const Error = ParseError || std.Io.Reader.Error;
```

If you write `!T` with no set, the compiler infers the set from each error that the body can make. Inside a program, this is the correct default. At the public boundary of a library, it is the wrong default. The inferred set is part of your interface, and the set changes without a warning when the body changes.

An error is only a value with a name. It does not contain a payload, a message or a stack trace. Thus you can compare errors, use them in a `switch`, and return them at no cost. When a failure needs detail, put the detail in a place where the caller can ask for it. Do not put it into the error.

## Four ways to handle an error

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `try x` | unwrap, or return the error to my caller |
| `x catch fallback` | unwrap, or use this value instead |
| `x catch \|err\| { ... }` | unwrap, or handle the error here |
| `if (x) \|v\| ... else \|err\| ...` | branch on both outcomes |

`try` is the most common form, and it is *only* a short form of `x catch |err|
return err`.

To handle some errors and return the other errors, use a `switch` inside the `catch`. The `switch` must have a prong for each error in the set. Thus, if a function that you call gets a new failure mode, each caller that lists the errors gets a compile error:

```zig
const config = load(path) catch |err| switch (err) {
    error.FileNotFound => Config.default,
    else => return err,
};
```

`catch unreachable` asserts that a call cannot fail. Safety builds check the assertion. In ReleaseFast, a failure is undefined behaviour.

Use `catch unreachable` only where the code shows, in the same place, why the call cannot fail. Do not use it to avoid an error that the signature says can occur.

## Errors that need cleanup

`errdefer` runs only on the error path. With `errdefer`, an initialiser with many steps can clean up correctly, and you do not copy the cleanup into each `catch`. [Defer](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/defer/) explains it.

`try` can return from the middle of a function. `errdefer` is the cleanup that you prepare before that return can occur.

## Find where an error comes from

An error contains no stack. Thus, in Debug and ReleaseSafe, Zig makes a separate **error return trace**. If an error goes out of `main`, Zig prints the chain of `try` sites that the error went through.

This trace gives you the same information as a stack trace, and often more. It shows where the code made the error, not only where the code saw the error. In ReleaseFast, Zig does not make the trace, thus the trace has no cost there.

To write an error to a [log](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/logging/) yourself, use `@errorName(err)`. It gives the name as a string. The `{!}` format specifier prints an error union directly, as `error.FileNotFound`.

## Why error unions are better than exceptions

The failure paths are in the type signature and in the control flow that you can see. No line has a hidden second exit, and no hidden code unwinds the stack. Each exit is visible. Thus `defer` is necessary for cleanup, and `defer` is also sufficient.

With exceptions, the main path of the code stays clean, and the code that handles errors is in a different place. Error unions put a `try` on each call that can fail. This adds noise. In return, each `try` shows the reader a place where the function can return early. Also, a function cannot fail in a way that its signature does not declare.

---

## Switch

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/switch/*

In Zig, `switch` can match single values, lists such as `10, 100`, and inclusive ranges such as `-1...1`. You can also use `switch` as an expression, and put its value directly into a `const`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "switch as a statement" {
    var x: i8 = 10;
    switch (x) {
        -1...1 => x = -x, // inclusive ranges
        10, 100 => x = @divExact(x, 10), // multiple values
        else => {},
    }
    try expect(x == 1);
}

test "switch as an expression" {
    const x: i8 = 10;
    const y: i8 = switch (x) {
        -1...1 => -x,
        10, 100 => @divExact(x, 10),
        else => 0,
    };
    try expect(y == 1);
}

const Direction = enum { north, south, east, west };

fn isVertical(d: Direction) bool {
    // No `else` branch: the compiler proves that the code handles each case.
    // Thus a new enum tag later causes a compile error, not a bug.
    return switch (d) {
        .north, .south => true,
        .east, .west => false,
    };
}

test "exhaustive switch over an enum" {
    try expect(isVertical(.north));
    try expect(!isVertical(.east));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.switch`)*

The Zig `switch` has no fallthrough, and it must be **exhaustive**. Each possible value needs a branch, or the program does not compile.

Because there is no fallthrough, an arm does not need a `break` at its end. Thus there is no bug from a `break` that you forgot. An arm for many values lists the values. In C, that was the usual reason to use fallthrough.

## Ranges and lists of values

```zig
switch (x) {
    -1...1 => ...,      // inclusive range
    10, 100 => ...,     // several values, one branch
    else => ...,
}
```

A `...` range includes the two ends. The `..` range in a `for` does not include the upper bound. The difference is intentional, and it is easy to make a mistake with it: `0..3` in a `for` gives three values, and `0...3` in a `switch` matches four.

Cases must not overlap. If two arms can match the same value, the code does not compile. There is no rule that the first match wins. Thus the order of the arms never changes the behaviour.

## A statement or an expression

The snippet has the two forms:

- In a statement, each arm does an action.
- In an expression, each arm produces a value, and the full `switch` has that value.

```zig
const y: i8 = switch (x) {
    -1...1 => -x,
    10, 100 => @divExact(x, 10),
    else => 0,
};
```

Use the expression form where possible, for the same reason as [loops as expressions](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/loops-as-expressions/). The result goes directly into a `const`, and each arm must produce a value.

## The benefit of exhaustiveness

When you switch over an enum and cover each tag, **do not write `else`**:

```zig
return switch (direction) {
    .north, .south => true,
    .east, .west => false,
};
```

If you add a `.up` variant later, this code becomes a compile error. The error points directly at the code that you must update. If you add `else => false`, the switch puts the new direction in the horizontal group, and you get no error.

With an `else` branch, the compiler cannot tell you about a new tag. Use `else` only when you want that result.

The error names the tag that you did not handle, and points at its declaration:

```
error: switch must handle all possibilities
note: unhandled enumeration value: 'west'
```

For an integer, "all possibilities" means all the values. A `switch` on a `u8` needs `else` or 256 arms. Thus `else` is usual on an integer, and suspicious on an enum.

## Switch on a tagged union

Each arm can capture the payload of the variant that it matched:

```zig
switch (value) {
    .int => |n| useInt(n),
    .text => |s| useText(s),
}
```

When the arm must change the payload, capture by reference with `|*n|`. A switch is the main way to use a tagged union. [Unions](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/unions/) and [payload captures](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/payload-captures/) have more about this topic.

## `inline else` and non-exhaustive enums

Two more forms are useful when code generates code, and you do not write each case.

`inline else` compiles a separate copy of the arm for each case that no other arm handles. In each copy, the tag is a comptime value:

```zig
switch (d) {
    inline else => |tag| doSomething(@tagName(tag)),
}
```

A usual `else` cannot do this, because at runtime the tag is only a number. With the inline form, code that uses reflection stays type-safe.

An enum with a `_` at the end is non-exhaustive. Values outside its named tags are legal. Usually the numbers come from a protocol or a C header. A switch on such an enum uses `_`, not `else`:

```zig
const Op = enum(u8) { get = 1, set = 2, _ };

switch (op) {
    .get => ...,
    .set => ...,
    _ => return error.UnknownOpcode,
}
```

`_` means "a value with no name". The exhaustiveness check for named tags still works. If you add `.delete` to the enum, this switch does not compile until you handle `.delete`. An `else` would hide the new tag.

## A switch can have a label

Give a switch a label. Then `continue :label value` runs the switch again with a new operand, and `break :label value` leaves the switch with a result. Thus a switch becomes a state machine with no loop around it. [Labelled switch](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-switch/) is the chapter about this form.

---

## Runtime Safety

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/runtime-safety/*

Zig inserts runtime checks for a group of mistakes that C leaves undefined. Examples are an out-of-bounds index, integer overflow, an invalid cast, and the unwrap of a null optional. When a check fails, the program panics with a clear message. It does not silently read the next data in memory.

Press **Run**. The program reads index 5 of an array that has three elements:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    _ = init;

    // Zig inserts checks for out-of-bounds access, integer overflow, invalid
    // casts, and more. In a build with safety checks, this code panics with
    // "index out of bounds". It does not read the memory after the array.
    const array = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    var index: usize = 5;
    _ = &index; // stop comptime evaluation
    const value = array[index];
    std.debug.print("never printed: {d}\n", .{value});
}

// This program panics intentionally. CI runs it and requires it to stop with
// exactly the message that this chapter quotes.
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.runtime-safety`)*

```
panic: index out of bounds: index 5, len 3
```

The message gives the index that the program used and the length that was the limit. The `std.debug.print` on the next line never runs, and the program reads no memory outside the array. In C, the same three lines produce a number. The number depends on the data that is in memory after the array.

## Integer overflow

Arithmetic gets the same treatment. This program adds 1 to a `u8` that holds 255:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    _ = init;

    var x: u8 = 255;
    _ = &x; // stop comptime evaluation

    // 256 does not fit in a u8. `+=` is the checked add. In this build, the
    // check runs and the program stops here. In ReleaseFast or ReleaseSmall,
    // there is no check, and the value is undefined. Zig does not guarantee
    // that the value wraps.
    x += 1;

    std.debug.print("never printed: {d}\n", .{x});
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.safety-overflow`)*

```
panic: integer overflow
```

C gives you 0 here, without a message, and the bug then causes a problem in a different part of the program. Zig stops at the line that is wrong.

Plain `+` does not guess if you want the value to wrap. A wrap is correct in a hash function or a checksum. Thus Zig gives the wrap a different operator, and the choice is visible where you write the operation:

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "+% wraps, and says so at the call site" {
    var x: u8 = 255;
    _ = &x;
    // `x + 1` is the checked add, and it stops the program. `+%` is a different
    // operator. It has a defined answer in each build mode.
    try expect(x +% 1 == 0);
}

test "+| saturates at the limit instead" {
    var x: u8 = 250;
    _ = &x;
    try expect(x +| 10 == 255);
}

test "@addWithOverflow reports rather than stops" {
    var x: u8 = 255;
    _ = &x;
    // A tuple: the wrapped value, and a u1 that is 1 when an overflow occurred.
    const result = @addWithOverflow(x, 1);
    try expect(result[0] == 0);
    try expect(result[1] == 1);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.safety-wrapping`)*

- `+%` wraps.
- `+|` saturates at the limit of the type.
- `@addWithOverflow` returns the wrapped value and a flag that tells if an overflow occurred.

All three have a defined result in each build mode, because you asked for that behaviour. Plain `+` means "this operation must not overflow, and tell me if it does".

## A null optional

`.?` on an optional is an assertion, not a conversion. It says that the value is not null. When the value is null, the check fails:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    _ = init;

    var maybe: ?u32 = null;
    _ = &maybe; // stop comptime evaluation

    // `.?` is a claim: "this is not null, give me the payload". Here the claim
    // is false. Thus the check stops the program. The program does not return
    // the unknown bits that are in the payload.
    const value = maybe.?;

    std.debug.print("never printed: {d}\n", .{value});
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.safety-null-unwrap`)*

```
panic: attempt to use null value
```

You will see this check more frequently than the others. `.?` is an easy choice when the alternative is to handle a case that you are sure cannot occur.

This check also has the best alternatives. `orelse` gives a default. `if (maybe) |value|` gives you the payload only on the branch where the payload exists. [Optionals](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/optionals/) has more about the two alternatives.

## Safety depends on the build mode

| Mode | Safety checks | Optimised |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Debug` | yes | no |
| `ReleaseSafe` | yes | yes |
| `ReleaseFast` | **no** | yes |
| `ReleaseSmall` | **no** | yes |

C never gives you this choice explicitly. `ReleaseSafe` keeps the checks, and it is a reasonable default for production. `ReleaseFast` removes the checks to make the program faster.

Where the build removes a check, the error that the check caught becomes **illegal behaviour**. Illegal behaviour is the same category as undefined behaviour in C, with the same results.

<aside>

**Runtime safety does not make incorrect code correct.** It makes some types of incorrect code fail with a message. Without the checks, the program continues with corrupted state.

Each panic on this page comes from a program that was wrong before the check failed. A read of index 5 of an array with three elements is a bug in `Debug` and a bug in `ReleaseFast`. The only difference is if you find the bug.

The checks do not define correct code. They report code that breaks the rules. If a program panics under `ReleaseSafe`, a build with `ReleaseFast` does not repair the bug. The bug stays in the program, and the program does not report it now.

</aside>

To change the setting for one scope, use `@setRuntimeSafety(true)`. For example, use it to keep bounds checks in one difficult function where speed is important, in a build that is otherwise `ReleaseFast`.

<aside>

The snippets on this site build as `ReleaseSmall`, where the checks are off. Three snippets on this page are the exception: the out-of-bounds read, the overflow and the null unwrap. The site builds these three as `ReleaseSafe` intentionally, because a chapter about a check must be able to show the check fail.

The site build runs all three on each change. It requires each one to stop with exactly the message above it. Thus a nightly check confirms those messages, and nobody has to remember them.

Each of the three costs about 1.1 MB. A usual snippet here is 79 KB. The extra size is the checks and the code that prints their messages. The browser downloads it only when you press Run on that snippet.

The snippet with `+%` and `+|` is a usual `ReleaseSmall` build. `+%`, `+|` and `@addWithOverflow` have a defined result in each mode, so they need no check to show their behaviour.

</aside>

---

## Pointers

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/pointers/*

A `*T` refers to exactly one `T`. Use `&` to get an address. Use `.*` to dereference the pointer. `.*` is a postfix operator, so a chain of operations reads from left to right, as field access does.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

fn increment(num: *u8) void {
    num.* += 1;
}

test "take an address and dereference" {
    var x: u8 = 1;
    increment(&x);
    try expect(x == 2);
}

test "pointers to const are const" {
    const x: u8 = 1;
    // Here `&x` is a `*const u8`. A write through it does not compile.
    const ptr: *const u8 = &x;
    try expect(ptr.* == 1);
}

test "pointers are never null" {
    // There is no null `*T`. Write `?*T` for a pointer that can be absent.
    // It uses no extra space, because the null address is the tag.
    var x: u8 = 5;
    const ptr: *u8 = &x;
    const maybe: ?*u8 = ptr;
    try expect(maybe != null);
    try expect(@sizeOf(?*u8) == @sizeOf(*u8));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.pointers`)*

## Exactly one

A `*T` is not a cursor into a sequence, and it has no pointer arithmetic: `p + 1` does not compile. Code that moves through memory needs a type that tells how much memory there is.

Thus there are three types. In Zig, the main purpose of pointer types is to help you select the correct one:

| Type | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `*T` | one `T`, and only one |
| `[*]T` | many `T`, count unknown, arithmetic allowed |
| `[]T` | many `T`, count carried alongside |

Usually, use `[]T`. It is a pointer and a length together. Thus an index into it can have a bounds check. You cannot forget the length, because the length is part of the value.

`[*]T` is for the C boundary, where the count is in a different place or in a sentinel. See [slices](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/slices/) and [many-item pointers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/many-item-pointers/).

## Never null

A `*T` cannot be null. If a pointer can be absent, its type says so: `?*T`. The compiler enforces this rule. It does not let you dereference the optional before you unwrap it.

The representation has no cost. Zig uses the null address as the `null` tag. Thus `?*T` has the same size as `*T`.

The result is that "did I check this pointer for null" is a question about the type, not about the code:

- A function that takes `*T` cannot receive nothing.
- A function that takes `?*T` cannot use the pointer before it says what occurs for null.

There is no third case, where the two types have the same syntax and one of them is a bug.

## Constness stays with the pointer

`&some_const` gives you a `*const T`, and you cannot assign through it. This rule is about what the *pointer* permits. It is a different rule from whether you can assign a new value to the pointer variable:

```zig
var p: *const u8 = &a;   // p can point elsewhere; p.* cannot be written
const q: *u8 = &b;       // q always points at b; q.* can be written
```

These are two different questions, and you write `const` in two different places. The `const` on the left of the colon is about the variable. The `const` inside the type is about what you can do through the pointer.

Const works in one direction. A `*T` coerces to a `*const T` without a cast, because it is always safe to remove the right to write. The opposite direction needs `@constCast`. If you use `@constCast` on memory that is really constant, the result is undefined behaviour, not a check that fails.

## Alignment is part of the type

A pointer carries the alignment that the compiler can trust. When this alignment is different from the natural alignment, the type is `*align(n) T`.

Usually you do not see the alignment. `&x` produces a correctly aligned pointer, and you do not have to write anything. You see the alignment when you cast a byte buffer to a wider type. `[]u8` gives no promise about alignment, and `*u32` requires an alignment of four bytes.

Use `@alignCast` to assert the alignment that you know is correct. In a safety build, the program checks the alignment and causes a panic if you are wrong. In ReleaseFast, the program trusts you. If you are wrong, the result is a misaligned load. On some targets a misaligned load causes a crash. On other targets it is slow, but the result is correct and there is no error.

## Get the address as a number

`@intFromPtr` gives you the address as a `usize`, and `@ptrFromInt` converts the number back to a pointer. The two builtins are for the cases that really need an integer: hardware access, pointer tags, or an address that you print when you debug.

They are not a general method to convert between types. When a pointer becomes an integer and then a pointer again, the compiler loses all the information that it had about the data at the address.

The address of a local has a meaning only while that local exists. If a function returns `&x`, and the frame of the function ends, the result is a dangling pointer. Nothing in the type system catches this bug. This is the one usual pointer bug that Zig does not remove. [The stack](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/the-stack/) has more about it.

---

## Pointer Sized Integers

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/pointer-sized-integers/*

In Zig, use `usize` for lengths, indices and byte offsets into memory. Use a fixed width such as `u64` for values that get their range from the problem, for example a file offset or a timestamp.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "usize matches pointer width" {
    try expect(@sizeOf(usize) == @sizeOf(*u8));
    try expect(@sizeOf(isize) == @sizeOf(*u8));
}

test "usize is the index and length type" {
    // `.len` is a usize. A value that you use as a slice index is also a usize.
    const array = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    const length: usize = array.len;
    try expect(length == 3);
    try expect(@TypeOf(array.len) == usize);
}

test "wasm32 is a 32-bit target" {
    // The build compiles these snippets to wasm32-wasi, so a pointer is 4 bytes.
    // On x86_64, the same source gets 8.
    try expect(@sizeOf(usize) == 4);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.pointer-sized-integers`)*

`usize` and `isize` are exactly as wide as a pointer on the target. `.len` is a `usize`, and a value that you use as a slice index is a `usize`.

## The width depends on the target, and this is intentional

The snippets on this site compile to `wasm32-wasi`. Thus `@sizeOf(usize)` is **4**. If you build the same source for `x86_64`, the size is 8. For this reason, the last test above asserts 4. The value 4 is a fact about the target, not about Zig.

This page is the one place on the site where an assertion shows the wasm target. When you run the snippet, you get the 32-bit answer. For this program, the browser is a 32-bit machine.

Be careful when you select between the two types:

- If you write `u64` where you mean `usize`, the code works on your machine. It fails on a 32-bit machine.
- If you write `usize` where you mean "a 64-bit counter", the value becomes narrower on wasm, and you get no error.

## Which type to use

Select the type from what the number *is*, not from how large you expect the number to become.

- **`usize`**: use it for a count of memory that exists, or an index into that memory. Examples are `.len`, an index, a byte offset into a buffer, and a capacity. The quantity of memory that the machine can address limits these values, and that limit is the definition of pointer width.
- **A fixed width** (`u32`, `u64`): use it for a value that gets its range from the problem, not from the machine. Examples are a file offset, a timestamp in milliseconds, a field in a wire protocol, and a hash. A file can be larger than the address space of a 32-bit machine. Thus a file offset is always `u64` and never `usize`.
- **`isize`**: almost never use it. It is for pointer differences, and for C interfaces that use `ssize_t`. Usually `ssize_t` is a length that can also be an error code.

When you select the wrong type, the code is correct on the machine that you tested on. It is wrong on the machine where you shipped it. Embedded targets are 16-bit, wasm is 32-bit, and your laptop is 64-bit. The same source must build for all three.

## Convert between the types

A conversion that can lose information on the target is never implicit. Thus code that builds for a 64-bit target must convert a `usize` to a `u32` explicitly:

```zig
const n: u32 = @intCast(slice.len);   // checked in safety builds
```

`@intCast` asserts that the value fits in the type:

- In Debug and ReleaseSafe, the assertion is a real check. A value that does not fit causes a panic.
- In ReleaseFast, the assertion is a promise from you. If the promise is false, the result is undefined behaviour.

Thus use `@intCast` when you know the limit, for example a length that you checked, or an index that you validated. Do not use it only to stop a type error.

When the value possibly does not fit, do the check yourself and return an error:

```zig
if (slice.len > std.math.maxInt(u32)) return error.TooLong;
const n: u32 = @intCast(slice.len);
```

A conversion in the other direction, from a narrower type such as `u32` to `usize`, cannot lose information. Thus Zig does this conversion implicitly, and you do not write `@intCast`. A `u64` is not narrower than `usize` on all targets, so a conversion from `u64` to `usize` still needs a cast.

## Where these types cause bugs

The first cause is subtraction. `usize` is unsigned. Thus, when `b > a`, `a - b` overflows. In a safety build, this causes a panic for integer overflow, not a large number.

A usual example is a loop that counts down from `items.len`. For this reason, a loop that counts down decrements the index inside the body, not in a continue expression. [For loops](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/for-loops/) shows that shape.

The second cause is arithmetic on `.len` in format strings and in buffer sizes. If you mix a `usize` length and a `u32` field, each expression needs an `@intCast`. To prevent this, select one type and convert at the boundary. Convert one time, where the value enters your code. The code then stays easy to read.

---

## Many-item Pointers

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/many-item-pointers/*

In Zig, `[*]T` is a many-item pointer. It points at an unknown number of `T`. You can use an index on it, but it has no `.len` and no bounds checks. When you know the length, slice the pointer with `many[0..count]`. The result is a `[]T` with bounds checks.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "many-item pointers support indexing" {
    var array = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4 };
    const many: [*]u8 = &array;

    // You can use an index and pointer arithmetic. But there is no `.len`,
    // thus there is no bounds check. You must make sure that the range is correct.
    try expect(many[0] == 1);
    try expect(many[3] == 4);
}

test "convert to a slice by supplying the length" {
    var array = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4 };
    const many: [*]u8 = &array;

    // `[*]T` does not have the length. Add the length, and you get a `[]T`.
    // The compiler adds bounds checks to a `[]T` again.
    const slice: []u8 = many[0..3];
    try expect(slice.len == 3);
}

test "single-item pointers do not index" {
    // A `*T` is one item. `ptr[1]` is a compile error. For this reason, Zig
    // has the two types `*T` and `[*]T`, and C has only `T*`.
    var x: u8 = 9;
    const single: *u8 = &x;
    try expect(single.* == 9);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.many-item-pointers`)*

C has one pointer type, `T*`, and C uses it for three different things: one item, many items, and "maybe nothing". Zig has a different type for each:

| Zig | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `*T` | exactly one `T` |
| `[*]T` | many `T`, count unknown |
| `[]T` | many `T`, count known (a [slice](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/slices/)) |
| `?*T` | one `T`, or nothing |

The different types have a purpose. In C, a function signature with a `char *` parameter gives you no information. A comment or a convention must tell you three things: if the function can use an index, how far, and if null is acceptable. In Zig, the type gives the three answers, and the compiler enforces them.

## What `[*]T` does not have

A many-item pointer supports an index and pointer arithmetic. But it has no `.len`, thus it has **no bounds checks**. The type is mainly for C interop, and for the code that makes the safe abstractions above it.

When you know the length, convert the pointer to a slice:

```zig
const slice: []u8 = many[0..count];
```

This one step gives you bounds checks, `for` iteration and `.len` again. Use slices in all places, except at the boundary where no length is available.

When you slice a `[*]T`, you tell the compiler something that it cannot check. `many[0..count]` makes a slice of exactly `count` elements, also if that number of elements does not exist. If you are wrong, no check fails. After that line, all accesses have checks again. Thus the unchecked statement is in one visible line, not in each access.

Also, `*T` does *not* support an index, and this is intentional. `ptr[1]` on a single-item pointer is a compile error. Thus the type system catches one type of C bug.

## Sentinel-terminated many-item pointers

`[*:0]T` is the one many-item pointer that knows where it ends. The data marks the end, so the pointer does not have to carry a length. This type is exactly a C string. translate-c gives you this type for `char *` parameters when the documentation says that they are null-terminated.

`std.mem.span` moves along the data to the sentinel and returns a slice. Thus the unsafe type exists for only one line at the boundary:

```zig
const name: []const u8 = std.mem.span(c_str);
```

[Sentinel termination](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/sentinel-termination/) has all of the sentinel types.

## Where many-item pointers come from

In usual Zig code, you do not often write `[*]T`. A `[*]T` comes from these places:

- **From C.** Each array parameter in a C header is a pointer. Thus translate-c produces `[*c]T`, the C pointer type. When you decide what the header really meant, you convert the `[*c]T` to `[*]T` or `?[*]T`.
- **From the internals of an allocator.** The code of a data structure has a block of memory and a count that the code itself keeps. `ArrayList` holds data of this shape and gives out slices.
- **From hardware or a mapped region.** The address is known, and the length comes from a different source.

All three are boundaries. To keep a program safe, convert at the boundary. Do not let the raw pointer move further into the code than the function that received it.

## `allowzero` and the null case

`[*]T` cannot be null, exactly like `*T`. Use `?[*]T` when the C side can return nothing. The optional uses no more space, because the null address is the tag. `allowzero` is a different modifier. It is for the rare targets where address zero is a correct mapped address. You need `allowzero` only on those targets.

---

## Slices

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/slices/*

A slice is a pointer plus a length. When you give a sequence to a function, use a slice by default.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

fn total(values: []const u8) u32 {
    var sum: u32 = 0;
    for (values) |v| sum += v;
    return sum;
}

test "slicing an array" {
    var array = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
    const slice = array[1..4]; // end is exclusive
    try expect(slice.len == 3);
    try expect(total(slice) == 9);
}

test "slices share memory" {
    var array = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    const slice = array[0..2];
    slice[0] = 100;
    try expect(array[0] == 100); // the slice is not a copy
}

test "strings are slices" {
    // A string literal is a `*const [N:0]u8` (a pointer to a
    // null-terminated array), which coerces to `[]const u8`.
    const message: []const u8 = "hello";
    try expect(message.len == 5);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, message[0..2], "he"));
}

test "slicing to the end" {
    const array = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4 };
    const rest = array[2..];
    try expect(rest.len == 2);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.slices`)*

## Two words, and the two are both important

`[]T` is exactly a `[*]T` and a `usize`, side by side. All other properties come from that structure:

- An index can have a bounds check, because the length is in the slice.
- `for` knows when to stop.
- A function that takes `[]const u8` cannot receive a buffer without the length of the real data in it.

Compare this with C. In C, the same job needs two parameters and a convention. Each function that does not give the length correctly causes a buffer overrun. A slice puts the two parts in one value. Thus an edit cannot separate the two parts.

## A slice is not a copy

`array[1..4]` gives a view into the same memory. A write through the slice changes the array. The upper bound is exclusive, as in `for` ranges. `array[2..]` makes a slice to the end.

A slice borrows memory. Thus the lifetime of a slice depends on the memory that it points at. A slice of a local array must not live longer than that array. Zig does not catch this error for you.

The type does not check the lifetime, and this is the one hazard of a slice. The slice does not stop you when you use an index on it. For the type, the slice still has a valid pointer and a valid length. But the memory that it points at now belongs to a different part of the program.

A usual example is a function that owns a stack buffer and returns a slice of that buffer. [Who owns this memory](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/who-owns-this-memory/) shows the shape of this problem.

The program *does* check the bounds. If you write `array[1..10]` on an array with three elements, and the two bounds are comptime-known, the compiler rejects the code. When the upper bound comes from a runtime value, the check occurs at runtime. It causes a panic in Debug and ReleaseSafe. In the two cases, the check is on the slice operation. It does not wait for the first access.

[Slice Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/slice-recipes/) shows how to reverse, rotate and shift a slice, and how to remove an element.

## `[]const T` vs `[]T`

In function parameters, use `[]const T`, unless the function changes the data. `[]const T` tells the reader the intent. It also accepts more callers, because `[]T` coerces to `[]const T`, but not in the opposite direction.

A signature that takes `[]const u8` says "I will read your bytes, and I will not keep them". Most functions do this. Also, the `const` decides if the function works on a literal. String literals are const. Thus a parameter of type `[]u8` cannot accept `"hello"`.

## Strings are slices

Zig has no special string type. A literal such as `"hello"` is a `*const [5:0]u8` (a pointer to a null-terminated array), and it coerces to `[]const u8`. There are three results:

- `.len` is the number of bytes, not the number of characters. Here, UTF-8 is bytes.
- To compare two strings, use `std.mem.eql(u8, a, b)`. Never use `==`, because `==` compares the pointers.
- The null terminator is there for C interop, but `.len` does *not* count it.

Zig omits a string type intentionally. A string in Zig is a slice of bytes. Thus each function that works on `[]const u8` also works on strings, and no function has two versions.

The cost is that there is no guarantee that the bytes are valid UTF-8. For this reason, [unicode](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/unicode/) is a separate topic. "The length" also has three different answers: bytes, code points, or what a reader calls characters.

## Where slices come from

Slices come from four places. When you know the source of a slice, you know who frees it:

- **A slice of an array or of a different slice.** It borrows memory. You do not free it, and its lifetime is the lifetime of the original.
- **An allocator.** `try allocator.alloc(u8, n)` gives you a `[]u8` that you own. On the next line, put a `defer allocator.free(...)`.
- **A literal.** It is static, it lives for the full program, and it is `const`.
- **A container.** `list.items` is a slice into memory that the list owns. When the list reallocates, the slice becomes invalid immediately. Do not keep the slice across an append.

The last case is an easy mistake. After the list grows, the slice is still a valid pair of numbers. But the numbers point at the old memory of the list.

---

## Enums

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/enums/*

A Zig enum is a type. Its value is exactly one tag from a fixed set of named tags. An enum can do three more things:

- It can set its integer tag type with `enum(u8)`.
- It can declare methods.
- It can accept values that are not named tags. A `_` at the end of the tag list makes the enum non-exhaustive.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const Direction = enum { north, south, east, west };

// You can set the tag type. The tag type fixes the numeric values.
const Value = enum(u8) { zero = 0, one = 1, hundred = 100 };

const Suit = enum {
    clubs,
    spades,
    diamonds,
    hearts,

    // Enums can have methods. They are functions in a namespace, not vtables.
    pub fn isRed(self: Suit) bool {
        return switch (self) {
            .diamonds, .hearts => true,
            .clubs, .spades => false,
        };
    }
};

test "enum values" {
    try expect(@intFromEnum(Value.zero) == 0);
    try expect(@intFromEnum(Value.hundred) == 100);
}

test "inferred enum literals" {
    // When the compiler knows the type, `.north` is sufficient.
    const d: Direction = .north;
    try expect(d == Direction.north);
}

test "enum methods" {
    try expect(Suit.hearts.isRed());
    try expect(!Suit.spades.isRed());
}

test "enums expose their tags at comptime" {
    const info = @typeInfo(Direction).@"enum";

    // Names and values are parallel arrays, not one array of field structs.
    try expect(info.field_names.len == 4);
    try expect(info.field_values.len == info.field_names.len);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, info.field_names[2], "east"));

    try expect(info.tag_type == u2);
    try expect(info.mode == .exhaustive);

    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, @tagName(Direction.east), "east"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.enums`)*

## Inferred literals

When the compiler knows the expected type, the dot at the start is sufficient:

```zig
const d: Direction = .north;
takeDirection(.south);
```

Thus `switch` prongs and struct literals stay easy to read, and you do not write the type name again in each place.

`.north` alone has its own type, the enum literal type. This type coerces to each enum that has a tag with the same name. Thus the same `.north` works for two unrelated enums in two different calls.

## Set the representation

```zig
const Value = enum(u8) { zero = 0, one = 1, hundred = 100 };
```

When you specify the tag type, you fix the size and the numeric values. This is important for wire formats and for C interop.

To convert, use `@intFromEnum` and `@enumFromInt`. In safety builds, Zig checks `@enumFromInt`, because not all integers are valid tags.

Without a tag type, the compiler selects the smallest integer that fits. It gives the tags numbers from zero. Thus `@intFromEnum` still works on a plain enum, and the values still have the order of the declaration. But do not write these numbers into a file format. When the numbers go out of your program, set the tag type.

## Non-exhaustive enums

A `_` at the end of the list says that values outside the named tags are legal:

```zig
const Opcode = enum(u8) { get = 1, set = 2, _ };
```

Use this type for a byte that comes from a network or a C library, where you do not control the set of values. `@enumFromInt` on such an enum cannot fail, because each value is legal.

A `switch` uses `_` for the unnamed values, not `else`. Thus the compiler still checks that the `switch` has a prong for each named tag. See [switch](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/switch/).

## Methods

Enums can declare functions. `Suit.hearts.isRed()` is exactly `Suit.isRed(Suit.hearts)`. The method syntax is a shorter way to give the receiver as the first argument. The call goes directly to that function, with no dynamic dispatch.

Enums can also contain constants and nested types. Thus an enum is a good place for the parsing and the formatting that belong to it.

For example, put a `fromString` that returns `?Suit` next to a `toString` that returns `[]const u8`. Then the full mapping is in one place. `std.meta.stringToEnum(Suit, text)` can also write the parsing half for you from the tag names.

## Reflection

`@typeInfo(T).@"enum"` gives the tags at comptime:

```zig
const info = @typeInfo(Direction).@"enum";
info.field_names[2];   // "east"
info.field_values[2];  // 2
info.tag_type;         // u2
info.mode;             // .exhaustive
```

These are **parallel arrays**, not one array of field structs. Older tutorials show `info.fields[i].name`. That shape does not exist now.

The change occurred between `0.17.0-dev.644` and `dev.1441`. When the compiler got that update, this change was the only break in this guide.

`@tagName` gives the name as a string. With `@tagName` and these arrays, generic code can print or parse enums without a table that you write by hand.

Use `inline for` on `field_names`, and you have a parser, a formatter or a table of all cases. The compiler makes them from the declaration, thus they always agree with the declaration. See [inline loops](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/inline-loops/).

## Enums and the alternatives

Use an enum when a value is exactly one item of a fixed, known set, and the value contains no other data. The other conditions need different types:

- If each case needs its own payload, use a [tagged union](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/unions/). A tagged union is an enum with data.
- If the cases are independent flags that you can combine, an enum is the wrong shape. Use a `packed struct` of `bool` fields. It gives you named bits in a single integer.

---

## Structs

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/structs/*

A Zig struct can give default values to its fields. It can also hold methods, and the first parameter of a method is the receiver. The layout of a struct is unspecified, unless the declaration is `extern` or `packed`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const Vec3 = struct {
    x: f32 = 0, // default value
    y: f32 = 0,
    z: f32 = 0,

    pub fn dot(a: Vec3, b: Vec3) f32 {
        return a.x * b.x + a.y * b.y + a.z * b.z;
    }

    // A `*Vec3` parameter lets the method change the receiver.
    pub fn scale(self: *Vec3, factor: f32) void {
        self.x *= factor;
        self.y *= factor;
        self.z *= factor;
    }
};

test "construct and read" {
    const v = Vec3{ .x = 1, .y = 2, .z = 3 };
    try expect(v.y == 2);
}

test "defaults fill in the rest" {
    const v = Vec3{ .x = 5 };
    try expect(v.y == 0 and v.z == 0);
}

test "methods" {
    const a = Vec3{ .x = 1, .y = 2, .z = 3 };
    const b = Vec3{ .x = 4, .y = 5, .z = 6 };
    try expect(Vec3.dot(a, b) == 32);
    try expect(a.dot(b) == 32); // same call, method syntax
}

test "mutating methods need a mutable receiver" {
    var v = Vec3{ .x = 1, .y = 1, .z = 1 };
    v.scale(3);
    try expect(v.x == 3);
}

test "field order is not guaranteed" {
    // Zig can change the order of fields to pack them, unless you select a
    // different layout: `extern struct` (C ABI) or `packed struct` (bit-level).
    try expect(@sizeOf(Vec3) == 12);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.structs`)*

## Defaults

A field can declare a default. Thus a literal must name only the fields that are different:

```zig
const v = Vec3{ .x = 5 };   // y and z default to 0
```

You must supply each field that has no default. Zig does not set it to zero for you.

When each field has a default, `.{}` makes the full struct. For this reason, code in the standard library usually gives `.{}` and one changed field to an options struct.

The compiler evaluates defaults at compile time, one time for each declaration. Think of a field with a default of an empty list. The field gets the same empty value each time. It does not get one shared mutable value, because the default is a value and not a constructor call.

## Methods and the receiver

A method with `self: Vec3` gets a copy. A method with `self: *Vec3` can change the original. To call a `*Vec3` method, you need a mutable value: `v` must be a `var`, and Zig takes the address for you.

Select the receiver carefully:

- `Vec3` for small value types that you want to copy.
- `*const Vec3` for large values that you only read.
- `*Vec3` to change the value.

A method has no special properties. `v.length()` is `Vec3.length(v)`. The only rule is that the first parameter is the receiver. There is no hidden `this`, and a method call never uses a vtable. The type at the call site always decides at compile time which function runs.

A struct can also hold declarations that are not methods. Thus a type can carry its own constants and nested types:

```zig
const Vec3 = struct {
    x: f32 = 0, y: f32 = 0, z: f32 = 0,

    pub const zero: Vec3 = .{};
    pub const Axis = enum { x, y, z };
};
```

Inside the body, `@This()` refers to the struct that the code declares. Thus the same code works in a file-level struct, and in an anonymous struct that has no name.

## Structs make generics

A function that returns a type is a generic container:

```zig
fn Stack(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        items: []T,
        len: usize = 0,
        pub fn push(self: *@This(), v: T) void { ... }
    };
}

const IntStack = Stack(i32);
```

`Stack(i32)` and `Stack(u8)` are different types. A function call at compile time produces each of them. Each generic type in the standard library has this shape. For this reason, `std.ArrayList(u8)` looks like a call: it is a call.

## Layout is not guaranteed

In a plain `struct`, the compiler can change the order of the fields and add padding as it decides. When the layout is important, state the layout:

| Declaration | Layout |
| --- | --- |
| `struct` | unspecified; optimiser's choice |
| `extern struct` | C ABI compatible |
| `packed struct` | bit-level, well-defined, backed by an integer |

Do not use `extern` or `packed` only as a precaution. They stop the packing that the optimiser can do. Use them only at real boundaries.

"Unspecified" has results:

- `@sizeOf` is not the sum of the field sizes.
- If you copy a plain struct into a file, a different compiler version possibly cannot read it back.
- The fields are not necessarily in the order that you wrote them.

If you need one of these properties, use `extern` or `packed`. See [struct layout](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/structs-are-layout/) for what the padding really does.

A struct with no fields has size zero, and an array of such structs also has size zero. This is useful. It lets a type carry only behaviour. It also lets a hash map with no values use no memory for each entry, other than the memory for the keys.

---

## Unions

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/unions/*

In Zig, you write a tagged union as `union(enum)`. A tagged union is a sum type. The value carries a tag that names its active field, and a `switch` on the value must handle each field. A bare `union` has no tag. A read of a field that is not the active field is illegal behaviour.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// A bare union has no tag: you must know which field is active.
const Payload = union {
    int: i64,
    float: f64,
};

const Tag = enum { int, float, none };

// A tagged union carries its tag, so `switch` can safely discriminate.
const Tagged = union(Tag) {
    int: i64,
    float: f64,
    none: void,
};

// `union(enum)` infers the tag enum for you.
const Inferred = union(enum) {
    text: []const u8,
    number: u32,
};

test "bare union" {
    var p = Payload{ .int = 42 };
    try expect(p.int == 42);
    // A read of `p.float` here is illegal behaviour: it is not the active field.
    p = Payload{ .float = 1.5 };
    try expect(p.float == 1.5);
}

test "switch on a tagged union" {
    var value = Tagged{ .int = 7 };
    switch (value) {
        .int => |*n| n.* += 1,
        .float => |*f| f.* *= 2,
        .none => {},
    }
    try expect(value.int == 8);
}

test "the tag is a real enum value" {
    const value = Tagged{ .float = 2.5 };
    try expect(@as(Tag, value) == .float);
}

test "inferred tag enum" {
    const v = Inferred{ .text = "hi" };
    switch (v) {
        .text => |t| try expect(t.len == 2),
        .number => unreachable,
    }
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.unions`)*

A union holds one of its fields at a time. The question is always: *which field*?

## A bare union does not know the active field

```zig
const Payload = union { int: i64, float: f64 };
```

A read of a field that is not the active field is illegal behaviour. Bare unions are for C interop, and for cases where a different part of the code already records the tag.

"Illegal behaviour" means more than "you get incorrect data":

- In a safety build, the program catches the access to the wrong field and panics.
- In ReleaseFast, the access is undefined, and the optimiser can assume that it never occurs.

Thus a bare union is a promise from you. Make that promise only when something outside the union already records the answer.

## A tagged union knows the active field

```zig
const Tagged = union(Tag) { int: i64, float: f64, none: void };
```

Now the value carries its tag. `switch` can safely select the correct field, and the switch must be exhaustive. A tagged union is the sum type of Zig, and almost always it is the correct choice. Error unions and optionals also use the same construct.

A pointer capture in a prong lets you change the value in place:

```zig
switch (value) {
    .int => |*n| n.* += 1,
    ...
}
```

A `void` field says "this case carries nothing". Thus a tagged union can have states without a payload, and you do not have to make a dummy payload.

## `union(enum)`

When you write `union(enum)`, the compiler makes the tag enum from the field names. Thus you do not have to declare and update a separate `enum` with the same names. Use the explicit form only when you need the enum as a named type, or when you must set its values.

To get the tag, use `@as(Tag, value)`, or compare directly against `.float` in a `switch`. `std.meta.activeTag(value)` does the same thing, and its name is easier to read outside a switch. `@tagName` changes the tag into a string for [logging](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/logging/).

Sometimes the compiler must select the variant at compile time, and the code does not write the variant literally. For this case, `@unionInit(T, "int", 5)` takes the field name as a comptime string. Generic code uses `@unionInit` when it examines a type and does not name a case.

## The cost of a tagged union

A tagged union is as large as its largest field plus the tag, plus the padding that alignment needs. Thus one very large variant sets the size for each value of the type, also for the values that carry nothing.

When the variants have very different sizes, the usual solution is to put the large variant behind a pointer. Then the union holds a pointer, not the payload.

The tag is a usual enum, and you can give it a type: `union(enum(u8))` makes the tag one byte. `packed union` is for the bit-level cases. As with `packed struct`, use it for real boundaries, not to save a byte.

## Where to use a tagged union

Use a tagged union in each place where a value has one of several shapes. Examples are a token from a lexer, a node in a syntax tree and a message from a protocol. A configuration value that can be a string or a number is also an example.

In code from other people, look for a struct with a "kind" field and some fields that are valid only for some kinds. That struct is a tagged union that a person wrote by hand, without the exhaustiveness check.

The [tiny language](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/) track builds a lexer, a parser and an interpreter with exactly this construct. Thus you can see a tagged union in a real program.

---

## Integer Rules

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/integer-rules/*

Zig integer types have an explicit width, such as `u8`, `i32` or `u3`. A conversion from a wider type to a narrower type needs `@intCast`.

For plain `+`, overflow is illegal behaviour, and safety builds panic on it. When you want a different result, use one of the two other operators:

- `+%` wraps.
- `+|` saturates.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "arbitrary bit widths" {
    // Each width from u0/i0 to u65535 is a real type.
    const small: u3 = 7;
    try expect(@as(u8, small) == 7);
    try expect(std.math.maxInt(u3) == 7);
}

test "widening is implicit, narrowing is not" {
    const a: u8 = 200;
    const b: u16 = a; // always safe, thus allowed
    try expect(b == 200);

    // `const c: u8 = b;` does not compile. Convert explicitly:
    const c: u8 = @intCast(b); // checked in safety builds
    try expect(c == 200);
}

test "wrapping and saturating operators" {
    const max: u8 = 255;
    // Plain `max + 1` is illegal behaviour (a panic in safety builds).
    try expect(max +% 1 == 0); // wrapping
    try expect(max +| 1 == 255); // saturating
}

test "overflow can be detected instead" {
    const max: u8 = 255;
    const result = @addWithOverflow(max, 1);
    try expect(result[0] == 0); // wrapped value
    try expect(result[1] == 1); // overflow bit set
}

test "comptime_int has no width" {
    // Literals have arbitrary precision until they get a type.
    const big = 1 << 100;
    try expect(big > 0);
    try expect(@TypeOf(1 + 1) == comptime_int);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.integer-rules`)*

## Any width that you want

`u3`, `i7`, `u64` and `u1000` are all real types. `u8` is not special. It is only the width of a byte. Packed structs use these widths to describe bitfields exactly.

The width is part of the type, and the width never depends on the platform. Zig has no `int` whose size changes with the compiler, and no integer promotion rules to remember. Your computer and the CI computer calculate the same results.

The only integer type that depends on the target is `usize`. It depends on the target on purpose, because it is the width of a pointer. See [pointer-sized integers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/pointer-sized-integers/).

`@sizeOf(u3)` is 1, because memory addresses are in bytes. Inside a `packed
struct`, the same `u3` uses exactly three bits. Unusual widths are for the description of a layout and for a limit on a value. Alone, they do not save memory.

## A wider type has no cost, a narrower type has a cost

A conversion from `u8` to `u16` is always safe. Thus Zig does it implicitly. The reverse conversion can lose data. Thus you must write it:

```zig
const c: u8 = @intCast(b);
```

In a build with safety checks, `@intCast` panics if the value does not fit. In `ReleaseFast`, a value that does not fit is illegal behaviour. In the two cases, the cast is visible in the source. Thus you cannot lose the top bits by accident.

The sign is also information. For Zig, a conversion from `i8` to `u8` is a narrowing, also when the widths are equal. The reason is that `u8` has no place for a negative value. Thus this conversion also needs `@intCast`.

`@bitCast` is the other conversion. It keeps the same bits and reads them as a different type. It never checks the value, because nothing can go wrong at the bit level. Use `@intCast` when you mean "this number", and `@bitCast` when you mean "these bits".

## You decide what overflow does

On overflow, plain `+` on integers **traps**. It does not wrap. If you want a different behaviour, ask for it:

| Operator | On overflow |
| --- | --- |
| `+` `-` `*` | illegal behaviour (panics in safety builds) |
| `+%` `-%` `*%` | wrap around |
| `+\|` `-\|` `*\|` | saturate at the type's limit |

You can also detect the overflow. `@addWithOverflow(a, b)` returns a tuple of the wrapped result and an overflow bit.

In C, overflow can corrupt a value, and you get no warning. In Zig, the behaviour is an explicit selection.

Each of the three behaviours is the correct answer for some data:

- Wrapping is correct for hashes, checksums and counters that must cycle.
- Saturating is correct for pixel arithmetic and audio mixing. In these cases, the correct answer above the limit really is the limit.
- The default trap is correct for all other data.

A number that does not fit its type now means that the code has a bug. It is better to find the bug immediately than three functions later.

A common mistake is unsigned subtraction. When `b > a`, `a - b` is an overflow, not a negative number, and it panics. When you count down from `.len`, put the decrement in a place where it cannot run at zero.

## Division and shifts also have rules

`/` on a signed integer that the compiler does not know at comptime does not compile at all. Rounding toward zero and rounding down give different results when an operand is negative. Thus Zig makes you write the one that you want: `@divTrunc`, `@divFloor`, `@divCeil` or `@divExact`.

`%` has the same rule, and you use `@rem` or `@mod`. C shows why the selection is important: for twenty years, the C answer to `-7 / 2` was implementation-defined.

On all platforms, a shift by more than the width is illegal behaviour. Also, the type of the shift amount has only enough bits for a legal shift. Thus `x << 8` on a `u8` does not compile.

## `comptime_int`

Literals have no width until they get one from an assignment. `1 << 100` is correct at compile time. It must fit only when it becomes a runtime value.

`comptime_int` has arbitrary precision. `comptime_float` does not, because it uses `f128`. Thus integer arithmetic at compile time is exact at all magnitudes. The error occurs only when you store the result in a location with a size.

For this reason, a `var` cannot hold a `comptime_int`. To refer to the limits of a type, use `std.math.maxInt(T)` and `minInt(T)`. Do not write the constant yourself.

---

## Floats

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/floats/*

Zig never converts between integers and floats implicitly. `@floatFromInt` and `@intFromFloat` do the conversion. `@intFromFloat` truncates toward zero.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "float widths" {
    const a: f16 = 1.5;
    const b: f32 = 1.5;
    const c: f64 = 1.5;
    try expect(a == 1.5 and b == 1.5 and c == 1.5);
    try expect(@sizeOf(f16) == 2 and @sizeOf(f64) == 8);
}

test "int and float do not mix implicitly" {
    const n: i32 = 3;
    const f: f32 = @floatFromInt(n);
    try expect(f == 3.0);

    // Truncates toward zero. Safety builds check the conversion.
    const back: i32 = @intFromFloat(3.9);
    try expect(back == 3);
}

test "comptime_float is f128, not magic" {
    // comptime_int really has arbitrary precision, but comptime_float uses
    // f128. Arithmetic at compile time gives you more bits, but the result
    // is still not exact:
    const x = 0.1 + 0.2;
    try expect(x != 0.3);

    // The same sum in f64 is not 0.3 either.
    const y: f64 = 0.1;
    const z: f64 = 0.2;
    try expect(y + z != 0.3);

    // Compare with a tolerance instead of ==.
    try expect(std.math.approxEqAbs(f64, y + z, 0.3, 1e-12));
}

test "special values" {
    const inf = std.math.inf(f32);
    const nan = std.math.nan(f32);
    try expect(std.math.isInf(inf));
    try expect(std.math.isNan(nan));
    try expect(nan != nan); // NaN is not equal to itself
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.floats`)*

Zig has `f16`, `f32`, `f64`, `f80` and `f128`. All of them are IEEE-754, except `f80`, the x87 extended format.

## No implicit mix of ints and floats

Zig does not do a conversion in either direction automatically:

```zig
const f: f32 = @floatFromInt(n);
const n: i32 = @intFromFloat(f);   // truncates toward zero
```

Zig does this on purpose. An implicit conversion from int to float loses precision for large integers, and you get no warning. An implicit conversion from float to int truncates, and you get no warning. The two conversions cause many bugs. Thus the two extra words are a good cost.

`@intFromFloat` truncates. It does not round. The target type must be able to hold the result. A value outside the range of the target, or a NaN, is illegal behaviour, and a safety build finds it.

If you do not know that the input is in range, clamp the input or check it first. If you want the saturating version, use `std.math.lossyCast`.

Between float types, `@floatCast` makes a value narrower. A change to a wider type is implicit, because it cannot lose data.

## `comptime_float` is `f128`

An earlier version of this page had this fact wrong. `comptime_int` really has arbitrary precision, but `comptime_float` does not: it uses `f128`. Arithmetic at compile time gives you more bits, but it does not give you exact decimal values:

```zig
const x = 0.1 + 0.2;
// x != 0.3, even at comptime
```

Comptime floats still have rounding error. Compare them with a tolerance:

```zig
std.math.approxEqAbs(f64, a, b, 1e-12)
```

`approxEqAbs` takes an absolute tolerance. It is correct when you know the magnitude of the numbers. `approxEqRel` takes a relative tolerance. It is correct when you do not know the magnitude.

For values near a billion, an absolute tolerance of `1e-12` is so strict that no result can meet it. For values near `1e-15`, the same tolerance is much too loose.

## NaN and infinity

`std.math.nan(f32)` and `std.math.inf(f32)` make these values. `isNan` and `isInf` test for them. Remember that `nan != nan`. This is the reason that `approxEqAbs` exists, and the reason to be careful with `==` on floats.

A NaN makes each comparison false. Thus a NaN can break code without an error. `a < b` and `a >= b` are both false when `a` or `b` is NaN.

Thus a NaN in a sort does more than put that value in a strange position. It breaks the order that the algorithm expects. Remove NaNs before the sort. Do not expect the comparator to handle them.

Division by zero follows IEEE and does not trap. `1.0 / 0.0` is infinity, and `0.0 / 0.0` is NaN. Integer division by zero is different: it is illegal behaviour.

## Which width to use

Use `f64` unless you have a reason to use a different width:

- `f32` uses half the memory, and graphics and audio pipelines expect it. It gives approximately seven decimal digits of precision. When a loop adds many values, this precision is quickly not sufficient.
- `f16` is for storage and for machine learning weights, not for arithmetic.
- `f80` and `f128` exist for the cases that need them. Most targets emulate them in software, thus they are slow.

Usually, the important precision question is not the width. Money in floats is wrong at all widths, because binary cannot represent 0.1 exactly. Use an integer count of the smallest unit.

---

## Labelled Blocks

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-blocks/*

In Zig, a labelled block computes a `const` with more than one statement. The block ends with `break :blk value`. The scope of the intermediate variables in the block ends at the closing brace.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "block as an expression" {
    // `break :label value` gives a value from the labelled block. Thus a
    // computation with many steps can still produce one const.
    const count = blk: {
        var sum: u32 = 0;
        for (0..10) |i| sum += i;
        break :blk sum;
    };
    try expect(count == 45);
    try expect(@TypeOf(count) == u32);
}

test "labels also name scopes for shadowing" {
    const outer_value: u32 = 1;
    const result = blk: {
        const outer_value_inner: u32 = 2;
        break :blk outer_value + outer_value_inner;
    };
    try expect(result == 3);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.labelled-blocks`)*

Give a label to a block, and use `break` with a value to leave the block:

```zig
const count = blk: {
    var sum: u32 = 0;
    for (0..10) |i| sum += i;
    break :blk sum;
};
```

You can use any name instead of `blk`. The important point is that a computation with many statements still produces one `const`. Thus the intermediate `var` cannot be visible in the outer scope, and you cannot use it again by accident later.

Use a labelled block when you need a few lines to compute a value, and you want the result to be immutable. Without a labelled block, programmers often use a mutable variable with a scope that is wider than necessary. Or they write a function that they use only one time.

## The label makes the block an expression

A block without a label is a statement. It groups code and starts a scope, but it has no value. The label gives `break` a name to use. The statement `break :blk x` gives the block a type. If you remove the label, you cannot get `x` out of the block.

The compiler also checks the opposite case. A label that no `break` uses is an error:

```
error: unused block label
```

[Labelled loops](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-loops/) get the same error, for the same reason. Usually, an unused label is a part of control flow that a programmer deleted, and the label stayed.

## `break :blk` is not `return`

In a block inside a function, it is easy to confuse the two statements. They do different things:

- `break :blk x` ends the block and gives `x` to the variable that receives the value of the block.
- `return x` ends the *function*.

Think of a block that computes one field of a struct. With `break`, the program sets the value of that field. With `return`, the program stops the construction of the full struct.

Blocks can be inside other blocks, and a `break` names the block that it leaves. Thus an inner block can break to an outer label and skip all the code between the two. In this case the code can be difficult to read. To make the code clear, select a good label name. A comment does not help as much.

## The block is a scope

The second test in the snippet shows this rule. The scope of each declaration inside the braces ends at the closing brace. This includes the `var` that did the work. Only the value that `break` gives out of the block continues to exist, and that value is a `const`.

This limit on scope is the real reason to use a labelled block. Compare the code without a block:

```zig
var sum: u32 = 0;
for (0..10) |i| sum += i;
// sum is mutable, in scope, and still writable fifty lines later
```

In this code, a mutable variable stays alive for the remainder of the function. Nothing shows that the code no longer writes to `sum`. A person who edits the function later must read all of it to know if the code still adds values to `sum`. In the block form, the closing brace gives the answer.

## Where real code uses labelled blocks

There are three usual places:

- **A `const` that needs more than one expression.** For example, to parse a value, to select a default, or to add the values in a table.
- **Switch arms that need statements.** When you use a `switch` as an expression, each arm must produce a value. An arm that needs three lines becomes a labelled block.
- **Comptime tables.** Put `comptime` before the block, and the full block runs during compilation. Thus the compiler can make a lookup table, and you do not have to type it:

  ```zig
  const squares = comptime blk: {
      var t: [5]u32 = undefined;
      for (&t, 0..) |*e, i| e.* = @intCast(i * i);
      break :blk t;
  };
  ```

  `squares` is a `[5]u32`, and the binary contains its value. No code runs at startup. The loop that made the table is not in the compiled program.

If you know C, a labelled block is the standard version of the statement expressions in GCC. If you know JavaScript, a labelled block replaces a function that you call immediately only to give a computation a private scope. The labelled block has no function and no call.

---

## Labelled Loops

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-loops/*

In Zig, `break :outer` leaves a labelled outer loop from inside a nested loop. `continue :outer` starts the next iteration of the outer loop. Thus you do not need a flag variable.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "break out of nested loops" {
    var found: ?[2]usize = null;
    outer: for (0..5) |i| {
        for (0..5) |j| {
            if (i * j == 6) {
                found = .{ i, j };
                break :outer; // leaves both loops
            }
        }
    }
    try expect(found.?[0] == 2);
    try expect(found.?[1] == 3);
}

test "continue an outer loop" {
    var count: u32 = 0;
    outer: for (0..4) |i| {
        for (0..4) |j| {
            if (j > i) continue :outer; // next i, skip the other j values
            count += 1;
        }
    }
    try expect(count == 10); // 1 + 2 + 3 + 4
}

test "labelled loops yield values too" {
    const first_square_over_20 = blk: {
        for (0..10) |i| {
            if (i * i > 20) break :blk i;
        }
        break :blk 0;
    };
    try expect(first_square_over_20 == 5);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.labelled-loops`)*

By default, `break` and `continue` affect the innermost loop. To select a different loop, give that loop a label:

```zig
outer: for (0..5) |i| {
    for (0..5) |j| {
        if (found) break :outer;      // leaves both loops
        if (skip) continue :outer;    // next i, abandon remaining j
    }
}
```

A label is an identifier and a colon, before the loop keyword. You can use any name. `outer` and `blk` are usual names, but the compiler does not require them. Usually, a label that tells what the loop examines (`rows:`, `candidates:`) is easier to read at the `break`. The `break` is where a reader looks.

## The cost of the alternative

Without labels, you need a flag to leave two loops at the same time:

```zig
var found = false;
for (rows) |row| {
    for (row) |cell| {
        if (matches(cell)) { found = true; break; }
    }
    if (found) break;
}
```

The flag adds three lines of bookkeeping. You must also repeat `if (found) break` at each level of nesting. The flag also continues to exist after the loop, so later code can read it. And the `break` in the inner loop does not tell you what it does until you read the next two lines.

In C, you use `goto` to jump past the loops. That method works, but then the label names a place in the code, not a loop.
