A loop with a name also keeps the code correct when a person edits it later. If you put one more level of nesting around either loop, a `break` without a label changes its meaning and gives no error. `break :outer` keeps its meaning.

## `continue :outer` runs the outer continue expression

A labelled `continue` does not jump to the top of the outer loop. It ends the current iteration of that loop. Thus the continue expression of the outer loop runs first, exactly as if the outer body got to its end:

```zig
outer: while (i < 3) : (i += 1) {
    while (j < 3) : (j += 1) {
        if (j == 1) continue :outer;   // i += 1 still happens
    }
}
```

If `continue :outer` did not run `i += 1`, that loop would not stop. But `continue :outer` runs `i += 1`, and the loop runs three times. The rule is that `continue` always means "this iteration is complete". It never means "return to the condition".

## An unused label is a compile error

If you give a label to a loop and never use the label, the program does not compile:

```
error: unused for loop label
```

Usually, a programmer adds a label together with a `break :outer`. Usually, the label becomes unused when a refactor deletes or moves that `break`. An unused label is a strong sign that the control flow for the label does not exist now. Zig treats an unused label as it treats an unused variable. You must use it or remove it.

## Labels are not only for loops

A label can also name a plain block, and `break :label value` gives a value from the block. The third test in the snippet uses a labelled block to change a search into one `const`:

1. The block runs the loop.
2. If the loop finds a match, the block breaks out with the index.
3. If the loop finds no match, the block gets to the end and gives a default.

[Labelled blocks](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-blocks/) has more about this construct. Together with `for` and `else`, the construct becomes the shorter form in [loops as expressions](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/loops-as-expressions/).

---

## Labelled Switch

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-switch/*

A `switch` can have a label, as a block or a loop can. When a switch has a label, two statements become available:

- `continue :label value` runs the switch again, with `value` as the new operand.
- `break :label value` leaves the switch, and the full switch has the value `value`.

With these two statements, you can write a state machine without a loop and without a state variable. This form came in Zig 0.14.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Tag = enum { identifier, number, equal, semicolon, invalid, eof };

const Token = struct { tag: Tag, start: usize, end: usize };

const State = enum { start, identifier, number };

// One token from `src`. The token starts at `index.*`.
//
// The source ends with a zero byte, as the source of std.zig.Tokenizer does.
// Thus the terminator marks the end of the input, and no prong checks a length.
fn next(src: [:0]const u8, index: *usize, out: *std.Io.Writer) !Token {
    var i = index.*;
    var start = i;

    const tag: Tag = state: switch (State.start) {
        .start => {
            try visit(out, "start", src, i);
            switch (src[i]) {
                0 => break :state .eof,
                ' ' => {
                    i += 1;
                    start = i;
                    continue :state .start;
                },
                'a'...'z', '_' => {
                    i += 1;
                    continue :state .identifier;
                },
                '0'...'9' => {
                    i += 1;
                    continue :state .number;
                },
                '=' => {
                    i += 1;
                    break :state .equal;
                },
                ';' => {
                    i += 1;
                    break :state .semicolon;
                },
                else => {
                    i += 1;
                    break :state .invalid;
                },
            }
        },
        .identifier => {
            try visit(out, "identifier", src, i);
            switch (src[i]) {
                'a'...'z', '_', '0'...'9' => {
                    i += 1;
                    continue :state .identifier;
                },
                else => break :state .identifier,
            }
        },
        .number => {
            try visit(out, "number", src, i);
            switch (src[i]) {
                '0'...'9' => {
                    i += 1;
                    continue :state .number;
                },
                else => break :state .number,
            }
        },
    };

    index.* = i;
    return .{ .tag = tag, .start = start, .end = i };
}

fn visit(out: *std.Io.Writer, state: []const u8, src: [:0]const u8, i: usize) !void {
    if (src[i] == 0) {
        try out.print("  {s:<10}  src[{d}] is the terminator\n", .{ state, i });
    } else {
        try out.print("  {s:<10}  src[{d}] = '{c}'\n", .{ state, i, src[i] });
    }
}

// The same tokenizer in the form that was necessary before Zig 0.14: a loop
// around a switch, and a variable that holds the state.
fn nextLoop(src: [:0]const u8, index: *usize) Token {
    var i = index.*;
    var start = i;
    var state: State = .start;

    const tag: Tag = while (true) {
        switch (state) {
            .start => switch (src[i]) {
                0 => break .eof,
                ' ' => {
                    i += 1;
                    start = i;
                },
                'a'...'z', '_' => {
                    i += 1;
                    state = .identifier;
                },
                '0'...'9' => {
                    i += 1;
                    state = .number;
                },
                '=' => {
                    i += 1;
                    break .equal;
                },
                ';' => {
                    i += 1;
                    break .semicolon;
                },
                else => {
                    i += 1;
                    break .invalid;
                },
            },
            .identifier => switch (src[i]) {
                'a'...'z', '_', '0'...'9' => i += 1,
                else => break .identifier,
            },
            .number => switch (src[i]) {
                '0'...'9' => i += 1,
                else => break .number,
            },
        }
    };

    index.* = i;
    return .{ .tag = tag, .start = start, .end = i };
}

const Instruction = union(enum) {
    push: i32,
    add,
    mul,
    halt,
};

// A small stack machine. The operand of each `continue` is the next
// instruction. The program knows the next instruction only at run time.
fn run(code: []const Instruction) i32 {
    var stack: [8]i32 = undefined;
    var sp: usize = 0;
    var ip: usize = 0;

    return vm: switch (code[ip]) {
        .push => |n| {
            stack[sp] = n;
            sp += 1;
            ip += 1;
            continue :vm code[ip];
        },
        .add => {
            sp -= 1;
            stack[sp - 1] += stack[sp];
            ip += 1;
            continue :vm code[ip];
        },
        .mul => {
            sp -= 1;
            stack[sp - 1] *= stack[sp];
            ip += 1;
            continue :vm code[ip];
        },
        .halt => stack[sp - 1],
    };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const src: [:0]const u8 = "n2 = 40;";
    try out.print("source: \"{s}\"\n", .{src});

    var index: usize = 0;
    var loop_index: usize = 0;
    var agree = true;
    while (true) {
        const token = try next(src, &index, out);
        const again = nextLoop(src, &loop_index);
        if (!std.meta.eql(token, again)) agree = false;

        try out.print("{s} \"{s}\"\n", .{ @tagName(token.tag), src[token.start..token.end] });
        if (token.tag == .eof) break;
    }
    try out.print("loop form agrees: {}\n\n", .{agree});

    // (2 + 3) * 4
    const program = [_]Instruction{ .{ .push = 2 }, .{ .push = 3 }, .add, .{ .push = 4 }, .mul, .halt };
    try out.print("(2 + 3) * 4 = {d}\n", .{run(&program)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.labelled-switch`)*

## The shape

```zig
const tag: Tag = state: switch (State.start) {
    .start => switch (src[i]) {
        'a'...'z' => {
            i += 1;
            continue :state .identifier;
        },
        '=' => {
            i += 1;
            break :state .equal;
        },
        // ...
    },
    .identifier => switch (src[i]) {
        'a'...'z', '0'...'9' => {
            i += 1;
            continue :state .identifier;
        },
        else => break :state .identifier,
    },
};
```

`State.start` is the first operand. Each prong is a state.

- `continue :state .identifier` means "go to the `.identifier` prong now".
- `break :state .equal` means "stop, and the answer is `.equal`".

The label is before `switch`. You can select any name for the label.

## See the jumps

The program above tokenizes `n2 = 40;`. Before each prong decides where to go, it prints its state and the byte that it examines.

- A line that starts with a state name is one entry into the switch.
- A line without an indent is a token that a `break` gives.

```
source: "n2 = 40;"
  start       src[0] = 'n'
  identifier  src[1] = '2'
  identifier  src[2] = ' '
identifier "n2"
  start       src[2] = ' '
  start       src[3] = '='
equal "="
  start       src[4] = ' '
  start       src[5] = '4'
  number      src[6] = '0'
  number      src[7] = ';'
number "40"
  start       src[7] = ';'
semicolon ";"
  start       src[8] is the terminator
eof ""
```

Read the first three lines:

1. `.start` sees `n`. A name can start with `n`, so `.start` continues into `.identifier`.
2. `.identifier` sees `2`. A name can contain `2`, so `.identifier` continues into itself.
3. Then `.identifier` sees a space and breaks with `.identifier`.

The tokenizer does not consume the space. The next call starts on the space, and `.start` continues into `.start` to skip it.

The source is a `[:0]const u8`. When the code reads one position after the last character, it gets the `0` terminator. Thus the `.start` prong ends the input when it matches `0`. It does not check a length.

`std.zig.Tokenizer` is the tokenizer that the Zig compiler uses on your code, and it has the same structure. Its `next` function is one labelled switch over a `State` enum, much larger than this one.

## What the labelled switch replaces

Before 0.14, the same tokenizer needed a loop around the switch. A variable held the state, and each transition had two steps. First the code set the variable, then the loop started its next iteration.

```zig
fn nextLoop(src: [:0]const u8, index: *usize) Token {
    var i = index.*;
    var start = i;
    var state: State = .start;

    const tag: Tag = while (true) {
        switch (state) {
            .start => switch (src[i]) {
                0 => break .eof,
                ' ' => {
                    i += 1;
                    start = i;
                },
                'a'...'z', '_' => {
                    i += 1;
                    state = .identifier;
                },
                '0'...'9' => {
                    i += 1;
                    state = .number;
                },
                '=' => {
                    i += 1;
                    break .equal;
                },
                ';' => {
                    i += 1;
                    break .semicolon;
                },
                else => {
                    i += 1;
                    break .invalid;
                },
            },
            .identifier => switch (src[i]) {
                'a'...'z', '_', '0'...'9' => i += 1,
                else => break .identifier,
            },
            .number => switch (src[i]) {
                '0'...'9' => i += 1,
                else => break .number,
            },
        }
    };

    index.* = i;
    return .{ .tag = tag, .start = start, .end = i };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `nextLoop` from `snippets/02-language/labelled-switch.zig`.*

The program runs the two versions on each token and checks that they agree:

```
loop form agrees: true
```

The two versions do the same thing. The language reference says this directly: a labelled switch has the same semantics as a `while (true)` around a `switch`. The difference is in how a person reads each version.

In the loop form, `state = .number;` is a line that sets a variable. To know that the line moves the machine, you must find the loop. You must also check that no code after the assignment runs before the next iteration.

In the labelled form, `continue :state .number` is the transition, and no code after it in the prong can run. Also, no `state` variable stays in scope, so other code cannot read or change the state.

## When the next state is only known at run time

The operand of `continue` does not have to be a literal. A bytecode interpreter selects the next prong from the next instruction:

```zig
fn run(code: []const Instruction) i32 {
    var stack: [8]i32 = undefined;
    var sp: usize = 0;
    var ip: usize = 0;

    return vm: switch (code[ip]) {
        .push => |n| {
            stack[sp] = n;
            sp += 1;
            ip += 1;
            continue :vm code[ip];
        },
        .add => {
            sp -= 1;
            stack[sp - 1] += stack[sp];
            ip += 1;
            continue :vm code[ip];
        },
        .mul => {
            sp -= 1;
            stack[sp - 1] *= stack[sp];
            ip += 1;
            continue :vm code[ip];
        },
        .halt => stack[sp - 1],
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `run` from `snippets/02-language/labelled-switch.zig`.*

```
(2 + 3) * 4 = 20
```

`Instruction` is a tagged union. Thus `.push => |n|` captures the payload, as in a usual switch. `.halt` has no `continue`. Thus its value is the value of the full switch, and `run` returns that value.

The language reference gives this dispatch loop as the reason for the feature. The reason comes from code generation:

- When the operand of `continue` is known at compile time, as `.identifier` is, the compiler can change it into a direct jump to that prong.
- When the operand is known only at run time, as `code[ip]` is, each `continue` can get its own branch.

A loop sends each iteration through one shared dispatch point. The CPU then predicts that one branch for all instructions together. With a branch at each `continue`, the CPU can learn that another `.push` usually follows a `.push`. The CPU learns this separately from what follows `.mul`.

The language lets the compiler do these things. Measure if a given backend and optimization mode does them. Do not assume it.

## Two compile errors

`continue` on a switch needs a value. Without a value, the switch has no operand:

```
error: cannot continue switch without operand
```

A label that no statement uses is a compile error, as on a loop:

```
error: unused switch label
```

## Related

A labelled switch uses the same label syntax as [labelled blocks](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-blocks/) and [labelled loops](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/labelled-loops/).

All the rules of a usual [switch](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/switch/) still apply, and exhaustiveness is one of them. If you add a tag to `State`, the tokenizer does not compile until a prong handles the new tag.

---

## Loops as Expressions

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/loops-as-expressions/*

In Zig, `for` and `while` loops are expressions. Thus a search can return its result directly. You do not need a mutable `result` variable before the loop.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

fn firstIndexOf(haystack: []const u8, needle: u8) ?usize {
    // The `else` branch runs only if the loop ends without a `break`. Thus
    // you cannot forget the "not found" case.
    return for (haystack, 0..) |c, i| {
        if (c == needle) break i;
    } else null;
}

test "for as an expression" {
    try expect(firstIndexOf("hello", 'l').? == 2);
    try expect(firstIndexOf("hello", 'z') == null);
}

test "while as an expression" {
    var i: u32 = 0;
    const result = while (i < 10) : (i += 1) {
        if (i == 4) break i * 10;
    } else 0;
    try expect(result == 40);
}

test "the else branch runs when nothing breaks" {
    var i: u32 = 0;
    const result = while (i < 3) : (i += 1) {
        if (i == 99) break @as(u32, 1);
    } else @as(u32, 2);
    try expect(result == 2);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.loops-as-expressions`)*

A loop can produce a value. `break x` gives `x`. If the loop ends and no `break` runs, the `else` branch gives the value.

```zig
return for (haystack, 0..) |c, i| {
    if (c == needle) break i;
} else null;
```

These lines are a complete linear search. The structure makes it impossible to forget the "not found" case: if you remove the `else`, the code does not compile.

Compare the usual alternative:

```zig
var result: ?usize = null;
for (haystack, 0..) |c, i| {
    if (c == needle) { result = i; break; }
}
return result;
```

The behaviour is the same. But now `result` is mutable, and it lives longer than necessary. Also, nothing makes you initialise it correctly.

## What `else` means on a loop

The `else` of a loop is not the `else` of an `if`. It runs when the loop ends *normally*: the `for` has no more elements, or the `while` condition becomes false. A `break` skips the `else`.

This rule makes the construct safe for searches. There are exactly two exits from the loop, and each exit produces a value.

The third test in the snippet shows this rule. It has a `break` that can never run:

```zig
const result = while (i < 3) : (i += 1) {
    if (i == 99) break @as(u32, 1);
} else @as(u32, 2);
```

`i` never gets to 99, the condition becomes false, and `result` is 2.

## The error when there is no `else`

The error can confuse you, because it does not mention `else`. A loop without an `else` has no value when it ends normally. Thus its type is `void`:

```
error: expected type '?usize', found 'void'
```

The error points at the full `for` expression. Read it as "this loop does not always produce a value". To correct the error, add the `else`.

Only a loop that cannot end normally does not need an `else`. `while (true)` has no condition that can become false. Thus `break` is the only exit, and the compiler knows this:

```zig
const v = while (true) : (i += 1) {
    if (i == 3) break i;
};
```

This code compiles, and `v` is `usize`. If you add an `else` to this loop, the `else` is dead code.

## The two arms must have one type

The `break` value and the `else` value are two arms of one expression. Thus they must resolve to one type. In the search above, the arms are `usize` and `null`. Together they become `?usize`, and that type is the return type of the function.

When the arms are integer literals without a type, they are comptime-known. They coerce to the type that the code around them needs. When no type is available, you must give one. Thus the test writes `@as(u32, 1)` and `@as(u32, 2)`, not `1` and `2`. `const result = ...` gives the literals no target type for their size and signedness.

If the arms really have different types, the error names the two types and points at the `break`. Because of this check, a search cannot return an index on one path and a boolean on a different path by accident.

## When to use a loop as an expression

Use the pattern when the loop answers exactly one question. For example: find a value, count until a condition, or decide if any element is acceptable. The value comes out at the place where the loop decides it. The compiler makes you handle the two results.

The pattern does not help when a loop has five `break` statements with five different meanings. Nothing prevents that code, but the result is more difficult to understand than an explicit variable. The reader must find each `break` to know the possible values of the expression. Use the pattern for one or two exits.

---

## Payload Captures

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/payload-captures/*

In Zig, `|value|` after `if`, `while`, `for`, `switch` or `catch` names the unwrapped payload. The payload is the non-null value, the success value, the active variant or the current element. `|*value|` captures a pointer instead. Thus writes change the original.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const Shape = union(enum) {
    circle: f32,
    rect: struct { w: f32, h: f32 },
};

test "capture an optional" {
    const maybe: ?u32 = 5;
    if (maybe) |value| {
        try expect(value == 5);
    } else {
        unreachable;
    }
}

test "capture an error union" {
    const result: anyerror!u32 = 7;
    if (result) |value| {
        try expect(value == 7);
    } else |_| {
        unreachable;
    }
}

test "capture a union payload in switch" {
    const s = Shape{ .rect = .{ .w = 2, .h = 3 } };
    const area = switch (s) {
        .circle => |r| 3.14 * r * r,
        .rect => |r| r.w * r.h,
    };
    try expect(area == 6);
}

test "capture by pointer to mutate" {
    var maybe: ?u32 = 5;
    if (maybe) |*value| {
        value.* += 1;
    }
    try expect(maybe.? == 6);
}

test "while captures until null" {
    // A `while` over an expression that returns an optional stops at null.
    var countdown: u32 = 3;
    var seen: u32 = 0;
    while (nextValue(&countdown)) |value| {
        seen += value;
    }
    try expect(seen == 6); // 3 + 2 + 1
}

fn nextValue(state: *u32) ?u32 {
    if (state.* == 0) return null;
    defer state.* -= 1;
    return state.*;
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.payload-captures`)*

The `|value|` syntax is one idea. Zig uses it in each place where a value is inside a wrapper:

| Construct | Captures |
| --- | --- |
| `if (optional) \|v\|` | the non-null payload |
| `if (error_union) \|v\| else \|e\|` | the value, or the error |
| `while (iter()) \|v\|` | each value until null |
| `switch (tagged_union) { .a => \|v\| ... }` | the active variant's payload |
| `for (slice) \|item\|` | each element |
| `catch \|err\|` | the error |

When you know the syntax for one wrapper type, you know it for all wrapper types in the language.

## Why the test and the unwrap are one construct

The capture makes these constructs safe. Zig has no `isSome()` with a separate `unwrap()`. An edit can move those two calls apart, and then the unwrap runs without the test.

In Zig, the payload has a name only inside the branch where the payload exists. Outside that branch, there is no name that you can use incorrectly.

The capture also explains why some operations do not exist:

- You cannot ask an optional "are you null" and get a bool that you can store in a variable.
- You cannot name the payload of a union variant that is not active.

The language gives you the payload exactly where it is valid, and in no other place.

## Capture a pointer to change the value

`|*value|` captures a pointer, not a copy. Thus you can change the original value in place:

```zig
if (maybe) |*value| value.* += 1;

switch (shape) {
    .circle => |*r| r.* *= 2,
    ...
}
```

Without the `*`, you get a copy. If you change the copy, the original does not change, and there is no error. This is one of the few places where Zig lets you write code that looks correct but has no effect.

To find this bug, ask what you hold:

- `|v|` is a value that you own. You can change it, and nothing else changes.
- `|*v|` is a pointer to the original. Thus writes change the original.

When the payload is large, the pointer form also prevents the copy. But use the pointer form for correctness, not for speed.

A pointer capture needs a location for the pointer. It works when the unwrapped value is in a mutable location: a `var`, a field or an element. A temporary value exists only for the duration of the expression. It has no fixed location, thus you cannot take its address. The compiler gives an error. It does not give you a pointer to memory that does not exist now.

## `_` is also a capture

Sometimes a construct requires a capture and you do not want the value. Then `_` discards the value, and you do not get the error for an unused variable:

```zig
while (it.next()) |_| : (n += 1) {}

if (result) |v| use(v) else |_| return default;
```

The last line is the usual way to say "the type of the error is not important to me". It is easier to read than a `catch` that ignores the error, because the discard is where the error arrives.

## More than one capture

A `for` can capture from more than one sequence. The captures are in the same order as the operands:

```zig
for (names, scores, 0..) |name, score, i| { ... }
```

Each capture can be a pointer capture, independently of the others. Thus `for (&items, extras) |*item, x|` changes the first sequence and reads the second.

The number of captures must be the same as the number of operands, and the compiler checks this. Thus, if you add a sequence and forget its capture, you get a compile error. You do not get a silent shift of each name by one position.

---

## Optionals

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/optionals/*

A `?T` holds a `T` or `null`. The compiler does not let you use the value before you handle the `null` case. Thus an accidental null dereference cannot occur.

These are real tests. Run executes the real `zig test` runner, compiled to WebAssembly.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "optional payload capture" {
    var maybe: ?i32 = null;
    try expect(maybe == null);

    maybe = 42;
    if (maybe) |value| {
        try expect(value == 42);
    } else {
        unreachable;
    }
}

test "orelse supplies a default" {
    const nothing: ?u32 = null;
    try expect((nothing orelse 7) == 7);
}

test "optional pointers are free" {
    // A `?*T` has the same size as a `*T`. The 0 address is the null value.
    try expect(@sizeOf(?*i32) == @sizeOf(*i32));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.optionals`)*

## Payload capture

The `if (maybe) |value|` form is *payload capture*. Inside the block, `value` is a plain `i32`, not an optional. The unwrap and the null check are the same syntax. Thus they cannot become different.

When you want only a fallback value, use the short form `orelse`:

```zig
const port = maybe_port orelse 8080;
```

On the right, `orelse` takes an expression, not only a value. That expression can exit:

```zig
const port = maybe_port orelse return error.MissingPort;
const item = list.pop() orelse break;
```

Read the two lines as "or else stop in this way". In the two lines, the usual path has no indent. Use this form when the function cannot continue after a null.

## Force the value with `.?`

`maybe.?` unwraps the value and asserts that the value exists. It is the same as `orelse unreachable`:

- In Debug and ReleaseSafe, the program checks the assertion, and a null causes a panic.
- In ReleaseFast, a null causes undefined behaviour.

Use `.?` where the invariant is local and visible. For example, use it immediately after you insert a key, when the next line reads that key. Do not use `.?` to stop a compiler error on a value from outside the function. In that case your assertion is about the code of a different person.

## Operations that Zig omits intentionally

Zig has no way to compare an optional to its payload without an unwrap. Zig has no implicit conversion from `?T` to `T`. Zig has no way to call a method on a `?T`.

Languages where null is a value of each type have all of these features. In those languages, each feature is a place where a null can pass without a check.

The cost is that a chain of optional lookups needs more code than an `a?.b?.c` operator. The benefit is that each `orelse` names the result when that step finds nothing. Usually that result is different at each step, and usually the code must state it.

## Optional pointers use no extra space

`?*T` has the same size as `*T`. Zig uses the null address as the `null` tag. Thus optional pointers have no cost: no extra byte, and no wrapper struct. The last test above uses `@sizeOf` to check exactly this.

This rule applies only to pointers. A `?u32` needs a tag byte together with the payload, because each bit pattern of a `u32` is a valid `u32`.

The rule is that an optional needs a tag only when the payload has no free bit pattern. A pointer has one free pattern, the null address, and `?T` uses it. A `u32` has no free pattern, thus `?u32` is larger than a `u32`.

Error unions do not get the same treatment. `error{A}!*u8` is two times the size of a `*u8`, because it must hold the error code and the pointer. Sometimes a function returns an error union for a value that is only "there or not". The programmer does this to avoid an explanation. The size is one more reason to use a `?T` for such a value.

## Optional or error

The two types both mean "you possibly do not get a value". To select one, decide if there is information to give about the failure.

- **`?T`**: use it when the absence is usual and needs no explanation. Examples are a lookup that found nothing, an iterator that ended, or a field that has no value.
- **`E!T`**: use it when the caller wants to know *why*. Examples are a file that did not exist, input with an incorrect format, or an allocation that failed.

A function that returns `?T` for a failure with a reason loses the reason. A function that returns `error{NotFound}!T` for a usual miss makes each caller write a `catch` for a case that is not exceptional. [Errors](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/errors/) has the other half of this topic.

---

## Comptime

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/comptime/*

`comptime` is the Zig solution for templates, macros, generics, reflection and constant folding. It uses one mechanism for all of them: **the compiler runs usual Zig code at compile time, and types are values there.**

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

fn fibonacci(n: u32) u32 {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);
}

// A generic function is only a function that takes a `type` parameter.
fn List(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        items: []T,

        pub fn first(self: @This()) ?T {
            return if (self.items.len == 0) null else self.items[0];
        }
    };
}

fn max(comptime T: type, a: T, b: T) T {
    return if (a > b) a else b;
}

test "evaluate at compile time" {
    // `comptime` makes the compiler evaluate the call during compilation.
    // The binary contains the answer, not the recursion.
    const small = comptime fibonacci(10);
    try expect(small == 55);
    try expect(@TypeOf(small) == u32);
}

test "the branch quota is a real limit" {
    // Comptime evaluation has a limit of 1000 backwards branches. Thus a
    // calculation that does not stop makes the build fail, and the compiler
    // does not hang. fibonacci(20) needs more, thus increase the limit.
    @setEvalBranchQuota(100_000);
    const result = comptime fibonacci(20);
    try expect(result == 6765);
}

test "types are comptime values" {
    const T = u16;
    const value: T = 300;
    try expect(@TypeOf(value) == u16);
}

test "generic data structure" {
    var backing = [_]i32{ 10, 20 };
    const list = List(i32){ .items = &backing };
    try expect(list.first().? == 10);

    // A different T makes a different type.
    try expect(List(i32) != List(u8));
}

test "generic function" {
    try expect(max(u8, 1, 2) == 2);
    try expect(max(f32, 1.5, 0.5) == 1.5);
}

test "comptime blocks can assert" {
    comptime {
        // A failed comptime assert is a compile error, not a test failure.
        std.debug.assert(@sizeOf(u32) == 4);
    }
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.comptime`)*

Zig has no second language for this. The code that runs during compilation is the same Zig, with the same syntax and the same standard library functions. To debug it, you read it. You do not expand a macro.

C++ templates, C macros and the declarative macros of Rust are each a separate language with separate rules. You cannot step through any of them.

## Types are values

A `type` is a usual comptime value. Because of this one fact, Zig does not need a separate language for generics:

```zig
fn max(comptime T: type, a: T, b: T) T {
    return if (a > b) a else b;
}
```

`comptime T: type` says that the compiler must know this parameter at compile time. The compiler makes a separately compiled function for each different `T`. The name of this process is monomorphisation, and it needs no special syntax.

Values that are not types can also be `comptime`. A function uses such a value to specialise on a configuration instead of a type:

```zig
fn hash(comptime seed: u64, data: []const u8) u64 { ... }
```

Each call with a different `seed` gets its own compiled copy, and the compiler folds the constant into that copy. These copies are also the cost. `comptime` parameters multiply the quantity of generated code. Use them for parameters that have a small number of different values, not for parameters that have a thousand values.

## Generic types are functions that return types

```zig
fn List(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct { items: []T, ... };
}
```

`List(i32)` and `List(u8)` are different types. `std.ArrayList` and `std.HashMap` are usual functions, the same as this one. The standard library gets no special syntax that you cannot use yourself.

When you call the same function with the same arguments, you get the same type. You do not get a new type for each call. Thus `List(u8)` in two different files is one type.

## What can and cannot run at compile time

Code that is pure computation can run at compile time. Examples are arithmetic, control flow, array construction, a walk over the fields of a type, and string formatting.

Code that touches the outside world cannot run at compile time. Comptime code cannot read a file, read the clock, allocate from a runtime allocator, or call C.

When you use a value that the compiler knows, the compiler evaluates the code, with or without `comptime`. The keyword makes the evaluation necessary. `comptime` before an expression tells the compiler to evaluate the expression now. If the compiler cannot, the build fails. Without the keyword, such code runs at runtime and you get no message. With the keyword, you get an error.

A related tool is `@compileError`. When the compiler reaches a branch with `@compileError`, the build fails with your message. With `@typeInfo`, a generic function can use `@compileError` to refuse a type that it cannot use. Then the user gets your message, not an error from inside the function body.

## The branch quota

Comptime evaluation has a limit of **1000 backwards branches**. Thus an accidental infinite loop makes the build fail, and the compiler does not hang. Real work is often more than this limit:

```zig
@setEvalBranchQuota(100_000);
const result = comptime fibonacci(20);
```

An increase of the quota is normal. If you must increase the quota to a very large number, the work possibly belongs at runtime.

## The work that comptime saves

When the compiler calculates something at comptime, the binary contains only the result, not the code. The compiler compares format strings with their arguments. It makes lookup tables. It removes dead configuration branches fully.

A check of a configuration value that the compiler knows does not become a branch in the output. Thus the CPU never has to predict the branch. A library can therefore have a dozen options, and none of the options costs a test at runtime. You can write a debug-only code path as usual code. You do not have to hide it behind conditional compilation.

The limit to remember is compile time. Each table that you generate and each type that you make is work for the compiler on each build. You can write a program that is fast at runtime and very slow to build. A comptime calculation that needs a large branch quota is a warning sign of this problem.

[Comptime](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/) is a full section on this subject. It builds a lookup table, reads the fields of a type and makes new types, with one program for each chapter.

---

## Interfaces

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/interfaces/*

Zig has no `interface` keyword. It has no `trait`, no `impl` and no `implements`. But the standard library has many interfaces. `std.mem.Allocator` is one, `std.Io` is one, and `std.Io.Writer` is one.

The standard library makes them from parts that you already know: `anytype`, tagged unions, function pointers and `@fieldParentPtr`. There are four common ways to put those parts together. Each way loses a different thing.

This chapter makes the same small interface in the four ways. Thus you can see the cost of each way.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// Two sinks. Neither sink knows about the other sink.

const Counter = struct {
    lines: usize = 0,
    bytes: usize = 0,

    pub fn write(self: *Counter, line: []const u8) void {
        self.lines += 1;
        self.bytes += line.len;
    }

    pub fn sink(self: *Counter) Sink {
        return .{ .ptr = self, .vtable = &vtable };
    }

    const vtable: Sink.VTable = .{ .write = writeOpaque };

    fn writeOpaque(ptr: *anyopaque, line: []const u8) void {
        const self: *Counter = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ptr));
        self.write(line);
    }
};

const Last = struct {
    buf: [32]u8 = undefined,
    len: usize = 0,

    pub fn write(self: *Last, line: []const u8) void {
        self.len = @min(line.len, self.buf.len);
        @memcpy(self.buf[0..self.len], line[0..self.len]);
    }

    pub fn text(self: *const Last) []const u8 {
        return self.buf[0..self.len];
    }

    pub fn sink(self: *Last) Sink {
        return .{ .ptr = self, .vtable = &vtable };
    }

    const vtable: Sink.VTable = .{ .write = writeOpaque };

    fn writeOpaque(ptr: *anyopaque, line: []const u8) void {
        const self: *Last = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ptr));
        self.write(line);
    }
};

// 1. anytype: the compiler checks the shape at each call site.

fn sendAll(target: anytype, lines: []const []const u8) void {
    comptime requireSink(@TypeOf(target));
    for (lines) |line| target.write(line);
}

fn requireSink(comptime T: type) void {
    if (!std.meta.hasMethod(T, "write")) {
        @compileError(@typeName(T) ++ " is not a sink: it has no write method");
    }
}

// 2. A tagged union: a closed list of implementations.

const AnySink = union(enum) {
    counter: Counter,
    last: Last,

    pub fn write(self: *AnySink, line: []const u8) void {
        switch (self.*) {
            inline else => |*s| s.write(line),
        }
    }
};

// 3. A pointer and a vtable: the shape of std.mem.Allocator and std.Io.

const Sink = struct {
    ptr: *anyopaque,
    vtable: *const VTable,

    pub const VTable = struct {
        write: *const fn (ptr: *anyopaque, line: []const u8) void,
    };

    pub fn write(self: Sink, line: []const u8) void {
        self.vtable.write(self.ptr, line);
    }
};

// 4. An embedded interface: the shape of std.Io.Writer.

const Out = struct {
    vtable: *const VTable,

    pub const VTable = struct {
        write: *const fn (out: *Out, line: []const u8) void,
    };

    pub fn write(self: *Out, line: []const u8) void {
        self.vtable.write(self, line);
    }
};

const Shouter = struct {
    shouted: usize = 0,
    interface: Out = .{ .vtable = &vtable },

    const vtable: Out.VTable = .{ .write = write };

    fn write(out: *Out, line: []const u8) void {
        const self: *Shouter = @fieldParentPtr("interface", out);
        for (line) |c| {
            if (c == '!') self.shouted += 1;
        }
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const lines = [_][]const u8{ "boot", "disk ok", "network down!" };

    try out.print("-- anytype\n", .{});
    var counter: Counter = .{};
    var last: Last = .{};
    sendAll(&counter, &lines);
    sendAll(&last, &lines);
    try out.print("counter: {d} lines, {d} bytes\n", .{ counter.lines, counter.bytes });
    try out.print("last: \"{s}\"\n", .{last.text()});

    try out.print("-- tagged union\n", .{});
    var mixed = [_]AnySink{ .{ .counter = .{} }, .{ .last = .{} } };
    for (&mixed) |*s| {
        for (lines) |line| s.write(line);
    }
    try out.print("counter: {d} lines\n", .{mixed[0].counter.lines});
    try out.print("last: \"{s}\"\n", .{mixed[1].last.text()});

    try out.print("-- vtable\n", .{});
    var counter2: Counter = .{};
    var last2: Last = .{};
    const sinks = [_]Sink{ counter2.sink(), last2.sink() };
    for (sinks) |s| {
        for (lines) |line| s.write(line);
    }
    try out.print("counter: {d} lines\n", .{counter2.lines});
    try out.print("last: \"{s}\"\n", .{last2.text()});
    try out.print("a Sink is two pointers: {}\n", .{@sizeOf(Sink) == 2 * @sizeOf(usize)});

    try out.print("-- embedded\n", .{});
    var shouter: Shouter = .{};
    const iface = &shouter.interface;
    for (lines) |line| iface.write(line);
    try out.print("shouted: {d}\n", .{shouter.shouted});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.interfaces`)*

## The task

A sink takes lines of text. The program has two sinks:

- `Counter` counts lines and bytes.
- `Last` keeps a copy of the most recent line.

The two types have a method with the same signature, `write(self, line: []const u8) void`. Neither type knows about the other type.

The question is how to write code that works with the two types.

## 1. `anytype`: a check at each call

```zig
fn sendAll(target: anytype, lines: []const []const u8) void {
    comptime requireSink(@TypeOf(target));
    for (lines) |line| target.write(line);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `sendAll` from `snippets/02-language/interfaces.zig`.*

`sendAll` never names a type. It calls `target.write` and expects that the method exists. The compiler checks this at each call.

`sendAll(&counter, ...)` compiles one copy of `sendAll` for `*Counter`. `sendAll(&last, ...)` compiles a second copy for `*Last`.

```
-- anytype
counter: 3 lines, 24 bytes
last: "network down!"
```

Each call to `write` is a direct call. The program does no lookup at runtime. Thus the optimizer can inline `write` into the loop.

This is how generic code works in Zig. [Comptime](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/comptime/) shows the `comptime T: type` form. `anytype` is the same idea, but the type comes from the argument. You do not pass the type yourself.

The standard library uses `anytype` in many places. `std.mem.sort` takes its `context` as `anytype`, and most functions that accept a callback do the same.

### Give the caller a better error

If you remove the first line of `sendAll` and pass an integer, the error points at `target.write` inside `sendAll`. The person who made the mistake must read your function to find what it needs.

`requireSink` runs first and gives the problem in words:

```zig
fn requireSink(comptime T: type) void {
    if (!std.meta.hasMethod(T, "write")) {
        @compileError(@typeName(T) ++ " is not a sink: it has no write method");
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `requireSink` from `snippets/02-language/interfaces.zig`.*

`std.meta.hasMethod` looks through one pointer. Thus `*Counter` passes the check and `*u32` fails it. Now the build stops with `*u32 is not a sink: it has no write method`.

`@compileError` stops the build. It does not return an error value, and no part of it gets into the program at runtime.

### The limits of `anytype`

You cannot put a `Counter` and a `Last` in the same array. No type means "any sink". Thus you have no type for the declaration of the array.

Also, each new type compiles one more copy of the function. For a three-line loop, the cost is too small to measure. For a large function that callers use with many types, the binary becomes larger.

## 2. A tagged union: a closed list

```zig
const AnySink = union(enum) {
    counter: Counter,
    last: Last,

    pub fn write(self: *AnySink, line: []const u8) void {
        switch (self.*) {
            inline else => |*s| s.write(line),
        }
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `AnySink` from `snippets/02-language/interfaces.zig`.*

`AnySink` is one type. Thus an array can hold the two kinds of sink.

`inline else` makes the compiler write one prong for each field. Inside each prong, `s` has the real type. Thus `s.write` is a direct call again.

```
-- tagged union
counter: 3 lines
last: "network down!"
```

The list of implementations is closed. A new kind of sink needs a new field in `AnySink`, and only the code that owns `AnySink` can add one.

Often this is exactly correct. The tokens of a parser, the instructions of a small VM and the values in a JSON document are all fixed lists. For this reason, `std.json.Value` is a `union(enum)`.

An `AnySink` is as large as its largest member, plus the tag. `Last` contains a 32-byte buffer. Thus each `AnySink` uses the space for that buffer, also an `AnySink` that holds a `Counter`.

[Unions](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/unions/) explains the type itself.

## 3. A pointer and a vtable: an open list

```zig
const Sink = struct {
    ptr: *anyopaque,
    vtable: *const VTable,

    pub const VTable = struct {
        write: *const fn (ptr: *anyopaque, line: []const u8) void,
    };

    pub fn write(self: Sink, line: []const u8) void {
        self.vtable.write(self.ptr, line);
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Sink` from `snippets/02-language/interfaces.zig`.*

A `Sink` holds two things:

- `ptr` points at the real object.
- `vtable` points at a table of functions that know how to use the object.

`*anyopaque` is a pointer to a value of unknown type. The `Sink` does not know what it points at, and it does not need to know.

Each implementation supplies the table, and a function that makes a `Sink` from the implementation:

```zig
const Counter = struct {
    lines: usize = 0,
    bytes: usize = 0,

    pub fn write(self: *Counter, line: []const u8) void {
        self.lines += 1;
        self.bytes += line.len;
    }

    pub fn sink(self: *Counter) Sink {
        return .{ .ptr = self, .vtable = &vtable };
    }

    const vtable: Sink.VTable = .{ .write = writeOpaque };

    fn writeOpaque(ptr: *anyopaque, line: []const u8) void {
        const self: *Counter = @ptrCast(@alignCast(ptr));
        self.write(line);
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Counter` from `snippets/02-language/interfaces.zig`.*

`writeOpaque` gets the `*anyopaque` and casts it back to `*Counter`. Then it calls the real `write`.

The cast is correct only because `sink()` stored a `*Counter` in `ptr`. The compiler cannot check this for you. If the table of one type is in a pair with the pointer of a different type, the cast still compiles.

`vtable` is a `const` declaration in the struct, not a field. It exists one time in the program. Each `Sink` that a `Counter` makes points at the same table.

Now two unrelated types fit in one array:

```
-- vtable
counter: 3 lines
last: "network down!"
a Sink is two pointers: true
```

This is the shape of `std.mem.Allocator`. In its source, the first two fields are `ptr: *anyopaque` and `vtable: *const VTable`. `std.Io` has the same structure, but its pointer has the name `userdata`.

Thus you can pass an `ArenaAllocator` or a `SafeAllocator` where the code wants an `Allocator`. A library that you do not know can also add its own allocator, and it does not change `std`. The list is open.

Each call goes through a function pointer. Usually the optimizer cannot inline a call through a function pointer.

Also, the `Sink` does not own the object. If the scope of `counter2` ends while a `Sink` still points at `counter2`, `ptr` becomes a dangling pointer.

The table holds the function pointers, and the `Sink` does not. Thus a `Sink` stays at two pointers when the interface gets more methods, because one table serves all `Counter` values.

## 4. An embedded interface: `@fieldParentPtr`

`std.Io.Writer` moves the interface into the object. The interface is not a separate value that points at the object. It is a field inside the object.

```zig
const Out = struct {
    vtable: *const VTable,

    pub const VTable = struct {
        write: *const fn (out: *Out, line: []const u8) void,
    };

    pub fn write(self: *Out, line: []const u8) void {
        self.vtable.write(self, line);
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Out` from `snippets/02-language/interfaces.zig`.*

```zig
const Shouter = struct {
    shouted: usize = 0,
    interface: Out = .{ .vtable = &vtable },

    const vtable: Out.VTable = .{ .write = write };

    fn write(out: *Out, line: []const u8) void {
        const self: *Shouter = @fieldParentPtr("interface", out);
        for (line) |c| {
            if (c == '!') self.shouted += 1;
        }
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Shouter` from `snippets/02-language/interfaces.zig`.*

The vtable function receives a `*Out`. That pointer points at the `interface` field inside a `Shouter`.

`@fieldParentPtr("interface", out)` subtracts the offset of the field from that address. It gives back the `*Shouter` that contains the field. The code has no `*anyopaque` and no stored pointer to the parent.

```
-- embedded
shouted: 1
```

The advantage is that the interface can hold its own state. `std.Io.Writer` keeps its buffer in the interface. `print` fills that buffer with usual code. It calls through the vtable only when the buffer is full or when you call `flush`. Thus most writes never make an indirect call.

You already used this shape. Each program on this site writes `const out = &file_writer.interface;` before it prints anything.

The `&` is important. `@fieldParentPtr` works only while the interface is still inside its parent.

If you copy the interface with `var copy = file_writer.interface;`, the vtable function subtracts the offset from the address of the copy. The result is memory that is not a `File.Writer`. This code compiles, and a safe build does not find the problem.

In a test on `Shouter`, a `ReleaseSafe` build ran without a panic and printed `shouted: 0`. The behaviour is undefined, thus a different build can do something worse.

Take the address of an embedded interface. Do not copy it.

[Linked lists in std](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/data-structures/std-lists/) use the same builtin for a different task: to find your struct from the list node inside it.

## Select a shape

| Shape | Who can add an implementation | How `write` is called | One array of mixed types | In `std` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `anytype` | anyone | directly, can inline | no | `std.mem.sort`'s `context` |
| tagged union | only the union's owner | switch, then directly | yes | `std.json.Value` |
| pointer and vtable | anyone | through a pointer | yes | `std.mem.Allocator`, `std.Io` |
| embedded interface | anyone | through a pointer, but often no call | yes, as pointers | `std.Io.Writer`, `std.Io.Reader` |

Use these rules:

- Start with `anytype`. It needs the least code, and it gives the fastest call.
- Change to a tagged union when you need a mixed list and you own each type in the list.
- Change to a vtable when code that you do not control must add an implementation.
- Use the embedded form only when the interface has its own state, as a writer has its buffer. Only then is the form worth its extra rules.

## If you know other languages

In Rust, generics with trait bounds do the job of `anytype`, and an `enum` is a tagged union. A Rust `&dyn Trait` is a data pointer and a vtable pointer. This is the same pair that `Sink` holds.

A Go interface value is also two words. One word points at the method table of the type, and the other word points at the data.

The difference in Zig is that you write the table yourself.

---

## Inline Loops

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/inline-loops/*

In Zig, `inline for` compiles the loop body one time for each iteration. Thus each iteration can handle a value of a different type. Code uses `inline for` to visit the elements of a tuple or the fields of a struct.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "inline for over a tuple" {
    // The elements of a tuple have different types. Thus the compiler must
    // compile the loop body separately for each element. `inline` does this.
    const tuple = .{ @as(u8, 1), @as(f32, 2.5), true };
    var count: usize = 0;
    inline for (tuple) |value| {
        if (@TypeOf(value) == bool) count += 10 else count += 1;
    }
    try expect(count == 12);
}

test "inline for over types" {
    const types = [_]type{ u8, u16, u32 };
    var total: usize = 0;
    inline for (types) |T| {
        total += @sizeOf(T);
    }
    try expect(total == 7);
}

test "the loop variable becomes comptime-known" {
    var sum: usize = 0;
    inline for (0..4) |i| {
        // `i` is comptime here. Thus you can use `i` where a comptime value
        // is necessary, for example the length of an array type.
        const arr: [i]u8 = undefined;
        sum += arr.len;
    }
    try expect(sum == 6); // 0 + 1 + 2 + 3
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.inline-loops`)*

`inline for` unrolls the loop at compile time. Sometimes this helps performance, but the main reason for `inline for` is **types**.

## Iterate over values of different types

The elements of a tuple have different types. The compiler compiles a normal loop body one time, thus a normal loop cannot handle the different types. The compiler compiles an `inline for` body separately for each iteration. Thus `@TypeOf(value)` can be different each time:

```zig
inline for (tuple) |value| {
    if (@TypeOf(value) == bool) { ... }
}
```

`std.debug.print` uses `inline for` to visit its arguments. Serialisation code uses it to visit the fields of a struct.

The `if` in that body is not a runtime branch. In each unrolled copy, the compiler knows `@TypeOf(value)` at comptime. Thus the condition becomes true or false during compilation, and the compiler generates only the branch that remains.

A chain of twelve `if` conditions on types has no runtime cost, because eleven of the arms do not exist in the output.

## The compiler knows the loop variable

Inside `inline for (0..4) |i|`, `i` is a comptime value. Thus you can use `i` where the compiler must have a comptime value, for example in array lengths, type construction or field names:

```zig
const arr: [i]u8 = undefined;   // only valid because i is comptime
```

A comptime loop variable is the thing that makes reflection work. `@typeInfo(T).@"struct".field_names` is a comptime array of strings. When you visit it with `inline for`, you get each name as a comptime string. `@field(value, name)` can then use that string to read the field.

A normal `for` gives you a runtime string. Zig has no runtime field lookup that can use a runtime string.

```zig
inline for (@typeInfo(@TypeOf(value)).@"struct".field_names) |name| {
    try writer.print("{s}={any}\n", .{ name, @field(value, name) });
}
```

Much of the generic code in the standard library has this shape.

## If you used an older version of Zig

Older Zig code uses `info.fields[i].name`. The current shape replaced it. Now `Type.Struct` has parallel arrays (`field_names`, `field_types`, `field_attrs`), not one array of field structs. A loop that needs only the names does not touch the other arrays.

## `inline while` and `inline else`

The same idea occurs on `while` and on `switch`:

- On `while`, the compiler must know the condition at comptime. Then the compiler can decide how many copies to make.
- On `switch`, `inline else` generates one arm for each case that is left. The tag is available as a comptime value.

Use them in the same conditions as `inline for`. Use them when the body must know a value at compile time, and the runtime version would know the value only at runtime.

## Use `inline` on purpose

An unrolled loop multiplies the generated code by the number of iterations. For a tuple with 3 elements, the cost is very small. For `inline for (0..10000)`, the compile time and the binary size increase badly. Use `inline` when you need comptime values. Do not use it as a habit to make code faster.

To use `inline` for speed is wrong for a second reason. The optimiser already unrolls the loops that it thinks are worth the cost. It uses cost information about the target that you do not have.

If you write `inline` to make a loop fast, you override a decision that was probably better than yours. The cost then shows as longer compile times, not in a benchmark.

A simple test is to ask if the body compiles without `inline`:

- If the body compiles without `inline`, you probably do not need `inline`.
- If the body does not compile, because it uses the loop variable where a comptime value is necessary, then `inline` is necessary. It is not an optimisation at all.

---

## Opaque

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/opaque/*

In Zig, `opaque {}` is the equivalent of the incomplete type in C. Use it for handles that code can hold only through a pointer. translate-c produces handles of this type from a C header.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// Usually this type replaces a C type that has no definition that you can
// see: `typedef struct Window Window;`
const Window = opaque {
    // Opaque types can still have methods.
    pub fn close(self: *Window) void {
        _ = self;
    }
};

const Handle = opaque {};

test "opaque types are only usable behind a pointer" {
    // `var w: Window = ...` is impossible, because the size is unknown. Only
    // pointers to a `Window` exist. C code uses C handles in the same way.
    var storage: u32 = 0;
    const handle: *Handle = @ptrCast(&storage);
    try expect(@TypeOf(handle) == *Handle);
}

test "distinct opaque types do not mix" {
    // *Window and *Handle are unrelated types. Thus the compiler does not let
    // you use one type where the other type is necessary. C's void* allows it.
    try expect(*Window != *Handle);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.opaque`)*

An `opaque {}` type has an unknown size and layout. You can never have a value of the type. You can have only a pointer to a value.

The compiler really does not know the size. If you ask for the size, the compiler refuses:

```
error: no size available for uninstantiable type
note: opaque declared here
```

Thus each of these fails, because each one needs a size:

- `@sizeOf` on the type.
- A local variable of the type.
- An array of the type.
- A struct field of the type.

Only a pointer works. The size of a pointer comes from the machine, not from the type that the pointer points at.

## Why an opaque type is useful

An opaque type is the Zig form of an incomplete type in C:

```c
typedef struct Window Window;   /* definition not provided */
Window *create_window(void);
```

The library gives you a `*Window`, and you can only give it back to the library. You cannot examine it, copy it, or put it on the stack. Its size is not part of the public interface.

The compiler enforces this rule. Thus the rule does not depend on callers who read the documentation.

When a library shows a struct definition, its layout cannot change. If the library adds a field, the size changes. Then each caller that put the struct on the stack has the wrong quantity of memory. An opaque type has no public layout. Thus the library can change its layout in a later version, and code that uses it does not have to compile again.

## Better than `void*`

The usual alternative in C is `void*`, which removes the type completely. Nothing prevents a `*File` where the code expects a `*Window`. Different opaque types stay different:

```zig
*Window != *Handle    // different types, checked by the compiler
```

You keep the rule that callers cannot look inside, and you keep type safety at the boundary. Opaque types can also have methods. Thus the handle still reads like an object: `window.close()`.

`opaque {}` has a body. The body can hold `pub fn` declarations, constants and nested types, exactly like a `struct`. But the body cannot hold fields, because fields give a type a size.

Thus the full public interface of a C handle library becomes one opaque type with methods. The code that calls it never learns more than it must.

## Where you find opaque types

Almost always, you find them at a C boundary. translate-c changes each incomplete type in a header into an opaque type. Thus the pointers that translate-c gives you stay different types, and they do not all become `?*anyopaque`. See [C headers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/cimport/) and [C pointers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/c-pointers/).

A related type is `anyopaque`. It is the type for "a pointer to a value whose type I removed". `anyopaque` is the direct translation of `void*` in C. A callback takes an `anyopaque` pointer when it receives user data of any type. `anyopaque` removes the type intentionally. An opaque type keeps the type and hides the layout.

To convert between the two, use `@ptrCast`. You must make sure that the conversion is correct. When the layout is unknown, the compiler cannot check the conversion. You accepted this condition when you selected a handle.

---

## Anonymous Structs

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/anonymous-structs/*

Zig has anonymous structs in two forms:

- A struct type that you write inline, at the place where you use it.
- A tuple. A tuple is a struct with numbered fields instead of named fields.

The argument list that you give to `print` is a tuple.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

fn describe(point: struct { x: i32, y: i32 }) i32 {
    return point.x + point.y;
}

test "anonymous struct literal" {
    // The compiler infers the type from the context. Thus you do not write the name.
    try expect(describe(.{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }) == 3);
}

test "tuples are anonymous structs with numeric fields" {
    const tuple = .{ @as(u8, 1), true, @as(f32, 2.5) };
    try expect(tuple.len == 3);
    try expect(tuple[0] == 1);
    try expect(tuple[1] == true);
    // The name of the field is `1`. `1` is not a valid identifier, thus the
    // field syntax needs `@""`. The two forms read the same field.
    try expect(tuple.@"1" == true);
    try expect(@field(tuple, "2") == 2.5);
}

test "tuples hold mixed types" {
    const pair = .{ @as(u32, 7), "seven" };
    try expect(pair[0] == 7);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, pair[1], "seven"));
}

test "this is how format arguments work" {
    // `.{ a, b }` in a print call is only a tuple. The compiler compares the
    // format string with the tuple at compile time.
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{s}={d}", .{ "x", 42 });
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, text, "x=42"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.anonymous-structs`)*

`.{ ... }` is a struct literal. The literal gets its type from the context. When the compiler knows the target type (a parameter, a field, a return type), you do not have to write the name:

```zig
describe(.{ .x = 1, .y = 2 });
```

The same dot at the start occurs in each place where the compiler can infer a type:

- `.north` for an enum tag.
- `.{ .ok = value }` for a union variant.
- `.{}` for a struct with a default value for each field.

These are one rule, not four. The dot means "you know the type, so I do not write the type again".

If the compiler does not know the target type, it has no type to infer. Then you must write the name of the type in the literal:

```zig
const p = Point{ .x = 1, .y = 2 };   // no context, so say the type
```

## Anonymous struct types

You can also write a struct type inline. The `describe` function in the snippet does this:

```zig
fn describe(point: struct { x: i32, y: i32 }) i32 {
    return point.x + point.y;
}
```

An inline type is useful for a shape that you use one time and that does not need a name. It is also useful when a function returns several values and you do not want to declare a type for them.

Two anonymous struct types that you write separately are different types, also when their fields are the same. Thus, use them for local convenience. Do not use them for types that cross an interface.

## Tuples

If you do not write the field names, you get a tuple. A tuple is a struct with numbered fields. A tuple has `.len`, you can use an index on it, and its fields can have different types:

```zig
const tuple = .{ @as(u8, 1), true, @as(f32, 2.5) };
tuple[0];     // 1
tuple.@"1";   // true
tuple.len;    // 3
```

The numbers are the field names. The name of the first field is `0`, the name of the second field is `1`, and so on.

A name cannot start with a digit, thus `tuple.1` does not parse. Put the name in `@""` instead. `tuple.@"1"` is usual field access. Zig uses the same escape for each name that is not a plain identifier.

`tuple[1]` is a shorter form of the same access. When the name is a string that you make at compile time, `@field(tuple, "1")` reads the same field.

The index must be a constant that the compiler knows. `tuple[i]` with a runtime `i` cannot work, because each element has its own type. With a runtime index, the type of the expression would depend on a runtime value. Zig does not allow that.

To visit each element, use [`inline for`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/inline-loops/). `inline for` compiles the body one time for each element. Thus each element can have a different type.

The `++` operator joins tuples. Helpers that look variadic use `++` to make an argument list at compile time.

## Format arguments are a tuple

```zig
std.mem.print(&buf, "{s}={d}", .{ "x", 42 });
```

The second argument is only a tuple. Zig has no mechanism for varargs. `print` takes one value, and that value is a struct. `print` visits the struct with `inline for`, and compares it with the format string at compile time. A `{d}` that does not match is a compile error, not a runtime error.

The arguments are a tuple, and some rules follow from that:

- The wrong number of arguments is a compile error, because the tuple has a length.
- A struct where `{d}` expects a number is a compile error, because the compiler knows the type of the field.
- Zig has no `printf` format-string vulnerability. The compiler compares the format string and the arguments before the program runs.

The tuple also explains the empty case. A call with no arguments still gives a tuple to `print`. Thus `.{}` occurs at the end of each `print` call that inserts no values.

---

## Sentinel Termination

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/sentinel-termination/*

In Zig, a string literal has the type `*const [N:0]u8`. `[:0]u8` is the slice form of a zero-terminated sequence, and `[*:0]u8` is the pointer form. You can give these types to C without a copy.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "sentinel-terminated array" {
    // `[3:0]u8` is three bytes plus a guaranteed 0 at index 3.
    const array: [3:0]u8 = .{ 1, 2, 3 };
    try expect(array.len == 3); // `.len` does not count the sentinel
    try expect(array[3] == 0); // but it is there
}

test "string literals are sentinel terminated" {
    const literal = "hi";
    try expect(@TypeOf(literal) == *const [2:0]u8);
    try expect(literal.len == 2);
    try expect(literal[2] == 0); // compatible with C at no extra cost
}

test "span recovers the length from a sentinel" {
    const c_string: [*:0]const u8 = "hello";
    // `[*:0]T` has no length, but the sentinel makes it recoverable.
    const slice = std.mem.span(c_string);
    try expect(slice.len == 5);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, slice, "hello"));
}

test "sentinel slices coerce to ordinary ones" {
    const sentinel_slice: [:0]const u8 = "abc";
    const plain: []const u8 = sentinel_slice;
    try expect(plain.len == 3);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.sentinel-termination`)*

A sentinel-terminated type guarantees a specific value immediately after the end. In the syntax, the value comes after a colon:

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `[3:0]u8` | 3 bytes, plus a guaranteed `0` at index 3 |
| `[:0]u8` | slice with a `0` after the last element |
| `[*:0]u8` | many-item pointer, terminated by `0` |

`.len` does **not** count the sentinel. But the sentinel is really in memory, and you can read it.

A `[:0]u8` has a length, as each slice has. Thus iteration over it has bounds checks, and `.len` is one instruction. The type *also* promises a zero after the last element. Thus you can give it to C without a copy. One value holds the length and the terminator.

## The sentinel can be a value other than zero

`0` is the usual case, because C strings are the usual case. But the value is part of the type: `[:255]u8` and `[: '\n']u8` are legal. You can use this form for any data that has a known terminator. Sometimes a protocol buffer or a line reader can use the type to state its rule, and a comment is not necessary.

## String literals have a sentinel

```zig
const literal = "hi";   // *const [2:0]u8
literal.len;            // 2
literal[2];             // 0
```

Thus, when you give a Zig string literal to a C function that wants `const char *`, you need no conversion and no copy. Usual Zig code still has the length. Thus the C compatibility has no cost for Zig code.

The type is a *pointer to an array*, not a slice. For this reason, a literal has a comptime-known length, and `@TypeOf("hi") != @TypeOf("hip")`.

A literal coerces to `[]const u8` or `[:0]const u8` when code uses it in a place that expects one of these types. This occurs almost always. Thus you see the difference only in error messages and in `@TypeOf`.

## Find the length

`[*:0]T` has no length, but the sentinel lets you find the length:

```zig
const slice = std.mem.span(c_string);   // scans to the sentinel
```

The scan is O(n), the same cost that C has for `strlen`. Do the scan one time at the boundary, and then use slices.

Two related functions are also useful:

- `std.mem.sliceTo(slice, 0)` cuts a value that already has a length at the first sentinel. Use it for a C struct field of fixed size that holds a name with padding.
- `std.mem.len` gives only the count, and does not make a slice.

## Make a sentinel-terminated value

Sometimes a C function wants a null-terminated string, and your string is a plain `[]const u8`. Then the terminator must be in memory. There are three methods:

- **A literal**, if the string does not change. A literal already has the terminator.
- **`allocator.dupeSentinel(u8, s, 0)`**. It copies the string, adds the terminator and returns a `[:0]u8`. Remember to free it. Older code used `dupeZ`. `dupeSentinel` replaced `dupeZ`, and the sentinel value is now an argument. It is not part of the name.
- **A stack buffer with an explicit sentinel slice**, `buf[0..n :0]`. This slice asserts that the byte at `buf[n]` is really zero. In a safety build, the program checks that assertion.

Be careful when you slice with a sentinel. `buf[0..n :0]` does not write the terminator. It states that the terminator is already there. You must write the terminator yourself.

## How this is different from C strings

In C, a scan is the only way to find the length. Thus each operation is O(n), and each buffer overrun starts with a terminator that is not there.

In Zig, the value carries the length, and the sentinel is an additional guarantee. Usual code uses the length. Only the C boundary uses the sentinel.

In C, the program reads a string without a terminator until the read finds a zero or fails. In Zig, this can occur only if you made the sentinel type incorrectly by hand.

---

## Vectors

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/vectors/*

Zig gives you SIMD as a type, `@Vector(N, T)`, not as a library of intrinsics. `std.simd.suggestVectorLength` selects `N` for the target.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "element-wise arithmetic" {
    const a: @Vector(4, i32) = .{ 1, 2, 3, 4 };
    const b: @Vector(4, i32) = .{ 10, 20, 30, 40 };
    const sum = a + b; // one operation across all lanes
    try expect(sum[0] == 11);
    try expect(sum[3] == 44);
}

test "reduce across lanes" {
    const v: @Vector(4, i32) = .{ 1, 2, 3, 4 };
    try expect(@reduce(.Add, v) == 10);
    try expect(@reduce(.Max, v) == 4);
}

test "splat fills every lane" {
    const v: @Vector(4, i32) = @splat(7);
    try expect(@reduce(.Add, v) == 28);
}

test "comparisons produce a vector of bools" {
    const a: @Vector(4, i32) = .{ 1, 5, 3, 7 };
    const b: @Vector(4, i32) = .{ 4, 4, 4, 4 };
    const mask = a > b; // @Vector(4, bool)
    try expect(@reduce(.Or, mask));
    try expect(!@reduce(.And, mask));

    // Select lane-wise between two vectors.
    const picked = @select(i32, mask, a, b);
    try expect(picked[0] == 4 and picked[1] == 5);
}

test "vectors and arrays convert" {
    const arr = [_]i32{ 1, 2, 3, 4 };
    const v: @Vector(4, i32) = arr;
    const back: [4]i32 = v;
    try expect(back[2] == 3);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.vectors`)*

`@Vector(N, T)` is a SIMD vector of `N` lanes. Arithmetic operators work element by element across all lanes at the same time. Where the target has vector instructions, the operators compile to real vector instructions:

```zig
const sum = a + b;   // one operation, four lanes
```

SIMD means "single instruction, multiple data". One machine instruction does the same arithmetic on many values at the same time. A 128-bit register holds four `i32` values, and one add instruction adds all four.

In Zig, you write that add with a usual operator on a vector type. You do not use an intrinsic with a name such as `_mm_add_epi32`.

## The builtins for vectors

| Builtin | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `@splat(x)` | fill every lane with `x` |
| `@reduce(.Add, v)` | collapse lanes to one value |
| `@select(T, mask, a, b)` | pick lane-wise between two vectors |
| `@shuffle` | rearrange lanes |

A comparison produces a `@Vector(N, bool)` mask, not one `bool`. Thus you use `@reduce(.Or, mask)` or `@select` to act on the result.

The mask replaces branches. If you wrote only scalar code before, this needs practice:

- A scalar loop says "if this element matches, do the action".
- A vector version computes the condition for all lanes at the same time. Then it uses the mask to select between two answers that it already computed.

There is no branch for each lane. For this reason, the vector version is fast. For the same reason, work that is different for each element does not vectorise.

## Select N

`std.simd.suggestVectorLength(T)` asks the target how many lanes of `T` fit in its widest register. It returns null when the target has no SIMD. Portable code uses this function, and does not hardcode 4 or 8. When the function returns null, the code uses a scalar loop.

This null is important on this site. SIMD in WebAssembly is an optional feature. Thus the site compiles the four chapters that teach vectors with SIMD explicitly on, and it compiles all other snippets without SIMD.

Without SIMD, the function returns null, and the compiler removes the vector path with no message. Then the page says that it shows SIMD, but the page ships a scalar loop.

## Convert between vectors and arrays

```zig
const v: @Vector(4, i32) = arr;   // array -> vector
const back: [4]i32 = v;           // vector -> array
```

The data is the same, and the type is different. Keep values in vector form during a computation, and convert at the edges.

The conversion does no arithmetic, but it can still take time. The values can move between usual registers and vector registers. Inside a loop, those moves can cost more time than the vector arithmetic saves. Load one time, compute, and store one time.

Vectors are not arrays:

- A vector has no `.len`. If you use `.len`, you get a compile error.
- An index works, with a runtime index or a comptime index. In a safety build, the index has a bounds check.
- You cannot slice a vector, or give it to a function by its length.

Use an array when you need these operations. Use a vector when you want arithmetic lane by lane.

## When to use vectors

Zig often auto-vectorises a plain loop. Use explicit vectors when you need the guarantee, or when the operation is not a simple loop. If the target has no SIMD, the code still works, because the compiler changes it to scalar operations.

First write the scalar loop and measure it. Only after that, change to vectors. If the loop was not the bottleneck, a vector version is more difficult to read and change, and it is not faster.

When vectors help, the gain is often large. For that reason, the two recipes below each process a large buffer in one pass.

Two how-to recipes use these builtins: [a SIMD dot product](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/simd-sum/) for arithmetic, and [a SIMD byte scan](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/simd-scan/) for search.

---

## Imports

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/imports/*

In Zig, each file is a struct. `pub` marks the declarations that other files can see. A declaration without `pub` is private to its file.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// A relative path imports another source file. The result is a struct type.
// The declarations of that type are the `pub` declarations of the file.
const shapes = @import("_shapes.zig");

test "use an imported declaration" {
    try expect(shapes.double(21) == 42);
}

test "imported types work like any other" {
    const c = shapes.Circle{ .radius = 2 };
    try expect(c.area() > 12.5 and c.area() < 12.6);
}

test "a file is a struct" {
    // `@This()` inside a file refers to the implicit struct type of the file.
    // Thus `@import` returns a value that you can use with `.`.
    try expect(@TypeOf(shapes) == type);
    try expect(shapes.pi > 3.14);
}

test "std is just another import" {
    // `@import("std")` uses the same mechanism. The compiler resolves the
    // name itself, and does not use a path.
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, "a", "a"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.imports`)*

`@import` takes a path and returns that file **as a struct type**:

```zig
const shapes = @import("_shapes.zig");
shapes.Circle{ .radius = 2 };
```
