Zig has no separate module system to learn. `@import` evaluates the file. Then you get its declarations with `.`, the same as for any other struct.

The result is a value, thus you select the name for it. `const s = @import("std")` works exactly as well as `const std = @import("std")`.

If you import the same file two times, you get the same type two times. Thus you get no problem with duplicate definitions, and you need no include guard.

## `pub` is the boundary

Only `pub` declarations are visible to the files that import a file:

```zig
pub const pi = 3.14159;   // visible
const secret = 42;        // not
```

Zig needs nothing more for visibility. Zig has no `private` keyword, no header files and no export lists.

To give a type a private implementation, put the type in its own file. To let two files see the internals of each other, merge the two files.

## A file can be the type

A file is a struct. Thus, if a file declares fields at the top level, the file *is* that struct. When you import the file, you get the type directly:

```zig
// Point.zig
x: f32,
y: f32,

pub fn magnitude(self: @This()) f32 { ... }
```

```zig
const Point = @import("Point.zig");
const p: Point = .{ .x = 3, .y = 4 };
```

This convention is the reason for the capitalised filenames in the standard library. `std.Io.Writer` is in `Writer.zig`, and the file has no wrapper declaration around it.

A lowercase filename means a namespace with many declarations. A capitalised filename means that the file is a single type. When you know this convention, the layout of the standard library is much easier to read.

## `@import("std")` is not special

The standard library uses the same mechanism. The compiler resolves the name `std` itself, and does not use it as a path. Package dependencies that `build.zig.zon` declares work the same way. You import them by their package name.

If the build declares a module with a name, the name resolves as that module. If not, the name resolves as a file path. Thus `@import("foo")` and `@import("foo.zig")` are different questions:

- `@import("foo")` asks the build system.
- `@import("foo.zig")` asks the filesystem, relative to the file that contains the import.

To add a dependency, change `build.zig` and `build.zig.zon`. Never change an include path.

Two more names are always available:

- `@import("root")` is the file at the root of the compilation. Library code uses it to get a configuration constant that the application declared.
- `@import("builtin")` is a file that the compiler generates. It describes the build: the target, the optimisation mode and the Zig version.

You did not write either of these two files.

## Import cycles

Two files can import each other. Zig resolves declarations lazily, thus this works. Zig does not accept a real cycle in *values*. For example, the initialiser of a `const` in A needs a `const` in B. The initialiser of that `const` in B needs the `const` in A.

Most cycles are types that refer to each other, and those cycles are correct. A `Node` in one file can hold a `?*Tree` from another file, and the `Tree` can hold `[]Node`. Zig resolves these types without an error, because the size of a pointer does not depend on the type that it points to.

A cycle is a problem only when the compiler cannot calculate a value without that same value. Then the error gives the loop.

## Import data, not code

`@embedFile("table.bin")` reads a file at compile time. It gives you a `*const
[N:0]u8`: a pointer to the contents, with a zero byte after the last byte.

Use it for a lookup table, a small template or a test fixture. Then the program can never fail because the data file is not next to the binary. Do not use it for large data, because the bytes go into the binary.

---

## Array Recipes

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/array-recipes/*

When arrays become larger than small examples, you need three things:

- A grid.
- A table that the compiler calculates at compile time.
- A fixed-size array that you take from a slice.

The three are language mechanics. None of them needs an allocator.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "a grid is an array of arrays" {
    const grid = [3][3]u8{
        .{ 1, 2, 3 },
        .{ 4, 5, 6 },
        .{ 7, 8, 9 },
    };

    // The two lengths are part of the type. The grid is one contiguous block
    // of nine bytes. The grid contains no pointers.
    try expect(grid.len == 3); // rows
    try expect(grid[0].len == 3); // columns
    try expect(@TypeOf(grid[0]) == [3]u8);
    try expect(@sizeOf(@TypeOf(grid)) == 9);

    try expect(grid[1][2] == 6); // row first, then column
}

test "walk a grid with nested for" {
    const grid = [2][3]u8{
        .{ 1, 2, 3 },
        .{ 4, 5, 6 },
    };

    var sum: u32 = 0;
    for (grid) |row| {
        for (row) |cell| sum += cell;
    }
    try expect(sum == 21);
}

test "the outer loop hands you a copy" {
    var grid = [2][2]u8{
        .{ 1, 2 },
        .{ 3, 4 },
    };

    // Arrays are values. Thus `row` is a copy, and a write to `row` changes
    // nothing in `grid`.
    for (grid) |row| {
        var mutable = row;
        mutable[0] = 99;
    }
    try expect(grid[0][0] == 1);

    // To write through the loop, use pointers at the two levels.
    for (&grid) |*row| {
        for (row) |*cell| cell.* += 10;
    }
    try expect(grid[0][0] == 11);
    try expect(grid[1][1] == 14);
}

test "one flat array, computed indices" {
    const width = 4;
    const height = 3;
    var cells: [width * height]u8 = @splat(0);

    // The type does not contain the shape. Thus you must keep the stride
    // correct yourself. Use a flat array when one of the dimensions is not
    // a compile-time constant.
    cells[1 * width + 2] = 7;

    try expect(cells[6] == 7);
    try expect(cells.len == 12);
}

test "build a lookup table at comptime" {
    // Declare undefined storage, fill it in a loop, and use break to return
    // the completed array from the block. The result is a constant in the
    // binary.
    const hex_digits = comptime blk: {
        var table: [16]u8 = undefined;
        for (&table, 0..) |*slot, i| {
            slot.* = if (i < 10) '0' + @as(u8, i) else 'a' + @as(u8, i - 10);
        }
        break :blk table;
    };

    try expect(hex_digits[0] == '0');
    try expect(hex_digits[10] == 'a');
    try expect(hex_digits[15] == 'f');
}

test "the table really is a compile-time constant" {
    const sizes = comptime blk: {
        var table: [4]usize = undefined;
        for (&table, 0..) |*slot, i| slot.* = i * 2;
        break :blk table;
    };

    // The compiler must know an array length at compile time. Thus this line
    // compiles only if the value came from comptime. The compile is the proof.
    const buf: [sizes[3]]u8 = @splat(0);
    try expect(buf.len == 6);
}

test "turn a slice back into an array" {
    const numbers = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
    const slice: []const u8 = &numbers;

    // .* on a slice with a comptime-known length copies a real array from the
    // slice. The length is then part of the type again.
    const first_three = slice[0..3].*;
    try expect(@TypeOf(first_three) == [3]u8);
    try expect(first_three.len == 3);

    // The result is a copy. Thus a write to the copy does not change the
    // original.
    var copy = first_three;
    copy[0] = 99;
    try expect(numbers[0] == 1);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.array-recipes`)*

## A grid is an array of arrays

`[3][3]u8` is nine bytes in one contiguous block. The two lengths are part of the type. `grid.len` is the number of rows, and `grid[0].len` is the number of columns.

`@sizeOf` shows that the grid contains no hidden pointer. Use the row index first, then the column index.

`[3][3]u8` is not the same type as `[][]u8`, a slice of slices. A slice of slices is a list of pointers to rows, and the rows can be at any location in memory. The nested array is one block, and it needs no allocation. The slice of slices has as many blocks as the code that made it.

## The outer loop gives you a copy

The [Arrays](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/arrays/) chapter states that arrays are values. In a nested loop, this rule has a direct effect.

`for (grid) |row|` copies each row. Thus a write through `row` changes nothing in `grid`. The compiler does not give an error, because the code is valid.

`for (&grid) |*row|` iterates over pointers, and then `for (row) |*cell|` gets the elements. The two levels must be pointers before a write can change the grid.

## Use one flat array

The other shape is `[width * height]T` with the index `y * width + x`. The type does not contain the geometry. Thus you must keep the stride correct yourself. In return, the dimensions do not have to be two separate compile-time constants.

Use the nested array when the shape is fixed and small. Use the flat array in these three conditions:

- The program calculates the width.
- You want to give the full array to a function that takes a `[]T`.
- The rows are so large that an accidental copy of one row is a problem.

## Make a table at compile time

To make the table, do these steps:

1. Declare storage that is `undefined`.
2. Fill the storage in a loop.
3. Use `break :blk` to return the completed array from the block.

Do these steps inside `comptime`. The result is a constant in the binary, and the program runs no initialization code at startup.

You can do a check of this. Use one of the entries of the table as an array length. The compiler must know each array length at compile time. Thus, if the code compiles, the value came from comptime.

## Change a slice back to an array

`slice[0..N].*` copies a real `[N]T` from the slice. The compiler must know `N` at compile time. The length moves back into the type. A function that expects `*const [4]u8` needs this.

The result is a copy. A write to the result does not change the original slice.

To join slices at runtime, use `std.mem.concat`. [String Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/string-recipes/) explains it. The operations that change slices in place are in [Slice Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/slice-recipes/).

---

## Slice Recipes

*Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/slice-recipes/*

A slice is a pointer and a length. Thus each recipe on this page writes to memory that already exists. No allocator is on this page.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;
const expectEqualStrings = std.testing.expectEqualStrings;

test "reverse in place" {
    var digits = [_]u8{ '1', '2', '3', '4' };
    std.mem.reverse(u8, &digits);
    try expectEqualStrings("4321", &digits);

    // This works on any []T. On UTF-8 bytes, it reverses the bytes. Thus it
    // breaks each character that has more than one byte: see Unicode Recipes.
}

test "rotate by n" {
    var buf = [_]u8{ 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e' };

    // The first two move to the end. Nothing allocates, and the length does
    // not change.
    std.mem.rotate(u8, &buf, 2);
    try expectEqualStrings("cdeab", &buf);
}

test "overlapping copies are @memmove, not @memcpy" {
    // @memcpy requires that the two ranges do not overlap. A shift inside one
    // slice always overlaps, and a release build does not report the mistake.
    var shift_left = [_]u8{ 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' };
    @memmove(shift_left[0..3], shift_left[1..4]);
    try expectEqualStrings("bcdd", &shift_left);

    // @memmove works in the two directions. Thus you cannot select the wrong
    // direction. std.mem.copyForwards and copyBackwards are deprecated, and
    // @memmove replaces them.
    var shift_right = [_]u8{ 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' };
    @memmove(shift_right[1..4], shift_right[0..3]);
    try expectEqualStrings("aabc", &shift_right);
}

test "remove an element from the middle" {
    var backing = [_]u8{ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 };
    var items: []u8 = &backing;

    // Move the tail one position lower over the gap. Then make the slice one
    // element shorter. The array keeps its length. Only the slice becomes shorter.
    const remove_at = 1;
    @memmove(items[remove_at .. items.len - 1], items[remove_at + 1 ..]);
    items = items[0 .. items.len - 1];

    try expect(items.len == 4);
    try expect(items[1] == 30);
    try expect(backing.len == 5); // not changed
}

test "sliceTo stops at a value" {
    // A different part of the program filled this buffer and terminated it.
    // Take the useful part. You do not have to scan for the terminator.
    var buf: [16]u8 = @splat(0);
    @memcpy(buf[0..5], "hello");

    try expectEqualStrings("hello", std.mem.sliceTo(&buf, 0));
}

test "min, max, and all the same" {
    const readings = [_]u8{ 12, 3, 40, 7 };

    // These functions return indices, not values. An index is what you need
    // when a second array holds the labels.
    try expect(std.mem.findMin(u8, &readings) == 1);
    try expect(std.mem.findMax(u8, &readings) == 2);
    try expect(readings[std.mem.findMax(u8, &readings)] == 40);

    try expect(std.mem.allEqual(u8, "aaaa", 'a'));
    try expect(!std.mem.allEqual(u8, &readings, 12));
}

test "dedup a sorted slice in place" {
    var values = [_]u8{ 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4 };

    // Two indices: one index reads, and one index writes the kept elements
    // forward. Nothing allocates. The result is a slice of the new length.
    var write: usize = 0;
    for (values, 0..) |value, read| {
        if (read > 0 and value == values[read - 1]) continue;
        values[write] = value;
        write += 1;
    }
    const unique = values[0..write];

    try expect(unique.len == 4);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, unique, &.{ 1, 2, 3, 4 }));
}

test "indices belong to the slice they came from" {
    const all = "abcdefgh";
    const mid = all[2..6]; // "cdef"

    // An offset from one slice has no meaning in a different slice. Thus each
    // find function is dangerous when you use a sub-slice.
    try expect(std.mem.find(u8, all, "de").? == 3);
    try expect(std.mem.find(u8, mid, "de").? == 1);

    // mid[1..3] is all[3..5]. To convert, add the offset of the sub-slice.
    try expectEqualStrings(mid[1..3], all[3..5]);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`02-language.slice-recipes`)*

## In place means that the length does not change

`std.mem.reverse` and `std.mem.rotate` write to the same bytes and return nothing. The two functions work on each `[]T`.

When you reverse a `[]const u8`, the function reverses the bytes, not the characters. Outside ASCII, this breaks each sequence of more than one byte, and the result is invalid UTF-8. [Unicode Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/unicode-recipes/) is about this problem and others.

## Copies that overlap

`@memcpy` requires that the source and the destination do not overlap. A shift of elements inside one slice always overlaps. A release build does not tell you about the error. The check is a safety check, so it is not in the build where the bug costs the most.

`@memmove` handles the overlap. It works in the two directions. Before `@memmove`, there was the pair `std.mem.copyForwards` and `std.mem.copyBackwards`. With `@memmove`, you do not have to select a direction, and you cannot select the wrong direction. The two older functions are now deprecated, and the builtin replaces them.

Use `@memcpy` when you know that the ranges do not overlap. Use `@memmove` when the ranges possibly overlap.

## Remove an element

To remove an element, do these steps:

1. Move the tail one position lower, over the gap.
2. Make the slice one element shorter.

The backing array always keeps its length. Only the slice becomes shorter. `orderedRemove` does these steps for you on an `ArrayList`. Here they are without the container.

## Stop at a value

`std.mem.sliceTo` takes the part of a buffer before the first occurrence of a value. Use it when a different part of the program filled a fixed buffer and terminated its own output. Most C interop is of this type.

## Min, max, and all equal

`std.mem.findMin` and `findMax` return **indices**, not values. This looks strange at first. It is correct when a second array holds labels in the same order as the first array. The functions are for this case. `std.mem.allEqual` checks if all elements of the slice are equal, and you do not need a loop.

## An index belongs to its slice

An offset from one slice has no meaning in a different slice. `std.mem.find` on a sub-slice returns a position relative to that sub-slice. If you use the position on the parent, you have a bug. The type system cannot see this bug, because the two slices are `[]const u8`.

To convert the position, add the offset of the sub-slice. Alternatively, search the parent and then make the result narrower. When you use sub-slices, this mistake is easy to make with each function in the `find` family.

[Sorting](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/sorting/) shows how to search a *sorted* slice, and how to sort a slice.

---

## Know What the Compiler Knows

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/compiler-knows/*

Each value in a Zig program is one of two kinds:

- A **comptime-known** value is a value that the compiler knows during compilation.
- A **runtime-known** value is a value that only the program knows when it runs.

Some places in the language accept only comptime-known values. An array length, a type and a `comptime` parameter are three of these places. Thus you must know which kind each value is.

[Comptime](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/comptime/) in Language Basics gives the idea in one page. This section starts at that point.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn square(x: u32) u32 {
    return x * x;
}

// A function does not decide where it runs. The caller decides.
// `@inComptime()` tells the function which case is true.
fn where() []const u8 {
    return if (@inComptime()) "compile time" else "runtime";
}

// A comptime parameter can be part of the return type.
// Each different `n` makes a different function.
fn repeat(comptime n: usize, char: u8) [n]u8 {
    return @splat(char);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    // 1. A `const` with a literal value is comptime-known.
    //    A `var` is runtime-known, even when its value never changes.
    const width = 8;
    var height: u32 = 3;
    _ = &height;
    try out.print("1. width: {s}, height: {s}\n", .{ @typeName(@TypeOf(width)), @typeName(@TypeOf(height)) });

    // A comptime-known value can be an array length. `height` cannot.
    const row: [width]u8 = @splat('#');
    try out.print("   row: {s}\n", .{&row});

    // 2. The same function, called two ways.
    const at_compile = comptime where();
    const at_run = where();
    try out.print("2. comptime where(): {s}\n", .{at_compile});
    try out.print("   where(): {s}\n", .{at_run});

    // 3. A labelled block after `comptime` runs during compilation.
    //    The binary contains only the array, not the loop.
    const squares = comptime blk: {
        var table: [6]u32 = undefined;
        for (&table, 0..) |*slot, i| slot.* = square(@intCast(i));
        break :blk table;
    };
    try out.print("3. squares: {any}\n", .{squares});

    // 4. A comptime parameter sets the length of the result.
    const three = repeat(3, 'a');
    const five = repeat(5, 'b');
    try out.print("4. {s} is a {s}\n", .{ &three, @typeName(@TypeOf(three)) });
    try out.print("   {s} is a {s}\n", .{ &five, @typeName(@TypeOf(five)) });

    // 5. A `comptime var` lives only during compilation. An `inline for`
    //    runs its body once for each item, so the counter sees each one.
    const words = .{ "red", "green", "blue" };
    comptime var total = 0;
    inline for (words) |word| total += word.len;
    try out.print("5. letters in {d} words: {d}\n", .{ words.len, total });
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.compiler-knows`)*

## `const` and `var`

The first part of the program declares two values:

```zig
const width = 8;
var height: u32 = 3;
```

The output shows their types:

```
1. width: comptime_int, height: u32
```

`width` is a `const` with a literal value. The compiler knows the value, and the type is `comptime_int`. A `comptime_int` has no fixed size. It becomes a sized integer when you use it in a place that needs one.

`height` is a `var`. The program never changes it, but the compiler does not use that fact. A `var` is runtime-known, always.

A `const` is not always comptime-known. `const n = readNumber();` is a `const`, but the value comes from a function that runs when the program runs. The rule is about the source of the value, not about the keyword.

## A runtime value where a type must go

`width` is comptime-known, thus `[width]u8` is a valid type. The program uses it for a row of 8 characters.

The next program tries the same thing with a `var`:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main() void {
    var n: usize = 4;
    _ = &n;
    // `n` never changes, but it is a `var`. Thus the compiler does not use
    // its value, and `[n]u8` is not a type that the compiler can make.
    const buf: [n]u8 = @splat(0);
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{buf.len});
}
```

The compiler says:

```
error: unable to resolve comptime value
note: types must be comptime-known
```

*Compiled by CI, but not runnable in the browser sandbox. (`25-comptime.runtime-length`)*

The length of an array is part of its type, and the compiler must know each type. A `var` cannot supply a value to a type.

To repair the program, use one of these two changes:

- Change `var` to `const`, if the value is a literal.
- Use a slice from an allocator, if the length is only known at runtime.

## The caller decides where a function runs

`where` is a usual function. It has no `comptime` keyword in its declaration. The program calls it two times:

```
2. comptime where(): compile time
   where(): runtime
```

The `comptime` keyword before a call tells the compiler to run the call during compilation. Without the keyword, the call runs when the program runs. Thus one function can run at both times. The function itself does not decide.

`@inComptime()` returns `true` when the code runs during compilation. Use it only when a function must do different work in the two cases. Most functions do not need it.

If a call has `comptime` in front of it, the compiler must be able to run it. A function that reads a file or the clock cannot run during compilation. The compiler then stops with an error, and the program does not build.

## A `comptime` block

```zig
const squares = comptime blk: {
    var table: [6]u32 = undefined;
    for (&table, 0..) |*slot, i| slot.* = square(@intCast(i));
    break :blk table;
};
```

The block runs during compilation. The block can contain a `var`, and the loop changes the array six times. The result of the block is the array, and the binary contains only the six numbers:

```
3. squares: { 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 }
```

The block uses `var` inside, but `squares` is a `const` with a comptime-known value. The block, not the `var`, decides the kind of the result.

## A `comptime` parameter in the return type

```zig
fn repeat(comptime n: usize, char: u8) [n]u8 {
    return @splat(char);
}
```

`n` is a `comptime` parameter. Thus the function can use `n` in its return type. Each call with a different `n` makes a separate copy of the function, and each copy has a different return type:

```
4. aaa is a [3]u8
   bbbbb is a [5]u8
```

`char` is a usual parameter. It can be a runtime value.

Each different value of `n` adds one copy to the binary. For a parameter with a small number of values, the cost is small. For a parameter with thousands of values, the binary becomes large.

## A `comptime var`

```zig
const words = .{ "red", "green", "blue" };
comptime var total = 0;
inline for (words) |word| total += word.len;
```

A `comptime var` exists only during compilation. The `inline for` runs its body one time for each word, and each copy of the body adds to the counter:

```
5. letters in 3 words: 12
```

A usual `for` cannot change a `comptime var`. The compiler compiles a usual loop body one time, and the body runs at runtime. A runtime loop cannot change a value that exists only during compilation. [Inline Loops](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/inline-loops/) gives more examples of `inline for`.

## Check yourself

`const limit = std.math.maxInt(u8);` Is `limit` comptime-known?

Yes. `std.math.maxInt` is a usual function. Its argument is a type, and a type is always comptime-known. The result is the same each time, and the compiler calculates it during compilation. Thus `[limit]u8` is a valid array type of 255 bytes.

The next chapter uses a `comptime` block to make a lookup table, and checks the table against the standard library.

---

## Build Lookup Tables

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/lookup-tables/*

A lookup table replaces a calculation with an array read. You calculate each answer one time and keep the answers in an array. Then the program reads the answer for an input from the array.

In many languages, you calculate the table with a separate script and paste the numbers into the source. In Zig, the compiler calculates the table from usual Zig code. The source keeps the calculation, and the binary keeps only the numbers.

This chapter builds the table for CRC-32. CRC-32 is the checksum in Zip files, PNG files and Ethernet frames. The program then compares its results with `std.hash.Crc32`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// The reflected CRC-32 polynomial. Zip, PNG and Ethernet use it.
const poly: u32 = 0xEDB88320;

// One entry for each possible byte. Each entry is the result of eight
// shift-and-xor steps on that byte. The steps run during compilation, and
// the binary contains only the 256 results.
const table: [256]u32 = blk: {
    // 256 bytes times 8 steps is more than 1000 backward branches.
    @setEvalBranchQuota(256 * 8 + 256);
    var t: [256]u32 = undefined;
    for (&t, 0..) |*entry, byte| {
        var c: u32 = @intCast(byte);
        for (0..8) |_| {
            c = if (c & 1 != 0) poly ^ (c >> 1) else c >> 1;
        }
        entry.* = c;
    }
    break :blk t;
};

// One table read for each byte of input, not eight steps.
fn crc32(data: []const u8) u32 {
    var crc: u32 = 0xFFFFFFFF;
    for (data) |byte| {
        crc = table[(crc ^ byte) & 0xFF] ^ (crc >> 8);
    }
    return ~crc;
}

// The same eight steps for one byte, at runtime, with each step printed.
// The table block above does exactly this work for each of the 256 bytes,
// during compilation.
fn traceEntry(out: *std.Io.Writer, byte: u8) !u32 {
    var c: u32 = byte;
    try out.print("  start   0x{x:0>8}\n", .{c});
    for (1..9) |step| {
        const low = c & 1;
        c = if (low != 0) poly ^ (c >> 1) else c >> 1;
        const what = if (low != 0) "shift, then xor" else "shift";
        try out.print("  step {d}  low bit {d}, {s: <16} 0x{x:0>8}\n", .{ step, low, what, c });
    }
    return c;
}

// A table can be a type check too. The compiler runs this block, and
// a false condition stops the build.
comptime {
    std.debug.assert(table[0] == 0);
    std.debug.assert(table[128] == poly);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    try out.print("table: {d} entries, {d} bytes\n", .{ table.len, @sizeOf(@TypeOf(table)) });
    for (table[0..4], 0..) |entry, i| {
        try out.print("  table[{d}] = 0x{x:0>8}\n", .{ i, entry });
    }

    const inputs = [_][]const u8{ "", "a", "hello, world", "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" };
    for (inputs) |input| {
        const ours = crc32(input);
        const theirs = std.hash.Crc32.hash(input);
        try out.print("\"{s}\"\n  ours 0x{x:0>8}, std 0x{x:0>8}, {s}\n", .{
            input,
            ours,
            theirs,
            if (ours == theirs) "same" else "DIFFERENT",
        });
    }

    // A table that the compiler made is also usable at compile time.
    const at_compile = comptime crc32("hello, world");
    try out.print("comptime crc32(\"hello, world\") = 0x{x:0>8}\n", .{at_compile});

    try out.print("\nthe 8 steps for byte 1\n", .{});
    const traced = try traceEntry(out, 1);
    try out.print("  table[1] = 0x{x:0>8}, same -> {}\n", .{ table[1], traced == table[1] });
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.lookup-tables`)*

## The calculation without a table

CRC-32 processes the input one bit at a time. For each bit, it does one shift and one conditional xor with a constant, the polynomial `0xEDB88320`. A byte has 8 bits, thus each byte of input costs 8 steps.

The result of the 8 steps depends only on one byte. A byte has 256 possible values. Thus there are only 256 possible results, and a table can hold all of them.

## Build the table

```zig
const table: [256]u32 = blk: {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(256 * 8 + 256);
    var t: [256]u32 = undefined;
    for (&t, 0..) |*entry, byte| {
        var c: u32 = @intCast(byte);
        for (0..8) |_| {
            c = if (c & 1 != 0) poly ^ (c >> 1) else c >> 1;
        }
        entry.* = c;
    }
    break :blk t;
};
```

`table` is a `const` at the top level of the file. The compiler always calculates a top-level `const` during compilation. Thus this block does not need the `comptime` keyword.

The output shows the first entries:

```
table: 256 entries, 1024 bytes
  table[0] = 0x00000000
  table[1] = 0x77073096
  table[2] = 0xee0e612c
  table[3] = 0x990951ba
```

The table in the zlib source, `crc32.h`, starts with the same four numbers. The table is 1024 bytes in the binary, because each of the 256 entries is a `u32`.

## Use the table

```zig
fn crc32(data: []const u8) u32 {
    var crc: u32 = 0xFFFFFFFF;
    for (data) |byte| {
        crc = table[(crc ^ byte) & 0xFF] ^ (crc >> 8);
    }
    return ~crc;
}
```

Each byte of input now costs one table read, one xor and one shift. The 8 steps for each bit are gone. They ran one time, in the compiler, for each of the 256 possible bytes.

The program also runs the 8 steps for byte 1 at runtime and prints each step. The figure plays that trace. The last register is `table[1]`, the same value that the compiler put in the table.

*Figure: A 32-bit register that starts at 1. Eight shift steps, two with an xor of the polynomial 0xEDB88320, give 0x77073096, entry 1 of a 256-entry table. The steps for byte 1, as the program above prints them. The bits that a step changed are filled. On a step that xors, the 1 bits of the polynomial are filled too.*

## Check the table against `std`

A table with one wrong entry gives a wrong checksum for some inputs and the correct checksum for others. Thus the program compares its result with `std.hash.Crc32.hash` for four inputs:

```
"The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
  ours 0x414fa339, std 0x414fa339, same
```

`0x414fa339` is also the published CRC-32 of this sentence. The `.expected` file pins the full output. Thus if a change to the table makes one result different, `zig build verify` fails.

The program also has a `comptime` block at the top level:

```zig
comptime {
    std.debug.assert(table[0] == 0);
    std.debug.assert(table[128] == poly);
}
```

During compilation, a failed `assert` is a compile error. These two checks stop the build before the program can run. Entry 128 is the byte `0x80`, and only its top bit is 1. Seven shifts move that bit to the bottom. Then the eighth step does the only xor, and the result is the polynomial.

## The branch quota

The compiler counts each backward branch during comptime evaluation. A backward branch is a jump back to the start of a loop. After 1000 of them, the compiler stops with an error. The limit makes sure that a loop which never ends gives an error, and the compiler does not run forever.

The table needs more than 1000. The inner loop runs 8 times for each of 256 bytes, and that is 2048 branches. The outer loop adds 256 more. Without `@setEvalBranchQuota`, the same block fails:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const table: [256]u32 = blk: {
    var t: [256]u32 = undefined;
    for (&t, 0..) |*entry, byte| {
        var c: u32 = @intCast(byte);
        for (0..8) |_| {
            c = if (c & 1 != 0) 0xEDB88320 ^ (c >> 1) else c >> 1;
        }
        entry.* = c;
    }
    break :blk t;
};

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("0x{x}\n", .{table[1]});
}
```

The compiler says:

```
error: evaluation exceeded 1000 backwards branches
note: use @setEvalBranchQuota() to raise the branch limit from 1000
```

*Compiled by CI, but not runnable in the browser sandbox. (`25-comptime.table-no-quota`)*

`@setEvalBranchQuota(256 * 8 + 256)` sets the limit for the current comptime evaluation. Calculate the number from the loops, as this program does. A number that you calculate tells the next reader why the limit has that value. A large round number such as `1_000_000` tells the reader nothing.

## A table is also comptime-known

The last line of the output is:

```
comptime crc32("hello, world") = 0xffab723a
```

`crc32` reads only `table`, and `table` is comptime-known. Thus the compiler can also run `crc32` during compilation, when the input is comptime-known. The binary then contains only the checksum.

## Check yourself

The program runs `crc32` at runtime on a string from a file. Does the binary contain the 8-step loop?

No. The 8-step loop is inside the block that builds `table`. That block runs only during compilation. At runtime, `crc32` contains only the loop over the input bytes and the table read.

The next chapter reads the fields of a type, and uses them to write a function that works for all struct types.

---

## Read a Type

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/read-a-type/*

`@typeInfo(T)` returns a description of the type `T`. The description is a usual Zig value of type `std.lang.Type`. It contains the names of the fields, the type of each field and the default values.

The description is comptime-known, thus a function can walk it with `inline for`. The function then has one copy of its body for each field. This is how one function can work with every struct type.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const Writer = std.Io.Writer;

const Config = struct {
    name: []const u8 = "server",
    port: u16 = 8080,
    verbose: bool = false,
    retries: u8,

    pub const max_port = 9000;

    pub fn isDefaultPort(self: Config) bool {
        return self.port == 8080;
    }
};

const Level = enum(u8) { debug, info, warn = 10, err };

const Shape = union(enum) {
    circle: f32,
    square: f32,
    empty: void,
};

// Print each field of a struct with its type and its default value.
fn describeStruct(out: *Writer, comptime T: type) !void {
    const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
    try out.print("{d} fields, {d} declarations\n", .{ info.field_names.len, info.decl_names.len });
    // The three arrays have the same length and the same order.
    inline for (info.field_names, info.field_types, info.field_attrs) |name, F, attrs| {
        try out.print("  {s}: {s}", .{ name, @typeName(F) });
        if (attrs.defaultValue(F)) |default| {
            if (F == []const u8) {
                try out.print(" = \"{s}\"", .{default});
            } else {
                try out.print(" = {any}", .{default});
            }
        } else {
            try out.print(" (no default)", .{});
        }
        try out.print("\n", .{});
    }
    inline for (info.decl_names) |decl| try out.print("  pub {s}\n", .{decl});
}

// Two values of one struct type. Print only the fields that are different.
fn diff(out: *Writer, old: anytype, new: @TypeOf(old)) !void {
    const T = @TypeOf(old);
    inline for (@typeInfo(T).@"struct".field_names, @typeInfo(T).@"struct".field_types) |name, F| {
        const a = @field(old, name);
        const b = @field(new, name);
        // `==` on a slice is not allowed. Compare the bytes instead.
        const same = if (F == []const u8) std.mem.eql(u8, a, b) else a == b;
        if (!same) {
            if (F == []const u8) {
                try out.print("  {s}: \"{s}\" -> \"{s}\"\n", .{ name, a, b });
            } else {
                try out.print("  {s}: {any} -> {any}\n", .{ name, a, b });
            }
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    try out.print("Config: ", .{});
    try describeStruct(out, Config);

    // Questions with a yes or no answer, all at compile time.
    try out.print("@hasField(Config, \"port\"): {}\n", .{@hasField(Config, "port")});
    try out.print("@hasField(Config, \"host\"): {}\n", .{@hasField(Config, "host")});
    try out.print("@hasDecl(Config, \"isDefaultPort\"): {}\n", .{@hasDecl(Config, "isDefaultPort")});
    try out.print("@FieldType(Config, \"port\"): {s}\n", .{@typeName(@FieldType(Config, "port"))});

    const level = @typeInfo(Level).@"enum";
    try out.print("Level: tag type {s}\n", .{@typeName(level.tag_type)});
    inline for (level.field_names, level.field_values) |name, value| {
        try out.print("  {s} = {d}\n", .{ name, value });
    }

    const shape = @typeInfo(Shape).@"union";
    try out.print("Shape: {d} variants\n", .{shape.field_names.len});
    inline for (shape.field_names, shape.field_types) |name, P| {
        try out.print("  {s}: {s}\n", .{ name, @typeName(P) });
    }

    const before: Config = .{ .retries = 3 };
    const after: Config = .{ .name = "api", .retries = 3, .verbose = true };
    try out.print("diff(before, after):\n", .{});
    try diff(out, before, after);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.read-a-type`)*

## The shape of the description

`std.lang.Type` is a tagged union with one variant for each kind of type. To get the description of a struct, take the `@"struct"` variant:

```zig
const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
```

The name has quotes because `struct` is a keyword. The `enum`, `union` and `fn` variants use the same syntax.

For a struct, `info` has three arrays of fields:

- `field_names` holds the name of each field.
- `field_types` holds the type of each field.
- `field_attrs` holds the default value, the alignment and the `comptime` flag of each field.

The three arrays have the same length. Item `i` in each array describes the same field. The fields are in the order of the source file.

## Walk the fields

```zig
inline for (info.field_names, info.field_types, info.field_attrs) |name, F, attrs| {
    try out.print("  {s}: {s}", .{ name, @typeName(F) });
    if (attrs.defaultValue(F)) |default| { ... }
}
```

A `for` with three arrays walks them together. The loop must be `inline`, because `F` is a type, and a type must be comptime-known in each copy of the body.

`attrs.defaultValue(F)` returns the default value as a `?F`. The result is `null` when the field has no default:

```
Config: 4 fields, 2 declarations
  name: []const u8 = "server"
  port: u16 = 8080
  verbose: bool = false
  retries: u8 (no default)
  pub max_port
  pub isDefaultPort
```

`decl_names` lists the declarations of the type. It lists only `pub` declarations. A declaration without `pub` is not in the list.

[Print Any Struct](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/struct-printer/) uses the same walk to print a value of any struct type.

## Questions with a yes or no answer

You do not always need the full description. Four builtins answer one question each:

```
@hasField(Config, "port"): true
@hasField(Config, "host"): false
@hasDecl(Config, "isDefaultPort"): true
@FieldType(Config, "port"): u16
```

The answers are comptime-known. Thus a generic function can use them in an `if`, and the compiler removes the branch that is not used.

Use `@hasDecl` to make a method optional. For example, a function can call `value.format(...)` when the type has a `format` method, and use a default output when it does not.

## Enums and unions

The description of an enum has `field_names` and `field_values`:

```
Level: tag type u8
  debug = 0
  info = 1
  warn = 10
  err = 11
```

The source sets `warn = 10`, and `err` follows with 11. The values in the description are the real values, not the position of each tag.

The description of a tagged union has `field_names` and `field_types`. The type of each variant is the type of its payload. A variant without a payload has the type `void`:

```
Shape: 3 variants
  circle: f32
  square: f32
  empty: void
```

## Use the walk: a diff for any struct

```zig
fn diff(out: *Writer, old: anytype, new: @TypeOf(old)) !void {
    const T = @TypeOf(old);
    inline for (@typeInfo(T).@"struct".field_names, @typeInfo(T).@"struct".field_types) |name, F| {
        const a = @field(old, name);
        const b = @field(new, name);
        const same = if (F == []const u8) std.mem.eql(u8, a, b) else a == b;
        ...
    }
}
```

`@field(old, name)` reads the field with the name `name`. The name must be comptime-known. In an `inline for`, each copy of the body has its own comptime-known `name`.

The type of `new` is `@TypeOf(old)`. Thus the two arguments must have the same type, and the compiler rejects a call with two different structs.

Zig does not allow `==` on two slices. Thus the function compares a `[]const u8` field with `std.mem.eql`. The `if` on `F == []const u8` is comptime-known, and each copy of the body contains only one of the two comparisons.

The program changes two fields of a `Config`, and `diff` prints the two changes:

```
diff(before, after):
  name: "server" -> "api"
  verbose: false -> true
```

`port` and `retries` have the same value in the two structs, thus `diff` prints nothing for them. If you add a field to `Config`, `diff` compares the new field too. You do not change `diff`.

## If you used an older version of Zig

Before version 0.17, the description of a struct had one `fields` array. Each item was a struct with a `name`, a `type` and a `default_value_ptr`. A loop was `inline for (info.fields) |f|`, and it read `f.name` and `f.type`.

Now the description has three separate arrays. [Zig 0.17](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/zig-0-17/) has a table of the changes for structs, enums and unions.

## Check yourself

A new field `tags: []const []const u8` goes into `Config`. Does `diff` still compile?

No. `F == []const u8` is false for `[]const []const u8`, thus `diff` uses `a == b`, and Zig does not allow `==` on slices. The compiler stops with an error at the line with `a == b`. To repair `diff`, add a branch for this type, or compare the slices item by item.

The next chapter goes in the other direction. It makes a new type from a description.

---

## Make a Type

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/make-a-type/*

The last chapter read the description of a type. This chapter goes in the other direction: a function makes a description, and a builtin changes the description into a new type.

Zig has one builtin for each kind of type that you can make:

- `@Int` makes an integer type.
- `@Struct` makes a struct type.
- `@Enum` makes an enum type.
- `@Union` makes a union type.
- `@Tuple` makes a tuple type.
- `@Pointer` and `@Fn` make pointer and function types.

The program uses four of them.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Config = struct {
    name: []const u8 = "server",
    port: u16 = 8080,
    verbose: bool = false,
};

// The same fields as `T`, but each field is optional, with a default of
// `null`. A patch sets only the fields that it wants to change.
fn Partial(comptime T: type) type {
    const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
    var types: [info.field_names.len]type = undefined;
    var attrs: [info.field_names.len]std.lang.Type.Struct.FieldAttributes = undefined;
    for (info.field_types, &types, &attrs) |F, *slot, *attr| {
        slot.* = ?F;
        // The attributes hold the address of the default, not the value.
        // `&@as(?F, null)` is the address of a comptime constant, thus the
        // address stays valid.
        attr.* = .{ .default_value_ptr = &@as(?F, null) };
    }
    return @Struct(.auto, null, info.field_names, &types, &attrs);
}

// Copy each field that the patch sets. Keep each field that it does not set.
fn apply(base: anytype, patch: Partial(@TypeOf(base))) @TypeOf(base) {
    var result = base;
    inline for (@typeInfo(@TypeOf(base)).@"struct".field_names) |name| {
        if (@field(patch, name)) |value| @field(result, name) = value;
    }
    return result;
}

// An enum with one tag for each field of `T`, numbered from 0.
fn FieldTag(comptime T: type) type {
    const names = @typeInfo(T).@"struct".field_names;
    var values: [names.len]u8 = undefined;
    for (&values, 0..) |*v, i| v.* = i;
    return @Enum(u8, .exhaustive, names, &values);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    // 1. An integer of any width from 1 to 65535 bits.
    const U12 = @Int(.unsigned, 12);
    try out.print("1. {s}: {d} bits, {d} bytes, max {d}\n", .{
        @typeName(U12),
        @bitSizeOf(U12),
        @sizeOf(U12),
        std.math.maxInt(U12),
    });

    // 2. A struct made from the fields of another struct.
    const Patch = Partial(Config);
    try out.print("2. Partial(Config):\n", .{});
    inline for (@typeInfo(Patch).@"struct".field_names, @typeInfo(Patch).@"struct".field_types) |name, F| {
        try out.print("   {s}: {s}\n", .{ name, @typeName(F) });
    }

    const base: Config = .{};
    const changed = apply(base, .{ .port = 9090 });
    try out.print("   apply(.{{ .port = 9090 }}): name \"{s}\", port {d}, verbose {}\n", .{
        changed.name,
        changed.port,
        changed.verbose,
    });

    // 3. An enum made from the field names. A `switch` on it must
    //    handle each field, so a new field makes the old switch fail.
    const Tag = FieldTag(Config);
    try out.print("3. FieldTag(Config):", .{});
    inline for (@typeInfo(Tag).@"enum".field_names) |name| try out.print(" .{s}", .{name});
    try out.print("\n", .{});
    const tag: Tag = .port;
    const label = switch (tag) {
        .name => "a string",
        .port => "a number",
        .verbose => "a flag",
    };
    try out.print("   .port is {s}\n", .{label});

    // 4. A tuple type from a list of types.
    const Pair = @Tuple(&.{ u8, bool });
    const pair: Pair = .{ 7, true };
    try out.print("4. @Tuple: {d} fields, values {d} and {}\n", .{
        @typeInfo(Pair).@"struct".field_names.len,
        pair[0],
        pair[1],
    });
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.make-a-type`)*

## An integer of any width

```zig
const U12 = @Int(.unsigned, 12);
```

`U12` is the same type as `u12`. `@Int` is useful when the width is a calculation, for example one bit for each item in a list:

```
1. u12: 12 bits, 2 bytes, max 4095
```

`@bitSizeOf` gives the 12 bits that the value uses. `@sizeOf` gives 2 bytes, because memory stores a value in whole bytes.

## A struct from another struct

`Partial(T)` has the same fields as `T`, but each field is optional, with a default of `null`. A value of `Partial(Config)` is a patch: it sets only the fields that it wants to change.

```zig
fn Partial(comptime T: type) type {
    const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
    var types: [info.field_names.len]type = undefined;
    var attrs: [info.field_names.len]std.lang.Type.Struct.FieldAttributes = undefined;
    for (info.field_types, &types, &attrs) |F, *slot, *attr| {
        slot.* = ?F;
        attr.* = .{ .default_value_ptr = &@as(?F, null) };
    }
    return @Struct(.auto, null, info.field_names, &types, &attrs);
}
```

`Partial` is a usual function with a `comptime` parameter. It runs during compilation because its result is a type. The loop is a usual `for`, not an `inline for`, because the loop body builds arrays and does not need one copy for each field.

`@Struct` takes five arguments:

1. The layout: `.auto`, `.@"extern"` or `.@"packed"`.
2. The backing integer of a packed struct, or `null`.
3. The field names. `Partial` uses the names of `T` without a change.
4. The field types.
5. The field attributes. `Partial` gives each field a default.

`default_value_ptr` is the address of the default value, not the value. `&@as(?F, null)` is the address of a comptime constant. The compiler puts each comptime constant that the program uses into the binary. Thus the address stays valid when the program runs.

The output shows the new fields:

```
2. Partial(Config):
   name: ?[]const u8
   port: ?u16
   verbose: ?bool
```

## Use the new type

```zig
fn apply(base: anytype, patch: Partial(@TypeOf(base))) @TypeOf(base) {
    var result = base;
    inline for (@typeInfo(@TypeOf(base)).@"struct".field_names) |name| {
        if (@field(patch, name)) |value| @field(result, name) = value;
    }
    return result;
}
```

The type of the `patch` parameter is a function call. The compiler calls `Partial` with the type of `base`, and the result is the type of the parameter.

The caller writes `.{ .port = 9090 }`. The compiler knows the type of the parameter, thus the literal becomes a `Partial(Config)`. The other two fields get their default, `null`:

```
   apply(.{ .port = 9090 }): name "server", port 9090, verbose false
```

`Partial(Config)` follows `Config`. If you add a field to `Config`, the patch type gets the same field. You do not change `Partial` or `apply`.

## An enum of the field names

```zig
fn FieldTag(comptime T: type) type {
    const names = @typeInfo(T).@"struct".field_names;
    var values: [names.len]u8 = undefined;
    for (&values, 0..) |*v, i| v.* = i;
    return @Enum(u8, .exhaustive, names, &values);
}
```

`FieldTag(Config)` is an enum with one tag for each field:

```
3. FieldTag(Config): .name .port .verbose
   .port is a number
```

The enum is exhaustive. Thus a `switch` on a `FieldTag(Config)` must have a branch for each tag. If you add a field to `Config`, each `switch` without the new tag stops the build. The compiler then shows you each place that must handle the new field.

The standard library has this function: `std.meta.FieldEnum`. Use the library function in real code. This program writes it to show `@Enum`.

## A tuple from a list of types

```zig
const Pair = @Tuple(&.{ u8, bool });
```

A tuple is a struct with fields that have numbers, not names. `@Tuple` takes a list of types:

```
4. @Tuple: 2 fields, values 7 and true
```

`@Tuple` is useful when a function must build an argument list for another function. `std.meta.ArgsTuple` uses it to make the tuple of argument types for a function.

## If you used an older version of Zig

Older code uses one builtin for all of these types: `@Type`. Its argument was a full `std.builtin.Type` value:

```zig
const U12 = @Type(.{ .int = .{ .signedness = .unsigned, .bits = 12 } });
```

On current Zig, `@Type` does not exist, and the compiler gives the error `invalid builtin function: '@Type'`. Use the builtin for the kind of type that you want. `@Int(.unsigned, 12)` replaces the line above.

`std.meta.Int` and `std.meta.Tuple` are also gone. Zig 0.16.0 already had the `@Int` and `@Tuple` builtins that replace them. [Zig 0.17](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/zig-0-17/) lists the other changes to reflection.

## Check yourself

`Partial(Partial(Config))` is a valid type. What is the type of its `port` field?

`??u16`, an optional of an optional. `Partial` adds `?` to each field type, and it does not look at the type first. For this type, `null` and `@as(?u16, null)` are two different values. To prevent this, `Partial` can check `@typeInfo(F) == .optional` and keep a type that is already optional.

---

## Dispatch with Comptime

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/dispatch/*

A program that reads commands must connect each command to the code for that command. The name of this connection is dispatch.

In Zig, the commands are often the tags of an enum. The compiler knows each tag, thus it can make the connection during compilation. If a tag has no handler, the build stops.

The program below reads five commands from a script. It connects each command to its handler in two ways, and the two results must agree.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Op = enum { add, sub, mul, neg };

// One function for each tag of `Op`, with the same name as the tag.
const Handlers = struct {
    pub fn add(a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
        return a + b;
    }
    pub fn sub(a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
        return a - b;
    }
    pub fn mul(a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
        return a * b;
    }
    pub fn neg(a: i64, _: i64) i64 {
        return -a;
    }
};

// 1. A switch with `inline else`. The compiler makes one branch for each
//    tag, and each branch calls its handler directly.
fn runSwitch(op: Op, a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
    return switch (op) {
        inline else => |tag| @field(Handlers, @tagName(tag))(a, b),
    };
}

// 2. A table of function pointers, built during compilation.
//    The program indexes it with the tag at runtime.
const Handler = *const fn (i64, i64) i64;
const table: std.EnumArray(Op, Handler) = blk: {
    var t: std.EnumArray(Op, Handler) = undefined;
    for (std.enums.values(Op)) |tag| {
        t.set(tag, @field(Handlers, @tagName(tag)));
    }
    break :blk t;
};

fn runTable(op: Op, a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
    return table.get(op)(a, b);
}

// 3. Data for each tag, in a table that the compiler checks: an
//    `EnumArray` must have a value for each tag.
const symbols: std.EnumArray(Op, []const u8) = .init(.{
    .add = "+",
    .sub = "-",
    .mul = "*",
    .neg = "neg",
});

const script =
    \\add 2 3
    \\mul 4 5
    \\neg 7 0
    \\sub 10 4
    \\div 8 2
;

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    var lines = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, script, '\n');
    while (lines.next()) |line| {
        var words = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
        const name = words.next() orelse continue;
        const a = try std.fmt.parseInt(i64, words.next().?, 10);
        const b = try std.fmt.parseInt(i64, words.next().?, 10);

        // `stringToEnum` compares the text with each tag name. The
        // compiler makes the list of names from `Op`.
        const op = std.meta.stringToEnum(Op, name) orelse {
            try out.print("{s}: unknown command\n", .{name});
            continue;
        };
        const by_switch = runSwitch(op, a, b);
        const by_table = runTable(op, a, b);
        try out.print("{s} {d} {d} = {d} (switch), {d} (table), symbol {s}\n", .{
            name, a, b, by_switch, by_table, symbols.get(op),
        });
    }
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.dispatch`)*

## Handlers with the same names as the tags

```zig
const Op = enum { add, sub, mul, neg };

const Handlers = struct {
    pub fn add(a: i64, b: i64) i64 { ... }
    pub fn sub(a: i64, b: i64) i64 { ... }
    pub fn mul(a: i64, b: i64) i64 { ... }
    pub fn neg(a: i64, _: i64) i64 { ... }
};
```

`Handlers` is a struct with no fields. It is a namespace for four functions. Each function has the same name as one tag of `Op`. The program uses this rule to find the handler for a tag.

## Dispatch with `inline else`

```zig
fn runSwitch(op: Op, a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
    return switch (op) {
        inline else => |tag| @field(Handlers, @tagName(tag))(a, b),
    };
}
```

`inline else` makes one branch for each tag. In each branch, `tag` is comptime-known. Thus `@tagName(tag)` is a comptime-known string, and `@field(Handlers, "add")` finds the function `Handlers.add`.

The compiler then has four usual branches, and each branch calls one function directly. The result is the same as a `switch` that you write by hand, with one line for each tag.

## Dispatch with a table

```zig
const Handler = *const fn (i64, i64) i64;
const table: std.EnumArray(Op, Handler) = blk: {
    var t: std.EnumArray(Op, Handler) = undefined;
    for (std.enums.values(Op)) |tag| {
        t.set(tag, @field(Handlers, @tagName(tag)));
    }
    break :blk t;
};
```

`std.EnumArray(Op, Handler)` is an array with one item for each tag of `Op`. The block fills it during compilation, with the address of each handler. At runtime, `table.get(op)` reads one item and calls the function at that address.

The two methods give the same results:

```
add 2 3 = 5 (switch), 5 (table), symbol +
mul 4 5 = 20 (switch), 20 (table), symbol *
neg 7 0 = -7 (switch), -7 (table), symbol neg
sub 10 4 = 6 (switch), 6 (table), symbol -
```

Select one method with these rules:

- Use `inline else` when the set of handlers does not change at runtime. Each call is direct, and the compiler can inline the handler.
- Use a table when the program must change a handler at runtime, or when it must keep the handlers in data.

## Data for each tag

```zig
const symbols: std.EnumArray(Op, []const u8) = .init(.{
    .add = "+",
    .sub = "-",
    .mul = "*",
    .neg = "neg",
});
```

`.init` takes a struct with one field for each tag. If the struct has no field for one tag, the compiler stops with the error `missing struct field`. Thus a table of data cannot become shorter than the enum.

## From a string to a tag

The script contains text, not tags. `std.meta.stringToEnum(Op, name)` compares the text with each tag name. It returns `null` when no tag has that name:

```
div: unknown command
```

`stringToEnum` is a usual generic function. The compiler makes the list of names from `Op`, thus the list always agrees with the enum.

## A new tag without a handler

Add a `div` tag to `Op`, and do not add a `div` function to `Handlers`:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Op = enum { add, neg, div };

const Handlers = struct {
    pub fn add(a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
        return a + b;
    }
    pub fn neg(a: i64, _: i64) i64 {
        return -a;
    }
};

fn run(op: Op, a: i64, b: i64) i64 {
    return switch (op) {
        inline else => |tag| @field(Handlers, @tagName(tag))(a, b),
    };
}

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{run(.add, 2, 3)});
}
```

The compiler says:

```
error: struct 'dispatch-new-tag.Handlers' has no member named 'div'
```

*Compiled by CI, but not runnable in the browser sandbox. (`25-comptime.dispatch-new-tag`)*

The `inline else` branch for `div` asks for `Handlers.div`, and that function does not exist. The build stops before the program can receive a `div` command. In the full program, the table and `symbols` also stop the build, each with its own error.

Without comptime, the same mistake gives a different result. A `switch` with an `else` branch accepts `div` and does the wrong thing at runtime.

## Check yourself

`runSwitch` has no `else` branch for unknown tags. Why does it not need one?

`op` has the type `Op`, and `inline else` makes a branch for each tag of `Op`. Thus the `switch` handles each possible value. An unknown command never reaches `runSwitch`: `stringToEnum` returns `null` for it first.

---

## Reject Bad Input with @compileError

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/compile-error/*

A generic function accepts `anytype`. Thus a caller can give it a type that the function cannot use. The compiler always finds this mistake, but the error message can be bad. It often points at a line inside the function, not at the call.

`@compileError("text")` stops the build with your text. Put it in a branch that the compiler reaches only for a bad type. Then the user of the function reads a message about their call.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// The item type of an array, a slice or a pointer to an array.
// Any other type stops the build with a message that names the type.
fn Item(comptime T: type) type {
    const I = switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .array => |info| info.child,
        .pointer => |info| switch (info.size) {
            .slice => info.child,
            .one => switch (@typeInfo(info.child)) {
                .array => |array| array.child,
                else => @compileError("sum: expected an array or a slice, found " ++ @typeName(T)),
            },
            else => @compileError("sum: expected an array or a slice, found " ++ @typeName(T)),
        },
        else => @compileError("sum: expected an array or a slice, found " ++ @typeName(T)),
    };
    switch (@typeInfo(I)) {
        .int, .float => {},
        else => @compileError(std.fmt.comptimePrint(
            "sum: the items of {s} are {s}, not numbers",
            .{ @typeName(T), @typeName(I) },
        )),
    }
    return I;
}

fn sum(values: anytype) Item(@TypeOf(values)) {
    var total: Item(@TypeOf(values)) = 0;
    for (values) |v| total += v;
    return total;
}

// A function that needs a method. The check runs before the body, thus
// the message names the method that the type does not have, not a line inside the loop.
fn describeAll(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: anytype) !void {
    const T = @typeInfo(@TypeOf(items)).pointer.child;
    const E = @typeInfo(T).array.child;
    if (!@hasDecl(E, "describe")) {
        @compileError(@typeName(E) ++ " needs a `pub fn describe`");
    }
    for (items) |item| try item.describe(out);
}

const Dog = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    pub fn describe(self: Dog, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
        try out.print("  dog {s}\n", .{self.name});
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const bytes = [_]u8{ 10, 20, 30 };
    const prices = [_]f64{ 1.5, 2.25 };
    const prices_slice: []const f64 = &prices;
    try out.print("sum(array of u8) = {d}\n", .{sum(bytes)});
    try out.print("sum(&array of u8) = {d}\n", .{sum(&bytes)});
    try out.print("sum(slice of f64) = {d}\n", .{sum(prices_slice)});

    // `comptimePrint` formats during compilation. The result is a string
    // constant, the same kind of value as a literal.
    const label = comptime std.fmt.comptimePrint("{d} dogs", .{2});
    try out.print("{s}:\n", .{label});
    const dogs = [_]Dog{ .{ .name = "Moti" }, .{ .name = "Raja" } };
    try describeAll(out, &dogs);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.compile-error`)*

## The same mistake, two messages

`sum` adds the items of an array or a slice. The two programs below call `sum` with a list of strings. The first `sum` has no check:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn sum(values: anytype) @typeInfo(@TypeOf(values)).array.child {
    var total: @typeInfo(@TypeOf(values)).array.child = 0;
    for (values) |v| total += v;
    return total;
}

pub fn main() void {
    const names = [_][]const u8{ "Moti", "Raja" };
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{sum(names)});
}
```

The compiler says:

```
error: expected type '[]const u8', found 'comptime_int'
```

*Compiled by CI, but not runnable in the browser sandbox. (`25-comptime.sum-unguarded`)*

The message is correct, but it does not help. It points at `total += v` inside `sum`, and it talks about a `comptime_int`. The caller did not write that line, and the caller did not use a `comptime_int`. The `0` that sets the start value of `total` is the `comptime_int`.

The second `sum` checks the type first:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn Item(comptime T: type) type {
    const I = switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .array => |info| info.child,
        .pointer => |info| switch (info.size) {
            .slice => info.child,
            else => @compileError("sum: expected an array or a slice, found " ++ @typeName(T)),
        },
        else => @compileError("sum: expected an array or a slice, found " ++ @typeName(T)),
    };
    switch (@typeInfo(I)) {
        .int, .float => {},
        else => @compileError(std.fmt.comptimePrint(
            "sum: the items of {s} are {s}, not numbers",
            .{ @typeName(T), @typeName(I) },
        )),
    }
    return I;
}

fn sum(values: anytype) Item(@TypeOf(values)) {
    var total: Item(@TypeOf(values)) = 0;
    for (values) |v| total += v;
    return total;
}

pub fn main() void {
    const names = [_][]const u8{ "Moti", "Raja" };
    std.debug.print("{any}\n", .{sum(names)});
}
```

The compiler says:

```
error: sum: the items of [2][]const u8 are []const u8, not numbers
note: generic function instantiated here
```

*Compiled by CI, but not runnable in the browser sandbox. (`25-comptime.sum-guarded`)*

The message names the argument type and the item type, and it says what is wrong. The note `generic function instantiated here` points at the call in `main`. That is the line that the caller must change.

## The check

```zig
fn Item(comptime T: type) type {
    const I = switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .array => |info| info.child,
        .pointer => |info| switch (info.size) { ... },
        else => @compileError("sum: expected an array or a slice, found " ++ @typeName(T)),
    };
    switch (@typeInfo(I)) {
        .int, .float => {},
        else => @compileError(std.fmt.comptimePrint(
            "sum: the items of {s} are {s}, not numbers",
            .{ @typeName(T), @typeName(I) },
        )),
    }
    return I;
}
```

`Item` returns the item type of `T`, or it stops the build. `sum` uses `Item` in its return type:

```zig
fn sum(values: anytype) Item(@TypeOf(values)) {
```

The compiler calculates the return type before it reads the body. Thus the check runs first, and the body never sees a bad type.

The check accepts three shapes: an array, a slice and a pointer to an array. The output shows all three:

```
sum(array of u8) = 60
sum(&array of u8) = 60
sum(slice of f64) = 3.75
```

## The message is a comptime string

`@compileError` takes a comptime-known string. There are two ways to build one:

- `++` joins strings that are comptime-known. `@typeName(T)` returns one.
- `std.fmt.comptimePrint` formats a string with the same syntax as `print`. Use it when the message contains a number, or when it has many parts.

`comptimePrint` is not only for errors. The program uses it to make the label `2 dogs` during compilation.

## Check for a method

```zig
if (!@hasDecl(E, "describe")) {
    @compileError(@typeName(E) ++ " needs a `pub fn describe`");
}
```

`describeAll` calls `describe` on each item. Without the check, a type with no `describe` method gives the error `no field or member function named 'describe'`. That error points at the line in the loop. With the check, the message says what the type must have.

`@hasDecl` sees only `pub` declarations. Thus the message says `pub fn`, and a method without `pub` fails the check.

[Interfaces](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/interfaces/) shows other ways to give a generic function an interface.

## When to add a check

Do not check each generic function. The compiler finds each type error without your help. Add a check when one of these conditions is true:

- Other people call the function, for example in a library.
- The error without a check points deep inside your code.
- The rule is not visible in the code, for example "the items must be numbers".

## Check yourself

`sum("abc")` calls `sum` with a string literal. Does the build stop?

No. The type of `"abc"` is `*const [3:0]u8`, a pointer to an array. `Item` accepts a pointer to an array, and the items are `u8`, an integer. Thus `sum("abc")` returns 97 + 98 + 99. That sum is 294, and it does not fit in a `u8`. In a build with safety checks, the program stops with an integer overflow.

A check accepts what its rules accept. If the function must refuse strings, the rules must say so.

---

## Parse Strings at Compile Time

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/parse-strings/*

A string that the compiler knows is data that comptime code can read. A comptime function can split it, check it and change it into a type.

This chapter parses a web route such as `/users/:user/posts/:post`. A segment that starts with `:` is a parameter. The result of the parse is two things:

- A `Params` struct with one field for each parameter.
- A `match` function that reads a path and fills a `Params`.

All of the parse happens during compilation. At runtime, only the match remains.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn segmentCount(comptime pattern: []const u8) usize {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, pattern, '/');
    var n: usize = 0;
    while (it.next()) |_| n += 1;
    return n;
}

// "/users/:user" becomes .{ "users", ":user" }.
fn segments(comptime pattern: []const u8) [segmentCount(pattern)][]const u8 {
    var result: [segmentCount(pattern)][]const u8 = undefined;
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, pattern, '/');
    for (&result) |*segment| segment.* = it.next().?;
    return result;
}

fn paramCount(comptime pattern: []const u8) usize {
    var n: usize = 0;
    for (segments(pattern)) |segment| {
        if (segment[0] == ':') n += 1;
    }
    return n;
}

// The names after each ':', in order. A name that occurs two times
// stops the build.
fn paramNames(comptime pattern: []const u8) [paramCount(pattern)][]const u8 {
    var names: [paramCount(pattern)][]const u8 = undefined;
    var i: usize = 0;
    for (segments(pattern)) |segment| {
        if (segment[0] != ':') continue;
        const name = segment[1..];
        for (names[0..i]) |earlier| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, earlier, name)) {
                @compileError("route " ++ pattern ++ ": parameter '" ++ name ++ "' occurs two times");
            }
        }
        names[i] = name;
        i += 1;
    }
    return names;
}

fn Route(comptime pattern: []const u8) type {
    const parts = segments(pattern);
    const names = paramNames(pattern);
    return struct {
        // One `[]const u8` field for each parameter in the pattern.
        pub const Params = @Struct(.auto, null, &names, &@splat([]const u8), &@splat(.{}));

        pub fn match(path: []const u8) ?Params {
            var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, path, '/');
            var params: Params = undefined;
            // One copy of the body for each segment of the pattern.
            inline for (parts) |part| {
                const got = it.next() orelse return null;
                if (part[0] == ':') {
                    @field(params, part[1..]) = got;
                } else if (!std.mem.eql(u8, got, part)) {
                    return null;
                }
            }
            if (it.next() != null) return null;
            return params;
        }
    };
}

const UserPost = Route("/users/:user/posts/:post");
const Health = Route("/health");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const fields = @typeInfo(UserPost.Params).@"struct".field_names;
    try out.print("UserPost.Params has {d} fields:", .{fields.len});
    inline for (fields) |name| try out.print(" {s}", .{name});
    try out.print("\n", .{});

    const paths = [_][]const u8{
        "/users/42/posts/7",
        "/users/tejas/posts/hello-world",
        "/users/42/posts",
        "/users/42/comments/7",
        "/users/42/posts/7/edit",
    };
    for (paths) |path| {
        if (UserPost.match(path)) |p| {
            // `p.user` and `p.post` are real fields. A wrong field name is a
            // compile error. A map gives `null` at runtime for a wrong key.
            try out.print("{s}: user={s} post={s}\n", .{ path, p.user, p.post });
        } else {
            try out.print("{s}: no match\n", .{path});
        }
    }

    try out.print("/health: {s}\n", .{if (Health.match("/health") != null) "match" else "no match"});
    try out.print("Health.Params has {d} fields\n", .{@typeInfo(Health.Params).@"struct".field_names.len});
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.parse-strings`)*

## Split the pattern

```zig
fn segments(comptime pattern: []const u8) [segmentCount(pattern)][]const u8 {
    var result: [segmentCount(pattern)][]const u8 = undefined;
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, pattern, '/');
    for (&result) |*segment| segment.* = it.next().?;
    return result;
}
```

`std.mem.tokenizeScalar` is the same function that a program uses at runtime. Comptime code can call it because it does not allocate memory and does not do I/O.

Comptime code has no allocator, thus the function cannot return a list that grows. It returns an array, and the array needs a length in its type. `segmentCount` calculates that length: it runs the same tokenizer and counts the segments. The pattern is comptime-known, thus the count is comptime-known too.

`paramCount` and `paramNames` use the same method. They count the segments that start with `:`, then they copy the names.

## Make the type

```zig
pub const Params = @Struct(.auto, null, &names, &@splat([]const u8), &@splat(.{}));
```

Each parameter becomes a field of type `[]const u8`. `@splat` makes an array with the same value in each item, with the length that `@Struct` needs. [Make a Type](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/make-a-type/) explains the five arguments of `@Struct`.

The output shows the fields of the new type:

```
UserPost.Params has 2 fields: user post
```

A route with no parameters gets a struct with no fields:

```
Health.Params has 0 fields
```

## Match a path

```zig
pub fn match(path: []const u8) ?Params {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, path, '/');
    var params: Params = undefined;
    inline for (parts) |part| {
        const got = it.next() orelse return null;
        if (part[0] == ':') {
            @field(params, part[1..]) = got;
        } else if (!std.mem.eql(u8, got, part)) {
            return null;
        }
    }
    if (it.next() != null) return null;
    return params;
}
```

`path` is a runtime value. `parts` is comptime-known. The `inline for` makes one copy of the body for each segment of the pattern. In each copy, the test `part[0] == ':'` is comptime-known. Thus each copy contains only one of the two branches: a store into a field, or a compare with fixed text.

For `/users/:user/posts/:post`, the result is the same as this function written by hand:

1. Compare the first segment with `users`.
2. Store the second segment in `params.user`.
3. Compare the third segment with `posts`.
4. Store the fourth segment in `params.post`.
5. Return `null` if there is a fifth segment.

The output shows a path that matches, and three paths that do not:

```
/users/42/posts/7: user=42 post=7
/users/tejas/posts/hello-world: user=tejas post=hello-world
/users/42/posts: no match
/users/42/comments/7: no match
/users/42/posts/7/edit: no match
```

## Typed fields, not a map

Many web frameworks return route parameters in a map from string to string. With a map, a misspelled key such as `params.get("usr")` returns `null` at runtime.

Here, `p.user` is a struct field. If you write `p.usr`, the build stops, because `Params` has no field with that name. If the pattern changes, each use of an old parameter name stops the build.

## Reject a bad pattern

A pattern can use one name two times, for example `/users/:id/friends/:id`. Then one field would hide the other. `paramNames` compares each name with the earlier names and stops the build:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn segmentCount(comptime pattern: []const u8) usize {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, pattern, '/');
    var n: usize = 0;
    while (it.next()) |_| n += 1;
    return n;
}

// "/users/:user" becomes .{ "users", ":user" }.
fn segments(comptime pattern: []const u8) [segmentCount(pattern)][]const u8 {
    var result: [segmentCount(pattern)][]const u8 = undefined;
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, pattern, '/');
    for (&result) |*segment| segment.* = it.next().?;
    return result;
}

fn paramCount(comptime pattern: []const u8) usize {
    var n: usize = 0;
    for (segments(pattern)) |segment| {
        if (segment[0] == ':') n += 1;
    }
    return n;
}

// The names after each ':', in order. A name that occurs two times
// stops the build.
fn paramNames(comptime pattern: []const u8) [paramCount(pattern)][]const u8 {
    var names: [paramCount(pattern)][]const u8 = undefined;
    var i: usize = 0;
    for (segments(pattern)) |segment| {
        if (segment[0] != ':') continue;
        const name = segment[1..];
        for (names[0..i]) |earlier| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, earlier, name)) {
                @compileError("route " ++ pattern ++ ": parameter '" ++ name ++ "' occurs two times");
            }
        }
        names[i] = name;
        i += 1;
    }
    return names;
}

fn Route(comptime pattern: []const u8) type {
    const parts = segments(pattern);
    const names = paramNames(pattern);
    return struct {
        // One `[]const u8` field for each parameter in the pattern.
        pub const Params = @Struct(.auto, null, &names, &@splat([]const u8), &@splat(.{}));

        pub fn match(path: []const u8) ?Params {
            var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, path, '/');
            var params: Params = undefined;
            // One copy of the body for each segment of the pattern.
            inline for (parts) |part| {
                const got = it.next() orelse return null;
                if (part[0] == ':') {
                    @field(params, part[1..]) = got;
                } else if (!std.mem.eql(u8, got, part)) {
                    return null;
                }
            }
            if (it.next() != null) return null;
            return params;
        }
    };
}

const Friend = Route("/users/:id/friends/:id");

pub fn main() void {
    if (Friend.match("/users/1/friends/2")) |p| std.debug.print("{s}\n", .{p.id});
}
```

The compiler says:

```
error: route /users/:id/friends/:id: parameter 'id' occurs two times
```

*Compiled by CI, but not runnable in the browser sandbox. (`25-comptime.route-duplicate`)*

The error occurs when the compiler evaluates `Route(...)`, not when a request arrives. A bad route that the program uses stops the build, even if no test sends a path to that route.

The compiler evaluates only the code that the program uses. If no code refers to a `Route` constant, the compiler does not evaluate it, and a bad pattern in it gives no error.

## The same method in `std`

`std.Io.Writer.print` parses its format string during compilation. That is why `print("{d}", .{"text"})` is a compile error, not a runtime error. `std.StaticStringMap(V).initComptime` takes a list of key and value pairs and builds a lookup structure during compilation.
