[Know the Limits](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/limits/) uses it on a file that the compiler reads.

## Check yourself

`Route("/files/:name")` matches `/files/report.pdf`. Does it match `/files/2026/report.pdf`?

No. The pattern has two segments, and the path has three. The `inline for` handles the two segments of the pattern. Then `it.next()` finds a third segment, and `match` returns `null`.

## Know the Limits

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/limits/*

Comptime code is usual Zig, but it runs inside the compiler. The compiler has no program, no operating system and no heap for that code. Thus some functions that work at runtime do not work during compilation.

This chapter gives the limits, and the tool to use for each one.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// Comptime code cannot open a file. `@embedFile` is the exception: the
// compiler reads the file and the bytes become a string constant.
const colors_txt = @embedFile("colors.txt");

// `parseColors` calls this function in its return type, before the quota
// line in its own body runs. Thus this function sets its own quota.
fn lineCount(comptime text: []const u8) usize {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(100_000);
    var n: usize = 0;
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, text, '\n');
    while (it.next()) |_| n += 1;
    return n;
}

const Entry = struct { []const u8, u24 };

// Parse "name=rrggbb" lines into key and value pairs. There is no runtime
// allocator at comptime, thus the result is an array with a size that
// the compiler calculates.
fn parseColors(comptime text: []const u8) [lineCount(text)]Entry {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(100_000);
    var entries: [lineCount(text)]Entry = undefined;
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, text, '\n');
    for (&entries) |*entry| {
        const line = it.next().?;
        const eq = std.mem.findScalar(u8, line, '=') orelse
            @compileError("colors.txt: no '=' in line: " ++ line);
        const value = std.fmt.parseInt(u24, line[eq + 1 ..], 16) catch
            @compileError("colors.txt: bad hex in line: " ++ line);
        entry.* = .{ line[0..eq], value };
    }
    return entries;
}

const colors = std.StaticStringMap(u24).initComptime(parseColors(colors_txt));

// Strings join with `++` during compilation. The result has a length
// that the compiler knows.
const names = blk: {
    var joined: []const u8 = "";
    for (parseColors(colors_txt), 0..) |entry, i| {
        joined = joined ++ (if (i == 0) "" else ", ") ++ entry[0];
    }
    break :blk joined;
};

fn List(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct { items: []T };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    try out.print("1. colors.txt: {d} bytes, {d} colors\n", .{ colors_txt.len, colors.keys().len });
    for ([_][]const u8{ "saffron", "blue", "purple" }) |name| {
        if (colors.get(name)) |rgb| {
            try out.print("   {s} = #{x:0>6}\n", .{ name, rgb });
        } else {
            try out.print("   {s}: not in the file\n", .{name});
        }
    }

    try out.print("2. names: {s} ({d} bytes)\n", .{ names, names.len });

    // The compiler keeps one result for each set of comptime arguments.
    // The same arguments give the same type. New arguments give a new copy.
    try out.print("3. List(u8) == List(u8): {}\n", .{List(u8) == List(u8)});
    try out.print("   List(u8) == List(u16): {}\n", .{List(u8) == List(u16)});
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.limits`)*

## No runtime allocator

An `ArrayList` needs an allocator, and an allocator asks the operating system for memory. During compilation, there is no operating system to ask:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const count = blk: {
    var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    list.append(std.heap.page_allocator, 1) catch unreachable;
    break :blk list.items.len;
};

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{count});
}
```

The compiler says:

```
error: unable to resolve comptime value
note: called at comptime from here
```

*Compiled by CI, but not runnable in the browser sandbox. (`25-comptime.comptime-alloc`)*

The error points inside the standard library, at the place where the allocator asks for memory. The notes `called at comptime from here` lead back to the `append` call.

Use these tools instead:

- An array with a length that a comptime function calculates. [Parse Strings at Compile Time](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/parse-strings/) uses this method.
- A `comptime var` of type `[]const u8`, extended with `++`.

The program joins the color names with `++`:

```
2. names: red, green, blue, saffron (25 bytes)
```

Each `++` makes a new comptime string, with a length that the compiler knows.

## No I/O, except `@embedFile`

Comptime code cannot open a file, read the clock or call the network. A build that reads the clock would give a different binary each time.

`@embedFile("colors.txt")` is the exception. The compiler reads the file and makes its bytes a string constant. The path is relative to the source file. The compiler notes the file as an input, thus a change to the file starts a new build.

The program parses the file during compilation:

```zig
const colors = std.StaticStringMap(u24).initComptime(parseColors(colors_txt));
```

`parseColors` splits the lines and parses each hex value. A line without `=`, or with a bad hex value, stops the build with `@compileError`. `StaticStringMap.initComptime` then builds a lookup structure from the pairs.

```
1. colors.txt: 51 bytes, 4 colors
   saffron = #f4c430
   blue = #0000ff
   purple: not in the file
```

The binary contains the map, not the text parser. The page runs this program in your browser, and the browser has no `colors.txt`. The program does not need the file at runtime.

## The branch quota

`parseColors` and `lineCount` both start with `@setEvalBranchQuota(100_000)`. The default limit is 1000 backward branches, and a file of 20 lines already needs more.

`lineCount` needs its own quota. `parseColors` calls `lineCount` in its return type, and the compiler calculates the return type before the body of `parseColors` runs. Thus the quota line in that body does not cover `lineCount`.

The branch count is difficult to calculate here. The tokenizer, `parseInt` and `initComptime` all add branches. Thus measure: make the file larger until the build fails. On 2026-10-24, this program built with a file of 400 lines.

[Build Lookup Tables](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/lookup-tables/) shows the error when a loop is longer than the limit, and how to calculate the limit from the loops.

## One copy for each set of arguments

```
3. List(u8) == List(u8): true
   List(u8) == List(u16): false
```

The compiler keeps the result of each comptime call. A second call with the same arguments returns the same type, and the compiler does no work again. A call with new arguments makes a new type, with new copies of each function that the program uses.

Each copy adds machine code to the binary. Each comptime calculation adds time to each build. The two costs grow with the number of different arguments:

- `List(u8)`, `List(u16)` and `List(Point)` give three copies. The cost is small.
- A `comptime` parameter that gets a different value for each call site can give hundreds of copies. Change it to a runtime parameter.

## Comptime cannot see runtime values

A comptime calculation cannot read a value that exists only at runtime. [Know What the Compiler Knows](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/compiler-knows/) shows the error for a `var` that sets an array length. The fix is always one of two:

- Make the value comptime-known.
- Move the calculation to runtime.

## Check yourself

`colors.txt` gets a fifth line, `teal=008080`. Which steps run again?

The compiler sees that an input changed and builds again. `parseColors` runs again during that build, and `initComptime` builds a new map with five pairs. The program code does not change. At runtime, the program only reads the new map.

---

## Project: Units of Measure

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/units/*

A program that calculates with physical values must keep the units correct. A value in metres plus a value in seconds has no meaning, but two `f64` values add without a complaint.

This project puts the unit into the type. The compiler then checks each calculation, and a wrong unit stops the build. At runtime, each value is one `f64` and nothing more.

The project uses these chapters:

- [Know What the Compiler Knows](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/compiler-knows/), for a struct value as a `comptime` parameter.
- [Reject Bad Input with @compileError](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/compile-error/), for the message.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// The power of each base unit. Metres per second squared is
// .{ .m = 1, .s = -2 }.
const Dim = struct {
    m: i8 = 0,
    s: i8 = 0,
    kg: i8 = 0,

    fn mul(a: Dim, b: Dim) Dim {
        return .{ .m = a.m + b.m, .s = a.s + b.s, .kg = a.kg + b.kg };
    }

    fn div(a: Dim, b: Dim) Dim {
        return .{ .m = a.m - b.m, .s = a.s - b.s, .kg = a.kg - b.kg };
    }

    fn eql(a: Dim, b: Dim) bool {
        return a.m == b.m and a.s == b.s and a.kg == b.kg;
    }

    // "kg*m/s^2". The compiler makes this text one time for each Dim.
    fn name(comptime d: Dim) []const u8 {
        comptime var top: []const u8 = "";
        comptime var bottom: []const u8 = "";
        inline for (.{ "kg", "m", "s" }) |unit| {
            const p = @field(d, unit);
            const text = if (@abs(p) == 1) unit else std.fmt.comptimePrint("{s}^{d}", .{ unit, @abs(p) });
            if (p > 0) top = top ++ (if (top.len == 0) "" else "*") ++ text;
            if (p < 0) bottom = bottom ++ (if (bottom.len == 0) "" else "*") ++ text;
        }
        if (top.len == 0) top = "1";
        return if (bottom.len == 0) top else top ++ "/" ++ bottom;
    }
};

fn Quantity(comptime dim: Dim) type {
    return struct {
        value: f64,

        const Self = @This();
        pub const unit = dim.name();

        pub fn add(a: Self, b: anytype) Self {
            const other = @TypeOf(b).dim_value;
            if (comptime !dim.eql(other)) {
                @compileError("cannot add " ++ Dim.name(other) ++ " to " ++ unit);
            }
            return .{ .value = a.value + b.value };
        }

        pub fn mul(a: Self, b: anytype) Quantity(dim.mul(@TypeOf(b).dim_value)) {
            return .{ .value = a.value * b.value };
        }

        pub fn div(a: Self, b: anytype) Quantity(dim.div(@TypeOf(b).dim_value)) {
            return .{ .value = a.value / b.value };
        }

        pub const dim_value = dim;
    };
}

const Metres = Quantity(.{ .m = 1 });
const Seconds = Quantity(.{ .s = 1 });
const Kilograms = Quantity(.{ .kg = 1 });

fn show(out: *std.Io.Writer, label: []const u8, q: anytype) !void {
    try out.print("{s} = {d} {s}\n", .{ label, q.value, @TypeOf(q).unit });
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const distance: Metres = .{ .value = 100 };
    const time: Seconds = .{ .value = 9.58 };
    const mass: Kilograms = .{ .value = 94 };

    const speed = distance.div(time);
    const accel = speed.div(time);
    const force = mass.mul(accel);
    const area = distance.mul(distance);

    try show(out, "distance", distance);
    try show(out, "speed", speed);
    try show(out, "acceleration", accel);
    try show(out, "force", force);
    try show(out, "area", area);
    try show(out, "distance + distance", distance.add(distance));
    try show(out, "area / distance", area.div(distance));

    // The same units give the same type, whatever path made them.
    try out.print("area / distance is Metres: {}\n", .{@TypeOf(area.div(distance)) == Metres});
    try out.print("size of a Quantity: {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(@TypeOf(force))});
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.units`)*

## A unit is a list of powers

```zig
const Dim = struct {
    m: i8 = 0,
    s: i8 = 0,
    kg: i8 = 0,
};
```

Each physical unit in this program is a product of three base units. `Dim` keeps the power of each one:

- Metres is `.{ .m = 1 }`.
- Metres per second is `.{ .m = 1, .s = -1 }`.
- Newtons, the unit of force, is `.{ .kg = 1, .m = 1, .s = -2 }`.

To multiply two units, add their powers. To divide, subtract the powers. `Dim.mul` and `Dim.div` do this. They are usual functions, and the compiler runs them.

## A type for each unit

```zig
fn Quantity(comptime dim: Dim) type {
    return struct {
        value: f64,
        ...
    };
}

const Metres = Quantity(.{ .m = 1 });
const Seconds = Quantity(.{ .s = 1 });
```

A `comptime` parameter can be a struct value, not only a type. Each different `Dim` makes a different type. Each type has one field, thus the size of a `Quantity` is the size of an `f64`:

```
size of a Quantity: 8 bytes
```

## Multiply and divide

```zig
pub fn div(a: Self, b: anytype) Quantity(dim.div(@TypeOf(b).dim_value)) {
    return .{ .value = a.value / b.value };
}
```

The return type is a calculation. The compiler reads the `Dim` of `b`, subtracts it from the `Dim` of `a`, and calls `Quantity` with the result. The body only divides two numbers.

The program calculates the values for a 100 m sprint in 9.58 s, by a runner of 94 kg:

```
distance = 100 m
speed = 10.438413361169102 m/s
acceleration = 1.0896047349863363 m/s^2
force = 102.4228450887156 kg*m/s^2
area = 10000 m^2
```

Each unit name in the output comes from the type. `Dim.name` builds the text during compilation, with `++` and `comptimePrint`. Each `Quantity` type keeps its name in the constant `unit`.

## The same unit is the same type

```
area / distance = 100 m
area / distance is Metres: true
```

`area.div(distance)` calculates `.{ .m = 2 }` minus `.{ .m = 1 }`, and the result is `.{ .m = 1 }`. The compiler keeps one type for each set of comptime arguments. Thus `Quantity(.{ .m = 1 })` from this calculation is the same type as `Metres`. A function that takes `Metres` accepts the result.

## Add two values

```zig
pub fn add(a: Self, b: anytype) Self {
    const other = @TypeOf(b).dim_value;
    if (comptime !dim.eql(other)) {
        @compileError("cannot add " ++ Dim.name(other) ++ " to " ++ unit);
    }
    return .{ .value = a.value + b.value };
}
```

Addition needs the same unit on both sides. The check is comptime, thus it costs nothing at runtime. Add seconds to metres:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// The power of each base unit. Metres per second squared is
// .{ .m = 1, .s = -2 }.
const Dim = struct {
    m: i8 = 0,
    s: i8 = 0,
    kg: i8 = 0,

    fn mul(a: Dim, b: Dim) Dim {
        return .{ .m = a.m + b.m, .s = a.s + b.s, .kg = a.kg + b.kg };
    }

    fn div(a: Dim, b: Dim) Dim {
        return .{ .m = a.m - b.m, .s = a.s - b.s, .kg = a.kg - b.kg };
    }

    fn eql(a: Dim, b: Dim) bool {
        return a.m == b.m and a.s == b.s and a.kg == b.kg;
    }

    // "kg*m/s^2". The compiler makes this text one time for each Dim.
    fn name(comptime d: Dim) []const u8 {
        comptime var top: []const u8 = "";
        comptime var bottom: []const u8 = "";
        inline for (.{ "kg", "m", "s" }) |unit| {
            const p = @field(d, unit);
            const text = if (@abs(p) == 1) unit else std.fmt.comptimePrint("{s}^{d}", .{ unit, @abs(p) });
            if (p > 0) top = top ++ (if (top.len == 0) "" else "*") ++ text;
            if (p < 0) bottom = bottom ++ (if (bottom.len == 0) "" else "*") ++ text;
        }
        if (top.len == 0) top = "1";
        return if (bottom.len == 0) top else top ++ "/" ++ bottom;
    }
};

fn Quantity(comptime dim: Dim) type {
    return struct {
        value: f64,

        const Self = @This();
        pub const unit = dim.name();

        pub fn add(a: Self, b: anytype) Self {
            const other = @TypeOf(b).dim_value;
            if (comptime !dim.eql(other)) {
                @compileError("cannot add " ++ Dim.name(other) ++ " to " ++ unit);
            }
            return .{ .value = a.value + b.value };
        }

        pub fn mul(a: Self, b: anytype) Quantity(dim.mul(@TypeOf(b).dim_value)) {
            return .{ .value = a.value * b.value };
        }

        pub fn div(a: Self, b: anytype) Quantity(dim.div(@TypeOf(b).dim_value)) {
            return .{ .value = a.value / b.value };
        }

        pub const dim_value = dim;
    };
}

const Metres = Quantity(.{ .m = 1 });
const Seconds = Quantity(.{ .s = 1 });
const Kilograms = Quantity(.{ .kg = 1 });

pub fn main() void {
    const distance: Metres = .{ .value = 100 };
    const time: Seconds = .{ .value = 9.58 };
    const wrong = distance.add(time);
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{wrong.value});
}
```

The compiler says:

```
error: cannot add s to m
```

*Compiled by CI, but not runnable in the browser sandbox. (`25-comptime.units-mismatch`)*

The message uses the unit names, not the type names. The `referenced by` list under the message names the line in `main` that called `add`.

## Limits of this design

- The program has three base units. To add a base unit such as amperes, add a field to `Dim`, and add it in `mul`, `div`, `eql` and `name`.
- A value in kilometres has the same `Dim` as a value in metres. This design checks the dimension, not the scale. A scale needs a second comptime value, for example a factor of 1000.
- `add` accepts any type with a `dim_value` declaration. A type from another library with the same declaration name also passes the check.

## Check yourself

What is the unit of `speed.mul(time)`, and which type is it?

`speed` is `.{ .m = 1, .s = -1 }` and `time` is `.{ .s = 1 }`. The product adds the powers: `.{ .m = 1, .s = 0 }`. That `Dim` is equal to `.{ .m = 1 }`, thus the result is the `Metres` type, and its name is `m`.

---

## Project: Parse Arguments from a Struct

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/args/*

A command-line program declares its options in one place and parses them in another. When you add an option, you must change both places, and the help text too. If you forget one, the three disagree.

In this project, a struct is the only declaration. The compiler reads the fields of the struct and makes the parser and the help text from them. A new field is a new option, with no other change.

The project uses [Read a Type](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/read-a-type/) for the fields and their defaults. [Command-Line Arguments](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/command-line/) shows how a real program gets its arguments. This page uses a fixed list of strings, so that the program can run in your browser.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Level = enum { debug, info, warn };

// Each field is one option. A field with a default is optional.
const Options = struct {
    port: u16 = 8080,
    host: []const u8 = "localhost",
    verbose: bool = false,
    level: Level = .info,
    name: []const u8,
};

const ParseError = error{ UnknownOption, MissingValue, BadValue, MissingOption };

fn parseValue(comptime T: type, text: []const u8) ParseError!T {
    return switch (@typeInfo(T)) {
        .int => std.fmt.parseInt(T, text, 10) catch error.BadValue,
        .@"enum" => std.meta.stringToEnum(T, text) orelse error.BadValue,
        .pointer => if (T == []const u8) text else @compileError("unsupported option type " ++ @typeName(T)),
        else => @compileError("unsupported option type " ++ @typeName(T)),
    };
}

fn parse(comptime T: type, args: []const []const u8) ParseError!T {
    const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
    var result: T = undefined;
    // One flag for each field: did an argument set it?
    var seen: [info.field_names.len]bool = @splat(false);

    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < args.len) : (i += 1) {
        const arg = args[i];
        if (!std.mem.startsWith(u8, arg, "--")) return error.UnknownOption;
        const key = arg[2..];
        var known = false;
        // The compiler unrolls this loop: one `if` for each field.
        inline for (info.field_names, info.field_types, 0..) |name, F, f| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, key, name)) {
                known = true;
                seen[f] = true;
                if (F == bool) {
                    @field(result, name) = true;
                } else {
                    i += 1;
                    if (i == args.len) return error.MissingValue;
                    @field(result, name) = try parseValue(F, args[i]);
                }
            }
        }
        if (!known) return error.UnknownOption;
    }

    // A field that no argument set gets its default, or is an error.
    inline for (info.field_names, info.field_types, info.field_attrs, 0..) |name, F, attrs, f| {
        if (!seen[f]) {
            @field(result, name) = attrs.defaultValue(F) orelse return error.MissingOption;
        }
    }
    return result;
}

// The help text, made during compilation from the same struct.
fn help(comptime T: type) []const u8 {
    comptime var text: []const u8 = "options:\n";
    const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
    inline for (info.field_names, info.field_types, info.field_attrs) |name, F, attrs| {
        const kind = switch (@typeInfo(F)) {
            .bool => "",
            .@"enum" => |e| blk: {
                var choices: []const u8 = "";
                for (e.field_names, 0..) |choice, c| choices = choices ++ (if (c == 0) "" else "|") ++ choice;
                break :blk " <" ++ choices ++ ">";
            },
            else => if (F == []const u8) " <text>" else " <" ++ @typeName(F) ++ ">",
        };
        const required = if (attrs.defaultValue(F) == null) " (required)" else "";
        text = text ++ "  --" ++ name ++ kind ++ required ++ "\n";
    }
    return text;
}

fn show(out: *std.Io.Writer, args: []const []const u8) !void {
    try out.print("args:", .{});
    for (args) |arg| try out.print(" {s}", .{arg});
    try out.print("\n", .{});
    if (parse(Options, args)) |o| {
        try out.print("  port={d} host={s} verbose={} level={t} name={s}\n", .{ o.port, o.host, o.verbose, o.level, o.name });
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("  error: {t}\n", .{err});
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    try out.print("{s}", .{comptime help(Options)});
    try show(out, &.{ "--name", "api" });
    try show(out, &.{ "--name", "api", "--port", "9090", "--verbose", "--level", "debug" });
    try show(out, &.{"--port"});
    try show(out, &.{ "--port", "99999", "--name", "x" });
    try show(out, &.{ "--level", "loud", "--name", "x" });
    try show(out, &.{ "--colour", "red" });
    try show(out, &.{"--verbose"});
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.args`)*

## The options are a struct

```zig
const Options = struct {
    port: u16 = 8080,
    host: []const u8 = "localhost",
    verbose: bool = false,
    level: Level = .info,
    name: []const u8,
};
```

The parser uses these rules:

- The name of a field is the name of an option: `port` is `--port`.
- A `bool` field is a flag. `--verbose` sets it to `true`, and it takes no value.
- Each other field takes the next argument as its value.
- A field with a default is optional. A field without a default must get a value from an argument.

## The help text

```
options:
  --port <u16>
  --host <text>
  --verbose
  --level <debug|info|warn>
  --name <text> (required)
```

`help` walks the fields during compilation and joins the lines with `++`. For an enum field, it lists the tag names from `@typeInfo`. The `main` function prints the text with `comptime help(Options)`, thus the binary contains the finished text.

## Match an argument to a field

```zig
inline for (info.field_names, info.field_types, 0..) |name, F, f| {
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, key, name)) {
        known = true;
        seen[f] = true;
        if (F == bool) {
            @field(result, name) = true;
        } else {
            i += 1;
            if (i == args.len) return error.MissingValue;
            @field(result, name) = try parseValue(F, args[i]);
        }
    }
}
```

`key` is a runtime string. The `inline for` makes one `if` for each field, and each `if` compares `key` with one comptime-known name. In each copy, `F` is a known type. Thus the `F == bool` test disappears, and each copy contains only one of the two branches.

`parseValue` has one branch for each kind of type: an integer, an enum or a string. A field of another type, for example an `f32`, stops the build with `unsupported option type f32`.

## Defaults and required options

```zig
inline for (info.field_names, info.field_types, info.field_attrs, 0..) |name, F, attrs, f| {
    if (!seen[f]) {
        @field(result, name) = attrs.defaultValue(F) orelse return error.MissingOption;
    }
}
```

`seen` has one `bool` for each field. After the arguments, each field that no argument set gets its default value. A field with no default gives `error.MissingOption`.

## The results

```
args: --name api
  port=8080 host=localhost verbose=false level=info name=api
args: --name api --port 9090 --verbose --level debug
  port=9090 host=localhost verbose=true level=debug name=api
args: --port
  error: MissingValue
args: --port 99999 --name x
  error: BadValue
args: --level loud --name x
  error: BadValue
args: --colour red
  error: UnknownOption
args: --verbose
  error: MissingOption
```

`99999` does not fit in a `u16`, thus `parseInt` fails, and the parser returns `error.BadValue`. `loud` is not a tag of `Level`. The last list does not set `--name`, and `name` has no default.

## Limits of this parser

- An option can occur two times. The second value replaces the first.
- There are no short names such as `-v`. A short name needs a second name for a field. One method is a declaration in the struct, for example `pub const short = .{ .verbose = 'v' };`, which `@hasDecl` can find.
- The errors do not say which option failed. A real parser returns a diagnostic with the argument, as well as the error.

## Check yourself

Add the field `threads: u8 = 4` to `Options`. Which parts of the program must change?

None. The help text gets the line `--threads <u8>`, and the parser accepts `--threads 8`. If no argument sets it, `threads` gets its default, 4. `parseValue` already handles each integer type.

## Project: A Typed Event Bus

*Comptime. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/event-bus/*

An event bus delivers each event to the functions that want it. In many languages, a handler registers with a string name, and the bus calls it at runtime with an untyped value. A misspelled name or a wrong type shows only when the event arrives.

In this project, a handler is a plain function, and its parameter type says which event it wants. The bus reads the parameter types during compilation. Thus a handler for an event that does not exist stops the build.

The project uses three earlier chapters:

- [Read a Type](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/read-a-type/), to read the parameter types of a function.
- [Dispatch with Comptime](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/dispatch/), for `inline else`.
- [Reject Bad Input with @compileError](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/metaprogramming/compile-error/), for the message.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const Writer = std.Io.Writer;

const Click = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };
const Key = struct { code: u8 };
const Resize = struct { width: u32, height: u32 };

const Event = union(enum) {
    click: Click,
    key: Key,
    resize: Resize,
};

// The payload type that a handler accepts: its second parameter.
fn Payload(comptime handler: anytype) type {
    const info = @typeInfo(@TypeOf(handler)).@"fn";
    if (info.param_types.len != 2) @compileError("a handler takes (*Writer, payload)");
    return info.param_types[1].?;
}

fn Bus(comptime E: type, comptime handlers: anytype) type {
    const variants = @typeInfo(E).@"union";
    // Each handler must accept the payload of one variant. A check here
    // gives one clear message, before any event exists.
    for (handlers, 0..) |handler, i| {
        const P = Payload(handler);
        for (variants.field_types) |V| {
            if (V == P) break;
        } else @compileError(std.fmt.comptimePrint(
            "handler {d} takes {s}, which is not a payload of {s}",
            .{ i, @typeName(P), @typeName(E) },
        ));
    }

    return struct {
        // The number of handlers for each variant, counted by the compiler.
        pub fn count(comptime tag: std.meta.Tag(E)) usize {
            var n: usize = 0;
            for (handlers) |handler| {
                if (Payload(handler) == @FieldType(E, @tagName(tag))) n += 1;
            }
            return n;
        }

        // One branch for each variant. Each branch calls only the handlers
        // for that variant, directly, in the order of the list.
        pub fn emit(out: *Writer, event: E) !void {
            switch (event) {
                inline else => |payload| {
                    inline for (handlers) |handler| {
                        if (comptime Payload(handler) == @TypeOf(payload)) {
                            try handler(out, payload);
                        }
                    }
                },
            }
        }
    };
}

var keys_pressed: usize = 0;

fn logClick(out: *Writer, c: Click) !void {
    try out.print("  logClick: ({d}, {d})\n", .{ c.x, c.y });
}

fn countKey(out: *Writer, k: Key) !void {
    keys_pressed += 1;
    try out.print("  countKey: code {d}, {d} so far\n", .{ k.code, keys_pressed });
}

fn quitOnEscape(out: *Writer, k: Key) !void {
    if (k.code == 27) try out.print("  quitOnEscape: escape, quit\n", .{});
}

const UiBus = Bus(Event, .{ logClick, countKey, quitOnEscape });

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    inline for (.{ .click, .key, .resize }) |tag| {
        try out.print("handlers for .{s}: {d}\n", .{ @tagName(tag), comptime UiBus.count(tag) });
    }

    const events = [_]Event{
        .{ .click = .{ .x = 10, .y = 20 } },
        .{ .key = .{ .code = 65 } },
        .{ .resize = .{ .width = 800, .height = 600 } },
        .{ .key = .{ .code = 27 } },
    };
    for (events) |event| {
        try out.print("emit .{t}\n", .{event});
        try UiBus.emit(out, event);
    }
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`25-comptime.event-bus`)*

## Events and handlers

```zig
const Event = union(enum) {
    click: Click,
    key: Key,
    resize: Resize,
};

fn logClick(out: *Writer, c: Click) !void { ... }
fn countKey(out: *Writer, k: Key) !void { ... }
fn quitOnEscape(out: *Writer, k: Key) !void { ... }

const UiBus = Bus(Event, .{ logClick, countKey, quitOnEscape });
```

Each variant of `Event` has its own payload type. Each handler takes a writer and one payload type. The list of handlers is a tuple of functions, and it is a `comptime` argument to `Bus`.

## Read the payload type of a handler

```zig
fn Payload(comptime handler: anytype) type {
    const info = @typeInfo(@TypeOf(handler)).@"fn";
    if (info.param_types.len != 2) @compileError("a handler takes (*Writer, payload)");
    return info.param_types[1].?;
}
```

The type of a function is a usual type, and `@typeInfo` describes it. `param_types` is a list of the parameter types. Each item is optional, because a parameter of a generic function has no fixed type. Here, the `.?` stops the build if the second parameter is `anytype`.

## Check each handler

```zig
for (handlers, 0..) |handler, i| {
    const P = Payload(handler);
    for (variants.field_types) |V| {
        if (V == P) break;
    } else @compileError(std.fmt.comptimePrint(
        "handler {d} takes {s}, which is not a payload of {s}",
        .{ i, @typeName(P), @typeName(E) },
    ));
}
```

The check runs when the compiler evaluates `Bus(...)`. The `else` of a `for` runs when the loop ends without a `break`. Thus the error occurs only when no variant has the payload type of the handler.

Give the bus a handler for a `Scroll` event, which `Event` does not have:

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const Writer = std.Io.Writer;

const Click = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };
const Key = struct { code: u8 };
const Resize = struct { width: u32, height: u32 };

const Event = union(enum) {
    click: Click,
    key: Key,
    resize: Resize,
};

// The payload type that a handler accepts: its second parameter.
fn Payload(comptime handler: anytype) type {
    const info = @typeInfo(@TypeOf(handler)).@"fn";
    if (info.param_types.len != 2) @compileError("a handler takes (*Writer, payload)");
    return info.param_types[1].?;
}

fn Bus(comptime E: type, comptime handlers: anytype) type {
    const variants = @typeInfo(E).@"union";
    // Each handler must accept the payload of one variant. A check here
    // gives one clear message, before any event exists.
    for (handlers, 0..) |handler, i| {
        const P = Payload(handler);
        for (variants.field_types) |V| {
            if (V == P) break;
        } else @compileError(std.fmt.comptimePrint(
            "handler {d} takes {s}, which is not a payload of {s}",
            .{ i, @typeName(P), @typeName(E) },
        ));
    }

    return struct {
        // The number of handlers for each variant, counted by the compiler.
        pub fn count(comptime tag: std.meta.Tag(E)) usize {
            var n: usize = 0;
            for (handlers) |handler| {
                if (Payload(handler) == @FieldType(E, @tagName(tag))) n += 1;
            }
            return n;
        }

        // One branch for each variant. Each branch calls only the handlers
        // for that variant, directly, in the order of the list.
        pub fn emit(out: *Writer, event: E) !void {
            switch (event) {
                inline else => |payload| {
                    inline for (handlers) |handler| {
                        if (comptime Payload(handler) == @TypeOf(payload)) {
                            try handler(out, payload);
                        }
                    }
                },
            }
        }
    };
}

const Scroll = struct { dy: i32 };

fn logClick(out: *Writer, c: Click) !void {
    try out.print("click ({d}, {d})\n", .{ c.x, c.y });
}

fn logScroll(out: *Writer, s: Scroll) !void {
    try out.print("scroll {d}\n", .{s.dy});
}

const UiBus = Bus(Event, .{ logClick, logScroll });

pub fn main() void {
    std.debug.print("{d}\n", .{UiBus.count(.click)});
}
```

The compiler says:

```
error: handler 1 takes event-bus-wrong.Scroll, which is not a payload of event-bus-wrong.Event
note: called at comptime here
```

*Compiled by CI, but not runnable in the browser sandbox. (`25-comptime.event-bus-wrong`)*

`handler 1` is the second item of the tuple, because the count starts at 0. The note `called at comptime here` points at the line that makes the bus.

## Deliver an event

```zig
pub fn emit(out: *Writer, event: E) !void {
    switch (event) {
        inline else => |payload| {
            inline for (handlers) |handler| {
                if (comptime Payload(handler) == @TypeOf(payload)) {
                    try handler(out, payload);
                }
            }
        },
    }
}
```

`inline else` makes one branch for each variant. In each branch, the `inline for` checks each handler, and the `if` is comptime-known. Thus each branch contains only the calls for its variant. The branch for `.key` contains two direct calls, in the order of the list. The branch for `.resize` contains no calls:

```
emit .key
  countKey: code 65, 1 so far
emit .resize
emit .key
  countKey: code 27, 2 so far
  quitOnEscape: escape, quit
```

At runtime, `emit` is one `switch` and some direct calls. There is no list of function pointers and no lookup by name.

## Count the handlers

```
handlers for .click: 1
handlers for .key: 2
handlers for .resize: 0
```

`count` runs during compilation. A program can use it in a test, for example to require at least one handler for each event. Then a new variant in `Event` without a handler stops the test.

## Limits of this design

- The program cannot change the list of handlers after it compiles. A plugin that registers a handler at runtime needs a list of function pointers.
- Two variants with the same payload type, for example `key_down: Key` and `key_up: Key`, cannot have different handlers. `Payload` connects a handler to a type, not to a variant. To separate them, give each variant its own payload type.
- Handlers share the writer and nothing else. A handler that needs state, such as `countKey`, uses a global variable here. A real bus passes a context pointer.

## Check yourself

Add the variant `scroll: Scroll` to `Event`, and do not add a handler. Does the program still compile?

Yes. The check requires each handler to match a variant. It does not require each variant to have a handler. `emit` makes a branch for `.scroll` with no calls, and `count(.scroll)` returns 0.

---

## The Io Interface

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/io-interface/*

Modern Zig has one idea in all of its standard library. Each operation that can block takes an `std.Io` parameter. Examples are a file read, a socket open, a sleep, and a clock read.

Nothing blocks secretly, as nothing allocates secretly. If the signature of a function has no `Io`, the function cannot do I/O.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// A function that takes an `Io` tells you in its signature that it can block.
// For example, it can read a clock, use a file, or wait on the network. The
// function does not decide *how* the blocking operation runs. The `Io` that
// the function receives decides.
fn elapsedNanos(io: std.Io) i96 {
    const start = std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now(io, .awake);
    var acc: u64 = 0;
    for (0..10_000) |i| acc +%= i;
    std.mem.doNotOptimizeAway(acc);
    const end = std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now(io, .awake);
    return start.durationTo(end).raw.toNanoseconds();
}

test "get an Io and pass it down" {
    // In a test, the instance is `std.testing.io`. In a program, it is
    // `init.io`, the field on the `std.process.Init` that `main` receives.
    // `std.Io.Threaded`, a real thread pool, is behind the two instances.
    const io = std.testing.io;
    try expect(elapsedNanos(io) >= 0);
}

fn double(out: *u32, value: u32) void {
    out.* = value * 2;
}

test "the same Io is what makes concurrency work" {
    // Each blocking operation goes through the interface. Thus the interface
    // can also *schedule* the operation. `io.async` starts a task, and the
    // Threaded io runs the task on a different thread. With an event-loop io,
    // the identical call suspends a coroutine. The caller does not change.
    const io = std.testing.io;

    var a: u32 = 0;
    var b: u32 = 0;
    var first = io.async(double, .{ &a, 10 });
    var second = io.async(double, .{ &b, 20 });
    first.await(io);
    second.await(io);

    try expect(a == 20 and b == 40);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.io-interface`)*

## What `Io` is

`std.Io` is an interface: a pointer and a vtable. This is exactly the shape of `std.mem.Allocator`. The vtable holds function pointers for the primitive operations: read, write, wait and schedule. A concrete implementation supplies these pointers.

The standard implementation is `std.Io.Threaded`, and a real thread pool is behind it. [Choose an Io](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/choosing-an-io/) tells you about the other implementations, and when to change to one of them.

The allocator uses the same dependency-injection pattern for memory, and `Io` uses it for blocking. For this reason, this chapter is next to [Allocators](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/allocators/). When you know the two interfaces, you know the pattern of most of the standard library.

## The source of an `Io`

You almost never make an `Io` yourself. The `Io` arrives at the top of your program, and you pass it down to the functions that need it:

| Context | The `Io` that you use |
| --- | --- |
| `main` | `init.io`, a field on the `std.process.Init` that `main` receives |
| A test | `std.testing.io` |
| A library function | the `Io` that the caller gives you: take `io: std.Io` |

A function that must block does not use a global value. It accepts an `Io`, and it gives the `Io` to the calls that block. For this reason, `std.Io.Dir.readFile`,
`std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now` and `Io.Mutex.lock` all take an `Io` as their first argument.

## The reason for one interface

Each I/O call now has this parameter. The parameter gives two benefits.

**The signature shows what the function does.** A function that takes an `Io` can block. A function that does not take an `Io` cannot block. The type of a function shows its effects, and you do not have to read its documentation. The allocator parameter gives you the same guarantee for memory.

**The caller selects the execution model.** Each blocking operation goes *through* the interface, thus the interface can also schedule it. `io.async` starts a task. On `Io.Threaded`, the task runs on a different thread. If you give the same code an event-loop `Io`, the identical call suspends a coroutine. The called function never changes.

This is the answer of Zig to the "function coloring" problem. No separate `async` version of `readFile` exists. There is one function, and it does what the given `Io` does.

The [Concurrency](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/) chapter adds `async` and `Group` to this idea. [Cancellation](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/) shows how to stop a task that runs. [Readers and
Writers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/readers-and-writers/),
[Filesystem](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/filesystem/) and
[Time](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/time/) each show one part of the same interface.

## If you used an older version of Zig

This change came in Zig 0.15, and more work on it came later. Older code wrote `std.fs.cwd().openFile(...)` or `std.time.timestamp()` with no `Io`. Now the same code goes through `std.Io.Dir` and `std.Io.Clock`.

The global I/O functions without an `Io` parameter are gone. The [migration
page](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/coming-from-older-zig/) gives a list of the specific renames.

---

## Allocators

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/allocators/*

Zig has no global allocator and no garbage collector. All code that needs heap memory takes an `std.mem.Allocator` parameter. Thus the signature of a function always shows if the function allocates.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "allocate a slice" {
    const allocator = std.testing.allocator;

    const numbers = try allocator.alloc(u32, 10);
    defer allocator.free(numbers);

    for (numbers, 0..) |*n, i| n.* = @intCast(i * i);
    try expect(numbers[9] == 81);
}

test "arena frees everything at once" {
    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.testing.allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    const allocator = arena.allocator();

    // It is not necessary to free each value. `deinit` frees all of them.
    for (0..100) |_| _ = try allocator.alloc(u8, 64);
}

test "fixed buffer needs no heap at all" {
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&buf);
    const allocator = fba.allocator();

    const slice = try allocator.alloc(u8, 100);
    try expect(slice.len == 100);
    try expect(allocator.alloc(u8, 1000) == error.OutOfMemory);
}

test "create and destroy a single value" {
    const allocator = std.testing.allocator;

    // Use alloc/free for slices. Use create/destroy for one value.
    const node = try allocator.create(Node);
    defer allocator.destroy(node);

    node.* = .{ .value = 42, .next = null };
    try expect(node.value == 42);
}

const Node = struct {
    value: u32,
    next: ?*Node,
};

test "dupe copies a slice into owned memory" {
    const allocator = std.testing.allocator;

    // A common use: keep a copy of a string when the original can disappear.
    const owned = try allocator.dupe(u8, "borrowed");
    defer allocator.free(owned);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, owned, "borrowed"));
}

test "resize in place, or realloc to move" {
    const allocator = std.testing.allocator;

    var slice = try allocator.alloc(u8, 4);
    // realloc keeps the contents. It can return a new pointer.
    slice = try allocator.realloc(slice, 8);
    defer allocator.free(slice);
    try expect(slice.len == 8);
}

test "SafeAllocator catches leaks in a real program" {
    // In a program, you own the allocator. std.testing.allocator wraps this
    // allocator for you. The name changed two times: GeneralPurposeAllocator,
    // then DebugAllocator, and now SafeAllocator. The function `init` takes
    // the allocator that supplies the pages. `deinit` returns the number of
    // allocations that the program did not free.
    var safe: std.heap.SafeAllocator = .init(std.heap.page_allocator, .{});
    defer std.debug.assert(safe.deinit() == 0);
    const allocator = safe.allocator();

    const data = try allocator.alloc(u8, 16);
    allocator.free(data); // without this line, deinit returns 1
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.allocators`)*

## Select an allocator

The `Allocator` interface is one type, but you select the strategy behind the interface:

| Allocator | Frees memory | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ArenaAllocator` | at `deinit()`, all at the same time | Request handlers, compilers, all work that occurs in phases |
| `FixedBufferAllocator` | never (bump pointer) | Embedded code, hot loops, code that has no heap |
| `SafeAllocator` | at each `free`, with leak detection | Development builds |
| `std.testing.allocator` | at each `free`, and the test fails on a leak | Tests |

The arena is correct for more programs than most people expect. Some programs do one unit of work and then discard all of the memory. For such a program, an arena changes hundreds of `free` calls into one `deinit`. An arena also removes a full category of leak.

## `defer` makes this easy to manage

```zig
const numbers = try allocator.alloc(u32, 10);
defer allocator.free(numbers);
```

`defer` runs when the scope ends. It runs on all paths, and an early `return` and an error return are two of these paths. In Zig code, the `free` is on the line directly *after* the `alloc`. Thus you see the two calls together.

The test above uses `std.testing.allocator`. If a test leaks memory, the test fails. Tests check for leaks by default. You do not have to remember to run a separate tool.

## The usual operations

| Call | Gives you | Use with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `alloc(T, n)` | a `[]T` of `n` items | `free` |
| `create(T)` | a `*T`, one value | `destroy` |
| `dupe(T, slice)` | an owned copy of `slice` | `free` |
| `realloc(slice, n)` | the slice with a new size, contents kept | `free` |

Each pair has a different use:

- Use `create` and `destroy` for one value. Examples are a node in a linked list, and a struct that must live longer than its stack frame.
- Use `alloc` and `free` for slices.
- Use `dupe` to keep a string when the original string will soon disappear. This is the fix for the dangling key that the Hash Maps chapter tells you about.

`realloc` can return a new pointer. Thus always assign the result again: `slice = try allocator.realloc(slice, n)`.

## `SafeAllocator` has two older names

The name of the allocator that checks for leaks changed two times. An older tutorial can use `std.heap.GeneralPurposeAllocator`. That name changed to `std.heap.DebugAllocator`, and on current master the name is `std.heap.SafeAllocator`. The two older names still resolve.

The second change also changed the shape of the type, not only its name:

```zig
// DebugAllocator: comptime config, backing allocator implied,
// deinit() returns .ok or .leak
var debug: std.heap.DebugAllocator(.{}) = .init;
defer std.debug.assert(debug.deinit() == .ok);
const allocator = debug.allocator();
```

```zig
// SafeAllocator: a plain struct, backing allocator passed in,
// deinit() returns how many allocations leaked
var safe: std.heap.SafeAllocator = .init(std.heap.page_allocator, .{});
defer std.debug.assert(safe.deinit() == 0);
const allocator = safe.allocator();
```

The new name says "safe" and not "debug", because the checks are also useful outside a development build. The allocator panics in these conditions:

- a double free
- a free through the wrong allocator
- most writes after a free

The cost is code size. On this site, five programs about data structures changed to `SafeAllocator`, and each `.wasm` became about 14 KB larger. If you do not want this bookkeeping, use `std.heap.smp_allocator` or an arena.

---

## ArrayList

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/arraylist/*

`std.ArrayList` is the array in Zig that can grow. On master, an `ArrayList` holds no allocator. Create the list with `.empty`. Then give the allocator to each method that can allocate, as in `list.append(gpa, x)`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "build up a list" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    // `.empty` replaces `init(allocator)`. The list does not store the
    // allocator. Thus each method that can allocate takes an allocator.
    var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);

    try list.append(gpa, 'h');
    try list.appendSlice(gpa, "ello");

    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, list.items, "hello"));
    try expect(list.items.len == 5);
}

test "items is a plain slice" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);

    for (0..5) |i| try list.append(gpa, @intCast(i * i));

    // `.items` is a `[]T` into the buffer of the list. It is valid until
    // the next reallocation. Thus do not keep it across an append.
    try expect(list.items[4] == 16);
}

test "pop and remove" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);

    try list.appendSlice(gpa, "abcd");
    try expect(list.pop().? == 'd');
    _ = list.orderedRemove(0); // moves the other items down
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, list.items, "bc"));
}

test "preallocate when the size is known" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);

    // One allocation, not a series of growth steps.
    try list.ensureTotalCapacity(gpa, 100);
    for (0..100) |_| list.appendAssumeCapacity('x');
    try expect(list.items.len == 100);
}

test "take ownership of the buffer" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    try list.appendSlice(gpa, "owned");

    // `toOwnedSlice` gives you the memory and makes the list empty. Thus
    // the caller frees the slice, and does not call deinit on the list.
    const slice = try list.toOwnedSlice(gpa);
    defer gpa.free(slice);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, slice, "owned"));
}

test "lock the buffer in place while holding a pointer into it" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var list: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer list.deinit(gpa);

    try list.appendSlice(gpa, &.{ 1, 2, 3 });

    // Between these two calls, the buffer must not move. Thus a pointer into
    // the buffer stays valid. In a safety build, an operation that
    // reallocates panics. It does not make `first` invalid without a report.
    list.lockPointers();
    const first = &list.items[0];
    first.* += 10;
    list.unlockPointers();

    try expect(list.items[0] == 11);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.arraylist`)*

## The list is unmanaged now

Of all the changes, this change most often breaks code that you find online. In the past, `std.ArrayList` stored its allocator:

```zig
var list = std.ArrayList(u8).init(allocator);   // old
defer list.deinit();
try list.append('a');
```

On master, `ArrayList` **is** the unmanaged variant. It holds no allocator. Thus you give an allocator to each method that can allocate:

```zig
var list: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;           // current
defer list.deinit(gpa);
try list.append(gpa, 'a');
```

You type more, but the allocator is visible at each call site that can fail. Also, the struct is two words smaller.

The second reason for the change is visible at scale. A program with ten thousand small lists stored ten thousand copies of the same allocator pointer and vtable. Now the program stores no copies. A struct with several list fields does not keep one allocator for each field.

`.empty` is a declaration on the type. Thus `var list: std.ArrayList(u8) =
.empty;` works by inference. If you know approximately how many items will come, use `try .initCapacity(gpa, n)`. It allocates one time at the start.

## The parts of a list

A list has an `items` slice, a `capacity`, and a safety field. A later section tells you about the safety field. Outside a safety build, the safety field costs nothing.

Thus a list is three words: a pointer, a length, and the number of elements that the buffer can hold before it must grow. An append past the capacity allocates a larger buffer, copies the elements, and frees the old buffer. For this reason, append returns an error, and growth has an amortised cost.

## `.items` is a borrowed slice

`list.items` points into the buffer of the list. An append can reallocate the buffer, and then each slice that you hold is not valid. Get `.items` when you need it. Do not keep it across changes to the list.

If you do nothing, no check finds this error. The old slice still has a valid pointer and a valid length, but it points into freed memory. It reads data that looks correct, or the program crashes. The result depends on what the allocator did next.

The same rule applies to a pointer to an element. After an append that grows the list, `&list.items[0]` is not valid.

The usual example is a loop that appends to the list that it iterates over. Collect the new items into a second list. Then append them after the loop.

## Lock the buffer in place

`lockPointers` and `unlockPointers` mark a region where the buffer must not move. Inside the region, an operation that reallocates or frees the buffer panics. Thus the operation does not make a pointer that you hold invalid:

```zig
list.lockPointers();
const first = &list.items[0];
first.* += 10;
list.unlockPointers();
```

The panic occurs when the buffer moves, not when you call the method. An `append` that fits in the current capacity moves nothing, and it passes. The same `append` panics on the iteration that must grow the buffer. Some methods always make pointers invalid, for example `insert`, `swapRemove` and `toOwnedSlice`. These methods assert directly.

The field behind the lock is a `std.debug.SafetyLock`. Outside a safety build, it checks nothing. Debug and ReleaseSafe have the check. ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall do not have it. The wasm behind the Run button on this page is ReleaseSmall.

## Allocate the capacity first when possible

Call `ensureTotalCapacity`, then call `appendAssumeCapacity`. This sequence makes one allocation and not a series of growth steps. The `AssumeCapacity` calls cannot fail, thus they need no `try`.

Speed is not the only reason. A loop of `try list.append(...)` has an error path on each iteration. Some code must not fail in the middle. In that code, reserve the space first. Then the full loop either occurs completely or does not occur.

In a safety build, `appendAssumeCapacity` panics if your capacity was wrong. Thus the safety build checks the assumption in the place where the assumption matters.

## Give the ownership to the caller

`toOwnedSlice(gpa)` gives you the buffer and makes the list empty. Then the caller frees the slice, and the list needs no `deinit`.

This is the idiomatic way to make a value of unknown size and return it. Use the list while the data grows. When the data is complete, return a plain `[]T`. The returned slice has the same length as the data, thus the caller does not keep the spare capacity of the list.

The opposite operation is `fromOwnedSlice`. It adopts a slice that you already have, and then the slice can continue to grow.

## When to use a different container

- If you remove elements from the front, a list costs O(n) for each removal. A [queue](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/queues/) does not.
- If you find values by a key and not by a position, use a [hash map](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/hash-maps/).
- If each element is a large struct and you usually use one field at a time, use a [MultiArrayList](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/multi-array-list/). It stores each field in a separate array, and it reads far fewer cache lines.

---

## Hash Maps

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/hash-maps/*

In Zig, a hash map is `std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(K, V)`. When the keys are strings, use `std.StringHashMapUnmanaged(V)`. `map.getOrPut(gpa, key)` inserts or updates an entry with one lookup.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "string keys" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var map: std.StringHashMapUnmanaged(u32) = .empty;
    defer map.deinit(gpa);

    try map.put(gpa, "one", 1);
    try map.put(gpa, "two", 2);

    try expect(map.get("one").? == 1);
    try expect(map.get("three") == null);
    try expect(map.count() == 2);
}

test "auto hash for simple keys" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    // AutoHashMap gets the hash and equality functions from the key type.
    var map: std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(u32, []const u8) = .empty;
    defer map.deinit(gpa);

    try map.put(gpa, 1, "one");
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, map.get(1).?, "one"));
}

test "getOrPut avoids hashing twice" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var counts: std.StringHashMapUnmanaged(u32) = .empty;
    defer counts.deinit(gpa);

    for ([_][]const u8{ "a", "b", "a" }) |word| {
        // One lookup, not a get and then a put.
        const entry = try counts.getOrPut(gpa, word);
        if (!entry.found_existing) entry.value_ptr.* = 0;
        entry.value_ptr.* += 1;
    }

    try expect(counts.get("a").? == 2);
    try expect(counts.get("b").? == 1);
}

test "iterate entries" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var map: std.AutoHashMapUnmanaged(u32, u32) = .empty;
    defer map.deinit(gpa);

    try map.put(gpa, 1, 10);
    try map.put(gpa, 2, 20);

    var total: u32 = 0;
    var it = map.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |entry| total += entry.value_ptr.*;
    try expect(total == 30);
}

test "remove" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var map: std.StringHashMapUnmanaged(u32) = .empty;
    defer map.deinit(gpa);

    try map.put(gpa, "gone", 1);
    try expect(map.remove("gone"));
    try expect(map.count() == 0);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.hash-maps`)*

## Select a map

| Type | For |
| --- | --- |
| `AutoHashMapUnmanaged(K, V)` | keys that Zig can hash automatically (integers, enums, simple structs) |
| `StringHashMapUnmanaged(V)` | `[]const u8` keys |
| `std.array_hash_map.Auto(K, V)` | when you need a stable insertion order |

These maps are unmanaged, like `ArrayList`. Create a map with `.empty`, and give the allocator to each method that allocates.

`AutoHashMap` refuses keys that it cannot hash safely, for example slices. The hash of the pointer is almost never what you want. For this reason, string keys have their own type.

The refusal is a compile error, not a surprise at runtime. It is a good example of what comptime reflection can do. The map examines your key type at compile time. If the key type contains a pointer and the map must follow that pointer, the map stops and tells you. It does not hash the address without a report.

Be careful with the third row. The iteration order of a plain hash map comes from the layout of the table, and the order changes when the map grows. An array hash map keeps the entries in a list next to the table. Thus an iteration gives you the insertion order, and the cost is one extra indirection.

Use an array hash map when a person will read the output, or when a test compares the output with a fixture. A test that iterates over a plain hash map will fail one day for no visible reason.

## Use `getOrPut`, not a get and then a put

This idiom counts words:

```zig
const entry = try counts.getOrPut(gpa, word);
if (!entry.found_existing) entry.value_ptr.* = 0;
entry.value_ptr.* += 1;
```

The idiom does one hash and one lookup, not two. `entry.value_ptr` points into the map. Thus a write through the pointer changes the stored value in place.

The pointer is valid only until the next insertion. This is the same rule as for `ArrayList.items`.

The entry also has `entry.key_ptr`, which is important for the string case below. On a new insert, the map stores *your* slice as the key. Use `key_ptr` to replace that slice with a copy that you own.

A full family of these functions exists:

- `put` overwrites the value.
- `putNoClobber` asserts that the key is new.
- `fetchPut` returns the old value.
- `getOrPutValue` supplies a default value in one call.

Each function makes a common intention into one operation, not a lookup and then a decision.

## The map does not copy the keys

The map stores your key as you give it. For a string key, the map holds a slice that points at memory that the map does not own. If the program frees that memory or uses the memory again, the map is corrupt. Thus do one of these two things:

- Keep the keys alive yourself.
- Duplicate each key when you insert it, and free the key when you remove it.

The version that duplicates the keys is short. Keep it as a template:

```zig
const entry = try map.getOrPut(gpa, name);
if (!entry.found_existing) {
    entry.key_ptr.* = try gpa.dupe(u8, name);
    entry.value_ptr.* = 0;
}
```

Before `deinit`, the teardown code iterates over the map and frees each `entry.key_ptr.*`. Code that uses maps often forgets this step, and the result is a leak. In a test, an allocator that checks for leaks finds this leak.

You do *not* need to copy the keys when a different value owns them and lives longer than the map. Examples are string literals, names interned in an arena, and slices of a buffer that you hold for the full time. Then the map can borrow the keys correctly, and a copy is a waste.

## The cost

A hash map is not free at small sizes. For a small number of entries, a linear search through a plain array is usually faster, and it is always simpler. The hash and the indirection cost more than a scan of eight elements.

The map is better when the count is so large that O(1) is better than O(n) by more than the constant. For cheap keys, this point is in the dozens. For expensive comparisons, the point is lower.

---

## Stacks

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/stacks/*

In Zig, push and pop are `append(gpa, x)` and `pop()` on a `std.ArrayList`. `pop()` returns `null` when the list is empty. When you know the maximum depth, a fixed array and a length index make a stack with no allocator.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "ArrayList is the stack you want" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var stack: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);

    try stack.append(gpa, 1);
    try stack.append(gpa, 2);
    try stack.append(gpa, 3);

    try expect(stack.pop().? == 3);
    try expect(stack.last().? == 2);
    try expect(stack.items.len == 2);
}

test "last is null on an empty stack, not a panic" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var stack: std.ArrayList(u32) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);

    try expect(stack.last() == null);
    try stack.append(gpa, 7);
    try expect(stack.last().? == 7);
}

test "pop returns null when empty" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var stack: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);

    try expect(stack.pop() == null);
}

test "a bounded stack needs no allocator at all" {
    // When you know the maximum, a fixed buffer does not use the heap.
    var buffer: [8]u32 = undefined;
    var len: usize = 0;

    for ([_]u32{ 10, 20, 30 }) |v| {
        buffer[len] = v;
        len += 1;
    }
    len -= 1;
    try expect(buffer[len] == 30);
}

test "balanced bracket check" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var stack: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);

    const input = "([]{})";
    var balanced = true;
    for (input) |c| switch (c) {
        '(', '[', '{' => try stack.append(gpa, c),
        ')' => balanced = balanced and stack.pop() == '(',
        ']' => balanced = balanced and stack.pop() == '[',
        '}' => balanced = balanced and stack.pop() == '{',
        else => {},
    };
    try expect(balanced and stack.items.len == 0);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.stacks`)*

Zig has no special `Stack` type, because it does not need one. An `ArrayList` that you use from the end is a stack:

| Operation | Call |
| --- | --- |
| push | `append(gpa, x)` |
| pop | `pop()` (returns `?T`) |
| peek | `last()` (returns `?T`) |
| size | `items.len` |

`pop()` and `last()` both return an optional. Thus the type handles the empty case. You do not have to remember a precondition.

In older tutorials, peek was `getLast()`, and it returned a `T`. It asserted that the list was not empty. Thus a call on an empty list was a safety-checked panic in a debug build, and undefined behaviour in a release build.

That function still exists. It is deprecated, and it still asserts. `last()` is the replacement. It returns `?T`, and thus the empty case is in the type.

`getLastOrNull()` is a deprecated alias for `last()`. There is also `lastPtr()`, which returns `?*T`. Use `lastPtr()` when you want to change the top element in place and not copy it.

The stack is cheap because it uses the end of the list, not the front. A removal from the end decrements the length one time. A removal from the front moves each of the other elements. For this reason, an array is a good fit for a stack, but not for a queue.

## When the depth has a limit

If you know the maximum, do not use an allocator. A fixed array and a length index are a complete stack that cannot fail. This is important for embedded targets and hot paths, and in Zig it is ordinary code.

```zig
var buf: [64]Frame = undefined;
var top: usize = 0;

buf[top] = frame; top += 1;   // push
top -= 1; const f = buf[top]; // pop
```

With no allocator, push needs no `try`, and this changes the shape of the code that uses the stack. A parser with a limit on the depth of nested brackets has no error path for "no more stack". It has only a check against the limit.

Write that check. With the check, the parser rejects input with too many levels. Without the check, the program crashes.

## Where to use a stack

Use a stack in almost all cases where the code must remember a point to return to:

- **Brackets that match**, in a parser or a linter. Push on an open bracket, pop on a close bracket, and compare.
- **Depth-first traversal** of a tree or a graph. Write it as a loop, so that deep input cannot overflow the stack of the machine.
- **Undo history**, where the code reverses the most recent action first.
- **An evaluator** for postfix expressions, which is exactly a stack machine.

The [tiny language](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/) track uses the second and fourth items of this list. It uses them to replace recursion with an explicit stack.

## Why not a linked list

A stack on a linked list allocates for each element, and puts the elements at many different places in memory. An `ArrayList` amortises to one allocation and keeps all the elements next to each other. This is faster for almost all real workloads. Use a linked list only when you need stable addresses or O(1) splicing.

The difference is more than a small constant factor. A pop from an array reads memory that the CPU already loaded. A pop from a linked list follows a pointer to memory that is not in the cache, and the CPU waits.

Textbooks show the two stacks as equal, because they compare instruction counts. Instruction counts decided performance until decades ago. Today they do not.

There is one real exception. If other code holds pointers to the elements, you cannot use an array, because when the array grows, all the elements move. In that case, the extra allocations give you a benefit.

---

## PriorityQueue

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/priority-queue/*

`std.PriorityQueue(T, Context, compareFn)` is the binary heap in Zig. `push` and `pop` are O(log n). `pop` returns the element that the comparator puts first, or `null` when the queue is empty.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;
const Order = std.math.Order;

fn ascU32(_: void, a: u32, b: u32) Order {
    return std.math.order(a, b);
}

test "min-heap: pop returns the smallest" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    // The comparator is part of the type. Order.lt means "a pops first".
    var pq: std.PriorityQueue(u32, void, ascU32) = .empty;
    defer pq.deinit(gpa);

    try pq.push(gpa, 30);
    try pq.push(gpa, 10);
    try pq.push(gpa, 20);

    try expect(pq.peek().? == 10); // read the top value, but do not remove it
    try expect(pq.pop().? == 10);
    try expect(pq.pop().? == 20);
    try expect(pq.pop().? == 30);
    try expect(pq.pop() == null);
}

const Job = struct {
    priority: u8,
    name: []const u8,
};

fn urgentFirst(_: void, a: Job, b: Job) Order {
    // Reverse the comparison to make a max-heap.
    return std.math.order(b.priority, a.priority);
}

test "structs with a priority field" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    var jobs: std.PriorityQueue(Job, void, urgentFirst) = .empty;
    defer jobs.deinit(gpa);

    try jobs.pushSlice(gpa, &.{
        .{ .priority = 1, .name = "compact logs" },
        .{ .priority = 9, .name = "page the human" },
        .{ .priority = 5, .name = "rebuild index" },
    });

    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, jobs.pop().?.name, "page the human"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, jobs.pop().?.name, "rebuild index"));
    try expect(jobs.count() == 1);
}

test "iteration order is not sorted order" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    var pq: std.PriorityQueue(u32, void, ascU32) = .empty;
    defer pq.deinit(gpa);
    try pq.pushSlice(gpa, &.{ 5, 1, 4, 2, 3 });

    // The storage array is a heap, not a sorted list. Only pop gives an order.
    var sum: u32 = 0;
    var it = pq.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |v| sum += v;
    try expect(sum == 15);
    try expect(pq.pop().? == 1);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.priority-queue`)*

## The comparator is part of the type

`std.PriorityQueue(T, Context, compareFn)` puts the order into the type. `std.sort` uses the same shape. The function returns a `std.math.Order`. Return `.lt` when the first argument must pop before the second argument.

Thus the comparator answers the question "which comes first". If you swap its two arguments, a min-heap becomes a max-heap.

The `Context` parameter is `void` when the comparison needs no external data. To compare against runtime data, give the parameter a real type. An example is distances to a target that you know only at runtime. Give the value to the queue through `initContext`.

The comparator is in the type and not in a field. Thus each comparison is a direct call that the optimiser can inline. Also, two queues with different orders are different types. You cannot use one of them where the code expects the other.

## It is unmanaged, as the other containers are

```zig
var q: std.PriorityQueue(u32, void, ascU32) = .empty;
defer q.deinit(gpa);

try q.push(gpa, 30);
const smallest = q.pop();     // ?u32
```

The rules are the same as for the other containers:

- Use `.empty` to create the queue.
- Give the allocator to each method that can allocate.
- `pop` returns an optional, thus the empty case is in the type.

Older code calls `init(allocator, {})` and uses `add` and `removeOrNull`. That is the older managed shape. Now the methods are `push` and `pop`, and you give the allocator to each call.

`pushSlice` adds several elements in one call. `count` gives the number of elements, and `capacity` gives the size of the storage. `update(old, new)` replaces an element and makes the heap order correct again. A Dijkstra implementation needs `update` when it finds a shorter path to a node that is already in the queue.

## When to use it

`push` and `pop` are O(log n), and `peek` is O(1). Use the queue when you must get the current best element from a set that changes again and again. Examples:

- A scheduler gets the most urgent job.
- Dijkstra gets the nearest node.
- A merge of sorted streams gets the next value.

Look for pushes and pops that occur in a mixed sequence. If the code adds all the elements and then removes all of them, one sort is faster and simpler. The heap is better when the code mixes pushes and pops. It never spends work to put the elements in full order before it must use them.

The heap is also the correct structure for "the largest k of n" when n is large. Push all the items, and keep the heap at a maximum size of k. Then the memory that you use is proportional to k. You do not sort n items and then discard most of them.

## What it is not

The storage is a heap, not a sorted array. `iterator` walks that storage in heap order, and heap order is not sorted order. Only `pop` gives you the elements in priority order.

If you must sort all the elements one time, an `ArrayList` and `std.sort` are a better choice. Use the queue when the code mixes insertions and removals.

The queue is also not stable. Two elements that the comparator calls equal come out in the order that the heap gives. That order can change when you insert other elements. If ties must break by the time of insertion, put a sequence number in the element. Compare the sequence number as a second key.

The name has the word "queue", but it is not a FIFO queue. If you want "first in, first out", use a [queue](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/queues/). A queue is O(1) and not O(log n).

---

## MultiArrayList

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/multi-array-list/*

`std.MultiArrayList(T)` is the struct-of-arrays container in Zig. Like an `ArrayList(T)`, it takes full structs through `append`. The call `items(.field)` returns one field of all the elements as a separate slice.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const Monster = struct {
    hp: u32,
    x: f32,
    y: f32,
};

test "append structs, read fields as plain slices" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    var monsters: std.MultiArrayList(Monster) = .empty;
    defer monsters.deinit(gpa);

    try monsters.append(gpa, .{ .hp = 10, .x = 1.0, .y = 2.0 });
    try monsters.append(gpa, .{ .hp = 25, .x = 3.0, .y = 4.0 });
    try monsters.append(gpa, .{ .hp = 40, .x = 5.0, .y = 6.0 });

    // items(.hp) is a real []u32. All the hp values are next to each other
    // in memory. A loop that uses only hp does not load x or y into the cache.
    var total: u32 = 0;
    for (monsters.items(.hp)) |hp| total += hp;
    try expect(total == 75);
}

test "get and set reassemble the struct" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    var monsters: std.MultiArrayList(Monster) = .empty;
    defer monsters.deinit(gpa);
    try monsters.append(gpa, .{ .hp = 10, .x = 1.0, .y = 2.0 });

    const m = monsters.get(0); // collects one element from the three arrays
    try expect(m.hp == 10 and m.x == 1.0);

    monsters.set(0, .{ .hp = 99, .x = 0.0, .y = 0.0 });
    try expect(monsters.items(.hp)[0] == 99);
}

test "mutate one column in place" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    var monsters: std.MultiArrayList(Monster) = .empty;
    defer monsters.deinit(gpa);
    try monsters.append(gpa, .{ .hp = 10, .x = 0, .y = 0 });
    try monsters.append(gpa, .{ .hp = 20, .x = 0, .y = 0 });

    // The slice is the real storage. It is not a copy.
    for (monsters.items(.hp)) |*hp| hp.* += 5;
    try expect(monsters.get(0).hp == 15);
    try expect(monsters.get(1).hp == 25);
}

test "cache the slice when touching several fields" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    var monsters: std.MultiArrayList(Monster) = .empty;
    defer monsters.deinit(gpa);
    try monsters.append(gpa, .{ .hp = 1, .x = 3.0, .y = 4.0 });

    // Each items() call calculates the field pointers again. slice() does
    // that work one time.
    const s = monsters.slice();
    const xs = s.items(.x);
    const ys = s.items(.y);
    try expect(xs[0] * xs[0] + ys[0] * ys[0] == 25.0);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.multi-array-list`)*

## The same API with a different storage

Ten monsters with `hp`, `x` and `y` become three arrays of ten values. They do not become ten structs next to each other. `get` still gives you full structs. You see the separate arrays only when you ask for one field.

The two layouts have names, and books and papers use these names:

- `ArrayList` is an array of structs, "AoS".
- `MultiArrayList` is a struct of arrays, "SoA".

The data is the same in the two layouts. Only the order of the bytes in memory is different.

## Why use it

`items(.hp)` gives you a real `[]u32`, with all the hp values next to each other. A loop that adds the hp values reads only that array. Thus the CPU loads no `x` or `y` bytes that it does not use.

When a program uses one field frequently and the struct is wide, this loop reads only the bytes that it needs. It does not move the full struct through the cache. This layout also lets the compiler vectorize changes to one field of all the elements.

The cache line gives the numbers. Memory comes from RAM in 64-byte blocks. The block size is the same when you need 64 bytes and when you need only 4. Take a 64-byte struct in AoS layout, and a loop that adds one `u32` field. The loop gets 64 bytes to use 4 bytes, thus fifteen sixteenths of the memory bandwidth is lost.

In SoA layout, the same loop uses all the bytes that it gets. On a large array, the layout causes all of the difference. Optimisation of the loop body cannot recover that difference.
