The layout has a second benefit. Each field array has one type, and its values are next to each other. Thus `@Vector` operations and the auto-vectoriser can operate on them. A loop over one field of an array of structs cannot vectorise, because the values are not adjacent.

## The costs

`get` and `set` collect or distribute the values across the separate arrays. Thus an operation on a full element is slightly more work than with a plain `ArrayList`. Use `MultiArrayList` when you iterate over columns much more frequently than you use full rows.

When a loop needs several fields, call `slice()` one time and get each `items(.field)` from the result. Each separate `items()` call calculates the field pointers again. `slice()` does that work one time. As with each list in this guide, the next append makes those slices invalid.

The other cost is readability, and that cost is real. Field access becomes `s.items(.hp)[i]` and not `list.items[i].hp`. Code that usually works with full entities becomes more difficult to read, and it gets no benefit. Select this layout after you measure. Use it only for the few arrays in a program that are both large and frequently used.

`MultiArrayList` also works only on structs with known fields. It uses the same comptime reflection as the other containers in this guide. It walks the field list of `T` and makes the arrays from that list. Thus the compiler checks `.hp` at compile time. A typo is a build error, and not a lookup at runtime.

## Where programs use it

Programs use it where the array is large and the code reads it one column at a time. Game entity systems are the usual example, and the term "SoA" comes from them.

Compilers are another example. The Zig compiler stores its abstract syntax tree in this layout, because each pass over the tree walks one field of all the nodes.

If you store thousands of small records and iterate over them one field at a time, use this container. If you store a few dozen items, use an `ArrayList` and put your attention on other parts of the program.

---

## Bit Sets and Enum Collections

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/bit-sets/*

`std.bit_set.Static(N)` stores a set of the integers `0..N` as bits, with no allocator. `EnumSet`, `EnumArray` and `EnumMap` change an enum into one of three containers:

- a set
- a table with a value for each tag
- a map with values for some tags

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "static bit set" {
    // 64 bits, stored inline. An allocator is not necessary.
    var seen: std.bit_set.Static(64) = .empty;

    seen.set(3);
    seen.set(40);
    try expect(seen.isSet(3));
    try expect(!seen.isSet(4));
    try expect(seen.count() == 2);

    // Gives the indices of the set bits in ascending order.
    var it = seen.iterator(.{});
    try expect(it.next().? == 3);
    try expect(it.next().? == 40);
    try expect(it.next() == null);
}

test "set algebra" {
    var a: std.bit_set.Static(16) = .empty;
    var b: std.bit_set.Static(16) = .empty;
    a.set(1);
    a.set(2);
    b.set(2);
    b.set(3);

    const both = a.intersectWith(b);
    try expect(both.count() == 1 and both.isSet(2));

    const either = a.unionWith(b);
    try expect(either.count() == 3);
}

test "ranges" {
    var mask: std.bit_set.Static(32) = .empty;
    mask.setRangeValue(.{ .start = 8, .end = 16 }, true);
    try expect(mask.count() == 8);
    try expect(mask.findFirstSet().? == 8);
}

const Perm = enum { read, write, execute };

test "EnumSet: a bit set keyed by an enum" {
    var perms = std.EnumSet(Perm).initMany(&.{ .read, .write });

    try expect(perms.contains(.read));
    try expect(!perms.contains(.execute));

    perms.insert(.execute);
    perms.remove(.write);
    try expect(perms.count() == 2);
}

const Light = enum { red, yellow, green };

test "EnumArray: one value per enum tag, no optionals" {
    // Each key exists. The initialization must give a value for each key.
    var durations = std.EnumArray(Light, u32).init(.{
        .red = 30,
        .yellow = 5,
        .green = 25,
    });

    try expect(durations.get(.red) == 30);
    durations.set(.yellow, 4);
    try expect(durations.get(.yellow) == 4);
}

test "EnumMap: some keys may be absent" {
    var overrides = std.EnumMap(Light, u32).init(.{ .red = 45 });

    try expect(overrides.get(.red).? == 45);
    try expect(overrides.get(.green) == null);

    overrides.put(.green, 20);
    try expect(overrides.count() == 2);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.bit-sets`)*

## A set that fits in registers

Older code calls this type `std.StaticBitSet`. The type stores the bits inline. When `N` is small, the type is one integer. When `N` is larger, the type is an array of words. The API is the same for the two layouts: `set`, `unset`, `isSet`, `count`.

If you know the size only at run time, use `std.bit_set.DynamicManaged`. This type takes an allocator.

Union and intersection are single instructions on the backing words. Thus `unionWith` and `intersectWith` are cheap. With `findFirstSet` and the ascending `iterator`, you can find the members without a scan of each index.

## Containers with an enum as the key

Three types change an enum into a container. The difference between them is the result for a key that you did not set:

| Type | Holds | A key that you did not set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EnumSet(E)` | membership only | not present |
| `EnumArray(E, V)` | a `V` for each tag | not possible: init sets all keys |
| `EnumMap(E, V)` | a `V` for some tags | `get` returns null |

An `EnumArray` always has a value for each tag. Thus its `get` returns `V`, not `?V`. The compiler makes you supply each field at initialization. Use `EnumArray` for lookup tables that must cover the full enum, for example a duration for each state of a traffic light.

`EnumMap` is the partial version. Use it when the absence of a key has a meaning. The three types use the same bit-set machinery. Thus they are compact, and they do not allocate.

The coverage of each tag is the main reason to use `EnumArray`. When you add a tag to the enum, each `EnumArray` initialiser becomes a compile error. The error gives the name of the tag that has no value. An exhaustive `switch` gives the same guarantee, for the same reason. A `HashMap` with the enum as the key compiles, and it returns null at runtime.

## What these types replace

These types replace a `[]bool`, or an array of booleans. The bit set uses eight times less memory. Also, it does a set operation in one instruction, not in a loop.

For example, take a record of which of 256 opcodes have an implementation. As a bit set, the record costs 32 bytes. As an array of `bool`, it costs 256 bytes. At that size, the difference is not important.

At sixty-four thousand flags, the bit set is 8 KB, and it stays in L1 on most machines. The array of `bool` is 64 KB, and it does not stay in L1. A test for "is any of these set" changes from a scan to a small number of `or` operations.

These types also replace a `flags: u32` that you write by hand, with named constants and manual `&` and `|`. That method works, and C uses it. But the bit positions are only in comments. Nothing stops a test of the wrong bit. To print the set, you must write a formatter. `EnumSet` gives the same layout, with names that the compiler checks.

## Iterate over a set

`iterator()` gives the indices of the set bits, in ascending order. It does not test each index. It skips a word of zeroes in one step. Take a sparse set over a large range. The time of the loop is proportional to the number of members, not to the size of the range.

`findFirstSet` returns the lowest member. A free-list allocator needs this operation. The bit set is the map of the available blocks, and the first set bit is the next block to give out. `toggleAll`, `unionWith`, `intersectWith` and `differenceWith` complete the set algebra.

## Select a size

`std.bit_set.Static(N)` stores its bits inline. Thus you can copy the type, and it has no pointers inside. It can be a struct field, and a function can return it by value. For these reasons, it is the default choice.

`DynamicManaged` is for an `N` that the program decides at run time. It takes an allocator, and it needs a `deinit`. Before you use it, make sure that you really have no upper limit. Usually, a static set with a large maximum size is simpler and smaller than a heap allocation and a pointer.

---

## Strings

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/strings/*

In Zig, a string is a `[]const u8`. The functions that search, trim, split and join strings are free functions in `std.mem`, for example `std.mem.find`, `std.mem.trim` and `std.mem.splitScalar`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;
const expectEqualStrings = std.testing.expectEqualStrings;

test "compare content, not pointers" {
    // The compiler rejects == on slices. Thus compare the contents with eql.
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, "zig", "zig"));
    try expect(std.mem.startsWith(u8, "build.zig", "build"));
    try expect(std.mem.endsWith(u8, "build.zig", ".zig"));
}

test "search" {
    // find returns the byte offset of the first match, or null.
    try expect(std.mem.find(u8, "hello world", "world").? == 6);
    try expect(std.mem.find(u8, "hello world", "moon") == null);
    try expect(std.mem.findScalarLast(u8, "a.b.c", '.').? == 3);
    try expect(std.mem.count(u8, "banana", "an") == 2);
}

test "trim strips a set of bytes, not a pattern" {
    // The second slice is the set of bytes to remove from the two ends.
    try expectEqualStrings("data", std.mem.trim(u8, "  data\n", " \n"));
    try expectEqualStrings("data  ", std.mem.trimStart(u8, "  data  ", " "));
    try expectEqualStrings("  data", std.mem.trimEnd(u8, "  data  ", " "));
}

test "split keeps empty fields, tokenize skips them" {
    // split: one entry for each field. "a,,b" has three fields, and one field
    // is empty. Use split for CSV-shaped input, where an empty field has a meaning.
    var fields = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, "a,,b", ',');
    try expectEqualStrings("a", fields.next().?);
    try expectEqualStrings("", fields.next().?);
    try expectEqualStrings("b", fields.next().?);
    try expect(fields.next() == null);

    // tokenize: a sequence of delimiters counts as one. Use it for whitespace.
    var words = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, "  one  two ", ' ');
    try expectEqualStrings("one", words.next().?);
    try expectEqualStrings("two", words.next().?);
    try expect(words.next() == null);
}

test "join and replace return new memory" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    const path = try std.mem.join(gpa, "/", &.{ "usr", "local", "bin" });
    defer gpa.free(path);
    try expectEqualStrings("usr/local/bin", path);

    const snake = try std.mem.replaceOwned(u8, gpa, "a-b-c", "-", "_");
    defer gpa.free(snake);
    try expectEqualStrings("a_b_c", snake);
}

test "case functions are ASCII-only on purpose" {
    // Real case mapping needs Unicode tables. The std library does not include them.
    try expect(std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase("Zig", "zIG"));

    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const lower = try std.ascii.allocLowerString(gpa, "MiXeD");
    defer gpa.free(lower);
    try expectEqualStrings("mixed", lower);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.strings`)*

## There is no string type

A string is `[]const u8`, a slice of bytes. Thus you cannot compare two strings with `==`, because the compiler rejects `==` on slices. To compare the contents, use `std.mem.eql(u8, a, b)`. To put two strings in order, use `std.mem.order(u8, a, b)`, which returns `.lt`, `.eq` or `.gt`.

All the other functions that you expect from a string class are free functions in `std.mem`. They work on all slice types. For this reason, each call gives the element type first.

## `indexOf` is now `find`

Zig renamed the search functions in the 0.17 development series:

```zig
// older tutorials
std.mem.indexOf(u8, haystack, needle);
std.mem.lastIndexOfScalar(u8, path, '.');

// current master
std.mem.find(u8, haystack, needle);
std.mem.findScalarLast(u8, path, '.');
```

All the functions in the family changed in the same way:

- `indexOfScalar` became `findScalar`.
- `indexOfAny` became `findAny`.
- `indexOfPos` became `findPos`.
- `lastIndexOf` became `findLast`.
- `indexOfNone` became `findNone`.

The old names still exist, as one-line aliases with the `Deprecated` mark in `std/mem.zig`. Code that uses the old names compiles and behaves in the same way. Nothing fails. Thus a guide can teach the old names for another year, and the authors do not see the problem.

## split or tokenize

The two functions look interchangeable until the input has two delimiters next to each other:

| Input `"a,,b"` with `,` | Yields |
| --- | --- |
| `splitScalar` | `"a"`, `""`, `"b"` |
| `tokenizeScalar` | `"a"`, `"b"` |

`split` keeps empty fields. CSV-shaped data needs this behaviour. `tokenize` treats a sequence of delimiters as one delimiter. Whitespace needs this behaviour.

The two functions have `Any` and `Sequence` variants:

- `splitAny` uses each byte of the delimiter string as a separate delimiter.
- `splitSequence` matches the full delimiter string.

## What allocates and what does not

`trim`, `split`, and `tokenize` return views into the original bytes. They do not copy. Thus the result is valid only while the original is valid.

`join`, `replaceOwned`, and `std.ascii.allocLowerString` make new strings. Thus they take an allocator, and you own the result.

## ASCII only

`std.ascii` stops at byte 127. Case mapping above byte 127 needs Unicode tables, and the standard library does not include these tables. The Unicode chapter shows what the standard library gives you.

[String Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/string-recipes/) shows a case-insensitive search, padding for a column, a join at runtime, and a replace without an allocator.

---

## Unicode

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/unicode/*

In Zig, a string is a slice of bytes. UTF-8 support is something that you select, through `std.unicode`. There, `Utf8View` validates the bytes and iterates over code points. Grapheme clusters, case folding and normalisation are not in the standard library.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;
const expectEqualStrings = std.testing.expectEqualStrings;

test "len counts bytes, not characters" {
    const s = "héllo"; // é is two bytes in UTF-8
    try expect(s.len == 6);
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints(s) == 5);
}

test "validate untrusted input first" {
    try expect(std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice("héllo"));
    // 0xff never occurs in well-formed UTF-8.
    try expect(!std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(&.{ 0xff, 0xfe }));
}

test "iterate codepoints" {
    // Utf8View.init validates one time. After that, the iterator cannot fail.
    const view = try std.unicode.Utf8View.init("héllo");
    var it = view.iterator();

    try expect(it.nextCodepoint().? == 'h');
    try expect(it.nextCodepoint().? == 'é');
    try expect(it.nextCodepoint().? == 'l');

    // nextCodepointSlice returns the raw bytes, not a u21.
    // Use it to slice the original string.
    var rest = view.iterator();
    _ = rest.nextCodepointSlice();
    const e_bytes = rest.nextCodepointSlice().?;
    try expect(e_bytes.len == 2);
}

test "encode a codepoint to bytes" {
    var buf: [4]u8 = undefined;
    const len = try std.unicode.utf8Encode('→', &buf);
    try expect(len == 3);
    try expectEqualStrings("→", buf[0..len]);
}

test "slicing bytes can split a character" {
    const s = "héllo";
    // s[0..2] cuts é in half: 'h', then the first byte of é without the
    // continuation byte that must follow it.
    try expect(!std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(s[0..2]));
    // When you need safe cut points, iterate over codepoint slices.
    try expect(std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(s[0..3]));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.unicode`)*

## `len` is bytes

`"héllo".len` is 6, not 5, because `é` encodes to two bytes. Nothing in the language layer knows about UTF-8. Source files must be valid UTF-8, but a `[]const u8` at runtime is only bytes. When you need a count of characters, `std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints` walks the encoding.

This is a design decision, not something that the designers forgot. Most code that handles text never needs the character boundaries. Copy, hash, equality comparison, a write to a socket, and a substring search all work on bytes. Thus they are faster and simpler. Only a small number of cases really need characters, and these cases ask for the UTF-8 code explicitly.

## Three different lengths

The word "length" has three answers. Bugs frequently occur when code uses the wrong answer.

- **Bytes.** `.len` gives you this length. You need it for buffers, offsets, and all data that you write to a file.
- **Code points.** `utf8CountCodepoints` gives you this length. A code point is one Unicode value, encoded in one to four bytes.
- **Grapheme clusters.** A grapheme cluster is what a person calls a character. A letter and its combining accent are two code points and one character. An emoji with a skin-tone modifier can be several code points.

The standard library gives you the first two lengths. Grapheme clusters need Unicode tables, and `std` does not include them. Thus "how many characters will this text use on screen" is a question for a library. Terminal width is a fourth, separate answer.

## Validate one time, then iterate

`Utf8View.init` checks the full slice first, and returns an error for malformed input. After that, its iterator cannot fail, thus the loop body stays clean. `nextCodepoint` gives `u21` values. `nextCodepointSlice` gives the raw bytes of each character. Use `nextCodepointSlice` when you slice the original string at character boundaries.

For input that you do not control (network data, file contents), run `utf8ValidateSlice` before you treat the bytes as text.

Validate one time, then iterate with no error path. Use this pattern in other code too. The alternative is a check for malformed input at each step. That check puts an error path in the middle of each loop, for a condition that the program already knew when the bytes arrived.

`utf8ByteSequenceLength` reads the first byte and tells you how many bytes the code point uses. All the functions above use it. Sometimes you want it directly, when you scan backward.

## A slice can cut a character in half

`s[0..2]` on `"héllo"` gives one valid byte and then half of `é`. Byte indices from `std.mem.find` (`indexOf` in older code) are always safe cut points when the needle is valid UTF-8. Other arithmetic on indices is not safe. If you truncate strings for display, iterate over code point slices and stop at the last full character.

[Unicode Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/unicode-recipes/) shows that function. It also shows how to find the character that contains a given byte, because std has no helper for that.

## What is not in std

The standard library has no case folding, no comparison for a locale, no normalisation and no collation. `std.ascii.toLower` exists and does exactly what its name says, but for ASCII only. That is correct for protocol keywords and incorrect for text in most languages.

The reason is size. Correct case conversion needs Unicode tables. The rules also depend on the language, in unexpected ways: the Turkish dotless i, the German sharp s, the Greek final sigma.

The position of Zig is this: a program that needs case conversion must depend on a library that keeps the tables current. The alternative is an old copy of the tables inside each binary that links `std`.

Thus, to compare text from a user, first decide what you really need. Byte equality is correct for identifiers and tokens. To find "the same word, typed in a different way", you need normalisation, and normalisation needs a library.

---

## Formatting

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/formatting/*

A format string is a string that is known at compile time. It has one `{}` placeholder for each argument. `{d}` prints a number, `{s}` prints a string, and `{any}` prints all other values.

The compiler checks the placeholders against the arguments. Thus a mismatch is a compile error, not wrong output at runtime.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "bufPrint formats into memory you own" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{s} is {d}", .{ "answer", 42 });
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, text, "answer is 42"));
}

test "common specifiers" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;

    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d}", .{255}), "255"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{x}", .{255}), "ff"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{X}", .{255}), "FF"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{b}", .{5}), "101"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{o}", .{8}), "10"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{c}", .{@as(u8, 'A')}), "A"));
}

test "width, alignment and fill" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;

    // {[fill][align][width]}: the align value is <, ^ or >.
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:5}", .{42}), "   42"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:<5}", .{42}), "42   "));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:^5}", .{42}), " 42  "));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:0>5}", .{42}), "00042"));
}

test "a width makes a signed integer carry its sign" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;

    // The same width with three types. A literal is `comptime_int`, and it
    // prints with no sign. The tests above depend on this result.
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:5}", .{42}), "   42"));

    // When you give a width, a signed value prints a `+` in front. The sign
    // is part of the number. Thus the fill goes in front of the sign, not
    // between the sign and the digits.
    const signed: i32 = 42;
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:5}", .{signed}), "  +42"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:<5}", .{signed}), "+42  "));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:0>5}", .{signed}), "00+42"));

    // An unsigned value has no sign. Thus a width adds the expected padding.
    const unsigned: u32 = 42;
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:5}", .{unsigned}), "   42"));

    // Without the width, the `+` does not appear. For this reason, you
    // usually see the problem only when you align a column of numbers.
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d}", .{signed}), "42"));
}

test "float precision" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d:.2}", .{3.14159}), "3.14"));
}

test "escaping braces" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try std.mem.print(&buf, "{{{d}}}", .{1}), "{1}"));
}

test "allocPrint when the length is unknown" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const text = try gpa.print("{d}-{d}", .{ 1, 2 });
    defer gpa.free(text);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, text, "1-2"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.formatting`)*

## The destination of the output

| Function | Writes to |
| --- | --- |
| `std.mem.print` | a buffer that you supply (no allocation) |
| `allocator.print` | new memory (the caller frees it) |
| `writer.print` | any writer |

`std.mem.print` returns a slice of the part that it filled. If the buffer is too small, it fails with `error.NoSpaceLeft`. It does not truncate the text.

## Specifiers

| Spec | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `{d}` | decimal |
| `{x}` / `{X}` | lower / upper hex |
| `{b}` / `{o}` | binary / octal |
| `{s}` | string |
| `{c}` | a byte as a character |
| `{any}` | structural dump |

## Width, alignment, precision

The form is `{[fill][align][width]}`. For alignment, use `<`, `^` or `>`:

```zig
"{d:5}"     // "   42"  (right by default for numbers)
"{d:<5}"    // "42   "
"{d:^5}"    // " 42  "
"{d:0>5}"   // "00042"
"{d:.2}"    // "3.14"
```

Right alignment is the default for each type, also for strings. This often causes mistakes: `{s:8}` puts the padding before the text, not after the text. A column of strings has three more rules for alignment. [String
Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/string-recipes/) gives these rules.

To write a literal brace, write it two times: `{{` and `}}`.

## A width makes a signed integer show its sign

The outputs above are the result of a literal, and a literal is `comptime_int`. If you give the same width to a signed value, a `+` appears in front of the value:

```zig
const signed: i32 = 42;
"{d:5}"    // "  +42"
"{d:<5}"   // "+42  "
"{d:0>5}"  // "00+42"
"{d}"      // "42"     no width, no sign
```

An unsigned value has no sign. Thus `{d:5}` on a `u32` adds padding to `"   42"`, as the table above shows.

The `+` is part of the width. The fill goes in front of the `+`, not between the sign and the digits. For this reason, `00042` becomes `00+42`.

A review usually does not find the bug that this causes. The format string is correct and the type is correct. The column is only one character narrower than the numbers in the column.

You see the bug when a heading does not align with a table that the program printed from an `i64`. If the value cannot be negative, the fix is a cast to the unsigned type.

## `bufPrint` and `allocPrint` moved

If you wrote Zig before, you know the first two rows of the table as `std.fmt.bufPrint` and `std.fmt.allocPrint`:

```zig
// older tutorials
const text = try std.fmt.bufPrint(&buf, "{d}", .{42});
const owned = try std.fmt.allocPrint(gpa, "{d}", .{42});

// current master
const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d}", .{42});
const owned = try gpa.print("{d}", .{42});
```

The two old names still resolve, and the error sets are the same. Now the definition of `std.fmt.BufPrintError` is `std.mem.PrintError`.

The buffer version moved to `std.mem`, because a function that fills a slice is a slice operation. The version that allocates became `Allocator.print`, a method next to `alloc` and `dupe`.

The new names do not say "print into a buffer" as `bufPrint` did. Also, `Allocator.print` does not look like a function that allocates. Thus read the receiver, not the verb:

- `mem` means that you supplied the memory.
- An allocator means that you own the result, and you must free it.

## The compiler checks the format string

The format string is a comptime parameter. Thus the compiler checks the argument count and each specifier against the argument types. A `{d}` for a string does not compile. A format string cannot fail at runtime.

---

## Advanced Formatting

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/advanced-formatting/*

In Zig, a custom `format` method takes only a `*std.Io.Writer`. `print` calls the method only when the format string asks for it with `{f}`. Width, fill and alignment go after a colon, as in `{d:0>4}`. The formatter does that work, not the type.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const Point = struct {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,

    // The `{f}` specifier uses a `format` method that takes a
    // `*std.Io.Writer`. Older Zig also gave a fmt string and options to the
    // method. That signature no longer applies.
    pub fn format(self: Point, writer: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
        try writer.print("({d}, {d})", .{ self.x, self.y });
    }
};

const Colour = enum { red, green, blue };

test "{f} calls a custom format method" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{f}", .{Point{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }});
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, text, "(1, 2)"));
}

test "{t} prints an enum tag name" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{t}", .{Colour.green});
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, text, "green"));
}

test "{any} falls back to a structural dump" {
    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{any}", .{[_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 }});
    // The exact text can change, but the text contains the elements.
    try expect(std.mem.find(u8, text, "1") != null);
}

test "format strings are checked at compile time" {
    // The wrong number of arguments is a compile error, not a runtime
    // error. A specifier that the type does not support is also a compile
    // error.
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const ok = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d} {s}", .{ 1, "two" });
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, ok, "1 two"));
}

test "writing to a list" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var out: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
    defer out.deinit();

    try out.writer.print("{f}", .{Point{ .x = 3, .y = 4 }});
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, out.written(), "(3, 4)"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.advanced-formatting`)*

## The shape of a custom `format` method changed

Zig 0.15 rewrote the `format` method. The method now takes only a writer:

```zig
pub fn format(self: Point, writer: *std.Io.Writer) std.Io.Writer.Error!void {
    try writer.print("({d}, {d})", .{ self.x, self.y });
}
```

The old signature also received the format string and an options struct. That signature no longer applies. A tutorial that shows `format(self,
comptime fmt: []const u8, options: FormatOptions, writer: anytype)` is older than the change.

The reason for the change explains the rest of this page. In the old design, the `format` method of each type had to parse the format string itself. Each method decided what `{d:>8}` meant for its type. Thus each implementation was slightly different, and most implementations ignored the options completely.

Now a type tells one time how it prints. The formatter controls the specifiers for width and alignment.

## `{f}` calls the method

`{}` and `{any}` do **not** use a custom `format` method. You must ask for the method with `{f}`:

```zig
try writer.print("{f}", .{point});   // (1, 2)
```

This rule is the other half of the same change. It often breaks code that you port from an older version. In the old design, `{}` found your method. Thus a type with a `format` method printed correctly in all places, and you did not have to ask.

Now `{}` prints the struct as the compiler sees it, and `{f}` asks for your method. The benefit is that the call site now shows which output you get: the type's own rendering or the generic dump. In the old design, you could not tell.

## Common specifiers

| Specifier | Prints |
| --- | --- |
| `{d}` | a number in decimal |
| `{x}` / `{X}` | hex, lower or upper case; also works on byte slices |
| `{b}` / `{o}` | binary, octal |
| `{s}` | a string, which is a `[]const u8` printed as text |
| `{c}` | one byte as a character |
| `{any}` | the generic dump, for any type |
| `{f}` | the type's own `format` method |
| `{t}` | the name of an enum tag or an error |
| `{!}` | an error union, as `error.Name` |
| `{*}` | the address in a pointer |

Width, fill and alignment come after a colon:

- `{d:0>4}` adds zeros on the left until the text has four characters.
- `{s:<20}` aligns the text on the left in a field of twenty characters.
- `{d:.2}` sets the number of decimal places for a float.

The compiler checks each specifier against the tuple that you give. A `{d}` for a string is a build error, not a runtime error. Four specifiers with three arguments is also a build error. Because of this check, the format string must be a comptime value.

## `{t}` for tag names

`{t}` prints the tag name of an enum or the name of an error. In older code, each call site called `@tagName`. `{t}` replaces that practice:

```zig
try writer.print("{t}", .{Colour.green});   // green
```

## Combine writers

`std.Io.Writer.Allocating` gives you an in-memory writer that can grow. It is the usual way to make a string from formatted parts:

```zig
var out: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
defer out.deinit();
try out.writer.print("{f}", .{point});
out.written();   // []const u8
```

For a string with a known maximum size, use `std.mem.print`. It writes into a buffer on the stack and returns the slice that it filled. It does not use an allocator. If the text is too long for the buffer, it returns an error.

- To format a number into a field of fixed size, use `std.mem.print`.
- When the length depends on the data, use `Allocating`.

```zig
var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
const text = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{d}%", .{percent});
```

These two functions replace `std.fmt.bufPrint` and `std.fmt.allocPrint`. The new names are `std.mem.print` and `Allocator.print`.

Both use the same `std.Io.Writer` interface that a file or a socket implements. Thus the same `print` call works with all of them. To test a function that takes a `*std.Io.Writer`, give the function a buffer. See [readers and writers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/readers-and-writers/).

---

## Parsing and Encoding

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/parsing-and-encoding/*

In Zig, `std.fmt.parseInt(T, text, base)` changes a string into an integer. It returns an error when the text is not a number, or when the number is too large for `T`. `std.fmt.bytesToHex` changes bytes into hex, and the codecs in `std.base64` change bytes into base64.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;
const expectError = std.testing.expectError;
const expectEqualStrings = std.testing.expectEqualStrings;

test "parseInt" {
    try expect(try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, "-42", 10) == -42);

    // Base 0 reads the prefix as a Zig literal does: 0x, 0o, 0b, or decimal.
    try expect(try std.fmt.parseInt(u32, "0xff", 0) == 255);
    try expect(try std.fmt.parseInt(u32, "0b1010", 0) == 10);

    // The function accepts underscore separators, as Zig literals do.
    try expect(try std.fmt.parseInt(u32, "1_000_000", 10) == 1_000_000);
}

test "parse failures are errors, not zeros" {
    try expectError(error.InvalidCharacter, std.fmt.parseInt(u8, "12a", 10));
    // The target type sets the limit: 300 is too large for a u8.
    try expectError(error.Overflow, std.fmt.parseInt(u8, "300", 10));
}

test "parseFloat" {
    try expect(try std.fmt.parseFloat(f64, "3.25") == 3.25);
    try expect(try std.fmt.parseFloat(f64, "-1e-3") == -0.001);
    try expect(std.math.isInf(try std.fmt.parseFloat(f32, "inf")));
}

test "hex" {
    const bytes = [_]u8{ 0xde, 0xad, 0xbe, 0xef };

    // bytesToHex returns an array of fixed size. The input gives the length
    // at compile time, thus the function needs no allocator.
    const hex = std.fmt.bytesToHex(bytes, .lower);
    try expectEqualStrings("deadbeef", &hex);

    var back: [4]u8 = undefined;
    _ = try std.fmt.hexToBytes(&back, "deadbeef");
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, &back, &bytes));
}

test "base64" {
    const codec = std.base64.standard;

    var enc_buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    const encoded = codec.Encoder.encode(&enc_buf, "zig");
    try expectEqualStrings("emln", encoded);

    var dec_buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    const n = try codec.Decoder.calcSizeForSlice(encoded);
    try codec.Decoder.decode(dec_buf[0..n], encoded);
    try expectEqualStrings("zig", dec_buf[0..n]);
}

test "url_safe base64 for tokens and file names" {
    // Standard base64 emits + and /. These characters break URLs and paths.
    const bytes = [_]u8{ 0xfb, 0xff };
    var buf: [8]u8 = undefined;
    try expectEqualStrings("+/8=", std.base64.standard.Encoder.encode(&buf, &bytes));
    try expectEqualStrings("-_8=", std.base64.url_safe.Encoder.encode(&buf, &bytes));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.parsing-and-encoding`)*

## A parse can fail, and the type shows it

`std.fmt.parseInt` returns an error union. Thus a bad character or a value out of range is a value that you must handle. It is never a silent zero.

The target type sets the limit. `parseInt(u8, "300", 10)` gives `error.Overflow`, because 300 is too large for a `u8`. With base `0`, the function reads the prefix as a Zig literal does: `0x`, `0o`, `0b`, or decimal. The function also accepts underscores.

Give a user a different report for each of the two errors:

- `error.InvalidCharacter` means that the text was not a number.
- `error.Overflow` means that the text was a number, but the type is too small.

A config parser that says "port must be a number" for `70000` does not help the user. The error already told you which problem occurred.

The target type does the bounds check, thus you do not write a separate range check. The check cannot disagree with the field that gets the value, because the type of the field *is* the range. A parse into `u16` for a port number rejects 70000, and you write no code for that check.

`parseFloat` accepts the usual decimal and scientific forms. It also accepts `inf` and `nan`.

The two functions parse the *full* string. Thus whitespace at the end or an unwanted newline causes an error. The function does not ignore the whitespace. When the input comes from a file or a terminal, remove the whitespace first with `std.mem.trim`. Input usually comes from one of these two places.

## Hex

`bytesToHex` returns an array of fixed size, not a slice. The reason is that the input gives the output length at compile time. Thus the function needs no allocator, and it cannot fail. `hexToBytes` does the opposite operation into a buffer that the caller supplies.

The function takes a case argument, `.lower` or `.upper`. Thus the format of a digest is always clear. The decoder accepts the two cases.

The return value is an array and not a slice. Thus, when a function needs a `[]const u8`, give it a reference to the array. A temporary value needs a `const` binding first, because without the binding there is nothing for the pointer to point at.

If you want to format the bytes in the output and not change them into a different value, use `{x}` on a byte slice. The format specifier does the same work directly in a `print`.

## base64: select the alphabet for the destination

`std.base64.standard` uses `+` and `/`. These characters are correct in a MIME body, but they are incorrect in a URL or a file name. `std.base64.url_safe` uses `-` and `_` in place of them.

Each codec has an `Encoder` and a `Decoder`. The decoder can fail, because the input can be invalid base64. Before you decode, calculate the size of the destination with `Decoder.calcSizeForSlice`.

| Codec | Emits | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `standard` | `A-Za-z0-9+/` | MIME, email, data URIs |
| `url_safe` | `A-Za-z0-9-_` | URLs, file names, tokens |
| `*_no_pad` | above, no `=` | fixed-width IDs |

People frequently do not calculate the size, and an incorrect guess does not cause a clear failure. Use these functions:

- To encode, use `Encoder.calcSize(n)`. It gives the exact output length: 4 bytes for each 3 input bytes, rounded up and padded.
- To decode, use `calcSizeForSlice`. It examines the padding and gives the exact answer.
- To allocate before you examine the input, use `calcSizeUpperBound`. It gives a safe value that can be too large.

The two decoder functions return an error for input that cannot be valid base64.

`encodeWriter` writes directly to a `std.Io.Writer`. Thus, when you encode a large payload into a response, you need no buffer between the two steps.

Base64 is not encryption, and it is not compression. It makes any bytes safe in a text field, and the result is one third larger.

---

## String Recipes

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/string-recipes/*

To pad a string in Zig, give it a width in the format spec, as in `{s:<8}`. To join strings at runtime, use `std.mem.concat`, which takes an allocator. For a case-insensitive search, use `std.ascii.findIgnoreCase`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;
const expectEqualStrings = std.testing.expectEqualStrings;

test "pad a string into a column" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;

    // There is no lpad or rjust. To pad a string, give {s} a width.
    // Right alignment is the default for all types, and strings too.
    try expectEqualStrings("[     zig]", try std.mem.print(&buf, "[{s:8}]", .{"zig"}));
    try expectEqualStrings("[zig     ]", try std.mem.print(&buf, "[{s:<8}]", .{"zig"}));
    try expectEqualStrings("[  zig   ]", try std.mem.print(&buf, "[{s:^8}]", .{"zig"}));

    // Put the fill byte before the alignment character.
    try expectEqualStrings("[.....zig]", try std.mem.print(&buf, "[{s:.>8}]", .{"zig"}));

    // The width is a minimum. It never truncates. If a value is wider than
    // the field, the formatter prints the full value and the column grows.
    try expectEqualStrings("[abcdefghij]", try std.mem.print(&buf, "[{s:>3}]", .{"abcdefghij"}));
}

test "the width can come from a value" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;

    // [1] takes the width from argument 1, not from the format string. Use it
    // when the column must be as wide as the longest row.
    const width: usize = 7;
    try expectEqualStrings("....zig", try std.mem.print(&buf, "{s:.>[1]}", .{ "zig", width }));
}

test "padding counts bytes, not characters" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;

    // Writer.alignBuffer calculates `width - buffer.len`, and len counts bytes.
    // The e-acute is two bytes. Thus this row gets one space less than it needs.
    const accented = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{s:>8}", .{"héllo"});
    try expect(accented.len == 8); // eight bytes
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints(accented) == 7); // seven columns

    var other: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const plain = try std.mem.print(&other, "{s:>8}", .{"world"});
    try expect(plain.len == 8);
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints(plain) == 8);

    // The spec is the same and the byte count is the same, but the two widths
    // on screen are different. A table of names loses its alignment when one
    // name has an accent.
}

test "concat is ++ with an allocator" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    // ++ works only when the compiler knows the two sides at compile time.
    const parts: []const []const u8 = &.{ "usr", "local", "bin" };
    const joined = try std.mem.concat(gpa, u8, parts);
    defer gpa.free(joined);
    try expectEqualStrings("usrlocalbin", joined);

    // joinZ adds the separator and a null terminator, for a C API.
    const path = try std.mem.joinZ(gpa, "/", parts);
    defer gpa.free(path);
    try expectEqualStrings("usr/local/bin", path);
    try expect(path[path.len] == 0);
}

test "measure the format before you allocate" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    // count runs the formatter with a writer that discards its output. Thus
    // the length is exact. You do not guess a size and grow the buffer later.
    const size = std.fmt.count("{d}:{d:0>2}", .{ 7, 5 });
    try expect(size == 4);

    const text = try gpa.alloc(u8, size);
    defer gpa.free(text);
    try expectEqualStrings("7:05", try std.mem.print(text, "{d}:{d:0>2}", .{ 7, 5 }));
}

test "replace without allocating" {
    // replacementSize gives the size of the destination. replace fills it and
    // returns the number of substitutions. replaceOwned does not give you that.
    const input = "a-b-c";
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;

    const size = std.mem.replacementSize(u8, input, "-", "__");
    try expect(size == 7);

    const count = std.mem.replace(u8, input, "-", "__", buf[0..size]);
    try expect(count == 2);
    try expectEqualStrings("a__b__c", buf[0..size]);
}

test "case-insensitive search" {
    // Use findIgnoreCase, not indexOfIgnoreCase. Zig removed indexOfIgnoreCase
    // and did not rename it. Thus old code that calls it does not compile.
    try expect(std.ascii.findIgnoreCase("Build.ZIG", "zig").? == 6);
    try expect(std.ascii.startsWithIgnoreCase("Build.zig", "BUILD"));
    try expect(std.ascii.endsWithIgnoreCase("Build.zig", ".ZIG"));

    // orderIgnoreCase sorts, and it does not allocate a lowercase copy first.
    try expect(std.ascii.orderIgnoreCase("apple", "Banana") == .lt);
}

test "classify a byte" {
    // trim cannot do this check: each byte must be a digit or a dash.
    const ok = for ("2026-07-30") |c| {
        if (!std.ascii.isDigit(c) and c != '-') break false;
    } else true;
    try expect(ok);

    try expect(std.ascii.isAlphabetic('z'));
    try expect(std.ascii.isWhitespace('\t'));
    try expect(std.ascii.isHex('f'));
    try expect(!std.ascii.isHex('g'));
}

test "build a string then take ownership of it" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;

    // ArrayList has no writer() on master. Writer.Allocating is the growable
    // buffer that you print into. toOwnedSlice gives the memory to the caller.
    var out: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
    defer out.deinit();

    for (0..3) |i| try out.writer.print("{d};", .{i});
    try expectEqualStrings("0;1;2;", out.written());

    const owned = try out.toOwnedSlice();
    defer gpa.free(owned);
    try expectEqualStrings("0;1;2;", owned);
    try expect(out.written().len == 0); // the writer kept nothing
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.string-recipes`)*

## Padding is a spec, not a function

Zig has no `lpad`, no `rjust` and no `String.padStart`. To pad a string, give `{s}` a width. The grammar is the one that [Formatting](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/formatting/) shows: `{[fill][align][width]}`. For a string, two things are different: the default, and the unit of the width.

Right alignment is the default for all types. Thus `{s:8}` puts the spaces *before* the text. This can surprise you if you know a language where strings align left and numbers align right. Write the alignment that you want:

```zig
"{s:8}"     // "     zig"
"{s:<8}"    // "zig     "
"{s:^8}"    // "  zig   "
"{s:.>8}"   // ".....zig"
```

The width is a minimum. If a value is wider than the field, the formatter prints the full value, and the column becomes wider. The formatter never truncates a value.

## The width counts bytes, not characters

The formatter does not decode the value first. The standard library says this in its own docs: alignment "is not Unicode-aware; appropriate only when used with raw bytes or ASCII."

A table of names stays aligned until one of the names has an accent. To count what a reader calls a character is a different problem. [Unicode Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/unicode-recipes/) shows how to solve it.

## Join at runtime

`++` is a compile-time operator. When the program knows the parts only at runtime, use `std.mem.concat`. It does the same work, and it takes an allocator. `joinZ` puts a separator between the parts and a null terminator at the end. Use it when you give the result to a C API.

If you prefer to calculate the buffer size yourself, use `std.fmt.count`. It runs the formatter with a writer that discards its output, and it returns the exact length. Then you make one allocation of the correct size, and you do not guess.

## Replace without an allocator

`std.mem.replaceOwned` is the easy form, and it allocates. The two functions below it do not allocate:

- `replacementSize` tells you the size of the result.
- `replace` fills memory that you already have.

`replace` also returns the number of substitutions that it made. The owned version does not give you that number.

## Ignore case, with care

`std.ascii` has the full family of functions: `startsWithIgnoreCase`, `endsWithIgnoreCase`, `findIgnoreCase`, and `orderIgnoreCase`. Use `orderIgnoreCase` to sort, because it does not allocate a lowercase copy first.

`findIgnoreCase` replaced a function that Zig removed. An older version had `indexOfIgnoreCase`, and Zig removed it fully. Thus code that uses the old name does not compile. It does not continue to work silently. The `std.mem` search functions are different: their old names still exist as aliases.

All of these functions stop at byte 127.

## When you want a String type

`std.mem` and `std.ascii` give you bytes and a set of functions that operate on them. They do not give you a type that behaves like a string class. If you want that shape, [zig-string](https://github.com/JakubSzark/zig-string) is a UTF-8 aware `String` with the usual methods. It has the MIT license, and its author still maintains it.

It is a dependency, not part of `std`, and on this site that difference is important. Each night, CI compiles and runs each snippet on this site against Zig master. An external library follows the compiler on its own schedule.

---

## Unicode Recipes

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/unicode-recipes/*

To truncate a UTF-8 string in Zig without a cut through a character, walk `nextCodepointSlice`. Stop before the slice that goes past the limit. To convert to and from UTF-16, use `std.unicode.utf8ToUtf16LeAlloc` and `utf16LeToUtf8Alloc`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;
const expectEqualStrings = std.testing.expectEqualStrings;

test "length from the first byte" {
    const s = "héllo";

    // The lead byte gives the length of the sequence. Thus you can decode
    // one character, and you do not scan forward for the next boundary.
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8ByteSequenceLength(s[0]) == 1);
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8ByteSequenceLength(s[1]) == 2);

    // Decode with the function for that length. The old utf8Decode took a
    // slice, and it is deprecated. It asserted that the length matched, and it
    // could not tell you when the length did not match.
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8Decode2(s[1..3].*) == 'é');

    // A continuation byte is not a start byte, and the function tells you so.
    try std.testing.expectError(error.Utf8InvalidStartByte, std.unicode.utf8ByteSequenceLength(s[2]));
}

test "how many bytes will this codepoint need" {
    // The same question for the encoder. Ask before you set the size of a buffer.
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8CodepointSequenceLength('a') == 1);
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8CodepointSequenceLength('é') == 2);
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8CodepointSequenceLength('€') == 3);
}

/// Cut `s` to `max_bytes` or less. Stop at the last full character, not in
/// the middle of a character. std has no function for this.
fn truncate(s: []const u8, max_bytes: usize) []const u8 {
    if (s.len <= max_bytes) return s;
    const view = std.unicode.Utf8View.init(s) catch return s[0..0];
    var it = view.iterator();
    var end: usize = 0;
    while (it.nextCodepointSlice()) |slice| {
        const next = end + slice.len;
        if (next > max_bytes) break;
        end = next;
    }
    return s[0..end];
}

test "truncate at a character boundary" {
    const s = "héllo";

    // Byte 2 is inside the e-acute. The simple cut gives invalid UTF-8.
    try expect(!std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(s[0..2]));

    // truncate moves back to the last full character.
    try expectEqualStrings("h", truncate(s, 2));
    try expect(std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(truncate(s, 2)));

    try expectEqualStrings("hé", truncate(s, 3));
    try expectEqualStrings("héllo", truncate(s, 99));
}

test "find the character that contains byte 2" {
    const s = "héllo";

    // Continuation bytes are 0b10xxxxxx. Walk back while the byte is a
    // continuation byte. The walk stops on the start byte of the character.
    var i: usize = 2;
    while (i > 0 and (s[i] & 0xC0) == 0x80) i -= 1;

    try expect(i == 1);
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8ByteSequenceLength(s[i]) == 2);
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8Decode2(s[i..][0..2].*) == 'é');
}

test "look ahead without consuming" {
    const view = try std.unicode.Utf8View.init("héllo");
    var it = view.iterator();

    // peek returns the bytes of the next n characters, and does not move the
    // cursor. Thus a parser can decide before it selects a branch.
    try expectEqualStrings("hé", it.peek(2));
    try expect(it.i == 0);

    try expect(it.nextCodepoint().? == 'h');
    try expectEqualStrings("él", it.peek(2));
}

test "a comptime view cannot fail" {
    // initComptime validates during compilation. Thus a literal needs no try,
    // and a malformed literal is a compile error, not a runtime branch.
    const view = comptime std.unicode.Utf8View.initComptime("héllo");
    var it = view.iterator();
    try expect(it.nextCodepoint().? == 'h');
}

test "print bytes you did not validate" {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;

    // fmtUtf8 puts U+FFFD in place of ill-formed sequences, and does not fail.
    // A log line needs this behaviour for untrusted input.
    const broken = [_]u8{ 'a', 0xff, 'b' };
    const shown = try std.mem.print(&buf, "{f}", .{std.unicode.fmtUtf8(&broken)});
    try expectEqualStrings("a\u{FFFD}b", shown);
}

test "cross to UTF-16 and back" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const s = "héllo";

    // Each Windows path goes through this conversion. The unit counts are
    // different: five UTF-16 units and six UTF-8 bytes.
    const wide = try std.unicode.utf8ToUtf16LeAlloc(gpa, s);
    defer gpa.free(wide);
    try expect(wide.len == 5);
    try expect(s.len == 6);

    const back = try std.unicode.utf16LeToUtf8Alloc(gpa, wide);
    defer gpa.free(back);
    try expectEqualStrings(s, back);
}

test "a combining mark is two codepoints" {
    // The two strings show as one character. The second string is e and a
    // combining acute accent. Thus the codepoint count is 2, but a reader sees 1.
    const composed = "é";
    const decomposed = "e\u{301}";

    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints(composed) == 1);
    try expect(try std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints(decomposed) == 2);
    try expect(!std.mem.eql(u8, composed, decomposed));

    // Nothing in std normalizes the two strings to one form, or counts what a
    // reader calls a character. You need a Unicode library for that.
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.unicode-recipes`)*

## Length from the first byte

UTF-8 puts the sequence length in the lead byte. Thus you can decode one character, and you do not have to scan forward to find the start of the next character. `utf8ByteSequenceLength` reads the length. `utf8Decode2`, `utf8Decode3` or `utf8Decode4` changes those bytes into a `u21`.

The length is in the name because each of those functions takes an array of fixed size. An older version had one `utf8Decode` that took a slice, and that function is now deprecated. It asserted that the length matched the lead byte, and it could not tell you when the length did not match. The new way is to get the length first and then decode that number of bytes. It is the same work, and the design prevents the mistake.

If you give `utf8ByteSequenceLength` a continuation byte, it returns `error.Utf8InvalidStartByte`. You want this check when an index comes from arithmetic and not from an iterator. `utf8CodepointSequenceLength` does the opposite work for the encoder. Use it to get the number of bytes that a codepoint needs, before you calculate the size of the buffer.

## Cut a string safely

The [Unicode](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/unicode/) chapter says to iterate over codepoint slices and stop at the last full character. This chapter shows that function:

1. Walk `nextCodepointSlice`.
2. Keep the end offset of the characters so far.
3. Stop before the first slice that would put the end past the limit.

The simple `s[0..max]` gives invalid UTF-8 when the cut is in the middle of a character. Nothing fails at the cut. The failure occurs where code decodes those bytes, possibly in a different program.

## Which character contains byte 7

The standard library has no helper for this, thus you must write it. All continuation bytes match `0b10xxxxxx`. Thus, walk back while `(b & 0xC0) == 0x80`. The walk stops on the start byte of the character that contains the byte.

You can remember this rule, and you do not need to look for it. A UTF-8 character is a maximum of four bytes. The design of the format makes sure that this walk is always short and never ambiguous.

## Look ahead, and views that cannot fail

`Utf8Iterator.peek(n)` returns the bytes of the next `n` characters, and does not move the cursor. A parser needs this before it selects a branch.

`Utf8View.initComptime` validates the bytes during compilation. A literal needs no `try`. A malformed literal is a compile error, not a runtime path that you must handle.

## Bytes that you did not validate

`std.unicode.fmtUtf8` prints ill-formed input with U+FFFD in place of the bad sequences. It does not return an error. A log line almost always needs this behaviour. When you debug bad input, you still need to see the input in the output.

## UTF-16 is for Windows

Windows paths are UTF-16. Thus each cross-platform program uses `utf8ToUtf16LeAlloc` and `utf16LeToUtf8Alloc` at that boundary. The counts of UTF-16 units are different from the byte counts. Because of that difference, the conversion is explicit and never automatic.

## What std does not do

The standard library has no support for grapheme clusters, no display width, no case folding, no normalization, and no case mapping above ASCII. A hand-written loop cannot solve this problem.

`é` can be one codepoint or two codepoints, and the two forms are not equal. To decide that they are the same string, you need the Unicode tables. Those tables are large, and they change with each Unicode revision. They belong in a library.

[zg](https://codeberg.org/atman/zg) by Sam Atman is the library to use. It divides the work into separate modules: graphemes, display width, letter case, case folding, normalization, word breaks, scripts, and emoji. Thus a program pays only for the tables that it uses. Codeberg is the upstream, not a mirror.

---

## Readers and Writers

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/readers-and-writers/*

In Zig, code reads bytes through `std.Io.Reader` and writes bytes through `std.Io.Writer`. Thus one parser or formatter works with a file, a socket or a fixed buffer.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "iterate lines with takeDelimiter" {
    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed("line one\nline two\n");

    // `takeDelimiter` consumes the delimiter and returns null at the end.
    // A line loop needs this behaviour.
    var count: usize = 0;
    while (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        count += 1;
        try expect(line.len == 8);
    }
    try expect(count == 2);
}

test "the Exclusive variant leaves the delimiter behind" {
    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed("line one\nline two\n");

    const first = try reader.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n');
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, first, "line one"));

    // The first call did NOT consume the '\n'. Thus the next call sees the
    // '\n' immediately and returns an empty slice. To loop over lines, use
    // `takeDelimiter`. Or call `toss(1)` to skip the delimiter.
    const second = try reader.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n');
    try expect(second.len == 0);

    reader.toss(1);
    const third = try reader.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n');
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, third, "line two"));
}

test "take a fixed number of bytes" {
    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed("abcdef");
    const chunk = try reader.take(3);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, chunk, "abc"));
}

test "write into a caller-owned buffer" {
    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    var writer: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&buf);

    try writer.writeAll("hello");
    try writer.print(" {d}", .{42});

    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, writer.buffered(), "hello 42"));
}

test "allocating writer grows as needed" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var writer: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
    defer writer.deinit();

    for (0..5) |i| try writer.writer.print("{d},", .{i});
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, writer.written(), "0,1,2,3,4,"));
}

test "a fixed writer reports when it runs out" {
    var buf: [4]u8 = undefined;
    var writer: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&buf);
    try std.testing.expectError(error.WriteFailed, writer.writeAll("too long"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.readers-and-writers`)*

Zig 0.15 replaced the old generic `Reader` and `Writer` with the non-generic `std.Io.Reader` and `std.Io.Writer`. Two of the changes are important in daily work:

1. **The buffer belongs to the interface**, not to the implementation. You supply the buffer. Thus there is no hidden allocation, and you control the size.
2. **Writers have a buffer**, thus you must call `flush`. A common mistake with the new API is to forget the flush.

The important word in the first sentence is "non-generic". The old `Writer` was a type parameter. Thus each function that took a writer was generic, and the compiler compiled it again for each writer type. A struct that stored a writer also had to be generic.

`std.Io.Writer` is a concrete type that holds a pointer and a vtable. Thus a function takes a `*std.Io.Writer` and needs nothing more. Compile times become shorter, error messages become shorter, and you can put a writer in a field.

## Create them

```zig
var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed("some bytes");
var writer: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&buf);

var growable: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
```

For files, `file.writerStreaming(io, &buf)` gives you a `File.Writer`. The `.interface` field of the `File.Writer` is the `std.Io.Writer` to use.

Learn to recognise that `.interface` field, because it is a pattern. The concrete type holds the state that a file writer needs. It also contains the generic interface as a field. Thus you give `&file_writer.interface` to each function that takes a writer.

Sometimes the compiler gives an error about a `File.Writer` where it expects a `*std.Io.Writer`. Almost always, the cause is that you forgot `.interface`.

## Flush, and where to put the flush

```zig
var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
var fw = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
defer fw.interface.flush() catch {};

try fw.interface.print("{d}\n", .{42});
```

No data goes to the file until the buffer is full or you flush. A program that prints and then exits without a flush prints nothing. The first time that you see this result, it can confuse you. For this reason, put the `defer` directly below the line that creates the writer.

You select the buffer size, and the size is important:

- A buffer of one byte causes a syscall for each write.
- Four kilobytes is a page, and it is a sensible default.
- A larger buffer helps for bulk output. It gives no benefit to a program that prints six lines.

## Read lines: select the correct variant

It is easy to confuse these three methods. An earlier version of this page had this error:

| Method | Consumes delimiter | At end of stream |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `takeDelimiter` | yes | returns `null` |
| `takeDelimiterExclusive` | **no** | error |
| `takeDelimiterInclusive` | yes, and includes it | error |

Thus, when you call `takeDelimiterExclusive` two times on `"a\nb\n"`, it returns `"a"` and then an **empty slice**. The reason is that the `\n` is still in the reader. For a line loop, use this code:

```zig
while (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| { ... }
```

If you use the exclusive form, call `toss(n)` to skip the bytes yourself.

The slice that a `take` returns points into the buffer of the reader. The slice is valid until the next read. To keep a line, copy it. `ArrayList.items` has the same rule: the slice is a borrowed view. This rule lets you read a large file with a small buffer.

## When the buffer is full

When the buffer of a `.fixed` writer is full, the writer fails with `error.WriteFailed`. It does not silently remove the extra bytes.

A reader has the same rule. When a line is longer than the buffer of the reader, the result is `error.StreamTooLong`, not a partial line. The interface does not give you data that looks complete but is not complete.

Sometimes the input comes from a source that you do not trust, and a line can have any length. In that case, the error is your length limit. Usually it is correct to treat the error as a protocol violation.

## Why one interface

With one interface, the parts work together. A parser that uses `*std.Io.Reader` gets its tests with `.fixed("literal input")`. Then the same parser, with no change, reads from a socket in production. A formatter that uses `*std.Io.Writer` writes to a file, a buffer, or a hash.

For this reason, the [networking](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/) chapters can run in a browser. The protocol code takes bytes and returns bytes. Only the chapters about sockets need a socket.

---

## JSON

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/json/*

`std.json.parseFromSlice` parses JSON into your own Zig struct. It matches the object keys to the field names. `std.json.Stringify.value` writes a value as JSON to any writer.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const Config = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    port: u16,
    debug: bool = false, // a default applies when the field is absent
};

test "parse into a struct" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const text =
        \\{ "name": "server", "port": 8080 }
    ;

    // The parse result owns its allocations. deinit frees all of them.
    const parsed = try std.json.parseFromSlice(Config, gpa, text, .{});
    defer parsed.deinit();

    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, parsed.value.name, "server"));
    try expect(parsed.value.port == 8080);
    try expect(parsed.value.debug == false);
}

test "unknown fields are rejected by default" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const text =
        \\{ "name": "x", "port": 1, "extra": true }
    ;
    try std.testing.expectError(
        error.UnknownField,
        std.json.parseFromSlice(Config, gpa, text, .{}),
    );

    // Turn off the check when the payload can have fields that you do
    // not model.
    const lenient = try std.json.parseFromSlice(Config, gpa, text, .{
        .ignore_unknown_fields = true,
    });
    defer lenient.deinit();
    try expect(lenient.value.port == 1);
}

test "dynamic values when the shape is unknown" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const parsed = try std.json.parseFromSlice(
        std.json.Value,
        gpa,
        \\{ "a": [1, 2, 3] }
    ,
        .{},
    );
    defer parsed.deinit();

    const array = parsed.value.object.get("a").?.array;
    try expect(array.items.len == 3);
    try expect(array.items[0].integer == 1);
}

test "serialise" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var out: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
    defer out.deinit();

    try std.json.Stringify.value(
        Config{ .name = "out", .port = 99, .debug = true },
        .{},
        &out.writer,
    );
    try expect(std.mem.find(u8, out.written(), "\"port\":99") != null);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.json`)*

## Parse into a struct

`parseFromSlice(T, gpa, text, .{})` puts JSON into your type by the field names of the type. The result owns each allocation that it made:

```zig
const parsed = try std.json.parseFromSlice(Config, gpa, text, .{});
defer parsed.deinit();
parsed.value.port;
```

Look at `parsed.value`. The payload is behind the owner, thus one `deinit` frees the full tree. The strings in `parsed.value` point into that arena, thus they become invalid with the arena. If a value must live longer than the parse, duplicate the value.

This design solves a problem that each JSON library has. A parsed document is a tree of small allocations with no single owner. To free the tree correctly, you must walk the tree.

The Zig solution is to allocate the full tree from an arena in the `Parsed(T)` wrapper. Then `deinit` is one call that releases all of the memory at the same time, and it cannot miss a node.

The cost is that the lifetime is all or nothing. If you keep one string from the document, the string does not keep the arena alive. After `deinit`, the arena is gone, and you have a dangling slice. Copy out the values that you need. Or keep the full `Parsed` alive while you use any part of it.

## How the types map to JSON

The compiler decides the mapping from your struct at compile time. The validation comes from this mapping.

| Zig | JSON |
| --- | --- |
| `bool`, integers, floats | the matching primitive |
| `[]const u8` | a string |
| `?T` | the value, or `null`, or absent |
| `[]T` | an array |
| a struct | an object, matched by field name |
| an enum | a string equal to a tag name |
| a tagged union | an object with one key, the tag name |

If a JSON value is too large for an integer field, the result is an error, not a truncation. A string in the place of a number is an error that gives the name of the field.

You write none of these checks. The compiler makes them from the struct definition. Thus the checks always match the struct.

## Absent fields and unknown fields

A field with a default is optional in the input. By default, an **unknown** field is an error:

```zig
error.UnknownField
```

This default finds typos in config files. Turn off the default only when you consume a payload that you do not model fully:

```zig
.{ .ignore_unknown_fields = true }
```

Know the difference between a field that can be absent and a field that can be null:

- `?u16` with no default accepts `null`, but the key must be present.
- `u16 = 8080` accepts an absent key.
- `?u16 = null` accepts the two conditions.

Say which one you mean. If you do not, a config file can get a default value without a report, when the parser must reject the file.

## When you do not know the shape

For a dynamic tree, parse into `std.json.Value`. Then walk `.object`, `.array`,
`.integer`, `.string`, and the other fields. When possible, use a concrete struct. Then the compiler checks the field names, and you get validation.

`std.json.Value` is a tagged union. Thus a walk of the tree is a `switch`, and the exhaustiveness check applies.

A usual compromise is a struct for the parts that are important to you. Give one field the type `std.json.Value` for the part that you pass through without change.

For input that is too large for memory, use `std.json.Scanner`. This is the streaming form. It emits tokens while it reads. Thus a fixed buffer can process a document of many gigabytes. `std.json.Scanner` is more difficult to use. Thus use it only when the document does not fit in memory.

## Write JSON

`std.json.Stringify.value(x, .{}, &writer)` serialises a value to any writer. To make a string, use it with `std.Io.Writer.Allocating`.

Options control the shape of the output. Use `.whitespace = .indent_2` for output that a person will read. Use the default for output that a machine will read.

The function writes to any `std.Io.Writer`. Thus it can serialise directly to a file or a socket, without an intermediate string.

---

## Filesystem

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/filesystem/*

Zig 0.16 moved the filesystem API onto `std.Io`. Of all the changes, this change most often makes older filesystem examples fail to compile.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = std.heap.page_allocator;

    var buf_out: [128]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf_out);
    const out = &stdout.interface;

    // `std.fs.cwd()` is now `std.Io.Dir.cwd()`. Each operation that uses
    // the disk takes the io instance explicitly.
    var dir = std.Io.Dir.cwd();

    // Create, write, close.
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, "example.txt", .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = file.writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    try writer.interface.writeAll("written by zig\n");
    try writer.interface.flush();

    // Read the full file again.
    const contents = try dir.readFileAlloc(io, "example.txt", gpa, .limited(1 << 20));
    defer gpa.free(contents);
    std.debug.assert(std.mem.eql(u8, contents, "written by zig\n"));
    try out.print("read back {d} bytes\n", .{contents.len});

    // Walk a directory. The number of entries depends on the contents of
    // the working directory. Thus count only the one file that this program
    // created. A value from the real contents of the directory can be
    // different on your machine and on the build that verified this page.
    var iterable = try dir.openDir(io, ".", .{ .iterate = true });
    defer iterable.close(io);
    var it = iterable.iterate();
    var found = false;
    while (try it.next(io)) |entry| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, entry.name, "example.txt")) found = true;
    }
    try out.print("example.txt listed in cwd: {}\n", .{found});

    try dir.deleteFile(io, "example.txt");
    try out.flush();
}

// This program runs in wasm. The two runners give the program an empty
// directory as its working directory. In CI, it is a temporary directory. In
// your browser, it is a directory in memory. Thus `Dir.cwd()` holds only the
// file that this program creates.
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.filesystem`)*

## What moved

| Was | Now |
| --- | --- |
| `std.fs.cwd()` | `std.Io.Dir.cwd()` |
| `std.fs.File` | `std.Io.File` |
| `dir.openFile(path, .{})` | `dir.openFile(io, path, .{})` |
| `file.close()` | `file.close(io)` |

The pattern is the same everywhere. Each function that can block takes the `io` instance as its first argument. You get the instance from `main`:

```zig
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
```

## The reason for the change

The signature of a function now tells you if the function does I/O. An `Allocator` parameter tells you in the same way that a function allocates. The *caller* decides how the I/O runs: threaded, evented or a different way. The standard library does not make the decision for you.

## Read a full file

```zig
const contents = try dir.readFileAlloc(io, path, gpa, .limited(1 << 20));
defer gpa.free(contents);
```

The limit is mandatory, not optional. No API can read an unlimited quantity of untrusted input into memory by accident.

## The location of the file

A WASI program can use only the directories that the host opens for it before it starts. The name for these directories is preopened directories.

The playground opens one empty directory for each run. In your browser, the directory is in memory. In CI, the directory is a temporary directory on disk.

Zig uses the first preopened directory as the current directory. Thus `Dir.cwd()` works, and this snippet runs in the two places. CI compares the output of the two runs with the same `.expected` file.

[A File Descriptor Is a Number](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/file-descriptors/) shows the other side. The host gives a WASI program its first descriptors. The program does not open them.

## A directory is a handle, not a string

`std.Io.Dir` is an open directory, and Zig resolves paths relative to it. This also makes the code safer. When Zig resolves a path against an open handle, a different program cannot change the path between the check and the use. That gap is the cause of a full family of security bugs.

In practice, open the directory one time and do all operations through the directory:

```zig
var dir = try std.Io.Dir.cwd().openDir(io, "data", .{ .iterate = true });
defer dir.close(io);

var it = dir.iterate();
while (try it.next(io)) |entry| {
    if (entry.kind != .file) continue;
    // entry.name is valid until the next next(io)
}
```

Look at `.iterate = true` in the open options. Without this option, you cannot iterate over the directory. On some platforms, iteration needs different permissions. Zig makes you say which permissions you want, and it does not ask for all of them.

`entry.name` points into the buffer of the iterator, and the next iteration replaces it. This is the same rule for a borrowed view as in all other places. To keep a name, copy it.

For a recursive walk, use `walk`. It goes down into each subdirectory for you, and it gives paths relative to the start directory. It needs an allocator, because the depth is not known before the walk.

## Handle each error

Filesystem calls fail for ordinary reasons, and the error set is the list of these reasons. Some examples are `error.FileNotFound`,
`error.AccessDenied`, `error.IsDir` and `error.NoSpaceLeft`. A real program handles each of these cases differently. A `switch` on the error is the way to do this.

Design your code for this fact: a check and then an action is not atomic. `if (exists) open()` can fail between the two lines. Thus do the operation, and then handle the error. When `openFile` returns `error.FileNotFound`, that result is the check. The check is atomic, and it needs no extra call.

## Write a file safely

If you write directly into the destination, a crash in the middle of the write can occur. Then a truncated file replaces the valid file. The fix is the same on all systems:

1. Write a temporary file in the same directory.
2. Flush the temporary file.
3. Rename the temporary file to the name of the target.

A rename is atomic in one filesystem. Thus a reader sees the old contents or the new contents, and never a mixture.

`dir.rename(io, "config.json.tmp", "config.json")` is the last step. Use this pattern for all data that a user does not want to lose. Keep the temporary file in the same directory. A rename across filesystems is a copy, and a copy is not atomic.

On master, the standard library has no `AtomicFile` helper. Older code that used one now writes the three steps by hand. The steps are four lines. When you write them yourself, the flush is visible. Code most often forgets the flush.

## Paths

`std.Io.Dir.path` holds the functions that only change strings. They need no `Io` instance: `join`, `dirname`, `basename`, `extension`, `isAbsolute`. These functions know the path separator of each system. Thus `join` makes backslashes on Windows and forward slashes on other systems. If you concatenate strings to make a path, you get this wrong.

Older code uses the name `std.fs.path`. It moved with the rest of the filesystem API.

There is a second reason to use these functions. `join` allocates, and it returns a slice that you must free. Thus you must decide the lifetime of the path. A path in a stack buffer can live longer than its frame, and `join` prevents this error.

---

## Command-Line Arguments

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/command-line/*

`main` receives a `std.process.Init`. A Zig program reads its command-line arguments from `init.minimal.args`, which is the `std.process.Args` inside that value.
