The program reads its environment from `init.environ_map`. The standard library has no argument parser, thus you write the loop for the flags.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;
const expectEqualStrings = std.testing.expectEqualStrings;

test "iterate arguments" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    // A real program iterates over `init.minimal.args` (see the page). This
    // test parses a fixed command line with the same iterator. Thus the test
    // gives the same result in the browser sandbox, which has no argv.
    var it = try std.process.Args.IteratorGeneral(.{}).init(gpa, "app --name zig -v");
    defer it.deinit();

    try expectEqualStrings("app", it.next().?); // argv[0] is the program name
    try expectEqualStrings("--name", it.next().?);
    try expectEqualStrings("zig", it.next().?);
    try expectEqualStrings("-v", it.next().?);
    try expect(it.next() == null); // no more arguments
}

test "a minimal flag parser" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    var it = try std.process.Args.IteratorGeneral(.{}).init(gpa, "app --verbose --out result.txt");
    defer it.deinit();

    _ = it.next(); // skip argv[0]
    var verbose = false;
    var out: []const u8 = "a.out";
    while (it.next()) |arg| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--verbose")) {
            verbose = true;
        } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, arg, "--out")) {
            // A flag that takes a value gets the next token itself.
            out = it.next() orelse return error.MissingValue;
        }
    }
    try expect(verbose);
    try expectEqualStrings("result.txt", out);
}

test "environment variables" {
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    // `init.environ_map` has exactly this type, and the real environment
    // fills it. This test makes the map by hand. Thus the test needs nothing
    // from outside.
    var env = std.process.Environ.Map.init(gpa);
    defer env.deinit();
    try env.put("EDITOR", "vim");

    try expectEqualStrings("vim", env.get("EDITOR").?);
    try expect(env.get("MISSING") == null);
    try expect(env.contains("EDITOR"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.command-line`)*

## The source of the real arguments

Your `main` receives a `std.process.Init`. This is the same value that holds `io`, `gpa`, and the arena. Its `minimal.args` field is a `std.process.Args`. `iterate` changes the field into an iterator. The `next` method of the iterator gives each argument as a `[:0]const u8`:

```zig
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var it = init.minimal.args.iterate();
    defer it.deinit();

    _ = it.next(); // argv[0]: the program's own path
    while (it.next()) |arg| {
        // ... handle arg ...
    }
}
```

The snippet above uses `Args.IteratorGeneral`. This iterator parses a fixed string, and its `next` has the identical shape. For this reason, the snippet can run in your browser. The WASI sandbox has no argv of its own, thus a real iterator returns nothing. The parse logic that you write is the same for the two iterators.

## You write the parser

The standard library has no `argparse`. For a small tool, the loop in the snippet is usually sufficient. Compare each argument to a flag. If the flag takes a value, get the next token.

The first argument is always the program path. Thus skip the first argument before you parse. Use a package (see the Build System section) only when you need subcommands, help text, and typed conversion.

## Environment variables

`init.environ_map` is a `std.process.Environ.Map`. The program makes this map from the real environment. It works like the other maps in this section: `get` returns an optional, and `contains` returns a bool.

An environment variable is often absent, and that is normal. Thus a `null` from `get` is a usual case that you handle, not an error.

## Start other programs

To run a subprocess, use `std.process.Child`. Like all code that uses the outside world, `std.process.Child` takes an `Io`. You can connect the stdin, stdout, and stderr of the child, or you can capture its output. A child needs a real OS process. Thus the browser sandbox cannot show an example.

## Conventions to follow

Users expect these conventions, thus your loop must follow them:

- `-v` is a short flag, and `--verbose` is its long form. Both forms must work.
- `--output=file` and `--output file` are both common. If you accept only one form, you annoy some users.
- Users expect combined short flags in a tool similar to a Unix tool. For example, `-abc` means `-a -b -c`.
- `--` ends the options. Each argument after it is a positional argument, also if it starts with a dash. This is the only way to give the name of a file called `-r`.
- By convention, `-` alone means standard input, not a file.

None of these conventions is difficult, and it is easy to forget each of them. Decide at the start which conventions you support. Then a bug report does not tell you about the gap.

## Fail correctly

The error reports of a command-line program are its user interface. Three rules cover most of it.

First, write errors to stderr, not to stdout. Another program can read the output through a pipe. Thus the output stream must contain only the data. A diagnostic in the data becomes a bug in a shell pipeline, and that bug is difficult to find.

Second, exit with a non-zero status on failure. When `main` returns an error, Zig does this for you. In a debug build, Zig also prints the error name and a return trace. To set a specific status, use `std.process.exit(2)`. By convention, 0 is success, 1 is a normal failure, and 2 is a usage error.

Third, tell the user what was wrong and what to do. "invalid argument" is a worse message than "unknown option --outpt (did you mean --output?)". The loop already knows which token failed. Thus the better message costs only a few lines.

## Arguments are untrusted input

All data on the command line came from outside the program:

- A number is a `parseInt` that can fail.
- A path can be absent.
- A count can be very large.

Check the value where it enters the program. Then convert it into a type that holds the constraint. The rest of the program then uses a `u16` port and not a string that somebody typed. See [parsing and
encoding](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/parsing-and-encoding/).

---

## Sorting

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/sorting/*

In Zig, `std.mem.sort` sorts a slice in place. The sort is stable, and it uses a less-than function that you supply. `std.mem.sortUnstable` is not stable, but it does less work.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const Person = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    age: u8,
};

fn byAge(_: void, a: Person, b: Person) bool {
    return a.age < b.age;
}

test "sort numbers" {
    var numbers = [_]u8{ 5, 3, 9, 1 };
    std.mem.sort(u8, &numbers, {}, std.sort.asc(u8));
    try expect(numbers[0] == 1 and numbers[3] == 9);

    std.mem.sort(u8, &numbers, {}, std.sort.desc(u8));
    try expect(numbers[0] == 9);
}

test "sort structs with a custom comparator" {
    var people = [_]Person{
        .{ .name = "c", .age = 30 },
        .{ .name = "a", .age = 10 },
        .{ .name = "b", .age = 20 },
    };
    // The `{}` is the context argument. The sort gives this value to each
    // comparison. It is useful when the order depends on external data.
    std.mem.sort(Person, &people, {}, byAge);
    try expect(people[0].age == 10);
}

test "sort strings lexicographically" {
    var words = [_][]const u8{ "pear", "apple", "fig" };
    std.mem.sort([]const u8, &words, {}, struct {
        fn lessThan(_: void, a: []const u8, b: []const u8) bool {
            return std.mem.order(u8, a, b) == .lt;
        }
    }.lessThan);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, words[0], "apple"));
}

test "binary search a sorted slice" {
    const sorted = [_]u8{ 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 };
    const index = std.sort.binarySearch(u8, &sorted, @as(u8, 7), struct {
        fn order(key: u8, item: u8) std.math.Order {
            return std.math.order(key, item);
        }
    }.order);
    try expect(index.? == 3);
}

test "sortUnstable is not stable, and it does less work" {
    var numbers = [_]u8{ 4, 2, 6 };
    // `std.mem.sort` is stable. When equal elements are interchangeable,
    // `sortUnstable` does not do the extra work.
    std.mem.sortUnstable(u8, &numbers, {}, std.sort.asc(u8));
    try expect(numbers[0] == 2);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.sorting`)*

```zig
std.mem.sort(T, slice, context, lessThanFn);
```

For simple orders, the standard library supplies the comparator: `std.sort.asc(T)` and `std.sort.desc(T)`.

The sort is in place and needs no allocator. Thus it takes a slice and not a list, because it changes the order of the elements that are already there. To sort the contents of an `ArrayList`, sort `list.items`.

## The context argument

The sort gives the third parameter to each comparison. The parameter is `{}` (the void value) when the order depends only on the elements. The parameter is useful when the comparison needs external data. An example is a sort of indices by the values that they point at:

```zig
std.mem.sort(usize, &indices, values, byReferencedValue);
```

With the context parameter, you do not need a global variable.

The pattern has more uses than you can see at first. Sort an array of indices, and not the data. Then you get several orders of one dataset, and you do not copy the data. You can also use it to sort data that is too large to move cheaply. The context is the data that the comparator needs for its work.

## Stable or not

| Function | Stable | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `std.mem.sort` | yes | equal elements keep their relative order |
| `std.mem.sortUnstable` | no | less work; prefer when elements are interchangeable |

Stability is important when you sort by one key after an earlier sort by a different key. For equal elements, stability keeps the earlier order.

A sort by more than one key uses this property. Sort by the least significant key first, then by the most significant key. Stability keeps the result of the earlier sort in each group.

For example, sort by name, then by department. The entries of each department are still in name order. If you do the same with `sortUnstable`, the second sort destroys the order from the first sort.

Sometimes elements are fully interchangeable, for example plain integers. Then you cannot see the effect of stability. In that case `sortUnstable` is the better choice, because it does less work and uses no extra memory.

## Comparators as anonymous structs

Zig has no closures. Thus a comparator that you use one time is usually a struct literal with a function in it:

```zig
std.mem.sort([]const u8, &words, {}, struct {
    fn lessThan(_: void, a: []const u8, b: []const u8) bool {
        return std.mem.order(u8, a, b) == .lt;
    }
}.lessThan);
```

`std.mem.order` returns `.lt`, `.eq` or `.gt`. `std.sort.binarySearch` also uses this type of result.

The comparator must be a strict "less than". If it returns true for equal elements, it breaks the order that the algorithm expects. Then the result is not only in an incorrect order. In an unchecked build, the sort can read out of bounds.

To compare on several fields, compare the first field. Compare the second field only when the first fields are equal.

## Search a sorted slice

`std.sort.binarySearch` finds an element in a slice that is already sorted. It takes a three-way comparison and not a less-than, because it must know which half to keep. `std.sort.isSorted` checks the invariant. It is a cheap assertion to put in a test.

Two related functions help when you do not need all the elements in order:

- `std.sort.lowerBound` and `upperBound` find insertion points. A query such as "how many are below this threshold" needs these functions.
- When you need only the few largest elements, a full sort is the wrong algorithm. A [priority queue](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/priority-queue/) keeps the top *k* and does not touch the other elements.

---

## Iterators

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/iterators/*

The iterators in the Zig standard library are plain structs with a `next` method. Examples are `std.mem.splitScalar`, `std.mem.tokenizeAny` and `std.mem.window`. They give slices of the original bytes, and they do not allocate.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// Zig has no Iterator trait. A type is iterable if it has a `next()` that
// returns an optional, because `while (it.next()) |x|` needs exactly that.
const Countdown = struct {
    remaining: u32,

    pub fn next(self: *Countdown) ?u32 {
        if (self.remaining == 0) return null;
        self.remaining -= 1;
        return self.remaining;
    }
};

test "write your own iterator" {
    var it = Countdown{ .remaining = 3 };
    var sum: u32 = 0;
    while (it.next()) |value| sum += value;
    try expect(sum == 3); // 2 + 1 + 0
}

test "split on a single byte" {
    var it = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, "a,b,c", ',');
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, it.next().?, "a"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, it.next().?, "b"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, it.next().?, "c"));
    try expect(it.next() == null);
}

test "split keeps empty fields, tokenize does not" {
    var split = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, "a,,b", ',');
    var split_count: u32 = 0;
    while (split.next()) |_| split_count += 1;
    try expect(split_count == 3); // "a", "", "b"

    var tokens = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, "a,,b", ',');
    var token_count: u32 = 0;
    while (tokens.next()) |_| token_count += 1;
    try expect(token_count == 2); // "a", "b"
}

test "tokenize on any of several separators" {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, "one two\tthree", " \t");
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, it.next().?, "one"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, it.next().?, "two"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, it.next().?, "three"));
}

test "window a slice, overlapping or not" {
    // If advance < size, the windows overlap.
    var windows = std.mem.window(u8, "abcd", 2, 1);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, windows.next().?, "ab"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, windows.next().?, "bc"));

    // If advance == size, the blocks do not overlap. There is no std.mem.chunk.
    var blocks = std.mem.window(u8, "abcd", 2, 2);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, blocks.next().?, "ab"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, blocks.next().?, "cd"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.iterators`)*

Zig has no `Iterator` trait, no `IntoIterator`, and no iterator protocol to implement. A type is iterable if it has a `next()` method that returns an optional. This loop needs exactly that method:

```zig
while (it.next()) |value| { ... }
```

To write your own iterator, make a struct with state and a `next` method.

```zig
const Countdown = struct {
    n: u32,
    fn next(self: *Countdown) ?u32 {
        if (self.n == 0) return null;
        self.n -= 1;
        return self.n + 1;
    }
};
```

Nothing registers the struct, and the struct implements nothing. `while (c.next()) |v|` works because the shapes match. The convention is the interface, and the compiler checks the convention when you use it.

An iterator is an ordinary struct, and this fact has two results:

- An iterator must be `var`, because `next` changes the state. If a function must advance the iterator, give the function a pointer.
- After one iteration, the iterator has no more values. To iterate a second time, make the iterator again.

## Split text

| Function | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `splitScalar(u8, s, ',')` | splits on one byte, **keeps** empty fields |
| `splitAny(u8, s, ",;")` | splits on any of several bytes |
| `splitSequence(u8, s, "::")` | splits on a separator of more than one byte |
| `tokenizeScalar(u8, s, ',')` | same, but **skips** empty fields |
| `tokenizeAny(u8, s, " \t")` | skips empty fields, any of several separators |

Remember the difference between split and tokenize:

- To parse CSV, use `split`. An empty field has a meaning.
- To split on whitespace, use `tokenize`. A series of spaces must not make empty tokens.

All of these functions give slices of the original string. They copy nothing and they allocate nothing. Thus a split of a megabyte of text costs no memory, and the parts stay valid while the original is valid. The usual problem also applies: if the program frees the source, each part that you kept is dangling.

Three more methods are available:

- `peek()` gets the next value, but does not consume it.
- `rest()` gives you all of the text that the iterator did not return. Use it when you parse a header field by field and the rest of the text is a body.
- `reset()` starts again from the beginning.

## Windows

`std.mem.window(T, s, size, advance)` gives views into the original bytes, and it copies nothing. Code that works on n-grams or on blocks needs this shape. You control the overlap:

- If `advance` is smaller than `size`, the windows overlap.
- If `advance` is equal to `size`, the windows do not overlap.

On master, there is no `std.mem.chunk`. For blocks that do not overlap, use `window(T,
s, n, n)`.

When the length is not a multiple of the window size, the last window is short. The function does not pad the last window, and it does not discard it. Thus code that expects a full window each time must check the length.

## No lazy adapter chains

Zig has no `.map().filter().take()`. Write the loop. The loop is usually shorter than the chain, and its cost is clear.

Zig has no chains because Zig has no closures. A `map` must take a function pointer and a context struct. That is three lines of setup for a task that one line in a loop body does directly. Chains are easy to read in languages where a lambda captures its environment automatically.

But the loss is real. You can write a chain of transformations over a large collection one time, and it reads the data in one pass. Careless nested loops make intermediate arrays. In Zig, write one loop that does all the steps for each element. In those other languages, the chain also compiles to this loop.

---

## Random Numbers

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/random-numbers/*

Zig has two random number generators:

- `std.Random.DefaultPrng` is fast, and you can give it a seed. Use it for tests and simulations.
- `std.Random.DefaultCsprng` is the secure generator. Use it for tokens and keys.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "a seeded generator is reproducible" {
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(42);
    const random = prng.random();

    const first = random.int(u32);

    // The same seed gives the same sequence. Thus the tests are deterministic.
    var again = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(42);
    try expect(again.random().int(u32) == first);
}

test "ranges" {
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(0);
    const random = prng.random();

    for (0..100) |_| {
        const die = random.intRangeAtMost(u8, 1, 6); // inclusive
        try expect(die >= 1 and die <= 6);

        const index = random.uintLessThan(usize, 10); // exclusive
        try expect(index < 10);
    }
}

test "floats and booleans" {
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(7);
    const random = prng.random();

    const f = random.float(f64); // [0, 1)
    try expect(f >= 0.0 and f < 1.0);

    _ = random.boolean();
}

test "shuffle a slice" {
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(1);
    var items = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };
    prng.random().shuffle(u8, &items);

    var sum: u32 = 0;
    for (items) |i| sum += i;
    try expect(sum == 15); // same elements, different order
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.random-numbers`)*

Zig has no global `rand()`. You create a generator, give it a seed, and give its `Random` interface to the code that needs it. Code gets allocators and I/O in the same way.

```zig
var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed);
const random = prng.random();
```

The two values in this code do different work. `prng` is the generator, and it owns the state. Thus `prng` must be a `var`, and it must exist longer than all the code that uses it.

`random` is the interface. It is a pointer to that state and a function pointer, the same shape as `Allocator`. Functions take the interface, never the generator. Thus you can give a real generator to a function in production, and a generator with a fixed seed in a test. The function does not know the difference.

## Seeds

A fixed seed gives a sequence that is the same each time. Tests need that. For values that nobody can predict, the entropy must come from the operating system. On master, the entropy comes through the `Io` interface, as all other operations that can block do:

```zig
var source: std.Random.IoSource = .{ .io = io };
const random = source.interface();
```

`std.Random.DefaultCsprng` is the cryptographically secure generator. Use it for tokens, keys, and all other values that an attacker must not predict. `DefaultPrng` is fast, but it is not secure. Do not use it for secrets.

Older code and tutorials use `std.crypto.random`. These generators replaced it. Zig no longer has a global secure generator. The same change removed the global stdout. Code now gets the capability as an argument, and does not import it.

The difference between the two generators is not statistical quality. `DefaultPrng` passes statistical tests. The problem is that a small number of outputs is sufficient to calculate its internal state again. Thus an attacker who sees a few session tokens can calculate the next token. The design of the secure generator makes sure that its output tells you nothing about the state.

In tests, a fixed seed is a useful feature. A seeded generator is better than no random values at all. It tries inputs that a hand-written test does not try, and it still fails in the same way each time. When a seeded test fails, print the seed. Then you can make the failure occur again at any time.

## Ranges

| Call | Range |
| --- | --- |
| `intRangeAtMost(T, lo, hi)` | `lo..=hi` inclusive |
| `intRangeLessThan(T, lo, hi)` | `lo..hi` |
| `uintLessThan(T, hi)` | `0..hi` |
| `float(T)` | `[0, 1)` |

These functions prevent modulo bias. `random.int(u8) % 6` does not prevent it, and its results are more frequently low values.

`shuffle` changes the order of a slice in place.

The bias is small, but it is real, and you can calculate it. A `u8` has 256 possible values, and the code wants 6 outcomes. 256 is not a multiple of 6. Thus four of the outcomes get 43 chances, and two outcomes get 42.

A dice roll with a bias of 2% is acceptable in a game. It is a problem in a simulation that you use to make conclusions. You do no extra work to prevent the bias. The standard library functions already reject the values that cause the bias, and draw a new value.

## Other functions on the interface

- `boolean()` gives the result of a coin flip.
- `weightedIndex` selects an index from a distribution.
- `enumValue(T)` gives a random tag of an enum.
- `bytes(buf)` fills a slice. Use it to make an identifier or a test payload in one call.

To select a random element of a slice, the correct call is `uintLessThan(usize, s.len)`. Use it and not `int(usize) % s.len`, for the reason above. Also, on an empty slice, `uintLessThan` fails, and the failure is easy to see. It does not divide by zero.

---

## Crypto

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/crypto/*

In Zig, a SHA-256 digest is one call to `std.crypto.hash.sha2.Sha256.hash`. To compare secrets such as MACs and tokens, use `std.crypto.timing_safe.eql`, not `std.mem.eql`. For passwords, use `std.crypto.pwhash`, not a plain hash.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "sha256" {
    var digest: [32]u8 = undefined;
    std.crypto.hash.sha2.Sha256.hash("abc", &digest, .{});

    // The SHA-256 of "abc", a well-known test value.
    var hex: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&hex, "{x}", .{digest});
    try expect(std.mem.startsWith(u8, text, "ba7816bf"));
}

test "incremental hashing" {
    var hasher = std.crypto.hash.sha2.Sha256.init(.{});
    hasher.update("a");
    hasher.update("bc");

    var digest: [32]u8 = undefined;
    hasher.final(&digest);

    var one_shot: [32]u8 = undefined;
    std.crypto.hash.sha2.Sha256.hash("abc", &one_shot, .{});
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, &digest, &one_shot));
}

test "compare secrets in constant time" {
    const a = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    const b = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    // `std.mem.eql` stops at the first difference. Thus its duration shows
    // how many bytes matched.
    try expect(std.crypto.timing_safe.eql([3]u8, a, b));
}

test "hmac" {
    const Hmac = std.crypto.auth.hmac.sha2.HmacSha256;
    var mac: [Hmac.mac_length]u8 = undefined;
    Hmac.create(&mac, "message", "key");
    try expect(mac.len == 32);
}

test "password hashing is deliberately slow" {
    // Use bcrypt, scrypt or argon2 for passwords. Do not use a bare hash.
    // This example does not run them, because they are slow by design.
    try expect(@hasDecl(std.crypto.pwhash, "argon2"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.crypto`)*

Zig includes a large crypto library in `std.crypto`. The library has hashes, AEADs, key exchange and signatures, and it has no external dependency.

In most languages, cryptography means that you link OpenSSL or a similar library. That adds a build dependency, a version to monitor, and a large quantity of C. In Zig, the crypto code is in the standard library, and the code is Zig code. It cross-compiles to each target that your program compiles to.

## Select the correct tool

The names are difficult to learn. This table shows which problem each tool solves.

| You want | Use | Do not use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A fingerprint of some data | `Sha256`, `Blake3` | a hash with "MD" or "SHA1" in its name |
| Proof that the data came from a person with the key | `hmac`, or an AEAD | a plain hash of key ++ data |
| Encryption, *and* detection of changes to the data | `aead` (`ChaCha20Poly1305`, `Aes256Gcm`) | a bare cipher |
| A stored password | `pwhash` (argon2) | any of the tools above |
| A fast hash for a hash map | `std.hash` | `std.crypto` |

Be careful with the last row. `std.hash` holds non-cryptographic hashes, for example Wyhash. They are much faster, and a hash table needs them.

Use `std.crypto.hash` when an attacker must not find two inputs with the same output. A crypto hash in a hash table is slow. A non-cryptographic hash is unsafe when an attacker can affect the data.

## One-shot and incremental

```zig
Sha256.hash(data, &digest, .{});          // one-shot

var hasher = Sha256.init(.{});            // incremental
hasher.update(part1);
hasher.update(part2);
hasher.final(&digest);
```

The two forms make the same digest. Use the incremental form when the input arrives in parts, or when the input is too large to hold in memory.

The digest is an array of fixed size: `[32]u8` for SHA-256. It contains raw bytes, not hex. To print it, use `{x}` or `std.fmt.bytesToHex`. To compare it with a hex string from a different source, convert one side. Do not compare the two values by eye.

## Constant-time comparison

```zig
std.crypto.timing_safe.eql([32]u8, a, b)
```

`std.mem.eql` returns when it finds the first difference. Thus its duration shows how many bytes matched. For MACs, tokens, and password hashes, this is a real attack. Use the timing-safe form for all secret data.

The steps of the attack make the danger clear:

1. The attacker sends tokens, and measures the time of each response.
2. The tokens are different only in the first byte.
3. One token takes slightly longer. Thus the attacker knows the first byte.
4. The attacker does the same for the second byte, and then for each next byte.

Thus 256^32 guesses become 32 × 256 guesses, which is a few thousand. The timing-safe version compares each byte on each call, and combines the results. Thus the duration gives no information.

## Passwords are a different problem

Do not hash passwords with SHA-256. `std.crypto.pwhash` supplies argon2, bcrypt, and scrypt. These functions are slow on purpose, and they use a salt. The slow speed is the feature: it makes an offline attack with many guesses expensive.

SHA-256 is fast by design. Usual hardware calculates billions of SHA-256 hashes each second. If a table of SHA-256 password hashes leaks, an attacker can get the passwords in some hours.

Argon2 has settings so that one hash takes a measurable part of a second and a set quantity of memory. Your login endpoint calculates one hash for each login, thus the cost is small. An attacker needs millions of guesses, thus the attacker's cost is millions of times larger.

The salt is the other half. The program stores the salt next to the hash, in the clear. The salt makes sure that two users with the same password get different hashes. Thus one precomputed table cannot crack the two hashes. `pwhash` makes and encodes the salt. This is the main reason to use `pwhash` and not to assemble the parts yourself.

## The limits of this page

This page does not give you enough information to design a protocol. The API for an AEAD does not tell you how to select a nonce. A bad nonce breaks the full construction.

Use a reviewed protocol when one exists. `std.crypto` gives implementations of primitives. It does not tell you how to combine them.

---

## Time

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/time/*

In Zig, you read the current time through the `Io` interface with `std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now(io, clock)`. Use `.real` for wall-clock time, and `.awake` to measure the duration of an operation. `std.time` keeps the constants and the calendar code.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "wall-clock time" {
    const io = std.testing.io;

    // .real is Unix time: nanoseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z.
    const now = std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now(io, .real);
    const secs = now.raw.toSeconds();

    // If this fails, the system clock has a date before November 2023.
    try expect(secs > 1_700_000_000);
}

fn busyWork() u64 {
    var acc: u64 = 0;
    for (0..100_000) |i| acc +%= i *% i;
    return acc;
}

test "measure elapsed time with the monotonic clock" {
    const io = std.testing.io;

    // .awake cannot move backward. Thus use it to measure time.
    // .real can jump when NTP or the administrator adjusts it.
    const start = std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now(io, .awake);
    std.mem.doNotOptimizeAway(busyWork());
    const end = std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now(io, .awake);

    const elapsed = start.durationTo(end);
    try expect(elapsed.raw.toNanoseconds() >= 0);
}

test "durations are values with unit conversions" {
    const d = std.Io.Duration.fromMilliseconds(1500);
    try expect(d.toMicroseconds() == 1_500_000);
    try expect(d.toSeconds() == 1); // truncates toward zero

    // With {f}, durations print in units that people can read.
    try std.testing.expectFmt("1.5s", "{f}", .{d});
    try std.testing.expectFmt("2m5s", "{f}", .{std.Io.Duration.fromSeconds(125)});
}

test "std.time still holds the constants and epoch math" {
    try expect(std.time.ns_per_s == 1_000_000_000);
    try expect(std.time.s_per_day == 86_400);

    // Divide a Unix timestamp into calendar parts, with no allocation and no locale.
    const es = std.time.epoch.EpochSeconds{ .secs = 86_400 + 3_600 };
    const year_day = es.getEpochDay().calculateYearDay();
    try expect(year_day.year == 1970);

    const month_day = year_day.calculateMonthDay();
    try expect(month_day.month == .jan);
    try expect(month_day.day_index == 1); // starts at zero: Jan 2nd

    try expect(es.getDaySeconds().getHoursIntoDay() == 1);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.time`)*

## To read a clock, you need an Io

A clock read is now an I/O operation. Thus it uses the same `Io` interface as files and sockets: `std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now(io, clock)`. In a test, the instance is `std.testing.io`. In a program, the instance is `init.io`. Zig removed the older free functions `std.time.timestamp` and `std.time.milliTimestamp`.

## Select the correct clock

- `.real` is wall-clock Unix time: nanoseconds since 1970. Use it for timestamps that you store or show. It can jump backward when NTP or an administrator corrects it.
- `.awake` is monotonic: it never moves backward. Use it to measure the duration of an operation. If the clock changes during a slow operation, the difference between two `.real` readings can be negative or absurd.

`durationTo` between two timestamps gives an `Io.Duration`.

## Durations are values

An `Io.Duration` holds a count of nanoseconds. It has conversion helpers (`fromMilliseconds`, `toSeconds`, and others) that truncate toward zero. When you format it with `{f}`, it prints units that people can read: `1.5s`, `2m5s`.

## std.time keeps the arithmetic

The constants (`ns_per_s`, `s_per_day`, and the others) and the calendar code are still in `std.time`. They need no `Io`, because they are pure math.

`std.time.epoch` divides a Unix timestamp into year, month, day, and time of day. It does not allocate, and it does not use a locale. Note that the day index starts at zero: day 1 is the second day of the month.

Use the named constants, and do not write `1_000_000_000`. The name `ns_per_s` tells the reader what the value means. In an expression such as `5 * std.time.ns_per_min`, a mistake by a factor of a thousand cannot hide from a reviewer.

## Measure elapsed time

```zig
const start = try std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now(io, .awake);
doWork();
const elapsed = start.durationTo(try std.Io.Clock.Timestamp.now(io, .awake));
```

Always use `.awake` for this measurement. The two clocks are separate because NTP or an administrator can move `.real` between your two clock reads. With `.real`, a benchmark can sometimes report a negative duration.

For a measurement that you do one time, one pair of reads is fine. If you want to make a conclusion from the measurement, one measurement is noise. Run the work enough times to make the total much larger than the resolution of the clock. Then report the total divided by the count.

## Timezones and formatting

`std.time.epoch` gives you UTC. The standard library has no timezone database, and no date formatting for a locale. The reason is the same as for Unicode case folding, which the standard library also does not have. The tables change several times each year, and each binary must not contain a frozen copy of them.

Thus the practical advice is simple:

- Store and send `.real` timestamps as integers, in UTC.
- Change them to local time and to a readable string only at the edge of the program. Do this with a library, and only where a person reads the result.

A program that uses UTC internally has no daylight-saving bugs.

## Wait

A sleep also goes through the `Io` instance. Thus you can cancel a sleep, and the same code works with threads and with an evented runtime. The interface exists to prevent a raw sleep that blocks the thread. [Cancellation](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/) shows a timeout that you can interrupt.

---

## Logging

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/logging/*

In Zig, `std.log` is the logging API. You set its level one time, in `std_options` in the root source file. The compiler removes a call below that level. The call is not skipped at run time.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// Zig reads `std_options` from the root of the program at compile time. The
// declaration has an effect here only because this snippet is an executable.
// A `zig test` file is not the root, and Zig ignores its std_options. The
// level .debug compiles in each level. By default, a release build removes
// the lower levels. A maximum for one scope overrides the global level.
pub const std_options: std.Options = .{
    .log_level = .debug,
    .log_scope_levels = &.{
        .{ .scope = .noisy, .level = .warn }, // .noisy logs only at warn and higher
    },
};

// A scoped logger puts the subsystem name on each line. Thus you can make the
// level of one area higher or lower, and not change the other areas.
const net = std.log.scoped(.net);

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) void {
    _ = init;

    // Each level goes to stderr through std.options.logFn. The configured
    // level decides at compile time if each call is in the build.
    std.log.debug("resolving host", .{});
    std.log.info("connected in {d}ms", .{12});
    std.log.warn("slow response, retrying", .{});
    std.log.err("giving up after {d} tries", .{3});

    net.info("scoped line, tagged (net)", .{});

    // logEnabled is known at comptime. Thus an unused level costs nothing.
    std.debug.assert(std.log.logEnabled(.debug, .default)); // on, because the level is .debug
    std.debug.assert(!std.log.logEnabled(.info, .noisy)); // capped at .warn
    std.debug.assert(std.log.logEnabled(.warn, .noisy));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.logging`)*

## Four levels, with a scope tag

`std.log` gives you `debug`, `info`, `warn`, and `err`. Each function takes a compile-time format string and its arguments. This is the same shape as in all other places.

`std.log.scoped(.name)` returns the same four functions, but each line gets a tag with a subsystem name. Thus a reader (or a filter) can see the source of a message. The default scope is `.default`.

The output above comes from the standard formatter, which writes to stderr. In your browser, the playground shows stdout and stderr together. For this reason, you can see the log lines.

## You set the level at the root, and the level is a compile-time gate

The full configuration is in one declaration. Zig reads the declaration from the **root** of the program:

```zig
pub const std_options: std.Options = .{
    .log_level = .debug,
    .log_scope_levels = &.{
        .{ .scope = .noisy, .level = .warn },
    },
};
```

The word "root" has two results, and both cause mistakes:

- The declaration must be in the root source file (the file with `main`). Zig **ignores** a `pub const
  std_options` in a library file or in a `zig test` file. In a test, the test runner is the root, not your file. For exactly this reason, the snippet in this chapter is a program and not a test.
- The compiler removes each call below the active level. The call is not skipped at run time. `std.log.debug` in a release build costs nothing, because the call is not in the build. `std.log.logEnabled(level, scope)` tells you the result, and its value is also known at comptime.

`log_scope_levels` sets a maximum level for each subsystem. In the example above, `.noisy` prints nothing below `warn`, but the global level is `.debug`. Make the level of one area higher or lower, and do not change the other areas.

## Replace the formatter

Each message goes through one function: `std.Options.logFn`. Override this function to change the format, add timestamps, send the messages to a file, or emit structured JSON:

```zig
pub const std_options: std.Options = .{
    .logFn = myLogFn,
};

fn myLogFn(
    comptime level: std.log.Level,
    comptime scope: @EnumLiteral(),
    comptime fmt: []const u8,
    args: anytype,
) void {
    // ... format `level`, `scope`, and `fmt`/`args` however you like ...
}
```

Each message goes through this one function. Thus you change the logging of a full program in one place. Libraries that call `std.log` also get the change, and they need no code of their own.

---

## Testing

*Standard Library. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/testing/*

Zig tests are `test` blocks, and `zig test` runs them. `std.testing` supplies the assertions, for example `expectEqual` and `expectError`. It also supplies `std.testing.allocator`, which fails a test that leaks memory.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

test "expectEqual prints both values on failure" {
    // expect(a == b) tells you only "false". expectEqual tells you
    // expected 42, found 41. The expected value comes first.
    try std.testing.expectEqual(42, 41 + 1);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(?u8, null), null);
}

test "slice and string comparisons show where they diverge" {
    try std.testing.expectEqualSlices(u8, &.{ 1, 2, 3 }, &.{ 1, 2, 3 });

    // On failure, this assertion prints the two strings and the index of the
    // first byte that is different.
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("hello", "hel" ++ "lo");

    try std.testing.expectStringStartsWith("zig build verify", "zig build");
}

fn parseDigit(c: u8) !u4 {
    if (c < '0' or c > '9') return error.NotADigit;
    return @intCast(c - '0');
}

test "expectError asserts the failure path" {
    // If no test runs an error path, the path can break and nobody sees it.
    // expectError makes the error path a normal assertion.
    try std.testing.expectError(error.NotADigit, parseDigit('x'));
    try std.testing.expectEqual(7, try parseDigit('7'));
}

test "floats compare within a tolerance" {
    const third: f64 = 1.0 / 3.0;
    // Never use == on calculated floats. Give the tolerance that you accept.
    try std.testing.expectApproxEqAbs(0.333, third, 0.001);
    try std.testing.expectApproxEqRel(1.0, third * 3.0, std.math.floatEps(f64));
}

const Config = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    retries: u8,
};

test "expectEqualDeep follows pointers and slices" {
    const a = Config{ .name = "prod", .retries = 3 };
    const b = Config{ .name = "prod", .retries = 3 };

    // expectEqual on these structs compares the slice pointers.
    // expectEqualDeep compares the data that the slices point at.
    try std.testing.expectEqualDeep(a, b);
}

test "expectFmt checks formatted output" {
    try std.testing.expectFmt("0x00ff", "0x{x:0>4}", .{255});
}

test "the test allocator reports leaks" {
    // std.testing.allocator fails the test if memory is still allocated
    // when the test returns. If you forget this free, the test fails with
    // a stack trace of the leaked allocation.
    const gpa = std.testing.allocator;
    const buf = try gpa.alloc(u8, 64);
    defer gpa.free(buf);

    // The allocator also finds a double free and a use after free in test builds.
    try std.testing.expect(buf.len == 64);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.testing`)*

## expect tells you nothing, and the others tell you what failed

When `try std.testing.expect(a == b)` fails, it says "expected true, found false". Then you must add print statements. The typed assertions put the values into the failure message:

| Assertion | Reports on failure |
| --- | --- |
| `expectEqual(expected, actual)` | both values |
| `expectEqualStrings` | both strings and the first differing byte |
| `expectEqualSlices(T, ...)` | both slices and the diverging index |
| `expectError(err, expr)` | which error, or that none was returned |

By convention, the expected value comes first. `expectEqual` gets its type from that first argument. For this reason, `@as(?u8, null)` sometimes needs the cast: the cast tells the comparison the type of `null`.

## Assert the error paths too

Bugs hide in failure paths that have no tests. With `expectError`, "this input is rejected" becomes a normal assertion. You can check it as easily as the success case. A parser test must check the digit that the parser accepts, and also the character that it refuses.

## Floats need a tolerance

Never compare calculated floats with `==`. Use one of these assertions:

- `expectApproxEqAbs` takes an absolute tolerance, for values near a known magnitude.
- `expectApproxEqRel` takes a relative tolerance.

`std.math.floatEps(f64)` is the natural limit for "as close as the type permits."

## expectEqualDeep for structures

Take two structs that hold slices. `expectEqual` on these structs compares the slice pointers, and almost always you do not want that. `expectEqualDeep` follows pointers and slices, and compares the content that they point at.

## The allocator is a test

`std.testing.allocator` fails the test if memory from the allocator is still live when the test returns. Thus, if you forget a `free`, the test fails. The leak does not become a slow leak in production.

The allocator also panics on a double free, on a free through the wrong allocator, and on most writes after a free. Put a `defer free` after each allocation, and let the allocator check them.

Use this allocator in each test. Memory bugs are frequently difficult to reproduce. A memory bug can stay hidden in the test that caused it, and it can cause a production incident weeks later. A test that uses this allocator is also a leak test, with no extra code.

`std.testing.checkAllAllocationFailures` does more. It runs your function again and again. Each time, the allocator fails at a different call, and the function checks that each partial failure still releases its memory. That test is too tedious to write by hand. It is the only way to know if your chain of `errdefer` statements is correct.

## How zig test finds and runs tests

A `test` block is a top-level declaration. `zig test` compiles the file into a runner, and the runner executes each test that it can see. "Can see" follows a rule. The compiler never compiles the tests in a file that no other file imports. Thus, when you add a test file to the tree, it does not run until other code imports it.

Put `std.testing.refAllDecls(@This())` at the bottom of a file to make the compiler analyse each declaration. This call includes the tests of imported files. It also finds code that does not compile now, but that no code calls at the moment.

`zig build test --test-filter <substring>` runs only the tests whose names match. Use it when you work on one failure again and again. Test names are plain strings. Thus it helps to write them as sentences that describe the behaviour. For example, a filter on `"rejects"` finds each negative case.

## Tests are documentation that is always current

A `test` next to the function that it uses is the usage example. A comment can become incorrect, but a test fails the build when it is no longer true. For that reason, the standard library has many of these tests, and your code can do the same. A reader who looks at an unfamiliar function reads the test before the doc comment, because the test cannot be out of date.

This site works in the same way. Before the site publishes a page, CI compiles and runs each snippet on the page. The guarantee is the same, on a larger scale. See [how CI verifies this guide](https://www.ziglang.in/verification/).

## Skipped tests and expected failures

`return error.SkipZigTest` skips a test at runtime. Use it for a case that applies only on some targets. The runner reports the test as skipped, not as passed. Thus a test that is always skipped stays visible in the output.

For code that must not compile, there is no assertion to write. The compile error already fails the build. When the type rejects a misuse, do not write that misuse in a test. Trust the type.

---

## Open, Read, Close

*Working with Files. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/open-read-close/*

Zig has three common ways to read a file:

- `readFileAlloc` reads the full file into new memory.
- `readFile` reads the file into a buffer that you supply.
- `openFile` gives you a handle. Then you decide how to read from the handle.

Each of the three functions needs a size limit. The functions are different in two ways: where the limit comes from, and what occurs when the file is larger than the limit.

The program below uses the three functions on the same 18-byte file.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Io = std.Io;

// The playground starts each run in an empty directory. Thus the program
// writes the file before it reads the file. The file is 18 bytes: three
// lines of 6, 5 and 4 characters, and a newline after each line.
const shopping = "apples\nbread\nmilk\n";

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = init.gpa;

    var out_buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const dir = Io.Dir.cwd();
    try dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "shopping.txt", .data = shopping });

    // 1. Read the full file into memory from the allocator.
    try out.print("1. readFileAlloc\n", .{});
    const whole = try dir.readFileAlloc(io, "shopping.txt", gpa, .limited(1024));
    defer gpa.free(whole);
    try out.print("   read {d} bytes\n", .{whole.len});

    // The function fails when the file size is equal to the limit, and also
    // when the file size is more than the limit.
    for ([_]usize{ 17, 18, 19 }) |limit| {
        if (dir.readFileAlloc(io, "shopping.txt", gpa, .limited(limit))) |bytes| {
            defer gpa.free(bytes);
            try out.print("   limit {d}: ok, {d} bytes\n", .{ limit, bytes.len });
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("   limit {d}: {t}\n", .{ limit, err });
        }
    }

    // 2. Read into a buffer that you supply. No allocator is necessary. A full
    //    buffer does not tell you if the file is longer than the buffer.
    try out.print("2. readFile\n", .{});
    var small: [8]u8 = undefined;
    const part = try dir.readFile(io, "shopping.txt", &small);
    try out.print("   8-byte buffer: {d} bytes \"{f}\"\n", .{ part.len, std.zig.fmtString(part) });
    var large: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const all = try dir.readFile(io, "shopping.txt", &large);
    try out.print("   64-byte buffer: {d} bytes\n", .{all.len});

    // 3. Open a handle. You must close the handle. Get the length of the
    //    file, then read exactly that number of bytes from offset 0.
    try out.print("3. openFile\n", .{});
    {
        const file = try dir.openFile(io, "shopping.txt", .{});
        defer file.close(io);

        // A file length is a u64. A length in memory is a usize, and a usize
        // is 32 bits on wasm32. If the value is too large, the cast fails.
        // It does not remove the high bits.
        const len = try file.length(io);
        const bytes = try gpa.alloc(u8, std.math.cast(usize, len) orelse return error.FileTooBig);
        defer gpa.free(bytes);
        const n = try file.readPositionalAll(io, bytes, 0);
        try out.print("   length {d}, read {d}\n", .{ len, n });
        try out.print("   first line: {s}\n", .{bytes[0..std.mem.findScalar(u8, bytes, '\n').?]});
    }

    // 4. A file that does not exist. The error gives the name of the
    //    problem. Thus the caller can use a default value for this error.
    try out.print("4. missing file\n", .{});
    if (dir.openFile(io, "settings.txt", .{})) |file| {
        file.close(io);
    } else |err| switch (err) {
        error.FileNotFound => try out.print("   settings.txt: FileNotFound, using defaults\n", .{}),
        else => return err,
    }

    try dir.deleteFile(io, "shopping.txt");
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`24-files.open-read-close`)*

## Write the file first

The playground starts each run in an empty directory. In your browser, the directory is in memory. In CI, the directory is a temporary directory on disk.

Thus the program writes `shopping.txt` before it reads the file. One call to `dir.writeFile` creates the file, writes the bytes and closes the file.

The file has three lines: `apples`, `bread` and `milk`. A newline follows each line. The three lines are 6 + 1, 5 + 1 and 4 + 1 bytes, thus the file is 18 bytes.

## Read the full file

`readFileAlloc` opens the file, reads all of the file, closes the file and returns the bytes.

The memory comes from the allocator that you give to the function. Free the memory with the same allocator.

The last argument is a limit, and the limit is necessary. No version of this function reads a quantity of data that has no limit. A file can be of any size. If a program accepts each file without a limit, one day the program will read a very large file into memory.

Be careful with the limit. The output shows the result of three limits:

```
   limit 17: StreamTooLong
   limit 18: StreamTooLong
   limit 19: ok, 18 bytes
```

A limit of 18 fails on an 18-byte file. The function fails when the file size is equal to the limit, and also when the file size is more than the limit.

Thus, if the largest file that you accept is 1 MiB, set the limit to 1 MiB plus one byte. Usually, a programmer selects a round number that is much larger than the expected files, for example `.limited(1 << 20)`.

## Read into a buffer that you supply

`readFile` does not need an allocator. The function reads into the buffer that you give to it. Then it returns the part of the buffer that it filled.

```
   8-byte buffer: 8 bytes "apples\nb"
   64-byte buffer: 18 bytes
```

The 8-byte buffer has space for 8 bytes. Thus the function read 8 bytes and stopped. The function did not return an error.

When the result fills the full buffer, the result does not tell you which of these two conditions is true:

- The file is exactly 8 bytes long.
- The file is longer than 8 bytes, and the program did not read the other bytes.

If you must know the difference, make the buffer one byte larger than the largest file that you accept. Then a full buffer always means that the file is too large.

The limit in `readFileAlloc` uses the same rule. This rule is the reason that a limit equal to the file size fails.

## Open a handle

`openFile` returns a `File`. You must close the file. Thus the next line is `defer file.close(io)`.

The `defer` statement runs when the block ends. It runs on all paths, and an early `return` from a `try` is one of these paths.

When the handle is open, the program gets the length of the file. Then it allocates memory of exactly that length.

```
   length 18, read 18
   first line: apples
```

Between these two steps, the program must change the type of the length:

- `file.length` returns a `u64`, because a file on disk can be larger than 4 GiB.
- `gpa.alloc` takes a `usize`. A `usize` has the same size as an address.

On a 64-bit computer, the two types have the same width. This program also runs as `wasm32`, where `usize` is 32 bits. Thus the compiler does not let you use a `u64` as a `usize`.

`std.math.cast(usize, len)` returns `null` when the value is too large for a `usize`. The program changes this `null` into `error.FileTooBig`.

Then the program reads the file with `readPositionalAll`. This function reads from a given offset until the buffer is full or the file ends. It returns the number of bytes that it read. In this example, the number is 18, which is equal to the length.

The two numbers can be different. Another program can make the file shorter after the call to `length` and before the read. Thus the program uses the count that the read returns. It does not use the length from the earlier call.

## A file that does not exist

When you open a file that does not exist, the result is `error.FileNotFound`.

```
   settings.txt: FileNotFound, using defaults
```

The program uses a `switch` on the error. For `FileNotFound`, the program has a correct action: it uses the default settings.

For each other error, the program returns the error to the caller with `return err`. This code cannot repair a permission problem or a full disk. Thus the code must not hide these errors.

Do not write `catch` without an error name, and do not use one action for all errors. If you do, a settings file that the program cannot read looks the same as a settings file that does not exist. Then no person gets a report about the problem.

## Select a function

- For a small file that you read one time, use `readFileAlloc`. It needs the least code.
- For a record of fixed size, or for a file that you know is small, use `readFile`. It does not need an allocator.
- For all other files, open a handle. With a handle, you can read the file in parts, move to a different position, and read a file that is larger than memory.

The next chapter uses a handle to read a file one line at a time.

## If you used an older version of Zig

Before version 0.16, these functions were on `std.fs.Dir`, and they did not have an `io` argument.

Now the functions are on `std.Io.Dir`. The `io` argument is the first argument after the directory.

[Filesystem](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/filesystem/) gives a list of the functions that moved.

---

## Read Line by Line

*Working with Files. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/read-lines/*

Usually, a program reads a text file one line at a time. To read the lines of a file, do these steps:

1. Open the file.
2. Put a reader with a buffer around the file.
3. Get the next line from the reader. Do this again until no lines remain.

The buffer can be small. The program below reads a file of almost 100 KB through a 256-byte buffer.

The program also shows three conditions that a line loop finds in real files:

- Different line endings.
- A line that is longer than the buffer.
- A line that the program must keep.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Io = std.Io;

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var out_buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const dir = Io.Dir.cwd();

    // 1. Three files with the same two lines and different endings.
    try out.print("1. line endings\n", .{});
    const endings = [_]struct { name: []const u8, data: []const u8 }{
        .{ .name = "unix.txt", .data = "one\ntwo\n" },
        .{ .name = "no-final.txt", .data = "one\ntwo" },
        .{ .name = "windows.txt", .data = "one\r\ntwo\r\n" },
    };
    for (endings) |e| {
        try dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = e.name, .data = e.data });
        try out.print("   {s}\n", .{e.name});
        try printLines(io, dir, e.name, out);
    }

    // 2. A line longer than the reader's buffer.
    try out.print("2. a long line\n", .{});
    try dir.writeFile(io, .{
        .sub_path = "long.txt",
        .data = "short\n" ++ @as([40]u8, @splat('x')) ++ "\nafter\n",
    });
    try readSkippingLong(io, dir, "long.txt", out);

    // 3. A file that is much larger than the buffer that reads it.
    try out.print("3. a large file\n", .{});
    try writeNumberedLines(io, dir, "big.txt", 10_000);
    try countLines(io, dir, "big.txt", out);

    for ([_][]const u8{ "unix.txt", "no-final.txt", "windows.txt", "long.txt", "big.txt" }) |name| {
        try dir.deleteFile(io, name);
    }
}

fn printLines(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = file.reader(io, &buf);

    var n: usize = 1;
    while (try reader.interface.takeDelimiter('\n')) |raw| : (n += 1) {
        // A file from Windows has "\r\n" at the end of each line. A split at
        // '\n' keeps the '\r' at the end of the line. Thus remove the '\r'.
        const line = std.mem.trimEnd(u8, raw, "\r");
        try out.print("     line {d}: \"{f}\" -> \"{s}\"\n", .{ n, std.zig.fmtString(raw), line });
    }
}

fn readSkippingLong(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    // The buffer is 16 bytes. The longest line that the reader can return
    // is 15 characters and the newline.
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = file.reader(io, &buf);
    const r = &reader.interface;

    var n: usize = 1;
    while (true) : (n += 1) {
        // The parentheses are necessary: `catch` handles the error, then
        // `orelse` handles the end of the file.
        const line = (r.takeDelimiter('\n') catch |err| switch (err) {
            error.StreamTooLong => {
                // The reader consumed no bytes. Skip to the end of this line,
                // then continue.
                const skipped = try r.discardDelimiterInclusive('\n');
                try out.print("   line {d}: StreamTooLong, skipped {d} bytes\n", .{ n, skipped });
                continue;
            },
            else => |e| return e,
        }) orelse break;
        try out.print("   line {d}: {s}\n", .{ n, line });
    }
}

fn writeNumberedLines(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, count: usize) !void {
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = file.writer(io, &buf);
    for (1..count + 1) |i| try writer.interface.print("line {d}\n", .{i});
    try writer.interface.flush();
}

fn countLines(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = file.reader(io, &buf);

    var lines: usize = 0;
    var bytes: usize = 0;
    var last: [16]u8 = undefined;
    var last_len: usize = 0;
    while (try reader.interface.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        lines += 1;
        bytes += line.len + 1;
        // `line` points into `buf`, and the next read writes over `buf`.
        // To keep the line after this iteration, copy the line.
        @memcpy(last[0..line.len], line);
        last_len = line.len;
    }
    try out.print("   file size {d} bytes, buffer {d} bytes\n", .{ try file.length(io), buf.len });
    try out.print("   {d} lines, {d} bytes, last line \"{s}\"\n", .{ lines, bytes, last[0..last_len] });
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`24-files.read-lines`)*

## The loop

```zig
fn printLines(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = file.reader(io, &buf);

    var n: usize = 1;
    while (try reader.interface.takeDelimiter('\n')) |raw| : (n += 1) {
        // A file from Windows has "\r\n" at the end of each line. A split at
        // '\n' keeps the '\r' at the end of the line. Thus remove the '\r'.
        const line = std.mem.trimEnd(u8, raw, "\r");
        try out.print("     line {d}: \"{f}\" -> \"{s}\"\n", .{ n, std.zig.fmtString(raw), line });
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `printLines` from `snippets/24-files/read-lines.zig`.*

`file.reader(io, &buf)` gives you a `File.Reader`. The general read methods are on its `interface` field, which is a `std.Io.Reader`.

`takeDelimiter('\n')` returns the next line without the `'\n'`. When the file has no more lines, the method returns `null`, and the `while` loop stops. Thus the full loop is one `while` with a capture.

[Readers and Writers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/readers-and-writers/#read-lines-select-the-correct-variant) compares `takeDelimiter` with the two methods that have similar names. For a line loop, use `takeDelimiter`.

## Line endings

The three files have the same two lines. Only the bytes at the end of each line are different.

```
   unix.txt
     line 1: "one" -> "one"
     line 2: "two" -> "two"
   no-final.txt
     line 1: "one" -> "one"
     line 2: "two" -> "two"
```

A file that ends with `'\n'` gives two lines, not three. No empty line comes after the last newline.

A file without a newline at the end also gives its last line. Thus the two files give the same result, and that result is correct.

Windows is different. Usually, a file from Windows has two bytes, `"\r\n"`, at the end of each line.

```
   windows.txt
     line 1: "one\r" -> "one"
     line 2: "two\r" -> "two"
```

The program splits each line at `'\n'`. Thus the `'\r'` stays at the end of the line. You can easily miss the `'\r'`, because a terminal does not show it. But `"one\r"` is not equal to `"one"`, and a number parser rejects `"42\r"`.

`std.mem.trimEnd(u8, raw, "\r")` removes the `'\r'`. On a line without a `'\r'`, the function returns the line with no change. Thus the same loop reads the two types of file.

## A line longer than the buffer

The reader can return only a line that fits in its buffer. In this example, the buffer is 16 bytes, and one line is 40 characters long.

```
   line 1: short
   line 2: StreamTooLong, skipped 41 bytes
   line 3: after
```

For the long line, `takeDelimiter` returns `error.StreamTooLong`. The method does not return the first 16 bytes as if they are the full line. Also, the method does not consume bytes. The reader has the same state as before the call.

Thus you must make a decision. In this example, the program skips the line with `discardDelimiterInclusive('\n')`. That method reads bytes up to the next newline, and the newline too, and discards them. It returns 41: forty `x` characters and the newline.

Then the loop continues, and the reader reads line 3 correctly.

```zig
fn readSkippingLong(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    // The buffer is 16 bytes. The longest line that the reader can return
    // is 15 characters and the newline.
    var buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = file.reader(io, &buf);
    const r = &reader.interface;

    var n: usize = 1;
    while (true) : (n += 1) {
        // The parentheses are necessary: `catch` handles the error, then
        // `orelse` handles the end of the file.
        const line = (r.takeDelimiter('\n') catch |err| switch (err) {
            error.StreamTooLong => {
                // The reader consumed no bytes. Skip to the end of this line,
                // then continue.
                const skipped = try r.discardDelimiterInclusive('\n');
                try out.print("   line {d}: StreamTooLong, skipped {d} bytes\n", .{ n, skipped });
                continue;
            },
            else => |e| return e,
        }) orelse break;
        try out.print("   line {d}: {s}\n", .{ n, line });
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `readSkippingLong` from `snippets/24-files/read-lines.zig`.*

The result of `takeDelimiter` can be an error or `null`. `catch` handles the error, and `orelse break` handles `null`, the end of the file. Put parentheses around the `catch` part, as the code above does.

Zig 0.17 accepted the line without the parentheses and read it as `(… catch …) orelse break`. Zig master does not accept the two operators together without parentheses. The error is `ambiguous operator precedence with operators ... catch ... orelse ...`. The parentheses make the old meaning explicit, and the program does not change.

Skip the line for a log file, where one bad line must not stop the program. For input from a user or from a different program, the error is frequently the correct result.

In that case, the buffer size is the longest line that you accept, and the reader rejects each longer line. If a line can truly have any length, use a larger buffer. Alternatively, copy each part of the line into an `ArrayList` when the reader reads it.

## A large file through a small buffer

The third file has 10,000 lines.

```
   file size 98894 bytes, buffer 256 bytes
   10000 lines, 98894 bytes, last line "line 10000"
```

The reader never holds more than 256 bytes of the file. When the buffer has no more bytes, the reader moves the bytes that it did not read to the start of the buffer. Then it reads more bytes from the file.

Thus the memory for this loop does not change with the size of the file. The same loop reads a 10 GB log with the same 256 bytes.

## Keep a line

```zig
fn countLines(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = file.reader(io, &buf);

    var lines: usize = 0;
    var bytes: usize = 0;
    var last: [16]u8 = undefined;
    var last_len: usize = 0;
    while (try reader.interface.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        lines += 1;
        bytes += line.len + 1;
        // `line` points into `buf`, and the next read writes over `buf`.
        // To keep the line after this iteration, copy the line.
        @memcpy(last[0..line.len], line);
        last_len = line.len;
    }
    try out.print("   file size {d} bytes, buffer {d} bytes\n", .{ try file.length(io), buf.len });
    try out.print("   {d} lines, {d} bytes, last line \"{s}\"\n", .{ lines, bytes, last[0..last_len] });
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `countLines` from `snippets/24-files/read-lines.zig`.*

`line` is a slice that points into `buf`. The slice is not a copy. The next call to `takeDelimiter` can put new bytes into `buf`, and then the old slice shows different bytes. Thus a line is valid only until the next read.

To keep the last line after the loop, the program copies the line into `last` with `@memcpy`. To keep all lines, copy each line with `gpa.dupe(u8, line)` and store the copies.

This rule is the reason that a small buffer can read a large file. The reader does not keep old lines. Thus the reader needs space only for the current line.

## Write the test file

`writeNumberedLines` writes the large file through a `File.Writer` with a 4 KB buffer. `print` writes into the buffer. Each time the buffer becomes full, the writer sends the buffer to the file.

The last call to `flush()` sends the bytes that remain. Without that call, the program never writes the last part of the file.

The next chapter gives more information about how to write a file.

---

## Write Text Files

*Working with Files. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/write-text/*

To write a file looks simple. You create the file, write some bytes and close the file. But some options change the bytes on disk, and the default values do not always do what you expect.

The program below writes six small files. Then it shows the contents of each file.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Io = std.Io;

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = init.gpa;

    var out_buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const dir = Io.Dir.cwd();

    // 1. By default, createFile truncates. With `.truncate = false`, the new
    //    bytes replace the start of the old bytes, and the other bytes stay.
    try out.print("1. truncate\n", .{});
    try writeText(io, dir, "note.txt", .{}, "first version\n");
    try writeText(io, dir, "note.txt", .{}, "v2\n");
    try show(io, gpa, dir, "note.txt", "   truncate = true: ", out);
    try writeText(io, dir, "note.txt", .{}, "first version\n");
    try writeText(io, dir, "note.txt", .{ .truncate = false }, "v2\n");
    try show(io, gpa, dir, "note.txt", "   truncate = false:", out);

    // 2. Create a file only if the file does not exist.
    try out.print("2. exclusive\n", .{});
    for (0..2) |attempt| {
        if (dir.createFile(io, "id.txt", .{ .exclusive = true })) |file| {
            file.close(io);
            try out.print("   attempt {d}: created\n", .{attempt + 1});
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("   attempt {d}: {t}\n", .{ attempt + 1, err });
        }
    }

    // 3. Append: open the file, then start the writer at the end. The mode
    //    is read_write because, on WASI, a request for the length needs read
    //    access. On Linux or macOS, write_only is sufficient.
    try out.print("3. append\n", .{});
    try writeText(io, dir, "log.txt", .{}, "started\n");
    for ([_][]const u8{ "loaded 3 items\n", "stopped\n" }) |line| {
        const file = try dir.openFile(io, "log.txt", .{ .mode = .read_write });
        defer file.close(io);
        var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
        var writer = file.writer(io, &buf);
        try writer.seekTo(try file.length(io));
        try writer.interface.writeAll(line);
        try writer.interface.flush();
    }
    try show(io, gpa, dir, "log.txt", "", out);

    // 4. The bytes stay in the buffer of the writer until a flush.
    try out.print("4. flush\n", .{});
    {
        const file = try dir.createFile(io, "lost.txt", .{});
        var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
        var writer = file.writer(io, &buf);
        try writer.interface.writeAll("this line never reaches the file\n");
        try out.print("   buffered {d} bytes, file length {d}\n", .{ writer.interface.buffered().len, try file.length(io) });
        file.close(io); // close without flush
    }
    try out.print("   after close: {d} bytes on disk\n", .{(try dir.statFile(io, "lost.txt", .{})).size});

    // 5. Replace a file in one step. The new contents go to a temporary
    //    file in the same directory. A rename then moves that file into place.
    try out.print("5. atomic replace\n", .{});
    try writeText(io, dir, "config.txt", .{}, "port = 8080\n");
    {
        var atomic = try dir.createFileAtomic(io, "config.txt", .{ .replace = true });
        defer atomic.deinit(io);

        var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
        var writer = atomic.file.writer(io, &buf);
        try writer.interface.writeAll("port = 9090\n");
        try writer.interface.flush();

        try show(io, gpa, dir, "config.txt", "   while writing:", out);
        try atomic.replace(io);
    }
    try show(io, gpa, dir, "config.txt", "   after replace:", out);

    // The same steps, but the program fails before `replace`. `deinit`
    // deletes the temporary file, and the old contents do not change.
    {
        var atomic = try dir.createFileAtomic(io, "config.txt", .{ .replace = true });
        defer atomic.deinit(io);
        try atomic.file.writeStreamingAll(io, "port = ");
        // ...an error occurs here, and the block returns before replace.
    }
    try show(io, gpa, dir, "config.txt", "   after a failed write:", out);
    try out.print("   files in the directory: {d}\n", .{try countEntries(io, dir)});

    for ([_][]const u8{ "note.txt", "id.txt", "log.txt", "lost.txt", "config.txt" }) |name| {
        try dir.deleteFile(io, name);
    }
}

fn writeText(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, options: Io.Dir.CreateFileOptions, text: []const u8) !void {
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, name, options);
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = file.writer(io, &buf);
    try writer.interface.writeAll(text);
    try writer.interface.flush();
}

fn show(io: Io, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, label: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const text = try dir.readFileAlloc(io, name, gpa, .limited(4096));
    defer gpa.free(text);
    if (label.len == 0) {
        var lines = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, std.mem.trimEnd(u8, text, "\n"), '\n');
        while (lines.next()) |line| try out.print("   {s}\n", .{line});
    } else {
        try out.print("{s} \"{f}\"\n", .{ label, std.zig.fmtString(text) });
    }
}

fn countEntries(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir) !usize {
    var d = try dir.openDir(io, ".", .{ .iterate = true });
    defer d.close(io);
    var it = d.iterate();
    var n: usize = 0;
    while (try it.next(io)) |_| n += 1;
    return n;
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`24-files.write-text`)*

## The helper

```zig
fn writeText(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, options: Io.Dir.CreateFileOptions, text: []const u8) !void {
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, name, options);
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = file.writer(io, &buf);
    try writer.interface.writeAll(text);
    try writer.interface.flush();
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writeText` from `snippets/24-files/write-text.zig`.*

Each write in this chapter uses the same three steps:

1. `createFile` opens the file for write operations. If the file does not exist, `createFile` creates the file.
2. `file.writer(io, &buf)` gives you a `File.Writer` with a 64-byte buffer.
3. The program writes through `writer.interface`. Then it calls `flush()`, which sends the bytes that remain in the buffer to the file.

The `options` argument controls what occurs when the file exists already.

## Truncate

By default, `createFile` truncates the file. The function removes the old contents before the program writes.

```
   truncate = true:  "v2\n"
   truncate = false: "v2\nst version\n"
```

With `.truncate = false`, the file keeps its old bytes. The writer starts at offset 0. Thus `"v2\n"` replaces the first three bytes of `"first version\n"`. The other bytes, `"st version\n"`, stay in the file.

For a text file, you almost never want this result. But it is useful for a file of records of fixed size, where you change one record and keep the other records. The [Random Access](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/random-access/) chapter shows this.

## Create only if new

`.exclusive = true` creates the file. If the file exists already, the call fails.

```
   attempt 1: created
   attempt 2: PathAlreadyExists
```

The check and the create occur in one step. This is important when two programs run at the same time.

If you check first with `statFile` and create the file after the check, the other program can create the file between your two calls. With `.exclusive = true`, only one of the two programs succeeds.

## Append

`createFile` does not have an append option, and `openFile` does not have one. Thus the program opens the file and starts the writer at the end.

```
   started
   loaded 3 items
   stopped
```

`writer.seekTo(try file.length(io))` moves the writer to the current end of the file. Then each new line goes after the old lines.

The program opens the file with `.mode = .read_write`, not `.write_only`. The reason is WASI, where this program runs. On WASI, Zig asks for the right to read the size of a file only when it opens the file for read operations. Thus, on WASI, `file.length` on a write-only file fails with `AccessDenied`. On Linux and macOS, `.write_only` works.

The append has one more limit. The seek to the end and the write are two separate steps. If two programs append to the same file at the same time, the two programs can seek to the same end. Then each program writes over the bytes of the other program.

[Two Writers, One File](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/filelock/) shows this problem, and the lock that prevents it.

## The forgotten flush

This part of the program writes a line. Then it closes the file, but it does not call `flush()`.

```
   buffered 33 bytes, file length 0
   after close: 0 bytes on disk
```

`writeAll` copied the 33 bytes into the buffer of the writer. No bytes went to the file, because the buffer was not full.

`close` closes the file, but it does not know about the buffer. Thus the bytes are lost, and you get no error.

To correct the problem, call `flush()` before you close the file. In a function that returns early on errors, put the call immediately after the last write. Then `try` reports a flush that fails.

## Replace a file in one step
