For example, a program writes a new `config.txt` while a different program reads the file. If the reader opens the file in the middle of the write, the reader gets half of the configuration. If the writer stops unexpectedly in the middle of the write, the file stays half written.

`createFileAtomic` prevents the two problems. The function writes to a new temporary file in the same directory. When you call `replace`, the function renames the temporary file to `config.txt`.

On Linux and macOS, a rename in one directory occurs in one step. A reader sees the old file or the new file, but never a mix of the two files.

```
   while writing: "port = 8080\n"
   after replace: "port = 9090\n"
```

During the write, `config.txt` still had the old contents.

The second block fails intentionally. It writes half a line and returns before `replace`.

```
   after a failed write: "port = 9090\n"
   files in the directory: 5
```

`deinit` runs from the `defer` statement and deletes the temporary file. The old contents do not change, and no temporary file stays in the directory.

Always call `deinit`, also after a `replace` that succeeds. In the two conditions, the call to `deinit` is safe.

The option `.replace = true` must agree with the call at the end:

- `replace` writes over a file that exists.
- `link` is the other choice. If the file exists already, `link` fails with `PathAlreadyExists`, the same as `.exclusive = true`.

## Select a function

- For a new file that you write one time, use `createFile` with the default options.
- For a log, open the file and seek to the end.
- For a file that a different program reads, or a file that must never be half written, use `createFileAtomic`.

In all of these conditions, flush before you close the file.

---

## Binary Files

*Working with Files. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/binary-files/*

A text file stores numbers as characters. The number 1200 is four bytes: `'1'`, `'2'`, `'0'`, `'0'`.

A binary file stores the number itself. As a `u32`, 1200 is also four bytes. But the bytes are the bits of the number, not digits.

Binary files are smaller and faster to read, because the program does not have to parse them. But a person cannot read them. Thus you must write down the format exactly.

The program below defines a small format for a list of players. It writes a file in that format and reads the file again. Then it gives the reader three bad files.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Io = std.Io;

// First, write down the format. All integers are little-endian.
//
//   header, 10 bytes
//     0  magic    4 bytes  "SCOR"
//     4  version  u16      1
//     6  count    u32      number of records
//
//   record, 9 bytes + name
//     0  id        u32
//     4  score     i32
//     8  name_len  u8
//     9  name      name_len bytes
const magic = "SCOR";
const version: u16 = 1;

const Player = struct {
    id: u32,
    score: i32,
    name: []const u8,
};

const players = [_]Player{
    .{ .id = 7, .score = 1200, .name = "ada" },
    .{ .id = 42, .score = -15, .name = "linus" },
    .{ .id = 300, .score = 0, .name = "grace" },
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var out_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const dir = Io.Dir.cwd();

    // 1. Byte order.
    try out.print("1. the number 0x01020304 as four bytes\n", .{});
    for ([_]std.lang.Endian{ .little, .big }) |endian| {
        var bytes: [4]u8 = undefined;
        std.mem.writeInt(u32, &bytes, 0x01020304, endian);
        try out.print("   {t:<7} {x}\n", .{ endian, bytes });
    }

    // 2. Write the file and dump each byte.
    try out.print("2. scores.bin\n", .{});
    try save(io, dir, "scores.bin", &players);
    try hexDump(io, dir, "scores.bin", out);

    // 3. Read the file again.
    try out.print("3. read back\n", .{});
    try printFile(io, dir, "scores.bin", out);

    // 4. Three files that are wrong in different ways.
    try out.print("4. bad files\n", .{});
    var good: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const bytes = try dir.readFile(io, "scores.bin", &good);

    try dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "photo.png", .data = "\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n\x00\x00" });
    var newer = bytes[0..10].*;
    std.mem.writeInt(u16, newer[4..6], 2, .little);
    try dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "newer.bin", .data = &newer });
    try dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "cut.bin", .data = bytes[0 .. bytes.len - 4] });

    for ([_][]const u8{ "photo.png", "newer.bin", "cut.bin" }) |name| {
        try out.print("   {s}: ", .{name});
        if (printFile(io, dir, name, out)) |_| {} else |err| try out.print("{t}\n", .{err});
    }

    for ([_][]const u8{ "scores.bin", "photo.png", "newer.bin", "cut.bin" }) |name| {
        try dir.deleteFile(io, name);
    }
}

fn save(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, list: []const Player) !void {
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = file.writer(io, &buf);
    const w = &fw.interface;

    try w.writeAll(magic);
    try w.writeInt(u16, version, .little);
    try w.writeInt(u32, @intCast(list.len), .little);

    for (list) |p| {
        try w.writeInt(u32, p.id, .little);
        try w.writeInt(i32, p.score, .little);
        try w.writeByte(@intCast(p.name.len));
        try w.writeAll(p.name);
    }
    try w.flush();
}

const FormatError = error{ NotScoresFile, UnsupportedVersion, Truncated, TooManyRecords, NameTooLong };

/// A record from the disk. The reader copies the name out of its buffer,
/// because the next read can write over that buffer.
const Record = struct {
    id: u32,
    score: i32,
    name_buf: [16]u8,
    name_len: u8,

    fn name(r: *const Record) []const u8 {
        return r.name_buf[0..r.name_len];
    }
};

const max_records = 8;

fn printFile(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var fr = file.reader(io, &buf);

    var records: [max_records]Record = undefined;
    const n = readRecords(&fr.interface, &records) catch |err| switch (err) {
        // The file ended in the middle of a value. For a reader of a
        // format, this is a bad file, not the normal end of input.
        error.EndOfStream => return error.Truncated,
        error.ReadFailed => return fr.err.?,
        else => |e| return e,
    };

    // Act on the data only now, after the check of the full file.
    for (records[0..n]) |*rec| {
        var num: [12]u8 = undefined;
        const score = try std.mem.print(&num, "{d}", .{rec.score});
        try out.print("   id {d:>3}  score {s:>5}  {s}\n", .{ rec.id, score, rec.name() });
    }
}

fn readRecords(r: *Io.Reader, records: []Record) !usize {
    // Check what the file says it is, before the reader uses the bytes after it.
    if (!std.mem.eql(u8, try r.takeArray(4), magic)) return FormatError.NotScoresFile;
    if (try r.takeInt(u16, .little) != version) return FormatError.UnsupportedVersion;

    // `count` comes from the file. Thus it is untrusted, the same as all data.
    const count = try r.takeInt(u32, .little);
    if (count > records.len) return FormatError.TooManyRecords;

    for (records[0..count]) |*rec| {
        rec.id = try r.takeInt(u32, .little);
        rec.score = try r.takeInt(i32, .little);
        rec.name_len = try r.takeByte();
        if (rec.name_len > rec.name_buf.len) return FormatError.NameTooLong;
        @memcpy(rec.name_buf[0..rec.name_len], try r.take(rec.name_len));
    }
    return count;
}

fn hexDump(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const bytes = try dir.readFile(io, name, &buf);
    var offset: usize = 0;
    while (offset < bytes.len) : (offset += 16) {
        const row = bytes[offset..@min(offset + 16, bytes.len)];
        try out.print("   {x:0>4}  ", .{offset});
        for (row) |b| try out.print("{x:0>2} ", .{b});
        try out.splatByteAll(' ', (16 - row.len) * 3 + 1);
        for (row) |b| try out.writeByte(if (std.ascii.isPrint(b)) b else '.');
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }
    try out.print("   {d} bytes\n", .{bytes.len});
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`24-files.binary-files`)*

## Write the format first

Before the code, the snippet writes down the format in a comment.

```
//   header, 10 bytes
//     0  magic    4 bytes  "SCOR"
//     4  version  u16      1
//     6  count    u32      number of records
//
//   record, 9 bytes + name
//     0  id        u32
//     4  score     i32
//     8  name_len  u8
//     9  name      name_len bytes
```

Each byte has a position, a size and a meaning. All integers are little-endian.

This table is the format. The code only obeys the table. A program in a different language can read the file if it obeys the same table.

## Byte order

A `u32` is four bytes, and a computer can store the four bytes in two orders.

```
   little  04030201
   big     01020304
```

- Little-endian puts the smallest byte first. x86 and ARM computers use this order.
- Big-endian puts the largest byte first. Network protocols frequently use this order.

The two orders are equally correct. The important thing is that the format says which order it uses, and that the code gives the order on each read and write.

For this reason, `writeInt` and `takeInt` both take the byte order as an argument. There is no default.

## Write the file

```zig
fn save(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, list: []const Player) !void {
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = file.writer(io, &buf);
    const w = &fw.interface;

    try w.writeAll(magic);
    try w.writeInt(u16, version, .little);
    try w.writeInt(u32, @intCast(list.len), .little);

    for (list) |p| {
        try w.writeInt(u32, p.id, .little);
        try w.writeInt(i32, p.score, .little);
        try w.writeByte(@intCast(p.name.len));
        try w.writeAll(p.name);
    }
    try w.flush();
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `save` from `snippets/24-files/binary-files.zig`.*

The program writes each field separately:

- `writeAll(magic)` writes the four letters `SCOR`.
- `writeInt(u16, version, .little)` writes the version as two bytes.
- The name is a string of any length. Thus the program first writes the length of the name as one byte, then the bytes of the name.

The name of this method is a length prefix. The length prefix tells the reader where one name ends and the next record starts.

Here is each byte of the file.

```
   0000  53 43 4f 52 01 00 03 00 00 00 07 00 00 00 b0 04  SCOR............
   0010  00 00 03 61 64 61 2a 00 00 00 f1 ff ff ff 05 6c  ...ada*........l
   0020  69 6e 75 73 2c 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 05 67 72 61  inus,........gra
   0030  63 65                                            ce
   50 bytes
```

You can find each field in the dump:

- `53 43 4f 52` is `SCOR`.
- `01 00` is version 1, and `03 00 00 00` is a count of 3. The small byte is first in the two values.
- Then the first record: id `07 00 00 00`, score `b0 04 00 00` (0x04b0 or 1200), name length `03`, and `ada`.

The score of Linus, -15, is `f1 ff ff ff`, because a computer stores negative numbers in two's complement.

## Why not write the struct directly

The program can copy the memory of a `Player` struct to the file in one call. That code is shorter, but it is incorrect.

A usual Zig struct has no fixed layout. The compiler can change the order of the fields and add padding. The integers in the struct are in the byte order of the computer that wrote them. Thus the bytes can change with a new compiler, a different target, or a different build mode.

[A Binary Wire Format](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/binary-roundtrip/) gives more information about this. The short rule: write the fields one at a time, and give the byte order each time.

## Read the file again

```zig
fn readRecords(r: *Io.Reader, records: []Record) !usize {
    // Check what the file says it is, before the reader uses the bytes after it.
    if (!std.mem.eql(u8, try r.takeArray(4), magic)) return FormatError.NotScoresFile;
    if (try r.takeInt(u16, .little) != version) return FormatError.UnsupportedVersion;

    // `count` comes from the file. Thus it is untrusted, the same as all data.
    const count = try r.takeInt(u32, .little);
    if (count > records.len) return FormatError.TooManyRecords;

    for (records[0..count]) |*rec| {
        rec.id = try r.takeInt(u32, .little);
        rec.score = try r.takeInt(i32, .little);
        rec.name_len = try r.takeByte();
        if (rec.name_len > rec.name_buf.len) return FormatError.NameTooLong;
        @memcpy(rec.name_buf[0..rec.name_len], try r.take(rec.name_len));
    }
    return count;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `readRecords` from `snippets/24-files/binary-files.zig`.*

The reader obeys the same table, in the same order. But the reader does not trust the file. The file can contain any data: a different format, a newer version of this format, or a file that a copy operation cut short.

Thus the reader checks each value before it uses the value:

1. First the magic. If the first four bytes are not `SCOR`, the file is not a file of this format, and the reader stops.
2. Then the version. A file from a newer program can have fields that this reader does not know. Thus the reader also stops for a newer version.
3. Then the count. The count comes from the file. Thus the count is also not trusted.

A bad file can say that it holds four billion records. Thus the reader compares the count with the number of records that it has space for. The name length gets the same check against the size of `name_buf`.

## Three bad files

```
   photo.png: NotScoresFile
   newer.bin: UnsupportedVersion
   cut.bin: Truncated
```

- `photo.png` starts with the PNG signature. Thus the magic check rejects the file.
- `newer.bin` is the header of this format, with the version changed to 2.
- `cut.bin` is the file of this format without the last four bytes.

In `cut.bin`, the reader reads the first two records correctly. The third record ends in the middle of its name.

When too few bytes remain, `take` returns `error.EndOfStream`. In a text file, the end of the stream is normal. It means that the input is complete.

In the middle of a record, the end of the stream means that the file is bad. Thus `printFile` changes `EndOfStream` into the error of this format, `error.Truncated`.

## Check all data, then act

```zig
fn printFile(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);

    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var fr = file.reader(io, &buf);

    var records: [max_records]Record = undefined;
    const n = readRecords(&fr.interface, &records) catch |err| switch (err) {
        // The file ended in the middle of a value. For a reader of a
        // format, this is a bad file, not the normal end of input.
        error.EndOfStream => return error.Truncated,
        error.ReadFailed => return fr.err.?,
        else => |e| return e,
    };

    // Act on the data only now, after the check of the full file.
    for (records[0..n]) |*rec| {
        var num: [12]u8 = undefined;
        const score = try std.mem.print(&num, "{d}", .{rec.score});
        try out.print("   id {d:>3}  score {s:>5}  {s}\n", .{ rec.id, score, rec.name() });
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `printFile` from `snippets/24-files/binary-files.zig`.*

`printFile` first reads all records into an array. It prints only after `readRecords` checked the full file.

The first version of this program printed each record when it read the record. For `cut.bin`, the program printed two players and then reported the error.

In a real program, an action on each record when the record arrives can cause damage. For example, the action is "update the database" and not "print". Then the program saves half of a bad file before it finds the error.

Thus read and check all data first. Act only when all of the data is valid.

`readRecords` has one more detail. `take(name_len)` returns a slice of the buffer of the reader, and the next read can write over that buffer. Thus the program copies the name into `name_buf` with `@memcpy`. [Read Line by Line](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/read-lines/#keep-a-line) has the same rule for lines.

---

## Random Access

*Working with Files. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/random-access/*

The earlier chapters read a file from the start to the end. That method works for text, where a line can have any length. To find line 500, the program must read the 499 lines before it.

If all records in a file have the same size, the program does not have to read the earlier records. Record 500 starts at byte `500 * size`. The program can read the record directly. It can also change the record and not touch the remainder of the file. The name of this method is random access.

The program below keeps a small file of bank accounts. Each account is 16 bytes.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Io = std.Io;

// One record is 16 bytes, little-endian, at offset `index * 16`.
//
//   0  id       u32
//   4  balance  i64   in cents
//   12 active   u8    1 or 0
//   13 unused   3 bytes, always zero
const record_size = 16;

const Account = struct {
    id: u32,
    balance: i64,
    active: bool,

    fn encode(a: Account) [record_size]u8 {
        var bytes: [record_size]u8 = @splat(0);
        std.mem.writeInt(u32, bytes[0..4], a.id, .little);
        std.mem.writeInt(i64, bytes[4..12], a.balance, .little);
        bytes[12] = @intFromBool(a.active);
        return bytes;
    }

    fn decode(bytes: *const [record_size]u8) Account {
        return .{
            .id = std.mem.readInt(u32, bytes[0..4], .little),
            .balance = std.mem.readInt(i64, bytes[4..12], .little),
            .active = bytes[12] != 0,
        };
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var out_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const dir = Io.Dir.cwd();
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, "accounts.db", .{ .read = true });
    defer file.close(io);

    // 1. Write five records. Each record is at its own offset.
    try out.print("1. five records\n", .{});
    for (0..5) |i| {
        const a: Account = .{ .id = @intCast(100 + i), .balance = @intCast(1000 * (i + 1)), .active = true };
        try writeRecord(io, file, i, a);
    }
    try list(io, file, out, true);

    // 2. Read one record directly.
    try out.print("2. record 3 only\n", .{});
    const a3 = try readRecord(io, file, 3);
    try out.print("   read 16 bytes at offset {d}: id {d}\n", .{ 3 * record_size, a3.id });

    // 3. Change one record in place. No other byte in the file moves.
    try out.print("3. update record 1\n", .{});
    var a1 = try readRecord(io, file, 1);
    a1.balance -= 750;
    try writeRecord(io, file, 1, a1);
    const updated = try readRecord(io, file, 1);
    try out.print("   record 1 is now id {d}  balance {d}\n", .{ updated.id, updated.balance });
    try list(io, file, out, false);

    // 4. Write past the end. A read of the gap gives zero bytes.
    try out.print("4. write record 7\n", .{});
    try writeRecord(io, file, 7, .{ .id = 107, .balance = 99, .active = true });
    try list(io, file, out, true);

    // 5. A reader that seeks, and not an offset on each call.
    try out.print("5. seek to the last record\n", .{});
    {
        var buf: [record_size]u8 = undefined;
        var reader = file.reader(io, &buf);
        const size = try reader.getSize();
        try reader.seekTo(size - record_size);
        const last = Account.decode(try reader.interface.takeArray(record_size));
        try out.print("   size {d}, seekTo({d}), id {d}\n", .{ size, size - record_size, last.id });
    }

    // 6. Make the file smaller to remove the last records.
    try out.print("6. setLength to 5 records\n", .{});
    try file.setLength(io, 5 * record_size);
    try list(io, file, out, false);

    // 7. A length that is not a whole number of records.
    try out.print("7. a torn write\n", .{});
    try file.writePositionalAll(io, "\x69\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00", 5 * record_size);
    try out.print("   file length {d}\n", .{try file.length(io)});
    if (list(io, file, out, false)) |_| {} else |err| try out.print("   {t}\n", .{err});

    try dir.deleteFile(io, "accounts.db");
}

fn writeRecord(io: Io, file: Io.File, index: usize, a: Account) !void {
    const bytes = a.encode();
    try file.writePositionalAll(io, &bytes, index * record_size);
}

fn readRecord(io: Io, file: Io.File, index: usize) !Account {
    var bytes: [record_size]u8 = undefined;
    const n = try file.readPositionalAll(io, &bytes, index * record_size);
    if (n != record_size) return error.NoSuchRecord;
    return Account.decode(&bytes);
}

fn list(io: Io, file: Io.File, out: *Io.Writer, show_records: bool) !void {
    const size = try file.length(io);
    if (size % record_size != 0) return error.PartialRecord;
    const count = std.math.cast(usize, size / record_size) orelse return error.FileTooBig;
    try out.print("   {d} bytes, {d} records\n", .{ size, count });
    if (!show_records) return;
    for (0..count) |i| {
        const a = try readRecord(io, file, i);
        if (a.id == 0) {
            try out.print("     [{d}] empty\n", .{i});
        } else {
            try out.print("     [{d}] id {d}  balance {d}\n", .{ i, a.id, a.balance });
        }
    }
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`24-files.random-access`)*

## One record, 16 bytes

```zig
const Account = struct {
    id: u32,
    balance: i64,
    active: bool,

    fn encode(a: Account) [record_size]u8 {
        var bytes: [record_size]u8 = @splat(0);
        std.mem.writeInt(u32, bytes[0..4], a.id, .little);
        std.mem.writeInt(i64, bytes[4..12], a.balance, .little);
        bytes[12] = @intFromBool(a.active);
        return bytes;
    }

    fn decode(bytes: *const [record_size]u8) Account {
        return .{
            .id = std.mem.readInt(u32, bytes[0..4], .little),
            .balance = std.mem.readInt(i64, bytes[4..12], .little),
            .active = bytes[12] != 0,
        };
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Account` from `snippets/24-files/random-access.zig`.*

A comment at the top of the snippet gives the layout, the same as the format in [Binary Files](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/binary-files/).

- `encode` changes an `Account` into exactly 16 bytes.
- `decode` changes 16 bytes back into an `Account`.

The balance is an `i64` count of cents, not a float. Money in a float gets rounding errors.

The record does not use bytes 13 to 15, and `encode` always sets them to zero. Unused bytes give a later version of the format space for a new field, with no change to the record size.

The bytes start from `@splat(0)`. Thus the program does not write old memory contents to the file.

## Read and write at an offset

```zig
fn writeRecord(io: Io, file: Io.File, index: usize, a: Account) !void {
    const bytes = a.encode();
    try file.writePositionalAll(io, &bytes, index * record_size);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writeRecord` from `snippets/24-files/random-access.zig`.*

`writePositionalAll(io, bytes, offset)` writes the bytes at that offset. The function does not use the current position of the file, and it does not move the position. Thus the offset of record `index` is `index * record_size`, and that is the full calculation.

```zig
fn readRecord(io: Io, file: Io.File, index: usize) !Account {
    var bytes: [record_size]u8 = undefined;
    const n = try file.readPositionalAll(io, &bytes, index * record_size);
    if (n != record_size) return error.NoSuchRecord;
    return Account.decode(&bytes);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `readRecord` from `snippets/24-files/random-access.zig`.*

`readPositionalAll` does the same for a read. It returns the number of bytes that it read. If the record is after the end of the file, that count is less than 16, and the function returns `error.NoSuchRecord`.

```
2. record 3 only
   read 16 bytes at offset 48: id 103
```

The program never read records 0, 1 and 2. For a file of five records, this saves nothing. For a file of five million records, it is the difference between one read and five million reads.

## Change one record

```
3. update record 1
   record 1 is now id 101  balance 1250
   80 bytes, 5 records
```

The program reads record 1 and subtracts 750 from the balance. Then it writes the 16 bytes back to the same offset.

The file is still 80 bytes. The program did not write the bytes before or after record 1 again.

Compare this with a text file. If a balance changes from `1000` to `999`, the line becomes one character shorter, and each byte after the line must move. With records of fixed size, a new value always fits in the old space.

## Write past the end

The file has five records, with the numbers 0 to 4. Now the program writes record 7.

```
4. write record 7
   128 bytes, 8 records
     [0] id 100  balance 1000
     [1] id 101  balance 1250
     [2] id 102  balance 3000
     [3] id 103  balance 4000
     [4] id 104  balance 5000
     [5] empty
     [6] empty
     [7] id 107  balance 99
```

The write succeeds, and the file becomes 128 bytes.

The program never wrote records 5 and 6. A read of each of these records gives 16 zero bytes. Thus their id is 0. The program uses id 0 for an empty slot. For this reason, real ids start at 100.

On most Linux and macOS filesystems, a gap of this type uses no space on disk. The filesystem records that the range is zero and does not store the range. The name of a file with gaps of this type is a sparse file.

## A reader that seeks

`readPositionalAll` takes the offset on each call. A `File.Reader` can do the same thing with a position that it keeps.

```
5. seek to the last record
   size 128, seekTo(112), id 107
```

1. `reader.getSize()` gets the file size.
2. `reader.seekTo(size - record_size)` moves the reader to the start of the last record.
3. `takeArray(record_size)` reads the 16 bytes from that position.

- To read some records in a sequence after one seek, use the reader.
- When each read is at a different position, use the positional calls.

## Make the file smaller

`file.setLength(io, 5 * record_size)` cuts the file to 80 bytes.

```
6. setLength to 5 records
   80 bytes, 5 records
```

Records 5, 6 and 7 are gone.

`setLength` can also make a file longer. The new bytes are zero, the same as the gap in part 4 of the output.

## A record that is too short

For example, the program stops unexpectedly in the middle of the write of a new record. Only part of the record gets to the disk. The last step of the program simulates this failure: it writes 6 bytes at the end.

```
7. a torn write
   file length 86
   PartialRecord
```

86 is not a multiple of 16.

```zig
fn list(io: Io, file: Io.File, out: *Io.Writer, show_records: bool) !void {
    const size = try file.length(io);
    if (size % record_size != 0) return error.PartialRecord;
    const count = std.math.cast(usize, size / record_size) orelse return error.FileTooBig;
    try out.print("   {d} bytes, {d} records\n", .{ size, count });
    if (!show_records) return;
    for (0..count) |i| {
        const a = try readRecord(io, file, i);
        if (a.id == 0) {
            try out.print("     [{d}] empty\n", .{i});
        } else {
            try out.print("     [{d}] id {d}  balance {d}\n", .{ i, a.id, a.balance });
        }
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `list` from `snippets/24-files/random-access.zig`.*

`list` first does this check, with `size % record_size`, and returns `error.PartialRecord`.

Without the check, the function calculates 5 records and ignores the six extra bytes. That hides the problem: the file is damaged, and the program never tells you.

A real program must decide what to do next:

- It can cut the file back to the last full record with `setLength`.
- It can refuse to start until a person examines the file.

In the two cases, the program must first find the problem.

[An Append-Only Record Store](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/flatdb/) recovers from exactly this case. [A Write-Ahead Log](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/kvstore/) handles a crash in the middle of a change.

## The size of a length

`file.length` returns a `u64`. `list` divides the length by 16. Then it changes the result to a `usize` with `std.math.cast`.

[Open, Read, Close](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/open-read-close/#open-a-handle) explains why. On `wasm32`, a `usize` is 32 bits, and a file can be larger than 32 bits can count.

---

## Read CSV

*Working with Files. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/csv-read/*

CSV looks like the easiest file format of all. Each line is a record, and commas separate the fields. Thus the first idea is to read a line and split the line at each `','`.

That method works until a field contains a comma. `2,"Widget, large",12.00` is three fields, not four. The quotes tell the reader that the comma in them is part of the text.

There are two more cases:

- A field can contain a quote, as two quotes: `"the ""best"" one"`.
- A quoted field can contain a newline. Thus one record can use two lines of the file.

A split at commas and newlines gives incorrect results for all three cases.

The Zig standard library does not include a CSV reader. Thus this chapter writes one. The reader is 150 lines, with comments and the code that prints the trace. At its centre is a state machine with four states.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Io = std.Io;
const Allocator = std.mem.Allocator;

/// Reads one record at a time. The fields that it returns stay valid until
/// the next call to `next`.
pub const CsvReader = struct {
    r: *Io.Reader,
    gpa: Allocator,
    /// The text of each field in the current record, with no space between.
    text: std.ArrayList(u8) = .empty,
    /// Where each field ends in `text`.
    ends: std.ArrayList(usize) = .empty,
    fields: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty,
    line: usize = 1,
    /// The line where a quoted field opened. The error for a quote that
    /// never closes gives this line.
    quote_line: usize = 0,
    /// If not null, the reader writes one row for each byte that it reads.
    trace: ?*Io.Writer = null,

    const State = enum {
        /// At the start of a field. A quote here opens a quoted field.
        field_start,
        /// In a field that did not start with a quote.
        unquoted,
        /// In a quoted field. Commas and newlines are usual text.
        quoted,
        /// The reader read a quote in a quoted field. The next byte decides:
        /// another quote is an escaped quote, and all other bytes end the field.
        quote_in_quoted,
    };

    const Error = error{ QuoteInUnquotedField, TextAfterClosingQuote, UnterminatedQuote };

    pub fn deinit(c: *CsvReader) void {
        c.text.deinit(c.gpa);
        c.ends.deinit(c.gpa);
        c.fields.deinit(c.gpa);
    }

    pub fn next(c: *CsvReader) !?[]const []const u8 {
        c.text.clearRetainingCapacity();
        c.ends.clearRetainingCapacity();
        c.fields.clearRetainingCapacity();

        var state: State = .field_start;
        var read_any = false;
        while (true) {
            const byte = c.r.takeByte() catch |err| switch (err) {
                error.EndOfStream => {
                    // End of input. In quotes, the end is an error. If the
                    // reader read no bytes, there is no record.
                    if (state == .quoted) {
                        c.line = c.quote_line;
                        return Error.UnterminatedQuote;
                    }
                    if (!read_any) return null;
                    try c.endField();
                    return try c.finish();
                },
                else => |e| return e,
            };
            read_any = true;
            const before = state;

            switch (state) {
                .field_start, .unquoted => switch (byte) {
                    ',' => {
                        try c.endField();
                        state = .field_start;
                    },
                    '\n' => {
                        try c.endField();
                        c.trace1(byte, before, .field_start);
                        c.line += 1;
                        return try c.finish();
                    },
                    // Part of a "\r\n" line ending. Discard it outside quotes.
                    '\r' => {},
                    '"' => if (state == .field_start) {
                        c.quote_line = c.line;
                        state = .quoted;
                    } else return Error.QuoteInUnquotedField,
                    else => {
                        try c.text.append(c.gpa, byte);
                        state = .unquoted;
                    },
                },
                .quoted => switch (byte) {
                    '"' => state = .quote_in_quoted,
                    else => {
                        if (byte == '\n') c.line += 1;
                        try c.text.append(c.gpa, byte);
                    },
                },
                .quote_in_quoted => switch (byte) {
                    // Two quotes in a sequence are one quote in the text.
                    '"' => {
                        try c.text.append(c.gpa, '"');
                        state = .quoted;
                    },
                    ',' => {
                        try c.endField();
                        state = .field_start;
                    },
                    '\n' => {
                        try c.endField();
                        c.trace1(byte, before, .field_start);
                        c.line += 1;
                        return try c.finish();
                    },
                    '\r' => {},
                    else => return Error.TextAfterClosingQuote,
                },
            }
            c.trace1(byte, before, state);
        }
    }

    fn endField(c: *CsvReader) !void {
        try c.ends.append(c.gpa, c.text.items.len);
    }

    /// Make the slices only here, when `text` does not grow any more. An
    /// earlier slice can point at memory that `append` moved.
    fn finish(c: *CsvReader) ![]const []const u8 {
        var start: usize = 0;
        for (c.ends.items) |end| {
            try c.fields.append(c.gpa, c.text.items[start..end]);
            start = end;
        }
        return c.fields.items;
    }

    fn trace1(c: *CsvReader, byte: u8, before: State, after: State) void {
        const w = c.trace orelse return;
        const shown: []const u8 = switch (byte) {
            '\n' => "'\\n'",
            '\r' => "'\\r'",
            else => &.{ '\'', byte, '\'' },
        };
        const n = c.ends.items.len;
        const field_ended = after == .field_start and (byte == ',' or byte == '\n');
        if (field_ended) {
            const start = if (n < 2) 0 else c.ends.items[n - 2];
            w.print("   {s:<4} {t:<15} -> {t:<15} field done: [{s}]\n", .{
                shown, before, after, c.text.items[start..c.ends.items[n - 1]],
            }) catch {};
        } else {
            const start = if (n == 0) 0 else c.ends.items[n - 1];
            w.print("   {s:<4} {t:<15} -> {t:<15} [{s}]\n", .{
                shown, before, after, c.text.items[start..],
            }) catch {};
        }
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = init.gpa;

    var out_buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    // 1. Each byte of one short line, and the state after the byte.
    try out.print("1. trace of: 7,\"say \"\"hi\"\"\",x\n", .{});
    {
        var r: Io.Reader = .fixed("7,\"say \"\"hi\"\"\",x\n");
        var csv: CsvReader = .{ .r = &r, .gpa = gpa, .trace = out };
        defer csv.deinit();
        const fields = (try csv.next()).?;
        try printRecord(out, fields);
    }

    // 2. A file with each case that the format allows.
    try out.print("2. products.csv\n", .{});
    const dir = Io.Dir.cwd();
    try dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "products.csv", .data = "id,name,price,note\r\n" ++
        "1,Pencil,0.50,\r\n" ++
        "2,\"Widget, large\",12.00,\"the \"\"best\"\" one\"\r\n" ++
        "3,Lamp,30.00,\"two\nlines\"\r\n" ++
        "4,Mug,8.25,no final newline" });
    {
        const file = try dir.openFile(io, "products.csv", .{});
        defer file.close(io);
        var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
        var fr = file.reader(io, &buf);
        var csv: CsvReader = .{ .r = &fr.interface, .gpa = gpa };
        defer csv.deinit();

        while (try csv.next()) |fields| try printRecord(out, fields);
    }
    try dir.deleteFile(io, "products.csv");

    // 3. Input that is not valid CSV, and the line where the error occurs.
    try out.print("3. errors\n", .{});
    for ([_][]const u8{
        "a,b\nc,d\"e\n",
        "a,\"b\"c\n",
        "a,b\nc,\"never closed\n",
    }) |input| {
        var r: Io.Reader = .fixed(input);
        var csv: CsvReader = .{ .r = &r, .gpa = gpa };
        defer csv.deinit();
        var records: usize = 0;
        while (csv.next()) |maybe| {
            if (maybe == null) break;
            records += 1;
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("   \"{f}\": {t} on line {d}\n", .{ std.zig.fmtString(input), err, csv.line });
            continue;
        }
        try out.print("   \"{f}\": {d} records\n", .{ std.zig.fmtString(input), records });
    }
}

fn printRecord(out: *Io.Writer, fields: []const []const u8) !void {
    try out.print("   {d} fields:", .{fields.len});
    for (fields) |f| {
        // Show a newline in a field as \n, so that a record stays on one line.
        try out.writeAll(" [");
        for (f) |b| if (b == '\n') try out.writeAll("\\n") else try out.writeByte(b);
        try out.writeByte(']');
    }
    try out.writeByte('\n');
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`24-files.csv-read`)*

## Four states

```zig
    const State = enum {
        /// At the start of a field. A quote here opens a quoted field.
        field_start,
        /// In a field that did not start with a quote.
        unquoted,
        /// In a quoted field. Commas and newlines are usual text.
        quoted,
        /// The reader read a quote in a quoted field. The next byte decides:
        /// another quote is an escaped quote, and all other bytes end the field.
        quote_in_quoted,
    };
```

*Quoted from the source: `State` from `snippets/24-files/csv-read.zig`.*

The reader looks at one byte at a time. The meaning of a byte changes with the current state:

- A comma in `field_start` or `unquoted` ends the field.
- A comma in `quoted` is only a comma.

Thus the reader keeps one variable, `state`. A `switch` on `state` handles each byte.

`quote_in_quoted` is the only state that is not easy to understand. In quotes, `"` can have two meanings:

- It can end the quoted field, as in `"abc",`.
- It can be the first half of an escaped quote, as in `"say ""hi"""`.

The reader cannot know which meaning is correct until it sees the next byte. Thus, after a quote, the reader goes to `quote_in_quoted` and waits for one more byte:

- Another `"` means an escaped quote. The reader adds one `"` to the text and returns to `quoted`.
- A comma or a newline means that the field ended.
- All other bytes cause an error.

## One line, byte by byte

The first part of the program reads `7,"say ""hi""",x` and prints one row for each byte.

```
   '7'  field_start     -> unquoted        [7]
   ','  unquoted        -> field_start     field done: [7]
   '"'  field_start     -> quoted          []
```

The first field is `7`. The comma ends the field. The quote starts a quoted field, and the reader does not add the quote to the text.

```
   ' '  quoted          -> quoted          [say ]
   '"'  quoted          -> quote_in_quoted [say ]
   '"'  quote_in_quoted -> quoted          [say "]
```

After `say `, two quotes come. The first quote moves the reader to `quote_in_quoted`, and the reader adds nothing to the text. The second byte is also a quote. Thus the reader adds one `"` to the text and returns to `quoted`.

```
   '"'  quote_in_quoted -> quoted          [say "hi"]
   '"'  quoted          -> quote_in_quoted [say "hi"]
   ','  quote_in_quoted -> field_start     field done: [say "hi"]
```

At the end of the field, there are three quotes in a sequence. The first two quotes are an escaped quote. A comma comes after the third quote. Thus the third quote was the quote that ends the field.

```
   3 fields: [7] [say "hi"] [x]
```

The brackets in the output show where each field starts and ends. The brackets are not part of the text.

## The reader

```zig
    pub fn next(c: *CsvReader) !?[]const []const u8 {
        c.text.clearRetainingCapacity();
        c.ends.clearRetainingCapacity();
        c.fields.clearRetainingCapacity();

        var state: State = .field_start;
        var read_any = false;
        while (true) {
            const byte = c.r.takeByte() catch |err| switch (err) {
                error.EndOfStream => {
                    // End of input. In quotes, the end is an error. If the
                    // reader read no bytes, there is no record.
                    if (state == .quoted) {
                        c.line = c.quote_line;
                        return Error.UnterminatedQuote;
                    }
                    if (!read_any) return null;
                    try c.endField();
                    return try c.finish();
                },
                else => |e| return e,
            };
            read_any = true;
            const before = state;

            switch (state) {
                .field_start, .unquoted => switch (byte) {
                    ',' => {
                        try c.endField();
                        state = .field_start;
                    },
                    '\n' => {
                        try c.endField();
                        c.trace1(byte, before, .field_start);
                        c.line += 1;
                        return try c.finish();
                    },
                    // Part of a "\r\n" line ending. Discard it outside quotes.
                    '\r' => {},
                    '"' => if (state == .field_start) {
                        c.quote_line = c.line;
                        state = .quoted;
                    } else return Error.QuoteInUnquotedField,
                    else => {
                        try c.text.append(c.gpa, byte);
                        state = .unquoted;
                    },
                },
                .quoted => switch (byte) {
                    '"' => state = .quote_in_quoted,
                    else => {
                        if (byte == '\n') c.line += 1;
                        try c.text.append(c.gpa, byte);
                    },
                },
                .quote_in_quoted => switch (byte) {
                    // Two quotes in a sequence are one quote in the text.
                    '"' => {
                        try c.text.append(c.gpa, '"');
                        state = .quoted;
                    },
                    ',' => {
                        try c.endField();
                        state = .field_start;
                    },
                    '\n' => {
                        try c.endField();
                        c.trace1(byte, before, .field_start);
                        c.line += 1;
                        return try c.finish();
                    },
                    '\r' => {},
                    else => return Error.TextAfterClosingQuote,
                },
            }
            c.trace1(byte, before, state);
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `next` from `snippets/24-files/csv-read.zig`.*

`next` reads until the end of one record and returns the fields of the record. At the end of the input, `next` returns `null`. Thus a `while` loop over `next` stops, the same as the line loop in [Read Line by Line](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/read-lines/).

`next` reads from a `*std.Io.Reader`, not from a file. The trace reads from `.fixed(...)`, which is a reader over a string in memory. The second part reads from a file, through `file.reader(io, &buf)`. `next` cannot see the difference, and it does not have to.

The reader discards a `'\r'` outside quotes. In this way, the reader handles `"\r\n"` line endings, which are common in CSV files from spreadsheets.

The reader handles the end of input in one location, at the top of the loop:

- If the reader is in quotes, the quote never closed. This is an error.
- If the reader read no bytes, there is no record. The reader returns `null`.
- If not, the last field ends at that position, also without a final newline.

## The fields, and when the reader makes them

The text of each field goes into one list, `text`, which becomes larger with each byte. `ends` records where each field stops. The reader makes the slices in `finish`, after it reads the full record.

```zig
    /// Make the slices only here, when `text` does not grow any more. An
    /// earlier slice can point at memory that `append` moved.
    fn finish(c: *CsvReader) ![]const []const u8 {
        var start: usize = 0;
        for (c.ends.items) |end| {
            try c.fields.append(c.gpa, c.text.items[start..end]);
            start = end;
        }
        return c.fields.items;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `finish` from `snippets/24-files/csv-read.zig`.*

This order is important. `text.append` can need more space, and then it moves the full list to a new location in memory. A slice from before the move still points to the old location.

Thus the reader waits until `text` gets no more bytes. The reader makes slices into `text` only after that.

The slices are valid until the next call to `next`. That call clears the lists and uses them again.

## A real file

```
   4 fields: [id] [name] [price] [note]
   4 fields: [1] [Pencil] [0.50] []
   4 fields: [2] [Widget, large] [12.00] [the "best" one]
   4 fields: [3] [Lamp] [30.00] [two\nlines]
   4 fields: [4] [Mug] [8.25] [no final newline]
```

Each line in the file ends with `"\r\n"`, and no field ends with a `'\r'`.

The first record is the header. The reader does not handle the header differently. The caller must decide what a header means.

The note for Pencil is empty. `1,Pencil,0.50,` ends with a comma. Thus there is a fourth field with no text.

The Lamp record uses two lines of the file, and its note contains a newline. The output shows the newline as `\n`, so that each record fits on one line.

The last line has no final newline, and the reader reads it correctly.

## Errors with line numbers

```
   "a,b\nc,d\"e\n": QuoteInUnquotedField on line 2
   "a,\"b\"c\n": TextAfterClosingQuote on line 1
   "a,b\nc,\"never closed\n": UnterminatedQuote on line 2
```

The first input has a quote in the middle of an unquoted field, `d"e`. RFC 4180, the standard for CSV, does not allow this. Some readers accept the quote and keep it. This reader stops, because the file is probably not what its writer intended.

The second input has text after the quote that ends the field, `"b"c`.

The third input opens a quote on line 2 and never closes it. The reader comes to the end of the input, and it is still in quotes. That end is on line 3, but the error gives line 2, where the quote opened. A person must look at line 2. Thus the reader keeps that line number in `quote_line`.

The count of lines is not the count of records. A newline in quotes is a new line of the file, but not a new record. Thus `line` also increases in the `quoted` state.

## What this reader does not do

- The reader reads bytes. It does not make sure that the text is valid UTF-8.
- It does not change fields to numbers. `"12.00"` stays text, and the caller parses it.
- It does not skip blank lines. A blank line is a record with one empty field.

Each of these is a decision for the program that uses the reader. The [next chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/csv-write/) writes CSV. It also makes sure that this reader reads the same data that the writer wrote.

---

## Write CSV

*Working with Files. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/csv-write/*

To write CSV needs less code than to read CSV. The writer writes most fields with no change. If a field contains a comma, a quote or a line break, the writer puts the field in quotes. It also writes each quote in the field two times.

The program below writes six records with this rule, and six more records without the rule. Then it reads the two files with the reader from [Read CSV](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/csv-read/). It compares each field with the field that it wrote.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const csv = @import("csv-read.zig");

const Io = std.Io;

/// A field needs quotes if it contains a special byte for a CSV reader:
/// the separator, a quote, or a line break.
fn needsQuotes(field: []const u8) bool {
    return std.mem.findAny(u8, field, ",\"\r\n") != null;
}

fn writeField(w: *Io.Writer, field: []const u8) !void {
    if (!needsQuotes(field)) return w.writeAll(field);

    try w.writeByte('"');
    for (field) |b| {
        // Write each quote in the field two times.
        if (b == '"') try w.writeByte('"');
        try w.writeByte(b);
    }
    try w.writeByte('"');
}

fn writeRecord(w: *Io.Writer, fields: []const []const u8) !void {
    for (fields, 0..) |field, i| {
        if (i > 0) try w.writeByte(',');
        try writeField(w, field);
    }
    // In RFC 4180, each record ends with "\r\n", and spreadsheet programs
    // expect "\r\n". A reader that accepts "\n" also accepts "\r\n".
    try w.writeAll("\r\n");
}

/// The mistake that this chapter prevents: a plain join with commas.
fn writeRecordNaive(w: *Io.Writer, fields: []const []const u8) !void {
    for (fields, 0..) |field, i| {
        if (i > 0) try w.writeByte(',');
        try w.writeAll(field);
    }
    try w.writeAll("\r\n");
}

const rows = [_][]const []const u8{
    &.{ "id", "name", "note" },
    &.{ "1", "Pencil", "" },
    &.{ "2", "Widget, large", "blue" },
    &.{ "3", "Lamp", "two\nlines" },
    &.{ "4", "Sign", "the \"best\" one" },
    &.{ "5", " padded ", "ends with a quote\"" },
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = init.gpa;

    var out_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const dir = Io.Dir.cwd();

    // 1. Write the rows and show the bytes. Show \r and \n as text.
    try out.print("1. the file\n", .{});
    try save(io, dir, "out.csv", writeRecord);
    try showBytes(io, dir, "out.csv", out);

    // 2. Read the file again with the reader from the previous chapter.
    //    Compare each field with the field that the program wrote.
    try out.print("2. round trip\n", .{});
    try roundTrip(io, gpa, dir, "out.csv", out);

    // 3. The same rows, with only commas between the fields.
    try out.print("3. naive join\n", .{});
    try save(io, dir, "naive.csv", writeRecordNaive);
    try showBytes(io, dir, "naive.csv", out);
    try roundTrip(io, gpa, dir, "naive.csv", out);

    try dir.deleteFile(io, "out.csv");
    try dir.deleteFile(io, "naive.csv");
}

fn save(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, comptime writeFn: anytype) !void {
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = file.writer(io, &buf);
    for (rows) |row| try writeFn(&fw.interface, row);
    try fw.interface.flush();
}

fn roundTrip(io: Io, gpa: std.mem.Allocator, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fr = file.reader(io, &buf);
    var reader: csv.CsvReader = .{ .r = &fr.interface, .gpa = gpa };
    defer reader.deinit();

    var i: usize = 0;
    while (reader.next()) |maybe| : (i += 1) {
        const got = maybe orelse break;
        const want = if (i < rows.len) rows[i] else &[_][]const u8{};
        if (got.len != want.len) {
            try out.print("   record {d}: field count {d}, wrote {d}\n", .{ i, got.len, want.len });
            continue;
        }
        for (got, want, 0..) |g, w, f| {
            if (!std.mem.eql(u8, g, w)) {
                try out.print("   record {d} field {d}: read [{f}], wrote [{f}]\n", .{ i, f, visible(g), visible(w) });
            }
        }
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("   record {d}: {t} on line {d}\n", .{ i, err, reader.line });
        return;
    }
    try out.print("   read {d} records, wrote {d}\n", .{ i, rows.len });
}

/// Formats a field and shows each newline as \n. Thus the field stays on
/// one line.
fn visible(field: []const u8) std.fmt.Alt([]const u8, writeVisible) {
    return .{ .data = field };
}

fn writeVisible(field: []const u8, w: *Io.Writer) Io.Writer.Error!void {
    for (field) |b| if (b == '\n') try w.writeAll("\\n") else try w.writeByte(b);
}

fn showBytes(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    const bytes = try dir.readFile(io, name, &buf);
    try out.writeAll("   ");
    for (bytes, 0..) |b, i| switch (b) {
        '\r' => try out.writeAll("\\r"),
        '\n' => try out.writeAll(if (i + 1 == bytes.len) "\\n\n" else "\\n\n   "),
        else => try out.writeByte(b),
    };
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`24-files.csv-write`)*

## When a field needs quotes

```zig
/// A field needs quotes if it contains a special byte for a CSV reader:
/// the separator, a quote, or a line break.
fn needsQuotes(field: []const u8) bool {
    return std.mem.findAny(u8, field, ",\"\r\n") != null;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `needsQuotes` from `snippets/24-files/csv-write.zig`.*

A field needs quotes if it contains a byte that has a special meaning for a CSV reader:

- A comma ends the field.
- A line break ends the record.
- A quote starts or ends a quoted field.

`std.mem.findAny` looks for the four bytes `,"\r\n`. It returns the position of the first of these bytes, or `null`.

The writer writes all other fields without quotes. Thus a file of plain numbers and names looks the same as in a text editor.

## Write one field

```zig
fn writeField(w: *Io.Writer, field: []const u8) !void {
    if (!needsQuotes(field)) return w.writeAll(field);

    try w.writeByte('"');
    for (field) |b| {
        // Write each quote in the field two times.
        if (b == '"') try w.writeByte('"');
        try w.writeByte(b);
    }
    try w.writeByte('"');
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writeField` from `snippets/24-files/csv-write.zig`.*

If a field has no special bytes, the function writes the field with no change. If not, it writes a quote, then the field, then one more quote.

When the function copies the field, it writes each `"` two times. The reader changes each pair back into one quote.

## Write a record

```zig
fn writeRecord(w: *Io.Writer, fields: []const []const u8) !void {
    for (fields, 0..) |field, i| {
        if (i > 0) try w.writeByte(',');
        try writeField(w, field);
    }
    // In RFC 4180, each record ends with "\r\n", and spreadsheet programs
    // expect "\r\n". A reader that accepts "\n" also accepts "\r\n".
    try w.writeAll("\r\n");
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writeRecord` from `snippets/24-files/csv-write.zig`.*

Commas separate the fields, and each record ends with `"\r\n"`. RFC 4180, the document that describes CSV, uses `"\r\n"`.

The reader in this guide removes a `'\r'` outside quotes. Thus the reader reads `"\r\n"` and `"\n"`.

Here is the file. The program shows `\r` and `\n` as text, so that you can see them.

```
   id,name,note\r\n
   1,Pencil,\r\n
   2,"Widget, large",blue\r\n
   3,Lamp,"two\n
   lines"\r\n
   4,Sign,"the ""best"" one"\r\n
   5, padded ,"ends with a quote"""\r\n
```

Only four fields have quotes: the field with the comma, the field with the newline, and the two fields with a `"` in them.

Record 3 continues on a second line of the file, because its note contains a newline.

The last field ends with a quote. Thus the field ends with three quotes: an escaped quote as two quotes, then the quote that ends the field.

## The round trip

```
2. round trip
   read 6 records, wrote 6
```

`roundTrip` reads the file with `CsvReader`. It compares each field with the field in the original row. No field is different. Thus the function prints only the count.

Test all writers in this way. A writer can make output that looks correct, but that does not agree with what its reader expects. When the real reader reads the output again, the test checks the writer and the reader together.

The snippet does not contain a copy of the reader. It imports the reader with `@import("csv-read.zig")`. Thus, if the reader changes, this test runs against the new version.

## Join with commas

The third part writes the same rows with `writeRecordNaive`. That function puts commas between the fields, and it does nothing more.

```
   2,Widget, large,blue\r\n
   3,Lamp,two\n
   lines\r\n
   4,Sign,the "best" one\r\n
```

Then the program reads the file again.

```
   record 2: field count 4, wrote 3
   record 3 field 2: read [two], wrote [two\nlines]
   record 4: field count 1, wrote 3
   record 5: QuoteInUnquotedField on line 6
```

Record 2 now has four fields. The comma in `Widget, large` became a separator, and the reader reported no error for it. A program that reads this file puts `large` in the note column, and `blue` in a column that does not exist.

The newline cuts record 3, and `lines` becomes a separate record. Thus each record after record 3 moves by one position.

Only record 5 fails with an error. The quote in `the "best" one` is in an unquoted field, and the reader rejects the quote.

Thus two of the three mistakes make incorrect data, and no error occurs.

## Spaces

Record 5 has a name with a space at each end, `" padded "`. The writer does not put the name in quotes, and the round trip keeps the two spaces.

RFC 4180 says that spaces are part of the field. Some other programs remove spaces from the ends of unquoted fields. If a file is for one of these programs, add `' '` to the bytes in `needsQuotes`. Then the writer puts quotes around fields with spaces.

## Formulas in spreadsheets

Frequently, a person opens a CSV file in a spreadsheet program. A spreadsheet uses a cell that starts with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` as a formula.

If a field comes from a user, a value such as `=HYPERLINK(...)` becomes a formula when a person opens the file. The name of this attack is [CSV injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/CSV_Injection).

The problem is not in the CSV format. The file is correct. The spreadsheet decides to run the text.

A common defence is to put a `'` before these fields when the file is for a spreadsheet. That change makes the data different. Thus the change must be in the program that knows who will open the file. It must not be in a general CSV writer such as this one.

---

## Directories

*Working with Files. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/directories/*

A directory is a list of names. Each name points to a file or to a different directory.

The program below makes a small project tree and lists the tree in two ways. Then it renames part of the tree and deletes all of the tree.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Io = std.Io;
const Allocator = std.mem.Allocator;

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = init.gpa;

    var out_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const cwd = Io.Dir.cwd();

    // 1. Create a small project tree. createDirPath makes each directory
    //    in the path that does not exist, the same as `mkdir -p`.
    try out.print("1. create\n", .{});
    try cwd.createDirPath(io, "project/src/util");
    try cwd.createDirPath(io, "project/docs");
    const files = [_]struct { path: []const u8, data: []const u8 }{
        .{ .path = "project/README.md", .data = "# project\n" },
        .{ .path = "project/src/main.zig", .data = "pub fn main() void {}\n" },
        .{ .path = "project/src/util/math.zig", .data = "pub fn add(a: u8, b: u8) u8 {\n    return a + b;\n}\n" },
        .{ .path = "project/docs/notes.txt", .data = "todo\n" },
    };
    for (files) |f| try cwd.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = f.path, .data = f.data });
    try out.print("   {d} files written\n", .{files.len});

    // createDir on a directory that exists is an error. createDirPath on
    // the same directory is not an error.
    if (cwd.createDir(io, "project", .default_dir)) |_| {
        try out.print("   createDir again: ok\n", .{});
    } else |err| try out.print("   createDir again: {t}\n", .{err});
    try cwd.createDirPath(io, "project/src");
    try out.print("   createDirPath again: ok\n", .{});

    // 2. One level, sorted.
    try out.print("2. list project/\n", .{});
    {
        var dir = try cwd.openDir(io, "project", .{ .iterate = true });
        defer dir.close(io);
        try listSorted(io, gpa, dir, out);
    }

    // 3. All levels, sorted, with sizes.
    try out.print("3. walk project/\n", .{});
    try walkSorted(io, gpa, cwd, "project", out);

    // 4. Rename a directory. All of its contents move with it.
    try out.print("4. rename project/docs -> project/doc\n", .{});
    try cwd.rename("project/docs", cwd, "project/doc", io);
    if (cwd.statFile(io, "project/doc/notes.txt", .{})) |st| {
        try out.print("   project/doc/notes.txt is {d} bytes\n", .{st.size});
    } else |err| return err;

    // 5. Delete. deleteDir removes only an empty directory.
    try out.print("5. delete\n", .{});
    if (cwd.deleteDir(io, "project")) |_| {
        try out.print("   deleteDir: ok\n", .{});
    } else |err| try out.print("   deleteDir: {t}\n", .{err});
    try cwd.deleteTree(io, "project");
    if (cwd.statFile(io, "project", .{})) |_| {
        try out.print("   deleteTree: project still exists\n", .{});
    } else |err| try out.print("   deleteTree: done, stat now gives {t}\n", .{err});
}

const Item = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    kind: Io.File.Kind,

    fn lessThan(_: void, a: Item, b: Item) bool {
        return std.mem.order(u8, a.name, b.name) == .lt;
    }
};

fn listSorted(io: Io, gpa: Allocator, dir: Io.Dir, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    var arena_state: std.heap.ArenaAllocator = .init(gpa);
    defer arena_state.deinit();
    const arena = arena_state.allocator();

    // The filesystem decides the order of the entries. Collect the entries
    // and sort them, so that the output is the same on all systems.
    var items: std.ArrayList(Item) = .empty;
    var it = dir.iterate();
    while (try it.next(io)) |entry| {
        // `entry.name` is valid only until the next call to `next`.
        try items.append(arena, .{ .name = try arena.dupe(u8, entry.name), .kind = entry.kind });
    }
    std.mem.sort(Item, items.items, {}, Item.lessThan);
    for (items.items) |item| try out.print("   {t:<9} {s}\n", .{ item.kind, item.name });
}

fn walkSorted(io: Io, gpa: Allocator, parent: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    var arena_state: std.heap.ArenaAllocator = .init(gpa);
    defer arena_state.deinit();
    const arena = arena_state.allocator();

    var dir = try parent.openDir(io, name, .{ .iterate = true });
    defer dir.close(io);

    var walker = try dir.walk(gpa);
    defer walker.deinit();

    var items: std.ArrayList(Item) = .empty;
    var total: u64 = 0;
    while (try walker.next(io)) |entry| {
        try items.append(arena, .{ .name = try arena.dupe(u8, entry.path), .kind = entry.kind });
        if (entry.kind == .file) {
            // `entry.dir` is the directory that holds this entry. Thus stat
            // by basename in that directory. Do not make a path from the top.
            total += (try entry.dir.statFile(io, entry.basename, .{})).size;
        }
    }
    std.mem.sort(Item, items.items, {}, Item.lessThan);
    for (items.items) |item| {
        const depth = std.mem.count(u8, item.name, "/");
        try out.splatByteAll(' ', 3 + 2 * depth);
        try out.print("{s}{s}\n", .{ std.Io.Dir.path.basename(item.name), if (item.kind == .directory) "/" else "" });
    }
    try out.print("   {d} entries, {d} bytes in files\n", .{ items.items.len, total });
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`24-files.directories`)*

## Create a tree

`createDirPath(io, "project/src/util")` creates `project`, then `project/src`, then `project/src/util`. The function skips each directory that exists already. A shell does the same with `mkdir -p`.

`createDir` creates exactly one directory, and the parent directory must exist already.

The two functions are also different when the directory exists already.

```
   createDir again: PathAlreadyExists
   createDirPath again: ok
```

`createDir` reports an error. `createDirPath` succeeds, because the path that the program asked for exists.

- To make sure that a directory exists before you write into it, use `createDirPath`.
- When the directory must be new, use `createDir`. This is the same as `.exclusive = true` for a file.

## List one level

`Dir.cwd()` is not open for a listing. Its doc comment says that iteration over `Dir.cwd()` is illegal behaviour. Thus first open the directory that you want with `.iterate = true`, then list that directory.

```zig
fn listSorted(io: Io, gpa: Allocator, dir: Io.Dir, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    var arena_state: std.heap.ArenaAllocator = .init(gpa);
    defer arena_state.deinit();
    const arena = arena_state.allocator();

    // The filesystem decides the order of the entries. Collect the entries
    // and sort them, so that the output is the same on all systems.
    var items: std.ArrayList(Item) = .empty;
    var it = dir.iterate();
    while (try it.next(io)) |entry| {
        // `entry.name` is valid only until the next call to `next`.
        try items.append(arena, .{ .name = try arena.dupe(u8, entry.name), .kind = entry.kind });
    }
    std.mem.sort(Item, items.items, {}, Item.lessThan);
    for (items.items) |item| try out.print("   {t:<9} {s}\n", .{ item.kind, item.name });
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `listSorted` from `snippets/24-files/directories.zig`.*

`dir.iterate()` returns an iterator. `it.next(io)` returns one entry at a time, or `null` at the end. Each entry has a `name` and a `kind`.

```
   file      README.md
   directory docs
   directory src
```

The filesystem decides the order of the entries. The order is not alphabetical, and it is not the order in which the program created the files. The order can be different on two computers. It can also be different between two runs on the same computer, after a program adds and deletes files.

In CI, this program runs on a real disk. In your browser, it runs in memory. The two give different orders.

Thus the program collects the names and sorts them before it prints them. All output that comes from a directory listing needs the same step. If not, a test of the output fails on some computers.

`README.md` is first, because the sort compares bytes. Uppercase letters have smaller byte values than lowercase letters.

The program copies the names with `arena.dupe`. `entry.name` points into the buffer of the iterator, and the next call to `next` can write over that buffer. The same rule applies to lines in [Read Line by Line](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/read-lines/#keep-a-line).

## Walk all levels

```zig
fn walkSorted(io: Io, gpa: Allocator, parent: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    var arena_state: std.heap.ArenaAllocator = .init(gpa);
    defer arena_state.deinit();
    const arena = arena_state.allocator();

    var dir = try parent.openDir(io, name, .{ .iterate = true });
    defer dir.close(io);

    var walker = try dir.walk(gpa);
    defer walker.deinit();

    var items: std.ArrayList(Item) = .empty;
    var total: u64 = 0;
    while (try walker.next(io)) |entry| {
        try items.append(arena, .{ .name = try arena.dupe(u8, entry.path), .kind = entry.kind });
        if (entry.kind == .file) {
            // `entry.dir` is the directory that holds this entry. Thus stat
            // by basename in that directory. Do not make a path from the top.
            total += (try entry.dir.statFile(io, entry.basename, .{})).size;
        }
    }
    std.mem.sort(Item, items.items, {}, Item.lessThan);
    for (items.items) |item| {
        const depth = std.mem.count(u8, item.name, "/");
        try out.splatByteAll(' ', 3 + 2 * depth);
        try out.print("{s}{s}\n", .{ std.Io.Dir.path.basename(item.name), if (item.kind == .directory) "/" else "" });
    }
    try out.print("   {d} entries, {d} bytes in files\n", .{ items.items.len, total });
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `walkSorted` from `snippets/24-files/directories.zig`.*

`dir.walk(gpa)` visits each entry below the directory, at all depths. The function needs an allocator, because it keeps a stack of the directories that it opened.

Each entry has these fields:

- `path`, relative to the start directory, for example `src/util/math.zig`.
- `basename`, the last part of that path.
- `dir`, the open directory that holds the entry.

```
   README.md
   docs/
     notes.txt
   src/
     main.zig
     util/
       math.zig
   7 entries, 87 bytes in files
```

The filesystem also decides the order of the walk. Thus the program also sorts by path here. When you sort full paths, each directory comes immediately before its contents.

To add the file sizes, the program calls `entry.dir.statFile(io, entry.basename, .{})`. This call asks the directory that holds the file for the details of the file. It uses only the name of the file.

Alternatively, the program can make the full path from the top. But that path becomes longer at each level. In a very deep tree, the path can become longer than the longest path that the system accepts.

## Rename a directory

`cwd.rename("project/docs", cwd, "project/doc", io)` renames the directory.

```
   project/doc/notes.txt is 5 bytes
```

The files in the directory move with the directory. The function copies nothing. Only the name in the parent directory changes. Thus the rename of a directory with a million files is as fast as the rename of an empty directory.

`rename` takes a directory for each side. Thus it can also move an entry into a different directory.

The two directories must be on the same filesystem. To move a file between two disks, a program must copy the file and then delete the original. `rename` does not do these steps for you.

## Delete

```
   deleteDir: DirNotEmpty
   deleteTree: done, stat now gives FileNotFound
```

`deleteDir` removes one empty directory. `project` still has files in it. Thus `deleteDir` fails with `DirNotEmpty`.

`deleteTree` removes the directory and all of the contents below it. It is the same as `rm -r` in a shell, and it has the same risk. An incorrect path deletes the incorrect tree, and you cannot undo the delete.

`deleteTree` also succeeds when the path does not exist. Thus `deleteTree` is safe as a cleanup step, also if no earlier step created the tree.

## Directories are handles

Each operation in this chapter goes through a `Dir` value. `cwd.openDir(io, "project", ...)` returns a new `Dir` for `project`, and `dir.close(io)` closes it.

Each path is relative to the `Dir` that the program gives the path to.

[Filesystem](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/filesystem/#a-directory-is-a-handle-not-a-string) explains why std uses open directories and not path strings.

---

## When Things Go Wrong

*Working with Files. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/failures/*

Each chapter in this section handles some errors. This chapter looks at the errors together.

A file operation can fail for reasons that the program does not control:

- A different program deleted the file.
- The path is incorrect.
- The disk is full.
- A different program changed something.

Zig does not hide these failures. Each failure is an error value with a name. The return type of the function gives a list of all the errors that the function can return.

The program below makes six operations fail intentionally. It prints the result of each operation.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Io = std.Io;

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var out_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &stdout.interface;
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    const dir = Io.Dir.cwd();
    try dir.writeFile(io, .{ .sub_path = "notes.txt", .data = "hello\n" });
    try dir.createDirPath(io, "archive");

    // 1. stat: what is at a path. stat does not open the path.
    try out.print("1. stat\n", .{});
    for ([_][]const u8{ "notes.txt", "archive" }) |path| {
        const st = try dir.statFile(io, path, .{});
        try out.print("   {s:<10} kind {t}", .{ path, st.kind });
        // The filesystem decides the size of a directory (4096 on ext4, 0 in
        // memory). The size tells you nothing about the contents.
        if (st.kind == .file) try out.print(", size {d}", .{st.size});
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }

    // 2. Six operations that fail, and the error each one returns.
    try out.print("2. six failures\n", .{});
    try out.print("   open a file that is not there:     {t}\n", .{fails(dir.openFile(io, "missing.txt", .{}), io)});
    try out.print("   create a file in a missing dir:    {t}\n", .{fails(dir.createFile(io, "drafts/new.txt", .{}), io)});
    try out.print("   open a directory as a file:        {t}\n", .{fails(dir.openFile(io, "archive", .{ .allow_directory = false }), io)});
    try out.print("   use a file as a directory:         {t}\n", .{fails(dir.openFile(io, "notes.txt/x", .{}), io)});
    try out.print("   deleteFile on a directory:         {t}\n", .{failsVoid(dir.deleteFile(io, "archive"))});
    try out.print("   deleteFile on a missing file:      {t}\n", .{failsVoid(dir.deleteFile(io, "missing.txt"))});

    // 3. The same errors as messages for a person.
    try out.print("3. messages\n", .{});
    for ([_][]const u8{ "missing.txt", "archive", "notes.txt/x", "notes.txt" }) |path| {
        try out.print("   {s:<12} ", .{path});
        loadNotes(io, dir, path, out) catch |err| try out.print("{s}\n", .{message(err)});
    }

    // 4. A write that fails halfway, with and without cleanup.
    try out.print("4. cleanup\n", .{});
    for ([_]bool{ false, true }) |cleanup| {
        exportReport(io, dir, "report.txt", cleanup) catch |err| {
            try out.print("   cleanup={}: {t}, ", .{ cleanup, err });
        };
        if (dir.statFile(io, "report.txt", .{})) |st| {
            try out.print("report.txt left behind, {d} bytes\n", .{st.size});
            try dir.deleteFile(io, "report.txt");
        } else |_| {
            try out.print("no report.txt\n", .{});
        }
    }

    try dir.deleteFile(io, "notes.txt");
    try dir.deleteDir(io, "archive");
}

/// The error that an operation returned. The operation must fail. Thus, on
/// a success, the function closes the file and returns a mistake.
fn fails(result: anytype, io: Io) anyerror {
    if (result) |file| {
        file.close(io);
        return error.UnexpectedSuccess;
    } else |err| return err;
}

fn failsVoid(result: anytype) anyerror {
    if (result) |_| return error.UnexpectedSuccess else |err| return err;
}

fn loadNotes(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, path: []const u8, out: *Io.Writer) !void {
    // Without `.allow_directory = false`, the open of a directory succeeds.
    // The error comes only at the first read, and each system gives a
    // different error.
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, path, .{ .allow_directory = false });
    defer file.close(io);
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const n = try file.readPositionalAll(io, &buf, 0);
    try out.print("loaded {d} bytes\n", .{n});
}

/// One sentence for each error that a person can correct. The function
/// gives the name of all other errors, because a hidden error helps nobody.
fn message(err: anyerror) []const u8 {
    return switch (err) {
        error.FileNotFound => "not found: check the name and the folder",
        error.IsDir => "that is a folder, not a file",
        error.NotDir => "part of the path is a file, not a folder",
        error.AccessDenied, error.PermissionDenied => "no permission to read it",
        error.NoSpaceLeft => "the disk is full",
        else => @errorName(err),
    };
}

/// Writes two lines of a report, then fails at the third line, as a real
/// check on the data can fail.
fn exportReport(io: Io, dir: Io.Dir, name: []const u8, cleanup: bool) !void {
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);
    // Runs only if this function returns an error. Deferred statements run
    // in reverse order. Thus this delete runs before `defer` closes the file.
    errdefer if (cleanup) dir.deleteFile(io, name) catch {};

    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var w = file.writer(io, &buf);
    try w.interface.writeAll("total: 3\n");
    try w.interface.writeAll("item 1\n");
    try w.interface.flush();
    return error.InvalidItem;
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`24-files.failures`)*

## What is at a path

`dir.statFile(io, path, .{})` asks what is at a path. It does not open the path.

```
   notes.txt  kind file, size 6
   archive    kind directory
```

The result is a `Stat`:

- `kind` tells you if the path is a file, a directory, or a different thing, for example a symbolic link.
- `size` is the length of a file in bytes.

For a directory, the size has no useful meaning. On Linux with ext4, the size is 4096. In the in-memory directory of the browser, the size is 0. Thus the program prints the size only for files.

`Stat` also has `mtime`, the time of the last change to the file, and `atime`, the time of the last read. This program does not print these times, for two reasons:

- A real time is different on each run. Thus CI cannot compare it.
- The in-memory directory in your browser does not store times. Each time in that directory is 0.

## Six failures

```
   open a file that is not there:     FileNotFound
   create a file in a missing dir:    FileNotFound
   open a directory as a file:        IsDir
   use a file as a directory:         NotDir
   deleteFile on a directory:         IsDir
   deleteFile on a missing file:      FileNotFound
```

`createFile` creates a file, but not the directory for the file. If `drafts` does not exist, the error is `FileNotFound`. This is the same error as for a file that does not exist.
