Look at what the check counts. `occupied` is the live entries *plus* the tombstones, not `count`. If you fill and empty a map many times, it collects tombstones, and it must still grow. The length of a probe depends on the number of slots that are not empty. It does not depend on the number of slots that hold real data.

Growth is also the only operation that removes tombstones. A rehash into a new buffer does not copy the tombstones.

## The tombstone

A delete cannot only empty the slot:

```zig
entry.* = .{ .state = .tombstone };
```

This line looks like an unnecessary complication, until you remove it. The snippet does the same deletes in the two ways:

```
removed 5 keys with tombstones
survivors still reachable: 9 of 9

same deletes, clearing the slot instead:
survivors still reachable: 7 of 9
lost by breaking the probe chain: 2
```

Two keys became unreachable. No error occurred, and no memory became corrupt. These are the steps of each failed lookup:

1. The lookup walked to the correct position for the key.
2. It found an empty slot, where a full slot was before.
3. It decided that the key was not in the map.
4. It returned null.

A probe chain is a run of occupied slots. If the home slot of a key is earlier in that run, the key needs all of the run to stay unbroken. When you empty a slot in the middle, you cut each chain that went through that slot. The tombstone says "continue, something was here before". The chain needs exactly that information.

The insert must also handle the tombstone correctly. The probe remembers the first tombstone that it sees, but it continues the walk, because the key can already exist farther along the chain. Only when the probe gets to an empty slot does it return to the tombstone and use it again. If the probe used the tombstone immediately, the same key could go into the map two times.

## Delete correctly without tombstones

One method is backward-shift deletion. After you remove an entry, walk forward through the rest of the run. Move an entry back to its home slot if the removal made space for it. This method keeps the table free of tombstones, but each delete costs more work. Robin Hood hashing usually uses this method. Thus tombstones are a design choice: cheaper deletes, or shorter probes.

## What std does differently

```zig
var std_map: std.StringHashMapUnmanaged(i32) = .empty;
try std_map.put(allocator, key, 1);
```

[Hash maps](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/hash-maps/) explains the API. The main structural difference is that `std` stores a separate array of one-byte metadata next to the entries. Each byte holds a few bits of the hash of the key, plus the empty and tombstone flags.

A probe scans that small byte array, not the full-size entries. Thus many more probe steps fit in a cache line. Also, a comparison of one byte can show that a key is not the correct key, before the probe touches the entry. Because of that layout, the same algorithm performs very differently in `std` and in a simple implementation like this one.

[ArrayList](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/arraylist/) uses the same pattern on master: the `Unmanaged` suffix, and an allocator argument on each method. The container does not store the allocator.

## The map borrows its keys

The map in this chapter stores `[]const u8` keys, but it does not copy them. Thus the caller must keep the strings alive. For the string literals in the snippet, this is not a problem, because they are in the binary. But if you store a key from a buffer that you use again later, the map points at the new data in that buffer.

`std.StringHashMap` has the same property. For this reason, helpers in the style of `putClone`, and arenas, are frequently used together with it. A container that borrows must tell you so, and this chapter tells you here.

---

## Async, Future and Group

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/*

Concurrency in Zig now goes through `std.Io`.
[The Io Interface](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/io-interface/) explains that
interface, and this section expects you to know it. Each chapter here takes an
`Io` and gives it to the functions that it calls.

Press Run. The program runs in your browser, on a target with **no threads**.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn slowDouble(out: *u32, value: u32) void {
    out.* = value * 2;
}

fn accumulate(total: *u32, mutex: *std.Io.Mutex, io: std.Io, amount: u32) void {
    // `Io.Mutex.lock` takes the io instance, like all other functions that can
    // block. It returns an error for one reason only: a task can cancel it.
    mutex.lock(io) catch return;
    defer mutex.unlock(io);
    total.* += amount;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // `io.async` starts a task and returns a Future to await.
    var a: u32 = 0;
    var b: u32 = 0;
    var first = io.async(slowDouble, .{ &a, 10 });
    var second = io.async(slowDouble, .{ &b, 20 });
    first.await(io);
    second.await(io);
    try out.print("doubled: {d} {d}\n", .{ a, b });

    // `io.async` can run the task inline. `io.concurrent` cannot: it promises
    // that the caller can continue while the task runs. It fails when the `Io`
    // cannot keep that promise. On this single-threaded wasm target, it fails.
    // This difference is the reason for two functions.
    var c: u32 = 0;
    if (io.concurrent(slowDouble, .{ &c, 30 })) |handle| {
        var pending = handle;
        pending.await(io);
        try out.print("concurrent: {d}\n", .{c});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("concurrent: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    }

    // A Group awaits many tasks together. Thus no task continues after the scope.
    var total: u32 = 0;
    var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;
    var group: std.Io.Group = .init;
    for (0..8) |_| {
        group.async(io, accumulate, .{ &total, &mutex, io, 1 });
    }
    try group.await(io);
    try out.print("total: {d}\n", .{total});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.concurrency`)*

## `io.async` returns a Future

```zig
var first = io.async(slowDouble, .{ &a, 10 });
var second = io.async(slowDouble, .{ &b, 20 });
first.await(io);
second.await(io);
```

The `Io` implementation decides the meaning of "async". A threaded
implementation runs these calls in parallel. The single-threaded WASI
implementation runs them inline. **Your code does not change.** For this
reason, you can run this page, and you cannot run the
[Threads](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/threads/) page.

## `async` can run a task inline, and `concurrent` cannot

`io.async` promises only one thing: the result is ready after you await it.
`io.async` can call the function immediately, complete it, and return a Future
that is already resolved. On this page, that occurs.

`io.concurrent` makes a stronger promise: the caller continues while the task
runs. Not all `Io` implementations can keep that promise. Thus
`io.concurrent` returns an error union:

```zig
if (io.concurrent(slowDouble, .{ &c, 30 })) |handle| {
    var pending = handle;
    pending.await(io);
} else |err| {
    // error.ConcurrencyUnavailable
}
```

The snippet above prints `concurrent: ConcurrencyUnavailable`. The
single-threaded wasm that runs the snippet has no second unit of concurrency
to give. If you give the same binary an `Io.Threaded`, it prints
`concurrent: 60`.

The difference has an effect on correctness, not on performance. If a task
must make progress *before* you await it, `io.async` can deadlock. For
example, a producer fills a queue, and the same thread must empty the queue
later. The producer runs first until it stops on a full queue. Then no code is
available to empty the queue.

For that case, do these steps:

- Use `concurrent`.
- Handle `error.ConcurrencyUnavailable`. Do not use `try` on it. If you use
  `try`, the program fails on the single-threaded targets, where `async`
  still works.

`Group` also has the two forms, `group.async` and `group.concurrent`, with the
same difference.

Use `async` as the default. `async` runs on all targets, and this page is one
of them.

## `Group` for many tasks

```zig
var group: std.Io.Group = .init;
for (0..8) |_| group.async(io, work, .{ ... });
try group.await(io);
```

A `Group` owns its tasks. When you await the group, it waits for all of the
tasks. When you cancel the group, it cancels all of the tasks. Thus a task
cannot continue after the end of the scope that started it. That property is
the meaning of "structured" here. A raw `Thread.spawn` does not give you this
property.

## Shared state still needs a lock

Concurrency is not parallelism. But when an implementation *is* parallel, a
change to shared data without synchronisation is a data race. Use
`std.Io.Mutex` for this. Like the other tools, it takes the io instance:

```zig
try mutex.lock(io);
defer mutex.unlock(io);
```

When you cancel a `Group`, it cancels each member. The [next
chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/) is about cancellation.

## How `Io` compares to `Allocator`

`Io` works in the same way as `Allocator`:

- A function that takes an `Allocator` lets the caller select the source of
  the memory.
- A function that takes an `Io` tells you that it can block. The caller
  selects how the function runs.

A library that uses `Io` in this way works without a change. It works on a
thread pool, an event loop, or a single-threaded wasm runtime.

The other chapters in this section use this design:

- [Queues](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/queues/) is for tasks that give work to other
  tasks.
- [Select](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/select/) is for the task that completes first.
- [Locks](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/locks/) is for the shared state below the tasks.
- [Choose an Io](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/choosing-an-io/) shows where the `Io`
  instance comes from.

---

## Cancellation

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/*

Sometimes you must stop a task that you started. For example, the client
closed the connection, the timeout occurred, or the user pressed Ctrl-C.

In Zig, cancellation is a request. It does not kill the task. You send the
request, and the task gets the request at its next *cancellation point*.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Sleeps for an hour, or until a caller cancels it. `io.sleep` is a
/// *cancellation point*: a function on `Io` that can return `error.Canceled`.
fn nap(io: std.Io) std.Io.Cancelable!void {
    try io.sleep(.fromSeconds(3600), .awake);
}

/// The same sleep, but it records how it ended. Then the program can examine
/// the group below after the sleep ends.
fn trackedNap(io: std.Io, status: *[]const u8) std.Io.Cancelable!void {
    io.sleep(.fromSeconds(3600), .awake) catch |err| {
        status.* = @errorName(err);
        return err;
    };
    status.* = "finished";
}

/// Pure computation calls nothing on `Io`. Thus it has no cancellation point,
/// and it spins forever. `io.checkCancel` is the point that you add.
fn count(io: std.Io, counter: *u64) std.Io.Cancelable!void {
    while (true) {
        try io.checkCancel();
        counter.* += 1;
    }
}

fn double(value: u32) u32 {
    return value * 2;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // `cancel` is `await` plus a cancellation request. It blocks until the task
    // is done, and it returns the value that the task returned.
    var sleeping = try io.concurrent(nap, .{io});
    if (sleeping.cancel(io)) |_| {
        try out.print("nap: finished\n", .{});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("nap: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    }

    // If you cancel a task that is already complete, the result is not an
    // error. The task has no cancellation point left, thus you get the result.
    var finished = io.async(double, .{21});
    try out.print("double: {d}\n", .{finished.cancel(io)});

    // The task sees the request only because it asks. If you remove the
    // `checkCancel`, this line never prints.
    var counter: u64 = 0;
    var counting = try io.concurrent(count, .{ io, &counter });
    if (counting.cancel(io)) |_| {
        try out.print("count: finished\n", .{});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("count: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    }

    // A Group cancels as a whole. Each member gets the request, and `cancel`
    // returns when all of the members stop.
    //
    // Use `concurrent`, not `async`. `async` can run the task on this thread.
    // The threaded `Io` does that when it has no spare capacity: `async_limit`
    // has a default of one less than the core count. A sleep on this thread
    // sleeps for an hour here, and the program never gets to `group.cancel`.
    //
    // The program hangs when the group is equal to or larger than the core
    // count. Thus it passes on a development computer and deadlocks on a
    // small one.
    var status: [3][]const u8 = @splat("still running");
    var group: std.Io.Group = .init;
    for (&status) |*slot| try group.concurrent(io, trackedNap, .{ io, slot });
    group.cancel(io);
    for (status, 0..) |s, i| try out.print("group task {d}: {s}\n", .{ i, s });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this program natively. To cancel a task that still runs, the Io must run the task in a different place. wasm32-wasi cannot do that. (`03-standard-library.cancellation`)*

## `cancel` is `await` plus a request

```zig
var sleeping = try io.concurrent(nap, .{io});
if (sleeping.cancel(io)) |_| { ... } else |err| { ... }
```

`Future.cancel` blocks until the task is done, exactly like `await`. Then it
returns the value that the task returned. The difference is that `cancel`
first asks the task to stop. Thus a cancelled task still runs its `defer`
statements and releases its resources. The task always stops before the runtime
removes its stack.

If you cancel a task that is already complete, the result is not an error. The
task has no cancellation point left to reach. Thus `cancel` only returns the
result. `cancel` and `await` are both idempotent, and neither is threadsafe.

## A cancellation point is a call on `Io`

The task gets the request at the next call on its `Io` that can return
`error.Canceled`. Examples are a sleep, a read, a lock and an accept. That is
the rule, and the rule has a result:

```zig
fn count(io: std.Io, counter: *u64) std.Io.Cancelable!void {
    while (true) {
        try io.checkCancel();
        counter.* += 1;
    }
}
```

Pure computation calls nothing on `Io`. Thus it has no cancellation point, and
you cannot cancel it. If you delete the `checkCancel` above, the loop runs
forever, and the task never gets the request.

`io.checkCancel` adds a cancellation point to code that has no other one. A
long computation loop needs one. The number of calls depends on how quickly
the loop must stop.

## Do not ignore `error.Canceled`

Only the *next* cancellation point reports the request. After that, the
request ends, and later points return normally. Thus, if a task catches
`error.Canceled` and continues, nothing tells the task again.

To ignore `error.Canceled` is a bug in almost all cases. Return the error to
the caller. Then the caller that asked for the cancellation can see that the
cancellation occurred.

Two functions change how the task gets requests:

- `io.recancel` makes a request that you handled active again. Then the next
  point reports it again.
- `io.swapCancelProtection(.blocked)` stops all delivery across a region that
  must not stop halfway, for example a rollback or a flush. The function
  returns the previous state. Restore that state in a `defer`.

Both functions are for the cleanup path. Do not use them to keep a cancelled
task in operation.

## A `Group` cancels as a whole

```zig
var group: std.Io.Group = .init;
for (&status) |*slot| try group.concurrent(io, trackedNap, .{ io, slot });
group.cancel(io);
```

Each member gets the request. `cancel` returns when all of the members
stop.

This is the main advantage of [structured
concurrency](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/), and it is the reason to
pass the extra parameter. For example, a server has one `Group` of connection
handlers. To stop, the server cancels the group. The server has no list of
threads to track. Also, no handler continues to run after the end of the
scope that started it.

A `Group` is also a cancellation boundary. Its tasks must return a value that
can coerce to `Cancelable!void`. If a member returns `error.Canceled`, the
error stops at the group and does not go out of the group.

`Group.await` returns `error.Canceled` when the task that awaits is itself
cancelled. It does not return the error because of a cancelled member. If you
must know how a member ended, record the result. The snippet does this: each
task writes its result into a slot.

## Use `concurrent` for a task that you intend to cancel

The loop above uses `group.concurrent`, not `group.async`. The difference
changes what the program does.

`async` can run the task on the thread that calls it. The threaded `Io` does
exactly that when it has no spare capacity. Its `async_limit` has a default of
one less than the number of logical cores. Past that limit, `async` runs the
task immediately. It does not schedule the task.

For a task that ends without help, that is correct. For this reason,
[`concurrency`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/) starts eight
`accumulate` tasks with `group.async`. Each task adds a number and returns.
Thus, if a task runs inline, the only loss is parallelism.

For a task that ends only when cancelled, the result is a deadlock.
`trackedNap` sleeps for an hour. If it runs inline, it sleeps for an hour on
the thread that must call `group.cancel` next. Thus the program never gets to
that call.

This problem is not a race. The deadlock occurs each time that the group is
equal to or larger than the core count. It never occurs below the core count.
With three sleepers, the program hangs on a computer with one, two or three
cores. It passes on four cores.

This type of bug is very difficult to find. The program passes on the
computer where you wrote it, and it hangs on the smaller computer where you
deploy it. This snippet had the bug. A CI runner with four cores and a
different program in operation found the bug.

`concurrent` makes a promise that `async` does not make. The task runs in a
different place, or the call fails with `error.ConcurrencyUnavailable`. For
the same reason, the program starts `nap` and `count` above with `io.concurrent`.

## Cancellation is why `lock` can fail

`Io.Mutex.lock`, `io.sleep` and
[`Io.RwLock.lock`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/locks/) all return `Cancelable!void`.
Older code had a plain `void` in those places. `Cancelable` is an error set
with one member, and that member is `error.Canceled`.

Thus, if the only error in a signature is `error.Canceled`, the signature
tells you one thing: the call is a cancellation point. When a call must not be
a cancellation point, the standard library puts that fact in the name:
`lockUncancelable`, `futexWaitUncancelable`.

---

## Select

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/select/*

`Future.await` waits for one task. `Group.await` waits for all of the tasks.
`std.Io.Select` is the third shape. It waits for the task that completes
first. Then you decide what to do with the other tasks. The most frequent case
that you will write is a request against a timeout.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The result of the winner arrives as this union. The tag is the arm that
/// made the result.
const Outcome = union(enum) {
    reply: u32,
    timeout: void,
};

fn request(io: std.Io, delay: std.Io.Duration) u32 {
    io.sleep(delay, .awake) catch return 0;
    return 42;
}

fn deadline(io: std.Io, after: std.Io.Duration) void {
    io.sleep(after, .awake) catch {};
}

/// Runs the two arms, reports the arm that completed first, and cancels the
/// other arm. The two durations are different by an hour. Thus the code
/// decides the winner, not the load on the computer.
fn race(
    io: std.Io,
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    reply_after: std.Io.Duration,
    timeout_after: std.Io.Duration,
) !void {
    var slots: [2]Outcome = undefined;
    var select: std.Io.Select(Outcome) = .init(io, &slots);

    try select.concurrent(.reply, request, .{ io, reply_after });
    try select.concurrent(.timeout, deadline, .{ io, timeout_after });

    switch (try select.await()) {
        .reply => |value| try out.print("reply: {d}\n", .{value}),
        .timeout => try out.print("timed out\n", .{}),
    }

    // The arm that lost still runs. A select owns its tasks. Thus a cancel of
    // the select stops the arm, and no task remains when this function returns.
    select.cancelDiscard();
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    try race(io, out, .fromMilliseconds(1), .fromSeconds(3600));
    try race(io, out, .fromSeconds(3600), .fromMilliseconds(1));

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this program natively. A race needs the arms to run at the same time. That needs io.concurrent, and single-threaded wasm cannot give it. (`03-standard-library.select`)*

## The union is the result

```zig
const Outcome = union(enum) {
    reply: u32,
    timeout: void,
};

var slots: [2]Outcome = undefined;
var select: std.Io.Select(Outcome) = .init(io, &slots);
```

Each arm is a field. `Select(U)` is a `Group` and a `Queue(U)` together. Thus
the buffer that you pass is the buffer of the queue. The buffer must have
space for each task that you spawn.

If you cancel with less space than that, the result is a deadlock. The
cancelled tasks still need a place to put their results.

```zig
try select.concurrent(.reply, request, .{ io, reply_after });
try select.concurrent(.timeout, deadline, .{ io, timeout_after });

switch (try select.await()) {
    .reply => |value| ...,
    .timeout => ...,
}
```

The field name is comptime, and the return type of the function must agree
with that field. Thus, if an arm returns the wrong type, the result is a
compile error, not a union with the wrong tag at run time.

`await` returns when one arm completes. Call `await` again for the next arm,
or stop.

## The other arms still run

```zig
select.cancelDiscard();
```

A select owns its tasks, the same as a `Group`. When `await` returns, the arm
that lost still runs. `cancelDiscard` sends a cancellation request to all of
the tasks. It waits until they are done, and it discards their results.

Use `cancel` instead when an arm can return a value that you must free.
`cancel` returns one outstanding result on each call. Call it in a loop until it
returns `null`.

If you do not cancel, the result is not a leak in the usual meaning. But you
cannot destroy the select while a task still points into its buffer. Thus you
get no advantage when you omit the cancel.

## Use `concurrent` for the arms

`select.async` exists, and it agrees with `Group.async`. But arms that can run
inline do not really race. On an `Io` that runs tasks inline, the first arm
that you spawn runs first until it completes. Thus it wins each time.

For a timeout arm, this means that the program sleeps for the full timeout
before the request starts. For that reason, the arms here use `concurrent`.
The snippet is native, because wasm cannot give `concurrent`.

The durations in the snippet are different by an hour in each direction. This
difference is intentional. The code decides the winner, not the load on the
computer. Thus the expected output is correct on CI.

If the difference is only some milliseconds, the winner can change from one
run to the next. Then the test can fail sometimes.

---

## Queues

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/queues/*

Tasks that only start and stop need a `Future`. Tasks that give work to other
tasks while they run need a queue. `std.Io.Queue` is the bounded channel:

- It has a fixed capacity.
- The two ends can block.
- The sender can close the queue.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // The queue owns no memory. The capacity is the buffer that you give it.
    var storage: [4]u32 = undefined;
    var queue: std.Io.Queue(u32) = .init(&storage);

    // `put` blocks when the queue is full, unless you ask for a minimum of
    // zero. Then it takes the elements that fit and returns their count.
    const accepted = try queue.put(io, &.{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }, 0);
    try out.print("accepted {d} of 6\n", .{accepted});

    // A close tells the receiver that no more elements will come. The queue
    // still delivers the elements in the buffer before it tells the receiver.
    queue.close(io);

    var total: u32 = 0;
    while (queue.getOne(io)) |value| {
        total += value;
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("drained {d}, then {s}\n", .{ total, @errorName(err) });
    }

    // A closed queue refuses new elements, also when the buffer is empty.
    queue.putOne(io, 7) catch |err| {
        try out.print("put after close: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    };

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.queues`)*

## Capacity is a buffer that you supply

```zig
var storage: [4]u32 = undefined;
var queue: std.Io.Queue(u32) = .init(&storage);
```

The queue allocates nothing. It is a ring over the array that you give it.
Thus you decide its capacity, its lifetime and its location, the same as with
`Io.Writer`. Usually, the queue is on the stack of the function that spawns
the two tasks.

## `put` and `get` take a minimum

```zig
const accepted = try queue.put(io, &.{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }, 0);
```

The last argument is the number of elements that the call must move before it
can return. `putAll` and `putOne` move all the elements or block. A minimum
of zero never blocks. The call moves the elements that fit and returns the
count. Above, the count is 4, because the capacity is 4. `get` works in
exactly the same way.

That parameter makes batches cheap. A consumer can ask for a minimum of one
and give a buffer of 64. Then one call gets all the elements that are in the
queue now. The call blocks only when the queue is empty.

## Close the queue to tell the receiver to stop

```zig
queue.close(io);
```

A closed queue rejects new elements immediately. But it delivers all the
elements that are already in the buffer before it reports `error.Closed`.
Thus the loop reads until the error, and it knows that it lost no elements:

```zig
while (queue.getOne(io)) |value| {
    total += value;
} else |err| { ... }
```

The consumer does not need to know how many elements will come. Thus a
producer can decide the number of elements while it sends them.

## Back pressure between two tasks

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Fills the queue and closes it. The capacity is two. Thus the function blocks
/// before it is done, and it continues when the consumer removes elements.
/// This is back pressure, and it needs no more code.
fn produce(io: std.Io, queue: *std.Io.Queue(u32)) void {
    for (1..6) |i| {
        queue.putOne(io, @intCast(i)) catch return;
    }
    queue.close(io);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var storage: [2]u32 = undefined;
    var queue: std.Io.Queue(u32) = .init(&storage);

    var producer = try io.concurrent(produce, .{ io, &queue });
    defer producer.await(io);

    // The consumer never asks how many elements will come. It reads until the
    // sender closes the queue. That is the reason for `error.Closed`.
    while (queue.getOne(io)) |value| {
        try out.print("got {d}\n", .{value});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("sender is done: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this program natively. The producer must make progress while the consumer waits. That needs io.concurrent, and single-threaded wasm cannot give it. (`03-standard-library.queue-worker`)*

The capacity is two, and the producer has five elements to send. Thus the
producer blocks before it is done. It continues when the consumer removes
elements from the queue.

No other code controls this behaviour. A full queue blocks the sender, and
that block *is* the back pressure. The pair runs at the speed of the slower
side.

This case needs
[`io.concurrent`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/), not `io.async`. A
producer that starts with `async` can run inline until it fills the queue and
blocks. The consumer that must empty the queue still waits for `async` to
return.

The two functions exist because of this deadlock. This deadlock is also the
reason that this snippet is native, and the snippet at the top of the page is
not.

## Cancellation

Each blocking call here is a cancellation point. `put`, `get`, and their
`One` and `All` forms return `Cancelable` errors. The `Uncancelable` variants
are for cleanup paths, and they do not report cancellation.

See [Cancellation](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/). The rule that you
return `error.Canceled` to the caller applies to a blocked producer, the same
as in all other code.

---

## Locks and Semaphores

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/locks/*

`Io.Mutex` is sufficient for most shared state. When it is not sufficient,
use `RwLock`, `Semaphore` or `Condition`. Each one takes the `Io` instance,
for the same reason as the mutex. A blocking call goes through the interface.
Thus you can cancel it, and it works on an implementation with no threads.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // An RwLock admits any number of readers at the same time, or exactly one writer.
    var rw: std.Io.RwLock = .init;

    try rw.lockShared(io);
    try rw.lockShared(io);
    try out.print("two readers: yes\n", .{});

    // `tryLock` never blocks. It tells you if it got the lock. Readers hold the
    // lock, thus a writer cannot get it.
    try out.print("writer while reading: {}\n", .{rw.tryLock(io)});

    rw.unlockShared(io);
    rw.unlockShared(io);

    // When the readers release the lock, the writer gets it.
    try out.print("writer once alone: {}\n", .{rw.tryLock(io)});
    rw.unlock(io);

    // A semaphore counts permits. It does not give exclusive access. With two
    // permits, two tasks continue, and the third task must wait.
    var sem: std.Io.Semaphore = .{ .permits = 2 };
    try sem.wait(io);
    try sem.wait(io);
    try out.print("permits taken: 2, left: {d}\n", .{sem.permits});

    // Use `waitTimeout` when a permit may never come. Then the task does not
    // wait forever. Here, no code releases a permit.
    const patience: std.Io.Timeout = .{ .duration = .{ .raw = .fromMilliseconds(1), .clock = .awake } };
    if (sem.waitTimeout(io, patience)) |_| {
        try out.print("third permit: taken\n", .{});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("third permit: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    }

    sem.post(io);
    try out.print("after post, left: {d}\n", .{sem.permits});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.locks`)*

## `RwLock`: many readers or one writer

```zig
try rw.lockShared(io);
try rw.lockShared(io);
```

Two readers hold the lock at the same time. A writer cannot get the lock with
them, and a reader cannot get the lock with a writer.

Use an `RwLock` only when these two conditions are true:

- Reads are much more frequent than writes.
- The reads hold the lock for a long time, and that time has an effect.

An `RwLock` does more bookkeeping than a `Mutex`. Thus, for a short critical
section, the plain mutex is usually faster.

`tryLock` and `tryLockShared` never block. They tell you if they got the
lock. The snippet uses them to show two results: while readers hold the lock,
the writer cannot get it. When the readers release the lock, the writer gets
it.

Unlock with the call that agrees with the lock:

- `unlockShared` for a shared lock.
- `unlock` for an exclusive lock.

## `Semaphore`: a count, not exclusion

```zig
var sem: std.Io.Semaphore = .{ .permits = 2 };
try sem.wait(io);
sem.post(io);
```

A semaphore counts permits. `wait` takes one permit, and it blocks while no
permit is available. `post` adds one permit.

A semaphore has no connection to the task that waited. This property makes a
semaphore different from a mutex. Use a semaphore to set a limit on the
number of tasks in one place at the same time. For example, you can set a
maximum number of active requests to a service that cannot accept more.

`waitTimeout` stops after a time. It does not wait forever:

```zig
const patience: std.Io.Timeout = .{ .duration = .{ .raw = .fromMilliseconds(1), .clock = .awake } };
if (sem.waitTimeout(io, patience)) |_| { ... } else |err| { ... }
```

When the time ends, `waitTimeout` returns `error.Timeout`. When a request
cancels the task, it returns `error.Canceled`. Thus you can always tell the
two cases apart.

`Io.Timeout` is a union of `.none`, a duration, or an absolute deadline. A
duration includes the clock that measures it. Here, the clock is `.awake`.

## `Condition`: wait for a predicate

`Io.Condition` is the third tool, and `Semaphore` uses it internally. To use
a condition, do these steps:

1. Hold a mutex.
2. Test the value that you need.
3. Wait for a signal. While you wait, the condition releases the mutex.

```zig
while (!ready) try cond.wait(io, &mutex);
```

The loop is necessary. A wakeup does not promise that the predicate is true.
It tells you only that a new check can be useful.

## Static initialisation, no deinit

`.init` on `Mutex` and `RwLock`, and a plain struct literal on `Semaphore`,
are compile-time constants. None of these types own memory or a handle. Thus
you have no deinit to call, and the construction cannot fail.

You can put a lock in a global or in a struct field. You can also put it on
the stack of the function that spawns the tasks that share the lock.

---

## Atomics

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/atomics/*

To add one to a number, the computer does three steps:

1. Read the number.
2. Add one.
3. Write the number back.

On one thread, the three steps cause no problem. With two threads, a different thread can act between the steps, and the program can lose an update.

This chapter shows the operations that prevent a lost update. It also shows the ordering argument that each of these operations takes.

The program runs in your browser. It starts no threads, and it does not need threads. An atomic operation does the same thing when no other thread runs.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Atomic = std.atomic.Value;

/// Two workers increment one plain counter. The code writes each step of the
/// read-modify-write in the order that a race can run the steps. This code has
/// no race. It shows the result that a race makes.
fn lostUpdate() u32 {
    var plain: u32 = 0;
    const a_read = plain; // worker A reads 0
    const b_read = plain; // worker B reads 0
    plain = b_read + 1; // worker B writes 1
    plain = a_read + 1; // worker A writes 1, over the value from B
    return plain;
}

/// The same two increments. No other operation can occur between the read and
/// the write.
fn atomicIncrements() u32 {
    var counter: Atomic(u32) = .init(0);
    _ = counter.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
    _ = counter.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
    return counter.load(.monotonic);
}

/// A multiplication needs a loop, because no `fetchMul` exists. Read the value,
/// calculate the new value, and swap only if no other thread changed it.
fn multiplyBy(counter: *Atomic(u32), factor: u32) void {
    var seen = counter.load(.monotonic);
    while (counter.cmpxchgWeak(seen, seen * factor, .monotonic, .monotonic)) |actual| {
        seen = actual;
    }
}

/// The `.release` store promises that the write to `payload` is visible to
/// each reader that gets `true` from an `.acquire` load.
fn publish(payload: *u32, ready: *Atomic(bool), value: u32) void {
    payload.* = value;
    ready.store(true, .release);
}

/// The other half of the pair. Null means that the writer did not publish yet.
fn consume(payload: *const u32, ready: *const Atomic(bool)) ?u32 {
    if (!ready.load(.acquire)) return null;
    return payload.*;
}

/// A lock is not a primitive. One compare-and-swap takes the lock, and one
/// ordered store releases the lock. The type needs nothing more.
/// `std.atomic.Mutex` is this type.
const SpinLock = enum(u8) {
    unlocked,
    locked,

    fn tryLock(self: *SpinLock) bool {
        return @cmpxchgStrong(SpinLock, self, .unlocked, .locked, .acquire, .monotonic) == null;
    }

    fn unlock(self: *SpinLock) void {
        @atomicStore(SpinLock, self, .unlocked, .release);
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    try out.print("two increments, plain:  {d}\n", .{lostUpdate()});
    try out.print("two increments, atomic: {d}\n", .{atomicIncrements()});

    // Each fetch operation returns the value from before the change. Thus the
    // counter can give tickets: no two callers get the same number.
    var counter: Atomic(u32) = .init(2);
    const before = counter.fetchAdd(10, .monotonic);
    try out.print("fetchAdd returned {d}, counter is now {d}\n", .{ before, counter.load(.monotonic) });

    multiplyBy(&counter, 3);
    try out.print("after the CAS loop: {d}\n", .{counter.load(.monotonic)});

    // A compare-and-swap returns null when it is successful. When it fails, it
    // returns the value that was really there.
    const wrong_guess = counter.cmpxchgStrong(0, 99, .monotonic, .monotonic);
    try out.print("cmpxchg against a wrong guess: {?d}\n", .{wrong_guess});

    var payload: u32 = 0;
    var ready: Atomic(bool) = .init(false);
    try out.print("before publish: {?d}\n", .{consume(&payload, &ready)});
    publish(&payload, &ready, 7);
    try out.print("after publish:  {?d}\n", .{consume(&payload, &ready)});

    var lock: SpinLock = .unlocked;
    try out.print("first tryLock:  {}\n", .{lock.tryLock()});
    try out.print("second tryLock: {}\n", .{lock.tryLock()});
    lock.unlock();
    try out.print("after unlock:   {}\n", .{lock.tryLock()});
    lock.unlock();

    // Ordering is an argument to each operation. The loop prints the orderings,
    // weakest first. No separate fence builtin exists.
    try out.print("orderings:", .{});
    for (std.meta.tags(std.lang.AtomicOrder)) |order| {
        try out.print(" .{t}", .{order});
    }
    try out.print("\n", .{});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.atomics`)*

## A lost update, step by step

A real race is difficult to show, because it occurs only sometimes. Thus the program writes the interleaving by hand.

Two workers each must add one. Both workers read before one of them writes.

```zig
/// Two workers increment one plain counter. The code writes each step of the
/// read-modify-write in the order that a race can run the steps. This code has
/// no race. It shows the result that a race makes.
fn lostUpdate() u32 {
    var plain: u32 = 0;
    const a_read = plain; // worker A reads 0
    const b_read = plain; // worker B reads 0
    plain = b_read + 1; // worker B writes 1
    plain = a_read + 1; // worker A writes 1, over the value from B
    return plain;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `lostUpdate` from `snippets/03-standard-library/atomics.zig`.*

Worker B does all of its work correctly. It reads zero, adds one, and stores one.

Then worker A stores one over the value from worker B. Worker A read zero, thus worker A calculated one.

```
two increments, plain:  1
```

The program did two increments, and the result is one.

The code above has no undefined behaviour, and no race occurs. The code runs the same sequence that a race can make. The program selects the order, thus the result is the same on each run.

## `fetchAdd` makes the three steps one operation

`std.atomic.Value(T)` contains one value. It gives the value operations that a different thread cannot divide.

```zig
/// The same two increments. No other operation can occur between the read and
/// the write.
fn atomicIncrements() u32 {
    var counter: Atomic(u32) = .init(0);
    _ = counter.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
    _ = counter.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
    return counter.load(.monotonic);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `atomicIncrements` from `snippets/03-standard-library/atomics.zig`.*

`fetchAdd` still reads, adds and writes. But no other core can see or change the value between those three parts.

```
two increments, atomic: 2
```

The wrapper adds no logic. On x86, that line is one `lock xadd` instruction. The hardware gives the guarantee.

## Each fetch returns the old value

`fetchAdd` returns the value that the counter held *before* the addition.

```
fetchAdd returned 2, counter is now 12
```

This design is intentional, and it is useful. With it, the counter can give tickets. If two threads call `fetchAdd(1, ...)`, each thread gets a different number. Each thread also knows which number it got.

If `fetchAdd` returned the new value, a caller could not know if it was the third caller or the fourth caller. Two callers can see the same total.

All the functions in the family work in this way: `fetchSub`, `fetchAnd`, `fetchOr`, `fetchXor`, `fetchMin`, `fetchMax`.

`swap` uses the same idea without arithmetic. It stores your value and returns the old value.

## Compare-and-swap is the general tool

No `fetchMul` exists. Also, no special operation exists for each problem. Instead, Zig has compare-and-swap. You can make each other operation on this page from compare-and-swap.

You give two values: the value that you think is there, and the new value. The swap occurs only if your first value is correct.

```zig
/// A multiplication needs a loop, because no `fetchMul` exists. Read the value,
/// calculate the new value, and swap only if no other thread changed it.
fn multiplyBy(counter: *Atomic(u32), factor: u32) void {
    var seen = counter.load(.monotonic);
    while (counter.cmpxchgWeak(seen, seen * factor, .monotonic, .monotonic)) |actual| {
        seen = actual;
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `multiplyBy` from `snippets/03-standard-library/atomics.zig`.*

Read the loop condition carefully. It works in the opposite way to its appearance.

`cmpxchgWeak` returns an optional.

**Null means that the swap was successful.** A payload means that the swap failed. The payload is the value that was really there.

Thus `while (...) |actual|` loops while the swap *fails*. On each turn, the loop gives the new value back for one more attempt.

The program shows a failure directly. It guesses a wrong value on purpose:

```
cmpxchg against a wrong guess: 36
```

The counter was 36, the guess was 0, and the swap did not occur. The returned 36 is the value that the counter really holds.

`cmpxchgWeak` can fail spuriously, also when your guess is correct. This helps on ARM and RISC-V. On these CPUs, the function compiles to a load-linked/store-conditional pair, and a context switch can interrupt that pair. Thus, if the function can sometimes fail falsely, the loop is tighter.

In a retry loop, a spurious failure costs one more turn. When there is no loop and a false failure is wrong, use `cmpxchgStrong`.

## Ordering is an argument, not a fence

Each operation in this chapter has a second argument. The chapter did not explain that argument yet.

The argument has six values. The program prints them, weakest first:

```
orderings: .unordered .monotonic .acquire .release .acq_rel .seq_cst
```

The ordering does not change the result on the atomic variable. The ordering controls what the compiler and the CPU can do with **the other memory around the operation**.

The compiler and the CPU can both change the order of your instructions. Usually, you cannot see the difference, and it costs nothing. When a different thread watches, the order that the thread sees changes what your program does.

`.monotonic` is the weakest ordering that a read-modify-write accepts. It makes the operation indivisible. It gives no promise about the memory near the operation. That is correct for a statistics counter. For such a counter, you need the total at the end, and no other data depends on the time of each increment.

Use a stronger ordering when the atomic is a **signal about other data**.

`.seq_cst` is the strongest ordering. Use it when you are not sure. It is slower, but it is always correct.

No `@fence` builtin exists to use with these orderings. The ordering is an argument of each operation.

The compiler rejects the combinations that have no meaning. Thus you do not have to remember them:

```
c.fetchAdd(1, .unordered)   error: @atomicRmw atomic ordering must not be unordered
c.load(.release)            error: @atomicLoad atomic ordering must not be release or acq_rel
c.store(1, .acquire)        error: @atomicStore atomic ordering must not be acquire or acq_rel
```

A load cannot release, because it has no data to publish. A store cannot acquire, because it reads no data.

Compare-and-swap takes two orderings: one for the success path and one for the failure path. The failure ordering must not be stricter than the success ordering:

```
c.cmpxchgStrong(0, 1, .monotonic, .acquire)
error: failure atomic ordering must be no stricter than success
```

## Acquire and release are a pair

The most common pattern has the name *publishing*. It has two halves:

- One thread writes some data, and then it sets a flag.
- A different thread sees the flag, and then it reads the data.

```zig
/// The `.release` store promises that the write to `payload` is visible to
/// each reader that gets `true` from an `.acquire` load.
fn publish(payload: *u32, ready: *Atomic(bool), value: u32) void {
    payload.* = value;
    ready.store(true, .release);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `publish` from `snippets/03-standard-library/atomics.zig`.*

The `.release` store makes a boundary. Each write above the store is visible to each thread that reads that `true` with `.acquire`.

```zig
/// The other half of the pair. Null means that the writer did not publish yet.
fn consume(payload: *const u32, ready: *const Atomic(bool)) ?u32 {
    if (!ready.load(.acquire)) return null;
    return payload.*;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `consume` from `snippets/03-standard-library/atomics.zig`.*

```
before publish: null
after publish:  7
```

Without the pair, a reader can see `ready` as true and `payload` as zero. The two writes go to different addresses. Without the pair, the store to `payload` can become visible second.

That bug is very difficult to find. The problem lasts for a few nanoseconds, it depends on the CPU, and it does not occur under a debugger.

On this page, the two calls run on one thread. Thus the output shows only the pattern. On targets with real threads, the guarantee is true, and this pattern is the one to learn.

`.acq_rel` is for an operation that does the two at the same time. Such an operation is a read-modify-write, not a plain load or store.

## A lock is a compare-and-swap

Usual tools, for example locks, use atomics as their parts.

```zig
/// A lock is not a primitive. One compare-and-swap takes the lock, and one
/// ordered store releases the lock. The type needs nothing more.
/// `std.atomic.Mutex` is this type.
const SpinLock = enum(u8) {
    unlocked,
    locked,

    fn tryLock(self: *SpinLock) bool {
        return @cmpxchgStrong(SpinLock, self, .unlocked, .locked, .acquire, .monotonic) == null;
    }

    fn unlock(self: *SpinLock) void {
        @atomicStore(SpinLock, self, .unlocked, .release);
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `SpinLock` from `snippets/03-standard-library/atomics.zig`.*

Those ten lines are a mutex that works.

`tryLock` changes `unlocked` to `locked`, and it tells you if it was successful. Only one caller can see `unlocked` and take the lock. The reason is that only one compare-and-swap can succeed against a given value.

`unlock` stores `unlocked` with `.release`. The store publishes all that the holder did inside the critical section. The next thread that takes the lock sees those changes. These orderings are the pattern from the previous section, applied to the lock.

```
first tryLock:  true
second tryLock: false
after unlock:   true
```

`std.atomic.Mutex` is this type, in the standard library, at approximately this length.

But `std.atomic.Mutex` does not wait. A caller that fails to get the lock either spins or stops the attempt. A real mutex must put the thread to sleep, and then something must wake the thread. The operating system does that part.

For that reason, [`Io.Mutex`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/locks/) takes an `Io`. `SpinLock` does not take an `Io`.

## When a mutex is the better answer

Atomics are for one machine word. You cannot update two related fields atomically together.

If your invariant includes a counter and a pointer, no combination of atomic operations protects it. Use a lock for that case.

Lock-free code is also not always fast. A contended `fetchAdd` moves a cache line between cores on each call. Eight threads that all update one counter can be slower than eight threads that take a mutex.

`std.atomic.cache_line` exists for this problem. With it, you can put separate counters on separate cache lines when a profiler shows contention between them.

Select the tool in this way:

- For a counter, a flag, or a single pointer that you swap as a unit, use an atomic.
- For data that has an invariant, use [`Io.Mutex`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/locks/).
- Before you write your own lock-free structure, try [`Io.Queue`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/queues/).

## What moved

Two things on this page are different from an older tutorial.

`AtomicOrder` is now in `std.lang`. `std.lang` contains the declarations that the standard library shares with the compiler. `std.builtin` stays as an alias. Thus `std.builtin.AtomicOrder` still resolves, and the snippet on this page uses `std.lang.AtomicOrder`.

`@fence` does not exist now. Code that called `@fence` could almost always put the ordering on the operation instead. Now the operation is the only place for an ordering.

The builtins are still available under the wrapper. `std.atomic.Value` calls `@atomicLoad`, `@atomicStore`, `@atomicRmw` and `@cmpxchgStrong`. `SpinLock` above uses two of these builtins directly, because `Value` is not designed for an `enum(u8)`.

Next: [Threads](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/threads/) shows the real threads that these guarantees are for. [Locks and Semaphores](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/locks/) shows the tools to prefer over atomics.

---

## Threads

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/threads/*

In Zig, `std.Thread.spawn` starts a real OS thread, and `join` waits until the
thread stops. Use `std.Io.Mutex` to protect shared data. `std.Thread.Mutex`
does not exist now.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn addTo(total: *u32, amount: u32) void {
    total.* += amount;
}

fn addLocked(total: *u32, mutex: *std.Io.Mutex, io: std.Io, amount: u32) void {
    mutex.lock(io) catch return;
    defer mutex.unlock(io);
    total.* += amount;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // One thread. The program joins it explicitly.
    var value: u32 = 0;
    const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, addTo, .{ &value, 42 });
    thread.join();
    try out.print("single: {d}\n", .{value});

    // Many threads that change one variable need synchronisation. Without the
    // mutex, this code is a data race, and the total is not reliable.
    var total: u32 = 0;
    var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;
    var threads: [8]std.Thread = undefined;
    for (&threads) |*t| {
        t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, addLocked, .{ &total, &mutex, io, 1 });
    }
    for (threads) |t| t.join();
    try out.print("locked total: {d}\n", .{total});

    // For a simple counter, use an atomic. It needs no lock.
    var counter = std.atomic.Value(u32).init(0);
    _ = counter.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
    _ = counter.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
    try out.print("atomic: {d}\n", .{counter.load(.monotonic)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this program natively. wasm32-wasi is single-threaded. Thus std.Thread.spawn does not compile for wasm32-wasi. (`03-standard-library.threads`)*

## Spawn and join

```zig
const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, function, .{ args... });
thread.join();
```

The arguments are a tuple, and the tuple must agree with the parameters of the
function. `join` blocks until the thread stops. `detach` releases the handle
and does not wait.

You must join or detach each thread that you spawn. If you discard a handle
and do not join or detach it, the resources of the thread leak. No destructor
finds this error. Thus put `defer thread.join()` on the line after the spawn.
The reason is the same as the reason for a `defer free` after an allocation.

If two threads write to the same memory without synchronisation, the result
is a data race. A data race is undefined behaviour, not only a wrong answer.
The optimiser can assume that a data race does not occur.

## Synchronisation moved to `std.Io`

This change breaks older code. On `std.Io.Mutex`, `lock` takes the io
instance:

```zig
var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;
try mutex.lock(io);
defer mutex.unlock(io);
```

`lock` can fail for one reason only: a task can *cancel* the call. Because of
this, the mutex works together with the other parts of `Io`.
See [Cancellation](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/) for the meaning of
cancellation.

The move changes more than the name. A mutex that knows the `Io` instance can
have a different implementation for each way that the program runs:

- Under a pool of OS threads, the mutex is a real futex.
- When all the code is on one thread, the mutex is a simple flag.
- Under green threads, the mutex yields to the scheduler.

Code that uses `std.Io.Mutex` works under all three without a change.

The rule for a mutex did not change, and the rule is still the difficult
part. Each access to the shared data, a read or a write, must hold the lock.
Also, the code must release the lock on each path out of the function. `defer`
does the second task. No tool checks the first task for you. Thus, design the
program so that it has the smallest possible quantity of shared state.

## Atomics for the simple cases

A counter does not need a mutex:

```zig
var counter = std.atomic.Value(u32).init(0);
_ = counter.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
```

Look at the `_ =`. `fetchAdd` returns the previous value, and Zig does not let
you discard the value silently.

The second argument is a memory ordering. The ordering controls the memory
around the operation, not the counter. `.monotonic` is correct for a total
that no thread reads until the end. `.monotonic` is wrong for a flag that
publishes data that the thread wrote before the flag.
[Atomics](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/atomics/) explains these subjects:

- the six orderings
- the compare-and-swap loop, which builds each operation that has no `fetch`
  function of its own
- the complete mutex that `std.atomic` makes from one compare-and-swap and one
  ordered store

## Prefer structured concurrency

For most work, [`Io.async` and
`Io.Group`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/) are a better choice than
raw threads that you spawn. They have these advantages:

- You can cancel them.
- A task that runs cannot continue after the end of their scope.
- They work on targets that have no threads, and this site runs on one of
  those targets.

A thread is a low-level resource, the same as a raw allocation. Most code
needs only this: "run these tasks at the same time and wait for them". That
need is a scope with a lifetime, not a handle that you must manage. Use
`std.Thread.spawn` when you need a long-lived worker with its own loop. For
all other work, use the structured forms.

---

## Migrate from `std.Thread`

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/coming-from-std-thread/*

Some code does not compile now, and the compiler gives this message:

```
error: struct 'Thread' has no member named 'Mutex'
```

Zig did not deprecate these names, and it did not rename them in place. `std.Thread.Mutex` does not exist now, and six related declarations also do not exist.

They moved to `std.Io`. The table below comes from the compiler, not from a changelog.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Move = struct {
    /// The old name on `std.Thread`.
    was: []const u8,
    /// The new name on `std.Io`.
    now: []const u8,
};

const moves = [_]Move{
    .{ .was = "Mutex", .now = "Mutex" },
    .{ .was = "RwLock", .now = "RwLock" },
    .{ .was = "Semaphore", .now = "Semaphore" },
    .{ .was = "Condition", .now = "Condition" },
    .{ .was = "ResetEvent", .now = "Event" },
    .{ .was = "WaitGroup", .now = "Group" },
    .{ .was = "Pool", .now = "Threaded" },
};

/// The declarations that stayed on `std.Thread`. They are about an OS thread,
/// not about a wait for a thread.
const kept = [_][]const u8{ "spawn", "getCpuCount", "getCurrentId", "yield", "detach" };

fn mark(present: bool) []const u8 {
    return if (present) "present" else "gone";
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    inline for (moves) |m| {
        try out.print("std.Thread.{s: <11} {s: <8}  std.Io.{s: <10} {s}\n", .{
            m.was,
            comptime mark(@hasDecl(std.Thread, m.was)),
            m.now,
            comptime mark(@hasDecl(std.Io, m.now)),
        });
    }

    try out.print("\n", .{});

    inline for (kept) |name| {
        try out.print("std.Thread.{s: <13} {s}\n", .{ name, comptime mark(@hasDecl(std.Thread, name)) });
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`03-standard-library.std-thread-today`)*

The program prints each line from `@hasDecl`. Thus, if the table becomes incorrect, the build finds the problem. If one of these names returns, the output changes and the nightly build fails.

## The split, and the reason for it

Seven declarations moved. Five stayed. Look at where each one went, and you can see the rule.

`spawn`, `detach`, `getCpuCount`, `getCurrentId` and `yield` are about an operating system thread. They are still on `std.Thread`, because that is their purpose.

All the declarations that moved have one thing in common. Each one of them **waits**:

- A mutex waits until a holder is done.
- A semaphore waits for a permit.
- A wait group waits until a count is zero.
- A pool waits for work.

Current Zig makes waits explicit. A function that can block must know how the program wants to block. The `Io` holds that knowledge. Thus each function that can block takes an `Io`.

A thread is still only a thread, and it does not need such an argument.

## The mutex, and why `lock` can fail

The old shape was a struct with a zero initialiser, and its methods could not fail: `var mutex: std.Thread.Mutex = .{};` and then `mutex.lock()`.

The new shape takes the `Io` on the two calls:

```zig
fn accumulate(total: *u32, mutex: *std.Io.Mutex, io: std.Io, amount: u32) void {
    // `Io.Mutex.lock` takes the io instance, like all other functions that can
    // block. It returns an error for one reason only: a task can cancel it.
    mutex.lock(io) catch return;
    defer mutex.unlock(io);
    total.* += amount;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `accumulate` from `snippets/03-standard-library/concurrency.zig`.*

Three things changed in four lines:

- The initialiser is `.init`, not `.{}`. `Io.Mutex` has state to set, not a zero value to accept.
- `lock` and `unlock` both take the `io`, for the same reason as all blocking calls.
- `lock` returns an error.

`lock` can fail for exactly one reason: the task that waits on the lock got a cancellation request. The lock cannot become poisoned, and a wrong use of the lock does not give an error.

Thus `catch return` is a reasonable answer in a worker that just got the request to stop. More often, you need `try`, and a caller that already knows what to do with a cancellation.

[Cancellation](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/) explains that subject. Cancellation is the reason that almost all signatures in this section have an error union.

## The pool is now the `Io` itself

`std.Thread.Pool` was a value that you built. You gave it work, and then you waited on it.

The replacement works in the opposite direction. You select an implementation one time, in `main`. `std.Io.Threaded` is the implementation that has a thread pool inside it. All the code below `main` takes the interface. That code never knows if a pool is behind the interface.

Thus you do not need to find a new `Pool` type. Do these steps instead:

1. Delete the pool.
2. Pass the `io` that you already have.
3. Start tasks with `io.async` or a `Group`.

Then the same code runs on an implementation that has no threads. Because of that, the other chapters in this section have Run buttons.

[Choose an Io](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/choosing-an-io/) explains the options.

## The rest of the table

`WaitGroup` became [`Io.Group`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/). You start tasks on the group and await the group. You do not count the tasks up and down by hand.

`RwLock`, `Semaphore` and `Condition` kept their names, and each one got an `io` parameter. [Locks and Semaphores](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/locks/) explains all three.

`ResetEvent` is now `Io.Event`. It is the only entry in the table with a name that really changed.

If you read [Atomics](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/atomics/), open `Io.Event` in the standard library. `Io.Event` is a three-state enum, one `@cmpxchgStrong` and an `@atomicLoad` with `.acquire`. These are the parts at the end of that chapter.

## Rewrite old code

The mechanical part is short:

1. Delete the pool and the wait group.
2. Add `io: std.Io` to each function that locks, waits or sleeps. Pass the `io` down from `main`.
3. Change `.{}` to `.init` on the primitives.
4. Put `try` in front of `lock`. Let the error go to the code that owns the cancellation.
5. Replace `std.Thread.spawn` with `io.async`, unless you really need an OS thread.
6. Before you depend on `async` or `concurrent`, read the difference between them.

Then ask one question: which functions in your codebase can block? Those functions take an `Io` now, and the compiler finds each one of them for you.

Next: read [The Io Interface](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/io-interface/) if that parameter is new to you. Read [Threads](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/threads/) for the five declarations that stayed.

---

## Choose an Io

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/choosing-an-io/*

Each other chapter in this section takes `init.io` and gives it to the
functions that it calls. This chapter shows where that value comes from. The
program makes the choice, and `main` is the only place in a codebase that must
make it.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

fn double(value: u32) u32 {
    return value * 2;
}

/// Usual library code. It never names an implementation. Thus it works with
/// the implementation that the caller made.
fn run(io: std.Io, label: []const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var future = io.async(double, .{21});
    try out.print("{s}: async {d}", .{ label, future.await(io) });

    if (io.concurrent(double, .{21})) |handle| {
        var pending = handle;
        try out.print(", concurrent {d}\n", .{pending.await(io)});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print(", concurrent {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // A thread pool. The implementation uses the allocator only to spawn
    // tasks. All other parts of the implementation do not allocate.
    var pool: std.Io.Threaded = .init(init.gpa, .{});
    defer pool.deinit();
    try run(pool.io(), "threaded", out);

    // The same implementation without concurrency. `async` still works,
    // because it can run the task inline. `concurrent` cannot work.
    var capped: std.Io.Threaded = .init(init.gpa, .{ .concurrent_limit = .nothing });
    defer capped.deinit();
    try run(capped.io(), "capped", out);

    // A static instance that spawns nothing. A target without threads gets
    // this instance, and it needs no allocator.
    var lone: std.Io.Threaded = .init_single_threaded;
    try run(lone.io(), "single-threaded", out);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this program natively. The program shows the difference between an implementation with threads and an implementation without threads. Thus it needs a host that has threads. (`03-standard-library.choosing-an-io`)*

## `Io.Threaded` is the default

```zig
var pool: std.Io.Threaded = .init(init.gpa, .{});
defer pool.deinit();
const io = pool.io();
```

`Io.Threaded` is a thread pool. It is portable to each target that Zig
supports. `init.io` gives you this implementation, except when the target has
no threads.

The implementation uses the allocator only to spawn tasks. If you never call
`async` or `concurrent`, you can pass `Allocator.failing`. The implementation
still works for plain I/O.

Two options are useful:

- `async_limit` sets the maximum size of the pool for `io.async`. Past that
  limit, tasks run inline. They do not wait for a thread.
- `concurrent_limit` sets the maximum for `io.concurrent`. Past that limit,
  the call returns `error.ConcurrencyUnavailable`.

The snippet makes a second instance with `.concurrent_limit = .nothing`. This
instance shows what code sees on a target that cannot give real concurrency.
You do not need a different host to see it.

## `init_single_threaded` spawns nothing

```zig
var lone: std.Io.Threaded = .init_single_threaded;
```

This instance is a compile-time constant. It needs no allocator, no threads
and no deinit. `async` still works, because `async` can run the task inline.
`concurrent` always fails, and cancellation requests do nothing.

A wasm build gets this instance. For this reason, each browser playground on
this site runs the same source as CI.

This instance is also a good way to test that library code still works
correctly with no threads. If your code needs `concurrent`, run it against
this instance and find the problem now.

## Evented implementations

The standard library has two more implementations: `std.Io.Uring` on Linux
and `std.Io.Kqueue` on Darwin and the BSDs. They do not park one thread for
each blocking call. Instead, they submit the operation to the kernel and
suspend the task. A task that suspends in this way costs a stack, not a
thread.

`std.Io.fiber` does the work of the suspension. It saves a small number of
registers and changes to a different stack. An implementation uses
`std.Io.fiber`. Application code does not call it.

This is the advantage of the `Io` parameter. You write a server against the
interface. The server runs on a thread pool during development and on
io_uring in production, without a change to one line. The decision between
the two stays in `main`.

## Library code names none of them

```zig
fn run(io: std.Io, ...) !void
```

The snippet calls this function three times with three different
implementations. The function does not know the difference.

To get this result in your library, do these steps:

1. Take an `Io` parameter.
2. Never use a global instead.
3. Handle `error.ConcurrencyUnavailable` where you ask for concurrency.

Then the caller makes the choice on this page. That is the reason that
blocking calls go through an interface.

`Io.Threaded.global_single_threaded` exists as a fallback for debug work. It
is also for code that really cannot take a parameter. If a library uses it,
the library removes the choice of implementation from the caller.

---

## A Batch Job Runner

*Concurrency. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/batch-runner/*

Each other chapter here shows one primitive at a time. This chapter is a full program.

A batch of order records goes in, four workers process the records, and a report comes out. Three of the records are malformed, each in a different way. A real batch runner cannot assume that its input is clean.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The batch. It is a `const`, not stdin. Thus CI checks the same bytes that
/// the chapter shows. Three records are malformed on purpose, each in a
/// different way, because a batch runner must handle bad input.
const input =
    \\1001,3,450
    \\1002,1,300
    \\1003,0,995
    \\1004,2,1250
    \\1005,x,100
    \\1006,4,275
    \\1007,7,880
    \\1008,2
    \\1009,1,1600
    \\1010,5,120
    \\1011,3,640
    \\1012,2,410
;

const worker_count = 4;
const capacity = 32;

/// The result for one record. Each worker writes only the slot that it
/// claimed. Thus this struct needs no lock.
const Result = struct {
    id: u32 = 0,
    total: u64 = 0,
    failure: ?[]const u8 = null,
};

/// The only state that the workers really share: the biggest order in the
/// batch and the record that it came from. The two fields must agree with each
/// other, and a single atomic cannot keep two fields in agreement.
const Largest = struct {
    value: u64 = 0,
    index: usize = 0,
};

/// Change one record into a `Result`. The function uses no `Io`, allocator or
/// shared state. Thus you can read it and test it alone.
fn parseOrder(line: []const u8) Result {
    var fields = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, line, ',');
    const id_text = fields.next() orelse return .{ .failure = "no id" };
    const id = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, id_text, 10) catch return .{ .failure = "bad id" };

    // The function reads the id before other parts can fail. Thus each line of
    // the report names its record.
    const quantity_text = fields.next() orelse return .{ .id = id, .failure = "missing quantity" };
    const price_text = fields.next() orelse return .{ .id = id, .failure = "missing price" };
    if (fields.next() != null) return .{ .id = id, .failure = "extra field" };

    const quantity = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, quantity_text, 10) catch
        return .{ .id = id, .failure = "bad quantity" };
    const price = std.fmt.parseInt(u64, price_text, 10) catch
        return .{ .id = id, .failure = "bad price" };
    if (quantity == 0) return .{ .id = id, .failure = "zero quantity" };

    return .{ .id = id, .total = @as(u64, quantity) * price };
}

/// Claim records until none remain. Each worker runs this same function. The
/// scheduler decides which records each worker gets.
fn worker(
    io: std.Io,
    records: []const []const u8,
    results: []Result,
    next: *std.atomic.Value(usize),
    largest: *Largest,
    mutex: *std.Io.Mutex,
) void {
    while (true) {
        // One atomic add gives one record to a worker. `fetchAdd` returns the
        // value from before the add. Thus no two workers can claim one index.
        const index = next.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
        if (index >= records.len) return;

        const result = parseOrder(records[index]);
        results[index] = result;
        if (result.failure != null) continue;

        mutex.lock(io) catch return;
        defer mutex.unlock(io);

        // The tie break on the index is necessary. Without it, if two records
        // have equal value, the answer is the record from the first worker.
        // Then the program can print a different line on a different
        // computer.
        if (result.total > largest.value or
            (result.total == largest.value and index < largest.index))
        {
            largest.* = .{ .value = result.total, .index = index };
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // The program divides the batch into records one time, in sequence,
    // before a worker starts. The slices that it gives to the workers make the
    // remainder parallel.
    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(input);
    var lines: [capacity][]const u8 = undefined;
    var count: usize = 0;
    while (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        if (line.len == 0) continue;
        lines[count] = line;
        count += 1;
    }
    const records = lines[0..count];

    var results: [capacity]Result = @splat(.{});
    var next: std.atomic.Value(usize) = .init(0);
    var largest: Largest = .{};
    var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;

    // Use `group.async`, not `group.concurrent`. These tasks all complete
    // without help. Thus an `Io` that runs one inline, because its pool is
    // busy, is still correct. A task that you intend to cancel needs
    // `concurrent`.
    var group: std.Io.Group = .init;
    for (0..worker_count) |_| {
        group.async(io, worker, .{ io, records, results[0..count], &next, &largest, &mutex });
    }
    try group.await(io);

    // The program prints after all workers are done. It prints in record
    // order, not in completion order. The work runs concurrently, but the
    // report has a fixed order.
    var ok: usize = 0;
    var value: u64 = 0;
    try out.print("  id     total  status\n", .{});
    for (results[0..count]) |result| {
        if (result.failure) |why| {
            try out.print("{d: >6} {s: >9}  {s}\n", .{ result.id, "-", why });
        } else {
            ok += 1;
            value += result.total;
            try out.print("{d: >6} {d: >9}  ok\n", .{ result.id, result.total });
        }
    }

    try out.print("\n{d} records, {d} ok, {d} failed\n", .{ count, ok, count - ok });
    try out.print("total value: {d}\n", .{value});
    try out.print("largest: record {d} (id {d}) at {d}\n", .{
        largest.index,
        results[largest.index].id,
        largest.value,
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this program natively. wasm32-wasi has a single thread. Thus each worker runs inline, and the program behaves like a plain for loop. (`03-standard-library.batch-runner`)*

The program has three items of state that the workers use. The program protects each item in a different way.

## Three kinds of state, three different answers

The results are one slot for each record.

```zig
/// The result for one record. Each worker writes only the slot that it
/// claimed. Thus this struct needs no lock.
const Result = struct {
    id: u32 = 0,
    total: u64 = 0,
    failure: ?[]const u8 = null,
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Result` from `snippets/03-standard-library/batch-runner.zig`.*

Each worker writes only the slot of the record that it claimed. Thus two workers never write the same bytes, and the slots need no lock and no atomic. This is the cheapest way to share state, and the first way to try.

The work index is a single number that each worker increments. It is one machine word, and one operation changes it. It does not have to agree with a different value. Thus an atomic is sufficient for the work index.

The largest order in the batch is the third kind of state.

```zig
/// The only state that the workers really share: the biggest order in the
/// batch and the record that it came from. The two fields must agree with each
/// other, and a single atomic cannot keep two fields in agreement.
const Largest = struct {
    value: u64 = 0,
    index: usize = 0,
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Largest` from `snippets/03-standard-library/batch-runner.zig`.*

The struct has two fields that must agree with each other. One is a value that belongs to an index. The other is an index that belongs to a value.

Atomic operations cannot keep that pair consistent. The end of [Atomics](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/atomics/) explains why. Thus the pair needs a mutex, and the pair is the only item in the program that needs one.

## Claim work with one atomic add

```zig
/// Claim records until none remain. Each worker runs this same function. The
/// scheduler decides which records each worker gets.
fn worker(
    io: std.Io,
    records: []const []const u8,
    results: []Result,
    next: *std.atomic.Value(usize),
    largest: *Largest,
    mutex: *std.Io.Mutex,
) void {
    while (true) {
        // One atomic add gives one record to a worker. `fetchAdd` returns the
        // value from before the add. Thus no two workers can claim one index.
        const index = next.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
        if (index >= records.len) return;

        const result = parseOrder(records[index]);
        results[index] = result;
        if (result.failure != null) continue;

        mutex.lock(io) catch return;
        defer mutex.unlock(io);

        // The tie break on the index is necessary. Without it, if two records
        // have equal value, the answer is the record from the first worker.
        // Then the program can print a different line on a different
        // computer.
        if (result.total > largest.value or
            (result.total == largest.value and index < largest.index))
        {
            largest.* = .{ .value = result.total, .index = index };
        }
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `worker` from `snippets/03-standard-library/batch-runner.zig`.*

Each worker runs the same function, and the workers compete for records.

`fetchAdd` returns the value from before the addition. Thus each worker gets an index that no other worker can get. That is how the program gives work to the workers.

When the returned index is past the end, the worker returns. Then the batch is done.

No code counts or divides the batch at the start. Thus no worker is idle because its share was the easy half.
