## The parser knows nothing about concurrency

```zig
/// Change one record into a `Result`. The function uses no `Io`, allocator or
/// shared state. Thus you can read it and test it alone.
fn parseOrder(line: []const u8) Result {
    var fields = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, line, ',');
    const id_text = fields.next() orelse return .{ .failure = "no id" };
    const id = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, id_text, 10) catch return .{ .failure = "bad id" };

    // The function reads the id before other parts can fail. Thus each line of
    // the report names its record.
    const quantity_text = fields.next() orelse return .{ .id = id, .failure = "missing quantity" };
    const price_text = fields.next() orelse return .{ .id = id, .failure = "missing price" };
    if (fields.next() != null) return .{ .id = id, .failure = "extra field" };

    const quantity = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, quantity_text, 10) catch
        return .{ .id = id, .failure = "bad quantity" };
    const price = std.fmt.parseInt(u64, price_text, 10) catch
        return .{ .id = id, .failure = "bad price" };
    if (quantity == 0) return .{ .id = id, .failure = "zero quantity" };

    return .{ .id = id, .total = @as(u64, quantity) * price };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `parseOrder` from `snippets/03-standard-library/batch-runner.zig`.*

`parseOrder` takes no `Io` and no allocator. It uses no shared state, and it does not know that concurrent work occurs. You can read it and test it alone.

A mistake in the concurrency cannot make the parse wrong. When this part has no concurrency, the full program is much easier to review. The networking chapters keep protocol code away from sockets for the same reason.

## The tie break is necessary

Look again at the comparison inside the lock.

A plain "greater than" is sufficient to find the largest value. It is not sufficient to find the value **the same way two times**.

If two records have equal value, the answer is the record from the worker that got there first. That worker changes with the computer, with the run, and with the load on the computer.

The tie break on the index gives the reduction a total order. Thus the result does not depend on the worker that arrived first.

Each reduction that workers share needs this rule. The reduction can find a maximum, a minimum, a first match or a best candidate. If two inputs can tie, something other than the order of arrival must decide between them.

## The run is concurrent, the report is not

The program prints nothing until all of the workers are done. Then the report reads the results in record order, not in the order that the workers made them.

This is intentional. Each program on this site runs each night, and CI compares its output with a recorded file. If the output depended on the scheduler, no person could check it.

The same rule applies outside this site. Sometimes the result of a concurrent program depends on the order in which its tasks ran. Then you cannot test the program, and you do not see when it starts to give wrong answers.

Make the result independent of the scheduler. Then you can change how the work runs later, and the result does not change.

## `group.async`, not `group.concurrent`

The workers start on a `Group`, and the selected function is important.

`group.async` can run a task inline when the pool is busy. That is correct for these workers. Each worker completes without help, thus a worker on the thread that calls `group.async` still completes its work.

`group.concurrent` promises a separate unit of concurrency. It returns an error when it cannot give one.

Use `concurrent` when a task possibly does not complete without help. In practice, this means each task that you intend to cancel. [Cancellation](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/) shows what goes wrong if you do not. It also shows how the problem occurred in the CI of this guide.

## What actually happened

I added instrumentation to a copy of this program. The copy recorded which thread claimed each record. I ran it on a computer with twelve cores.

All twelve records went to one thread. That result occurred on each run, with each setting for the work per record.

The first worker starts before the second worker exists. Twelve records is much too little work. The first worker is already done when the second worker starts.

A larger batch changes the result. At two hundred records, the same binary gives a different answer on each run: one thread, then three, then two. The runs were seconds apart on a computer with no other load. At five thousand records, the result is four threads each time.

Thus, **the work index makes the batch safe to share, but it does not make the batch parallel**. The safety comes from the structure, thus it is true at all sizes. The work runs in parallel only when the work is sufficient to keep the first worker busy while the other workers start.

This is also why the report does not depend on the scheduler. The same program, with the same input on the same computer, divided the work differently two seconds apart. A report that showed threads would be wrong when you read it.

## When this shape is the wrong one

A work index is correct for a fixed batch that you know at the start. For other work, use a different shape:

- For work that arrives while the program runs, use [`Io.Queue`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/queues/). Producers and consumers run at the same time. The capacity of the queue limits how far the producers can go ahead of the consumers.
- For work with a deadline, put [Select](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/select/) around the group. Then cancel the work that is not complete.
- For work where each job is a network round trip, use many more workers than cores. The workers block for most of their time, and they do not compute.

Next: [Choose an Io](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/choosing-an-io/) explains the choice that this program makes in one line. The other chapters assume that choice.

# Track: Groundwork

What the machine does, from zero. The track assumes no C and no earlier systems work.

## Everything Is Bytes

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/everything-is-bytes/*

A computer stores one kind of thing: numbers from 0 to 255. One of these
numbers is a **byte**. Letters do not have a separate place in memory.
Decimals, dates and pictures do not have a separate place either. All of them
are bytes.

Then how does the machine know that one byte is the letter `A` and another
byte is the number 65?

The machine does not know. The two are the same byte. The difference is the
**type**. A type is an agreement about how to read a sequence of bytes: how
many bytes go together, and what the pattern means. The agreement is in your
program, not in the memory. If you change the agreement, the same bytes have a
different meaning.

Many things that look strange later have this cause. For example, the
operating system sees a file and an image as the same thing. Also, a network
can send numbers and receive text.

## The program

Press **Run**. The program runs in your browser. The build for this site
compiled and ran the same file before this page went on the site.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Point = struct { x: u8, y: u8 };

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // A letter is a number. 'A' is 65, in a form that a person can read
    // more easily.
    const letter: u8 = 'A';
    try out.print("'A' is the number {d}\n\n", .{letter});

    // @sizeOf gives the space that each type uses.
    try out.print("a u8 takes {d} byte\n", .{@sizeOf(u8)});
    try out.print("a u32 takes {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(u32)});
    try out.print("a Point takes {d} bytes\n\n", .{@sizeOf(Point)});

    // std.mem.asBytes gives the bytes of the value.
    const n: u32 = 1;
    try out.writeAll("the u32 1, byte by byte:");
    for (std.mem.asBytes(&n)) |byte| try out.print(" {d}", .{byte});
    try out.writeAll("\n\n");

    // No conversion occurs here. The four bytes do not change. Only the
    // rule for how to read the bytes changes.
    const number: u32 = 0x41424344;
    const letters: [4]u8 = @bitCast(number);
    try out.print("read as a number: {d}\n", .{number});
    try out.writeAll("read as letters:  ");
    for (letters) |c| try out.print("{c}", .{c});
    try out.writeAll("\n");

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.everything-is-bytes`)*

## What just happened

**`'A'` printed as 65.** In Zig, `'A'` does not make a letter. `'A'` is a
different way to write the number 65, and a person can read it more easily.
You can use one in place of the other: `letter == 65` is true.

**`@sizeOf` gave the number of bytes that each type uses.** A `u8` is one
byte, and a `u32` is four bytes. The `Point` in the program is two bytes,
because it holds two `u8` fields next to each other. `@sizeOf` answers a
physical question: if you ask for a million of these values, how much memory
do you ask for?

**The `u32` that holds 1 printed as `1 0 0 0`.** The value has four bytes, and
the useful byte is first. This machine stores the smallest place value at the
lowest address. The name of this order is **little-endian**. The hardware
selected this order, and arithmetic does not need it. Most machines that you
will use have the same order.

The byte order is important in exactly two places, and you will see both much
later:

- when you read a file that a different program wrote
- when you send bytes across a network

**The last pair shows the same bytes read in two ways.** `0x41424344` printed
as the number 1094861636, and then as the letters `DCBA`. No conversion
occurred between those two lines. `@bitCast` copies no bytes and does no
arithmetic.

`@bitCast` tells the compiler: read the four bytes as four `u8` values, not as
one `u32`. The bytes did not move. Only the agreement changed.

(`0x41` is 65, the number for `A`. In memory, the first byte is `0x44`, the
number for `D`, because of the little-endian order above. Thus the letters
print in the reverse order.)

The figure shows the four bytes from the program, and reads them once as a
`u32` and once as four `u8` values.

*Figure: Four bytes in memory, 68, 67, 66, 65, read once as the u32 1094861636 and once as the letters DCBA. The bytes from the program above. The same four bytes give a number or four letters, and only the type decides which.*

## Check yourself

If `Point` held two `u32` fields instead of two `u8` fields, what would
`@sizeOf(Point)` print?

Eight. A struct is its fields, one after the other, and its size is the space
that the fields need. The size is not always exactly the sum. The [memory
layout](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/memory-layout/) recipe gives the reasons. But at the
start, the sum is a good model.

## If you know C

In C, a programmer uses a union or a pointer cast to do the work of
`@bitCast`:

```c
uint32_t n = 0x41424344;
char *letters = (char *)&n;      /* the same four bytes, read as chars */
```

The C version uses a pointer. The C version lets you read five bytes, or read
four bytes that do not exist. `@bitCast` makes sure at compile time that the
source and the destination have the same size. Thus a `@bitCast` from a `u32`
to a `[5]u8` does not compile.

You will see this pattern frequently. Zig lets you do the same operation, but
Zig stops the mistake that usually comes with the operation.

Next: [Numbers Have a Size](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/numbers-have-a-size/),
which asks the same question about arithmetic.

---

## Numbers Have a Size

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/numbers-have-a-size/*

In Python or JavaScript, a number is only a number. You add one to the number
and you get one more. You can do that again and again, with no limit.

At the level of the machine, a number is a fixed number of bytes. A fixed
number of bytes can hold only a fixed number of different patterns. One byte
has 256 patterns. No person selected this limit. The limit comes from a simple
count: eight switches have 256 possible settings, and no 257th setting.

Thus a `u8` counts from 0 to 255. What occurs after 255?

A language can do one of three things, and many well-known bugs come from the
difference between them:

- The value wraps to 0.
- The program stops.
- The operation reports that the result did not fit, and lets you decide.

Zig makes you write which one you want.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // The name gives the size. A u8 is an unsigned 8-bit integer. Thus a u8
    // can hold 256 patterns and no more.
    try out.print("u8  counts {d} to {d}\n", .{ std.math.minInt(u8), std.math.maxInt(u8) });
    try out.print("i8  counts {d} to {d}\n", .{ std.math.minInt(i8), std.math.maxInt(i8) });
    try out.print("u32 counts {d} to {d}\n\n", .{ std.math.minInt(u32), std.math.maxInt(u32) });

    const top: u8 = 255;

    // One way past the top: use a different operator that wraps. The answer
    // is 0, and 0 is the answer that you asked for.
    try out.print("255 +% 1 = {d}\n", .{top +% 1});

    // A second way: ask for an answer that can be absent. Then handle the
    // case where the answer is absent.
    if (std.math.add(u8, top, 1)) |sum| {
        try out.print("255 + 1 = {d}\n\n", .{sum});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("255 + 1 = {t}\n\n", .{err});
    }

    // The size that you select decides the memory for a million values.
    try out.print("a million u8  = {d} bytes\n", .{1_000_000 * @sizeOf(u8)});
    try out.print("a million u32 = {d} bytes\n", .{1_000_000 * @sizeOf(u32)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.numbers-have-a-size`)*

## What just happened

**The names describe the storage.** `u8` is an **u**nsigned **8**-bit
integer: eight switches, no sign, thus 0 to 255. `i8` has the same eight
switches, but it uses one pattern for the sign. Thus `i8` goes up only to 127,
but it goes down to -128. `u32` has thirty-two switches, thus it counts past
four billion.

After you see a few of these names, you can read the range directly from the
name. Zig also has `u1` to `u65535`, if you need an unusual size.

**`255 +% 1` gave 0.** The value wrapped. This result is not a bug, because
`+%` is a different operator from `+`. With the `%`, you tell the compiler: "I
know that this can overflow, and I want the value to wrap". Hash functions and
checksums need exactly this behaviour.

**`std.math.add` returned `Overflow` instead of a number.** The return type of
`std.math.add` says that the answer can be absent. Thus the program must
handle both cases before it can use the result. You cannot read a sum by
accident when the sum does not exist.

## Check yourself

The program does not use a plain `+` on `top`. What would occur if it did?

The result would not be 0, and it would not be 256. `top` is a `const` with a
known value. Thus the compiler can do the addition, see that 256 does not fit
in a `u8`, and reject the program. You get a compile error, and the program
does not run.

Sometimes the numbers are known only when the program runs. Then the compiler
cannot decide before the program runs. The compiler adds a check that runs
with the program.

Some builds keep these checks. In those builds, an overflow stops the program
with a message that gives the line. [A different
chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/when-checks-are-off/) tells which builds
keep the checks. In short, the builds that you use during development keep
them.

## If you know C

This difference in behaviour between the two languages is large. Because of
this difference, this material is easier to learn in Zig.

```c
unsigned char x = 255;
x = x + 1;        /* x is now 0. No warning, no error, nothing. */

int y = 2147483647;
y = y + 1;        /* undefined behaviour: the compiler may assume it cannot happen */
```

The first line wraps, and gives no message. The second line is more dangerous.
In C, signed overflow is undefined behaviour. Thus an optimiser can assume
that signed overflow never occurs, and it can delete the check that you wrote
for it. A beginner can spend days on a bug like this, and many beginners
decide that they are bad programmers.

The C behaviours have these equivalents in Zig:

- The silent wrap of C is `+%` in Zig, and you must type the `%`.
- The undefined behaviour of C is a crash that you can see, in Debug and
  ReleaseSafe builds.

[Integer Rules](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/integer-rules/) gives the full rules,
and what changes in a release build.

Next: [Memory Is Numbered](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/memory-is-numbered/).
In that chapter, each value gets an address.

---

## Memory Is Numbered

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/memory-is-numbered/*

Memory is one long row of boxes, and each box holds one byte. The boxes have
numbers, in order from one end. The number of a box is its **address**.

Think of a street. Each house has a number, and the numbers are in order. If
you know the number, you can go to the house.

A house number is not a house. You can write a house number on a piece of
paper, and give the paper to a different person. That person can go to the
same house and paint the door. The paint goes on the real house, not on the
paper.

The piece of paper is a **pointer**. A pointer is a variable, and its value is
an address. All the other facts about pointers come from this fact.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var row = [_]u32{ 10, 20, 30, 40 };

    // @intFromPtr does no work. It shows the address as the number that it is.
    const first = @intFromPtr(&row[0]);
    try out.print("row[0] sits at address {d}\n\n", .{first});

    for (&row, 0..) |*slot, i| {
        const here = @intFromPtr(slot);
        try out.print(
            "row[{d}] = {d}, {d} bytes along from row[0]\n",
            .{ i, slot.*, here - first },
        );
    }
    try out.print("\n@sizeOf(u32) = {d}\n\n", .{@sizeOf(u32)});

    // A pointer holds one of these numbers and nothing else.
    const p: *u32 = &row[2];
    try out.print("a *u32 is {d} bytes wide\n", .{@sizeOf(*u32)});
    try out.print("this one holds {d}\n", .{@intFromPtr(p)});
    try out.print("reading through it gives {d}\n\n", .{p.*});

    // A write through the pointer changes that box in the row, not a copy.
    p.* = 99;
    try out.print("after p.* = 99, row[2] = {d}\n", .{row[2]});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.memory-is-numbered`)*

Your numbers will not be the same as the numbers below. They also change if
you press Run two times, or if you open this page tomorrow. This is correct.
The loader decides the position of a program in memory when the program loads,
not when you write the program. The **spacing** between the addresses does not
change.

## What just happened

**Four `u32` values printed at offsets 0, 4, 8 and 12.** The values are four
bytes apart, because a `u32` is four bytes wide. An array puts its elements
directly next to each other, with no gap. Thus the machine does not search for
`row[2]`. The machine calculates the address of `row[0]` plus two times four,
and goes directly to that address.

To find element 999,999 of a large array, the machine does the same arithmetic
as for element 0. Not all data structures have this property.

**`@intFromPtr` did nothing.** `@intFromPtr` does no work and makes no new
information. A pointer is already a number. With `@intFromPtr`, you tell Zig
that you want to see the pointer as a number. Zig makes you ask, because when
you can do arithmetic on an address, you can also make a mistake in that
arithmetic.

**The pointer was 4 bytes wide.** This page runs your program as 32-bit
WebAssembly. On that target, 4 bytes are sufficient to give a number to each
box. If you compile the same file for your laptop, the same line prints 8. A
pointer is exactly as wide as an address on the machine that runs the
program. The term "64-bit" describes this width.

**`p.* = 99` changed `row[2]`, not a copy of `row[2]`.** The pointer held the
address of that box. Thus a write through the pointer wrote to that box, and
the array shows the change. This write is the door that the other person
painted.

## Check yourself

If the array held `u8` values instead of `u32` values, what would the four
offsets be?

The offsets would be 0, 1, 2 and 3. Each box now holds one byte, thus the
boxes are one address apart. The addresses did not become smaller. The boxes
became smaller, thus more boxes fit into the same length of street.

## If you know C

The concept and the layout are the same, but the notation is different. C
writes the type as `int *p`, and reads through the pointer with a prefix `*p`.
Zig writes `*u32`, and reads through the pointer with a postfix `.*`. Thus Zig
code reads from left to right, as a field access does.

Two differences are important now:

- A Zig `*u32` can never be null. Thus you cannot forget a null check. When a
  pointer can be absent, its type says so. The compiler does not let you read
  the pointer before you unwrap it.
- Zig does not let you do arithmetic on a `*u32`. Pointer arithmetic without
  a length causes buffer overruns. In Zig, a pointer and a length go
  together, as a [slice](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/slices/).

[Pointers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/pointers/) gives the details at the level of
the language, which include the null question and the rules for constness.

Next: [The Stack](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/the-stack/). That chapter tells
who decides the addresses, and for how long the addresses stay valid.

---

## The Stack

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/the-stack/*

The last chapter said that each value has an address. This chapter answers the
next question: who decides the address, and for how long is the address valid?

For a local variable, the machine decides, and the method costs very little.
The machine keeps one number: the position where the used part of memory ends
now. A function call moves that mark forward, to make space for the local
variables of the call. A return moves the mark back. To make space costs one
addition, and to give the space back costs one subtraction. Thus you do not
have to plan for the cost of a function call.

The region that a call gets is its **frame**, and the sequence of frames is
the **stack**. A stack of plates is similar in one way only: the plate that
you put down last is the plate that you take first. A call cannot return
before the calls that it made return. Thus the program always releases the
frames in the reverse order.

This rule has a result, and a large group of bugs comes from it: **when the
call returns, that memory is not yours any more.** Nothing erases or marks the
memory. The mark only moves back, and the next call gets the same bytes.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

var main_local: usize = 0;
var outer_local: usize = 0;
var inner_local: usize = 0;
var outer_local_again: usize = 0;

fn inner() void {
    var value: u32 = 3;
    _ = &value; // keep the value in memory, not in a register
    inner_local = @intFromPtr(&value);
}

fn outer(record: *usize) void {
    var value: u32 = 2;
    _ = &value;
    record.* = @intFromPtr(&value);
    inner();
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var value: u32 = 1;
    _ = &value;
    main_local = @intFromPtr(&value);

    outer(&outer_local);

    // Each call gets its own region for its local variables. Three calls are
    // live at the same time here, and no two of them share a place.
    try out.print("main and outer used different addresses:  {}\n", .{main_local != outer_local});
    try out.print("outer and inner used different addresses: {}\n", .{inner_local != outer_local});

    // The direction of the regions depends on the target. The language has
    // no rule for the direction. Most machines count downward. This machine
    // does not, and nothing in the chapter depends on the answer.
    try out.print("deeper calls got higher addresses here:   {}\n", .{inner_local > main_local});

    // outer() returned, thus its region is free again.
    outer(&outer_local_again);
    try out.print("\nthe second call to outer reused the same address: {}\n", .{outer_local == outer_local_again});

    try out.print("\nso a pointer to outer's local, kept after it returned,\n", .{});
    try out.print("would now be pointing at the second call's data.\n", .{});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.the-stack`)*

## What just happened

**Three calls were live at the same time, and no two of them shared an
address.** `main` called `outer`, and `outer` called `inner`. Each call had a
local variable at a different place. Nothing controlled this. Each call only
moved the mark forward by the size of the space that the call needed.

**The direction that the program prints is not a rule.** On this target, the
frames go upward. On most machines that you will use, the frames go downward.
For this reason, many texts say "the stack grows down".

The direction is a detail of the target. The program cannot see the direction
unless it looks for it, and nothing above depends on the answer. The program
prints the direction because this target is different from the textbook.

**The second call to `outer` got the same address as the first call.** The
first call finished, and the mark moved back. The next call that needed that
much space got exactly the same bytes. The old values stayed there until the
new call wrote over them.

Thus, if a pointer to the local of `outer` stayed in use after the call, the
pointer would look correct. It would point at real memory that the program can
read. But that memory now belongs to a different call. A read through the
pointer would give a number that had a meaning before. A write through the
pointer would corrupt the call that now uses that frame.

The name of this pointer is a **dangling pointer**. The pointer did not
change. The pointer is a number, and the number is still valid. The owner of
the memory changed, and a number cannot hold the owner.

## Check yourself

Think of a second local variable in `outer`, for example `var other: u32 = 9;`
next to `value`. Would `other` be at a higher address or a lower address than
`value`?

Each guess is acceptable, because the correct answer is that **you cannot
know**. The compiler can arrange a frame in any order. If the compiler can
keep a value in a register, the value possibly gets no address at all. For
this reason, the program above has `_ = &value;` next to each local. When the
program takes the address, the value must be in memory, and the program has an
address to print. Without that line, an optimised build could make the
question have no meaning.

## If you know C

C works in the same way, and you can write the same bug:

```c
int *broken(void) {
    int x = 42;
    return &x;      /* returns a pointer into a frame that is about to end */
}
```

C compilers usually give a warning for that exact code. Zig rejects the code
with an error: `error: returning address of expired local variable`.

Neither language finds the same bug in a less obvious form. For example, the
code can store the address in a struct field and return the struct. Nothing
checks this case, thus you must be careful. The
[Pointers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/pointers/) chapter says this directly. A
slice of a local array must not stay in use after the array ends, and the
compiler will not tell you.

Instead, Zig gives you [`defer`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/defer/) and the
ownership rules in the next chapter. With these two tools, you answer the
question "who owns this, and how long does it live" one time, in a function
signature. You do not answer it in each caller.

Next: [Who Owns This
Memory](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/who-owns-this-memory/). That chapter is
about memory that must stay valid after the call returns.

---

## Who Owns This Memory

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/who-owns-this-memory/*

A frame ends when the call returns. What do you do when the answer must stay
valid after the call that calculated it?

You ask for memory that does not belong to a frame. A second pool of memory
exists for this purpose. Its usual name is the **heap**, and its rules are
different:

- Frame memory costs nothing, is automatic, and has a short life.
- Heap memory needs a request. It stays valid until the program gives it
  back. If the program never gives it back, the program holds the memory
  until the program exits. The name for this problem is a **leak**.

Thus some part of the program must give the memory back. Memory management is
the answer to one question: **who owns this memory, and when does the owner
release it?** Each method that you know is an answer to this question:

- A garbage collector answers "nobody, the runtime decides later".
- Rust answers "the compiler tracks it".
- C answers "you do, and nothing helps you".
- Zig answers "you do, and the type signature shows it".

The last part makes Zig different. In Zig, **a function that allocates takes
an allocator as an argument**. Zig has no global `malloc` that a function can
use. Thus a function that needs memory cannot hide the request. The allocator
is in the signature, and you can see it at each call site. A function without
that parameter cannot allocate without your knowledge.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Fills a buffer from the caller. This function allocates nothing. Thus the
/// function owns nothing, and the caller has nothing to release.
fn writeGreeting(into: []u8, name: []const u8) []u8 {
    return std.mem.print(into, "hello, {s}", .{name}) catch into[0..0];
}

/// Returns memory of its own. The doc comment holds the rule: the caller owns
/// the result, and must free it with the same allocator.
fn makeGreeting(allocator: std.mem.Allocator, name: []const u8) ![]u8 {
    return allocator.print("hello, {s}", .{name});
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // This memory is in the frame of this call, and it ends when main
    // returns. For the same reason, the function above cannot return memory
    // from its own frame.
    var scratch: [64]u8 = undefined;
    try out.print("{s}\n", .{writeGreeting(&scratch, "stack")});

    // This memory needs a request. Nothing in Zig allocates without an
    // allocator argument. Thus each place that can allocate says so.
    var safe: std.heap.SafeAllocator = .init(std.heap.page_allocator, .{});
    const allocator = safe.allocator();

    {
        const greeting = try makeGreeting(allocator, "heap");
        defer allocator.free(greeting); // runs at the end of this block
        try out.print("{s}\n", .{greeting});
    }

    // deinit answers one question: how many allocations did the program not free?
    try out.print("allocations never freed: {d}\n\n", .{safe.deinit()});

    // The same program without the `defer`. At the end, the program asks the
    // allocator if the program freed all its memory, and the allocator answers.
    var leaky: std.heap.SafeAllocator = .init(std.heap.page_allocator, .{});
    {
        const greeting = try makeGreeting(leaky.allocator(), "forgotten");
        try out.print("{s}\n", .{greeting});
    }
    try out.print("allocations never freed: {d}\n", .{leaky.deinit()});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.who-owns-this-memory`)*

## What just happened

**The first function allocated nothing.** `writeGreeting` takes a buffer from
the caller and writes into the buffer. The function owns nothing. Thus it has
nothing to release, and it cannot leak. Use this method more frequently than
a beginner in systems programming expects. Many jobs look as if they need the
heap, but they only need the caller to supply the space.

**The second function returns memory that it asked for.** `makeGreeting`
takes an `std.mem.Allocator` and returns a slice from that allocator. The
caller now owns the slice. The type system does not make this rule true. Thus
the rule is in the place where the reader looks: the doc comment on the
function.

**`defer` gives the memory back.** Put `defer allocator.free(greeting);` on
the line after the allocation. Then the release occurs when the block ends,
in all the ways that the block can end. The two lines are next to each other,
thus you can see the pair at one time. The other method is a cleanup section
at the bottom of the function, and a hope that each path gets to it.

**The allocator answered the question at the end.** `SafeAllocator` records
the memory that it gave out. A call to `deinit` reports how many allocations
the program did not free. The count is 0 the first time. The count is 1 in the
block that has no `defer`.

`deinit` also writes a description of the leaked block to standard error. For
this reason, use this allocator during development.

This report is the reason to learn ownership in Zig and not in C. You do not
find a leak in production three months later, when a server fails. The leak is
a number that the program prints before it exits. In tests, a leak makes the
build fail: `std.testing.allocator` fails each test that leaks.

## Check yourself

In the block that leaks, why does an earlier call to `deinit` not help?

`deinit` does not free the allocation. `deinit` is the audit. The function
that frees memory is `allocator.free`, and the block never calls it. An
earlier call to `deinit` would ask the question earlier and get the same
answer. The allocator would also be unusable for the code after the call.

The correct repair is to add the `defer`. The report tells you that the code
broke a rule. The report does not tell you the correct repair.

## If you know C

The two languages are almost the same here, but they are different in one
place:

```c
char *greeting = malloc(32);   /* where did this memory come from? */
if (!greeting) return NULL;    /* and who checks? */
/* ... */
free(greeting);                /* and who remembers, on every path out? */
```

The Zig `allocator.alloc` is `malloc`, but the call site names the source of
the memory. The failure is in the return type. Thus `try` handles the failure,
and you cannot forget the null check, because no null exists. Also, `defer`
puts the `free` next to the `alloc`, not at each exit from the function. Thus
the usual C ladder of `goto cleanup` labels is not necessary.

[Allocators](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/allocators/) tells about the other
allocators in Zig:

- arenas that free all their memory at one time
- fixed buffers that never use the heap
- the allocator above, which finds leaks

Next: [Off the End](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/off-the-end/). That chapter
tells what occurs when you read memory that you own, but not the part that you
wanted.

---

## Off the End

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/off-the-end/*

An array of four numbers uses a length of memory, and that length has an end.
What is at the address immediately after the end? Something is always there: a
different variable, part of a frame, or the internal parts of the program.
Memory continues after the end of your array. Only your right to use the
memory stops there.

Thus what must `row[4]` do?

Only three answers are possible, and each language selects one:

- Read the value that is there, and continue.
- Stop the program.
- Refuse the request, and make the caller check first.

The third answer needs nothing from the language except an `if`. Thus the
program starts with the third answer.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const builtin = @import("builtin");

/// Reads an element, and does not assume that the caller checked first.
fn at(numbers: []const u32, index: usize) !u32 {
    if (index >= numbers.len) return error.OutOfBounds;
    return numbers[index];
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const row = [_]u32{ 10, 20, 30, 40 };

    // A slice is a pointer and a length together. Thus a function that
    // receives a slice always knows where the data stops.
    const slice: []const u32 = &row;
    try out.print("the slice has {d} elements\n", .{slice.len});
    try out.print("a slice is {d} bytes: a pointer and a length\n\n", .{@sizeOf([]const u32)});

    // Valid index.
    if (at(slice, 2)) |value| {
        try out.print("element 2 is {d}\n", .{value});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("element 2: {t}\n", .{err});
    }

    // One past the end. The function reads nothing, and tells the caller.
    if (at(slice, 4)) |value| {
        try out.print("element 4 is {d}\n", .{value});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("element 4: {t}\n", .{err});
    }

    // For `slice[i]`, the language adds this comparison. The build decides
    // if the comparison is present.
    try out.print("\nsafety checks in this build: {}\n", .{builtin.optimize.runtimeSafety()});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.off-the-end`)*

## What just happened

**The slice knew where it ended.** A slice is a pointer and a length that go
together as one value. Thus a function that receives a slice always knows the
size. For this reason, `[]const u32` is the usual way to pass a sequence, and
a bare pointer is not. The pointer alone tells the function where the data
starts, but not where to stop.

**The slice printed as 8 bytes.** The pointer uses four bytes and the length
uses four bytes, on this 32-bit WebAssembly build. If you compile the program
for your own machine, it prints 16. The reason is the same reason that a
pointer on your machine is 8 bytes and not 4.

**The checked read returned an error instead of a number.** `at` compares the
index with `.len`. When the index is too large, `at` returns
`error.OutOfBounds`. The function read nothing.

The return type told the caller that the answer can be absent. Thus the caller
had to handle both cases before it could use the result. All of this cost one
comparison.

**Then the last line said `safety checks in this build: false`.**

## About the last line

When you write `slice[i]` directly, Zig adds the same comparison for you. If
the comparison fails, the program stops with a message that gives the index
and the length. Debug and ReleaseSafe builds have this check. ReleaseFast and
ReleaseSmall builds do not have it. In those builds, the compiler removes the
check for speed and size.

The wasm that you ran is a ReleaseSmall build, because the site sends
ReleaseSmall builds to the browser of the reader. Thus on this page,
`slice[4]` would not stop the program. It would read four bytes that are not
yours, and give them to you as a number.

The program below does that read. This program is the exception on this site.
Its build is ReleaseSafe and not ReleaseSmall. Thus the check is present, and
the program must stop. Press **Run**.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    _ = init;

    const row = [_]u32{ 10, 20, 30, 40 };
    const slice: []const u32 = &row;

    // `index` is a `var`, and the compiler cannot fold its value. Thus the
    // compiler does not reject this line. The compiler cannot know the index.
    // Thus the check that stops the read runs when the program runs.
    var index: usize = 4;
    _ = &index;

    std.debug.print("value: {d}\n", .{slice[index]});
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.past-the-end`)*

```
panic: index out of bounds: index 4, len 4
```

The program read nothing. The program gave the index that it got and the
length that it had permission to use. Then it stopped on the line that asked.
Compare this result with the silent wrong answer of the ReleaseSmall build
above. The mistake is the same. The only difference is if the build contains
the check.

The run also says that it cannot print a stack trace, because debug info is
not available for this target. The wasm that your browser gets has no symbols.
Thus the runtime cannot change a return address into a file and a line. On
your own machine, the same panic shows the sequence of calls that caused it.

The message above is not from memory. The build for this site runs this
program on each change, and the program must stop with exactly that text. If a
future version of Zig changes the words of the panic, this page will not
publish. Thus the page cannot teach you a message that you will never see.

This snippet is about 1.1 MB, and the program at the top of this page is 46
KB. The difference is the cost of the safety checks and of the code that
describes them. For this reason, the other snippets on the site do not have
the checks. Your browser downloads this snippet only when you press Run.

[When the Checks Are Off](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/when-checks-are-off/)
gives the general rule: what each build mode turns off, and what you promise
when you select a build mode.

## Check yourself

The program checks `index >= numbers.len`. Why does it not check
`index > numbers.len`?

The indexes of four elements are 0, 1, 2 and 3. Index 4 is the first index
after the end, thus the program must reject index 4. A mistake of one at
exactly this boundary is frequent, and it has a name: the fencepost error. For
this reason, use `for (slice) |item|` instead of an index and a counter when
you do not need the number.

## If you know C

You will see this difference early.

```c
int row[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
int x = row[4];        /* reads something. no error, no warning, no crash */
```

A C array does not hold a length. Thus a function that receives `int *row`
cannot check anything. The code must pass the length as a separate value, and
the programmer must keep the length correct. A read past the end is undefined
behaviour. In practice, the read usually works, sometimes returns a value that
has no meaning, and sometimes corrupts memory. That corruption can cause a
failure much later, in an unrelated part of the program.

Zig has two answers to this problem:

- The slice holds the length. Thus the length always agrees with the data.
- The safety check changes "usually works" into a message with a line number.

Because of these two answers, you can learn this material. You see the mistake
at the time that you make it, not an hour later.

Zig still has the C pointer without a length, for code that calls C. Zig gives
it a different syntax on purpose: [many-item
pointers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/many-item-pointers/).

Next: [When the Checks Are
Off](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/when-checks-are-off/). That chapter tells
what you promise when you turn a check off.

---

## When the Checks Are Off

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/when-checks-are-off/*

The last chapter ended on a difficult fact: the program that you ran said that
its safety checks were absent. The reason for this absence is the difference
between systems programming and all the levels above it.

A high-level language answers each question. If you read past the end of a
list, Python raises `IndexError`. Python does this always, on each machine, in
each configuration. This guarantee has a cost, and you pay the cost when you
need the guarantee and when you do not.

A systems language does not answer some questions, on purpose. This does not
mean "answered in a way that you cannot predict". It means **not answered**.
The specification says: if your program does this thing, the language makes no
promise about what occurs next. The name for this is **undefined behaviour**.

Undefined behaviour is not a special word for "crash" or for "garbage value".
It is neither of these.

Think of undefined behaviour as a promise that you made. When the language
leaves integer overflow undefined, the language tells the compiler to assume
that overflow never occurs. The compiler uses that assumption, because the
assumption makes the generated code fast. The compiler can delete a check that
you wrote, because your check can be true only in a situation that you
promised would not occur.

Thus undefined behaviour is worse than a wrong answer. A wrong answer stays in
one place. A broken promise can change code in a different place.

Zig uses this method: **the checks exist, and for each build you decide if you
pay for them.**

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const builtin = @import("builtin");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // Each program can see its build mode.
    try out.print("build mode: {t}\n", .{builtin.optimize});
    try out.print("safety checks present: {}\n\n", .{builtin.optimize.runtimeSafety()});

    var a: u8 = 200;
    var b: u8 = 100;
    _ = &a;
    _ = &b;

    // Four ways to say what must occur when 300 does not fit in a u8. None of
    // them change with the build mode, because none of them use a check that
    // a release build can remove.

    // 1. Wrap, on purpose.
    try out.print("a +% b            = {d}\n", .{a +% b});

    // 2. Refuse, with an error that the caller must handle.
    if (std.math.add(u8, a, b)) |sum| {
        try out.print("std.math.add      = {d}\n", .{sum});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("std.math.add      = {t}\n", .{err});
    }

    // 3. Give the answer and a flag, with no error to handle.
    const result = @addWithOverflow(a, b);
    try out.print("@addWithOverflow  = {d}, overflowed: {d}\n", .{ result[0], result[1] });

    // 4. Saturate at the limit.
    try out.print("a +| b            = {d}\n", .{a +| b});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.when-checks-are-off`)*

## What just happened

**The program read its own build mode.** Each Zig program can use
`builtin.optimize`. `builtin.optimize.runtimeSafety()` asks the direct
question: does this build have the checks? Print these two values as a habit.
Almost all bugs of the type "why is it different on the server" has this
cause.

The four modes, and the promise of each mode:

- **Debug**: all the safety checks are present, and there is no optimisation.
  Debug is the default for `zig run` and `zig build`. Thus you use Debug for
  all of your daily work. Overflow, out-of-bounds access, invalid casts and
  the other checked errors stop the program with a message and a line number.
- **ReleaseSafe**: the compiler optimises the build, and the safety checks
  stay. Use
  this mode for most server software. The checks have a cost, but the
  cost is small. A program that stops with a clear message is better than a
  program that continues with corrupt state.
- **ReleaseFast**: the compiler optimises the build and removes the checks.
  You promise that none of the checked situations occur.
- **ReleaseSmall**: the compiler optimises the build for size and removes
  the checks. The promise is the same.

The snippets on this site are ReleaseSmall builds, because each reader
downloads them. For that reason, the output above says `small` and `false`.

**The four operators gave the same result in each mode.** `+%`,
`std.math.add`, `@addWithOverflow` and `+|` behave the same in all four
modes. Each of them states in the source what must occur when the value does
not fit. They do not use a check that a release build can remove. When
overflow is important, write in the source what you want. Then the build mode
does not change the answer.

## The one that depends on the build

The program below adds the same two values as the four lines above, with a
plain `+`. It is the one snippet on this page that is a ReleaseSafe build and
not a ReleaseSmall build. Thus the check is still in it. Press **Run**.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    _ = init;

    var a: u8 = 200;
    var b: u8 = 100;
    _ = &a;
    _ = &b;

    // 300 does not fit in a u8. In this build, the check runs and the program
    // stops here. ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall have no check, and the value is
    // undefined. The value does not always wrap.
    const sum = a + b;

    std.debug.print("sum: {d}\n", .{sum});
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.the-one-that-depends`)*

```
panic: integer overflow
```

Compare this result with the four operators above. Each of those operators
answered the question in the source. Thus each operator behaves the same in
all four modes. The plain `+` asked the build mode for the answer. Thus the
answer depends on the build:

| Build | `a + b` where the sum does not fit |
| --- | --- |
| Debug | stops, with the message above |
| ReleaseSafe | stops, with the message above |
| ReleaseFast | undefined |
| ReleaseSmall | undefined |

The last two rows do **not** say "wraps". The value can wrap on your machine
today. Code that depends on that wrap is exactly the broken promise at the top
of this page. If you want the value to wrap, use `+%`. The `+%` operator costs
nothing.

This page shows you the panic, but it cannot show you the other half, and
there is a reason.

In a safety build, the behaviour is defined. Thus the build for this site runs
this program on each change, and the program must stop with that exact
message. In a release build, no answer is defined. Thus no correct result
exists to compare with.

A guide could print the output of its compiler on that day, and call that
output the result. That guide would teach you to trust the thing that this
chapter warns you about.

## Check yourself

ReleaseSafe keeps the checks, and the compiler optimises it. Then why does a
programmer ship ReleaseFast?

The checks do not always cost little in the place where speed is important. A
bounds check inside a loop that runs a billion times per frame has a cost that
you can measure. In some programs, that speed is the most important thing.

The decision is for each program, and sometimes for each function. For this
reason, Zig lets you turn safety off for one block with
`@setRuntimeSafety(false)`. You do not have to select all or nothing for the
full binary. Start in ReleaseSafe, and make a change only where you measured
the cost.

## If you know C

Undefined behaviour is the same idea in C, and C has much more of it:

- signed overflow
- a read of an uninitialised variable
- a read through a null pointer
- most pointer arithmetic that goes outside an object
- strict-aliasing violations
- about two hundred more

By default, C checks almost none of these. For this reason, sanitiser tools
exist, and `-fsanitize=undefined` finds problems in code that worked for ten
years.

Zig is different in three places:

- The default build mode has the checks on. Thus you see the mistake the
  first time that you run the code. You do not have to know about a special
  flag and add it later.
- Where C leaves a common operation undefined, Zig usually gives a different
  syntax for each intent. The four operators above are an example.
- You must write an uninitialised variable as `= undefined`. Thus you can
  search for each one with grep.

[Runtime Safety](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/runtime-safety/) gives the list for
Zig: what Zig checks, and what each check finds. [Integer
Rules](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/integer-rules/) gives the integer rules in
detail.

Next: [Strings Are Bytes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/strings-are-bytes/). In
that chapter, the bytes from chapter one become text.
