## Strings Are Bytes

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/strings-are-bytes/*

Chapter one said that everything is bytes. With text, that fact starts to have
a cost.

In the language that you know, a string is a thing. A string knows its length,
and you can compare two strings with `==`. When you ask for the length, you
get the number of letters that you count with your eyes. A different person
made all of that for you. In Zig, nobody made it.

Zig has only a sequence of bytes. Thus Zig has the same question that C had to
answer first. If you get the address of some text, **how do you know where the
text ends?**

C put a zero byte after the last character. This method costs little: one byte
for each string, and a pointer is all that you must pass. But to find the
length, the code must read all the text and look for the zero. If the zero is
not there, the read does not stop at the end of the text.

Zig keeps the zero for code that calls C, but Zig does not depend on it.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const greeting = "hello";

    // The type shows all that the memory stores: a pointer to five bytes, and
    // a zero after them. The length does not count the zero.
    try out.print("\"hello\" is a {s}\n", .{@typeName(@TypeOf(greeting))});
    try out.print("greeting.len       = {d}\n", .{greeting.len});
    try out.print("the array occupies = {d} bytes\n\n", .{@sizeOf(@TypeOf(greeting.*))});

    // An index gives a number, because the memory stores only a number.
    try out.print("greeting[0] = {d}, which prints as '{c}'\n\n", .{ greeting[0], greeting[0] });

    // Two separate literals with the same contents. Zig does not allow `==`
    // on slices. std.mem.eql compares the contents.
    const a: []const u8 = "cat";
    const b: []const u8 = "cat";
    try out.print("std.mem.eql(a, b) = {}\n\n", .{std.mem.eql(u8, a, b)});

    // A length in bytes is not a count of characters. On this string, you can
    // see the difference.
    const word = "héllo";
    try out.print("\"héllo\".len = {d} bytes\n", .{word.len});
    try out.print("codepoints  = {d}\n", .{try std.unicode.utf8CountCodepoints(word)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.strings-are-bytes`)*

## What just happened

**The type printed as `*const [5:0]u8`.** Read it as: a pointer to an array of
5 bytes, with a sentinel `0` after them. The type does not say "a string".
The type describes a specific number of specific bytes at a specific place.

**`.len` was 5, and the array was 6 bytes.** The terminator is really there,
and it uses memory, but the length does not count it, on purpose. Thus Zig
knows the length without a search. Zig can also give the pointer to a C
function that expects the zero. You get both answers to the question above,
and you do not have to select one.

**The index gave 104, not `'h'`.** The two are the same byte. The memory
stores `104`, and `'h'` is a way to print it. This fact is the point of
chapter one again, in a place where it is important.

**The comparison needed `std.mem.eql`.** Zig does not let you write `a == b`
on two slices. The compiler rejects it: `operator == not allowed for type
'[]const u8'`. You can compare two pointers with `==`, and the answer tells
you if they point at the same place. That question is valid, but it is not
the question that you wanted to ask. If you know a managed language, make
this a firm habit: **compare contents with `std.mem.eql`.**

**`"héllo".len` was 6 for five letters.** UTF-8 uses one byte for each ASCII
letter, and two to four bytes for each other character. Thus `é` uses two
bytes. A count of bytes and a count of characters are different questions,
with different answers. `.len` answers the question about bytes, because the
machine can answer that question without an inspection of the bytes.

## Check yourself

You have a `[]const u8`, and you want its third character. What is the problem
with `text[2]`?

If the text is ASCII, there is no problem. If the text can contain other
characters, `text[2]` is the third *byte*. That byte can be the middle of a
two-byte character, and then you get half of the character.

The correct method is to iterate over the codepoints with
`std.unicode.Utf8View`. [Unicode](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/unicode/) tells
about this method. But usually, you do not want the character at an index. You
want to search, split or compare, and all of these operations work on bytes.

## If you know C

You already know the terminator and its cost:

```c
char *name = "hello";
strlen(name);            /* walks the string every time you ask */
if (name == "hello")     /* compares pointers, and compiles without complaint */
strcpy(dest, name);      /* writes until the zero, wherever that turns out to be */
```

The `strcpy` line caused real damage. `strcpy` trusts a terminator that it
cannot check. If the terminator is not there, `strcpy` continues to write.

A Zig slice holds the length next to the pointer. Thus functions do not have
to trust anything. `[:0]const u8` is the type for the case where a C function
also needs the zero. [Sentinel
Termination](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/sentinel-termination/) gives the full set
of types, and how to get a C string back into Zig.

Next: [Structs Are Layout](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/structs-are-layout/).
That chapter tells what occurs when you put several values together.

---

## Structs Are Layout

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/structs-are-layout/*

When you put some values together under one name, you get a struct. In a
managed language, that is all. At the level of the machine, there is a second
part: the values must go to a place in memory, in some order. The machine has
a preference about the place.

The name of that preference is **alignment**. A processor reads memory in
blocks. If a four-byte number starts at an address that is divisible by four,
the processor can read the number in one operation. If the number goes across
the boundary, the processor needs two reads and some extra instructions. On
some processors, that read is not permitted. Thus the rule for a number is:
the number starts at an address that is divisible by its own size.

Apply that rule to a struct with fields of different sizes, and the result can
be a surprise: **the struct is larger than its fields**. The name of the gaps
that keep each field aligned is **padding**. You pay for the padding when you
know about it and when you do not.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// `extern` gives the layout of C: the fields are in the order of the source.
// Padding makes each field start at an address that the machine prefers for
// its type. Learn this layout first, because other languages and file formats
// use it.
const Row = extern struct {
    flag: u8,
    count: u32,
    tag: u8,
};

// The same three fields, largest first.
const Packed = extern struct {
    count: u32,
    flag: u8,
    tag: u8,
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    try out.print("the fields hold {d} bytes of data\n", .{@sizeOf(u8) + @sizeOf(u32) + @sizeOf(u8)});
    try out.print("but @sizeOf(Row) = {d}\n\n", .{@sizeOf(Row)});

    // The start and the size of each field. The gaps are the padding.
    try out.print("flag  starts at byte {d}, size {d}\n", .{ @offsetOf(Row, "flag"), @sizeOf(u8) });
    try out.print("count starts at byte {d}, size {d}\n", .{ @offsetOf(Row, "count"), @sizeOf(u32) });
    try out.print("tag   starts at byte {d}, size {d}\n\n", .{ @offsetOf(Row, "tag"), @sizeOf(u8) });

    // Only the order of the fields changed.
    try out.print("same fields, largest first: {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(Packed)});
    try out.print("count starts at byte {d}, size {d}\n", .{ @offsetOf(Packed, "count"), @sizeOf(u32) });
    try out.print("flag  starts at byte {d}, size {d}\n", .{ @offsetOf(Packed, "flag"), @sizeOf(u8) });
    try out.print("tag   starts at byte {d}, size {d}\n\n", .{ @offsetOf(Packed, "tag"), @sizeOf(u8) });

    // Without `extern`, Zig can put the fields in any order. Zig usually
    // selects the smaller layout.
    const Auto = struct { flag: u8, count: u32, tag: u8 };
    try out.print("Zig's own layout for them:  {d} bytes\n", .{@sizeOf(Auto)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.structs-are-layout`)*

## What just happened

**Six bytes of data used twelve bytes.** The fields are `u8`, `u32` and `u8`.
The offsets show the reason: `flag` at 0, `count` at **4**, `tag` at 8.
`count` could not start at byte 1, because 1 is not divisible by 4. Thus
three bytes are not used.

Then the compiler adds padding at the end, and the struct becomes 12 bytes.
Thus in an array of these structs, each `count` is also aligned.

**The same fields, with the largest first, used eight bytes.** The struct lost
no fields. `count` is at 0, `flag` at 4, `tag` at 5, and two bytes of padding
are at the end.

The order of the fields decides the size. In C, you alone must get the order
correct. Four bytes on one struct are not important. Four bytes on ten million
rows are 40 MB.

The figure places the fields one at a time, at the offsets that the program
printed. Select an order to compare the two layouts at the same step.

*Figure: The struct with flag, count and tag in 12 bytes. In the declared order it uses 12 bytes with padding; largest first it uses 8. The offsets and sizes the program above prints. Select an order and step through the fields. The steps have the same names, thus you can switch at any step.*

**The layout that Zig selected also used eight bytes.** Here Zig is different
from C. A plain `struct` in Zig has **no guaranteed layout**. The compiler can
put the fields in any order, and it usually packs them for you. With `extern
struct`, you ask for the rules of C. Use `extern struct` when the layout must
agree with something outside your program: a C library, a file format, or a
network packet. Inside your own program, let the compiler decide.

## Check yourself

If you add a `u64` field to `Packed`, what will `@sizeOf` become?

16. The `u64` needs an address that is divisible by 8. `count` uses four
bytes, and `flag` and `tag` use two more, thus 6 bytes are already used. Thus
the `u64` starts at 8 and ends at 16. The alignment of the struct also becomes
8, because a struct takes the alignment of its field with the largest
alignment. This rule makes arrays of the struct work. One 8-byte field added
to an 8-byte struct cost 8 bytes. This result is the usual case, not a
surprise.

## If you know C

The rules, the padding and the arithmetic are the same. The two languages have
two differences.

First, C guarantees the order of the declarations. Thus you can find the
layout of a struct from its source, and you can trust that layout. Zig gives
that guarantee only for `extern struct` and `packed struct`. For a plain
struct, the compiler decides.

This default is better, because most structs never go outside your program.
When the compiler packs them, you get better performance at no cost. The
default is wrong in exactly one place: at a boundary with C, if you assume the
C layout. Use `extern struct` there, and the two languages agree.

Second, C gives you `offsetof` from `<stddef.h>`. In Zig, `@offsetOf` is a
builtin, and it needs no include. The program above used `@offsetOf` to show
the gaps. Thus you do not have to trust a statement about them.

The [memory layout](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/memory-layout/) recipe tells about the other
layout controls: `align`, `packed struct` for bit fields, and the C ABI in
detail.

Next: [Errors Are Values](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/errors-are-values/).
That chapter is about what a function returns when it cannot do the work that
you asked for.

---

## Errors Are Values

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/errors-are-values/*

In a higher-level language, a failure has a place to go. You raise or throw an
exception. Then code that you did not write unwinds the calls between your
code and the code that can handle the failure. This method works because a
runtime monitors the program.

In Zig, nothing monitors the program. No runtime is under your program to
catch anything, and the machine does not know what an exception is. Thus a
failure must move in the same way as each other result: as a value, in the
return.

Then one question decides if the language is easy to use: **what stops the
caller when it ignores the failure?**

The answer decides if the errors of a language work in practice. If code that
ignores a failure is shorter than code that handles it, programmers ignore it.
Then the program continues with a number that means "this did not occur".

Zig puts the failure in the **type**. A function that can fail does not return
a `u16`. It returns "a `u16` or an error", and these are different types. You
cannot use the `u16` before you say what occurs in the error case. Until you
do, you do not have a `u16`.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The return type says two things: on success a u16, on failure one of a
/// known set of errors. A caller can see both, and does not have to read the
/// body.
fn parsePort(text: []const u8) !u16 {
    const value = try std.fmt.parseInt(u16, text, 10);
    if (value < 1024) return error.ReservedPort;
    return value;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const inputs = [_][]const u8{ "8080", "http", "99999", "80" };

    for (inputs) |text| {
        // `if` on a call that can fail separates the two cases. Neither branch
        // can see the value of the other branch. Thus you cannot read a result
        // that the function did not make.
        if (parsePort(text)) |port| {
            try out.print("{s: <6} -> port {d}\n", .{ text, port });
        } else |err| {
            // An error is an ordinary value. You can compare it, use it in a
            // switch, and pass it to other code, as any other value. This
            // switch has no `else` prong, because no other error can occur.
            // The compiler found the full set of errors that parsePort can
            // return. The compiler rejects an `else` prong as unreachable.
            const reason = switch (err) {
                error.InvalidCharacter => "not a number",
                error.Overflow => "too large for a u16",
                error.ReservedPort => "below 1024, needs privileges",
            };
            try out.print("{s: <6} -> {t}: {s}\n", .{ text, err, reason });
        }
    }

    // When a default is the correct answer, say so in one word. Do not write
    // a branch that only looks as if it handles the error.
    const port = parsePort("nonsense") catch 8080;
    try out.print("\nfalling back: {d}\n", .{port});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.errors-are-values`)*

## What just happened

**The return type is `!u16`.** The `!` means "a `u16` or an error". The
caller receives one value in one of two states. The language does not let you
use the value as a number until you handle the other state.

**`if` separated the two states.** `if (parsePort(text)) |port| ... else
|err|` gives a `port` to the success branch and an `err` to the failure
branch. Neither branch can see the value of the other branch. At no time does
a variable hold a result that the function did not make.

**`try` is the short way to pass the error to the caller.** Inside
`parsePort`, the line `try std.fmt.parseInt(...)` means: if that call failed,
return its error to my caller, and if not, give me the number. The usual case
needs only three letters. Nothing unwinds, and nothing searches. The failure
path is an ordinary return.

**The errors were values.** A `switch (err)` on them works as a switch on any
other value. Also, the switch has **no `else` prong**. The compiler found
without help that `parsePort` can return exactly three errors. Thus the
compiler rejected an `else` prong as unreachable code.

You can later change the function so that it can fail in a fourth way. Then
each switch like this one does not compile until you update it. The compiler
checks the set of failures. You do not have to keep a list of them in a
comment.

**`catch 8080` handled the error in one word.** When a default is really
correct, `catch` says so without a full branch. `catch` also lets you put an
error aside on purpose:

- `catch unreachable` asserts that the error cannot occur.
- `catch |e| std.debug.panic(...)` stops the program on purpose.

You can see all three at the call site. But you cannot say nothing.

## Check yourself

`parsePort("99999")` reported `Overflow`, but `parsePort` does not mention
overflow. Where did that error come from?

The error came from `std.fmt.parseInt`, and `try` passed it directly through.
The compiler infers the error set of `parsePort`. The set is the union of the
error that `parsePort` returns itself (`error.ReservedPort`) and all the
errors that its `try` lines can pass up. Because of the inferred set, the
switch has three prongs for a function with one `return error` line. Also
because of the inferred set, you can trust the set. The set comes from the
code, not from a comment that a person remembered to update.

## If you know C

C has the same limit and gives no help with it. Thus each C function has a
different convention:

```c
int fd = open(path, O_RDONLY);       /* -1 means failure, errno says why */
long n = strtol(text, &end, 10);     /* 0 might be failure or might be zero */
void *p = malloc(size);              /* NULL means failure */
```

Three functions have three encodings. In each case, the failure is a value
that looks exactly like a success. Nothing stops you when you assign `fd` and
use it. The `strtol` case is the worst. To tell a real 0 from a failed parse,
you must check `errno` and the end pointer, and almost nobody does.

The Zig `!u16` solves the same problem, but the type system owns the encoding,
not you. There is one convention, and it is in the signature. In C, a
programmer skips the check as a habit. In Zig, a skipped check is a compile
error.

[Errors](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/errors/) gives the details at the level of the
language: error sets as types, `errdefer`, and how error returns work together
with cleanup.

Next: [Talking to the Operating
System](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/talking-to-the-os/), the last chapter in
this track.

---

## Talk to the Operating System

*Systems from Scratch. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/talking-to-the-os/*

Each chapter before this one was about the inside of your program: its bytes,
its memory and its failures. This chapter is about the edge, because a program
cannot do anything from the inside alone. A program cannot read a file, write
to your terminal or open a connection. It can only calculate.

For each operation that goes outside the program, the program asks the
operating system. The name of that request is a **system call**. Your program
stops. The kernel does the operation, with privileges that your program does
not have. Then control returns to your program with a result.

That is the boundary, and all I/O goes across it.

The arrangement has three parts. It is older than almost all the other tools
that you use, and it did not change:

- The operating system gives your program some things when the program
  starts. The program does not ask for them.
- Your program asks for all other things by number. It uses a small integer,
  not a name, to refer to each thing that it opened.
- When the program ends, it gives back one number. The operating system
  guarantees only that number to the parent process.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // Three streams were already open when main started. Nothing in this
    // program opened them, and the numbers are not random: each process starts
    // with the same three.
    try out.print("stdin  is descriptor {d}\n", .{std.Io.File.stdin().handle});
    try out.print("stdout is descriptor {d}\n", .{std.Io.File.stdout().handle});
    try out.print("stderr is descriptor {d}\n\n", .{std.Io.File.stderr().handle});

    // The streams go to different places. For this reason, there are two
    // output streams. This line is the result of the program.
    try out.writeAll("this line went to stdout: the program's output\n");
    try out.flush();

    // This line is for the person who watches. If you redirect the program
    // into a file, this line still shows on the terminal.
    var err_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var err_writer = std.Io.File.stderr().writerStreaming(io, &err_buf);
    try err_writer.interface.writeAll("this line went to stderr: not part of the output\n");
    try err_writer.interface.flush();

    // A normal return from main gives a status of 0. By convention, 0 means
    // success. An error return makes the status non-zero. The operating system
    // guarantees only the status to the parent process.
    try out.writeAll("\nreturning from main reports success to whoever ran us\n");
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`15-groundwork.talking-to-the-os`)*

## What just happened

**Three streams were already open.** The program did not open them, and it
cannot select their numbers. Descriptor 0 is standard input, 1 is standard
output, and 2 is standard error. This is true for each process on each system
that comes from Unix. A shell uses this fact to connect two programs, and the
two programs do not have to agree on anything first.

**A descriptor is an integer and nothing else.** A descriptor is not a handle
object with methods inside it. It is a number. The kernel uses the number to
find the thing that you opened, in a table that the kernel keeps for your
process. When you open a file, you get the next free number.

This is the practical meaning of the phrase "everything is a file". A file, a
socket, a pipe and a terminal are all numbers into that table, and `read`
works on all of them.

**The program has two output streams, on purpose.** stdout is the *result* of
the program. If you pipe this program into a different program, the second
program reads these bytes. stderr is for the person who watches. You can see
the difference only when you redirect the output. Run the program on your
machine as `zig run talking-to-the-os.zig > out.txt`. The stdout lines go into
the file, but the stderr line still shows on your terminal. A tool that mixes
the two streams is difficult to use from scripts.

**The return from `main` reported 0.** A process ends with a status. By
convention, 0 means success, and each other value means a specific type of
failure. One small integer cannot hold much information. Thus programs also
write to stderr. The status says *that* the program failed. stderr says *what*
occurred.

## Check yourself

This program ran in your browser. The browser has no operating system, no
process table and no kernel to call. Then why did the descriptors print 0, 1
and 2?

The page runs the program under **WASI**. WASI is an interface with the same
shape as the real operating system: the same numbers and the same calls. But
WASI in the browser is JavaScript code, and it works with the browser, not
with a kernel.

The program cannot see the difference. An interface is exactly that promise.
Because of WASI, most of the snippets in this guide run on the page. Three
chapters in [the OS section](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/) need a real kernel: pipes, signals
and the start of new processes. Those chapters say so, and they do not have a
Run button.

## Where to go next

This chapter is the end of the track. You now have the model that the rest of
the guide assumes.

Perhaps you came here before the rest of the guide. Then [Getting
Started](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/) installs a compiler, and shows how to run
these programs on your own machine. After that, [Language
Basics](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/) teaches the same topics for the language: the
exact meaning of `*T`, how optionals remove null, and what `comptime` is.

If you already read those sections, go to [the operating system](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/)
next. That section uses the descriptors above to open files, start processes
and connect pipes. If you prefer to learn when you build something, [Data
Structures](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/data-structures/) starts with a linked list. A linked list
is the smallest program that makes you really answer the ownership question
from [chapter five](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/who-owns-this-memory/).

## If you know C

You already know all of this, with the names `open`, `read`, `write`, `close`
and `exit`. A Zig `std.Io.File` is a descriptor and some flag bits. You can
make one from the number 1, and write to standard output with it. The [file
descriptors](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/file-descriptors/) chapter does exactly that.

You will see two differences immediately:

- A failed call returns an error. It does not set a global `errno`. Thus the
  error works with `try`, as all other errors do.
- The permission to do I/O comes as an argument. `main` receives an `init`,
  and the writers above come from `init.io`. Zig has no global `stdout` that a
  function can use. Thus a function that does not take an `Io` cannot touch
  the outside world without your knowledge.

# Track: Systems

Zig and the world outside the process: networks, builds, C, wasm and pixels.

## A File Descriptor Is a Number

*Operating System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/file-descriptors/*

Open a file, accept a connection, or create a pipe. Each of these operations
gives you a small non-negative integer, and you hold only that integer. Your
side has no object.

The kernel keeps one table for each process, and the number is an index into
that table. Each later call identifies the thing that you opened, because you
give the number back to the call.

Press Run.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // A `std.Io.File` is a handle and one flag bit. The handle is the number.
    // Its type is the descriptor type of the platform.
    try out.print("File.Handle = {s}\n", .{@typeName(std.Io.File.Handle)});
    try out.print("a File is {d} bytes\n\n", .{@sizeOf(std.Io.File)});

    // Each process starts with these three. No code opened them. They were
    // already open when main started.
    try out.print("stdin  {d}\n", .{std.Io.File.stdin().handle});
    try out.print("stdout {d}\n", .{std.Io.File.stdout().handle});
    try out.print("stderr {d}\n\n", .{std.Io.File.stderr().handle});
    try out.flush();

    // The File that `stdout()` returns is not special. Build a File from the
    // number 1, and the File writes to the same stream.
    const by_hand: std.Io.File = .{ .handle = 1, .flags = .{ .nonblocking = false } };
    var hand_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var hand_writer = by_hand.writerStreaming(io, &hand_buf);
    try hand_writer.interface.writeAll("written through a hand-built File\n");
    try hand_writer.interface.flush();

    try out.print("same handle: {}\n", .{by_hand.handle == std.Io.File.stdout().handle});
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`14-os.file-descriptors`)*

## What a `File` is

```zig
handle: Handle,
flags: Flags,

pub const Handle = std.posix.fd_t;
```

This is the full declaration of `std.Io.File` in the standard library,
without its methods. A `File` is a descriptor and one bit. The bit tells if
the file was opened non-blocking.

On all POSIX targets and on WASI, `fd_t` is `i32`. On Windows, `fd_t` is a
`HANDLE`. For this reason, the declaration uses the name of the type and does
not write out the type.

The struct holds nothing more. Thus you can build a `File` from a raw number,
and the operation needs no cast:

```zig
const by_hand: std.Io.File = .{ .handle = 1, .flags = .{ .nonblocking = false } };
```

That value and `std.Io.File.stdout()` are the same eight bytes. When you write
through either value, the bytes go to the same place.

## The three that you get

A process starts with descriptors 0, 1 and 2 already open. No code in your
program opened them. The shell, or the parent process, prepared them before
your first instruction ran:

| Number | Name | Convention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | standard input | where the program reads from |
| 1 | standard output | where its results go |
| 2 | standard error | where its diagnostics go |

The numbers are a convention. But the kernel and all programs agree on the
convention, so in practice the convention is as strict as a rule. `zig build`,
the `2>&1` of your shell, and the redirect that a CI system applies to your
test run all use this convention.

Nothing else about the numbers is certain. The next descriptor that you open
gets the lowest free number. In a new process, that number is 3. After any
open or close, the number can be different. Code that hardcodes 4 works until
a library opens a log file before your function runs.

## The sandbox keeps the numbers

This chapter runs in your browser. The browser has no kernel, no descriptor
table and no processes. But the numbers are still 0, 1 and 2, because WASI
copied the interface.

The host gives descriptors to a module. The module identifies the descriptors
by number. It reads and writes through calls that take that number as their
first argument.

The descriptor number is not a detail of the Linux implementation that went
into the API by accident. The number is the API. The API is so thin that a
wasm runtime in a browser tab can implement it. A program for
a kernel cannot see the difference.

## Where descriptors come from next

The rest of this section uses descriptors in four ways:

- It writes to the descriptors that you got at startup.
- It gives changed copies to a child process.
- It holds one end of a pipe.
- It closes a descriptor to show that the program has no more data.

Sockets in [Network Programming](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/what-is-a-socket/) are
the same integers again, with a different call that creates them.

---

## The Three Standard Streams

*Operating System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/standard-streams/*

The output of the snippet below is not in the order in which the program
wrote it.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    // Two writers, both for descriptor 1. One holds bytes until the program
    // flushes it. The other has no buffer, so it writes the bytes at once.
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var buffered = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    var unbuffered = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &.{});

    try buffered.interface.writeAll("written first, into a buffer\n");
    try unbuffered.interface.writeAll("written second, straight to the fd\n");
    try buffered.interface.flush();

    const out = &buffered.interface;

    // "Is the stream a terminal?" is a question about the descriptor. A
    // program asks it before it decides to write colour. Through a pipe, or
    // into a CI log file, the answer is no. The browser runner says yes.
    try out.print("\nstdout is a tty: {}\n", .{try std.Io.File.stdout().isTty(io)});
    try out.print("stderr is a tty: {}\n", .{try std.Io.File.stderr().isTty(io)});

    // Descriptor 2 exists for two reasons. A diagnostic stays visible when you
    // redirect the output of the program. Also, the diagnostic is not in a
    // buffer when the process stops. Progress, warnings and errors go here.
    // Results go to 1.
    var err_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var err_writer = std.Io.File.stderr().writerStreaming(io, &err_buf);
    try err_writer.interface.writeAll("this line went to stderr\n");
    try err_writer.interface.flush();

    try out.writeAll("this line went to stdout\n");
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`14-os.standard-streams`)*

## Two writers, one descriptor

```zig
var buffered = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
var unbuffered = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &.{});

try buffered.interface.writeAll("written first, into a buffer\n");
try unbuffered.interface.writeAll("written second, straight to the fd\n");
try buffered.interface.flush();
```

Both writers write to descriptor 1:

- The first writer has a 1 KB buffer. It holds bytes until the program
  flushes the buffer.
- The second writer has an empty slice, so it has no place to keep bytes.
  Thus each write goes out immediately.

The second line gets to the terminal first. When you read the source from top
to bottom, you cannot see that.

The descriptor has no buffer. Your writer holds the buffer, on your side of
the call. Thus the fix is `flush`, not a flag on the file.
[Hello, World](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/getting-started/hello-world/) explains the mechanics.
Here, see this fact: two writers on one descriptor have two independent
buffers, and neither writer knows about the other.

Interleaved output often goes wrong in this way. A program prints progress to
standard error without a buffer, and it prints results to standard output with
a buffer. Then the log shows the work in an order that did not occur.

## Which stream a line belongs on

Descriptor 1 is for the output that the program must make. Descriptor 2 is for
all the messages that the program has about that work.

A pipe tests the split. `zig build 2>/dev/null | wc -l` must count results,
not warnings. It does this only if each line went to the correct stream.

Put on descriptor 2 all the text that a reader wants to remove from the data.
Examples are progress, warnings, errors, and the name of the file that the
program processes.

The output of standard error also stays after a crash. For this reason,
standard error usually has no buffer, or a line buffer. If a diagnostic is
still in a buffer when the process stops, you never see the diagnostic. After
a crash, you need the diagnostic most.

## `isTty`, and why programs ask it

```zig
std.Io.File.stdout().isTty(io)
```

The answer is true in the playground above, because the browser runner
reports both streams as a terminal. The answer is false in a CI log and
through a pipe. It is true in your terminal. The answer depends on the
descriptor, not on the program.

A good tool asks this question before it does one of these things:

- It writes colour escapes.
- It draws a progress bar again in the same place.
- It prints a table with the size of the window.

A tool that does not ask writes escape sequences into log files.

## Both streams in the playground

The playground puts 1 and 2 into one pane, because a browser has one place for
text. Under CI, the streams stay separate. The runner sends each stream to its
own file. It compares only standard output with the recorded expectation.

Thus the stderr line in this snippet is not in the expectation that gates the
snippet. That is the correct split for a test. The test checks what the
program made, and it ignores the messages that the program printed during the
work.

---

## The Environment

*Operating System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/environment/*

The environment is a list of `KEY=value` strings. The parent process selected
the list, and the kernel copied the list into your address space at startup.
The environment belongs only to your process. After startup, a change that you
make to the environment does not get to any other process that runs.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // The real environment. The startup code parsed it into a map before
    // main. This program runs in a wasm sandbox that has no parent process.
    // Thus the count is the real value, not a placeholder.
    const env = init.environ_map;
    try out.print("inherited variables: {d}\n", .{env.count()});
    try out.print("PATH: {?s}\n\n", .{env.get("PATH")});

    // A put into the map does not change any other process. The map is the
    // copy that belongs to this program. A child gets a copy at spawn time.
    try env.put("ZIG_GUIDE", "live");
    try env.put("EDITOR", "vim");
    try out.print("after two puts: {d}\n", .{env.count()});
    try out.print("ZIG_GUIDE: {?s}\n", .{env.get("ZIG_GUIDE")});
    try out.print("contains EDITOR: {}\n", .{env.contains("EDITOR")});

    _ = env.swapRemove("EDITOR");
    try out.print("after removing it: {?s}\n\n", .{env.get("EDITOR")});

    // A name must not be empty and must not contain '='. You cannot escape
    // the separator. Thus you cannot read back a key that contains '='.
    try out.print("\"HOME\" valid: {}\n", .{std.process.Environ.Map.validateKeyForPut("HOME")});
    try out.print("\"A=B\" valid: {}\n", .{std.process.Environ.Map.validateKeyForPut("A=B")});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`14-os.environment`)*

## The map is ready at startup

```zig
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const env = init.environ_map;
    const path = env.get("PATH");
}
```

`init.environ_map` is a `*std.process.Environ.Map`. The startup code filled
the map from the raw block before the call to `main`. The startup code
allocated the map with the same `gpa` that is on `init`. You do not free the
map, and you do not build the map.

In the playground above, the count is 0. The count is the real result, not a
stub. A wasm module in a browser tab has no parent process, so the module
inherits no environment. Thus the environment is really empty.

In the playground, `env.get("PATH")` returns `null`. A program must be ready
for this result on all platforms. If you did not set a variable yourself, the
variable can be absent.

## Your copy belongs to you

```zig
try env.put("ZIG_GUIDE", "live");
```

This line changes the map of this program and nothing else. It does not
change the shell that started your program. Alone, it does not change the
environment of a child process either.

A child process inherits a copy of a block. The block is the one that existed
when you spawned the child. When you spawn the child, you select the block. If
you give `null`, the child gets the environment of the parent.

Many people expect the other direction to work, but it does not work. No call
lets a program change the environment of its parent. Thus a tool that must
change your shell prints text, and the shell evaluates that text. The
kernel copied the environment at fork time, and the copies have no connection.

## Two rules for keys

A name must not be empty. A name must not contain `=` or a NUL byte. The map
can tell you if a key is valid:

```zig
std.process.Environ.Map.validateKeyForPut("A=B") // false
```

You cannot escape the separator. A block is a flat list of `KEY=VALUE`
strings, and the split occurs at the first `=`. Thus you can write a key that
contains `=`, but you cannot read the key back as you intended.

All bytes after the first `=` are the value. The value can contain newlines,
spaces and more `=` signs. For this reason, `PATH` works, and a value never
needs quotes at this level. The quotes that you write in a shell belong to
the shell. The shell removes the quotes before the string gets to your
program.

## Case, and the platform that is different

On POSIX, names are case-sensitive. On Windows, names are case-insensitive,
and the block is UTF-16. Thus on Windows, `Path` and `PATH` are the same
variable. `Environ.Map` follows the target platform of the build.

Code that reads one spelling and writes a different spelling works on
Windows. On all other platforms, the code is wrong, and no error tells you.
Thus select the usual upper-case spelling, and use the same spelling in both
places.

---

## Spawn a Process

*Operating System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/spawning/*

To run another program, you make three decisions:

- What to run.
- What the program inherits.
- What to do with the number that the program leaves when it ends.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = init.gpa;

    var args = init.minimal.args.iterate();
    defer args.deinit();
    _ = args.next(); // argv[0]

    // With an argument, this program is the child. The program runs itself.
    // Thus it does not need a system binary to be installed.
    if (args.next()) |mode| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, mode, "ok")) {
            var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
            var w = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
            try w.interface.writeAll("hello from the child\n");
            try w.interface.flush();
            std.process.exit(0);
        }
        // A program reports failure with a number, and only a number. If there
        // is a reason, the program writes the reason to stderr.
        std.process.exit(3);
    }

    var path_buf: [std.Io.Dir.max_path_bytes]u8 = undefined;
    const len = try std.process.executablePath(io, &path_buf);
    const self = path_buf[0..len];

    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // `run` spawns, collects both streams to the end, and waits. Use it when
    // the output is small and you want all of the output.
    const ok = try std.process.run(gpa, io, .{ .argv = &.{ self, "ok" } });
    defer gpa.free(ok.stdout);
    defer gpa.free(ok.stderr);
    try out.print("child stdout: {s}", .{ok.stdout});
    try out.print("child term:   {f}\n\n", .{ok.term});

    const failed = try std.process.run(gpa, io, .{ .argv = &.{ self, "fail" } });
    defer gpa.free(failed.stdout);
    defer gpa.free(failed.stderr);
    try out.print("failing child: {f}\n", .{failed.term});
    try out.print("succeeded:     {}\n", .{failed.term.success()});

    // A status is a `u8`. Thus there are only 256 values, and only 0 means
    // success. The program decides the meaning of the other values.
    switch (failed.term) {
        .exited => |code| try out.print("exit code:     {d}\n", .{code}),
        else => try out.print("killed or stopped rather than exited\n", .{}),
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this snippet natively. A WASI sandbox cannot create a process, and a browser tab has nothing to create a process from. (`14-os.spawning`)*

## The snippet runs itself

```zig
const len = try std.process.executablePath(io, &path_buf);
const ok = try std.process.run(gpa, io, .{ .argv = &.{ path_buf[0..len], "ok" } });
```

The snippet does not use `/bin/echo`, and this is intentional. A chapter that
runs a system binary fails on each computer that keeps that binary in a
different place. This site claims that CI ran each snippet today.

`executablePath` gives the program that runs its own path. A first argument
tells the copy which part of the program to run.

Real programs also do this. A supervisor can start itself again with a flag to
spawn workers. Thus the supervisor is sure that the workers have the same
version as the supervisor.

## `run` against `spawn`

`std.process.run` does four things in one call:

1. It spawns the child.
2. It reads standard output and standard error to end of file.
3. It waits for the child.
4. It gives you the two buffers.

Use `run` when the output is small and you want all of the output. Do not use
`run` when the output is large, or when you must react to the output when it
arrives.

`.stdout_limit` sets the maximum quantity of output that `run` collects. If
the output is more than that limit, `run` returns `error.StreamTooLong`. Thus
`run` does not fill memory while a child continues to write.

`std.process.spawn` returns immediately when the child exists. After that, you
control everything: the streams that you asked for, when to read them, and
when to wait. [Pipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/pipes/) uses that call.

Both functions go through `Io`. The creation of a process is an operation on
the interface. It is not a free function that calls the kernel without your
knowledge. Thus, with a different `Io` implementation, a program spawns in the
way that the implementation spawns.

## The status code

```zig
switch (failed.term) {
    .exited => |code| ...,
    .signal => |sig| ...,
    .stopped, .unknown => ...,
}
```

`Term` is a union, because the question "how did the process end?" has more
than one answer. A process that exited selected its own status. A process that
was killed selected nothing. The shell reports the signal number as an exit
code with the `128 + n` convention, and this loses that difference.

A program can select from 256 codes, and only 0 means success. These three
ask the same question and get the same one-bit answer:

- `&&` in a shell.
- A step that fails in CI.
- `Term.success()`.

Put all other information for the caller on standard error, because a code has
no space for it.

The child in the snippet exits with 3, and the snippet itself exits with 0.
This is intentional. Each snippet on this site must exit with 0 to pass the
gate. Thus this page can show you a nonzero code only from a child that fails
under a parent that succeeds.

## What a child inherits

By default, a child inherits three things:

- The environment.
- The working directory.
- Descriptors 0, 1 and 2.

The descriptors are the reason that the output of a child appears in your
terminal, and no code makes this occur. The child got the same descriptor 1
that you got.

You can override each one at the spawn call:

- `environ_map` replaces the environment.
- `cwd` changes the directory.
- `stdin`, `stdout` and `stderr` each take `inherit`, `ignore`, `close`, an
  open `file`, or a `pipe`.

When you replace the environment, the search for the program does not change.
The search still uses the `PATH` of the parent. If you set a different `PATH`
in the environment of the child, the search for the child does not change.

---

## Pipes Are the Child's Streams

*Operating System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/pipes/*

A pipe is a one-way buffer in the kernel, with a descriptor at each end. Write
into one end, and read from the other end. A pipe carries only bytes. It has
no message boundaries and no types. You cannot ask how much data will come.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = init.gpa;

    var args = init.minimal.args.iterate();
    defer args.deinit();
    _ = args.next(); // argv[0]

    // The child half: read standard input to end of file. Write it back in upper case.
    if (args.next() != null) {
        var in_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
        var reader = std.Io.File.stdin().readerStreaming(io, &in_buf);
        var out_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
        var writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);

        while (try reader.interface.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
            var upper: [64]u8 = undefined;
            const shouted = std.ascii.upperString(upper[0..line.len], line);
            try writer.interface.print("{s}\n", .{shouted});
        }
        try writer.interface.flush();
        std.process.exit(0);
    }

    var path_buf: [std.Io.Dir.max_path_bytes]u8 = undefined;
    const len = try std.process.executablePath(io, &path_buf);

    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // `.pipe` on a stream means: do not give the stream of the parent to the
    // child. Make a new pipe, and give the other end to the parent as a `File`.
    var child = try std.process.spawn(io, .{
        .argv = &.{ path_buf[0..len], "child" },
        .stdin = .pipe,
        .stdout = .pipe,
    });

    // Both ends are ordinary descriptors, after the three that the process
    // started with. The numbers depend on the other files that this process
    // has open. Thus the test checks that the numbers are new. It does not
    // check that they are 4.
    const fresh = child.stdin.?.handle > 2 and child.stdout.?.handle > 2;
    try out.print("both ends are fresh descriptors: {}\n\n", .{fresh});
    try out.flush();

    var to_child_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var to_child = child.stdin.?.writerStreaming(io, &to_child_buf);
    try to_child.interface.writeAll("one\ntwo\nthree\n");
    try to_child.interface.flush();

    // The close tells the child that the input is complete. The child is
    // blocked in a read. The read ends only when no write end of that pipe
    // exists. If the parent keeps this descriptor open and then waits for
    // output, the parent waits forever.
    child.stdin.?.close(io);
    child.stdin = null;

    var from_child_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var from_child = child.stdout.?.readerStreaming(io, &from_child_buf);
    const reply = try from_child.interface.allocRemaining(gpa, .limited(4096));
    defer gpa.free(reply);

    try out.print("{s}", .{reply});
    try out.print("\nterm: {f}\n", .{try child.wait(io)});
    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this snippet natively. The snippet makes the pipe when it spawns a process, and a WASI sandbox cannot spawn a process. (`14-os.pipes`)*

## There is no `std.posix.pipe`

The standard library does not have a `std.posix.pipe` function. `pipe2`
exists inside the `Io` implementations, `std.Io.Threaded` and `std.Io.Uring`.
There, `pipe2` is a detail of how the implementations schedule work.

The standard library gives you the useful case. Ask for a pipe on a stream of
a child, and you get the other end back as an `Io.File`.

```zig
var child = try std.process.spawn(io, .{
    .argv = &.{ self, "child" },
    .stdin = .pipe,
    .stdout = .pipe,
});
```

The `|` of the shell does the same thing. `.pipe` on a stream has this
meaning: do not give my stream to the child, make a new pipe, and give me the
other end. Then `child.stdin` and `child.stdout` are ordinary files. All
that you know about readers and writers applies to them without change.

The descriptors are new numbers after the three that the process started with.
Nothing makes the numbers certain. Thus the snippet checks that the numbers
are more than 2. It does not check that they are 4 and 5.

The numbers can be different with a different `Io` implementation. A test
that asserts exact numbers fails on a computer that opened one more file at
startup.

## Close the pipe to send the message

```zig
try to_child.interface.flush();
child.stdin.?.close(io);
child.stdin = null;
```

The child reads until end of file. On a pipe, end of file means that all of
the write ends are closed, and the parent holds one write end. Assume that a
parent writes, does not close the pipe, and then waits for output. That parent
waits forever.

In that case, the child is blocked in a read that cannot return. The parent
is blocked in a read from a child that will never write. Neither process
failed, and neither process can continue.

This is the classic pipe deadlock. The deadlock has a second form. A pipe
holds a fixed quantity of data, by default 64 KB on Linux. Assume that a
parent writes more than that before it reads anything. The parent fills the
buffer and is blocked in its own write. At the same time, the child fills its
output pipe and is blocked in its own write.

`std.process.run` prevents both forms, because it drains the pipes and waits
in the correct order. Thus use `std.process.run` when the output fits in
memory.

After the close, you must set `child.stdin = null`. `Child.wait` closes the
streams that it still holds. If a program closes a descriptor two times, a
bug occurs much later. The bug occurs after the kernel gives the number to a
different file that you use.

## `SIGPIPE`, the other direction

Assume that you write to a pipe, and the read end no longer exists. Then the
kernel sends `SIGPIPE`. The default action of `SIGPIPE` is to kill your
process.

That default is the reason that `head` works. In `producer | head -3`, the
producer stops when `head` stops its reads. No person writes code to make
this occur.

For the same reason, a server that runs for a long time ignores the signal.
Instead, the server handles the `error.BrokenPipe` from the write. If a client
disconnects in the middle of a reply, only that connection must end. The
process that serves all the other connections must continue.
[Signals](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/signals/) is the next chapter.

---

## Signals

*Operating System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/signals/*

A signal is a call from the operating system to a function in your program,
at a time that you did not select. A signal is not a queue that you poll, and
it is not a message that you receive.

The kernel stops your thread between two instructions. The handler runs on
the stack of that thread. Then the next instruction runs, as if nothing
occurred.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const posix = std.posix;

/// The handler here does one thing: it sets this flag. The flag is a
/// `std.atomic.Value`, because the handler can run between any two
/// instructions of the code below. A write to a plain `bool` there is a data
/// race with the code that the handler interrupted.
var caught: std.atomic.Value(u32) = .init(0);

fn onUsr1(sig: posix.SIG) callconv(.c) void {
    _ = sig;
    caught.store(1, .seq_cst);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // `sigaction` returns nothing. In the past, it returned an error union,
    // and the handler took a `c_int`. Both changed. Thus a handler from an
    // older tutorial does not compile. It does not fail at run time.
    var action: posix.Sigaction = .{
        .handler = .{ .handler = onUsr1 },
        .mask = posix.sigemptyset(),
        .flags = 0,
    };
    posix.sigaction(.USR1, &action, null);

    try out.print("caught before: {d}\n", .{caught.load(.seq_cst)});
    try posix.raise(.USR1);
    try out.print("caught after:  {d}\n\n", .{caught.load(.seq_cst)});

    // A block delays a signal. It does not discard the signal. If you raise
    // USR1 while it is blocked, it stays pending. The kernel sends it
    // immediately when you unblock it.
    caught.store(0, .seq_cst);
    var mask = posix.sigemptyset();
    posix.sigaddset(&mask, .USR1);
    posix.sigprocmask(posix.SIG.BLOCK, &mask, null);

    try posix.raise(.USR1);
    try out.print("while blocked: {d}\n", .{caught.load(.seq_cst)});
    try out.flush();

    posix.sigprocmask(posix.SIG.UNBLOCK, &mask, null);
    try out.print("once unblocked: {d}\n\n", .{caught.load(.seq_cst)});

    // Give the signal back to the default disposition of the kernel. For USR1,
    // that default is "terminate the process". Thus a USR1 kills a program
    // that never installed a handler for it.
    var default: posix.Sigaction = .{
        .handler = .{ .handler = posix.SIG.DFL },
        .mask = posix.sigemptyset(),
        .flags = 0,
    };
    posix.sigaction(.USR1, &default, null);
    try out.writeAll("USR1 restored to its default disposition\n");

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this snippet natively. A WASI sandbox has no signals, because it has no kernel to send them. (`14-os.signals`)*

## Two things changed, and both cause compile errors

```zig
var action: std.posix.Sigaction = .{
    .handler = .{ .handler = onUsr1 },
    .mask = std.posix.sigemptyset(),
    .flags = 0,
};
std.posix.sigaction(.USR1, &action, null);
```

`sigaction` returns `void`. In the past, it returned an error union. Thus a
`try` in front of the call now causes an error about a value that is not an
error. Also, a handler now takes a `std.posix.SIG`, not a `c_int`:

```zig
fn onUsr1(sig: std.posix.SIG) callconv(.c) void
```

Each handler from before this change has the signature `fn (c_int)
callconv(.C) void`, and it does not compile. Here, a compile error is the
better result.

The enum parameter has two more advantages:

- The compiler checks a `switch` over the signal in a shared handler.
- You cannot confuse `.USR1` with the integer 10 on one platform and 30 on a
  different platform.

## Set a flag. Do nothing else.

```zig
var caught: std.atomic.Value(u32) = .init(0);

fn onUsr1(_: std.posix.SIG) callconv(.c) void {
    caught.store(1, .seq_cst);
}
```

The handler interrupted code that can be anywhere. Assume that the code was
inside `malloc` and held the lock of the allocator. If your handler allocates,
the handler waits for a lock that its own thread holds. The result is a
deadlock with one thread. It can occur one time in ten thousand runs, in
production, under load.

The same problem applies to all calls that take a lock or allocate, and these
are most of the calls that you want. `std.debug.print` locks standard error. A
logger allocates. An insert into a hash map can allocate. Only a small set of
calls is safe in a handler. That set does not include the calls that you use
to find why the handler does not work.

Thus the handler stores to an atomic and returns. All the real work occurs in
the main loop. The main loop reads the flag between two units of work, when it
has time to handle the flag.

The flag is an atomic, not a plain `bool`. The reason is that the handler runs
between two instructions of code that can read the same variable. On a
weakly ordered computer, a torn or reordered read at that point is a real bug.

## A block delays a signal and does not discard it

```zig
std.posix.sigprocmask(std.posix.SIG.BLOCK, &mask, null);
try std.posix.raise(.USR1);   // pending, not delivered
std.posix.sigprocmask(std.posix.SIG.UNBLOCK, &mask, null);
// handler runs here
```

The kernel holds a blocked signal as pending until you unblock it. Then the
kernel sends the signal. With this method, a program protects a section from
interruptions, and it does not lose the notification.

The same method is the base of `signalfd`. Block a signal permanently, then
read it as data on a descriptor. Then a normal event loop can wait for the
interruption. Most servers handle signals in this way.

Pending is one bit, not a count. If you raise ten `SIGUSR1` signals while the
signal is blocked, the kernel sends the signal one time. A handler that
increments a counter counts deliveries, not signals. If a program must know
how many events occurred, the program must count the events in a different
place.

## Defaults that you inherit

Each signal has a disposition before your program changes it. For most
signals, the disposition is to terminate the process.

`SIGUSR1` is the example in the snippet. Its name means "user defined", and by
default it is fatal. Thus if a program never installs a handler, the program
stops when a `SIGUSR1` arrives.

Remember these three:

| Signal | Default | Sent when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SIGINT` | terminate | someone pressed Ctrl-C |
| `SIGTERM` | terminate | something asked you to stop politely |
| `SIGPIPE` | terminate | you wrote to a pipe that has no reader |

A program that runs for a long time must handle `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM`. To
handle them, set a flag. The main loop then changes the flag into a clean
shutdown.

You cannot handle or block `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP`. Thus an operator can
always stop a process that does not respond.

---

## Exit the Process

*Operating System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/exiting/*

The snippet writes two lines and registers two `defer` statements. Only one
line comes out.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // The program registers these now. The exit below skips each of them.
    defer std.debug.print("this defer never runs\n", .{});
    defer out.flush() catch {};

    try out.writeAll("first line, flushed by hand\n");
    try out.flush();

    try out.writeAll("second line, still sitting in the buffer\n");

    // The process stops here. This is not a return. No defer runs, and the
    // program flushes no buffer. Thus the program loses the second line above, and
    // it loses the memory that held the line.
    std.process.exit(0);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`14-os.exiting`)*

## What `exit` skips

```zig
defer std.debug.print("this defer never runs\n", .{});
defer out.flush() catch {};

try out.writeAll("second line, still sitting in the buffer\n");
std.process.exit(0);
```

`std.process.exit` is `noreturn`. It never returns to the caller, so no code
between the call and the end of `main` runs. No `defer` runs at any depth of
the stack, no `errdefer` runs, and the program flushes nothing.

Look at the lost line. Those bytes were in a buffer in the memory of your
process. The operating system never received the bytes, and then the process
ended. Output often disappears in this way from a program that "definitely
printed it".

The second `defer` above is the one that flushes. It looks like it protects
the output. But it never runs, so it protects nothing.

When `main` returns normally, every `defer` runs. Thus an error return from
`main` and `exit(1)` are not the same:

- An error return unwinds the stack and runs the cleanup.
- `exit(1)` stops the process immediately.

## The status that you leave

`exit` takes a `u8`. Zero means success, and you decide the meaning of each
other value. This is the same one-bit protocol that the parent sees as `Term`
in [Spawn a Process](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/spawning/).

When `main` returns an error, Zig sets a nonzero status for you. In debug
builds, Zig also prints the error name with a stack trace. For a tool, that
is the correct default.

Select a specific code only for a program whose callers make a decision on
the code. `grep` returns 1 for "no match" and 2 for "something went wrong". A
shell script can act on that difference, but it cannot act on an error
message.

## `cleanExit`, and why it does nothing in Debug

```zig
pub fn cleanExit(io: Io) void {
    if (builtin.mode == .debug) return;
    _ = io.lockStderr(&.{}, .no_color) catch {};
    exit(0);
}
```

A program that is about to exit does not have to free anything. The kernel
takes back the full address space. A walk through a tree of allocations to
release memory that will disappear soon only makes the program slower to
stop.

`std.process.cleanExit` is that shortcut, with the one condition that makes
the shortcut safe:

- In Debug, the function returns and lets your teardown code run. Thus the
  leak detector still sees a program that freed everything, and it can still
  tell you about the leak that is important.
- In release builds, the function exits immediately.

The Zig compiler itself calls `cleanExit`.

Because the behavior changes with the build mode, this page describes the call
and does not run it. Assume that the output of a snippet changes between
`-Doptimize=Debug` and `ReleaseSmall`, which this site ships. Then the snippet
passes CI, but readers who use the other build mode see the wrong output.

## `abort` is not an exit

`std.process.abort` ends the process abnormally. It raises `SIGABRT`, which
runs a handler if you installed one. Then it makes sure that the process
stops in all cases. It sets no status code and runs no cleanup. Usually, it
leaves a core dump.

Use `abort` for a broken invariant, where more work can cause damage and
there is nothing useful to report. Do not use `abort` for a file that does not
exist. Use `exit` when the program has no more work. Use `abort` when the
program gets to a state that must be impossible.

---

## What a Socket Is

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/what-is-a-socket/*

A socket is a [file descriptor](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/file-descriptors/) with an address.
That is almost the full definition. When two sockets have a connection, all the
work uses the reader and writer interface from [Readers and
Writers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/readers-and-writers/). A file uses the same
interface.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // An address is only data. The parse does not use the network and
    // opens nothing. It fails only if the text is not an address.
    const wanted = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    try out.print("asked for port:  {d}\n", .{wanted.getPort()});

    // Port 0 tells the kernel to select a free port. The kernel gives the
    // port when it binds the socket, and the socket records the port. A
    // fixed port makes a test suite fail when two copies run at one time.
    var server = try wanted.listen(io, .{});
    defer server.deinit(io);

    const bound = server.socket.address;
    try out.print("kernel gave me:  {s}\n", .{if (bound.getPort() == 0) "port 0" else "a real port"});
    try out.print("still loopback:  {}\n\n", .{bound.getPort() != wanted.getPort()});

    // `.stream` is TCP: an ordered and reliable byte stream on a
    // connection. `.dgram` is UDP, which has none of these three properties.
    var client = try bound.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
    defer client.close(io);

    var accepted = try server.accept(io);
    defer accepted.close(io);

    try out.writeAll("connected. two handles now refer to one conversation.\n\n");

    // After this point, the code does not use sockets. The reader and
    // writer interfaces that a file uses move the bytes. Thus the next
    // protocol chapters can run without a network.
    var write_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = client.writer(io, &write_buf);
    try writer.interface.writeAll("ping\n");
    try writer.interface.flush();

    var read_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = accepted.reader(io, &read_buf);
    const line = try reader.interface.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n');
    try out.print("server read:     \"{s}\"\n", .{line});

    // No other code closes a socket for you. You must close each socket.
    // Each socket is a file descriptor. If a server does not close its
    // sockets, it cannot accept connections at the process limit. This
    // occurs a long time before the server has no more memory.
    try out.writeAll("closing: the defers above release three descriptors\n");

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this snippet natively, and binds a real loopback socket. Browser wasm has no sockets. (`11-networking.what-is-a-socket`)*

## An address is data

`IpAddress.parse` does not use the network. It opens nothing and sends
nothing. It fails only if the text is not an address. No network action
occurs until you call `listen`, `bind` or `connect`.

```zig
const wanted = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
```

## Port 0 tells the kernel to select a port

If you ask for port 0, the kernel gives the socket a free port when it binds
the socket. The socket records the port in `server.socket.address`.

A test that uses a fixed port such as 8080 can fail in three conditions:

- Two copies of the test run at the same time.
- The server from the last run is still active.
- A different program on the computer already uses port 8080.

Each snippet in this section binds port 0 and reads the port that it gets.
Thus all of the snippets can run on the same CI computer at the same time.

## Stream or datagram

```zig
var client = try bound.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
```

`.stream` is TCP. TCP keeps the bytes in order, is reliable, and uses a
connection. `.dgram` is UDP,
and UDP has none of these three properties.
[UDP Datagrams](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/udp-message/), at the end of this section,
gives more information about UDP. You select the mode one time, on the socket.
Each difference between the two protocols comes from that mode.

## After the connection, the code does not use sockets

```zig
var writer = client.writer(io, &write_buf);
try writer.interface.writeAll("ping\n");
try writer.interface.flush();
```

When the connection exists, no part of the code is specific to networks.
Thus five of the chapters between this chapter and the UDP chapter run in your
browser, without sockets. A protocol parser that uses `std.Io.Reader` works
on a socket, on a file and on a byte array in a test. You write the parser
one time only.

## You must close each socket

Each socket is a file descriptor, and each process has a limit on file
descriptors. If a server does not close one socket for each connection, the
server cannot accept new connections when it reaches that limit. This occurs a long time before the server has no
more memory. The symptom is an error from `accept`, and the error does not
tell you about the leak. Put a `defer` immediately after the line that makes
the socket. Then the program always closes the socket.

Next: [A TCP Round Trip](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/tcp-echo/). That chapter adds an
accept loop to this program.

---

## A TCP Round Trip

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/tcp-echo/*

In current Zig, a TCP server uses three calls:
`std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse`, then `address.listen(io, .{})`, then
`server.accept(io)`. A TCP client uses `addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream })`.
The reader of a connected stream is the same `std.Io.Reader` that you use for
files.

## The problem

You want a TCP server and a client that talks to the server, in Zig, with the
current API. Old tutorials cause many problems on this topic. The network
code moved from `std.net` to `std.Io.net`, and each operation now takes the
`Io` instance. If you copy code from a guide of last year, the compiler
rejects the code.

The recipe runs the two halves in one process. You can use the same method
for an integration test of any protocol code.

## The plan

1. Parse `127.0.0.1` with **port 0**, and call `listen`. Port 0 tells the OS
   to select a free ephemeral port. `server.socket.address` holds the port
   that the OS selected. Thus no code uses a fixed port that another program
   can already use.
2. Start a thread for the server half. The thread calls `accept`, reads a
   line and sends a reply.
3. In the main thread, `connect` to the recorded address. Send a line and
   read the reply.
4. Join the thread. CI runs exactly this program and compares the output.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// The server half: accept one client, read one line, and send the line
// back in uppercase. A real server runs this code one time per connection.
fn serve(server: *std.Io.net.Server, io: std.Io) void {
    var conn = server.accept(io) catch return;
    defer conn.close(io);

    var read_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = conn.reader(io, &read_buf);
    const line = reader.interface.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n') catch return;

    var upper_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    const upper = std.ascii.upperString(&upper_buf, line);

    var write_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = conn.writer(io, &write_buf);
    writer.interface.print("{s}\n", .{upper}) catch return;
    writer.interface.flush() catch return;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // Port 0 asks the OS for a free port. The socket records the port that
    // it got. Thus no code here uses a fixed port that is possibly in use.
    const any_port = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    var server = try any_port.listen(io, .{});
    defer server.deinit(io);
    const addr = server.socket.address;

    const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, serve, .{ &server, io });

    // The client half. After this point, all code uses the reader and
    // writer interface. A socket stream and a file operate the same way.
    var stream = try addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
    defer stream.close(io);

    var write_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = stream.writer(io, &write_buf);
    try writer.interface.writeAll("hello over tcp\n");
    try writer.interface.flush();

    var read_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = stream.reader(io, &read_buf);
    const reply = try reader.interface.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n');

    try out.print("sent:     hello over tcp\n", .{});
    try out.print("received: {s}\n", .{reply});

    thread.join();
    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this snippet natively, and sends real bytes over loopback. Browser wasm has no sockets. (`11-networking.tcp-echo`)*

## What changed from std.net

If you learned to write network code in Zig before the change to `std.Io`, use
this table:

| Then | Now |
| --- | --- |
| `std.net.Address.parseIp(...)` | `std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse(...)` |
| `address.listen(.{})` | `address.listen(io, .{})` |
| `listener.accept()` | `server.accept(io)` |
| `std.net.tcpConnectToAddress(addr)` | `addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream })` |
| `stream.reader()` / `.writer()` | `stream.reader(io, &buf)` / `.writer(io, &buf)`, then `.interface` |

All rows follow one rule. Each operation that can block uses the `io` parameter,
and you must supply the buffers.

## One interface for sockets and files

`stream.reader(io, &buf).interface` is the same `std.Io.Reader` that you use
for files and stdin. Thus `takeDelimiterExclusive('\n')` reads a line from a
socket in the same way as from a file. Protocol code that uses the interface
does not know that a socket is below it. For this reason, you can test the
protocol code with `std.Io.Reader.fixed` in unit tests.

## Why a thread

`accept` blocks until a client connects, and `connect` blocks until the
server accepts. Thus one thread cannot do the two halves together, unless it
uses details of the connection queue in the kernel. A second thread lets each
half run as straight-line code. On the wasm target, this code does not
compile, because wasm has no sockets and no threads. For this reason, CI runs
this snippet natively.

## Variations

- **Many clients:** put the accept-and-serve body in a loop and start one
  thread for each connection. Or give the accepted streams to a
  [worker queue](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/worker-queue/).
- **Timeouts:** `connect` takes an `Io.Timeout` in its options. Reads can use
  `receiveTimeout` at the socket level.
- **Structured protocols:** for binary data, length-prefixed frames are better
  than lines of text. See [the wire format recipe](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/binary-roundtrip/).

---

## Bytes Have No Edges

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/short-reads/*

If a server ignores the subject of this chapter, the server can work in tests
and fail under load.

TCP is a byte stream. TCP keeps the bytes in order and delivers all of the
bytes. TCP does not make a promise about how it groups the bytes. The sender
made three writes, and these writes can arrive as one read or as seventeen
reads. The socket API does not tell you which of these occurred. TCP does not
record where one write ended and where the next write started.

Press Run. The program delivers the same bytes one byte at a time, and then
all together. The parser cannot see a difference.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// All the bytes that arrived, and the quantity that the parser gave out.
///
/// Two indices do all the work. `len` increases when the network delivers
/// bytes. `at` increases when the parser removes a complete message from the
/// front. No bytes move, thus the slices that `next` returns stay valid.
const Incoming = struct {
    buf: [256]u8 = undefined,
    len: usize = 0,
    at: usize = 0,

    /// The bytes from the last read. A socket gives you a slice of any size.
    /// The slice can be a part of a message, or two messages, or both.
    fn feed(self: *Incoming, chunk: []const u8) void {
        @memcpy(self.buf[self.len..][0..chunk.len], chunk);
        self.len += chunk.len;
    }

    /// `null` means "not yet, read more". If a parser cannot say that, the
    /// parser must think that the full message arrived in one part. That
    /// assumption is the bug.
    fn next(self: *Incoming) ?[]const u8 {
        const avail = self.buf[self.at..self.len];
        if (avail.len < 2) return null;

        const want = std.mem.readInt(u16, avail[0..2], .big);
        if (avail.len < 2 + want) return null;

        self.at += 2 + want;
        return avail[2..][0..want];
    }
};

/// Frame a payload as the sender does: first the length, then the bytes.
fn frame(out: []u8, payload: []const u8) []u8 {
    std.mem.writeInt(u16, out[0..2], @intCast(payload.len), .big);
    @memcpy(out[2..][0..payload.len], payload);
    return out[0 .. 2 + payload.len];
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // Three messages, one after the other on the wire, as the sender sends
    // them. Only the length of a message shows where the message ends.
    var wire: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var used: usize = 0;
    for ([_][]const u8{ "hello", "hi", "goodbye" }) |payload| {
        used += frame(wire[used..], payload).len;
    }
    try out.print("{d} bytes on the wire for 3 messages\n\n", .{used});

    // One byte for each read. This is the worst case that a real network
    // can make, and a real network can do it. If a parser works
    // here, the parser works for all sizes of parts.
    var incoming: Incoming = .{};
    for (wire[0..used], 1..) |byte, fed| {
        incoming.feed(&.{byte});
        while (incoming.next()) |message| {
            try out.print("after {d} bytes: \"{s}\"\n", .{ fed, message });
        }
    }

    // The same bytes in one read make the same messages. The parser does
    // not know which of the two cases occurred. The parser has this design
    // because the size of the parts is not a part of the protocol.
```
