```zig
    var at_once: Incoming = .{};
    at_once.feed(wire[0..used]);
    var count: usize = 0;
    while (at_once.next()) |_| count += 1;
    try out.print("\none read of {d} bytes: {d} messages\n", .{ used, count });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.short-reads`)*

## The bug

```zig
// Wrong, and it works on your machine every time.
var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
const n = try socket.read(&buf);
const message = parse(buf[0..n]);
```

This code is correct only when the full message arrives in one read. On
loopback, with a small message and a computer that has no other load, the
full message always arrives in one read. In these conditions, the full
message possibly does not arrive in one read:

- The message is larger than one packet (the MTU).
- The network has a high load.
- The sender uses two writes.
- The connection uses a proxy.

The failure occurs in production. It looks like data corruption, not like a
message that is too short.

## Two indices and no copies

```zig
const Incoming = struct {
    buf: [256]u8 = undefined,
    len: usize = 0,   // bytes received
    at: usize = 0,    // bytes handed out
};
```

`len` increases when the network delivers bytes. `at` increases when the
parser removes a complete message from the front. The parser does not move
bytes, thus the slices that `next` returns stay valid. You can give a message
to a handler and not copy the message first.

The other method is to compact the buffer after each message: you move the
other bytes to the front. Then each slice that the parser returned before
points at the wrong bytes. This is a use-after-free. A `[256]u8` hides the
error from you, because the memory is still there and you can still read it.

## `null` means "not yet"

```zig
fn next(self: *Incoming) ?[]const u8 {
    const avail = self.buf[self.at..self.len];
    if (avail.len < 2) return null;

    const want = std.mem.readInt(u16, avail[0..2], .big);
    if (avail.len < 2 + want) return null;

    self.at += 2 + want;
    return avail[2..][0..want];
}
```

The function has two `null` returns, for the two ways that a message can be
incomplete:

- There are not sufficient bytes to know the length.
- There are not sufficient bytes for that length.

If a parser cannot say "not yet", the parser must think that the message is
complete. That assumption is the bug from the start of this chapter.

Also look at the `while` in the caller. One read can complete more than one
message. If a handler processes only one message for each read, a fast
client makes the number of messages in the buffer increase. Then the handler
never gets to the end of the buffer.

## The result

The parser does not know how the bytes arrived in parts. Thus the size of the
parts is not a part of your protocol. You can test the parser with a byte
array, and [Three Ways to Frame](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/framing/) does that next.
That test has value. The parser cannot see the delivery patterns that the
test does not simulate.

---

## Three Ways to Frame

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/framing/*

The previous chapter showed that a stream has no message boundaries. Framing
adds the boundaries again. There are three ways to frame a message. Each
protocol that you know selects one of these three ways. The hex below shows
each of the three.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// ---------------------------------------------------------------- length

/// Two bytes of length, then exactly that number of bytes. Before the
/// receiver reads one byte of payload, it knows how much to wait for.
fn writeLengthPrefixed(w: *std.Io.Writer, payload: []const u8) !void {
    var header: [2]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(u16, &header, @intCast(payload.len), .big);
    try w.writeAll(&header);
    try w.writeAll(payload);
}

fn readLengthPrefixed(r: *std.Io.Reader) ![]const u8 {
    const header = try r.take(2);
    const len = std.mem.readInt(u16, header[0..2], .big);
    return r.take(len);
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------- delimiter

/// A byte that cannot occur in the payload ends the message. The delimiter
/// is cheap to write and easy to read by hand. The cost is that the payload
/// can never contain that byte.
fn writeDelimited(w: *std.Io.Writer, payload: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeAll(payload);
    try w.writeByte('\n');
}

// ------------------------------------------------------- self-describing

/// The payload tells the receiver how to read the payload. Here, one tag
/// byte selects a fixed-width integer or a length-prefixed string. RESP,
/// protobuf and all tagged formats work in this way.
const Value = union(enum) {
    int: i32,
    text: []const u8,
};

fn writeTagged(w: *std.Io.Writer, value: Value) !void {
    switch (value) {
        .int => |n| {
            try w.writeByte('i');
            var b: [4]u8 = undefined;
            std.mem.writeInt(i32, &b, n, .big);
            try w.writeAll(&b);
        },
        .text => |s| {
            try w.writeByte('s');
            try writeLengthPrefixed(w, s);
        },
    }
}

fn printValue(w: *std.Io.Writer, value: Value) !void {
    switch (value) {
        .int => |n| try w.print("int {d}\n", .{n}),
        .text => |s| try w.print("text \"{s}\"\n", .{s}),
    }
}

fn readTagged(r: *std.Io.Reader) !Value {
    const tag = try r.takeByte();
    return switch (tag) {
        'i' => .{ .int = std.mem.readInt(i32, (try r.take(4))[0..4], .big) },
        's' => .{ .text = try readLengthPrefixed(r) },
        else => error.BadTag,
    };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var wire: [64]u8 = undefined;

    // Length prefix. The framing does not change the payload. The payload
    // can contain any byte, also the newline that the next method cannot
    // carry.
    {
        var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&wire);
        try writeLengthPrefixed(&w, "PING");
        try out.print("length:    {x}\n", .{w.buffered()});

        var r: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(w.buffered());
        try out.print("           read back \"{s}\"\n\n", .{try readLengthPrefixed(&r)});
    }

    // Delimiter. A person can read it on the wire, thus HTTP and SMTP use it.
    {
        var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&wire);
        try writeDelimited(&w, "PING");
        try out.print("delimiter: {x}\n", .{w.buffered()});

        var r: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(w.buffered());
        try out.print("           read back \"{s}\"\n\n", .{try r.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n')});
    }

    // Self-describing. The cost is a tag byte. Then the receiver does not
    // need an agreement about the type of the payload before the message.
    {
        var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&wire);
        try writeTagged(&w, .{ .int = 4096 });
        try writeTagged(&w, .{ .text = "PING" });
        try out.print("tagged:    {x}\n", .{w.buffered()});

        var r: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(w.buffered());
        try out.writeAll("           read back ");
        try printValue(out, try readTagged(&r));
        try out.writeAll("           read back ");
        try printValue(out, try readTagged(&r));
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }

    // A limit of the delimiter method. The payload contains the delimiter,
    // thus the reader stops too early and does not report an error. The
    // message is too short, and the reader uses the rest as the next message.
    {
        var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&wire);
        try writeDelimited(&w, "two\nlines");

        var r: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(w.buffered());
        const first = try r.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n');
        try out.print("delimiter with a '\\n' in the payload: \"{s}\"", .{first});
        try out.print(" ({d} of {d} bytes)\n", .{ first.len, "two\nlines".len });
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.framing`)*

## Length prefix

```
00 04 50 49 4e 47
^^^^^ length      ^^^^^^^^^^^ payload
```

Before the receiver reads one byte of payload, the receiver knows exactly how
many bytes to wait for. This property makes the parser in the last chapter
possible. For this reason, a length prefix is the default selection for all
binary data.

The framing does not change the payload. Thus the payload can contain any
byte, and also the newline that the next method cannot carry. The cost is
that you must know the length before you start to write. Thus you must put
the full message in a buffer, or know its size before you start.

## Delimiter

```
50 49 4e 47 0a
^^^^^^^^^^^ payload  ^^ '\n'
```

A delimiter is cheap to write and cheap to read. A person can also read it
on the wire. For these reasons, HTTP, SMTP, IMAP and Redis use a delimiter
for their text parts. You can debug the protocol with `nc`, because you can
read the bytes.

The cost is that the delimiter byte can never occur in a payload. The last
line of the output shows what occurs when the payload contains the byte. The
reader stops too early and does not report an error. For the reader, the
message ended at the correct place for the end of a message. The reader uses
the other bytes as the next message.

Real protocols solve this problem in one of two ways:

- They escape the delimiter byte in the payload.
- They put a length prefix on the body only.

HTTP uses the second way: headers with delimiters, then `Content-Length` and
a raw body.

## Self-describing

```
69 00 00 10 00   73 00 04 50 49 4e 47
^^ 'i'           ^^ 's'
```

A tag byte tells the receiver how to read the bytes after the tag. Here, `i`
means a fixed-width integer and `s` means a length-prefixed string. Thus the
receiver does not need an agreement before the message about the contents of
the field.

RESP, protobuf wire types, MessagePack and CBOR use this shape. The cost is
one byte for each value. You also need a `switch` that rejects unknown tags.
The `switch` must not trust an unknown tag.

## Select a method

The other two methods are special cases of a length prefix. A delimiter is a
length that you must search for. A tag is a length that also carries its
meaning. If you design a new protocol, and it is not necessary for a person
to read it, use a length prefix.

If you want to debug the protocol by hand, use a delimiter for the envelope
and a length for the body. HTTP used that combination for thirty years.

---

## A Text Protocol, Both Directions

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/text-protocols/*

A text protocol is delimiter framing with a grammar in it. This protocol uses
the reply syntax of Redis, because that syntax is small and useful. The first
byte of a reply tells the reader how to read the rest of the reply.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// All the commands that the server knows. The verb is an enum, not a
/// string, thus the switch below is exhaustive. If you add a command and do
/// not handle it, the compiler gives an error. Thus no request can do
/// nothing and report nothing.
const Verb = enum { get, set, del, ping };

const Command = struct {
    verb: Verb,
    args: [2][]const u8 = .{ "", "" },
    count: usize = 0,
};

/// On the wire, commands are not case-sensitive, as in Redis, SMTP and HTTP
/// methods. Normalise the case one time, here. Then later code need not.
fn parse(line: []const u8) !Command {
    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    const word = it.next() orelse return error.EmptyCommand;

    var lower: [16]u8 = undefined;
    if (word.len > lower.len) return error.UnknownCommand;
    const verb = std.meta.stringToEnum(Verb, std.ascii.lowerString(lower[0..word.len], word)) orelse
        return error.UnknownCommand;

    var cmd: Command = .{ .verb = verb };
    while (it.next()) |arg| {
        if (cmd.count == cmd.args.len) return error.TooManyArguments;
        cmd.args[cmd.count] = arg;
        cmd.count += 1;
    }
    return cmd;
}

/// The reply side. The first byte tells the reader how to read the rest.
/// This is the self-describing framing from the previous chapter, for text.
fn reply(w: *std.Io.Writer, cmd: Command) !void {
    switch (cmd.verb) {
        .ping => try w.writeAll("+PONG\r\n"),
        .set => if (cmd.count == 2) try w.writeAll("+OK\r\n") else try w.writeAll("-ERR wrong number of arguments\r\n"),
        .get => if (cmd.count == 1)
            try w.print("${d}\r\n{s}\r\n", .{ cmd.args[0].len, cmd.args[0] })
        else
            try w.writeAll("-ERR wrong number of arguments\r\n"),
        .del => try w.print(":{d}\r\n", .{cmd.count}),
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // A conversation as it arrives: lines that end in CRLF, in one buffer.
    // The network does not deliver the lines one at a time.
    const conversation =
        "PING\r\n" ++
        "set name alice\r\n" ++
        "GET name\r\n" ++
        "DEL a b\r\n" ++
        "SET oops\r\n" ++
        "FLY me to the moon\r\n";

    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(conversation);
    var wire: [128]u8 = undefined;

    // `takeDelimiter` consumes the '\n' and returns null at the end. Thus
    // this is the full read loop. The '\r' is still on the line. Remove it,
    // but do not think that it is always there. Many clients do not send it.
    while (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) |raw| {
        const line = std.mem.trimEnd(u8, raw, "\r");

        var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&wire);
        if (parse(line)) |cmd| {
            try reply(&w, cmd);
        } else |err| {
            // An error is also a reply. If the server closes the connection,
            // the client cannot know which command was bad.
            try w.print("-ERR {s}\r\n", .{@errorName(err)});
        }

        // Escape the CRLF in the reply. Then you can see the framing, and
        // the terminal does not change the CRLF into line breaks.
        try out.print("{s: <20} -> ", .{line});
        for (w.buffered()) |byte| switch (byte) {
            '\r' => try out.writeAll("\\r"),
            '\n' => try out.writeAll("\\n"),
            else => try out.writeByte(byte),
        };
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.text-protocols`)*

## The verb is an enum, not a string

```zig
const Verb = enum { get, set, del, ping };

const verb = std.meta.stringToEnum(Verb, lowered) orelse return error.UnknownCommand;
```

Convert the verb one time, at the edge. Then each `switch` after the
conversion can be exhaustive. If you add a command to the enum and do not
handle the command, the compiler rejects the program. If the verb stays a
`[]const u8`, the same mistake gives a request that does nothing and reports
nothing. Then a user finds the problem later.

`parse` is the one place where this conversion can occur. It is the only
place that knows that the bytes came from outside the program.

## Normalise at the edge

On the wire, commands are not case-sensitive, as in Redis, SMTP and HTTP
methods. Change the command to lowercase one time, in `parse`. Then no later
code must remember that `GET`, `get` and `Get` are the same command. If many
functions must remember this rule, one of the functions will possibly get it
wrong.

## Errors are replies

```zig
} else |err| {
    try w.print("-ERR {s}\r\n", .{@errorName(err)});
}
```

Do not close the connection because of a malformed command. The client is
still connected and can still send valid commands. The client does not know
which command you rejected, unless you tell it. If you close the socket on a
parse error, each typo causes a new connection. Under load, that becomes many
new connections at the same time.

`@errorName` sends the names of your internal errors to the connected client.
For a guide, that is satisfactory. For a service on a public port, decide if
you want to show these names.

## The `\r` is not optional and not guaranteed

```zig
const line = std.mem.trimEnd(u8, raw, "\r");
```

The specification says CRLF. Real clients send LF only, and so does a person
who types into `nc`. Read until `\n`, then remove a `\r` if there is one.

- If you require the `\r`, you reject the clients that send LF only.
- If you think that the `\r` is not there, the last character is wrong for
  the clients that send CRLF.

## Escape the framing when you print it

The output above shows `\r\n` as text, and the line does not end there. If
the program prints a raw reply, the terminal changes the framing into line
breaks. Then you cannot see the bytes that the server sent. To debug a
protocol, you must see the exact bytes, and a terminal hides characters such
as `\r`.

---

## Binary Protocols and Byte Order

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/binary-protocols/*

Each binary protocol starts with a fixed-size header. Thus the receiver can
read a known number of bytes before it knows other information. To write a
header, you must obey two rules. The rules are easy to state, and they are
also easy to forget.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Each message in this example protocol starts with this header. The
/// header is always ten bytes. Thus the receiver can read a fixed quantity
/// before it knows other data. Compare `@sizeOf(Header)`, which is not ten.
const Header = struct {
    magic: u16,
    version: u8,
    kind: Kind,
    length: u32,
    checksum: u16,

    const Kind = enum(u8) { request = 1, response = 2 };
    const magic_value: u16 = 0x5A47; // "ZG"
    const wire_size = 10;

    /// One field at a time, with the endianness at each call. This needs
    /// more code than a cast of the bytes of the struct. It is the only
    /// method that works with a different compiler, a different target, or
    /// a peer in a different language.
    fn write(self: Header, w: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
        try w.writeInt(u16, self.magic, .big);
        try w.writeInt(u8, self.version, .big);
        try w.writeInt(u8, @intFromEnum(self.kind), .big);
        try w.writeInt(u32, self.length, .big);
        try w.writeInt(u16, self.checksum, .big);
    }

    fn read(r: *std.Io.Reader) !Header {
        const magic = try r.takeInt(u16, .big);
        if (magic != magic_value) return error.NotOurProtocol;

        const version = try r.takeInt(u8, .big);
        const kind = try r.takeInt(u8, .big);
        return .{
            .magic = magic,
            .version = version,
            // `std.enums.fromInt` returns null, not an error. It replaced
            // `std.meta.intToEnum`, which does not exist now. An attacker
            // can control a tag byte from the wire. Thus `@enumFromInt` on
            // the byte is undefined behaviour.
            .kind = std.enums.fromInt(Kind, kind) orelse return error.UnknownKind,
            .length = try r.takeInt(u32, .big),
            .checksum = try r.takeInt(u16, .big),
        };
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const payload = "hello";
    const header: Header = .{
        .magic = Header.magic_value,
        .version = 1,
        .kind = .request,
        .length = payload.len,
        .checksum = 0xBEEF,
    };

    // The struct in memory is larger than the message on the wire, because
    // the compiler can pad and change the order. You cannot send a struct
    // as it is, because you do not control the padding bytes.
    try out.print("@sizeOf(Header) = {d}, on the wire = {d}\n\n", .{
        @sizeOf(Header),
        Header.wire_size,
    });

    var wire: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&wire);
    try header.write(&w);
    try w.writeAll(payload);

    try out.print("wire: {x}\n", .{w.buffered()});
    try out.print("      ^^^^ magic  ^^ version  ^^ kind  ^^^^^^^^ length\n\n", .{});

    var r: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(w.buffered());
    const back = try Header.read(&r);
    const body = try r.take(back.length);
    try out.print("decoded: version {d}, {s}, {d} bytes: \"{s}\"\n\n", .{
        back.version,
        @tagName(back.kind),
        back.length,
        body,
    });

    // Write as big-endian, read as little-endian. No function returns an
    // error. The length is only wrong. It is so large that the receiver
    // tries to allocate or wait for 83 million bytes.
    var swapped: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(w.buffered()[4..8]);
    try out.print("length read as big-endian:    {d}\n", .{
        std.mem.readInt(u32, w.buffered()[4..8], .big),
    });
    try out.print("length read as little-endian: {d}\n", .{
        try swapped.takeInt(u32, .little),
    });

    // The other half of a header check. If a peer does not use your
    // protocol, reject the peer on the first two bytes. Do this before
    // the parser trusts a length.
    var junk: std.Io.Reader = .fixed("GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n");
    if (Header.read(&junk)) |_| {
        try out.writeAll("\nan HTTP request into this parser: accepted\n");
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("\nan HTTP request into this parser: {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.binary-protocols`)*

## A struct is not a wire format

```
@sizeOf(Header) = 12, on the wire = 10
```

The struct is larger than the message. Zig can pad a struct, and Zig can
change the order of its fields. You do not control the padding bytes. They
contain the data that was in that memory before. If you send the struct, you
send two bytes of other data. Also, the layout that you send is the layout
that your compiler selected for your target today.

```zig
// Do not do this.
try socket.writeAll(std.mem.asBytes(&header));
```

`extern struct` makes the layout fixed. It is the correct tool for calls to
C, as [ABI](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/abi/) shows. But `extern struct` does not
make the byte order fixed, thus it is not sufficient here.

Write the fields:

```zig
try w.writeInt(u16, self.magic, .big);
try w.writeInt(u8, self.version, .big);
```

This method needs more code. It is also the only method that still works
with a different compiler, a different target, or a peer in a different
language.

## Say which end first

```
length read as big-endian:    5
length read as little-endian: 83886080
```

No function returned an error. The length is only wrong, but it is wrong in
a dangerous way. If a receiver trusts this length, the receiver tries to wait
for 83 megabytes, or to allocate 83 megabytes. The cause is one message of
five bytes.

By convention, network byte order is big-endian. Obey the convention, also
when the two ends are little-endian computers today. One day, one of the two
ends will possibly not be little-endian. State the endianness at each call.
`readInt` and `writeInt` require the argument, thus you cannot forget it.

The [Byte Order](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/integer-rules/) rules are most
important here. Inside your process, byte order is never a problem.

## Reject before you trust

```
an HTTP request into this parser: NotOurProtocol
```

The parser checks the magic number before it reads a length. When a port on
the internet opens, it receives HTTP requests, TLS handshakes and scanner
probes in a few minutes. If you let the parser accept them, each of these
messages will parse as *something*. Two bytes of magic make the parser
reject them immediately.

The same rule applies to the tag byte:

```zig
.kind = std.enums.fromInt(Kind, kind) orelse return error.UnknownKind,
```

An attacker can control a byte from the wire. If you use `@enumFromInt` on a
value that is not a valid tag, the behaviour is undefined.
`std.enums.fromInt` returns null for that value. `std.enums.fromInt` replaced
`std.meta.intToEnum`, which does not exist now. If your code uses
`std.meta.intToEnum`, change it to `std.enums.fromInt`.

---

## Serve Many Clients

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/many-clients/*

If a server handles one connection at a time, one slow client can stop the
server. There are two usual solutions, and each solution has a cost:

- One thread for each connection. Each thread costs a stack, and the server
  cannot scale past some thousands of threads.
- A single-threaded event loop. The loop can scale, but each function that
  you write must use callbacks.

Zig uses neither of these two solutions. This page runs the Zig solution in
your browser, on a target that has no threads.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// A connection without the transport. The handler below reads bytes and
/// writes bytes. It does not know if the bytes came from a socket. Thus this
/// page can run in a browser that has no sockets. Chapter two puts a
/// `std.Io.net.Server` in front of the same handler.
const Connection = struct {
    request: []const u8,
    reply: [64]u8 = undefined,
    reply_len: usize = 0,

    fn written(self: *const Connection) []const u8 {
        return self.reply[0..self.reply_len];
    }
};

/// Not `!void`, by design. A task in a Group cannot return an error to a
/// caller. Thus a failure in a connection must become a part of the reply
/// for that connection. One bad client must not stop the server.
fn handle(conn: *Connection, counter: *usize, mutex: *std.Io.Mutex, io: std.Io) void {
    var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&conn.reply);

    var it = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, conn.request, ' ');
    const verb = it.next() orelse "";

    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "ECHO")) {
        w.print("+{s}\r\n", .{it.rest()}) catch {};
    } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "COUNT")) {
        // Shared state, thus it needs the lock. The implementation decides
        // if `io.async` is parallel. If code is correct only with the
        // single-threaded implementation, the code has a race when you
        // deploy it on a threaded implementation.
        mutex.lock(io) catch return;
        defer mutex.unlock(io);
        counter.* += 1;
        w.print(":{d}\r\n", .{counter.*}) catch {};
    } else {
        w.print("-ERR unknown command '{s}'\r\n", .{verb}) catch {};
    }

    conn.reply_len = w.buffered().len;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var conns = [_]Connection{
        .{ .request = "ECHO first" },
        .{ .request = "COUNT" },
        .{ .request = "ECHO second" },
        .{ .request = "COUNT" },
        .{ .request = "SUBSCRIBE news" },
        .{ .request = "COUNT" },
    };

    var counter: usize = 0;
    var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;

    // A Group owns its tasks. The await waits for each task, and no task
    // continues after this scope. A bare `Thread.spawn` for each connection
    // does not give you this. Thus a server with a Group can stop, and it
    // does not leak connections that it forgot.
    var group: std.Io.Group = .init;
    for (&conns) |*conn| {
        group.async(io, handle, .{ conn, &counter, &mutex, io });
    }
    try group.await(io);

    // Print the replies in the order of the connections, not in the order
    // that the tasks completed. The implementation selected that order. A
    // threaded Io and the single-threaded Io of this page can complete the
    // tasks in different orders.
    for (&conns, 1..) |*conn, n| {
        try out.print("conn {d}: {s: <16} -> ", .{ n, conn.request });
        for (conn.written()) |byte| switch (byte) {
            '\r' => try out.writeAll("\\r"),
            '\n' => try out.writeAll("\\n"),
            else => try out.writeByte(byte),
        };
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }

    try out.print("\nCOUNT reached {d} across {d} connections\n", .{ counter, conns.len });
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.many-clients`)*

## The handler does not know about sockets

```zig
const Connection = struct {
    request: []const u8,
    reply: [64]u8 = undefined,
    reply_len: usize = 0,
};
```

The struct has no transport, by design. `handle` reads bytes and writes
bytes. It does not know where the bytes came from. Thus this page runs
without a network below it. If you put a `std.Io.net.Server` in front of the
same function, you get [the TCP round trip](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/tcp-echo/).

Write protocol code for `Reader` and `Writer`, not for a socket. Then the
tests are fast, and the browser can run the example.

## `io.async`, not `Thread.spawn`

```zig
var group: std.Io.Group = .init;
for (&conns) |*conn| {
    group.async(io, handle, .{ conn, &counter, &mutex, io });
}
try group.await(io);
```

The `Io` implementation decides what "async" means. `std.Io.Threaded` runs
the tasks on a thread pool. This page runs on the single-threaded WASI
implementation, which runs the tasks inline. **The source does not change.**
For this reason, you cannot run the [Threads](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/threads/)
page here, but you can run this page.

If you used an older version of Zig, you possibly look for the `async` and
`await` keywords. Zig removed these keywords. `io.async` replaced them, as a
library function and not as syntax.
[Concurrency](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/) shows the general
shape.

## A Group so nothing outlives the scope

`Group` owns its tasks. When you await the group, it waits for all of its
tasks. When you cancel the group, it cancels all of its tasks. Thus a
connection handler cannot continue after the end of the server that started
it. A bare `Thread.spawn` for each connection does not give you this
guarantee. To stop the server cleanly, you must then record each thread that
you started.

[Cancellation](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/) shows what a
handler sees when you cancel its group.

## A handler cannot return an error

```zig
fn handle(conn: *Connection, counter: *usize, mutex: *std.Io.Mutex, io: std.Io) void {
```

Look at the `void`. There is no caller that can receive an error, because
the caller continued to the next connection. Thus a failure in a connection
must become a part of the reply for that connection. The [text protocol
chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/text-protocols/) came to the same result from the
other direction. If one client sends bad data, no other client must see an
effect.

## Shared state still needs a lock

```zig
mutex.lock(io) catch return;
defer mutex.unlock(io);
counter.* += 1;
```

This page uses the single-threaded implementation, and that implementation
works without the mutex. Do not trust that result. Some code is correct only
with the implementation that you used for the tests. That code has a data
race, and the race can occur after you deploy the code. The cause is that the
`Io` in production is the threaded implementation.

`lock` takes the `io` and returns an error. The function can block, thus a
cancel can stop it.

## Why the replies print in order

The tasks completed in the order that the implementation selected. The loop
that prints the replies runs after the tasks, and it uses the order of the
connections. Thus the output is the same with each implementation. If the
handlers printed the replies, the lines would have a different order on a
threaded `Io`.

The `COUNT` values are the exception. They show the order in which the tasks
got the mutex. If you run this program natively, the values can have a
different order.

---

## Failure Is Ordinary

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/network-errors/*

On a network, failure is normal. A client can stop in the middle of a
request, and a computer can stop. Also, each connection ends when it
succeeds. These events will occur. The important question is if your code can
see the difference between them.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The client half of the clean-shutdown case: send a full message, then
/// close. The server must see the message and then a normal end.
fn sendThenClose(address: std.Io.net.IpAddress, io: std.Io) void {
    var stream = address.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream }) catch return;
    defer stream.close(io);

    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = stream.writer(io, &buf);
    writer.interface.writeAll("complete\n") catch return;
    writer.interface.flush() catch return;
}

/// The truncated case: half of a message, then close. The bytes are valid.
/// But there are not sufficient bytes to make a message.
fn sendPartialThenClose(address: std.Io.net.IpAddress, io: std.Io) void {
    var stream = address.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream }) catch return;
    defer stream.close(io);

    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = stream.writer(io, &buf);
    writer.interface.writeAll("truncat") catch return;
    writer.interface.flush() catch return;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const any_port = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    var server = try any_port.listen(io, .{});
    const address = server.socket.address;

    // 1. The peer completed its message and closed the connection. Each
    //    connection does this at the end. If you make it a failure, you log
    //    an error for each successful conversation.
    {
        const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, sendThenClose, .{ address, io });
        defer thread.join();

        var conn = try server.accept(io);
        defer conn.close(io);

        var read_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
        var reader = conn.reader(io, &read_buf);
        const line = try reader.interface.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n');
        try out.print("clean close:  read \"{s}\", then ", .{line});

        // The delimiter is not consumed yet. Skip it and read again.
        reader.interface.toss(1);
        if (reader.interface.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n')) |_| {
            try out.writeAll("more data\n");
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("{s} (expected: the client is done)\n", .{@errorName(err)});
        }
    }

    // 2. The peer closed the connection in the middle of a message. It is
    //    easy to make a mistake here. Read the doc comment on
    //    `takeDelimiterExclusive`. The comment says: "End-of-stream is
    //    treated equivalent to a delimiter." If a client stops in the middle of a line, you get a
    //    fragment. The fragment looks the same as a complete message. There
    //    is no error and no flag to check.
    {
        const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, sendPartialThenClose, .{ address, io });
        defer thread.join();

        var conn = try server.accept(io);
        defer conn.close(io);

        var read_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
        var reader = conn.reader(io, &read_buf);
        const fragment = try reader.interface.takeDelimiterExclusive('\n');
        try out.print("truncated:    Exclusive returned \"{s}\" and no error\n", .{fragment});
    }

    // 3. The same half of a message, but this call requires the delimiter.
    //    `takeDelimiterInclusive` returns the byte as a part of the slice.
    //    Thus it cannot invent a delimiter. The end of the stream without
    //    the delimiter is `EndOfStream`, and you discard the bytes.
    {
        const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, sendPartialThenClose, .{ address, io });
        defer thread.join();

        var conn = try server.accept(io);
        defer conn.close(io);

        var read_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
        var reader = conn.reader(io, &read_buf);
        if (reader.interface.takeDelimiterInclusive('\n')) |line| {
            try out.print("truncated:    Inclusive returned \"{s}\"\n", .{line});
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("truncated:    Inclusive returned {s}, so the ", .{@errorName(err)});
            try out.print("{d} buffered bytes get discarded\n", .{reader.interface.buffered().len});
        }
    }

    // 4. No program listens. The code closes the listener first, thus the
    //    port is real and not in use. The kernel replies for the computer,
    //    and the connect fails immediately. It does not wait.
    server.deinit(io);
    if (address.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream })) |stream| {
        var s = stream;
        s.close(io);
        try out.writeAll("refused:      connected anyway\n");
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("refused:      {s}\n", .{@errorName(err)});
    }

    try out.writeAll(
        \\
        \\None of these are bugs in your program, and all of them will happen.
        \\The one worth remembering is the second: a truncated message came
        \\back as a successful read, and only the choice of call decided
        \\whether the server acted on half a request.
        \\
    );

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Built and run natively by CI, over real loopback sockets. Browser wasm has no sockets. (`11-networking.network-errors`)*

## The clean close

```
clean close:  read "complete", then EndOfStream (expected: the client is done)
```

`EndOfStream` after a complete message is the normal end of a successful
conversation. If you make it a failure, you log an error for each client that
operates correctly. Then the log has no value.

## The truncated message

```
truncated:    Exclusive returned "truncat" and no error
```

The client sent `"truncat"` and then stopped. The client did not send a
newline. But `takeDelimiterExclusive` returned the bytes as a message, with
success. The result has no error and no flag to check.

This is not a bug in the standard library. The documentation says:

> End-of-stream is treated equivalent to a delimiter, unless it would result
> in a length 0 return value, in which case `error.EndOfStream` is returned
> instead.

That behaviour is correct for a text file, because the last line of a text
file often has no newline at the end. The behaviour is wrong for a socket. On
a socket, the absence of the delimiter is the only sign that the sender did not
complete the message. If your protocol does an action on the data that it
reads, this default does an action on half of a request.

## The call that does not invent a delimiter

```
truncated:    Inclusive returned EndOfStream, so the 7 buffered bytes get discarded
```

`takeDelimiterInclusive` returns the delimiter as a part of the slice. Thus
the function cannot invent a delimiter. If there is no delimiter, the result
is `EndOfStream`, and you discard the fragment.

The rule is short: **on a stream that can carry a partial message, use
`takeDelimiterInclusive`, and remove the delimiter in your code.** Use
`takeDelimiterExclusive` only when a truncated last record is acceptable. On
a socket, a truncated record is almost never acceptable.

## Refused

```
refused:      ConnectionRefused
```

No program listened on the port. Thus the kernel on the other computer sent
the answer, and the connect failed immediately. This is the good case. In the
bad case, the host does not answer. Then the connect waits until a timeout
that you did not set. The default timeout is some minutes long.

## What to do for each error

| What happened | What it means | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EndOfStream`, message complete | The client completed its work | Close, do not log an error |
| `EndOfStream`, message partial | The client stopped in the middle of a request | Discard the fragment, close |
| `ConnectionRefused` | No program listens there | Fail fast, wait before you try again |
| `ConnectionResetByPeer` | The peer closed abruptly, or crashed | Same as a partial message |
| `BrokenPipe` on write | The peer is gone, and you still write | Stop, close, do not try the write again |

A loopback test does not cause the last two errors. For this reason, the last
two errors are in the table and not in the snippet.

---

## UDP Datagrams

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/udp-message/*

In Zig, a UDP socket comes from `std.Io.net.IpAddress.bind` with `.mode
= .dgram`. There is no `listen` and no `accept`. Each `send` names its
destination. Each `receive` returns the data and the address of the sender.

## The problem

Some traffic does not need a connection: metrics, discovery pings, game
state and sensor readings. The loss of one message is acceptable. The cost of
the ordering and retransmission in TCP is not acceptable. For this traffic,
use UDP. The API of UDP is very different from TCP, thus the "listen and
accept" model does not apply.

There is nothing to accept. A socket binds to an address, and messages arrive
at any time.

## The plan

1. Call `bind` with `.mode = .dgram`, not `listen`. If you bind to port 0,
   the OS selects an ephemeral port and records it in `socket.address`.
2. Send with `socket.send(io, &destination, bytes)`. Each message has a
   destination, because there is no connection to remember the destination.
3. Receive with `socket.receive(io, &buffer)`. This function returns the data
   slice and the address of the sender.
4. To reply, send to that address. There is no connection for the answer,
   thus the reply is only one more `send`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // A datagram socket binds, and does not listen. There is no connection
    // to accept. There is only an address that can receive messages.
    const any_port = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    const receiver = try any_port.bind(io, .{ .mode = .dgram });
    defer receiver.close(io);

    const sender = try any_port.bind(io, .{ .mode = .dgram });
    defer sender.close(io);

    // Send first, receive second, on one thread. The kernel keeps the
    // datagram until a program asks for it. Thus the send and the receive
    // are independent steps.
    // `receiver.address` holds the ephemeral port that the OS selected.
    try sender.send(io, &receiver.address, "reading: 21.4C");

    var data_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    const msg = try receiver.receive(io, &data_buf);

    try out.print("got {d} bytes: \"{s}\"\n", .{ msg.data.len, msg.data });

    // Each datagram is one unit. This second message cannot merge with the
    // first message. Bytes on a TCP stream can merge.
    try sender.send(io, &receiver.address, "reading: 21.6C");
    const second = try receiver.receive(io, &data_buf);
    try out.print("got {d} bytes: \"{s}\"\n", .{ second.data.len, second.data });

    // The message holds the address of the sender in `second.from`. A send
    // to that address is a reply, with no accept and no connection. The
    // receiver knows only the address in the packet about the sender. The
    // receiver needs no more data.
    var upper_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    const reply = std.ascii.upperString(&upper_buf, second.data);
    try receiver.send(io, &second.from, reply);

    var reply_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    const answer = try sender.receive(io, &reply_buf);
    try out.print("reply: \"{s}\"\n", .{answer.data});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this snippet natively, and sends real datagrams over loopback. Browser wasm has no sockets. (`11-networking.udp-message`)*

## Why this program needs no threads

The snippet sends a message and reads it. Then it sends one more message and
reads that message. All of this occurs on one thread. No code must wait when
a datagram arrives, because the kernel keeps the datagrams on the bound
socket until a program reads them.

UDP works in this way: the sender and the
receiver never meet. They only share an address. (The queue has a limit.
When the queue is full, the kernel drops datagrams, and UDP permits that.)

## Message boundaries are real

Two `send` calls gave exactly two `receive` results, of 14 bytes each. TCP
can deliver those 28 bytes as one read or as three reads. A datagram socket
never merges or splits messages. Protocol designers select UDP for this
property. The property comes with a limit: if a datagram is larger than the
receive buffer, the kernel truncates the datagram. `msg.flags.trunc` shows
the truncation.

## Reply without a connection

The last step changes the message to uppercase and sends it back. Look at
what this step does not need. In TCP, a server that sends an answer must
`accept` and keep a socket for that client. Here, the receiver knows one
thing about the sender: the address in `second.from`. The receiver sends to
that address, and then its work is complete.

Request and response over UDP need only a receive and then a send. DNS works
in this way: one datagram asks, one datagram answers, and no connection ever
exists.

## Variations

- **Timeouts:** `receiveTimeout` returns `error.Timeout` and does not block
  forever. Use it to wait a maximum of one second for a reply.
- **Broadcast:** to send to broadcast addresses on a LAN, set
  `.allow_broadcast = true` in the bind options.

---

## Lost Datagrams

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/packet-loss/*

A network that carries UDP datagrams does three things to them. It loses some
datagrams, it delivers some datagrams two times, and it delivers some
datagrams in the wrong order.

## The problem

UDP does not promise to deliver anything. The
[previous chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/udp-message/) sent datagrams over
loopback. On loopback, datagrams always arrive, thus none of these failures
occurred.

It is difficult to learn how to handle failures that you never see. Thus this
chapter makes the failures. The snippet is a channel that operates
incorrectly by design. A seeded random generator controls the channel, thus
each run has the same failures. The next two chapters send their traffic
through the same type of channel, and they fix each problem in turn.

## The plan

1. Make a `FlakyChannel` with one method: put a datagram in, and see what
   comes out. Sometimes nothing comes out. Sometimes the datagram comes out
   two times. Sometimes an older datagram arrives late.
2. Send ten numbered datagrams through the channel.
3. Let the receiver count what arrived and name each failure.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// A channel that operates incorrectly, as a real network does. Each
/// datagram is one byte. A seeded generator decides the fate of each
/// datagram. Thus each run of this program sees exactly the same network.
const FlakyChannel = struct {
    prng: std.Random.DefaultPrng,
    /// A datagram that the channel keeps, to deliver after a later datagram.
    delayed: ?u8 = null,

    fn init(seed: u64) FlakyChannel {
        return .{ .prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(seed) };
    }

    /// Put one datagram in. Returns the output at the far end now: nothing,
    /// the datagram, the datagram two times, or an older datagram late.
    fn transmit(self: *FlakyChannel, datagram: u8, out: *[3]u8) []const u8 {
        var n: usize = 0;
        const fate = self.prng.random().uintLessThan(u8, 10);
        switch (fate) {
            // Dropped. The channel does not report the drop.
            0, 1 => {},
            // Duplicated: a retry in a lower layer sent the datagram again.
            2 => {
                out[n] = datagram;
                out[n + 1] = datagram;
                n += 2;
            },
            // Delayed: the channel keeps the datagram. It will arrive after a
            // newer datagram.
            3 => self.delayed = datagram,
            else => {
                out[n] = datagram;
                n += 1;
            },
        }
        // A datagram that the channel kept arrives now, after the newer
        // datagram. This is reordering.
        if (fate != 3) {
            if (self.delayed) |old| {
                out[n] = old;
                n += 1;
                self.delayed = null;
            }
        }
        return out[0..n];
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var channel = FlakyChannel.init(4);

    // The receiver keeps a count for each datagram, and it records the
    // highest number. This data is sufficient to name each failure later.
    var seen: [10]u8 = @splat(0);
    var highest: u8 = 0;
    var late: [10]bool = @splat(false);

    for (0..10) |i| {
        const seq: u8 = @intCast(i);
        try out.print("send {d}\n", .{seq});
        var slots: [3]u8 = undefined;
        for (channel.transmit(seq, &slots)) |got| {
            try out.print("  got {d}\n", .{got});
            if (got < highest) late[got] = true;
            if (got > highest) highest = got;
            seen[got] += 1;
        }
    }

    // What the receiver can say after the run. During the run, the receiver
    // cannot know "lost" from "not sent yet". In the two cases, nothing
    // arrives.
    try out.writeAll("\n");
    for (seen, 0..) |count, seq| {
        if (count == 0) try out.print("never arrived: {d}\n", .{seq});
        if (count > 1) try out.print("arrived twice: {d}\n", .{seq});
        if (late[seq]) try out.print("arrived late:  {d}\n", .{seq});
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.packet-loss`)*

## Silence looks the same as no traffic

The channel dropped datagram 0, and the trace for datagram 0 is empty. The
receiver does not see a gap at the position of datagram 0. The receiver sees
nothing. The receiver also sees nothing before the traffic starts and between
datagrams. Thus the receiver cannot see a loss at the time of the loss.

After the run, this receiver can name the lost datagram. There are two
reasons for this:

- The snippet numbered the datagrams.
- The snippet told the receiver that ten datagrams will arrive.

A real receiver does not know these two facts until the
protocol tells it. The next chapter adds these facts to the protocol.

## The cause of duplicates

The channel duplicated datagram 1, but the sender sent it one time only. Real
networks do this, but the fix for loss is a much more frequent cause. If a
sender sends a message again after a silence, the sender cannot know which
of these two conditions is true:

- The datagram of the sender was lost.
- The reply was lost.

In the second condition, the receiver gets the message two times. Thus each
protocol that tries again must expect its own retries to arrive. Two chapters
after this one, the receiver handles this problem. It uses the same sequence
numbers that it uses to find gaps.

## Reordering is only delay

Datagram 4 arrived after datagram 5. Nothing exchanged the two datagrams. The
channel kept datagram 4, and datagram 5 arrived before it. On real networks,
two datagrams can use different routes, and the second datagram can arrive
first.

Reordering makes the detection of loss more difficult. A gap in the numbers
can be a lost datagram, or a slow datagram that is still on the way. TCP has
exactly this problem. The TCP solution is to wait a short time, then stop the
wait and send again. The retransmission chapter of this section adds this
timeout logic.

## Variations

- **Change the probability:** the fate roll gives each datagram a 2 in 10
  probability that the channel drops it. Increase the value, and the summary
  becomes longer. A channel that drops half of all datagrams is similar to
  wifi at the edge of its range.
- **Change the seed:** a different seed is a different network. The failures
  occur to different datagrams, but the types of failure stay the same.
- **No corruption here:** real networks also change bits. But UDP carries a
  checksum, thus the network stack discards corrupted datagrams before your
  program sees them. Corruption arrives at your program as loss.

---

## Sequence Numbers and Acks

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/sequence-numbers/*

A sequence number on each message lets a receiver find loss and duplicates.
A cumulative ack ("I have everything through N") tells the sender what to send
again. The acks in TCP use the same design.

## The problem

At the end of the previous chapter, the receiver could not see the difference
between loss and silence. The fix costs one byte: put a number on each
message. If a receiver expects 2 and gets 3, the receiver now knows that a
message is lost. The network did not report the loss. If a receiver gets 4
two times, the receiver knows that the second 4 is a retry, not a new message.

Detection is only half of the work. The receiver knows about the gap, but the
sender has the lost message. Thus the receiver sends a report back. This
report is an acknowledgement in the other direction. It tells the sender how
much of the stream the receiver has. The reply gives the loss to the sender,
and only the sender can fix the loss.

## The plan

1. Use the same channel that operates incorrectly, but with a script. The
   channel drops datagram 2 and duplicates datagram 4. Thus you can check
   each line of the output by hand.
2. Make a `Watcher` with one field: the next number that it expects. A number
   below that value is a duplicate. An equal number is in order. A number
   above that value is a gap, and the gap has exact edges.
3. Make a receiver that sends acks. It answers each arrival with "I have
   everything through N". Make a sender that reads these answers.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The network that operates incorrectly, with a script and not random. It
/// drops datagram 2 and duplicates datagram 4. It uses a script because
/// this chapter is about the logic of the receiver. You can check each line
/// of the output against these two rules.
fn transmit(seq: u8, out: *[2]u8) []const u8 {
    if (seq == 2) return out[0..0];
    out[0] = seq;
    if (seq == 4) {
        out[1] = seq;
        return out[0..2];
    }
    return out[0..1];
}

/// To find problems, the receiver needs only one number: the sequence number
/// that it expects next. Below it: seen before. Equal: in order. Above it:
/// the numbers between the two never arrived.
const Watcher = struct {
    next: u8 = 0,

    const Verdict = union(enum) { in_order, duplicate, gap_after: u8 };

    fn accept(self: *Watcher, seq: u8) Verdict {
        if (seq < self.next) return .duplicate;
        const expected = self.next;
        self.next = seq + 1;
        if (seq == expected) return .in_order;
        return .{ .gap_after = expected };
    }
};

/// For acks, the receiver records what it *has*, without gaps from the
/// start. It moves forward only on the exact next number. It answers each
/// arrival with that count. The answer is cumulative: "I have everything
/// through N" also confirms all that the earlier acks confirmed.
const AckSender = struct {
    have: ?u8 = null,

    fn accept(self: *AckSender, seq: u8) ?u8 {
        const want = if (self.have) |h| h + 1 else 0;
        if (seq == want) self.have = seq;
        return self.have;
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // First: the receiver names each failure when it occurs.
    try out.writeAll("-- numbering finds the failures --\n");
    var watcher = Watcher{};
    for (0..6) |i| {
        const seq: u8 = @intCast(i);
        try out.print("send {d}\n", .{seq});
        var slots: [2]u8 = undefined;
        for (transmit(seq, &slots)) |got| {
            switch (watcher.accept(got)) {
                .in_order => try out.print("  got {d}, in order\n", .{got}),
                .duplicate => try out.print("  got {d} again, dropped\n", .{got}),
                .gap_after => |from| if (from == got - 1) {
                    try out.print("  got {d}: gap, {d} never arrived\n", .{ got, from });
                } else {
                    try out.print(
                        "  got {d}: gap, {d} through {d} never arrived\n",
                        .{ got, from, got - 1 },
                    );
                },
            }
        }
    }

    // Second: the receiver sends a report, and the sender learns.
    try out.writeAll("\n-- acks tell the sender --\n");
    var acker = AckSender{};
    var acked_through: ?u8 = null;
    for (0..6) |i| {
        const seq: u8 = @intCast(i);
        var slots: [2]u8 = undefined;
        const arrivals = transmit(seq, &slots);
        if (arrivals.len == 0) {
            try out.print("send {d}: no ack came back\n", .{seq});
            continue;
        }
        for (arrivals) |got| {
            const ack = acker.accept(got);
            acked_through = ack;
            if (ack) |a| {
                try out.print("send {d}: ack \"have 0 through {d}\"\n", .{ seq, a });
            } else {
                try out.print("send {d}: ack \"have nothing\"\n", .{seq});
            }
        }
    }

    // The sender knows only the acks. The sender never saw the drop. It
    // sees only which of its messages got no confirmation.
    if (acked_through) |a| {
        try out.print("\nsender: confirmed through {d}, so {d} through 5 need resending\n", .{ a, a + 1 });
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.sequence-numbers`)*

## One counter, three verdicts

The `Watcher` is one `u8` and a comparison. Detection with sequence numbers
needs only these two things. Each result in the first half of the trace comes
from one rule: numbers arrive in order unless the network causes a problem.
The comparison that finds gaps also finds the duplicate of 4.

The last chapter said that retries cause duplicates. This receiver already
handles duplicates, one chapter before retries occur.

The scripted channel does not change the order of datagrams, by design. With
reordering, "3 arrived and 2 did not" can mean that 2 is lost or only late.
The receiver cannot know which yet. Sequence numbers find that a problem
exists. To decide that the problem is loss, you need a timeout. The timeout
is the first step of the next chapter.

## Acks are cumulative by design

The receiver that sends acks never says "I got 3". It says "I have everything through
1", also while 3, 4 and 5 arrive. These words have two effects:

- Acks repair themselves. If one ack is lost, the next arrival repeats all of
  the information in the lost ack.
- The sender must record only one number.

Look at the last line of the trace. The sender got "through 1" and decided
that it must send 2 through 5 again. The sender never saw the drop. It found the
loss from the replies only. TCP uses this design for acks. The version in
this snippet is different mainly in the byte layout.

The trace also shows the cost: 3, 4 and 5 arrived, but a simple sender like
this one sends them again. A real receiver keeps the out-of-order arrivals in
a buffer, thus the resends are cheap. A real sender also has better recovery.
The shape of the exchange does not change.

## Acks use the same network

In this snippet, the acks always arrive. This is the one simplification, and
it keeps the trace easy to read. On a real network, the ack for 2 can
disappear, as 2 can disappear. The sender cannot see a difference between
these two cases. The sender uses the same tool for the two cases. The
duplicate check in the receiver makes this safe: if the sender sends a
received message again, it wastes time but causes no harm.

The next chapter puts these parts in a loop, and the clock decides when to
use them.

## Variations

- **Change the script:** drop 0, not 2. Then the first ack becomes "have
  nothing". The sender gets the same quantity of information from that ack.
- **Wrap-around:** a `u8` sequence number gets to 255 and wraps. Real
  protocols select a counter size so that an old number cannot occur again while
  its datagram can still be on the network. TCP uses 32 bits.
- **Selective acks:** "I have 0 through 1, and also 3 through 5" names the
  exact hole, but the reply is more complex. TCP added this as the SACK
  option, fifteen years after the first release of cumulative acks.

---

## Retransmission and the Window

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/retransmission/*

Retransmission sends a message again when its ack does not arrive before a
timeout. A sliding window keeps many messages in flight, thus one loss does
not stop the stream. Together with sequence numbers and cumulative acks, these
two methods are the core mechanism of TCP.

## The problem

The sender now knows which messages got no confirmation. The sender must
still recover these messages. Something must decide *when* to stop the wait
for an ack and send the message again. The data cannot make that decision.
Silence does not tell how long it will continue, thus the sender can only use
the clock. The sender waits a fixed time, then it sends again.

That fixes the delivery, but it causes a speed problem. If a sender sends one
message and waits for its ack, the sender spends most of its time in the wait.
The fix is a window: many messages in flight at the same time, each with its
own timer.

In this snippet, time is a counter that has the name tick. It is not a real
clock. The tick counter makes each run the same. The round trip of the ack
also costs no time. Thus the only delay in the trace comes from the timeout
policy.

## The plan

1. The scripted network drops transmissions by position: the 2nd and 4th data
   transmission, and the 4th ack. A retry is a new transmission, thus the
   network can also drop a retry.
2. The receiver is the receiver from the
   [previous chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/sequence-numbers/), with one change.
   It records what arrived and answers with a cumulative ack. It also keeps
   the arrivals that are out of order.
3. The sender records `base` (all messages below it have a confirmation) and
   `next`. It also records when it last sent each message in flight. After
   three ticks without an ack, the sender sends the message again.
4. Run the same 8 messages two times: first with a window of 1, then with a
   window of 4.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const message_count = 8;
const timeout_ticks = 3;

/// The network, with a script by position. It drops the 2nd and 4th data
/// transmission and the 4th ack. The count starts at 1. It counts positions
/// because the network does not know which message a transmission carries.
/// A retry is a new transmission, thus the network can also drop a retry.
const Wire = struct {
    data_sent: usize = 0,
    acks_sent: usize = 0,

    fn deliverData(self: *Wire) bool {
        self.data_sent += 1;
        return self.data_sent != 2 and self.data_sent != 4;
    }

    fn deliverAck(self: *Wire) bool {
        self.acks_sent += 1;
        return self.acks_sent != 4;
    }
};

/// The receiver records what it has, and it answers each arrival with a
/// cumulative ack, as in the previous chapter. But this receiver also keeps
/// the arrivals that are out of order. Thus it does not need them again.
const Receiver = struct {
    got: [message_count]bool = @splat(false),

    fn accept(self: *Receiver, seq: u8) ?u8 {
        self.got[seq] = true;
        var have: ?u8 = null;
        for (self.got, 0..) |g, i| {
            if (!g) break;
            have = @intCast(i);
        }
        return have;
    }
};

/// The state of the sender. All messages below `base` have a confirmation.
/// All messages from `base` to `next` are in flight. Each message in flight
/// records when the sender last sent it. Thus the clock can find a message
/// that is late.
const Sender = struct {
    base: u8 = 0,
    next: u8 = 0,
    sent_at: [message_count]usize = @splat(0),

    fn onAck(self: *Sender, have: ?u8) void {
        if (have) |h| {
            if (h + 1 > self.base) self.base = h + 1;
        }
    }
};

fn run(out: *std.Io.Writer, window: u8) !void {
    try out.print("-- window = {d} --\n", .{window});
    var wire = Wire{};
    var receiver = Receiver{};
    var sender = Sender{};

    var tick: usize = 1;
    while (sender.base < message_count and tick <= 40) : (tick += 1) {
        // First, the work of the clock: send again each message that is in
        // flight for too long.
        var seq = sender.base;
        while (seq < sender.next) : (seq += 1) {
            // An ack inside this loop can move `base` past a message that the
            // loop did not reach yet. That message has a confirmation now.
            if (seq < sender.base) continue;
            if (tick - sender.sent_at[seq] < timeout_ticks) continue;
            try out.print("tick {d:2}: {d} timed out, resend", .{ tick, seq });
            try transmit(out, &wire, &receiver, &sender, seq, tick);
        }
        // Then fill the window with new messages.
        while (sender.next < message_count and sender.next - sender.base < window) {
            const s = sender.next;
            sender.next += 1;
            try out.print("tick {d:2}: send {d}", .{ tick, s });
            try transmit(out, &wire, &receiver, &sender, s, tick);
        }
    }
    try out.print(
        "delivered {d} messages in {d} ticks, {d} transmissions\n\n",
        .{ sender.base, tick - 1, wire.data_sent },
    );
}

/// One transmission and, if it arrives, the ack that comes directly back.
/// The full round trip is inside one tick. Only a loss makes it longer.
fn transmit(
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    wire: *Wire,
    receiver: *Receiver,
    sender: *Sender,
    seq: u8,
    tick: usize,
) !void {
    sender.sent_at[seq] = tick;
    if (!wire.deliverData()) {
        try out.writeAll(" .. lost\n");
        return;
    }
    const had_it = receiver.got[seq];
    const have = receiver.accept(seq);
    if (!wire.deliverAck()) {
        try out.writeAll(" .. delivered, ack lost\n");
        return;
    }
    sender.onAck(have);
    if (had_it) {
        try out.writeAll(" .. receiver had it already, ack repeated\n");
    } else if (have) |h| {
        try out.print(" .. ack: have 0 through {d}\n", .{h});
    } else {
        try out.writeAll(" .. ack: have nothing\n");
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    try run(out, 1);
    try run(out, 4);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.retransmission`)*

## The timeout is a guess

Message 1 is lost at tick 1, and the sender sends it again at tick 4, because
the rule is three ticks of silence. Nothing confirmed the loss. The sender
guessed that the ack was so late that it would never arrive.

The two traces also show that the guess can be wrong. In the first trace,
message 3 arrives correctly, but its *ack* is lost. Thus the sender sends
again a message that the receiver already has. The sender can never see the
difference between a lost message and a lost ack.

The second trace shows a different cause. Message 2 arrives at tick 1, but
message 1 does not arrive. A cumulative ack cannot confirm message 2 before
message 1 arrives. Then the ack for the resend of message 1 is lost. Thus
at tick 4, message 2 still has no confirmation, and the sender sends it
again.

A wrong guess is safe because of the duplicate check in the receiver, from the
last chapter. The receiver ignores the second copy and repeats the ack. Thus
retransmission does not need certainty. It needs a receiver that accepts
duplicates without harm.

If the timeout has a bad value, you pay one of two costs:

- If the timeout is too long, each loss stops the stream.
- If the timeout is too short, the network fills with copies of messages that
  arrived correctly.

Here, three ticks is a constant, because the delay of the network never
changes. On a real network, the delay changes all the time. Thus TCP measures
the round trip and calculates the timeout from it. The timeout is still a
guess.

## What the window gives

The messages, the network and the losses are the same in the two runs. A
window of 1 takes 10 ticks, and a window of 4 takes 4 ticks. The difference
is in the ticks around a loss. With one message in flight, the loss of
message 1 stops all traffic. The stream waits during ticks 2 and 3, and it
delivers nothing.

With four messages in flight, messages 2 and 4 arrive while message 1
waits for its timeout. Message 3 is also lost, and its timer expires at the
same tick as the timer of message 1. Thus one round of resends at tick 4
recovers the two losses.

The two runs use the same number of transmissions, 11. In this run, the
window does not save transmissions. The window saves time, because the two
losses overlap and one timeout recovers both of them.

At tick 4, the resend of message 3 gets the ack "have 0 through 4". The timer
of message 4 also expired at tick 4. But that ack confirms message 4, thus
the loop does not send message 4 again. For this reason, the loop compares
each message with `base` again before it sends the message. The loop starts
at the old `base`, and an ack inside the loop can move `base` forward.

TCP adjusts the window all the time. TCP makes the window larger while
messages arrive. TCP makes the window smaller when a loss shows that the
network is possibly full. The name of that policy is congestion control, and
the policy is sufficiently large to fill a book. The mechanism below it is
the dozen lines in this snippet.

## What you built

Sequence numbers, cumulative acks, duplicate detection, timeout
retransmission and a sliding window are the core mechanism of TCP. You built
them in three short chapters, on a protocol that promises nothing.

Each guarantee of TCP comes from records and waits: the timeout stops, the
resends and the management of the window. When a connection feels slow on a
bad link, this mechanism is the cause.

For some traffic, the loss of a message is better than a wait of three ticks.
A position update in a game has no value when a newer update exists. UDP
exists for this type of traffic, where the recovery of a message costs more
than its loss.

QUIC, the transport below HTTP/3, runs on UDP, thus QUIC can do this work
itself. It does not use the TCP of the kernel. The recovery decisions move
into the application, where you can tune them for each stream. At this
level, the protocol that carries most of the web today runs the loop that you
just read.

## Variations

- **Give the ack a travel time:** let an ack need one tick to travel. Then a
  window of 1 sends only one message for each round trip. This occurs also on
  a perfect network. The other function of the window is to keep the link
  full, and on long links that function is most important.
- **Make the timeout 1 tick:** the recovery becomes faster, and the number of
  transmissions increases. This is the cost of a timeout that is too short.
- **Drop more acks:** the stream still completes. With cumulative acks, each
  later ack repairs the loss of an earlier ack.

---

## An HTTP Round Trip

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/http-roundtrip/*

The Zig standard library has the two halves of HTTP, with no dependencies:

- `std.http.Server` answers requests over any reader and writer.
- `std.http.Client.fetch` makes a request in one call.

The two halves use the `std.Io` reader and writer interfaces.

## The problem

Zig rebuilt the two halves on the `std.Io` interfaces. Most of the example
code that you can find for each half is older than that change.

As in [TCP](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/tcp-echo/), the recipe runs the server and the
client in one process. CI runs the recipe and compares the output. Thus, if
the page becomes out of date, CI fails.

## The plan

1. Listen on an ephemeral TCP port, as in the TCP recipe. HTTP is a layer on
   a TCP socket. HTTP does not need a different type of socket.
2. On the server thread, give the reader and writer of the accepted stream to
   `std.http.Server.init`. Then use a loop: `receiveHead()` gives a request,
   `request.head.target` selects the route, and `respond()` sends the answer.
3. On the client side, make a `std.http.Client`. Call `fetch()` with a URL
   and a `response_writer`. One call does the connect, the request, the
   redirects and the delivery of the body.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// The life of one connection. HTTP is a layer on the plain TCP stream. To
// make the layer, give the reader and writer of the stream to std.http.Server.
fn serve(listener: *std.Io.net.Server, io: std.Io) void {
    var conn = listener.accept(io) catch return;
    defer conn.close(io);

    var read_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var write_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = conn.reader(io, &read_buf);
    var writer = conn.writer(io, &write_buf);
    var http_server = std.http.Server.init(&reader.interface, &writer.interface);

    // With keep-alive, many requests can arrive on this connection. The
    // loop ends when the client completes its work and the stream closes.
    while (true) {
        var request = http_server.receiveHead() catch return;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, request.head.target, "/hello")) {
            request.respond("hello from zig\n", .{}) catch return;
        } else {
            request.respond("no such page\n", .{
                .status = .not_found,
            }) catch return;
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    const gpa = std.heap.page_allocator;

    var buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // The same setup as the TCP recipe: port 0, the OS selects a port, and
    // the socket records the port.
    const any_port = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    var listener = try any_port.listen(io, .{});
    defer listener.deinit(io);
    const port = listener.socket.address.getPort();

    const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, serve, .{ &listener, io });
    defer thread.join();

    var client: std.http.Client = .{ .allocator = gpa, .io = io };
    defer client.deinit();

    // fetch() does the full request: connect, send, follow the response,
    // and decompress if necessary. The body goes to the writer that you
    // give. `Allocating` collects the body into memory.
    var url_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var body: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
    defer body.deinit();

    const ok = try client.fetch(.{
        .location = .{ .url = try std.mem.print(
            &url_buf,
            "http://127.0.0.1:{d}/hello",
            .{port},
        ) },
        .response_writer = &body.writer,
    });
    try out.print("GET /hello -> {d}\n", .{@intFromEnum(ok.status)});
    try out.print("body: {s}", .{body.written()});

    // The second request uses the same keep-alive connection from the pool.
    const missing = try client.fetch(.{
        .location = .{ .url = try std.mem.print(
            &url_buf,
            "http://127.0.0.1:{d}/nope",
            .{port},
        ) },
    });
    try out.print("GET /nope  -> {d}\n", .{@intFromEnum(missing.status)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this snippet natively: a real client fetches from a real server over loopback. Browser wasm has no sockets. (`11-networking.http-roundtrip`)*

## The layers are real

`std.http.Server.init(&reader.interface, &writer.interface)` takes the same
two interfaces that each stream in current Zig has. The HTTP layer never sees
the socket. If you give it a pipe or a fixed buffer, it works in the same way.
The standard library tests it with a fixed buffer. If you know the TCP recipe,
only two parts are new: the parse of the head and the format of the response.
Both parts are in `std.http`.

The server loop also shows keep-alive. The two fetches in the snippet arrive
on one TCP connection, as two iterations of the `receiveHead` loop. The loop
ends when the connection pool of the client closes the stream.

## What fetch does for you

`fetch` is the one-call path. It does these steps:

1. It parses the URL.
2. It takes a connection from the pool, or it opens a connection.
3. It sends the request.
4. It follows redirects. For GET, the default maximum is three redirects.
5. If necessary, it decompresses the body.
6. It writes the body into the writer that you supply.

The result contains the status code. For streamed bodies, headers for each
request, or requests that stay open for a long time, use `client.request()`.
That function does the same steps, but you write each step in your code.

## Status is data, not an error

The 404 arrives as `FetchResult.status`, not as a Zig error. Errors are
for a failure of the transport, for example a refused connection or a
malformed response. Your application decides if a 404 is a failure. Use the
status enum to select the action: `.ok`, `.not_found`, or the numeric value
with `@intFromEnum`.

## Variations

- **POST:** set `.payload = body` in the fetch options. When a payload is
  present, the default method is POST.
- **Serve files:** use the router with reads from
  [Filesystem](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/filesystem/). `respond` takes any byte
  slice.
- **HTTPS:** `fetch` handles `https://` URLs with the bundled TLS client. The
  call site does not change.

---

## The WebSocket Handshake

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-handshake/*

HTTP is request and response. The client asks, the server answers, and the
server cannot speak first. A chat, a live score or a game needs messages in
both directions at any time. WebSocket gives a TCP connection to the two
sides for that purpose, and it starts as an ordinary HTTP request.

The client sends a `GET` with an `Upgrade: websocket` header. The server
answers `101 Switching Protocols`. After the empty line at the end of that
answer, the connection carries WebSocket frames, not HTTP. This chapter is
about the handshake. [WebSocket Frames](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-frames/)
is about the frames.

The program below plays both sides in memory. The server is
`std.http.Server`, the same type as in
[An HTTP Round Trip](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/http-roundtrip/).

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// RFC 6455 fixes this string. Each server appends it to the key of the
/// client, so the answer proves that the server read the request.
const guid = "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11";

/// The value of `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` for a key: the SHA-1 of the key and
/// the GUID, encoded in base64. A client computes the same value to check
/// the answer of the server.
fn acceptFor(key: []const u8) [28]u8 {
    var sha1 = std.crypto.hash.Sha1.init(.{});
    sha1.update(key);
    sha1.update(guid);
    var digest: [std.crypto.hash.Sha1.digest_length]u8 = undefined;
```
