```zig
    sha1.final(&digest);
    var accept: [28]u8 = undefined;
    _ = std.base64.standard.Encoder.encode(&accept, &digest);
    return accept;
}

/// The value of one header in a request, or null.
fn header(request: *const std.http.Server.Request, name: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    var it = request.iterateHeaders();
    while (it.next()) |h| {
        if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(h.name, name)) return h.value;
    }
    return null;
}

/// What the server decides about one request. std finds the upgrade and the
/// key. The checks of the key and the version are for your code to do.
const Decision = union(enum) {
    upgrade: []const u8,
    refuse: std.http.Status,
    plain_http,
};

fn decide(request: *const std.http.Server.Request) Decision {
    switch (request.upgradeRequested()) {
        // HTTP lets a server ignore an upgrade that it does not support.
        .none, .other => return .plain_http,
        .websocket => |maybe_key| {
            const key = maybe_key orelse return .{ .refuse = .bad_request };
            const version = header(request, "sec-websocket-version") orelse "";
            if (!std.mem.eql(u8, version, "13")) return .{ .refuse = .upgrade_required };
            return .{ .upgrade = key };
        },
    }
}

/// Show the bytes of an HTTP head, one line for each header, with the CR LF
/// at the end of each line written out.
fn printHead(out: *std.Io.Writer, bytes: []const u8) !void {
    var lines = std.mem.splitSequence(u8, bytes, "\r\n");
    while (lines.next()) |line| {
        if (lines.peek() == null) break;
        try out.print("  {s}\\r\\n\n", .{line});
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // The worked example from section 1.3 of RFC 6455.
    const key = "dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==";
    try out.print("key:    {s}\n", .{key});
    try out.print("accept: {s}\n\n", .{&acceptFor(key)});

    // The client sends an ordinary GET with four extra headers.
    const request_bytes =
        "GET /chat HTTP/1.1\r\n" ++
        "Host: example.com\r\n" ++
        "Upgrade: websocket\r\n" ++
        "Connection: Upgrade\r\n" ++
        "Sec-WebSocket-Key: " ++ key ++ "\r\n" ++
        "Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n" ++
        "\r\n";
    try out.print("client sends:\n", .{});
    try printHead(out, request_bytes);

    // The server reads from a Reader and writes to a Writer. Here both are
    // buffers in memory. Over a socket, they are the reader and the writer of
    // the stream, and nothing below changes.
    var in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(request_bytes);
    var response_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var response: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&response_buf);
    var server = std.http.Server.init(&in, &response);

    var request = try server.receiveHead();
    const accepted_key = switch (decide(&request)) {
        .upgrade => |k| k,
        else => return error.NotAnUpgrade,
    };
    var ws = try request.respondWebSocket(.{ .key = accepted_key });
    try ws.flush();

    try out.print("\nserver answers:\n", .{});
    try printHead(out, response.buffered());

    // The client checks the status and the accept value. If either is wrong,
    // the client must close the connection and not send frames.
    const answer = response.buffered();
    const status_ok = std.mem.startsWith(u8, answer, "HTTP/1.1 101 ");
    const expected = acceptFor(key);
    const accept_ok = std.mem.find(u8, answer, &expected) != null;
    try out.print("\nclient checks: status 101 {s}, accept {s}\n", .{
        if (status_ok) "ok" else "WRONG",
        if (accept_ok) "ok" else "WRONG",
    });

    // The checks that std.http.Server leaves to you. Each request goes to a
    // new server, and `decide` gives the answer.
    try out.print("\nother requests:\n", .{});
    const cases = [_]struct { name: []const u8, bytes: []const u8 }{
        .{ .name = "no key", .bytes = "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nSec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n\r\n" },
        .{ .name = "version 8", .bytes = "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nSec-WebSocket-Key: " ++ key ++ "\r\nSec-WebSocket-Version: 8\r\n\r\n" },
        .{ .name = "upgrade to h2c", .bytes = "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nUpgrade: h2c\r\n\r\n" },
        .{ .name = "POST with upgrade", .bytes = "POST / HTTP/1.1\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nSec-WebSocket-Key: " ++ key ++ "\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n" },
        .{ .name = "no upgrade", .bytes = "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n" },
    };
    for (cases) |case| {
        var case_in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(case.bytes);
        var sink_buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
        var sink: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&sink_buf);
        var case_server = std.http.Server.init(&case_in, &sink);
        const case_request = try case_server.receiveHead();
        switch (decide(&case_request)) {
            .upgrade => try out.print("  {s:<18} -> upgrade\n", .{case.name}),
            .refuse => |status| try out.print("  {s:<18} -> refuse with {d} {s}\n", .{
                case.name, @intFromEnum(status), status.phrase().?,
            }),
            .plain_http => try out.print("  {s:<18} -> ordinary HTTP request\n", .{case.name}),
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.websocket-handshake`)*

## The request

```
client sends:
  GET /chat HTTP/1.1\r\n
  Host: example.com\r\n
  Upgrade: websocket\r\n
  Connection: Upgrade\r\n
  Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==\r\n
  Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n
  \r\n
```

Four headers make this request an upgrade request:

- `Upgrade: websocket` names the protocol that the client wants.
- `Connection: Upgrade` tells each proxy on the path that the `Upgrade`
  header is for this connection.
- `Sec-WebSocket-Key` is 16 random bytes in base64. The client makes a new
  key for each connection.
- `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13` is the version from RFC 6455. No other version
  is in use.

The key is not a secret and it is not security. The key lets the client
check that the server read this request and understood it.

## The answer

The server appends a fixed GUID to the key. RFC 6455 defines the GUID. Then
the server computes the SHA-1 of the result and encodes the 20 bytes in
base64.

```zig
/// The value of `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` for a key: the SHA-1 of the key and
/// the GUID, encoded in base64. A client computes the same value to check
/// the answer of the server.
fn acceptFor(key: []const u8) [28]u8 {
    var sha1 = std.crypto.hash.Sha1.init(.{});
    sha1.update(key);
    sha1.update(guid);
    var digest: [std.crypto.hash.Sha1.digest_length]u8 = undefined;
    sha1.final(&digest);
    var accept: [28]u8 = undefined;
    _ = std.base64.standard.Encoder.encode(&accept, &digest);
    return accept;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `acceptFor` from `snippets/11-networking/websocket-handshake.zig`.*

The key in the program is the example from section 1.3 of RFC 6455. The RFC
gives the answer, and CI compares the output with it on each run:

```
key:    dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=
```

In std, `respondWebSocket` does this computation and writes the answer:

```
server answers:
  HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\n
  connection: upgrade\r\n
  upgrade: websocket\r\n
  sec-websocket-accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=\r\n
  \r\n
```

`respondWebSocket` writes into the buffer of the writer. It does not send
the bytes. Call `flush` on the `WebSocket` value that it returns, as the
program does. Otherwise the client waits for an answer that is still in your
buffer.

The client must check two things:

1. The status is 101. Any other status means that the server refused, or
   that the server does not know WebSocket.
2. The `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value is the value that the client computes
   from its own key.

If one check fails, the client closes the connection and sends no frames.

## What std checks, and what it does not

`request.upgradeRequested()` reads the headers and returns one of three
values:

- `.websocket` with the key, or with `null` if the request has no key.
- `.other` with the name of a different protocol, for example `h2c`.
- `.none` for an ordinary request. A `POST` and an HTTP/1.0 request always
  give `.none`, because RFC 6455 requires a `GET` on HTTP/1.1.

The function does not check the version, and it does not refuse a request
without a key. Those checks are for your code:

```zig
fn decide(request: *const std.http.Server.Request) Decision {
    switch (request.upgradeRequested()) {
        // HTTP lets a server ignore an upgrade that it does not support.
        .none, .other => return .plain_http,
        .websocket => |maybe_key| {
            const key = maybe_key orelse return .{ .refuse = .bad_request };
            const version = header(request, "sec-websocket-version") orelse "";
            if (!std.mem.eql(u8, version, "13")) return .{ .refuse = .upgrade_required };
            return .{ .upgrade = key };
        },
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `decide` from `snippets/11-networking/websocket-handshake.zig`.*

```
other requests:
  no key             -> refuse with 400 Bad Request
  version 8          -> refuse with 426 Upgrade Required
  upgrade to h2c     -> ordinary HTTP request
  POST with upgrade  -> ordinary HTTP request
  no upgrade         -> ordinary HTTP request
```

The two refusals are different. A request without a key is not a valid
upgrade request, thus the answer is 400. A request with the wrong version is valid HTTP for a
version that the server does not speak. RFC 6455 tells the server to answer
426 with a `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13` header, so that the client can try
again. Use the `extra_headers` option of `respond` to add the header.

An upgrade to a protocol that the server does not know is not an error.
HTTP lets a server ignore the `Upgrade` header and answer the request as
ordinary HTTP.

## The layers are the same

The server in the program reads from `std.Io.Reader.fixed` and writes to
`std.Io.Writer.fixed`. Over a socket, the reader and the writer come from
the stream, as in [A TCP Round Trip](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/tcp-echo/). Nothing
else changes. [A WebSocket Server on a Socket](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-server/)
runs the same handshake over a real connection.

`std.http.Client` has no WebSocket support. A client must write the request
and check the answer itself. [A WebSocket Client](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-client/)
does that.

---

## WebSocket Frames

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-frames/*

After the [handshake](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-handshake/), the
connection carries frames. A frame is a length-prefixed message, as in
[Three Ways to Frame](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/framing/), with a header of two to
fourteen bytes. The header tells the receiver four things:

- the type of the frame: text, binary, ping, pong or close
- if the frame is the last part of a message
- the length of the payload
- if the sender masked the payload, and with which mask

The program writes frames with std, decodes a header, masks a client frame
by hand, and gives eight frames to the reader of `std.http.Server`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const WebSocket = std.http.Server.WebSocket;

fn printBytes(out: *std.Io.Writer, bytes: []const u8) !void {
    for (bytes, 0..) |b, i| {
        if (i > 0) try out.writeByte(' ');
        try out.print("{x:0>2}", .{b});
    }
}

/// A frame from a client. The server writes frames with std, but std has no
/// client, so this is the other half. RFC 6455 requires a client to mask
/// each frame, and a server must refuse a frame without the mask.
fn writeClientFrame(
    w: *std.Io.Writer,
    opcode: WebSocket.Opcode,
    fin: bool,
    mask: [4]u8,
    payload: []const u8,
) !void {
    try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header0{ .opcode = opcode, .fin = fin }));
    if (payload.len <= 125) {
        try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header1{
            .payload_len = @enumFromInt(payload.len),
            .mask = true,
        }));
    } else if (payload.len <= 0xffff) {
        try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header1{ .payload_len = .len16, .mask = true }));
        try w.writeInt(u16, @intCast(payload.len), .big);
    } else {
        try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header1{ .payload_len = .len64, .mask = true }));
        try w.writeInt(u64, payload.len, .big);
    }
    try w.writeAll(&mask);
    // The mask is four bytes. Each byte i of the payload gets an XOR with byte
    // i % 4 of the mask. The same XOR on the receiver gives the payload back.
    for (payload, 0..) |b, i| try w.writeByte(b ^ mask[i % 4]);
}

/// Print the fields of a packed struct with the bits that each one uses.
fn printLayout(out: *std.Io.Writer, comptime T: type) !void {
    try out.print("  {s}:", .{@typeName(T)[std.mem.findScalarLast(u8, @typeName(T), '.').? + 1 ..]});
    const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
    inline for (info.field_names, info.field_types) |name, F| {
        const low = @bitOffsetOf(T, name);
        const high = low + @bitSizeOf(F) - 1;
        if (low == high) {
            try out.print(" {s}={d}", .{ name, low });
        } else {
            try out.print(" {s}={d}-{d}", .{ name, low, high });
        }
    }
    try out.print("\n", .{});
}

/// Give one frame to std, as a server reads it, and print the result.
fn serverReads(out: *std.Io.Writer, name: []const u8, frame: []const u8) !void {
    var in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(frame);
    var unused: [0]u8 = undefined;
    var sink: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&unused);
    var ws: WebSocket = .{ .key = "", .input = &in, .output = &sink };
    try out.print("  {s:<26} -> ", .{name});
    if (ws.readSmallMessage()) |msg| {
        try out.print("{t} \"{s}\"\n", .{ msg.opcode, msg.data });
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("error.{t}\n", .{err});
    }
}

var big: [70000]u8 = @splat('x');

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // ------------------------------------------------ the three length forms

    // A server frame from std. The length field has 7 bits. The values 126
    // and 127 mean that a 16-bit or a 64-bit length follows.
    try out.print("server frames, header bytes:\n", .{});
    var frame_buf: [70016]u8 = undefined;
    for ([_]usize{ 5, 125, 126, 200, 70000 }) |len| {
        var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&frame_buf);
        var ws: WebSocket = .{ .key = "", .input = undefined, .output = &w };
        try ws.writeMessage(big[0..len], .text);
        const header_len: usize = switch (frame_buf[1] & 0x7f) {
            126 => 4,
            127 => 10,
            else => 2,
        };
        try out.print("  {d:>5} bytes: ", .{len});
        try printBytes(out, frame_buf[0..header_len]);
        try out.print("\n", .{});
    }

    // ----------------------------------------------------- the header bits

    // The first two bytes are two packed structs in std. Zig packs the
    // first field into the lowest bits.
    try out.print("\nthe header structs in std, field=bits, bit 0 first:\n", .{});
    try printLayout(out, WebSocket.Header0);
    try printLayout(out, WebSocket.Header1);

    // A @bitCast reads the fields of one byte.
    try out.print("\nthe first two bytes, 81 85:\n", .{});
    const h0: WebSocket.Header0 = @bitCast(@as(u8, 0x81));
    const h1: WebSocket.Header1 = @bitCast(@as(u8, 0x85));
    try out.print("  byte 0 = {b:0>8}: fin={} rsv=0 opcode={t}\n", .{ @as(u8, 0x81), h0.fin, h0.opcode });
    try out.print("  byte 1 = {b:0>8}: mask={} length={d}\n", .{ @as(u8, 0x85), h1.mask, @intFromEnum(h1.payload_len) });

    // ------------------------------------------------------------ the mask

    // The example from section 5.7 of RFC 6455: "Hello", masked.
    const mask = [4]u8{ 0x37, 0xfa, 0x21, 0x3d };
    var hello_buf: [16]u8 = undefined;
    var hello_w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&hello_buf);
    try writeClientFrame(&hello_w, .text, true, mask, "Hello");
    const hello = hello_w.buffered();

    try out.print("\nmask a client frame, mask ", .{});
    try printBytes(out, &mask);
    try out.print(":\n", .{});
    for ("Hello", 0..) |c, i| {
        try out.print("  {d}  '{c}' {x:0>2} ^ {x:0>2} = {x:0>2}\n", .{ i, c, c, mask[i % 4], c ^ mask[i % 4] });
    }
    try out.print("frame: ", .{});
    try printBytes(out, hello);
    const rfc = [_]u8{ 0x81, 0x85, 0x37, 0xfa, 0x21, 0x3d, 0x7f, 0x9f, 0x4d, 0x51, 0x58 };
    try out.print("\nthe same as RFC 6455: {}\n", .{std.mem.eql(u8, hello, &rfc)});

    // ------------------------------------------------ what std.http accepts

    // Each frame goes to readSmallMessage, as a server reads it.
    try out.print("\nstd reads each frame:\n", .{});
    try serverReads(out, "masked text", hello);

    var f: [32]u8 = undefined;
    var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&f);
    try writeClientFrame(&w, .ping, true, mask, "are you there");
    try serverReads(out, "masked ping", w.buffered());

    w = .fixed(&f);
    try writeClientFrame(&w, .pong, true, mask, "");
    try writeClientFrame(&w, .text, true, mask, "after");
    try serverReads(out, "pong, then text", w.buffered());

    try serverReads(out, "unmasked text", &.{ 0x81, 0x05, 'H', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o' });

    w = .fixed(&f);
    try writeClientFrame(&w, .text, false, mask, "Hel");
    try writeClientFrame(&w, .continuation, true, mask, "lo");
    try serverReads(out, "\"Hel\" + \"lo\" in 2 frames", w.buffered());

    w = .fixed(&f);
    try writeClientFrame(&w, .continuation, true, mask, "lo");
    try serverReads(out, "continuation alone", w.buffered());

    // The length says 300 bytes. The reader has a buffer of 10 bytes.
    try serverReads(out, "300 bytes, 10-byte buffer", &.{ 0x81, 0xfe, 0x01, 0x2c, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 });

    w = .fixed(&f);
    try writeClientFrame(&w, .connection_close, true, mask, &.{ 0x03, 0xe8 });
    try serverReads(out, "close, code 1000", w.buffered());

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.websocket-frames`)*

## Two bytes of header

The first byte holds the `fin` bit, three reserved bits and a 4-bit opcode.
The second byte holds the `mask` bit and a 7-bit length. std declares each
byte as a `packed struct(u8)`: `WebSocket.Header0` and `WebSocket.Header1`
in `std.http.Server`. The program reads the layout of the two structs with
`@bitOffsetOf` and prints it:

```
the header structs in std, field=bits, bit 0 first:
  Header0: opcode=0-3 rsv3=4 rsv2=5 rsv1=6 fin=7
  Header1: payload_len=0-6 mask=7
```

Zig puts the first field of a packed struct in the lowest bits. RFC 6455
draws the frame with the highest bit first. Thus the fields in std are in
the reverse order of the diagram in the RFC: `opcode` is the first field in
Zig, and the RFC draws it last in the byte.

A `@bitCast` turns a byte into the struct, and the program prints the
fields:

```
the first two bytes, 81 85:
  byte 0 = 10000001: fin=true rsv=0 opcode=text
  byte 1 = 10000101: mask=true length=5
```

*Figure: The bytes 81 and 85 as 16 bits, with each field of Header0 and Header1 marked in turn. The layout and the two bytes from the program above. Step through the fields from bit 7 to bit 0.*

## Three length forms

The length field has 7 bits, thus it holds 0 to 127. The values 0 to 125
are the length. The value 126 means that a 16-bit length follows. The value
127 means that a 64-bit length follows. Both are big-endian, as in
[Binary Protocols and Byte Order](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/binary-protocols/).

```
server frames, header bytes:
      5 bytes: 81 05
    125 bytes: 81 7d
    126 bytes: 81 7e 00 7e
    200 bytes: 81 7e 00 c8
  70000 bytes: 81 7f 00 00 00 00 00 01 11 70
```

A message of 125 bytes has a header of two bytes. A message of 126 bytes
has a header of four bytes. The `payload_len` field in std is a
non-exhaustive enum. Thus a `switch` on the field has three cases: `.len16`,
`.len64`, and `else` for a length in the field itself.

## The mask

A client must mask each frame that it sends. The client selects four random
bytes, sends the bytes after the length, and XORs each payload byte with one
mask byte. Byte `i` uses mask byte `i % 4`. The receiver does the same XOR
and gets the payload back, because `x ^ m ^ m == x`.

```zig
/// A frame from a client. The server writes frames with std, but std has no
/// client, so this is the other half. RFC 6455 requires a client to mask
/// each frame, and a server must refuse a frame without the mask.
fn writeClientFrame(
    w: *std.Io.Writer,
    opcode: WebSocket.Opcode,
    fin: bool,
    mask: [4]u8,
    payload: []const u8,
) !void {
    try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header0{ .opcode = opcode, .fin = fin }));
    if (payload.len <= 125) {
        try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header1{
            .payload_len = @enumFromInt(payload.len),
            .mask = true,
        }));
    } else if (payload.len <= 0xffff) {
        try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header1{ .payload_len = .len16, .mask = true }));
        try w.writeInt(u16, @intCast(payload.len), .big);
    } else {
        try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header1{ .payload_len = .len64, .mask = true }));
        try w.writeInt(u64, payload.len, .big);
    }
    try w.writeAll(&mask);
    // The mask is four bytes. Each byte i of the payload gets an XOR with byte
    // i % 4 of the mask. The same XOR on the receiver gives the payload back.
    for (payload, 0..) |b, i| try w.writeByte(b ^ mask[i % 4]);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writeClientFrame` from `snippets/11-networking/websocket-frames.zig`.*

The mask does not make the data secret. The mask is in the frame. The mask
protects proxies on the path. Without the mask, a script in a browser could
send bytes that look like an HTTP request to a proxy. The proxy could then
store a wrong answer in its cache. With a random mask, the script cannot control the
bytes on the wire.

The program masks "Hello" with the mask from section 5.7 of RFC 6455:

```
mask a client frame, mask 37 fa 21 3d:
  0  'H' 48 ^ 37 = 7f
  1  'e' 65 ^ fa = 9f
  2  'l' 6c ^ 21 = 4d
  3  'l' 6c ^ 3d = 51
  4  'o' 6f ^ 37 = 58
frame: 81 85 37 fa 21 3d 7f 9f 4d 51 58
the same as RFC 6455: true
```

*Figure: The payload "Hello", the four mask bytes repeated under it, and the XOR of each pair. The mask trace from the program above. The figure stops at byte 4 and asks you which mask byte it uses.*

The server does not mask its frames. The direction decides the rule:

- A frame from a client must have the mask. A server closes the connection
  if the frame has no mask.
- A frame from a server must not have the mask. A client closes the
  connection if the mask is present.

std has no client, thus `writeClientFrame` is in the program. The mask in
the program is a constant, so that CI can compare the output. A real client
selects a new random mask for each frame.
[A WebSocket Client](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-client/) does that.

## What std reads, and what it refuses

`WebSocket.readSmallMessage` reads one frame, checks it, removes the mask,
and returns the opcode and the payload. The program gives it eight frames:

```
std reads each frame:
  masked text                -> text "Hello"
  masked ping                -> ping "are you there"
  pong, then text            -> text "after"
  unmasked text              -> error.MissingMaskBit
  "Hel" + "lo" in 2 frames   -> error.MessageOversize
  continuation alone         -> error.UnexpectedOpCode
  300 bytes, 10-byte buffer  -> error.MessageOversize
  close, code 1000           -> error.ConnectionClose
```

Each line shows one property of the reader in std:

- **A ping returns to your code.** std does not answer it. Send the pong
  with `writeMessage(data, .pong)`.
- **std skips a pong.** The reader reads the next frame and returns that
  frame.
- **std requires the mask**, as the RFC says for a server.
- **std refuses a message in fragments.** A frame without the `fin` bit gives
  `error.MessageOversize`, and a continuation frame gives
  `error.UnexpectedOpCode`. The RFC lets a sender split a message into
  frames, and a browser can do it. std reads only complete messages.
- **The whole frame must fit in the buffer of the reader.** std returns
  the payload as a slice of that buffer. Thus the size of the buffer is the
  largest message that the server accepts. The name `readSmallMessage` says
  this.
- **A close frame is an error value.** std stops after the first two bytes
  of the frame. Thus your code does not get the status code of the close
  frame. The rest of the frame stays unread in the stream. std does not send
  the close answer either.

These limits are the right size for the reason that std has this code. The
build system of Zig talks to its web interface (`zig build --webui`) over a
WebSocket, with small messages in both directions. For a server that
accepts messages from any browser, you must fill the gaps yourself.
[A WebSocket Server on a Socket](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-server/) shows
how to answer a ping and a close.

---

## A WebSocket Client

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-client/*

`std.http.Client` has no WebSocket support. Thus a Zig program that
connects to a WebSocket server needs its own client. The client is about 170
lines. It has five tasks:

1. Send the upgrade request with a random key, and check the answer.
2. Mask each frame with a new random mask.
3. Put a message in fragments together.
4. Answer each ping with a pong, also in the middle of a message.
5. Complete the close handshake.

The client reads from a `std.Io.Reader` and writes to a `std.Io.Writer`. It
never sees a socket. Thus the program below runs in your browser: it plays
the server in memory with `std.http.Server`, and you can see the bytes in
each direction.
[A WebSocket Server on a Socket](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-server/)
imports this file and uses the same client over a real TCP connection.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const Opcode = std.http.Server.WebSocket.Opcode;
const Header0 = std.http.Server.WebSocket.Header0;
const Header1 = std.http.Server.WebSocket.Header1;

const guid = "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11";

pub fn acceptFor(key: []const u8) [28]u8 {
    var sha1 = std.crypto.hash.Sha1.init(.{});
    sha1.update(key);
    sha1.update(guid);
    var digest: [std.crypto.hash.Sha1.digest_length]u8 = undefined;
    sha1.final(&digest);
    var accept: [28]u8 = undefined;
    _ = std.base64.standard.Encoder.encode(&accept, &digest);
    return accept;
}

pub const Client = struct {
    in: *std.Io.Reader,
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    /// The source of the key and of each mask. RFC 6455 requires a new,
    /// unpredictable mask for each frame.
    random: std.Random,
    key: [24]u8 = undefined,
    /// True after this side sends a close frame.
    closing: bool = false,
    /// The type of the message in fragments, and its bytes so far. These are
    /// fields, not locals: a ping can arrive between two fragments, and
    /// `receive` returns for the ping before the message is complete.
    fragment: ?Opcode = null,
    fragment_len: usize = 0,

    pub const Event = union(enum) {
        text: []const u8,
        binary: []const u8,
        /// The client answered the ping with a pong. The event is for the log.
        ping: []const u8,
        pong: []const u8,
        /// The status code of the close frame. 1005 means that it had none.
        close: u16,
    };

    pub const Error = error{
        UpgradeRefused,
        BadAccept,
        MaskedServerFrame,
        ProtocolError,
        MessageTooBig,
        InvalidUtf8,
    } || std.Io.Reader.DelimiterError || std.Io.Writer.Error;

    /// Send the HTTP request that asks for the upgrade. The key is 16
    /// random bytes in base64.
    pub fn sendHandshake(c: *Client, host: []const u8, path: []const u8) Error!void {
        var nonce: [16]u8 = undefined;
        c.random.bytes(&nonce);
        _ = std.base64.standard.Encoder.encode(&c.key, &nonce);
        try c.out.print(
            "GET {s} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {s}\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\n" ++
                "Sec-WebSocket-Key: {s}\r\nSec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n\r\n",
            .{ path, host, &c.key },
        );
        try c.out.flush();
    }

    /// Read the answer of the server. Frames start after the empty line.
    pub fn finishHandshake(c: *Client) Error!void {
        const status = try c.in.takeDelimiterInclusive('\n');
        if (!std.mem.startsWith(u8, status, "HTTP/1.1 101 ")) return error.UpgradeRefused;
        const expected = acceptFor(&c.key);
        var accept_ok = false;
        while (true) {
            const line = std.mem.trimEnd(u8, try c.in.takeDelimiterInclusive('\n'), "\r\n");
            if (line.len == 0) break;
            const colon = std.mem.findScalar(u8, line, ':') orelse return error.ProtocolError;
            const name = line[0..colon];
            const value = std.mem.trim(u8, line[colon + 1 ..], " ");
            if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(name, "sec-websocket-accept")) {
                accept_ok = std.mem.eql(u8, value, &expected);
            }
        }
        if (!accept_ok) return error.BadAccept;
    }

    /// Send one frame. A client masks each frame with a new mask.
    pub fn send(c: *Client, opcode: Opcode, payload: []const u8) Error!void {
        var mask: [4]u8 = undefined;
        c.random.bytes(&mask);
        try c.out.writeByte(@bitCast(Header0{ .opcode = opcode, .fin = true }));
        if (payload.len <= 125) {
            try c.out.writeByte(@bitCast(Header1{ .payload_len = @enumFromInt(payload.len), .mask = true }));
        } else if (payload.len <= 0xffff) {
            try c.out.writeByte(@bitCast(Header1{ .payload_len = .len16, .mask = true }));
            try c.out.writeInt(u16, @intCast(payload.len), .big);
        } else {
            try c.out.writeByte(@bitCast(Header1{ .payload_len = .len64, .mask = true }));
            try c.out.writeInt(u64, payload.len, .big);
        }
        try c.out.writeAll(&mask);
        for (payload, 0..) |b, i| try c.out.writeByte(b ^ mask[i % 4]);
        try c.out.flush();
    }

    /// Start the close handshake. The server answers with its own close
    /// frame, which `receive` returns as `.close`.
    pub fn close(c: *Client, code: u16) Error!void {
        var payload: [2]u8 = undefined;
        std.mem.writeInt(u16, &payload, code, .big);
        try c.send(.connection_close, &payload);
        c.closing = true;
    }

    /// Return the next event. A message in fragments is put together in
    /// `buffer`, thus give the same buffer to each call. A ping gets its pong
    /// here, also in the middle of a message.
    pub fn receive(c: *Client, buffer: []u8) Error!Event {
        while (true) {
            const header = try c.in.takeArray(2);
            const h0: Header0 = @bitCast(header[0]);
            const h1: Header1 = @bitCast(header[1]);
            // The mask is for frames from a client. A server must not mask.
            if (h1.mask) return error.MaskedServerFrame;
            const len: u64 = switch (h1.payload_len) {
                .len16 => try c.in.takeInt(u16, .big),
                .len64 => try c.in.takeInt(u64, .big),
                else => @intFromEnum(h1.payload_len),
            };

            switch (h0.opcode) {
                .ping, .pong, .connection_close => {
                    // A control frame is short and never in fragments.
                    if (len > 125 or !h0.fin) return error.ProtocolError;
                    const payload = try c.in.take(@intCast(len));
                    switch (h0.opcode) {
                        .ping => {
                            var copy: [125]u8 = undefined;
                            @memcpy(copy[0..payload.len], payload);
                            try c.send(.pong, copy[0..payload.len]);
                            return .{ .ping = payload };
                        },
                        .pong => return .{ .pong = payload },
                        else => {
                            const code: u16 = if (payload.len >= 2) std.mem.readInt(u16, payload[0..2], .big) else 1005;
                            // If the server closes first, send the same code back.
                            if (!c.closing) try c.close(code);
                            return .{ .close = code };
                        },
                    }
                },
                .text, .binary => {
                    if (c.fragment != null) return error.ProtocolError;
                    c.fragment = h0.opcode;
                    c.fragment_len = 0;
                },
                .continuation => if (c.fragment == null) return error.ProtocolError,
                _ => return error.ProtocolError,
            }

            const used = c.fragment_len;
            if (len > buffer.len - used) return error.MessageTooBig;
            try c.in.readSliceAll(buffer[used..][0..@intCast(len)]);
            c.fragment_len += @intCast(len);
            if (!h0.fin) continue;

            const data = buffer[0..c.fragment_len];
            const opcode = c.fragment.?;
            c.fragment = null;
            if (opcode == .binary) return .{ .binary = data };
            if (!std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(data)) return error.InvalidUtf8;
            return .{ .text = data };
        }
    }
};

// Everything below is the demonstration. It plays the server in memory, so
// the bytes of each direction are visible.

/// A server frame that std cannot write: the first frame of a message, or a
/// continuation. std writes complete messages only.
fn writeServerFrame(w: *std.Io.Writer, opcode: Opcode, fin: bool, payload: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeByte(@bitCast(Header0{ .opcode = opcode, .fin = fin }));
    try w.writeByte(@bitCast(Header1{ .payload_len = @enumFromInt(payload.len), .mask = false }));
    try w.writeAll(payload);
}

/// List the frames that the server wrote, after the HTTP head. All of them
/// are short and unmasked, thus each header is two bytes.
fn printServerFrames(out: *std.Io.Writer, bytes: []const u8) !void {
    const body = bytes[(std.mem.find(u8, bytes, "\r\n\r\n").? + 4)..];
    try out.print("server sends 101, then these frames:\n", .{});
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < body.len) {
        const h0: Header0 = @bitCast(body[i]);
        const len = body[i + 1];
        const payload = body[i + 2 ..][0..len];
        try out.print("  {t:<16} fin={d} ", .{ h0.opcode, @intFromBool(h0.fin) });
        if (h0.opcode == .connection_close) {
            try out.print("code {d}\n", .{std.mem.readInt(u16, payload[0..2], .big)});
        } else {
            try out.print("\"{s}\"\n", .{payload});
        }
        i += 2 + len;
    }
}

fn printEvent(out: *std.Io.Writer, event: Client.Event) !void {
    switch (event) {
        .text => |t| try out.print("  text \"{s}\"\n", .{t}),
        .binary => |b| try out.print("  binary, {d} bytes\n", .{b.len}),
        .ping => |p| try out.print("  ping \"{s}\", answered with a pong\n", .{p}),
        .pong => |p| try out.print("  pong \"{s}\"\n", .{p}),
        .close => |code| try out.print("  close {d}, answered with close {d}\n", .{ code, code }),
    }
}

/// Give the client a server answer, and print what the client decides.
fn clientRejects(out: *std.Io.Writer, name: []const u8, key: [24]u8, head: []const u8, frames: []const u8) !void {
    var answer: [256]u8 = undefined;
    @memcpy(answer[0..head.len], head);
    @memcpy(answer[head.len..][0..frames.len], frames);
    var in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(answer[0 .. head.len + frames.len]);
    var unused: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var sink: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&unused);
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(1);
    var c: Client = .{ .in = &in, .out = &sink, .random = prng.random(), .key = key };
    var buffer: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const result = if (c.finishHandshake()) c.receive(&buffer) else |err| err;
    if (result) |event| {
        try out.print("  {s:<24} -> accepted: ", .{name});
        try printEvent(out, event);
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("  {s:<24} -> error.{t}\n", .{ name, err });
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // A fixed seed gives the same key and masks on each run, thus CI can
    // compare the output. A real client takes its seed from `io.random`.
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(2026);

    // Two wires, one for each direction.
    var to_server_buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var to_server: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&to_server_buf);
    var to_client_buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var to_client: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&to_client_buf);
    var client_in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed("");

    var client: Client = .{ .in = &client_in, .out = &to_server, .random = prng.random() };

    // 1. The client asks for the upgrade.
    try client.sendHandshake("example.com", "/chat");
    try out.print("client key: {s}\n", .{&client.key});

    // 2. The server, with std. It answers 101, then sends four frames.
    var server_in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(to_server.buffered());
    var http = std.http.Server.init(&server_in, &to_client);
    var request = try http.receiveHead();
    const key = request.upgradeRequested().websocket.?;
    var ws = try request.respondWebSocket(.{ .key = key });
    try ws.writeMessage("welcome", .text);
    try writeServerFrame(&to_client, .text, false, "Hel");
    try writeServerFrame(&to_client, .ping, true, "beat");
    try writeServerFrame(&to_client, .continuation, true, "lo");
    try ws.writeMessage(&.{ 0x03, 0xe8 }, .connection_close);
    try ws.flush();
    try printServerFrames(out, to_client.buffered());

    // 3. The client reads the answer and the frames.
    client_in = .fixed(to_client.buffered());
    to_server = .fixed(&to_server_buf);
    try client.finishHandshake();
    try out.print("\nclient: status 101 and accept ok\n", .{});
    try client.send(.text, "hi");
    try out.print("client sends \"hi\": ", .{});
    for (to_server.buffered(), 0..) |b, i| {
        if (i > 0) try out.writeByte(' ');
        try out.print("{x:0>2}", .{b});
    }
    try out.print("\nclient receives:\n", .{});
    var message_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    while (true) {
        const event = try client.receive(&message_buf);
        try printEvent(out, event);
        if (event == .close) break;
    }

    // 4. std reads what the client sent: the text, the pong, the close.
    var reply_in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(to_server.buffered());
    ws.input = &reply_in;
    try out.print("\nstd reads the frames of the client:\n", .{});
    while (true) {
        if (ws.readSmallMessage()) |msg| {
            try out.print("  {t} \"{s}\"\n", .{ msg.opcode, msg.data });
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("  error.{t}\n", .{err});
            break;
        }
    }

    // 5. Server answers that the client must refuse.
    try out.print("\nthe client refuses:\n", .{});
    var head_buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    const ok = try std.mem.print(&head_buf, "HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\nSec-WebSocket-Accept: {s}\r\n\r\n", .{&acceptFor(&client.key)});
    const k = client.key;
    try clientRejects(out, "200 OK", k, "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n\r\n", "");
    try clientRejects(out, "wrong accept", k, "HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\nSec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=\r\n\r\n", "");
    try clientRejects(out, "no accept", k, "HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\n\r\n", "");
    try clientRejects(out, "masked server frame", k, ok, "\x81\x82\x00\x00\x00\x00hi");
    try clientRejects(out, "continuation first", k, ok, "\x80\x02lo");
    try clientRejects(out, "ping of 126 bytes", k, ok, "\x89\x7e\x00\x7e");
    try clientRejects(out, "text that is not UTF-8", k, ok, "\x81\x02\xc3\x28");
    try clientRejects(out, "70 bytes, 64-byte buffer", k, ok, "\x82\x46");

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.websocket-client`)*

## The handshake

The key is 16 random bytes in base64. The client keeps the key, because it
needs the key again to check the answer.

```zig
    /// Send the HTTP request that asks for the upgrade. The key is 16
    /// random bytes in base64.
    pub fn sendHandshake(c: *Client, host: []const u8, path: []const u8) Error!void {
        var nonce: [16]u8 = undefined;
        c.random.bytes(&nonce);
        _ = std.base64.standard.Encoder.encode(&c.key, &nonce);
        try c.out.print(
            "GET {s} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {s}\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\n" ++
                "Sec-WebSocket-Key: {s}\r\nSec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n\r\n",
            .{ path, host, &c.key },
        );
        try c.out.flush();
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `sendHandshake` from `snippets/11-networking/websocket-client.zig`.*

The program makes the random numbers with `std.Random.DefaultPrng` and a
fixed seed. Thus the key is the same on each run, and CI can compare the
output. A real client takes the seed from `io.random`, as the server chapter
does. The RFC requires a key and masks that a script cannot predict.

The request and the answer are split into two functions, because a server
must read the request before it answers. Over a socket, call the two
functions one after the other.

```zig
    /// Read the answer of the server. Frames start after the empty line.
    pub fn finishHandshake(c: *Client) Error!void {
        const status = try c.in.takeDelimiterInclusive('\n');
        if (!std.mem.startsWith(u8, status, "HTTP/1.1 101 ")) return error.UpgradeRefused;
        const expected = acceptFor(&c.key);
        var accept_ok = false;
        while (true) {
            const line = std.mem.trimEnd(u8, try c.in.takeDelimiterInclusive('\n'), "\r\n");
            if (line.len == 0) break;
            const colon = std.mem.findScalar(u8, line, ':') orelse return error.ProtocolError;
            const name = line[0..colon];
            const value = std.mem.trim(u8, line[colon + 1 ..], " ");
            if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(name, "sec-websocket-accept")) {
                accept_ok = std.mem.eql(u8, value, &expected);
            }
        }
        if (!accept_ok) return error.BadAccept;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `finishHandshake` from `snippets/11-networking/websocket-client.zig`.*

`finishHandshake` reads the head line by line with
`takeDelimiterInclusive`. After the empty line, the next byte in the reader
is the first byte of the first frame. The reader can hold frames that came
in the same TCP packet as the answer, and the client keeps them for
`receive`.

## Send a frame

```zig
    /// Send one frame. A client masks each frame with a new mask.
    pub fn send(c: *Client, opcode: Opcode, payload: []const u8) Error!void {
        var mask: [4]u8 = undefined;
        c.random.bytes(&mask);
        try c.out.writeByte(@bitCast(Header0{ .opcode = opcode, .fin = true }));
        if (payload.len <= 125) {
            try c.out.writeByte(@bitCast(Header1{ .payload_len = @enumFromInt(payload.len), .mask = true }));
        } else if (payload.len <= 0xffff) {
            try c.out.writeByte(@bitCast(Header1{ .payload_len = .len16, .mask = true }));
            try c.out.writeInt(u16, @intCast(payload.len), .big);
        } else {
            try c.out.writeByte(@bitCast(Header1{ .payload_len = .len64, .mask = true }));
            try c.out.writeInt(u64, payload.len, .big);
        }
        try c.out.writeAll(&mask);
        for (payload, 0..) |b, i| try c.out.writeByte(b ^ mask[i % 4]);
        try c.out.flush();
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `send` from `snippets/11-networking/websocket-client.zig`.*

`send` is `writeClientFrame` from
[WebSocket Frames](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-frames/), with a random mask
for each frame. The program prints one frame. The mask is the four bytes
after `81 82`:

```
client sends "hi": 81 82 cd 0a 77 67 a5 63
```

## Receive: fragments and control frames

A sender can split one message into frames. The first frame has the opcode
`text` or `binary` and no `fin` bit. Each next frame has the opcode
`continuation`. The last frame has the `fin` bit. The server in the program
sends a message in two fragments, with a ping between them:

```
server sends 101, then these frames:
  text             fin=1 "welcome"
  text             fin=0 "Hel"
  ping             fin=1 "beat"
  continuation     fin=1 "lo"
  connection_close fin=1 code 1000
```

RFC 6455 lets a control frame (ping, pong or close) arrive between two
fragments. A server that sends a large message must still answer a ping from
the client. Control frames have two rules of their own: the payload is 125
bytes or fewer, and a control frame is never in fragments.

*Figure: 5 frames from a server, including a text message in two fragments with a ping between them, and what the client does for each frame. The frames and the events from the program above, one step for each frame.*

```zig
    /// Return the next event. A message in fragments is put together in
    /// `buffer`, thus give the same buffer to each call. A ping gets its pong
    /// here, also in the middle of a message.
    pub fn receive(c: *Client, buffer: []u8) Error!Event {
        while (true) {
            const header = try c.in.takeArray(2);
            const h0: Header0 = @bitCast(header[0]);
            const h1: Header1 = @bitCast(header[1]);
            // The mask is for frames from a client. A server must not mask.
            if (h1.mask) return error.MaskedServerFrame;
            const len: u64 = switch (h1.payload_len) {
                .len16 => try c.in.takeInt(u16, .big),
                .len64 => try c.in.takeInt(u64, .big),
                else => @intFromEnum(h1.payload_len),
            };

            switch (h0.opcode) {
                .ping, .pong, .connection_close => {
                    // A control frame is short and never in fragments.
                    if (len > 125 or !h0.fin) return error.ProtocolError;
                    const payload = try c.in.take(@intCast(len));
                    switch (h0.opcode) {
                        .ping => {
                            var copy: [125]u8 = undefined;
                            @memcpy(copy[0..payload.len], payload);
                            try c.send(.pong, copy[0..payload.len]);
                            return .{ .ping = payload };
                        },
                        .pong => return .{ .pong = payload },
                        else => {
                            const code: u16 = if (payload.len >= 2) std.mem.readInt(u16, payload[0..2], .big) else 1005;
                            // If the server closes first, send the same code back.
                            if (!c.closing) try c.close(code);
                            return .{ .close = code };
                        },
                    }
                },
                .text, .binary => {
                    if (c.fragment != null) return error.ProtocolError;
                    c.fragment = h0.opcode;
                    c.fragment_len = 0;
                },
                .continuation => if (c.fragment == null) return error.ProtocolError,
                _ => return error.ProtocolError,
            }

            const used = c.fragment_len;
            if (len > buffer.len - used) return error.MessageTooBig;
            try c.in.readSliceAll(buffer[used..][0..@intCast(len)]);
            c.fragment_len += @intCast(len);
            if (!h0.fin) continue;

            const data = buffer[0..c.fragment_len];
            const opcode = c.fragment.?;
            c.fragment = null;
            if (opcode == .binary) return .{ .binary = data };
            if (!std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(data)) return error.InvalidUtf8;
            return .{ .text = data };
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `receive` from `snippets/11-networking/websocket-client.zig`.*

The state of the message in fragments is in two fields of `Client`:
`fragment` and `fragment_len`. The first version of this client kept that
state in local variables of `receive`. That version failed on this exact
input. `receive` returned for the ping, the locals were lost, and the next
call saw a `continuation` with no message open. It returned
`error.ProtocolError`.

The bug gives a rule. If a function can return in the middle of
a message, keep the state of the message outside the function.

The client prints each event:

```
client receives:
  text "welcome"
  ping "beat", answered with a pong
  text "Hello"
  close 1000, answered with close 1000
```

A text message must be valid UTF-8, and the client checks it after the last
fragment. The check must wait for the last fragment, because a fragment
boundary can split one character.

## The close handshake

A close is a handshake too. One side sends a close frame with a 2-byte
status code. The other side answers with a close frame, and then the TCP
connection closes. 1000 is a normal close. 1009 means that a message was too
big. The client reports a close frame with no code as 1005.

If the server closes first, `receive` answers with the same code. If the
client calls `close`, the `closing` field stops a second close frame, and
`receive` returns the answer of the server.

std reads the frames of the client and confirms the order:

```
std reads the frames of the client:
  text "hi"
  error.ConnectionClose
```

The pong for "beat" is between those two frames. std skips pong frames, thus
it does not show in the list.

## What the client refuses

```
the client refuses:
  200 OK                   -> error.UpgradeRefused
  wrong accept             -> error.BadAccept
  no accept                -> error.BadAccept
  masked server frame      -> error.MaskedServerFrame
  continuation first       -> error.ProtocolError
  ping of 126 bytes        -> error.ProtocolError
  text that is not UTF-8   -> error.InvalidUtf8
  70 bytes, 64-byte buffer -> error.MessageTooBig
```

The "wrong accept" line uses the accept value from the RFC example. That
value is correct for the key in the RFC, and wrong for the key of this
client. Thus a server that sends a fixed answer fails the check.

After an error, the client must close the TCP connection. The RFC calls this
"fail the WebSocket connection". A real client also sends a close frame
first, with code 1002 for a protocol error or 1007 for text that is not
UTF-8.

## What this client does not do

- **TLS.** A `wss://` URL is WebSocket over TLS. Connect with TLS first,
  then give the reader and the writer of the TLS stream to the client.
  Nothing in the client changes.
- **Compression.** The `permessage-deflate` extension sets a reserved bit
  and compresses each message. The client does not ask for it in the
  handshake, thus a correct server does not use it.
- **Large messages.** The caller supplies the buffer, and a message larger
  than the buffer gives `error.MessageTooBig`. A client that streams a large
  message must return each fragment to the caller.

---

## A WebSocket Server on a Socket

*Networking. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-server/*

The last three chapters used buffers in memory. This chapter uses a real
TCP connection on loopback. The server is `std.http.Server` with its
WebSocket support. The client is the client from
[A WebSocket Client](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-client/). The program
imports that file with `@import("websocket-client.zig")`.

The client runs here without a change. It reads from the reader of a TCP
stream in place of a fixed buffer. That is the purpose of the rule of this
section: parse from a `Reader`, never from a socket.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const Client = @import("websocket-client.zig").Client;

/// The largest message this server accepts. readSmallMessage needs the
/// whole frame in the buffer of the reader, thus this buffer is the limit.
const max_message = 512;

/// One connection. The server thread writes what it decides into `log`,
/// and main prints the log after the thread ends. If both threads printed,
/// the order of the lines would change from run to run.
fn handle(conn: std.Io.net.Stream, io: std.Io, log: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var read_buf: [max_message]u8 = undefined;
    var write_buf: [max_message + 16]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = conn.reader(io, &read_buf);
    var writer = conn.writer(io, &write_buf);
    var http = std.http.Server.init(&reader.interface, &writer.interface);

    var request = try http.receiveHead();
    const key = switch (request.upgradeRequested()) {
        .websocket => |k| k orelse return request.respond("", .{ .status = .bad_request }),
        .none, .other => return request.respond("use a WebSocket client\n", .{}),
    };
    var ws = try request.respondWebSocket(.{ .key = key });
    try ws.flush();
    try log.print("upgraded {s}\n", .{request.head.target});

    while (true) {
        const msg = ws.readSmallMessage() catch |err| {
            const code: u16 = switch (err) {
                // The client started the close handshake.
                error.ConnectionClose => 1000,
                // 1009 means "message too big". A fragmented message gives
                // this error too, because std reads single frames only.
                error.MessageOversize => 1009,
                else => return err,
            };
            var payload: [2]u8 = undefined;
            std.mem.writeInt(u16, &payload, code, .big);
            try ws.writeMessage(&payload, .connection_close);
            try log.print("{t}: sent close {d}\n", .{ err, code });
            // std stops in the middle of the frame that caused the error,
            // thus the rest of the frame is unread. Read until the client
            // closes the TCP connection. If the server closed with unread
            // bytes, the kernel would send a reset to the client.
            _ = reader.interface.discardRemaining() catch {};
            return;
        };
        switch (msg.opcode) {
            .text, .binary => {
                try ws.writeMessage(msg.data, msg.opcode);
                try log.print("echo {t}, {d} bytes\n", .{ msg.opcode, msg.data.len });
            },
            .ping => {
                try ws.writeMessage(msg.data, .pong);
                try log.print("ping: sent pong\n", .{});
            },
            else => unreachable,
        }
    }
}

fn serve(listener: *std.Io.net.Server, io: std.Io, log: *std.Io.Writer) void {
    for (0..2) |_| {
        const conn = listener.accept(io) catch return;
        defer conn.close(io);
        handle(conn, io, log) catch |err| log.print("connection failed: {t}\n", .{err}) catch {};
    }
}

fn printEvent(out: *std.Io.Writer, event: Client.Event) !void {
    switch (event) {
        .text => |t| if (t.len <= 20)
            try out.print("  got text \"{s}\"\n", .{t})
        else
            try out.print("  got text, {d} bytes\n", .{t.len}),
        .binary => |b| try out.print("  got binary, {d} bytes\n", .{b.len}),
        .ping => |p| try out.print("  got ping \"{s}\"\n", .{p}),
        .pong => |p| try out.print("  got pong \"{s}\"\n", .{p}),
        .close => |code| try out.print("  got close {d}\n", .{code}),
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const any_port = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    var listener = try any_port.listen(io, .{});
    defer listener.deinit(io);
    const addr = listener.socket.address;

    var log_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var log: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&log_buf);
    const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, serve, .{ &listener, io, &log });

    // The key and the masks are not in the output, thus a real seed is
    // correct here.
    var seed: [8]u8 = undefined;
    io.random(&seed);
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(std.mem.readInt(u64, &seed, .little));

    var message_buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;

    // Connection 1: text, a ping, a long text, and a normal close.
    {
        var stream = try addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
        defer stream.close(io);
        var read_buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
        var write_buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
        var reader = stream.reader(io, &read_buf);
        var writer = stream.writer(io, &write_buf);
        var client: Client = .{ .in = &reader.interface, .out = &writer.interface, .random = prng.random() };

        try client.sendHandshake("127.0.0.1", "/echo");
        try client.finishHandshake();
        try out.print("connection 1:\n", .{});

        try client.send(.text, "hello");
        try printEvent(out, try client.receive(&message_buf));
        try client.send(.ping, "beat");
        try printEvent(out, try client.receive(&message_buf));
        const long: [400]u8 = @splat('z');
        try client.send(.text, &long);
        try printEvent(out, try client.receive(&message_buf));
        try client.close(1000);
        try printEvent(out, try client.receive(&message_buf));
    }

    // Connection 2: a message larger than the server accepts.
    {
        var stream = try addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
        defer stream.close(io);
        var read_buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
        var write_buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
        var reader = stream.reader(io, &read_buf);
        var writer = stream.writer(io, &write_buf);
        var client: Client = .{ .in = &reader.interface, .out = &writer.interface, .random = prng.random() };

        try client.sendHandshake("127.0.0.1", "/echo");
        try client.finishHandshake();
        try out.print("connection 2:\n", .{});

        const big: [1000]u8 = @splat(7);
        try client.send(.binary, &big);
        try printEvent(out, try client.receive(&message_buf));
    }

    thread.join();
    try out.print("server log:\n", .{});
    var lines = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, log.buffered(), '\n');
    while (lines.next()) |line| {
        if (line.len > 0) try out.print("  {s}\n", .{line});
    }
    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this snippet natively: the server and the client talk over a real loopback socket. Browser wasm has no sockets. (`11-networking.websocket-server`)*

The program makes two connections. The first sends a text, a ping and a
long text, and then closes normally. The second sends a message that is too
big for the server.

```
connection 1:
  got text "hello"
  got pong "beat"
  got text, 400 bytes
  got close 1000
connection 2:
  got close 1009
```

## One connection

```zig
/// One connection. The server thread writes what it decides into `log`,
/// and main prints the log after the thread ends. If both threads printed,
/// the order of the lines would change from run to run.
fn handle(conn: std.Io.net.Stream, io: std.Io, log: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var read_buf: [max_message]u8 = undefined;
    var write_buf: [max_message + 16]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = conn.reader(io, &read_buf);
    var writer = conn.writer(io, &write_buf);
    var http = std.http.Server.init(&reader.interface, &writer.interface);

    var request = try http.receiveHead();
    const key = switch (request.upgradeRequested()) {
        .websocket => |k| k orelse return request.respond("", .{ .status = .bad_request }),
        .none, .other => return request.respond("use a WebSocket client\n", .{}),
    };
    var ws = try request.respondWebSocket(.{ .key = key });
    try ws.flush();
    try log.print("upgraded {s}\n", .{request.head.target});

    while (true) {
        const msg = ws.readSmallMessage() catch |err| {
            const code: u16 = switch (err) {
                // The client started the close handshake.
                error.ConnectionClose => 1000,
                // 1009 means "message too big". A fragmented message gives
                // this error too, because std reads single frames only.
                error.MessageOversize => 1009,
                else => return err,
            };
            var payload: [2]u8 = undefined;
            std.mem.writeInt(u16, &payload, code, .big);
            try ws.writeMessage(&payload, .connection_close);
            try log.print("{t}: sent close {d}\n", .{ err, code });
            // std stops in the middle of the frame that caused the error,
            // thus the rest of the frame is unread. Read until the client
            // closes the TCP connection. If the server closed with unread
            // bytes, the kernel would send a reset to the client.
            _ = reader.interface.discardRemaining() catch {};
            return;
        };
        switch (msg.opcode) {
            .text, .binary => {
                try ws.writeMessage(msg.data, msg.opcode);
                try log.print("echo {t}, {d} bytes\n", .{ msg.opcode, msg.data.len });
            },
            .ping => {
                try ws.writeMessage(msg.data, .pong);
                try log.print("ping: sent pong\n", .{});
            },
            else => unreachable,
        }
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `handle` from `snippets/11-networking/websocket-server.zig`.*

The function has three parts:

1. `receiveHead` reads the HTTP request, as in
   [An HTTP Round Trip](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/http-roundtrip/).
2. `upgradeRequested` and `respondWebSocket` do the handshake. A request
   with no key gets a 400. An ordinary request gets an ordinary answer.
3. The loop reads messages with `readSmallMessage` and answers each one.

The [handshake chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-handshake/) also
checks the version header. This server does not, to keep the function
short.

## The size of the buffer is the limit

`readSmallMessage` returns the payload as a slice of the buffer of the
reader. Thus the whole frame must fit in that buffer, and `max_message` is
the largest message that the server accepts. Here it is 512 bytes. The
400-byte text fits. The 1000-byte binary message does not, and std returns
`error.MessageOversize`.

The server answers with close code 1009, "message too big". A message in
fragments gives the same error, because std reads single frames only. For
this server, a message in two fragments is too big. If your clients send
fragments, read the frames yourself, as the client does.

The limit has a second purpose. Without a limit, a client can announce a
length of 2<sup>63</sup> bytes, and a server that allocates for the length
fails. A fixed buffer refuses that frame before it reads the payload.

## Ping and close are your work

std returns a ping to your code, and the server answers with
`writeMessage(msg.data, .pong)`. A client can send pings to check
that the connection is alive. If no pong arrives, the client can close the
connection.

std returns a close frame as `error.ConnectionClose`. The server sends its
own close frame. The close handshake has one more problem: std stops after
the first two bytes of the close frame. Thus the mask and the status code of
the client are still unread in the stream.

If a TCP socket closes with unread bytes in its receive buffer, the kernel
sends a reset (RST) in place of a normal close. The client can then get
an error for a reset connection before it reads the close frame from the
server. Thus the server calls `discardRemaining` on its reader. The call
reads and discards bytes until the client closes the connection.

RFC 6455 says that the server should close the TCP connection first. This
server lets the client close first, because std does not give the length of
the rest of the frame. To close first, read the frame yourself and discard
exactly the rest of it.

## The log comes from the server thread

```
server log:
  upgraded /echo
  echo text, 5 bytes
  ping: sent pong
  echo text, 400 bytes
  ConnectionClose: sent close 1000
  upgraded /echo
  MessageOversize: sent close 1009
```

The server thread writes into a buffer, and `main` prints the buffer after
`thread.join()`. If both threads printed, the order of the lines could
change from run to run, and CI could not compare the output.

## One client at a time

This server serves one connection and then the next. A WebSocket
connection stays open for a long time, thus a real server needs a task for
each connection. [Serve Many Clients](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/many-clients/) shows
the pattern with `std.Io`. Use it with the `handle` function above.

## When std is not enough

The WebSocket support in std is small. It exists for the web interface of
the Zig build system (`zig build --webui`). This list shows what a server
for the open internet needs in addition:

| Need | std.http.Server | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Messages in fragments | refused | read the frames yourself |
| Large messages | refused | a larger buffer, or stream the frames |
| Answer to a ping | your code | `writeMessage(data, .pong)` |
| Close handshake | your code | send close, then drain |
| Compression | no | `permessage-deflate` |
| A client | no | [write one](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-client/) |

[websocket.zig](https://github.com/karlseguin/websocket.zig) by Karl Seguin
is a complete library for Zig, under the MIT licence. It has a server and a
client. It answers ping and close frames, supports compression, and runs
connections on a thread pool. On 2026-10-26, its readme said that it is for
Zig 0.17.0, with branches for older versions. This guide tracks Zig master,
thus no snippet here depends on the library. Check the readme for the
version that it supports today.

---

## Build Modes

*Build System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/build-system/build-modes/*

Zig has four build modes: `Debug`, `ReleaseSafe`, `ReleaseFast` and `ReleaseSmall`. The modes are different in two ways:

- Some modes keep the runtime safety checks in the binary, and some modes remove them.
- The optimiser makes the code fast in some modes, and small in a different mode.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const builtin = @import("builtin");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "the current mode is known at compile time" {
    // The build makes these snippets as .small. Master changed the mode tags
    // to lowercase: .Debug/.ReleaseSafe/.ReleaseFast/.ReleaseSmall are now
    // .debug/.safe/.fast/.small.
    try expect(builtin.optimize == .small);
}

test "safety checks follow the mode" {
    // True in .debug and .safe. False in .fast and .small.
    const safety_on = switch (builtin.optimize) {
        .debug, .safe => true,
        .fast, .small => false,
    };
    try expect(!safety_on); // because this build is .small
}

test "safety can be forced back on for a scope" {
    // Use this call to keep the bounds checks in one risky function of a
    // ReleaseFast build.
    @setRuntimeSafety(true);
    var index: usize = 1;
    _ = &index;
    const array = [_]u8{ 1, 2, 3 };
    try expect(array[index] == 2);
}

test "branch hints and unreachable" {
    // In safety builds, `unreachable` panics. In ReleaseFast, `unreachable`
    // is a promise to the optimiser. If the program gets to it, the result
    // is illegal behaviour.
    const value: u8 = 2;
    switch (value) {
        1, 2, 3 => {},
        else => unreachable,
    }
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`04-build-system.build-modes`)*

| Mode | Safety checks | Optimised | Size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Debug` | yes | no | large |
| `ReleaseSafe` | yes | yes | medium |
| `ReleaseFast` | **no** | yes | medium |
| `ReleaseSmall` | **no** | yes | small |

Select the mode with `-O`:

```bash
zig build-exe main.zig -OReleaseSafe
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe
```

## The purpose of each mode

- **`Debug`** is the default. Use it while you develop. The compiler does almost no optimisation, thus the compilation is fast. All safety checks are on. The compiler fills `undefined` memory with `0xaa`, thus a read of memory without a value is easy to see. The binaries are large and the code is slow. That is not a problem while you edit the code.
- **`ReleaseSafe`** is the mode to ship, if you do not have a reason to use a different mode. It has full optimisation, and it keeps the checks.
- **`ReleaseFast`** removes the checks. Use it when a measurement shows that the checks make the program too slow. That occurs less frequently than people expect.
- **`ReleaseSmall`** makes the code small instead of fast, and it also removes the checks. Embedded targets use this mode. This site also uses it. A snippet here is about 60 KB. The same snippet in `ReleaseSafe` is more than one megabyte. The browser of the reader must download the file before the snippet can run.

These numbers come from measurements of this project. They are not estimates. Thus only five snippets on this site use `.safe`. These five snippets show a panic, and the panic is the lesson.

## Use `ReleaseSafe` more frequently

In C and C++, a release build is usually a build without checks. Zig keeps the two choices separate. `ReleaseSafe` has optimisation, *and* it keeps the bounds checks, the overflow checks and the null-unwrap checks. For most software, the cost is small. Without the checks, memory can become corrupt and nothing tells you.

Use `ReleaseFast` when you measured that the checks are important to the speed. Do not use it as the default.

The two costs are very different:

- A check that stays in the binary costs a compare and a predictable branch. On modern hardware, that cost is almost zero, unless the speed of the code is already limited by memory.
- A check that the compiler removes costs nothing until an index is wrong. Then the cost is a corrupt heap and a bug that you cannot reproduce.

Thus a default without checks is a bad exchange. You remove a small cost that you always pay, and you get a large cost that occurs rarely. For decades, C and C++ gave no other choice.

## When the checks go, the rules stay

In `ReleaseFast` and `ReleaseSmall`, an index out of bounds is **illegal behaviour**. Illegal behaviour is the same category as undefined behaviour in C. The check only reported that the code broke the rule. When you remove the check, the rule stays. If code works only because Debug found the panic, the code is already wrong.

If a program works in ReleaseFast, the result does not show that the program is correct. It only shows that nothing found the problem until now. The optimiser can assume that the code obeys the rules. The optimiser uses that assumption to delete branches that you think are in the code.

## Change the mode for one scope

```zig
@setRuntimeSafety(true);
```

This call keeps the checks in one function of a build that has no other checks. Use it for a function that parses input that you cannot trust.

The opposite also works: put `@setRuntimeSafety(false)` in one hot function of a safe build. Use this approach when you can. The unsafe code stays small, and it is easy to find and examine. The other approach removes the checks from the full program to make one loop faster.

## Get the mode at compile time

`@import("builtin").optimize` is a comptime value. Thus code for one mode has no cost at runtime: the compiler does not compile the branch that cannot run.

The tags are lowercase: `.debug`, `.safe`, `.fast`, `.small`. Before, the tags were `.Debug`, `.ReleaseSafe`, `.ReleaseFast` and `.ReleaseSmall`. Thus a comparison from an older tutorial does not compile.

The name of the field also changed from `mode` to `optimize`. `builtin.mode` still works at this time, and the std source marks it for removal after 0.18.0. On the command line, both forms work: `-O ReleaseFast` and `-O fast` make the same build.

Because the mode is a comptime value, expensive assertions are practical. You can put a check of a full data structure behind `if (builtin.optimize == .debug)`. In a release build, that check is not in the binary.

`std.debug.assert` is a different tool. It becomes `unreachable`. Thus it follows the safety checks and not the name of the mode, and it still fires in `ReleaseSafe`.

---

## Emit an Executable

*Build System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/build-system/emitting-an-executable/*

For a single file, you do not need a build script:

```bash
zig build-exe main.zig          # an executable
zig build-lib  main.zig         # a static library
zig build-obj  main.zig         # an object file
zig run        main.zig         # build and run in one step
zig test       main.zig         # build and run its tests
```

## Useful flags

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-O<Mode>` | optimisation mode |
| `-target <triple>` | cross-compile |
| `--name <n>` | output name |
| `-femit-bin=<path>` | where to write the binary |
| `-fstrip` | drop debug info |
| `-fsingle-threaded` | assume no threads |

## You will use `zig run` most

The only difference between `run` and `build-exe` is the location of the binary:

```
zig run foo.zig
      │
      ├── compile
      ├── binary into the cache
      └── execute it

zig build-exe foo.zig
      │
      └── compile
             │
             ▼
           ./foo
```

`build-exe` puts an artifact in your working directory. You can then run the artifact, ship it or link it.

`run` puts the same artifact in the cache and runs it immediately. Thus there is nothing to delete after the run, and nothing to add to `.gitignore`.

For a program of a few hundred lines or fewer, `zig run main.zig` is sufficient, and there is no build step to remember. Put the arguments for the program after `--`:

```bash
zig run main.zig -- --verbose input.txt
```

The cache is content-addressed. If nothing changed, a second `zig run` does not compile again. Thus `zig run` is fast enough to use as a script interpreter. You can work on a tool in a single file this way for a long time.

`zig test` works in the same way, and it does not need a `main`. For Zig, a file that contains only `test` blocks is a complete program that can run.

## The output of each command

- `build-exe` makes a file that the OS can run. Thus it needs an entry point, and it links.
- `build-lib` makes a `.a` file (or a `.lib` file) that other code links. With `-dynamic`, it makes a shared library.
- `build-obj` stops before the link and gives you a single object file. Use it when Zig is one part of a build that a different tool controls.

`build-obj` is an easy way to add Zig to a codebase that you already have. Compile one module with `build-obj`. Then link the object file into a C or C++ project, the same as all other object files. Nothing else in the project must change.

## Build for WebAssembly

Most snippets on this site build with this target and this mode:

```bash
zig build-exe main.zig -target wasm32-wasi -OReleaseSmall
```

For a freestanding wasm module without WASI, use `-target wasm32-freestanding`. The browser-canvas example is this type of module. Add `-fno-entry` and give each export explicitly:

```bash
zig build-exe main.zig -target wasm32-freestanding \
  -OReleaseSmall -fno-entry --export=add
```

The two targets are different in what the module expects from the host:

- `wasm32-wasi` expects an interface like a filesystem, and a `main`.
- `wasm32-freestanding` expects nothing. Thus there is no entry point to call. Instead, you give the names of the functions that the host can call.

`-OReleaseSmall` is very important here, because the browser downloads the artifact before it runs.

## When to change to `build.zig`

Move to a build script when you have one of these:

- more than one artifact
- dependencies
- generated files
- a named test step

Then `zig build --help` shows the steps and options that the script defines.

Usually, the change is necessary at the second target or at the first dependency. While one command line builds the program, the command line is simpler than a script. When you start to keep a note of the flags, that note must become `build.zig`.

---

## Cross-compilation

*Build System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/build-system/cross-compilation/*

In Zig, cross-compilation is not a special mode. Cross-compilation is a flag:

```bash
zig build-exe main.zig -target x86_64-linux-gnu
zig build-exe main.zig -target aarch64-macos
zig build-exe main.zig -target x86_64-windows-gnu
zig build-exe main.zig -target wasm32-wasi
```

You do not install a cross toolchain, and you do not make a sysroot. Zig includes the libc sources for the targets that it supports. Zig builds the parts that it needs when it needs them.

```bash
zig targets       # everything available
```

## One source file, three platforms

The source does not change. Only the flag changes:

```
                 hello.zig
                     │
   ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
   │                 │                 │
   ▼                 ▼                 ▼
x86_64-linux-gnu  x86_64-windows-gnu  aarch64-linux-musl
   │                 │                 │
   ▼                 ▼                 ▼
 hello            hello.exe          hello
```

Run this command on a Linux computer:

```bash
zig build-exe hello.zig -target x86_64-windows-gnu
file hello.exe
```

```
hello.exe: PE32+ executable (console) x86-64, for MS Windows
```

`file` reads the container format, and the container format is Windows. The compiler that made `hello.exe` is the same binary that you use for a native build. The Linux computer has no Windows SDK, no MinGW and no Wine.

Change the triple to `aarch64-linux-musl`. Then `file` reports a statically linked ARM64 ELF.

## The triple

`<arch>-<os>-<abi>`, with `native` allowed in any position:

```
x86_64-linux-gnu
x86_64-linux-musl      # static linking without glibc's version requirements
aarch64-macos-none
wasm32-wasi
native-native-musl
```

Each of the three fields answers a question, and each question is more specific than the last:

- The **architecture** tells which instructions the CPU understands.
- The **OS** tells what the binary asks the system for, and the container format of the binary.
- The **ABI** tells which C library and which calling conventions the binary expects when it runs.

Be careful with the ABI field. `musl` makes a fully static binary. `gnu` links against glibc and gets the version compatibility rules of glibc. Thus the two `x86_64-linux` lines above are two different builds.

## Build for a specific CPU

```bash
zig build-exe main.zig -target x86_64-linux -mcpu=znver3
zig build-exe main.zig -mcpu=baseline        # maximum portability
```

`baseline` is the safe choice. It assumes only the minimum features of the architecture. When you give the name of a specific CPU, the optimiser can use the instructions of that CPU. The cost is that the binary does not run on older CPUs.

## In `build.zig`

```zig
const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
```

This line gives `-Dtarget=` to each person who runs your build. Thus users can cross-compile your project, and you do not have to do more work.

## Why this is unusual
