If you cross-compiled C before, you know the usual steps. Many of those steps are not necessary here.

The usual method needs three things:

- A cross toolchain for each target.
- A sysroot that contains the headers and libraries of that platform.
- A build system that can find the toolchain and the sysroot.

To prepare one of these takes a day. To keep several of them up to date is work that does not stop. Because of that cost, many teams decide to build only on Linux. Also, CI matrices use most of their time to install compilers.

Zig includes the libc sources for the targets that it supports, and it compiles the parts that it needs when it needs them. Thus the toolchain and the system headers are already in the single binary that you downloaded. To build a Windows executable on a Mac, use the same command as a native build, with one more flag: `-target x86_64-windows`.

## What still needs care

Cross-compilation gives you a binary. You must still test the binary.

Cross-compilation also does not remove the platform differences that the code must handle. Examples are path separators, line endings, and the size of `usize`: 4 bytes on wasm and 8 bytes on your laptop.

A successful build shows that the code compiles for that target. That is most of the value. But code that compiles is not always code that works.

The second limit is a system library that the target has and your computer does not have. To link against that library, you need the real headers. Then cross-compilation needs more preparation.

## Compile C too

`zig cc` is a C compiler that can replace your current C compiler, and it has the same cross-compilation support. Thus some projects use Zig only as a build tool for their C code.

`zig cc` accepts the flags that a C compiler accepts. Thus you can put it into a `Makefile` or a `configure` command as `CC=zig cc`, and you get the cross-compilation support with it. Some C projects build only on the type of computer that their authors used. After that change, such a project can usually build for four platforms. The source of the project does not change. `zig c++` does the same for C++.

---

## Zig Build

*Build System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/build-system/zig-build/*

`build.zig` is not a configuration file. `build.zig` is a Zig program that makes a graph of steps. Then `zig build` runs the steps in the graph.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
        .name = "myapp",
        .root_module = b.createModule(.{
            .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
            .target = target,
            .optimize = optimize,
        }),
    });
    b.installArtifact(exe);

    const run = b.addRunArtifact(exe);
    const run_step = b.step("run", "Run the app");
    run_step.dependOn(&run.step);
}
```

## The module comes first

`addExecutable` takes a `root_module`. It does not take a source file directly.

Older examples give `.root_source_file`, `.target` and `.optimize` directly to `addExecutable`. Zig removed that form. Make the module first.

## Steps and options

```bash
zig build              # the default step
zig build run          # a step you declared
zig build --help       # lists your steps and options
zig build -Dtarget=wasm32-wasi -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall
```

`b.option(...)` declares your own flags. Your flags then show in the `--help` output.

## Why a program and not a configuration file

Many people say that a build script must be declarative. But each declarative build system adds a way to run ordinary code, and the difficult parts of the build go into that code. For example, Make runs shell commands, and CMake has its own language. Zig lets you write the build in Zig from the start.

Thus all that you know about Zig applies in `build.zig`. You can use loops, functions and a `switch` on the target.

The build of this site is an example. The build reads a directory and examines the first lines of each file to find its type. Then the build makes a compile step and a run step for each snippet. The code is thirty lines of ordinary Zig. In a declarative system, the same work needs a plugin.

The cost is that a build script can do anything. A build script can be slow, or it can break the cache. The next section is about the cache.

## Configure time and run time

People often confuse these two times. `build()` runs **one time** to make the graph. The steps run after `build()` is complete.

The cache layer cannot see what `build()` examines directly. For example, the cache cannot see a directory that `build()` reads, or a check that a file exists.

If `build()` examines something directly, tell the build system with this call:

```zig
b.graph.poisonCache();
```

Without the call, the build system keeps the configuration in the cache. Then your `build()` does not run again when the thing that it examined changes.

The `build.zig` of this guide finds snippets in a directory, and it needs this call. Before the call was in the file, the build ignored a new snippet and gave no message.

To prevent the problem, give the inputs to the graph as files that the graph knows about. Do not let `build()` examine the inputs itself:

- The build system tracks `b.path("src/main.zig")`. A step that depends on the file runs again when the file changes.
- The build system does not track `std.Io.Dir.cwd().openFile(...)` inside `build()`. When the file changes, nothing in the build sees the change.

## Steps are a graph, not a list

`dependOn` is the only way to put steps in order. These results come from that rule:

- Independent steps run in parallel on all cores, because no declaration gives an order between them.
- A step runs a maximum of one time in each build, if one or many other steps depend on it.
- `zig build test` runs only the part of the graph that the `test` step needs. It does not run the full file.

Thus, to make one step run before a different step, add a `dependOn` between the two steps. If you move lines in the file, the order does not change. The order of declarations in `build()` has no meaning.

## Dependencies

`build.zig.zon` declares the dependencies. In `build.zig`, `b.dependency("name", .{})` gets one dependency. The fetch uses the content address of each package, and it verifies the hash.

`zig fetch --save <url>` adds an entry and records the hash. Use this command. Do not edit the file manually.

The hash covers the contents. Thus, if a dependency changes after you add it, the build fails. The build does not fetch the changed contents. Packages go into a global cache that all projects share.

The `build.zig` of a dependency runs as a part of your build. Thus a dependency can supply modules (`dep.module("name")`) and artifacts (`dep.artifact("name")`). You connect these modules and artifacts to your own targets.

There is no separate format for a package manifest, and there is no install step. The fetch, the build and the link are all parts of the same graph.

---

## Dependencies

*Build System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/build-system/dependencies/*

The Zig build system includes a package manager. There is no separate tool, and there is no central registry. A dependency is a URL and a hash. Zig fetches the dependency into a global cache and verifies the hash when the files arrive.

Two files work together:

- `build.zig.zon` declares the packages that you depend on.
- `build.zig` gets each package and connects its modules to your artifacts.

## The path of a dependency

```
 build.zig.zon
      │
      │ declares
      ▼
  Dependency
      │
      │ downloaded, hash checked
      ▼
Global Zig cache
      │
      │ requested by
      ▼
   build.zig
      │
      ▼
executable / module
```

The two files answer two different questions:

- `build.zig.zon` answers **what do I depend on?**
- `build.zig` answers **where must the build use that dependency?**

The two files are separate. Thus, on each computer, a checkout and `zig build` give the same set of dependencies. The manifest records what you depend on. The build script connects each dependency to your code.

You cannot edit one file into a state where the other file disagrees and nothing tells you. If `build.zig` uses a name that the manifest does not declare, the result is an error, not an empty module.

## `build.zig.zon`

The manifest is a ZON literal. ZON is Zig Object Notation, and it has the same syntax as a Zig struct literal. A minimal manifest:

```zig
.{
    .name = .myproject,
    .version = "0.1.0",
    .fingerprint = 0x1234567890abcdef, // generated once by `zig init`
    .dependencies = .{
        .mecha = .{
            .url = "https://github.com/Hejsil/mecha/archive/<commit>.tar.gz",
            .hash = "mecha-0.9.0-...",
        },
    },
    .paths = .{
        "build.zig",
        "build.zig.zon",
        "src",
    },
}
```

You rarely write the `.url` and `.hash` pair manually. Run this command:

```bash
zig fetch --save https://github.com/Hejsil/mecha/archive/<commit>.tar.gz
```

`zig fetch` downloads the archive, calculates its hash, and writes the `.dependencies` entry for you.

The hash is content-addressed. The same bytes always give the same hash. If the hash is different on a later fetch, the result is a hard error. Thus a dependency cannot change after you add it.

## Connect the dependency in `build.zig`

A declared dependency does nothing until `build.zig` asks for it. Do these steps:

1. Get the dependency with `b.dependency`.
2. Get a named module from the dependency with `.module`.
3. Add that module to the module that imports it.

```zig
pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    // The name matches the key in build.zig.zon's .dependencies.
    const mecha = b.dependency("mecha", .{
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });

    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
        .name = "myproject",
        .root_module = b.createModule(.{
            .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
            .target = target,
            .optimize = optimize,
            .imports = &.{
                // "mecha" is the name `@import` will use in your source;
                // `mecha.module("mecha")` is the module the dependency exposes.
                .{ .name = "mecha", .module = mecha.module("mecha") },
            },
        }),
    });
    b.installArtifact(exe);
}
```

`build.zig` gives `target` and `optimize` to `b.dependency`. Thus the dependency builds for the same target and mode as the code that uses it. Almost always, that is the correct result.

## Use the dependency in code

When the build imports a module under a name, `@import` gets the module in the same way as a module of the standard library:

```zig
const mecha = @import("mecha");
```

If you import a name that `build.zig` does not declare, the result is a compile error. The error gives the name of the module that is not declared. It is not a runtime failure that is difficult to understand.

The same mechanism connects your own internal modules. Thus you import a dependency and a local module in the same way.

## Where the files are

Zig puts fetched packages in a global cache. On Linux, the cache is under `~/.cache/zig`. All projects share the cache, and the hash is the key for each package.

Your repository contains only `build.zig.zon`, the small manifest. You do not commit a `vendor/` directory. You do not run a separate install step such as `npm install`.

---

## Generate Documentation

*Build System. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/build-system/generating-documentation/*

Zig makes HTML documentation from doc comments.

```bash
zig build-lib src/root.zig -femit-docs
zig build docs        # if your build.zig declares it
```

## The comment forms

| Syntax | Attaches to |
| --- | --- |
| `///` | the declaration that follows |
| `//!` | the file or module that contains it (must be at the top) |
| `//` | ordinary comment, not documentation |

```zig
//! A module for working with points.

/// A point in two dimensions.
pub const Point = struct {
    /// Horizontal position, in pixels.
    x: i32,
};
```

Doc comments are Markdown. Only `pub` declarations are in the output.

If a `///` comment is in a position where it cannot attach to a declaration, the result is a compile error, not a warning. Thus, if a doc comment becomes separate from its declaration, the compiler tells you.

## The output

The generator does one thing. It copies the signature from the source and puts your `///` text below the signature.

```
Source

  /// Adds two integers.
  pub fn add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 { ... }

        │
        │  zig build-lib -femit-docs
        ▼

Generated page

  add(a: i32, b: i32) i32
  Adds two integers.
```

The signature is already on the page. The generator makes the signature from the code, thus the signature is always correct. If your comment repeats the signature, the comment can become incorrect, and the generated signature above it stays correct.

## In `build.zig`

```zig
const docs = b.addInstallDirectory(.{
    .source_dir = lib.getEmittedDocs(),
    .install_dir = .prefix,
    .install_subdir = "docs",
});
b.step("docs", "Generate documentation").dependOn(&docs.step);
```

## What to write in a doc comment

The generated page already shows the signature. Thus do not repeat the signature in prose. Write what the signature cannot show and what a caller must know:

- **The owner of the return value.** If the function allocates, tell which allocator frees the memory and when. In most doc comments, this sentence is the most useful one.
- **The meaning of the errors.** The error set is visible. The cause of each error in the set is not visible.
- **The constraints that the type cannot express.** For example, a slice must be in sorted order, two lengths must be equal, or a pointer must stay valid during the call.
- **The cost**, when the cost is not clear. O(n) and O(1) change how a caller uses the function.

In the example above, "Adds two integers" tells the reader nothing new. The reader can see that from `add(a: i32, b: i32) i32`. The signature cannot tell the reader that the addition has an overflow check, and that it panics on overflow and does not wrap. Write that sentence instead.

## Only `pub` declarations are in the output

Thus the doc build is a check of your interface. When you generate the docs, you can find problems in the public list. For example, the list can show a type that you wanted to keep private, or a helper without a comment. Without the docs, you possibly never examine that list.

The output is a static site: HTML, the source and a search index. The site needs no server, and you can publish it at any location that can hold files. The `addInstallDirectory` call above installs the site for that purpose.

## Doctests

Tests are ordinary language constructs. Thus a `test` block next to a function is both a test and an example. A comment can become incorrect without a message from the build, but a test cannot. This full guide uses the same method.

Give a test the name of the function that it tests, for example `test myFunction { ... }`. The name connects the test and the function. Thus the example stays with the documentation. It is not in a separate file that nobody updates.

Use a test as the main form of documentation, not as an extra. A prose example in a comment tells how the function behaves, but nothing checks the example. Someone wrote the example for the signature on one day. A test that says the same thing gets a check on each build. The two disagree eventually. When the two disagree, the test is correct.

---

## ABI

*Working with C. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/abi/*

To pass a struct from Zig to C, declare it as `extern struct`. An
`extern struct` uses the field order and padding of the C ABI. A
`packed struct` gives exact bits with no padding, for registers and wire
formats.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// `extern struct` guarantees the C layout: the order of the declaration, and
// the C rules for padding.
const CPoint = extern struct {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
};

// `packed struct` has exact bits and no padding. An integer holds the bits.
const Flags = packed struct {
    a: bool,
    b: bool,
    rest: u6,
};

// The compiler can change the order of the fields of a plain struct, and add
// padding in any way that it selects.
const Loose = struct {
    small: u8,
    big: u64,
};

test "extern struct follows C layout" {
    try expect(@sizeOf(CPoint) == 8);
    try expect(@offsetOf(CPoint, "x") == 0);
    try expect(@offsetOf(CPoint, "y") == 4);
}

test "packed struct is exactly its bits" {
    try expect(@bitSizeOf(Flags) == 8);
    try expect(@sizeOf(Flags) == 1);

    const f = Flags{ .a = true, .b = false, .rest = 0 };
    // Packed structs convert to their backing integer.
    try expect(@as(u8, @bitCast(f)) == 1);
}

test "plain structs make no layout promise" {
    // Zig can put these fields in any order for packing. Do not assume offsets.
    try expect(@sizeOf(Loose) >= 9);
}

test "extern union and enum" {
    const E = extern union { i: i32, f: f32 };
    try expect(@sizeOf(E) == 4);

    // An enum with a C ABI tag type.
    const Colour = enum(c_int) { red, green, blue };
    try expect(@intFromEnum(Colour.green) == 1);
}

// `callconv(.c)` lets C call a Zig function.
export fn addFromC(a: c_int, b: c_int) callconv(.c) c_int {
    return a + b;
}

test "exported function is callable from Zig too" {
    try expect(addFromC(2, 3) == 5);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`05-working-with-c.abi`)*

A plain Zig `struct` makes **no layout promise**. The compiler can put the
fields in a different order and add padding in any way that it prefers. This
freedom is a feature, because it lets the optimiser pack the fields. But you
cannot give a plain `struct` to C.

## The three layouts

| Declaration | Layout | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `struct` | unspecified | ordinary Zig code |
| `extern struct` | C ABI: declaration order, C padding | C interop |
| `packed struct` | exact bits, no padding, integer-backed | wire formats, registers |

```zig
const CPoint = extern struct { x: i32, y: i32 };   // offsets 0 and 4
const Flags = packed struct { a: bool, b: bool, rest: u6 };  // exactly 8 bits
```

A `packed struct` converts to and from its backing integer with `@bitCast`.
Thus a `packed struct` is the natural way to describe hardware registers and
protocol headers.

## What "ABI" means

The application binary interface is a set of agreements. Two pieces of code
that are compiled separately need these agreements to call each other:

- The position of the fields of a struct.
- The registers that hold each argument.
- The side that cleans the stack.
- The form of a name in the symbol table.

The source language does not specify these items. The platform decides them.
The two sides must agree before they meet, because at that time no type
information remains to check.

Because nothing remains to check, a mistake here makes no noise. An incorrect
field offset is not a compile error in either language. The result is a
program that reads the wrong four bytes and continues.

## Verify the layout

`@sizeOf`, `@offsetOf` and `@bitSizeOf` are comptime values. Thus you can
assert a layout assumption at compile time:

```zig
comptime {
    std.debug.assert(@offsetOf(CPoint, "y") == 4);
}
```

Add these assertions at each real C boundary. An assertion changes a silent
mismatch into a build failure.

A stronger version of the same idea is to not write the declaration by hand.
translate-c reads the header and makes the struct. Thus the struct and the
header cannot become different. See [import C](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/cimport/).
Write an `extern` declaration by hand only when no header exists. Those cases
are exactly the cases that need the assertions.

## Bit order is not portable

`packed struct` gives you exact bit positions. A hardware register or a
protocol header needs exact bit positions. But a `packed struct` does not
always agree with the bitfields of a C compiler. In C, the order of bits in a
unit is implementation-defined. Thus two compilers can put the bits of the
same header in different positions.

For a wire format, this is not a problem. It is even an advantage, because
you define the layout. You do not copy the layout of a different program. If
you must match a C bitfield exactly, do not assume. Compare the layout with
the C compiler that you use.

Byte order is a different question, and `packed struct` says nothing about
it. A protocol header that you read from a socket needs `std.mem.bigToNative`
or an explicit decode, one byte at a time. `@bitCast` gives you the byte order
of the host.

## Calling conventions

`callconv(.c)` gives a function the C calling convention. `export` gives the
function an unmangled symbol name:

```zig
export fn add(a: c_int, b: c_int) callconv(.c) c_int {
    return a + b;
}
```

C needs nothing more to call Zig. To call C from Zig, declare the C function
with `extern`:

```zig
extern "c" fn abs(n: c_int) c_int;
```

`export` does the two jobs. It gives the function an unmangled symbol name
and the C calling convention. Thus the `callconv(.c)` above only states what
`export` already gives. The extra `callconv(.c)` costs nothing, and it shows
what you intend.

With `@export(&add, .{ .name = "add" })`, you must supply the convention
yourself. `@export` exports a function, and the function keeps the convention
that it declares.

Zig errors also do not cross the boundary. If an `export` function returns
`!void`, C has no representation for the return type. Thus a function for C
callers returns a status code, and keeps its error handling inside.

## Do not `extern` everything

An `extern struct` stops the packing that the optimiser can do for a plain
struct. Use `extern struct` at the boundary, and use ordinary structs inside.

An `extern struct` also makes your layout fixed, as part of the interface. You
can add a field to a plain struct, and the only result is a recompile. An
`extern struct` that C code allocates is a promise about size. If you change
the size, all code that was compiled against the old size breaks.

---

## C Primitive Types

*Working with C. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/c-primitive-types/*

In Zig, a C `int` is `c_int` and a C `long` is `c_long`. The sizes of these
types follow the C ABI of the target. Use them at the C boundary, because
`long` is 8 bytes on 64-bit Linux and 4 bytes on Windows.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "c types are separate from fixed-width ones" {
    // `c_int` has the size of `int` on this target. Use `c_int` only at the
    // C boundary. In all other places, use i32, u64 and the other fixed types.
    try expect(@sizeOf(c_int) == 4);
    try expect(@sizeOf(c_char) == 1);
    try expect(c_int != i32); // different types, also at the same size
}

test "c_long varies by target" {
    // 4 bytes on wasm32 and Windows, 8 bytes on 64-bit Linux. The type
    // exists because of this difference. Thus do not hardcode i64.
    try expect(@sizeOf(c_long) == 4); // wasm32
}

test "converting at the boundary" {
    const n: i32 = 42;
    const c: c_int = @intCast(n);
    try expect(c == 42);
}

test "the C ABI integer for pointers" {
    try expect(@sizeOf(usize) == @sizeOf(*anyopaque));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`05-working-with-c.c-primitives`)*

Zig has these C types:

- `c_char`, `c_short`, `c_int`, `c_long` and `c_longlong`.
- An `unsigned` type for each of these types except `c_char`. There is no
  `c_uchar`.
- `c_longdouble`.

The C ABI of the target sets the size of each type.

## Why not use `i32`

A C `long` does not have one size. If code uses `i64` for a C `long`, the code
is correct on one platform and wrong on a different platform. Nothing tells
you about the error. A bug of this type appears only after a port.

`c_int` and `i32` are **different types**, also when they have the same size.
Thus the compiler does not let you use one type for the other by accident.

## What C guarantees, and what it does not

C does not specify the size of its integer types. C specifies minimum ranges
and an order of sizes. The platform sets the actual widths, and a document
called the ABI records them. For this reason, the table below has three
answers and not one:

| C type | 64-bit Linux/macOS | 64-bit Windows | wasm32 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `int` | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| `long` | 8 | **4** | **4** |
| `long long` | 8 | 8 | 8 |
| `size_t` | 8 | 8 | **4** |
| pointer | 8 | 8 | **4** |

`long` causes the most problems, because the two most common desktop
platforms do not agree about its size. `c_long` gives the correct size on all
targets that Zig supports.

`c_char` has a second problem in addition to the width. The platform also
decides if `c_char` is signed or unsigned, and the answer is different on x86
Linux and ARM Linux. Zig also models this difference. For this reason,
`c_char` is a separate type, and not an alias for `i8` or `u8`.

## Keep the C types at the boundary

Convert at the edge, and use fixed-width types inside the program:

```zig
export fn process(count: c_int) callconv(.c) void {
    const n: u32 = @intCast(count);   // now in Zig's world
    ...
}
```

If you use `c_int` in all of your program, an assumption that depends on the
target spreads to all parts of the program.

The conversion is also the correct place for validation. A `c_int` from C can
be negative. If your code uses the value as a count, reject a negative value
on the line of the conversion. In a safety build, `@intCast` panics when the
value does not fit. A panic is better than a program that continues. But at a
boundary where the value comes from outside, an explicit check that returns
an error is better again.

## `anyopaque`

`anyopaque` is Zig's `void` in the C sense: the type that a `void*` points
to. Thus C's `void *ptr` becomes `*anyopaque`, and C's `void f(void)` returns
Zig's `void`. Zig keeps the two meanings of C's `void` separate.

The same rule applies in other places. C uses one keyword for "nothing", and
also for "something whose type I do not tell you". Code must use the context
to find which meaning is correct. Zig gives the two meanings different names.
Thus the ambiguity stops at the point of translation. Your program does not
get the ambiguity.

In the same way, C's `void*` is "a pointer to unknown data". It is also the
generic pointer that all other pointers convert to. In Zig, `*anyopaque` has
only the first meaning. For the conversion, you use `@ptrCast`, and you can
see the conversion in the code.

For handles that you control, use a separate [`opaque
{}`](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/opaque/) type, not `*anyopaque`. A separate type
prevents the use of one type of handle in place of a different type of
handle.

---

## C Pointers

*Working with C. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/c-pointers/*

Zig's C pointer type is `[*c]T`. A `[*c]T` can be null, has no length and has
no bounds checks. Convert it to a slice or a `*T` at the C boundary. Do not
use it in the rest of the program.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

test "a C pointer is the permissive one" {
    var value: i32 = 42;
    // A [*c]T can be null, you can index it, and it coerces freely. It has
    // none of the guarantees of the other pointer types in Zig.
    const c_ptr: [*c]i32 = &value;
    try expect(c_ptr.* == 42);
    try expect(c_ptr[0] == 42);
}

test "it coerces to and from the safe types" {
    var array = [_]i32{ 1, 2, 3 };
    const many: [*]i32 = &array;
    const c_ptr: [*c]i32 = many;
    const back: [*]i32 = c_ptr;
    try expect(back[2] == 3);
}

test "null is representable" {
    const c_ptr: [*c]i32 = null;
    try expect(c_ptr == null);
}

test "convert at the boundary and use real types inside" {
    var array = [_]i32{ 10, 20, 30 };
    const c_ptr: [*c]i32 = &array;

    // The pointer does not carry the length. Supply the length one time.
    // Then use a slice, which has bounds checks.
    const slice: []i32 = c_ptr[0..3];
    try expect(slice.len == 3);
    try expect(slice[1] == 20);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`05-working-with-c.c-pointers`)*

`[*c]T` is Zig's model of C's `T*`. The main reason for the type is that
translate-c can then convert headers automatically.

## A C pointer has no guarantees

| Property | `*T` | `[]T` | `[*c]T` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| can be null | no | no | **yes** |
| carries a length | n/a | yes | no |
| bounds checked | n/a | yes | no |
| indexable | no | yes | yes |
| coerces freely | no | no | **yes** |

The last row is the dangerous row. A `[*c]T` converts to and from the safe
pointer types, and the compiler does not complain. At a C boundary, this
conversion is convenient. In all other places, the conversion causes damage.
The conversion removes the guarantees that the rest of the language depends
on, and nothing tells you.

## Why the type is necessary

A C header cannot tell the translator which of the three things a `T*` is.
Look at `void process(int *data, size_t n)`. A human reads the two parameters
together, and decides that `data` is an array of `n` items. Look at
`int *out`. A human reads the name, and decides that `out` is one item that
the function writes through. But the declaration itself is the same in the
two examples.

Thus translate-c cannot select a type. `[*c]T` is the type that means "any one
of these three things". Each safe pointer type would be a guess. A wrong guess
causes more damage than no guess.

## Read the header, not the signature

Thus at a C boundary, your task is to decide what the C function really
promises. Then write that promise as a Zig type. Ask four questions. Usually,
the documentation of the header is the only place with the answers:

- **How many items?** One, or `n`, or all items until a terminator.
- **Can the pointer be null?** Frequently yes, and frequently null has a
  specific meaning.
- **Who owns the memory?** Does the function keep the pointer after it
  returns? Must the caller free the result, and with which free function?
- **Does the function write to the memory?** A C declaration without `const`
  does not prove that the function writes. It also does not prove the opposite.

The type that you get from translate-c answers none of these questions.
Answer them one time, in the wrapper. Then the rest of the program can use the
answers. When no person answers the questions, C programs get bugs.

## Convert at the boundary

When you know the length, make a slice. After that, use only the slice:

```zig
const slice: []i32 = c_ptr[0..count];
```

The slice gives you bounds checks, `for` loops and `.len`. If the pointer can
be null, check it one time and change it into an optional. Do not send the
uncertainty to other parts of the program.

In practice, you write a thin Zig wrapper for each C function that you use. The signature of the wrapper states what the C function really
promises:

```zig
pub fn process(data: []i32) void {
    c.process(data.ptr, data.len);
}
```

The wrapper has three lines, and all of the program above the wrapper uses a
slice. The unchecked assumption is in one place, where you can compare it
with the header. It is not at each call site.

## Which pointer type to use

If the pointer type does not come from translate-c or from an `extern`
declaration, do not write `[*c]`. Use one of these types:

- `*T` for one item.
- `[*]T` for many items.
- `[]T` when you know the count.
- `?` when the value can be absent.

Sometimes a `[*c]` occurs in a compile error deep inside your own code, far
from any C. Then a `[*c]` came out of a boundary, and your code passed it
to other code from there. Fix the problem at that boundary, not at the place of the
error.

---

## Import C

*Working with C. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/cimport/*

Zig reads C headers directly. You do not need a binding generator, and you
do not maintain an intermediate `.zig` file.

The change is the place where Zig reads the header. Before, a builtin in your
source read the header. Now a step in your build reads the header.

## `@cImport` is gone

If you come from an older tutorial, this line does not compile:

```zig
// Removed from the language. Every tutorial written before 2026 shows this.
const c = @cImport({
    @cDefine("_GNU_SOURCE", {});
    @cInclude("stdio.h");
    @cInclude("string.h");
});
```

On current Zig, the line fails with
`error: invalid builtin function: '@cImport'`. `@cInclude` and `@cDefine` are
also removed.

Headers now come from `b.addTranslateC`, which makes an ordinary Zig module.
Import the module by the name that you gave to it:

```zig
const c = @import("c");

pub fn main() void {
    // Zig string literals are already null-terminated. Thus you can give
    // them to a `[*c]const u8` parameter without a change.
    _ = c.printf("hello from C\n");

    const len = c.strlen("abc");
    _ = c.printf("strlen(\"abc\") = %d\n", @as(c_int, @intCast(len)));
}
```

*This snippet translates the real stdio.h and string.h and links the host libc. Thus CI builds and runs it natively. Browser wasm has no headers and no libc. (`05-working-with-c.libc-from-zig`)*

All declarations of the header are still members of `c`. The difference is
that the source file does not name a header now. The build names the header.

The translate step takes one C file as its root. If a project needs several
headers, write one header that includes them:

```c
// src/c.h
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
```

```zig
// build.zig
const translate = b.addTranslateC(.{
    .root_source_file = b.path("src/c.h"),
    .target = target,
    .optimize = optimize,
    .link_libc = true,
});
translate.defineCMacro("_GNU_SOURCE", null);
```

`defineCMacro` replaces `@cDefine`. A `null` value means a macro without a
value. Then `translate.createModule()` gives the module. Give that module to
the code that needs it.

The extra step has an advantage. The build now caches and configures a C

again on each compile.

## Tell the build where to look

There are three separate jobs, in three places.

The translate step must find the headers:

```zig
translate.addIncludePath(b.path("vendor/include"));
translate.linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3", .{});
```

The module that calls the C code needs libc and the compiled C code:

```zig
const module = b.createModule(.{
    .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
    .target = target,
    .optimize = optimize,
    .link_libc = true,
    .imports = &.{.{ .name = "c", .module = translate.createModule() }},
});
module.linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3", .{});
```

Or compile the C code yourself. Zig includes a C compiler. Thus you can copy
the source files of a dependency into your project:

```zig
module.addCSourceFile(.{ .file = b.path("vendor/thing.c"), .flags = &.{"-std=c99"} });
```

Look at the type that has these methods. `addCSourceFile`, `addIncludePath`
and `linkSystemLibrary` are methods on `std.Build.Module`, not on the
executable. `exe.linkLibC()` does not exist now. For libc, set
`.link_libc = true` in the options of the module. Code that calls
`exe.addIncludePath` or `exe.linkLibC` is from the same time as `@cImport`. That
code fails in the same way.

## A full project

The parts above have a meaning only together. This is the smallest project
that uses all of the parts. Your Zig code calls a C function from a C file in
your project. No system library is necessary.

```
project/
├── build.zig
├── src/
│   └── main.zig
└── vendor/
    ├── calc.c
    └── calc.h
```

```c
// vendor/calc.h
int calc_add(int a, int b);
```

```c
// vendor/calc.c
#include "calc.h"
int calc_add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
```

`src/main.zig` is a real snippet in this guide. Thus CI compiles and runs it
on each push:

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// The removed `@cImport` builtin made this module before. Now the build names
// the header. Thus this file does not name a header.
const c = @import("c");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // `calc_add` is an ordinary member of the module. The translation of the
    // header makes the name. The compiled `calc.c` lets the name link.
    try out.print("calc_add(2, 3) = {d}\n", .{c.calc_add(2, 3)});
    try out.flush();
}
```

*This snippet translates a vendored header and compiles a vendored .c file. The two steps need a host C compiler. CI builds and runs the snippet on each push. (`05-working-with-c.translate-c`)*

CI builds the snippet against the two C files above. The C files are next to
the snippet in `snippets/05-working-with-c/`. Your own project writes the
build below by hand. This repo makes the same steps from a marker on the
snippet.

```zig
// build.zig
const translate = b.addTranslateC(.{
    .root_source_file = b.path("vendor/calc.h"),
    .target = target,
    .optimize = optimize,
    .link_libc = true,
});

const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
    .name = "demo",
    .root_module = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
        .link_libc = true,
        .imports = &.{.{ .name = "c", .module = translate.createModule() }},
    }),
});
exe.root_module.addCSourceFile(.{ .file = b.path("vendor/calc.c") });
b.installArtifact(exe);
```

The project has one header. Thus the header is the root of the translate step,
and no include path is necessary. If the root is your own header that
`#include`s several headers, `translate.addIncludePath` lets Zig find those
headers.

To read the header and to compile the C code are separate jobs. If you omit
one job, the failure is different from the failure for the other job:

```
 vendor/calc.h
       │
       │ addTranslateC reads it, once, as a build step
       ▼
   module "c"
       │
       │ imported by src/main.zig as @import("c")
       ▼
  src/main.zig
       │
       │ addCSourceFile compiles vendor/calc.c
       ▼
 build.zig links both
       │
       ▼
   executable
```

The translate step decides which declarations Zig can see. If the header does
not exist, the error gives the name of the header.

`addCSourceFile` puts the compiled function in the binary. If you forget
`addCSourceFile`, the code compiles without errors. Then the link fails with
`ld.lld: undefined symbol: calc_add`. This error is more difficult to
understand than the other error, so learn to recognise it. The line does not
come from memory. When the C file is removed from the snippet above, the build gives exactly
that line.

To use a system library in place of the vendored file, change two lines:

- `linkSystemLibrary("sqlite3", .{})` on the translate step, so that the
  translate step finds the header.
- The same call on the module, so that the build links the library.

## What translates and what does not

Types, functions and simple `#define` constants translate correctly.
**Function-like macros do not translate correctly.** They are C syntax, not C
semantics, and Zig cannot always give them a meaning. If you need a
function-like macro, write it again in Zig.

The command `zig translate-c header.h` still exists. It prints exactly what
the build step makes. To see the result for a given header, this command is
the fastest method.

## Strings

C strings are `[*c]const u8` and null-terminated. Zig string literals are
already null-terminated. Thus you can give a literal to C without a
conversion. For a C string that comes to Zig, `std.mem.span(ptr)` finds the
terminator and returns a slice.

## Binding generators in other languages

Other languages use a separate tool for the same problem:

- Python has ctypes, cffi and a generator.
- Rust has bindgen.
- Go has cgo, with its own dialect of comments.

Each of these tools reads the header and writes code in a third file. You must
then make that file again, commit it, and keep it the same as the header.

Zig reads the header as part of the build. The build makes the binding again
when the header changes. Thus the binding is always the same as its header.
You do not commit a generated file, and you do not make one again by hand. If
you update the C library, a changed signature is a compile error on the same
day.

Because the build makes the binding again each time, the X11 chapter of this
guide can link against the real system Xlib in CI. The X11 snippet does not
run. But CI translates the header and type-checks the calls. Thus a change in libX11 makes
the build fail. Without this check, nobody would see the change until a person
read the page.

## Error handling across the boundary

C reports a failure with a return value and with a global `errno`. After
translation, neither of the two has a useful meaning. Thus the wrapper that you
write for a C library is also the place where the C conventions become Zig
errors:

```zig
pub fn open(path: [:0]const u8) !Handle {
    const h = c.thing_open(path.ptr);
    if (h == null) return error.OpenFailed;
    return .{ .ptr = h.? };
}
```

Write a wrapper of this type one time for each function. The work is
repetitive, and it is all the work that the wrapper must do. In return, the
rest of the program uses `try`. No caller has a return code that it can
forget to check.

Ownership is the other half. Each C library has its own rules about who frees
which memory. In the wrapper, those rules become `defer` and `errdefer` in the
scope of the Zig caller. Usually, a handle type with a `deinit` method is the
correct shape, because then you can see the pair of calls.

## Why the snippets here have no Run button

CI compiles and runs the two programs above on each push, with the compiler
that the footer names. Neither program runs in your browser.

To translate a header, you need real C headers and a libc for the target. The
wasm sandbox of these pages has neither. Thus the two programs are host
builds. CI runs them on Linux and diffs their output. The page shows you the
source without a Run button. The page does not ship a `.wasm` that cannot
work.

Only the `build.zig` on this page is an illustration, not a checked file. Your
project writes those steps by hand. This repo generates the steps from a
marker on the snippet. Thus the two cannot be the same file. But the calls
are the same calls, and each run of `zig build` compiles them. That compile
found the most recent API changes that broke this page.

For more C code that CI verifies on each run, see these chapters:

- [SQLite from Zig](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/databases/sqlite-basic/), which links the
  real libsqlite3.
- [The X11 chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/on-screen/), which links the real Xlib.

## What WebAssembly Is

*WebAssembly. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/webassembly/what-is-wasm/*

WebAssembly (wasm) is a binary instruction format for a stack machine. Wasm is
a compile *target*, not a language. You write Zig, C or Rust, and the compiler
emits a `.wasm` module. An engine (a browser, Node, wasmtime) loads that
module and runs it in a sandbox at almost native speed.

This site is an example. Each snippet that you read is Zig compiled to
`wasm32-wasi`. The Run button gives that exact module to a WASI shim in your
browser. Press the button below, and the code reports the target of its build.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const builtin = @import("builtin");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &fw.interface;

    try out.print("cpu arch: {t}\n", .{builtin.target.cpu.arch});
    try out.print("os tag:   {t}\n", .{builtin.target.os.tag});
    try out.print("pointer:  {d} bits\n", .{@bitSizeOf(usize)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`08-webassembly.hello-wasm`)*

## Module, instance, linear memory

Three terms explain most of the model.

A **module** is the compiled `.wasm` file. It contains code and a description
of its imports and exports. A module does nothing alone, like a shared library
that is not loaded.

An **instance** is a module that an engine loaded and connected. The
instantiation resolves the imports of the module, which are functions that the
host supplies. It also gives the module its memory. You can instantiate the
same module more than one time. Each instance has its own state.

**Linear memory** is the heap of the instance. It is one flat, contiguous
array of bytes, with addresses from zero, and the module and the host both see
it. It starts at a number of 64 KiB pages and can grow. A Zig pointer inside a
wasm module is only an offset into this array. The module cannot touch any
other memory.

## Only numbers go through a call

A call can carry only these types: `i32`, `i64`, `f32` and `f64`. Later
proposals added `v128` for SIMD and reference types for host objects. But a
JavaScript host still gives numbers. A call cannot give or return a string, a
struct or an array.

Larger data goes as bytes in linear memory. An `i32` offset and, usually, an
`i32` length identify the bytes. A Zig `[]const u8` slice becomes a pointer
and a length. At the wasm boundary, that is two `i32` values. The [linear
memory recipe](../linear-memory/) shows the full pattern.

## The sandbox

A wasm module has no ambient authority. By default, it gets access to nothing.
Alone, it cannot open a file, read the clock or make a network call. It can do
only what its imports let it do. If a module gets no imports, it can only
calculate.

The capability comes from the host, not from the binary. Thus the same `.wasm`
runs without change in a browser tab and on a server. For the same reason, it
is reasonable to run a module that you do not trust. It is not reasonable to
run a native binary that you do not trust.

## Three ways that Zig compiles to wasm

The difference is the target triple that you give. The triple decides what the
sandbox can get to.

| Target | What it gives you | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `wasm32-freestanding` | Only wasm itself. No libc, no OS. You export functions and manage memory. | Modules that a JavaScript or native host controls. |
| `wasm32-wasi` | A system interface with the shape of POSIX: files, args, clock, stdout, an entry point. | Command-line programs that run under Node, wasmtime or Wasmer. |
| `wasm32-emscripten` | The Emscripten runtime and its libc/JS glue. | A port of a large C/C++ codebase that expects that environment. |

This guide verifies against `wasm32-wasi`, because the guide needs stdout to
compare. The [freestanding recipe](../freestanding/) shows the smaller target.

## Command and reactor

There are two shapes of module. The difference is if the module has an entry
point.

A **command** has a `_start` function. The engine calls `_start` one time. It
runs to completion like a `main`, and then the instance is complete. Each WASI
program in this guide is a command. A Zig file with `pub fn main` compiles to a
command.

A **reactor** has no entry point. The engine instantiates the reactor, and then
calls its exported functions when necessary, many times. The instance stays
alive between calls. Use this shape when JavaScript calls into Zig. To build a
reactor, use `-fno-entry` and give the names of the functions to export.

The shape that you need decides which recipe applies. The next pages build
each shape.

---

## Recipe: A WASI Command

*WebAssembly. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/webassembly/wasi-command/*

To run a Zig program as WebAssembly outside the browser, do these steps:

1. Build the program with `zig build-exe -target wasm32-wasi`.
2. Run the `.wasm` under a WASI runtime, for example `wasmtime`, `wasmer` or
   the `node:wasi` module of Node.

The program itself needs no code that is specific to wasm.

## The problem

You have a Zig program with a `main`. You want a single `.wasm` that runs the
same on Linux, macOS and Windows, without a new compilation. WASI makes this
possible.

WASI is the system interface for a wasm command. The command calls WASI for
the OS operations (here, stdout) that pure wasm cannot do.

## The plan

1. Write an ordinary Zig program. Nothing in it is specific to wasm.
2. Build the program for `wasm32-wasi`.
3. Run the `.wasm` under a WASI runtime.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const document =
    \\zig compiles to wasm
    \\wasm runs in the browser
    \\the browser runs this page
;

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fw = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &fw.interface;

    var lines: usize = 0;
    var words: usize = 0;
    var it = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, document, '\n');
    while (it.next()) |line| {
        lines += 1;
        var w = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
        while (w.next()) |_| words += 1;
    }

    try out.print("lines: {d}\n", .{lines});
    try out.print("words: {d}\n", .{words});
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`08-webassembly.wasi-command`)*

The source is a normal program. It splits an embedded document and counts
lines and words. It writes the totals to stdout through the `Io` instance that
`main` receives. The code has no setup that is specific to wasm.

## Build the program

```bash
zig build-exe wasi-command.zig -target wasm32-wasi -O ReleaseSmall
```

This command emits `wasi-command.wasm`. `-O ReleaseSmall` is more important
here than on a native build. The module is a file that you ship or fetch, and
the debug build is approximately thirty times larger. For exactly this reason,
the `build.zig` of this guide uses that mode by default.

## Run the program

The module does not need a browser. Any WASI runtime runs it:

```bash
wasmtime wasi-command.wasm
# lines: 3
# words: 14

wasmer wasi-command.wasm      # same output
node --experimental-wasi-unstable-preview1 run.mjs   # via node:wasi
```

CI and the Run button on this page use the Node path. The runner
(`tools/run-wasi.mjs` in this repo) is about a hundred lines. It opens the
module, builds a WASI import object, and calls `_start`.

## What WASI does

The program prints through a buffered writer over stdout. On a native build,
the flush lowers to a `write` syscall. On `wasm32-wasi`, the flush lowers to a
call to an imported function, `fd_write`. The module does not contain
`fd_write`. The runtime supplies it at instantiation.

If you change the runtime, stdout goes to a different place, and the module
stays the same byte for byte. Under wasmtime, stdout goes to a real terminal.
Under the shim of this page, stdout goes to a captured buffer.

The runtime decides which capabilities to give. A runtime can refuse to
preopen directories. Then the same program can print, but it cannot read a
file. That refusal is a real example of the sandbox from the
[overview](../what-is-wasm/).

## Variations

- **Arguments and env:** WASI gives `argv` and environment variables when the
  runtime decides to give them. Read them from the `std.process.Init` that
  `main` receives, in the same way as on native. On WASI, the argument
  iterator needs an allocator, so use `Args.Iterator.initAllocator`.
- **Files:** `std.Io.Dir` works, but only inside directories that the runtime
  preopened. The design makes all other files on disk unreachable.
- **Exit status:** when `main` returns an error, the exit code is non-zero,
  and the runtime reports it. Thus wasm commands work in shell pipelines like
  all other tools.

---

## Recipe: Call Zig from JavaScript

*WebAssembly. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/webassembly/export-to-js/*

To call Zig from JavaScript, do these steps:

1. Mark the function `export fn`.
2. Build for `wasm32-freestanding` with `-fno-entry` and `--export=<name>`.
3. After `WebAssembly.instantiate` returns, call the function as
   `instance.exports.<name>`.

## The problem

Usual uses are a hot loop, a parser, or math that is slow in the JavaScript
engine. The module has no `main`. JavaScript instantiates the module one time,
and then calls its functions when necessary. That is the reactor shape from the
[overview](../what-is-wasm/).

## The plan

1. Mark each function that the host must call with `export fn`.
2. Build for `wasm32-freestanding` with `-fno-entry`, and give the names of the
   exports.
3. Instantiate in JavaScript and call `instance.exports.<name>`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

export fn add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 {
    return a + b;
}

export fn fib(n: u32) u64 {
    var a: u64 = 0;
    var b: u64 = 1;
    var i: u32 = 0;
    while (i < n) : (i += 1) {
        const next = a + b;
        a = b;
        b = next;
    }
    return a;
}

test add {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 5), add(2, 3));
}

test fib {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 55), fib(10));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`08-webassembly.export-to-js`)*

Here, the Run button runs the `test` blocks of the file, because this guide
verifies each snippet in that way. In real use, nothing calls these functions
as Zig tests. The functions exist for calls from outside. The tests only prove
that the functions return the values that the text below gives.

## Export the functions

`export fn` does two things:

- It makes sure that dead-code elimination does not remove the function.
- It puts the function in the export table of the module, under its exact Zig
  name.

There is no name mangling and no wrapper. `add` in Zig is `add` in the export
table.

The signatures use only `i32` and `u32`/`u64`, and this is intentional. Those
types map directly to the numeric types of wasm. Thus you do not have to think
about marshalling at the boundary. `fib` returns a `u64`, and a JavaScript host
receives a `u64` as a `BigInt`.

## Build the reactor

```bash
zig build-exe export-to-js.zig \
  -target wasm32-freestanding \
  -O ReleaseSmall -fno-entry \
  --export=add --export=fib
```

`-fno-entry` tells the linker that there is no `_start`. This module is a
reactor, not a command. `--export=` gives the name of each function to expose.

`export fn` marks the functions in the source. But on a freestanding link, the
linker still removes the symbols, unless something roots them. `--export` is
that root.

You can give `-rdynamic` instead. Then the module exports each public symbol,
also compiler internals like the stack pointer. When you give the names, the
module contains only what you intended to ship.

The result is very small. These two functions and the memory are about 135
bytes.

## Call the functions

```js
const bytes = await fetch("export-to-js.wasm").then((r) => r.arrayBuffer());
const { instance } = await WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes, {});

console.log(instance.exports.add(2, 3));    // 5
console.log(instance.exports.fib(10));      // 55n  (the u64 return is a BigInt)
```

The second argument to `instantiate` is the imports object. Here, the object is
empty, because this module imports nothing. The module only calculates. When a
module needs something from the host, you supply it in that object. The
[browser recipe](../browser-instantiate/) shows this.

## Variations

- **Give data that is larger than a number:** strings, slices and structs do
  not fit in a wasm value. They go through linear memory as an offset and a
  length. The [next recipe](../linear-memory/) shows that handshake.
- **Use a different export name:** the Zig name and the name for the host can be
  different. In that case, use `@export(&foo, .{ .name = "bar" })`, and give
  `foo` a `callconv(.c)`. `@export` does not add a calling convention, but
  `export fn` does. `bar` is the name in the export table.
- **Many instances:** each `WebAssembly.instantiate` gives a new instance with
  its own memory. Thus if two workers call the same module, their states stay
  separate.

---

## Recipe: Pass Data Across the Boundary

*WebAssembly. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/webassembly/linear-memory/*

A string cannot go between JavaScript and a Zig wasm module as a value. Thus
the string goes through the linear memory of the module:

1. The exported `alloc` function of the module returns an offset.
2. The host writes the bytes at that offset.
3. The host calls into the module with the offset and a length.

## The problem

The [last recipe](../export-to-js/) gave numbers to the module, and a number
fits in a wasm value. A string does not fit. A slice, a struct and a buffer do
not fit either. Linear memory is the only place where both sides can see them.
The two sides must agree on the meaning of the bytes there.

## The plan

1. Export an `alloc` function, so that the host can reserve space in linear
   memory.
2. Export the memory. The reactor build does this automatically.
3. The host writes bytes at the returned offset, then calls in with `(offset,
   len)`. The host reads a result back from memory at an offset that the
   module reports.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// A small arena that gives scratch space to the host. A real module exports
// a general allocator. This arena keeps each step visible in the code.
var scratch: [4096]u8 = undefined;
var used: usize = 0;

export fn alloc(len: usize) [*]u8 {
    const start = used;
    used += len;
    return scratch[start..].ptr;
}

export fn reset() void {
    used = 0;
}

// Sum the bytes that the host put at ptr[0..len].
export fn sumBytes(ptr: [*]const u8, len: usize) u32 {
    var total: u32 = 0;
    for (ptr[0..len]) |b| total += b;
    return total;
}

// Change to upper case in place. Thus the host reads the answer from the
// same offset.
export fn upperInPlace(ptr: [*]u8, len: usize) void {
    for (ptr[0..len]) |*b| b.* = std.ascii.toUpper(b.*);
}

test "the round trip a JS host would drive" {
    reset();

    // Host: reserve space, and copy bytes into linear memory.
    const msg = "zig";
    const dst = alloc(msg.len);
    @memcpy(dst[0..msg.len], msg);

    // Host: call in with (offset, length).
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 'z' + 'i' + 'g'), sumBytes(dst, msg.len));

    // Host: change the bytes in place, then read them back.
    upperInPlace(dst, msg.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqualStrings("ZIG", dst[0..msg.len]);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`08-webassembly.linear-memory`)*

The test in the snippet is the script of the host, written in Zig. It does
these steps:

1. Reserve space.
2. Copy bytes in.
3. Call `sumBytes`.
4. Change the bytes in place with `upperInPlace`.
5. Read the bytes back.

A JavaScript host does the same steps through `instance.exports` and a
typed-array view. The [browser recipe](../browser-instantiate/) shows how to
build the module as a reactor and call it. This page covers the memory
protocol itself.

## Why an offset and not a pointer

Inside a wasm module, a Zig `[*]u8` is an offset into linear memory, counted
from zero. It is not an address in the process of the host. When `alloc`
returns `[*]u8`, JavaScript sees a plain integer. The integer tells where in
the shared array the bytes go.

The host never dereferences a wasm pointer directly. The host uses that number
as an index into the memory buffer.

## The JavaScript side

`WebAssembly.Memory` gives an `ArrayBuffer`, and you look at it through typed
arrays. The protocol only writes into the buffer and reads back from it:

```js
const { instance } = await WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes, {});
const { alloc, reset, sumBytes, upperInPlace, memory } = instance.exports;

function pass(str) {
  const utf8 = new TextEncoder().encode(str);
  const ptr = alloc(utf8.length);
  // A fresh view each time: growing memory detaches the old ArrayBuffer.
  new Uint8Array(memory.buffer, ptr, utf8.length).set(utf8);
  return { ptr, len: utf8.length };
}

reset();
const { ptr, len } = pass("zig");
console.log(sumBytes(ptr, len));        // 330  (z + i + g)

upperInPlace(ptr, len);
const out = new Uint8Array(memory.buffer, ptr, len);
console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(out));   // "ZIG"
```

## The one trap

`memory.buffer` can change. Any allocation can grow the linear memory of the
module. When the memory grows, the old `ArrayBuffer` becomes *detached*, and
each typed array over it reads as empty.

Thus make the `Uint8Array` view immediately before you use it. Never keep the
view across a call that can allocate. For this reason, the `pass` helper above
makes a new view each time.

## Who owns the memory

In this snippet, the module owns the memory. `alloc` gives out slices of a
fixed 4 KiB buffer, and `reset` takes back all of the buffer at one time. This
is a bump allocator.

A bump allocator is sufficient for the work of one request. In that
work, the host fills a buffer, calls the module, and continues. For data
that must stay longer, do one of these:

- Export a real allocator, with `free`.
- Let the host keep a record of the offsets that it got.

In both cases, the rule stays the same. The module manages its linear memory.
The host only uses offsets that the module gave out.

## Variations

- **Return a string:** the module cannot return a slice. Return an offset, and
  give the length through a second export. Or write both into a small struct
  in memory, and return the offset of that struct.
- **Strings are UTF-8 on both ends:** Zig source is UTF-8, and the
  `TextEncoder` of JavaScript emits UTF-8. Thus bytes that you copy across
  need no new encoding.
- **Grow on demand:** `alloc` here cannot fail in a useful way. A real `alloc`
  calls `@wasmMemoryGrow` when the buffer is full. The [freestanding
  recipe](../freestanding/) shows this.

---

## Recipe: A Freestanding Module

*WebAssembly. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/webassembly/freestanding/*

`wasm32-freestanding` is the smallest wasm target of Zig, with no WASI and no
libc. The module has no `main`, no stdout, no files and no OS heap. Its host
controls the module through exports.

## The problem

You want the smallest possible module, with no dependency on a system
interface. A JavaScript host or a native embedder controls the module. Thus
the files and clocks of WASI only add weight that the module does not use.

## The plan

1. Write functions that do not need an OS: no files, no stdout, no `main`.
2. Supply your own memory, because no system allocator is available.
3. Build for `wasm32-freestanding`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// Freestanding has no OS heap. Thus give the allocator a fixed backing store
// inside the linear memory of the module.
var heap: [64 * 1024]u8 = undefined;
var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&heap);

export fn sumRange(n: u32) u64 {
    var total: u64 = 0;
    var i: u32 = 1;
    while (i <= n) : (i += 1) total += i;
    return total;
}

// Ask the engine for one more 64 KiB page of linear memory, and report the
// previous size in pages. This is a wasm builtin. It needs no OS.
export fn growOnePage() i32 {
    return @wasmMemoryGrow(0, 1);
}

test sumRange {
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u64, 55), sumRange(10));
}

test "a fixed buffer allocator needs no OS" {
    const a = fba.allocator();
    const s = try a.alloc(u8, 8);
    defer a.free(s);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 8), s.len);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`08-webassembly.freestanding`)*

The tests here run because the guide builds each snippet for `wasm32-wasi` to
verify it. For freestanding, the source does not change, because no line in it
touches WASI. Only the target in the build command is different. The next
section gives that command.

## Build for freestanding

```bash
zig build-exe freestanding.zig \
  -target wasm32-freestanding \
  -O ReleaseSmall -fno-entry \
  --export=sumRange --export=growOnePage
```

These are the same reactor flags as in the [JavaScript
recipe](../export-to-js/). The only change is `-target wasm32-freestanding` in
place of `wasm32-wasi`.

That one change removes the full WASI import layer. The module imports nothing
at all. It needs no runtime, only a bare wasm engine.

## What freestanding removes

Freestanding removes everything that has the shape of an OS, because there is
no OS:

- **No `main` / `_start`.** There is no entry point to call. The host gets into
  the module through the exports.
- **No stdout, files, clock or sockets.** Files and clocks are now behind
  `std.Io`, and freestanding has no `Io` implementation to give to the code.
  There is nothing to lower the calls onto. Thus a use of them is a compile
  error, not a failure at run time.
- **No OS heap.** There is no `mmap` under the code. But
  `std.heap.page_allocator` still works. On wasm, it uses `@wasmMemoryGrow`,
  not the OS. The general-purpose allocator works on top of it.

The snippet uses the simpler method. It gives a `FixedBufferAllocator` a 64
KiB static array. That array is in linear memory, which is the only memory
that exists. The allocator never calls the OS, because there is no OS to call.

## The memory builtins

Freestanding does not limit you to the memory that the module started with.
Two wasm builtins manage linear memory directly, with no runtime under them:

- `@wasmMemorySize(0)` returns the current size in 64 KiB pages.
- `@wasmMemoryGrow(0, n)` asks the engine for `n` more pages. It returns the
  previous size, or `-1` if the engine refuses.

`growOnePage` in the snippet uses the second builtin. When its buffer is full,
a real allocator calls this builtin. Then it divides the new pages into
allocations.

This is the layer under the fixed buffer. When a freestanding module needs
more memory than it got at compile time, the bytes come from here.

## When to select freestanding and not WASI

Select freestanding when a host can give the module all that it needs, and you
want the module itself to carry nothing extra. A browser is such a host. A
native program that embeds wasmtime is also such a host.

Select WASI when the module is a full program that must run from a shell and do
the work of an OS program. The [command recipe](../wasi-command/) covers that
case. This recipe covers the opposite case.

---

## Recipe: Load wasm in the Browser

*WebAssembly. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/webassembly/browser-instantiate/*

To load a Zig wasm module in the browser, give `fetch("module.wasm")` and an
imports object to `WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming`. Then call the functions
on `instance.exports`. The module calls back into JavaScript through `extern`
functions. The imports object supplies these functions by name.

## The problem

You have a reactor module and a web page. The page must load the `.wasm` and
call its functions. The module must be able to call back into JavaScript when
necessary. This site does the same for each Run button. This page shows all
the parts together.

## The plan

1. `fetch` the `.wasm`, and give the stream to `instantiateStreaming`.
2. Give an **imports** object that supplies each function that the module
   imports.
3. Call the **exports** of the module, and let the module call your imports.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// The host (JavaScript) supplies this function at instantiation. The imports
// object of the host must match the module name "env" and the symbol "log".
extern "env" fn log(ptr: [*]const u8, len: usize) void;

fn hostPrint(msg: []const u8) void {
    log(msg.ptr, msg.len);
}

// The host calls this function. It then calls back to the host through
// the import.
export fn greet() void {
    hostPrint("hello from wasm");
}
```

*This module imports a host `log` function, and the WASI of Node does not supply it. Thus CI compiles the module but does not run it here. The JavaScript below runs it in a browser. (`08-webassembly.browser-import`)*

This module imports and exports. It exports `greet`, and the page calls
`greet`. Then `greet` calls out through `log`, which the module *imports*.
`log` is an `extern` declaration with no body.

The host must supply `log`, or the instantiation fails. For this reason, the
guide cannot run this snippet through its WASI shim. Also for this reason, the
page above shows the snippet without a Run button.

## Fetch and instantiate

`WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming` compiles the module during the download.
This is faster than a download of the full file into a buffer first:

```js
const decoder = new TextDecoder();
let memory;   // filled in once the instance exists

const imports = {
  env: {
    // The module's `extern "env" fn log(ptr, len)` resolves to this.
    log(ptr, len) {
      const bytes = new Uint8Array(memory.buffer, ptr, len);
      console.log(decoder.decode(bytes));
    },
  },
};

const { instance } = await WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(
  fetch("browser-import.wasm"),
  imports,
);
memory = instance.exports.memory;

instance.exports.greet();   // logs "hello from wasm"
```

## Imports resolve by name

The module declared `extern "env" fn log(...)`. Those two names are the
contract: the module name `env` and the field `log`. The imports object must
have exactly `imports.env.log`. If it does not, the instantiation throws a
`LinkError` that gives the name of the absent import.

If you rename either side, the import does not resolve. The engine checks this
interface at instantiation.

Note that `log` reads the string from `memory` with the offset and length that
the module gave. The module put "hello from wasm" in its linear memory, and it
gave the location of the string. The host decodes the string at that location.
It is the [boundary protocol](../linear-memory/) again, but now the module is
the caller.

## Order of operations

There is a small circular dependency here:

- The import `log` needs `memory` to read the string.
- `memory` exists only after the engine creates the instance.
- To create the instance, the engine needs the imports object.

This works because instantiation only *defines* `log`, and does not *call*
`log`. When `greet` runs and calls `log`, `memory` already has its value. The
usual solution is the one above: a closure that reads `memory` only when it
runs.

## A note on `instantiateStreaming`

`instantiateStreaming` needs the server to send the file with
`Content-Type: application/wasm`. If your host sends the wrong type, the call
rejects. To fix this, change the server configuration, or use the buffered
fallback:

```js
const bytes = await fetch(url).then((r) => r.arrayBuffer());
const { instance } = await WebAssembly.instantiate(bytes, imports);
```

The [JavaScript recipe](../export-to-js/) used the same path. The runner of
this site also uses it, because the runner already has the bytes.

## Variations

- **Many imports:** put them in groups by module name. Use `imports.env` for
  your own hooks. A WASI shim adds its own namespace next to it.
- **Give complex data back:** here, `log` takes an offset and a length. Each
  structured value (a JSON string, a packed struct) goes across in the same
  way. The host decodes it from `memory`.
- **This site, exactly:** the playground fetches the verified `.wasm`. It
  builds a WASI import object, not a single `log`, and it calls `_start`. The
  imports are different, but the mechanism is the same.
