## Write an Image File

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/image-files/*

A buffer is useful as a picture when you can look at it. PPM is the shortest way to save a buffer: a short text header, then the pixel bytes. The format has nothing more, and it needs no library.

PPM is part of the Netpbm family. The family has six formats, on two axes: what a pixel is, and whether the data is text or binary.

| | ASCII | Binary | A pixel is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **PBM** (bitmap) | `P1` | `P4` | one bit, black or white |
| **PGM** (graymap) | `P2` | `P5` | one gray sample |
| **PPM** (pixmap) | `P3` | `P6` | three samples: R, G, B |

Write `P6`. `P3` holds the same pixels as decimal numbers in text. `P3` is larger and slower. But if you want to read your own image in an editor, it is useful to make a `P3` file one time.

## The header

```
P6\n64 32\n255\n<6144 raw bytes>
```

The header has four fields, then the data: the magic, the width, the height, and the maxval (the largest value that a sample can have). Any mix of spaces, tabs and newlines can separate the fields. Thus `P6 64 32 255 ` is as valid as the form above.

Then there is one strict rule:

> **Exactly one whitespace byte follows the maxval.** All the bytes after that single byte are pixel data.

If you write `"255\n\n"`, each pixel moves by one byte. The image shows diagonal noise. No parser can find the mistake, because `0x0A` is a legal pixel value. At the end, the snippet below decodes a file with exactly this defect, so that you can see what the reader gets.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const canvas = @import("_canvas.zig");

var pixels: [canvas.width * canvas.height]u32 = undefined;

// The header is at most a few dozen bytes. The body is three bytes per pixel.
var file_bytes: [64 + canvas.width * canvas.height * 3]u8 = undefined;

fn drawScene() void {
    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            const r: u8 = @intCast((x * 255) / (canvas.width - 1));
            const g: u8 = @intCast((y * 255) / (canvas.height - 1));
            canvas.putPixel(&pixels, @intCast(x), @intCast(y), canvas.rgb(r, g, 80));
        }
    }
}

/// Write the header, then the body, and return the part of the slice that
/// the function used.
///
/// The header uses the same constants that set the size of the buffer.
/// A hardcoded "P6\n64 32\n255\n" works only until somebody changes one of
/// the constants. Then the header and the data do not agree, and the image
/// tears diagonally. No part of the program reports an error.
fn encodeP6(out: []u8) ![]const u8 {
    const header = try std.mem.print(out, "P6\n{d} {d}\n255\n", .{
        canvas.width, canvas.height,
    });

    var n = header.len;
    for (pixels) |p| {
        const c = canvas.channels(p);
        out[n + 0] = c.r;
        out[n + 1] = c.g;
        out[n + 2] = c.b;
        n += 3;
    }
    return out[0..n];
}

const Image = struct { w: usize, h: usize, data: []const u8 };

/// A reader that is sufficient for the files that this code writes. It does
/// not remove `#` comments. A general parser must remove them.
fn decodeP6(bytes: []const u8) !Image {
    if (!std.mem.startsWith(u8, bytes, "P6")) return error.NotP6;

    var it = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, bytes[2..], " \t\r\n");
    const w = try std.fmt.parseInt(usize, it.next() orelse return error.Truncated, 10);
    const h = try std.fmt.parseInt(usize, it.next() orelse return error.Truncated, 10);
    const maxval = try std.fmt.parseInt(usize, it.next() orelse return error.Truncated, 10);
    if (maxval != 255) return error.UnsupportedMaxval;

    // Exactly one whitespace byte follows maxval. All the bytes after it are
    // pixel data. The tokenizer stops before that byte, thus the `+ 1`.
    const data_start = 2 + it.index + 1;
    if (data_start + w * h * 3 > bytes.len) return error.Truncated;
    return .{ .w = w, .h = h, .data = bytes[data_start..] };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    drawScene();
    const file = try encodeP6(&file_bytes);

    try out.print("total bytes: {d}\n", .{file.len});
    try out.print("header:      {d} bytes, body {d}x{d}x3 = {d}\n", .{
        file.len - canvas.width * canvas.height * 3,
        canvas.width,
        canvas.height,
        canvas.width * canvas.height * 3,
    });

    try out.writeAll("first 16:   ");
    for (file[0..16]) |b| try out.print(" {X:0>2}", .{b});
    try out.writeAll("\n");
    try out.writeAll("as text:     ");
    for (file[0..16]) |b| {
        try out.writeByte(if (b >= 0x20 and b < 0x7F) b else '.');
    }
    try out.writeAll("\n\n");

    const decoded = try decodeP6(file);
    try out.print("decoded:     {d}x{d}, {d} bytes of pixel data\n", .{
        decoded.w, decoded.h, decoded.w * decoded.h * 3,
    });
    try out.print("pixel (0,0): {d} {d} {d}\n", .{
        decoded.data[0], decoded.data[1], decoded.data[2],
    });
    const last = (canvas.width * canvas.height - 1) * 3;
    try out.print("last pixel:  {d} {d} {d}\n", .{
        decoded.data[last], decoded.data[last + 1], decoded.data[last + 2],
    });

    // One extra newline after maxval moves each pixel by one byte. No parser
    // can find this mistake, because 0x0A is a legal pixel value.
    const shifted = decodeP6("P6\n2 1\n255\n\n\x01\x02\x03\x04\x05\x06") catch unreachable;
    try out.print("shifted by one: first pixel reads {d} {d} {d}\n", .{
        shifted.data[0], shifted.data[1], shifted.data[2],
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.ppm-write`)*

## The pixel data

The pixels go from left to right and from top to bottom. There is no padding, no alignment and no row header. Each pixel is three samples in the order R, G, B.

The maxval sets the size of a sample:

- **A maxval below 256** gives one byte for each sample. `640 * 480 * 3` is 921,600 bytes.
- **A maxval from 256 to 65535** gives *two* bytes for each sample, **big-endian**. This is the only place where PPM has a byte order, and it causes bugs on little-endian computers.

With a maxval that is not 255, the samples use a different scale. With a maxval of 100, a sample of 50 is mid-gray. Use 255, unless you have a reason to use a different value.

A `#` starts a comment. The comment continues to the end of the line, and it can be at any place where whitespace can be. It is easy to write a comment, but it is difficult to read comments. A strict parser must remove the comments while it reads the header fields. Many simple parsers do this incorrectly. Thus, if the file goes to other programs, do not write comments.

## Format the header from the constants

```zig
const header = try std.mem.print(out, "P6\n{d} {d}\n255\n", .{ width, height });
```

The header uses the same `width` and `height` that set the size of the buffer. A hardcoded `"P6\n640 480\n255\n"` works only until somebody changes a constant. Then the header and the data do not agree, and the image tears diagonally. No part of the program reports an error.

## On disk

The version that writes a file does two writes: the header, then the pixels.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const width: usize = 640;
const height: usize = 480;

// Three bytes per pixel, 921,600 bytes in total. Global, not on the stack.
var pixels: [width * height * 3]u8 = undefined;

fn putPixel(x: usize, y: usize, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) void {
    if (x >= width or y >= height) return;
    const i = (y * width + x) * 3;
    pixels[i + 0] = r;
    pixels[i + 1] = g;
    pixels[i + 2] = b;
}

fn drawScene() void {
    for (0..height) |y| {
        for (0..width) |x| {
            const r: u8 = @intCast((x * 255) / (width - 1));
            const g: u8 = @intCast((y * 255) / (height - 1));
            putPixel(x, y, r, g, 80);
        }
    }

    // The circle comes second, thus it is on top. This code has no depth buffer
    // and no transparency. A later write replaces an earlier write.
    const cx: i32 = @intCast(width / 2);
    const cy: i32 = @intCast(height / 2);
    const radius: i32 = 100;
    var y: i32 = cy - radius;
    while (y <= cy + radius) : (y += 1) {
        var x: i32 = cx - radius;
        while (x <= cx + radius) : (x += 1) {
            const dx = x - cx;
            const dy = y - cy;
            if (dx * dx + dy * dy <= radius * radius) {
                putPixel(@intCast(x), @intCast(y), 255, 220, 40);
            }
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf_out: [128]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf_out);
    const out = &stdout.interface;

    drawScene();

    var dir = std.Io.Dir.cwd();

    // The program writes a real file, reads it again and deletes it. Thus the
    // example leaves no file on the computer that ran it.
    defer dir.deleteFile(io, "output.ppm") catch {};

    // A createFile handle is write-only by default. With `.read = true`, the
    // check at the end can read through this handle and not open the file again.
    const file = try dir.createFile(io, "output.ppm", .{ .read = true });
    defer file.close(io);

    var header_buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const header = try std.mem.print(&header_buf, "P6\n{d} {d}\n255\n", .{ width, height });

    try file.writeStreamingAll(io, header);
    try file.writeStreamingAll(io, &pixels);

    // To know that the two writes above went in the correct order, read the
    // header again. An image viewer shows the problem later. This check makes
    // the build fail now.
    var check: [15]u8 = undefined;
    _ = try file.readPositionalAll(io, &check, 0);

    try out.writeAll("header read back:\n");
    try out.writeAll(check[0..header.len]);
    try out.print("bytes on disk: {d}\n", .{header.len + pixels.len});
    try out.flush();
}

// This program runs in wasm. The runner gives it an empty working directory:
// a temporary directory in CI, and a directory in memory in your browser. In
// both, the program really writes the file and reads it again.
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.ppm-file`)*

Look at the order of the drawing. The background comes first, then the circle on top. The circle replaces the pixels that were there before. This is the painter's algorithm. Until [Alpha Blending](../blending/), it is the only compositing model in this section.

The `defer` that deletes `output.ppm` makes sure that the build that verifies this page leaves no files. When you run the program yourself, remove that one line. If you do not, the program deletes the file before you can look at it.

To look at the result, use one of these tools:

- Most Linux viewers open PPM directly (`feh output.ppm`).
- ImageMagick and the netpbm tools convert PPM to other formats:

```bash
magick output.ppm output.png
pnmtopng output.ppm > output.png
```

To examine only the header, and not the full file, use this command:

```bash
head -c 20 output.ppm | xxd
# 00000000: 5036 0a36 3430 2034 3830 0a32 3535 0a00  P6.640 480.255..
```

`5036` is `P6`. The `0a` immediately before the pixel data is the one necessary whitespace byte.

## When to use a different format

PPM is not compressed. A 4K frame is 24 MB, and a sequence of frames quickly fills a disk. PPM is the correct tool when you want to get pixels out of a program that you write. It is the wrong tool when you want to store or share the pixels. When the image is correct, convert the image, or write a PNG directly. [Write a PNG](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/png/) does this with the zlib in the Zig standard library.

Video is the exception. `ffmpeg` reads a stream of PPM files, one after the other. Thus PPM is a good pipe format for a software renderer that makes frames:

```bash
./renderer | ffmpeg -f image2pipe -i - out.mp4
```

---

## Write a PNG

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/png/*

A PPM file is easy to write, but it is large. The 64 by 32 test picture of this section is 6157 bytes as a PPM. As a PNG, the picture is 680 bytes, and all image viewers and browsers open it.

A PNG needs two things in addition to the pixels: zlib compression and a CRC-32 checksum. The Zig standard library has both. Thus a PNG writer is about a hundred lines.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const canvas = @import("_canvas.zig");
const flate = std.compress.flate;

var scene: [canvas.width * canvas.height]u32 = undefined;
var gradient: [canvas.width * canvas.height]u32 = undefined;

/// All PNG files start with these eight bytes. The `\r\n`, `\x1a` and `\n`
/// find a file that a text copy damaged. A line-ending conversion or a
/// truncation changes these bytes, and then a reader refuses the file.
const signature = "\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n";

/// One scanline: a filter byte, then R, G, B for each pixel in the row.
const row_len = 1 + canvas.width * 3;
var rows: [canvas.height * row_len]u8 = undefined;

const Filter = enum(u8) {
    /// The bytes as they are.
    none = 0,
    /// Each byte minus the same channel of the pixel to its left.
    sub = 1,
};

fn filterRows(pixels: []const u32, filter: Filter) void {
    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        const row = rows[y * row_len ..][0..row_len];
        row[0] = @intFromEnum(filter);
        const data = row[1..];
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            const c = canvas.channels(pixels[y * canvas.width + x]);
            data[x * 3 ..][0..3].* = .{ c.r, c.g, c.b };
        }
        if (filter == .sub) {
            // Go backward, thus the byte to the left still holds its raw
            // value at the time of the subtraction. The first pixel has no
            // left neighbour and does not change. `-%=` wraps, because the
            // format says so.
            var i = data.len;
            while (i > 3) {
                i -= 1;
                data[i] -%= data[i - 3];
            }
        }
    }
}

/// The compressor keeps about 224 KB of state and needs a 64 KB window. Thus
/// both are here, not on the stack. Decompression needs a window of the same
/// size, thus the check below uses this window again.
var compressor: flate.Compress = undefined;
var window: [flate.max_window_len]u8 = undefined;
var compressed: [16 * 1024]u8 = undefined;

/// zlib-compress `data`: a 2-byte header, deflate, and an Adler-32 checksum.
fn deflate(data: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    var out: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&compressed);
    compressor = try .init(&out, &window, .zlib, .default);
    try compressor.writer.writeAll(data);
    try compressor.finish();
    return out.buffered();
}

/// Length, type, data, and a CRC-32 of the type and the data.
fn writeChunk(w: *std.Io.Writer, kind: *const [4]u8, data: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeInt(u32, @intCast(data.len), .big);
    try w.writeAll(kind);
    try w.writeAll(data);
    var crc = std.hash.Crc32.init();
    crc.update(kind);
    crc.update(data);
    try w.writeInt(u32, crc.final(), .big);
}

fn writePng(w: *std.Io.Writer, idat: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeAll(signature);

    var ihdr: [13]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, ihdr[0..4], canvas.width, .big);
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, ihdr[4..8], canvas.height, .big);
    ihdr[8] = 8; // bits per channel
    ihdr[9] = 2; // colour type 2: RGB, no alpha
    ihdr[10] = 0; // compression method: zlib, the only method
    ihdr[11] = 0; // filter method: the five filters, the only set
    ihdr[12] = 0; // no interlacing
    try writeChunk(w, "IHDR", &ihdr);
    try writeChunk(w, "IDAT", idat);
    try writeChunk(w, "IEND", "");
}

/// Read the file again as a viewer does: read the chunks, check each CRC,
/// inflate the pixels, remove the filter, and compare with the drawing.
fn check(out: *std.Io.Writer, png: []const u8, pixels: []const u32) !void {
    if (!std.mem.startsWith(u8, png, signature)) return error.BadSignature;
    var at: usize = signature.len;
    var idat: []const u8 = &.{};
    while (at < png.len) {
        const len = std.mem.readInt(u32, png[at..][0..4], .big);
        const kind = png[at + 4 ..][0..4];
        const data = png[at + 8 ..][0..len];
        const stored = std.mem.readInt(u32, png[at + 8 + len ..][0..4], .big);
        var crc = std.hash.Crc32.init();
        crc.update(kind);
        crc.update(data);
        const ok = crc.final() == stored;
        try out.print("    {s} {d: >5} bytes  crc {s}\n", .{ kind, len, if (ok) "ok" else "BAD" });
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, kind, "IDAT")) idat = data;
        at += 12 + len;
    }

    var in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(idat);
    var inflate: flate.Decompress = .init(&in, .zlib, &window);
    var raw: [canvas.height * row_len]u8 = undefined;
    try inflate.reader.readSliceAll(&raw);

    var same = true;
    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        const row = raw[y * row_len ..][0..row_len];
        const data = row[1..];
        if (row[0] == @intFromEnum(Filter.sub)) {
            // Forward this time: each byte adds back the byte to its left,
            // which the loop already decoded.
            for (3..data.len) |i| data[i] +%= data[i - 3];
        }
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            const got = canvas.rgb(data[x * 3], data[x * 3 + 1], data[x * 3 + 2]);
            if (got != pixels[y * canvas.width + x]) same = false;
        }
    }
    try out.print("  decoded pixels match the drawing: {}\n", .{same});
}

/// Try the two filters and keep the smaller result. Write the file, then read
/// the file again from disk and check it.
fn save(io: std.Io, out: *std.Io.Writer, name: []const u8, pixels: []const u32) !void {
    try out.print("{s}\n", .{name});

    filterRows(pixels, .none);
    const none_len = (try deflate(&rows)).len;
    filterRows(pixels, .sub);
    const sub_len = (try deflate(&rows)).len;
    try out.print("  compressed, filter none: {d} bytes\n", .{none_len});
    try out.print("  compressed, filter sub:  {d} bytes\n", .{sub_len});

    const best: Filter = if (sub_len < none_len) .sub else .none;
    filterRows(pixels, best);
    const idat = try deflate(&rows);

    const dir = std.Io.Dir.cwd();
    {
        const file = try dir.createFile(io, name, .{});
        defer file.close(io);
        var file_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
        var writer = file.writer(io, &file_buf);
        try writePng(&writer.interface, idat);
        try writer.interface.flush();
    }

    var read_buf: [16 * 1024]u8 = undefined;
    const png = try dir.readFile(io, name, &read_buf);
    try out.print("  wrote it with filter {s}: {d} bytes on disk\n", .{ @tagName(best), png.len });
    try check(out, png, pixels);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // Flat areas and hard edges.
    canvas.scene(&scene);
    // Each pixel is different from its neighbours, by the same quantity.
    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            gradient[y * canvas.width + x] = canvas.rgb(@intCast(x * 4), @intCast(y * 8), 128);
        }
    }

    try out.print("scanlines: {d} rows of {d} bytes = {d} bytes\n", .{ canvas.height, row_len, rows.len });
    try save(io, out, "scene.png", &scene);
    try save(io, out, "gradient.png", &gradient);

    try canvas.announce(out, "gradient.png", &gradient);
    try canvas.announce(out, "scene.png", &scene);
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.png-write`)*

The two pictures under the output are the two PNG files that the program wrote. Your browser decoded the files with its own PNG decoder. No code from this site decoded those files.

## The shape of the file

A PNG is an 8-byte signature and then a list of chunks.

```
signature   89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A
IHDR        width, height, and what kind of pixels
IDAT        the pixels, compressed
IEND        nothing, it marks the end
```

The signature is the same in all PNG files.

```zig
/// All PNG files start with these eight bytes. The `\r\n`, `\x1a` and `\n`
/// find a file that a text copy damaged. A line-ending conversion or a
/// truncation changes these bytes, and then a reader refuses the file.
const signature = "\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n";
```

*Quoted from the source: `signature` from `snippets/09-graphics/png-write.zig`.*

`50 4E 47` is the text `PNG`. The other bytes find a file that a text copy damaged:

- A tool that converts line endings changes `0D 0A`.
- A tool that removes the top bit changes `89`.

In both cases, a reader refuses the file at the first eight bytes.

## A chunk

All chunks have the same four parts:

```
length   4 bytes, big-endian, the size of the data only
type     4 letters, like IHDR
data     length bytes
crc      4 bytes, CRC-32 of the type and the data
```

```zig
/// Length, type, data, and a CRC-32 of the type and the data.
fn writeChunk(w: *std.Io.Writer, kind: *const [4]u8, data: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeInt(u32, @intCast(data.len), .big);
    try w.writeAll(kind);
    try w.writeAll(data);
    var crc = std.hash.Crc32.init();
    crc.update(kind);
    crc.update(data);
    try w.writeInt(u32, crc.final(), .big);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writeChunk` from `snippets/09-graphics/png-write.zig`.*

The CRC covers the type and the data. It does not cover the length.

All numbers in a PNG are big-endian. Thus each call to `writeInt` gets `.big`.

`std.hash.Crc32` is the same CRC-32 that zip and Ethernet use. Call `init`, then call `update` as many times as necessary, then call `final`.

## The header chunk

```zig
fn writePng(w: *std.Io.Writer, idat: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeAll(signature);

    var ihdr: [13]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, ihdr[0..4], canvas.width, .big);
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, ihdr[4..8], canvas.height, .big);
    ihdr[8] = 8; // bits per channel
    ihdr[9] = 2; // colour type 2: RGB, no alpha
    ihdr[10] = 0; // compression method: zlib, the only method
    ihdr[11] = 0; // filter method: the five filters, the only set
    ihdr[12] = 0; // no interlacing
    try writeChunk(w, "IHDR", &ihdr);
    try writeChunk(w, "IDAT", idat);
    try writeChunk(w, "IEND", "");
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writePng` from `snippets/09-graphics/png-write.zig`.*

`IHDR` is always 13 bytes, and it must be the first chunk.

Colour type 2 means three bytes for each pixel, in the order R, G, B, with no alpha.

The two fields that are always 0 identify the compression method and the filter method. The format defines only one of each. Thus 0 is the only legal value.

## Scanlines and the filter byte

The writer does not compress the pixels in their original form. It cuts them into rows, and each row starts with one extra byte, the **filter byte**. Thus one row here is 1 + 64 × 3 = 193 bytes. Before compression, the 32 rows are 6176 bytes.

The filter byte tells how the writer changed the bytes of the row before compression:

- Filter 0, None, keeps the bytes as they are.
- Filter 1, Sub, stores each byte minus the same channel of the pixel to its left.

```zig
fn filterRows(pixels: []const u32, filter: Filter) void {
    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        const row = rows[y * row_len ..][0..row_len];
        row[0] = @intFromEnum(filter);
        const data = row[1..];
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            const c = canvas.channels(pixels[y * canvas.width + x]);
            data[x * 3 ..][0..3].* = .{ c.r, c.g, c.b };
        }
        if (filter == .sub) {
            // Go backward, thus the byte to the left still holds its raw
            // value at the time of the subtraction. The first pixel has no
            // left neighbour and does not change. `-%=` wraps, because the
            // format says so.
            var i = data.len;
            while (i > 3) {
                i -= 1;
                data[i] -%= data[i - 3];
            }
        }
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `filterRows` from `snippets/09-graphics/png-write.zig`.*

## The worked example

In the gradient picture, the red channel increases by 4 at each pixel.

```
red bytes, filter none:  0  4  8 12 16 20 ...
red bytes, filter sub:   0  4  4  4  4  4 ...
```

After Sub, the row is the same few bytes again and again. zlib compresses repeated bytes well.

The output shows the result. Without a filter, the compressed gradient is 3801 bytes. With Sub, it is 133 bytes.

## A filter can also make the file larger

The scene picture shows the opposite result: 623 bytes with no filter, and 709 bytes with Sub. The scene has large flat areas and hard edges. Its rows already repeat, and Sub breaks some of those repeats. Thus `save` tries the two filters and keeps the smaller result.

Real encoders select a filter for each row. There are five filters:

- None.
- Sub.
- Up subtracts the byte above.
- Average subtracts the average of the left byte and the byte above.
- Paeth subtracts one of the left, above and above-left bytes: the one that is the best guess.

## Wrapping subtraction

Sub can give a negative number. If a pixel with red 10 is to the right of a pixel with red 200, Sub stores 10 − 200.

The format says that this value wraps around 256: 10 − 200 + 256 = 66. The decoder adds the value back with the same wrap: 66 + 200 − 256 = 10.

In Zig, you must write this wrap on purpose. A plain `-` on two `u8` values that goes below zero is integer overflow. Zig checks integer overflow in safe builds. The wrapping operators `-%` and `+%` tell Zig that the wrap is intentional.

## Compression

`std.compress.flate.Compress` writes deflate. The `.zlib` container adds the 2-byte header and the Adler-32 checksum that a PNG expects.

```zig
/// zlib-compress `data`: a 2-byte header, deflate, and an Adler-32 checksum.
fn deflate(data: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    var out: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&compressed);
    compressor = try .init(&out, &window, .zlib, .default);
    try compressor.writer.writeAll(data);
    try compressor.finish();
    return out.buffered();
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `deflate` from `snippets/09-graphics/png-write.zig`.*

The compressor keeps about 224 KB of state and needs a 64 KB window buffer. That is too much for the stack. Thus both are global variables.

`finish` writes the end of the stream. Without `finish`, the data stops before the end, and a reader reports a truncated file.

## Read the file again

The program reads its own file from disk and checks the file as a viewer does.

```zig
/// Read the file again as a viewer does: read the chunks, check each CRC,
/// inflate the pixels, remove the filter, and compare with the drawing.
fn check(out: *std.Io.Writer, png: []const u8, pixels: []const u32) !void {
    if (!std.mem.startsWith(u8, png, signature)) return error.BadSignature;
    var at: usize = signature.len;
    var idat: []const u8 = &.{};
    while (at < png.len) {
        const len = std.mem.readInt(u32, png[at..][0..4], .big);
        const kind = png[at + 4 ..][0..4];
        const data = png[at + 8 ..][0..len];
        const stored = std.mem.readInt(u32, png[at + 8 + len ..][0..4], .big);
        var crc = std.hash.Crc32.init();
        crc.update(kind);
        crc.update(data);
        const ok = crc.final() == stored;
        try out.print("    {s} {d: >5} bytes  crc {s}\n", .{ kind, len, if (ok) "ok" else "BAD" });
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, kind, "IDAT")) idat = data;
        at += 12 + len;
    }

    var in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(idat);
    var inflate: flate.Decompress = .init(&in, .zlib, &window);
    var raw: [canvas.height * row_len]u8 = undefined;
    try inflate.reader.readSliceAll(&raw);

    var same = true;
    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        const row = raw[y * row_len ..][0..row_len];
        const data = row[1..];
        if (row[0] == @intFromEnum(Filter.sub)) {
            // Forward this time: each byte adds back the byte to its left,
            // which the loop already decoded.
            for (3..data.len) |i| data[i] +%= data[i - 3];
        }
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            const got = canvas.rgb(data[x * 3], data[x * 3 + 1], data[x * 3 + 2]);
            if (got != pixels[y * canvas.width + x]) same = false;
        }
    }
    try out.print("  decoded pixels match the drawing: {}\n", .{same});
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `check` from `snippets/09-graphics/png-write.zig`.*

The `check` function does these steps:

1. It reads each chunk and checks its CRC.
2. It inflates the pixels.
3. It removes the filter.
4. It compares the result with the drawing.

To remove Sub, the function goes forward through the row. Each byte adds back the byte to its left, which the function already decoded.

This check proves only that the writer and the reader of this program agree. The writer and the reader can have the same mistake. Thus the page checks the files two more times, with decoders that share no code with this one:

- CI decodes each file with zlib from Node and the five filters, written from the specification.
- Your browser decodes each file with its own PNG decoder.

Both must give pixels with a hash equal to the hash in the `wrote` line that the program printed.

## What this writer does not do

This writer writes one kind of PNG: 8 bits for each channel, RGB, no interlacing.

It does not write alpha (colour type 6), 16-bit channels, palettes, or the chunks for colour space and text.

A viewer shows a PNG with no colour space chunk as sRGB. Thus the bytes that you write are the encoded bytes from [Linear Light](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/linear-light/), not linear values.

## Explain before you read the answer

A row has 64 pixels, all with the same colour `(30, 60, 90)`. The row goes through the Sub filter. What bytes come after the filter byte?

The answer is `30 60 90` for the first pixel, then 189 zeros.

The first pixel has no left neighbour, thus it does not change. Each other byte is equal to the byte three places to its left. Thus the difference is zero.

---

## Lines

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/lines/*

A line between two pixels is a question about rounding. Almost everywhere, the ideal line goes between pixel centres. At each step, the algorithm must decide on which side to put the pixel.

The obvious answer is to calculate `y = y0 + slope * (x - x0)` and round the result. This method works, but it costs a float multiply and a rounding for each pixel. On long lines, the result drifts, because the error accumulates. Bresenham's algorithm asks the same question with an integer error term. The algorithm updates the error term by addition. It does not drift, because it never rounds a value.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const canvas = @import("_canvas.zig");

var pixels: [canvas.width * canvas.height]u32 = undefined;

/// The error term `err` records twice the distance from the ideal line to the
/// pixel centre, scaled so that it stays an integer. At each step, it decides
/// if the minor axis is far enough behind to advance too.
///
/// This is the symmetric form: `dy` stays negative, thus the same two ifs
/// move the two axes. There is no special case for steep lines, and no swap
/// of the endpoints.
fn drawLine(x0: i32, y0: i32, x1: i32, y1: i32, color: u32) usize {
    var x = x0;
    var y = y0;

    const dx: i32 = @intCast(@abs(x1 - x0));
    const dy: i32 = -@as(i32, @intCast(@abs(y1 - y0)));
    const sx: i32 = if (x0 < x1) 1 else -1;
    const sy: i32 = if (y0 < y1) 1 else -1;

    var err = dx + dy;
    var drawn: usize = 0;

    while (true) {
        canvas.putPixel(&pixels, x, y, color);
        drawn += 1;
        if (x == x1 and y == y1) break;

        const e2 = 2 * err;
        // Two independent tests, not an if/else. On a perfect diagonal, the
        // two tests are both true, and the line moves on the two axes at once.
        if (e2 >= dy) {
            err += dy;
            x += sx;
        }
        if (e2 <= dx) {
            err += dx;
            y += sy;
        }
    }

    return drawn;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    canvas.fill(&pixels, canvas.rgb(0, 0, 40));

    const cx: i32 = @intCast(canvas.width / 2);
    const cy: i32 = @intCast(canvas.height / 2);
    const w: i32 = @intCast(canvas.width);
    const h: i32 = @intCast(canvas.height);

    // A fan of lines to points at equal distances along the border. All slopes,
    // from almost horizontal to almost vertical, use the same code path.
    var i: i32 = 0;
    while (i < 16) : (i += 1) {
        const t = @divTrunc(i * (w - 1), 16);
        _ = drawLine(cx, cy, t, 0, canvas.rgb(255, 200, 60));
        _ = drawLine(cx, cy, w - 1 - t, h - 1, canvas.rgb(120, 200, 255));
    }

    // A border of four lines, to show that the endpoints are exact.
    _ = drawLine(0, 0, w - 1, 0, canvas.rgb(255, 255, 255));
    _ = drawLine(w - 1, 0, w - 1, h - 1, canvas.rgb(255, 255, 255));
    _ = drawLine(w - 1, h - 1, 0, h - 1, canvas.rgb(255, 255, 255));
    _ = drawLine(0, h - 1, 0, 0, canvas.rgb(255, 255, 255));

    try canvas.dump(out, &pixels);

    // A line sets max(|dx|, |dy|) + 1 pixels: exactly one for each step of the
    // major axis, at all slopes.
    const probe = canvas.rgb(0, 0, 40);
    try out.print("\n(0,0)->(40,10): {d} pixels\n", .{drawLine(0, 0, 40, 10, probe)});
    try out.print("(0,0)->(10,30): {d} pixels\n", .{drawLine(0, 0, 10, 30, probe)});
    try out.print("(0,0)->(20,20): {d} pixels\n", .{drawLine(0, 0, 20, 20, probe)});
    try out.print("(40,10)->(0,0): {d} pixels (same line, drawn backwards)\n", .{
        drawLine(40, 10, 0, 0, probe),
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.lines`)*

## The error term

`err` records how far the ideal line is from the pixel that the loop plotted last. The code scales the value, so that it stays a whole number.

At each step, the major axis always advances. The minor axis advances only when the accumulated error shows that the line is a full pixel behind. The scale factor of two comes from the comparison of `2 * err` with `dx` and `dy`. With this factor, the comparison uses a half-pixel threshold, and the code does not divide.

The form in the snippet keeps `dy` negative:

```zig
const dx: i32 = @intCast(@abs(x1 - x0));
const dy: i32 = -@as(i32, @intCast(@abs(y1 - y0)));
```

When `dy` is negative, the eight cases (four quadrants, shallow and steep) become one loop. Many textbooks swap the endpoints, or swap `x` and `y` for steep lines. Then they need two loops that are almost the same. This version needs neither change.

The two tests are intentionally not an `if`/`else`:

```zig
if (e2 >= dy) { err += dy; x += sx; }
if (e2 <= dx) { err += dx; y += sy; }
```

On an exact diagonal, the two tests are both true, and the line moves on the two axes at the same time. If you change the second test into an `else`, the diagonals get a stair-step.

## The pixel count

A line sets `max(|dx|, |dy|) + 1` pixels: exactly one for each step of the major axis, at all slopes. The snippet prints this count for three slopes.

When you write your own version, check this invariant. There are two possible errors: an off-by-one at the end, or a double step on diagonals. Both errors show in the count before they show in the picture.

The count is correct only because the error term is symmetric. Check that a line drawn backwards gives the same count. If it does not, a renderer that draws shared edges from the two directions leaves seams.

## What this version does not do

**No thickness.** All lines here are one pixel wide. A thick line is a rectangle, or a polygon with round joins. Neither is a small change.

**No antialiasing.** Each pixel is fully on or fully off. Thus the diagonals in the output have visible steps. Xiaolin Wu's line algorithm is Bresenham with the error term used again as a coverage value. [Antialiasing](../antialiasing/) applies the same idea to a circle.

**No clipping other than in `putPixel`.** Think of a line that starts far outside one edge and ends far outside a different edge. The loop still goes through each pixel between the endpoints, and `putPixel` discards most of them. At this size, the cost is small. At larger sizes, the cost is a waste. The Cohen-Sutherland algorithm cuts the endpoints to the buffer before the loop starts.

---

## Circles

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/circles/*

A point is inside a circle when the distance from the point to the centre is not more than the radius:

```
sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy) <= r
```

Square the two sides, and the square root goes away:

```
dx*dx + dy*dy <= r*r
```

Now the two sides are integers, and the test is two multiplies and a compare. This method is useful in many areas, not only in graphics. If you must *compare* two lengths, do not call `sqrt`. Hit testing, nearest neighbour searches and collision detection all use squared distances.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const canvas = @import("_canvas.zig");

var pixels: [canvas.width * canvas.height]u32 = undefined;

/// Scans each pixel in the buffer. This is the simple version, and it does
/// too much work: at r = 7 it tests 2048 pixels to fill about 150.
fn fillCircleNaive(cx: i32, cy: i32, r: i32, color: u32) usize {
    var tested: usize = 0;
    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            tested += 1;
            const dx = @as(i32, @intCast(x)) - cx;
            const dy = @as(i32, @intCast(y)) - cy;
            if (dx * dx + dy * dy <= r * r) {
                canvas.putPixel(&pixels, @intCast(x), @intCast(y), color);
            }
        }
    }
    return tested;
}

/// The same circle, with a loop over only its bounding box. `putPixel`
/// clips, thus a circle that goes past an edge needs no extra code here.
fn fillCircle(cx: i32, cy: i32, r: i32, color: u32) usize {
    var tested: usize = 0;
    var y = cy - r;
    while (y <= cy + r) : (y += 1) {
        var x = cx - r;
        while (x <= cx + r) : (x += 1) {
            tested += 1;
            const dx = x - cx;
            const dy = y - cy;
            if (dx * dx + dy * dy <= r * r) {
                canvas.putPixel(&pixels, x, y, color);
            }
        }
    }
    return tested;
}

/// An outline is the same test two times: inside the outer radius and outside
/// the inner radius. The algorithm is the same, and the result is a band.
fn strokeCircle(cx: i32, cy: i32, r: i32, thickness: i32, color: u32) void {
    const outer = r * r;
    const inner = (r - thickness) * (r - thickness);
    var y = cy - r;
    while (y <= cy + r) : (y += 1) {
        var x = cx - r;
        while (x <= cx + r) : (x += 1) {
            const dx = x - cx;
            const dy = y - cy;
            const d2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;
            if (d2 <= outer and d2 > inner) {
                canvas.putPixel(&pixels, x, y, color);
            }
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    canvas.fill(&pixels, canvas.rgb(0, 0, 40));

    strokeCircle(20, 16, 13, 2, canvas.rgb(120, 200, 255));
    const naive = fillCircleNaive(20, 16, 7, canvas.rgb(255, 220, 40));
    const boxed = fillCircle(45, 16, 10, canvas.rgb(180, 255, 140));

    // This circle goes past two edges at the same time: the right edge and the
    // bottom edge. No code here checks for that. The clip in putPixel does.
    _ = fillCircle(62, 30, 8, canvas.rgb(255, 120, 120));

    try canvas.dump(out, &pixels);

    try out.print("\nfull-buffer scan, r=7:  {d} pixels tested\n", .{naive});
    try out.print("bounding box,     r=10: {d} pixels tested\n", .{boxed});
    try out.print("a circle of r=10 covers about {d} pixels\n", .{
        (314 * 10 * 10) / 100,
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.circles`)*

## The bounding box

The simple version scans the full buffer to fill one circle. At 64x32, the scan does 2048 tests for a shape of about 150 pixels. At 640x480, a circle of radius 100 costs 307,200 tests to fill 31,000 pixels.

A better version loops `y` and `x` over `[centre - r, centre + r]`. This version tests `(2r+1)^2` pixels. The snippet prints this count next to the count for the simple version.

The change is only three lines, because `putPixel` clips. When a circle is near an edge, its bounding box goes outside the buffer, and `fillCircle` does not check for this. To show this, the last circle in the snippet goes past two sides of the buffer at the same time.

If the clipping is not in one place, each shape routine needs its own `@min`/`@max` against the buffer size. Then, at some time, one of those routines will be wrong.

## An outline is the same test two times

```zig
if (d2 <= outer and d2 > inner) putPixel(...);
```

The pixels inside the outer radius and outside the inner radius make a band. The band needs no new algorithm and no special case, and the thickness is a parameter.

The midpoint circle algorithm draws a one-pixel outline faster. It calculates only one octant and mirrors the octant eight ways. It is the circle version of Bresenham, and you should read it one time. But if you want to fill a shape, the squared-distance test is simpler, and the compiler can vectorize it.

## What the circles do not have

The edge is hard: a pixel is in or out, with no value between. This is the staircase that you see in the output. To correct the edge, calculate the fraction of each pixel that is inside the circle, and use that fraction as an alpha value. [Antialiasing](../antialiasing/) does exactly this, on the same shape.

## Exercises

1. **Ellipses.** Scale one axis before you square it: `(dx*dx) * ry*ry + (dy*dy) *
   rx*rx <= rx*rx * ry*ry`. The values are still integers, and there is still no square root.
2. **Rounded rectangles.** Draw a rectangle, and apply the circle test only in the four corner boxes.
3. **A span fill.** For each row, find the two x values where the circle crosses the row. Then write that run of pixels directly. One `@memset` for each row is much faster than a test for each pixel, and production rasterizers use this method.

---

## Alpha Blending

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/blending/*

Each chapter before this one draws a shape on top of the old pixels. A later
write replaces an earlier write. This method is the painter's algorithm, and
it is sufficient for opaque shapes. When the shape on top is not opaque, use
blending instead.

The standard operator is **source over destination**. It operates on one
channel at a time:

```
out = (src * a + dst * (255 - a)) / 255
```

At `a = 255`, the output is the source. At `a = 0`, the output does not
change. Between these two values, the output is a weighted average. The sum
of the weights is exactly one. Thus the blend alone never makes the result
brighter or darker.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const canvas = @import("_canvas.zig");

var pixels: [canvas.width * canvas.height]u32 = undefined;

/// The source-over operator on one channel:
///
///     out = (src * a + dst * (255 - a)) / 255
///
/// The `+ 127` rounds to the nearest value. Without it, the division removes
/// the fraction. A division by 256 with a shift looks faster. But at a = 255
/// the shift gives 254. Thus blending code that uses the shift cannot make
/// pure white.
fn blendChannel(src: u8, dst: u8, a: u8) u8 {
    const s = @as(u32, src) * @as(u32, a);
    const d = @as(u32, dst) * (255 - @as(u32, a));
    return @intCast((s + d + 127) / 255);
}

fn blend(src: u32, dst: u32, a: u8) u32 {
    const s = canvas.channels(src);
    const d = canvas.channels(dst);
    return canvas.rgb(
        blendChannel(s.r, d.r, a),
        blendChannel(s.g, d.g, a),
        blendChannel(s.b, d.b, a),
    );
}

/// Read, blend, then write the result. The difference from `putPixel` is that
/// the destination is now an input. A later draw does not erase an earlier
/// draw, and the order of the draws changes the result.
fn blendPixel(x: i32, y: i32, color: u32, a: u8) void {
    if (x < 0 or y < 0) return;
    const ux: usize = @intCast(x);
    const uy: usize = @intCast(y);
    if (ux >= canvas.width or uy >= canvas.height) return;

    const i = uy * canvas.width + ux;
    pixels[i] = blend(color, pixels[i], a);
}

fn blendCircle(cx: i32, cy: i32, r: i32, color: u32, a: u8) void {
    var y = cy - r;
    while (y <= cy + r) : (y += 1) {
        var x = cx - r;
        while (x <= cx + r) : (x += 1) {
            const dx = x - cx;
            const dy = y - cy;
            if (dx * dx + dy * dy <= r * r) blendPixel(x, y, color, a);
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            const g: u8 = @intCast((x * 90) / (canvas.width - 1));
            canvas.putPixel(&pixels, @intCast(x), @intCast(y), canvas.rgb(20, g, 60));
        }
    }

    // Three discs at 60% opacity. Where two discs overlap, the background
    // shows through both discs. The overlap is brighter than each disc alone.
    blendCircle(24, 13, 11, canvas.rgb(255, 80, 80), 153);
    blendCircle(40, 13, 11, canvas.rgb(80, 255, 120), 153);
    blendCircle(32, 24, 11, canvas.rgb(120, 160, 255), 153);

    try canvas.dump(out, &pixels);

    const white = canvas.rgb(255, 255, 255);
    const black = canvas.rgb(0, 0, 0);

    try out.writeAll("\nwhite over black:\n");
    for ([_]u8{ 0, 64, 128, 192, 255 }) |a| {
        const result = canvas.channels(blend(white, black, a));
        try out.print("  a={d:>3} -> {d:>3} (shift-by-256 would give {d:>3})\n", .{
            a, result.r, (@as(u32, 255) * a) >> 8,
        });
    }

    // Blending is not commutative. Half of red on top of blue is not equal to
    // half of blue on top of red. Thus the draw order is still important.
    const red = canvas.rgb(255, 0, 0);
    const blue = canvas.rgb(0, 0, 255);
    const r_over_b = canvas.channels(blend(red, blue, 64));
    const b_over_r = canvas.channels(blend(blue, red, 64));
    try out.print("\nred over blue  at a=64: {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ r_over_b.r, r_over_b.g, r_over_b.b });
    try out.print("blue over red  at a=64: {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ b_over_r.r, b_over_r.g, b_over_r.b });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.blending`)*

## Do not skip the division

A division by 256 with a shift is faster than a division by 255. But the
error is visible:

```zig
(255 * a) >> 8   // a = 255 gives 254, not 255
```

The output above shows both columns. An opaque white composite gives 254.
For this reason, much older blending code cannot make pure white. The error
increases each time that you blend onto the same pixel again.

The expression `(s + d + 127) / 255` rounds to the nearest value. The cost is
one division, and the compiler usually changes that division into a multiply
and a shift.

If you want a fast version that is also correct, the usual method is:

```zig
const t = @as(u32, src) * a + 128;
const blended: u8 = @intCast((t + (t >> 8)) >> 8);
```

This version is exact for all 8-bit inputs. Use it only when a profile shows
that the division is important.

## Read, blend, write

The only change in structure from `putPixel` is that the destination is now
an input:

```zig
const i = uy * width + ux;
pixels[i] = blend(color, pixels[i], a);
```

With this one change, the draw order changes the colour. Before, the draw
order decided only which shape hid which shape.

In the output, three discs at 60% opacity overlap. Each overlap has a
different colour, because each overlap is the result of two blends in
sequence.

## Blending is not commutative

The snippet composites red over blue and blue over red at the same alpha. The
two answers are different. For this reason, renderers draw from back to
front. If a renderer draws translucent geometry in a random order, the
colours are also random.

Use one of these methods:

- Sort by depth, and draw from far to near.
- Use an order-independent technique.

## Premultiplied alpha

The operator above is the simple model, and the model has a known weakness.
Some operations use colours that carry their own alpha: filters, changes of
scale, and averages. These operations give wrong results at the edges. The
cause is that a fully transparent pixel still adds its colour to the average.

**Premultiplied alpha** stores `(r*a, g*a, b*a, a)` instead. Then the
operator needs one less multiply:

```
out = src + dst * (255 - a) / 255
```

Systems that scale or filter use premultiplied alpha for this reason, for
example a GPU, a compositor or a browser. The cost is a conversion at the
boundary, because most image files store straight alpha.

## sRGB bytes are not linear light

All the code on this page averages the bytes as the file stores them. These
bytes are not linear light. sRGB applies a transfer curve of approximately
`x^2.2`. Thus a value of 128 is about 22% of the light of 255, not 50%.

A blend in sRGB space makes a 50% composite of black and white too dark. The
eye expects a lighter result, and the difference is visible.

To blend correctly, convert to linear, blend, and then convert the result to
sRGB again.
Alternatively, use 16-bit linear values for all steps.
[Linear Light](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/linear-light/) builds both conversions as
lookup tables.

Almost all 8-bit graphics code blends in sRGB and accepts the error. The code
on this page also does this. This tradeoff is deliberate. In your code, make
sure that a blend in sRGB is a choice and not a mistake.

---

## Linear Light

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/linear-light/*

For the colour halfway between black and white, most code writes 128. The
value 128 is half of 255. But when a screen shows 128, the screen gives about
22% of the light that it gives for 255.

The bytes in an image are not amounts of light. The bytes are an encoding of
the light. Thus decode the bytes to light, mix the light, and then encode the
result again.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const canvas = @import("_canvas.zig");

var pixels: [canvas.width * canvas.height]u32 = undefined;

/// Change an sRGB byte to linear light, 0.0 to 1.0. The constants 0.04045,
/// 12.92, 0.055 and 2.4 come from the sRGB standard. Do not adjust them.
fn decode(byte: u8) f64 {
    const c = @as(f64, @floatFromInt(byte)) / 255.0;
    return if (c <= 0.04045) c / 12.92 else std.math.pow(f64, (c + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4);
}

/// Change linear light, 0.0 to 1.0, to sRGB, 0.0 to 1.0. This function is the
/// inverse of `decode`.
fn encode(light: f64) f64 {
    return if (light <= 0.0031308) light * 12.92 else 1.055 * std.math.pow(f64, light, 1.0 / 2.4) - 0.055;
}

/// The program keeps linear light in 16 bits: 0 is black and 65535 is full
/// white. Eight bits are not sufficient. The dark bytes 0 to 6 would all
/// become 0.
const Light = u16;

/// One entry for each byte. A block that initialises a `const` runs at compile
/// time. Thus the program contains a table of 512 bytes, and it does not call
/// `pow` at run time.
const to_light: [256]Light = blk: {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(1_000_000);
    var table: [256]Light = undefined;
    for (&table, 0..) |*entry, byte| {
        entry.* = @intFromFloat(@round(decode(@intCast(byte)) * 65535.0));
    }
    break :blk table;
};

/// The conversion from light to a byte. 65536 entries would be 64 KB. Thus the
/// index of the table is the top 12 bits of the light value. Each entry holds
/// the byte for the middle of its range of 16 light values.
const to_byte: [4096]u8 = blk: {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(10_000_000);
    var table: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    for (&table, 0..) |*entry, i| {
        const middle = @as(f64, @floatFromInt(i * 16 + 8)) / 65535.0;
        entry.* = @intFromFloat(@round(encode(middle) * 255.0));
    }
    break :blk table;
};

fn toLight(byte: u8) Light {
    return to_light[byte];
}

fn toByte(light: Light) u8 {
    return to_byte[light >> 4];
}

/// Mix two stored bytes directly. The weight of `a` is (n - k), and the weight
/// of `b` is k. The result rounds to the nearest byte. Most 8-bit code mixes
/// colours in this way.
fn mixBytes(a: u8, b: u8, k: u32, n: u32) u8 {
    return @intCast((@as(u32, a) * (n - k) + @as(u32, b) * k + n / 2) / n);
}

/// The same mix on light: decode, mix, encode.
fn mixLight(a: u8, b: u8, k: u32, n: u32) u8 {
    const la: u32 = toLight(a);
    const lb: u32 = toLight(b);
    return toByte(@intCast((la * (n - k) + lb * k + n / 2) / n));
}

fn mixColor(comptime mix: fn (u8, u8, u32, u32) u8, a: u32, b: u32, k: u32, n: u32) u32 {
    const ca = canvas.channels(a);
    const cb = canvas.channels(b);
    return canvas.rgb(mix(ca.r, cb.r, k, n), mix(ca.g, cb.g, k, n), mix(ca.b, cb.b, k, n));
}

/// Four bands of eight rows. Each band is a ramp from left to right.
fn drawBands() void {
    const black = canvas.rgb(0, 0, 0);
    const white = canvas.rgb(255, 255, 255);
    const red = canvas.rgb(255, 0, 0);
    const green = canvas.rgb(0, 255, 0);
    const n = canvas.width - 1;

    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            const k: u32 = @intCast(x);
            const color = switch (y / 8) {
                0 => mixColor(mixBytes, black, white, k, n),
                1 => mixColor(mixLight, black, white, k, n),
                2 => mixColor(mixBytes, red, green, k, n),
                else => mixColor(mixLight, red, green, k, n),
            };
            pixels[y * canvas.width + x] = color;
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    try out.writeAll("halfway from black to white\n");
    try out.print("  mixing bytes: {d}\n", .{mixBytes(0, 255, 1, 2)});
    try out.print("  mixing light: {d}\n", .{mixLight(0, 255, 1, 2)});

    const red = canvas.rgb(255, 0, 0);
    const green = canvas.rgb(0, 255, 0);
    const by_bytes = canvas.channels(mixColor(mixBytes, red, green, 1, 2));
    const by_light = canvas.channels(mixColor(mixLight, red, green, 1, 2));
    try out.writeAll("halfway from red to green\n");
    try out.print("  mixing bytes: {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ by_bytes.r, by_bytes.g, by_bytes.b });
    try out.print("  mixing light: {d} {d} {d}\n", .{ by_light.r, by_light.g, by_light.b });

    // Byte 128 holds about 22% of the light of byte 255, not 50%.
    try out.print("light in byte 128: {d}%\n", .{(@as(u32, toLight(128)) * 100 + 32767) / 65535});

    // Each byte must return as the same byte. If the steps of the encode
    // table were too large, the dark bytes would fail this check first.
    var exact: u32 = 0;
    for (0..256) |i| {
        const byte: u8 = @intCast(i);
        if (toByte(toLight(byte)) == byte) exact += 1;
    }
    try out.print("bytes that survive byte -> light -> byte: {d} of 256\n", .{exact});

    // The same conversion, but with 8-bit light instead of 16-bit light.
    var seen: [256]bool = @splat(false);
    var kept: u32 = 0;
    for (0..256) |i| {
        const light8 = (@as(u32, toLight(@intCast(i))) * 255 + 32767) / 65535;
        if (!seen[light8]) kept += 1;
        seen[light8] = true;
    }
    try out.print("distinct bytes left after 8-bit light: {d} of 256\n", .{kept});

    try out.print("tables: {d} bytes, built by the compiler\n", .{@sizeOf(@TypeOf(to_light)) + @sizeOf(@TypeOf(to_byte))});

    drawBands();
    try canvas.writePicture(init.io, out, "linear-light.ppm", &pixels);
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.linear-light`)*

## The worked example

The program finds the colour halfway from black to white in two ways:

- Mix the bytes: (0 + 255) / 2 is 128, after the program rounds the result.
- Mix the light: the average of 0% light and 100% light is 50%. When the
  program encodes 50% light again, the result is byte 188.

The output shows both values. The values 128 and 188 are very different.

The change from red to green shows the same problem in colour:

- A mix of the bytes gives `128 128 0`, a dark olive.
- A mix of the light gives `188 188 0`, a yellow.

The third and fourth bands of the picture show these two ramps.

## Why images store encoded bytes

The human eye does not see light linearly. In a dark area, a person sees a
small change much more easily than the same change in a bright area.

For this reason, the sRGB encoding gives more of its 256 values to dark tones.
Thus the steps between bytes look approximately equal to a person.

For the same reason, the first band in the picture looks even, and the second
band looks mostly pale. The second band has equal steps of light, and to the
human eye most of those steps look bright.

Thus there are two different tasks:

- To store or show a colour, use the encoded bytes.
- To add or average light, use linear values.

Blending, blurs, changes of image scale and antialiasing all add or average
light. Do these operations in linear light.

## The conversion

The sRGB standard defines the curve in two parts. Near black, the curve is a
short straight line. For the other values, the curve is a power curve.

```zig
/// Change an sRGB byte to linear light, 0.0 to 1.0. The constants 0.04045,
/// 12.92, 0.055 and 2.4 come from the sRGB standard. Do not adjust them.
fn decode(byte: u8) f64 {
    const c = @as(f64, @floatFromInt(byte)) / 255.0;
    return if (c <= 0.04045) c / 12.92 else std.math.pow(f64, (c + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `decode` from `snippets/09-graphics/linear-light.zig`.*

The numbers 0.04045, 12.92, 0.055 and 2.4 come from the standard. Copy them
exactly.

A plain `x^2.2` curve is close, but the two curves are different near black.
The function `encode` uses the same curve in the opposite direction.

## Tables built by the compiler

`pow` is slow, and a byte has only 256 possible values. Thus the program
calculates all 256 answers one time and keeps the answers in a table.

```zig
/// One entry for each byte. A block that initialises a `const` runs at compile
/// time. Thus the program contains a table of 512 bytes, and it does not call
/// `pow` at run time.
const to_light: [256]Light = blk: {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(1_000_000);
    var table: [256]Light = undefined;
    for (&table, 0..) |*entry, byte| {
        entry.* = @intFromFloat(@round(decode(@intCast(byte)) * 65535.0));
    }
    break :blk table;
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `to_light` from `snippets/09-graphics/linear-light.zig`.*

The code is an ordinary loop inside a block. But the block initialises a
top-level `const`. Thus Zig runs the block at compile time. The finished
program contains the 256 numbers, and it never calls `pow` for these numbers.

`@setEvalBranchQuota` increases the limit of the compiler on the quantity of
work that a compile-time block can do. `pow` has loops inside it, thus the
default limit is too low. Without the call, the build fails with an error
that names `@setEvalBranchQuota`.

## Why light needs 16 bits

The table stores light as a `u16`, not a `u8`. The output shows the result
with 8 bits.

Only 183 of the 256 bytes return as different values. The bytes 0 to 6 all
become 0. Thus seven dark greys become black.

The dark tones need small steps in linear light, because the encoding gives
many bytes to the dark tones. With 16 bits, each byte returns as the same
byte after the conversion to light and back. The output checks all 256 bytes.

## Encode light as bytes

The encode step needs a second table. If the index of the table is the full
16-bit value, the table needs 65536 entries.

Thus the index of this table is the top 12 bits. Each entry covers 16 light
values. Each entry holds the byte for the middle of its 16 light values.

```zig
/// The conversion from light to a byte. 65536 entries would be 64 KB. Thus the
/// index of the table is the top 12 bits of the light value. Each entry holds
/// the byte for the middle of its range of 16 light values.
const to_byte: [4096]u8 = blk: {
    @setEvalBranchQuota(10_000_000);
    var table: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    for (&table, 0..) |*entry, i| {
        const middle = @as(f64, @floatFromInt(i * 16 + 8)) / 65535.0;
        entry.* = @intFromFloat(@round(encode(middle) * 255.0));
    }
    break :blk table;
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `to_byte` from `snippets/09-graphics/linear-light.zig`.*

Sixteen light values for each entry are a sufficiently small step, also near
black:

- Near black, one byte is about 20 light values wide.
- The middle of an entry is never more than 8 light values from a value that
  the entry covers.
- 8 light values are less than half a byte. Thus the rounding still gives the
  correct byte.

The round-trip line in the output is the proof. If the steps of the table
were too large, the dark bytes would fail first.

## Mix in linear light

With the two tables, a mix in linear light is two lookups, the same
arithmetic, and one more lookup.

```zig
/// The same mix on light: decode, mix, encode.
fn mixLight(a: u8, b: u8, k: u32, n: u32) u8 {
    const la: u32 = toLight(a);
    const lb: u32 = toLight(b);
    return toByte(@intCast((la * (n - k) + lb * k + n / 2) / n));
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `mixLight` from `snippets/09-graphics/linear-light.zig`.*

Compare `mixLight` with `mixBytes` in the snippet above. The arithmetic is
the same. Only the type of number in the arithmetic is different.

The [Alpha Blending](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/blending/) chapter blends the bytes
directly, and the chapter tells you this. To blend in linear light, do these
steps:

1. Decode both colours with `toLight`.
2. Do the same blend in 16 bits.
3. Encode the result with `toByte`.

## What linear light does not fix

Linear light describes how light adds, for example two torches that point at
one wall. Paint does not operate in this way, because pigments absorb light.

Yellow paint mixed with blue paint makes green. Yellow light mixed with blue
light makes grey, in linear light or in bytes.

Thus a linear mix is correct for a screen and for a camera. A linear mix is
not a model of paint.

## Explain before you read the answer

Draw a checkerboard of single black and white pixels. Look at the checkerboard
from the other side of the room, so that the squares become one blur. Which
grey looks the same: byte 128 or byte 188?

The answer is 188. Half of the pixels give full light, and half of the pixels
give no light. Your eye averages the light, thus your eye sees 50% light. 50%
light is byte 188, not 128.

---

## Rasterize Triangles

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/triangles/*

The triangle is the primitive that a GPU actually draws. All other shapes
become triangles before they arrive at the rasterizer. A quad that you draw also
becomes triangles. Three vertices are always coplanar and always convex. For
this reason, the inside test is fast enough to run for each pixel.

The test is one function, and the rasterizer calls it three times:

```zig
fn edge(a: Point, b: Point, p: Point) i32 {
    return (b.x - a.x) * (p.y - a.y) - (b.y - a.y) * (p.x - a.x);
}
```

The function calculates the 2D cross product of `b - a` and `p - a`. The
result is two times the signed area of the triangle `(a, b, p)`.

- The **sign** of the result tells you on which side of the line `ab` the
  point `p` is.
- The **magnitude** of the result is exactly the barycentric weight that
  interpolation needs.

Thus a rasterizer calculates the value one time and uses it two times.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const canvas = @import("_canvas.zig");

var pixels: [canvas.width * canvas.height]u32 = undefined;

const Point = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };

/// Two times the signed area of triangle (a, b, p). The value is positive on
/// one side of the line ab, negative on the other side, and zero on the line.
/// The sign alone is the inside test. The magnitude is the barycentric weight.
fn edge(a: Point, b: Point, p: Point) i32 {
    return (b.x - a.x) * (p.y - a.y) - (b.y - a.y) * (p.x - a.x);
}

fn fillTriangle(a: Point, b: Point, c: Point, ca: u32, cb: u32, cc: u32) void {
    // Make the winding the same for all triangles. Then "inside" is always
    // the side where the values are zero or more. Without this step, a
    // triangle with the other winding disappears.
    var v0 = a;
    var v1 = b;
    const v2 = c;
    var col0 = ca;
    var col1 = cb;
    const col2 = cc;
    const area = edge(v0, v1, v2);
    if (area < 0) {
        std.mem.swap(Point, &v0, &v1);
        std.mem.swap(u32, &col0, &col1);
    }
    const total = edge(v0, v1, v2);
    if (total == 0) return; // degenerate: three collinear points make no face

    const min_x = @min(v0.x, @min(v1.x, v2.x));
    const max_x = @max(v0.x, @max(v1.x, v2.x));
    const min_y = @min(v0.y, @min(v1.y, v2.y));
    const max_y = @max(v0.y, @max(v1.y, v2.y));

    var y = min_y;
    while (y <= max_y) : (y += 1) {
        var x = min_x;
        while (x <= max_x) : (x += 1) {
            const p = Point{ .x = x, .y = y };
            const w0 = edge(v1, v2, p);
            const w1 = edge(v2, v0, p);
            const w2 = edge(v0, v1, p);
            if (w0 < 0 or w1 < 0 or w2 < 0) continue;

            // The three edge values, divided by the total, are the barycentric
            // coordinates. Their sum is 1. Each coordinate is the weight for
            // the colour of one vertex: the nearer the pixel, the larger the
            // weight.
            const g0 = canvas.channels(col0);
            const g1 = canvas.channels(col1);
            const g2 = canvas.channels(col2);
            canvas.putPixel(&pixels, x, y, canvas.rgb(
                mix(w0, w1, w2, g0.r, g1.r, g2.r, total),
                mix(w0, w1, w2, g0.g, g1.g, g2.g, total),
                mix(w0, w1, w2, g0.b, g1.b, g2.b, total),
            ));
        }
    }
}

fn mix(w0: i32, w1: i32, w2: i32, c0: u8, c1: u8, c2: u8, total: i32) u8 {
    const sum = w0 * @as(i32, c0) + w1 * @as(i32, c1) + w2 * @as(i32, c2);
    return @intCast(@divTrunc(sum, total));
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    canvas.fill(&pixels, canvas.rgb(0, 0, 30));

    // Gouraud shading in three lines: one colour for each vertex, and the
    // colours interpolate across the face.
    fillTriangle(
        .{ .x = 4, .y = 28 },
        .{ .x = 30, .y = 2 },
        .{ .x = 40, .y = 26 },
        canvas.rgb(30, 30, 60),
        canvas.rgb(255, 255, 255),
        canvas.rgb(120, 120, 160),
    );

    // This triangle has the other winding and one flat colour. The triangle
    // still appears, because fillTriangle makes the winding the same.
    fillTriangle(
        .{ .x = 62, .y = 4 },
        .{ .x = 44, .y = 20 },
        .{ .x = 62, .y = 30 },
        canvas.rgb(255, 200, 60),
        canvas.rgb(255, 200, 60),
        canvas.rgb(255, 200, 60),
    );

    try canvas.dump(out, &pixels);
    try canvas.writePicture(init.io, out, "triangle.ppm", &pixels);

    const a = Point{ .x = 0, .y = 0 };
    const b = Point{ .x = 10, .y = 0 };
    try out.print("\nedge value below the line ab: {d}\n", .{edge(a, b, .{ .x = 5, .y = 4 })});
    try out.print("edge value on the line ab:    {d}\n", .{edge(a, b, .{ .x = 5, .y = 0 })});
    try out.print("edge value above the line ab: {d}\n", .{edge(a, b, .{ .x = 5, .y = -4 })});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.triangle`)*

## Inside is three signs

A point is inside the triangle when all three edge functions have the same
sign. The snippet first makes the winding the same for all triangles. Then
"the same sign" means "all values are zero or more", and the second case is
not necessary:

```zig
if (edge(v0, v1, v2) < 0) {
    std.mem.swap(Point, &v0, &v1);
    std.mem.swap(u32, &col0, &col1);
}
```

If you swap two vertices, also swap their colours. If you do not, the shading
shows a mirror image on the triangles that have the other winding. When this
code gets more attributes, it is easy to forget to keep each vertex with its
attributes.

A production pipeline usually does not change the winding. It rejects one
winding on purpose. This method is *backface culling*. With backface culling,
a renderer quickly discards the far side of a closed mesh before it touches a
pixel.

## Barycentric coordinates at no extra cost

Divide the three edge values by their total. The result is three weights, and
the sum of the weights is one. Each weight measures how near the pixel is to
the vertex opposite that edge.

Multiply a value at each vertex by these weights. Then the value interpolates
linearly across the face:

```zig
const sum = w0 * c0 + w1 * c1 + w2 * c2;
return @intCast(@divTrunc(sum, total));
```

The snippet uses colour as the example. Press Run, and the picture under the
output shows the colours. The left triangle is Gouraud shading in three
lines.

The same three weights also interpolate texture coordinates, normals and
depth. This is the main reason that edge functions replaced scanline methods.
The inside test and the interpolation of attributes use the same arithmetic.

For a perspective projection, do the interpolation in `1/w` space. If you do
not, the textures warp visibly along the diagonal of a quad. This correction
is the origin of the name "perspective-correct" interpolation.

## Shared edges, and the top-left rule

Two triangles that share an edge have a problem. Think of a pixel whose
centre is exactly on the shared edge. For both triangles, the edge value of
that pixel is zero:

- With `>= 0`, the rasterizer draws the pixel two times.
- With `> 0`, the rasterizer leaves a gap.

When the code uses blending, a pixel drawn two times is visible. A gap is
always visible.

The solution is a rule that decides the tie only from the edge. The rule does
not look at the triangle that the code draws. For a top edge or a left edge,
zero counts as inside. For other edges, zero does not count as inside.

This rule is the **top-left rule**, and all hardware rasterizers use it. This
snippet does not use the rule, because it draws no shared edges. But code
that joins triangles into a mesh needs the rule.

## Why an incremental loop is faster

`edge` is affine in `p`. Thus a step of one pixel to the right adds a
constant, and a step of one row down adds a different constant.

A production rasterizer calculates the three edge values one time, at the
corner of the bounding box. Then it adds the constants for each pixel. This
method removes all multiplies from the inner loop.

After that change, the values for four or eight pixels fit in a SIMD
register. Then the rasterizer tests the full group of pixels at the same
time.

The version on this page is easy to read. The change to the fast version is
mechanical.

## Exercises

1. **Backface culling.** When the winding is negative, return early instead
   of a swap. Then draw the faces of a cube, and see the back faces
   disappear.
2. **Two triangles that share an edge.** Blend them at 50%, and look for the
   bright seam. Then add the top-left rule, and see the seam disappear.
3. **A depth buffer.** Interpolate a `z` value at each vertex with the same
   weights. Keep a second array with the nearest `z` for each pixel. Reject
   each pixel that is behind that `z`. This method replaces the painter's
   algorithm, and it works correctly for geometry that intersects.

## Antialiasing

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/antialiasing/*

A pixel is not a point. A pixel is a small square of the image. The edge of a
shape usually crosses the square. Usually the square is not fully outside or
fully inside the shape.

A test at only the centre of the pixel gives a yes-or-no answer. But the real
answer is a fraction. The staircase on each hard edge is this rounding error,
and you can see it.

Do the same test at sixteen points inside the pixel. Then the answer is a
count from 0 to 16. This count is the **coverage**, and the coverage is
exactly the alpha value for the composite.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const canvas = @import("_canvas.zig");

var pixels: [canvas.width * canvas.height]u32 = undefined;

const samples = 4; // 4x4 = 16 tests per pixel

fn blendChannel(src: u8, dst: u8, a: u32) u8 {
    return @intCast((@as(u32, src) * a + @as(u32, dst) * (255 - a) + 127) / 255);
}

/// Coverage in 0..16: the number of sub-positions inside this pixel that are
/// in the circle. The sub-positions are at the centres of a 4x4 grid, with an
/// offset of half a sub-pixel. Thus the samples are symmetric about the
/// centre of the pixel.
///
/// The code multiplies all values by `samples * 2` to keep integers. A
/// sub-position is at an odd multiple of half a sub-pixel. Thus two times
/// that value is a whole number.
fn coverage(x: i32, y: i32, cx: i32, cy: i32, r: i32) u32 {
    const scale = samples * 2;
    const rs = r * scale;
    var hits: u32 = 0;
    var sy: i32 = 0;
    while (sy < samples) : (sy += 1) {
        var sx: i32 = 0;
        while (sx < samples) : (sx += 1) {
            const px = x * scale + 2 * sx + 1;
            const py = y * scale + 2 * sy + 1;
            const dx = px - (cx * scale + samples);
            const dy = py - (cy * scale + samples);
            if (dx * dx + dy * dy <= rs * rs) hits += 1;
        }
    }
    return hits;
}

fn hardCircle(cx: i32, cy: i32, r: i32, color: u32) void {
    var y = cy - r - 1;
    while (y <= cy + r + 1) : (y += 1) {
        var x = cx - r - 1;
        while (x <= cx + r + 1) : (x += 1) {
            const dx = x - cx;
            const dy = y - cy;
            if (dx * dx + dy * dy <= r * r) canvas.putPixel(&pixels, x, y, color);
        }
    }
}

fn smoothCircle(cx: i32, cy: i32, r: i32, color: u32) void {
    var y = cy - r - 1;
    while (y <= cy + r + 1) : (y += 1) {
        var x = cx - r - 1;
        while (x <= cx + r + 1) : (x += 1) {
            const hits = coverage(x, y, cx, cy, r);
            if (hits == 0) continue;
            if (x < 0 or y < 0) continue;
            const ux: usize = @intCast(x);
            const uy: usize = @intCast(y);
            if (ux >= canvas.width or uy >= canvas.height) continue;

            // 16 hits means fully inside. Fewer hits mean a partial pixel.
            // The fraction is exactly the alpha for the composite.
            const alpha = (hits * 255) / (samples * samples);
            const i = uy * canvas.width + ux;
            const s = canvas.channels(color);
            const d = canvas.channels(pixels[i]);
            pixels[i] = canvas.rgb(
                blendChannel(s.r, d.r, alpha),
                blendChannel(s.g, d.g, alpha),
                blendChannel(s.b, d.b, alpha),
            );
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    canvas.fill(&pixels, canvas.rgb(0, 0, 30));

    const ink = canvas.rgb(255, 230, 150);
    hardCircle(16, 16, 12, ink);
    smoothCircle(47, 16, 12, ink);

    try canvas.dump(out, &pixels);

    try out.writeAll("\nleft: hard test. right: 16 samples per pixel.\n");
    try out.writeAll("\ncoverage across the right circle's edge, row y=16:\n");
    var x: i32 = 56;
    while (x <= 61) : (x += 1) {
        const hits = coverage(x, 16, 47, 16, 12);
        try out.print("  x={d}: {d:>2}/16 -> alpha {d:>3}\n", .{ x, hits, (hits * 255) / 16 });
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.antialias`)*

The two circles have the same radius and the same colour:

- The left circle uses the hard test from [Circles](../circles/).
- The right circle tests a 4x4 grid of samples in each pixel. It blends by
  the fraction of samples that passed.

The table in the output goes across the edge of the right circle on one row.
A pixel that is half covered gets alpha 127.

## The arithmetic stays integer

The sub-positions are at the centres of a 4x4 grid inside the pixel. Thus
the sub-positions are at odd multiples of half a sub-pixel. The code
multiplies each coordinate by `2 * samples`, and then the sub-positions are
whole numbers. Thus the distance test is the same comparison of squared
integers as before:

```zig
const scale = samples * 2;
const px = x * scale + 2 * sx + 1;
```

The `+ 1` is the offset of half a sub-pixel. Without the `+ 1`, the samples
are at the corners. Then the full edge moves by half a sub-pixel, which is
one eighth of a pixel here. This error is small and always in the same
direction. When two antialiased shapes must touch, you can see the error.

## The cost

The code does sixteen inside tests for each pixel. The bounding box must also
become one pixel larger on each side, or the code skips pixels that are
partially covered. Because of this cost, supersampling is often the first
technique that people use, and the technique that they replace later.

There are other techniques:

- For a circle, the distance from the centre already tells you how far into
  the edge a pixel is. A ramp one pixel wide on that distance gives a good
  edge with one test.
- Signed distance fields use the same idea for shapes of all types.
- A font rasterizer calculates the coverage of polygon edges analytically.
  Text with samples at this quality would be much too slow.

Supersampling has one advantage that these techniques do not have: it needs
no knowledge of the shape. You can antialias any inside test, whatever its
code. Do the test more times for each pixel. Thus supersampling is a good
first choice, and it can stay the answer for offline rendering.

## Where the result is wrong

On this page, blending occurs in sRGB, as in all other chapters of this
section. Thus a half-covered pixel is darker than half the light of a covered
pixel. For this reason, thin antialiased strokes look thinner than they are.
This problem is very important for text rasterizers. Refer to the note at the
end of [Alpha Blending](../blending/).

## Exercises

1. **Change the sample count.** Use 2x2 samples, and the ramp gets four
   levels instead of sixteen. In the character dump, it is easy to count the
   bands.
2. **Rotate the sample grid.** A regular grid gives the worst result on edges
   that are almost horizontal or almost vertical. For this reason, hardware
   uses rotated grid patterns. Move the samples, and compare the top of the
   circle.
3. **Antialias a line.** Xiaolin Wu's algorithm is Bresenham's algorithm, with
   the error term used again as coverage. It is the idea of this page applied
   to [Lines](../lines/), with no extra samples.

## Per-Pixel Transforms
