```zig
        'Z' => .{ 0b11111, 0b00001, 0b00010, 0b00100, 0b01000, 0b10000, 0b11111 },
        'I' => .{ 0b11111, 0b00100, 0b00100, 0b00100, 0b00100, 0b00100, 0b11111 },
        'G' => .{ 0b01110, 0b10001, 0b10000, 0b10111, 0b10001, 0b10001, 0b01110 },
        '2' => .{ 0b01110, 0b10001, 0b00001, 0b00010, 0b00100, 0b01000, 0b11111 },
        '0' => .{ 0b01110, 0b10001, 0b10011, 0b10101, 0b11001, 0b10001, 0b01110 },
        '6' => .{ 0b00110, 0b01000, 0b10000, 0b11110, 0b10001, 0b10001, 0b01110 },
        ' ' => .{ 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 },
        else => null,
    };
}

fn putPixel(x: i32, y: i32, ink: u8) void {
    if (x < 0 or y < 0) return;
    const ux: usize = @intCast(x);
    const uy: usize = @intCast(y);
    if (ux >= width or uy >= height) return;
    pixels[uy * width + ux] = ink;
}

/// Draw one glyph. The function tests each bit and skips the zeroes. Thus text
/// draws *over* a background and not in a box. A glyph has no background of
/// its own. It has only the pixels that it sets.
fn drawGlyph(g: Glyph, x: i32, y: i32, ink: u8) void {
    for (g, 0..) |row, dy| {
        var bit: u3 = 0;
        while (bit < glyph_width) : (bit += 1) {
            const mask = @as(u8, 1) << @intCast(glyph_width - 1 - bit);
            if (row & mask != 0) {
                putPixel(x + @as(i32, bit), y + @as(i32, @intCast(dy)), ink);
            }
        }
    }
}

/// Move the pen by the glyph width plus one column of spacing. A proportional
/// font stores an advance for each glyph. That one change is most of the
/// difference between a terminal font and a text engine.
fn drawText(text: []const u8, x: i32, y: i32, ink: u8) i32 {
    var pen = x;
    for (text) |c| {
        if (glyphFor(c)) |g| drawGlyph(g, pen, y, ink);
        pen += glyph_width + 1;
    }
    return pen;
}

fn dump(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    for (0..height) |y| {
        try out.print("{s}\n", .{pixels[y * width ..][0..width]});
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const end = drawText("ZIG 2026", 1, 1, '#');
    _ = drawText("206", 1, 9, '*');

    try dump(out);
    try out.print("\n\"ZIG 2026\" is {d} glyphs and ended at column {d}\n", .{ 8, end });
    try out.print("each glyph is {d}x{d} bits, so the whole font above is {d} bytes\n", .{
        glyph_width, glyph_height, 7 * glyph_height,
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.font`)*

## What just happened

**Each glyph is seven bytes.** Each row uses five bits, and there are seven
rows. The source writes the rows in binary, so you can see the shape. Look at
`Z` in the code, and you can read the letter from the ones.

**The program skipped the zeroes. It did not draw them.** That one `if` lets
text compose with other drawings. A glyph has no background of its own, so it
draws *over* the pixels that are already there. If the program fills the
zeroes with a background colour, each character is in an opaque box. This
mistake is immediately visible.

**The pen moved by a fixed amount.** The step is always six columns per
character. A font of this type is a **monospaced** font, and for this reason
terminal output aligns in columns. A proportional font stores an advance width
for each glyph. That one change is most of the difference between this program
and a text engine. With that change, the width of a string is a sum and not a
multiplication.

**The full font is 49 bytes.** There are seven glyphs at seven bytes each. For
this reason, machines with only kilobytes of memory used this method. A
bootloader or an embedded display still uses this method.

## Check yourself

The glyphs here are 5x7. What must change to draw them at twice the size?

The data does not change, and one line of the loop changes: write a 2x2 block
of pixels and not one pixel. This method works. It is also the reason that
doubled bitmap text has visibly blocky edges. The data never had the
information for the pixels between.

A *good* larger size needs a different glyph format. Store the glyph as
outlines, which are curves that control points define. Then rasterise the
outlines at the requested size. TrueType uses this method.

Outlines are also the reason that fonts need *hinting*. At small sizes, the
outline rarely aligns with the pixel grid. Thus the shapes need small
adjustments. Without the adjustments, a stem can be half in one column and half
in the next column.

## If you know C

The font table is `static const unsigned char font[][7]`, with the character as
the index. The classic version uses `c - 32` as the index directly, to skip the
control characters. This method is fast. But it is an out-of-bounds read when
a byte above 127 arrives, and all non-ASCII input contains such bytes. The
version above uses a switch that returns null for each character that it does
not know.

The other traditional detail is the storage order. Fonts were column-major as
frequently as they were row-major. Some displays used vertical strips of
eight pixels, and eight pixels are exactly one byte. The storage order followed
the order that the hardware read.

Next: sprites, which use the same copy with more than one bit per pixel.

---

## Sprites and Transparency

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/sprite/*

A sprite is a small image that a program copies onto a larger image. The copy
is a nested loop, and you can write it in a minute.

A sprite is different from a rectangle because of one part: the part that
decides which pixels to skip. Without that part, each sprite is a box. Then a
spaceship moves a square of background with it.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const width: usize = 40;
const height: usize = 14;
var canvas: [width * height]u8 = @splat('.');

/// A sprite is a small image and a rule for the pixels that are transparent.
/// Here the rule is a key colour: one value that means "skip". The 8-bit and
/// 16-bit consoles used this method, because a per-pixel alpha channel costs
/// memory that those machines did not have.
const Sprite = struct {
    w: usize,
    h: usize,
    pixels: []const u8,
    transparent: u8,
};

const ship = Sprite{
    .w = 7,
    .h = 5,
    .transparent = ' ',
    .pixels = "   A   " ++
        "  AAA  " ++
        " AABAA " ++
        "AAAAAAA" ++
        " A   A ",
};

fn blit(sprite: Sprite, x: i32, y: i32) void {
    for (0..sprite.h) |sy| {
        for (0..sprite.w) |sx| {
            const value = sprite.pixels[sy * sprite.w + sx];
            // All of transparency is this one comparison. Without it, a
            // sprite is a rectangle, and the sprite hides all of the pixels
            // behind its corners.
            if (value == sprite.transparent) continue;

            const dx = x + @as(i32, @intCast(sx));
            const dy = y + @as(i32, @intCast(sy));
            if (dx < 0 or dy < 0) continue;
            const ux: usize = @intCast(dx);
            const uy: usize = @intCast(dy);
            if (ux >= width or uy >= height) continue;

            canvas[uy * width + ux] = value;
        }
    }
}

fn fillBackground() void {
    for (0..height) |y| {
        for (0..width) |x| {
            canvas[y * width + x] = if ((x / 4 + y / 2) % 2 == 0) '.' else ',';
        }
    }
}

fn dump(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    for (0..height) |y| try out.print("{s}\n", .{canvas[y * width ..][0..width]});
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    fillBackground();

    // Three copies of one sprite. The program does not copy the data in
    // memory. A sprite is data, and a loop draws it. Thus the second copy
    // costs no memory.
    blit(ship, 2, 2);
    blit(ship, 14, 6);
    // This copy is over the edge intentionally, to show the clipping.
    blit(ship, 36, 9);

    try dump(out);

    try out.print("\nthe sprite is {d}x{d} = {d} bytes\n", .{ ship.w, ship.h, ship.w * ship.h });
    var opaque_count: usize = 0;
    for (ship.pixels) |p| {
        if (p != ship.transparent) opaque_count += 1;
    }
    try out.print("{d} of those pixels are drawn, {d} are skipped\n", .{
        opaque_count,
        ship.w * ship.h - opaque_count,
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.sprite`)*

## What just happened

**The background shows through the corners.** Inside the bounding box of the
sprite, you can see the checkerboard at each pixel where the sprite has the
transparent value. The program drew 18 of the 35 pixels and skipped 17. The
program prints these counts, so you can see the ratio: almost half of a sprite
is usually empty.

**Transparency is one comparison.** The program uses a **key colour**: one
value that means "skip". Each 8-bit and 16-bit console used this method. The
reason is that a per-pixel alpha channel costs one byte per pixel, and those
machines did not have that memory.

The method has one well-known disadvantage: the artwork cannot use the key
colour. For this reason, much sprite art of that time did not use one specific
shade of magenta.

**The program clipped the third copy.** The program drew the third copy
partly off the right edge, and the loop skipped the cells outside the canvas.
No extra code does the clipping. The clipping comes from the bounds check.

**The program stores the sprite one time and draws it three times.** The
program does not make a copy of the sprite data in memory. A sprite is data, and a loop draws it. Thus the second
and third copies cost only the loop.

## Check yourself

Key-colour transparency is binary: the program draws a pixel or it does not.
What does an alpha channel add, and what is its cost?

An alpha channel adds partial transparency. Thus an edge pixel can be half
sprite and half background. This is the difference between a jagged outline
and a smooth outline.

The cost has two parts:

- Memory: one more byte per pixel.
- Arithmetic: the program does not only copy. Each pixel becomes a blend of
  the source and the destination, with alpha as the weight.

The [blending](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/blending/) chapter makes exactly that blend.
For this reason, the blending chapter comes before this chapter.

The other cost is order. If opaque sprites do not overlap, you can draw them
in any order. You must draw translucent sprites from back to front, because
blending is not commutative.

## If you know C

The usual optimisation is a `memcpy` for each row. You can use it only when
there is no transparency, because `memcpy` cannot skip. This trade-off
controls all of 2D blitting. An opaque rectangle is a fast copy of rows. An
image with holes is a loop over each pixel.

Hardware sprite units existed for this reason. The machines that made this
method famous had silicon that read a sprite and a key colour. The silicon
composited the sprite during the scan-out, and the CPU did not touch those
pixels. Sometimes people say that a 1985 console did something that a faster
PC could not do. Usually, they mean this hardware.

Next: a scene graph, which moves many sprites at the same time.

---

## A Scene Graph

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/scene/*

To draw one sprite, you must know where the sprite goes. To draw fifty sprites that belong together, you must know where all fifty go. When the group moves, all fifty numbers must stay correct. A scene graph solves this problem.

Do not store where each thing is. Store where each thing is **relative to its parent**, and calculate the rest. An arm is always at "shoulder plus two", and the shoulder can go to any position.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const width: usize = 44;
const height: usize = 12;
var canvas: [width * height]u8 = @splat('.');

/// The position of a node is **local**: it is relative to its parent, not to
/// the canvas. An arm is always at "shoulder plus two", and the shoulder can
/// move to any position.
const Node = struct {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
    w: i32 = 1,
    h: i32 = 1,
    ink: u8 = '#',
    first: ?u32 = null,
    next: ?u32 = null,
};

fn fill(x: i32, y: i32, w: i32, h: i32, ink: u8) void {
    var row: i32 = 0;
    while (row < h) : (row += 1) {
        var col: i32 = 0;
        while (col < w) : (col += 1) {
            const px = x + col;
            const py = y + row;
            if (px < 0 or py < 0) continue;
            const ux: usize = @intCast(px);
            const uy: usize = @intCast(py);
            if (ux >= width or uy >= height) continue;
            canvas[uy * width + ux] = ink;
        }
    }
}

/// Walk the tree and add up the offsets. Each node draws at the position of
/// its parent plus its own offset. Then the node gives that total to its
/// children. The walk adds one time for each level, and that addition is the
/// transform.
///
/// A real engine stores a 3x3 matrix, not two integers. Thus a node can also
/// rotate and scale. To combine the values, the walk multiplies matrices. It
/// does not add numbers. The structure of the walk is the same.
fn draw(nodes: []const Node, index: u32, ox: i32, oy: i32) void {
    const node = nodes[index];
    const x = ox + node.x;
    const y = oy + node.y;
    fill(x, y, node.w, node.h, node.ink);

    var child = node.first;
    while (child) |c| : (child = nodes[c].next) draw(nodes, c, x, y);
}

fn clear() void {
    @memset(&canvas, '.');
}

fn dump(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    for (0..height) |y| try out.print("{s}\n", .{canvas[y * width ..][0..width]});
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // Index 0 is the body. The other nodes are children of the body, and
    // their positions are relative to the body. Only index 0 refers to the
    // canvas.
    var nodes = [_]Node{
        .{ .x = 4, .y = 3, .w = 6, .h = 4, .ink = '#', .first = 1 }, // body
        .{ .x = -3, .y = 1, .w = 3, .h = 1, .ink = '=', .next = 2 }, // left arm
        .{ .x = 6, .y = 1, .w = 3, .h = 1, .ink = '=', .next = 3 }, // right arm
        .{ .x = 1, .y = -2, .w = 4, .h = 2, .ink = 'o', .next = null }, // head
    };

    clear();
    draw(&nodes, 0, 0, 0);
    try out.writeAll("body at (4, 3)\n");
    try dump(out);

    // Two numbers change. Each child follows the body, because no child
    // stores its position on the canvas.
    nodes[0].x = 26;
    nodes[0].y = 5;

    clear();
    draw(&nodes, 0, 0, 0);
    try out.writeAll("\nbody moved to (26, 5), and only that line changed\n");
    try dump(out);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.scene`)*

## What just happened

**Two lines changed and four shapes moved.** `nodes[0]` went from (4, 3) to (26, 5). The program did not change other items in the array. The head and the two arms followed the body, because no child knew its position on the canvas.

**The transform is an addition.** Each node draws at the position of its parent plus its own offset. Then the node gives that total to its children. The walk adds one time for each level, and the total grows as the walk goes down the tree.

The layout engine uses the same downward walk for the same reason. The position of a child depends on its parent. The position of a parent does not depend on its child.

**The order in the array is not the order in the tree.** The program stores the nodes in a flat array and links them by index. The order of the siblings sets the order of the paint. This is the painter's algorithm again: a later sibling covers an earlier sibling.

## What a real scene graph stores

Two integers only let a node move. A full scene graph stores a **matrix** for each node, usually 3x3 for 2D. With a matrix, a node can also rotate and scale. To combine a parent with a child, the walk multiplies two matrices. It does not add two numbers.

The matrices give scene graphs their main benefit. A rotation on the parent turns each child around the *origin of the parent*, and no child knows about the rotation. When a robot turns its shoulder, the full arm moves. No part of the arm refers to the rotation.

The structure of the walk does not change. Add the parent value to each node, draw the node, and then do the same steps for each child.

## Check yourself

The walk calculates each position again on each frame. Is that a waste of time?

Usually it is not, and a cache has its own cost. If you keep a cache of the world position of each node, a parent that moves makes the cache incorrect for its full subtree. In an animated scene, most parents move on most frames. Thus the program must clear the cache approximately as frequently as it reads the cache.

Usually, an engine that keeps this cache solves a different problem. The engine needs the world position for a task other than the drawing, for example hit tests or physics. Without the cache, each query must walk from the root. The cache is a good choice when the reads are more frequent than the writes. The same question applies to [an index in a database](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/indexes/).

## If you know C

The tree is `struct Node { int x, y; struct Node *first, *next; }` and the walk is the same recursion. Two known risks apply.

Deep recursion on a scene with deep nesting overflows the stack. A scene graph that a program loads from a file can have any depth. If the file is malformed, the graph can also have a cycle. A production loader checks the depth and rejects cycles. Another solution is to write the walk again with an explicit stack.

The flat array in this program has the usual advantage over pointers:

- The full scene is one allocation.
- One call frees the scene.
- The walk reads contiguous memory.

Contiguous memory makes the walk faster. This is important when the walk occurs sixty times each second.

Next: a chart. A chart is a scene where the positions come from data.

---

## A Bar Chart

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/chart/*

In this section, a chart is the first drawing where the programmer does not select the shape. The data sets the height of each bar. Thus a function changes a number into a height in pixels, and charts go wrong in that function.

The function is one division. The difficult part is to select the value to divide by.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const width: usize = 48;
const height: usize = 17;
var canvas: [width * height]u8 = @splat(' ');

const plot_left: usize = 5;
// Keep two rows below the plot: one row for the axis, one row for the labels.
const plot_bottom: usize = height - 3;
const plot_top: usize = 1;

fn put(x: usize, y: usize, ink: u8) void {
    if (x >= width or y >= height) return;
    canvas[y * width + x] = ink;
}

/// Map a value to pixels. The denominator sets the scale. When the function
/// divides by the largest value, the tallest bar fills the plot. Thus you can
/// compare two charts only if the two charts use the same scale.
fn barHeight(value: u32, max: u32, rows: usize) usize {
    if (max == 0) return 0;
    return @intCast(@as(usize, value) * rows / max);
}

fn drawAxes() void {
    var y = plot_top;
    while (y <= plot_bottom) : (y += 1) put(plot_left - 1, y, '|');
    var x = plot_left - 1;
    while (x < width - 1) : (x += 1) put(x, plot_bottom + 1, '-');
    put(plot_left - 1, plot_bottom + 1, '+');
}

fn drawBar(slot: usize, value: u32, max: u32, ink: u8) void {
    const rows = plot_bottom - plot_top + 1;
    const h = barHeight(value, max, rows);
    const x = plot_left + slot * 5;

    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < h) : (i += 1) {
        const y = plot_bottom - i;
        put(x, y, ink);
        put(x + 1, y, ink);
        put(x + 2, y, ink);
    }
}

fn dump(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    for (0..height) |y| try out.print("{s}\n", .{canvas[y * width ..][0..width]});
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const labels = [_]u8{ 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'g' };
    const values = [_]u32{ 12, 31, 24, 8, 40, 19, 27 };

    var max: u32 = 0;
    for (values) |v| max = @max(max, v);

    drawAxes();
    for (values, 0..) |v, i| {
        drawBar(i, v, max, '#');
        put(plot_left + i * 5 + 1, plot_bottom + 2, labels[i]);
    }
    // Write the scale on the chart. Without the scale, the reader cannot tell
    // what the heights of the bars mean.
    put(0, plot_top, '4');
    put(1, plot_top, '0');
    put(0, plot_bottom, '0');

    try dump(out);

    try out.print("\nmax is {d}, plot is {d} rows tall\n", .{ max, plot_bottom - plot_top + 1 });
    for (values, 0..) |v, i| {
        try out.print("  {c} = {d: >3}  ->  {d} rows\n", .{
            labels[i],
            v,
            barHeight(v, max, plot_bottom - plot_top + 1),
        });
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.chart`)*

## What just happened

**Each bar is `value * rows / max`.** The largest value is the denominator, thus the largest bar fills the plot exactly. This scale is not the only possible scale, and the choice has a result. You cannot compare two charts that use this scale, because each chart used a different scale and did not tell you.

**The integer division truncates, and the table shows the truncation.** 12 of 40 over 14 rows is 4.2, and the program draws 4. Each bar is up to one row shorter than the correct height, and never taller. You cannot see this bias in the picture. If a chart has only a small number of pixels for each bar, the bias can show small differences incorrectly.

**The program draws the axis, and also the scale.** `40` is at the top and `0` is at the bottom. Without these labels, the picture shows a shape and makes no claim. The reader cannot tell if the tallest bar is 40 or 40,000. The reader also cannot tell if the baseline is zero.

## The lie that a bar chart can tell

If the vertical axis starts at a value other than zero, the bars are not proportional to their values. A bar that is two times as tall as another bar does not mean two times the value. The reader can see this problem only in the axis labels. A quick look at a chart does not read the labels.

For a **bar** chart, a vertical axis that does not start at zero is an error. The length of the bar is the encoding, thus the area and the value must be proportional. For a **line** chart, the same axis is frequently correct. A line shows change, not magnitude. A truncated axis lets you see a small change.

The rule comes from the meaning of the mark. When you write the mapping function yourself one time, the rule becomes clear.

## Check yourself

The chart divides by the largest value in the data. When is that division wrong?

The division is wrong when the reader compares this chart with a different chart. Examples are all dashboards, all sets of small multiples, and all charts that update over time. If the scale changes when the data changes, a bar can grow while its value becomes smaller.

To fix the problem, use a fixed denominator. Select a scale for the domain, not for the data, and use that scale for all of the charts. A shared axis on a set of small multiples uses the same logic. Charts that code makes frequently do not have this shared scale.

## If you know C

The drawing is easy. The arithmetic needs the care. The multiplication overflows if the product is too large for the type. With a `u32` count and a large plot, usual data can cause this overflow. Thus the multiplication needs a wider type, or a different order of operations.

The other hazard in C is the empty case. When each value is 0, `max` is 0, and the division is a division by zero. In C, the result is undefined behaviour. In a safety build of Zig, the result is a panic that the runtime catches. The function above returns 0 for that case explicitly. A chart where all values are zero is a valid chart, and the chart must draw without a crash.

---

## A Canvas Is a View

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/sub-canvas/*

Until now, each drawing routine in this section assumed that it owned the full buffer. The type says so. There is one width, and the width is a constant. The pixel at the end of a row is immediately before the pixel at the start of the next row.

Frequently you want to draw into a region of the buffer instead. Examples are a panel inside a window, a cell inside a chart, or a widget inside a toolbar. The region has its own origin and its own edges, and these are different from the origin and the edges of the buffer. You have two choices:

- Give an offset and a clip rectangle to each routine, and apply them in each routine.
- Change the value that each routine gets.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const root_width: usize = 60;
const root_height: usize = 18;

var framebuffer: [root_width * root_height]u32 = undefined;

fn rgb(r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) u32 {
    return (@as(u32, r) << 16) | (@as(u32, g) << 8) | @as(u32, b);
}

const backdrop = rgb(40, 44, 52);
const amber = rgb(247, 164, 29);
const green = rgb(63, 185, 80);
const paper = rgb(240, 246, 243);
const violet = rgb(120, 60, 180);

/// These four fields make a canvas different from a slice.
///
/// `width` and `height` give the size of this region. `stride` gives the
/// distance between two vertically adjacent pixels **in the buffer that
/// holds them**. That distance is the full width of the parent. The width of
/// this region does not change it. A region works only if these two values
/// stay separate.
///
/// Without `stride`, a routine can only address pixels with
/// `y * width + x`. That address is correct only for a canvas that owns the
/// full buffer.
const Canvas = struct {
    pixels: []u32,
    width: usize,
    height: usize,
    stride: usize,

    /// For a canvas over a full buffer, you cannot see the difference: the
    /// stride is equal to the width.
    fn init(pixels: []u32, w: usize, h: usize) Canvas {
        return .{ .pixels = pixels, .width = w, .height = h, .stride = w };
    }

    /// A window onto a part of this canvas. The window shares the memory of
    /// this canvas, and the function copies nothing. The child does not know
    /// its position. The child has no x or y, thus a drawing routine has no
    /// parent coordinate that it can get wrong.
    fn sub(self: Canvas, x: usize, y: usize, w: usize, h: usize) Canvas {
        const cx = @min(x, self.width);
        const cy = @min(y, self.height);
        const cw = @min(w, self.width - cx);
        const ch = @min(h, self.height - cy);

        // Here a slice cannot describe the shape of the data. A rectangle
        // inside a wider buffer is not contiguous. Thus no `[]u32` can
        // describe exactly these pixels. This slice starts at the first pixel
        // of the region and ends at the last pixel of its bottom row. Each gap
        // between two rows belongs to the parent. The length is only a bound
        // on the buffer.
        const span = if (ch == 0) 0 else (ch - 1) * self.stride + cw;

        return .{
            .pixels = self.pixels[cy * self.stride + cx ..][0..span],
            .width = cw,
            .height = ch,
            .stride = self.stride,
        };
    }

    /// This clip protects the parent. `width` and `height` belong to this
    /// region. Thus the clip rejects only pixels that the region does not own.
    /// The clip rejects these pixels also when the slice above permits the
    /// write.
    fn set(self: Canvas, x: usize, y: usize, color: u32) void {
        if (x >= self.width or y >= self.height) return;
        self.pixels[y * self.stride + x] = color;
    }

    fn fill(self: Canvas, color: u32) void {
        for (0..self.height) |y| {
            for (0..self.width) |x| self.set(x, y, color);
        }
    }

    fn rect(self: Canvas, x: usize, y: usize, w: usize, h: usize, color: u32) void {
        for (0..h) |row| {
            for (0..w) |col| self.set(x + col, y + row, color);
        }
    }
};

/// Ten characters, from dark to light. The other chapters in this section use
/// the same ramp for their dumps. Thus you can compare these pictures with
/// those pictures.
const ramp = " .:-=+*#%@";

fn dump(canvas: Canvas, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var row: [root_width]u8 = undefined;
    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            // Use `stride`, not `width`. With `width` here, a view reads the
            // wrong pixels.
            const color = canvas.pixels[y * canvas.stride + x];
            const luma = (((color >> 16) & 0xff) * 77 +
                ((color >> 8) & 0xff) * 150 +
                (color & 0xff) * 29) >> 8;
            row[x] = ramp[(luma * (ramp.len - 1)) / 255];
        }
        try out.writeAll(row[0..canvas.width]);
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const root = Canvas.init(&framebuffer, root_width, root_height);
    root.fill(backdrop);

    // Two panels side by side, and one panel two levels deep. The same `fill`
    // that filled the full screen also fills each panel.
    const left = root.sub(2, 2, 26, 14);
    const right = root.sub(32, 2, 26, 14);
    left.fill(amber);
    right.fill(green);

    const inset = right.sub(3, 3, 14, 6);
    inset.fill(paper);

    // A bar 40 wide inside a panel that is 26 wide. The parent does not
    // change. The clip in `set` rejects each column past the edge of the
    // panel. Thus the bar stops at the border of the panel. The bar does not
    // go into the panel next to it.
    left.rect(4, 5, 40, 3, violet);

    try out.writeAll("the whole framebuffer\n");
    try dump(root, out);

    // The same pixels, addressed as a region. The program copies nothing. The
    // dump reads the memory of the parent through different bounds.
    try out.writeAll("\nthe right panel alone, same memory\n");
    try dump(right, out);

    try out.writeAll("\n           width  height  stride\n");
    const rows = [_]struct { name: []const u8, canvas: Canvas }{
        .{ .name = "root", .canvas = root },
        .{ .name = "left", .canvas = left },
        .{ .name = "right", .canvas = right },
        .{ .name = "inset", .canvas = inset },
    };
    for (rows) |r| {
        try out.print("{s:<10}{d:>6}{d:>8}{d:>8}\n", .{
            r.name,
            r.canvas.width,
            r.canvas.height,
            r.canvas.stride,
        });
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.sub-canvas`)*

## What just happened

**The bar is 40 pixels wide inside a panel that is 26 pixels wide.** The bar stops at the edge of the panel. The program does not change the panel next to it. Neither `rect` nor the caller refers to the position of the panel to get this result.

**The three sub-canvases share one buffer and one stride with the root.** The table at the end shows this in four rows. `width` is different for each region. `stride` is 60 for all of them, and also for the region two levels deep. All of the canvases address the same memory, and the shape of that memory did not change.

**The child does not know its position.** `Canvas` has no `x` and no `y`. A sub-canvas is its pixels, its size, and the distance between its rows. A drawing routine needs nothing more. The canvas stores no parent coordinate, thus no routine can forget to add a parent coordinate.

**The dump of the right panel copied nothing.** The second picture is the same memory as the first picture. The program reads that memory through different bounds.

## The stride gives what the width cannot give

For a canvas over a full buffer, the stride and the width are the same number. Thus the earlier chapters did not need to tell them apart. When a canvas is a region, the two numbers are different. In a region, the pixel below a pixel is one full buffer row after it. The width of the region does not set that distance.

Thus the addressing has two parts:

- `width` and `height` give the bounds of the region: what the region *is*.
- `stride` gives the *spacing* of the rows.

With the width as the stride, each row after the first starts a small distance to the left of the row above. The picture shears diagonally across the screen. The result looks like a bug in the drawing code, but the bug is in the addressing.

## A rectangle is not a slice

Zig asks a question here that C does not ask.

`sub` must return a `[]u32`, and no `[]u32` describes exactly these pixels. A rectangle inside a wider buffer is not contiguous. The returned slice starts at the first pixel of the region and ends at the last pixel of its bottom row. Thus the slice covers the region, and also the gap at the end of each row. That gap belongs to the parent.

That bound gives less protection than it appears to give. If an index is past the end of the framebuffer, the bounds check catches the error. If code writes into the panel next to the region, nothing catches the error, because those pixels are inside the slice.

The clip in `set` keeps the panels apart. The clip compares against the `width` and the `height` of the region. Thus two different mechanisms give two different guarantees, and only the bounds check comes from the language. If you do not use `set` and you index `pixels` directly, you keep the bounds check. But you lose the clip that keeps the drawing inside the region.

## Check yourself

The slice contains pixels that the region does not own. What stops `fill` from a write to those pixels?

`fill` calls `set`, and `set` rejects each `x` that is equal to or more than `width`. The pixels in the gap are at the end of a row. To get to one of them, a call must give an `x` past the right edge of the region. `set` refuses exactly this case. You can get to the pixels through the slice, but not through the API.

The protection comes from one comparison in `set`, and a person wrote that comparison by hand. The slice bound and the type do not give this protection. When a widget paints over the widget next to it, examine that comparison first.

## If you know C

This struct is `Olivec_Canvas` from [olive.c](https://github.com/tsoding/olive.c), the 2D graphics library of Alexey Kutepov that has no dependencies. Each field is the same, and `sub` is `olivec_subcanvas`. The C version has a bare pointer with no length. Thus the bounds check above does not exist. Only the clip stops a widget from a write over the other parts of the window.

If the comparison in the clip is wrong, the code writes into the pixels of a different widget and gives no error. The symptom is a smear in a part of the screen where the code is correct.

The same design also occurs outside graphics libraries. A GUI toolkit gives a widget a region for its paint, and a stride that the widget does not own. A compositor gives a client a buffer with a stride that the client did not select. Usually the compositor rounds the stride up for alignment. This is the common case where the stride is larger than the width for a canvas that is not a sub-canvas.

Next: read pixels from one canvas, and paint them onto a different canvas.

---

## Texture Mapping

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/texture/*

At the end of [the triangles chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/triangles/), the triangle had three barycentric weights. That chapter also showed that the weights interpolate each value that you attach to the corners. That chapter attached colours. Attach a pair of coordinates into a different image instead, and the result is a textured triangle. No line of the rasteriser changes.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const dst_width: usize = 60;
const dst_height: usize = 16;

var framebuffer: [dst_width * dst_height]u32 = undefined;

fn rgb(r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) u32 {
    return (@as(u32, r) << 16) | (@as(u32, g) << 8) | @as(u32, b);
}

const backdrop = rgb(0, 0, 0);
const dark = rgb(40, 44, 52);
const light = rgb(240, 246, 243);
const amber = rgb(247, 164, 29);

/// The canvas from the previous chapter, with only the parts that this
/// chapter uses. The program writes to the canvas, thus the canvas has a
/// stride.
const Canvas = struct {
    pixels: []u32,
    width: usize,
    height: usize,
    stride: usize,

    fn set(self: Canvas, x: usize, y: usize, color: u32) void {
        if (x >= self.width or y >= self.height) return;
        self.pixels[y * self.stride + x] = color;
    }

    fn fill(self: Canvas, color: u32) void {
        for (0..self.height) |y| {
            for (0..self.width) |x| self.set(x, y, color);
        }
    }
};

/// The program only reads a texture, thus a texture has no stride: no code
/// samples a rectangle from the middle of a texture. A separate type, not
/// `Canvas`, shows that data only comes out of a texture. The compiler makes
/// sure of that rule, because a `Texture` has no `set`.
const Texture = struct {
    pixels: []const u32,
    width: usize,
    height: usize,
};

var texels: [8 * 8]u32 = undefined;

/// Checks that are two texels wide, thus the pattern stays visible when the
/// program scales the texture down. One amber corner shows when a tile flips
/// or wraps.
fn buildTexture() Texture {
    for (0..8) |y| {
        for (0..8) |x| {
            const check = ((x / 2) + (y / 2)) % 2 == 0;
            texels[y * 8 + x] = if (check) light else dark;
        }
    }
    for (0..2) |y| {
        for (0..2) |x| texels[y * 8 + x] = amber;
    }
    return .{ .pixels = &texels, .width = 8, .height = 8 };
}

/// A corner of a triangle: its position on the canvas, and the position that
/// it reads in the texture. `u` and `v` go from 0 to 1 across the image, for
/// any number of pixels in the image. Thus the same coordinates address a
/// texture of any size.
const Vertex = struct { x: f32, y: f32, u: f32, v: f32 };

/// Twice the signed area of the triangle abp. Positive on one side of the line
/// ab and negative on the other. The sign is the inside test.
fn edge(ax: f32, ay: f32, bx: f32, by: f32, px: f32, py: f32) f32 {
    return (bx - ax) * (py - ay) - (by - ay) * (px - ax);
}

/// Nearest-neighbour sample. `wrap` sets the meaning of a coordinate outside
/// 0..1: repeat the image, or keep the edge texel.
fn sample(tex: Texture, u: f32, v: f32, wrap: bool) u32 {
    const w: i32 = @intCast(tex.width);
    const h: i32 = @intCast(tex.height);
    var tx: i32 = @intFromFloat(@floor(u * @as(f32, @floatFromInt(w))));
    var ty: i32 = @intFromFloat(@floor(v * @as(f32, @floatFromInt(h))));

    if (wrap) {
        // Use `@mod`, not `%`. The remainder operator keeps the sign of the
        // dividend. Thus a u of -0.1 would index backwards out of the texture.
        tx = @mod(tx, w);
        ty = @mod(ty, h);
    } else {
        tx = @max(0, @min(w - 1, tx));
        ty = @max(0, @min(h - 1, ty));
    }

    return tex.pixels[@intCast(ty * w + tx)];
}

/// The same barycentric rasteriser as the triangles chapter, with one change:
/// the three weights interpolate `u` and `v`, not a colour.
fn triangle(dst: Canvas, tex: Texture, a: Vertex, b: Vertex, c: Vertex, wrap: bool) void {
    const area = edge(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y, c.x, c.y);
    if (area == 0) return;

    const min_x: usize = @intFromFloat(@max(0, @floor(@min(a.x, @min(b.x, c.x)))));
    const min_y: usize = @intFromFloat(@max(0, @floor(@min(a.y, @min(b.y, c.y)))));
    const max_x: usize = @intFromFloat(@max(0, @ceil(@max(a.x, @max(b.x, c.x)))));
    const max_y: usize = @intFromFloat(@max(0, @ceil(@max(a.y, @max(b.y, c.y)))));

    var y = min_y;
    while (y <= max_y and y < dst.height) : (y += 1) {
        var x = min_x;
        while (x <= max_x and x < dst.width) : (x += 1) {
            // Sample at the centre of the pixel. Thus a shared edge between two
            // triangles does not lose a line of pixels.
            const px = @as(f32, @floatFromInt(x)) + 0.5;
            const py = @as(f32, @floatFromInt(y)) + 0.5;

            const w0 = edge(b.x, b.y, c.x, c.y, px, py) / area;
            const w1 = edge(c.x, c.y, a.x, a.y, px, py) / area;
            const w2 = edge(a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y, px, py) / area;
            if (w0 < 0 or w1 < 0 or w2 < 0) continue;

            // The interpolation. The three weights apply to the texture
            // coordinates of the corners exactly as they apply to colours.
            const u = w0 * a.u + w1 * b.u + w2 * c.u;
            const v = w0 * a.v + w1 * b.v + w2 * c.v;
            dst.set(x, y, sample(tex, u, v, wrap));
        }
    }
}

/// Four corners and two triangles. The two triangles share the diagonal.
fn quad(dst: Canvas, tex: Texture, corners: [4]Vertex, wrap: bool) void {
    triangle(dst, tex, corners[0], corners[1], corners[2], wrap);
    triangle(dst, tex, corners[0], corners[2], corners[3], wrap);
}

const ramp = " .:-=+*#%@";

fn dump(canvas: Canvas, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var row: [dst_width]u8 = undefined;
    for (0..canvas.height) |y| {
        for (0..canvas.width) |x| {
            const color = canvas.pixels[y * canvas.stride + x];
            const luma = (((color >> 16) & 0xff) * 77 +
                ((color >> 8) & 0xff) * 150 +
                (color & 0xff) * 29) >> 8;
            row[x] = ramp[(luma * (ramp.len - 1)) / 255];
        }
        try out.writeAll(std.mem.trimEnd(u8, row[0..canvas.width], " "));
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const tex = buildTexture();
    const dst = Canvas{
        .pixels = &framebuffer,
        .width = dst_width,
        .height = dst_height,
        .stride = dst_width,
    };

    // Left: the image one time, from corner to corner. Right: the same
    // rectangle, but the coordinates go to 2, not 1. Thus the sampler goes
    // past the edge of the texture in each direction. The wrap returns the
    // sampler to the start of the texture, and the image shows two times.
    dst.fill(backdrop);
    quad(dst, tex, .{
        .{ .x = 2, .y = 0, .u = 0, .v = 0 },
        .{ .x = 26, .y = 0, .u = 1, .v = 0 },
        .{ .x = 26, .y = 16, .u = 1, .v = 1 },
        .{ .x = 2, .y = 16, .u = 0, .v = 1 },
    }, false);
    quad(dst, tex, .{
        .{ .x = 32, .y = 0, .u = 0, .v = 0 },
        .{ .x = 56, .y = 0, .u = 2, .v = 0 },
        .{ .x = 56, .y = 16, .u = 2, .v = 2 },
        .{ .x = 32, .y = 16, .u = 0, .v = 2 },
    }, true);
    try out.writeAll("uv 0..1, and uv 0..2 wrapped\n");
    try dump(dst, out);

    // A trapezoid: the top edge is shorter than the bottom edge. Thus no one
    // affine map covers all four corners. Each triangle gets its own map, and
    // the two maps do not agree on the shared diagonal.
    dst.fill(backdrop);
    quad(dst, tex, .{
        .{ .x = 19, .y = 0, .u = 0, .v = 0 },
        .{ .x = 41, .y = 0, .u = 1, .v = 0 },
        .{ .x = 57, .y = 16, .u = 1, .v = 1 },
        .{ .x = 3, .y = 16, .u = 0, .v = 1 },
    }, false);
    try out.writeAll("\nthe same uv on a trapezoid, and the seam it produces\n");
    try dump(dst, out);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.texture`)*

## What just happened

**The interpolation uses the same three weights.** The program calculates `w0`, `w1` and `w2` exactly as it did for Gouraud shading. The only change is the values that the weights multiply:

```zig
const u = w0 * a.u + w1 * b.u + w2 * c.u;
const v = w0 * a.v + w1 * b.v + w2 * c.v;
```

**The coordinates go from 0 to 1, not from 0 to 8.** The texture is a square of 8 by 8 pixels, and only `sample` refers to that size. With normalized coordinates, the same four corners address a texture of 16 pixels or of 4096 pixels. The geometry does not know which texture it has.

**A coordinate past 1 is not an error.** The square on the right asks for coordinates up to 2. Wrapping changes that range into two copies of the image in each direction. A clamp would stretch the edge texels into a smear. The two choices are both reasonable, and you must tell the sampler which one to use.

**The trapezoid has a seam.** Look along its diagonal. The program draws a shape with four corners as two triangles, and each triangle gets its own affine interpolation. When the shape is not a parallelogram, the two maps do not agree along the edge that they share.

## The seam is not a bug in the rasteriser

The seam comes from a limit of an affine map. The three corners of a triangle set a linear relation between position and texture coordinate. The three corners set this relation exactly, and no freedom remains. Four corners are one constraint too many. Thus two triangles solve two separate problems, and the two answers meet at the diagonal but do not agree.

If you draw a parallelogram, the seam does not occur. For a parallelogram, one affine map does satisfy all four corners. Thus the two triangles agree because of their construction.

The seam is the same defect as perspective in 3D. In 2D, the defect is easier to see. A wall that goes away into the distance is a trapezoid on the screen. Thus the texture coordinates change non-linearly across the wall.

Games of the mid nineties interpolated those coordinates linearly, and that caused the floors that wobbled. The fix is to interpolate the reciprocals together with the coordinates, and to divide at each pixel. The name of that fix is "perspective correct". For much of the hardware of that time, the fix cost too much.

## Why a texture is not a canvas

Here, `Texture` is a separate type, with `pixels`, `width` and `height` and no `stride`. The absence of `stride` is a deliberate difference from [the canvas](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/sub-canvas/). No code in this program samples a rectangle from the middle of a larger image. Thus the type does not need a second width.

The separate type gives a guarantee. `Texture` has no `set`, and its pixels are `[]const u32`. Thus the type shows which image the code reads and which image the code writes. If you give the destination where the source must go, the code does not compile.

The alternative is one type for the two ends. olive.c uses that alternative, and it is not wrong. With one type, you can use a rendered canvas as a texture immediately. Render-to-texture works this way, and a compositor uses a window this way. The cost is that nothing stops a write through a handle that you wanted to use only for reads.

## Check yourself

The sampler floors the scaled coordinate to select a texel. If wrapping is off, what occurs at exactly `u = 1.0`?

`u * 8` is `8`, the floor of 8 is `8`, and the last valid index of the texture is `7`. The clamp catches this value and returns texel 7. For that reason, the branch reads `@min(w - 1, tx)`, not `@min(w, tx)`.

In this program, no pixel gets to that value. `u` is exactly 1 only on the line through the other two corners, where the weight of the `u = 0` corner becomes 0. For the left square, that line is `x = 26`. The centres of the pixels are at half-integers. Thus each pixel centre is half a pixel away from that line.

Thus the picture above never tests the guard, and nothing here would show an error in the guard. Also, the snippet on this page ships without the bounds check. Suppose that the guard is wrong, and you move one vertex to a half-integer. Then the read goes past the end of the texture. A safety build catches that read with a panic. This build returns a pixel from the memory after the texture.

## If you know C

The rasteriser has the shape that you would write in C, with one difference: it uses `@mod`, not `%`.

In C, `%` keeps the sign of the dividend. Thus `-1 % 8` is `-1`, and a texture coordinate that becomes slightly negative indexes backwards out of the array. The symptom is one wrong row or column along one edge. You can easily think that this symptom is an off-by-one error in the geometry.

Zig does not let you write that error by accident. The reason is not that Zig selects the other answer. `%` on signed integers is a compile error:

```
error: remainder division with 'i32' and 'i32': signed integers
and floats must use @rem or @mod
```

`@rem(-1, 8)` is `-1`, the same as C. `@mod(-1, 8)` is `7`, because it takes the sign of the divisor. A sampler needs this wrapping. Zig has the two functions, and neither one is the default. Thus you must select one.

Next: move the shape, not the pixels inside the shape.

---

## Transforms

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/transform/*

[The scene graph](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/scene/) stored two integers for each node, and that chapter gave the limit: two integers only let a node move. A full scene graph stores a matrix. Thus a node can also turn and change its size. To combine a parent with a child, the walk then multiplies two matrices. This chapter builds that matrix.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const width: usize = 58;
const height: usize = 17;

var framebuffer: [width * height]u8 = undefined;

/// A 2D affine transform: the top two rows of a 3x3 matrix.
///
///     | a c e |     x' = a*x + c*y + e
///     | b d f |     y' = b*x + d*y + f
///     | 0 0 1 |
///
/// For an affine transform, the bottom row is always `0 0 1`. Thus the struct
/// does not store the bottom row, because it is a constant. Six numbers hold
/// each possible combination of move, turn, scale and shear.
const Transform = struct {
    a: f32 = 1,
    b: f32 = 0,
    c: f32 = 0,
    d: f32 = 1,
    e: f32 = 0,
    f: f32 = 0,

    const identity: Transform = .{};

    fn translate(dx: f32, dy: f32) Transform {
        return .{ .e = dx, .f = dy };
    }

    fn scale(sx: f32, sy: f32) Transform {
        return .{ .a = sx, .d = sy };
    }

    fn rotate(radians: f32) Transform {
        const cos = @cos(radians);
        const sin = @sin(radians);
        return .{ .a = cos, .b = sin, .c = -sin, .d = cos };
    }

    /// `self.then(next)` is the transform that applies `self` first. As
    /// matrices, the transform is `next * self`, because a point is a column
    /// on the right, and the matrix nearest the point acts first. With `then`,
    /// you read a chain from left to right, in the order of the operations.
    /// That is the reason for the name.
    fn then(self: Transform, next: Transform) Transform {
        return .{
            .a = next.a * self.a + next.c * self.b,
            .b = next.b * self.a + next.d * self.b,
            .c = next.a * self.c + next.c * self.d,
            .d = next.b * self.c + next.d * self.d,
            .e = next.a * self.e + next.c * self.f + next.e,
            .f = next.b * self.e + next.d * self.f + next.f,
        };
    }

    fn apply(self: Transform, x: f32, y: f32) struct { x: f32, y: f32 } {
        return .{
            .x = self.a * x + self.c * y + self.e,
            .y = self.b * x + self.d * y + self.f,
        };
    }
};

/// The shape, in its own coordinates. The shape is an arrow because an arrow
/// has no symmetry. A rotated square looks like a square, and thus shows
/// nothing.
const shape = [_][2]f32{
    .{ 0, -3 },
    .{ 2, 0 },
    .{ 1, 0 },
    .{ 1, 3 },
    .{ -1, 3 },
    .{ -1, 0 },
    .{ -2, 0 },
};

fn clear() void {
    @memset(&framebuffer, ' ');
}

fn plot(x: i32, y: i32, ink: u8) void {
    if (x < 0 or y < 0) return;
    const ux: usize = @intCast(x);
    const uy: usize = @intCast(y);
    if (ux >= width or uy >= height) return;
    framebuffer[uy * width + ux] = ink;
}

/// Bresenham. Thus the program draws each edge of the shape as a line. It
/// does not sample the edge.
fn line(x0: i32, y0: i32, x1: i32, y1: i32, ink: u8) void {
    var x = x0;
    var y = y0;
    const dx: i32 = @intCast(@abs(x1 - x0));
    const dy: i32 = -@as(i32, @intCast(@abs(y1 - y0)));
    const sx: i32 = if (x0 < x1) 1 else -1;
    const sy: i32 = if (y0 < y1) 1 else -1;
    var err = dx + dy;

    while (true) {
        plot(x, y, ink);
        if (x == x1 and y == y1) break;
        const e2 = 2 * err;
        if (e2 >= dy) {
            err += dy;
            x += sx;
        }
        if (e2 <= dx) {
            err += dx;
            y += sy;
        }
    }
}

/// A character cell is approximately two times as tall as it is wide. Thus
/// the last operation on each point is a non-uniform scale that cancels that
/// difference. The program combines the scale here with `then`. It does not
/// multiply by two at the call site, and that is the main reason for `then`.
/// The transforms above stay in square units, where a rotation keeps the
/// shape. The uneven aspect of the display is one matrix, and the program
/// applies it after all the other matrices.
const aspect = Transform.scale(2, 1);

/// Transform each point, then draw the outline through the results. The
/// program never changes the shape. The shape is one array, and the program
/// draws it through different matrices.
fn draw(t: Transform, ink: u8) void {
    const view = t.then(aspect);
    for (shape, 0..) |point, i| {
        const next = shape[(i + 1) % shape.len];
        const p = view.apply(point[0], point[1]);
        const q = view.apply(next[0], next[1]);
        line(
            @intFromFloat(@round(p.x)),
            @intFromFloat(@round(p.y)),
            @intFromFloat(@round(q.x)),
            @intFromFloat(@round(q.y)),
            ink,
        );
    }
}

fn dump(out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    for (0..height) |y| {
        const row = framebuffer[y * width ..][0..width];
        try out.writeAll(std.mem.trimEnd(u8, row, " "));
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }
}

const quarter_turn: f32 = std.math.pi / 2.0;

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // Rotate then move, compared with move then rotate. The same quarter turn
    // and the same offset, combined in the two possible orders. Then the
    // program moves the two shapes by the same distance to put them on the
    // canvas. This move changes the position of the pair, but not the
    // distance between the two shapes.
    const view = Transform.translate(13, 6);
    const spin_then_move = Transform.rotate(quarter_turn)
        .then(Transform.translate(7, 0))
        .then(view);
    const move_then_spin = Transform.translate(7, 0)
        .then(Transform.rotate(quarter_turn))
        .then(view);

    clear();
    draw(spin_then_move, '#');
    draw(move_then_spin, 'o');
    try out.writeAll("# rotate then move, o move then rotate\n");
    try dump(out);

    // Three transforms turn a shape about a point that is not the origin.
    // Move the point to the origin, turn, and move the point back.
    // No rotate function takes a centre, because these three steps do the
    // same work.
    const pivot_x: f32 = 16;
    const pivot_y: f32 = 7;
    clear();
    for ([_]f32{ 0, 1, 2 }, "123") |steps, ink| {
        const about_pivot = Transform.translate(-pivot_x, -pivot_y)
            .then(Transform.rotate(quarter_turn * steps))
            .then(Transform.translate(pivot_x, pivot_y));
        // Put the arrow five units to the right of the pivot, then turn the
        // arrow about the pivot. Thus the arrow moves in an orbit. The arrow
        // does not turn at its own position.
        draw(Transform.translate(pivot_x + 5, pivot_y).then(about_pivot), ink);
    }
    plot(@intFromFloat(pivot_x * 2), @intFromFloat(pivot_y), '+');
    try out.writeAll("\n+ is the pivot; 1, 2 and 3 are quarter turns about it\n");
    try dump(out);

    // A scale uses the same six numbers, and it combines in the same way.
    clear();
    draw(Transform.scale(1, 1).then(Transform.translate(5, 8)), '.');
    draw(Transform.scale(1.6, 1.6).then(Transform.translate(13, 8)), '+');
    draw(Transform.scale(2.2, 2.2).then(Transform.translate(23, 8)), '#');
    try out.writeAll("\nthe same seven points at three scales\n");
    try dump(out);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`09-graphics.transform`)*

## What just happened

**Six numbers cover all cases.** A move, a turn, a scale and a shear are four ways to fill the same six slots. A routine that applies a transform does not know which of the four it got.

**The order changes the answer.** The two arrows in the first picture come from the same quarter turn and the same offset, combined in the two possible orders. The rotation is about the origin. Thus, if the move occurs first, the turn also turns the offset. The shape goes a quarter circle to a different position. The picture shows that matrix multiplication is not commutative.

**A turn about a point is three transforms.** No `rotate` function takes a centre. Do these three steps:

1. Move the pivot to the origin.
2. Turn.
3. Move the pivot back.

The three steps combine into one matrix, and that matrix costs the same as one rotation. The arrows with the numbers 1, 2 and 3 move around the `+`, but the program has no code for an orbit. Each arrow is this matrix with a different angle.

**The program never changes the shape.** `shape` is one `const` array of seven points. The program draws it eight times in the three pictures. Each difference is in the matrix.

## Read a composition

In practice, transforms are difficult because the usual notation is in the reverse order of the operations. With matrices, to apply `A` and then `B` to a column vector, you write `B * A * p`. The matrix nearest the point acts first. Thus you read the chain from right to left.

`then` hides that reverse order. `a.then(b)` means `a` first, and the function calculates `b * a` internally. The reversal occurs one time, in one function. A person who reads the call does not have to reverse the order mentally:

```zig
const about_pivot = Transform.translate(-pivot_x, -pivot_y)
    .then(Transform.rotate(quarter_turn * steps))
    .then(Transform.translate(pivot_x, pivot_y));
```

The code gives the three operations in the order that they occur. The code builds the same matrix that a graphics textbook writes as `T * R * T⁻¹`.

The program combines the aspect ratio of the display in the same way. A character cell is approximately two times as tall as it is wide. Thus each point gets a final non-uniform scale of `(2, 1)`.

The transforms above do not include this scale. Thus a rotation in this program keeps the angles of the shape correct. The program calculates the shape in square units. At the end, one matrix squashes the shape, and that matrix is the same as all the other matrices.

## The purpose of the bottom row

The matrix is 3x3, but the program stores only six numbers. The row that the program does not store is always `0 0 1`. Thus the program does not need to store it.

The row exists because translation is not a linear operation. A 2x2 matrix multiply can rotate, scale and shear, and each of those operations keeps the origin at the same position. A matrix made only from `a`, `b`, `c` and `d` cannot move a point away from the origin. A third coordinate, always 1, gives translation a column. The last column is that column. The multiply multiplies its entries by the 1 and adds them, and a move does exactly that.

This extra coordinate is the meaning of homogeneous coordinates. With the extra coordinate, translation becomes a multiply, the same as the other operations. Thus a chain of moves, turns and scales becomes one matrix. The program multiplies each point by that one matrix. The point does not go through each step of the chain.

Perspective goes one step more. Put values other than 0 and 1 in the bottom row, and divide by the third coordinate after the multiply. The division makes the far end of a wall smaller. The trapezoid in [texture mapping](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/texture/) did not have this division.

## Check yourself

`then` multiplies to build a new matrix. Why not apply each transform to the points, one after the other?

For seven points, the result is the same. The reason applies to seven thousand points, or to a long chain. A composition costs one multiply for each *transform*. An application costs one multiply for each *point*.

If you combine the chain first, each point pays for only one matrix, for any number of operations in the chain. For the same reason, the scene graph adds the offsets as it goes down the tree. It does not walk again from the root for each node.

The second reason is accuracy. Each application rounds. Thus five transforms, applied one after the other, round five times for each point. A composition rounds while it builds the matrix, and the program transforms each point one time.

## If you know C

The struct is the six-float affine matrix from all the 2D graphics APIs that you know. Examples are the matrices of Cairo and Direct2D, the six arguments to the web canvas `setTransform`, and the `AffineTransform` of Java. The order and the names of the fields are different, but the six numbers are the same.

The Zig version has two differences. First, the trigonometry uses builtins, not libc calls. Thus this snippet has no dependency to link, and the snippet runs in a browser without changes. The program above runs on this page in that way.

Second, the default field values in the struct declaration are important. `identity` is `.{}`, and each constructor sets only the fields that it needs. `translate` writes `e` and `f`, and the other four fields keep the `1, 0, 0, 1` of the identity. In C, each constructor needs four more assignments. If you forget one, you get a common bug: a translate that sets the scale to zero and gives no error.

Next: the same buffer, but the program gives it to a display server, not to a file.

---

## Onto the Screen

*Graphics. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/on-screen/*

A file write goes in one direction: you make bytes, and then the work is complete. A window needs messages in the two directions. The display server decides when you can paint, asks if your program is still alive, and reports input. If your program does not do its part of this exchange, the window stays blank, freezes, or the server kills it.

Three things are different from [Write an Image File](../image-files/).

**The pixels are wider.** X11 and Wayland both want 32 bits per pixel, not 24. On a little-endian computer, both want a `u32` that holds `0x00RRGGBB`. In memory, this value is B, G, R, X. When you write full `u32` values, the byte order is correct without more work. For this reason, the framebuffer in this section uses 32 bits from the first chapter.

**Two programs can share the buffer.** A file write is a copy. To put pixels on screen, a copy is not always necessary. Wayland's `wl_shm` gives the compositor a file descriptor for the same pages that you drew into, and no copy occurs. X11's `XPutImage` copies the pixels to the server. The `MIT-SHM` extension exists to prevent that copy.

**One drawing is not sufficient.** The server tells you when to paint, and it asks again later.

## Xlib, the short version

Open a display, create a window and map it. Then answer the events. Xlib needs much less setup code than Wayland. It still runs on all Linux desktops, also under XWayland on a Wayland desktop.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// translate-c makes this module from the headers named above. `@cImport`
/// is not in the language now. C now comes through a build-system step.
const c = @import("c");

const width: c_uint = 640;
const height: c_uint = 480;

fn drawFrame(pixels: []u32) void {
    for (0..height) |y| {
        for (0..width) |x| {
            const r: u32 = @intCast((x * 255) / (width - 1));
            const g: u32 = @intCast((y * 255) / (height - 1));
            // 0x00RRGGBB. On a little-endian computer, this value is in memory
            // as B, G, R, X. A 24-bit TrueColor visual expects that order.
            pixels[y * width + x] = (r << 16) | (g << 8) | 80;
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    _ = init;

    const display = c.XOpenDisplay(null) orelse return error.NoDisplay;
    defer _ = c.XCloseDisplay(display);

    // Xlib's `DefaultScreen`, `RootWindow`, `DefaultVisual` and similar names
    // are function-like macros that read a private struct. translate-c cannot
    // give them a meaning. Each macro has a real function behind it.
    const screen = c.XDefaultScreen(display);
    const root = c.XRootWindow(display, screen);
    const visual = c.XDefaultVisual(display, screen);
    const depth = c.XDefaultDepth(display, screen);
    const gc = c.XDefaultGC(display, screen);

    if (depth != 24 and depth != 32) return error.UnsupportedVisual;

    const window = c.XCreateSimpleWindow(
        display,
        root,
        0,
        0,
        width,
        height,
        0,
        c.XBlackPixel(display, screen),
        c.XBlackPixel(display, screen),
    );
    defer _ = c.XDestroyWindow(display, window);

    _ = c.XStoreName(display, window, "Zig pixels");
    _ = c.XSelectInput(display, window, c.ExposureMask | c.KeyPressMask);

    // Without this call, the close button closes the connection. It does not
    // send an event that the program can use.
    var wm_delete = c.XInternAtom(display, "WM_DELETE_WINDOW", 0);
    _ = c.XSetWMProtocols(display, window, &wm_delete, 1);

    // XCreateImage takes ownership. XDestroyImage frees this memory with
    // `free()`. Thus the memory must come from the C allocator, not a Zig one.
    const data: [*]u32 = @ptrCast(@alignCast(std.c.malloc(width * height * 4) orelse
        return error.OutOfMemory));
    drawFrame(data[0 .. width * height]);

    const image = c.XCreateImage(
        display,
        visual,
        @intCast(depth),
        c.ZPixmap,
        0,
        @ptrCast(data),
        width,
        height,
        32, // bitmap_pad: rows start on 32-bit boundaries
        0, // bytes_per_line: 0 means "calculate it from width"
    ) orelse {
        std.c.free(data);
        return error.ImageFailed;
    };
    // XDestroyImage is another macro. It calls through the function table of
    // the image, and Zig can call through that table directly.
    defer _ = image.*.f.destroy_image.?(image);

    _ = c.XMapWindow(display, window);

    var event: c.XEvent = undefined;
    while (true) {
        _ = c.XNextEvent(display, &event);
        switch (event.type) {
            // X11 keeps no copy of your pixels. Each time the window becomes
            // visible again, the server asks the client to paint it again.
            // Thus the program keeps the image. It does not blit it one time.
            c.Expose => _ = c.XPutImage(display, window, gc, image, 0, 0, 0, 0, width, height),

            c.KeyPress => {
                if (c.XLookupKeysym(&event.xkey, 0) == c.XK_Escape) return;
            },

            c.ClientMessage => {
                if (event.xclient.data.l[0] == @as(c_long, @intCast(wm_delete))) return;
            },

            else => {},
        }
    }
}

// Marked `//! norun`: this program opens a window and then waits for a
// keypress. A CI step cannot wait for a keypress. CI still compiles it and
// links it against the real libX11 on each run. Thus a change in the Xlib
// headers, or in how Zig translates them, makes the build fail.
```

*Opens a window and waits for a keypress. A CI step cannot wait for a keypress. CI compiles the snippet and links it against the real libX11 on each run. (`09-graphics.x11-window`)*

When you write your own version, four details in that code are important.

**`@cImport` does not exist now.** C headers now come through a build-system step. In this repo, `//! link: X11` and `//! cinclude:` configure that step. `build.zig` makes a header, runs `addTranslateC` on it, and gives the result to the snippet as `@import("c")`. In your own project, use `b.addTranslateC(...)` and then `translate.createModule()`. [Import C](../../working-with-c/cimport/) shows the general shape.

**Xlib's `Default*` macros do not work after translation.** `DefaultScreen(dpy)`, `RootWindow`, `DefaultVisual` and `DefaultGC` all expand to member accesses on a private struct. translate-c cannot give those accesses a meaning. Each macro has a real function behind it (`XDefaultScreen`, `XRootWindow`, and others), thus call those functions.

`XDestroyImage` has the same problem, but a different solution. The macro expands to a call through the function table of the image. Zig can make that call directly:

```zig
_ = image.*.f.destroy_image.?(image);
```

**`XCreateImage` takes ownership of your pixels.** `XDestroyImage` frees them with `free()`. Thus the buffer must come from `std.c.malloc`, not from a Zig allocator. If you give it a block from a `GeneralPurposeAllocator`, the program calls `free` on a pointer that the C allocator never owned.

**X11 keeps no copy of your pixels.** Each time the window becomes visible again, the server sends `Expose`, and the client must paint again. For this reason, the program keeps the image. It does not blit the image one time and then discard it.

The close button also needs a registration. Register `WM_DELETE_WINDOW` through `XSetWMProtocols`. If you do not, a click on the close button closes the connection. You get no event that the program can use.

## What Wayland changes

Wayland is the newer protocol, and it is the default on most current Linux desktops. The drawing code is the same. All the code around it is different. All the differences go in the same direction: the compositor does less work for you.

**Discovery is a handshake.** You connect and ask for the registry. Then the compositor advertises its globals. You bind the globals that you need: `wl_compositor`, `wl_shm`, `xdg_wm_base`, `wl_seat`. This takes two roundtrips, not one, because the second roundtrip runs the listeners that you registered inside the first.

**A surface is not a window.** A bare `wl_surface` is only a rectangle of pixels. To make a window, put it in an `xdg_surface` and then in an `xdg_toplevel`. The toplevel holds the title and the app id.

**The first commit has no buffer.** The first commit asks the compositor for the initial `configure`. If you attach a buffer before that handshake is complete, the result is a protocol error. The `configure` handler does these steps:

1. It acks the serial.
2. It attaches the buffer.
3. It damages the surface.
4. It commits.

The window appears at that last commit.

**You must answer `xdg_wm_base.ping` with `pong`.** The ping is the check of the compositor that your client is alive. If you ignore the ping, the compositor kills your client as unresponsive. It is easy to forget the ping, because nothing fails until the compositor sends one.

**The shell protocol is not in the library.** `xdg-shell` comes as XML. At build time, `wayland-scanner` changes the XML into a header and glue code. A normal `addSystemCommand` step with `addOutputFileArg2` does this work. Thus the generated files can stay in the Zig cache, and you do not add them to the repo.

**There are no window decorations.** A compositor *can* offer to draw them through `zxdg_decoration_manager_v1`, but it does not have to. GNOME's Mutter does not advertise that global. A client that only posts a buffer gets exactly that buffer: no titlebar, no close button, and no way to move the window.

To draw your own decorations, do these steps:

1. Allocate a taller buffer.
2. Paint a strip.
3. Track the pointer.
4. Change a drag into a move request.

The compositor controls the window positions, not you.

The cursor image is also the work of the client. Until you call `wl_pointer.set_cursor`, the pointer is undefined. Thus, without a loaded cursor theme, the pointer disappears over your window.

Because of these differences, the X11 version above is one file, and a Wayland version is not.

## What neither version here does

**Animation.** The program shows one static frame. On Wayland, a `wl_surface_frame` callback controls the redraws, so that they occur at the same rate as the compositor. On X11, a timer or an idle loop controls the redraws.

**Resize.** A complete client allocates a new buffer at each `ConfigureNotify` or `configure`. If you use a fixed buffer again, X11 leaves the extra area unpainted, and Wayland scales the buffer.

**Double buffering.** If you write into a buffer that the compositor can read at the same time, you get a torn frame. A complete client keeps two buffers and waits for `wl_buffer.release`.

**Format negotiation.** The Wayland protocol makes `XRGB8888` mandatory. Thus you can safely assume it. The X11 code above checks only that the default visual is 24-bit or 32-bit. That is true on all desktops from the last twenty years. But it is not the same as a check of the formats that the server really offers.

# Track: Cookbook

Recipes for tasks. Each recipe is a complete program that CI compiled and ran.

## Recipe: Word Frequencies

*How-To. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/word-frequency/*

To count words in Zig, divide the text into words with `std.mem.tokenizeAny`. Count the words into a `StringHashMapUnmanaged(u32)` with `getOrPut`. Then copy the entries into an `ArrayList`, and sort the list with `std.mem.sort`.

## The problem

You have a block of text, and you want the five most common words. These are the conditions:

- Upper case and lower case are the same.
- The program ignores punctuation.
- The order is stable, thus two runs always give the same order for words with equal counts.

Log analysis, tag clouds and all types of "top N by count" reports use this shape.

Be careful about one thing. A hash map is the correct tool to count, but a hash map **has no order**. To rank the words, you need a second structure.

## The plan

1. **Tokenize.** Use whitespace and punctuation as delimiters. `tokenizeAny` never gives an empty token.
2. **Count** with `getOrPut`. This function does one lookup for each word, not a `get` and then a `put`.
3. **Rank.** Sort a copy of the entries with a comparator. When two counts are equal, the comparator uses alphabetical order.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Count = struct { word: []const u8, n: u32 };

fn moreFrequent(_: void, a: Count, b: Count) bool {
    if (a.n != b.n) return a.n > b.n;
    // For equal counts, use alphabetical order. Thus the ranking is deterministic.
    return std.mem.lessThan(u8, a.word, b.word);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    // An arena is correct for this job. The map, the list and the copied keys
    // have the same lifetime. Thus one `deinit` frees all of them at one time.
    var arena_state = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.heap.page_allocator);
    defer arena_state.deinit();
    const gpa = arena_state.allocator();

    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const text =
        \\the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
        \\The dog barks, and the fox runs.
    ;

    // Step 1: count. `getOrPut` does one hash lookup, for a new word and for
    // a word that the map already has.
    var counts: std.StringHashMapUnmanaged(u32) = .empty;
    defer counts.deinit(gpa);

    var lower_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var words = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, text, " \n\t.,!?");
    while (words.next()) |raw| {
        const word = std.ascii.lowerString(&lower_buf, raw);
        const entry = try counts.getOrPut(gpa, word);
        if (!entry.found_existing) {
            // `word` is in a buffer that the loop uses again. Thus keys must own their bytes.
            entry.key_ptr.* = try gpa.dupe(u8, word);
            entry.value_ptr.* = 0;
        }
        entry.value_ptr.* += 1;
    }

    // Step 2: a hash map has no order. Move the entries into a list. Then
    // the program can sort them.
    var ranked: std.ArrayList(Count) = .empty;
    defer ranked.deinit(gpa);

    var it = counts.iterator();
    while (it.next()) |entry| {
        try ranked.append(gpa, .{ .word = entry.key_ptr.*, .n = entry.value_ptr.* });
    }

    // Step 3: rank the words, and report the top five.
    std.mem.sort(Count, ranked.items, {}, moreFrequent);

    for (ranked.items[0..@min(5, ranked.items.len)]) |c| {
        try out.print("{d:>2}  {s}\n", .{ c.n, c.word });
    }
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`06-cookbook.word-frequency`)*

## Why the program copies the keys

`lowerString` writes each word in lower case into the same buffer, which the program uses again for each word. If the map stores that slice as a key, all of the keys point to one buffer. Then the last word overwrites all of the keys. `gpa.dupe` gives each key its own bytes.

The copy of the keys is the only ownership decision in this recipe, and the arena makes the copy cheap. The map, the list and the copied keys all have the same lifetime. Thus one `arena_state.deinit()` frees all of them. No key needs its own `free`, and no memory leaks.

## Why sort a copy

`counts.iterator()` goes through the entries in hash order. That order is effectively random, and it can change between compiler versions.

The program moves the `(word, count)` pairs into an `ArrayList`. That costs one pass, and it gives you a plain slice. `std.mem.sort` needs a slice.

The comparator sorts by count, from the largest to the smallest, and then in alphabetical order. Without the second rule, the order of equal counts depends on hash order, and the output can change from one run to the next. CI compares the output of this page character by character. Thus the output must be the same on each run.

## Variations

- **Top N of a large set:** at a large scale, a sort of all the words to get five is wasteful. `std.PriorityQueue` gives you the heap. To keep the heap at five items, remove the smallest item after each push. The standard library sorts only full slices. Thus you must write the partial selection yourself. Do either of these only when profiling shows that you need it.
- **Unicode:** `std.ascii.lowerString` works only on ASCII, by design. Real case-folding needs a Unicode library, and [Unicode Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/unicode-recipes/) gives the name of one. The standard library intentionally does not guess.

---

## Recipe: Load a JSON Config

*How-To. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/json-config/*

In Zig, `std.json.parseFromSlice` loads a JSON config into a struct. If the file does not have a field, and the field has a default value, the field keeps that default. Put checks such as a port range in a separate `validate` function, because the parser checks only types and field names.

## The problem

Your program reads a JSON config file, and users edit the file by hand. Thus each type of failure will occur:

- fields that are not in the file
