## Why a bit set is better than a hash set here

In the snippet, the intersection compiles to one `and` instruction on a u24. `count()` is a popcount. The iterator goes directly to the bits that are set, and it does not examine buckets.

`Static` selects its representation from the size. Up to the pointer width, it uses one integer. For a larger size, it uses an array of words. Thus a set for the days of a year works in the same way, but on several words.

There is a cost. The members must be small integers that you can count at compile time. When the keys are strings or have no limit, use [hash maps](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/hash-maps/).

## Variations

- **A universe with a size from runtime:** `std.bit_set.DynamicManaged` takes an allocator and a length that the program selects at runtime.
- **Difference and complement:** `differenceWith` gives the hours when ana is free and raj is not free. `complement()` changes each bit of the set to its opposite value.
- **First fit:** `findFirstSet()` returns the lowest member. Use it to get the earliest common hour without an iterator.

---

## Recipe: Reproducible Randomness

*How-To. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/seeded-random/*

For repeatable randomness in Zig, make a generator from a fixed seed with `std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(42)`. Give `prng.random()` to the code that needs it. On the same Zig version, the same seed gives the same output on all platforms.

## The problem

Your program makes something random: a game map, test data or a shuffled playlist. Then a bug report comes. You need the exact map that the user saw, not a new random map. Or a test fails one time in fifty runs, and you need that run again.

In each of these cases, the randomness must come from a seed that you control. Zig has no hidden global generator. Thus the code always gives the generator explicitly.

## The plan

1. Make a deterministic generator from a seed.
2. Give its `std.Random` interface to the code that needs randomness. That code cannot see a difference between a seeded generator and a generator with a new seed.
3. Store or log the seed. When you use the seed again, you get again all of the data that came from the seed.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Side = 8;

// All of the values come from the Random interface in the argument. Thus
// the caller controls the seed, and with it the determinism.
fn generateCave(random: std.Random, grid: *[Side][Side]u8) void {
    for (grid) |*row| {
        for (row) |*cell| {
            // 40% wall, 60% floor.
            cell.* = if (random.uintLessThan(u8, 10) < 4) '#' else '.';
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // Save only the seed. Put the seed in a bug report, and the program
    // builds exactly the same cave again.
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(42);
    var cave: [Side][Side]u8 = undefined;
    generateCave(prng.random(), &cave);

    try out.print("seed 42:\n", .{});
    for (cave) |row| try out.print("  {s}\n", .{&row});

    // The same seed and a new generator give a world with identical bytes.
    var replay = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(42);
    var again: [Side][Side]u8 = undefined;
    generateCave(replay.random(), &again);
    try out.print("same seed reproduces: {}\n", .{
        std.mem.eql(u8, std.mem.asBytes(&cave), std.mem.asBytes(&again)),
    });

    // A different seed gives a different world.
    var other = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(43);
    var different: [Side][Side]u8 = undefined;
    generateCave(other.random(), &different);
    try out.print("different seed differs: {}\n", .{
        !std.mem.eql(u8, std.mem.asBytes(&cave), std.mem.asBytes(&different)),
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`06-cookbook.seeded-random`)*

## Give the `std.Random` interface

`generateCave` takes `std.Random`, not a concrete generator. In production, you can make the seed from the clock or from entropy. In a test or a replay, you give a fixed seed.

The code that makes the cave is the same in both cases. The call site decides if the output is reproducible, and the algorithm does not change.

You can also nest seeds. A world seed can make a seed for each system (terrain, loot, weather). The program draws these seeds from the master generator. Then you can replay each subsystem by itself.

## What a seed promises

With the same seed and the same Zig version, the output is identical on all platforms, wasm too. This page is the proof: CI compares the cave above, byte for byte, with an expected output that is in the repository.

On a different Zig version, the sequence can change if the default PRNG algorithm changes. If saved seeds must work after compiler upgrades, give the name of an algorithm explicitly (for example `std.Random.Xoshiro256`). Do not use `DefaultPrng`.

## Do not use a PRNG for secrets

A seeded PRNG is predictable on purpose. Keys, tokens and all other data that an attacker must not guess need entropy from the operating system.

On master, that entropy comes through `std.Random.IoSource`, which fills bytes from the `Io` interface. You can also use a `std.Random.DefaultCsprng` that gets its seed from `IoSource`.

There is no global secure generator now. Zig removed `std.crypto.random`. Thus the code gives the capability as an argument, as it does for each other effect.

The rule:

- If a replay of the values can be useful, use a PRNG.
- If a replay of the values is a vulnerability, use the secure generator.

See [Random Numbers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/random-numbers/) for more information about both generators.

---

## Recipe: Split Work Across Threads

*How-To. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/parallel-sum/*

To divide work among threads in Zig, give each `std.Thread.spawn` worker its own chunk of the slice and its own output slot. Then `join` all of the threads and add the slots. Current master does not have `std.Thread.Pool`.

## The problem

You have a large slice and a computation for each element, and one core does all of the work. The usual solution is to give each thread a chunk.

The usual problem in practice is shared data. When threads write to common state, you need locks. Locks cause contention and can cause a deadlock.

This recipe gets parallel work with no locks. The threads share no data.

## The plan

1. Divide the slice into one chunk for each worker. Use ceiling division, thus the last chunk gets the remainder.
2. Give each thread its own input chunk and its own output slot. No two threads use the same data. Thus no shared mutable state needs protection.
3. `join` each thread. Then combine the slots on the main thread.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// Each worker owns its chunk and its slot. The workers share no data. Thus
// no data needs synchronization before the join.
fn sumChunk(chunk: []const u64, slot: *u64) void {
    var sum: u64 = 0;
    for (chunk) |x| sum += x;
    slot.* = sum;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var numbers: [1000]u64 = undefined;
    for (&numbers, 1..) |*n, i| n.* = i;

    // With a fixed number of workers, the output of this demo is the same on
    // each machine. A real program starts from std.Thread.getCpuCount().
    const workers = 4;
    var slots: [workers]u64 = undefined;
    var threads: [workers]std.Thread = undefined;

    // Use ceiling division, thus the last chunk gets the remainder.
    const chunk_size = (numbers.len + workers - 1) / workers;
    for (&threads, &slots, 0..) |*t, *slot, w| {
        const start = w * chunk_size;
        const end = @min(start + chunk_size, numbers.len);
        t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, sumChunk, .{ numbers[start..end], slot });
    }

    // join is the synchronization. After join returns, the writes of that
    // thread are visible here.
    for (threads) |t| t.join();

    var total: u64 = 0;
    for (slots) |s| total += s;
    try out.print("total: {d}\n", .{total});
    try out.print("check: {d}\n", .{@as(u64, 1000 * 1001 / 2)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this program natively. wasm32-wasi has a single thread. Thus std.Thread.spawn does not compile for that target. (`06-cookbook.parallel-sum`)*

## Why the program needs no locks

Exactly one thread writes slot `w`. The main thread reads the slot only after `join` returns. `join` is the synchronization point. It guarantees that the writes of the joined thread are visible to the thread that called `join`.

The pattern works for each workload of the map type:

1. Divide the inputs.
2. Give each worker a private output.
3. Merge the outputs after the join.

The alternative is that each thread adds to one shared total. That needs a mutex or an atomic on the hot path. Private slots move that cost to one merge loop at the end.

## What replaced the pool

Older tutorials use `std.Thread.Pool` with a `WaitGroup`. Current master has neither of these. `std.Thread.spawn` and `join` are the primitives. The fan-out of tasks moves to the `std.Io` interface (`io.async` and `Io.Group`).

For a fixed number of workers with a long life, use spawn and join directly, as here. For structured task concurrency, see [Concurrency](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/async-future-group/).

## Variations

- **Thread count:** real code starts from `std.Thread.getCpuCount()`, not from a constant. The quantity of work that is useful to divide sets the maximum.
- **Work that is not equal:** chunks of equal size assume an equal cost for each element. When the items are very different, static chunks leave threads with no work. The [atomic work index](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/work-index/) recipe solves that problem.
- **False sharing:** adjacent `u64` slots can be on the same cache line. False sharing does not change correctness, and for a demo it is not important. If profiling shows that the merge pattern is hot, add padding to make each slot the size of a cache line.

---

## Recipe: An Atomic Work Index

*How-To. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/work-index/*

An atomic work index in Zig is a shared `std.atomic.Value(usize)`. Each thread increments it with `fetchAdd(1, .monotonic)` to claim its next job. A thread that completes its work early claims the next job, and no lock is necessary.

## The problem

Static chunks (one part of the slice for each thread) balance the load only when all items have the same cost. Item 7 can take a hundred times longer than item 8. Then the thread with the chunk of item 7 completes last, and the other threads have no work.

You want each thread to get the next job when it is free, as workers take tickets from a dispenser.

A mutex around a `next_job` counter works, but the counter is the full critical section. Atomics do the same work without a lock.

## The plan

1. Share two atomics. `next` is the index of the next job that no thread claimed. `total` is the result so far.
2. Each worker runs a loop. It claims an index, and stops when the index is past the end. If the index is not past the end, the worker processes the job and adds the result to `total` with another `fetchAdd`.
3. Spawn the workers, `join` them, and read the total.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const jobs = blk: {
    var j: [100]u64 = undefined;
    for (&j, 1..) |*x, i| x.* = i;
    break :blk j;
};

fn worker(next: *std.atomic.Value(usize), total: *std.atomic.Value(u64)) void {
    while (true) {
        // fetchAdd gives each index exactly one time, with no lock. Two threads
        // can race here, but they never get the same job.
        const i = next.fetchAdd(1, .monotonic);
        if (i >= jobs.len) return;

        const result = jobs[i] * jobs[i]; // the "work"
        _ = total.fetchAdd(result, .monotonic);
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var next = std.atomic.Value(usize).init(0);
    var total = std.atomic.Value(u64).init(0);

    var threads: [4]std.Thread = undefined;
    for (&threads) |*t| {
        t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, worker, .{ &next, &total });
    }
    for (threads) |t| t.join();

    // The threads completed in a random order. But each job ran exactly one
    // time. Thus the sum is the same on each run.
    try out.print("sum of squares 1..100: {d}\n", .{total.load(.monotonic)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this program natively. wasm32-wasi has a single thread. Thus std.Thread.spawn does not compile for that target. (`06-cookbook.work-index`)*

## Why fetchAdd cannot give one job to two threads

`fetchAdd` is one indivisible read-modify-write. It returns the old value and stores the incremented value. No other thread can run between the read and the write. Two threads in a race on the same counter always get two different indices.

That guarantee is the main reason to use an atomic here, more than speed. The absence of a lock is an extra benefit.

Both atomics use `.monotonic` ordering, because each atomic is independent. No thread reads `total` before `join`, and `join` already gives the visibility guarantee.

When one atomic must publish writes to *other* memory, the ordering becomes more difficult. Keep counters independent, and the simplest ordering stays correct.

## When threads claim more indices than there are jobs

Each worker stops when it claims an index past the end. With 4 threads, exactly 4 claims are past the end, and the counter ends after `jobs.len`. This is normal and causes no problem.

Do not use the final value of the counter as the number of completed jobs. If you need that number, count the completions separately.

## Variations

- **Claim a batch:** `fetchAdd(16, ...)` gives sixteen jobs for each claim. When jobs are very small, this decreases the contention on the counter.
- **Results for each job:** when each job makes data and not a number to add, write to `results[i]`. Only the thread that claimed `i` writes that slot. Thus the write needs no lock.
- **Compare with chunks:** the [parallel sum](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/parallel-sum/) recipe is the static version. Use it when the cost of each item is the same, because it never uses a shared counter.

---

## Recipe: A Producer/Consumer Queue

*How-To. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/worker-queue/*

A producer/consumer queue in Zig is `std.Io.Queue(T)`. Workers block on `getOne`. After the producer calls `close`, the workers get the items that remain, and then they get `error.Closed`.

## The problem

One part of your program finds work. A different part does the work. The usual solution is a queue between the two parts.

Versions that people write by hand usually get extra parts: a mutex, a condition variable and a "no more work" flag. They also often get a subtle bug: at shutdown, workers wait forever.

On current Zig master, `std.Io.Queue(T)` does all of this. It is a bounded, thread-safe channel. It has a put and a get that block, and a close protocol.

## The plan

1. Make a `std.Io.Queue(u64)` on a fixed buffer that you supply. The length of the buffer is the capacity of the queue. If a producer is more items ahead than the capacity, the producer blocks until the workers take more items. The name of this behavior is backpressure.
2. Spawn workers that loop on `getOne`. `getOne` blocks until an item arrives.
3. Produce the items, then call `close`. The workers get the items that remain. Then `getOne` returns `error.Closed`, and each worker stops its loop.
4. `join` the workers.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Queue = std.Io.Queue(u64);

fn consumer(q: *Queue, io: std.Io, total: *std.atomic.Value(u64)) void {
    while (true) {
        // Blocks until an item arrives. After close(), the queue still delivers
        // the items that remain. Only then does getOne return Closed.
        const job = q.getOne(io) catch return;
        _ = total.fetchAdd(job * job, .monotonic);
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // The queue borrows its storage: eight slots. If a producer is more than
    // eight items ahead, the producer blocks. This backpressure prevents an
    // overload of slow workers by a fast producer.
    var storage: [8]u64 = undefined;
    var queue: Queue = .init(&storage);

    var total = std.atomic.Value(u64).init(0);
    var workers: [3]std.Thread = undefined;
    for (&workers) |*t| {
        t.* = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, consumer, .{ &queue, io, &total });
    }

    // Produce twenty jobs, then close the queue. The close tells the workers
    // to stop. It needs no sentinel values and no stop flag, and no worker
    // leaks.
    for (1..21) |job| try queue.putAll(io, &.{job});
    queue.close(io);

    for (workers) |t| t.join();
    try out.print("processed total: {d}\n", .{total.load(.monotonic)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this program natively. wasm32-wasi has a single thread. Thus std.Thread.spawn does not compile for that target. (`06-cookbook.worker-queue`)*

## Close is the shutdown protocol

Shutdown is the usual place where worker queues fail. Usual solutions are a sentinel value for each worker, or a flag and a broadcast. It is easy to make an error in each of these.

`close` makes shutdown part of the contract of the queue:

1. A put after close fails.
2. The queue still delivers the items that it already has.
3. Only then does a get return `error.Closed`.

Thus the worker loop is two lines with no special cases, and no worker can wait through the shutdown.

## Why the queue takes `io`

Each operation that blocks goes through the `std.Io` interface, and the queue does too. The rest of the standard library now follows the same design.

The code that supplies the `Io` implementation decides how a block works: with OS threads here, or with an event loop in a different program. Operations that block also become cancellation points. When you give `io` to the worker, the same worker code works across different execution models.

## Variations

- **Batching:** `put` and `get` move slices, not only single items. They return the number of items that they moved. `putAll` blocks until all of the items are in the queue. Batches divide the cost of synchronization across many items.
- **More than one producer:** put is thread-safe. Thus many producers can put items into one queue. Close the queue one time, from the coordinator that knows when production is complete.
- **A channel for results:** for a full pipeline, give the workers a second queue for their results. Close that queue after the `join` of the workers.

---

## Recipe: Struct Memory Layout

*How-To. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/memory-layout/*

In Zig, `@sizeOf`, `@alignOf` and `@offsetOf` report the real size, alignment and field offsets of a struct. A plain struct can change the order of its fields. Use `extern struct` to match C, and use `packed struct` for exact bits.

## The problem

You must know how a struct is in memory:

- the size of the struct
- the position of each field
- if you can give the struct to C or to hardware

Do not guess from the field types. The default layout can change the order of the fields and add padding.

## The plan

1. Examine a type with `@sizeOf`, `@alignOf` and `@offsetOf`.
2. Put a field on a specified boundary with `align(N)`.
3. Use `packed struct` for fields at the bit level with no padding. Then use `@bitCast` to change the struct to an integer.
4. Use `extern struct` when the layout must match the C ABI.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// Default (auto) layout. The compiler selects the offsets for this target.
// It can add padding, so that each field is on its natural alignment.
const Padded = struct {
    a: u8,
    b: u64,
    c: u32,
};

// One field must be on a 16-byte boundary. The alignment of the struct is
// the largest alignment of its fields.
const Aligned = struct {
    a: u8 align(16),
    b: u8,
};

// Packed: no padding, fields in declaration order, and integers smaller than
// a byte. For hardware registers, use @bitCast to change the struct to an
// unsigned integer of the same width.
const Register = packed struct {
    enable: bool, // bit 0
    mode: u3, // bits 1..3
    reserved: u4, // bits 4..7
    value: u8, // bits 8..15
};

// Extern: follows the C ABI of the platform. Thus it can cross an FFI boundary.
const CStruct = extern struct {
    a: u8,
    b: u32,
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    try out.print("Padded:   size={d} align={d} offsets a={d} b={d} c={d}\n", .{
        @sizeOf(Padded),   @alignOf(Padded),
        @offsetOf(Padded, "a"), @offsetOf(Padded, "b"), @offsetOf(Padded, "c"),
    });

    try out.print("Aligned:  size={d} align={d} offset b={d}\n", .{
        @sizeOf(Aligned), @alignOf(Aligned), @offsetOf(Aligned, "b"),
    });

    const reg = Register{ .enable = true, .mode = 0b101, .reserved = 0, .value = 42 };
    const raw: u16 = @bitCast(reg);
    try out.print("Register: size={d} raw=0x{X:0>4}\n", .{ @sizeOf(Register), raw });

    try out.print("CStruct:  size={d} offset b={d}\n", .{
        @sizeOf(CStruct), @offsetOf(CStruct, "b"),
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`06-cookbook.memory-layout`)*

## The default layout changes the order of fields

The declaration of `Padded` is `a: u8, b: u64, c: u32`. A C programmer expects this layout: `a` at offset 0, seven bytes of padding, `b` at 8 and `c` at 16. The total is 24 bytes.

The default layout of Zig is not specified, and the current compiler uses that freedom. The compiler puts `b` at 0, `c` at 8 and `a` at 12. The total is 16 bytes. With the largest field first, the padding decreases from eleven bytes to three bytes.

These numbers are specific to this compiler and this target. Do not depend on the field order of an `auto` struct. If a byte offset is important, read it with `@offsetOf`, or use a layout that guarantees the order.

## `align(N)` increases the alignment of the full struct

`Aligned` puts `a` on a 16-byte boundary. The alignment of a field cannot decrease the alignment of the struct. It can only increase it. Thus the full struct gets an alignment of 16 and a size of 16 bytes.

Use this when a buffer must align with a cache line, or when a device expects a specific boundary.

## Packed structs give you bits

A `packed struct` has no padding and keeps the fields in the order of the declaration. It also allows integers smaller than a byte. `Register` puts a `bool`, a `u3`, a `u4` and a `u8` into exactly two bytes. `@bitCast` gives the same bits as an integer, with no copy.

The fields fill the integer from the least significant bit. Thus the first field is bit 0, and the last field is in the high byte. The result is `0x2A0B`. Use this method to build the value of a hardware register, or to decode the value.

## Extern structs match C

An `extern struct` follows the C ABI of the platform. The fields stay in order, and the padding follows the rules of C. Thus `CStruct` is 8 bytes, with `b` at offset 4.

Use this layout across an FFI boundary. The [ABI chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/abi/) shows in full how to send these structs to C and get them back from C.

## Variations

- **`std.debug.print("{}", .{@typeInfo(T)})`** shows the fields of a type and their declared types. Use it when you want all of the information at comptime.
- **`@sizeOf` and `@bitSizeOf`:** the second function reports the width in bits. Packed fields use that number of bits.
- **Write the bytes and read them back:** first, set the layout with `packed` or `extern`. Then [the binary round-trip recipe](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/binary-roundtrip/) writes the struct as raw bytes and reads it back, with a known endianness.

---

## Recipe: SQLite From Zig

*How-To / Databases. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/databases/sqlite-basic/*

Zig calls the C API of SQLite directly. A translate-c build step changes `sqlite3.h` into a module, and the program imports that module as `@import("c")`. The program links `sqlite3`. Zig removed `@cImport`, thus older examples that use it do not compile now.

## The problem

You want a real database from Zig, and SQLite is the usual first database. SQLite is a C library with no server. Thus you need only a header and a linked library.

Zig calls C directly, thus you do not have to install a binding layer. The work is to learn the open/prepare/bind/step/finalize shape of SQLite, and to change its integer return codes into Zig errors.

## The plan

1. Import the C API. On current Zig, this is a translate-c step in the build, imported as `@import("c")`. It is not the old `@cImport` (see below).
2. Call `sqlite3_open(":memory:", &db)`. With an in-memory database, the example is deterministic, and it leaves no file.
3. Use `sqlite3_exec` for statements with no results, for example `CREATE TABLE`.
4. For inserts, call `sqlite3_prepare_v2` one time. Then bind, step and reset for each row.
5. Step a `SELECT`, and read the columns until the step returns `SQLITE_DONE`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// Zig removed @cImport from the language. build.zig translates sqlite3.h with a
// translate-c step and gives the result to this file with the name "c".
const c = @import("c");

// SQLite reports success as SQLITE_OK. All other values are error codes.
// Change an error code into a Zig error. Then `try` works, and no code ignores it.
fn check(db: ?*c.sqlite3, rc: c_int, ok: c_int) !void {
    if (rc == ok) return;
    std.debug.print("sqlite error: {s}\n", .{c.sqlite3_errmsg(db)});
    return error.Sqlite;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // ":memory:" is a real database that never uses the disk. Thus the run is
    // deterministic, and it leaves no file.
    var db: ?*c.sqlite3 = null;
    try check(db, c.sqlite3_open(":memory:", &db), c.SQLITE_OK);
    defer _ = c.sqlite3_close(db);
    try out.writeAll("opened :memory:\n");

    // sqlite3_exec runs SQL with no results. err_msg is separate from the
    // return code, and the program must free it.
    var err_msg: [*c]u8 = null;
    try check(db, c.sqlite3_exec(db,
        "CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, email TEXT);",
        null, null, &err_msg), c.SQLITE_OK);
    try out.writeAll("created table users\n");

    // SQLite compiles a prepared statement one time. Then the program binds
    // and steps it for each row. The ? placeholders keep values out of the
    // SQL text. Thus they prevent injection.
    const users = [_]struct { name: []const u8, email: []const u8 }{
        .{ .name = "Ziggy Stardust", .email = "ziggy@ziglang.in" },
        .{ .name = "Grace Hopper", .email = "grace@ziglang.in" },
        .{ .name = "Alan Turing", .email = "alan@ziglang.in" },
    };

    var insert: ?*c.sqlite3_stmt = null;
    try check(db, c.sqlite3_prepare_v2(db,
        "INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (?, ?);", -1, &insert, null), c.SQLITE_OK);
    defer _ = c.sqlite3_finalize(insert);

    for (users) |u| {
        // A null destructor is SQLITE_STATIC. The string will exist after the
        // step, thus SQLite does not have to copy it.
        _ = c.sqlite3_bind_text(insert, 1, u.name.ptr, @intCast(u.name.len), null);
        _ = c.sqlite3_bind_text(insert, 2, u.email.ptr, @intCast(u.email.len), null);
        try check(db, c.sqlite3_step(insert), c.SQLITE_DONE);
        _ = c.sqlite3_reset(insert); // use the compiled statement again
    }
    try out.print("inserted {d} rows\n", .{users.len});

    // A step of a SELECT gives SQLITE_ROW for each row, until SQLITE_DONE.
    var query: ?*c.sqlite3_stmt = null;
    try check(db, c.sqlite3_prepare_v2(db,
        "SELECT id, name, email FROM users ORDER BY id;", -1, &query, null), c.SQLITE_OK);
    defer _ = c.sqlite3_finalize(query);

    while (c.sqlite3_step(query) == c.SQLITE_ROW) {
        const id = c.sqlite3_column_int(query, 0);
        const name = std.mem.span(c.sqlite3_column_text(query, 1));
        const email = std.mem.span(c.sqlite3_column_text(query, 2));
        try out.print("{d} | {s} | {s}\n", .{ id, name, email });
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*The program links the system libsqlite3. Thus CI builds and runs it natively. Browser wasm cannot link a C library. (`06-cookbook.sqlite-basic`)*

## Zig removed `@cImport`: use translate-c

If you come from an older tutorial, the first line does not compile. Before, Zig translated C headers inline with `@cImport` and `@cInclude`. Zig removed that builtin.

Now headers come through a step of the build system, `b.addTranslateC`. This step makes a usual Zig module that you import by name.

The `build.zig` of this guide does this from a marker on the snippet:

1. It makes a header that includes `sqlite3.h`.
2. It translates that header.
3. It links `sqlite3`.
4. It gives the module to the snippet.

As a result, the build caches and configures C imports as it does each other dependency. It does not run them again on each compile.

## Return codes become errors

Each SQLite call returns an `int`. The setup calls return `SQLITE_OK`, and a step returns `SQLITE_ROW` or `SQLITE_DONE`.

If the codes stay integers, it is easy to ignore them. That is how C programs skip error handling.

The `check` helper compares the code with the expected code. If the codes are different, it returns a Zig error. Thus `try` makes the check necessary, and `sqlite3_errmsg` explains each failure. This is the main thing that a Zig wrapper adds to the raw API.

## Prepared statements, not string building

The insert uses `?` placeholders and `sqlite3_bind_text`. It never joins strings. Placeholders keep user data out of the SQL grammar. Thus a name that contains a quote is data, not syntax.

A bind with `SQLITE_STATIC` as the destructor argument is a promise: the string will exist after the step. Thus SQLite does not copy the string. The promise is true here, because the values are string literals.

`sqlite3_reset` returns the compiled statement to its start. Thus the next row uses the same statement, and SQLite does not compile it again.

## Read columns

When you step a `SELECT`, the step returns `SQLITE_ROW` one time for each row. Read the columns by index and type: `sqlite3_column_int` for the id, and `sqlite3_column_text` for the strings.

The text accessor returns a C pointer. Thus `std.mem.span` changes it into a Zig slice for the print. The loop ends when `sqlite3_step` returns `SQLITE_DONE`.

## Variations

- **On disk:** give a filename in place of `":memory:"` to keep the data. All of the other code is the same.
- **Transactions:** put a batch of inserts between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` with `sqlite3_exec`. Then the inserts are atomic and much faster.
- **Other C libraries:** the same `//! link:` marker works for each system library with a header of the same name. For the layout rules on the C side, see [struct memory layout](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/memory-layout/) and the [ABI chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/working-with-c/abi/).

---

## Recipe: A Redis RESP Round Trip

*How-To / Databases. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/databases/redis-resp/*

A Redis command in RESP is `*` and the argument count. Then each argument follows as `$`, its byte length and its bytes. Each line ends in `\r\n`. A Zig program can write and parse that format directly, with no client library.

## The problem

Redis uses RESP, a small text protocol over TCP. You do not need a client library to communicate with Redis. A command is an array of strings, each with its length before it. A reply is one line with a tag.

This recipe implements a small part of both ends, sufficient to run `SET` and `GET`. Thus you can see the exact bytes that go over the wire.

The recipe does not depend on a `redis-server` that runs. It runs a small RESP server in the same process, as [the TCP recipe](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/tcp-echo/) does. CI runs the full exchange and compares the output. Thus CI verifies the protocol code, but no external database is necessary.

## The plan

1. Encode a command as RESP. Write `*<n>` for the argument count. Then, for each argument, write `$<len>` and the bytes. End each line with `\r\n`.
2. On the server, parse that array. Send `SET` and `GET` to a `StringHashMap`, and reply in RESP.
3. On the client, send a command. Decode the one-line reply by its first byte: `+` simple string, `-` error, `:` integer, `$` bulk string.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// A RESP command is an array of bulk strings: `*<n>\r\n`, then
// `$<len>\r\n<bytes>\r\n` for each argument. A real redis-server accepts
// exactly this format.
fn sendCommand(w: *std.Io.Writer, args: []const []const u8) !void {
    try w.print("*{d}\r\n", .{args.len});
    for (args) |a| {
        try w.print("${d}\r\n", .{a.len});
        try w.writeAll(a);
        try w.writeAll("\r\n");
    }
    try w.flush();
}

// takeDelimiterInclusive consumes the '\n' (the Exclusive form leaves it in the
// stream). The trim removes the "\r\n" at the end of each RESP line.
fn line(r: *std.Io.Reader) ![]const u8 {
    return std.mem.trimEnd(u8, try r.takeDelimiterInclusive('\n'), "\r\n");
}

// --- server: a key-value store for one connection, with RESP ---

const Store = std.StringHashMapUnmanaged([]const u8);

fn serve(server: *std.Io.net.Server, io: std.Io) void {
    serveImpl(server, io) catch {};
}

fn serveImpl(server: *std.Io.net.Server, io: std.Io) !void {
    var conn = try server.accept(io);
    defer conn.close(io);

    var arena = std.heap.ArenaAllocator.init(std.heap.page_allocator);
    defer arena.deinit();
    const a = arena.allocator();
    var store: Store = .empty;

    var rbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var wbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = conn.reader(io, &rbuf);
    var writer = conn.writer(io, &wbuf);
    const r = &reader.interface;
    const w = &writer.interface;

    while (true) {
        // Parse one command array. A clean EOF stops the loop.
        const header = line(r) catch break;
        if (header.len == 0 or header[0] != '*') break;
        const n = try std.fmt.parseInt(usize, header[1..], 10);

        var argv: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;
        for (0..n) |_| {
            const len_line = try line(r);
            const len = try std.fmt.parseInt(usize, len_line[1..], 10);
            const data = try a.alloc(u8, len);
            try r.readSliceAll(data);
            try r.discardAll(2); // trailing \r\n
            try argv.append(a, data);
        }
        if (argv.items.len == 0) continue;

        const cmd = argv.items[0];
        if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(cmd, "SET") and argv.items.len == 3) {
            try store.put(a, try a.dupe(u8, argv.items[1]), try a.dupe(u8, argv.items[2]));
            try w.writeAll("+OK\r\n");
        } else if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(cmd, "GET") and argv.items.len == 2) {
            if (store.get(argv.items[1])) |val| {
                try w.print("${d}\r\n", .{val.len});
                try w.writeAll(val);
                try w.writeAll("\r\n");
            } else {
                try w.writeAll("$-1\r\n"); // RESP nil
            }
        } else if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(cmd, "QUIT")) {
            try w.writeAll("+OK\r\n");
            try w.flush();
            break;
        } else {
            try w.writeAll("-ERR unknown command\r\n");
        }
        try w.flush();
    }
}

// --- client: send a command, and decode the one-line RESP reply ---

fn printReply(r: *std.Io.Reader, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    const l = try line(r);
    switch (l[0]) {
        '+' => try out.print("  simple: {s}\n", .{l[1..]}),
        '-' => try out.print("  error:  {s}\n", .{l[1..]}),
        ':' => try out.print("  int:    {s}\n", .{l[1..]}),
        '$' => {
            const len = try std.fmt.parseInt(isize, l[1..], 10);
            if (len < 0) {
                try out.writeAll("  bulk:   (nil)\n");
            } else {
                var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
                const data = buf[0..@intCast(len)];
                try r.readSliceAll(data);
                try r.discardAll(2);
                try out.print("  bulk:   \"{s}\"\n", .{data});
            }
        },
        else => try out.print("  ?       {s}\n", .{l}),
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // Start the small server on a port that the OS selects. Then connect to it.
    const any_port = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    var server = try any_port.listen(io, .{});
    defer server.deinit(io);
    const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, serve, .{ &server, io });

    var stream = try server.socket.address.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
    defer stream.close(io);

    var rbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var wbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = stream.reader(io, &rbuf);
    var writer = stream.writer(io, &wbuf);
    const r = &reader.interface;
    const w = &writer.interface;

    try out.writeAll("> SET framework zig\n");
    try sendCommand(w, &.{ "SET", "framework", "zig" });
    try printReply(r, out);

    try out.writeAll("> GET framework\n");
    try sendCommand(w, &.{ "GET", "framework" });
    try printReply(r, out);

    try out.writeAll("> GET missing\n");
    try sendCommand(w, &.{ "GET", "missing" });
    try printReply(r, out);

    try out.writeAll("> QUIT\n");
    try sendCommand(w, &.{"QUIT"});
    try printReply(r, out);

    thread.join();
    try out.flush();
}
```

*A RESP server and client in one program, with no other parts. CI builds and runs it natively. It needs no redis-server, and browser wasm has no sockets. (`06-cookbook.redis-resp`)*

## The wire format

`SET framework zig` goes out as `*3\r\n$3\r\nSET\r\n$9\r\nframework\r\n$3\r\nzig\r\n`. A RESP command contains only these parts: a count, then each argument as a byte length and the bytes.

The length is explicit. Thus the parser never has to guess where a value ends. A value can contain any byte, `\r\n` too.

Replies are more simple. One byte at the start gives the type. Thus `+OK\r\n` is success, and `$3\r\nzig\r\n` is the three-byte string `zig`. A key that does not exist gives the RESP nil, `$-1\r\n`, and the client prints it as `(nil)`.

## Read lines: be careful with the delimiter

The reader helper uses `takeDelimiterInclusive('\n')` and removes the `\r\n` at the end. This is intentional.

The exclusive variant returns the line without the terminator, but it leaves that terminator in the stream. In a loop that reads one line after the other with that variant, each later call reads an empty string.

The `Inclusive` form consumes the delimiter. You want that behavior when you parse a stream of lines that end in `\r\n`.

For a bulk string, the code does not read a line. It reads exactly the number of bytes that the length gives. Then it discards the two framing bytes at the end.

## Use a real Redis

To use a real server, replace the listener in the process with a connection to `127.0.0.1:6379`. Connect exactly as [the TCP recipe](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/tcp-echo/) does.

The encoder and the decoder here use real RESP. Thus the same `sendCommand` and reply parser work with `redis-server` without a change. The parser handles the four reply types that most commands return. For commands such as `KEYS` or `HGETALL`, add the array case (`*`).

## Variations

- **Pipelining:** send several commands before you read the replies. RESP allows this, and it decreases the number of round trips. The replies come in the same order as the commands.
- **Binary values:** bulk strings have their length before them. Thus you can store raw bytes without escape characters.
- **A persistent store:** for a database that keeps data on disk from Zig, see [SQLite from Zig](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/databases/sqlite-basic/).

---

## Recipe: The PostgreSQL Wire Protocol

*How-To / Databases. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/databases/postgres-wire/*

A Zig program can use the PostgreSQL wire protocol with no driver. After the startup message, each message has three parts: a one-byte type, a big-endian `Int32` length that counts itself, and the payload.

## The problem

A Postgres driver is mostly a codec for one TCP protocol. When you see that protocol without a driver, you see the real cost of a query, and the cause of a hang.

This recipe implements a part of both ends, sufficient to complete a startup handshake and run one query. Thus the exact bytes are on the page.

The other database recipes run a mock backend in the same process, and this recipe does too. Thus CI runs the full exchange and compares the output, without a `postgres` that runs. The framing is the real protocol. Only the authentication and the query engine are stubs.

## The plan

1. All of the integers are big-endian. Write one `putInt` and one `getInt`, and use them everywhere.
2. Send a `StartupMessage`. It has no type byte, only a length and a list of parameters that ends in a null.
3. Read the reply stream of the backend until `ReadyForQuery` (`Z`). Decode each message by its type byte.
4. Send a `Query` (`Q`). Then read `RowDescription` (`T`), `DataRow` (`D`), `CommandComplete` (`C`) and the next `ReadyForQuery`.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// PostgreSQL frames all integers big-endian (network order).
fn putInt(comptime T: type, w: *std.Io.Writer, v: T) !void {
    var b: [@divExact(@typeInfo(T).int.bits, 8)]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(T, &b, v, .big);
    try w.writeAll(&b);
}

fn getInt(comptime T: type, r: *std.Io.Reader) !T {
    var b: [@divExact(@typeInfo(T).int.bits, 8)]u8 = undefined;
    try r.readSliceAll(&b);
    return std.mem.readInt(T, &b, .big);
}

// After startup, each message starts with a type byte. Then an Int32 length
// follows. The length counts itself but not the type byte. Then the payload
// follows: that length minus four bytes.
fn sendMsg(w: *std.Io.Writer, tag: u8, payload: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeAll(&.{tag});
    try putInt(i32, w, @intCast(payload.len + 4));
    try w.writeAll(payload);
}

const Msg = struct { tag: u8, payload: []const u8 };

fn readMsg(r: *std.Io.Reader, buf: []u8) !Msg {
    var tb: [1]u8 = undefined;
    try r.readSliceAll(&tb);
    const len = try getInt(i32, r);
    const payload = buf[0..@intCast(len - 4)];
    try r.readSliceAll(payload);
    return .{ .tag = tb[0], .payload = payload };
}

// A small reader for a message payload.
const Cursor = struct {
    b: []const u8,
    i: usize = 0,
    fn int(self: *Cursor, comptime T: type) T {
        const n = @divExact(@typeInfo(T).int.bits, 8);
        const v = std.mem.readInt(T, self.b[self.i..][0..n], .big);
        self.i += n;
        return v;
    }
    fn cstr(self: *Cursor) []const u8 {
        const start = self.i;
        while (self.b[self.i] != 0) self.i += 1;
        defer self.i += 1; // move past the terminator
        return self.b[start..self.i];
    }
};

// --- the mock backend ---

fn serve(server: *std.Io.net.Server, io: std.Io) void {
    serveImpl(server, io) catch {};
}

fn sendParam(w: *std.Io.Writer, name: []const u8, val: []const u8) !void {
    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    var fb = std.Io.Writer.fixed(&buf);
    try fb.writeAll(name);
    try fb.writeAll("\x00");
    try fb.writeAll(val);
    try fb.writeAll("\x00");
    try sendMsg(w, 'S', fb.buffered());
}

fn serveImpl(server: *std.Io.net.Server, io: std.Io) !void {
    var conn = try server.accept(io);
    defer conn.close(io);

    var rbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var wbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = conn.reader(io, &rbuf);
    var writer = conn.writer(io, &wbuf);
    const r = &reader.interface;
    const w = &writer.interface;

    // StartupMessage has no type byte: an Int32 length, then the body. The demo
    // does no authentication. Thus it reads the body and discards it.
    const slen = try getInt(i32, r);
    try r.discardAll(@intCast(slen - 4));

    var p: [128]u8 = undefined;
    var fb = std.Io.Writer.fixed(&p);
    try putInt(i32, &fb, 0); // AuthenticationOk
    try sendMsg(w, 'R', fb.buffered());
    try sendParam(w, "server_version", "16.0");
    try sendParam(w, "client_encoding", "UTF8");
    fb = std.Io.Writer.fixed(&p);
    try putInt(i32, &fb, 4242); // BackendKeyData: pid
    try putInt(i32, &fb, 99887766); // secret
    try sendMsg(w, 'K', fb.buffered());
    try sendMsg(w, 'Z', "I"); // ReadyForQuery: idle
    try w.flush();

    // One simple Query. The reply has one text column and one row.
    var mbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    const q = try readMsg(r, &mbuf);
    if (q.tag == 'Q') {
        fb = std.Io.Writer.fixed(&p);
        try putInt(i16, &fb, 1); // RowDescription: one field
        try fb.writeAll("greeting\x00");
        try putInt(i32, &fb, 0); // table oid
        try putInt(i16, &fb, 0); // column number
        try putInt(i32, &fb, 25); // type oid: text
        try putInt(i16, &fb, -1); // type is variable length
        try putInt(i32, &fb, -1); // no type modifier
        try putInt(i16, &fb, 0); // text format
        try sendMsg(w, 'T', fb.buffered());

        fb = std.Io.Writer.fixed(&p);
        try putInt(i16, &fb, 1); // DataRow: one column
        try putInt(i32, &fb, 3); // its length
        try fb.writeAll("zig");
        try sendMsg(w, 'D', fb.buffered());

        try sendMsg(w, 'C', "SELECT 1\x00"); // CommandComplete
        try sendMsg(w, 'Z', "I");
        try w.flush();
    }

    _ = readMsg(r, &mbuf) catch {}; // Terminate, or the client closes the connection
}

// --- the client ---

fn sendStartup(w: *std.Io.Writer, user: []const u8) !void {
    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var fb = std.Io.Writer.fixed(&buf);
    try putInt(i32, &fb, 196608); // protocol 3.0 == 3 << 16
    try fb.writeAll("user\x00");
    try fb.writeAll(user);
    try fb.writeAll("\x00");
    try fb.writeAll("\x00"); // end of parameters
    const body = fb.buffered();
    try putInt(i32, w, @intCast(4 + body.len)); // length counts itself
    try w.writeAll(body);
    try w.flush();
}

fn statusName(b: u8) []const u8 {
    return switch (b) {
        'I' => "idle",
        'T' => "in transaction",
        'E' => "failed transaction",
        else => "?",
    };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    const any_port = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    var server = try any_port.listen(io, .{});
    defer server.deinit(io);
    const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, serve, .{ &server, io });

    var stream = try server.socket.address.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
    defer stream.close(io);

    var rbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var wbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = stream.reader(io, &rbuf);
    var writer = stream.writer(io, &wbuf);
    const r = &reader.interface;
    const w = &writer.interface;

    var mbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;

    try out.writeAll("> startup (user=zig)\n");
    try sendStartup(w, "zig");
    while (true) {
        const m = try readMsg(r, &mbuf);
        var c = Cursor{ .b = m.payload };
        switch (m.tag) {
            'R' => if (c.int(i32) == 0) try out.writeAll("auth:    ok\n"),
            'S' => try out.print("param:   {s}={s}\n", .{ c.cstr(), c.cstr() }),
            'K' => try out.print("backend: pid={d}\n", .{c.int(i32)}),
            'Z' => {
                try out.print("ready:   {s}\n", .{statusName(m.payload[0])});
                break;
            },
            else => {},
        }
    }

    try out.writeAll("> query: SELECT 'zig' AS greeting\n");
    try sendMsg(w, 'Q', "SELECT 'zig' AS greeting\x00");
    try w.flush();
    while (true) {
        const m = try readMsg(r, &mbuf);
        var c = Cursor{ .b = m.payload };
        switch (m.tag) {
            'T' => {
                const n = c.int(i16);
                try out.print("fields:  {d} ({s})\n", .{ n, c.cstr() });
            },
            'D' => {
                _ = c.int(i16); // column count
                const len = c.int(i32);
                try out.print("row:     {s}\n", .{c.b[c.i..][0..@intCast(len)]});
            },
            'C' => try out.print("done:    {s}\n", .{c.cstr()}),
            'Z' => {
                try out.print("ready:   {s}\n", .{statusName(m.payload[0])});
                break;
            },
            else => {},
        }
    }

    try sendMsg(w, 'X', ""); // Terminate
    try w.flush();
    thread.join();
    try out.flush();
}
```

*A client and a mock backend in one program, with no other parts. CI builds and runs it natively. It needs no postgres server, and browser wasm has no sockets. (`06-cookbook.postgres-wire`)*

## Two message shapes

After the first message, each Postgres message has the same frame:

1. a one-byte type
2. an `Int32` length that counts itself but not the type byte
3. `length - 4` bytes of payload

`sendMsg` and `readMsg` encode exactly that frame. Thus the other code works only with payloads.

The startup message is the one exception. It is older than the type-byte convention. Thus it is only a length and a body. Because of this difference, `sendStartup` and `readMsg` are separate.

## The handshake is a stream, not a call

When you send the startup message, you do not get one reply. The backend replies with a sequence of messages:

1. `AuthenticationOk`.
2. One `ParameterStatus` for each server setting (`server_version`, `client_encoding`, and usually about twelve more).
3. `BackendKeyData`, with the process id and the secret that a client uses to cancel queries.
4. `ReadyForQuery`.

The client loops until it sees `Z`. That message tells the client that the connection is ready to use. A real driver caches the parameters and the cancel key here.

## Read a result

A query replies with the same stream shape:

- `RowDescription` gives the names of the columns and their types.
- `DataRow` contains one row as column values, each with its length before it. A length of -1 means SQL `NULL`.
- `CommandComplete` reports the tag.
- `ReadyForQuery` closes the batch.

The `Cursor` helper moves through a payload with an index. It reads integers and null-terminated strings. These messages need only that parse.

## Flush, or the program hangs

Each send here has a flush after it, because the first version of this recipe hung without the flush. The socket writer has a buffer. Thus a message that you "sent" stays in your buffer until you flush.

If both sides then block on a read, neither side can continue. This is a common deadlock in wire protocols. It is easy to cause this deadlock when a flush does not immediately follow a send.

## Variations

- **Real authentication:** the backend can reply to the startup with `AuthenticationCleartextPassword` or with an MD5 or SCRAM challenge, in place of `AuthenticationOk`. The client replies with a `PasswordMessage`, and the loop continues.
- **Prepared statements:** the extended-query protocol replaces `Q` with `Parse`, `Bind` and `Execute`. With this protocol, parameters stay out of the SQL text.
- **A local database:** to keep data without a server or a protocol, [SQLite from Zig](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/databases/sqlite-basic/) links the C library directly.

# Track: From Scratch

Rebuild the tools that you use every day, one program at a time, with only code that you wrote.

## String Primitives

*Survive the Terminal. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/terminal/strings/*

The other chapters in this track need four operations on text: measure, compare,
copy and trim. Write these four functions one time. You learn more from that
than from a description, because three of the four functions have a well-known
mistake.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Walk the string until the zero byte. C calls this function `strlen`. Its
/// cost is the reason that a slice holds its length. Each call is O(n). A call
/// inside a loop changes an O(n) job into O(n^2) work.
fn strLen(s: [*:0]const u8) usize {
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (s[i] != 0) i += 1;
    return i;
}

fn strEq(a: []const u8, b: []const u8) bool {
    if (a.len != b.len) return false;
    for (a, b) |x, y| {
        if (x != y) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

/// Copy `src` into `dest` and terminate the copy. If `src` is too large for
/// `dest`, return null. Do not write a part of `src`.
///
/// The `+ 1` is for the terminator. A 5-byte string needs 6 bytes of space.
/// A version that checks `src.len > dest.len` compiles and passes a simple
/// test. But that version writes one byte past the end of the buffer.
fn strCopy(dest: []u8, src: []const u8) ?[:0]u8 {
    if (src.len + 1 > dest.len) return null;
    @memcpy(dest[0..src.len], src);
    dest[src.len] = 0;
    return dest[0..src.len :0];
}

fn isSpace(c: u8) bool {
    return c == ' ' or c == '\t' or c == '\n' or c == '\r';
}

/// Trim both ends, and do not move a byte. A trim does not need a copy. The
/// result is a slice of the bytes that you already have.
fn strTrim(s: []const u8) []const u8 {
    var start: usize = 0;
    var end: usize = s.len;
    while (start < end and isSpace(s[start])) start += 1;
    while (end > start and isSpace(s[end - 1])) end -= 1;
    return s[start..end];
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const greeting = "hello";
    try out.print("strLen(\"hello\")   = {d}\n", .{strLen(greeting)});
    try out.print("greeting.len      = {d}   (already known, no walk)\n\n", .{greeting.len});

    try out.print("strEq(\"cat\",\"cat\") = {}\n", .{strEq("cat", "cat")});
    try out.print("strEq(\"cat\",\"cot\") = {}\n", .{strEq("cat", "cot")});
    try out.print("strEq(\"cat\",\"cats\")= {}\n\n", .{strEq("cat", "cats")});

    // Six bytes of space for five bytes of text.
    var room: [6]u8 = undefined;
    if (strCopy(&room, "hello")) |copied| {
        try out.print("copied \"{s}\" into 6 bytes, terminator at index {d}\n", .{ copied, copied.len });
    }
    var tight: [5]u8 = undefined;
    try out.print("copying \"hello\" into 5 bytes -> {s}\n\n", .{
        if (strCopy(&tight, "hello") == null) "refused" else "wrote",
    });

    // This buffer is separate from `buf`. An earlier version gave `buf` here.
    // Then `buf` held the data of the writer and the data of `escape`, and
    // this garbled the first line of output. Both slices hold a length. Thus the
    // mistake garbled the output, and did not write past the end of a buffer.
    var scratch: [64]u8 = undefined;
    for ([_][]const u8{ "  padded  ", "\tboth\n", "none", "   ", "" }) |sample| {
        try out.print("trim(\"{s}\") -> \"{s}\"\n", .{ escape(sample, &scratch), strTrim(sample) });
    }

    try out.flush();
}

/// Show whitespace as visible text, so that you can check the trim by eye.
fn escape(s: []const u8, scratch: []u8) []const u8 {
    var n: usize = 0;
    for (s) |c| {
        const replacement: []const u8 = switch (c) {
            '\t' => "\\t",
            '\n' => "\\n",
            else => &[_]u8{c},
        };
        @memcpy(scratch[n..][0..replacement.len], replacement);
        n += replacement.len;
    }
    return scratch[0..n];
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`18-terminal.strings`)*

## What just happened

**`strLen` walks the string, and `.len` does not.** Both printed 5. `strLen`
counted bytes until it found a zero. `.len` read a number that the slice
already holds.

For a five-byte greeting, the difference is almost zero. In a loop, the
difference can be large:

```c
for (int i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++)   /* walks the string on every iteration */
```

The loop does an O(n) job with O(n²) work. This is a common performance bug in
C. You cannot write this bug with a slice, because no call exists that you can
repeat by accident.

**`strEq` compares the lengths first.** When the lengths are different, a
comparison of the contents is unnecessary work. More important, a loop without
the length check reads past the end of the shorter string. `"cat"` against
`"cats"` is false after one comparison.

**The copy refused the text and did not truncate it.** A buffer of six bytes
accepted `"hello"`, and a buffer of five bytes did not. The check is
`src.len + 1 > dest.len`. The `+ 1` is necessary because a 5-byte string needs
6 bytes: the terminator is also a byte.

Another version of the check is `src.len > dest.len`. That version looks
correct and compiles. It also passes a test with short strings. But it writes
exactly one byte past the end of the buffer.

That one byte is the classic C buffer overflow. It does not need a bad pointer
or malicious input. It needs only an off-by-one error in a bounds check, after
a reviewer read the check two times and approved it.

**The trim returned a view.** `"  padded  "` became `"padded"`, and the
function copied nothing and allocated nothing. The obvious implementation moves
the bytes to the front, and that work is unnecessary. The trimmed text is
already in the input. The function only returns a slice that covers a smaller
part of the input.

## Check yourself

`strTrim` takes `[]const u8` and returns `[]const u8`. Can it take a
null-terminated C string and return a null-terminated C string?

Not without a copy of the string or a write to the string. To trim the front is
easy, because the function can point further into the string. To trim the back,
the string must end earlier, and a C string ends at its zero byte.

Thus the function must write a zero over the first trailing space, and that
write changes the data of the caller. `strtok` does exactly this, and this
behavior makes `strtok` difficult to use. A slice can describe a shorter part
of the same bytes and not change them. For this reason, a slice does not need
a terminator.

## If you know C

You wrote these four functions before, possibly more than one time:

```c
size_t str_len(const char *s) { size_t i = 0; while (s[i]) i++; return i; }
int    str_eq(const char *a, const char *b) { return strcmp(a, b) == 0; }
void   str_copy(char *d, const char *s) { while ((*d++ = *s++)); }   /* no bounds at all */
```

The third function is `strcpy`, and it does not know the size of the
destination. The problem is in the signature, not in the implementation. The
caller never gives the size to the function, so the function cannot check the
size.

`strncpy` was the fix, and it added a new problem. It does not terminate the
result when the source is too long. Thus the safer replacement for `strncpy` is
`strlcpy`, and `strlcpy` is not in the C standard.

That is three attempts at one function. All three are difficult to use because
a `char *` is a pointer with no length. Each function above takes a slice. Thus
the length is not a separate argument that a caller can give incorrectly.

Next: [tokenize a command line](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/terminal/tokenize/). A shell does this
step first.

---

## Tokenize a Command Line

*Survive the Terminal. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/terminal/tokenize/*

A shell reads a line and must change it into two things: a program to run, and
a list of arguments for that program. `execve` takes an array of strings. Thus
the line must become an array before the shell can do anything.

This chapter looks like the `cut` chapter, but the rule is the opposite. `cut`
splits a record on a delimiter, and two delimiters in a row mean an empty field.
A command line splits on *separation*, and two spaces in a row mean nothing.
`ls   -la` is two arguments, not four.

The rule is different because the meaning is different. In a data format, the
delimiter is structure. On a command line, the delimiter is whitespace.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Split on runs of whitespace. The function returns slices of `line`. Thus
/// it copies nothing and allocates nothing. The result is valid only while
/// `line` is valid.
///
/// A run of spaces makes no empty argument. `cut` needs the opposite rule.
/// A command line is not a delimited record. The spaces only separate the
/// arguments. Thus `ls   -la` is two arguments.
fn tokenize(line: []const u8, out: [][]const u8) ![][]const u8 {
    var n: usize = 0;
    var i: usize = 0;

    while (i < line.len) {
        while (i < line.len and isSpace(line[i])) i += 1;
        if (i == line.len) break;

        const start = i;
        while (i < line.len and !isSpace(line[i])) i += 1;

        if (n == out.len) return error.TooManyArguments;
        out[n] = line[start..i];
        n += 1;
    }
    return out[0..n];
}

fn isSpace(c: u8) bool {
    return c == ' ' or c == '\t' or c == '\n' or c == '\r';
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var argv: [8][]const u8 = undefined;

    const lines = [_][]const u8{
        "ls -la /tmp",
        "  spaced   out   ",
        "single",
        "",
        "   ",
    };

    for (lines) |line| {
        const args = try tokenize(line, &argv);
        try out.print("\"{s}\"\n  {d} args:", .{ line, args.len });
        for (args) |arg| try out.print(" [{s}]", .{arg});
        try out.writeAll("\n");
    }

    // A shell runs the first token with exec. It gives the other tokens to
    // that program as arguments.
    const args = try tokenize("grep -n main build.zig", &argv);
    try out.print("\ncommand: {s}\n", .{args[0]});
    for (args[1..], 1..) |arg, i| try out.print("  argv[{d}] = {s}\n", .{ i, arg });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`18-terminal.tokenize`)*

## What just happened

**`"  spaced   out   "` gave exactly two arguments.** Whitespace at the start, at
the end and in runs needs no extra code, because the loop has two phases:

1. Skip the whitespace.
2. Take all the bytes that are not whitespace.

Neither phase can make an empty token. Thus the code has no empty tokens to
handle.

Compare this loop with the [cut](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/cut/) chapter. In that
chapter, a loop that collapsed runs of delimiters was the bug. Both chapters
split a line of text. `cut` must keep the empty fields, and the tokenizer must
remove them, because the two inputs mean different things.

**An empty line and a line of only whitespace gave zero arguments.** A shell
needs this result. When you press Enter on an empty line, the shell must do
nothing. It must not try to run a program with an empty name. The loop handles
this case without a special check at the top, and the code for that is short.

**The program copied nothing.** Each argument is a slice of the line. The array
of slices is the argv that a shell gives to the next program, and the program
moved no bytes to make the array.

The cost is the usual cost of slices: the arguments are valid only while the
line buffer is valid. This cost is important when a shell must remember a
command for its history.

**The first token is the command.** It is not a special case. It is position
0. For this reason, `argv[0]` is the program name in each C program that you
wrote. The shell put the command there, and the convention stayed.

## Check yourself

This tokenizer splits `echo "hello world"` into three arguments. What does a
real shell do, and what does that mean for the loop?

A real shell gives two arguments: `echo` and `hello world`. Quotes add an
exception to the whitespace rule, and thus the loop needs state. Inside a quoted
run, whitespace is an ordinary character.

That state is one more bit, with the same shape as the bit that `wc` uses. With
that state, the tokenizer is not a simple split. It is a small parser.

Add escapes with backslashes, then variable expansion, then globs. Then the
"small parser" is most of a shell. At that point, a shell that you write from
zero must get a real lexer or remove support for quotes.

## If you know C

The C version tokenizes **in place**. This is the classic method:

```c
char *argv[8];
int argc = 0;
char *p = line;
while (*p) {
    while (*p == ' ') *p++ = '\0';    /* overwrite separators with terminators */
    if (*p) argv[argc++] = p;
    while (*p && *p != ' ') p++;
}
```

The loop writes `\0` over each run of spaces. This changes one buffer into
several C strings, and the program can give them directly to `execve` with no
allocation.

The method is clever, but it destroys the input. The original line is gone.
Thus a shell that needs the line for its history must copy the line first.

Slices give the same result with zero allocations, and they do not change the
input. A slice can describe a part of a buffer, and it does not need a
terminator to mark the end. The line stays complete, and the tokens point into
the line.

The C version is better in one place: its tokens are already null-terminated
and ready for `execve`. For that boundary, Zig has `[:0]const u8` and [sentinel
termination](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/language-basics/sentinel-termination/). That chapter
explains the subject.

Next: [the read-eval-print loop](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/terminal/repl/). All of this code runs
inside that loop.

---

## The Read-Eval-Print Loop

*Survive the Terminal. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/terminal/repl/*

Read a line. Find what the line means. Print the result. Return to the start.
Each shell, each database prompt and each language REPL runs this loop, and
the loop is four lines of code.

The end of the loop is less obvious. The loop can end in **two** ways, and the
two ways are completely different. A loop that handles only one of them has a
bug, and you can easily miss that bug before a release. The two ways are:

- The user asks the loop to stop: the user types `quit`.
- The input stops. On a terminal, the user presses Ctrl-D. In a pipeline, the
  input reaches the end of the file. This occurs each time a person writes
  `echo "help" | yourshell`.

A loop that looks only for `quit` runs forever at the first end of input. The
read continues to return an empty result, and an empty result is not `quit`.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Action = enum { printed, quit };

/// The "eval" half. It is separate from the loop, so that you can test it
/// without a terminal. For the same reason, this page can run the loop.
fn eval(line: []const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !Action {
    const trimmed = std.mem.trim(u8, line, " \t\r");

    if (trimmed.len == 0) return .printed; // a newline alone is not an error
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, trimmed, "quit")) return .quit;

    if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, trimmed, "echo ")) {
        try out.print("{s}\n", .{trimmed["echo ".len..]});
    } else if (std.mem.eql(u8, trimmed, "help")) {
        try out.writeAll("echo <text> | help | quit\n");
    } else {
        // Do not exit on unknown input. A REPL that exits on a typo is not
        // usable.
        try out.print("unknown command: {s}\n", .{trimmed});
    }
    return .printed;
}

/// The loop. It has two exits: the user asks to stop, or the input ends.
fn repl(input: []const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(input);

    while (true) {
        try out.writeAll("> ");

        // takeDelimiter returns null at the end of input (EOF). On a terminal,
        // the user presses Ctrl-D for EOF. A loop that checks only for "quit"
        // runs forever when a user presses Ctrl-D the first time.
        const line = try reader.takeDelimiter('\n') orelse {
            try out.writeAll("\n(end of input)\n");
            return;
        };

        try out.print("{s}\n", .{line});
        switch (try eval(line, out)) {
            .quit => {
                try out.writeAll("(bye)\n");
                return;
            },
            .printed => {},
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    try out.writeAll("--- session that quits\n");
    try repl(
        \\help
        \\echo hello there
        \\
        \\nonsense
        \\quit
        \\
    , out);

    try out.writeAll("\n--- session that hits end of input\n");
    try repl("echo still here\n", out);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`18-terminal.repl`)*

## What just happened

**Two sessions, two exits.** The first session ended on `quit` and printed
`(bye)`. The second session came to the end of its input and printed
`(end of input)`. Both are normal ends, and neither is an error. The code paths
are different.

**The empty line did nothing and did not stop the loop.** When a user presses
Enter at a blank prompt, that is not a command and not an error. A REPL that
uses either of these two meanings annoys the user quickly.

**An unknown command printed a message, and the loop continued.** This is the
difference between a REPL and a batch program. A batch program usually stops
when it gets bad input. A REPL that exits on a typo is not usable. The input is
the same in both cases. The correct behavior depends on one question: does a
person wait at the prompt?

This page can run the loop because of the way the loop reads input. The loop
reads through a `std.Io.Reader`, and here the reader gets its bytes from a
string, not from a terminal. If you change the source of the bytes, the rest
of the loop stays the same. You test a REPL in the same way. Without this
method, a REPL is difficult to test.

## Check yourself

The demo prints `> ` and then echoes the line that it read. A real terminal
does not do that. Why not, and why must this demo do it?

A terminal echoes the characters while you type them. The characters appear
because the terminal driver shows them, not because the program printed them.
This page has no keyboard. The input is a string, and nothing shows that
string. When the demo echoes the line, the transcript is easy to read.

That difference is also important in real programs. A password prompt must
turn *off* the echo of the terminal before the read. That is a call to the
terminal driver, separate from the read. Thus a password read needs more than
a line read.

## If you know C

The loop is the same. C makes the end of the loop easy to get wrong:

```c
while (1) {
    write(1, "> ", 2);
    ssize_t n = read(0, buf, sizeof buf - 1);
    if (n <= 0) break;          /* forget this and Ctrl-D spins forever */
    buf[n] = '\0';
    ...
}
```

When `read` returns 0, the input is at its end, and that is not an error. A
check for only `n < 0` does not see the end, and the loop runs forever on an
empty read. Almost each programmer who writes a shell makes this mistake at
least one time.

The `sizeof buf - 1` is the same off-by-one as in the [strings
chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/terminal/strings/). It keeps space for the terminator, because
`read` does not write the terminator.

## Where this section ends

This section has three primitives:

- Measure and copy text.
- Split a line into arguments.
- Loop until something stops the loop.

A shell needs these three primitives *before* it can run a program.

The next steps need a real kernel. Thus they are in the operating system
section, not here. One chapter starts a process. The chapter after it is about
pipes, where the output of one program becomes the input of another program.
Neither chapter can run on this page, and both chapters tell you this.

---

## cat

*Unix Tools. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/cat/*

`cat` copies its input to its output. That is the full specification, and it
is a good place to start.

Each program that moves bytes has the same loop:

1. Keep a fixed buffer.
2. Read into a part of the buffer.
3. Write exactly that part.
4. Do the steps again.

The loop never asks **how large is the input?** It never needs to know. A
program with this loop copies a four-byte file and a four-gigabyte file with
the same code and the same memory. At no time does the program hold more than
one full buffer.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// All of `cat`. Fill a buffer, write exactly the filled part, and do it again.
/// No line here knows the size of the input, and no line needs to know it.
fn cat(in: *std.Io.Reader, out: *std.Io.Writer, buffer: []u8) !usize {
    var copied: usize = 0;
    while (true) {
        // A read returns the bytes that it has, not the number that you asked
        // for. A common bug is to think that the buffer is now full.
        // A return of 0 means that the input ended. It is not an error.
        const n = try in.readSliceShort(buffer);
        if (n == 0) return copied;
        try out.writeAll(buffer[0..n]);
        copied += n;
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var stdout_buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &stdout_buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const input = "the quick brown fox\njumps over the lazy dog\n";

    // Four bytes at a time. This shows that the size controls memory, not
    // correctness. Real cat uses 128 KB to make fewer syscalls. A smaller
    // buffer is not wrong.
    var small: [4]u8 = undefined;
    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(input);
    const copied = try cat(&reader, out, &small);

    try out.print("\ncopied {d} bytes through a {d}-byte buffer\n", .{ copied, small.len });
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`16-unix-tools.cat`)*

## What just happened

**The buffer is four bytes, and the program still copied 44.** The small
buffer shows that the size of the buffer does not change the correctness. The
size controls only the quantity of memory and the number of syscalls.

Real `cat` reads 128 KB at a time. Each read is a trip into the kernel, and
fewer trips are faster. A smaller buffer still gives the correct output.

**The read returns the bytes that it has, which can be fewer than you asked
for.** `readSliceShort` fills the buffer *up to* its size and tells you how
many bytes it actually got.

A common bug in programs like this one is to think that the buffer is now
full. Then you write the full buffer, with the old bytes from the last read,
and the output contains garbage. The bug appears only under load, because only
under load does a read return fewer bytes.

A write can also be partial. Thus the loop calls `writeAll`, not a single
write.

**End of input is a read that returns zero bytes.** The end of a file is not
a problem, so the reader does not report it as an error. The loop stops when
a read returns nothing.

## Check yourself

The program never checks if the input contains text. Does the program work on
a JPEG?

Yes, and without changes. No part of the loop examines a byte. Thus the loop
has no idea of a character, a line or an encoding that it can get wrong.

For the same reason, `cat` on a binary file makes your terminal show garbage,
and `cat` does not fail. The bytes arrive without changes. The terminal is the
part that tries to interpret them.

## If you know C

The loop is the same, and it has the same two traps:

```c
char buf[4096];
ssize_t n;
while ((n = read(0, buf, sizeof buf)) > 0)
    write(1, buf, n);       /* n, never sizeof buf */
```

It is normal for `read` to return fewer bytes than you requested. It is also
normal for `write` to write fewer bytes than you gave it. Thus a correct C
version needs its own loop around the write. The `writeAll` function of Zig is
that loop, already written.

C makes you check for `-1` and examine `errno`, but Zig does not. In Zig, a
failure is an error in the return type. Thus `try` handles the failure, and
you cannot confuse `-1` with a byte count.

Next: [wc](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/wc/). It is the same loop with one bit of memory
added.

---

## wc

*Unix Tools. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/wc/*

To count bytes is trivial. To count lines is almost as easy: add one for each
`\n`. Words are more difficult, because a word is not a single byte in the
input. A word is a pattern *between* bytes.

If you try to count words directly, you need rules for many usual cases:

- Two spaces between words.
- A space at the start.
- A tab in place of a space.
- A line that ends without a newline.

If you handle each case as a special case, the code becomes complex, and soon
one case is wrong.

Instead, count **transitions**. Keep one bit that tells if the program is
inside a word now. Each time that bit changes from false to true, a word
starts. The difficult cases need no special code. A run of twelve spaces sets
the bit to false twelve times, and false is already false.

This one bit and the rule that changes it are a **state machine**, and a very
small one.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Counts = struct { lines: usize = 0, words: usize = 0, bytes: usize = 0 };

fn isSpace(c: u8) bool {
    return c == ' ' or c == '\t' or c == '\n' or c == '\r' or c == 11 or c == 12;
}

/// One pass, one byte at a time, one bit of state. `in_word` is the state
/// machine. The function counts a word when the input moves from a space into
/// a non-space. Thus runs of spaces cost nothing, and it reads each byte once.
fn count(text: []const u8) Counts {
    var c: Counts = .{};
    var in_word = false;

    for (text) |ch| {
        c.bytes += 1;
        if (ch == '\n') c.lines += 1;

        if (isSpace(ch)) {
            in_word = false;
        } else if (!in_word) {
            in_word = true;
            c.words += 1;
        }
    }
    return c;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const samples = [_][]const u8{
        "hello world\n",
        "  hello   world  \n",
        "one\ntwo\nthree\n",
        "no newline at the end",
        "",
    };

    for (samples) |text| {
        const c = count(text);
        try out.print("{d:>3} {d:>3} {d:>3}  ", .{ c.lines, c.words, c.bytes });
        try printEscaped(out, text);
        try out.writeAll("\n");
    }

    try out.flush();
}

/// Show the sample with its whitespace visible, so that you can check the counts.
```
