```zig
fn printEscaped(out: *std.Io.Writer, text: []const u8) !void {
    try out.writeAll("\"");
    for (text) |ch| {
        if (ch == '\n') try out.writeAll("\\n") else try out.writeByte(ch);
    }
    try out.writeAll("\"");
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`16-unix-tools.wc`)*

## What just happened

Each sample tests one of the cases above.

**`"hello world\n"` and `"  hello   world  \n"` both give 2 words.** The byte
counts are different, 12 and 18, but the word count is the same. No code has
a special case for whitespace at the start or for repeated whitespace. The
transition never occurs two times in sequence, because the bit is already set.

**`"no newline at the end"` reports 0 lines and 5 words.** This is correct.
`wc` counts newline *characters*. Thus if the last line of a file has no
terminator, the file has one line fewer than you count with your eyes. Real
`wc` does exactly this. If `wc` reports "0 lines" for a file that clearly has
text in it, the file has no newline at the end.

**The empty input gives three zeroes** without special code, because a loop
over nothing runs zero times.

The counter never examines a byte two times, and it never needs the full input
in memory. Thus it works with the loop from the previous chapter:

1. Read one full buffer.
2. Send the buffer through the same state.
3. Do the steps again.

To count a file that is larger than memory, you need nothing new.

## Check yourself

Give this program the six-byte string `"héllo"`. How many words does it
report?

One. The `é` is two bytes, and neither byte is whitespace. Thus the program sets
the bit one time, and the bit stays set.

The word count is one of the few text operations that is correct on raw UTF-8
without knowledge of UTF-8. It only asks if a byte is one of six ASCII
whitespace values. UTF-8 makes sure that those bytes never appear inside a
multi-byte character.

An operation that needs *character* counts is a more difficult problem. That
problem is the subject of [Strings Are
Bytes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/strings-are-bytes/).

## If you know C

The C version has the same bit and the same loop:

```c
int in_word = 0;
for (...) {
    if (isspace(c)) in_word = 0;
    else if (!in_word) { in_word = 1; words++; }
}
```

In C, be careful with `isspace(c)` and a plain `char`. On a platform where
`char` is signed, a byte above 127 becomes negative. If you give `isspace` a
negative value that is not `EOF`, the result is undefined behaviour.

The fix is `isspace((unsigned char)c)`. Nobody can see this bug for years,
because it appears only on input that is not ASCII.

A `u8` in Zig cannot be negative, so the problem does not exist.

Next: [grep](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/grep/), where the program must answer a
question, and not only report on what it saw.

---

## grep

*Unix Tools. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/grep/*

`grep` prints the lines that contain a pattern. This chapter builds two parts
of `grep` by hand: the search, and the exit code. The exit code is also a
feature, and people often forget it.

The obvious substring search is two nested loops:

1. Go to the first position.
2. Compare the bytes one by one, until the pattern ends.
3. If the pattern ended, that is a match.
4. If a byte is different, stop and go to the next start position.

In the worst case, the search is O(n×m). The worst case needs input like
`aaaaaaaaab` with the pattern `aaab`, and a normal line of text does not
look like that. There are faster algorithms, for example Boyer-Moore. Here,
they are less important than you possibly expect, because the simple search is
fast enough on a line of text.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The simple search, written out here, so that you can see it one time.
/// Try each start position, compare forward, and stop at the first mismatch.
/// O(n*m) in the worst case, and good enough for a line of text.
fn find(haystack: []const u8, needle: []const u8) ?usize {
    if (needle.len == 0) return 0;
    if (needle.len > haystack.len) return null;

    var start: usize = 0;
    while (start + needle.len <= haystack.len) : (start += 1) {
        var i: usize = 0;
        while (i < needle.len and haystack[start + i] == needle[i]) : (i += 1) {}
        if (i == needle.len) return start;
    }
    return null;
}

/// Returns true if a line matched. The exit code reports this result.
/// The contract of grep is that "found nothing" is not an error. A shell
/// pipeline must see the difference between those two results.
fn grep(text: []const u8, pattern: []const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !bool {
    var lines: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(text);
    var matched = false;
    var number: usize = 0;

    while (try lines.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        number += 1;
        if (find(line, pattern) != null) {
            matched = true;
            try out.print("{d}:{s}\n", .{ number, line });
        }
    }
    return matched;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const text =
        \\the quick brown fox
        \\jumps over the lazy dog
        \\the end
        \\
    ;

    for ([_][]const u8{ "the", "fox", "cat" }) |pattern| {
        try out.print("--- grep \"{s}\"\n", .{pattern});
        const matched = try grep(text, pattern, out);
        // 0 when a line matched, 1 when no line matched. Neither is an error.
        try out.print("exit {d}\n\n", .{@intFromBool(!matched)});
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`16-unix-tools.grep`)*

## What just happened

**The program did three searches, and the third search found nothing.** Look
at the output: `exit 1`. The program printed no error and nothing on stderr.
Only the exit status changed.

With the exit status, other programs can use `grep`. If you think only about
the search, you do not think of this design. A shell must ask "does this file
contain the pattern?", and the shell does not need the output. The shell asks
with `if grep -q pattern file; then`.

For this to work, "found nothing" must be a *result that grep can report*,
not a failure. `grep` uses three values:

- 0 when it found a match.
- 1 when it found no match.
- 2 for a real error, for example a file that does not exist.

One small integer carries all three results, as
[Talk to the Operating System](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/talking-to-the-os/)
describes.

**The program counted to get the line number.** The search does not know the
line number. Nothing in the input marks the start of line 2. The loop over
`takeDelimiter('\n')` counts each line. It is the same streaming loop as in the
last two chapters.

**The match compares bytes, and this has a limit.** A search for `é` works,
because the program compares its two bytes like all other bytes. A search
that ignores case does not work. A change to upper case is correct for a byte
only in ASCII. With `-i` on UTF-8, real `grep` must know Unicode case folding,
which is a much larger problem than the search.

## Check yourself

The search returns `?usize`, the position of a match, not `bool`. Here, the
program only compares the result with null. Why not return `bool`?

Usually, a caller needs the position next, and to return the position costs
nothing. `grep -o` prints only the part that matched. `grep --color`
highlights that part. A replace tool must know where to splice.

If the function returns `bool`, it discards information that the loop already
had. As a habit, return the position of what you found, not only a yes or no.

## If you know C

The search is the same, and the C standard library can do it for you:

```c
char *hit = strstr(line, pattern);   /* NULL when absent */
```

Two differences are important. First, `strstr` needs two null-terminated
strings. Thus `strstr` cannot search a slice of a larger buffer until you cut
the slice, and usually that means a copy. The Zig version takes lengths, so a
search of a part of a buffer needs no copy.

Second, `strstr` returns a pointer *into* the haystack. That pointer is a
position and an alias at the same time. To get the index, you write
`hit - line`. This pointer arithmetic is valid only because both pointers
point into the same array. A `?usize` gives the same information without the
alias.

The standard library has this function as `std.mem.find`.
[String Recipes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/string-recipes/) covers it. This
chapter writes out the function, so that you can see the loop.

Next: [sort](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/sort/), the first tool that cannot stream.

---

## sort

*Unix Tools. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/sort/*

The first three tools never held more than one full buffer. `sort` cannot do
that. You cannot know which line comes first until you see the last line.
Thus in this chapter, the streaming loop stops. The chapter has a question
that the earlier tools did not have.

**Where are the lines in memory?**

To read the lines, the program must hold all of them. To sort the lines, the
program must move them. After the sort, something must still point at the
correct bytes. This is the ownership question from [Who Owns This
Memory](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/who-owns-this-memory/). `sort` is the first
program where you cannot avoid the question.

There are two answers that work:

- Copy each line into memory that you allocated.
- Keep the full input in one buffer, and sort a list of *pointers into the
  buffer*.

For all input that fits, the real `sort` uses the second answer. To move an
8-byte pointer costs less than to move a 200-byte line, and the preparation
costs nothing.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Sort the lines of `text`, and return slices that point back into `text`.
/// The function copies nothing. Thus the result is valid only while `text` is
/// valid. The caller frees exactly one thing: the list of pointers.
fn sortLines(allocator: std.mem.Allocator, text: []const u8) ![][]const u8 {
    var lines: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;
    errdefer lines.deinit(allocator);

    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(text);
    while (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        try lines.append(allocator, line);
    }

    const slice = try lines.toOwnedSlice(allocator);
    std.mem.sort([]const u8, slice, {}, lessThan);
    return slice;
}

/// Byte order, as in `LC_ALL=C sort`. Thus "Zebra" comes before "apple":
/// upper case is 65..90, and lower case is 97..122.
fn lessThan(_: void, a: []const u8, b: []const u8) bool {
    return std.mem.order(u8, a, b) == .lt;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // A fixed buffer, so this program never uses the heap. The C version builds
    // this arena by hand. Here, the bookkeeping is already written.
    var storage: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&storage);

    const text =
        \\banana
        \\Zebra
        \\apple
        \\cherry
        \\apple
        \\
    ;

    const sorted = try sortLines(fba.allocator(), text);
    defer fba.allocator().free(sorted);

    for (sorted) |line| try out.print("{s}\n", .{line});

    try out.print("\n{d} lines, {d} bytes of pointers, 0 bytes of copied text\n", .{
        sorted.len,
        sorted.len * @sizeOf([]const u8),
    });
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`16-unix-tools.sort`)*

## What just happened

**The program copied nothing.** The last line shows this: 40 bytes of pointers
and zero bytes of copied text. Each entry in the sorted list is a slice that
points back into the original input. Thus the sort of five lines moved five
pointers, and the text stayed exactly where it was.

The contract of the function states the cost of that decision: the result is
valid only while the input buffer is valid. Assume that a function owns the
buffer and returns those slices. Then you have the dangling pointer from [The
Stack](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/the-stack/), but now you have a full array
of dangling pointers.

**`Zebra` sorted before `apple`.** This is not a bug. It is byte order. `Z` is
90 and `a` is 97, so each capital letter sorts before each lower-case letter.
`LC_ALL=C sort` does the same.

Plain `sort` uses the collation of the locale, and the collation puts `apple`
first. For this reason, the two commands give different results on the same
file. An order that is easier for people than byte order is a question about
the locale, not about the sort.

**Both copies of `apple` stayed.** A sort does not remove duplicates. `sort -u`
removes them, in a separate pass. The question "are these adjacent lines
equal?" is cheap only after the sort.

**The full program used no heap.** `FixedBufferAllocator` gives out parts of a
4 KB array on the stack. When the array is full, the allocator returns
`error.OutOfMemory`, as all other allocators do. That is the correct failure
for a tool with a fixed memory budget. A C version uses an arena for the same
job, and the programmer writes the bookkeeping by hand.

## Check yourself

The input has five lines, and the program allocated one thing. What was it?
What must change to sort a file that is too large for memory?

The program allocated the *list of slices*, not the lines. For a file that is
larger than memory, do these steps:

1. Sort the part that fits.
2. Write that sorted run to a temporary file.
3. Do steps 1 and 2 again until no input remains.
4. Merge the sorted runs. Keep only one line from each run in memory at a
   time.

That is an external merge sort. The real `sort` changes to this method for
large files. Because of the merge step, `sort` always could handle files that
are larger than the computer that it runs on.

## If you know C

The table of pointers is the same, and in C you build it by hand:

```c
char *lines[MAX_LINES];       /* pointers into one big buffer */
...
qsort(lines, n, sizeof(char *), cmp);
```

Zig removes two problems. The first problem: the comparator of `qsort` gets
`const void *` and starts with a cast. The classic bug is in that cast.

The argument is a pointer to the array *element*. Thus for an array of
`char *`, the argument is a `char **`. If you get that one indirection wrong,
the code compiles without a warning and sorts garbage. `std.mem.sort` is
generic over the element type, so the comparator gets the two elements
themselves.

The second problem: `MAX_LINES` is a real limit. A C version must select the
limit in advance and check it on each append. `ArrayList` grows and asks the
allocator for memory, and the allocator can refuse.

Next: [cut](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/cut/), which returns to one line at a time.

---

## cut

*Unix Tools. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/cut/*

`cut -d: -f2` takes the second field from each line. It is the smallest tool
here. Its correctness depends fully on its edge cases. Thus the chapter must
state exactly what a split is.

Split `a:b:c` at `:`, and you get three fields. One rule covers all the other
cases: **n delimiters make n+1 fields, always.** The split does not merge a
run of delimiters, and it does not skip empty fields.

With that rule, the difficult inputs have clear answers. With a different
rule, you must add more and more special cases to fix them.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Field `n` of `line`. The count starts at 1, as in cut. Returns null when
/// the line has fewer fields. Null is different from an empty field, and the
/// two must stay different.
fn field(line: []const u8, delimiter: u8, n: usize) ?[]const u8 {
    if (n == 0) return null;

    var it = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, line, delimiter);
    var i: usize = 1;
    while (it.next()) |part| : (i += 1) {
        if (i == n) return part;
    }
    return null;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const rows = [_][]const u8{
        "alice:30:london",
        "bob:25:paris",
        // An empty field in the middle: two delimiters with nothing between them.
        "carol::berlin",
        // Fewer fields than the program asks for.
        "dave",
    };

    for ([_]usize{ 1, 2 }) |n| {
        try out.print("--- field {d}\n", .{n});
        for (rows) |row| {
            if (field(row, ':', n)) |value| {
                try out.print("{s} -> \"{s}\"\n", .{ row, value });
            } else {
                try out.print("{s} -> (no such field)\n", .{row});
            }
        }
        try out.writeAll("\n");
    }

    // A split never adds or loses a field: n delimiters give n+1 fields, also
    // when some of the fields are empty.
    var it = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, "carol::berlin", ':');
    var parts: usize = 0;
    while (it.next()) |_| parts += 1;
    try out.print("\"carol::berlin\" has {d} fields\n", .{parts});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`16-unix-tools.cut`)*

## What just happened

**`carol::berlin` has three fields, and the middle field is empty.** There are
two delimiters and three fields, as the rule says. Many splitters that look
correct get this case wrong.

A programmer can want to treat a run of delimiters as one delimiter, because a
split at whitespace usually works that way. For a delimited data format, that
is wrong, and no error shows the mistake. Each field after the run moves by
one. Field 3 of a CSV row becomes field 2, and the data is corrupt, but no
error tells you.

**An empty field and an absent field print differently.** In
`carol::berlin`, field 2 is `""`. In `dave`, field 2 is `(no such field)`. For
this reason, the function returns `?[]const u8`, not `[]const u8`:

- An empty string is a field that exists and is empty.
- Null means that there is no field.

If you merge the two, a caller cannot see the difference between "this record
has no email" and "the email of this record is blank". A program that acts on
the record must know which of the two it has.

Each field is a slice of its line, as in the last chapter. The program copies
no bytes. For this reason, `cut` runs at the speed of the disk.

## Check yourself

The real `cut` has a special case for a line that has no delimiter.
`cut -d: -f2` prints the full line, not nothing. Does the rule above explain
this behavior, or is it an exception?

It is an exception. By the rule, zero delimiters means one field. Thus field 1
is the full line, and field 2 does not exist. The program above follows the
rule: `dave` gives `"dave"` for field 1 and no field 2.

POSIX makes `cut` print a line that has no delimiter without change, for all
field numbers. POSIX gives a reason. If you drop a line that you did not
parse, the result is worse than if you send the line on. The `-s` flag
disables the exception.

## If you know C

C has `strtok`. Do not use `strtok` for this work:

```c
char *field = strtok(line, ":");
while (field) field = strtok(NULL, ":");
```

`strtok` has three problems:

- It **changes the input**. It writes `\0` over each delimiter. Thus it
  destroys the line that you got, and you cannot use the original line after
  the loop.
- It **merges runs of delimiters**. Thus `carol::berlin` gives two fields, not
  three. That is the bug described above, built into the standard library.
- It keeps its position in a **static variable**. Thus it is not reentrant.
  Two loops that use it at the same time corrupt each other.

`strtok_r` fixes only the third problem. The merge is intentional, because
the authors of `strtok` made it for whitespace. Programmers still use `strtok` on data
formats because it is a habit.

The `splitScalar` function of Zig returns slices of the original. It does not
change the input, it does not merge delimiters, and it keeps no static state.

Next: [printf](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/printf/), where a number must become text.

---

## printf

*Unix Tools. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/printf/*

Each tool before this one moved bytes that already existed. `printf` makes new
bytes. For the number 42, some code must make the two characters `4` and `2`.
Nothing in the computer does this for you. 42 is a bit pattern, `"42"` is two
bytes, and you write the arithmetic for the conversion.

The algorithm is division:

1. Divide the number by ten.
2. The remainder is the last digit.
3. The quotient is the rest of the number.
4. Do the steps again until the quotient is zero.

These steps give you all the digits correctly, but in reverse order, because
you get the last digit first.

Thus write the digits into the **end** of a buffer, and move to the front.
When you stop, the number is the tail of the buffer. Return a slice from the
position where you stopped. You never have to reverse the digits in a second
pass.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Write `value` as decimal into `buf`, and return the part that it used.
///
/// The digits come out in reverse. The only cheap way to get a digit is
/// `value % 10`, and that gives you the *last* digit. Thus the function writes
/// the digits into the end of the buffer. It takes the slice from the
/// position where it stopped.
fn decimal(buf: []u8, value: i64) []const u8 {
    if (value == 0) {
        buf[0] = '0';
        return buf[0..1];
    }

    const negative = value < 0;
    // Negate in a wider type. The most negative i64 has no positive
    // equivalent, so `-value` in the same type is an overflow. Printf code
    // that people write by hand often gets this wrong.
    var n: u64 = if (negative) @as(u64, @intCast(-@as(i128, value))) else @intCast(value);

    var i = buf.len;
    while (n > 0) {
        i -= 1;
        buf[i] = '0' + @as(u8, @intCast(n % 10));
        n /= 10;
    }
    if (negative) {
        i -= 1;
        buf[i] = '-';
    }
    return buf[i..];
}

/// The scanner: copy bytes until '%', then dispatch on the next byte.
fn format(out: *std.Io.Writer, comptime fmt: []const u8, args: []const i64) !void {
    var arg: usize = 0;
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < fmt.len) : (i += 1) {
        if (fmt[i] != '%') {
            try out.writeByte(fmt[i]);
            continue;
        }
        i += 1;
        if (i == fmt.len) break;
        switch (fmt[i]) {
            'd' => {
                var digits: [24]u8 = undefined;
                try out.writeAll(decimal(&digits, args[arg]));
                arg += 1;
            },
            // With %%, you print the character that the scanner looks for.
            '%' => try out.writeByte('%'),
            else => {
                // Unknown specifier: print it back. Do not guess.
                try out.writeByte('%');
                try out.writeByte(fmt[i]);
            },
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var digits: [24]u8 = undefined;
    for ([_]i64{ 0, 7, 42, -1, 1234567890, std.math.minInt(i64) }) |n| {
        try out.print("{s}\n", .{decimal(&digits, n)});
    }
    try out.writeAll("\n");

    try format(out, "%d + %d = %d\n", &.{ 2, 3, 5 });
    try format(out, "100%% of %d\n", &.{7});
    try format(out, "unknown %q stays put\n", &.{});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`16-unix-tools.printf`)*

## What just happened

**Zero needed its own line of code.** The loop runs while the value is more
than zero. Thus for zero, the loop never runs, and you get an empty string. An
integer formatter that you write by hand needs this special case at the top.
Without the special case, a count of 0 prints as nothing.

**The most negative number printed correctly.** This is the main trap in this
program. The obvious way to handle a negative number is to keep the sign and
negate: `n = -value`. For `i64`, that works for all values except one.

The range is -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807. Thus the smallest
value has no positive equivalent, and `-value` overflows. In C, that is
undefined behaviour. In practice, C gives you the same negative number back.
After that, the loop makes garbage or does not stop.

The program negates in a wider type before it narrows the value. Thus the
intermediate value has space. In a build with safety checks on, a mistake here
stops the program, and the program does not print nonsense. That is [the main
reason](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/when-checks-are-off/) to develop in a
safety build.

**The scanner is a state machine with two states**: it copies bytes, or it
holds a `%`. A format string needs nothing more. `%%` exists because `%` is
special. Thus you need a way to say that you want the character itself.

**An unknown specifier printed itself back.** `%q` came out as `%q`. The
program did not drop it or guess its meaning. When you cannot know the
intention, print the input without change. This helps the user find the typo.

## Check yourself

The buffer for the digits is 24 bytes. Where does that number come from, and
what occurs if the buffer is too small?

The largest `i64` has 19 digits. With a sign, that is 20, so 24 has more space
than necessary. If the buffer is too small, the writes go past the front of
the buffer. In a safety build, the program catches an index-out-of-bounds. In
a release build, the writes go into memory that you do not own.

You must calculate this buffer size by hand, and the size must be correct.
Thus real implementations write the bound next to the buffer. They do not
select a round number.

## If you know C

You wrote this loop before, and you know the problem of `INT_MIN`:

```c
if (value < 0) { *p++ = '-'; value = -value; }   /* UB at INT_MIN */
```

The usual C fix is to do the arithmetic on a negative accumulator, so that no
negation is necessary. The Zig fix here is to widen first, which is easier to
read.

C also makes you build the argument list. `printf` is variadic, so you need
`va_list`, `va_arg`, and a promise to the compiler. The promise is that the
types in the format string match the arguments that you gave. The language
does not check the promise.

`%d` with a `long` is undefined behaviour. In this way, a `printf` that looks
correct often corrupts a program. Modern compilers give a warning through
`__attribute__((format))`. But compiler authors added that warning later,
outside the language itself.

Zig intentionally has no variadic functions. `std.fmt` takes a tuple, and the
compiler checks the format string against the tuple at compile time. A
mismatch is a build error, not a problem at run time. The chapter about this
is [Formatting](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/formatting/).

Next: [make](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/make/), the last tool, and the only tool that is
really an algorithm.

---

## make

*Unix Tools. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/make/*

People know `make` as a language with strange rules about tabs. Remove the
syntax, and two small ideas remain. This chapter builds both ideas, so that
the tool is easier to understand.

The first idea: **the targets make a graph.** `app` needs `main.o` and
`util.o`, and each object needs its `.c` file. To build in the correct order,
visit a node only after all of the nodes that it depends on. That is a
topological sort.

The second idea: **a timestamp decides if work occurs.** A target is stale if
one of its dependencies is newer than the target. Because of this one
comparison, `make` is faster than a shell script that builds everything again.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Rule = struct {
    target: []const u8,
    needs: []const []const u8,
    /// In place of the mtime of the file. Higher is newer. 0 means absent.
    stamp: u64,
};

/// Visit the dependencies before the target that depends on them, and do not
/// loop. This is all of the order logic of make. State 1 ("visit in progress")
/// changes an infinite recursion into an error that you can report.
fn order(
    rules: []const Rule,
    target: []const u8,
    state: []u8,
    out: *std.ArrayList([]const u8),
    allocator: std.mem.Allocator,
) !void {
    const idx = indexOf(rules, target) orelse return; // a source file, not a rule
    switch (state[idx]) {
        2 => return, // already scheduled
        1 => return error.CircularDependency,
        else => {},
    }
    state[idx] = 1;
    for (rules[idx].needs) |need| try order(rules, need, state, out, allocator);
    state[idx] = 2;
    try out.append(allocator, target);
}

fn indexOf(rules: []const Rule, name: []const u8) ?usize {
    for (rules, 0..) |rule, i| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, rule.target, name)) return i;
    }
    return null;
}

fn stampOf(rules: []const Rule, name: []const u8, sources: []const Rule) u64 {
    if (indexOf(rules, name)) |i| return rules[i].stamp;
    if (indexOf(sources, name)) |i| return sources[i].stamp;
    return 0;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var storage: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&storage);
    const allocator = fba.allocator();

    const sources = [_]Rule{
        .{ .target = "main.c", .needs = &.{}, .stamp = 30 },
        .{ .target = "util.c", .needs = &.{}, .stamp = 10 },
    };
    const rules = [_]Rule{
        .{ .target = "main.o", .needs = &.{"main.c"}, .stamp = 20 },
        .{ .target = "util.o", .needs = &.{"util.c"}, .stamp = 20 },
        .{ .target = "app", .needs = &.{ "main.o", "util.o" }, .stamp = 25 },
    };

    // `@splat`, not the `**` repeat operator. The language removed `**`.
    var state: [rules.len]u8 = @splat(0);
    var scheduled: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty;
    defer scheduled.deinit(allocator);
    try order(&rules, "app", &state, &scheduled, allocator);

    try out.writeAll("build order:\n");
    for (scheduled.items) |target| try out.print("  {s}\n", .{target});

    // A target is stale when one of its dependencies is newer than the target.
    // Because of this one comparison, make is faster than a shell script.
    try out.writeAll("\nwhat actually needs rebuilding:\n");
    for (scheduled.items) |target| {
        const i = indexOf(&rules, target).?;
        var stale = false;
        for (rules[i].needs) |need| {
            if (stampOf(&rules, need, &sources) > rules[i].stamp) stale = true;
        }
        try out.print("  {s: <7} {s}\n", .{ target, if (stale) "rebuild" else "up to date" });
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`16-unix-tools.make`)*

The stamps are in place of file modification times, and a higher stamp is
newer. `main.c` is 30 and `main.o` is 20. Thus someone edited the source after
the last build of the object. `util.c` is 10 and `util.o` is 20, so `util.o`
is current.

## What just happened

**The build order put the objects before the binary.** No line declared that
order. The order is the result of two rules: visit the dependencies first, and
append each target only on the return. This is depth-first post-order, and it
is how you write a topological sort in code.

**Only `main.o` needed a new build.** Its source is newer than `main.o`.
`util.o` is newer than its source, so the program skipped `util.o`. Here,
`make` saves time. On a large project, almost all targets are current, and
the check costs one integer comparison for each target.

**The `state` array is the cycle check.** The program marks each target 1
while it visits the dependencies of that target. It marks the target 2 when the
visit is complete. If the program finds a target that is still 1, the graph has
a loop.

In that case, the program returns `error.CircularDependency`. It does not
recurse until the stack overflows. Real `make` also finds the loop. It prints
`Circular b <- a dependency dropped`, removes the edge, and continues.

**The program does not model one thing.** When `make` builds `main.o` again,
the timestamp of `main.o` becomes *now*. Then `app` is stale too. Real `make`
calculates again after each step, so the stale state moves up the graph. The
program above never runs a command. Thus it reports only one snapshot of the
stale targets.

## Check yourself

`make` is famously strict about a rule: a recipe line starts with a tab, not
spaces. You built the tool above. Does that rule do any work?

The rule does almost no work, and the author of `make` said this too. The tab shows the
difference between a recipe line and a continuation of the rule. A better
parser can find that difference without the tab.

The rule stays because a change can break each Makefile that exists. Many
things in Unix stay the same for this reason. The graph and the timestamps are
the design. The tab is an early decision that nobody could change later.

## If you know C

Almost certainly, you wrote a Makefile but never wrote `make`. The
translation is direct. The prerequisites of a rule are its edges. `$@` and
`$<` are the target and the first prerequisite of the node that you are at.

A C implementation must do one thing that this program skips. It must get the
timestamp with `stat`, and it must handle a file that does not exist. A target
that does not exist has no mtime. That target must compare as "older than
everything", so that `make` builds it. The C version uses 0 for this case, and
that is the correct simplification.

## Where to go next

This is the last of the seven programs. Together, the programs use these
ideas:

- A fixed buffer with a streaming loop.
- A state machine.
- A search.
- An ownership decision.
- A delimiter.
- A conversion.
- A graph.

[Groundwork](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/) gives the same treatment to the
language itself, and it starts from what a byte is. For a larger project, see
the [ORM](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/). It is one library with an open design, with one
decision in each chapter.

---

## A Lexer

*Tiny Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/lexer/*

A compiler is a short pipeline of programs. Each program takes the output of
the program before it, and knows almost nothing about the other programs. This
section builds that pipeline. The first stage changes characters into words.

Source code comes in as bytes. `let total = 0;` is fourteen bytes. Nothing in
the bytes says that `let` is a keyword, or that `total` is one name and not
five letters. The stage that makes these decisions is the *lexer*, and its work
is called *lexing*.

When lexing is a separate pass, each later stage is easier to write. The parser
never sees a space and never counts a digit. The parser also never checks if
an identifier starts with a keyword.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub const Kind = enum {
    number,
    identifier,
    plus,
    minus,
    star,
    slash,
    lparen,
    rparen,
    lbrace,
    rbrace,
    semi,
    comma,
    assign,
    eq,
    lt,
    kw_let,
    kw_print,
    kw_if,
    kw_else,
    kw_while,
    kw_fn,
    kw_return,
    eof,
    invalid,
};

pub const Token = struct {
    kind: Kind,
    /// A slice into the source. The token owns no memory.
    text: []const u8,
    value: i64 = 0,
    line: usize = 1,
};

/// The words that are not identifiers. The lexer checks this table after it
/// scans a full word. Thus `letter` lexes as an identifier, not as `let` and
/// then `ter`. The scan is greedy first, and the lookup uses the full word.
fn keyword(word: []const u8) ?Kind {
    const table = .{
        .{ "let", Kind.kw_let },
        .{ "print", Kind.kw_print },
        .{ "if", Kind.kw_if },
        .{ "else", Kind.kw_else },
        .{ "while", Kind.kw_while },
        .{ "fn", Kind.kw_fn },
        .{ "return", Kind.kw_return },
    };
    inline for (table) |entry| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, word, entry[0])) return entry[1];
    }
    return null;
}

fn isDigit(c: u8) bool {
    return c >= '0' and c <= '9';
}

fn isAlpha(c: u8) bool {
    return (c >= 'a' and c <= 'z') or (c >= 'A' and c <= 'Z') or c == '_';
}

/// Put the tokens of `source` into `out`. Return the part of `out` that has tokens.
pub fn tokenize(source: []const u8, out: []Token) ![]Token {
    var i: usize = 0;
    var line: usize = 1;
    var n: usize = 0;

    while (i < source.len) {
        const c = source[i];

        // Whitespace has no meaning, except that it separates tokens. Thus the
        // lexer drops the whitespace here, and the parser never sees it.
        if (c == '\n') {
            line += 1;
            i += 1;
            continue;
        }
        if (c == ' ' or c == '\t' or c == '\r') {
            i += 1;
            continue;
        }

        if (n == out.len) return error.TooManyTokens;
        const start = i;

        if (isDigit(c)) {
            var value: i64 = 0;
            while (i < source.len and isDigit(source[i])) : (i += 1) {
                value = value * 10 + (source[i] - '0');
            }
            out[n] = .{ .kind = .number, .text = source[start..i], .value = value, .line = line };
        } else if (isAlpha(c)) {
            while (i < source.len and (isAlpha(source[i]) or isDigit(source[i]))) : (i += 1) {}
            const word = source[start..i];
            out[n] = .{ .kind = keyword(word) orelse .identifier, .text = word, .line = line };
        } else {
            i += 1;
            // Lookahead is necessary only here, because `=` and `==` start the same.
            const kind: Kind = switch (c) {
                '+' => .plus,
                '-' => .minus,
                '*' => .star,
                '/' => .slash,
                '(' => .lparen,
                ')' => .rparen,
                '{' => .lbrace,
                '}' => .rbrace,
                ';' => .semi,
                ',' => .comma,
                '<' => .lt,
                '=' => blk: {
                    if (i < source.len and source[i] == '=') {
                        i += 1;
                        break :blk .eq;
                    }
                    break :blk .assign;
                },
                else => .invalid,
            };
            out[n] = .{ .kind = kind, .text = source[start..i], .line = line };
        }
        n += 1;
    }

    if (n == out.len) return error.TooManyTokens;
    out[n] = .{ .kind = .eof, .text = "", .line = line };
    return out[0 .. n + 1];
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const source =
        \\let total = 0;
        \\while (total < 10) {
        \\  total = total + 3;
        \\}
        \\print total;
    ;

    var storage: [128]Token = undefined;
    const tokens = try tokenize(source, &storage);

    try out.print("{d} tokens\n\n", .{tokens.len});
    for (tokens) |token| {
        try out.print("line {d}  {t: <12} \"{s}\"", .{ token.line, token.kind, token.text });
        if (token.kind == .number) try out.print("  value {d}", .{token.value});
        try out.writeAll("\n");
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`17-tiny-lang.lexer`)*

## What just happened

**The whitespace is gone.** The parser in the next chapter never sees a space,
a tab or a newline. The lexer reads these characters and makes no token for
them, thus each later stage is simpler. The line number stays, and each token
holds it. An error message without a line number is almost useless, and the
lexer is the last stage that knows the line.

**`total` became one token, not five.** The scan is greedy: it takes as many
characters as it can. When a letter starts a word, the scan continues to take
letters and digits until it finds a different character. Because of this one
rule, `total3` is one identifier. `3total` is a number and then an identifier,
and the parser correctly rejects it.

**A keyword is an identifier that the lexer finds in the keyword table.** The
scanner does not try to match `let` first. It scans the full word, and then it
searches the table for the word. Only this order works. If the scanner matched
`let` first, it would lex `letter` as `let` and then `ter`. Each language with
keywords uses this order.

**`=` and `==` are the reason for lookahead.** After the scanner reads `=`, it
examines the next character. Then it decides which token it made. One
character of lookahead is enough for this language, and for most languages.
When a language needs more lookahead, the design has a real cost. That cost is
the reason that `>>` in old C++ template syntax was a well-known problem.

**The lexer allocated nothing.** The `text` of each token is a slice that
points back into the source. The lexer copied no bytes to make the tokens.
When the program frees the source, the tokens become invalid. The
[sort](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/sort/) chapter made the same decision to borrow
memory, and a compiler makes the same decision too.

## Check yourself

The lexer never rejects `let let = 3;` or `4 5 6`. Should the lexer reject
them?

No, because the split is intentional. The job of a lexer is to identify the
*words*. The lexer does not check if the sentence has a meaning. Both inputs
are valid streams of tokens. Both inputs are also errors, and the parser
reports them. Because there are two separate stages, an error message can tell
you which stage failed.

## If you know C

In C, a lexer is a `switch` on the current character inside a loop. It has an
enum of token types, and a struct that holds a pointer, a length and a line
number. The code above does the same. There are some small differences.

A C token holds `char *start; int len;` as two fields, and you must keep the
two fields correct manually. A Zig slice is those two fields, and the language
keeps them together.

Also, a C keyword lookup is usually a chain of `strcmp` calls. The version here
uses a comptime `inline for` over a table. The compiler generates the
comparisons, but you write the table one time. Neither version uses a hash,
and with seven keywords neither version needs one.

The next chapter is a parser. The parser takes this flat list and finds the
structure in it.

---

## A Parser

*Tiny Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/parser/*

The lexer made a flat list. `1 + 2 * 3` is five tokens in a row, and a row has
no shape. Nothing in the row tells you which operation occurs first. The job of
the parser is to find the shape, and the shape is a tree.

In the tree for `1 + 2 * 3`, the `+` is at the top, because the `+` is the
*last* operation. The right operand of the `+` is all of `2 * 3`. A tree runs
from the deepest node to the top, thus the deepest node runs first. This means
that **precedence is depth**.

This fact gives a more useful view of the problem. You do not need a rule that
says `*` binds tighter than `+`. You need `*` to be deeper in the tree. It is
possible to write a parser that puts `*` deeper, and that parser never reads a
table.

## The method

Write one function for each precedence level, with the loosest level first.
Each function gets its operands from the function for the next tighter level.

```
comparison  ->  sum   ( "<" | "==" sum )*
sum         ->  product   ( "+" | "-" product )*
product     ->  unary   ( "*" | "/" unary )*
unary       ->  "-" unary | primary
primary     ->  number | name | "(" comparison ")"
```

`sum` cannot see a `*`. `sum` asks `product` for each operand. `product` reads
each multiplication and returns a complete subtree. Thus the multiplication is
inside the operand of the addition, and that is exactly the meaning of "binds
tighter". The call chain *is* the precedence table.

This method is called **recursive descent**. Most production compilers use it,
because the code is easy to read.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const lex = @import("lexer.zig");

pub const Kind = enum {
    number,
    variable,
    binary,
    unary,
    let,
    assign,
    print,
    @"if",
    @"while",
    block,
    fn_decl,
    call,
    ret,
};

/// Children are a linked list, not a slice. Thus the full tree is in one flat
/// array, and each node has a fixed size. `first` starts the list, and `next`
/// continues it.
pub const Node = struct {
    kind: Kind,
    op: lex.Kind = .eof,
    value: i64 = 0,
    name: []const u8 = "",
    /// The operand, the condition, or the value for the assignment.
    a: ?u32 = null,
    /// The second operand, or the body of an if or a while.
    b: ?u32 = null,
    /// The else branch.
    c: ?u32 = null,
    first: ?u32 = null,
    next: ?u32 = null,
};

/// The error set is explicit, not inferred. These functions are mutually
/// recursive: `primary` calls `expression` again for a group in parentheses.
/// An inferred error set cannot close a cycle, and the compiler reports a
/// dependency loop.
pub const Error = error{ UnexpectedToken, TooManyNodes, TooManyTokens };

pub const Parser = struct {
    tokens: []const lex.Token,
    pos: usize = 0,
    nodes: []Node,
    used: u32 = 0,

    fn peek(p: *Parser) lex.Kind {
        return p.tokens[p.pos].kind;
    }

    fn accept(p: *Parser, kind: lex.Kind) bool {
        if (p.peek() != kind) return false;
        p.pos += 1;
        return true;
    }

    fn expect(p: *Parser, kind: lex.Kind) Error!lex.Token {
        if (p.peek() != kind) return error.UnexpectedToken;
        defer p.pos += 1;
        return p.tokens[p.pos];
    }

    fn add(p: *Parser, node: Node) Error!u32 {
        if (p.used == p.nodes.len) return error.TooManyNodes;
        p.nodes[p.used] = node;
        p.used += 1;
        return p.used - 1;
    }

    // Each level reads its own operators, and gets its operands from the next
    // level. That call order *is* the precedence. `product` binds tighter than
    // `sum`, because `sum` asks `product` for both sides before it examines `+`.

    pub fn expression(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        return p.comparison();
    }

    fn comparison(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        var left = try p.sum();
        while (p.peek() == .lt or p.peek() == .eq) {
            const op = p.peek();
            p.pos += 1;
            const right = try p.sum();
            left = try p.add(.{ .kind = .binary, .op = op, .a = left, .b = right });
        }
        return left;
    }

    fn sum(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        var left = try p.product();
        while (p.peek() == .plus or p.peek() == .minus) {
            const op = p.peek();
            p.pos += 1;
            const right = try p.product();
            left = try p.add(.{ .kind = .binary, .op = op, .a = left, .b = right });
        }
        return left;
    }

    fn product(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        var left = try p.unary();
        while (p.peek() == .star or p.peek() == .slash) {
            const op = p.peek();
            p.pos += 1;
            const right = try p.unary();
            left = try p.add(.{ .kind = .binary, .op = op, .a = left, .b = right });
        }
        return left;
    }

    fn unary(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        if (p.accept(.minus)) {
            return p.add(.{ .kind = .unary, .op = .minus, .a = try p.unary() });
        }
        return p.primary();
    }

    fn primary(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        const token = p.tokens[p.pos];
        switch (token.kind) {
            .number => {
                p.pos += 1;
                return p.add(.{ .kind = .number, .value = token.value });
            },
            .identifier => {
                p.pos += 1;
                // One token of lookahead decides between a name and a call.
                // The expression grammar needs lookahead only here.
                if (p.peek() != .lparen) {
                    return p.add(.{ .kind = .variable, .name = token.text });
                }
                p.pos += 1;
                const node = try p.add(.{ .kind = .call, .name = token.text });
                var last: ?u32 = null;
                while (p.peek() != .rparen) {
                    const arg = try p.expression();
                    if (last) |l| p.nodes[l].next = arg else p.nodes[node].first = arg;
                    last = arg;
                    if (!p.accept(.comma)) break;
                }
                _ = try p.expect(.rparen);
                return node;
            },
            // Parentheses need no precedence rule of their own. They start
            // again at the loosest level, and thus they change the order of
            // operations.
            .lparen => {
                p.pos += 1;
                const inner = try p.expression();
                _ = try p.expect(.rparen);
                return inner;
            },
            else => return error.UnexpectedToken,
        }
    }

    pub fn statement(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        if (p.accept(.kw_let)) {
            const name = try p.expect(.identifier);
            _ = try p.expect(.assign);
            const value = try p.expression();
            _ = try p.expect(.semi);
            return p.add(.{ .kind = .let, .name = name.text, .a = value });
        }
        if (p.accept(.kw_print)) {
            const value = try p.expression();
            _ = try p.expect(.semi);
            return p.add(.{ .kind = .print, .a = value });
        }
        if (p.accept(.kw_if)) {
            _ = try p.expect(.lparen);
            const cond = try p.expression();
            _ = try p.expect(.rparen);
            const then = try p.block();
            const other: ?u32 = if (p.accept(.kw_else)) try p.block() else null;
            return p.add(.{ .kind = .@"if", .a = cond, .b = then, .c = other });
        }
        if (p.accept(.kw_fn)) {
            const name = try p.expect(.identifier);
            _ = try p.expect(.lparen);
            const node = try p.add(.{ .kind = .fn_decl, .name = name.text });
            var last: ?u32 = null;
            while (p.peek() == .identifier) {
                const param = try p.expect(.identifier);
                const child = try p.add(.{ .kind = .variable, .name = param.text });
                if (last) |l| p.nodes[l].next = child else p.nodes[node].first = child;
                last = child;
                if (!p.accept(.comma)) break;
            }
            _ = try p.expect(.rparen);
            p.nodes[node].b = try p.block();
            return node;
        }
        if (p.accept(.kw_return)) {
            const value: ?u32 = if (p.peek() == .semi) null else try p.expression();
            _ = try p.expect(.semi);
            return p.add(.{ .kind = .ret, .a = value });
        }
        if (p.accept(.kw_while)) {
            _ = try p.expect(.lparen);
            const cond = try p.expression();
            _ = try p.expect(.rparen);
            const body = try p.block();
            return p.add(.{ .kind = .@"while", .a = cond, .b = body });
        }
        const name = try p.expect(.identifier);
        _ = try p.expect(.assign);
        const value = try p.expression();
        _ = try p.expect(.semi);
        return p.add(.{ .kind = .assign, .name = name.text, .a = value });
    }

    fn block(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        _ = try p.expect(.lbrace);
        const node = try p.add(.{ .kind = .block });
        try p.statementsUntil(node, .rbrace);
        _ = try p.expect(.rbrace);
        return node;
    }

    fn statementsUntil(p: *Parser, parent: u32, stop: lex.Kind) Error!void {
        var last: ?u32 = null;
        while (p.peek() != stop and p.peek() != .eof) {
            const child = try p.statement();
            if (last) |l| p.nodes[l].next = child else p.nodes[parent].first = child;
            last = child;
        }
    }

    pub fn program(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        const node = try p.add(.{ .kind = .block });
        try p.statementsUntil(node, .eof);
        return node;
    }
};

/// Print the tree as an S-expression. An S-expression is the shape without the
/// syntax. Only the nesting remains, thus the precedence is visible.
pub fn show(nodes: []const Node, index: u32, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    const node = nodes[index];
    switch (node.kind) {
        .number => try out.print("{d}", .{node.value}),
        .variable => try out.print("{s}", .{node.name}),
        .unary => {
            try out.writeAll("(neg ");
            try show(nodes, node.a.?, out);
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
        .binary => {
            const symbol = switch (node.op) {
                .plus => "+",
                .minus => "-",
                .star => "*",
                .slash => "/",
                .lt => "<",
                .eq => "==",
                else => "?",
            };
            try out.print("({s} ", .{symbol});
            try show(nodes, node.a.?, out);
            try out.writeAll(" ");
            try show(nodes, node.b.?, out);
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
        .let, .assign => {
            try out.print("({s} {s} ", .{ if (node.kind == .let) "let" else "set", node.name });
            try show(nodes, node.a.?, out);
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
        .print => {
            try out.writeAll("(print ");
            try show(nodes, node.a.?, out);
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
        .@"if" => {
            try out.writeAll("(if ");
            try show(nodes, node.a.?, out);
            try out.writeAll(" ");
            try show(nodes, node.b.?, out);
            if (node.c) |else_branch| {
                try out.writeAll(" ");
                try show(nodes, else_branch, out);
            }
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
        .@"while" => {
            try out.writeAll("(while ");
            try show(nodes, node.a.?, out);
            try out.writeAll(" ");
            try show(nodes, node.b.?, out);
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
        .call => {
            try out.print("(call {s}", .{node.name});
            var arg = node.first;
            while (arg) |a| : (arg = nodes[a].next) {
                try out.writeAll(" ");
                try show(nodes, a, out);
            }
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
        .ret => {
            try out.writeAll("(return");
            if (node.a) |value| {
                try out.writeAll(" ");
                try show(nodes, value, out);
            }
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
        .fn_decl => {
            try out.print("(fn {s} (", .{node.name});
            var param = node.first;
            var first = true;
            while (param) |pa| : (param = nodes[pa].next) {
                if (!first) try out.writeAll(" ");
                try out.print("{s}", .{nodes[pa].name});
                first = false;
            }
            try out.writeAll(") ");
            try show(nodes, node.b.?, out);
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
        .block => {
            try out.writeAll("(block");
            var child = node.first;
            while (child) |c| : (child = nodes[c].next) {
                try out.writeAll(" ");
                try show(nodes, c, out);
            }
            try out.writeAll(")");
        },
    }
}

pub fn parse(source: []const u8, tokens: []lex.Token, nodes: []Node) !struct { root: u32, used: u32 } {
    const stream = try lex.tokenize(source, tokens);
    var p: Parser = .{ .tokens = stream, .nodes = nodes };
    return .{ .root = try p.program(), .used = p.used };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var tokens: [128]lex.Token = undefined;
    var nodes: [128]Node = undefined;

    // Precedence, without the syntax. Nothing reads a table. `*` is deeper
    // than `+` because `sum` called `product` first.
    try out.writeAll("precedence\n");
    for ([_][]const u8{ "1 + 2 * 3;", "(1 + 2) * 3;", "1 - 2 - 3;", "0 - -4;" }) |line| {
        const stream = try lex.tokenize(line, &tokens);
        var p: Parser = .{ .tokens = stream, .nodes = &nodes };
        const root = try p.expression();
        try out.print("  {s: <14} ", .{line});
        try show(&nodes, root, out);
        try out.writeAll("\n");
    }

    const source =
        \\let total = 0;
        \\while (total < 10) {
        \\  total = total + 3;
        \\}
        \\print total;
    ;

    const tree = try parse(source, &tokens, &nodes);
    try out.print("\nthe program, as a tree ({d} nodes)\n  ", .{tree.used});
    try show(&nodes, tree.root, out);
    try out.writeAll("\n");

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`17-tiny-lang.parser`)*

## What just happened

**`1 + 2 * 3` became `(+ 1 (* 2 3))`**, and `(1 + 2) * 3` became
`(* (+ 1 2) 3)`. A simple left-to-right order uses the same five tokens as the
first case, but it makes a completely different tree.

**Parentheses needed no precedence rule.** When `primary` sees a `(`, it starts
again at the *loosest* level, and then it expects a `)`. Nothing more is
necessary. Parentheses work for each expression, because they start the chain
again.

**`1 - 2 - 3` became `(- (- 1 2) 3)`, not `(- 1 (- 2 3))`.** Subtraction is
left-associative, and the loop makes it left-associative. Each level reads its
operators in a `while` loop, and puts the result so far into the left side. If
the function called itself for the right side instead, the same grammar would
make the other tree. Then the answer would be 2, not -4. A parser for a
right-associative operator, for example exponentiation in languages that have
it, intentionally uses that method.

**The full tree is one flat array.** A node holds indices, not pointers. The
children of a node are a linked list, through the `first` and `next` fields.
Thus the parser allocates nothing more than the array that it gets. Each node
has a fixed size, and the program can copy or discard the full tree in one
step. Production compilers also do this, for the cache behaviour as much as
for the simplicity.

**The code gives the error set explicitly, and Zig does not infer it.** These
functions are mutually recursive, because `primary` calls `expression` again
for a group in parentheses. Zig cannot infer an error set around a cycle. The
first version of this snippet did not compile. The error was `dependency loop
with length 6`, which names the cycle and does not point at one function.

## Check yourself

The grammar says `while (cond) { ... }`, and the grammar requires the
parentheses.
With recursive descent, can the language remove the parentheses and accept
`while cond { ... }`?

Yes, and many languages do this. Here, the parentheses do no parsing work. The
condition ends where the block starts. The expression parser stops at the
brace with no extra code, because a brace is not an operator that the parser
recognises.

The parentheses give you a better error message when the condition is
malformed. They also keep the grammar unambiguous if you add a construct
later, where a brace after an expression has a different meaning. Rust
requires the braces and warns about the parentheses for exactly this reason.

## If you know C

The shape is the same in C. The parser is one of the places where a C
implementation and a Zig implementation are the most similar. In C, the nodes
are a `struct Node` with a `kind` enum, a union of payloads, and `struct Node *`
children.

There are two differences. First, indices instead of pointers are a choice in
both languages. In C, you make that choice when you want to grow the node
array. Then the growth does not make each reference into the array invalid. Here, the choice also lets the full tree live in a fixed array, with
no allocator.

Second, in practice a C union payload has no tag. The `kind` field tells you
which member is live, and nothing checks that the field and the member agree.
This mismatch is the classic cause of a compiler bug that occurs on only one
node type. Zig gives you tagged unions for exactly this problem.

The version above avoids the question, because each node has the same fields.
That design is fine with thirteen node kinds, and it would not be fine with
fifty.

The next chapter is an interpreter. The interpreter walks this tree and
produces an answer.

---

## A Tree-Walking Interpreter

*Tiny Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/interpreter/*

After two stages, the source is a tree. In this chapter, the tree runs. The
code for this stage is smaller than the parser.

To evaluate `(+ 1 (* 2 3))`, start at the top. The node is a `+`, thus evaluate
its two children and add them. The left child is `1`, and its value is `1`. The
right child is a `*`, thus evaluate *its* two children and multiply them. There
is no third rule.

The function calls itself one time for each child, thus the recursion has the
same shape as the tree. The recursion stops at numbers and names.

This is a **tree-walking interpreter**. Most languages start this way, and some
languages never needed anything more.

## Two kinds of node

The grammar already separates expressions from statements, and the interpreter
keeps the same split:

- `eval` takes a node and returns an `i64`. Expressions produce values.
- `exec` takes a node and returns nothing. Statements produce effects.

Because the two functions are separate, you can never use a statement as a
value: `exec` has nothing to return. The grammar does not let `print` appear
inside an expression. Thus no code has to check for a `print` in an expression
at run time.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const lex = @import("lexer.zig");
const ast = @import("parser.zig");

pub const Error = error{
    UndefinedVariable,
    TooManyVariables,
    DivideByZero,
    WriteFailed,
};

/// Names to values, in a flat array with a linear search. At this size, the
/// array is the correct choice. At a thousand names, it is the wrong choice.
/// Real interpreters resolve a name to a slot number one time, at compile
/// time. Then this search never occurs at run time.
pub const Env = struct {
    names: [32][]const u8 = undefined,
    values: [32]i64 = undefined,
    count: usize = 0,

    fn find(env: *Env, name: []const u8) ?usize {
        for (env.names[0..env.count], 0..) |candidate, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, candidate, name)) return i;
        }
        return null;
    }

    fn define(env: *Env, name: []const u8, value: i64) Error!void {
        if (env.find(name)) |i| {
            env.values[i] = value;
            return;
        }
        if (env.count == env.names.len) return error.TooManyVariables;
        env.names[env.count] = name;
        env.values[env.count] = value;
        env.count += 1;
    }

    fn get(env: *Env, name: []const u8) Error!i64 {
        const i = env.find(name) orelse return error.UndefinedVariable;
        return env.values[i];
    }
};

pub const Interpreter = struct {
    nodes: []const ast.Node,
    env: Env = .{},
    out: *std.Io.Writer,

    /// Expressions produce a value. Each case does two steps: evaluate the
    /// children, then combine the results. The recursion follows the shape of
    /// the tree exactly, thus this interpreter is short.
    pub fn eval(vm: *Interpreter, index: u32) Error!i64 {
        const node = vm.nodes[index];
        return switch (node.kind) {
            .number => node.value,
            .variable => vm.env.get(node.name),
            .unary => -(try vm.eval(node.a.?)),
            .binary => blk: {
                const left = try vm.eval(node.a.?);
                const right = try vm.eval(node.b.?);
                break :blk switch (node.op) {
                    .plus => left + right,
                    .minus => left - right,
                    .star => left * right,
                    // The language must define division by zero. The machine does not define it.
                    .slash => if (right == 0) error.DivideByZero else @divTrunc(left, right),
                    .lt => @intFromBool(left < right),
                    .eq => @intFromBool(left == right),
                    else => 0,
                };
            },
            else => 0,
        };
    }

    /// Statements produce an effect. `exec` returns nothing. The grammar
    /// already made this distinction.
    pub fn exec(vm: *Interpreter, index: u32) Error!void {
        const node = vm.nodes[index];
        switch (node.kind) {
            .let, .assign => try vm.env.define(node.name, try vm.eval(node.a.?)),
            .print => try vm.out.print("{d}\n", .{try vm.eval(node.a.?)}),
            .@"if" => {
                if (try vm.eval(node.a.?) != 0) {
                    try vm.exec(node.b.?);
                } else if (node.c) |other| {
                    try vm.exec(other);
                }
            },
            // The loop in the interpreted language is a loop in the
            // interpreter. The interpreter has no other way to repeat code.
            .@"while" => while (try vm.eval(node.a.?) != 0) {
                try vm.exec(node.b.?);
            },
            .block => {
                var child = node.first;
                while (child) |c| : (child = vm.nodes[c].next) try vm.exec(c);
            },
            else => {},
        }
    }
};

fn run(source: []const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var tokens: [256]lex.Token = undefined;
    var nodes: [256]ast.Node = undefined;
    const tree = try ast.parse(source, &tokens, &nodes);

    var interp: Interpreter = .{ .nodes = &nodes, .out = out };
    try interp.exec(tree.root);
}

fn report(out: *std.Io.Writer, label: []const u8, result: anyerror!void) !void {
    if (result) |_| {
        try out.print("{s} -> no error\n", .{label});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("{s} -> {t}\n", .{ label, err });
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const program =
        \\let total = 0;
        \\let i = 1;
        \\while (i < 6) {
        \\  total = total + i * i;
        \\  i = i + 1;
        \\}
        \\print total;
        \\if (total == 55) { print 1; } else { print 0; }
    ;

    try out.writeAll("sum of squares 1..5\n");
    try run(program, out);

    // Integer division truncates toward zero. Division by zero is an error
    // that the language defines, not a crash that it gets from the host.
    try out.writeAll("\ndivision\n");
    // The second statement shows the difference. Truncation toward zero
    // gives -3, and floor division would give -4.
    try run("print 7 / 2; print (0 - 7) / 2;", out);
    try report(out, "7 / 0", run("print 7 / 0;", out));

    // The interpreter finds an undefined name at the point where the program uses it.
    try report(out, "print nope;", run("print nope;", out));

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`17-tiny-lang.interpreter`)*

## What just happened

**`while` in the interpreted language is `while` in the interpreter.** Look at
the `.@"while"` case. The case is a Zig loop, and the body of the loop calls
`exec`. The interpreted language gets its loop from Zig, the language of the
interpreter.

The same is true for `if`, and for recursion when the next chapter adds
functions. This property defines a tree-walking interpreter. It is also the
main limit of a tree-walking interpreter: it can only give the control flow
that the host language already has.

**The interpreter finds names with a search through an array.** `Env` compares
each string in its list with the name. This method works with 32 variables, and
it is too slow with a thousand. The reason is that the search occurs *each time
the program reads a variable*, also inside the loop.

Real interpreters solve this problem. Before the program runs, they resolve
each name to a slot number one time. Then a variable read at run time is an
array index. The compiler later in this section does exactly that. The compiler
emits `load` with a slot number, and at that point the name is gone.

**Division by zero is a choice that the language makes.** The divide
instruction of the machine traps. Thus the language must say what division by
zero means. Here, division by zero is an error in the return type. The error
passes through `try` and leaves `run`, the same as other errors. To return an
error and not crash is the choice that
[Errors Are Values](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/errors-are-values/) describes,
now in a language that you wrote.

**`(0 - 7) / 2` printed -3, not -4.** The result truncates toward zero because
the implementation used `@divTrunc`, and floor division would give -4. Both answers
are reasonable: C and Zig truncate, and Python uses floor division. Your
language decides this question, not arithmetic. If you do not choose
intentionally, you get the behaviour of the host language.

**The interpreter found the undefined name at the point where the program used
it.** The parser did not find the error, because the parser does not ask what
names mean. To find the error earlier, a language needs a separate pass between
the parser and the run. That pass is called a resolver. For this type of
mistake, a "compile-time error" is an error from the resolver.

## Check yourself

The `.let` and `.assign` cases do exactly the same thing. Should the two cases
do the same thing?

No. This simplification causes a real bug. `let x = 1;` declares a variable.
`x = 1;` assigns to a variable that must already exist. In the code here, an
assignment to an undeclared name silently creates the name. Thus a typo in a
variable name makes a new variable, not an error.

This bug is the reason that JavaScript added `"use strict"` and Visual Basic
added `Option Explicit`. The fix is two lines: `assign` should find the name,
and fail if the name does not exist. The code here keeps the bug, so that you can
see it.

## If you know C

In C, a tree-walking interpreter is the same recursive `switch`. There are two
differences, and you saw both of them before.

In C, `eval` must return the value and the error. The usual methods are a
sentinel value, an out-parameter, or a global error flag. With each of the
three, "divide by zero" can silently return 0, or set a flag that nobody
checks. `Error!i64` makes the failure part of the return type. Thus a caller
that ignores the failure does not compile.

Also, in C the environment is a linked list of `{char *name; long value; struct
Env *next;}`. The program allocates each node when it needs the node. That
design works until you ask which code frees the list. The version here is a
fixed array inside the interpreter. The array lives as long as the
interpreter, thus there is nothing to free. This is the cheapest correct
design, but it stops working when the language gets closures.

The next chapter adds functions. With functions, the environment is no longer
one flat thing.

---

## Functions and Frames

*Tiny Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/functions/*

The interpreter so far has one set of variables. Functions break that design
immediately. Two calls to the same function must not share one set of
variables. A recursive call must have several sets alive at the same time, one
set for each call.

Thus a call needs its own storage, and that storage is a **frame**. A frame is
the run-time equivalent of the machine-level idea in
[The Stack](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/the-stack/). The difference is that
here you build the frame yourself, and the hardware does not supply it. A call
pushes a frame, a return pops the frame, and the array of frames is the call
stack.

The second problem is less obvious. `return` can be anywhere: inside an `if`,
inside a `while`, or inside a block inside both. `return` must leave all of
those statements and arrive at the call site. The `exec` function is
recursive. Thus `return` must unwind an unknown number of Zig frames.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const lex = @import("lexer.zig");
const ast = @import("parser.zig");

pub const Error = error{
    UndefinedVariable,
    UnknownFunction,
    WrongArgCount,
    TooManyVariables,
    DivideByZero,
    StackOverflow,
    WriteFailed,
    /// Not a failure. `return` must leave all the nested blocks, loops and
    /// ifs around it. An error is the only mechanism that unwinds through any
    /// number of calls. This is the one place where this language uses an
    /// error for control flow, and exactly one caller catches it.
    Return,
};

/// The variables of one call. Frame 0 holds the globals. Thus the lookup
/// searches the current frame first and frame 0 second. Locals shadow
/// globals, and nothing else shadows anything.
const Frame = struct {
    names: [16][]const u8 = undefined,
    values: [16]i64 = undefined,
    count: usize = 0,

    fn find(f: *Frame, name: []const u8) ?usize {
        for (f.names[0..f.count], 0..) |candidate, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, candidate, name)) return i;
        }
        return null;
    }

    fn define(f: *Frame, name: []const u8, value: i64) Error!void {
        if (f.find(name)) |i| {
            f.values[i] = value;
            return;
        }
        if (f.count == f.names.len) return error.TooManyVariables;
        f.names[f.count] = name;
        f.values[f.count] = value;
        f.count += 1;
    }
};

pub const Interpreter = struct {
    nodes: []const ast.Node,
    out: *std.Io.Writer,

    /// Declared functions, by name. Each `fn` statement adds its function when it executes.
    fn_names: [16][]const u8 = undefined,
    fn_nodes: [16]u32 = undefined,
    fn_count: usize = 0,

    /// The call stack, as an array. The depth limit here is intentional. The
    /// limit is a fixed number in the code, not the depth that the stack of
    /// the host allows.
    frames: [64]Frame = undefined,
    depth: usize = 0,
    returned: i64 = 0,

    fn frame(vm: *Interpreter) *Frame {
        return &vm.frames[vm.depth];
    }

    fn lookup(vm: *Interpreter, name: []const u8) Error!i64 {
        if (vm.frame().find(name)) |i| return vm.frame().values[i];
        if (vm.frames[0].find(name)) |i| return vm.frames[0].values[i];
        return error.UndefinedVariable;
    }

    fn call(vm: *Interpreter, index: u32) Error!i64 {
        const node = vm.nodes[index];

        var found: ?u32 = null;
        for (vm.fn_names[0..vm.fn_count], 0..) |candidate, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, candidate, node.name)) found = vm.fn_nodes[i];
        }
        const decl_index = found orelse return error.UnknownFunction;
        const decl = vm.nodes[decl_index];

        // The interpreter evaluates the arguments in the frame of the *caller*,
        // before the new frame exists. If you reverse the order, a parameter
        // can see the value that it will get.
        var args: [8]i64 = undefined;
        var count: usize = 0;
        var arg = node.first;
        while (arg) |a| : (arg = vm.nodes[a].next) {
            if (count == args.len) return error.WrongArgCount;
            args[count] = try vm.eval(a);
            count += 1;
        }

        if (vm.depth + 1 == vm.frames.len) return error.StackOverflow;
        vm.depth += 1;
        defer vm.depth -= 1;
        vm.frame().* = .{};

        var param = decl.first;
        var bound: usize = 0;
        while (param) |pa| : (param = vm.nodes[pa].next) {
            if (bound == count) return error.WrongArgCount;
            try vm.frame().define(vm.nodes[pa].name, args[bound]);
            bound += 1;
        }
        if (bound != count) return error.WrongArgCount;

        // A function that ends without a `return` gives 0. Only this code
        // catches `error.Return`. Thus `error.Return` is a jump to this exact
        // point, not a failure.
        vm.returned = 0;
        vm.exec(decl.b.?) catch |err| switch (err) {
            error.Return => {},
            else => return err,
        };
        return vm.returned;
    }

    pub fn eval(vm: *Interpreter, index: u32) Error!i64 {
        const node = vm.nodes[index];
        return switch (node.kind) {
            .number => node.value,
            .variable => vm.lookup(node.name),
            .call => vm.call(index),
            .unary => -(try vm.eval(node.a.?)),
            .binary => blk: {
                const left = try vm.eval(node.a.?);
                const right = try vm.eval(node.b.?);
                break :blk switch (node.op) {
                    .plus => left + right,
                    .minus => left - right,
                    .star => left * right,
                    .slash => if (right == 0) error.DivideByZero else @divTrunc(left, right),
                    .lt => @intFromBool(left < right),
                    .eq => @intFromBool(left == right),
                    else => 0,
                };
            },
            else => 0,
        };
    }

    pub fn exec(vm: *Interpreter, index: u32) Error!void {
        const node = vm.nodes[index];
        switch (node.kind) {
            .fn_decl => {
                if (vm.fn_count == vm.fn_names.len) return error.TooManyVariables;
                vm.fn_names[vm.fn_count] = node.name;
                vm.fn_nodes[vm.fn_count] = index;
                vm.fn_count += 1;
            },
            .ret => {
                vm.returned = if (node.a) |value| try vm.eval(value) else 0;
                return error.Return;
            },
            .let, .assign => try vm.frame().define(node.name, try vm.eval(node.a.?)),
            .print => try vm.out.print("{d}\n", .{try vm.eval(node.a.?)}),
            .@"if" => {
                if (try vm.eval(node.a.?) != 0) {
                    try vm.exec(node.b.?);
                } else if (node.c) |other| {
                    try vm.exec(other);
                }
            },
            .@"while" => while (try vm.eval(node.a.?) != 0) {
                try vm.exec(node.b.?);
            },
            .block => {
                var child = node.first;
                while (child) |c| : (child = vm.nodes[c].next) try vm.exec(c);
            },
            else => {},
        }
    }
};

fn run(source: []const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var tokens: [512]lex.Token = undefined;
    var nodes: [512]ast.Node = undefined;
    const tree = try ast.parse(source, &tokens, &nodes);

    var interp: Interpreter = .{ .nodes = &nodes, .out = out };
    interp.frames[0] = .{};
    try interp.exec(tree.root);
}

fn report(out: *std.Io.Writer, label: []const u8, result: anyerror!void) !void {
    if (result) |_| {
        try out.print("{s} -> no error\n", .{label});
    } else |err| {
```
