```zig
        try out.print("{s} -> {t}\n", .{ label, err });
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    try out.writeAll("recursion\n");
    try run(
        \\fn fact(n) {
        \\  if (n < 2) { return 1; }
        \\  return n * fact(n - 1);
        \\}
        \\fn fib(n) {
        \\  if (n < 2) { return n; }
        \\  return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
        \\}
        \\print fact(5);
        \\print fib(10);
    , out);

    // The parameter is a local. Thus it shadows the global with the same name,
    // and the global does not change when the call returns.
    try out.writeAll("\nshadowing\n");
    try run(
        \\let x = 100;
        \\fn bump(x) { return x + 1; }
        \\print bump(1);
        \\print x;
    , out);

    try out.writeAll("\nlimits\n");
    try report(out, "recursion with no base case", run("fn loop(n) { return loop(n); } print loop(1);", out));
    try report(out, "calling something undeclared", run("print nope(1);", out));
    try report(out, "too few arguments", run("fn two(a, b) { return a; } print two(1);", out));

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`17-tiny-lang.functions`)*

## What just happened

**`fact(5)` gave 120 and `fib(10)` gave 55.** Thus several values of `n` were
alive at the same time, and no value of `n` changed a different one. `fib(10)`
alone makes 177 calls. Each call got a frame, used the frame, and released
the frame.

**`bump(1)` printed 2, and the global `x` stayed 100.** The interpreter
defines the parameter in the new frame. Thus the parameter shadows the global, and does not
overwrite it. Look at `lookup`: it searches the current frame first, the
globals second, and nothing else. Those two lines are the complete rule for
scope in this language.

**`return` is an error in the implementation.** `error.Return` is not a
failure, and it does not mean that an operation failed. It is the only
mechanism in Zig that unwinds through recursive calls of any depth. Exactly one
place catches it: the code immediately after the body runs. Nothing else
catches `error.Return`, thus it works as a jump to a known point.

Interpreters use this method intentionally. Interpreters in languages with
exceptions do the same thing with a `ReturnException`. Here, the method is
safe because the error set is explicit. The return signal is visible in each
signature that can produce it. A caller that does not handle the signal does
not compile.

**The interpreter evaluates the arguments before it pushes the frame.** This
order is necessary, because the arguments are expressions in the scope of the
*caller*. If the interpreter evaluated them after the push, a parameter would
see the new, empty frame and not the frame of the caller. That bug does not
cause a crash. It gives wrong answers that look reasonable.

**The stack depth is 64, and the interpreter enforces the limit.** `loop(n)`
calls itself with no end, and stops with `StackOverflow`. It does not use all
of the stack of the host and crash the full program. This is the advantage of
your own call stack. The limit is a number that you chose and can report, not
a segfault somewhere in the runtime.

## Check yourself

The interpreter registers `fn` declarations when the `fn` statement executes.
What occurs if a function calls a function that you declare after it?

The call works if the call occurs after both declarations ran. In the program
above, `fib` refers to itself. This is correct, because the declaration already
ran when `print fib(10);` runs. But a program that calls `f()` at the top and
declares `f` at the bottom fails with `UnknownFunction`.

Languages that allow this order use a separate pass. The pass collects the
declarations before anything runs, and it is called hoisting. Hoisting is one
more thing that a compiler does and that you must tell an interpreter to do.

## If you know C

C makes the frame for you. Locals are on the machine stack, and `return` is an
instruction. The work in this chapter is the work that the C compiler does for
you. Thus an interpreter is a good way to understand what your compiler emits.

Compare two more things with C. In C, the stack depth is the size that the OS
gave the thread. If a program uses more than that size, the result is a
segfault with no useful message, because nothing checks the depth. The
interpreter above checks on each call. The check costs one comparison, and it
gives you an error that you can report with a line number.

Also, a C `return` unwinds nothing, because there is nothing to unwind: a
change to one register pops the frame. In C, the equivalent of this chapter is
`setjmp`/`longjmp`. C programs use these functions for exactly this type of
problem. They also have all the usual cautions: when you jump past code, that
code can leave its state inconsistent.

The next chapter is a compiler. The compiler emits instructions, and the
program does not walk the tree when it runs.

---

## A Bytecode Compiler

*Tiny Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/compiler/*

The interpreter walks the tree each time the program runs. Inside a loop, the
interpreter walks the same subtree on each iteration. It follows the same
indices, it switches on the same node kinds, and it compares the same variable
names with the same strings. None of that work depends on the values. Thus
that work never needs to occur more than one time.

A compiler removes that repeated work. The compiler walks the tree **one
time**. It does not calculate an answer. It writes down the steps, and the
steps are **bytecode**. Then, to run the program, a loop goes over a flat
array, not over a tree.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const lex = @import("lexer.zig");
const ast = @import("parser.zig");

pub const Op = enum {
    push,
    load,
    store,
    add,
    sub,
    mul,
    div,
    lt,
    eq,
    neg,
    print,
    jmp,
    jmp_if_false,
    halt,
};

/// One instruction. `arg` is a literal value, a slot number or a jump target.
/// The opcode decides which. A real VM packs the instruction into bytes. A
/// struct uses more memory, but you do not have to write a decoder. That
/// trade is good for code that people read.
pub const Instr = struct {
    op: Op,
    arg: i64 = 0,
};

pub const Error = error{
    TooManyInstructions,
    TooManySlots,
    UndefinedVariable,
    DivideByZero,
    WriteFailed,
};

pub const Chunk = struct {
    code: []Instr,
    len: u32 = 0,
    /// Names, in the order that the compiler first saw them. The index is the
    /// slot number. After the compile step, the compiler never needs the names.
    slots: [32][]const u8 = undefined,
    slot_count: u32 = 0,
};

pub const Compiler = struct {
    nodes: []const ast.Node,
    chunk: *Chunk,

    fn emit(c: *Compiler, op: Op, arg: i64) Error!u32 {
        if (c.chunk.len == c.chunk.code.len) return error.TooManyInstructions;
        c.chunk.code[c.chunk.len] = .{ .op = op, .arg = arg };
        c.chunk.len += 1;
        return c.chunk.len - 1;
    }

    /// Resolve a name to a number, one time, here. This is the fix that the
    /// interpreter chapter promised. At run time a variable is an array index,
    /// and the string comparison on each read does not occur.
    fn slot(c: *Compiler, name: []const u8) Error!i64 {
        for (c.chunk.slots[0..c.chunk.slot_count], 0..) |candidate, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, candidate, name)) return @intCast(i);
        }
        if (c.chunk.slot_count == c.chunk.slots.len) return error.TooManySlots;
        c.chunk.slots[c.chunk.slot_count] = name;
        c.chunk.slot_count += 1;
        return @intCast(c.chunk.slot_count - 1);
    }

    /// Post-order: emit the operands, then the operator. This order is all
    /// that you need to translate a tree for a stack machine. When `add` runs,
    /// its two inputs are already the top of the stack.
    pub fn compile(c: *Compiler, index: u32) Error!void {
        const node = c.nodes[index];
        switch (node.kind) {
            .number => _ = try c.emit(.push, node.value),
            .variable => _ = try c.emit(.load, try c.slot(node.name)),
            .unary => {
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                _ = try c.emit(.neg, 0);
            },
            .binary => {
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                try c.compile(node.b.?);
                _ = try c.emit(switch (node.op) {
                    .plus => .add,
                    .minus => .sub,
                    .star => .mul,
                    .slash => .div,
                    .lt => .lt,
                    else => .eq,
                }, 0);
            },
            .let, .assign => {
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                _ = try c.emit(.store, try c.slot(node.name));
            },
            .print => {
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                _ = try c.emit(.print, 0);
            },
            .@"if" => {
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                // The target is not known yet, because the compiler did not
                // emit the then-branch yet. Emit a placeholder, remember its
                // position, and write the target later. That is backpatching.
                // Because of backpatching, a compiler can work in one pass.
                const skip_then = try c.emit(.jmp_if_false, 0);
                try c.compile(node.b.?);
                if (node.c) |other| {
                    const skip_else = try c.emit(.jmp, 0);
                    c.chunk.code[skip_then].arg = c.chunk.len;
                    try c.compile(other);
                    c.chunk.code[skip_else].arg = c.chunk.len;
                } else {
                    c.chunk.code[skip_then].arg = c.chunk.len;
                }
            },
            .@"while" => {
                // The backward jump needs no patch. The compiler emitted the
                // start of the loop before it emits the jump.
                const start = c.chunk.len;
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                const exit = try c.emit(.jmp_if_false, 0);
                try c.compile(node.b.?);
                _ = try c.emit(.jmp, start);
                c.chunk.code[exit].arg = c.chunk.len;
            },
            .block => {
                var child = node.first;
                while (child) |ch| : (child = c.nodes[ch].next) try c.compile(ch);
            },
            else => {},
        }
    }
};

pub fn compileSource(source: []const u8, tokens: []lex.Token, nodes: []ast.Node, chunk: *Chunk) !void {
    const tree = try ast.parse(source, tokens, nodes);
    var c: Compiler = .{ .nodes = nodes, .chunk = chunk };
    try c.compile(tree.root);
    _ = try c.emit(.halt, 0);
}

pub fn disassemble(chunk: *const Chunk, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    for (chunk.code[0..chunk.len], 0..) |instr, i| {
        try out.print("{d:0>3}  {t: <13}", .{ i, instr.op });
        switch (instr.op) {
            .push => try out.print(" {d}", .{instr.arg}),
            .load, .store => try out.print(" {d}    ; {s}", .{ instr.arg, chunk.slots[@intCast(instr.arg)] }),
            .jmp, .jmp_if_false => try out.print(" {d}", .{instr.arg}),
            else => {},
        }
        try out.writeAll("\n");
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var tokens: [256]lex.Token = undefined;
    var nodes: [256]ast.Node = undefined;
    var code: [128]Instr = undefined;

    try out.writeAll("an expression\n");
    {
        var chunk: Chunk = .{ .code = &code };
        try compileSource("print 1 + 2 * 3;", &tokens, &nodes, &chunk);
        try disassemble(&chunk, out);
    }

    try out.writeAll("\na loop\n");
    {
        var chunk: Chunk = .{ .code = &code };
        try compileSource(
            \\let total = 0;
            \\while (total < 10) {
            \\  total = total + 3;
            \\}
            \\print total;
        , &tokens, &nodes, &chunk);
        try disassemble(&chunk, out);
        try out.print("\n{d} slots: ", .{chunk.slot_count});
        for (chunk.slots[0..chunk.slot_count], 0..) |name, i| {
            try out.print("{d}={s} ", .{ i, name });
        }
        try out.writeAll("\n");
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`17-tiny-lang.compiler`)*

## What just happened

**`1 + 2 * 3` became push, push, push, mul, add.** The operands come first,
and then the operator. That order is a post-order traversal, and it is all
that you need to translate a tree for a stack machine. When an operator runs,
its two inputs are the top two values on the stack, because the code for the
children put them there. No instruction ever names its operands.

**Variables became numbers.** The listing shows `load 0` with a comment that
says `total`, and the comment is only for you. The
[interpreter chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/interpreter/) showed that the
interpreter does a linear search over names each time it reads a variable.
That chapter promised this fix. The search still occurs here, one time for
each mention, at compile time. At run time, a variable is an array index.

This change is a large part of the reason that compiled languages are faster.

**The compiler patched the forward jump.** When the compiler emits
`jmp_if_false`, it does not know the target address, because the body that the
jump skips does not exist yet. Thus the compiler writes a placeholder and
remembers its position. When the length of the body is known, the compiler
writes the real target. This method is called **backpatching**. It lets a
compiler emit code in one pass over the tree, not two.

Look at the loop. The compiler patched `jmp_if_false 11`, and it did not patch
`jmp 2`. The backward jump needed no patch, because the start of the loop is
already in the code when the compiler emits the jump to it. Forward jumps need
a patch, and backward jumps do not.

**The slot table is not in the program.** The program prints the table at the
end so that you can read the disassembly, but the bytecode holds only numbers.
After the compile step, the names are debug information. A stack trace can use
them, but the program does not need them to run.

## What this compiler does not do

The compiler ignores `fn`, `return` and calls. The `else` prong in `compile`
silently skips them. Thus a program that uses functions compiles to bytecode
without those functions, and no error tells you.

This is a real limit of the code. To compile functions, you must design a
**calling convention**. A calling convention decides these things:

- where the arguments go
- how the code addresses a frame
- how the code stores the return address
- which side removes the arguments after the call

Each of those is a decision with alternatives. Thus calls get
[their own chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/calls/). Read this compiler first. The
compiler in that chapter is the same, plus the part that makes calls work.

## Check yourself

The compiler emits `store` for both `let x = 1;` and `x = 1;`, and it resolves
both to the same slot. What does that mean for a variable that you declare
inside a `while` body?

There is only one copy of the variable. The compiler allocates slots by
*name*, for the full program. Thus a variable inside a loop uses the same slot
again on each iteration. Two variables with the same name in different
functions would collide.

Real compilers give each scope its own range of slots, and free the slots when
the scope ends. Slots for each scope make locals cheap. This is the same
bookkeeping that the frames chapter did at run time. This compiler has one
flat namespace, which is enough for a language without functions.

## If you know C

C compiles to machine code, not to bytecode, but the middle of the pipeline has
the same shape. A person who knows compiler output can recognise the
disassembly above. A real back end is different in two ways.

First, a real back end has **registers**. A value can stay in a register
across several operations, and the code does not push and pop the value.

The decision about which values go in which registers is called register
allocation. A large part of the complexity of a real compiler is in register
allocation. A stack machine does not have this problem at all. That is the
reason that many bytecode VMs are stack machines, and the reason that they are
slower. Lua and Dalvik made the other choice, and allocate registers.

Second, a real back end optimises. Optimisation is possible because the
bytecode is now a data structure that you can change. `push 1, push 2, add`
can become `push 3` before anything runs. This compiler does none of that, but
it could. That possibility is the reason that compiled code can run faster than
interpreted code, and not only because some of its work occurred earlier.

The next chapter is the virtual machine. The virtual machine runs the bytecode
that this compiler wrote.

---

## A Virtual Machine

*Tiny Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/vm/*

The compiler made an array of instructions. This chapter runs that array. The
program that runs the array is the smallest program in the section.

The machine has an instruction pointer, which is an index into the array. The
machine does these steps in a loop:

1. Read the instruction at the instruction pointer.
2. Move the instruction pointer forward.
3. Do what the instruction says.
4. Do the steps again.

This loop is called **fetch, decode, execute**. A physical processor runs the
same loop. Thus this program is called a virtual machine, not an interpreter.

The machine needs only a stack and a table of slots. Instructions never name
their operands. The instructions take the operands from the top of the stack,
and put the result back on the stack.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const lex = @import("lexer.zig");
const ast = @import("parser.zig");
const comp = @import("compiler.zig");

pub const Error = error{
    StackOverflow,
    StackUnderflow,
    DivideByZero,
    WriteFailed,
};

pub const Vm = struct {
    chunk: *const comp.Chunk,
    out: *std.Io.Writer,

    stack: [64]i64 = undefined,
    top: usize = 0,
    /// One value for each slot that the compiler allocated. A variable read is
    /// now an array index. The name of the variable is not in the VM.
    globals: [32]i64 = @splat(0),
    /// The number of instructions that ran. It makes the cost of the loop visible.
    steps: usize = 0,

    fn push(vm: *Vm, value: i64) Error!void {
        if (vm.top == vm.stack.len) return error.StackOverflow;
        vm.stack[vm.top] = value;
        vm.top += 1;
    }

    fn pop(vm: *Vm) Error!i64 {
        if (vm.top == 0) return error.StackUnderflow;
        vm.top -= 1;
        return vm.stack[vm.top];
    }

    pub fn run(vm: *Vm) Error!void {
        // The instruction pointer is an index, not a pointer. A change to the
        // index is the only control flow that this machine has. A jump is an
        // assignment.
        var ip: usize = 0;

        while (true) {
            const instr = vm.chunk.code[ip];
            ip += 1;
            vm.steps += 1;

            switch (instr.op) {
                .push => try vm.push(instr.arg),
                .load => try vm.push(vm.globals[@intCast(instr.arg)]),
                .store => vm.globals[@intCast(instr.arg)] = try vm.pop(),
                .neg => try vm.push(-(try vm.pop())),
                // Order is important. The code pushed the right operand last,
                // thus the VM pops it first. If you reverse the order, `+`
                // looks correct and `-` is silently wrong.
                .add, .sub, .mul, .div, .lt, .eq => {
                    const right = try vm.pop();
                    const left = try vm.pop();
                    try vm.push(switch (instr.op) {
                        .add => left + right,
                        .sub => left - right,
                        .mul => left * right,
                        .div => if (right == 0) return error.DivideByZero else @divTrunc(left, right),
                        .lt => @intFromBool(left < right),
                        else => @intFromBool(left == right),
                    });
                },
                .print => try vm.out.print("{d}\n", .{try vm.pop()}),
                .jmp => ip = @intCast(instr.arg),
                .jmp_if_false => if (try vm.pop() == 0) {
                    ip = @intCast(instr.arg);
                },
                .halt => return,
            }
        }
    }
};

fn execute(source: []const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !usize {
    var tokens: [256]lex.Token = undefined;
    var nodes: [256]ast.Node = undefined;
    var code: [128]comp.Instr = undefined;

    var chunk: comp.Chunk = .{ .code = &code };
    try comp.compileSource(source, &tokens, &nodes, &chunk);

    var vm: Vm = .{ .chunk = &chunk, .out = out };
    try vm.run();
    return vm.steps;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    try out.writeAll("source -> bytecode -> answer\n");
    const loop =
        \\let total = 0;
        \\while (total < 10) {
        \\  total = total + 3;
        \\}
        \\print total;
    ;
    const steps = try execute(loop, out);
    try out.print("{d} instructions executed\n", .{steps});

    // The same programs the tree-walking interpreter ran, for comparison.
    try out.writeAll("\nsum of squares 1..5\n");
    _ = try execute(
        \\let total = 0;
        \\let i = 1;
        \\while (i < 6) {
        \\  total = total + i * i;
        \\  i = i + 1;
        \\}
        \\print total;
        \\if (total == 55) { print 1; } else { print 0; }
    , out);

    try out.writeAll("\narithmetic\n");
    _ = try execute("print 1 + 2 * 3; print (1 + 2) * 3; print 1 - 2 - 3; print (0 - 7) / 2;", out);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`17-tiny-lang.vm`)*

## What just happened

**The answers are exactly the same as the answers of the tree-walking
interpreter.** The sum of squares gives 55 and 1, and the arithmetic results
are the same. Compilation and interpretation do the same calculation. The
compiler only makes its decisions earlier. If the answers were different, one
of the two would have a bug.

**A jump is an assignment.** `ip = instr.arg` is the full implementation of
`while`, `if` and `else`. All the structure that the parser found is gone. The
tree became a flat array, and control flow is arithmetic on an index. This
change is the meaning of "lowering". It is the reason that a disassembly is
hard to read and fast to run.

**Operand order is an easy bug to make in this loop.** The code pushed the
right operand last, thus the loop must pop it first. If you reverse the order,
`+` and `*` still look correct, because the order does not change their result.
But `-` and `/` give wrong answers with no error. A test suite of `2 + 3`
would pass.

**45 instructions for a five-line program.** The program prints the count so
that you can see the cost. Each instruction is one dispatch through the
switch, and that is the cost of a bytecode VM. Real VMs use computed goto or a
JIT, because this switch runs billions of times.

Nothing in the program at run time knows that a variable ever had a name. Thus
a stack trace from a stripped binary is full of addresses. Debug information
is a separate thing that you choose to keep.

## The state of this language

This VM has no `call` and no `ret`. Thus a program that uses functions
compiles to bytecode without those functions, and no error tells you. This
limit stays for one more chapter. A calling convention is four separate
decisions, and each decision has alternatives:

- where the arguments are
- how the code addresses a frame
- which code restores the instruction pointer
- which code removes the arguments

[A Calling Convention](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/calls/) makes those decisions, and runs
`fact(5)` through compiled bytecode. Read this VM first. The VM in that chapter
is the same dispatch loop, with `load_local`, `call` and `ret` added, and `div`
and `neg` removed.

## Check yourself

The VM checks for stack overflow and underflow on each push and pop. A real VM
usually does not. Why is that safe?

The compiler makes the bytecode, and the compiler emits only sequences that
balance. The compiler emits `add` only after two operands. Thus a correct
compiler cannot make an `add` that underflows. Real VMs move the check to the
time when they *load* the bytecode. They verify the bytecode one time, not on
each instruction. The JVM bytecode verifier exists for this purpose.

The checks are here because they are cheap at this size. Also, a bad chunk
that a person wrote manually should report an error. The chunk should not
read memory that the VM does not own.

## If you know C

The dispatch loop is a switch. The usual method to make it faster is computed
goto, which is a GCC extension. With computed goto, each instruction ends with
a direct jump to the next handler, and does not return to the top of the
switch. It helps because the branch predictor gets one indirect jump for each
opcode, not one shared jump. It is a common optimisation in real interpreters.

The stack is the other difference. The VM here checks each push and pop. In C,
a push past the end of the stack array reads and writes past the array, with
no warning. This loop runs millions of times. Thus a bug there corrupts data
far away, and the problem appears much later.

## Where to go next

That is the full pipeline:

1. Characters become tokens.
2. Tokens become a tree.
3. The interpreter walks the tree, or the compiler lowers the tree to
   instructions.
4. The VM runs the instructions.

The compilers and interpreters that you use follow the same steps, with many
more cases.

To learn about the machine under the language, read
[Groundwork](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/systems-from-scratch/). Groundwork explains what a byte, an
address and a stack frame are. To continue to build tools, read
[the Unix toolbox](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/unix-tools/), which has seven more programs of the
same type.

---

## A Calling Convention

*Tiny Language. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/calls/*

The compiler and the VM stopped before functions. Calls are not difficult to
implement. But to implement them, you must answer four questions that have no
obvious answers. The set of answers is called a **calling convention**.

1. Where do the arguments go?
2. How does the callee find its own variables?
3. Where does the machine go when the function returns?
4. Which side removes the arguments after the call?

Each question has more than one answer, and real machines make different
choices. Code that uses one convention cannot call code that uses a different
convention. Thus you cannot link a library that uses a different convention.

## The answers in this convention

**The caller pushes the arguments on the stack, in order.** This answer is the
oldest and the simplest. Real machines put the first few arguments in
registers, because registers are faster. For example, the System V AMD64 ABI
passes the first six integer arguments in `rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9`.

**A local is a slot that the code counts from the frame base.** When a call
starts, the base points at the first argument that the caller pushed. Thus
parameter 0 is at base + 0. No code has to tell the callee where its arguments
are, because the arguments are already on the stack at its base. No code
copies the arguments.

**The call saves the return address.** The instruction pointer already points
past the `call` when the VM pushes the frame. Thus the save costs no extra
work.

**The callee removes the arguments.** On `ret`, the callee resets the top of
the stack to the frame base, which discards the arguments. Then the callee
pushes the result. The other choice is that the caller removes the arguments,
and C uses that choice. C does this because of variadic functions: `printf`
cannot remove arguments when nothing tells it how many there are.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const lex = @import("lexer.zig");
const ast = @import("parser.zig");

pub const Op = enum {
    push,
    load, // global slot
    store, // global slot
    load_local, // slot relative to the frame base
    add,
    sub,
    mul,
    lt,
    eq,
    print,
    jmp,
    jmp_if_false,
    call, // arg = function index
    ret,
    halt,
};

pub const Instr = struct { op: Op, arg: i64 = 0 };

const Func = struct { name: []const u8, entry: u32, params: [4][]const u8, param_count: u8 };

pub const Error = error{ TooMuchCode, TooManySlots, TooManyFuncs, UnknownFunction, WriteFailed };

pub const Chunk = struct {
    code: [256]Instr = undefined,
    len: u32 = 0,
    globals: [16][]const u8 = undefined,
    global_count: u32 = 0,
    funcs: [8]Func = undefined,
    func_count: u32 = 0,
};

const Compiler = struct {
    nodes: []const ast.Node,
    chunk: *Chunk,
    /// The function that the compiler compiles now, or null at the top level.
    /// Its parameters are the only names that resolve to a local slot.
    current: ?*const Func = null,

    fn emit(c: *Compiler, op: Op, arg: i64) Error!u32 {
        if (c.chunk.len == c.chunk.code.len) return error.TooMuchCode;
        c.chunk.code[c.chunk.len] = .{ .op = op, .arg = arg };
        c.chunk.len += 1;
        return c.chunk.len - 1;
    }

    fn globalSlot(c: *Compiler, name: []const u8) Error!i64 {
        for (c.chunk.globals[0..c.chunk.global_count], 0..) |g, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, g, name)) return @intCast(i);
        }
        if (c.chunk.global_count == c.chunk.globals.len) return error.TooManySlots;
        c.chunk.globals[c.chunk.global_count] = name;
        c.chunk.global_count += 1;
        return @intCast(c.chunk.global_count - 1);
    }

    /// The slot of a parameter is its position, counted from the frame base.
    /// That rule is the convention. The caller pushes the arguments, and the
    /// callee uses them as slots 0, 1, 2. Nothing tells the callee where they are.
    fn localSlot(c: *Compiler, name: []const u8) ?i64 {
        const f = c.current orelse return null;
        for (f.params[0..f.param_count], 0..) |p, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, p, name)) return @intCast(i);
        }
        return null;
    }

    fn funcIndex(c: *Compiler, name: []const u8) Error!i64 {
        for (c.chunk.funcs[0..c.chunk.func_count], 0..) |f, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, f.name, name)) return @intCast(i);
        }
        return error.UnknownFunction;
    }

    fn compile(c: *Compiler, index: u32) Error!void {
        const node = c.nodes[index];
        switch (node.kind) {
            .number => _ = try c.emit(.push, node.value),
            .variable => {
                if (c.localSlot(node.name)) |slot| {
                    _ = try c.emit(.load_local, slot);
                } else {
                    _ = try c.emit(.load, try c.globalSlot(node.name));
                }
            },
            .binary => {
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                try c.compile(node.b.?);
                _ = try c.emit(switch (node.op) {
                    .plus => .add,
                    .minus => .sub,
                    .star => .mul,
                    .lt => .lt,
                    else => .eq,
                }, 0);
            },
            // The caller pushes the arguments in order, and they stay on the
            // stack. The frame base of the callee points at the first argument.
            // Thus no code copies the arguments.
            .call => {
                var arg = node.first;
                while (arg) |a| : (arg = c.nodes[a].next) try c.compile(a);
                _ = try c.emit(.call, try c.funcIndex(node.name));
            },
            .let, .assign => {
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                _ = try c.emit(.store, try c.globalSlot(node.name));
            },
            .print => {
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                _ = try c.emit(.print, 0);
            },
            .ret => {
                if (node.a) |value| try c.compile(value) else _ = try c.emit(.push, 0);
                _ = try c.emit(.ret, 0);
            },
            .@"if" => {
                try c.compile(node.a.?);
                const skip = try c.emit(.jmp_if_false, 0);
                try c.compile(node.b.?);
                if (node.c) |other| {
                    const over = try c.emit(.jmp, 0);
                    c.chunk.code[skip].arg = c.chunk.len;
                    try c.compile(other);
                    c.chunk.code[over].arg = c.chunk.len;
                } else {
                    c.chunk.code[skip].arg = c.chunk.len;
                }
            },
            // The body is inline, with a jump around it. Thus a run straight
            // through the program does not go into a function that no code
            // called.
            .fn_decl => {
                if (c.chunk.func_count == c.chunk.funcs.len) return error.TooManyFuncs;
                const over = try c.emit(.jmp, 0);

                var f: Func = .{ .name = node.name, .entry = c.chunk.len, .params = undefined, .param_count = 0 };
                var param = node.first;
                while (param) |p| : (param = c.nodes[p].next) {
                    f.params[f.param_count] = c.nodes[p].name;
                    f.param_count += 1;
                }
                // The compiler registers the function before it compiles the
                // body. Thus a function can call itself.
                c.chunk.funcs[c.chunk.func_count] = f;
                c.chunk.func_count += 1;

                const saved = c.current;
                c.current = &c.chunk.funcs[c.chunk.func_count - 1];
                try c.compile(node.b.?);
                c.current = saved;

                // A function that gets to the end without a `return` gives 0.
                _ = try c.emit(.push, 0);
                _ = try c.emit(.ret, 0);
                c.chunk.code[over].arg = c.chunk.len;
            },
            .block => {
                var child = node.first;
                while (child) |ch| : (child = c.nodes[ch].next) try c.compile(ch);
            },
            else => {},
        }
    }
};

const Frame = struct { return_ip: u32, base: usize, args: usize };

pub const Vm = struct {
    chunk: *const Chunk,
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    stack: [128]i64 = undefined,
    top: usize = 0,
    globals: [16]i64 = @splat(0),
    frames: [32]Frame = undefined,
    depth: usize = 0,
    steps: usize = 0,

    fn push(vm: *Vm, v: i64) !void {
        if (vm.top == vm.stack.len) return error.StackOverflow;
        vm.stack[vm.top] = v;
        vm.top += 1;
    }

    fn pop(vm: *Vm) !i64 {
        if (vm.top == 0) return error.StackUnderflow;
        vm.top -= 1;
        return vm.stack[vm.top];
    }

    pub fn run(vm: *Vm) !void {
        var ip: u32 = 0;
        while (true) {
            const instr = vm.chunk.code[ip];
            ip += 1;
            vm.steps += 1;

            switch (instr.op) {
                .push => try vm.push(instr.arg),
                .load => try vm.push(vm.globals[@intCast(instr.arg)]),
                .store => vm.globals[@intCast(instr.arg)] = try vm.pop(),
                .load_local => try vm.push(vm.stack[vm.frames[vm.depth - 1].base + @as(usize, @intCast(instr.arg))]),
                .add, .sub, .mul, .lt, .eq => {
                    const r = try vm.pop();
                    const l = try vm.pop();
                    try vm.push(switch (instr.op) {
                        .add => l + r,
                        .sub => l - r,
                        .mul => l * r,
                        .lt => @intFromBool(l < r),
                        else => @intFromBool(l == r),
                    });
                },
                .print => try vm.out.print("{d}\n", .{try vm.pop()}),
                .jmp => ip = @intCast(instr.arg),
                .jmp_if_false => if (try vm.pop() == 0) {
                    ip = @intCast(instr.arg);
                },
                // The call: remember the return address, and the start of the
                // arguments for this frame. No code copies the arguments. The
                // arguments that the caller pushed *are* the locals of the callee.
                .call => {
                    const f = vm.chunk.funcs[@intCast(instr.arg)];
                    if (vm.depth == vm.frames.len) return error.StackOverflow;
                    vm.frames[vm.depth] = .{
                        .return_ip = ip,
                        .base = vm.top - f.param_count,
                        .args = f.param_count,
                    };
                    vm.depth += 1;
                    ip = f.entry;
                },
                // The return: take the value, and discard the arguments and all
                // else that this call put on the stack. Then push the
                // value and jump to the caller. Here the callee removes the
                // arguments, because this calling convention chose that.
                .ret => {
                    const value = try vm.pop();
                    const frame = vm.frames[vm.depth - 1];
                    vm.depth -= 1;
                    vm.top = frame.base;
                    try vm.push(value);
                    ip = frame.return_ip;
                },
                .halt => return,
            }
        }
    }
};

fn compileSource(source: []const u8, tokens: []lex.Token, nodes: []ast.Node, chunk: *Chunk) !void {
    const tree = try ast.parse(source, tokens, nodes);
    var c: Compiler = .{ .nodes = nodes, .chunk = chunk };
    try c.compile(tree.root);
    _ = try c.emit(.halt, 0);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var tokens: [512]lex.Token = undefined;
    var nodes: [512]ast.Node = undefined;
    var chunk: Chunk = .{};

    const source =
        \\fn square(n) { return n * n; }
        \\fn fact(n) {
        \\  if (n < 2) { return 1; }
        \\  return n * fact(n - 1);
        \\}
        \\print square(7);
        \\print fact(5);
    ;

    try compileSource(source, &tokens, &nodes, &chunk);

    try out.print("{d} instructions, {d} functions\n", .{ chunk.len, chunk.func_count });
    for (chunk.funcs[0..chunk.func_count]) |f| {
        try out.print("  {s} takes {d}, entry at {d}\n", .{ f.name, f.param_count, f.entry });
    }

    try out.writeAll("\nsquare's body\n");
    const square = chunk.funcs[0];
    for (chunk.code[square.entry .. square.entry + 5], square.entry..) |instr, i| {
        try out.print("  {d:0>3}  {t: <11} {d}\n", .{ i, instr.op, instr.arg });
    }

    try out.writeAll("\noutput\n");
    var vm: Vm = .{ .chunk = &chunk, .out = out };
    try vm.run();
    try out.print("\n{d} instructions executed\n", .{vm.steps});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`17-tiny-lang.calls`)*

## What just happened

**The body of `square` is four instructions:** `load_local 0` two times, `mul`
and `ret`. Each function gets an epilogue, and the `push 0` after the body in
the listing is that epilogue. The epilogue is for the case where control
reaches the end of the function without a `return`. The body has no name
lookup and copies no arguments. The compiler made the parameter `n` into slot
0, thus at run time a read of `n` is one array index from the frame base.

**`fact(5)` recursed through compiled bytecode and gave 120.** Each call pushed
a frame, and each `ret` popped one. The recursion works because each call has
its own frame base. Five frames existed at the same time, at different stack
offsets. The frames chapter showed the same thing in the tree-walking
interpreter.

**A jump goes around each function body.** The compiler emits each body
inline, in the middle of the program. Without the jump, a straight run through
the program would go into `square`, although no code called `square`. The
compiler patches the jump when it knows the length of the body. This is the
same backpatching that the compiler chapter used for `if`.

**The compiler registers the function before it compiles the body.** This
order makes recursion possible. When the compiler gets to `fact(n - 1)` inside
`fact`, the compiler must already know that `fact` exists.

## Check yourself

The compiler resolves a name to a local slot only if the name is a parameter
of the function around it. What occurs with `let x = 1;` inside a function
body?

The variable becomes a **global**, and all calls share it. That is wrong, and
it is one of the limits that this compiler still has. The same silent `else`
prong drops `while` loops, and compiles `/` as an equality test.

Real locals need a scope resolver. The resolver walks the body first, collects
each declaration, and gives each declaration a slot above the parameters. The
frame then has space for both. The base pointer addresses all of the frame in
the same way.

With that resolver, a function has its own scope, not only arguments. The
resolver is the next thing to build if you continue this work. Without the
resolver, the tree-walking interpreter and this compiler still accept
different programs. A language with two back ends often has gaps like this.

## If you know C

You saw the output of this convention each time you read a disassembly. The
prologue and epilogue that GCC emits are exactly the bookkeeping above:

```
push rbp          ; save the caller's frame pointer
mov  rbp, rsp     ; this frame's base
sub  rsp, 32      ; room for locals
...
leave             ; undo it
ret               ; jump back
```

`rbp` is the frame base. A local at `[rbp-8]` is the slot arithmetic above,
and a real register does the work. A debugger can print a stack trace because
each frame stores the previous frame pointer. The debugger follows that chain
and gets the call history. The chain is the frame array from this chapter,
stored as a linked list in memory.

The convention is also the reason that a stack overflow in C is a segfault, not
an error. Nothing checks the depth, because a check would cost an instruction
on each call. This VM checks. The cost is acceptable here, because the VM
already pays for a dispatch through the switch.

If you did not read [the virtual machine chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/vm/), read
it next. This chapter uses the same dispatch loop, with `load_local`, `call`
and `ret` added, and `div` and `neg` removed.
