## Parse an HTTP Request

*Web Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/request/*

An HTTP request is text. A request is small, and you can read it aloud:

```
POST /submit?id=7 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Length: 13

name=ada&ok=1
```

A request has a request line, some headers, a blank line, and a body. That is
the full format, and you can implement it without a library.

The difficult part is the blank line. The purpose of the blank line seems
simple, but it is not.

HTTP gives **no length at the start**. A server that
reads from a socket cannot know how many bytes are in this request. Thus the
server cannot ask for that number of bytes. The server must read until the
header section ends. After that, `Content-Length` tells the server the size of
the body.

This is the framing problem from the [networking](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/framing/)
section. The HTTP solution is a delimiter: `\r\n\r\n`.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub const Request = struct {
    method: []const u8,
    target: []const u8,
    version: []const u8,
    /// Slices into the original bytes. The parser copies nothing.
    headers: [][2][]const u8,
    body: []const u8,

    /// Header names are case-insensitive, and the parser must handle this.
    /// curl sends `Host`, some proxies send `HOST`, and a hand-written client
    /// sends `host`. An exact comparison fails when the case is different.
    pub fn header(r: Request, name: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
        for (r.headers) |pair| {
            if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(pair[0], name)) return pair[1];
        }
        return null;
    }
};

pub const Error = error{ Malformed, TooManyHeaders };

pub fn parse(bytes: []const u8, storage: [][2][]const u8) Error!Request {
    // The header section ends at the first blank line. All bytes after it are
    // the body. To find that boundary is the framing problem. HTTP gives no
    // length at the start, thus the parser reads until it finds CRLF CRLF.
    const split = std.mem.find(u8, bytes, "\r\n\r\n") orelse return error.Malformed;
    const head = bytes[0..split];
    const body = bytes[split + 4 ..];

    var lines = std.mem.splitSequence(u8, head, "\r\n");

    const request_line = lines.next() orelse return error.Malformed;
    var parts = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, request_line, ' ');
    const method = parts.next() orelse return error.Malformed;
    const target = parts.next() orelse return error.Malformed;
    const version = parts.next() orelse return error.Malformed;
    if (parts.next() != null) return error.Malformed;

    var count: usize = 0;
    while (lines.next()) |line| {
        if (line.len == 0) continue;
        const colon = std.mem.findScalar(u8, line, ':') orelse return error.Malformed;
        if (count == storage.len) return error.TooManyHeaders;
        storage[count] = .{
            line[0..colon],
            // Remove optional whitespace after the colon, and only after it. A
            // space before the colon is malformed. If the parser accepts that
            // space, request smuggling can occur.
            std.mem.trimStart(u8, line[colon + 1 ..], " \t"),
        };
        count += 1;
    }

    return .{
        .method = method,
        .target = target,
        .version = version,
        .headers = storage[0..count],
        .body = body,
    };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const raw =
        "POST /submit?id=7 HTTP/1.1\r\n" ++
        "Host: example.com\r\n" ++
        "content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded\r\n" ++
        "Content-Length: 13\r\n" ++
        "\r\n" ++
        "name=ada&ok=1";

    var storage: [16][2][]const u8 = undefined;
    const request = try parse(raw, &storage);

    try out.print("method  {s}\n", .{request.method});
    try out.print("target  {s}\n", .{request.target});
    try out.print("version {s}\n\n", .{request.version});

    for (request.headers) |pair| try out.print("  {s}: {s}\n", .{ pair[0], pair[1] });

    // The lookup uses a different case from the case that the client sent.
    try out.print("\nlookup \"Content-Type\" -> {s}\n", .{request.header("Content-Type").?});
    try out.print("lookup \"Missing\"      -> {s}\n\n", .{
        if (request.header("Missing") == null) "absent" else "present",
    });

    try out.print("body ({d} bytes) {s}\n", .{ request.body.len, request.body });
    const declared = request.header("content-length").?;
    try out.print("Content-Length says {s}, and it agrees: {}\n\n", .{
        declared,
        request.body.len == try std.fmt.parseInt(usize, declared, 10),
    });

    for ([_][]const u8{
        "GET /only-one-line\r\n\r\n",
        "GET /extra parts HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n",
        "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nBadHeader\r\n\r\n",
        "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n",
    }) |bad| {
        if (parse(bad, &storage)) |_| {
            try out.writeAll("accepted, which is wrong\n");
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("rejected: {t}\n", .{err});
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`19-web-server.request`)*

## What the program did

**The parse is a split, then a split, then a loop.** The parser does these
steps:

1. Find the blank line, to separate the head from the body.
2. Split the head on `\r\n`.
3. Use the first line as the request line.
4. Read each of the other lines as `name: value`.

The parser needs no state machine and no buffering, because the full request is
already in memory.

**The parser found `Content-Type`, but the client sent `content-type`.** Header
names are case-insensitive, and the parser must handle this from the start.
`curl` sends `Host`, HTTP/2 clients use lowercase for all names, and a
hand-written client sends the text that its author typed. A parser that
compares names exactly works with the client that you used for the test. It
fails with the other clients.

**The parser removes whitespace after the colon, but not before the colon.**
`Host: example.com` and `Host:example.com` are both correct.
`Host : example.com` is malformed. To accept it anyway seems safe, but it is
not safe.

Sometimes two systems in a chain do not agree about which requests
are valid. Then an attacker can make one system see a request that the other
system did not see. Request smuggling uses this problem. Strict parsing
prevents it.

**The parser copied nothing.** Each field is a slice of the original bytes.
The request is a view of the buffer that the socket filled. Thus parsing
allocates nothing. The request is valid for exactly as long as that buffer is
valid.

**The parser rejected four malformed requests:**

- A request line with no version.
- A request line with too many parts.
- A header with no colon.
- A request that stops before the blank line.

The parser returns an error for each request, and it does not guess.

## Check yourself

The parser takes `[]const u8` and has no socket. Why is this important?

The answer: because of this property, this page can run the parser. The same
property lets you do three more things without a network:

- Unit-test the parser.
- Fuzz the parser with a corpus of malformed requests.
- Use the parser again in a client. A *response* has the same shape: a status
  line, headers, a blank line, a body.

The status line needs its own split. This parser wants exactly three fields,
and a reason phrase such as `Not Found` contains a space. A parser that reads
from a socket is testable only when a server runs.

All protocol parsers in this guide use this design. Thus most of the networking
chapters run in a browser. The next chapter puts a socket in front of this
parser, and the parser does not change.

## If you know C

The C version uses `strstr` for the blank line and `strtok` for the other
parts. Both choices have a cost.

`strtok` writes `\0` over each delimiter, and thus it destroys the buffer while
it reads. For a request, this is frequently acceptable, because you do not need
the request again. But `strtok` also joins a sequence of delimiters into one.
Thus an empty header line disappears, and that empty line marks the end of the
headers. For this reason, parsers that use `strtok` usually find the blank line
in a separate step.

Also, each field is a `char *` into the buffer, with no length. Thus "header
value" and "the rest of the request after this point" have the same type. Because
of this, a bug can read a request body as a header value.

Next: [the server](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/server/), which is this parser with a
socket in front of it.

---

## An HTTP Server

*Web Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/server/*

The parser takes bytes and returns a request. A server is the parser, plus a
source for the bytes and a destination for the answer. This chapter has little
new code, because the parser is already complete.

## The program

This program has no Run button. The program binds a listening socket, and the
browser sandbox has no sockets. Thus the build makes the program for the host
and runs the program there. CI runs the program on each change. The program
serves two real requests over a real port, and CI checks what the client
received. Without the Run button, the verification is the same.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const http = @import("request.zig");

/// Serve exactly one connection, then return. A real server puts this function
/// in a loop, and gives each connection to a thread or to an event loop. The
/// work for each connection does not change.
fn serve(server: *std.Io.net.Server, io: std.Io) void {
    var conn = server.accept(io) catch return;
    defer conn.close(io);

    var read_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = conn.reader(io, &read_buf);

    // Read until the blank line. HTTP does not give a length at the start.
    // Thus the server cannot know how much to read. The server reads until it
    // finds the end of the header section. After that, Content-Length gives
    // the size of a body.
    var raw: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var used: usize = 0;
    while (std.mem.find(u8, raw[0..used], "\r\n\r\n") == null) {
        const line = reader.interface.takeDelimiterInclusive('\n') catch break;
        if (used + line.len > raw.len) break;
        @memcpy(raw[used..][0..line.len], line);
        used += line.len;
    }

    var storage: [16][2][]const u8 = undefined;
    const request = http.parse(raw[0..used], &storage) catch {
        respond(&conn, io, 400, "text/plain", "bad request\n");
        return;
    };

    if (std.mem.eql(u8, request.target, "/")) {
        respond(&conn, io, 200, "text/html", "<h1>hello</h1>\n");
    } else {
        respond(&conn, io, 404, "text/plain", "not found\n");
    }
}

/// A response is a status line, headers, a blank line, and the body. The
/// Content-Length is necessary. Without it, the client cannot know that the
/// body ended, and the client waits.
fn respond(conn: *std.Io.net.Stream, io: std.Io, status: u16, content_type: []const u8, body: []const u8) void {
    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var writer = conn.writer(io, &buf);
    const w = &writer.interface;

    const reason: []const u8 = switch (status) {
        200 => "OK",
        400 => "Bad Request",
        else => "Not Found",
    };

    w.print("HTTP/1.1 {d} {s}\r\n", .{ status, reason }) catch return;
    w.print("Content-Type: {s}\r\n", .{content_type}) catch return;
    w.print("Content-Length: {d}\r\n", .{body.len}) catch return;
    w.writeAll("Connection: close\r\n\r\n") catch return;
    w.writeAll(body) catch return;
    w.flush() catch return;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // Port 0 asks the OS for a free port. Thus the server cannot use the same
    // port as a different program on the machine.
    const any_port = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    var server = try any_port.listen(io, .{});
    defer server.deinit(io);
    const addr = server.socket.address;

    for ([_][]const u8{ "/", "/nope" }) |target| {
        const thread = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, serve, .{ &server, io });

        var stream = try addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
        defer stream.close(io);

        var write_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
        var writer = stream.writer(io, &write_buf);
        try writer.interface.print(
            "GET {s} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n",
            .{target},
        );
        try writer.interface.flush();

        var read_buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
        var reader = stream.reader(io, &read_buf);

        // Read until the peer closes the connection. Do not read line by line.
        // The server sent `Connection: close`, thus the end of the stream is
        // the end of the response. Only this framing rule needs no header.
        var response: [2048]u8 = undefined;
        var got: usize = 0;
        while (true) {
            const n = reader.interface.readSliceShort(response[got..]) catch break;
            if (n == 0) break;
            got += n;
        }

        try out.print("--- GET {s}\n", .{target});
        var lines = std.mem.splitSequence(u8, response[0..got], "\r\n");
        while (lines.next()) |line| {
            if (line.len == 0) continue;
            try out.print("{s}\n", .{line});
        }

        thread.join();
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*This program binds a real socket. Thus CI builds and runs the program on the host, not in your browser. CI checks the output below on each build. (`19-web-server.server`)*

```
--- GET /
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 15
Connection: close
<h1>hello</h1>

--- GET /nope
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Length: 10
Connection: close
not found
```

## What the program did

**The server reads until it finds a blank line.** The server does not read a
fixed number of bytes, and it does not read only one line. A loop reads lines
until the collected bytes contain `\r\n\r\n`. This is the framing rule from the
last chapter, and here the rule is important in practice. The bytes now come
slowly from a socket, and the server cannot know how many bytes will come.

**`Content-Length` on the response has a purpose.** Without the header, the
client cannot know that the body ended. Thus the client waits, and the request
seems to stop.

The alternative is to close the connection. Then the end of the stream marks
the end of the body. `Connection: close` tells the client about this choice,
and the client in this program uses it. Chunked encoding is the third way.
Chunked encoding exists for a response with a length that is not known when the
server sends the headers. The other two ways do not work for that response.

**The routing is one `eql`.** The target `/` gets HTML, and all other targets
get a 404. At this level, routing is only a comparison with the target.

**The status line has a number and a phrase.** The number is for programs, and
the phrase is for people. No program reads the phrase. You can send
`HTTP/1.1 200 Fine`, and all clients will accept it.

**Each `serve` call handles one connection, then returns.** A production server
puts this function in a loop. The loop gives each connection to a thread or to
an event loop. The [many clients](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/many-clients/) chapter shows
these designs. The work for each connection does not change, thus you can study
that work alone.

## Check yourself

The server does not check the method. `POST /` gets the same HTML as `GET /`.
This behaviour is incorrect, but why is it also a risk?

The answer: the HTTP rules define `GET` as safe and idempotent, and software
that you do not control relies on this rule. Browsers prefetch links, proxies
cache responses, and crawlers follow each URL that they find. Suppose a server
does an action on `GET`. Then a caching proxy, the link preview in a browser,
and at some time a search engine will do that action. The usual example is an
admin panel with `GET /delete?id=5` links, and a crawler that visited those
links.

A check of the method is one comparison. The check is important because of what
other software expects from `GET`.

## If you know C

In C, the sequence is `socket`, `bind`, `listen`, then `accept` in a loop, and
`read`/`write` on the returned descriptor. The sequence here is the same. The
difference is that a failed call is an error in the return type, not `-1` plus
`errno`.

This version prevents two hazards that are specific to C:

- A read into a fixed buffer must keep space for a terminator if the program
  uses the result as a string. If you forget the space, you get the off-by-one
  error from the strings chapter, on a buffer that holds bytes from an
  attacker.
- On a socket, `write` can write only part of the data, the same as on a pipe.
  Thus the C version needs its own loop around `write`. `writeAll` is that loop.

The C version shows one thing clearly that this version hides: a socket is
only a file descriptor. `read` and `write` work on a socket because they work
on all file descriptors. The [file descriptors](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/os/file-descriptors/)
chapter gives the details.

## The next chapters in this section

This chapter has the protocol and the socket. A production server adds more
parts. In approximately the order that a server needs them, the parts are:

1. Files from disk, with a guard against path traversal.
2. Routing with query strings and percent-decoding.
3. Form bodies.
4. Cookies and sessions.
5. A template engine, so the HTML is not in string literals.

Each part is a chapter. Each part is mostly parsing, thus most of the chapters
will run in the page.

---

## Serve Files Safely

*Web Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/static/*

A static file server has four steps of logic:

1. Take the request target.
2. Open that file under the document root.
3. Read the file.
4. Send the file.

A static file server is also a common way to give your `/etc/passwd` to an
attacker. The cause is a one-line mistake in the order of the steps.

The target comes percent-encoded. `%20` is a space, and `%2e` is a full stop.
Thus a check on the string `/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd` finds no `..` at all. A
moment later, the string decodes to `/../../etc/passwd`.

**Decode first, then check.** A guard that runs before the decode examines a
string that is different from the string that the filesystem gets.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub const Reject = error{ Traversal, BadEncoding, TooLong };

fn hexValue(c: u8) ?u8 {
    return switch (c) {
        '0'...'9' => c - '0',
        'a'...'f' => c - 'a' + 10,
        'A'...'F' => c - 'A' + 10,
        else => null,
    };
}

/// `%20` becomes a space, and `+` stays a plus. (In a query string, `+` means
/// a space. In a path, `+` does not. If you mix the two rules, you get a
/// separate small bug.)
pub fn percentDecode(dest: []u8, src: []const u8) Reject![]u8 {
    var n: usize = 0;
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < src.len) {
        if (n == dest.len) return error.TooLong;
        if (src[i] == '%') {
            if (i + 2 >= src.len) return error.BadEncoding;
            const hi = hexValue(src[i + 1]) orelse return error.BadEncoding;
            const lo = hexValue(src[i + 2]) orelse return error.BadEncoding;
            dest[n] = hi * 16 + lo;
            i += 3;
        } else {
            dest[n] = src[i];
            i += 1;
        }
        n += 1;
    }
    return dest[0..n];
}

/// Change a request target into a path under the document root, or refuse.
///
/// The order is important. The decode occurs first. A check that runs before
/// the decode sees `%2e%2e`, which looks harmless. But the filesystem still
/// gets `..`. Directory traversal bugs occur in code that checked the
/// incorrect string.
pub fn safePath(dest: []u8, target: []const u8) Reject![]const u8 {
    // A query string is not part of the path.
    const raw = if (std.mem.findScalar(u8, target, '?')) |q| target[0..q] else target;

    const decoded = try percentDecode(dest, raw);

    // A nul byte makes the name shorter for code that later uses it as a C
    // string. Thus `/safe.txt\x00../../etc/passwd` can pass a suffix check
    // and still open a different file.
    if (std.mem.findScalar(u8, decoded, 0) != null) return error.Traversal;

    // Reject, and do not normalise. You can change `a/../b` into `b`, but
    // that is a second thing to make correct. A rule that refuses each `..`
    // component has no edge cases, and no legitimate URL needs `..`.
    var parts = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, decoded, '/');
    while (parts.next()) |part| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, part, "..")) return error.Traversal;
    }

    if (decoded.len == 0 or std.mem.eql(u8, decoded, "/")) return "/index.html";
    return decoded;
}

/// Get the Content-Type from the extension. A static server knows only the
/// extension. In the past, browsers guessed the type from the bytes. For that
/// reason, people invented `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
pub fn mimeFor(path: []const u8) []const u8 {
    const dot = std.mem.findScalarLast(u8, path, '.') orelse return "application/octet-stream";
    const ext = path[dot + 1 ..];
    const table = .{
        .{ "html", "text/html; charset=utf-8" },
        .{ "css", "text/css" },
        .{ "js", "text/javascript" },
        .{ "json", "application/json" },
        .{ "png", "image/png" },
        .{ "txt", "text/plain; charset=utf-8" },
    };
    inline for (table) |entry| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, ext, entry[0])) return entry[1];
    }
    return "application/octet-stream";
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var scratch: [256]u8 = undefined;

    const targets = [_][]const u8{
        "/",
        "/index.html",
        "/style.css?v=3",
        "/a%20file.txt",
        // The three traversal attempts.
        "/../etc/passwd",
        "/static/../../etc/passwd",
        "/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd",
        // Encoded nul.
        "/safe.txt%00.png",
        // Malformed encoding.
        "/bad%zz",
    };

    for (targets) |target| {
        if (safePath(&scratch, target)) |path| {
            try out.print("ok       {s: <28} -> {s: <18} {s}\n", .{ target, path, mimeFor(path) });
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("refused  {s: <28} -> {t}\n", .{ target, err });
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`19-web-server.static`)*

## What the program did

**The guard refused three traversal attempts, and one attempt used percent-encoding.**
The three attempts are:

- The plain `/../etc/passwd`.
- The hidden `/static/../../etc/passwd`.
- The encoded `/%2e%2e/%2e%2e/etc/passwd`.

The third attempt is the one that gets through servers in production. The
guard refuses it here for one reason: `percentDecode` runs before any code
looks for `..`.

**Reject, and do not normalise.** You can change `a/../b` into `b`. But then you
must maintain a path normaliser.

A path normaliser is a second thing that you
must make exactly correct, and path normalisers have their own history of bugs.
A rule that refuses each `..` component is one rule with no edge cases. No
legitimate URL contains a `..` component, because the browser resolves `..`
before it sends the URL.

**The guard also refused the nul byte.** `/safe.txt%00.png` decodes to a name
that contains a zero byte. Code after the guard can use the name as a C string.
That code sees `/safe.txt` and stops. Thus a check on the extension can pass,
and the program opens a different file.

Zig strings have a length, thus the nul
byte has no effect here. But the program can give the path to a C library, and
the guard costs one comparison.

**The content type comes from the extension, not from the bytes.** A static
server knows only the extension. In the past, browsers guessed the type from
the content. Thus the browser *rendered* a `.txt` upload that contained HTML as
HTML. Each feature for user uploads became a stored XSS problem.

`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` tells the browser not to guess. Send this
header.

## Check yourself

The guard refuses `..`, but it accepts `/etc/passwd`, which has no dots. Why is
that correct, and when does it become incorrect?

The answer: the program joins the path to a document root. `www` +
`/etc/passwd` is `www/etc/passwd`, and that file almost certainly does not
exist. The slash at the start is part of the URL, not part of the filesystem.

The guard becomes incorrect when the join uses a function that keeps an
absolute path as absolute and discards the prefix. Several languages have a
`path.join` that does exactly this, for example Python `os.path.join` and Node
`path.resolve`. Then a "harmless" absolute path becomes a full filesystem read.

The guard must not be the only protection between a request and the disk. But a
directory handle is not a second guard:

- `openat` resolves `..` the same as any other path.
- `openat` ignores the directory completely when the path is absolute.

`std.Io.Dir` has `resolve_beneath` in its open options. The documentation says
that this option changes a path that escapes into `error.AccessDenied`. The
documentation also says that the option has no effect on an operating system
that does not support it.

Linux is one of those systems. The option uses a BSD `O_`
flag, and Linux has the same idea as an `openat2` resolve flag. Thus on Linux
the option silently does nothing. If you set the option and open
`../outside.txt`, the file opens.

## If you know C

The usual version of this bug is a check on the raw buffer:

```c
if (strstr(target, "..")) return forbidden();   /* runs before decoding */
url_decode(path, target);
int fd = open(path, O_RDONLY);
```

This code has two problems, and the order is only the first problem. The check
also matches the pattern in all positions. Thus it refuses a legitimate file
that has the pattern in its name. Then the maintainer usually makes the check
more complex, and more complex checks let the encoded variant through.

The other hazard that is specific to C: `open` takes a `char *`. Thus a nul in
the decoded path silently makes the path shorter. For this reason, the guard
above rejects a nul and does not ignore it. In Zig, the slice keeps its length.
But when the path goes into C code, the length does not go with it.

The usual design is `openat` with a directory handle. In Zig, this is
`dir.openFile`, which resolves the path relative to a `Dir`. It is not a
sandbox. A `..` can still climb out of the directory, and an absolute path
ignores the directory. Thus the check above must always run, on all platforms,
with or without `resolve_beneath`.

Next: [routes and query strings](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/routes/), which is the
other part of the meaning of a target.

---

## Routes and Query Strings

*Web Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/routes/*

A request target is two parts with a `?` between them. Before the `?` is a
path. The path decides *what runs*. After the `?` is a query string. The query
string is input to the code that runs.

The two parts have different parsing
rules and different uses. If a program uses the two parts as one string, many
bugs occur.

Routing is the first part, and routing is simpler than many people expect: a
comparison with a table. A framework adds shorter ways to write the table. The
decision that the framework makes is the same.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const path_util = @import("static.zig");

pub const Param = struct { name: []const u8, value: []const u8 };

/// In a query string, `+` means a space. In a path, `+` does not mean a space.
/// Thus this function is separate from the path decoder. It is not a flag.
fn decodeQueryValue(dest: []u8, src: []const u8) ![]u8 {
    var swapped: [256]u8 = undefined;
    if (src.len > swapped.len) return error.TooLong;
    for (src, 0..) |c, i| swapped[i] = if (c == '+') ' ' else c;
    return path_util.percentDecode(dest, swapped[0..src.len]);
}

/// Parse `a=1&b=hello+world&flag` into pairs. A key with no `=` gets an empty
/// value. HTML checkboxes and flags come in this form.
pub fn parseQuery(target: []const u8, dest: []u8, out: []Param) ![]Param {
    const q = std.mem.findScalar(u8, target, '?') orelse return out[0..0];
    var used: usize = 0;
    var n: usize = 0;

    var pairs = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, target[q + 1 ..], '&');
    while (pairs.next()) |pair| {
        if (pair.len == 0) continue;
        if (n == out.len) return error.TooManyParams;

        const eq = std.mem.findScalar(u8, pair, '=');
        const raw_name = if (eq) |e| pair[0..e] else pair;
        const raw_value = if (eq) |e| pair[e + 1 ..] else "";

        const name = try decodeQueryValue(dest[used..], raw_name);
        used += name.len;
        const value = try decodeQueryValue(dest[used..], raw_value);
        used += value.len;

        out[n] = .{ .name = name, .value = value };
        n += 1;
    }
    return out[0..n];
}

pub fn find(params: []const Param, name: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    // The last value wins. Real servers do not agree about this rule, and an
    // attacker can use the disagreement. Suppose a proxy uses the first `user`
    // and the origin uses the last. Then one request has two meanings.
    var result: ?[]const u8 = null;
    for (params) |p| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, p.name, name)) result = p.value;
    }
    return result;
}

const Route = struct { method: []const u8, path: []const u8 };

/// Routing is a comparison. A framework adds more parts on top of this
/// comparison. The table gets patterns, then a compiler changes the patterns
/// into a tree. The decision does not change.
pub fn route(method: []const u8, target: []const u8) ?usize {
    const path = if (std.mem.findScalar(u8, target, '?')) |q| target[0..q] else target;
    const table = [_]Route{
        .{ .method = "GET", .path = "/" },
        .{ .method = "GET", .path = "/search" },
        .{ .method = "POST", .path = "/submit" },
    };
    for (table, 0..) |r, i| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, r.method, method) and std.mem.eql(u8, r.path, path)) return i;
    }
    return null;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var scratch: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var params: [8]Param = undefined;

    const targets = [_][]const u8{
        "/search?q=hello+world&page=2",
        "/search?q=a%26b&empty=&flag",
        "/search?q=first&q=second",
        "/",
    };

    for (targets) |target| {
        const found = try parseQuery(target, &scratch, &params);
        try out.print("{s}\n", .{target});
        for (found) |p| try out.print("  {s} = \"{s}\"\n", .{ p.name, p.value });
        if (found.len == 0) try out.writeAll("  (no parameters)\n");
    }

    try out.writeAll("\nlast value wins\n");
    const dup = try parseQuery("/search?q=first&q=second", &scratch, &params);
    try out.print("  q -> \"{s}\"\n", .{find(dup, "q").?});

    try out.writeAll("\nrouting\n");
    for ([_][2][]const u8{
        .{ "GET", "/" },
        .{ "GET", "/search?q=x" },
        .{ "POST", "/submit" },
        .{ "GET", "/submit" },
        .{ "GET", "/missing" },
    }) |pair| {
        if (route(pair[0], pair[1])) |i| {
            try out.print("  {s: <5} {s: <14} -> handler {d}\n", .{ pair[0], pair[1], i });
        } else {
            try out.print("  {s: <5} {s: <14} -> 404\n", .{ pair[0], pair[1] });
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`19-web-server.routes`)*

## What the program did

**`hello+world` became `hello world`, and `%26` became a literal `&`.** Both
results are important.

In a query string, a plus sign means a space. This rule applies only in the
query string, not in the path. Thus the decoder is a separate function, not a
flag.

The program decoded `%26` *after* the split on `&`. Thus a value that contains
an ampersand stayed one value, and did not become two parameters. Decode after
you split on the structural characters. That order is the opposite of the order
in the last chapter. The reason is the same: decode at the point where the
result is data and not structure.

**`empty=` and `flag` both gave an empty value.** `empty=` is a parameter with
an empty value. `flag` has no `=`. This parser stores both values as `""`.

This choice has a cost: you cannot know the difference between a field that the user
cleared and a key that had no value. An optional value keeps the difference. A
browser always sends the first form. Thus keys without a value come from
hand-written URLs and from APIs.

**`q` occurred two times, and the last value won.** Servers do not agree about
this rule. Some servers use the first value, some use the last value, and some
make a list.

An attacker can use this disagreement. Suppose a caching proxy uses
the first value and the origin server uses the last value. Then one request has
two different meanings for two systems. Parameter-pollution bugs come from this
difference. Select a rule, and know which rule you selected.

**Routing ignored the query.** `GET /search?q=x` matched the `/search` route.
The path decides the handler, and the query is the input to the handler. Also,
`GET /submit` gave a 404 and `POST /submit` matched. The method is part of the
route. It is not a detail for a later check.

## Check yourself

The routing table is a linear scan over three entries. When is that shape
incorrect?

The answer: later than you think, and the reason for a change is usually not
speed. A linear scan of a few dozen exact-match routes costs almost nothing. The
syscall that delivered the request costs much more.

*Patterns* make a different structure necessary. When a route contains a
placeholder, the comparison is not equality. Then a server must match a hundred
patterns against each request. The server has two choices:

- Compile the patterns into a tree that walks the path one time.
- Accept a hundred partial matches for each request.

A production router is that tree. The tree exists because of patterns, not
because of scale.

## If you know C

The parsing is the same, and the difference is the memory. The C version has
two choices:

- Decode in place. This works because a decoded string is never longer than its
  encoded form.
- Allocate memory for each value. Then the code must free each value.

Many programmers decode in place, but that choice destroys the original target.
You possibly need that target for [logging](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/logging/).
Also, the code must decode after the split. If the code writes a decoded `&`
into the buffer before the split, the code makes a parameter boundary that the
client did not send. This is the same point about order as above. In C, the
point is more important, because C lets you write the decoded bytes into the
buffer that you still parse.

Another problem in C: `strtok` on `&` joins a sequence of delimiters into one.
Thus `a=1&&b=2` loses the empty parameter, and `a=1&` loses the last one. This
loss is important only if code after the parser counts parameters. You do not
see that type of dependency until something breaks.

Next: form bodies. A form body uses the same encoding, but it comes by a
different path.

---

## Form Bodies

*Web Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/forms/*

A submitted HTML form comes as `name=Ada+Lovelace&role=engineer`. That text is
exactly a query string without the `?`. This is intentional. HTML specifies one
encoding. The method decides if the encoding goes in the URL or in the body.

Thus the parser is the parser from the last chapter. The new parts are around
the parser, because a body is not a URL. A body can be megabytes, and it comes
after the headers.

Also, **the client tells you the size of the body**. This chapter is about what
the server does with that number, because the client can lie.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const routes = @import("routes.zig");

pub const Field = routes.Param;

/// A urlencoded body is a query string without the `?`. The HTML
/// specification gives forms one encoding. The method decides where that
/// encoding goes.
pub fn parseForm(body: []const u8, dest: []u8, out: []Field) ![]Field {
    var joined: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    if (body.len + 1 > joined.len) return error.TooLong;
    joined[0] = '?';
    @memcpy(joined[1..][0..body.len], body);
    return routes.parseQuery(joined[0 .. body.len + 1], dest, out);
}

/// The number of body bytes to read. If a server trusts this number without a
/// limit, the client decides how much memory the server uses.
pub fn bodyLength(declared: ?[]const u8, limit: usize) !usize {
    const text = declared orelse return 0;
    const n = std.fmt.parseInt(usize, text, 10) catch return error.Malformed;
    if (n > limit) return error.TooLarge;
    return n;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var scratch: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var fields: [8]Field = undefined;

    const bodies = [_][]const u8{
        "name=Ada+Lovelace&role=engineer",
        "note=100%25+done&tags=a%26b",
        "consent=on&newsletter=",
        "",
    };

    for (bodies) |body| {
        const parsed = try parseForm(body, &scratch, &fields);
        try out.print("\"{s}\"\n", .{body});
        for (parsed) |f| try out.print("  {s} = \"{s}\"\n", .{ f.name, f.value });
        if (parsed.len == 0) try out.writeAll("  (no fields)\n");
    }

    try out.writeAll("\nContent-Length, with a ceiling of 1 MB\n");
    for ([_]?[]const u8{ "13", null, "99999999", "twelve" }) |declared| {
        const label = declared orelse "(absent)";
        if (bodyLength(declared, 1 << 20)) |n| {
            try out.print("  {s: <10} -> read {d} bytes\n", .{ label, n });
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("  {s: <10} -> {t}\n", .{ label, err });
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`19-web-server.forms`)*

## What the program did

**The program uses the same parser without a change.** `parseForm` puts a `?` at
the front and calls `parseQuery`. There is one encoding, thus there is one
parser. No second implementation exists that can become different from the
first.

**`100%25+done` became `100% done`.** The rules are the same as for a query
string: `+` is a space, and `%25` is a literal percent. A form that contains a
percent sign is a good test. If the code is incorrect, the value looks almost
correct.

**The program compared `Content-Length` with a ceiling.** The program refused
`99999999` before it read one byte of the body. Without that check, this
sequence occurs:

1. The client says that the body is 4 GB.
2. The server allocates or reads toward 4 GB.
3. The server stops with a failure.

The check costs nothing. Without the check, the client controls how much memory
the server uses.

A GET has no body and sends no length. Suppose the length is absent, and the
server uses "no limit" for it. Then the server waits forever on a connection that has no more data
to send.

**The program rejected `twelve`, and did not use zero for it.** A malformed
length is a malformed request. To use 0 as a default seems kind to the client.
But then the body that the client sent stays in the socket buffer. The next
request on a keep-alive connection reads that body as its own request line.

That is request smuggling. This is the second time in this section that bad
input, when accepted, causes the vulnerability.

## Check yourself

The parser handles `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. What does a form with a
file upload send, and why can that form not use this encoding?

The answer: the form sends `multipart/form-data`, which is a completely
different format. Each field becomes a section. A boundary string separates the
sections. The client selects the boundary and gives it in the `Content-Type`
header.

The format exists for two reasons:

- The urlencoded form of a megabyte of binary is approximately three times
  larger. Each byte that is not a letter, a digit or one of `*-._` becomes
  three characters.
- A file has its own filename and content type, and the urlencoded format has
  no place for them.

Thus a server that supports uploads has two body parsers. The multipart parser
must handle these problems:

- A boundary that occurs inside the data.
- Sections that come split across reads.
- A filename that the server must never trust as a path.

Each of these problems caused real bugs. [File
Uploads](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/multipart/) is the chapter that builds this parser.

## If you know C

The body comes on the same descriptor as the headers. A common mistake in C is
to read the body with the same call:

```c
read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);   /* may return the headers AND part of the body */
```

When you find the blank line, you have probably already read some of the body.
Thus the parser must use the data that is in the buffer, and only then read
more. Some code expects "headers, then a new read for the body". That code is
correct on a fast loopback, and incorrect over a real network.

The other mistake is `atoi(content_length)`. It returns 0 for `"twelve"` and
also for `"0"`. It also cannot report overflow. `parseInt` returns an error.
Thus the compiler makes you handle the malformed case.

Next: [cookies and sessions](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/sessions/). With cookies and
sessions, the server knows who sent the form.

---

## Cookies and Sessions

*Web Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/sessions/*

HTTP has no memory. Each request comes with no information about the requests
before it. Because of this property, you can restart, replicate and
load-balance a server, and no user sees a difference.

A cookie is the smallest possible solution to this problem. The server sends
`Set-Cookie: session=abc`, and the client sends `Cookie: session=abc` on each
later request. That is the full mechanism. The server trusts a string that the
client stores and can edit.

Thus a session cookie holds an **identifier**, not information. If you put
`user=admin` in a cookie, any person can log in as admin if they edit the
cookie.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub const Cookie = struct { name: []const u8, value: []const u8 };

/// `Cookie: a=1; b=2`. One header, with semicolons between items, and no
/// encoding. A client cannot send a value that contains `;`. For this reason,
/// session ids are hex.
pub fn parseCookies(header: []const u8, out: []Cookie) ![]Cookie {
    var n: usize = 0;
    var parts = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, header, ';');
    while (parts.next()) |part| {
        const item = std.mem.trim(u8, part, " \t");
        if (item.len == 0) continue;
        const eq = std.mem.findScalar(u8, item, '=') orelse continue;
        if (n == out.len) return error.TooManyCookies;
        out[n] = .{ .name = item[0..eq], .value = item[eq + 1 ..] };
        n += 1;
    }
    return out[0..n];
}

pub fn find(cookies: []const Cookie, name: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    for (cookies) |c| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, c.name, name)) return c.value;
    }
    return null;
}

/// Hex, because a cookie value cannot contain `;` or whitespace, and hex never
/// contains them. 16 bytes is 128 bits. No person can guess that many ids.
pub fn sessionId(random: std.Random, dest: *[32]u8) []const u8 {
    var raw: [16]u8 = undefined;
    random.bytes(&raw);
    return std.mem.print(dest, "{x}", .{&raw}) catch unreachable;
}

/// The attributes give the security. Without them, any script on the page can
/// read a session cookie. The browser sends the cookie on each cross-site
/// request, and the cookie goes in clear text.
pub fn setCookie(out: *std.Io.Writer, name: []const u8, value: []const u8) !void {
    try out.print("Set-Cookie: {s}={s}", .{ name, value });
    try out.writeAll("; HttpOnly"); // no script can read it, thus XSS cannot steal it
    try out.writeAll("; Secure"); // HTTPS only, thus a network observer cannot read it
    try out.writeAll("; SameSite=Lax"); // the browser does not send it on cross-site POSTs, to stop CSRF
    try out.writeAll("; Path=/");
    try out.writeAll("; Max-Age=3600\r\n");
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var storage: [8]Cookie = undefined;

    const headers = [_][]const u8{
        "session=deadbeef; theme=dark",
        "  spaced = value ; other=1",
        "novalue; session=abc",
        "",
    };

    for (headers) |header| {
        const cookies = try parseCookies(header, &storage);
        try out.print("\"{s}\"\n", .{header});
        for (cookies) |c| try out.print("  {s} -> \"{s}\"\n", .{ c.name, c.value });
        if (cookies.len == 0) try out.writeAll("  (none)\n");
    }

    const cookies = try parseCookies("session=deadbeef; theme=dark", &storage);
    try out.print("\nlookup session -> {s}\n", .{find(cookies, "session").?});
    try out.print("lookup missing -> {s}\n\n", .{
        if (find(cookies, "missing") == null) "absent" else "present",
    });

    // A fixed seed, thus this page prints the same text each time. A real
    // server must not do this. If a person can predict a session id, that
    // person can take the session. Use `std.Random.IoSource` over the `Io`
    // that you already have. (Older code uses `std.crypto.random`. Zig
    // removed it.)
    var prng: std.Random.DefaultPrng = .init(0x5eed);
    var hex: [32]u8 = undefined;
    try out.print("a session id (seeded, therefore insecure)\n  {s}\n\n", .{
        sessionId(prng.random(), &hex),
    });

    try setCookie(out, "session", "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef");

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`19-web-server.sessions`)*

## What the program did

**The parse is a split on `;`, then on `=`.** There is no percent-decoding,
because cookies have no encoding. Thus a value cannot contain a semicolon or a
space. For this reason, session ids are hex. Hex never contains those
characters, thus the problem does not occur.

**The parser ignored `novalue`.** An item with no `=` is not a cookie. The
parser removes the item, and it does not make an empty value.

**The second line kept its inner spaces.** `  spaced = value ` gave the name
`spaced ` and the value ` value`, with the spaces. The parser removes
whitespace around each *pair*, not inside the pair. The grammar does not allow
those spaces, and browsers never send them. Thus a strict rule here costs
nothing.

A parser that removes spaces inside the pair accepts input that a stricter
parser later in the chain rejects. When two parsers do not agree about the same
bytes, an attacker can use the difference.

The program uses a fixed seed. Thus the output is the same on each build. A
real server must never do this.

If the ids are predictable, any person can
calculate a valid session. Use `std.Random.IoSource`, which gets bytes from the
operating system through the `Io` interface. Sixteen bytes is 128 bits. With
that many possible ids, no person can guess an id.

**The security comes from the attributes on the cookie.** Each attribute stops
a specific attack:

- With `HttpOnly`, JavaScript cannot read the cookie. Thus a cross-site
  scripting bug cannot copy the id. A script on the page can still act as the
  user while the page is open. Thus this attribute does not fix XSS.
- `Secure` stops the cookie on plain HTTP. On plain HTTP, any device on the path
  can read the cookie.
- With `SameSite=Lax`, the browser does not send the cookie on cross-site
  POSTs. This stops most cross-site request forgery.
- `Max-Age` gives the cookie an end. After that end, the browser does not send
  the cookie. A stolen id stops working only when the server expires the id. You
  must build that part.

Without these attributes, there are several well-known ways to steal the
session.

## Check yourself

The server stores the id and finds the session in its own memory. What breaks
when you run a second copy of the server behind a load balancer?

The answer: a request that goes to the other machine has a session id that the
other machine never saw. Thus the session of the user ends at random times. When there
is more than one process, the session storage must move to a shared place, for
example Redis or a database.

There is also a different method: put the data in the cookie and sign the
cookie. Then each server can verify the cookie without shared state. A signed
cookie or a JWT works this way. This method removes the lookup, but it adds a
new problem: you cannot revoke something that you do not store.

## If you know C

In C, programmers usually do this parsing with `strtok`. `strtok` has two
problems:

- It writes `\0` over each delimiter, and this destroys the header.
- It joins a sequence of delimiters into one. Here, this loses nothing, but in
  other formats it loses data.

C makes the random number more difficult. The usual random function in C is
`rand()`: a linear congruential generator, with the clock as the seed. Thus a
person who knows approximately when the session started can calculate the id.
This problem was a real vulnerability in real products more than one time. The
correct source is `/dev/urandom` or `getrandom()`. People use `rand()` anyway,
because it is one call and needs no error handling.

Zig does not give that easy path. Zig removed `std.crypto.random`. Thus you give
the secure source to the code as a parameter, the same as any other capability:
`std.Random.IoSource` over the `Io` that you already have. That costs one line
of setup, and there is no easy insecure option that you can use by mistake.

Next: [a template engine](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/templates/), so the HTML is not in
string literals.

---

## A Template Engine

*Web Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/templates/*

Until now, each response was a string literal in Zig source. That method does
not work for long. People must edit HTML without a new compile. Also, when a
program makes a page from joined strings, the markup and the data are the same
type of thing.

A template engine keeps the markup and the data separate. The engine reads a
file with holes in it, fills the holes, and sends the result. To fill the holes
is a substring search, and you can write that code in an afternoon.

The important part is what occurs when the value contains `<`.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub const Binding = struct { name: []const u8, value: []const u8 };

/// The five characters that can end an HTML text node or an attribute value.
/// Escaping decides if the browser shows a name or runs it.
fn writeEscaped(out: *std.Io.Writer, text: []const u8) !void {
    for (text) |c| {
        switch (c) {
            '&' => try out.writeAll("&amp;"),
            '<' => try out.writeAll("&lt;"),
            '>' => try out.writeAll("&gt;"),
            '"' => try out.writeAll("&quot;"),
            '\'' => try out.writeAll("&#39;"),
            else => try out.writeByte(c),
        }
    }
}

fn lookup(bindings: []const Binding, name: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    for (bindings) |b| {
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, b.name, name)) return b.value;
    }
    return null;
}

/// The engine escapes `{{name}}`, but not `{{{name}}}`. To turn off escaping,
/// you need three braces. Thus the safe form is shorter to type, and the
/// dangerous form is easy to see in a diff.
pub fn render(template: []const u8, bindings: []const Binding, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < template.len) {
        if (i + 1 < template.len and template[i] == '{' and template[i + 1] == '{') {
            const raw = i + 2 < template.len and template[i + 2] == '{';
            const open = i + if (raw) @as(usize, 3) else 2;
            const close_tag: []const u8 = if (raw) "}}}" else "}}";

            const close = std.mem.find(u8, template[open..], close_tag) orelse {
                // An unterminated placeholder is a typo. It is more useful to
                // print the typo than to hide the rest of the page.
                try out.writeAll(template[i..]);
                return;
            };

            const name = std.mem.trim(u8, template[open .. open + close], " ");
            if (lookup(bindings, name)) |value| {
                if (raw) try out.writeAll(value) else try writeEscaped(out, value);
            } else {
                // A binding that does not exist is not an empty string. A marker is
                // better than a page that silently shows a blank in the place
                // of a price.
                try out.print("[missing:{s}]", .{name});
            }
            i = open + close + close_tag.len;
        } else {
            try out.writeByte(template[i]);
            i += 1;
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const bindings = [_]Binding{
        .{ .name = "title", .value = "Guest book" },
        .{ .name = "name", .value = "<script>alert('xss')</script>" },
        .{ .name = "note", .value = "Tom & Jerry \"quoted\"" },
        .{ .name = "banner", .value = "<em>welcome</em>" },
    };

    const template =
        \\<h1>{{title}}</h1>
        \\<p>from {{ name }}</p>
        \\<p>{{note}}</p>
        \\<div>{{{banner}}}</div>
        \\<p>{{absent}}</p>
        \\<p>{{unclosed
    ;

    try render(template, &bindings, out);
    try out.writeAll("\n");
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`19-web-server.templates`)*

## What the program did

**The script tag became harmless.** The binding for `name` was
`<script>alert('xss')</script>`, and the page got `&lt;script&gt;...`. A
browser shows that text as text. Without escaping, a guest book runs the
JavaScript of any person in the session of each visitor. That script can then
use the session cookie from the last chapter.

**Escaping is the default. To stop escaping, you must type more.** The engine
escapes `{{name}}`, and it does not escape `{{{banner}}}`. You need an extra
brace to turn off escaping. Thus the safe form is shorter to type.

The dangerous
form uses three braces, and three braces are easy to see in a code review.
Template engines that made escaping opt-*in* all have lists of security
vulnerabilities (CVEs).

**The engine escapes five characters, not three.** `&`, `<` and `>` are the
obvious ones. The two quote characters are important because a value is not
always in a text node. An attribute is a different context. In an attribute, a
quote ends the attribute, and all text after the quote is markup. An escaper
that handles only the first three characters is safe in one context and broken
in the other context.

**A binding that does not exist printed `[missing:absent]`, not an empty string.** Suppose
a page shows a blank in the place of a price. That bug gets into production,
because the blank looks like a design choice. A person sees a visible marker
the first time that they look at the page.

**The engine printed the unterminated `{{unclosed` without a change.** The text
is a typo in the template. It is more useful to show the typo than to hide the
rest of the page. If the engine hides the page, it searches for a `}}` that
does not exist.

## Check yourself

The escaper is correct for HTML text and for quoted attribute values. Where is
the escaper incorrect?

The answer: inside a `<script>` block and inside a URL.

- `<a href="{{link}}">` with the value `javascript:alert(1)` has correct
  escaping, and the script still runs. In a URL, the problem is the *scheme*,
  not the characters.
- A value in JavaScript needs JavaScript escaping. Inside a string literal,
  `</script>` ends the block, and the quotes have no effect on that.
- The escaper is also incorrect in an unquoted attribute. In
  `<a href={{link}}>`, the value ends at the first space. Thus a value such as
  `x onmouseover=alert(1)` becomes new markup, and it uses none of the five
  escaped characters.

Thus production engines are **context-aware**. They parse enough of the HTML to
know if a hole is in text, an attribute, a URL or a script. Then they use a
different escaper for each context. The Go `html/template` package does this,
and it is the standard reference. A single escaper is much better than no
escaper, but it is not sufficient alone.

## If you know C

Substitution in C is a loop with a search. The loop uses much pointer
arithmetic to calculate how much to copy between holes. This code is one of the
easier things to write in C, because all values are a length and an offset.

The escaping is more difficult, because of the size. The escaped string is
longer than the input. If the input is all double quotes, the escaped string is
six times longer, because `&quot;` is six characters. Thus the output buffer
cannot have the length of the input. You have three choices:

- Calculate the size in a first pass.
- Make the buffer larger while you write.
- Write directly to the socket.

The version above writes directly to the writer. Thus it never needs to know
the size. Usually that is the correct choice, because the full escaped text is
never necessary in memory.

## The state of this section

The seven chapters until now do these tasks:

- Parse a request.
- Answer over a socket.
- Serve files, and keep the rest of the disk safe.
- Route.
- Read forms.
- Remember users.
- Render pages, and do not run the text that users typed.

Together, the chapters make a small web server.

The parts that are not in this section are mostly about scale, not about new ideas: keep-alive,
chunked bodies, compression, TLS, and concurrency.
[Many clients](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/many-clients/) shows concurrency. File
uploads have their own chapter, [File Uploads](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/multipart/),
because `multipart/form-data` is a second body format. It is not a variation of
the first format.

---

## File Uploads

*Web Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/multipart/*

Each other format in this section has a delimiter that the specification
fixes. `&` separates query parameters, `;` separates cookies, and `\r\n\r\n`
ends the headers. You can write the delimiter into the parser.

`multipart/form-data` cannot do that. The bytes of a file can be any value,
and they can include any delimiter that you select. Thus the **client**
selects a string, checks that the data does not contain the string, and
announces the string:

```
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----zig42
```

The parser reads the delimiter from a header, and then searches for the
delimiter. For this reason, the multipart parser is separate from the
urlencoded parser. It is not a variation of the urlencoded parser.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub const Part = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    filename: ?[]const u8,
    content_type: ?[]const u8,
    data: []const u8,
};

pub const Error = error{ NoBoundary, Malformed, TooManyParts };

/// `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc123`. The client selects the
/// boundary and announces it here. Each other format in this section uses a
/// fixed delimiter. Here the delimiter is data.
pub fn boundaryOf(content_type: []const u8) Error![]const u8 {
    const at = std.mem.find(u8, content_type, "boundary=") orelse return error.NoBoundary;
    const rest = content_type[at + "boundary=".len ..];
    const end = std.mem.findScalar(u8, rest, ';') orelse rest.len;
    const value = std.mem.trim(u8, rest[0..end], " \"");
    if (value.len == 0) return error.NoBoundary;
    return value;
}

/// All text after the last slash or backslash, and never `..`.
///
/// The filename comes from the client. In an upload handler, the filename is
/// a dangerous string. If code joins it to a directory without this function,
/// the client can write to any place where the process can write. That is
/// worse than the read in the [path chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/static/).
pub fn safeFilename(raw: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    var name = raw;
    if (std.mem.findScalarLast(u8, name, '/')) |i| name = name[i + 1 ..];
    // Also remove backslashes. A Windows client sends `C:\Users\me\photo.png`.
    // A parser that removes only `/` keeps the full path as one filename.
    if (std.mem.findScalarLast(u8, name, '\\')) |i| name = name[i + 1 ..];
    if (name.len == 0) return null;
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, name, ".") or std.mem.eql(u8, name, "..")) return null;
    if (std.mem.findScalar(u8, name, 0) != null) return null;
    return name;
}

fn attribute(header: []const u8, key: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    const at = std.mem.find(u8, header, key) orelse return null;
    const rest = header[at + key.len ..];
    if (rest.len == 0 or rest[0] != '"') return null;
    const end = std.mem.findScalar(u8, rest[1..], '"') orelse return null;
    return rest[1 .. 1 + end];
}

pub fn parse(body: []const u8, boundary: []const u8, out: []Part, scratch: []u8) Error![]Part {
    // The delimiter is CRLF + "--" + boundary. The CRLF is part of the
    // delimiter, not part of the data before it. If a parser forgets this, it
    // adds two bytes to each uploaded file. In a text field, you cannot see
    // the two bytes. In an image, they corrupt the data.
    const delim = std.mem.print(scratch, "\r\n--{s}", .{boundary}) catch return error.Malformed;

    // The first boundary has no CRLF before it. Thus the parser starts as if
    // the CRLF is there.
    var cursor: usize = if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, body, delim[2..])) delim.len - 2 else return error.Malformed;

    var n: usize = 0;
    while (true) {
        if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, body[cursor..], "--")) break; // closing delimiter
        if (!std.mem.startsWith(u8, body[cursor..], "\r\n")) return error.Malformed;
        cursor += 2;

        const head_end = std.mem.findPos(u8, body, cursor, "\r\n\r\n") orelse return error.Malformed;
        const head = body[cursor..head_end];
        const data_start = head_end + 4;

        const next = std.mem.findPos(u8, body, data_start, delim) orelse return error.Malformed;

        var disposition: []const u8 = "";
        var content_type: ?[]const u8 = null;
        var lines = std.mem.splitSequence(u8, head, "\r\n");
        while (lines.next()) |line| {
            if (std.ascii.startsWithIgnoreCase(line, "content-disposition:")) disposition = line;
            if (std.ascii.startsWithIgnoreCase(line, "content-type:")) {
                content_type = std.mem.trim(u8, line["content-type:".len..], " ");
            }
        }

        if (n == out.len) return error.TooManyParts;
        out[n] = .{
            .name = attribute(disposition, "name=") orelse return error.Malformed,
            .filename = attribute(disposition, "filename="),
            .content_type = content_type,
            .data = body[data_start..next],
        };
        n += 1;
        cursor = next + delim.len;
    }
    return out[0..n];
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const content_type = "multipart/form-data; boundary=----zig42";
    const boundary = try boundaryOf(content_type);
    try out.print("boundary announced by the client: {s}\n\n", .{boundary});

    const body =
        "------zig42\r\n" ++
        "Content-Disposition: form-data; name=\"title\"\r\n" ++
        "\r\n" ++
        "My holiday\r\n" ++
        "------zig42\r\n" ++
        "Content-Disposition: form-data; name=\"photo\"; filename=\"../../etc/passwd\"\r\n" ++
        "Content-Type: image/png\r\n" ++
        "\r\n" ++
        "PNG\r\ndata\r\n" ++
        "------zig42--\r\n";

    var parts: [8]Part = undefined;
    var scratch: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const parsed = try parse(body, boundary, &parts, &scratch);

    try out.print("{d} parts\n\n", .{parsed.len});
    for (parsed) |part| {
        try out.print("name         {s}\n", .{part.name});
        try out.print("filename     {s}\n", .{part.filename orelse "(none, so it is a field)"});
        if (part.filename) |raw| {
            try out.print("  as sent    {s}\n", .{raw});
            try out.print("  safe form  {s}\n", .{safeFilename(raw) orelse "(refused)"});
        }
        try out.print("content-type {s}\n", .{part.content_type orelse "(unset)"});
        try out.print("data         {d} bytes: \"{s}\"\n\n", .{ part.data.len, part.data });
    }

    // The data of the second part ends at "data", not at "data\r\n". Those two
    // bytes are part of the delimiter.
    try out.print("the photo is {d} bytes, and \"PNG\\r\\ndata\" is {d}\n\n", .{
        parsed[1].data.len,
        "PNG\r\ndata".len,
    });

    try out.writeAll("filenames a client might send\n");
    for ([_][]const u8{
        "holiday.png",
        "../../etc/passwd",
        "C:\\Users\\me\\photo.png",
        "..",
        "",
    }) |raw| {
        try out.print("  {s: <24} -> {s}\n", .{ raw, safeFilename(raw) orelse "(refused)" });
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`19-web-server.multipart`)*

## What the program did

**The body has two parts, and only one part is a file.** Both parts come in
the same way. The difference is a `filename` attribute in the
`Content-Disposition` header. If the attribute is present, the part is a file.
If the attribute is absent, the part is an ordinary field.

A form can contain
the two types together. Thus an upload handler is also a form handler.

**The photo is 9 bytes, not 11.** The data is `PNG\r\ndata`, and the body has
`\r\n` immediately before the next boundary line. Those two bytes are part of
the **delimiter**, not part of the file.

A parser that keeps the two bytes adds `\r\n` to each uploaded file. In a text
field, you will never see the difference. In a PNG, the two bytes corrupt the
last chunk. In a ZIP, they break the central directory. A checksum comparison
fails, and an examination of the file does not show the cause. The demo prints
the two numbers, thus you can check this yourself.

**The filename came as `../../etc/passwd`.** An attacker tries exactly this,
and the sanitised form is `passwd`. This is the same traversal as in the static
files chapter, but in the opposite direction. That chapter was about an
unauthorised **read**. This chapter is about an unauthorised **write**, to any
place where the process can write. The usual result is a web shell: a script
that the attacker puts into a directory that the server also serves.

**The sanitiser also removes backslashes.** A Windows client can legitimately
send `C:\Users\me\photo.png`. A parser that removes only `/` stores a file with
a path in its name. On a Unix server, that name is only ugly. If the name
reaches a Windows filesystem, the name is a traversal again.

**The safe filename is not the sent filename.** You can show the string from
the client as a name. You must not use the string as a name to open. The two
uses need different handling. When code mixes the two uses, `..` gets to the
filesystem.

## Limits of this parser

The parser needs the full body in memory. Real uploads are too large for that.
A program cannot keep a 2 GB file in a buffer before it parses the file. Thus a
production parser is a state machine, and reads give data to the state machine.
The parser sends out each part while the data streams through, and writes file
data directly to disk.

That design changes the code very much, but it changes none of the decisions
above:

- The client still selects the boundary.
- The last `\r\n` is still part of the delimiter.
- The filename is still untrusted.

One problem becomes more difficult. A boundary can come split across two reads.
Thus the matcher must keep partial state. Framing is the same problem for all
protocols.

## Check yourself

The client promises that the boundary is not in the data. What must a server
do if the boundary is in the data?

The answer: nothing special. If the boundary is inside a file, the parser
splits that file at exactly that point. The parser reads the data after that
point as the head of another part. Usually the result is a parse error, not two
files. Nothing tells you which result occurred, because there is no length to
compare. If the file data also contains a `Content-Disposition` line and a
blank line, you cannot see the split.

This is a real weakness of the design, and no validation fixes it. Long, random
boundaries make a collision unlikely. Browsers make a fixed prefix plus 16
random characters. Thus an accidental collision does not occur in practice. A
deliberate collision needs an attacker who already controls the boundary. That
attacker can already send all the parts that they want.

## If you know C

The search uses `memmem`, not `strstr`, because file data contains nul bytes.
Thus all C string functions are incorrect here. Suppose code calls `strlen` on
the contents of a part. Then `strlen` stops at the first nul byte, and the code
loses the rest of the file.

The other hazard in C is the filename. `basename()` is the obvious tool, and it
has two problems:

- The POSIX version can change its argument.
- No version rejects `..`, because `basename("..")` is `".."`.

Then `open(dir_fd, name)` with that name writes into the parent directory. The
sanitiser above rejects `..` explicitly. If the sanitiser returned a plausible
name for a dangerous input, it would hide the problem. When it returns nothing,
the caller must handle the problem.

## The end of this section

The section has eight chapters. Together, they make a small web server with
these parts:

- A request parser.
- A socket.
- Static files with a traversal guard.
- Routing.
- Urlencoded forms.
- Sessions.
- Templates.
- Uploads.

The parts that remain are mostly about scale, not about new ideas. [Many
clients](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/many-clients/) shows the concurrency part.
