## An Append-Only Record Store

*Data and Storage. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/flatdb/*

The simplest database is a file that you only append to. To write a record,
seek to the end and write. The write does not touch the data that is already on
disk.

This rule seems to be a limitation, but it gives three benefits together:

- A write that crashes in the middle leaves a partial record at the end. All
  the data before the partial record does not change.
- Two readers can read while a writer appends, because the bytes that they
  read never change.
- The full history stays in the file. Thus the file can answer the question
  "what did this look like on Tuesday".

The rule also causes two problems, and each log-structured store must solve
them. This chapter is about those two problems.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// One record on each line, with `|` between the fields. The separator is
/// the main design decision. It makes a second decision necessary: what
/// occurs when a value contains `|`.
pub const Record = struct {
    op: enum { put, delete },
    key: []const u8,
    value: []const u8,
};

/// Escape the separator and the newline, so that a record can hold them.
/// Without this function, a value that contains `|` silently becomes two
/// fields. You cannot see the corruption until some code reads the value.
fn writeEscaped(out: *std.Io.Writer, text: []const u8) !void {
    for (text) |c| switch (c) {
        '|' => try out.writeAll("\\p"),
        '\n' => try out.writeAll("\\n"),
        '\\' => try out.writeAll("\\\\"),
        else => try out.writeByte(c),
    };
}

fn unescape(dest: []u8, text: []const u8) ![]const u8 {
    var n: usize = 0;
    var i: usize = 0;
    while (i < text.len) : (n += 1) {
        if (n == dest.len) return error.TooLong;
        if (text[i] == '\\' and i + 1 < text.len) {
            dest[n] = switch (text[i + 1]) {
                'p' => '|',
                'n' => '\n',
                else => '\\',
            };
            i += 2;
        } else {
            dest[n] = text[i];
            i += 1;
        }
    }
    return dest[0..n];
}

pub fn append(log: *std.Io.Writer, record: Record) !void {
    try log.writeAll(if (record.op == .put) "put|" else "del|");
    try writeEscaped(log, record.key);
    try log.writeAll("|");
    try writeEscaped(log, record.value);
    try log.writeAll("\n");
}

/// Read the log forward, and keep the last record for each key. A delete is
/// a record in the file. An append-only file has no other way to show a
/// removal.
pub fn lookup(log: []const u8, key: []const u8, scratch: []u8) !?[]const u8 {
    var result: ?[]const u8 = null;
    var used: usize = 0;

    var lines = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, log, '\n');
    while (lines.next()) |line| {
        if (line.len == 0) continue;
        var fields = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, line, '|');
        const op = fields.next() orelse continue;
        const raw_key = fields.next() orelse continue;
        const raw_value = fields.next() orelse "";

        var key_buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
        const this_key = try unescape(&key_buf, raw_key);
        if (!std.mem.eql(u8, this_key, key)) continue;

        if (std.mem.eql(u8, op, "del")) {
            result = null;
        } else {
            const value = try unescape(scratch[used..], raw_value);
            used += value.len;
            result = value;
        }
    }
    return result;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // A buffer in place of the file. Each write is an append. No code here
    // can seek backwards, and this demo stays within that limit.
    var file: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var log: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&file);

    try append(&log, .{ .op = .put, .key = "alice", .value = "engineer" });
    try append(&log, .{ .op = .put, .key = "bob", .value = "designer" });
    try append(&log, .{ .op = .put, .key = "alice", .value = "architect" });
    try append(&log, .{ .op = .delete, .key = "bob", .value = "" });
    try append(&log, .{ .op = .put, .key = "carol", .value = "a|b\nc" });

    const written = log.buffered();
    try out.print("the log, {d} bytes:\n", .{written.len});
    try out.print("{s}\n", .{written});

    var scratch: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var live: usize = 0;
    for ([_][]const u8{ "alice", "bob", "carol", "dave" }) |key| {
        if (try lookup(written, key, &scratch)) |value| {
            live += 1;
            try out.print("{s: <6} -> \"{s}\"\n", .{ key, value });
        } else {
            try out.print("{s: <6} -> (absent)\n", .{key});
        }
    }

    try out.print("\n5 records written, {d} keys live, and the file only ever grew\n", .{live});
    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`20-storage.flatdb`)*

## What the program did

**The program wrote `alice` two times, and the read gives the second value.**
No code updated the first record. The reader scans forward and keeps the last
record for each key. Thus "update" means "append a newer record".

The old
value is still in the file. The old value can be a useful audit log. It can
also be a leak, if the old value was a secret.

**The program deleted `bob` with a new record.** The store never modifies the
file, thus it also cannot remove data. The store must write a removal as a new
record. That record is a **tombstone**, and all log-structured databases have
tombstones: LSM trees, Kafka topics, Git. For the same reason, a delete in such
a store makes the file larger.

**The value for `carol` contained a `|` and a newline, and the value stayed
correct.** The separator causes this problem. If `|` is the field separator, a
value that contains `|` becomes two fields. A value that contains a newline
becomes two records. Neither case gives an error. Both cases give incorrect data
on read, and the data looks correct.

The escape scheme has three rules. The design of the scheme had to be complete
before the program wrote the first record. If you change the scheme later, all
the files that exist are in the old format. For this reason, real formats use one of
two methods:

- Escape the data. CSV does this, and doubles the quotes.
- Put a length prefix on the data. Write the byte count, then the bytes, and
  never scan for a delimiter.

[Binary protocols](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/binary-protocols/) use length prefixes.
Length prefixes are the better answer when a human does not read the file.

**A read of one key read the full file.** Each lookup is a full scan. With
five records, the scan costs almost nothing. With five million records, the
scan is the full cost of the system. The solution is an index, two chapters
after this one.

## Check yourself

The store keeps the *last* record for a key. What must change, so that the
store can answer "what was the value for alice before she became an architect"?

The answer: almost nothing. The information is already in the file, and the
reader discards it. To return a history, collect the matches and do not write
over one variable. Because the store keeps the history, append-only stores are
a good fit for these uses:

- Audit trails.
- Event sourcing.
- All uses where you must answer "how did the data get to this state".

A store that updates data in place loses this history.

## If you know C

The append is `open(path, O_WRONLY | O_APPEND)` and a `write`. `O_APPEND` does
more work than it seems to do. It makes the seek to the end and the write into
one atomic operation. Thus two processes that append to the same file cannot
interleave a record. Without `O_APPEND`, you seek, then you write, and the
problem of the next chapter occurs immediately.

That atomic operation has two limits:

- A `write` can return after it wrote fewer bytes than you asked for. The rest
  of the bytes need a second call, and a different writer can write before that
  call.
- On NFS, the guarantee does not apply. The protocol has no append, thus the
  client simulates the append, and the race occurs again.

For this reason, the program builds each record in memory and writes it one
time.

Next: [what occurs when two writers meet](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/filelock/). `O_APPEND`
solved that problem here, but the program did not ask it to.

---

## Two Writers, One File

*Data and Storage. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/filelock/*

To increment a counter in a file, you need three operations, not one:

1. Read the value.
2. Add one.
3. Write the value back.

There is a gap between the read and the write. During that gap, the value on
disk is stale, and a different writer can read it.

Two writers, each with 200 increments, must give 400. They will not.

## The program

This program has no Run button. It needs real threads and a real filesystem.
Thus the build makes the program for the host and runs it there. The program
also has no pinned output. That is unusual on this site, and the chapter
explains the reason.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const rounds = 200;

/// Read a counter, add one, and write it back. That is three steps. The other
/// writer can change the file between the read and the write.
fn increment(dir: *std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io, name: []const u8, lock: ?*std.Io.Mutex) void {
    for (0..rounds) |_| {
        if (lock) |m| m.lock(io) catch return;
        defer if (lock) |m| m.unlock(io);

        var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
        const current = blk: {
            const file = dir.openFile(io, name, .{}) catch break :blk @as(u64, 0);
            defer file.close(io);
            var reader = file.readerStreaming(io, &buf);
            const text = reader.interface.allocRemaining(std.heap.page_allocator, .unlimited) catch break :blk @as(u64, 0);
            defer std.heap.page_allocator.free(text);
            break :blk std.fmt.parseInt(u64, std.mem.trim(u8, text, " \n"), 10) catch 0;
        };

        var out_buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
        const text = std.mem.print(&out_buf, "{d}", .{current + 1}) catch continue;

        const file = dir.createFile(io, name, .{ .truncate = true }) catch continue;
        defer file.close(io);
        var writer = file.writerStreaming(io, &buf);
        writer.interface.writeAll(text) catch continue;
        writer.interface.flush() catch continue;
    }
}

fn run(dir: *std.Io.Dir, io: std.Io, name: []const u8, lock: ?*std.Io.Mutex) !u64 {
    {
        const file = try dir.createFile(io, name, .{ .truncate = true });
        defer file.close(io);
        var buf: [8]u8 = undefined;
        var writer = file.writerStreaming(io, &buf);
        try writer.interface.writeAll("0");
        try writer.interface.flush();
    }

    const a = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, increment, .{ dir, io, name, lock });
    const b = try std.Thread.spawn(.{}, increment, .{ dir, io, name, lock });
    a.join();
    b.join();

    var buf: [32]u8 = undefined;
    const file = try dir.openFile(io, name, .{});
    defer file.close(io);
    var reader = file.readerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const text = try reader.interface.allocRemaining(std.heap.page_allocator, .unlimited);
    defer std.heap.page_allocator.free(text);
    return std.fmt.parseInt(u64, std.mem.trim(u8, text, " \n"), 10) catch 0;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var buf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // The files are in the working directory, with names that no other code
    // uses. The program removes them at the end. A new directory is one more
    // thing to remove on each exit path, and this demo does not need one.
    var dir = std.Io.Dir.cwd();
    defer dir.deleteFile(io, "storage-unlocked.tmp") catch {};
    defer dir.deleteFile(io, "storage-locked.tmp") catch {};

    const expected = rounds * 2;

    const lost = try run(&dir, io, "storage-unlocked.tmp", null);
    try out.print("two threads, {d} increments each\n\n", .{rounds});
    try out.print("without a lock: {d}, expected {d}\n", .{ lost, expected });
    try out.print("  updates lost: {}\n\n", .{lost < expected});

    var mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init;
    const kept = try run(&dir, io, "storage-locked.tmp", &mutex);
    try out.print("with a lock:    {d}, expected {d}\n", .{ kept, expected });
    try out.print("  updates lost: {}\n", .{kept < expected});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*This program needs real threads and a real filesystem. Thus CI builds and runs it on the host. The output is intentionally different on each run. Thus, different from each other snippet here, it has no expected output to check. (`20-storage.filelock`)*

This is one run on the computer that built this page:

```
two threads, 200 increments each

without a lock: 183, expected 400
  updates lost: true

with a lock:    400, expected 400
  updates lost: false
```

## What the program did

**More than half of the increments disappeared.** The program did not crash,
report an error or write a log line. The file contains a number that is too
small, and no part of the system saw the problem. Each lost update was the same
sequence: one thread read 91, the other thread read 91, and both threads wrote
92.

**If you run the program again, you get a different number.** Because the
result changes, races are expensive to fix. You can bisect a bug that occurs
again in the same way. This bug gives a different value each time. It
disappears under a debugger, because the timing changes. It is worst on the
computer with the most cores, and that computer is usually production.

The value changes on each run. This is also the reason that this snippet has
no expected output. If the build pinned one number, the nightly would fail on a tree with no
changes. That failure would be a false report from the build, not a bug in the
code.

**The lock made the result exact.** The result is 400 each time. The fix makes
the read-modify-write indivisible. The fix works because the gap between the
read and the write does not exist now. The gap does not only become smaller.

**The lock here is in-process.** A `std.Io.Mutex` controls threads in one
program, and it knows nothing about a second copy of the program. For a second
copy, the operating system must hold the lock, thus you must lock the file. The
same three-line fix applies, at a level where each process can see it.

## Check yourself

Suppose that you make the write atomic. For example, you write to a temporary
file and rename it over the original. Does this fix the problem?

The answer is no. With an atomic rename, no reader ever sees a half-written
file. That solves a real problem, but a different problem. It does nothing for
this problem, because both threads still read 91 before either thread writes.
The lost update occurs between the read and the write. A change to the write
cannot close a gap that opened before the write.

An atomic write and exclusive access across the read-modify-write are two
separate properties, and a store needs both. Some systems confuse the two
properties. These systems have careful `rename` steps and corrupted counters.

## If you know C

There are two calls, and their differences are important:

- `flock` locks the open file description. Thus a child gets the lock across
  `fork`, and the kernel releases the lock when the last descriptor closes.
- `fcntl` locks are per-process. The kernel releases them when any descriptor
  for the file closes, also a descriptor that you opened separately. This second
  behaviour surprises many people.

On Linux, both locks are **advisory** by default. They work only if each writer
asks for the lock. This is intentional. File locks control programs that agree
to use them. No mode protects a file from a program that ignores the lock.

The other hazard that is specific to C: `read` and `write` on the same
descriptor share a file offset. Two threads that use one `fd` mix their
positions. Thus the fix in C is usually `pread`/`pwrite`. These calls take an
offset, and they do not change the shared offset.

Next: [an index](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/indexes/). With an index, a read of one key
does not need a read of the full file.

---

## An Index Over the Log

*Data and Storage. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/indexes/*

A read of one key from the append-only store reads the full file. The read must
do this. The newest record for a key can be the last record in the file. Thus
a scan cannot stop early, because then the answer can be stale.

An index solves that problem. People usually describe an index as a thing that
makes lookups fast, but that description hides what an index is. An index is a
**second data structure**. A program builds it from the first, and it holds no data of
its own. It maps a key to the *location* of the record. The rest of this
chapter comes from those two facts.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const store = @import("flatdb.zig");

/// Maps a key to the byte offset of the newest record for that key. An index
/// does not copy the data. It maps each key to the location of the data.
pub const Index = struct {
    keys: [64][]const u8 = undefined,
    offsets: [64]usize = undefined,
    count: usize = 0,

    fn put(ix: *Index, key: []const u8, offset: usize) !void {
        for (ix.keys[0..ix.count], 0..) |existing, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, existing, key)) {
                ix.offsets[i] = offset;
                return;
            }
        }
        if (ix.count == ix.keys.len) return error.IndexFull;
        ix.keys[ix.count] = key;
        ix.offsets[ix.count] = offset;
        ix.count += 1;
    }

    pub fn get(ix: Index, key: []const u8) ?usize {
        for (ix.keys[0..ix.count], 0..) |existing, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, existing, key)) return ix.offsets[i];
        }
        return null;
    }
};

/// Build the index again from the log. The index is *derived*: the log holds
/// the true data, and you can always build the index again from the log. Thus
/// you can delete an index to save space, and a corrupt index loses no data.
pub fn build(log: []const u8) !Index {
    var ix: Index = .{};
    var offset: usize = 0;

    while (offset < log.len) {
        const end = std.mem.findScalarPos(u8, log, offset, '\n') orelse break;
        const line = log[offset..end];

        var fields = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, line, '|');
        const op = fields.next() orelse break;
        const key = fields.next() orelse break;

        // The index contains tombstones, the same as other records. If the
        // index ignored them, it would point to an older live record. Then a
        // deleted key would seem to be present on read.
        _ = op;
        try ix.put(key, offset);
        offset = end + 1;
    }
    return ix;
}

/// Read one record from a known offset. The read does not touch the data
/// before that offset.
fn readAt(log: []const u8, offset: usize, scratch: []u8) !?[]const u8 {
    const end = std.mem.findScalarPos(u8, log, offset, '\n') orelse log.len;
    var fields = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, log[offset..end], '|');
    const op = fields.next() orelse return null;
    _ = fields.next();
    const raw_value = fields.next() orelse "";
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, op, "del")) return null;
    @memcpy(scratch[0..raw_value.len], raw_value);
    return scratch[0..raw_value.len];
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var file: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var log: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&file);

    // Sufficient records to show the difference in the output.
    var name_buf: [16][8]u8 = undefined;
    var names: [16][]const u8 = undefined;
    for (0..16) |i| {
        names[i] = try std.mem.print(&name_buf[i], "key{d:0>2}", .{i});
        try store.append(&log, .{ .op = .put, .key = names[i], .value = "first" });
    }
    // Write each key again. Thus the newest record for each key is in the
    // second half of the file. A scan must get to the end to know that it has
    // the newest record.
    for (0..16) |i| {
        try store.append(&log, .{ .op = .put, .key = names[i], .value = "second" });
    }
    const written = log.buffered();

    var ix = try build(written);
    try out.print("log is {d} bytes, {d} records, {d} distinct keys\n\n", .{
        written.len,
        32,
        ix.count,
    });

    // Two buffers, not one. Both lookups return slices into the buffer that
    // they get. If the lookups use the same buffer, the second call silently
    // writes over the first answer. Then the comparison below compares a
    // value with itself.
    var scan_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var seek_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const target = "key03";

    // A scan reads all the data, because the last record for a key can be the
    // last record in the file.
    try out.print("scan for {s}: read {d} bytes\n", .{ target, written.len });
    const scanned = try store.lookup(written, target, &scan_buf);

    const offset = ix.get(target).?;
    const end = std.mem.findScalarPos(u8, written, offset, '\n') orelse written.len;
    const seeked = try readAt(written, offset, &seek_buf);
    try out.print("index for {s}: offset {d}, read {d} bytes\n", .{ target, offset, end - offset });
    try out.print("  both say \"{s}\": {}\n\n", .{
        seeked orelse "",
        std.mem.eql(u8, scanned orelse "", seeked orelse ""),
    });

    try out.print("the index costs {d} entries and one update per write\n", .{ix.count});
    try out.print("and it is derived: delete it and `build` reconstructs it\n", .{});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`20-storage.index`)*

## What the program did

**The read became 16 bytes, not 528 bytes.** The answer is the same, and the
index went directly to offset 307. That offset is in the second half of the
file. The demo shows this case intentionally. The program wrote each key two
times. Thus the newest record is far from the first record, and a scan cannot
know that it is complete until it gets to the end.

**The index holds offsets, not values.** It has 16 entries for 32 records. The
index answers "where", and the log still answers "what". Because the index
stores only offsets, an index over a terabyte of records can fit in memory.

**You can build the index again from the log.** `build` reads the file one time
and makes the full index again. The index is derived data, and the log is the
source of truth. This has three results:

- A corrupt index is an inconvenience, not a loss of data.
- You can delete an index to get the space back.
- To add a new index to a database that exists, you need one full scan.

**The index also contains tombstones.** If the index ignored delete records,
it would point to an older live record. Then a deleted key would seem to be
present on read. The comment in the code states this, because to ignore
tombstones looks like an optimisation.

## The cost of an index

Each write now does two things. The store appends the record, and it updates
the index. If the index is on disk, each write that you asked for needs a
second write. The name of this effect is **write amplification**. For this
reason, an insert into a table with six indexes is slow. You asked for one
write, and the disk does seven.

Each storage engine makes this trade. Reads become faster in proportion to the
quantity that you index. Writes become slower in the same proportion. No
configuration prevents this. You can only select if reads or writes pay the
cost.

## Check yourself

This index is a linear scan over 16 entries, and that is not clearly better
than a scan of the log. When does the index start to be important, and what
replaces the linear scan?

The answer: the index is already important, because the entries are in memory
and the log is on disk. Memory is several orders of magnitude faster than disk,
before you compare the algorithms. The replacement for the linear scan depends
on the question:

- Use a hash map if each lookup uses only one exact key.
- Use a B-tree if you also need ranges, order, or "the next 50 keys after this
  one". A hash map scatters keys that are near each other, and a B-tree keeps
  them adjacent.

For this reason, relational databases almost always use B-trees for indexes.
Both structures serve `WHERE id = 7` well, but only one structure serves
`ORDER BY id LIMIT 50`. [The data structures
section](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/data-structures/bst/) explains the structure. That section
builds a search tree. Then it shows how sorted input makes the tree as tall as
a list, and then each lookup walks each node.

## If you know C

In C, the index in memory is a hash table that you wrote, or a hash table from a
library. The difficult case is when the index is too large for memory. Then the
index goes on disk, and each design decision changes.

The program reads an on-disk index one block at a time, because the disk has no
smaller unit. Thus the shape of the structure must follow the block size. The
block size is the reason that B-trees have a high branching factor, and the
reason that disks do not use binary trees. A binary tree with a million keys
has 20 levels, and needs 20 reads. A B-tree with 200 keys in each block needs
three.

C also makes you see another fact: the offsets are valid only for the file that
they came from. If you store the index in its own file, you have two files that
must agree. A crash between the two writes makes the two files inconsistent.
The next chapter solves that problem.

Next: [a write-ahead log](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/kvstore/). With a write-ahead log, two
files that must agree stay correct after a power loss between the two writes.

---

## A Write-Ahead Log

*Data and Storage. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/kvstore/*

The last chapter ended on a problem that it could not solve: two files that
must agree, and a crash between the two writes. This problem is not specific to
files. It occurs with each change that is not one indivisible action.

The answer is old and simple. All databases, all journalling filesystems and
most message queues use it. **Write down what you will do, then do it.** If the
power fails before you finish, the note is still there when the program starts
again. Then you do the change again.

That note is a **write-ahead log**. Recovery is a read of the note.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// Adler-style: two sums, one of the bytes and one of the sums. Thus the
/// order of the bytes is important. The function is hand-written because this
/// track builds the parts that it uses. The necessary property is easy to
/// state: if you change a byte, the number changes.
fn checksum(bytes: []const u8) u32 {
    var a: u32 = 1;
    var b: u32 = 0;
    for (bytes) |c| {
        a = (a + c) % 65521;
        b = (b + a) % 65521;
    }
    return (b << 16) | a;
}

/// `<checksum>|<op>|<key>|<value>\n`. The checksum is first, so that a reader
/// can read it before the data that it describes. The newline marks the end
/// of a record. Thus a write that stopped in the middle leaves a last line
/// without a newline.
pub fn append(wal: *std.Io.Writer, op: []const u8, key: []const u8, value: []const u8) !void {
    var body: [256]u8 = undefined;
    const payload = try std.mem.print(&body, "{s}|{s}|{s}", .{ op, key, value });
    try wal.print("{d}|{s}\n", .{ checksum(payload), payload });
}

pub const Store = struct {
    keys: [32][]const u8 = undefined,
    values: [32][]const u8 = undefined,
    count: usize = 0,

    fn set(s: *Store, key: []const u8, value: []const u8) !void {
        for (s.keys[0..s.count], 0..) |k, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, k, key)) {
                s.values[i] = value;
                return;
            }
        }
        if (s.count == s.keys.len) return error.Full;
        s.keys[s.count] = key;
        s.values[s.count] = value;
        s.count += 1;
    }

    fn remove(s: *Store, key: []const u8) void {
        for (s.keys[0..s.count], 0..) |k, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, k, key)) {
                s.keys[i] = s.keys[s.count - 1];
                s.values[i] = s.values[s.count - 1];
                s.count -= 1;
                return;
            }
        }
    }

    pub fn get(s: Store, key: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
        for (s.keys[0..s.count], 0..) |k, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, k, key)) return s.values[i];
        }
        return null;
    }
};

pub const Recovery = struct { store: Store, applied: usize, discarded: usize };

/// Build the store again from a replay of the log. Stop at the first record
/// that fails verification. Do not skip the record and continue, because a
/// log is a sequence. A record after a broken record can depend on it.
pub fn replay(wal: []const u8) Recovery {
    var store: Store = .{};
    var applied: usize = 0;
    var offset: usize = 0;
    // The end of the part of the log that is known good. The value moves
    // only after the program verifies *and* applies a record. Thus a record
    // that fails its checksum counts as discarded, and is not silently used.
    var good: usize = 0;

    while (offset < wal.len) {
        // No newline means that the process stopped during a write. All the
        // data before the partial record is intact. The replay ignores the
        // partial record, as if the program never wrote it.
        const end = std.mem.findScalarPos(u8, wal, offset, '\n') orelse break;
        const line = wal[offset..end];
        offset = end + 1;

        const bar = std.mem.findScalar(u8, line, '|') orelse break;
        const declared = std.fmt.parseInt(u32, line[0..bar], 10) catch break;
        const payload = line[bar + 1 ..];
        if (checksum(payload) != declared) break;

        var fields = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, payload, '|');
        const op = fields.next() orelse break;
        const key = fields.next() orelse break;
        const value = fields.next() orelse "";

        if (std.mem.eql(u8, op, "set")) {
            store.set(key, value) catch break;
        } else {
            store.remove(key);
        }
        applied += 1;
        good = offset;
    }

    return .{ .store = store, .applied = applied, .discarded = wal.len - good };
}

fn report(out: *std.Io.Writer, label: []const u8, wal: []const u8) !void {
    const r = replay(wal);
    try out.print("{s}\n", .{label});
    try out.print("  {d} records applied, {d} trailing bytes discarded\n", .{ r.applied, r.discarded });
    for ([_][]const u8{ "a", "b", "c" }) |key| {
        try out.print("  {s} -> {s}\n", .{ key, r.store.get(key) orelse "(absent)" });
    }
    try out.writeAll("\n");
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    var file: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var wal: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&file);

    try append(&wal, "set", "a", "one");
    try append(&wal, "set", "b", "two");
    try append(&wal, "set", "a", "uno");
    try append(&wal, "set", "c", "three");
    const full = wal.buffered();

    try out.print("the log:\n{s}\n", .{full});
    try report(out, "clean shutdown", full);

    // The power fails during the last write. The bytes that got to the disk
    // are a line with no newline at the end.
    const torn = full[0 .. full.len - 8];
    try report(out, "crash during the last write", torn);

    // A byte changes in the middle of the log. The newline framing cannot
    // see this change, but the checksum can see it.
    var damaged: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    @memcpy(damaged[0..full.len], full);
    // Inside the second record. The third and fourth records are still
    // readable, but the replay refuses them.
    damaged[30] = 'X';
    try report(out, "a byte corrupted in the second record", damaged[0..full.len]);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`20-storage.kvstore`)*

## What the program did

**A clean shutdown replayed all four records.** The program built the
in-memory store again from the log alone. The log is the database. The
in-memory store is a fast cache of the log.

**The crash lost the record that was in the middle of a write, and nothing
else.** To simulate a power failure, the program truncated the log. This left
a last line with no newline. The replay stopped there, and the first three
records were correct. `c` is absent, and that is correct: that write did not
complete, thus it did not occur.

A WAL works because of this property. When the process stops, you can find a
partial record at the **end** of an append-only file. A record is complete only
after the program writes its terminator. The data before the partial record
does not change, because no write touched that data.

**The checksum found the corrupted byte, and the replay stopped.** The newline
framing cannot see this problem. The record has its terminator, but its content
is incorrect. Only the checksum sees the problem.

The stop had a cost. Records three and four were readable, but the replay
refused them. This is intentional. A log is a **sequence**, and a record after
a damaged record can depend on the lost record. If you apply the readable
records that remain, you get a store that never existed at any time.

A store without its last records is the better result. A store that you build
from the readable records that are left looks correct, and you cannot see that it
is incorrect.

## What this program cannot show you

`fsync`. A write to a file puts the bytes in the page cache of the operating
system. The kernel writes them to the disk later, at a time that it selects. If
the power fails between these two times, the write is lost. On recovery, the
log shows that the write did not occur.

`fsync` is the call that says "write this to the disk now, and do not return
until the data is on the disk". A WAL without `fsync` protects you when your
process stops, but not when the computer stops. `fsync` is also slow. For this
reason, databases have a durability setting, and the fast setting is fast.

This page cannot demonstrate `fsync`, because there is no disk here. The
mechanism above is complete, but the durability guarantee is not complete.

## Check yourself

The log grows forever. Each `set` appends, also for a key that the program
wrote a thousand times. In a real system, what prevents a full disk?

The answer: a **checkpoint**. Then recovery loads the last checkpoint, and
replays only the records after the checkpoint. A checkpoint also makes the start
fast. Without checkpoints, a database that ran for a year must replay a year of
history each time it starts.

This is the same idea as the tombstones from the first chapter, at a larger
scale. An append-only structure needs a periodic process to get back the space
of dead records. In an LSM tree, the name of that process is compaction.

## If you know C

In C, the sequence is `write` and then `fsync`. The two hazards are order and
false success.

**Order:** the log write must get to the disk **before** the change that it
describes. It must come before the change, not at the same time. Suppose the
program updates the database file first, and the computer stops. Then the log
has no record of a change that already occurred, and recovery cannot undo the
change. For this reason, the name is write-*ahead*.

If the order is incorrect,
the system passes each test. Then it loses data the first time that the
computer stops at the incorrect moment.

**False success:** in the past, `fsync` sometimes returned success when the data
was not durable. This occurred on several combinations of filesystem,
controller and drive, with write caching on. PostgreSQL has a well-known report
about a related discovery. The error handling on a failed `fsync` was also
different in different kernel versions, and some versions could lose data
silently. Thus `fsync` alone does not make data durable. The filesystem, the
controller and the drive must also keep their promise.

Next: a query engine. The query engine is the first part here that must decide
*how* to answer, not only what to answer.

---

## A Query Engine

*Data and Storage. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/storage/minidb/*

Until now, each part of this section got exact instructions. Append this
record. Find this key. Replay this log.

A query is different. `SELECT name FROM people WHERE id = 3` says **what** you
want, and says nothing about how to get it. Some part of the engine must
decide if it examines one row or all rows. The query does not contain that
decision.

Thus a query engine has two halves:

- A parser, which changes text into a structure.
- A **planner**, which changes that structure into a strategy.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Row = struct { id: []const u8, name: []const u8, role: []const u8 };

const people = [_]Row{
    .{ .id = "1", .name = "alice", .role = "engineer" },
    .{ .id = "2", .name = "bob", .role = "designer" },
    .{ .id = "3", .name = "carol", .role = "engineer" },
    .{ .id = "4", .name = "dave", .role = "manager" },
    .{ .id = "5", .name = "erin", .role = "designer" },
    .{ .id = "6", .name = "frank", .role = "engineer" },
    .{ .id = "7", .name = "grace", .role = "manager" },
    .{ .id = "8", .name = "heidi", .role = "designer" },
};

/// `SELECT <column> FROM <table> WHERE <column> = <value>`. The shape is fixed.
/// Thus the parser checks for each expected token in order. A full expression
/// grammar needs precedence climbing.
const Query = struct {
    select: []const u8,
    table: []const u8,
    where_column: []const u8,
    where_value: []const u8,
};

const ParseError = error{ Unexpected, Incomplete };

fn parse(sql: []const u8) ParseError!Query {
    var words = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, sql, " \t");

    const expect = struct {
        fn word(it: *std.mem.TokenIterator(u8, .any), want: []const u8) ParseError![]const u8 {
            const got = it.next() orelse return error.Incomplete;
            if (want.len > 0 and !std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(got, want)) return error.Unexpected;
            return got;
        }
    };

    _ = try expect.word(&words, "select");
    const select = try expect.word(&words, "");
    _ = try expect.word(&words, "from");
    const table = try expect.word(&words, "");
    _ = try expect.word(&words, "where");
    const column = try expect.word(&words, "");
    _ = try expect.word(&words, "=");
    const value = try expect.word(&words, "");
    if (words.next() != null) return error.Unexpected;

    return .{ .select = select, .table = table, .where_column = column, .where_value = value };
}

fn columnOf(row: Row, name: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, name, "id")) return row.id;
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, name, "name")) return row.name;
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, name, "role")) return row.role;
    return null;
}

const Plan = enum { index_lookup, table_scan };

/// Query planning in a small form. Does a structure already know the answer
/// to the filter, or must the engine examine each row? A real planner asks the
/// same question with statistics. An index that matches most rows is slower
/// than the scan that it replaces.
fn plan(query: Query, indexed_column: ?[]const u8) Plan {
    const indexed = indexed_column orelse return .table_scan;
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, query.where_column, indexed)) return .index_lookup;
    return .table_scan;
}

const Result = struct { examined: usize, matched: usize };

fn execute(query: Query, indexed_column: ?[]const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !Result {
    const chosen = plan(query, indexed_column);
    try out.print("  plan: {s}\n", .{switch (chosen) {
        .index_lookup => "index lookup",
        .table_scan => "table scan",
    }});

    var examined: usize = 0;
    var matched: usize = 0;
    try out.writeAll("  rows: ");

    switch (chosen) {
        // `id` is the row number, thus it is the index here. The lookup
        // touches only one row. The method of the lookup does not change that.
        .index_lookup => {
            const n = std.fmt.parseInt(usize, query.where_value, 10) catch 0;
            if (n >= 1 and n <= people.len) {
                examined = 1;
                const row = people[n - 1];
                if (columnOf(row, query.select)) |value| {
                    matched = 1;
                    try out.print("{s}", .{value});
                }
            }
        },
        .table_scan => {
            for (people) |row| {
                examined += 1;
                const cell = columnOf(row, query.where_column) orelse continue;
                if (!std.mem.eql(u8, cell, query.where_value)) continue;
                if (columnOf(row, query.select)) |value| {
                    if (matched > 0) try out.writeAll(", ");
                    try out.print("{s}", .{value});
                    matched += 1;
                }
            }
        },
    }

    if (matched == 0) try out.writeAll("(none)");
    try out.print("\n  examined {d} of {d}\n\n", .{ examined, people.len });
    return .{ .examined = examined, .matched = matched };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const queries = [_][]const u8{
        "SELECT name FROM people WHERE id = 3",
        "SELECT name FROM people WHERE role = engineer",
        "SELECT role FROM people WHERE name = grace",
    };

    try out.writeAll("with an index on id\n\n");
    for (queries) |sql| {
        try out.print("{s}\n", .{sql});
        _ = try execute(try parse(sql), "id", out);
    }

    // The same first query with no index. The answer is the same, and the
    // work is eight times more.
    try out.writeAll("with no index at all\n\n");
    try out.print("{s}\n", .{queries[0]});
    _ = try execute(try parse(queries[0]), null, out);

    try out.writeAll("rejected\n");
    for ([_][]const u8{
        "SELECT name FROM people",
        "SELECT name FROM people WHERE id 3",
        "DELETE FROM people WHERE id = 3",
        "SELECT name FROM people WHERE id = 3 AND role = x",
    }) |sql| {
        if (parse(sql)) |_| {
            try out.print("  {s} -> accepted, which is wrong\n", .{sql});
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("  {s: <46} {t}\n", .{ sql, err });
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`20-storage.minidb`)*

## What the program did

**The same query ran in two ways and gave the same answer.** With an index,
`WHERE id = 3` examined 1 row. Without an index, it examined 8 rows. The result
and the SQL were the same, and the second run did eight times the work. The
query did not change, because the query never said how.

Declarative languages have this design. The same design also causes a problem:
you cannot see the cost when you read the code. For this reason,
all databases have an EXPLAIN command. This program prints two lines: the plan
and the rows examined. When a query is slow, you spend most of your time on
those two lines.

**`WHERE role = engineer` used a scan, because `role` has no index.** The
planner is one comparison: is the filtered column the column of the index? A
real planner asks the same question, and then asks a second question. The
section below describes the second question.

**The parser is a sequence of expectations, not a precedence climb.** The
grammar is fixed. Thus the parse is: expect `SELECT`, take a word, expect
`FROM`, take a word. Compare that with the [recursive descent
parser](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/parser/) in the language section.

That parser needed
one function for each precedence level, because arithmetic nests. The SQL
`WHERE` clause also nests when it gets `AND`, `OR` and parentheses. At that
point, this parser becomes that parser.

**The parser rejected four malformed queries, and one of them was a
`DELETE`.** The parser has no special rule against a delete. It expected the
word `SELECT` and got a different word. For a grammar of this size, that is a
fair way to reject a query, and that is the meaning of "SQL subset".

## The question that this planner does not ask

Suppose there is an index on `role`. Must `WHERE role = engineer` use it?

Probably not. Three of eight rows match. Thus an index lookup needs three
jumps into the table and a read of the index. A scan is one straight pass that
reads each row in order. Disks and caches strongly prefer the straight pass.

Real planners make this decision with **statistics**:

- Approximately how many rows match this value?
- How large is the table?
- How expensive is a random read, compared with a sequential read?

Because of these statistics, EXPLAIN output has numbers in it, and databases
have a command to refresh the statistics. Also because of statistics, a query
that was fast last month can become slow after the data changes, and no person
changed the query.

An index is faster only *for selective filters*. A planner without statistics
cannot know if a filter is selective.

## Check yourself

The planner selects the index for `WHERE id = 3`, because `id` has an index.
What must the planner know to handle `WHERE id = 3 AND role = engineer`?

The answer: each condition alone can control the plan, and then the other
condition becomes a filter after the lookup. Thus the planner must select one
of two plans:

- Use the `id` index, and check `role` on the one row that it finds.
- Scan, and check both conditions.

The planner must select the first plan, because `id` is more selective.

With two indexes, the choice is more difficult. With a join, the choice becomes
the main problem of query optimisation. The number of possible plans grows
factorially with the number of tables. Thus planners search, and do not make a
list of all plans. Because of the search, the same query can get a different
plan on a different day.

## The end of this section

These five chapters built append-only records, a lock, an index, a write-ahead
log and a query planner. All databases have these parts.

If you prefer to use one of these parts and not to build it, the database
recipes connect to SQLite, Redis and PostgreSQL from Zig. The ORM builds the
layer above them.
