## An HTML Parser

*The Browser. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/html/*

Each parser in this guide until now can refuse its input. The HTTP request parser rejects a header that has no colon. The language parser reports `UnexpectedToken`. When a parser refuses, it tells you that the input is not what it claims to be.

An HTML parser cannot refuse. No HTML document fails to parse, and this rule is intentional. The specification defines the exact tree for each possible byte sequence. This includes sequences that no author would write intentionally.

The reason is historical, and it explains most of the strange parts of this parser:

- Before anybody wrote a standard, the web already had millions of pages.
- Most of these pages had errors in their markup. All of them looked correct in the browsers that people used.
- A new browser that rejected these pages would look broken.

Thus the standard describes what the old browsers already did, and their error recovery too. "Be lenient" became a written rule.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");

pub const Kind = enum { element, text };

pub const Attr = struct { name: []const u8, value: []const u8 };

pub const Node = struct {
    kind: Kind,
    /// The tag name of an element. For text, the name is empty.
    name: []const u8 = "",
    text: []const u8 = "",
    attrs: [4]Attr = undefined,
    attr_count: u8 = 0,
    first: ?u32 = null,
    next: ?u32 = null,

    pub fn attr(n: Node, name: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
        for (n.attrs[0..n.attr_count]) |a| {
            if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(a.name, name)) return a.value;
        }
        return null;
    }
};

/// Elements that can never have children. `<br>` does not wait for a `</br>`.
/// The element is complete without an end tag. If a parser pushes it onto
/// the stack of open elements, the remainder of the document goes inside it.
fn isVoid(name: []const u8) bool {
    inline for (.{ "br", "img", "hr", "input", "meta", "link" }) |v| {
        if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(name, v)) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

/// The next `<p>` closes an open `<p>`, because a paragraph cannot contain a
/// paragraph. HTML has a table of these rules. Because of these rules, a
/// document with no end tags still gives a sensible tree.
fn closedBy(open: []const u8, starting: []const u8) bool {
    return std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(open, "p") and
        (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(starting, "p") or std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(starting, "div"));
}

pub const Error = error{TooManyNodes};

pub const Parser = struct {
    source: []const u8,
    nodes: []Node,
    used: u32 = 0,
    pos: usize = 0,
    /// The elements that are open and not yet closed. The parser builds the
    /// tree: it appends each node to the element at the top.
    open: [16]u32 = undefined,
    depth: usize = 0,

    fn add(p: *Parser, node: Node) Error!u32 {
        if (p.used == p.nodes.len) return error.TooManyNodes;
        p.nodes[p.used] = node;
        p.used += 1;
        return p.used - 1;
    }

    fn appendChild(p: *Parser, child: u32) void {
        const parent = p.open[p.depth - 1];
        if (p.nodes[parent].first) |first| {
            var last = first;
            while (p.nodes[last].next) |n| last = n;
            p.nodes[last].next = child;
        } else {
            p.nodes[parent].first = child;
        }
    }

    fn closeUntil(p: *Parser, name: []const u8) void {
        // Walk down the stack and find an open element with the same name. If
        // there is none, the end tag is stray. The parser ignores it, and it
        // is not an error. That is what "no parse errors" means in practice.
        var i = p.depth;
        while (i > 1) : (i -= 1) {
            if (std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(p.nodes[p.open[i - 1]].name, name)) {
                p.depth = i - 1;
                return;
            }
        }
    }

    pub fn parse(p: *Parser) Error!u32 {
        const root = try p.add(.{ .kind = .element, .name = "document" });
        p.open[0] = root;
        p.depth = 1;

        while (p.pos < p.source.len) {
            if (p.source[p.pos] == '<') {
                const end = std.mem.findScalarPos(u8, p.source, p.pos, '>') orelse break;
                const inner = p.source[p.pos + 1 .. end];
                p.pos = end + 1;
                if (inner.len == 0) continue;

                if (inner[0] == '/') {
                    p.closeUntil(std.mem.trim(u8, inner[1..], " "));
                    continue;
                }

                var it = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, inner, " \t");
                const name = it.next() orelse continue;

                if (closedBy(p.nodes[p.open[p.depth - 1]].name, name)) p.depth -= 1;

                var node: Node = .{ .kind = .element, .name = name };
                while (it.next()) |pair| {
                    if (node.attr_count == node.attrs.len) break;
                    const eq = std.mem.findScalar(u8, pair, '=') orelse {
                        node.attrs[node.attr_count] = .{ .name = pair, .value = "" };
                        node.attr_count += 1;
                        continue;
                    };
                    node.attrs[node.attr_count] = .{
                        .name = pair[0..eq],
                        .value = std.mem.trim(u8, pair[eq + 1 ..], "\"'"),
                    };
                    node.attr_count += 1;
                }

                const index = try p.add(node);
                p.appendChild(index);
                if (!isVoid(name) and p.depth < p.open.len) {
                    p.open[p.depth] = index;
                    p.depth += 1;
                }
            } else {
                const end = std.mem.findScalarPos(u8, p.source, p.pos, '<') orelse p.source.len;
                const raw = p.source[p.pos..end];
                p.pos = end;
                const text = std.mem.trim(u8, raw, " \t\n\r");
                // Here, whitespace between tags is not content. A real browser
                // keeps it, because in a `<p>` it is a space between words.
                if (text.len == 0) continue;
                const index = try p.add(.{ .kind = .text, .text = text });
                p.appendChild(index);
            }
        }
        return root;
    }
};

pub fn show(nodes: []const Node, index: u32, indent: usize, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    const node = nodes[index];
    for (0..indent) |_| try out.writeAll("  ");
    switch (node.kind) {
        .text => try out.print("\"{s}\"\n", .{node.text}),
        .element => {
            try out.print("<{s}", .{node.name});
            for (node.attrs[0..node.attr_count]) |a| try out.print(" {s}={s}", .{ a.name, a.value });
            try out.writeAll(">\n");
        },
    }
    var child = node.first;
    while (child) |c| : (child = nodes[c].next) try show(nodes, c, indent + 1, out);
}

pub fn parseInto(source: []const u8, nodes: []Node) Error!struct { root: u32, used: u32 } {
    var p: Parser = .{ .source = source, .nodes = nodes };
    const root = try p.parse();
    return .{ .root = root, .used = p.used };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    // This source has four intentional mistakes. The HTML specification tells
    // a parser how to recover from each one, thus a browser shows the page.
    const source =
        \\<h1 class="title">Hello</h1>
        \\<p>First paragraph
        \\<p>Second, and the first was never closed
        \\<div id=main>
        \\  <img src="cat.png">
        \\  text after a void element
        \\</div>
        \\</span>
    ;

    var nodes: [64]Node = undefined;
    const tree = try parseInto(source, &nodes);

    try show(&nodes, tree.root, 0, out);
    try out.print("\n{d} nodes, and every one of the four mistakes above was recovered from\n", .{tree.used});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`21-browser.html`)*

## What just happened

The input has four things that would be errors in XML. The parser made a sensible tree from all four.

**The first `<p>` has no end tag**, and it did not swallow the second `<p>`. The two paragraphs are siblings in the tree. HTML says that a start tag `<p>` closes an open `<p>`. A paragraph cannot contain a paragraph, thus the parser closes the first one for you. The real specification has a table of these rules for list items, table cells and about a dozen more elements.

**`<img>` is complete without an end tag.** It is a **void element**. A void element can never have children. Thus the parser adds it to the tree, but does not push it onto the stack of open elements. If you push it, each node after `<img>` becomes a child of the image. Then the remainder of the document is inside an image.

**`</span>` closed nothing.** No `span` element was open, thus the parser ignores the end tag. The rule does not change: find an open element with the same name, and do nothing if there is no such element.

**`id=main` has no quotes, and it is legal.** An attribute value needs quotes when it is empty. It also needs quotes when it contains a space, a quote, `=`, `<`, `>` or a backtick. All other values can be without quotes.

**The stack makes the tree.** The language parser uses recursion, but this parser does not. The parser pushes an element when it opens, and pops the element when it closes. It appends each node to the element at the top of the stack. A stack is a good fit for a format where the parser can repair the nesting at each step.

## Check yourself

The parser trims whitespace between tags. If no text remains, the parser discards the whitespace. Where is this behaviour wrong?

It is wrong inside a paragraph. `<p>Hello <b>world</b></p>` has a space before `<b>`, and the page needs that space. Without the space, the text on the page is `Helloworld`. A real browser keeps that whitespace. It collapses a run of whitespace into one space. Then it discards the whitespace where the reader cannot see it.

The rules for these cases have many details, and it is easy to make a mistake with them. They cause the unexpected gaps between inline-block elements. They are also the reason that minifiers are careful when they remove newlines in HTML, but not in CSS. This parser discards all of the whitespace, so that the tree is easy to read. A layout engine needs the information that the parser discards.

## If you know C

The tokenizer is a state machine over bytes. The C version is the same `switch` that you would write for the parsers in the Unix tools section. The large part is the tree.

Each node needs children, and the children change when the parser repairs the nesting. Thus C code usually uses one allocation for each node and a linked list for each list of children. Then the code must free all of these allocations when the program discards the document.

The version here uses indices into one flat array. To free the full document, the program discards the array. A node is one struct of fixed size, and it needs no allocation.

Real HTML parsers are also very large. The tokenizer in the specification has about 80 states. The tree construction stage has more than twenty "insertion modes", and each mode has different rules. Nobody wanted this complexity. The complexity comes from a byte-by-byte record of what twenty years of browsers actually did.

Next: a stylesheet, which tells the browser how these nodes must look.

---

## A Stylesheet and the Cascade

*The Browser. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/css/*

A stylesheet is a list of rules. A rule is a selector and some declarations. The parser is simple: split on `{`, then split on `;`, then split on `:`.

The difficult part is this: **several rules match the same element, and the rules give different values**. Something must decide which rule wins. That decision is the cascade, the C in CSS.

## The rule

The cascade makes two comparisons, in this order:

1. **Specificity.** How precisely does the selector describe the element?
2. **Source order.** If the specificity is equal, the later rule wins.

The cascade has no other comparisons. When CSS seems unpredictable, the cause is usually a wrong idea about specificity.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const dom = @import("html.zig");

/// Three counts. Compare them from left to right, and never add them into
/// one number. The common 100/10/1 weights are a simplification that gives
/// wrong answers. The "Check yourself" in the chapter shows where.
pub const Specificity = struct {
    ids: u16 = 0,
    classes: u16 = 0,
    tags: u16 = 0,

    pub fn beats(a: Specificity, b: Specificity) bool {
        if (a.ids != b.ids) return a.ids > b.ids;
        if (a.classes != b.classes) return a.classes > b.classes;
        return a.tags > b.tags;
    }
};

pub const Selector = struct {
    tag: ?[]const u8 = null,
    class: ?[]const u8 = null,
    id: ?[]const u8 = null,

    pub fn specificity(s: Selector) Specificity {
        return .{
            .ids = if (s.id != null) 1 else 0,
            .classes = if (s.class != null) 1 else 0,
            .tags = if (s.tag != null) 1 else 0,
        };
    }

    /// Each component that is present must match. A component that is absent
    /// matches all values. Thus `*` needs no special case.
    pub fn matches(s: Selector, node: dom.Node) bool {
        if (node.kind != .element) return false;
        if (s.tag) |t| {
            if (!std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(node.name, t)) return false;
        }
        if (s.id) |want| {
            const got = node.attr("id") orelse return false;
            if (!std.mem.eql(u8, got, want)) return false;
        }
        if (s.class) |want| {
            const got = node.attr("class") orelse return false;
            var classes = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, got, " ");
            var found = false;
            while (classes.next()) |c| {
                if (std.mem.eql(u8, c, want)) found = true;
            }
            if (!found) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
};

pub const Declaration = struct { property: []const u8, value: []const u8 };

pub const Rule = struct {
    selector: Selector,
    decls: [8]Declaration = undefined,
    decl_count: u8 = 0,
    /// The position in the stylesheet. When two specificities are equal, the
    /// position decides. Thus the advice "put your overrides last" works.
    order: u16 = 0,
};

fn parseSelector(text: []const u8) Selector {
    var s: Selector = .{};
    var rest = std.mem.trim(u8, text, " \t\n");
    if (rest.len == 0) return s;

    // The tag name, if the selector does not start with a marker.
    if (rest[0] != '.' and rest[0] != '#' and rest[0] != '*') {
        const end = std.mem.findAny(u8, rest, ".#") orelse rest.len;
        s.tag = rest[0..end];
        rest = rest[end..];
    } else if (rest[0] == '*') {
        rest = rest[1..];
    }

    while (rest.len > 0) {
        const marker = rest[0];
        rest = rest[1..];
        const end = std.mem.findAny(u8, rest, ".#") orelse rest.len;
        const name = rest[0..end];
        if (marker == '.') s.class = name else s.id = name;
        rest = rest[end..];
    }
    return s;
}

pub fn parse(source: []const u8, out: []Rule) ![]Rule {
    var n: usize = 0;
    var rest = source;

    while (std.mem.findScalar(u8, rest, '{')) |open| {
        const close = std.mem.findScalar(u8, rest, '}') orelse break;
        if (n == out.len) return error.TooManyRules;

        var rule: Rule = .{ .selector = parseSelector(rest[0..open]), .order = @intCast(n) };

        var decls = std.mem.splitScalar(u8, rest[open + 1 .. close], ';');
        while (decls.next()) |decl| {
            const colon = std.mem.findScalar(u8, decl, ':') orelse continue;
            if (rule.decl_count == rule.decls.len) break;
            rule.decls[rule.decl_count] = .{
                .property = std.mem.trim(u8, decl[0..colon], " \t\n"),
                .value = std.mem.trim(u8, decl[colon + 1 ..], " \t\n"),
            };
            rule.decl_count += 1;
        }

        out[n] = rule;
        n += 1;
        rest = rest[close + 1 ..];
    }
    return out[0..n];
}

/// The cascade: find each declaration that matches. Specificity decides the
/// winner first, and source order decides second. A third tiebreak is not
/// necessary, because each rule in the sheet has a different position.
pub fn cascade(rules: []const Rule, node: dom.Node, property: []const u8) ?[]const u8 {
    var best: ?Declaration = null;
    var best_spec: Specificity = .{};
    var best_order: u16 = 0;

    for (rules) |rule| {
        if (!rule.selector.matches(node)) continue;
        for (rule.decls[0..rule.decl_count]) |decl| {
            if (!std.mem.eql(u8, decl.property, property)) continue;
            const spec = rule.selector.specificity();
            const wins = best == null or spec.beats(best_spec) or
                (!best_spec.beats(spec) and rule.order >= best_order);
            if (wins) {
                best = decl;
                best_spec = spec;
                best_order = rule.order;
            }
        }
    }
    return if (best) |d| d.value else null;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const stylesheet =
        \\p { color: black; margin: 0 }
        \\.warning { color: orange }
        \\p.warning { color: red; margin: 8 }
        \\#urgent { color: crimson }
        \\p { margin: 4 }
    ;

    var rules_buf: [16]Rule = undefined;
    const rules = try parse(stylesheet, &rules_buf);

    try out.print("{d} rules\n", .{rules.len});
    var text: [32]u8 = undefined;
    for (rules) |rule| {
        const s = rule.selector.specificity();
        var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&text);
        if (rule.selector.tag) |t| try w.print("{s}", .{t});
        if (rule.selector.class) |c| try w.print(".{s}", .{c});
        if (rule.selector.id) |i| try w.print("#{s}", .{i});
        try out.print("  order {d}  specificity {d},{d},{d}  {s}\n", .{
            rule.order, s.ids, s.classes, s.tags, w.buffered(),
        });
    }

    const html = "<p class=\"warning\" id=\"urgent\">Careful</p><p>Ordinary</p>";
    var nodes: [16]dom.Node = undefined;
    const tree = try dom.parseInto(html, &nodes);

    try out.writeAll("\nwhat each element gets\n");
    var child = nodes[tree.root].first;
    while (child) |c| : (child = nodes[c].next) {
        const node = nodes[c];
        if (node.kind != .element) continue;
        try out.print("  <{s} class={s} id={s}>\n", .{
            node.name,
            node.attr("class") orelse "-",
            node.attr("id") orelse "-",
        });
        for ([_][]const u8{ "color", "margin" }) |property| {
            try out.print("    {s: <7} {s}\n", .{ property, cascade(rules, node, property) orelse "(unset)" });
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`21-browser.css`)*

## What just happened

**`<p class="warning" id="urgent">` got `color: crimson`.** Each rule in the sheet matched the element, and four of the rules set a colour: black, orange, red and crimson. `#urgent` won, because an id beats any number of classes. That is specificity.

**The same element got `margin: 8`, from `p.warning`.** Three rules set a margin. Two of them are the plain `p`, with a specificity of 0,0,1. `p.warning` has 0,1,1, and it beats both. The class component makes the decision.

**The plain `<p>` got `margin: 4`, from the last rule.** Two rules with the same selector `p` set a margin. The specificity is equal, thus the source order makes the decision, and the later rule wins. This is the reason for the advice "put your overrides at the bottom".

**Specificity is three numbers, not one.** The output shows the three numbers separately: `0,1,1` for `p.warning` and `1,0,0` for `#urgent`. The cascade compares them from left to right, as you compare version numbers. Thus any id beats any number of classes.

## Check yourself

Many texts describe specificity as one score: 100 for an id, 10 for a class and 1 for a tag, added together. Where does this score give the wrong answer?

It gives the wrong answer at eleven classes. Eleven classes get a score of 110, and 110 beats the 100 of an id. In a real browser, the id wins. The comparison is one component at a time. Thus an id beats any number of classes, however large the middle number is.

The single score is a shortcut that teachers use. It gives the correct answer for each realistic stylesheet, and thus people continue to use it. But when you build a program that *computes* specificity, one number is a bug. For this reason, the implementation above uses a struct with three fields.

## What this one leaves out

**Inheritance.** For some properties, for example `color`, a child that does not set the property inherits the value from its parent. For other properties, for example `margin`, the child does not inherit. The specification gives this rule for each property. The next chapter needs inheritance, because a paragraph in a styled div must get its colour from some place.

**Combinators.** `div p` matches a `p` that has a `div` ancestor. `div > p` matches only when the `div` is the parent. Both need the tree, not only the node. Thus the match becomes a walk up through the ancestors.

For this reason, real engines match selectors from right to left. They start from the element and walk up. They do not find all the candidates and then search down.

`!important` is above specificity. It exists because of user stylesheets. A reader who needs larger text must be able to overrule the page.

## If you know C

The parser is `strtok` on braces and semicolons, with no surprises. The match needs more thought, because it is the hot loop of a browser.

The simple method tests each rule against each element. The cost is the number of rules times the number of nodes. For a real stylesheet on a real page, that cost is much too slow.

Instead, engines put the rules in an index by the rightmost component. The index is a set of hash maps, with the tag, the class and the id as keys. Then an element tests only the few rules that can match it. This index is the reason that the shape of your selectors has an effect on performance. It is also the reason that a selector that ends in `*` is the slow one.

The other concern for a C programmer is that each string here points into the stylesheet source. Thus the source must live longer than the parsed rules. The remainder of this track makes the same decision to borrow. In a browser, this is the reason that the bytes of a stylesheet stay alive for as long as the page.

Next: layout, which changes this tree of styled nodes into rectangles with positions.

---

## Layout

*The Browser. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/layout/*

After two chapters, the program has a tree of nodes and a way to ask how each node must look. Neither of them tells where each node goes. Layout is the stage that changes the tree into rectangles with positions. The earlier stages parse text. Layout is the first stage of a browser that calculates geometry.

The algorithm is not symmetric:

- **Width goes down.** A block fills the width that it gets. Thus a parent can decide the widths of its children before it knows anything about them.
- **Height goes up.** A block is as tall as its contents. Thus a parent cannot know its height until the layout of each child is complete.

One pass goes down for the widths, and one pass goes up for the heights. Many surprises in CSS sizes come from this difference.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const dom = @import("html.zig");
const style = @import("css.zig");

pub const Box = struct {
    node: u32,
    x: i32 = 0,
    y: i32 = 0,
    width: i32 = 0,
    height: i32 = 0,
    padding: i32 = 0,
    margin: i32 = 0,
    first: ?u32 = null,
    next: ?u32 = null,
};

/// Each line of text has this height. A real engine measures the font and
/// breaks the text into lines that fit the width. The number of lines gives
/// the height. That is inline layout. It is a different algorithm from the
/// block layout below.
const line_height: i32 = 20;

pub const Engine = struct {
    nodes: []const dom.Node,
    rules: []const style.Rule,
    boxes: []Box,
    used: u32 = 0,

    fn number(e: Engine, node: dom.Node, property: []const u8, default: i32) i32 {
        const text = style.cascade(e.rules, node, property) orelse return default;
        return std.fmt.parseInt(i32, text, 10) catch default;
    }

    fn add(e: *Engine, box: Box) !u32 {
        if (e.used == e.boxes.len) return error.TooManyBoxes;
        e.boxes[e.used] = box;
        e.used += 1;
        return e.used - 1;
    }

    /// Pass one goes down. The parent decides the width of a block, because a
    /// block fills the space that it gets. The pass does not look at the
    /// children. Thus this pass can run before the children exist.
    pub fn buildWidths(e: *Engine, node_index: u32, available: i32) !u32 {
        const node = e.nodes[node_index];
        const margin = e.number(node, "margin", 0);
        const padding = e.number(node, "padding", 0);

        const explicit = style.cascade(e.rules, node, "width");
        const width = if (explicit) |text|
            std.fmt.parseInt(i32, text, 10) catch available
        else
            available - 2 * margin - 2 * padding;

        const box = try e.add(.{
            .node = node_index,
            .width = width,
            .margin = margin,
            .padding = padding,
        });

        var last: ?u32 = null;
        var child = node.first;
        while (child) |c| : (child = e.nodes[c].next) {
            const child_box = try e.buildWidths(c, width);
            if (last) |l| e.boxes[l].next = child_box else e.boxes[box].first = child_box;
            last = child_box;
        }
        return box;
    }

    /// Pass two goes up. The height of a block is the height that its children
    /// need. The pass cannot know that height before the layout of the children.
    /// The pass gives positions on the way down, and adds heights on the way up.
    pub fn placeAndSize(e: *Engine, box_index: u32, x: i32, y: i32) i32 {
        const box = &e.boxes[box_index];
        box.x = x + box.margin + box.padding;
        box.y = y + box.margin + box.padding;

        if (e.nodes[box.node].kind == .text) {
            box.height = line_height;
            return box.height + 2 * box.margin + 2 * box.padding;
        }

        var cursor = box.y;
        var child = box.first;
        while (child) |c| : (child = e.boxes[c].next) {
            cursor += e.placeAndSize(c, box.x, cursor);
        }

        const explicit = style.cascade(e.rules, e.nodes[box.node], "height");
        box.height = if (explicit) |text|
            std.fmt.parseInt(i32, text, 10) catch (cursor - box.y)
        else
            cursor - box.y;

        return box.height + 2 * box.margin + 2 * box.padding;
    }
};

fn show(e: Engine, index: u32, depth: usize, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    const box = e.boxes[index];
    const node = e.nodes[box.node];
    for (0..depth) |_| try out.writeAll("  ");
    const label = if (node.kind == .text) "#text" else node.name;
    // Format each number into a string first, then add the padding. If an
    // integer has a width, this compiler prints a sign with it (`{d:<4}` on 7
    // is "+7  "). A box tree must not show a column of plus signs.
    var cell: [4][8]u8 = undefined;
    try out.print("{s: <8} x={s: <5} y={s: <5} w={s: <5} h={s}\n", .{
        label,
        try std.mem.print(&cell[0], "{d}", .{box.x}),
        try std.mem.print(&cell[1], "{d}", .{box.y}),
        try std.mem.print(&cell[2], "{d}", .{box.width}),
        try std.mem.print(&cell[3], "{d}", .{box.height}),
    });
    var child = box.first;
    while (child) |c| : (child = e.boxes[c].next) try show(e, c, depth + 1, out);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const html =
        \\<div id=page>
        \\<h1>Title</h1>
        \\<div class=box><p>One</p><p>Two</p></div>
        \\<p>Footer</p>
        \\</div>
    ;
    const sheet =
        \\#page { padding: 10 }
        \\.box { margin: 5; padding: 5 }
        \\h1 { height: 40 }
    ;

    var nodes: [32]dom.Node = undefined;
    const tree = try dom.parseInto(html, &nodes);

    var rules_buf: [8]style.Rule = undefined;
    const rules = try style.parse(sheet, &rules_buf);

    var boxes: [32]Box = undefined;
    var engine: Engine = .{ .nodes = &nodes, .rules = rules, .boxes = &boxes };

    const viewport: i32 = 400;
    const root = try engine.buildWidths(tree.root, viewport);
    _ = engine.placeAndSize(root, 0, 0);

    try out.print("viewport is {d} wide\n\n", .{viewport});
    try show(engine, root, 0, out);

    try out.writeAll("\nwidths were decided before any child was measured;\n");
    try out.writeAll("heights could not be known until every child was placed.\n");

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`21-browser.layout`)*

## What just happened

**The widths become smaller at each level: 400, then 380, then 360.** The viewport gives 400. `#page` has a padding of 10 on each side, thus its content is 380. `.box` is inside `#page`, and it has a margin of 5 and a padding of 5. These use 20 more, thus the children of `.box` get 360. The pass did not look at a child at any point.

**The heights add up from the bottom.** The two paragraphs inside `.box` are 20 each, thus `.box` is 40. `#page` contains these boxes:

- an `h1` that is 40 tall
- the `.box`, which is 40 tall, with a margin of 5 and a padding of 5 on each side
- a footer that is 20 tall

40 plus 60 plus 20 is 120. No part of the program can know this number before the layout of the children.

**The `h1` has an explicit height of 40, and it kept that height.** Its text is 20 tall. An explicit height overrides the measured height. Thus content can overflow a box, and that is the reason for the `overflow` property.

**The positions come from a cursor.** The program puts each child at the current y. Then the cursor moves down by the full outer height of that child. This one loop is normal flow. It is the reason that blocks stack vertically by default.

## Why `height: 100%` does not do what people expect

`width: 100%` works because the widths go down. The width of the parent is already known when the program calculates the size of the child.

`height: 100%` asks the child to be as tall as its parent. But the program calculates the height of the parent *from its children*. The question is circular. CSS says that the question has no answer, unless the parent has a definite height of its own. When there is no answer, the browser ignores the declaration.

Thus the usual fix is an explicit height on each ancestor. Viewport units also work, because the viewport has a definite height. That height does not depend on the contents of the viewport.

## What this leaves out

**Inline layout.** In this program, text is always one line that is 20 pixels tall. A real engine measures the text in its font and breaks the text into lines that fit the width. The number of lines gives the height. Inline layout is a different algorithm, and it runs inside the block algorithm. In inline layout, the whitespace that the [HTML chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/html/) discarded becomes important.

**All layout that is not normal flow.** Floats, absolute positions, flexbox and grid are each a different layout algorithm. `display` and `position` select the algorithm for each element. Flexbox reverses the asymmetry above. That is the reason flexbox solved problems that were difficult for ten years.

## Check yourself

The program runs `buildWidths` to the end, then runs `placeAndSize` to the end. Why can the program not use one pass?

The height of a parent needs the heights of its children. The width of a child needs the width of its parent. One pass would have to move in both directions at the same time. Two passes in opposite directions make each pass simple.

Real engines run both passes, and they call the two passes together *reflow*. The heights go up. Thus, a change to the height of one element causes a new calculation for each ancestor in the chain.

A script can change the document, and then the old boxes are out of date. The browser tries to run layout again one time for each frame, not one time for each change.

When JavaScript reads a computed size, such as `offsetHeight`, the browser cannot follow that plan. The browser cannot answer from boxes that are out of date. It must run layout *immediately*, in the middle of your script.

If a loop reads a size and also writes to the page, each iteration causes a full layout. This problem has the name *layout thrashing*. It is the same two passes from this chapter. They run a thousand times, because the script asks a thousand questions.

## If you know C

The walk through the tree is simple. The arithmetic needs care. Each value here is a signed integer, and the box model adds values together.

A negative margin is a real CSS feature, and it makes a box wider than its parent. A chain of negative margins can make a width negative. A production engine clamps the value at zero after each subtraction.

Layout is also the hot path. A page has tens of thousands of boxes. Layout runs on each resize, on each animation frame that changes the geometry, and on each DOM change. Thus engines pack their box structs, and they cache the result for each node with a dirty bit.

The flat array in this program also helps the speed. When layout walks a tree of pointers to random locations on the heap, layout is slower.

Next: paint, which changes these rectangles into pixels.

---

## Paint

*The Browser. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/render/*

Layout made rectangles with positions. The paint stage fills them in. It is the simplest stage in the pipeline.

The canvas is a rectangle of memory. Each box writes its colour into the cells that it covers. The painter visits the parents first, then the children in document order. Thus a box that the painter paints later covers the previous contents. The painter does not use a depth buffer or a visibility test. It does not clip a box against the boxes that are already on the canvas.

This method is the **painter's algorithm**. A painter on a canvas paints the later layers over the earlier layers, and this algorithm does the same. It is the correct choice here, because the order is already known. The document tells which element is in front of which element.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const dom = @import("html.zig");
const style = @import("css.zig");
const layout = @import("layout.zig");

pub const cols = 50;
pub const rows = 15;

/// The framebuffer. A real framebuffer holds four bytes for each pixel, and
/// the browser gives it to the compositor. This one holds one character for
/// each cell, so that you can read the result in a terminal. Nothing else
/// about the algorithm changes.
pub const Canvas = struct {
    cells: [rows][cols]u8 = @splat(@splat('.')),

    pub fn fill(c: *Canvas, x: i32, y: i32, w: i32, h: i32, ink: u8) void {
        var row = y;
        while (row < y + h) : (row += 1) {
            if (row < 0 or row >= rows) continue;
            var col = x;
            while (col < x + w) : (col += 1) {
                if (col < 0 or col >= cols) continue;
                c.cells[@intCast(row)][@intCast(col)] = ink;
            }
        }
    }

    pub fn show(c: Canvas, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
        for (c.cells) |row| try out.print("{s}\n", .{&row});
    }
};

/// Parents first, then children, in document order. That order is the
/// painter's algorithm: paint all boxes, and a box painted later covers the
/// previous contents. There is no depth test, and the painter does not clip
/// a box against another box. The only clip is at the edges of the canvas.
pub fn paint(
    engine: layout.Engine,
    rules: []const style.Rule,
    box_index: u32,
    canvas: *Canvas,
) void {
    const box = engine.boxes[box_index];
    const node = engine.nodes[box.node];

    if (node.kind == .element) {
        const ink = if (style.cascade(rules, node, "background")) |text|
            text[0]
        else
            ' ';
        if (ink != ' ') {
            canvas.fill(
                @divTrunc(box.x, 8),
                @divTrunc(box.y, 10),
                @divTrunc(box.width, 8),
                @divTrunc(box.height, 10),
                ink,
            );
        }
    } else {
        // Paint the characters of the text. Clip them to the edges of the canvas.
        const text = node.text;
        const x = @divTrunc(box.x, 8);
        const y = @divTrunc(box.y, 10);
        if (y >= 0 and y < rows) {
            for (text, 0..) |ch, i| {
                const col = x + @as(i32, @intCast(i));
                if (col >= 0 and col < cols) canvas.cells[@intCast(y)][@intCast(col)] = ch;
            }
        }
    }

    var child = box.first;
    while (child) |c| : (child = engine.boxes[c].next) paint(engine, rules, c, canvas);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const html =
        \\<div id=page><h1>Title</h1><div class=box><p>One</p><p>Two</p></div></div>
    ;
    const sheet =
        \\#page { padding: 10; background: - }
        \\.box { margin: 5; padding: 5; background: o }
        \\h1 { height: 40; background: = }
    ;

    var nodes: [32]dom.Node = undefined;
    const tree = try dom.parseInto(html, &nodes);

    var rules_buf: [8]style.Rule = undefined;
    const rules = try style.parse(sheet, &rules_buf);

    var boxes: [32]layout.Box = undefined;
    var engine: layout.Engine = .{ .nodes = &nodes, .rules = rules, .boxes = &boxes };
    const root = try engine.buildWidths(tree.root, 400);
    _ = engine.placeAndSize(root, 0, 0);

    var canvas: Canvas = .{};
    paint(engine, rules, root, &canvas);
    try canvas.show(out);

    try out.writeAll("\n#page painted first, then h1 over it, then .box,\n");
    try out.writeAll("then the text of each paragraph over that.\n");

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`21-browser.render`)*

## What just happened

**The program made three fills and wrote three runs of text, in order. You can see the order in the picture.**

1. `#page` filled its area with `-`.
2. `h1` filled a part of that area with `=`.
3. `.box` filled a lower part with `o`.
4. The program wrote the text over the fills.

The paragraphs have no `background` rule, thus they did not fill. Each step wrote over the step before it, and nothing did a check first.

**The canvas is an array.** A real framebuffer has four bytes for each pixel, not one character. The fill loop writes RGBA instead of a letter. The remainder of the structure is the same. The [pixel buffers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/pixel-buffers/) chapter builds the full version.

**Clipping is a bounds check.** Each write tests if the cell is inside the canvas. The check stops a box that is off the edge, so that the box cannot write outside the buffer. Without the check, a stylesheet could cause a buffer overflow.

**The program paints text, but it does not do a layout of the text.** The text starts at the corner of the box and continues to the right. Real text needs glyphs from a font at a size, with hinting and subpixel positioning. The [font](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/) work in the graphics section is closer to that.

## Why this order and not another

One alternative is to paint the children first, and then let the parents fill the area around them. That alternative fails immediately. The background of a parent would need the combined shape of all its children. That question is much more difficult than "fill this rectangle".

The other alternative is to skip each part that a later box will cover. That is a real optimisation, with the name occlusion culling. Browsers do a limited version of it. It needs to know which boxes are opaque, and `background: rgba(0,0,0,0.5)` makes that more difficult. Thus the general case stays the same: paint all boxes in order, and accept that the program paints some pixels two times.

## Check yourself

With `z-index`, the browser can paint an element in front of an element that comes after it in the document. How does `z-index` fit into one ordered walk?

It does not fit. Stacking contexts solve this problem. An element with a `z-index`, and with a `position` that is not `static`, makes a *stacking context*. The browser paints the subtree of that element as a unit. It sorts the units by `z-index`, then paints them in that order.

Thus the walk is still ordered. But the order comes from a sort, not from the document, and the sort is over groups, not single elements. For this reason, a child can never paint outside the stacking context of its parent, however large its `z-index` is. This surprises many people, until they know how the paint stage works.

## If you know C

The fill loop is the same as in any framebuffer, and so are the notes about performance:

- Write full rows instead of single cells, so that the compiler can vectorise the loop.
- Keep the buffer row-major, so that the writes are sequential.

The main danger here is the bounds check. A box with a negative position, or a width larger than the canvas, is normal, not a corner case. A stylesheet can make one easily. Content that overflows its container does it all the time.

C code that calculates `row * width + col` and writes without a clamp lets a stylesheet control an out-of-bounds write. That is a serious security bug.

The version above clamps each cell. It is slow, and it is clearly correct. Production code clamps the rectangle one time and then writes without a check. That method is fast, but the clamp must be correct.

Next: the scripting engine, and then the full pipeline from start to end.

---

## A Scripting Engine

*The Browser. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/script/*

Many people think that the DOM is a part of JavaScript. It is not. The JavaScript specification does not mention `document`, `window`, `fetch` or an element.

The specification defines a language: values, functions, objects and control flow. A browser **embeds** that language, and then adds a set of names to its global scope. These names are **host objects**. They are the only connection between a script and a page.

Node has a different set of names. A game engine that embeds a scripting language has a third set. The language is the same in all of them.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const dom = @import("html.zig");

/// The smallest evaluator that can show the binding: names, integers, `+`
/// and `print`. The Tiny Language section builds the real language, with a
/// lexer, a parser, an interpreter and a bytecode VM. This file does not
/// import it, because each snippet on this site compiles alone. Also, in a
/// browser, the language and the host are separate libraries.
///
/// The script and the page meet in one place: `Env`.
const Env = struct {
    names: [8][]const u8 = undefined,
    values: [8]i64 = undefined,
    count: usize = 0,

    fn define(e: *Env, name: []const u8, value: i64) !void {
        if (e.count == e.names.len) return error.Full;
        e.names[e.count] = name;
        e.values[e.count] = value;
        e.count += 1;
    }

    fn get(e: Env, name: []const u8) !i64 {
        for (e.names[0..e.count], 0..) |n, i| {
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, n, name)) return e.values[i];
        }
        return error.UndefinedVariable;
    }
};

/// `print <expr>;`. An expression is a chain of names and numbers, with `+`
/// between them. That is sufficient to show that a script reads the values
/// from the host and nothing more.
fn eval(env: Env, expr: []const u8) !i64 {
    var total: i64 = 0;
    var terms = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, expr, "+ \t");
    while (terms.next()) |term| {
        total += std.fmt.parseInt(i64, term, 10) catch try env.get(term);
    }
    return total;
}

fn run(env: Env, script: []const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var lines = std.mem.tokenizeAny(u8, script, ";\n");
    while (lines.next()) |raw| {
        const line = std.mem.trim(u8, raw, " \t");
        if (line.len == 0) continue;
        if (!std.mem.startsWith(u8, line, "print ")) return error.Unsupported;
        try out.print("  {d}\n", .{try eval(env, line["print ".len..])});
    }
}

/// Count the elements with a given tag, at all levels of the tree.
fn countTag(nodes: []const dom.Node, index: u32, tag: []const u8) u32 {
    var total: u32 = 0;
    const node = nodes[index];
    if (node.kind == .element and std.ascii.eqlIgnoreCase(node.name, tag)) total += 1;
    var child = node.first;
    while (child) |c| : (child = nodes[c].next) total += countTag(nodes, c, tag);
    return total;
}

/// The link between the page and the script. The evaluator does not know
/// what an element is. The host walks the document and defines ordinary
/// variables. About the page, the script sees only the values in this
/// function. That is a "host object": it is not part of the language. The
/// program that embeds the language installs it.
fn bind(env: *Env, nodes: []const dom.Node, root: u32) !void {
    try env.define("paragraphs", countTag(nodes, root, "p"));
    try env.define("headings", countTag(nodes, root, "h1"));
    try env.define("images", countTag(nodes, root, "img"));
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const html =
        \\<h1>Gallery</h1>
        \\<p>One</p>
        \\<p>Two</p>
        \\<p>Three</p>
        \\<img src=a.png>
        \\<img src=b.png>
    ;

    var doc: [32]dom.Node = undefined;
    const tree = try dom.parseInto(html, &doc);

    var env: Env = .{};
    try bind(&env, &doc, tree.root);

    try out.writeAll("what the host put in scope\n");
    for ([_][]const u8{ "paragraphs", "headings", "images" }) |name| {
        try out.print("  {s: <11} {d}\n", .{ name, try env.get(name) });
    }

    // The script has no syntax for documents, and it needs none. `paragraphs`
    // is an ordinary variable. The host set its value with a walk of a tree.
    const script =
        \\print paragraphs;
        \\print paragraphs + images;
        \\print headings + paragraphs + images;
    ;

    try out.writeAll("\nwhat the script printed\n");
    try run(env, script, out);

    // A name that the host did not define is an ordinary undefined variable.
    // There is no separate category of "DOM error".
    try out.writeAll("\nasking for something not in scope\n");
    if (run(env, "print stylesheets;", out)) |_| {
        try out.writeAll("  accepted, which is wrong\n");
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("  {t}\n", .{err});
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`21-browser.script`)*

## What just happened

**The host walked the document and defined three ordinary variables.** `paragraphs` is 3, because a walk through the tree counted three `<p>` elements. For the evaluator, `paragraphs` is a name with an integer value. It looks the same as a variable that the script declared.

**The script has no syntax for documents, and it needs none.** `print paragraphs + images` is arithmetic. No part of the grammar knows what an image is. To give the page a new capability, the host defines one more name. The language does not change.

**A name that the host did not define is an ordinary undefined variable.** The request for `stylesheets` gave `UndefinedVariable`. A typo in a local name gives the same error. There is no separate type of "DOM error". For the same reason, in a real browser, `document.foo is not a function` and `myTypo is not defined` come from the same code.

**The evaluator here is intentionally very small.** It supports names, integers, `+` and `print`. That is sufficient to show where the language and the host meet.

[The Tiny Language section](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/lexer/) builds a fuller language, with a lexer, a parser, a tree-walking interpreter and a bytecode VM. In a browser, the language and the host are two separate libraries, and the build links them together, as in this program. V8 does not contain a DOM. Chrome supplies the DOM.

## What a real binding adds

**Writes, not only reads.** A script that can only read the page cannot do much. `element.textContent = "x"` changes the tree. Then layout and paint run again, with the two passes from [the layout chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/layout/).

**Objects instead of flat names.** A real script uses `document.querySelectorAll("p").length` instead of `paragraphs`. For that, the language must have objects, and the host must put functions on those objects. That is more code, but the idea is the same.

**Events.** In the program above, nothing runs two times. A real engine keeps the environment alive. It calls back into the environment when an event occurs. Thus the variables of the script live longer than the script.

Then the host has a problem with lifetimes. A listener that holds a reference to a removed element keeps that element alive. This is a common memory leak on the web. It occurs because the language and the host both hold objects that point to each other.

## Check yourself

The language does not know what an element is. Then how does a script get a *type error* when it calls a method on the wrong thing?

For the language, host objects are ordinary objects. A script can call a method that does not exist on a host object. That call fails in the same way as on any other object.

The engine does not know that `document` is special. It knows only two facts. The thing with the name `document` has no property `queryselectorAll`, because you misspelled `querySelectorAll`. And a call to `undefined` is an error.

Thus these error messages usually tell you little about your mistake. The engine that reports them does not know what a document is.

Next: [the whole pipeline](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/browser/), with each stage in one program.

---

## The Whole Pipeline

*The Browser. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/browser/*

Each stage has a chapter. This chapter runs the stages one after the other. The pipeline answers the question "how does a browser work?", and here you can see the answer in about 50 lines of code.

```
bytes ─► tree ─► boxes with widths ─► boxes with positions ─► pixels
        (HTML)      (CSS + layout)         (layout)            (paint)
```

There are five stages. Each stage uses only what the previous stage made. This separation is the reason that a person can build a browser at all. The HTML parser knows nothing about pixels. The painter knows nothing about tags.

## The program

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const dom = @import("html.zig");
const style = @import("css.zig");
const layout = @import("layout.zig");
const render = @import("render.zig");

/// All the stages that a page needs, in the order that they run. Each stage
/// uses only what the previous stage made. Thus each stage has a chapter of
/// its own, and you can replace one stage without a change to the others.
fn open(html: []const u8, sheet: []const u8, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    // 1. Bytes to a tree. This stage cannot fail.
    var nodes: [64]dom.Node = undefined;
    const tree = try dom.parseInto(html, &nodes);

    // 2. Bytes to rules. This stage does not look at the tree.
    var rules_buf: [16]style.Rule = undefined;
    const rules = try style.parse(sheet, &rules_buf);

    // 3. Tree and rules to boxes with widths, from the top down.
    var boxes: [64]layout.Box = undefined;
    var engine: layout.Engine = .{ .nodes = &nodes, .rules = rules, .boxes = &boxes };
    const root = try engine.buildWidths(tree.root, 400);

    // 4. Give the boxes positions and heights, from the bottom up.
    _ = engine.placeAndSize(root, 0, 0);

    // 5. Boxes to pixels, from back to front.
    var canvas: render.Canvas = .{};
    render.paint(engine, rules, root, &canvas);
    try canvas.show(out);

    try out.print("\n{d} nodes, {d} rules, {d} boxes\n", .{ tree.used, rules.len, engine.used });
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [8192]u8 = undefined;
    var stdout_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &stdout_writer.interface;

    const html =
        \\<div id=page>
        \\<h1>Zig</h1>
        \\<div class=row><p>alpha</p><p>beta</p></div>
        \\<p class=note>footer</p>
        \\</div>
    ;

    const sheet =
        \\#page { padding: 10; background: . }
        \\h1 { height: 30; background: # }
        \\.row { margin: 5; padding: 5; background: o }
        \\.note { background: - }
    ;

    try out.writeAll("as written\n\n");
    try open(html, sheet, out);

    // The same document, with a change to one declaration and to nothing
    // else. This property makes a stylesheet useful.
    const restyled =
        \\#page { padding: 10; background: . }
        \\h1 { height: 60; background: # }
        \\.row { margin: 5; padding: 5; background: o }
        \\.note { background: - }
    ;

    try out.writeAll("\nwith h1 twice as tall, and nothing else touched\n\n");
    try open(html, restyled, out);

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`21-browser.browser`)*

## What just happened

**One declaration changed, and the page changed its arrangement.** `h1 { height: 30 }` became `height: 60`, and each box below the `h1` moved down. Nothing else in the stylesheet or the document changed.

This is the reason that stylesheets exist. The height of the box is an input to layout. The program calculates each position below the box. It does not store the positions. When you change the input and run the two passes again, you get a new set of positions. The program writes no value two times, thus no two copies can disagree.

**The program prints the counts for each render.** The counts are 11 nodes, 4 rules and 11 boxes. Here, the box tree and the node tree have the same size. Usually they do not. Some elements make no box. One element can make several boxes, for example one box for each line of text or one for each table cell.

**You can replace each stage.** The renderer writes characters. A renderer that writes RGBA changes nothing in the earlier stages. The layout engine does block flow. To add flexbox, you add a different function that makes the same `Box` values. The stages are separate, thus browsers can rewrite one stage at a time.

## What a real browser adds, largest first

**Each stage is incremental.** The program above caches nothing. A second render does all five stages again. A real engine records which nodes changed, which boxes need a new layout, and which regions need new paint. A page can have fifty thousand nodes.

A cursor that blinks must not cause a new render of all of these nodes. The code that records these changes is larger than the pipeline.

**Each stage is concurrent.** The browser parses the page while bytes still arrive. Images decode on other threads. The paint stage runs on a compositor thread, so that the page scrolls smoothly when JavaScript is busy. The pipeline keeps the same shape. The browser only runs several copies of the pipeline at the same time.

The versions here show the shape of each stage without the details. The details take years to build:

- the 80 tokenizer states of the HTML parser
- the dozen layout modes of CSS
- text shaping
- bidirectional text
- thirty years of old pages that must continue to work

## Check yourself

The diagram shows the pipeline in one direction, but a script can change the document. What does that do to the diagram?

A script changes the tree. Then the old boxes are out of date, thus layout and paint must run again. The browser tries to do this one time for each frame, not one time for each change.

A script can read a size such as `offsetHeight` in a loop that also writes to the page. Then each iteration causes a full layout. This problem has the name *layout thrashing*, and [the layout chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/browser/layout/) explains it.

## Where this section ends

This section has six chapters:

- a parser that cannot fail
- a cascade that decides between rules
- two passes that change a tree into rectangles
- a painter that fills the rectangles
- a scripting engine that connects at one point
- this chapter, which joins the stages

Together, they have the shape of a browser. The section leaves out each part that makes a real browser difficult to build.

If you liked the graphics part, [the graphics section](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/) does rasterisation fully. It has real pixel buffers, lines and triangles, antialiasing and image files. If you liked the language part, [the Tiny Language section](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/tiny-lang/lexer/) builds the scripting engine that this section only shows in outline.
