# Track: Projects

One library at a time, designed in public, with one decision in each chapter.

## What Is an Ecto-Style ORM?

*An Ecto-Style ORM. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/what-is-ecto/*

This group builds a small ORM in the style of **Ecto**, the database library
of Elixir. Most readers here never wrote Elixir. Thus this page explains that
style, and the reasons to copy it, before the next chapters build it in Zig.

## The idea in one sentence

Ecto divides database work into parts that are plain data and pure functions.
Each real database operation goes through one explicit gateway, the **Repo**.

## What that looks like

In Ecto, an application defines a schema, builds queries as values, and gives
the queries to the Repo:

```elixir
# Elixir (Ecto), for flavor only
defmodule User do
  schema "users" do
    field :name, :string
    field :age, :integer
  end
end

query = from u in User, where: u.age > 18
adults = Repo.all(query)
```

These lines contain three separate ideas:

1. **The schema is a declaration**, not a class with behavior. It gives the
   shape of a row and nothing more.
2. **A query is a value.** When you build a query, no SQL runs. You can
   compose the query, give it to other functions, and examine it. The query
   touches the database only when you give it to the Repo.
3. **The Repo is the only gateway.** There is no `user.save()`. Records do
   not know how to save themselves. One object owns the connection, and all
   operations go through that object.

## Why this maps so well to Zig

Each of these ideas matches a Zig feature closely:

| Ecto idea | Zig mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| schema as declaration | a plain struct, read by `@typeInfo` at compile time |
| query as a value | a builder struct; a chain is functions that return the struct |
| Repo as the gateway | `Repo(Adapter)`, a type function with one stateful field |
| validations on the schema | a `rules` declaration, found with `@hasDecl` |

Zig is better than the original in one way. Ecto checks some things when the
query runs. Zig can check the same things when the query **compiles**. In the
[query builder chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/query-builder/), a misspelled field in a
filter is a compile error, not a database error at runtime.

## Why not Active Record?

The other well-known ORM shape is Active Record (Rails, Django). In Active
Record, the record is an object that saves itself: `user.save()` and
`User.find(1)`. The two designs are different in only one thing.

```
Active Record

  user.save()
       │
       └── the object knows about the database

Ecto style

  User        Query
   │            │
   └──── data ──┘
         │
        Repo
         │
      Database
```

That one difference is the location of the database behavior. In Active
Record, the record knows how to save itself. Thus a `User` holds a connection
everywhere that the `User` goes.

In the design that these chapters build, a `User` stays data. It has no methods
that touch a socket, and it does not know that a database exists. `Repo` owns
persistence, and only `Repo` does.

This design adds extra code between the parts. In return, you can test each
part alone:

- A schema is a struct.
- A query is a value that you can examine and not run.
- The Repo is the single seam that you replace in a test.

The [Repo chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/repo/) uses this seam with a driver that records SQL
and never opens a connection. Active Record is convenient. The cost is a test
suite that needs a live database, even to check a validation rule.

## Where each idea lives in this group

- Schema as declaration: [A Type Function as the Front Door](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/schema-to-sql/)
- Query as a value: [A Typed Query Builder](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/query-builder/)
- Declared validations: [Validation from Declarations](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/validation-rules/)
- Writes derived from the schema: [Write Rows](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/insert-update/)
- One gateway, replaced by a fake in tests: [The Repo](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/repo/)
- User code inside a safe start and end: [Transactions and errdefer](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/transactions/)

The Elixir example above is the only unverified code in this group. It is a
reference point, and you do not run it. CI compiles and runs each Zig snippet
in the chapters that follow.

---

## A Type Function as the Front Door

*An Ecto-Style ORM. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/schema-to-sql/*

These pages build a small ORM in the style of Ecto from Elixir. Each page takes
one pattern and makes it into a snippet that is small enough to verify. A full
ORM adds drivers, pools and migrations around these same basic parts.

## The problem

A Zig library has a difficult interface question: how does the caller give you
*the data shape of the caller*? Dynamic languages take a dict or use reflection
at runtime. C takes void pointers and trusts you.

The Zig answer is a function that runs at compile time. The function takes a
`type` and returns a new `type` that wraps the first type.

In the ORM, the caller defines a plain struct. Then `Table(User, "users")`
becomes the typed gateway of the caller to all the operations that the library
can do with that struct.

## The pattern

1. Accept `comptime T: type`, and the configuration that goes with it (the
   table name).
2. Read `@typeInfo(T)` one time, at compile time.
3. Return a struct whose declarations hold all the derived data: metadata,
   generated SQL, and later the query and insert functions.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// The public API of the library is one function from a type to a type.
// Callers define plain structs. The compiler derives all other parts.
fn Table(comptime T: type, comptime name: []const u8) type {
    const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
    return struct {
        pub const Row = T;
        pub const table_name = name;
        pub const column_count = info.field_names.len;

        // The compiler makes the full CREATE TABLE statement. At runtime,
        // the statement is a plain string constant in the binary.
        pub const create_sql = blk: {
            var sql: []const u8 = "CREATE TABLE " ++ name ++ " (";
            for (info.field_names, info.field_types, 0..) |field, Field, i| {
                if (i > 0) sql = sql ++ ", ";
                sql = sql ++ field ++ " " ++ sqlType(Field);
            }
            break :blk sql ++ ")";
        };

        fn sqlType(comptime Field: type) []const u8 {
            return switch (Field) {
                i32, i64, u32, bool => "INTEGER",
                f32, f64 => "REAL",
                []const u8 => "TEXT",
                else => @compileError("no SQL mapping for " ++ @typeName(Field)),
            };
        }
    };
}

// A caller writes only this struct. The caller does not register
// anything, run a code generator or use reflection at runtime. The struct
// is the schema.
const User = struct {
    id: i64,
    name: []const u8,
    active: bool,
};
const Users = Table(User, "users");

test "the schema compiles to exact SQL" {
    try expect(std.mem.eql(
        u8,
        Users.create_sql,
        "CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER, name TEXT, active INTEGER)",
    ));
}

test "metadata is comptime-known" {
    try expect(Users.column_count == 3);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, Users.table_name, "users"));
    // Row is the type of the caller, with no change. The library only adds
    // new declarations next to it.
    const u = Users.Row{ .id = 1, .name = "ada", .active = true };
    try expect(u.id == 1);
}

test "a second table is a distinct type with its own SQL" {
    const Post = struct {
        id: i64,
        title: []const u8,
        score: f64,
    };
    const Posts = Table(Post, "posts");
    try expect(std.mem.eql(
        u8,
        Posts.create_sql,
        "CREATE TABLE posts (id INTEGER, title TEXT, score REAL)",
    ));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`07-building-libraries.schema-to-sql`)*

## The SQL exists before the program runs

A comptime block makes `create_sql` with `++` concatenation. At runtime,
`create_sql` is one string constant in the binary. No formatting, allocation
or reflection remains to do.

The test compares `create_sql` with the exact expected SQL text. This site
uses the same type of gate on each snippet: a comparison character by
character.

Look at the location of the errors. If a schema field has a type that the
library cannot map, the mapping function gives a compile error. The user of
your library sees the error at build time. The message is a message that you
wrote, and it names the type of the user. These messages are part of your
API, so design them.

## The type of the caller does not change

`Table` wraps the type of the caller and does not change it. `Users.Row` is the
`User` of the caller, with no change. Thus the code of the caller continues to
make and pass plain structs.

This is important. Some libraries make callers use *the library struct* in place
of their own struct. Then that struct goes into each function signature that
the callers own.

## In a full ORM

The `Table` on this page is the start of the real one. To make it larger, add
declarations to the returned struct:

- `insert_sql` with placeholders.
- Metadata for each column (primary key, nullability), read from sentinel types.
- The query builder from the [next page](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/query-builder/).

The current members of the public API do not change. The API only gets new
members.

---

## A Typed Query Builder

*An Ecto-Style ORM. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/query-builder/*

A typed query builder in Zig takes columns as `std.meta.FieldEnum(T)`. Thus a
misspelled column is a compile error. The builder writes values as numbered
placeholders (`$1`, `$2`), and the values never touch the SQL text. The builder
is a plain value, and you can chain its calls without an allocator.

## The problem

Each database library has the same two failure modes:

- A query names a column that does not exist. You find the error at runtime,
  in production, as a database error.
- A value goes into the SQL string directly. You find the error as an
  injection.

A Zig library can prevent both at the type level, and the code for this is
small.

## The pattern

1. `std.meta.FieldEnum(T)` changes the field names of the schema struct into an
   enum. A filter takes that enum. Thus `.where(.emial, .eq)` is a compile
   error, and the error shows the misspelled name.
2. The builder is a plain value. `where` copies the builder, appends to a
   bounded array, and returns the copy. Thus the caller can make many queries
   from one base query.
3. `render` writes numbered placeholders, and the values go to the driver
   separately.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

fn Query(comptime T: type) type {
    return struct {
        // FieldEnum changes the fields of the struct into an enum. Thus a
        // filter on a misspelled column is a compile error, not an SQL error
        // at runtime.
        pub const Field = std.meta.FieldEnum(T);
        pub const Op = enum {
            eq,
            lt,
            gt,

            fn sql(op: Op) []const u8 {
                return switch (op) {
                    .eq => " = ",
                    .lt => " < ",
                    .gt => " > ",
                };
            }
        };

        const Filter = struct { field: Field, op: Op };

        table: []const u8,
        // The builder has a bounded array, and it is a value, not a pointer.
        // Thus you can chain its calls without an allocator. The limit of
        // eight filters is a choice. The library makes that choice and
        // documents it.
        filters: [8]Filter = undefined,
        filter_count: usize = 0,

        pub fn where(q: @This(), field: Field, op: Op) @This() {
            var next = q;
            next.filters[next.filter_count] = .{ .field = field, .op = op };
            next.filter_count += 1;
            return next;
        }

        // Values never go into the SQL text. The statement holds numbered
        // placeholders, and the values go to the driver separately. Values
        // outside the SQL text make injection impossible.
        pub fn render(q: @This(), w: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
            try w.print("SELECT * FROM {s}", .{q.table});
            for (q.filters[0..q.filter_count], 1..) |f, n| {
                try w.writeAll(if (n == 1) " WHERE " else " AND ");
                try w.print("{t}{s}${d}", .{ f.field, f.op.sql(), n });
            }
        }
    };
}

const User = struct {
    id: i64,
    name: []const u8,
    age: u8,
};

fn rendered(q: anytype, buf: []u8) ![]const u8 {
    var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(buf);
    try q.render(&w);
    return w.buffered();
}

test "no filters" {
    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    const q = Query(User){ .table = "users" };
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, try rendered(q, &buf), "SELECT * FROM users"));
}

test "filters chain, placeholders number themselves" {
    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    const q = (Query(User){ .table = "users" })
        .where(.name, .eq)
        .where(.age, .gt);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(
        u8,
        try rendered(q, &buf),
        "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = $1 AND age > $2",
    ));
}

test "the field argument is an enum, not a string" {
    // `.email` does not compile, because User has no field with that name.
    // The check costs nothing at runtime, because the enum exists only at
    // compile time.
    const q = (Query(User){ .table = "users" }).where(.id, .lt);
    try expect(q.filter_count == 1);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`07-building-libraries.query-builder`)*

## What the enum gives you

The `Field` enum exists only at compile time. At runtime, a filter is an
integer tag. `{t}` formats the tag name back into SQL. Thus the enum checks the
column and also supplies its name. That gives three properties:

- A typo does not compile.
- The check costs nothing at runtime.
- No string table must stay the same as the schema.

The same method works in code that is not an ORM. A library can accept "one of
the fields of this struct" as an argument, for example a sorter, a serializer
or a diff tool. That library can take `FieldEnum(T)` in place of a string, and
move the failure to compile time.

## Why the builder is by-value

`where` returns a changed copy. Thus, in practice, the builder is immutable.
When one call site adds its filters, it cannot corrupt a shared base query.

The bounded array keeps the copy cheap and the API free of allocators. The cost
is a fixed capacity. State that trade-off in the documentation of your library
as a design decision. Do not hide it as an implementation detail.

## In a full ORM

The real builder adds operators, `ORDER BY`, joins and an `insert` path. It
pairs each placeholder with a typed value list for the driver.

This section comes from a draft. The draft writes PostgreSQL and SQLite
dialects from the same builder. The dialect switch is in `render`, in the same
place as the SQL format code of this snippet.

---

## Validation from Declarations

*An Ecto-Style ORM. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/validation-rules/*

A Zig library finds optional behavior for each type with `@hasDecl` at compile
time. A schema that declares `pub const rules = .{ ... }` gets validation. A
schema without that declaration gets no validation code.

## The problem

Your library needs optional behavior for each type: validation rules on one
schema, custom serialization on another schema, and nothing on a third schema.
The classical answers are interfaces and inheritance, and Zig has neither.

Zig has a method that is better for libraries. The caller *declares* the
behavior that it supports. The library *asks* for that declaration at compile
time.

## The pattern

1. The convention: a schema can declare `pub const rules = .{ ... }`, with the
   names of its own fields.
2. The library checks `@hasDecl(T, "rules")` before it touches `rules`. If the
   declaration does not exist, there is no validation and no generated code.
3. `inline for` walks the rules. On each rule struct, `@hasField` decides which
   checks apply. Each lookup resolves at compile time. The work at runtime is
   only the comparisons.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const Violation = struct {
    field: []const u8,
    rule: []const u8,
};

// The half in the library: walk the fields of the value. When the schema
// declares a rule for a field, apply the rule. A schema without rules always
// passes. An unknown rule name makes the build fail. The library does not
// ignore it.
fn validate(value: anytype) ?Violation {
    const T = @TypeOf(value);
    if (!@hasDecl(T, "rules")) return null;

    const info = @typeInfo(@TypeOf(T.rules)).@"struct";
    inline for (info.field_names) |field| {
        const rule = @field(T.rules, field);
        const v = @field(value, field);
        const R = @TypeOf(rule);

        if (@hasField(R, "min_len")) {
            if (v.len < rule.min_len) return .{ .field = field, .rule = "min_len" };
        }
        if (@hasField(R, "max")) {
            if (v > rule.max) return .{ .field = field, .rule = "max" };
        }
    }
    return null;
}

// The half in the caller: the rules are on the schema as one declaration,
// and they name the fields directly. A rule for a field that does not exist
// does not compile, because @field(value, ...) cannot resolve.
const User = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    age: u8,

    pub const rules = .{
        .name = .{ .min_len = 3 },
        .age = .{ .max = 130 },
    };
};

test "a valid value passes" {
    try expect(validate(User{ .name = "ada", .age = 36 }) == null);
}

test "violations name the field and the rule" {
    const short = validate(User{ .name = "al", .age = 36 }).?;
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, short.field, "name"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, short.rule, "min_len"));

    const old = validate(User{ .name = "methuselah", .age = 200 }).?;
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, old.field, "age"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, old.rule, "max"));
}

test "a schema without rules is fine" {
    const Point = struct { x: f32, y: f32 };
    try expect(validate(Point{ .x = 1, .y = 2 }) == null);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`07-building-libraries.validation-rules`)*

## Errors occur in the correct build

The compiler finds two mistakes when the caller builds. The library author
does no work for this:

- A rule for a field that does not exist: `@field(value, "nmae")` cannot resolve.
- A `min_len` rule on an integer field: `v.len` does not exist on `u8`.

For this reason, use declarations and not registration functions. A call to
`registerValidator("name", ...)` at runtime can fail only at runtime. The
compiler analyzes a declaration against the schema while it has both open.

## The standard library does the same thing

This pattern did not start in the ORM. `std.json` looks for `jsonStringify` on
your type. The format functions look for a `format` declaration.

When your library uses the same shape (a documented declaration name, found
with `@hasDecl`), Zig users already know how to use the library.

## In a full ORM

This page comes from a draft. The draft runs validation inside insert and
update, and returns a typed error set with the violation attached.

The draft also adds rules across fields, for example unique-together and
conditional requirements. These rules are declarations that use the same
discovery pattern. The core stays the twenty lines on this page. The extra
features are more rules.

---

## Write Rows

*An Ecto-Style ORM. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/insert-update/*

A Zig ORM can derive its INSERT and UPDATE statements from the schema struct
at compile time. The same walk over the fields also builds the values, as an
array of tagged-union `Value`s. Thus the statement and its values always have
the same length and the same order.

## The problem

The [query builder](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/query-builder/) reads rows. Writes are the other
half. An INSERT must name each column and give a number to each placeholder. An
UPDATE must separate the key columns from the data columns.

If you write those statements by hand for each table, the work repeats, and the
statements easily become out of date. The schema already has the data to make
them.

## The pattern

1. Derive `insert_sql` at compile time. Make the column list and the
   placeholder list from the same fields.
2. Derive `update_sql` with a stated convention: the first field is the key. A
   convention that a library documents is part of its API, so select it
   carefully.
3. Pair each statement with `bind`. `bind` changes a row into an array of
   tagged-union `Value`s, one for each placeholder, in the same field order.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// The value type that the driver gets. The SQL text and the values go to
// the driver separately, and the values have the form of this union.
const Value = union(enum) {
    int: i64,
    text: []const u8,
    boolean: bool,
};

fn Table(comptime T: type, comptime name: []const u8) type {
    const info = @typeInfo(T).@"struct";
    return struct {
        // "INSERT INTO users (id, name, active) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)"
        pub const insert_sql = blk: {
            var cols: []const u8 = "";
            var params: []const u8 = "";
            for (info.field_names, 0..) |field, i| {
                if (i > 0) {
                    cols = cols ++ ", ";
                    params = params ++ ", ";
                }
                cols = cols ++ field;
                params = params ++ std.fmt.comptimePrint("${d}", .{i + 1});
            }
            break :blk "INSERT INTO " ++ name ++ " (" ++ cols ++ ") VALUES (" ++ params ++ ")";
        };

        // "UPDATE users SET name = $2, active = $3 WHERE id = $1":
        // the first field is the key, by a convention in the docs.
        pub const update_sql = blk: {
            var sets: []const u8 = "";
            for (info.field_names[1..], 2..) |field, n| {
                if (n > 2) sets = sets ++ ", ";
                sets = sets ++ field ++ std.fmt.comptimePrint(" = ${d}", .{n});
            }
            break :blk "UPDATE " ++ name ++ " SET " ++ sets ++
                " WHERE " ++ info.field_names[0] ++ " = $1";
        };

        // The runtime half: one Value for each column, in placeholder order.
        // The inline for resolves each @field at compile time. Thus, at
        // runtime, this loop is a fixed sequence of stores.
        pub fn bind(row: T) [info.field_names.len]Value {
            var values: [info.field_names.len]Value = undefined;
            inline for (info.field_names, 0..) |field, i| {
                values[i] = switch (@TypeOf(@field(row, field))) {
                    i64 => .{ .int = @field(row, field) },
                    []const u8 => .{ .text = @field(row, field) },
                    bool => .{ .boolean = @field(row, field) },
                    else => @compileError("no Value mapping for field " ++ field),
                };
            }
            return values;
        }
    };
}

const User = struct {
    id: i64,
    name: []const u8,
    active: bool,
};
const Users = Table(User, "users");

test "insert statement is derived, not written" {
    try expect(std.mem.eql(
        u8,
        Users.insert_sql,
        "INSERT INTO users (id, name, active) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)",
    ));
}

test "update keys on the first field" {
    try expect(std.mem.eql(
        u8,
        Users.update_sql,
        "UPDATE users SET name = $2, active = $3 WHERE id = $1",
    ));
}

test "bind produces one typed value per placeholder" {
    const values = Users.bind(.{ .id = 7, .name = "ada", .active = true });
    try expect(values.len == 3);
    try expect(values[0].int == 7);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, values[1].text, "ada"));
    try expect(values[2].boolean == true);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`07-building-libraries.insert-update`)*

## The statement and its values always agree

The placeholders of `insert_sql` and the output of `bind` come from one walk
over one list of fields. If you add a column to the struct, both change
together at the next compile.

A common ORM bug is a statement with four placeholders that gets five values.
Here you cannot write that bug, because both come from one list.

`comptimePrint` formats the numbers during compilation. Thus even `$3` is in
the constant. At runtime, `bind` is a fixed sequence of stores. The
`inline for` leaves no loop in the binary.

## The Value union is the wire contract

Drivers do not take Zig structs. They take a statement and a list of typed
values. The value union is the element type of that list.

The compile error in the mapping arm checks the types of the schema against
the types of the driver. If a field type has no wire mapping, the build fails,
and the error names the field.

## In a full ORM

The draft does more:

- It adds `RETURNING` clauses to inserts.
- It skips auto-managed columns. The library gives the values of these columns,
  not the caller.
- It marks the key column explicitly, not by position.

All three changes walk the same field list at compile time.

---

## The Adapter Seam

*An Ecto-Style ORM. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/adapters/*

A Zig ORM can support several SQL dialects without interfaces or a vtable.
Each dialect is a struct of `pub` declarations. The renderer takes the dialect
as a `comptime Dialect: type` parameter. The compiler makes the selection, so
no dispatch occurs at runtime.

## The problem

The SQL dialects are different:

- PostgreSQL gives numbers to its placeholders (`$1`).
- SQLite uses positional question marks.
- MySQL puts identifiers in backticks.

An ORM that supports more than one database needs a seam. The seam is the one
place in the code that holds the dialect differences, and no other place holds
them. The query builder above the seam must not know which database is below
it.

In a language with interfaces, you define `IDialect`. The Zig answer is
structural. A dialect is any type with the correct declarations, and the code
gives it as a `comptime` parameter.

## The pattern

1. Define each dialect as a small struct of `pub` declarations: a
   `placeholder` writer and a `quote` string.
2. The renderer takes `comptime Dialect: type`. It calls
   `Dialect.placeholder(...)` where the difference is important.
3. Each dialect makes its own copy of the renderer, with the calls inlined.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// A dialect is any type with these declarations. It does not implement an
// interface or use a vtable. The requirement is structural. If a dialect does
// not have a declaration, the call site that uses it gives a compile error.
const Postgres = struct {
    pub fn placeholder(w: *std.Io.Writer, n: usize) !void {
        try w.print("${d}", .{n});
    }
    pub const quote = "\"";
};

const Sqlite = struct {
    pub fn placeholder(w: *std.Io.Writer, _: usize) !void {
        try w.writeAll("?");
    }
    pub const quote = "\"";
};

const Mysql = struct {
    pub fn placeholder(w: *std.Io.Writer, _: usize) !void {
        try w.writeAll("?");
    }
    pub const quote = "`"; // different from the other dialects
};

// The renderer takes the dialect as a comptime parameter. Each dialect
// makes its own copy of this function, with the calls inlined. No dispatch
// occurs at runtime.
fn renderSelect(
    comptime Dialect: type,
    w: *std.Io.Writer,
    table: []const u8,
    filters: []const []const u8,
) !void {
    const q = Dialect.quote;
    try w.print("SELECT * FROM {s}{s}{s}", .{ q, table, q });
    for (filters, 1..) |field, n| {
        try w.writeAll(if (n == 1) " WHERE " else " AND ");
        try w.print("{s} = ", .{field});
        try Dialect.placeholder(w, n);
    }
}

fn rendered(comptime Dialect: type, buf: []u8) ![]const u8 {
    var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(buf);
    try renderSelect(Dialect, &w, "users", &.{ "name", "age" });
    return w.buffered();
}

test "postgres numbers its placeholders" {
    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    try expect(std.mem.eql(
        u8,
        try rendered(Postgres, &buf),
        "SELECT * FROM \"users\" WHERE name = $1 AND age = $2",
    ));
}

test "sqlite uses positional question marks" {
    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    try expect(std.mem.eql(
        u8,
        try rendered(Sqlite, &buf),
        "SELECT * FROM \"users\" WHERE name = ? AND age = ?",
    ));
}

test "mysql differs only where it differs" {
    var buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
    try expect(std.mem.eql(
        u8,
        try rendered(Mysql, &buf),
        "SELECT * FROM `users` WHERE name = ? AND age = ?",
    ));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`07-building-libraries.adapters`)*

## Requirements are structural, and errors are precise

No code declares "Mysql implements Dialect". The requirement is exactly the set
of declarations that the renderer touches. If a dialect does not have one of
those declarations, the compile fails at the line that needed it.

The standard library uses the same contract style for its `Io`
implementations. The [driver of the repo](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/repo/) uses it for
databases.

The three tests are the specification of the seam. The same call makes three
exact SQL strings. The only differences between them are the placeholders and
the quotes. When a new difference occurs (for example, the `LIMIT` syntax), it
becomes a new declaration. Each dialect must supply the declaration, or the
build fails.

## When to use comptime dispatch, and when not

With a dialect selected at compile time, one binary supports only the dialects
that it compiled with. That trade-off is good for an ORM, because an
application knows its database.

If users must select a dialect from a config file at startup, you need dispatch
at runtime. Use a tagged union over the dialects, or a vtable as in
`std.mem.Allocator`. Start with comptime. If you change the dispatch later, the
seam stays in the same place.

## In a full ORM

The adapters of the draft hold more than syntax. The same seam also holds these
parts:

- The connection setup.
- The wire protocol (libpq for PostgreSQL, embedded C for SQLite).
- The type encoding.

The surface of the dialect becomes larger, but all of it stays behind the seam.

---

## Migrations as Data

*An Ecto-Style ORM. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/migrations/*

Database migrations are easiest to test as data. The history is an append-only
list of `{version, up, down}` entries. A pure function, `plan(current, target)`,
returns the steps to run. A separate loop runs the plan. Thus you can test each
case of the planner without a database.

## The problem

Schemas change after they ship. Most mature ORMs handle this in the same way:

- Each change is a versioned migration with an up and a down.
- The list is append-only.
- The database records its current version.

The design question is the location of the logic. The code that calculates
what to run often becomes mixed with the code that runs it. Then you cannot
test anything without a database.

## The pattern

1. The history is data: an ordered array of `{version, up, down}`. Do not edit
   an entry after a release, because the database of a user already ran it.
2. The planner is a pure function. `plan(current, target)` returns the steps
   to run, in order. An upgrade walks forward. A downgrade walks the affected
   range, with the newest entry first.
3. A separate, simple loop runs the plan. That loop belongs to the
   [repo](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/repo/).

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const Migration = struct {
    version: u32,
    up: []const u8,
    down: []const u8,
};

// The full history, in order. The list is append-only. Do not edit a
// released migration, because the database of a user already ran it.
const history = [_]Migration{
    .{
        .version = 1,
        .up = "CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER, name TEXT)",
        .down = "DROP TABLE users",
    },
    .{
        .version = 2,
        .up = "CREATE TABLE posts (id INTEGER, title TEXT)",
        .down = "DROP TABLE posts",
    },
    .{
        .version = 3,
        .up = "ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN active INTEGER",
        .down = "ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN active",
    },
};

const Step = struct { version: u32, sql: []const u8 };

// The planner is a pure function from (current, target) to steps. You can
// test all the difficult cases (no-op, partial upgrade, rollback order)
// without a database.
fn plan(current: u32, target: u32, buf: []Step) []Step {
    var n: usize = 0;
    if (target > current) {
        for (history) |m| {
            if (m.version > current and m.version <= target) {
                buf[n] = .{ .version = m.version, .sql = m.up };
                n += 1;
            }
        }
    } else {
        // A downgrade runs the down steps with the newest step first.
        var i = history.len;
        while (i > 0) {
            i -= 1;
            const m = history[i];
            if (m.version <= current and m.version > target) {
                buf[n] = .{ .version = m.version, .sql = m.down };
                n += 1;
            }
        }
    }
    return buf[0..n];
}

test "a fresh database applies everything in order" {
    var buf: [8]Step = undefined;
    const steps = plan(0, 3, &buf);
    try expect(steps.len == 3);
    try expect(steps[0].version == 1);
    try expect(steps[2].version == 3);
    try expect(std.mem.startsWith(u8, steps[0].sql, "CREATE TABLE users"));
}

test "partial upgrade takes only the gap" {
    var buf: [8]Step = undefined;
    const steps = plan(1, 3, &buf);
    try expect(steps.len == 2);
    try expect(steps[0].version == 2);
    try expect(steps[1].version == 3);
}

test "rollback runs down steps newest-first" {
    var buf: [8]Step = undefined;
    const steps = plan(3, 1, &buf);
    try expect(steps.len == 2);
    try expect(steps[0].version == 3);
    try expect(std.mem.startsWith(u8, steps[0].sql, "ALTER TABLE users DROP"));
    try expect(steps[1].version == 2);
}

test "already there is a no-op" {
    var buf: [8]Step = undefined;
    try expect(plan(3, 3, &buf).len == 0);
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`07-building-libraries.migrations`)*

## Pure functions make the edge cases cheap

The four tests cover the cases that go wrong in real systems:

- The new, empty database.
- The partial upgrade.
- The rollback, in reverse order. Forward order corrupts the database.
- The no-op.

Each test is an assertion about a function from two integers to a slice. The
tests need no fixtures, containers or cleanup. If the planner and the executor
are one function, each of those tests needs a live database, and programmers
never write most of them.

The split also gives you `--dry-run` with no extra work: print the plan, and do
not run it. If your library can plan an operation and not do it, users can
examine the plan before they run it.

## Append-only is a social contract, not a technical one

The code does not stop a person who edits migration 2 after the release. The
guarantee comes from convention and review.

A library can help to enforce the convention. The draft stores a checksum of
each applied migration. If a person changed the history after the database
applied it, the draft refuses to continue. That check is also pure logic over
data, and you can test it in the same way.

## In a full ORM

In the draft, the migrations are Zig files that the build finds. Each file has
an up and a down. A CLI creates, applies and rolls back migrations.

A `schema_migrations` table holds the applied version. Only two parts touch the
database: the code that reads that table and the code that runs the plan.

---

## The Repo

*An Ecto-Style ORM. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/repo/*

The Repo is the one stateful object in an Ecto-style ORM. It is also the only
part that talks to the database. In Zig, it is `Repo(Driver)`, and the driver
is a comptime parameter. Thus a test can give it a driver that records the SQL
and does not run it.

## The problem

Each part so far (schema, statements, dialects, plans) is pure. At some point,
the library must talk to a real database, and that point decides if you can
test the library.

- If database calls are in all parts of the code, each test needs Postgres.
- If the calls are behind one seam, you can test the full ORM against a fake.

The Ecto answer is the Repo, which holds the connection. Each operation goes
through the Repo. This page builds the skeleton of the Repo.

## The pattern

1. `Repo(Driver)` is a type function, as all other parts of this library are.
   The driver is a comptime parameter with a structural contract: an `exec`
   function that takes SQL.
2. The methods of the Repo combine the pure parts (the derived SQL of a Table)
   with one effect (`driver.exec`).
3. The test driver *records* the SQL and does not run it. The assertions read
   the log: the SQL that the database gets, and the order of that SQL.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

// The test double for a database driver. It records each statement that the
// repo tells it to run. The test suite of the ORM runs against this driver.
// Only integration tests need a real database.
const RecordingDriver = struct {
    gpa: std.mem.Allocator,
    log: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty,

    pub fn exec(d: *RecordingDriver, sql: []const u8) !void {
        try d.log.append(d.gpa, try d.gpa.dupe(u8, sql));
    }

    pub fn deinit(d: *RecordingDriver) void {
        for (d.log.items) |sql| d.gpa.free(sql);
        d.log.deinit(d.gpa);
    }
};

// Repo(Driver) is the composition root of the library. The driver arrives
// as a comptime parameter, in the same way that an allocator arrives as a
// runtime parameter. The caller selects the policy, and the library gives
// the mechanism.
fn Repo(comptime Driver: type) type {
    return struct {
        driver: *Driver,

        pub fn createTable(r: @This(), comptime T: type) !void {
            try r.driver.exec(T.create_sql);
        }

        pub fn insert(r: @This(), comptime T: type, row: T.Row) !void {
            // A real repo puts values into the parameter slots of the
            // statement. A record of the template shows exactly the SQL that
            // the database gets.
            _ = row;
            try r.driver.exec(T.insert_sql);
        }
    };
}

// A minimal Table. It has only enough code to show that the composition works.
fn Table(comptime T: type, comptime name: []const u8) type {
    return struct {
        pub const Row = T;
        pub const create_sql = "CREATE TABLE " ++ name;
        pub const insert_sql = "INSERT INTO " ++ name;
    };
}

const User = struct { id: i64 };
const Users = Table(User, "users");

test "the repo drives the driver in order" {
    var driver = RecordingDriver{ .gpa = std.testing.allocator };
    defer driver.deinit();

    const repo = Repo(RecordingDriver){ .driver = &driver };
    try repo.createTable(Users);
    try repo.insert(Users, .{ .id = 1 });
    try repo.insert(Users, .{ .id = 2 });

    try expect(driver.log.items.len == 3);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, driver.log.items[0], "CREATE TABLE users"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, driver.log.items[1], "INSERT INTO users"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, driver.log.items[2], "INSERT INTO users"));
}

test "a failing driver surfaces its error unchanged" {
    const FailingDriver = struct {
        pub fn exec(_: *@This(), _: []const u8) !void {
            return error.ConnectionLost;
        }
    };
    var driver = FailingDriver{};
    const repo = Repo(FailingDriver){ .driver = &driver };
    try std.testing.expectError(error.ConnectionLost, repo.createTable(Users));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`07-building-libraries.repo`)*

## `RecordingDriver` is the test suite of the ORM

`RecordingDriver` is thirteen lines. With it, you can test each feature of the
library (inserts, transactions, migrations). Each test has one form: "for these
calls, exactly this SQL, in exactly this order". These tests check the behavior of
your library, and the database is not part of them.

A thin layer of integration tests against real SQLite and Postgres then tests
the drivers. No other test needs the drivers.

Look at the second test. A driver error (`error.ConnectionLost`) comes out
through the repo with no change. To pass errors through is a design decision,
so test it. If a library wraps or hides driver errors, the caller cannot react
to a specific error.

## Comptime parameter, runtime state

`Repo(Driver)` fixes the driver *type* at compile time. The driver *value*
arrives at runtime through the struct field, and it holds the connection
state.

This split follows the allocator convention of the standard library. The compiler
fixes the type of the driver, and the program gives its settings and state at
runtime. The split also makes the fake free at runtime. The repo that
compiles against `RecordingDriver` never contains a branch that asks which
driver it has.

## In a full ORM

The `repo.zig` file of the draft adds more to the Repo:

- The query path (`all`, `get`, `one`).
- The decode of results back into schema structs.
- Validation before writes.
- A pool checkout around each operation.

Each of these runs against `RecordingDriver` in its tests. Below them, the
shape of the skeleton on this page does not change.

---

## Transactions and errdefer

*An Ecto-Style ORM. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/transactions/*

In Zig, a transaction wrapper does these steps:

1. Run `BEGIN`.
2. Register an `errdefer` that runs `ROLLBACK`.
3. Run the work of the caller.
4. Run `COMMIT`.

An error at any point after the `errdefer`, also in `COMMIT`, rolls the
transaction back and returns the original error.

## The problem

A transaction wrapper has one job: no path can leave the transaction open.
Languages solve this problem with `defer`, context managers or RAII.

The bugs are in the paths that a programmer forgot: the early return, the error
between two statements, the failed COMMIT. The designers of Zig made `errdefer`
for this case, and a library API is a good place to use it.

## The pattern

This is the full contract:

```zig
try r.driver.exec("BEGIN");
errdefer r.driver.exec("ROLLBACK") catch {};
try body.run(r);
try r.driver.exec("COMMIT");
```

The `errdefer` covers each `try` after it. On success, the `errdefer` does not
run. No path reaches the end of the function with the transaction open. You can
verify that when you read four lines, and you do not have to examine each
return.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const expect = std.testing.expect;

const RecordingDriver = struct {
    gpa: std.mem.Allocator,
    log: std.ArrayList([]const u8) = .empty,

    pub fn exec(d: *RecordingDriver, sql: []const u8) !void {
        try d.log.append(d.gpa, try d.gpa.dupe(u8, sql));
    }

    pub fn deinit(d: *RecordingDriver) void {
        for (d.log.items) |sql| d.gpa.free(sql);
        d.log.deinit(d.gpa);
    }
};

fn Repo(comptime Driver: type) type {
    return struct {
        driver: *Driver,

        // These four lines are the transaction contract. errdefer runs on
        // each error return between BEGIN and COMMIT. Thus no path leaves
        // the transaction open: not an early return, not a failure inside
        // the callback, and not a failed COMMIT.
        pub fn transaction(r: @This(), body: anytype) !void {
            try r.driver.exec("BEGIN");
            errdefer r.driver.exec("ROLLBACK") catch {};
            try body.run(r);
            try r.driver.exec("COMMIT");
        }
    };
}

const R = Repo(RecordingDriver);

test "success path commits" {
    var driver = RecordingDriver{ .gpa = std.testing.allocator };
    defer driver.deinit();

    const body = struct {
        fn run(_: @This(), repo: R) !void {
            try repo.driver.exec("INSERT INTO users");
        }
    }{};
    try (R{ .driver = &driver }).transaction(body);

    try expect(driver.log.items.len == 3);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, driver.log.items[0], "BEGIN"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, driver.log.items[1], "INSERT INTO users"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, driver.log.items[2], "COMMIT"));
}

test "a failing body rolls back and the error escapes" {
    var driver = RecordingDriver{ .gpa = std.testing.allocator };
    defer driver.deinit();

    const body = struct {
        fn run(_: @This(), repo: R) !void {
            try repo.driver.exec("INSERT INTO users");
            return error.ValidationFailed;
        }
    }{};
    try std.testing.expectError(
        error.ValidationFailed,
        (R{ .driver = &driver }).transaction(body),
    );

    // The work ran, and then the wrapper rolled it back. No commit occurred.
    try expect(driver.log.items.len == 3);
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, driver.log.items[0], "BEGIN"));
    try expect(std.mem.eql(u8, driver.log.items[2], "ROLLBACK"));
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`07-building-libraries.transactions`)*

## Why the ROLLBACK discards its own error

The wrapper discards the error from the ROLLBACK on purpose. A real library
must document this decision.

The wrapper already returns with the error of the caller, and that error
explains the problem. A second error, "and also the rollback failed", in place
of the first error, hides the cause. A production library logs the rollback
failure, but it still returns the original error.

## The callback shape

`body` is `anytype` with a `run` method. In the snippet, it takes the place of
a closure. The work of the caller runs *inside* the frame of the wrapper. Thus
`errdefer` can see the errors of that work.

The same shape occurs each time that a library puts user code between a start
and an end:

- Handlers with one arena for each request.
- File locks.
- The pool checkout of the draft (acquire, run, always release).

## In a full ORM

Real transactions nest: the inner one uses SAVEPOINT in place of BEGIN. The
draft keeps the depth in a counter on the connection. The `errdefer` shape is
the same at each depth.

The tests with `RecordingDriver` from [the previous
page](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/repo/) extend easily to this case. They assert the
BEGIN/SAVEPOINT/ROLLBACK sequences for the nested cases.
