## What You Will Build

*A URL Shortener. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/url-shortener/what-we-are-building/*

A URL shortener works like this: you give it a long address, and it gives you
a short address. When a person follows the short address, the person gets to
the long address. A URL shortener is a common first service. It is small
enough to complete. But it needs all the parts that a larger service needs: a
database, a schema, validation, and an HTTP surface with all four verbs.

The completed service has five routes:

| Route | Action | Operation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /links` | shorten a URL, answer with the slug | Create |
| `GET /{slug}` | redirect, and count the hit | Read |
| `GET /links/{slug}` | report target and hit count | Read |
| `PUT /links/{slug}` | point the slug to a different target | Update |
| `DELETE /links/{slug}` | retire the slug | Delete |

The storage is PostgreSQL, with one table:

```sql
CREATE TABLE links (
  id     bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  slug   text UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  target text NOT NULL,
  hits   bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
```

## The design

Each chapter in this project builds one box in this diagram, from the bottom
to the top:

```
Browser / curl
      │
      ▼
 HTTP Server
      │
      ▼
   Routes ──────────► Slug logic
      │
      ▼
    Store
      │
      ▼
Postgres Client
      │
  TCP socket
      │
      ▼
  PostgreSQL
```

The diagram has two halves:

- All the boxes above `Store` are about HTTP: what a request means, and what
  to answer.
- All the boxes below `Store` are about Postgres: how to send the query, and
  how to read the answer.

`Store` is the line between the two halves. Because of `Store`, most of this
code runs without a network.

## One request, from start to end

This service uses no JSON. The body of a `POST` is the URL, and the answer is
the slug. Thus the parsing stays in the chapters that are about parsing.

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/links \
  --data 'https://ziglang.org'
```

```
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Length: 2

1
```

The slug is `1` because the slug is the row id in base62. It is not a random
string. When you follow the slug, you get the redirect. The redirect is the
main task of the service:

```bash
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/1
```

```
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://ziglang.org
Content-Length: 0
```

The record of the slug reports the target and how many times people followed
the slug:

```bash
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/links/1
```

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Length: 34

1 -> https://ziglang.org (1 hits)
```

The expected output of the routes chapter contains these same exchanges, and
CI replays them on each build.

## Decision one: no driver

The service talks to Postgres directly, over the Postgres wire protocol. The
[cookbook recipe](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/databases/postgres-wire/) showed each byte of
that protocol. Each message is a tag, a length, and a payload. This project
changes that recipe into a client that a program can use. The client does
these tasks:

- Connect.
- Authenticate.
- Send SQL.
- Iterate over rows.
- Continue after errors.

That is what a driver is. When the driver is small enough to read, you can see
all of the path between your code and the database.

## Decision two: the seams

Almost no part of this project needs a network. This follows the rule for all
of the guide: protocol code parses from a `Reader`, never from a socket.

- The tests of the Postgres client use scripted bytes.
- The slug logic is arithmetic.
- The HTTP handlers take request bytes and return response bytes. They use a
  store interface with an in-memory implementation. This is the same seam that
  the [ORM's Repo chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/repo/) used.

Thus those three chapters run in your browser, and CI checks them the same as
each other snippet on this site.

Only the last chapter opens sockets. That chapter puts the client, the slugs
and the routes into one file. It replaces the in-memory store with a store that
writes SQL. Then it serves the full service against a real database. CI
compiles that file on each run. You run the file on your computer, where a real
Postgres can answer.

## What this project does not include

This small project does not include some features. You can add each of these
features behind one of the seams in this design.

- **Connection pooling.** One connection serves all requests. This is
  sufficient for a tutorial.
- **The extended query protocol.** Real drivers send parameters separately from
  the SQL. This project quotes values into the SQL text, and does this
  carefully. The client chapter states the tradeoff exactly.
- **SCRAM authentication.** The client uses cleartext password auth. A default
  local Postgres accepts that auth from loopback. The client chapter states
  what production adds.
- **Users and rate limits.** No part of this service knows who you are.

The [web server track](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/server/) explains the HTTP side in
full. This project uses the ideas from that track in a smaller form, and stays
on the storage path.

---

## A Postgres Client

*A URL Shortener. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/url-shortener/pg-client/*

A PostgreSQL client in Zig uses the wire protocol directly. `PgClient` does
these tasks:

- It sends the startup message.
- It answers the password request from the server.
- It returns rows through an iterator.
- It changes an `ErrorResponse` into a Zig error, and keeps the connection.

The client reads from a `Reader`. Thus its tests use scripted bytes, not a
database.

## The problem

The [cookbook recipe](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/how-to/databases/postgres-wire/) showed that the
wire protocol is only messages with a tag and a length prefix. But a recipe is
not a client. The service in this project needs a client that it can call
without attention to bytes.

The client must keep the connection after an error. A shortener gets
constraint violations in normal operation. If a client stopped the connection
on each error, the client would connect again all the time.

## The plan

1. `PgClient` holds a reader, a writer, and the last known state of the
   server. The client never opens a socket. The owner of the connection gives
   the streams to the client.
2. `connect` sends the startup message and does the handshake. If the server
   asks for a password, `connect` sends the password.
3. `query` returns `Rows`, an iterator. The column names come in the
   `RowDescription` message. The values come in `DataRow` messages, one
   message for each row.
4. An `ErrorResponse` becomes a Zig error. The client keeps the SQL state code
   and the message. First, the iterator reads all messages until
   `ReadyForQuery`. Thus the connection is immediately usable again.

The demo talks to a scripted backend. The backend is the server half of two
conversations, written into a buffer before the demo starts. The client cannot
see a difference, because it parses a `Reader` and does not know the source of
the bytes. This guide uses the same seam in other chapters. With this seam, a
driver can have regression tests without a database in CI.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// ------------------------------------------- framing, the same as the recipe
// Postgres frames all data big-endian: a tag byte, an Int32 length that
// counts itself but not the tag, then the payload.

fn putInt(comptime T: type, w: *std.Io.Writer, v: T) !void {
    var b: [@divExact(@typeInfo(T).int.bits, 8)]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(T, &b, v, .big);
    try w.writeAll(&b);
}

fn sendMsg(w: *std.Io.Writer, tag: u8, payload: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeAll(&.{tag});
    try putInt(i32, w, @intCast(payload.len + 4));
    try w.writeAll(payload);
}

const Cursor = struct {
    b: []const u8,
    i: usize = 0,
    fn int(self: *Cursor, comptime T: type) T {
        const n = @divExact(@typeInfo(T).int.bits, 8);
        const v = std.mem.readInt(T, self.b[self.i..][0..n], .big);
        self.i += n;
        return v;
    }
    fn cstr(self: *Cursor) []const u8 {
        const start = self.i;
        while (self.b[self.i] != 0) self.i += 1;
        defer self.i += 1;
        return self.b[start..self.i];
    }
};

// ------------------------------------------------------------- the client

const max_columns = 8;

/// A Postgres connection: a reader, a writer, and the state of the last
/// server message. It never uses a socket. The owner of the connection
/// gives the two streams to it. Thus the demo below can give a script.
const PgClient = struct {
    r: *std.Io.Reader,
    w: *std.Io.Writer,
    msg_buf: [512]u8 = undefined,
    asked_for_password: bool = false,
    /// From the last ReadyForQuery: 'I' idle, 'T' in transaction, 'E' failed.
    ready_status: u8 = 0,
    err_code: [5]u8 = undefined,
    err_msg: [256]u8 = undefined,
    err_msg_len: usize = 0,

    const Msg = struct { tag: u8, payload: []const u8 };

    fn readMsg(self: *PgClient) !Msg {
        var tag: [1]u8 = undefined;
        try self.r.readSliceAll(&tag);
        var len_bytes: [4]u8 = undefined;
        try self.r.readSliceAll(&len_bytes);
        const len = std.mem.readInt(i32, &len_bytes, .big);
        const payload = self.msg_buf[0..@intCast(len - 4)];
        try self.r.readSliceAll(payload);
        return .{ .tag = tag[0], .payload = payload };
    }

    /// Startup and authentication, until the first ReadyForQuery. The
    /// server selects the auth method. This client supports "none" and
    /// "cleartext password", and loopback setups use these methods. SCRAM,
    /// the production method, is one more case here.
    fn connect(r: *std.Io.Reader, w: *std.Io.Writer, user: []const u8, database: []const u8, password: []const u8) !PgClient {
        var body_buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
        var body: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&body_buf);
        try putInt(i32, &body, 196608); // protocol 3.0
        for ([_][]const u8{ "user", user, "database", database }) |s| {
            try body.writeAll(s);
            try body.writeAll("\x00");
        }
        try body.writeAll("\x00");
        // The startup message alone has no tag byte.
        try putInt(i32, w, @intCast(4 + body.buffered().len));
        try w.writeAll(body.buffered());
        try w.flush();

        var client = PgClient{ .r = r, .w = w };
        while (true) {
            const m = try client.readMsg();
            var c = Cursor{ .b = m.payload };
            switch (m.tag) {
                'R' => switch (c.int(i32)) {
                    0 => {}, // AuthenticationOk
                    3 => { // AuthenticationCleartextPassword
                        client.asked_for_password = true;
                        var pw_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
                        var pw: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&pw_buf);
                        try pw.writeAll(password);
                        try pw.writeAll("\x00");
                        try sendMsg(w, 'p', pw.buffered());
                        try w.flush();
                    },
                    else => return error.UnsupportedAuth,
                },
                'S', 'K' => {}, // parameters and cancel key: the client ignores them
                'E' => {
                    client.storeError(m.payload);
                    return error.ConnectFailed;
                },
                'Z' => {
                    client.ready_status = m.payload[0];
                    return client;
                },
                else => {},
            }
        }
    }

    fn storeError(self: *PgClient, payload: []const u8) void {
        // ErrorResponse is a list of fields: a type byte and a C string.
        // The list ends at a zero byte. The useful fields are code and message.
        var c = Cursor{ .b = payload };
        while (c.b[c.i] != 0) {
            const kind = c.b[c.i];
            c.i += 1;
            const text = c.cstr();
            switch (kind) {
                'C' => @memcpy(&self.err_code, text[0..5]),
                'M' => {
                    const n = @min(text.len, self.err_msg.len);
                    @memcpy(self.err_msg[0..n], text[0..n]);
                    self.err_msg_len = n;
                },
                else => {},
            }
        }
    }

    fn errorMessage(self: *const PgClient) []const u8 {
        return self.err_msg[0..self.err_msg_len];
    }

    fn query(self: *PgClient, sql: []const u8) !Rows {
        var sql_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
        var q: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&sql_buf);
        try q.writeAll(sql);
        try q.writeAll("\x00");
        try sendMsg(self.w, 'Q', q.buffered());
        try self.w.flush();
        return .{ .client = self };
    }
};

/// Row iteration. Column values are slices into the message buffer of the
/// client. They are valid until the next call, exactly like the zero-copy
/// row of a real driver. Copy the values that you keep.
const Rows = struct {
    client: *PgClient,
    column_count: usize = 0,
    names: [max_columns][24]u8 = undefined,
    name_lens: [max_columns]usize = @splat(0),

    const Row = struct { values: [max_columns][]const u8, count: usize };

    fn name(self: *const Rows, i: usize) []const u8 {
        return self.names[i][0..self.name_lens[i]];
    }

    fn next(self: *Rows) !?Row {
        while (true) {
            const m = try self.client.readMsg();
            var c = Cursor{ .b = m.payload };
            switch (m.tag) {
                'T' => { // RowDescription: the names come now, the values come in 'D' messages
                    self.column_count = @intCast(c.int(i16));
                    for (0..self.column_count) |i| {
                        const n = c.cstr();
                        const len = @min(n.len, self.names[i].len);
                        @memcpy(self.names[i][0..len], n[0..len]);
                        self.name_lens[i] = len;
                        // table oid, attnum, type oid, typlen, typmod,
                        // format: 18 bytes that this client does not use.
                        c.i += 18;
                    }
                },
                'D' => {
                    var row = Row{ .values = undefined, .count = @intCast(c.int(i16)) };
                    for (0..row.count) |i| {
                        const len = c.int(i32);
                        if (len < 0) {
                            row.values[i] = "<null>";
                            continue;
                        }
                        row.values[i] = c.b[c.i..][0..@intCast(len)];
                        c.i += @intCast(len);
                    }
                    return row;
                },
                'C' => {}, // CommandComplete. The tag repeats the command that the client sent.
                'E' => {
                    self.client.storeError(m.payload);
                    // Read until ReadyForQuery, to keep the connection usable.
                    while ((try self.client.readMsg()).tag != 'Z') {}
                    self.client.ready_status = 'I';
                    return error.QueryFailed;
                },
                'Z' => {
                    self.client.ready_status = m.payload[0];
                    return null;
                },
                else => {},
            }
        }
    }
};

// ---------------------------------------------------- a scripted backend

/// The server half of two conversations, written into a buffer before the
/// demo starts. The client cannot see a difference. It parses a `Reader`, and
/// bytes from a script look the same as bytes from a socket. This site uses
/// the same method frequently. With this method, a driver can have
/// regression tests without a database in CI.
fn scriptBackend(w: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    var pbuf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var p: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&pbuf);

    // Connection: ask for a password, accept it, then send ready.
    try putInt(i32, &p, 3); // AuthenticationCleartextPassword
    try sendMsg(w, 'R', p.buffered());
    p = .fixed(&pbuf);
    try putInt(i32, &p, 0); // AuthenticationOk
    try sendMsg(w, 'R', p.buffered());
    try sendMsg(w, 'S', "server_version\x0016.4\x00");
    try sendMsg(w, 'Z', "I");

    // The SELECT: three columns, one row, then complete.
    p = .fixed(&pbuf);
    try putInt(i16, &p, 3);
    for ([_][]const u8{ "id", "target", "hits" }) |col| {
        try p.writeAll(col);
        try p.writeAll("\x00");
        try putInt(i32, &p, 0); // table oid
        try putInt(i16, &p, 0); // column number
        try putInt(i32, &p, 25); // type oid: text
        try putInt(i16, &p, -1); // variable length
        try putInt(i32, &p, -1); // no modifier
        try putInt(i16, &p, 0); // text format
    }
    try sendMsg(w, 'T', p.buffered());
    p = .fixed(&pbuf);
    try putInt(i16, &p, 3);
    for ([_][]const u8{ "7", "https://ziglang.org", "41" }) |val| {
        try putInt(i32, &p, @intCast(val.len));
        try p.writeAll(val);
    }
    try sendMsg(w, 'D', p.buffered());
    try sendMsg(w, 'C', "SELECT 1\x00");
    try sendMsg(w, 'Z', "I");

    // The INSERT: the server rejects it, but then sends ready again.
    try sendMsg(w, 'E', "SERROR\x00C23505\x00" ++
        "Mduplicate key value violates unique constraint \"links_slug_key\"\x00\x00");
    try sendMsg(w, 'Z', "I");
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var backend_bytes: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var backend: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&backend_bytes);
    try scriptBackend(&backend);

    var sent: [512]u8 = undefined; // what the client sends. The demo does not check it.
    var to_server: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&sent);
    var from_server: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(backend.buffered());

    var client = try PgClient.connect(&from_server, &to_server, "shortener", "links", "hunter2");
    try out.print("connect: password asked: {}, ready: {c}\n", .{
        client.asked_for_password, client.ready_status,
    });

    try out.writeAll("\nquery: SELECT id, target, hits FROM links WHERE slug = 'zig1'\n");
    var rows = try client.query("SELECT id, target, hits FROM links WHERE slug = 'zig1'");
    while (try rows.next()) |row| {
        try out.writeAll("  row:");
        for (0..row.count) |i| {
            try out.print(" {s}={s}", .{ rows.name(i), row.values[i] });
        }
        try out.writeAll("\n");
    }

    try out.writeAll("\nquery: INSERT INTO links (slug, target) VALUES ('zig1', ...)\n");
    var failing = try client.query("INSERT INTO links (slug, target) VALUES ('zig1', 'https://example.com')");
    _ = failing.next() catch {
        try out.print("  error {s}: {s}\n", .{ client.err_code, client.errorMessage() });
    };
    try out.print("  connection after the failure: ready: {c}\n", .{client.ready_status});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`22-url-shortener.pg-client`)*

## The server selects the auth method

The client does not decide how to authenticate. It answers the request in the
`R` message:

- Code 0 means that the server accepted the client.
- Code 3 means: send the password in clear text. Loopback setups use this
  method, and this client supports it.

A standard Postgres asks for SCRAM. SCRAM is a challenge-response exchange
that never sends the password on the wire. SCRAM fits into the same `switch`
as one more case. The [final chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/url-shortener/the-server/) tells
you how to configure a local server to use the method that this client knows.

## The client lends rows, and does not give them

The column values from `next` are slices into the message buffer of the
client. They are valid until the client reads the next message. Real drivers
work the same way, for the same reason: the alternative is one allocation for
each row.

This design has a cost. The caller must follow a rule: copy the
values that you keep. The store in the server chapter copies each value that
it returns. The comment on `drain` in that file states this rule in one line.

## An error is a message, not a disconnection

Look at the failed INSERT at the end of the trace. The server sends an
`ErrorResponse` with a five-character SQL state (`23505` is a unique
violation), then a `ReadyForQuery`. For the server, only the transaction
failed, and the connection is still correct.

The client stores the code and the message, reads until the server is ready,
and returns `error.QueryFailed`. The routes can then change "duplicate slug"
into a response, and they do not need to connect again.

## Variations

- **More of the handshake:** the scripted backend sends one
  `ParameterStatus`, and a real server sends a dozen. The client ignores them.
  Most drivers ignore most of them.
- **Null:** a column can be null on the wire (length -1). Null is not the empty
  string. This client uses a marker for null. A real driver shows the
  difference in the type.
- **The script is a test:** write a script for a bug that you found before.
  For example, use a truncated row or an error in the middle of the results.
  Then you have a regression test that is faster than any integration suite.

---

## Slugs Are Arithmetic

*A URL Shortener. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/url-shortener/slugs/*

The slug of a URL shortener can be the database row id in base62. Then each
slug is unique, and the service needs no collision check. The service must
check the target URL before it stores the URL, because a shortener is an open
redirect by design.

## The problem

The service needs a short name for each stored URL. One attractive design is a
random string. The service checks the string against the database for
collisions, and tries again if necessary.

A simpler design uses a value that the database already has. The database
gives each row a unique integer, the `bigserial` id. A slug that is only that
integer in a compact form is unique, because the ids are unique.

A compact form needs a larger base. Base 10 writes a billion as ten
characters. Base 62 uses the digits and both alphabets, and it writes a
billion as six characters.

## The plan

1. `encode`: divide the id by 62 again and again. Write one character for each
   remainder. The one-billionth link is still six characters.
2. `decode`: the opposite operation, for the redirect path. With the id, the
   lookup can use the primary key. Reject all characters outside the alphabet
   before they get to a query.
3. `checkTarget`: the targets that the service accepts for a redirect. This is
   security logic.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// 62 characters that go through a URL without a change. They need no
// escaping, and they include no punctuation that looks like another
// character. Copy and paste does not change them.
const alphabet = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

/// The row id, written in base 62. The database already makes sure that ids
/// are unique, thus the slugs are also unique. The code needs no random
/// value, collision check or retry loop. An id fits in 11 characters, also at
/// the u64 limit.
fn encode(id: u64, buf: *[11]u8) []const u8 {
    var rest = id;
    var i: usize = buf.len;
    while (true) {
        i -= 1;
        buf[i] = alphabet[@intCast(rest % 62)];
        rest /= 62;
        if (rest == 0) break;
    }
    return buf[i..];
}

/// The opposite direction, for the redirect handler: from slug to id. With
/// the id, the database lookup can use the primary key. This function rejects
/// all characters outside the alphabet, before they get to a query.
fn decode(slug: []const u8) !u64 {
    if (slug.len == 0 or slug.len > 11) return error.BadSlug;
    var id: u64 = 0;
    for (slug) |ch| {
        const digit = std.mem.findScalar(u8, alphabet, ch) orelse
            return error.BadSlug;
        id = try std.math.add(u64, try std.math.mul(u64, id, 62), digit);
    }
    return id;
}

/// The URLs that the service accepts. The scheme check is necessary. If a
/// redirect service stores `javascript:` URLs, it sends each visitor to code
/// from the person who sent the URL.
fn checkTarget(url: []const u8) !void {
    const has_scheme = std.mem.startsWith(u8, url, "https://") or
        std.mem.startsWith(u8, url, "http://");
    if (!has_scheme) return error.SchemeNotAllowed;
    for (url) |ch| {
        // Control characters can let a stored URL smuggle bytes into the
        // HTTP response that redirects to it. A space makes the URL
        // invalid.
        if (ch <= ' ' or ch == 0x7f) return error.BadCharacter;
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var out_buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &out_buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var buf: [11]u8 = undefined;

    // The mapping, at the sizes that a shortener actually gets.
    try out.writeAll("-- encode --\n");
    for ([_]u64{ 0, 7, 61, 62, 100_000, 1_000_000_000, std.math.maxInt(u64) }) |id| {
        try out.print("id {d} -> \"{s}\"\n", .{ id, encode(id, &buf) });
    }

    // The redirect route needs the encoding to be reversible. Thus the test
    // checks this property, and does not assume it.
    for ([_]u64{ 0, 1, 61, 62, 3843, 1 << 20, 1 << 40, std.math.maxInt(u64) }) |sample| {
        if (try decode(encode(sample, &buf)) != sample) return error.RoundtripBroken;
    }
    try out.writeAll("\nroundtrip: decode(encode(id)) == id held for every size tried\n");

    try out.writeAll("\n-- decode rejects --\n");
    for ([_][]const u8{ "zig_1", "", "zzzzzzzzzzzz" }) |slug| {
        _ = decode(slug) catch |err| {
            try out.print("\"{s}\" -> {t}\n", .{ slug, err });
        };
    }

    try out.writeAll("\n-- target validation --\n");
    const targets = [_][]const u8{
        "https://ziglang.org/download/",
        "http://old-but-fine.example",
        "javascript:alert(1)",
        "https://zig lang.org",
        "ziglang.org",
    };
    for (targets) |t| {
        if (checkTarget(t)) {
            try out.print("ok      {s}\n", .{t});
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("{t}: {s}\n", .{ err, t });
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`22-url-shortener.slugs`)*

## Why the scheme check is necessary

A shortener sends visitors to the targets of its stored URLs. Only the check
on the stored URLs stops attackers from the misuse of the shortener.

- A stored `javascript:` URL changes the redirect into script execution in the
  browser of the visitor.
- Control characters can let a stored URL smuggle extra bytes into the HTTP
  response that carries the redirect.

Thus the check allows exactly two schemes. It refuses the space, all characters
below the space, and DEL. The [routes chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/url-shortener/routes/)
runs the check on create and also on update, before any code touches storage.

## What the id shows

If the slugs come from the sequence, there is one cost: a person can guess the
slugs. `4c92` tells any person that `4c91` probably exists. It also tells them
approximately how many links the service gave.

This project accepts that cost, because it is a demonstration of the
mechanism. Some services must have links that no person can guess, or must not
show their size. Such a service encodes a permutation of the id, not the id
itself. A permutation keeps the slugs unique and mixes the order. The change
stays inside these two functions.

## Variations

- **Sixty-two, not sixty-four:** base64 needs `+` and `/`, or the URL-safe
  replacements for them. Base62 uses two fewer characters, and its slugs stay
  correct after any copy and paste.
- **Case is important:** `q0U` and `Q0u` are different links. Suppose people
  read the links aloud on a phone. Then the shortener must not use the
  uppercase letters, and its slugs become approximately 15 percent longer.

---

## Routes Over a Seam

*A URL Shortener. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/url-shortener/routes/*

All five CRUD routes of a URL shortener fit in one Zig function. `handle`
takes request bytes and a store, and writes a complete HTTP response. An
in-memory store is behind the seam. Thus the tests of each route need no
server, no socket and no database.

## The problem

In the HTTP surface, create, read, update and delete become routes. This layer
also has the most cases that you must make correct:

- The slug that does not exist.
- The URL that fails validation.
- The method that no code handles.

If you test those cases against a live server and database, you must start
the server and the database for each case.

The solution is the same seam that the [ORM's Repo chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/orm/repo/)
built. Put the storage behind an interface. Then give the handler the
implementation that it needs at that time. The in-memory store needs no server
and no database. Thus this chapter runs in your browser.

## The plan

1. A `Store` that holds links in a fixed array. The store has only the methods
   that the routes can use: create and find.
2. `handle`: parse the request line, dispatch on the method and the path, and
   write a complete HTTP response. The request parsing is the minimum that
   works. The [web server track](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/web-server/request/) shows the full
   parsing.
3. A demo that runs all five routes and the failure cases, and prints each
   exchange.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// From the slugs chapter, without a change.
const alphabet = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

fn encode(id: u64, buf: *[11]u8) []const u8 {
    var rest = id;
    var i: usize = buf.len;
    while (true) {
        i -= 1;
        buf[i] = alphabet[@intCast(rest % 62)];
        rest /= 62;
        if (rest == 0) break;
    }
    return buf[i..];
}

fn checkTarget(url: []const u8) !void {
    const has_scheme = std.mem.startsWith(u8, url, "https://") or
        std.mem.startsWith(u8, url, "http://");
    if (!has_scheme) return error.SchemeNotAllowed;
    for (url) |ch| {
        if (ch <= ' ' or ch == 0x7f) return error.BadCharacter;
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------- store

/// All the operations that the routes can ask of storage, and no other
/// operations. The final chapter replaces this struct with a struct whose
/// methods write SQL, and no line of the handler changes. The recording
/// driver of the ORM uses the same split for the same reason: you can test
/// the route logic without a database.
const Store = struct {
    const Link = struct {
        id: u64 = 0,
        slug_buf: [11]u8 = undefined,
        slug_len: usize = 0,
        target_buf: [256]u8 = undefined,
        target_len: usize = 0,
        hits: u64 = 0,
        live: bool = false,

        fn slug(self: *const Link) []const u8 {
            return self.slug_buf[0..self.slug_len];
        }
        fn target(self: *const Link) []const u8 {
            return self.target_buf[0..self.target_len];
        }
    };

    links: [16]Link = @splat(.{}),
    next_id: u64 = 1,

    fn create(self: *Store, target: []const u8) ?*Link {
        for (&self.links) |*link| {
            if (link.live) continue;
            const id = self.next_id;
            self.next_id += 1;
            link.* = .{ .id = id, .live = true };
            // encode fills the end of its buffer, and the slug must be at
            // the front. The ranges can overlap, and @memmove handles that.
            const s = encode(id, &link.slug_buf);
            @memmove(link.slug_buf[0..s.len], s);
            link.slug_len = s.len;
            @memcpy(link.target_buf[0..target.len], target);
            link.target_len = target.len;
            return link;
        }
        return null;
    }

    fn find(self: *Store, slug: []const u8) ?*Link {
        for (&self.links) |*link| {
            if (link.live and std.mem.eql(u8, link.slug(), slug)) return link;
        }
        return null;
    }
};

// -------------------------------------------------------------- handler

fn respond(w: *std.Io.Writer, status: []const u8, extra_header: []const u8, body: []const u8) !void {
    try w.print("HTTP/1.1 {s}\r\n", .{status});
    if (extra_header.len > 0) try w.print("{s}\r\n", .{extra_header});
    try w.print("Content-Length: {d}\r\n\r\n{s}", .{ body.len, body });
}

/// One request in, one response out, and no other effects. The request
/// parsing here is the minimum that works. The web server track shows the
/// full parsing, with headers.
fn handle(store: *Store, request: []const u8, w: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    const line_end = std.mem.find(u8, request, "\r\n") orelse return error.BadRequest;
    var line = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, request[0..line_end], ' ');
    const method = line.next() orelse return error.BadRequest;
    const path = line.next() orelse return error.BadRequest;
    const body_start = std.mem.find(u8, request, "\r\n\r\n") orelse return error.BadRequest;
    const body = request[body_start + 4 ..];

    var scratch: [300]u8 = undefined;

    // Create: the body is the URL to shorten, and the answer is the slug.
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "POST") and std.mem.eql(u8, path, "/links")) {
        checkTarget(body) catch |err| {
            const msg = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "{t}\n", .{err});
            return respond(w, "400 Bad Request", "", msg);
        };
        const link = store.create(body) orelse
            return respond(w, "507 Insufficient Storage", "", "full\n");
        const msg = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "{s}\n", .{link.slug()});
        return respond(w, "201 Created", "", msg);
    }

    // The management routes use the same prefix and the same lookup.
    if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, path, "/links/")) {
        const link = store.find(path["/links/".len..]) orelse
            return respond(w, "404 Not Found", "", "no such link\n");
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "GET")) {
            const msg = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "{s} -> {s} ({d} hits)\n", .{
                link.slug(), link.target(), link.hits,
            });
            return respond(w, "200 OK", "", msg);
        }
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "PUT")) {
            checkTarget(body) catch |err| {
                const msg = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "{t}\n", .{err});
                return respond(w, "400 Bad Request", "", msg);
            };
            @memcpy(link.target_buf[0..body.len], body);
            link.target_len = body.len;
            return respond(w, "200 OK", "", "updated\n");
        }
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "DELETE")) {
            link.live = false;
            return respond(w, "204 No Content", "", "");
        }
        return respond(w, "405 Method Not Allowed", "", "");
    }

    // The main route of the service: all other paths are slugs.
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "GET")) {
        if (store.find(path[1..])) |link| {
            link.hits += 1;
            const loc = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "Location: {s}", .{link.target()});
            return respond(w, "302 Found", loc, "");
        }
    }
    return respond(w, "404 Not Found", "", "no such link\n");
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------- demo

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var out_buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &out_buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var store = Store{};

    const requests = [_][]const u8{
        "POST /links HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s\r\n\r\nhttps://ziglang.org",
        "POST /links HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s\r\n\r\njavascript:alert(1)",
        "GET /1 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s\r\n\r\n",
        "GET /links/1 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s\r\n\r\n",
        "PUT /links/1 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s\r\n\r\nhttps://ziglang.org/download/",
        "GET /1 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s\r\n\r\n",
        "DELETE /links/1 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s\r\n\r\n",
        "GET /1 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: s\r\n\r\n",
    };

    for (requests) |request| {
        const line_end = std.mem.find(u8, request, "\r\n").?;
        try out.print("> {s}\n", .{request[0..line_end]});

        var response_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
        var response: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&response_buf);
        try handle(&store, request, &response);

        // Print the response without the HTTP \r, with a prefix on each line.
        var lines = std.mem.splitSequence(u8, response.buffered(), "\r\n");
        while (lines.next()) |l| {
            const line = std.mem.trimEnd(u8, l, "\n");
            if (line.len > 0) try out.print("< {s}\n", .{line});
        }
        try out.writeAll("\n");
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`22-url-shortener.routes`)*

## Read the trace as a contract

The demo is the specification of the service, with one exchange for each case:

- Create answers 201 with the slug.
- The bad scheme answers 400, before the storage gets the request.
- The redirect answers 302 and counts the hit.
- Update changes the target of the same slug.
- Delete answers 204.
- A slug that does not exist now answers 404.

The final chapter replaces the store with SQL. After that change, this trace
must stay true.

## The order of the routes is important

The handler matches `/links` and `/links/{slug}` before the general slug route.
Thus a link with the slug `links` is not reachable. The alphabet from the slugs
chapter makes that collision impossible now: `links` decodes to a very large
id, not to an early id.

But route shadowing occurs with no warning. Suppose a person adds `/stats` to a
slug space that grows. No part of the system gives a warning. Keep all reserved
paths under one prefix, as `/links/...` does. This is an easy way to prevent the
problem.

## Variations

- **No allocation:** the store is a fixed array, and the handler builds each
  response in a buffer that the caller owns. A service of this size can decide
  its limits at the start. When the array is full, the service answers 507.
- **Add a route:** a `GET /links` listing is one more branch and one more store
  method. The handler cannot go around the seam. It must ask the store for all
  the data that it needs.

---

## The Server

*A URL Shortener. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/url-shortener/the-server/*

A URL shortener in Zig fits in one file. The file contains a Postgres wire
client, base62 slugs, and a CRUD `handle` function behind a store seam. An
accept loop serves the routes on real sockets. The server runs against a local
Postgres that one `docker run` command starts.

## The problem

Three chapters built three parts, and the tests of each part used bytes. The
last part cannot run in a browser: real sockets on both sides. All the
code is in one file. Thus you can read the full service from the top to the
bottom.

CI compiles this file on each run. Thus the file stays correct against Zig
master, the same as each other snippet. CI cannot run the file, because CI has
no Postgres server. You can run the file on your computer against a local
Postgres.

## The plan

1. Connect to Postgres on 127.0.0.1:5432. Use the `PgClient` from the client
   chapter again, with only the parts that the server calls.
2. `SqlStore`: the store interface from the routes chapter, with SQL behind
   it. `sqlQuote` puts values into the statement text, and doubles each `'`.
   Thus a value cannot end its own quotes.
3. The same `handle` function, behind the same seam.
4. An accept loop: parse one request, answer it, and close the connection. One
   Postgres connection serves all requests.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

// ------------------------------------------------- wire framing, again
// The same as in the client chapter. In a multi-file project, this block is
// the module that the chapters share. In a one-file server that you read
// from the top to the bottom, it is forty lines of repeated code.

fn putInt(comptime T: type, w: *std.Io.Writer, v: T) !void {
    var b: [@divExact(@typeInfo(T).int.bits, 8)]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(T, &b, v, .big);
    try w.writeAll(&b);
}

fn sendMsg(w: *std.Io.Writer, tag: u8, payload: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeAll(&.{tag});
    try putInt(i32, w, @intCast(payload.len + 4));
    try w.writeAll(payload);
}

const Cursor = struct {
    b: []const u8,
    i: usize = 0,
    fn int(self: *Cursor, comptime T: type) T {
        const n = @divExact(@typeInfo(T).int.bits, 8);
        const v = std.mem.readInt(T, self.b[self.i..][0..n], .big);
        self.i += n;
        return v;
    }
    fn cstr(self: *Cursor) []const u8 {
        const start = self.i;
        while (self.b[self.i] != 0) self.i += 1;
        defer self.i += 1;
        return self.b[start..self.i];
    }
};

// ------------------------------------------------------ the pg client
// The PgClient from the client chapter, with only the parts that this
// server calls.

const PgClient = struct {
    r: *std.Io.Reader,
    w: *std.Io.Writer,
    msg_buf: [512]u8 = undefined,
    ready_status: u8 = 0,
    err_code: [5]u8 = undefined,
    err_msg: [256]u8 = undefined,
    err_msg_len: usize = 0,

    const Msg = struct { tag: u8, payload: []const u8 };

    fn readMsg(self: *PgClient) !Msg {
        var tag: [1]u8 = undefined;
        try self.r.readSliceAll(&tag);
        var len_bytes: [4]u8 = undefined;
        try self.r.readSliceAll(&len_bytes);
        const len = std.mem.readInt(i32, &len_bytes, .big);
        const payload = self.msg_buf[0..@intCast(len - 4)];
        try self.r.readSliceAll(payload);
        return .{ .tag = tag[0], .payload = payload };
    }

    fn connect(r: *std.Io.Reader, w: *std.Io.Writer, user: []const u8, database: []const u8, password: []const u8) !PgClient {
        var body_buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
        var body: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&body_buf);
        try putInt(i32, &body, 196608); // protocol 3.0
        for ([_][]const u8{ "user", user, "database", database }) |s| {
            try body.writeAll(s);
            try body.writeAll("\x00");
        }
        try body.writeAll("\x00");
        try putInt(i32, w, @intCast(4 + body.buffered().len));
        try w.writeAll(body.buffered());
        try w.flush();

        var client = PgClient{ .r = r, .w = w };
        while (true) {
            const m = try client.readMsg();
            var c = Cursor{ .b = m.payload };
            switch (m.tag) {
                'R' => switch (c.int(i32)) {
                    0 => {},
                    3 => {
                        var pw_buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
                        var pw: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&pw_buf);
                        try pw.writeAll(password);
                        try pw.writeAll("\x00");
                        try sendMsg(w, 'p', pw.buffered());
                        try w.flush();
                    },
                    // A default Postgres wants SCRAM. The server chapter
                    // tells you how to allow password auth for this demo.
                    else => return error.UnsupportedAuth,
                },
                'S', 'K', 'N' => {},
                'E' => {
                    client.storeError(m.payload);
                    return error.ConnectFailed;
                },
                'Z' => {
                    client.ready_status = m.payload[0];
                    return client;
                },
                else => {},
            }
        }
    }

    fn storeError(self: *PgClient, payload: []const u8) void {
        var c = Cursor{ .b = payload };
        while (c.b[c.i] != 0) {
            const kind = c.b[c.i];
            c.i += 1;
            const text = c.cstr();
            switch (kind) {
                'C' => @memcpy(&self.err_code, text[0..5]),
                'M' => {
                    const n = @min(text.len, self.err_msg.len);
                    @memcpy(self.err_msg[0..n], text[0..n]);
                    self.err_msg_len = n;
                },
                else => {},
            }
        }
    }

    fn query(self: *PgClient, sql: []const u8) !Rows {
        var sql_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
        var q: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&sql_buf);
        try q.writeAll(sql);
        try q.writeAll("\x00");
        try sendMsg(self.w, 'Q', q.buffered());
        try self.w.flush();
        return .{ .client = self };
    }

    /// Run a statement, and keep no part of the result.
    fn exec(self: *PgClient, sql: []const u8) !void {
        var rows = try self.query(sql);
        while (try rows.next()) |_| {}
    }
};

const Rows = struct {
    client: *PgClient,

    const Row = struct { values: [4][]const u8, count: usize };

    fn next(self: *Rows) !?Row {
        while (true) {
            const m = try self.client.readMsg();
            var c = Cursor{ .b = m.payload };
            switch (m.tag) {
                'D' => {
                    var row = Row{ .values = undefined, .count = @intCast(c.int(i16)) };
                    for (0..row.count) |i| {
                        const len = c.int(i32);
                        if (len < 0) {
                            row.values[i] = "";
                            continue;
                        }
                        row.values[i] = c.b[c.i..][0..@intCast(len)];
                        c.i += @intCast(len);
                    }
                    return row;
                },
                'E' => {
                    self.client.storeError(m.payload);
                    while ((try self.client.readMsg()).tag != 'Z') {}
                    self.client.ready_status = 'I';
                    return error.QueryFailed;
                },
                'Z' => {
                    self.client.ready_status = m.payload[0];
                    return null;
                },
                else => {}, // T, C, N: this server does not need them
            }
        }
    }

    /// Read the other messages, to make the connection ready again. Call
    /// this function after you copy the values that you keep. Row values are
    /// in the message buffer of the client, and this function writes over it.
    fn drain(self: *Rows) !void {
        while (try self.next()) |_| {}
    }
};

// -------------------------------------------------- slugs, from before

const alphabet = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

fn encode(id: u64, buf: *[11]u8) []const u8 {
    var rest = id;
    var i: usize = buf.len;
    while (true) {
        i -= 1;
        buf[i] = alphabet[@intCast(rest % 62)];
        rest /= 62;
        if (rest == 0) break;
    }
    return buf[i..];
}

fn checkTarget(url: []const u8) !void {
    const has_scheme = std.mem.startsWith(u8, url, "https://") or
        std.mem.startsWith(u8, url, "http://");
    if (!has_scheme) return error.SchemeNotAllowed;
    for (url) |ch| {
        if (ch <= ' ' or ch == 0x7f) return error.BadCharacter;
    }
}

// ------------------------------------------------------- the sql store
// The same interface that the routes chapter used in memory, with SQL
// behind it. The store quotes values into the statement text: each ' in the
// value becomes ''. Thus the value cannot end its own quotes. This quoting
// is the simple-protocol tradeoff that the intro names. A production driver
// uses the extended protocol, which sends values outside the SQL.

fn sqlQuote(w: *std.Io.Writer, s: []const u8) !void {
    try w.writeByte('\'');
    for (s) |ch| {
        if (ch == '\'') try w.writeAll("''") else try w.writeByte(ch);
    }
    try w.writeByte('\'');
}

const SqlStore = struct {
    client: *PgClient,

    fn ensureSchema(self: *SqlStore) !void {
        try self.client.exec(
            \\CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS links (
            \\  id     bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
            \\  slug   text UNIQUE NOT NULL,
            \\  target text NOT NULL,
            \\  hits   bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
            \\)
        );
    }

    /// The slug comes from the id, and the id comes from the sequence of
    /// the table. Thus ask the sequence first, then insert a complete row.
    /// That is two statements. A production service puts them in a
    /// transaction. Then a crash between them cannot lose an id.
    fn create(self: *SqlStore, target: []const u8, slug_buf: *[11]u8) ![]const u8 {
        var rows = try self.client.query("SELECT nextval('links_id_seq')");
        const row = (try rows.next()) orelse return error.NoRow;
        const id = try std.fmt.parseInt(u64, row.values[0], 10);
        try rows.drain();

        const slug = encode(id, slug_buf);
        var stmt_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
        var stmt: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&stmt_buf);
        try stmt.print("INSERT INTO links (id, slug, target) VALUES ({d}, ", .{id});
        try sqlQuote(&stmt, slug);
        try stmt.writeAll(", ");
        try sqlQuote(&stmt, target);
        try stmt.writeAll(")");
        try self.client.exec(stmt.buffered());
        return slug;
    }

    const LinkInfo = struct {
        target_buf: [256]u8,
        target_len: usize,
        hits: u64,

        fn target(self: *const LinkInfo) []const u8 {
            return self.target_buf[0..self.target_len];
        }
    };

    fn lookup(self: *SqlStore, slug: []const u8) !?LinkInfo {
        var stmt_buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
        var stmt: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&stmt_buf);
        try stmt.writeAll("SELECT target, hits FROM links WHERE slug = ");
        try sqlQuote(&stmt, slug);
        var rows = try self.client.query(stmt.buffered());
        const row = (try rows.next()) orelse return null;
        var info = LinkInfo{ .target_buf = undefined, .target_len = row.values[0].len, .hits = 0 };
        @memcpy(info.target_buf[0..info.target_len], row.values[0]);
        info.hits = try std.fmt.parseInt(u64, row.values[1], 10);
        try rows.drain();
        return info;
    }

    /// The read for the redirect and its hit count, in one statement. It
    /// needs no second round trip. When two requests race, no update is lost.
    fn follow(self: *SqlStore, slug: []const u8, target_buf: *[256]u8) !?[]const u8 {
        var stmt_buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
        var stmt: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&stmt_buf);
        try stmt.writeAll("UPDATE links SET hits = hits + 1 WHERE slug = ");
        try sqlQuote(&stmt, slug);
        try stmt.writeAll(" RETURNING target");
        var rows = try self.client.query(stmt.buffered());
        const row = (try rows.next()) orelse return null;
        const target = target_buf[0..row.values[0].len];
        @memcpy(target, row.values[0]);
        try rows.drain();
        return target;
    }

    fn update(self: *SqlStore, slug: []const u8, target: []const u8) !bool {
        var stmt_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
        var stmt: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&stmt_buf);
        try stmt.writeAll("UPDATE links SET target = ");
        try sqlQuote(&stmt, target);
        try stmt.writeAll(" WHERE slug = ");
        try sqlQuote(&stmt, slug);
        try stmt.writeAll(" RETURNING id");
        var rows = try self.client.query(stmt.buffered());
        const found = (try rows.next()) != null;
        try rows.drain();
        return found;
    }

    fn remove(self: *SqlStore, slug: []const u8) !bool {
        var stmt_buf: [128]u8 = undefined;
        var stmt: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&stmt_buf);
        try stmt.writeAll("DELETE FROM links WHERE slug = ");
        try sqlQuote(&stmt, slug);
        try stmt.writeAll(" RETURNING id");
        var rows = try self.client.query(stmt.buffered());
        const found = (try rows.next()) != null;
        try rows.drain();
        return found;
    }
};

// ------------------------------------------------------------ the http
// The handler from the routes chapter, with the SQL store behind the seam.
// The shape does not change. Only the store calls are different, because
// the in-memory version returned pointers and SQL returns copies.

fn respond(w: *std.Io.Writer, status: []const u8, extra_header: []const u8, body: []const u8) !void {
    try w.print("HTTP/1.1 {s}\r\n", .{status});
    if (extra_header.len > 0) try w.print("{s}\r\n", .{extra_header});
    try w.print("Connection: close\r\nContent-Length: {d}\r\n\r\n{s}", .{ body.len, body });
}

fn handle(store: *SqlStore, request: []const u8, w: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    const line_end = std.mem.find(u8, request, "\r\n") orelse return error.BadRequest;
    var line = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, request[0..line_end], ' ');
    const method = line.next() orelse return error.BadRequest;
    const path = line.next() orelse return error.BadRequest;
    const body_start = std.mem.find(u8, request, "\r\n\r\n") orelse return error.BadRequest;
    const body = request[body_start + 4 ..];

    var scratch: [300]u8 = undefined;

    if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "POST") and std.mem.eql(u8, path, "/links")) {
        checkTarget(body) catch |err| {
            const msg = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "{t}\n", .{err});
            return respond(w, "400 Bad Request", "", msg);
        };
        var slug_buf: [11]u8 = undefined;
        const slug = try store.create(body, &slug_buf);
        const msg = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "{s}\n", .{slug});
        return respond(w, "201 Created", "", msg);
    }

    if (std.mem.startsWith(u8, path, "/links/")) {
        const slug = path["/links/".len..];
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "GET")) {
            const info = (try store.lookup(slug)) orelse
                return respond(w, "404 Not Found", "", "no such link\n");
            const msg = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "{s} -> {s} ({d} hits)\n", .{
                slug, info.target(), info.hits,
            });
            return respond(w, "200 OK", "", msg);
        }
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "PUT")) {
            checkTarget(body) catch |err| {
                const msg = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "{t}\n", .{err});
                return respond(w, "400 Bad Request", "", msg);
            };
            if (!try store.update(slug, body))
                return respond(w, "404 Not Found", "", "no such link\n");
            return respond(w, "200 OK", "", "updated\n");
        }
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "DELETE")) {
            if (!try store.remove(slug))
                return respond(w, "404 Not Found", "", "no such link\n");
            return respond(w, "204 No Content", "", "");
        }
        return respond(w, "405 Method Not Allowed", "", "");
    }

    if (std.mem.eql(u8, method, "GET")) {
        var target_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
        if (try store.follow(path[1..], &target_buf)) |target| {
            const loc = try std.mem.print(&scratch, "Location: {s}", .{target});
            return respond(w, "302 Found", loc, "");
        }
    }
    return respond(w, "404 Not Found", "", "no such link\n");
}

// -------------------------------------------------------------- wiring

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;

    var out_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &out_buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // One connection to Postgres. It serves each request in sequence.
    const pg_addr = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 5432);
    var pg_stream = try pg_addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
    defer pg_stream.close(io);
    var pg_rbuf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var pg_wbuf: [1024]u8 = undefined;
    var pg_reader = pg_stream.reader(io, &pg_rbuf);
    var pg_writer = pg_stream.writer(io, &pg_wbuf);

    var client = PgClient.connect(
        &pg_reader.interface,
        &pg_writer.interface,
        "shortener",
        "shortener",
        "hunter2",
    ) catch |err| {
        if (err == error.ConnectFailed) {
            try out.print("postgres refused: {s}\n", .{client_err_hint});
            try out.flush();
        }
        return err;
    };
    var store = SqlStore{ .client = &client };
    try store.ensureSchema();

    const http_addr = try std.Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 8080);
    var server = try http_addr.listen(io, .{});
    defer server.deinit(io);
    try out.writeAll("listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080\n");
    try out.flush();

    while (true) {
        var conn = server.accept(io) catch continue;
        defer conn.close(io);
        serveOne(io, &store, &conn) catch |err| {
            try out.print("request failed: {t}\n", .{err});
            try out.flush();
        };
    }
}

const client_err_hint =
    "check the docker run line in the server chapter; a stock Postgres asks for " ++
    "SCRAM auth, which this client does not speak";

fn serveOne(io: std.Io, store: *SqlStore, conn: *std.Io.net.Stream) !void {
    var rbuf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var wbuf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = conn.reader(io, &rbuf);
    var writer = conn.writer(io, &wbuf);

    // Read header lines until the blank line, then exactly Content-Length
    // bytes of body. Only HTTP knows where a request starts and ends. If the
    // code reads only the bytes that are there now, it fails on the first
    // request that comes split. The short-reads chapter explains this.
    var request_buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var used: usize = 0;
    var content_length: usize = 0;
    while (true) {
        const line = try reader.interface.takeDelimiterInclusive('\n');
        if (used + line.len + content_length > request_buf.len) return error.RequestTooBig;
        @memcpy(request_buf[used..][0..line.len], line);
        used += line.len;
        if (std.mem.eql(u8, line, "\r\n")) break;
        if (std.ascii.startsWithIgnoreCase(line, "content-length:")) {
            const value = std.mem.trim(u8, line["content-length:".len..], " \r\n");
            content_length = try std.fmt.parseInt(usize, value, 10);
        }
    }
    try reader.interface.readSliceAll(request_buf[used..][0..content_length]);

    try handle(store, request_buf[0 .. used + content_length], &writer.interface);
    try writer.interface.flush();
}
```

*This program needs a Postgres that answers on localhost, and CI does not have one. CI compiles the program against Zig master on each run. The commands below run the program against a temporary database. (`22-url-shortener.the-server`)*

## Run it

A standard Postgres asks for SCRAM authentication, and this client does not
support SCRAM. The container flag `POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=password` selects
the cleartext method that the client knows. That method is acceptable on
loopback, and nowhere else.

```bash
docker run --rm -d --name shortener-pg \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=shortener -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=hunter2 \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=shortener -e POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=password \
  -p 5432:5432 postgres:16

zig run the-server.zig
```

Then, in a different terminal, use the full CRUD surface:

```bash
curl -X POST --data-binary 'https://ziglang.org' localhost:8080/links
# 1
curl -i localhost:8080/1
# HTTP/1.1 302 Found, Location: https://ziglang.org
curl localhost:8080/links/1
# 1 -> https://ziglang.org (1 hits)
curl -X PUT --data-binary 'https://ziglang.org/download/' localhost:8080/links/1
curl -X DELETE localhost:8080/links/1
```

When you finish, `docker stop shortener-pg` removes the database.

## What changed behind the seam, and what did not change

Compare `handle` here with the routes chapter. The dispatch, the status codes
and the bodies are the same, because the seam did not change.

The ownership changed. The in-memory store gave pointers into its own array.
SQL gives bytes in a message buffer, and the next query writes over that
buffer. Thus each store method copies the values that it returns. Each method
also reads all of the row iterator before it returns control.

The redirect is also better. `UPDATE ... SET hits = hits + 1 ... RETURNING
target` reads the target and counts the hit in one statement. Thus two visitors
at the same time cannot lose an update.

## SQL quotes are a defense with a known limit

`sqlQuote` doubles each `'`. Thus a value cannot end its own string literal,
and this stops the usual injection. The simple query protocol makes this
method necessary.

To keep this method correct for all time is a burden, and real drivers do not
use it. They use the extended protocol. In the extended protocol, values go in
separate messages and are never part of the SQL text. The extended protocol
adds more message types, but no new concepts. `Parse`, `Bind` and `Execute`
go into the `switch` of the client chapter.

## What to build next

- **Pooling:** with one Postgres connection, the server can do only one query
  at a time. A pool is a fixed array of clients and a free list. The
  [many-clients chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/many-clients/) gives the concurrency
  model.
- **The extended protocol:** replace `sqlQuote` with real parameters. The
  Postgres manual describes the messages. The framing code does not change.
- **SCRAM:** add one more arm in the auth `switch`. Then the loopback-only
  configuration above is not necessary.

## A Game You Can Test

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/what-we-are-building/*

Press Play. To change lane, use the arrow keys or `A` and `D`. Space starts a
run. `M` stops the sound.

*Interactive: the game, compiled to WebAssembly. The same build that runs on the desktop, compiled to WebAssembly. It runs on the web page of this chapter.*

The game has three lanes. Blocks move toward you. Coins add to the score. The
game becomes faster until you lose. A run lasts approximately half a minute.

## Games are difficult to test

The behaviour of a game is inside a loop. The loop reads the keyboard, sends
commands to a GPU and runs sixty times each second. A test must not contain any
of these three things.

Thus most small games have no tests. The developer plays the game and adjusts
it. The difficulty becomes the level that the developer could play that week.

This game has fifty-five tests. No test needs a window.

## One rule makes the tests possible

The rules of the game are in one module. That module does not import raylib, a
library for windows, or a clock. The module never allocates. It changes a seed
and a list of inputs into a list of states.

```zig
/// Edge-triggered: each field means "pressed during this tick", not "held".
/// A key that the player holds must not slide the player across the board.
pub const Input = struct {
    left: bool = false,
    right: bool = false,
    confirm: bool = false,

    pub const none: Input = .{};
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Input` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

All other code reads from that state. The renderer draws the world. The audio
code plays a note when an event occurs. The renderer and the audio code cannot
change the result of a run.

The [networking chapters](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/) use the same design. Their
protocol code parses from a `Reader` and not from a socket. If code runs only
inside the full program, nobody tests that code.

## What the tests do

A bot plays the course for four minutes of game time at each seed. The bot must
never crash. If the generator can make a row that nobody can pass, this test
finds the row. The test also found a bug in the bot. The bot steered into blocks
whose centres were behind the player but whose bodies were not.

The same bot runs again with a delay before each action. The delay is a model of
human reaction time. The test checks the average length of a run. A machine with
no reaction time can survive a course, but that result does not tell you if a
person can play the course. This test found a difficulty curve that stopped its
increase after sixty seconds. A good player never lost.

A third test runs two worlds from one seed and one script of inputs. The test
compares the two worlds on each tick.

## Where the code is

```
src/
  sim/        the rules. imports nothing.
  render/     what it looks like. reads the world, never writes it.
  audio/      what it sounds like. holds no raylib either.
  platform/   raylib input and the audio device
  main.zig    window and the fixed timestep loop
```

The full project is on GitHub at
[examples/lane-dodger](https://github.com/rajeshpillai/zig-guide/tree/main/examples/lane-dodger).
Each code block in these chapters shows the path of its file, and the path is a
link to the file. The build of this page reads the blocks from disk. Thus a
chapter cannot describe a function that somebody deleted months ago.

The chapters explain the full game, in the order that you would build it.

## The chapters

- [Vendor raylib](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-build/): how to add raylib to a Zig
  project. Also, why this project depends on the C of raylib and not on its
  build script.
- [The world](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-world/): the field, the two positions of
  the player, and the order of work in a tick.
- [The loop](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-loop/): a fixed timestep, and why `step`
  has no `dt` parameter.
- [Handles](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/entities/): a pool of entities that never
  allocates. The code refers to an entity by a handle and not by a pointer.
- [Draw it](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/drawing/): field units on a window, the road,
  and a particle system that does not use raylib.
- [Input](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/input/): the game records key presses one time in
  each frame and gives them to exactly one tick.
- [Difficulty](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/fair-by-design/): the space between rows comes
  from what is possible. Nobody adjusted it by feel.
- [Sound](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/sound/): five effects, and no audio files.
- [Build it from scratch](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/build-it/): the order in which to
  write the files, and the two points where you can stop and check your work.
