## Vendor raylib

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-build/*

raylib is a C library for windows, drawing and sound. This chapter connects
raylib to a Zig project.

## The one line version, and why it fails

raylib has a `build.zig`. With that file, the dependency should be one line:

```zig
const raylib = b.dependency("raylib", .{ .target = target, .optimize = optimize });
```

On Zig master today, that line itself does not compile. The failure occurs
before the build compiles any of the C of raylib.

```
raylib/build.zig:95:10: error: member function expected 1 argument(s), found 2
raylib/build.zig:762:23: error: no field named 'build_root' in struct 'Build'
```

When you name a package in `build.zig.zon`, the build runner imports the
`build.zig` of that package. The build compiles the build script of each
dependency before it compiles any of your code. Thus, if the build script of a
dependency does not support Zig master yet, your build fails before it gets to
your code.

Both errors are in the Wayland detection of raylib, and this project does not use
Wayland. That fact does not help. The full build script must type-check before
the build gets to your code.

`raylib-zig`, the usual binding, is more out of date. It pins raylib 5.5, and it
calls three standard library functions that do not exist on master now.

Neither project does something wrong. Both projects track releases. This guide
tracks master. The breakage comes from that difference. Thus it is better to
know about the breakage before you add the dependency.

## Depend on the C instead

The C of raylib changes much more slowly than the build API of Zig. Thus this
project depends on the C.

### 1. Fetch the source

Clone raylib at a pinned commit into a directory that the build can read. Pin the
commit, because a dependency without a pin can change without your knowledge.

```bash
git init vendor/raylib
git -C vendor/raylib remote add origin https://github.com/raysan5/raylib.git
git -C vendor/raylib fetch --depth 1 origin <commit>
git -C vendor/raylib checkout FETCH_HEAD
```

Keep `src/` and the licence. Delete all other files. The `examples/` directory of
raylib is 72 MB by itself, and the build compiles none of it. In this project,
`fetch-raylib.sh` does these steps and records the commit that it fetched.

Add `vendor/` to `.gitignore`. The script is the record. The vendored copy is
not the record.

### 2. Do not declare it in `build.zig.zon`

`vendor/raylib` stays a plain directory of C files. The build runner imports the
build script of each declared package, and it never looks at a plain directory.
Thus nothing reads the `build.zig` of raylib.

### 3. Compile the C

```zig
const mod = b.createModule(.{
    .target = target,
    .optimize = optimize,
    .link_libc = true,
});
const lib = b.addLibrary(.{ .name = "raylib", .linkage = .static, .root_module = mod });

mod.addCMacro("PLATFORM_DESKTOP_GLFW", "");
mod.addCMacro("GRAPHICS_API_OPENGL_33", "");
mod.addCMacro("_GLFW_X11", "");

mod.addIncludePath(b.path("vendor/raylib/src/platforms"));
mod.addIncludePath(b.path("vendor/raylib/src/external/glfw/include"));
mod.addCSourceFiles(.{
    .root = b.path("vendor/raylib/src"),
    .files = &.{ "rcore.c", "rshapes.c", "rtextures.c", "rtext.c", "raudio.c", "rglfw.c" },
    .flags = &.{"-std=gnu99"},
});

for ([_][]const u8{ "GL", "X11", "Xrandr", "Xinerama", "Xi", "Xcursor" }) |name| {
    mod.linkSystemLibrary(name, .{});
}
```

The build compiles six C files. `rglfw.c` is the copy of GLFW that raylib
includes, and GLFW is the layer that makes the windows. The other files are the modules of
raylib. The `SUPPORT_MODULE_*` macros turn these modules on and off.

On Debian or Ubuntu, these packages supply the system libraries:

```bash
sudo apt-get install libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxinerama-dev \
                     libxi-dev libxcursor-dev libgl1-mesa-dev
```

You do not need an ALSA package. The audio backend of raylib loads libasound at
runtime, and does not include its header. Thus the game compiles without
libasound, and it is silent when no device exists.

### 4. Change `raylib.h` into a Zig module

The language does not have `@cImport` now. C headers now come through a build
step.

```zig
const translated = b.addTranslateC(.{
    .root_source_file = b.path("vendor/raylib/src/raylib.h"),
    .target = target,
    .optimize = optimize,
    .link_libc = true,
});
const rl = translated.createModule();
rl.linkLibrary(lib);

exe_mod.addImport("rl", rl);
```

### 5. Use it

```zig
const rl = @import("rl");

pub fn main() void {
    rl.InitWindow(540, 960, "Lane Dodger");
    defer rl.CloseWindow();

    while (!rl.WindowShouldClose()) {
        rl.BeginDrawing();
        rl.ClearBackground(rl.RAYWHITE);
        rl.DrawText("hello", 20, 20, 24, rl.BLACK);
        rl.EndDrawing();
    }
}
```

translate-c does not change the names. Thus the documentation of raylib applies
directly.

## The full function

```zig
fn raylibModule(
    b: *std.Build,
    target: std.Build.ResolvedTarget,
    optimize: std.lang.Optimize,
    platform: Platform,
    emsdk: ?[]const u8,
) Raylib {
    const mod = b.createModule(.{
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
        .link_libc = true,
        // In the debug modes, Zig instruments C with UBSan by default and
        // links its own runtime to catch the reports. That runtime comes with
        // a Zig link. emcc does the link for the web build. Thus the
        // instrumentation would leave a few dozen undefined `__ubsan_*`
        // symbols. This project did not write this C. It is a pinned upstream
        // release.
        .sanitize_c = .off,
    });
    const lib = b.addLibrary(.{
        .name = "raylib",
        .linkage = .static,
        .root_module = mod,
    });

    inline for (.{
        .{ "_GNU_SOURCE", "" },
        .{ "GL_SILENCE_DEPRECATION", "199309L" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RSHAPES", "1" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RTEXTURES", "1" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RTEXT", "1" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RAUDIO", "1" },
        // The 3D model loader adds cgltf, m3d and par_shapes. This game draws
        // only rectangles, thus the build turns the module off.
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RMODELS", "0" },
    }) |macro| mod.addCMacro(macro[0], macro[1]);

    switch (platform) {
        .desktop => {
            mod.addCMacro("PLATFORM_DESKTOP_GLFW", "");
            mod.addCMacro("GRAPHICS_API_OPENGL_33", "");
            mod.addCMacro("_GLFW_X11", "");
        },
        .web => {
            mod.addCMacro("PLATFORM_WEB", "");
            // WebGL 2. ES2 also works, and it also works on older phones. All
            // browsers where a person would play this game support ES3 today.
            mod.addCMacro("GRAPHICS_API_OPENGL_ES3", "");
        },
    }

    mod.addIncludePath(b.path(raylib_root ++ "/platforms"));
    mod.addIncludePath(b.path(raylib_root ++ "/external/glfw/include"));
    if (emsdk) |sdk| {
        mod.addIncludePath(.{ .cwd_relative = b.pathJoin(
            &.{ sdk, "upstream", "emscripten", "cache", "sysroot", "include" },
        ) });
    }

    // rglfw.c is the desktop GLFW that raylib includes. On the web,
    // Emscripten supplies GLFW for the canvas. Thus the web build does not
    // compile rglfw.c.
    const sources: []const []const u8 = switch (platform) {
        .desktop => &.{
            "rcore.c", "rshapes.c", "rtextures.c", "rtext.c", "raudio.c", "rglfw.c",
        },
        .web => &.{
            "rcore.c", "rshapes.c", "rtextures.c", "rtext.c", "raudio.c",
        },
    };
    mod.addCSourceFiles(.{
        .root = b.path(raylib_root),
        .files = sources,
        .flags = &.{"-std=gnu99"},
    });

    if (platform == .desktop) {
        for ([_][]const u8{ "GL", "X11", "Xrandr", "Xinerama", "Xi", "Xcursor" }) |name| {
            mod.linkSystemLibrary(name, .{});
        }
    }

    const translated = b.addTranslateC(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path(raylib_root ++ "/raylib.h"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
        .link_libc = true,
    });
    if (emsdk) |sdk| {
        translated.addIncludePath(.{ .cwd_relative = b.pathJoin(
            &.{ sdk, "upstream", "emscripten", "cache", "sysroot", "include" },
        ) });
    }
    const rl = translated.createModule();
    rl.linkLibrary(lib);
    return .{ .module = rl, .lib = lib };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `raylibModule` from `examples/lane-dodger/build.zig`.*

The macros are a copy of the macros in the build script of raylib. That is the
cost of this method. When raylib changes its configuration, this function must
change too. The list of macros is a dozen lines. A mismatch fails at compile
time. A mismatch does not silently make a different library.

## The same source, on a canvas

The platform choice has an effect in two places: the raylib module above, and a
separate `addWeb` step that runs `emcc`.

The desktop build uses `PLATFORM_DESKTOP_GLFW` with OpenGL 3.3 and the copy of
GLFW that raylib includes. The web build uses `PLATFORM_WEB` with GLES 3, and it
does not compile `rglfw.c`. Emscripten supplies its own GLFW, which it connects
to the canvas.

Zig compiles the game and raylib to a static library for `wasm32-emscripten`.
`emcc` does the link. Emscripten supplies the JavaScript glue, the GL context and
the canvas configuration.

```zig
/// Build the game for a browser canvas.
///
/// Zig compiles the game code and the raylib code to a static library for
/// `wasm32-emscripten`. `emcc` does the link, because only Emscripten can emit
/// the JavaScript glue, the GL context and the canvas configuration. The same
/// split is the reason for `Game.frame` in `main.zig`. emcc gives the loop to
/// the browser and never returns.
fn addWeb(
    b: *std.Build,
    optimize: std.lang.Optimize,
    options: *std.Build.Step.Options,
) void {
    const step = b.step("web", "Build the browser version with Emscripten");

    const emsdk = b.option([]const u8, "emsdk", "Path to an activated emsdk") orelse
        b.graph.environ_map.get("EMSDK") orelse
    {
        step.dependOn(&b.addFail(
            "no Emscripten SDK found: pass -Demsdk=/path/to/emsdk, or source emsdk_env.sh",
        ).step);
        return;
    };

    const target = b.resolveTargetQuery(.{
        .cpu_arch = .wasm32,
        .os_tag = .emscripten,
    });

    const game = gameModule(b, target, optimize, options, .web, emsdk);
    const lib = b.addLibrary(.{
        .name = "lane-dodger",
        .linkage = .static,
        .root_module = game.module,
    });

    const emcc = b.addSystemCommand(&.{b.pathJoin(&.{ emsdk, "upstream", "emscripten", "emcc" })});
    emcc.addArtifactArg(lib);
    emcc.addArtifactArg(game.raylib);
    emcc.addArgs(&.{
        // Emscripten supplies GLFW 3 for the canvas. The GLFW that raylib
        // includes is a desktop library for windows. This build does not
        // compile it.
        "-sUSE_GLFW=3",
        // The canvas can have any size, and the page selects the size. Growth
        // costs a small quantity of speed. Without growth, the program must
        // reserve memory for the worst case at the start.
        "-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1",
        // A factory function, and not a global `Module`. Thus the page can
        // start the game at the time that it selects, and give the game its
        // own canvas.
        //
        // This output is not an ES6 module, and that is intentional. The guide
        // puts the game in a page that Vite builds. Vite rewrites `import()`
        // also for a file that it only serves from `public/`. It adds
        // `?import`, then it cannot transform a 190 KB Emscripten bundle. A
        // plain `<script>` tag loads a classic script that defines one global,
        // and no bundler changes that tag.
        "-sMODULARIZE=1",
        "-sEXPORT_NAME=createLaneDodger",
        // emscripten_set_main_loop controls the loop. Thus the build needs
        // none of the code that unwinds the stack.
        "-sASYNCIFY=0",
        "-sSTACK_SIZE=1048576",
        // Here the build compiles raylib against GLES 3, which emits
        // `#version 300 es` shaders. These shaders need a WebGL 2 context.
        // Emscripten creates a WebGL 1 context unless you tell it to do
        // otherwise. The symptom is a game that loads, runs, and compiles no
        // shader.
        "-sMIN_WEBGL_VERSION=2",
        "-sMAX_WEBGL_VERSION=2",
    });
    if (optimize != .debug) emcc.addArgs(&.{ "-O3", "--closure", "0" });
    emcc.addArg("-o");
    const out = emcc.addOutputFileArg("lane-dodger.js");

    // emcc writes the wasm next to the js, with the same basename.
    const install_js = b.addInstallFileWithDir(out, .{ .custom = "web" }, "lane-dodger.js");
    const install_wasm = b.addInstallFileWithDir(
        out.dirname().path(b, "lane-dodger.wasm"),
        .{ .custom = "web" },
        "lane-dodger.wasm",
    );
    // The page that holds the canvas. The page comes with the two artefacts.
    // Thus `zig build web` makes a directory that you can play with no other
    // configuration.
    const install_page = b.addInstallFileWithDir(
        b.path("web-shell/index.html"),
        .{ .custom = "web" },
        "index.html",
    );
    step.dependOn(&install_js.step);
    step.dependOn(&install_wasm.step);
    step.dependOn(&install_page.step);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `addWeb` from `examples/lane-dodger/build.zig`.*

Two flags in that function prevent silent failures.

`-sMIN_WEBGL_VERSION=2`. GLES 3 emits `#version 300 es` shaders, and these
shaders need a WebGL 2 context. Emscripten creates a WebGL 1 context unless you
tell it to do otherwise. The symptom is a game that loads, runs, reports no
error, and compiles no shader.

`.sanitize_c = .off` on the raylib module. In the debug modes, Zig instruments C
with UBSan and links its own runtime to catch the reports. That runtime comes
with a Zig link. Here `emcc` does the link. Thus the instrumentation leaves
dozens of undefined `__ubsan_*` symbols.

## Run it

```bash
cd examples/lane-dodger
./fetch-raylib.sh
zig build run -Doptimize=ReleaseFast
```

The browser build is a `.wasm` file of 200 KB, and approximately the same
quantity of JavaScript. The browser build needs the Emscripten SDK:

```bash
zig build web -Doptimize=ReleaseFast
python3 -m http.server -d zig-out/web 8080
```

## The World

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-world/*

The simulation never uses pixels. It uses a fixed field of 360 by 640 units. The
renderer maps the field onto the window, whatever the size of the window.

```zig
/// The play field, in simulation units. The field is portrait, because the
/// player uses a thumb to play.
pub const field_w: f32 = 360;
```

*Quoted from the source: `field_w` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/config.zig`.*

This design has two results:

- A change to the size of the window cannot change the difficulty, because a
  wider window does not show more road.
- A test can assert that a block is at `y = 520`, and the test opens nothing.

The three lanes divide the width. Thus a lane is 120 units wide.

```zig
/// The centre of a lane, in field units.
pub fn laneCenter(lane: u8) f32 {
    return (@as(f32, @floatFromInt(lane)) + 0.5) * lane_w;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `laneCenter` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/config.zig`.*

Thus `laneCenter(0)` is 60, `laneCenter(1)` is 180 and `laneCenter(2)` is 300.
These three numbers are the only x positions where an object stops.

The player is at a fixed height near the bottom. The world moves toward the
player.

```zig
/// The player is at a fixed height, and the world moves toward the player.
pub const player_y: f32 = 520;
```

*Quoted from the source: `player_y` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/config.zig`.*

## The player has two positions

One position is the lane that the player steers toward. The other position is
where the body of the player really is.

```zig
pub const Player = struct {
    /// The lane that the player steers toward. It changes immediately when the
    /// player presses a key.
    lane: u8,
    /// Where the player really is. It slides toward the lane centre. Thus the
    /// player can change direction during a slide. Also, if the player touches
    /// a block during a slide, the result is a real crash.
    x: f32,
    x_prev: f32,
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Player` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

`lane` changes immediately when the player presses a key. `x` slides toward the
centre of that lane during `lane_change_time`. After each press, the two values
are different for approximately a tenth of a second. That difference gives the
game its feel.

```zig
/// The seconds for a slide of one full lane. This number has a large effect on
/// how the controls feel. If it is too slow, the game is unfair. If it is
/// too fast, a lane change costs nothing to cancel.
pub const lane_change_time: f32 = 0.11;
```

*Quoted from the source: `lane_change_time` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/config.zig`.*

The slide has a constant speed. It does not start slowly or stop slowly.

```zig
    fn movePlayer(w: *World, dt: f32) void {
        w.player.x_prev = w.player.x;
        const target = config.laneCenter(w.player.lane);
        // A constant speed, and not a slow start and stop. Thus two lanes cost
        // exactly two times one lane. The fairness budget in config.zig needs
        // that.
        const rate = config.lane_w / config.lane_change_time;
        const delta = target - w.player.x;
        const max_move = rate * dt;
        w.player.x += std.math.clamp(delta, -max_move, max_move);
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `movePlayer` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

A slide that starts and stops slowly looks smoother. But with that slide, a move
of two lanes costs less than two times a move of one lane.
[The spacing rule](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/fair-by-design/) needs a move of two lanes
to cost exactly two times a move of one lane. A constant speed looks less smooth,
but it keeps the spacing rule correct.

Because `x` is continuous, the player really occupies the space between lanes.
If the player touches a block during a slide, the game counts a crash.

## The other objects in the field

Blocks and coins have the same shape of data. A tag tells them apart.

```zig
pub const Entity = struct {
    kind: Kind,
    lane: u8,
    y: f32,
    /// The position at the end of the previous tick. Thus the renderer can
    /// interpolate between ticks, and does not show the steps of the
    /// simulation.
    y_prev: f32,
    /// For blocks: true when this block became level with the player. A near
    /// miss gives points one time, on the tick when it occurs.
    passed: bool = false,
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Entity` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

`y_prev` is not simulation state. The renderer needs it to
[draw between two ticks](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-loop/).

## The world

```zig
pub const World = struct {
    phase: Phase,
    rng: Rng,
    seed: u64,

    entities: EntityPool,
    player: Player,
    events: EventBuffer,

    /// The seconds of play in the current run.
    time: f32,
    /// The units that the world moved in the current run.
    distance: f32,
    /// The units until the game puts down the next row.
    to_next_row: f32,
    /// The seconds since the crash.
    death_time: f32,

    score: u32,
    /// The score from coins and near misses. The code calculates the distance
    /// score from `distance`. Thus rounding cannot make the total drift.
    bonus: u32,
    combo: u32,
    coins: u32,
    best: u32,

    // ...
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `World` (fields only) from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

`seed` and `best` stay after a restart. The restart clears all other fields. The
game calculates `score` again on each tick, and does not add to it. The distance
points come from `distance` on each tick. Only coins and near misses add to
`bonus`. If the game added a fraction of a point 120 times each second, the
total would drift.

## The order in a tick

```zig
    fn stepPlaying(w: *World, input: Input) void {
        const dt = config.tick_dt;

        w.steer(input);
        w.movePlayer(dt);

        const moved = w.speed() * dt;
        w.advanceEntities(moved);
        w.spawnIfDue(moved);
        w.collide();

        w.distance += moved;
        w.time += dt;
        w.score = w.bonus + @as(u32, @intFromFloat(w.distance * config.points_per_unit));
        if (w.score > w.best) w.best = w.score;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `stepPlaying` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

A tick does these steps:

1. If a press arrived, move the target lane.
2. Slide `x` toward that lane at a constant speed.
3. Move each entity down by `speed * dt`.
4. When a block first gets to the height of the player, give points for a near
   miss.
5. Destroy each object below the field. A coin that the player did not collect
   sets the combo to zero.
6. If the world moved the full gap, spawn a row.
7. Test the box of the player against the box of each entity.
8. Calculate the score again as the bonus plus the distance.

The order has a reason. First the player moves, then the world moves, then the
tick tests the player against the world. If the tick tested collisions before
the world moved, a block could move through the player on the tick when the
block arrives.

`steer` reads the input and moves the target lane by one.

```zig
    fn steer(w: *World, input: Input) void {
        const from = w.player.lane;
        var lane: i32 = from;
        if (input.left) lane -= 1;
        if (input.right) lane += 1;
        const clamped: u8 = @intCast(std.math.clamp(lane, 0, config.lane_count - 1));
        if (clamped != from) {
            w.player.lane = clamped;
            w.events.push(.{ .lane_changed = .{ .from = from, .to = clamped } });
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `steer` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

One press moves the target one lane. The clamp keeps the player on the board. Two
fast presses set a target that is two lanes away. Then `movePlayer` slides there
continuously.

## Collision

```zig
    fn collide(w: *World) void {
        var it = w.entities.iterator();
        while (it.next()) |entry| {
            const e = entry.value;
            const ex = config.laneCenter(e.lane);
            switch (e.kind) {
                .block => {
                    if (overlaps(
                        w.player.x,
                        config.player_y,
                        config.player_half_w,
                        config.player_half_h,
                        ex,
                        e.y,
                        config.block_half_w,
                        config.block_half_h,
                    )) {
                        w.phase = .dead;
                        w.death_time = 0;
                        w.combo = 0;
                        w.events.push(.{ .crashed = .{ .x = w.player.x, .y = config.player_y } });
                        return;
                    }
                },
                .coin => {
                    if (overlaps(
                        w.player.x,
                        config.player_y,
                        config.player_half_w,
                        config.player_half_h,
                        ex,
                        e.y,
                        config.coin_half,
                        config.coin_half,
                    )) {
                        if (w.combo < config.max_combo) w.combo += 1;
                        const points = config.coin_points * w.combo;
                        w.bonus += points;
                        w.coins += 1;
                        w.events.push(.{ .coin = .{
                            .x = ex,
                            .y = e.y,
                            .combo = w.combo,
                            .points = points,
                        } });
                        w.entities.destroy(entry.handle);
                    }
                },
            }
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `collide` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

Both tests look for an overlap of two boxes whose sides are parallel to the
axes.

```zig
fn overlaps(
    ax: f32,
    ay: f32,
    ahw: f32,
    ahh: f32,
    bx: f32,
    by: f32,
    bhw: f32,
    bhh: f32,
) bool {
    return @abs(ax - bx) < ahw + bhw and @abs(ay - by) < ahh + bhh;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `overlaps` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

A block stops the run. A coin adds to the combo, gives points, and the game
destroys the coin. The combo has a maximum. The combo goes to zero when a coin
falls off the bottom and the player did not collect it.

## The game has its own random numbers

The world has its own generator.

```zig
pub fn next(self: *Rng) u32 {
    const old = self.state;
    self.state = old *% 6364136223846793005 +% self.inc;
    const xorshifted: u32 = @truncate(((old >> 18) ^ old) >> 27);
    const rot: u5 = @truncate(old >> 59);
    return std.math.rotr(u32, xorshifted, rot);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `next` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/rng.zig`.*

The generator is thirty lines of PCG32, and not a call into the standard
library. The reason is reproducibility. A seed and a list of inputs must replay
to the identical run. Then the replay test can assert exact scores. A player
can report a bad run as a seed and not as a video. The standard library can
change the algorithm of its generators between releases, and this guide tracks
Zig master.

Each run moves the stream forward and does not use the seed again. Thus the
second game of a session is not a replay of the first game.

---

## The Loop Takes No dt

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-loop/*

The usual game loop reads the clock and gives the elapsed time to the world.

```zig
while (running) {
    const dt = getFrameTime();
    world.update(dt);   // do not do this
    draw(world);
}
```

This loop causes three problems.

**The same inputs do not give the same run.** The value of `dt` is the time that
the machine gave. A 60 Hz laptop and a 165 Hz monitor move the world in
different steps. If you add 1/60 sixty times, the result is not the same number
as when you add 1/165 one hundred and sixty-five times.

**A slow frame becomes an advantage.** The score in this game measures survival.
A frame that takes 50 ms moves the world 50 ms forward in one jump. The game
tests for collision at the two ends of that jump, and not between them. If the
game stops for a moment, the player can move through a block.

**No run can replay.** To report a crash, you must record a video of the crash.
A seed and a list of key presses do not make the same crash on a different
machine.

## Fixed steps

`step` has no `dt` parameter. It moves the world forward by one tick, and a tick
always has the same size.

```zig
    /// Move the world forward by one fixed tick.
    ///
    /// This function has no `dt` parameter, on purpose. With a variable
    /// timestep, the same inputs would give different runs on different
    /// machines. Then the replay tests below could not work. Also, in a game
    /// that gives points for survival time, a slow frame would become an
    /// advantage. The caller collects real time and calls this function a
    /// whole number of times. `src/main.zig` shows how.
    pub fn step(w: *World, input: Input) void {
        switch (w.phase) {
            .ready => if (input.confirm) w.start(),
            .playing => w.stepPlaying(input),
            .dead => {
                w.death_time += config.tick_dt;
                w.player.x_prev = w.player.x;
                w.driftEntities();
                if (w.death_time >= config.death_hold and input.confirm) w.start();
            },
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `step` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

A caller cannot use `step` incorrectly. A caller cannot get half a tick. To get
ten ticks, a caller calls `step` ten times.

The tick rate is 120 Hz. This rate is more than each common refresh rate. Thus
the simulation is never the cause when the motion of the game looks rough.

## The accumulator

Real time arrives in parts of different sizes. The loop saves the time and uses
it one tick at a time.

```zig
/// Move a world forward by whole ticks, and react to the report of each tick.
fn advance(
    world: *sim.World,
    system: *particles.System,
    shake: *Shake,
    audio: ?*Audio,
    accumulator: *f32,
    latch: ?*input.Latch,
) void {
    while (accumulator.* >= config.tick_dt) {
        accumulator.* -= config.tick_dt;
        const tick_input = if (latch) |l| l.take() else bot.play(world);
        world.step(tick_input);
        react(world, system, shake, audio);
        world.events.reset();
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `advance` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/main.zig`.*

The input goes to the first tick of the frame. The input for the other ticks is
empty. A key press is an edge trigger. If one press went to three ticks, one tap
would move the player across three lanes.

The loop clamps the frame time before the time goes into the accumulator.

```zig
/// The largest real-time step that the loop accepts. A larger step means that
/// the game was paused, the laptop was asleep, or a breakpoint stopped the
/// program. If the loop ran ten seconds of ticks at one time to recover the
/// time, the player would die before the player could react.
const max_frame_time: f32 = 0.25;
```

*Quoted from the source: `max_frame_time` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/main.zig`.*

Without the clamp, the loop can get ten seconds at one time. A paused game or a
laptop that wakes from sleep can cause this. Ten seconds is 1200 ticks. The time
to run these ticks gives another large `dt`, and that `dt` gives more ticks. The
game stops and does not respond, and it does not move forward. The usual name for
this problem is the spiral of death.

## The leftover time

After the tick loop, some time always remains, and this time is less than one
tick. If the renderer ignores this time, the game moves in visible steps at 120
Hz on a 165 Hz display.

Thus the loop tells the renderer how far it is into the next tick. The renderer
draws between the last two states.

```zig
const alpha = self.accumulator / config.tick_dt;
```

```zig
/// Interpolate between the last two simulation ticks. Without this, the game
/// moves in visible steps at 120 Hz on a 144 Hz display.
fn lerp(previous: f32, current: f32, alpha: f32) f32 {
    return previous + (current - previous) * alpha;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `lerp` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/draw.zig`.*

Because the renderer draws between states, `Entity` has a `y_prev` field that no
rule reads. `y_prev` is not simulation state. The renderer needs it to draw a
frame between two ticks.

## One frame, not a loop

On the desktop, the loop is a `while` loop. In a browser, the loop cannot be a
`while` loop. Emscripten calls a function one time for each animation frame, and
Emscripten never returns into your code. A `while` loop cannot run there, and its
local variables have no place to live.

Thus the code keeps "one frame" separate from "run frames continuously". `Game`
is a struct with a `frame` method. Only the caller is different.

```zig
pub fn main() void {
    run();
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `main` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/main.zig`.*

The game state is a variable at file scope, and not a local variable.
`emscripten_set_main_loop` never returns. Thus a local variable in `main` does not
exist when the first frame starts.

Use this split also for a game that you never put in a browser. If you can call a
frame one time, you can also call it six hundred times. A bot can be at the
controls, with no open window. [The difficulty tests](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/fair-by-design/)
use this method.

---

## Handles, Not Pointers

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/entities/*

The game creates blocks and coins above the screen. It destroys them after they
leave the bottom. This occurs several times each second while the game runs.

## The storage is a fixed array

A run of any length allocates one time at startup, and never again. The
simulation has no allocator. That is one reason why the simulation imports
nothing.

Forty-eight slots are more than the field can hold. At the smallest spacing and
the highest speed, approximately three rows are on the screen. Each row has a
maximum of three entities, thus approximately nine entities exist at one time. A
test asserts that the peak stays less than the capacity and more than six. Thus
the test finds a change that stops the spawns without an error.

## An index is not sufficient

The usual way to refer to an entity is by its index. This causes a bug that is
very difficult to reproduce.

An event says "the player collected coin 12". One frame later, the pool frees
slot 12 and gives it to a new block. Any code that still has the number 12 now
reads a block and thinks that the block is a coin. The program does not crash.
The score is wrong approximately one time each hour, usually when nobody looks.

A pointer instead of an index does not help, because the pool uses the slot again
in both cases.

## Generational handles

A handle contains the slot index and the generation of that slot at the time
when the pool made the handle. When the pool frees a slot, it increments the
generation of the slot. Thus no handle to the old occupant resolves after that.

```zig
pub fn Pool(comptime T: type, comptime capacity_in: u16) type {
    return struct {
        const Self = @This();

        pub const capacity = capacity_in;

        pub const Handle = struct {
            index: u16,
            generation: u32,

            /// A handle that never resolves. The pool never gives out
            /// generation 0, because live slots start at generation 1.
            pub const none: Handle = .{ .index = 0, .generation = 0 };

            pub fn eql(a: Handle, b: Handle) bool {
                return a.index == b.index and a.generation == b.generation;
            }
        };

        const Slot = struct {
            value: T,
            /// Odd while the slot is live, even while it is free.
            generation: u32,
            /// The index of the next free slot. It is valid only while this
            /// slot is free.
            next_free: u16,
        };

        slots: [capacity]Slot,
        free_head: u16,
        live: u16,

        pub const empty = init: {
            var self: Self = .{
                .slots = undefined,
                .free_head = 0,
                .live = 0,
            };
            for (&self.slots, 0..) |*slot, i| {
                slot.* = .{
                    .value = undefined,
                    .generation = 0,
                    .next_free = @intCast(i + 1),
                };
            }
            break :init self;
        };

        /// Returns null when the pool is full. The caller decides what a full
        /// pool means. The spawner uses a full pool as back-pressure and does
        /// not do the spawn. This is always safe, because the course stays
        /// solvable.
        pub fn create(self: *Self, value: T) ?Handle {
            if (self.free_head >= capacity) return null;
            const index = self.free_head;
            const slot = &self.slots[index];
            self.free_head = slot.next_free;
            slot.generation += 1; // even -> odd: now live
            slot.value = value;
            self.live += 1;
            return .{ .index = index, .generation = slot.generation };
        }

        pub fn destroy(self: *Self, handle: Handle) void {
            const slot = self.resolve(handle) orelse return;
            slot.generation += 1; // odd -> even: now free
            slot.next_free = self.free_head;
            self.free_head = handle.index;
            self.live -= 1;
        }

        pub fn get(self: *Self, handle: Handle) ?*T {
            const slot = self.resolve(handle) orelse return null;
            return &slot.value;
        }

        pub fn contains(self: *const Self, handle: Handle) bool {
            if (handle.index >= capacity) return false;
            const slot = &self.slots[handle.index];
            return slot.generation == handle.generation and slot.generation % 2 == 1;
        }

        fn resolve(self: *Self, handle: Handle) ?*Slot {
            if (handle.index >= capacity) return null;
            const slot = &self.slots[handle.index];
            if (slot.generation != handle.generation) return null;
            if (slot.generation % 2 == 0) return null;
            return slot;
        }

        pub const Entry = struct { handle: Handle, value: *T };

        pub const Iterator = struct {
            pool: *Self,
            index: u16 = 0,

            pub fn next(self: *Iterator) ?Entry {
                while (self.index < capacity) {
                    const i = self.index;
                    self.index += 1;
                    const slot = &self.pool.slots[i];
                    if (slot.generation % 2 == 1) return .{
                        .handle = .{ .index = i, .generation = slot.generation },
                        .value = &slot.value,
                    };
                }
                return null;
            }
        };

        pub fn iterator(self: *Self) Iterator {
            return .{ .pool = self };
        }

        pub fn clear(self: *Self) void {
            var it = self.iterator();
            while (it.next()) |entry| self.destroy(entry.handle);
        }
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `Pool` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/pool.zig`.*

The generation is odd while a slot is live, and even while the slot is free. One
counter tells you two things: which occupant has the slot, and if the slot is in
use. The pool never gives out generation zero. Thus a handle of all zeros is a
null handle.

`create` returns an optional, and does not assert. Here a full pool is not an
error. The spawner uses a full pool as back pressure and does not do that spawn.
This is safe because the player can always pass the course in both cases.

The name of the test is the name of the bug:

```zig
test "a stale handle does not resolve to the slot's new occupant" {
    var pool: TestPool = .empty;
    const old = pool.create(1).?;
    pool.destroy(old);
    const new = pool.create(2).?;
    // The pool uses the freed slot again. This is the purpose of the pool.
    try std.testing.expectEqual(old.index, new.index);
    // The stale handle must not see the new value.
    try std.testing.expect(pool.get(old) == null);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(i32, 2), pool.get(new).?.*);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `a stale handle does not resolve to the slot's new occupant` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/pool.zig`.*

The first assertion proves that the pool really used the slot again. Without that
assertion, the test can pass when the pool gives out a new slot, and then the test
does not test the bug.

## One pool, two users

The pool is generic, thus other code can use it. The particle system uses the
same pool with a capacity of 256 and a different element type. The particles are
part of the renderer and not part of the simulation. Because the code has one
pool type for both users, the renderer got storage with a fixed capacity and no
allocator, at no extra cost.

## Events

The simulation reports what occurred. The simulation does not know what other
code does with that report.

```zig
/// What the simulation did in this tick. The parts of the program that react
/// to it read this: particles, screen shake, sound. The simulation does not
/// know that those parts exist. Thus a new sound cannot change the physics.
pub const Event = union(enum) {
    started,
    lane_changed: struct { from: u8, to: u8 },
    coin: struct { x: f32, y: f32, combo: u32, points: u32 },
    coin_missed,
    near_miss: struct { x: f32, y: f32 },
    crashed: struct { x: f32, y: f32 },
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Event` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

The events collect in a fixed buffer, and the caller empties the buffer one time
in each frame. The buffer counts the events that it had to drop. A test asserts
that this count is zero across forty thousand ticks. If the event stream lost
events, the only symptom would be some particles that do not
appear.

One function contains the full reaction to a tick:

```zig
/// Change the reports from the simulation into what the player sees and
/// feels. No code here can change the result of the run.
fn react(
    world: *const sim.World,
    system: *particles.System,
    shake: *Shake,
    audio: ?*Audio,
) void {
    if (audio) |sound| {
        for (world.events.slice()) |event| sound.onEvent(event);
    }
    for (world.events.slice()) |event| switch (event) {
        .coin => |c| {
            system.burst(c.x, c.y, 10, palette.coin, 190);
            shake.kick(1.5 + @as(f32, @floatFromInt(c.combo)) * 0.4);
        },
        .near_miss => |n| {
            system.graze(n.x, n.y);
            shake.kick(3);
        },
        .crashed => |c| {
            system.debris(c.x, c.y);
            shake.kick(16);
        },
        .lane_changed => |l| {
            const direction: f32 = if (l.to > l.from) 1 else -1;
            system.dust(world.player.x, config.player_y, direction);
        },
        .coin_missed, .started => {},
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `react` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/main.zig`.*

A coin becomes ten amber dots and a small shake of the screen. A crash becomes
debris. The simulation cannot see any of these effects.

## What this split gives you

The sound came after the game was already playable. The sound did not change a
rule of the game, because it reads the same events that the particles read.

```zig
    /// The one entry point that the game uses. It takes the same events as the
    /// particles and the screen shake.
    pub fn onEvent(self: *Audio, event: sim.Event) void {
        switch (event) {
            .coin => |c| {
                // Each combo step increases the pitch of the one coin sound.
                // Thus the game does not need eight coin sounds.
                // A semitone is 2^(1/12). This value is a little less than one
                // semitone for each step. Thus a full combo ends approximately
                // a fifth above its start.
                const step = std.math.pow(f32, 2.0, @as(f32, @floatFromInt(c.combo - 1)) / 14.0);
                self.cue(.coin, 0.85, step);
            },
            .near_miss => self.cue(.near_miss, 0.6, 1),
            .lane_changed => self.cue(.lane, 0.5, 1),
            .crashed => self.cue(.crash, 1, 1),
            .started => self.cue(.start, 0.8, 1),
            .coin_missed => {},
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `onEvent` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/platform/audio.zig`.*

It is easy to make an event system too large. Here, six variants in a tagged
union, a fixed buffer and one loop are sufficient. To test the design, ask this
question: to add a reaction, must you change the code that caused the event?
Here you do not. The same property lets
[the difficulty tests](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/fair-by-design/) run the full game
with no renderer and no audio device.

---

## Draw It

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/drawing/*

The simulation uses a fixed field of 360 by 640. The window can have any size
that the reader gives it. One struct maps between the field and the window.

```zig
/// Field units to screen pixels.
pub const View = struct {
    scale: f32,
    origin_x: f32,
    origin_y: f32,
    shake_x: f32 = 0,
    shake_y: f32 = 0,

    pub fn init(screen_w: f32, screen_h: f32) View {
        const scale = @min(screen_w / config.field_w, screen_h / config.field_h);
        return .{
            .scale = scale,
            .origin_x = (screen_w - config.field_w * scale) * 0.5,
            .origin_y = (screen_h - config.field_h * scale) * 0.5,
        };
    }

    pub fn x(self: View, field_x: f32) f32 {
        return self.origin_x + field_x * self.scale + self.shake_x;
    }

    pub fn y(self: View, field_y: f32) f32 {
        return self.origin_y + field_y * self.scale + self.shake_y;
    }

    pub fn len(self: View, value: f32) f32 {
        return value * self.scale;
    }

    fn rect(self: View, cx: f32, cy: f32, half_w: f32, half_h: f32) rl.Rectangle {
        return .{
            .x = self.x(cx - half_w),
            .y = self.y(cy - half_h),
            .width = self.len(half_w * 2),
            .height = self.len(half_h * 2),
        };
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `View` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/draw.zig`.*

The scale is the smaller of the two ratios. Thus the renderer letterboxes the
field. A
wider window gets bars on the sides. It does not get more road.

If the view filled the window, a wide window would show blocks earlier. Then a
player could get an advantage when the player changes the size of the window.

The transform adds `shake_x` and `shake_y` at the end. Thus the screen shake
moves the full field, and it costs nothing in other places.

## A frame

```zig
pub fn frame(
    world: *const sim.World,
    system: *particles.System,
    view: View,
    alpha: f32,
    /// The total distance that the road moved. Only the animation of the road
    /// stripes uses it.
    scroll: f32,
    /// False behind the title screen. There, the visible score would be the
    /// score of the attract mode, and not the score of the player.
    show_hud: bool,
) void {
    rl.ClearBackground(color(palette.background));
    drawRoad(view, scroll);
    drawEntities(world, view, alpha);
    drawParticles(system, view);
    if (world.phase != .dead) drawPlayer(world, view, alpha);
    if (show_hud) drawHud(world, view);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `frame` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/draw.zig`.*

The order is from back to front: road, entities, particles, player, HUD. This
file reads the world and never writes it. No code in this file can change the
result of a run.

## The road

```zig
fn drawRoad(view: View, scroll: f32) void {
    const road = view.rect(
        config.field_w * 0.5,
        config.field_h * 0.5,
        config.field_w * 0.5,
        config.field_h * 0.5,
    );
    rl.DrawRectangleRec(road, color(palette.road));

    // The lines between the lanes.
    for (1..config.lane_count) |i| {
        const lane_x = view.x(@as(f32, @floatFromInt(i)) * config.lane_w);
        rl.DrawRectangleV(
            .{ .x = lane_x - view.len(1), .y = view.y(0) },
            .{ .x = view.len(2), .y = view.len(config.field_h) },
            color(palette.lane_line),
        );
    }

    // Dashes move down each line. Thus the speed is visible also when the
    // field is empty.
    const period: f32 = 80;
    const offset = @mod(scroll, period);
    for (1..config.lane_count) |i| {
        const lane_x = view.x(@as(f32, @floatFromInt(i)) * config.lane_w);
        var dash_y: f32 = -period + offset;
        while (dash_y < config.field_h) : (dash_y += period) {
            rl.DrawRectangleV(
                .{ .x = lane_x - view.len(2), .y = view.y(dash_y) },
                .{ .x = view.len(4), .y = view.len(36) },
                color(palette.stripe),
            );
        }
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `drawRoad` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/draw.zig`.*

The dashes move with the distance that the player travelled. When the field is
empty, the dashes are the only thing on the screen that shows the speed. In the
first few seconds, the field is empty more frequently than you think.

## The entities

```zig
fn drawEntities(world: *const sim.World, view: View, alpha: f32) void {
    var it = @constCast(&world.entities).iterator();
    while (it.next()) |entry| {
        const e = entry.value;
        const cx = config.laneCenter(e.lane);
        const cy = lerp(e.y_prev, e.y, alpha);
        switch (e.kind) {
            .block => {
                const body = view.rect(cx, cy, config.block_half_w, config.block_half_h);
                rl.DrawRectangleRounded(body, 0.28, 6, color(palette.block_dark));
                const face = view.rect(
                    cx,
                    cy - config.block_half_h * 0.28,
                    config.block_half_w * 0.9,
                    config.block_half_h * 0.55,
                );
                rl.DrawRectangleRounded(face, 0.4, 6, color(palette.block));
                const gloss = view.rect(
                    cx,
                    cy - config.block_half_h * 0.55,
                    config.block_half_w * 0.7,
                    config.block_half_h * 0.14,
                );
                rl.DrawRectangleRounded(gloss, 1, 6, color(palette.block_top));
            },
            .coin => {
                // A slow spin. The code makes the width smaller, and does not
                // really rotate the coin. The minimum width is 55%. A coin that
                // turns its full edge to the player is not visible for a few
                // frames. A player does not try to get a coin that the player
                // cannot see.
                const spin = 0.55 + 0.45 * @abs(@cos(cy * 0.028));
                const half_w = config.coin_half * spin;
                rl.DrawEllipse(
                    @intFromFloat(view.x(cx)),
                    @intFromFloat(view.y(cy)),
                    view.len(half_w),
                    view.len(config.coin_half),
                    color(palette.coin_dark),
                );
                rl.DrawEllipse(
                    @intFromFloat(view.x(cx)),
                    @intFromFloat(view.y(cy)),
                    view.len(half_w * 0.62),
                    view.len(config.coin_half * 0.62),
                    color(palette.coin),
                );
            },
        }
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `drawEntities` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/draw.zig`.*

The renderer draws each entity between its last two positions. It uses the
`alpha` value that the [loop](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-loop/) gives it. Without
`alpha`, the game moves in visible steps at 120 Hz on a faster display.

The coin spin makes the width smaller, and it does not rotate the coin. The
minimum width is 55 percent, thus the coin is always visible. An earlier version
used the full range. Then the coin turned its edge to the player and was not
visible for a few frames. Players do not try to get a coin that they cannot see.

## The player

```zig
fn drawPlayer(world: *const sim.World, view: View, alpha: f32) void {
    const cx = lerp(world.player.x_prev, world.player.x, alpha);
    const cy = config.player_y;

    // Tilt toward the turn. The tilt shows where the player wants to go. It
    // makes the slide look like a steered movement, and not like a pull.
    const drift = (config.laneCenter(world.player.lane) - cx) / config.lane_w;
    const lean = std.math.clamp(drift, -1, 1) * config.player_half_w * 0.55;

    const shadow = view.rect(cx, cy + config.player_half_h * 0.75, config.player_half_w * 0.9, config.player_half_h * 0.22);
    rl.DrawRectangleRounded(shadow, 1, 6, color(palette.background.alpha(0.55)));

    const nose: rl.Vector2 = .{ .x = view.x(cx + lean), .y = view.y(cy - config.player_half_h) };
    const left: rl.Vector2 = .{ .x = view.x(cx - config.player_half_w), .y = view.y(cy + config.player_half_h) };
    const right: rl.Vector2 = .{ .x = view.x(cx + config.player_half_w), .y = view.y(cy + config.player_half_h) };
    // raylib needs counter-clockwise winding. If not, raylib culls the
    // triangle.
    rl.DrawTriangle(nose, left, right, color(palette.player));

    const core: rl.Vector2 = .{ .x = view.x(cx + lean * 0.5), .y = view.y(cy) };
    const core_left: rl.Vector2 = .{ .x = view.x(cx - config.player_half_w * 0.45), .y = view.y(cy + config.player_half_h * 0.7) };
    const core_right: rl.Vector2 = .{ .x = view.x(cx + config.player_half_w * 0.45), .y = view.y(cy + config.player_half_h * 0.7) };
    rl.DrawTriangle(core, core_left, core_right, color(palette.player_dark));
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `drawPlayer` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/draw.zig`.*

The renderer calculates the lean from the distance between the target lane and
the actual position. That distance is exactly the gap that
[the previous chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-world/) described. The lean costs
three lines. The lean is the main reason that the movement looks deliberate.

## Colours are plain data

```zig
pub const Color = struct {
    r: u8,
    g: u8,
    b: u8,
    a: u8 = 255,

    pub fn alpha(self: Color, value: f32) Color {
        const clamped = if (value < 0) 0 else if (value > 1) 1 else value;
        return .{ .r = self.r, .g = self.g, .b = self.b, .a = @intFromFloat(clamped * 255) };
    }

    pub fn mix(a: Color, b: Color, t: f32) Color {
        const clamped = if (t < 0) 0 else if (t > 1) 1 else t;
        return .{
            .r = lerp(a.r, b.r, clamped),
            .g = lerp(a.g, b.g, clamped),
            .b = lerp(a.b, b.b, clamped),
            .a = lerp(a.a, b.a, clamped),
        };
    }

    fn lerp(a: u8, b: u8, t: f32) u8 {
        const af: f32 = @floatFromInt(a);
        const bf: f32 = @floatFromInt(b);
        return @intFromFloat(af + (bf - af) * t);
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Color` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/palette.zig`.*

The palette file has no raylib types. `draw.zig` converts the colours at the
edge:

```zig
fn color(c: palette.Color) rl.Color {
    return .{ .r = c.r, .g = c.g, .b = c.b, .a = c.a };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `color` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/draw.zig`.*

The reason is the particle system below. The particle system needs colours. When
raylib stays out of the particle system, you can test the particle system
without a window.

## Particles

The particles are presentation. The simulation reports that the player collected
a coin. The particle system changes that report into ten amber dots that fly
outward.

```zig
pub const System = struct {
    pub const capacity = 256;
    const Pool = sim.Pool(Particle, capacity);

    pool: Pool,
    rng: Rng,

    pub fn init(seed: u64) System {
        return .{ .pool = .empty, .rng = .init(seed, 0xBEEF) };
    }

    pub fn clear(self: *System) void {
        self.pool.clear();
    }

    pub fn live(self: *const System) u16 {
        return self.pool.live;
    }

    /// The oldest particles stay. When the pool is full, the system drops new
    /// particles. Nobody sees a spark that is not there, but a frame that stops
    /// to make space is visible.
    fn emit(self: *System, p: Particle) void {
        _ = self.pool.create(p);
    }

    pub fn update(self: *System, dt: f32) void {
        var it = self.pool.iterator();
        while (it.next()) |entry| {
            const p = entry.value;
            p.life -= dt;
            if (p.life <= 0) {
                self.pool.destroy(entry.handle);
                continue;
            }
            p.vy += p.gravity * dt;
            p.x += p.vx * dt;
            p.y += p.vy * dt;
        }
    }

    pub fn iterator(self: *System) Pool.Iterator {
        return self.pool.iterator();
    }

    /// A ring of sparks, used for coins.
    pub fn burst(self: *System, x: f32, y: f32, count: usize, color: Color, speed: f32) void {
        for (0..count) |i| {
            const turn = @as(f32, @floatFromInt(i)) / @as(f32, @floatFromInt(count));
            const angle = turn * std.math.tau + self.rng.float() * 0.4;
            const magnitude = speed * (0.6 + self.rng.float() * 0.8);
            const life = 0.35 + self.rng.float() * 0.3;
            self.emit(.{
                .x = x,
                .y = y,
                .vx = @cos(angle) * magnitude,
                .vy = @sin(angle) * magnitude,
                .life = life,
                .life_max = life,
                .size = 3 + self.rng.float() * 3,
                .gravity = 420,
                .color = color,
            });
        }
    }

    /// A wider, slower and heavier burst, for the crash.
    pub fn debris(self: *System, x: f32, y: f32) void {
        for (0..28) |_| {
            const angle = (self.rng.float() - 0.5) * std.math.pi * 1.6 - std.math.pi / 2.0;
            const magnitude = 120 + self.rng.float() * 340;
            const life = 0.5 + self.rng.float() * 0.6;
            self.emit(.{
                .x = x,
                .y = y,
                .vx = @cos(angle) * magnitude,
                .vy = @sin(angle) * magnitude,
                .life = life,
                .life_max = life,
                .size = 3 + self.rng.float() * 5,
                .gravity = 900,
                .color = if (self.rng.chance(0.5)) palette.block else palette.block_top,
            });
        }
    }

    /// A short horizontal smear behind the player, when the player moves to a
    /// new lane.
    pub fn dust(self: *System, x: f32, y: f32, direction: f32) void {
        for (0..6) |_| {
            const life = 0.18 + self.rng.float() * 0.16;
            self.emit(.{
                .x = x,
                .y = y + (self.rng.float() - 0.5) * 30,
                .vx = -direction * (60 + self.rng.float() * 120),
                .vy = (self.rng.float() - 0.5) * 40,
                .life = life,
                .life_max = life,
                .size = 2 + self.rng.float() * 3,
                .gravity = 0,
                .color = palette.player_dark,
            });
        }
    }

    /// Two vertical streaks that mark a block that moved past near the player.
    pub fn graze(self: *System, x: f32, y: f32) void {
        for (0..8) |_| {
            const life = 0.25 + self.rng.float() * 0.2;
            self.emit(.{
                .x = x + (self.rng.float() - 0.5) * 40,
                .y = y + (self.rng.float() - 0.5) * 50,
                .vx = (self.rng.float() - 0.5) * 60,
                .vy = 260 + self.rng.float() * 200,
                .life = life,
                .life_max = life,
                .size = 2 + self.rng.float() * 2,
                .gravity = 0,
                .color = palette.good,
            });
        }
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `System` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/particles.zig`.*

The particle system uses the same [pool](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/entities/) as the
entities, with a different element type and a capacity of 256.

A full pool drops new particles. It does not stop a frame to make space. A
player can see a stopped frame, but cannot see a spark that is not there.

```zig
    /// A ring of sparks, used for coins.
    pub fn burst(self: *System, x: f32, y: f32, count: usize, color: Color, speed: f32) void {
        for (0..count) |i| {
            const turn = @as(f32, @floatFromInt(i)) / @as(f32, @floatFromInt(count));
            const angle = turn * std.math.tau + self.rng.float() * 0.4;
            const magnitude = speed * (0.6 + self.rng.float() * 0.8);
            const life = 0.35 + self.rng.float() * 0.3;
            self.emit(.{
                .x = x,
                .y = y,
                .vx = @cos(angle) * magnitude,
                .vy = @sin(angle) * magnitude,
                .life = life,
                .life_max = life,
                .size = 3 + self.rng.float() * 3,
                .gravity = 420,
                .color = color,
            });
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `burst` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/particles.zig`.*

None of this code uses raylib. Thus the tests check the behaviour without a
window:

- Particles expire and free their slots.
- A full pool stays inside its capacity.
- Gravity pulls the particles down.

## Text over a moving field

The HUD is at the top of the field, and the blocks enter at exactly that
position. During each run, the score is on top of a bright red rectangle for some
of the time.

```zig
/// Text with a hard drop shadow.
///
/// The HUD is at the top of the field, and the blocks enter at exactly that
/// position. Thus, during each run, the score is on top of a bright red
/// rectangle for some of the time. A shadow costs less than a strip of the
/// field that only the HUD uses. The shadow also keeps the full field
/// available for play.
fn shadowed(text: [*:0]const u8, px: i32, py: i32, size: i32, c: palette.Color) void {
    const offset = @max(@divTrunc(size, 14), 1);
    rl.DrawText(text, px + offset, py + offset, size, color(palette.background.alpha(0.75)));
    rl.DrawText(text, px, py, size, color(c));
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `shadowed` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/draw.zig`.*

A shadow of one pixel costs less than a strip of the field that only the HUD
uses. The shadow also keeps the full field available for play.
