## Input

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/input/*

The simulation runs at a fixed 120 Hz. The window runs at the rate of the
display. The two rates do not divide evenly. Thus a rendered frame can need zero
ticks, one tick, or three ticks from the simulation.

A press must get to exactly one of these ticks:

- If the game drops a press, the game ignores the player.
- If the game gives a press to more than one tick, one tap moves the player
  across three lanes.

```zig
pub const Latch = struct {
    left: bool = false,
    right: bool = false,
    confirm: bool = false,

    /// The caller calls this one time for each rendered frame, before the tick
    /// loop.
    pub fn poll(self: *Latch) void {
        if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_LEFT) or
            rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_A)) self.left = true;
        if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_RIGHT) or
            rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_D)) self.right = true;
        if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_SPACE) or
            rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_ENTER)) self.confirm = true;

        // Touch and mouse: tap a side of the screen to steer. On a phone, the
        // player uses these taps.
        if (rl.IsMouseButtonPressed(rl.MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT)) {
            const x = rl.GetMousePosition().x;
            if (x < @as(f32, @floatFromInt(rl.GetScreenWidth())) * 0.5) {
                self.left = true;
            } else {
                self.right = true;
            }
            self.confirm = true;
        }
    }

    /// Give the latched presses to one tick, then clear them.
    pub fn take(self: *Latch) sim.Input {
        const input: sim.Input = .{
            .left = self.left,
            .right = self.right,
            .confirm = self.confirm,
        };
        self.* = .{};
        return input;
    }

    pub fn pending(self: *const Latch) bool {
        return self.left or self.right or self.confirm;
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Latch` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/platform/input.zig`.*

`poll` runs one time in each rendered frame, before the tick loop. `take` gives
the latched presses to one tick and clears them.

## Why the fields are booleans and not key states

`IsKeyPressed` is true on the frame when a key goes down. It is false while the
key stays down. The game needs that behaviour. If the player holds `D`, the
player must move one lane. The player must not slide across the board at a
hundred lanes each second.

The simulation states this rule in its own type:

```zig
/// Edge-triggered: each field means "pressed during this tick", not "held".
/// A key that the player holds must not slide the player across the board.
pub const Input = struct {
    left: bool = false,
    right: bool = false,
    confirm: bool = false,

    pub const none: Input = .{};
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Input` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

A test checks the rule:

```zig
test "a held direction moves exactly one lane" {
    // Input is edge-triggered. If the game read a held key as a press on each
    // tick, the player would cross the board in two frames.
    var w: World = .init(1);
    w.start();
    const start_lane = w.player.lane;
    w.step(.{ .right = true });
    try std.testing.expectEqual(start_lane + 1, w.player.lane);
    for (0..60) |_| w.step(.none);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(start_lane + 1, w.player.lane);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `a held direction moves exactly one lane` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/tests.zig`.*

## A frame that needs no ticks

If a frame makes no ticks, nothing calls `take`. The latch keeps its presses for
the next frame. Thus the game remembers a tap between two ticks, and does not
lose it.

If a frame makes three ticks, the first tick gets the press. The other two ticks
get nothing. This works because `take` clears the latch.

## Touch

The same poll reads the mouse. It divides the window into a left half and a
right half.

A tap on the left half steers left. A tap on the right half steers right. A tap
on either half is also the confirm that starts a run. A phone needs only these
controls. The touch input needed only one more branch in `poll`, because the
simulation already uses lanes and not keys.

## What the platform layer does not do

Mute is a key press, and the key press never gets to the simulation:

```zig
if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_M)) self.audio.toggleMute();
```

Mute changes only the audio device. No code in `sim/` knows that sound exists. A
mute key inside the simulation would change that.

---

## Difficulty You Can Prove

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/fair-by-design/*

The course generator puts down rows of blocks. The rows must become more
difficult, and they must stay possible.

A mistake here does not look like a bug. Each row still has an open lane and the
game still runs, but nobody can survive the course. The only sign is that people
stop their play.

## The spacing has a minimum

Between the arrival of one row and the next row, the player can have to cross
the full board. That costs two lane changes. Also, the player cannot start while
the current row is level with the player. A move to the side into a block next
to you is a crash.

The smallest spacing that a player can still survive is the sum of these two
times.

```zig
/// The smallest row spacing that a player can still survive at this speed. It
/// is the time to cross the full board, plus the time that the current row is
/// level with the player. Below this value, the game is impossible, however
/// open the rows look.
pub fn fairnessFloor(speed: f32) f32 {
    return 2 * config.lane_change_time + blockedSeconds(speed);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `fairnessFloor` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

The second term becomes smaller when the game becomes faster, because a faster
row is next to you for less time. The first term does not change with the speed.

## Calculate the spacing, do not adjust it by hand

The first version had two constants that a person selected: an easy spacing and
a hard spacing. The game interpolated between them. This method worked. But it
had three numbers that had to agree, and nothing in the code said so. If you
changed the lane change time, the hard spacing became impossible without an
error.

Now the code calculates the spacing from the minimum, and the spacing decays
toward the minimum.

```zig
/// The seconds between rows. The value decays toward the minimum, and never
/// gets to it.
///
/// Thus the difficulty increases for as long as a person plays. The margin
/// above the impossible spacing is a named constant. It does not come by
/// chance from two endpoints that a person selected and a third number that
/// agrees with them.
pub fn rowGapSeconds(speed: f32, time: f32) f32 {
    const floor = fairnessFloor(speed) + config.gap_safety;
    const decay = std.math.exp(-time / config.gap_tau);
    if (config.row_gap_easy <= floor) return floor;
    return floor + (config.row_gap_easy - floor) * decay;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `rowGapSeconds` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

The decay never gets to the minimum, and this fixes a second problem. The
earlier curve got to its most difficult setting at sixty seconds and then stayed
there. A sufficiently good player never lost.

One named constant now holds the margin above the impossible spacing.

```zig
/// The margin that the row spacing keeps above the point where a player can
/// no longer survive.
///
/// The physics of the game sets a minimum for the spacing. Between the arrival
/// of one row and the next row, the player must be able to cross the full
/// board (`2 * lane_change_time`). Also, the player cannot start while the
/// current row is level with the player (`2 * (player_half_h + block_half_h) / speed`).
/// If the rows are closer than that sum, no player can survive. That failure
/// would be silent, because each row would still leave a lane open. But
/// nobody could get to that lane.
///
/// Thus `sim.rowGapSeconds` calculates that minimum, adds this margin, and
/// decays toward it. The game always becomes more difficult, and it always
/// stays solvable. A designer adjusts this margin, and the margin sets only
/// the quantity of extra space. The code calculates the minimum, and the
/// minimum decides if a player can survive.
pub const gap_safety: f32 = 0.06;
```

*Quoted from the source: `gap_safety` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/config.zig`.*

## Prove it with play

All of this is still an argument about four constants. That type of argument is
easy to get wrong. Thus a program plays the game.

```zig
/// The lane where the bot wants to be.
pub fn targetLane(w: *const sim.World) u8 {
    const current = w.player.lane;
    const pos = position(w);
    const view = look(w);

    var best: ?u8 = null;
    var best_cost: f32 = std.math.floatMax(f32);

    for (0..config.lane_count) |i| {
        const lane: u8 = @intCast(i);
        const lane_f: f32 = @floatFromInt(i);

        if (view.blocked_now[lane]) continue;
        if (view.next) |next| {
            if (next.blocked[lane]) continue;
        }
        if (!pathClear(pos, lane_f, view.blocked_now)) continue;

        const distance = @abs(lane_f - pos);
        const travel = distance * config.lane_change_time;
        if (view.next) |next| {
            if (travel + margin > next.seconds) continue;
        }

        var cost = distance;
        // Prefer a lane that is still good one row later. Then the bot does
        // not always have to solve the problem that it just made.
        if (view.after) |after| {
            if (after.blocked[lane]) cost += 1.5;
        }
        // Take a coin when the coin is on the path and the time is
        // sufficient. The bot limits its effort for coins. A dodge that fails
        // stops the run, but a coin that the bot does not get costs only a
        // multiplier.
        if (view.next) |next| {
            if (next.coin_lane == lane and next.seconds > travel * 2) cost -= 0.5;
        }
        if (cost < best_cost) {
            best_cost = cost;
            best = lane;
        }
    }

    // The bot cannot get to a safe lane. The spacing rule in config.zig must
    // make this impossible, and the tests check that. But if the policy
    // panicked here, a bad adjustment would crash the program.
    return best orelse current;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `targetLane` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/bot.zig`.*

The policy looks at the next two rows. It does three things:

- It selects a lane that is open in the first row.
- It does not start a move across the board that it cannot complete in time.
- It does not take a path that slides through a block that is level with it now.

Then a test runs the bot for four minutes of game time at each seed.

```zig
test "solvable course: the bot survives a long run at every seed" {
    // This test proves that the generator is fair. Four minutes is well after
    // the point where the difficulty ramp saturates. Thus the test includes the
    // smallest spacing that the game makes.
    for (0..24) |seed| {
        const w = playWithBot(seed, 240);
        std.testing.expectEqual(sim.Phase.playing, w.phase) catch |err| {
            std.debug.print(
                "seed {d}: crashed after {d:.1}s at score {d}\n",
                .{ seed, w.time, w.score },
            );
            return err;
        };
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `solvable course: the bot survives a long run at every seed` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/tests.zig`.*

The test failed on its first run, at seed 21, after 8.2 seconds of play.

## What the test found

The bot steered into blocks that it thought were behind it. It ignored each
block whose centre was behind the centre of the player. It measured this
distance with only the half height of the block. The correct number is the sum
of the two half heights. Each body is 52 units tall. Thus a block whose centre
is 41 units behind you still overlaps you.

```zig
/// The vertical half-span in which a block and the player overlap. A block is
/// dangerous from `+reach` in front of the player to `-reach` behind the
/// player. If this value used only the half-height of the block, the result
/// would be the off-by-one-body bug that the fairness test found.
const reach = config.player_half_h + config.block_half_h;
```

*Quoted from the source: `reach` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/bot.zig`.*

The title of the regression test states the case:

```zig
test "the bot will not slide into a block that is still level with it" {
    // The regression that the fairness test found. A block whose centre is
    // behind the centre of the player can still overlap the player. If the bot
    // thinks that the block is behind it, the bot steers into the side of the
    // block.
    var w: sim.World = .init(1);
    w.start();
    w.entities.clear();
    const beside: u8 = w.player.lane + 1;
    _ = w.entities.create(.{
        .kind = .block,
        .lane = beside,
        // Behind the centre of the player, but well inside the overlap band.
        .y = config.player_y + reach * 0.8,
        .y_prev = config.player_y + reach * 0.8,
    });
    try std.testing.expect(targetLane(&w) != beside);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `the bot will not slide into a block that is still level with it` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/bot.zig`.*

Each unit test passed while this bug existed. The collision code was correct by
itself. The generator and the spacing were also correct. The error was in the
logic that connected these parts. Only a full run of the game tests that logic.

## Solvable and playable are different

A bot with no reaction time can survive a course. That result proves that the
course is solvable. It does not tell you if a person can play the course.

Thus the same policy runs again with a delay before it.

```zig
/// A player who sees the danger and then needs a moment to act. The model
/// contains only latency. The player acts now on the decision from the world
/// as it was `delay` ticks ago.
///
/// With this model, the tests can tell you something about whether the game
/// is *fun*. The bot proves that the course is solvable. But the bot has no
/// reaction time, and a course that only a machine can pass is not a game.
/// With a delay before the same policy, the test asks if the game is fair to a
/// person.
const Human = struct {
    delay: usize,
    buffer: [64]u8 = @splat(config.lane_count / 2),
    index: usize = 0,

    fn init(reaction_seconds: f32) Human {
        return .{ .delay = @intFromFloat(reaction_seconds * config.tick_hz) };
    }

    fn play(self: *Human, w: *const World) Input {
        self.buffer[self.index % self.buffer.len] = bot.targetLane(w);
        const decided = self.buffer[(self.index + self.buffer.len - self.delay) % self.buffer.len];
        self.index += 1;
        if (decided < w.player.lane) return .{ .left = true };
        if (decided > w.player.lane) return .{ .right = true };
        return .none;
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Human` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/tests.zig`.*

The model contains only latency. The bot acts now on the decision that it made
from the world as the world was some ticks ago. An earlier version counted down a
timer and reset the timer each time that the ideal lane changed. When the policy
could not choose between two lanes, that version livelocked. The model reported
that the game was much more difficult than it really was. Some time passed
before anybody saw that the fault was in the model and not in the game.

The numbers from the model are the difficulty curve:

| Reaction | Mean run |
| --- | --- |
| 100 ms | 58 s |
| 150 ms | 46 s |
| 200 ms | 30 s |
| 250 ms | 26 s |
| 300 ms | 24 s |

Thus a slow, calm player gets half a minute, and a fast player gets a minute. All
players lose at some time. That part took the most work.

The test asserts the shape and not the values. Thus you can adjust the numbers
and not rewrite the test.

```zig
test "a run lasts about as long as a hyper casual run should" {
    // A quarter second is a slow, calm player. That player must get a real
    // run, and not a game over screen after a few seconds.
    const casual = meanSurvival(0.25, 24, 300);
    std.testing.expect(casual > 12 and casual < 70) catch |err| {
        std.debug.print("casual player averaged {d:.1}s\n", .{casual});
        return err;
    };

    // A fast player must last longer. If not, skill makes no difference.
    const sharp = meanSurvival(0.10, 24, 300);
    std.testing.expect(sharp > casual * 1.5) catch |err| {
        std.debug.print("sharp {d:.1}s vs casual {d:.1}s\n", .{ sharp, casual });
        return err;
    };

    // A fast player must still lose. This check finds the difficulty curve
    // that saturated, where a fast player never died.
    std.testing.expect(sharp < 180) catch |err| {
        std.debug.print("sharp player averaged {d:.1}s: the game stops getting harder\n", .{sharp});
        return err;
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `a run lasts about as long as a hyper casual run should` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/tests.zig`.*

The last assertion found the flat difficulty curve. A fast player had an average
of the full limit of three hundred seconds, and every other test passed.

## Two smaller rules

**The start is easy.** During a grace window, no row blocks more than one lane.
In the first few seconds, one small move is sufficient for each row.

This rule is a decision, not a measurement. The reaction time model already
knows the controls perfectly. Thus the model cannot show the problems of a
player who still looks for the keys. When the window is off, the modelled 200 ms
average moves by three tenths of a second.

```zig
/// The seconds at the start when no row blocks more than one lane.
///
/// This value is a decision, not a measurement. The reaction time model in the
/// tests already knows the controls. Thus the model cannot show a new player
/// who still looks for the keys. When the window is off, the modelled 200 ms
/// average moves from 29.5 s to 29.2 s. In the grace window, each row leaves
/// two lanes open. Thus one lane change is always sufficient to pass the row.
pub const grace_seconds: f32 = 7;
```

*Quoted from the source: `grace_seconds` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/config.zig`.*

**Coins show the safe lane.** The spawner puts a coin only in a lane that its own
row leaves open. When a row blocks two of the three lanes, the coin is in the one
gap. A player who follows the coins follows the safe path, and nobody has to tell
the player. The rule is four statements in the spawner. The game has no other
tutorial.

```zig
    fn spawnRow(w: *World) void {
        const d = w.difficulty();

        // Shuffle the lanes, then block a prefix of them. Because the code
        // blocks a prefix of a shuffle, the blocked lanes are always
        // different. The count is always less than `lane_count`. Thus a free
        // lane always remains.
        var lanes: [config.lane_count]u8 = undefined;
        for (&lanes, 0..) |*lane, i| lane.* = @intCast(i);
        var i: usize = lanes.len;
        while (i > 1) {
            i -= 1;
            const j = w.rng.below(@intCast(i + 1));
            std.mem.swap(u8, &lanes[i], &lanes[j]);
        }

        const two = w.time > config.grace_seconds and w.rng.chance(lerp(
            config.two_block_chance_easy,
            config.two_block_chance_hard,
            d,
        ));
        const blocked: usize = if (two) 2 else 1;
        std.debug.assert(blocked <= config.max_blocked_lanes);

        for (lanes[0..blocked]) |lane| {
            _ = w.entities.create(.{
                .kind = .block,
                .lane = lane,
                .y = config.spawn_y,
                .y_prev = config.spawn_y,
            });
        }

        // The coin goes in a lane that this row leaves open. This keeps the
        // row fair, and it also teaches the player. When a row blocks two of
        // three lanes, the coin is in the one gap. Thus, if the player follows
        // the coins, the player plays correctly.
        const free = lanes[blocked..];
        if (free.len > 0 and w.rng.chance(config.coin_chance)) {
            const lane = free[w.rng.below(@intCast(free.len))];
            _ = w.entities.create(.{
                .kind = .coin,
                .lane = lane,
                .y = config.spawn_y,
                .y_prev = config.spawn_y,
            });
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `spawnRow` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`.*

---

## Sound Without Sound Files

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/sound/*

This project has no audio files. The five effects are arithmetic. The game
generates them when it starts.

To record or license five short sounds would take less time than to write a
synthesiser. But that choice also adds three costs:

- A folder of binary files that nobody can diff.
- A licence question for each file.
- An audio editor for each change.

When the game generates the sounds, a sound changes when a number changes.

## One oscillator with an envelope

```zig
/// One oscillator with an envelope. A sound is a stack of a few layers.
pub const Layer = struct {
    shape: Shape,
    /// The frequency at the start and at the end of the layer. The sweep is
    /// exponential. Thus the slide is even in pitch, and not in hertz. `noise`
    /// ignores these values.
    from: f32,
    to: f32,
    /// Seconds. `delay` starts a layer later than the others. The arpeggios
    /// use `delay`.
    duration: f32,
    delay: f32 = 0,
    gain: f32 = 0.5,
    /// The seconds of fade in. Never zero. A waveform that starts at full
    /// amplitude starts with a step, and a step is a click.
    attack: f32 = 0.004,
    /// The shape of the decay. 1 is a straight line to silence. A higher value
    /// gives a faster drop at the start and a longer tail.
    curve: f32 = 2.5,
    /// A one-pole low pass. 1 means no filter. It removes the high hiss from
    /// the noise burst.
    lowpass: f32 = 1,
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Layer` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/audio/synth.zig`.*

Each layer has a frequency sweep, an amplitude envelope, and an optional low
pass. The low pass removes the high hiss from noise. `delay` starts a layer
later than the others. The arpeggios use `delay`, thus they need no sequencer
code.

The coin has two layers: a triangle, and a quieter sine one octave higher.

```zig
/// The five sounds of the game. The pitch for the combo steps changes at
/// playback, and is not part of the samples. Thus the game has one coin sound
/// and not eight.
pub const coin: []const Layer = &.{
    .{ .shape = .triangle, .from = 900, .to = 1350, .duration = 0.085, .gain = 0.55 },
    .{ .shape = .sine, .from = 1800, .to = 2700, .duration = 0.07, .gain = 0.22 },
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `coin` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/audio/synth.zig`.*

The crash has six layers. The last three layers are the descending triad that plays
over the game over screen:

```zig
/// An impact, then a descending triad.
///
/// One event, one sound. The alternative was two sounds. The thud would play
/// at the crash, and the sting would play when the retry prompt appears. Then
/// the game must record if it played the sting yet, for a run that is already
/// lost. A layer can have a delay. Thus the pause is in the waveform.
pub const crash: []const Layer = &.{
    .{ .shape = .noise, .from = 1, .to = 1, .duration = 0.45, .gain = 0.5, .lowpass = 0.12, .curve = 2 },
    .{ .shape = .square, .from = 220, .to = 55, .duration = 0.4, .gain = 0.28, .curve = 1.6 },
    .{ .shape = .sine, .from = 130, .to = 40, .duration = 0.5, .gain = 0.35, .curve = 1.4 },
    .{ .shape = .triangle, .from = 587, .to = 587, .duration = 0.12, .delay = 0.38, .gain = 0.3 },
    .{ .shape = .triangle, .from = 466, .to = 466, .duration = 0.12, .delay = 0.49, .gain = 0.3 },
    .{ .shape = .triangle, .from = 349, .to = 349, .duration = 0.3, .delay = 0.6, .gain = 0.34, .curve = 1.8 },
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `crash` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/audio/synth.zig`.*

The six layers are one sound, and not two sounds. As two sounds, the thud would
play at impact and the sting would play when the retry prompt appears. Then the
code must record if the sting played yet, for a run that is already over. A layer
can have a delay, thus the pause is in the waveform.

## The renderer

```zig
/// Render `layers` into `out`. Returns the number of samples that it wrote.
///
/// The envelope is exactly zero at the two ends of each layer. This prevents
/// clicks. If a clip starts or stops at a point above zero on a waveform, the
/// clip makes a discontinuity. A discontinuity is a click, and the click is
/// much louder and more unpleasant than its sound.
pub fn render(layers: []const Layer, out: []i16, seed: u64) usize {
    var total: f32 = 0;
    for (layers) |layer| total = @max(total, layer.delay + layer.duration);

    const count = @min(out.len, @as(usize, @intFromFloat(total * @as(f32, sample_rate))));
    if (count == 0) return 0;

    var mixed: [max_samples]f32 = @splat(0);
    const window = mixed[0..@min(count, mixed.len)];

    var rng: Rng = .init(seed, 0x5040);
    for (layers) |layer| {
        var filtered: f32 = 0;
        var phase: f32 = 0;
        const offset: usize = @intFromFloat(layer.delay * @as(f32, sample_rate));
        const length: usize = @intFromFloat(layer.duration * @as(f32, sample_rate));
        if (length == 0) continue;

        for (0..length) |i| {
            const index = offset + i;
            if (index >= window.len) break;

            const t = @as(f32, @floatFromInt(i)) / @as(f32, sample_rate);
            const progress = @as(f32, @floatFromInt(i)) / @as(f32, @floatFromInt(length));

            // An exponential sweep is even in pitch, and not in hertz.
            const frequency = layer.from * std.math.pow(f32, layer.to / layer.from, progress);
            phase += std.math.tau * frequency / @as(f32, sample_rate);
            if (phase > std.math.tau) phase -= std.math.tau;

            var value: f32 = switch (layer.shape) {
                .sine => @sin(phase),
                .triangle => 1 - 4 * @abs(@round(phase / std.math.tau) - phase / std.math.tau),
                .square => if (phase < std.math.pi) 1 else -1,
                .noise => rng.float() * 2 - 1,
            };
            if (layer.lowpass < 1) {
                filtered += layer.lowpass * (value - filtered);
                value = filtered;
            }

            mixed[index] += value * layer.gain * envelope(t, layer);
        }
    }

    // A soft clip, and not a hard clip. Layers on top of each other go past
    // the limit. tanh bends the peaks, and does not cut them flat.
    for (window, 0..) |value, i| {
        const shaped = std.math.tanh(value);
        out[i] = @intFromFloat(std.math.clamp(shaped, -1, 1) * 32_600);
    }
    return window.len;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `render` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/audio/synth.zig`.*

The frequency sweep is exponential and not linear. Pitch is logarithmic. Thus a
linear sweep sounds as if it becomes faster near the end.

The renderer adds the layers together, then soft clips the sum with `tanh`. It
does not clamp the sum. Layers on top of each other go past the limit, and a
clamp cuts the peaks flat. You hear the flat peaks as distortion.

## The envelope, and the click

```zig
fn envelope(t: f32, layer: Layer) f32 {
    if (t < layer.attack) return t / layer.attack;
    const remaining = layer.duration - layer.attack;
    if (remaining <= 0) return 0;
    const decayed = 1 - (t - layer.attack) / remaining;
    if (decayed <= 0) return 0;
    return std.math.pow(f32, decayed, layer.curve);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `envelope` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/audio/synth.zig`.*

The envelope is exactly zero at the two ends of each layer.

If a clip starts at full amplitude, the clip starts with a step. The step goes
from silence to the value of the waveform at that point. A step of this type is
a broadband impulse. The speaker plays it as a click, and the click is usually
louder than the effect. The same problem occurs at the end.

A fade in of four
milliseconds is sufficient. The decay has a shape that stops at zero, and the
code does not cut the decay at zero.

## Test a waveform

The synthesiser contains no raylib types. It fills a buffer with samples and
stops. Thus the tests check the sounds without an audio device. CI has no
speakers.

```zig
test "no sound begins or ends with a click" {
    // If a clip starts or stops at a point above zero on a waveform, the clip
    // has a step change. A step change is a click, and the click is louder and
    // more unpleasant than its effect. The envelope prevents the click, at the
    // two ends.
    var buffer: [max_samples]i16 = undefined;
    for (all, 0..) |layers, index| {
        const written = render(layers, &buffer, 2);
        testing.expect(@abs(@as(i32, buffer[0])) < 400) catch |err| {
            std.debug.print("sound {d} starts at {d}\n", .{ index, buffer[0] });
            return err;
        };
        testing.expect(@abs(@as(i32, buffer[written - 1])) < 400) catch |err| {
            std.debug.print("sound {d} ends at {d}\n", .{ index, buffer[written - 1] });
            return err;
        };
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `no sound begins or ends with a click` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/audio/synth.zig`.*

The next test checks the mix. The exact frequencies are a matter of taste, and
they can change. The relation between the sounds must not change. The crash is
the low, long and loud sound. The lane tick plays on each input, and it must not
be louder than a pickup.

```zig
test "the sounds sit in the right places against each other" {
    // The exact frequencies are a design decision, and they can change. The
    // order must not change. The crash is the low, long and loud sound. The
    // lane tick is the short and quiet sound. If that order changed, you would
    // hear it in one second, but a diff would not show it.
    var buffer: [max_samples]i16 = undefined;

    const written_coin = render(coin, &buffer, 7);
    const coin_hz = brightness(buffer[0..written_coin], sample_rate);
    const coin_peak = peak(buffer[0..written_coin]);

    const written_crash = render(crash, &buffer, 7);
    const crash_hz = brightness(buffer[0..written_crash], sample_rate);
    const crash_peak = peak(buffer[0..written_crash]);

    const written_lane = render(lane, &buffer, 7);
    const lane_peak = peak(buffer[0..written_lane]);

    // The coin is a chime and the crash is a thud.
    try testing.expect(coin_hz > crash_hz * 2);
    // The coin is in the band of its sweep.
    try testing.expect(coin_hz > 800 and coin_hz < 1600);

    // The crash is the longest sound of the game, and the loudest.
    try testing.expect(written_crash > written_coin * 4);
    try testing.expect(crash_peak >= coin_peak);

    // The lane tick is the shortest sound, and it must be quieter than a
    // pickup. It plays on each input. If an input sound is as loud as a reward
    // sound, players turn off the sound of the game.
    try testing.expect(written_lane < written_coin);
    try testing.expect(lane_peak < coin_peak);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `the sounds sit in the right places against each other` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/audio/synth.zig`.*

Here, brightness is the number of zero crossings each second. This number is
only an approximate estimate of pitch. But it is sufficient to tell a chime from
a thud.

The measurements show that the five sounds are as intended. The coin is at
approximately 1130 Hz for 85 ms. The crash lasts 900 ms, with 81 percent of its
energy below 500 Hz. The lane tick is the shortest and the quietest sound. If you
prefer to listen, `zig build sounds` writes all of the sounds as `.wav` files.

## Play the sounds

```zig
/// One sound and a few aliases of it, played round robin.
///
/// If a sound already plays, raylib starts that sound again from the start.
/// Thus one handle can make only one note at a time. Coins arrive quickly, one
/// after the other. With one handle, each coin sound would stop the sound of
/// the previous coin. The aliases fix this problem. They use the same sample
/// data, and each alias has its own playback position.
const Voice = struct {
    /// Four is sufficient for the fastest series of coins that the spacing
    /// allows.
    const max_aliases = 4;

    sounds: [max_aliases]rl.Sound = undefined,
    count: usize = 0,
    next: usize = 0,

    fn load(layers: []const synth.Layer, scratch: []i16, aliases: usize, seed: u64) Voice {
        const written = synth.render(layers, scratch, seed);
        const wave: rl.Wave = .{
            .frameCount = @intCast(written),
            .sampleRate = synth.sample_rate,
            .sampleSize = 16,
            .channels = 1,
            .data = @ptrCast(scratch.ptr),
        };
        // raylib converts the frames and copies them into its own buffer. Thus
        // the code can use the scratch array again for the next sound.
        var voice: Voice = .{ .count = @min(aliases, max_aliases) };
        voice.sounds[0] = rl.LoadSoundFromWave(wave);
        for (1..voice.count) |i| voice.sounds[i] = rl.LoadSoundAlias(voice.sounds[0]);
        return voice;
    }

    fn play(self: *Voice, volume: f32, pitch: f32) void {
        if (self.count == 0) return;
        const sound = self.sounds[self.next];
        self.next = (self.next + 1) % self.count;
        rl.SetSoundVolume(sound, volume);
        rl.SetSoundPitch(sound, pitch);
        rl.PlaySound(sound);
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Voice` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/platform/audio.zig`.*

If a sound already plays, raylib starts that sound again from the start. Thus one
handle can make only one note at a time. During a combo, coins arrive quickly,
one after the other. Each coin would stop the sound of the previous coin. An
alias uses the same sample data as the sound, but each alias has its own
playback position.

The combo ladder is a pitch multiplier on the one coin sound. It is not eight
recordings:

```zig
    /// The one entry point that the game uses. It takes the same events as the
    /// particles and the screen shake.
    pub fn onEvent(self: *Audio, event: sim.Event) void {
        switch (event) {
            .coin => |c| {
                // Each combo step increases the pitch of the one coin sound.
                // Thus the game does not need eight coin sounds.
                // A semitone is 2^(1/12). This value is a little less than one
                // semitone for each step. Thus a full combo ends approximately
                // a fifth above its start.
                const step = std.math.pow(f32, 2.0, @as(f32, @floatFromInt(c.combo - 1)) / 14.0);
                self.cue(.coin, 0.85, step);
            },
            .near_miss => self.cue(.near_miss, 0.6, 1),
            .lane_changed => self.cue(.lane, 0.5, 1),
            .crashed => self.cue(.crash, 1, 1),
            .started => self.cue(.start, 0.8, 1),
            .coin_missed => {},
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `onEvent` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/platform/audio.zig`.*

## Optional at runtime

The device does not open in these cases:

- A machine with no sound card.
- A container with no ALSA.
- A browser tab that nobody clicked yet.

In each of these cases, each call above does nothing.

```zig
    /// Opens the device and renders each sound into it. You can safely call
    /// this function when no device exists. Then `ready` stays false, and all
    /// other calls do nothing.
    pub fn init(seed: u64) Audio {
        var audio: Audio = .{};
        rl.InitAudioDevice();
        if (!rl.IsAudioDeviceReady()) return audio;
        audio.ready = true;

        // One buffer for all sounds, because `LoadSoundFromWave` copies.
        var scratch: [synth.max_samples]i16 = undefined;
        const table = .{
            .{ Cue.coin, synth.coin, 4 },
            .{ Cue.near_miss, synth.near_miss, 2 },
            .{ Cue.lane, synth.lane, 3 },
            .{ Cue.crash, synth.crash, 1 },
            .{ Cue.start, synth.start, 1 },
        };
        inline for (table) |entry| {
            audio.voices.set(entry[0], .load(entry[1], &scratch, entry[2], seed));
        }

        rl.SetMasterVolume(0.55);
        return audio;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `init` from `examples/lane-dodger/src/platform/audio.zig`.*

The sound in this game is decoration. Thus the game must start when a mixer does
not open. To check this, the real binary runs with an ALSA configuration that has
an error on purpose.

The sound reads the same [event stream](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/entities/) as the
particles. The tests that were already there continued to pass during the work on the
sound.

---

## Build It From Scratch

*Lane Dodger. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/build-it/*

The other chapters explain what each part does. This chapter gives the order in
which to write the parts.

You can stop and check your work at two points. The first point comes before you
draw anything, and it runs the full game.

## What you need

You need Zig master, and not 0.16. The game uses `std.process.Init`,
`std.Io.Dir`, `std.mem.printSentinel` and `@splat` on arrays. All of these came
after 0.16. `build.zig.zon` gives the exact minimum version.

```bash
zig version    # 0.17.0-dev.1676 or newer
```

You also need Git and a C compiler. On Debian or Ubuntu, the game also needs the
X development headers:

```bash
sudo apt-get install libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxinerama-dev \
                     libxi-dev libxcursor-dev libgl1-mesa-dev
```

You do not need an ALSA package. The audio backend of raylib loads libasound at
runtime, and does not include its header.

## Part one: the project structure

**1. Make the directory tree.**

```bash
mkdir -p lane-dodger/src/{sim,render,audio,platform,tools}
cd lane-dodger
```

**2. Tell Git to ignore the raylib copy.** Add one line to `.gitignore`:

```
vendor/
```

The fetch script below records which raylib commit the game uses. The copy that
the script downloads is 13 MB, thus the copy stays out of Git.

**3. Write the package file.**

```zig
.{
    .name = .lane_dodger,
    .version = "0.1.0",
    .fingerprint = 0x10128392faa1179,
    .minimum_zig_version = "0.17.0-dev.1676",
    .dependencies = .{},
    .paths = .{
        "build.zig",
        "build.zig.zon",
        "src",
    },
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `examples/lane-dodger/build.zig.zon`.*

`zig build` does not accept the fingerprint, and prints the correct value. Paste
that value into the file.

raylib is *not* in `.dependencies`. This is intentional, and
[Vendor raylib](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-build/) gives the reason.

**4. Write the fetch script.**

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Vendor raylib's C sources at a pinned commit.
#
# raylib is used as a plain directory of C files, not as a Zig package. That is
# deliberate: the build runner imports the build.zig of every package named in
# build.zig.zon, and raylib's own build.zig chases Zig master a few weeks behind
# it. Pulling raylib in as a package therefore breaks whenever Zig moves and
# raylib has not caught up, which for a repo that tracks master is most weeks.
# The C sources have no such problem, so we compile them ourselves.
set -euo pipefail

REPO="https://github.com/raysan5/raylib.git"
# raylib 6.0.0-dev. Bump deliberately, then re-run `zig build test`.
COMMIT="9f3cadf1e618f125bd9b282c7759f8cb26ce17fc"

here="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
dest="$here/vendor/raylib"

if [ -f "$dest/.commit" ] && [ "$(cat "$dest/.commit")" = "$COMMIT" ]; then
  echo "raylib already at $COMMIT"
  exit 0
fi

rm -rf "$dest"
mkdir -p "$dest"
git -C "$dest" init -q
git -C "$dest" remote add origin "$REPO"
git -C "$dest" fetch -q --depth 1 origin "$COMMIT"
git -C "$dest" checkout -q FETCH_HEAD
rm -rf "$dest/.git"

# Keep only what we compile. raylib's examples/ alone is 72 MB and none of it
# is built here.
find "$dest" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -name src ! -name LICENSE -exec rm -rf {} +
rm -rf "$dest/src/external/RGFW"

echo "$COMMIT" > "$dest/.commit"
echo "raylib vendored at $COMMIT"
```

*Quoted from the source: `examples/lane-dodger/fetch-raylib.sh`.*

```bash
chmod +x fetch-raylib.sh && ./fetch-raylib.sh
```

**5. Write the build script.**

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The C sources of raylib. `fetch-raylib.sh` vendors them at a pinned commit.
const raylib_root = "vendor/raylib/src";

/// The screen that a headless `-Dframes` run shows at its end. Thus CI can take
/// a screenshot of the title and of the game over screen with nobody at the
/// keyboard. With these screenshots, CI checks what the game draws.
pub const Demo = enum { title, play, crash };

/// The raylib build for a desktop window is different from the build for a
/// canvas. It has a different platform backend and a different GL. On the web
/// it does not use the GLFW that raylib includes, because Emscripten supplies
/// its own GLFW.
const Platform = enum { desktop, web };

pub fn build(b: *std.Build) void {
    const target = b.standardTargetOptions(.{});
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{});

    // A headless smoke run. CI uses it, and you can use it after a change to
    // check that the game still draws, without a person who watches.
    // `-Dframes=N` plays N frames with the bot at the controls, then exits.
    // `-Dshot=path` saves the last frame. These are build options and not
    // environment variables. Thus `zig build --help` shows them, and their
    // values are comptime-known.
    const options = b.addOptions();
    const frames = b.option(
        usize,
        "frames",
        "Play this many frames with the bot, then exit (headless smoke test)",
    );
    options.addOption(?usize, "auto_frames", frames);
    // By default, a headless run has no sound, because nobody listens. A CI
    // container has no audio device, and an attempt to open one only puts
    // driver warnings in the log. `-Daudio=true` turns the sound on again.
    // That option lets you test the path for a machine with no sound card.
    options.addOption(bool, "audio", b.option(
        bool,
        "audio",
        "Enable sound (default: on, except in a -Dframes run)",
    ) orelse (frames == null));
    options.addOption(?[]const u8, "screenshot", b.option(
        []const u8,
        "shot",
        "Write a screenshot to this path before exiting",
    ));
    options.addOption(Demo, "demo", b.option(
        Demo,
        "demo",
        "What the headless run should show: title, play (bot drives) or crash",
    ) orelse .play);

    addTests(b, target, optimize);
    addSoundDump(b, target, optimize);
    addDesktop(b, target, optimize, options);
    addWeb(b, optimize, options);
}

/// The simulation is a separate module, and it imports nothing: not raylib, a
/// window or a clock. Thus `zig build test` can run the full game headless.
/// Also, the rules of the game stay in one place, and not in parts of a draw
/// loop.
fn simModule(
    b: *std.Build,
    target: std.Build.ResolvedTarget,
    optimize: std.lang.Optimize,
) *std.Build.Module {
    return b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/sim/sim.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
}

fn addTests(
    b: *std.Build,
    target: std.Build.ResolvedTarget,
    optimize: std.lang.Optimize,
) void {
    const sim = simModule(b, target, optimize);
    const sim_tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = sim });

    // The particles are presentation. But they contain no raylib types, thus
    // the tests can also check them headlessly.
    const particles = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/render/particles.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    particles.addImport("sim", sim);
    const particle_tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = particles });

    // The synthesiser also contains no raylib types. It fills a buffer with
    // samples. Thus the tests check the waveforms without an audio device. CI
    // has no speakers.
    const synth = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/audio/synth.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    synth.addImport("sim", sim);
    const synth_tests = b.addTest(.{ .root_module = synth });

    const step = b.step("test", "Run the headless simulation tests");
    step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(sim_tests).step);
    step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(particle_tests).step);
    step.dependOn(&b.addRunArtifact(synth_tests).step);
}

/// `zig build sounds` writes the sound effects to `zig-out/sounds` as `.wav`
/// files. Thus you can listen to each effect and adjust it. You do not have to
/// play the game until the effect occurs.
fn addSoundDump(
    b: *std.Build,
    target: std.Build.ResolvedTarget,
    optimize: std.lang.Optimize,
) void {
    const synth = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/audio/synth.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    synth.addImport("sim", simModule(b, target, optimize));

    const module = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/tools/dump_sounds.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    module.addImport("synth", synth);

    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "dump-sounds", .root_module = module });
    const run = b.addRunArtifact(exe);
    const wavs = run.addOutputDirectoryArg("sounds");

    const install = b.addInstallDirectory(.{
        .source_dir = wavs,
        .install_dir = .{ .custom = "sounds" },
        .install_subdir = ".",
    });
    b.step("sounds", "Write the sound effects to zig-out/sounds as .wav").dependOn(&install.step);
}

/// The root module of the game, connected to a raylib build for `platform`.
const Game = struct {
    module: *std.Build.Module,
    raylib: *std.Build.Step.Compile,
};

fn gameModule(
    b: *std.Build,
    target: std.Build.ResolvedTarget,
    optimize: std.lang.Optimize,
    options: *std.Build.Step.Options,
    platform: Platform,
    emsdk: ?[]const u8,
) Game {
    const module = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    const raylib = raylibModule(b, target, optimize, platform, emsdk);
    module.addImport("sim", simModule(b, target, optimize));
    module.addImport("rl", raylib.module);
    module.addOptions("build_options", options);
    return .{ .module = module, .raylib = raylib.lib };
}

fn addDesktop(
    b: *std.Build,
    target: std.Build.ResolvedTarget,
    optimize: std.lang.Optimize,
    options: *std.Build.Step.Options,
) void {
    const game = gameModule(b, target, optimize, options, .desktop, null);
    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "lane-dodger", .root_module = game.module });
    b.installArtifact(exe);

    const run = b.addRunArtifact(exe);
    run.step.dependOn(b.getInstallStep());
    b.step("run", "Build and play the game").dependOn(&run.step);
}

/// Build the game for a browser canvas.
///
/// Zig compiles the game code and the raylib code to a static library for
/// `wasm32-emscripten`. `emcc` does the link, because only Emscripten can emit
/// the JavaScript glue, the GL context and the canvas configuration. The same
/// split is the reason for `Game.frame` in `main.zig`. emcc gives the loop to
/// the browser and never returns.
fn addWeb(
    b: *std.Build,
    optimize: std.lang.Optimize,
    options: *std.Build.Step.Options,
) void {
    const step = b.step("web", "Build the browser version with Emscripten");

    const emsdk = b.option([]const u8, "emsdk", "Path to an activated emsdk") orelse
        b.graph.environ_map.get("EMSDK") orelse
    {
        step.dependOn(&b.addFail(
            "no Emscripten SDK found: pass -Demsdk=/path/to/emsdk, or source emsdk_env.sh",
        ).step);
        return;
    };

    const target = b.resolveTargetQuery(.{
        .cpu_arch = .wasm32,
        .os_tag = .emscripten,
    });

    const game = gameModule(b, target, optimize, options, .web, emsdk);
    const lib = b.addLibrary(.{
        .name = "lane-dodger",
        .linkage = .static,
        .root_module = game.module,
    });

    const emcc = b.addSystemCommand(&.{b.pathJoin(&.{ emsdk, "upstream", "emscripten", "emcc" })});
    emcc.addArtifactArg(lib);
    emcc.addArtifactArg(game.raylib);
    emcc.addArgs(&.{
        // Emscripten supplies GLFW 3 for the canvas. The GLFW that raylib
        // includes is a desktop library for windows. This build does not
        // compile it.
        "-sUSE_GLFW=3",
        // The canvas can have any size, and the page selects the size. Growth
        // costs a small quantity of speed. Without growth, the program must
        // reserve memory for the worst case at the start.
        "-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH=1",
        // A factory function, and not a global `Module`. Thus the page can
        // start the game at the time that it selects, and give the game its
        // own canvas.
        //
        // This output is not an ES6 module, and that is intentional. The guide
        // puts the game in a page that Vite builds. Vite rewrites `import()`
        // also for a file that it only serves from `public/`. It adds
        // `?import`, then it cannot transform a 190 KB Emscripten bundle. A
        // plain `<script>` tag loads a classic script that defines one global,
        // and no bundler changes that tag.
        "-sMODULARIZE=1",
        "-sEXPORT_NAME=createLaneDodger",
        // emscripten_set_main_loop controls the loop. Thus the build needs
        // none of the code that unwinds the stack.
        "-sASYNCIFY=0",
        "-sSTACK_SIZE=1048576",
        // Here the build compiles raylib against GLES 3, which emits
        // `#version 300 es` shaders. These shaders need a WebGL 2 context.
        // Emscripten creates a WebGL 1 context unless you tell it to do
        // otherwise. The symptom is a game that loads, runs, and compiles no
        // shader.
        "-sMIN_WEBGL_VERSION=2",
        "-sMAX_WEBGL_VERSION=2",
    });
    if (optimize != .debug) emcc.addArgs(&.{ "-O3", "--closure", "0" });
    emcc.addArg("-o");
    const out = emcc.addOutputFileArg("lane-dodger.js");

    // emcc writes the wasm next to the js, with the same basename.
    const install_js = b.addInstallFileWithDir(out, .{ .custom = "web" }, "lane-dodger.js");
    const install_wasm = b.addInstallFileWithDir(
        out.dirname().path(b, "lane-dodger.wasm"),
        .{ .custom = "web" },
        "lane-dodger.wasm",
    );
    // The page that holds the canvas. The page comes with the two artefacts.
    // Thus `zig build web` makes a directory that you can play with no other
    // configuration.
    const install_page = b.addInstallFileWithDir(
        b.path("web-shell/index.html"),
        .{ .custom = "web" },
        "index.html",
    );
    step.dependOn(&install_js.step);
    step.dependOn(&install_wasm.step);
    step.dependOn(&install_page.step);
}

/// Compile raylib from its C sources, and return a Zig module for `raylib.h`.
///
/// raylib has its own build.zig, and this project does not use it on purpose.
/// When you name a package in build.zig.zon, the build runner imports the
/// build.zig of that package. If the build script of a dependency does not
/// support Zig master yet, your build fails before it compiles one line of
/// your code. The build script of raylib had that problem, and the build
/// script of raylib-zig also had it. The C of raylib changes much more slowly.
///
/// The macros below are a copy of the macros that the build.zig of raylib
/// sets for each of these targets.
const Raylib = struct {
    /// `@import("rl")`: raylib.h, run through translate-c.
    module: *std.Build.Module,
    /// The compiled archive. Zig links the archive into an executable
    /// automatically. But a static library records the dependency and does
    /// not include the archive. Thus the web build must give the archive to
    /// emcc.
    lib: *std.Build.Step.Compile,
};

fn raylibModule(
    b: *std.Build,
    target: std.Build.ResolvedTarget,
    optimize: std.lang.Optimize,
    platform: Platform,
    emsdk: ?[]const u8,
) Raylib {
    const mod = b.createModule(.{
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
        .link_libc = true,
        // In the debug modes, Zig instruments C with UBSan by default and
        // links its own runtime to catch the reports. That runtime comes with
        // a Zig link. emcc does the link for the web build. Thus the
        // instrumentation would leave a few dozen undefined `__ubsan_*`
        // symbols. This project did not write this C. It is a pinned upstream
        // release.
        .sanitize_c = .off,
    });
    const lib = b.addLibrary(.{
        .name = "raylib",
        .linkage = .static,
        .root_module = mod,
    });

    inline for (.{
        .{ "_GNU_SOURCE", "" },
        .{ "GL_SILENCE_DEPRECATION", "199309L" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RSHAPES", "1" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RTEXTURES", "1" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RTEXT", "1" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RAUDIO", "1" },
        // The 3D model loader adds cgltf, m3d and par_shapes. This game draws
        // only rectangles, thus the build turns the module off.
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RMODELS", "0" },
    }) |macro| mod.addCMacro(macro[0], macro[1]);

    switch (platform) {
        .desktop => {
            mod.addCMacro("PLATFORM_DESKTOP_GLFW", "");
            mod.addCMacro("GRAPHICS_API_OPENGL_33", "");
            mod.addCMacro("_GLFW_X11", "");
        },
        .web => {
            mod.addCMacro("PLATFORM_WEB", "");
            // WebGL 2. ES2 also works, and it also works on older phones. All
            // browsers where a person would play this game support ES3 today.
            mod.addCMacro("GRAPHICS_API_OPENGL_ES3", "");
        },
    }

    mod.addIncludePath(b.path(raylib_root ++ "/platforms"));
    mod.addIncludePath(b.path(raylib_root ++ "/external/glfw/include"));
    if (emsdk) |sdk| {
        mod.addIncludePath(.{ .cwd_relative = b.pathJoin(
            &.{ sdk, "upstream", "emscripten", "cache", "sysroot", "include" },
        ) });
    }

    // rglfw.c is the desktop GLFW that raylib includes. On the web,
    // Emscripten supplies GLFW for the canvas. Thus the web build does not
    // compile rglfw.c.
    const sources: []const []const u8 = switch (platform) {
        .desktop => &.{
            "rcore.c", "rshapes.c", "rtextures.c", "rtext.c", "raudio.c", "rglfw.c",
        },
        .web => &.{
            "rcore.c", "rshapes.c", "rtextures.c", "rtext.c", "raudio.c",
        },
    };
    mod.addCSourceFiles(.{
        .root = b.path(raylib_root),
        .files = sources,
        .flags = &.{"-std=gnu99"},
    });

    if (platform == .desktop) {
        for ([_][]const u8{ "GL", "X11", "Xrandr", "Xinerama", "Xi", "Xcursor" }) |name| {
            mod.linkSystemLibrary(name, .{});
        }
    }

    const translated = b.addTranslateC(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path(raylib_root ++ "/raylib.h"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
        .link_libc = true,
    });
    if (emsdk) |sdk| {
        translated.addIncludePath(.{ .cwd_relative = b.pathJoin(
            &.{ sdk, "upstream", "emscripten", "cache", "sysroot", "include" },
        ) });
    }
    const rl = translated.createModule();
    rl.linkLibrary(lib);
    return .{ .module = rl, .lib = lib };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `examples/lane-dodger/build.zig`.*

Nothing compiles yet. `build.zig` names files that do not exist, and that is
correct. Zig reads a source file only when a step that needs the file runs.

## Part two: the simulation

Write these nine files in this order. Each file uses only the files above it.

- `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/config.zig`: Every tunable number, and the field geometry. [The World](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-world/).
- `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/rng.zig`: PCG32, so a seed replays exactly. [The World](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-world/).
- `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/pool.zig`: Fixed-capacity storage with generational handles. [Handles, Not Pointers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/entities/).
- `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/sim.zig`: The world, the tick, collision and spawning. [The World](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-world/).
- `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/bot.zig`: A policy that plays the game. [Difficulty You Can Prove](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/fair-by-design/).
- `examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/tests.zig`: The tests that play the game. [Difficulty You Can Prove](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/fair-by-design/).
- `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/palette.zig`: Colours as plain data, no raylib. [Draw It](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/drawing/).
- `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/particles.zig`: Sparks and debris, using the same pool. [Draw It](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/drawing/).
- `examples/lane-dodger/src/audio/synth.zig`: Five sound effects, generated. [Sound Without Sound Files](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/sound/).

### The first checkpoint

```bash
zig build test
```

The command runs fifty-five tests:

- A bot plays four minutes of the game at each seed.
- A second bot plays the game with a human reaction time.
- Two worlds replay from one seed, and the test compares them on each tick.

You did not write drawing code, input code or `main.zig` yet. You do not need a
window or an audio device. But the game is already sufficiently complete to play
and to check. The design has this arrangement so that this checkpoint exists.

If the tests pass, the rules are correct. The other files draw the game,
read the input and play the sound.

## Part three: the game you can see

Write four more files.

- `examples/lane-dodger/src/render/draw.zig`: The view transform and every raylib call. [Draw It](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/drawing/).
- `examples/lane-dodger/src/platform/input.zig`: Keys and taps, read one time in each frame. [Input](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/input/).

## How one tap becomes a frame

```
you press D
   |
   v
Latch.poll()            once per rendered frame, sets latch.right
   |
   v
Game.frame()            adds real elapsed time to the accumulator
   |
   v
while accumulator >= 1/120:
     Input = latch.take()      first tick gets the press, the rest get nothing
     World.step(input)         steer, move, spawn, collide, score
     react(events)             particles, screen shake, a note
   |
   v
alpha = accumulator / (1/120)      what is left over, less than one tick
   |
   v
draw.frame(world, alpha)    draws between the last two ticks
```

The press gets to exactly one tick. If a frame needs no ticks, the frame keeps
the press for the next frame. If a frame needs three ticks, the frame gives the
press to the first tick.

## If the build fails

**`error: invalid fingerprint`.** This error is normal on the first run. Paste
the value that the compiler prints into `build.zig.zon`.

**`error: unable to find module 'rl'`**, or the compiler cannot find the raylib
headers.
`fetch-raylib.sh` did not run, or it ran in the wrong directory. Make sure that
`vendor/raylib/src/raylib.h` exists.

**`ld: cannot find -lX11`** and similar errors. The X development headers are not on
your system. Install the packages in the list above. The runtime libraries alone are
not sufficient. You need the `-dev` packages.

**`root source file struct 'std' has no member named ...`.** Your Zig is too old,
or too new. This game tracks master, thus both of these problems can occur.
Compare `zig version` with `minimum_zig_version`.

**The tests pass but the window is black.** You use Wayland without XWayland, or
a container with no display. To make sure that the program itself runs, try
`xvfb-run -a ./zig-out/bin/lane-dodger`.

**The game builds, but it plays badly.** All the numbers are in
[`src/sim/config.zig`](https://github.com/rajeshpillai/zig-guide/blob/main/examples/lane-dodger/src/sim/config.zig).
Change `lane_change_time` first. Do not make the row spacing smaller by hand.
`sim.zig` calculates a minimum from the other numbers, and
[the tests](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/fair-by-design/) tell you when the spacing is
less than that minimum.

---

## A Paint Program You Can Test

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/a-paint-program/*

Press Start painting and draw.

*Interactive: the paint program, compiled to WebAssembly. Select a brush, a size and a colour. Draw on the bottom or the top layer, erase, fill, undo, and save a PNG. It runs on the web page of this chapter.*

You can use a mouse or a finger. If your pen has pressure, the line is thicker when you push harder.

Try the Calligraphy brush. Lines in one direction are thin, and lines across them are wide.

Draw on the bottom layer. Then select the top layer, draw again, and erase there. Where you erase, you see the bottom layer.

## One rule

The program has two parts:

- The **engine** calculates the value of each pixel. The engine is about 2,100 lines of Zig, and about 1,050 more lines of tests.
- The **front end** changes mouse and pen events into calls to the engine. Then it copies the pixels from the engine to the canvas.

The rule is that the engine never sees a mouse, a window or a clock. Points go in, and pixels come out.

The main type of the engine is a document. A document holds the layers, the current stroke, the history, and the data for the screen:

```zig
pub const Document = struct {
    gpa: std.mem.Allocator,
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    /// Bottom first. Each one is `width * height` premultiplied pixels.
    layers: [][]Rgba,
    visible: []bool,
    active_layer: u32 = 0,
    /// The coverage of the current stroke.
    mask: Mask,
    /// The grain below the full picture, for brushes with less than full
    /// contact. The document makes it one time, thus each stroke touches the
    /// same hills.
    paper: Paper,
    /// The picture on the screen: each visible layer over white paper, with
    /// the current stroke applied. Always opaque.
    display: []Rgba,
    /// The part of `display` that is out of date.
    stale: Rect = .empty,
    history: History,
    stroke: ?Active = null,
    /// False after an action if the history could not keep its undo step. A
    /// front end can tell the user. Otherwise, Undo silently skips that action.
    history_ok: bool = true,

    // ...
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Document` (fields only) from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

A front end calls a small number of methods on the document. A stroke is one `beginStroke` call, some `moveStroke` calls, and one `endStroke` call. Each call takes a point: an `x`, a `y` and a pressure.

After these calls, `render` updates `display` and returns the rectangle that changed. The front end copies that rectangle to the screen. The front end does nothing more.

## What the rule gives you

The engine needs no window. Thus a test can draw.

A test can start a stroke, move it, end it, and then examine the pixels. This test makes sure that a stroke looks the same while you draw it and after you release the pointer:

```zig
test "a stroke shows while drawing, and looks the same after it is committed" {
    var d = try newDoc();
    defer d.deinit();
    _ = d.render();
    const blank = d.displayHash();

    d.beginStroke(.{ .radius = 6, .color = .{ 200, 30, 30 } }, .brush, .{ .x = 10, .y = 10 });
    d.moveStroke(.{ .x = 50, .y = 30 });
    _ = d.render();
    const preview = d.displayHash();
    try testing.expect(preview != blank);

    d.endStroke();
    _ = d.render();
    try testing.expectEqual(preview, d.displayHash());
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `a stroke shows while drawing, and looks the same after it is committed` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

There are 80 tests of this type, and no test opens a window.

## The same pixels in all builds

The engine runs in three places: in your browser, in a native window, and in the tests.

A test proves something about the browser only if the browser build draws the same pixels as the test build. Thus the engine contains a fixed drawing. The drawing uses each tool. It has a soft wash, a calligraphy nib, a ribbon, a dry bristle brush, an oil brush and spray. It also has a fill, an eraser, and an undo and redo.

```zig
/// The display hash after `draw` on a new 640 by 400 document with two layers.
/// If a change to the engine changes the picture on purpose, run the tests,
/// examine the new picture, and update this value.
pub const hash: u32 = 0x3870db57;
```

*Quoted from the source: `hash` from `examples/paint/src/engine/demo.zig`.*

A native test draws the picture. Then the test compares a hash of the pixels with that number.

Before the site build, the browser build draws the same picture and compares its hash with the same number. If one pixel is different between the two builds, the build fails, and the site does not publish this page.

## The browser build

The engine is plain Zig with no dependencies. Thus the browser build needs no other tools. It uses the same compiler, with the target `wasm32-freestanding`:

```zig
/// The browser build. The function is public, thus the build.zig of the
/// guide can call it with its own path to `src/`. Both builds use one definition.
pub fn addWeb(b: *std.Build, src: std.Build.LazyPath, optimize: std.lang.Optimize) *std.Build.Step.Compile {
    const wasm_target = b.resolveTargetQuery(.{ .cpu_arch = .wasm32, .os_tag = .freestanding });
    const engine = b.createModule(.{
        .root_source_file = src.path(b, "engine.zig"),
        .target = wasm_target,
        .optimize = optimize,
    });
    const exe = b.addExecutable(.{
        .name = "paint",
        .root_module = b.createModule(.{
            .root_source_file = src.path(b, "web.zig"),
            .target = wasm_target,
            .optimize = optimize,
            .imports = &.{.{ .name = "engine", .module = engine }},
        }),
    });
    // A library of exported functions, not a program with a main. The page
    // calls the functions.
    exe.entry = .disabled;
    exe.rdynamic = true;
    return exe;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `addWeb` from `examples/paint/build.zig`.*

`freestanding` means that there is no operating system. The engine does not need an operating system, because it never opens a file or reads a clock.

The result is about 150 KB. About half of that size is the JSON parser that reads brush presets. The [Projects and Presets](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/projects-and-presets/) chapter gives the measurement.

## The chapters

The chapters follow the engine from the pointer to the PNG file:

1. **Strokes**: change pointer samples at irregular distances into dabs at equal distances.
2. **Smoothing, pressure and scatter**: make a stroke look as if a hand drew it, and make it repeatable.
3. **The tip**: soft edges, flat tips, and tips that turn.
4. **Bristles and paper**: separate tracks for each hair, and a dry brush on the grain of the paper.
5. **Oil**: a brush that collects the paint below it, and becomes dry.
6. **Flow and opacity**: why the engine first puts a stroke in a separate buffer.
7. **Layers and the eraser**: premultiplied alpha, and why the eraser needs it.
8. **Undo**: keep only the pixels that changed, inside a memory budget.
9. **Fill**: a flood fill that uses a queue instead of recursion.
10. **Save a PNG**: write the picture as a PNG.
11. **Projects and presets**: keep the layers in a file format of this program, and brushes in JSON. Examine both when the program reads them again.
12. **Watercolour**: water and pigment that spread and dry on a grid. This is a separate experiment that you can run.
13. **A native window**: the same engine with raylib, and a cross-compiled build for Windows.

Each chapter shows the tests that examine it.

## Explain before you read the answer

The front end sends each pointer sample from the browser to the engine.

Some browsers send a fast movement as a small number of samples that are far apart. Other browsers send the same movement as many samples that are near each other.

Does the same movement draw the same stroke in both browsers?

Yes, it does. The engine does not put one mark for each sample. The engine moves along the path and puts a mark at a fixed distance, for all sets of samples. The next chapter shows how.

---

## Strokes

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/strokes/*

A brush stroke is a row of marks. Each mark is a **dab**, and a dab is one stamp of the brush tip.

If many dabs are near each other at equal distances, they look like one continuous line.

## The obvious answer is wrong

While you hold the button, the pointer sends its position again and again. Each position report is a **sample**.

The obvious answer is one dab for each sample. That answer fails, because the samples do not come at equal distances.

The browser sends a sample when it can, about one time for each screen frame:

- A slow movement gives samples that are one or two pixels apart.
- A fast movement gives samples that are 40 pixels apart, with nothing between them.

Thus one dab for each sample draws a solid line when you move slowly. When you move fast, it draws a row of separate dots.

## Distance and lerp

The stroke code needs two small tools first.

The distance between two points is the length of the straight line between them:

```zig
/// Straight-line distance, in pixels. A movement backwards gives the same distance.
pub fn distance(a: Point, b: Point) f32 {
    return std.math.hypot(b.x - a.x, b.y - a.y);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `distance` from `examples/paint/src/engine/geometry.zig`.*

From (10, 20) to (40, 60), the change in x is 30, and the change in y is 40. The distance is √(900 + 1600) = 50 pixels. A movement in the opposite direction gives negative changes, but the distance is the same.

`lerp` gives the value at a fraction `t` of the distance from `a` to `b`:

```zig
/// The value a fraction `t` of the way from `a` to `b`. `t` is not clamped:
/// `t = 1.5` goes past `b`.
pub fn lerp(a: f32, b: f32, t: f32) f32 {
    return a + (b - a) * t;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `lerp` from `examples/paint/src/engine/geometry.zig`.*

From 20 to 100, `t = 0.25` gives 40. `t = 0` gives 20, and `t = 1` gives 100.

`t = 1.5` gives 140, which is after the end. `lerp` does not clamp, and the stroke code never needs a clamp.

## Move along the path

The solution is to ignore the positions of the samples.

Between two samples, the pointer moved along a line. The stroke code moves along that line and puts a dab after each `gap` pixels.

The gap comes from the brush. The gap is a fraction of the radius. Thus a large brush puts its dabs farther apart than a small brush:

```zig
    /// The gap between dabs, in pixels. Never below half a pixel, or a tiny
    /// brush would put thousands of dabs on one short segment.
    fn gap(s: Stroke) f32 {
        return @max(s.brush.spacing * s.brush.radius, 0.5);
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `gap` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

A spacing of 0.25 on a brush of radius 40 gives a gap of 10 pixels.

## The distance that remains

If the code examines each segment separately, there is still a problem.

For example, the gap is 10, and the pointer moves 6 pixels. A dab does not fit in 6 pixels. Then the pointer moves 6 more pixels. If each segment starts its count at zero, a dab does not fit in the second segment either. The pointer moved 12 pixels, and the stroke has no dab after the first dab.

Thus the code keeps the distance from the last dab. This distance is the **carry**. After the first 6-pixel movement, the carry is 6.

The next segment does not need a full gap before its first dab. It needs only the 4 pixels that complete the interval: 10 − 6 = 4.

Each new sample goes through the function `move`:

```zig
    /// The pointer moved to `p`. Put each dab that is on the path.
    pub fn move(s: *Stroke, p: Point, sink: anytype) void {
        // Smoothing: move part of the distance to the real point.
        s.filtered = geometry.lerpPoint(s.filtered, p, s.brush.follow);

        const a = s.last;
        const b = s.filtered;
        const d = geometry.distance(a, b);
        // Two samples at the same position: there is no distance to move. A
        // division by `d` below would give NaN.
        if (d == 0) return;
        s.direction = std.math.atan2(b.y - a.y, b.x - a.x);

        const step = s.gap();
        // The first dab on this segment completes the interval that remains
        // from the last segment.
        var at = step - s.carry;
        while (at <= d) : (at += step) {
            // The load decreases with distance, not with each dab or sample. One
            // gap farther along the path uses `drain * step / 100` of a load.
            s.load = @max(s.load - s.brush.drain * step / 100.0, 0);
            s.emit(geometry.lerpPoint(a, b, at / d), sink);
        }
        s.carry = d - (at - step);
        s.last = b;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `move` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

`at` is the distance along this segment to the position of the next dab. Its first value is `step - s.carry`, which is 4 pixels in the example.

The loop puts a dab and adds a gap. The loop continues while `at` is inside the segment.

When the loop ends, `at` is one gap after the last dab. Thus `at - step` is the position of the last dab. `d - (at - step)` is the length of the segment after the last dab, and that length is the new carry.

After the loop, the carry is always less than one gap.

## Two small details

Two samples can have exactly the same position. Then the distance is 0, and `at / d` is a division by zero, which gives NaN. A NaN position puts a dab nowhere, and it makes all of the calculations after it incorrect. Thus `move` returns immediately when `d == 0`.

A stroke must also make a mark when you click without a movement. Thus `begin` puts the first dab at the start point, and sets the carry to 0:

```zig
    /// Start a stroke at `p` and put the first dab there, so a click with no
    /// movement still leaves a mark.
    pub fn begin(brush: Brush, p: Point, sink: anytype) Stroke {
        const b = brush.sanitized();
        var s: Stroke = .{
            .brush = b,
            .random = .init(b.seed),
            .filtered = p,
            .last = p,
            .carry = 0,
            .direction = 0,
            .loaded = .{ @floatFromInt(b.color[0]), @floatFromInt(b.color[1]), @floatFromInt(b.color[2]) },
            .load = 1,
        };
        s.emit(p, sink);
        return s;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `begin` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

## The destination of the dabs

`move` does not draw. It calls `sink.dab(...)`, and the caller decides what to do.

`sink` is `anytype`, thus any value with a `dab` method is correct. Zig examines this at compile time, separately for each type that a caller gives.

The document gives a painter that stamps each dab into the stroke buffer. A test gives a recorder that only keeps a list:

```zig
/// A sink for tests. It keeps the dabs that it receives.
const Recorder = struct {
    dabs: [256]Dab = undefined,
    len: usize = 0,
    /// The paint that `sample` returns for each dab.
    under: ?Sample = null,

    fn dab(r: *Recorder, d: Dab) void {
        r.dabs[r.len] = d;
        r.len += 1;
    }

    fn sample(r: *Recorder, x: f32, y: f32) ?Sample {
        _ = x;
        _ = y;
        return r.under;
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Recorder` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

The stroke code is the same in the two cases. Only the action on the dabs changes.

## Checks

This test is the example from above: three movements of 6 pixels with a gap of 10.

```zig
test "carry after three moves of 6 pixels with a gap of 10 is 8" {
    // Radius 40 at spacing 0.25 is a gap of 10 pixels.
    const brush: Brush = .{ .radius = 40, .spacing = 0.25 };
    var rec: Recorder = .{};
    var s = Stroke.begin(brush, .{ .x = 0, .y = 0 }, &rec);
    s.move(.{ .x = 6, .y = 0 }, &rec);
```
