```zig
    s.move(.{ .x = 18, .y = 0 }, &rec);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f32, 8), s.carry);

    // A dab at the start, and one at x = 10. Not one per sample.
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 2), rec.len);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f32, 0), rec.dabs[0].x);
    try std.testing.expectApproxEqAbs(@as(f32, 10), rec.dabs[1].x, 1e-4);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `carry after three moves of 6 pixels with a gap of 10 is 8` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

The first dab is at 0, and the second dab is at 10, one gap after the first. The second movement, from 6 to 12, puts the second dab 4 pixels into that movement.

The next test shows why the carry is necessary. The test draws one movement of 100 pixels. Then it draws the same 100 pixels as movements of 3 pixels. The two strokes must give the same dabs:

```zig
test "the spacing does not depend on how the movement was cut up" {
    const brush: Brush = .{ .radius = 20, .spacing = 0.25 };
    var one: Recorder = .{};
    var s1 = Stroke.begin(brush, .{ .x = 0, .y = 0 }, &one);
    s1.move(.{ .x = 100, .y = 0 }, &one);

    var many: Recorder = .{};
    var s2 = Stroke.begin(brush, .{ .x = 0, .y = 0 }, &many);
    var x: f32 = 0;
    while (x < 100) {
        x = @min(x + 3, 100);
        s2.move(.{ .x = x, .y = 0 }, &many);
    }

    try std.testing.expectEqual(one.len, many.len);
    for (one.dabs[0..one.len], many.dabs[0..many.len]) |a, b| {
        try std.testing.expectApproxEqAbs(a.x, b.x, 1e-3);
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `the spacing does not depend on how the movement was cut up` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

Without the carry, the second stroke puts a dab at the end of each 3-pixel movement, or at none of them.

This test examines the repeated sample:

```zig
test "a repeated sample adds no dab and does not divide by zero" {
    var rec: Recorder = .{};
    var s = Stroke.begin(.{}, .{ .x = 5, .y = 5 }, &rec);
    s.move(.{ .x = 5, .y = 5 }, &rec);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 1), rec.len);
    try std.testing.expect(!std.math.isNan(s.carry));
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `a repeated sample adds no dab and does not divide by zero` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

## Record and replay a stroke

A stroke is only its list of samples.

If you keep the list, you can draw the stroke again. With the same brush, the list draws the same dabs. With a different brush, it draws the same path in a different style.

The demo picture from the [first chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/a-paint-program/) is a replay of this type. Its samples are in the code. Thus a test can draw the picture and compare the pixels.

## Explain before you read the answer

You complete a stroke with a carry of 7 and lift the pen. Then you start a new stroke in a different position.

Must the new stroke start with a carry of 7?

No, it must not. The carry is the distance from the last dab of this stroke. A new stroke has no last dab. It starts its own spacing, with a dab at the point where the pen touches the surface. That is why `begin` sets `carry = 0`.

---

## Smoothing, Pressure and Scatter

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/smoothing-pressure-scatter/*

The last chapter changed samples into dabs at equal distances. This chapter changes the dabs. There are three changes, and each change is a small number of lines:

- **Smoothing** moves the path, to make a shaky hand steady.
- **Pressure** changes the size of each dab.
- **Jitter and scatter** change the size and position of each dab at random. A brush such as a spray can uses them.

The third change has a condition. The random values must repeat exactly. If they do not repeat, no test can compare two pictures.

## Smoothing

A hand is not steady, and a mouse is less steady than a hand.

Smoothing keeps a second position, the **filtered** position. For each new sample, smoothing moves the filtered position only part of the distance to the sample:

```zig
    /// The pointer moved to `p`. Put each dab that is on the path.
    pub fn move(s: *Stroke, p: Point, sink: anytype) void {
        // Smoothing: move part of the distance to the real point.
        s.filtered = geometry.lerpPoint(s.filtered, p, s.brush.follow);

        const a = s.last;
        const b = s.filtered;
        const d = geometry.distance(a, b);
        // Two samples at the same position: there is no distance to move. A
        // division by `d` below would give NaN.
        if (d == 0) return;
        s.direction = std.math.atan2(b.y - a.y, b.x - a.x);

        const step = s.gap();
        // The first dab on this segment completes the interval that remains
        // from the last segment.
        var at = step - s.carry;
        while (at <= d) : (at += step) {
            // The load decreases with distance, not with each dab or sample. One
            // gap farther along the path uses `drain * step / 100` of a load.
            s.load = @max(s.load - s.brush.drain * step / 100.0, 0);
            s.emit(geometry.lerpPoint(a, b, at / d), sink);
        }
        s.carry = d - (at - step);
        s.last = b;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `move` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

The first line of `move` does all of the smoothing. `follow` is the fraction of the distance to move.

## An example

The filtered x is 100. A sample comes at x = 120. `follow` is 0.25.

The filtered x moves a quarter of the distance: 100 + (120 − 100) × 0.25 = 105.

The next sample is at 120 again. The filtered x moves a quarter of the distance that remains: 105 + 15 × 0.25 = 108.75.

A small movement of a few pixels gets the same calculation. Thus the movement becomes a quarter of its size. At `follow = 1`, the filtered point moves directly to the sample, and there is no smoothing.

The cost is a delay. The stroke is behind the pointer. When you release the pointer, the stroke ends before the last position of the pointer. A lower `follow` gives a steadier line and a longer delay. That is why the Ink brush in the studio uses 0.35, and the Spray brush uses 1.

## Pressure

A pen sends its pressure as a value from 0 to 1. A mouse has no pressure, and browsers send 0.5 while the button is down.

The `pressure` setting of the brush tells how much effect the pen has, from 0 (no effect) to 1 (full effect). This function calculates the size of each dab:

```zig
    fn emit(s: *Stroke, p: Point, sink: anytype) void {
        const b = s.brush;

        // Pressure: at `pressure = 0` the size ignores the pen.
        // At 1, a light touch draws at a quarter of the size.
        const p2 = p.pressure * p.pressure;
        var radius = b.radius * geometry.lerp(1.0, 0.25 + 0.75 * p2, b.pressure);

        // Three random numbers for each dab, also if the code does not use them.
        // Thus a change to scatter does not change the size of each later dab.
        const u_size = s.random.next();
        const u_angle = s.random.next();
        const u_reach = s.random.next();

        radius *= 1.0 - b.jitter * u_size;

        // Scatter across a disc. The square root spreads the offsets equally
        // over the area. Without it, the offsets collect at the centre.
        const theta = 2.0 * std.math.pi * u_angle;
        const reach = b.scatter * b.radius * @sqrt(u_reach);
        const x = p.x + @cos(theta) * reach;
        const y = p.y + @sin(theta) * reach;

        // Pickup: before the dab, the brush takes part of the paint that is
        // already below it. The brush carries the colour to the next dab. Thus
        // paint moves along the stroke. Thin paint gives less, and empty paper
        // gives nothing: a brush cannot collect the paper.
        if (b.pickup > 0) {
            if (sink.sample(x, y)) |under| {
                const t = b.pickup * under.cover;
                for (&s.loaded, under.color) |*c, u| c.* = geometry.lerp(c.*, @floatFromInt(u), t);
            }
        }

        sink.dab(.{
            .x = x,
            .y = y,
            .radius = radius,
            // When the tip follows the direction, the brush angle is an offset from
            // the direction. 0 puts the tip along the stroke, and 90 puts it across.
            .angle = (if (b.follow_direction) s.direction else 0) + b.angle * std.math.pi / 180.0,
            .direction = s.direction,
            .color = .{
                @intFromFloat(@round(s.loaded[0])),
                @intFromFloat(@round(s.loaded[1])),
                @intFromFloat(@round(s.loaded[2])),
            },
            .load = s.load,
        });
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `emit` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

The size at full effect is `0.25 + 0.75 × p²`, where `p` is the pressure of the pen.

At full pressure, the size is 1, which is the full radius. At no pressure, the size is 0.25, which is a quarter of the radius. Because of the square, light pressure has less effect. This feels more like a real pen than a straight line does.

Then the brush setting selects a value between that size and the full size with a `lerp`. At setting 0, the dab always has the full size, and the engine ignores the pen.

For a radius of 20, at setting 1:

- Pressure 1 gives 20 × (0.25 + 0.75) = 20 pixels.
- Pressure 0.5 gives 20 × (0.25 + 0.1875) = 8.75 pixels.
- Pressure 0 gives 20 × 0.25 = 5 pixels.

## Random numbers that repeat

The Spray brush changes the size and position of each dab at random.

Usually, a program gets random numbers from the operating system, and the numbers are different each time the program runs. That causes two problems:

- A test cannot draw with the spray brush and compare the result with a number.
- A recorded stroke draws differently each time that you replay it.

Thus the engine makes its own random numbers from a **seed**. The same seed gives the same numbers in the same order, on all computers:

```zig
pub const Random = struct {
    /// Always between 1 and 2^31 - 2. A zero state always stays zero.
    state: u32,

    const modulus: u64 = 2147483647; // 2^31 - 1, a prime
    const multiplier: u64 = 16807; // 7^5

    pub fn init(seed: u32) Random {
        const s: u32 = @intCast(seed % modulus);
        return .{ .state = if (s == 0) 1 else s };
    }

    /// The next value, from 0.0 to 1.0.
    pub fn next(r: *Random) f32 {
        // The product needs 46 bits, thus the code calculates it in u64. In u32
        // it would overflow, and Zig would stop the program in a safe build.
        r.state = @intCast((@as(u64, r.state) * multiplier) % modulus);
        return @as(f32, @floatFromInt(r.state - 1)) / 2147483646.0;
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Random` from `examples/paint/src/engine/random.zig`.*

This is the "minimal standard" generator of Park and Miller, from 1988. Each step multiplies the state by 16807. Then it keeps the remainder after a division by 2³¹ − 1.

The product can need 46 bits. Thus the code calculates it in a `u64`, because a `u32` overflows. In safe builds, Zig examines integer overflow. Thus an overflow stops the program with a message, and it does not silently give incorrect numbers.

Each brush has a seed. After each stroke, the studio adds one to the seed. Thus two spray strokes look different, but a replayed stroke looks the same.

## Jitter and scatter

In `emit`, the code takes three random numbers for each dab.

**Jitter** makes the dab smaller by a random quantity. At jitter 0.6, a dab is between 40% and 100% of its size.

**Scatter** moves the dab to a random point in a disc around its position on the path. The radius of the disc is `scatter` multiplied by the brush radius.

The random point is an angle and a distance. The angle is `2π × u`. The distance is `R × √v`.

The square root is necessary. Without the square root, half of the dabs are within half of the radius. But that inner circle is only a quarter of the area of the disc. The dabs collect at the centre.

With the square root, half of the dabs are within `R × √0.5`, about 71% of the radius. That circle is exactly half of the area, and the dabs spread equally.

The code takes the three numbers even when jitter and scatter are off. If the code takes them only when it uses them, the sequence moves when you turn scatter on. Then the jitter of each subsequent dab also changes.

## Checks

```zig
test "the first values from seed 1 are the published ones" {
    // Park and Miller give 16807, 282475249 and 1622650073 as the first three
    // states from seed 1. Thus this test finds an incorrect multiplication.
    var r = Random.init(1);
    _ = r.next();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 16807), r.state);
    _ = r.next();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 282475249), r.state);
    _ = r.next();
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1622650073), r.state);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `the first values from seed 1 are the published ones` from `examples/paint/src/engine/random.zig`.*

```zig
test "scatter stays inside the disc, and the same seed repeats it" {
    const brush: Brush = .{ .radius = 10, .scatter = 2, .seed = 7 };
    var a: Recorder = .{};
    var b: Recorder = .{};
    var sa = Stroke.begin(brush, .{ .x = 0, .y = 0 }, &a);
    var sb = Stroke.begin(brush, .{ .x = 0, .y = 0 }, &b);
    sa.move(.{ .x = 200, .y = 0 }, &a);
    sb.move(.{ .x = 200, .y = 0 }, &b);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(a.len, b.len);
    for (a.dabs[0..a.len], b.dabs[0..b.len], 0..) |da, db, i| {
        try std.testing.expectEqual(da, db);
        // The position of the dab on the path, before scatter, is i * gap.
        const along: f32 = @as(f32, @floatFromInt(i)) * 2.5;
        const off = std.math.hypot(da.x - along, da.y);
        try std.testing.expect(off <= 20.001);
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `scatter stays inside the disc, and the same seed repeats it` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

## Explain before you read the answer

A random number `u` is 0.25, and a second random number `v` is 0.25. The scatter radius `R` is 20 pixels.

Where does the dab move?

The angle is 2π × 0.25 = π/2, which is a quarter turn. The distance is 20 × √0.25 = 10 pixels.

A quarter turn from the x axis points along the y axis. On a screen, y increases downwards. Thus the dab moves 10 pixels straight down.

---

## The Tip

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/the-tip/*

A dab tells where the brush touched and how large the dab was. The **tip** decides which pixels the dab covers, and how much it covers them.

For each pixel, the answer is a number from 0 to 1, the **coverage**. 1 is full coverage, 0 is no coverage, and 0.5 is half coverage.

The engine calculates the coverage for three types of tip:

- A round tip with a soft edge.
- A flat tip, which is an ellipse.
- A flat tip at an angle. The angle is fixed, or it follows the stroke.

## Which pixels to examine

A dab can touch only the pixels within its radius from its centre. Thus the code examines the square around the dab, cut at the edges of the image, and no other pixels:

```zig
    /// The pixels that a circle of `radius` around (`x`, `y`) can touch, cut
    /// to a `w` by `h` image. The function calculates in `f32` and clamps
    /// before the conversion, because a dab can start far outside the image.
    pub fn around(x: f32, y: f32, radius: f32, w: u32, h: u32) Rect {
        const fw: f32 = @floatFromInt(w);
        const fh: f32 = @floatFromInt(h);
        return .{
            .x0 = @intFromFloat(std.math.clamp(@floor(x - radius), 0, fw)),
            .y0 = @intFromFloat(std.math.clamp(@floor(y - radius), 0, fh)),
            .x1 = @intFromFloat(std.math.clamp(@ceil(x + radius), 0, fw)),
            .y1 = @intFromFloat(std.math.clamp(@ceil(y + radius), 0, fh)),
        };
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `around` from `examples/paint/src/engine/geometry.zig`.*

A 20-pixel dab examines a 40 by 40 square, which is 1,600 pixels. The full 640 by 400 image is 256,000 pixels. Thus, for each dab, the square is 160 times less work.

The code calculates the square in `f32` and clamps it before it changes it to an integer. A dab can start far outside the image. A direct conversion from a negative `f32` to a `u32` is illegal behaviour, and Zig examines it in safe builds.

## A soft round tip

For a round tip, the coverage depends only on the distance `d` from the centre of the dab to the centre of the pixel.

The **hardness** of the brush is the solid part of the radius. With radius 20 and hardness 0.6:

- Inside 12 pixels (0.6 × 20), the coverage is 1.
- From 12 to 20 pixels, the coverage decreases in a straight line from 1 to 0.
- After 20 pixels, the coverage is 0.

At 16 pixels, which is the middle of the soft band, the coverage is 0.5.

At hardness 1, the band has no width. Then the edge of each dab is a staircase of full pixels. Thus the band is never narrower than one pixel. One pixel is sufficient to make the edge smooth.

## Pixel centres

A pixel is a small square, not a point. Pixel (5, 3) covers x from 5 to 6 and y from 3 to 4. Its centre is (5.5, 3.5).

The tip measures the distance to the centre. If the tip used the corner, each dab would be half a pixel up and to the left of its correct position. The [Scale and Resample](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/resample/) chapter shows how the same half-pixel mistake moves a full image.

## Make the tip flat and turn it

A calligraphy nib is not round. It is flat.

A flat tip is an ellipse. It has the full width along one axis, and `aspect` multiplied by that width along the other axis. With radius 20 and aspect 0.25, the tip is 40 pixels wide and 10 pixels high.

To draw an ellipse, the code changes the problem back into a circle:

1. Take the offset of the pixel from the centre, `dx` and `dy`.
2. Turn the offset by the angle of the tip. Then `u` is along the tip, and `v` is across it.
3. Divide `v` by the aspect.

Now a point on the edge of the ellipse is exactly on the circle with the original radius. Thus the coverage rule of the round tip works without a change.

This function is the full tip, with all three types:

```zig
    /// Add one dab of the tip.
    ///
    /// `hardness` is the solid fraction of the radius, `aspect` makes the tip
    /// an ellipse, and `flow` is how much one dab adds.
    pub fn stamp(m: *Mask, dab: Dab, hardness: f32, aspect: f32, flow: f32) void {
        m.stampOn(null, 1, dab, hardness, aspect, flow);
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `stamp` from `examples/paint/src/engine/mask.zig`.*

The code calculates `@cos` and `@sin` one time for each dab, not one time for each pixel. A 20-pixel dab examines 1,600 pixels and uses the same two numbers for all of them.

## Follow the direction

A nib at a fixed angle gives calligraphy. Lines along the nib are thin, and lines across the nib are wide, with no change in pressure. The Calligraphy brush in the studio does this, at −45 degrees.

A tip can also turn with the stroke. The stroke knows its direction already. Each `move` calculates the direction from its segment:

```zig
s.direction = std.math.atan2(b.y - a.y, b.x - a.x);
```

`atan2` takes the change in y and the change in x, and returns the angle, from −π to π. A movement to the right gives 0. A movement down the page gives π/2, which is a quarter turn, because y increases downwards on a screen.

With `follow_direction`, the angle of the dab is that direction plus the angle of the brush:

- At 0, the flat tip is along the stroke, and it draws a thin line.
- At 90, the flat tip is across the stroke, and it draws a wide ribbon. The Ribbon brush does this.

## Checks

This test is the soft tip from the example. The tip is solid to 12 pixels, half at 16, and empty after 20.

```zig
test "radius 20, hardness 0.6 is solid to 12 and half at 16" {
    var m = try Mask.init(std.testing.allocator, 64, 64);
    defer m.deinit(std.testing.allocator);
    // Put the centre on a pixel corner. Then the centre of the pixel at
    // (32 + k, 32) is k + 0.5 pixels from the dab.
    m.stamp(.{ .x = 32, .y = 32, .radius = 20, .angle = 0, .direction = 0, .color = .{ 0, 0, 0 }, .load = 1 }, 0.6, 1, 1);
    const at = struct {
        fn f(mm: Mask, k: u32) f32 {
            return @as(f32, @floatFromInt(mm.at(32 + k, 32))) / full;
        }
    }.f;
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f32, 1), at(m, 11)); // 11.5 from the centre
    try std.testing.expectApproxEqAbs(@as(f32, 0.5), at(m, 15), 0.07); // 15.5
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f32, 0), at(m, 20)); // 20.5, outside
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `radius 20, hardness 0.6 is solid to 12 and half at 16` from `examples/paint/src/engine/mask.zig`.*

The test puts the centre of the dab on a pixel corner. Thus the centre of the pixel at offset `k` is `k + 0.5` pixels away. That is why the checks use 11, 15 and 20.

This test examines the flat tip, and then the same tip after a quarter turn:

```zig
test "aspect 0.25 makes a tip 40 wide and 10 high" {
    var m = try Mask.init(std.testing.allocator, 64, 64);
    defer m.deinit(std.testing.allocator);
    m.stamp(.{ .x = 32, .y = 32, .radius = 20, .angle = 0, .direction = 0, .color = .{ 0, 0, 0 }, .load = 1 }, 1, 0.25, 1);
    try std.testing.expect(m.at(32 + 18, 32) > 0);
    try std.testing.expect(m.at(32, 32 + 6) == 0);
    try std.testing.expect(m.at(32, 32 + 3) > 0);
    // After a quarter turn, the same tip is tall, not wide.
    var t = try Mask.init(std.testing.allocator, 64, 64);
    defer t.deinit(std.testing.allocator);
    t.stamp(.{ .x = 32, .y = 32, .radius = 20, .angle = std.math.pi / 2.0, .direction = 0, .color = .{ 0, 0, 0 }, .load = 1 }, 1, 0.25, 1);
    try std.testing.expect(t.at(32, 32 + 18) > 0);
    try std.testing.expect(t.at(32 + 6, 32) == 0);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `aspect 0.25 makes a tip 40 wide and 10 high` from `examples/paint/src/engine/mask.zig`.*

This test uses a dab that is mostly outside the image. The dab must touch only the pixels inside the image:

```zig

    var m = try Mask.init(std.testing.allocator, 8, 8);
    defer m.deinit(std.testing.allocator);
    m.stamp(.{ .x = -3, .y = 4, .radius = 5, .angle = 0, .direction = 0, .color = .{ 0, 0, 0 }, .load = 1 }, 1, 1, 1);
```

## Explain before you read the answer

The Calligraphy brush has an aspect of 0.2 and an angle of −45 degrees.

You draw a line from the bottom left to the top right of the page. Is the line thin or wide?

The line is thin. On the screen, y increases downwards, thus −45 degrees points up and to the right. That is the direction of your line. The long side of the nib is along the line, and the line is only as wide as the short side.

---

## Bristles and Paper

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/bristles-and-paper/*

A real brush is not a solid disc. It is a bundle of hairs.

When the brush has much paint, the hairs push together and make one solid mark. When the brush is almost dry, each hair makes its own thin track. The tracks break at each dip in the surface of the paper.

The Dry brush in the studio does both. It needs two new brush settings:

- **bristles**: the number of hairs, from 0 (a solid tip) to 16.
- **contact**: how much of the paper the brush touches, from 0 to 1.

## Hairs across the stroke

A bristle brush stamps one small round dab for each hair, instead of one large dab.

The hairs are in a row across the stroke, at right angles to its movement. If the stroke moves in direction `θ`, the direction straight across the stroke is:

```
(−sin θ, cos θ)
```

For a movement to the right, θ is 0, and the result is (0, 1): straight down the page. For a movement down the page, θ is a quarter turn, and the result is (−1, 0): to the left. In both cases, the direction is across the stroke.

Each hair has an **offset** from −1 (one edge of the tip) to 1 (the other edge). The position of the hair is the centre of the dab, plus the product of the direction across, the offset and the radius.

With radius 20 and offset −0.5, a stroke that moves to the right puts that hair 10 pixels above the centre.

```zig
        pub fn dab(p: Painter, d: Dab) void {
            const b = p.brush;
            const doc = p.doc;
            if (b.bristles == 0) {
                doc.mask.stampOn(&doc.paper, b.contact, d, b.hardness, b.aspect, b.flow);
                doc.stale = doc.stale.join(Rect.around(d.x, d.y, d.radius, doc.width, doc.height));
                return;
            }

            // A bristle brush is a row of thin hairs across the stroke. Each
            // hair is a small round dab on the line at right angles to the
            // direction of movement.
            const across_x = -@sin(d.direction);
            const across_y = @cos(d.direction);
            const count: f32 = @floatFromInt(b.bristles);
            // Each hair is half as wide as its space. Thus the tracks stay apart,
            // also after the small random movements in `Hairs`.
            const hair_radius = @max(d.radius / count * 0.5, 0.75);
            for (p.hairs.offset[0..b.bristles], p.hairs.flow[0..b.bristles]) |offset, flow| {
                var hair = d;
                hair.x += across_x * offset * d.radius;
                hair.y += across_y * offset * d.radius;
                hair.radius = hair_radius;
                doc.mask.stampOn(&doc.paper, b.contact, hair, b.hardness, 1, b.flow * flow);
            }
            doc.stale = doc.stale.join(Rect.around(d.x, d.y, d.radius + hair_radius, doc.width, doc.height));
        }
```

*Quoted from the source: `dab` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

The direction comes from the stroke. Each dab now has its direction of movement, and also the angle of the tip. The two values are separate because you can turn a tip to any angle, but the hairs must always spread across the path.

## The positions of the hairs

Hairs at exactly equal distances look like a comb. Thus the code moves each hair by a small random distance. It also gives each hair its own part of the flow, so that some tracks are fainter than others:

```zig
    /// The position of each hair of a bristle brush across the tip, and how
    /// much paint the hair carries. The code makes the hairs from the seed of
    /// the brush. Thus the same brush always has the same hairs, and a painter
    /// can make them again on each call. It does not have to store them.
    const Hairs = struct {
        /// From -1 (one edge of the tip) to 1 (the other).
        offset: [max_bristles]f32,
        /// A part of the flow of the brush, from 0.55 to 1.
        flow: [max_bristles]f32,

        fn layOut(b: Brush) Hairs {
            var h: Hairs = undefined;
            var random: Random = .init(b.seed +% 0x9e37);
            const n: f32 = @floatFromInt(@max(b.bristles, 1));
            for (0..max_bristles) |i| {
                const even = -1.0 + (2.0 * @as(f32, @floatFromInt(i)) + 1.0) / n;
                // Equal distances, then a movement of up to a third of the gap.
                // Thus the tracks are not a perfect comb.
                h.offset[i] = even + (random.next() - 0.5) * (2.0 / n) / 3.0;
                h.flow[i] = 0.55 + 0.45 * random.next();
            }
            return h;
        }
    };
```

*Quoted from the source: `Hairs` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

The code makes the layout from the seed of the brush. The same brush always has the same hairs. Thus the program does not store the layout. The painter makes the layout again on each call.

This decision also prevents a bug that this file had before. The code puts the first dab of a stroke before the document stores the stroke. Thus the painter must not get any data from the stored stroke.

Each hair is half as wide as its space. A test found a problem at 90%: after the random movements, the hairs touched each other, and five hairs made only three tracks.

## Paper

Real paper has a surface of very small hills and dips.

The engine stores the surface as a grid of **heights**, with one height for each cell of 4 by 4 pixels. The heights are random, from a seed. The code makes them one time, when it makes the document:

```zig
pub const Paper = struct {
    /// Width and height of one cell, in pixels.
    cell: u32,
    columns: u32,
    rows: u32,
    /// One height per cell, row by row: 0 is the bottom of a dip, 255 the
    /// top of a hill.
    heights: []u8,

    pub fn init(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, width: u32, height: u32, cell: u32, seed: u32) !Paper {
        const columns = (width + cell - 1) / cell;
        const rows = (height + cell - 1) / cell;
        const heights = try gpa.alloc(u8, @as(usize, columns) * rows);
        var random: Random = .init(seed);
        for (heights) |*h| h.* = @intFromFloat(@round(random.next() * 255.0));
        return .{ .cell = cell, .columns = columns, .rows = rows, .heights = heights };
    }

    pub fn deinit(p: *Paper, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        gpa.free(p.heights);
    }

    /// The height below pixel (`x`, `y`). All pixels in a cell have one
    /// height, thus the grain is `cell` pixels across.
    pub fn at(p: Paper, x: u32, y: u32) u8 {
        const column = @min(x / p.cell, p.columns - 1);
        const row = @min(y / p.cell, p.rows - 1);
        return p.heights[@as(usize, row) * p.columns + column];
    }

    /// Whether a brush with this `contact` (0 to 1) reaches the paper at
    /// (`x`, `y`). Full contact reaches every height. Less contact reaches
    /// only the hills: at 0.3, only heights in the top 30%.
    pub fn touches(p: Paper, x: u32, y: u32, contact: f32) bool {
        const threshold = (1.0 - contact) * 255.0;
        return @as(f32, @floatFromInt(p.at(x, y))) >= threshold;
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Paper` from `examples/paint/src/engine/paper.zig`.*

The paper does not move. If you draw two strokes across the same area, both strokes touch the same hills. Real grain does the same.

To find the height below a pixel, divide by the cell size:

```
column = x / 4
row    = y / 4
index  = row × columns + column
```

The pixel at (22, 10) is in column 5 and row 2. A 640-pixel document has 160 columns. Thus the cell of the pixel is number 2 × 160 + 5 = 325.

## Contact

A wet brush pushes into the dips. A dry brush touches only the tops of the hills.

**Contact** tells how deep the brush goes. A pixel gets paint only if its paper is sufficiently high:

```zig
    /// Whether a brush with this `contact` (0 to 1) reaches the paper at
    /// (`x`, `y`). Full contact reaches every height. Less contact reaches
    /// only the hills: at 0.3, only heights in the top 30%.
    pub fn touches(p: Paper, x: u32, y: u32, contact: f32) bool {
        const threshold = (1.0 - contact) * 255.0;
        return @as(f32, @floatFromInt(p.at(x, y))) >= threshold;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `touches` from `examples/paint/src/engine/paper.zig`.*

At contact 0.3, the brush touches only heights in the top 30%. A height of 0.8 gets paint, and a height of 0.4 does not. At contact 0.9, both heights get paint. At 1, all heights get paint. That is why all of the other brushes work exactly as before.

The check is inside the loop of the tip, immediately after the distance test:

```zig
if (paper) |pp| if (!pp.touches(x, y, contact)) continue;
```

If the brush does not touch a pixel, the pixel gets no coverage from this dab. Another dab of the same stroke does not change the result, because that dab touches the same paper.

```zig
test "a dry brush skips the paper's dips, the same ones every time" {
    var d = try newDoc();
    defer d.deinit();

    d.beginStroke(dry, .brush, .{ .x = 0, .y = 24 });
```

```zig
    var d = try newDoc();
    defer d.deinit();
```

## Explain before you read the answer

A bristle brush moves along the track of one hair. The hair touches a pixel whose paper is too low for the contact of the brush.

Does the track of the hair continue after the gap?

Yes, it does. The gap is in the paint, not in the stroke. The stroke continues along the path and puts more dabs. The next dab on higher paper paints again. The result is the broken line of a dry brush.

---

## Oil: Pickup and Paint Load

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/oil/*

Each brush in the previous chapters puts down one colour. The colour is the same at the end of a stroke and at the start.

A brush with oil paint is different. Two things change while the brush moves:

- **Pickup.** The brush collects some of the paint below it. Thus its colour moves towards the colour below it.
- **Load.** The brush becomes dry. It has less paint after each centimetre, and the stroke becomes fainter.

Select the Oil brush in the studio. Paint some colours, and then pull the Oil brush across them.

## The brush carries paint

For these two effects, the stroke must keep two values from one dab to the next. The values are the colour on the brush and the quantity of paint that remains.

Thus the stroke has two new fields:

```zig
pub const Stroke = struct {
    brush: Brush,
    random: Random,
    /// The smoothed pointer position.
    filtered: Point,
    /// The end of the last segment. The next dabs start from here.
    last: Point,
    /// The distance since the last dab, in pixels. Always less than `gap`.
    carry: f32,
    /// The direction of movement, in radians. 0 (to the right) until the first move.
    direction: f32,
    /// The colour on the brush. It is in `f32`, thus small pickups accumulate,
    /// and the rounding does not remove them. Starts as the brush colour.
    loaded: [3]f32,
    /// The paint left on the brush. Every stroke starts with a full brush.
    load: f32,

    /// Start a stroke at `p` and put the first dab there, so a click with no
    /// movement still leaves a mark.

    // ...
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Stroke` (fields only) from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

The first value of `loaded` is the brush colour. The first value of `load` is 1, which is a full brush. Each stroke starts with a full brush.

## Pickup

Before each dab, the brush examines the paint below it. Then it moves its colour part of the distance to that paint:

```
loaded = loaded + (under − loaded) × pickup
```

This is `lerp` again, one time each for red, green and blue.

For example, the loaded red is 200, the paint below it has red 100, and `pickup` is 0.2. The new loaded red is 200 + (100 − 200) × 0.2 = 180. Over the same paint again, the result is 180 + (100 − 180) × 0.2 = 164.

The brush carries the colour to the next dab. Thus the paint from one area moves a short distance along the stroke, and that is the smear.

The pickup occurs in `emit`:

```zig
    fn emit(s: *Stroke, p: Point, sink: anytype) void {
        const b = s.brush;

        // Pressure: at `pressure = 0` the size ignores the pen.
        // At 1, a light touch draws at a quarter of the size.
        const p2 = p.pressure * p.pressure;
        var radius = b.radius * geometry.lerp(1.0, 0.25 + 0.75 * p2, b.pressure);

        // Three random numbers for each dab, also if the code does not use them.
        // Thus a change to scatter does not change the size of each later dab.
        const u_size = s.random.next();
        const u_angle = s.random.next();
        const u_reach = s.random.next();

        radius *= 1.0 - b.jitter * u_size;

        // Scatter across a disc. The square root spreads the offsets equally
        // over the area. Without it, the offsets collect at the centre.
        const theta = 2.0 * std.math.pi * u_angle;
        const reach = b.scatter * b.radius * @sqrt(u_reach);
        const x = p.x + @cos(theta) * reach;
        const y = p.y + @sin(theta) * reach;

        // Pickup: before the dab, the brush takes part of the paint that is
        // already below it. The brush carries the colour to the next dab. Thus
        // paint moves along the stroke. Thin paint gives less, and empty paper
        // gives nothing: a brush cannot collect the paper.
        if (b.pickup > 0) {
            if (sink.sample(x, y)) |under| {
                const t = b.pickup * under.cover;
                for (&s.loaded, under.color) |*c, u| c.* = geometry.lerp(c.*, @floatFromInt(u), t);
            }
        }

        sink.dab(.{
            .x = x,
            .y = y,
            .radius = radius,
            // When the tip follows the direction, the brush angle is an offset from
            // the direction. 0 puts the tip along the stroke, and 90 puts it across.
            .angle = (if (b.follow_direction) s.direction else 0) + b.angle * std.math.pi / 180.0,
            .direction = s.direction,
            .color = .{
                @intFromFloat(@round(s.loaded[0])),
                @intFromFloat(@round(s.loaded[1])),
                @intFromFloat(@round(s.loaded[2])),
            },
            .load = s.load,
        });
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `emit` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

The code keeps `loaded` in `f32`, not in bytes. A small pickup moves each channel by less than 1. In bytes, the rounding removes that change. Then a brush with a low pickup never changes colour.

## The brush cannot collect paper

The first version of the code took its sample from the picture on the screen: the layer over white paper.

The oil stroke in the demo is red, and it starts on empty paper. After a small number of dabs, the brush was white. Then it painted white over the dark stroke below it. The brush collected the paper.

Paper is not paint. Thus the code now takes the sample from the layer. The sample gives the quantity of paint and also its colour:

```zig
        /// The paint that is already on the active layer at (`x`, `y`): its
        /// colour, and how much of the pixel it covers. The function reads the
        /// layer, not the stroke buffer. Thus a brush collects the paint below it,
        /// and never collects the current stroke. Empty paper is not paint, thus
        /// it gives nothing.
        pub fn sample(p: Painter, x: f32, y: f32) ?Sample {
            const doc = p.doc;
            if (!(x >= 0 and y >= 0)) return null;
            const ux: u32 = @intFromFloat(@min(x, @as(f32, @floatFromInt(doc.width - 1))));
            const uy: u32 = @intFromFloat(@min(y, @as(f32, @floatFromInt(doc.height - 1))));
            const px = doc.layers[doc.active_layer][@as(usize, uy) * doc.width + ux];
            if (px.a == 0) return null;
            // Layers are premultiplied. Thus the colour of the paint is each
            // channel divided by the alpha.
            const a: u32 = px.a;
            return .{
                .color = .{
                    @intCast((@as(u32, px.r) * 255 + a / 2) / a),
                    @intCast((@as(u32, px.g) * 255 + a / 2) / a),
                    @intCast((@as(u32, px.b) * 255 + a / 2) / a),
                },
                .cover = @as(f32, @floatFromInt(a)) / 255.0,
            };
        }
```

*Quoted from the source: `sample` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

Empty paper returns `null`, thus the brush collects nothing. If paint covers half of a pixel, the paint has half of the effect: the code multiplies the pickup by `cover`.

Layers are premultiplied, as the [Layers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/layers-and-the-eraser/) chapter explains. If red 200 covers half of a pixel, the layer stores red 100. To get the colour of the paint, `sample` divides by the alpha.

The sample also comes from the layer, and never from the stroke buffer. Thus the brush collects paint that was there before the stroke. It never collects the current stroke.

## A stroke of many colours

The stroke buffer in [Flow and Opacity](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/flow-and-opacity/) held one number for each pixel, the coverage. The colour was the brush colour, the same at all pixels.

With pickup, two dabs of one stroke can have different colours. Thus the buffer now also keeps a colour for each pixel:

```zig
pub const Mask = struct {
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    coverage: []u16,
    /// The colour that the stroke puts at each pixel. For most brushes, it is
    /// the brush colour at all pixels. A brush with pickup changes colour
    /// along the stroke. Thus the buffer must keep the colour for each pixel.
    /// The value has a meaning only where `coverage` is above 0. Thus the
    /// code never clears it.
    color: [][3]u8,
    /// Each pixel outside this rectangle is 0. With this rectangle, the
    /// commit, the clear and the redraw touch only the part of the image that
    /// the stroke touched.
    dirty: Rect = .empty,

    // ...
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Mask` (fields only) from `examples/paint/src/engine/mask.zig`.*

When a dab adds coverage to a pixel, the colour of the pixel changes. The new colour is the average of the old colour and the colour of the dab. The weight of each colour is the coverage that it added.

For example, a red dab at 50% flow covers half of a pixel. A blue dab at 50% covers half of the remainder, which is a quarter. Red added two times as much as blue. Thus the colour is two thirds red and one third blue.

That weighted average is the same result as blue paint on red paint. When the two colours are the same, the average is exactly that colour, with no rounding error. Thus each brush without pickup draws the same pixels as before this change.

A test proved this. Before the change, the demo picture had a fixed hash. After the change, all of the tests ran, and the hash did not change. Only after that did the demo get an oil stroke and a new fixed hash.

## The brush becomes dry

The load decreases with distance. It does not decrease with time or with pointer samples. The [Strokes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/strokes/) chapter shows why samples are a bad measurement.

The stroke already moves along the path one gap at a time. Thus each gap uses a fixed part of the load:

```zig
s.load = @max(s.load - s.brush.drain * step / 100.0, 0);
```

`drain` is the part of a full load that the brush uses in each 100 pixels. With `drain` 0.2, 150 pixels of stroke use 0.3. Then 0.7 of a full load remains.

The load never goes below 0. The code multiplies the flow of each dab by the load. Thus a stroke becomes fainter smoothly while the brush becomes empty.

## Checks

This test is the pickup example, with 200, then 180, then 164:

```zig
test "pickup: the loaded red goes 200, 180, 164 over a red of 100 at 0.2" {
    var rec: Recorder = .{ .under = .{ .color = .{ 100, 0, 0 } } };
    var s = Stroke.begin(.{ .radius = 40, .spacing = 0.25, .pickup = 0.2, .color = .{ 200, 0, 0 } }, .{ .x = 0, .y = 0 }, &rec);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 180), rec.dabs[0].color[0]);
    s.move(.{ .x = 10, .y = 0 }, &rec);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 164), rec.dabs[1].color[0]);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `pickup: the loaded red goes 200, 180, 164 over a red of 100 at 0.2` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

*Quoted from the source: `pickup from paint that half covers the paper is half as strong` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

This test is the drain example. It cuts the stroke into samples in two ways, and the two results must be the same:

```zig
test "drain 0.2 over 150 pixels uses 0.3 of a load, whatever the samples" {
    // A gap of 10 pixels. 150 pixels of stroke is 15 gaps.
    const brush: Brush = .{ .radius = 40, .spacing = 0.25, .drain = 0.2 };
    var one: Recorder = .{};
    var s1 = Stroke.begin(brush, .{ .x = 0, .y = 0 }, &one);
    s1.move(.{ .x = 150, .y = 0 }, &one);
    var many: Recorder = .{};
    var s2 = Stroke.begin(brush, .{ .x = 0, .y = 0 }, &many);
    var x: f32 = 0;
    while (x < 150) {
        x = @min(x + 7, 150);
        s2.move(.{ .x = x, .y = 0 }, &many);
    }
    try std.testing.expectApproxEqAbs(@as(f32, 0.7), s1.load, 1e-5);
    try std.testing.expectApproxEqAbs(s1.load, s2.load, 1e-5);
    // The load never goes below empty.
    s1.move(.{ .x = 2000, .y = 0 }, &one);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(f32, 0), s1.load);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `drain 0.2 over 150 pixels uses 0.3 of a load, whatever the samples` from `examples/paint/src/engine/stroke.zig`.*

This test examines how the stroke buffer mixes colours:

```zig
test "two colours mix by the coverage each one added" {
    var m = try Mask.init(std.testing.allocator, 16, 16);
    defer m.deinit(std.testing.allocator);
    const at: Dab = .{ .x = 8, .y = 8, .radius = 6, .angle = 0, .direction = 0, .color = .{ 200, 0, 0 }, .load = 1 };
    m.stamp(at, 1, 1, 0.5);
```

## Explain before you read the answer

Set `pickup` to 1. Then pull the brush from a blue area onto empty paper.

What does the brush paint?

Over the blue, each dab takes all of the blue below it. Thus the brush paints blue on blue, and nothing seems to change. On the paper, there is nothing to collect. Thus the brush keeps the last blue that it took, and paints that blue on the paper. The stroke pulls the blue out of its area, as a finger does through wet paint.

---

## Flow and Opacity

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/flow-and-opacity/*

A brush has two settings, and both seem to mean "how much paint":

- **Flow** is the quantity that one dab adds.
- **Opacity** is the maximum coverage of the full stroke.

The two settings are different. The difference is visible when dabs overlap. Each stroke is a set of dabs that overlap, thus the difference is visible in all strokes.

## The problem

For example, the code draws each dab directly onto the layer at 50%.

Two dabs overlap at a pixel. The first dab covers 50% of the pixel. The second dab covers half of the remainder, thus the pixel has 75% coverage. Along a slow stroke, ten dabs overlap, and the pixel is almost at 100%.

Thus a stroke "at 50%" is solid in the middle. It is darker where it crosses itself, and darker again where you moved slowly.

That result is correct for flow. An airbrush adds paint in the same way. The result is incorrect for opacity. Opacity must be a limit, and the full stroke must never go past that limit.

## The stroke buffer

The solution is to keep the stroke off the layer until the stroke is complete.

While you draw, the dabs go into a separate buffer. The buffer holds one number for each pixel: how much of that pixel the stroke covers.

```zig
pub const Mask = struct {
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    coverage: []u16,
    /// The colour that the stroke puts at each pixel. For most brushes, it is
    /// the brush colour at all pixels. A brush with pickup changes colour
    /// along the stroke. Thus the buffer must keep the colour for each pixel.
    /// The value has a meaning only where `coverage` is above 0. Thus the
    /// code never clears it.
    color: [][3]u8,
    /// Each pixel outside this rectangle is 0. With this rectangle, the
    /// commit, the clear and the redraw touch only the part of the image that
    /// the stroke touched.
    dirty: Rect = .empty,

    // ...
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Mask` (fields only) from `examples/paint/src/engine/mask.zig`.*

When you release the pointer, the stroke goes onto the layer one time. The code multiplies its coverage by the opacity.

Dabs that overlap only increase the coverage towards 1. The opacity applies one time after that. Thus, where the coverage is 1, the stroke covers exactly 50%, and no more.

## Add coverage

Each dab adds `flow` multiplied by the part that has no coverage. In the stamp loop:

```zig
const new = old + ((full - old) * add + full - 1) / full;
m.coverage[i] = @intCast(new);
```

`full - old` is the part that has no coverage. `add` is the coverage of the dab at this pixel, multiplied by the flow.

After `n` dabs of flow `f`, the coverage is 1 − (1 − f)ⁿ. For example, two dabs at 20% flow give 1 − 0.8² = 0.36, not 0.40.

With each dab, the coverage moves nearer to 1. The coverage never goes past 1, for any number of dabs.

## Why 16 bits

The coverage is a `u16`: 0 is no coverage, and 65535 is full coverage.

Eight bits are not sufficient. The Airbrush in the studio has a flow of 4%. In 8 bits, 4% of 255 is 10.2, and the rounding makes it 10.

There is a worse problem. The soft edge of a tip contains small fractions of that 10. The rounding makes them 0, 1, 2 and 3, and the edge has visible steps.

In 16 bits, 4% is 2621, and the steps are too small to see.

## The rounding bug that a test found

The line above rounds the step **up**: it adds `full - 1` before the division.

The first version rounded to the nearest value, and a test found the problem. The test stamps 200 dabs at 30% flow and expects full coverage. With the rounding to the nearest value, the coverage stopped at 65534.

At 65534, the part without coverage is 1. One dab adds 30% of 1, which is 0.3, and the rounding makes 0.3 into 0. Thus each subsequent dab added nothing, and the stroke never gave a pixel full coverage.

When the code rounds up, the step is at least 1 while some part has no coverage. The step still never goes past full, because the step after rounding up is never larger than the gap that it fills.

## Put the stroke on the layer

`endStroke` does three things:

1. It keeps the old pixels for undo.
2. It applies the stroke to each pixel that the buffer touched.
3. It clears the buffer.

```zig
    /// Put the stroke onto its layer, once, and keep the old pixels for undo.
    pub fn endStroke(d: *Document) void {
        const active = d.stroke orelse return;
        const r = d.mask.dirty;
        const layer = d.layers[active.layer];

        d.history_ok = d.history.record(d.gpa, active.layer, layer, d.width, r);

        var y = r.y0;
        while (y < r.y1) : (y += 1) {
            var x = r.x0;
            while (x < r.x1) : (x += 1) {
                const i = @as(usize, y) * d.width + x;
                layer[i] = applyStroke(active, layer[i], d.mask.coverage[i], d.mask.color[i]);
            }
        }
        d.mask.clear();
        d.stroke = null;
        d.stale = d.stale.join(r);
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `endStroke` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

`endStroke` examines only `mask.dirty`, the rectangle that the dabs of the stroke touched. A short stroke in a corner touches only that corner, not the full layer.

`applyStroke` does the work for each pixel:

```zig
    /// One pixel of a layer with the stroke applied. The preview on the screen
    /// and the commit both call this function. Thus the stroke that you see
    /// while you draw is exactly the stroke that you get when you release it.
    fn applyStroke(active: Active, below: Rgba, coverage: u16, color: [3]u8) Rgba {
        const amount = (@as(u32, coverage) * active.opacity + 32767) / 65535;
        return switch (active.tool) {
            .brush => pixel.paint(below, color, amount),
            .eraser => pixel.erase(below, amount),
        };
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `applyStroke` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

## What you see while you draw

The stroke is not on the layer until you release the pointer. But you must see the stroke while you draw.

Thus the code applies the stroke while it builds the screen. When it builds a pixel of the active layer, it runs the same `applyStroke` first:

```zig
    /// One screen pixel: white paper, then each visible layer from the
    /// bottom up.
    fn composite(d: *const Document, x: u32, y: u32) Rgba {
        const i = @as(usize, y) * d.width + x;
        var out: Rgba = .white;
        for (d.layers, d.visible, 0..) |layer, visible, li| {
            if (!visible) continue;
            var p = layer[i];
            if (d.stroke) |active| {
                if (active.layer == li) p = applyStroke(active, p, d.mask.coverage[i], d.mask.color[i]);
            }
            out = pixel.over(p, out);
        }
        return out;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `composite` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

The preview and the commit call the same function with the same numbers. Thus the stroke cannot change when you release the pointer. A test makes sure of this. It calculates the hash of the screen immediately before `endStroke` and immediately after it, and the two hashes must be the same.

## Cancel a stroke

Something can interrupt a stroke. The browser can take the pointer away when a dialog opens, or the window can lose focus in the middle of a stroke.

If the code commits half of a stroke, the result is a mark that the person did not complete. If the code does not change the buffer, an unwanted image of the stroke stays on the screen.

The stroke is still only in the buffer. Thus it is easy to cancel the stroke: clear the buffer and draw that rectangle again.

```zig
    /// Drop the current stroke, and change no layer. A front end calls this
    /// function when it loses the pointer during a stroke.
    pub fn cancelStroke(d: *Document) void {
        if (d.stroke == null) return;
        d.stale = d.stale.join(d.mask.dirty);
        d.mask.clear();
        d.stroke = null;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `cancelStroke` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

## Explain before you read the answer

You draw one stroke at 50% opacity. Then you draw a second stroke at 50% across the first stroke.

Where the strokes cross, is the colour 50% or 75%?

The colour is 75%. Each stroke has its own buffer, thus each stroke has a limit of 50%. But the second stroke goes over the result of the first stroke, as a second layer of paint does. The result is the first 50%, plus 50% of the 50% that had no coverage.

---

## Layers and the Eraser

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/layers-and-the-eraser/*

A **layer** is a sheet of clear plastic that you can paint on.

Put two sheets on white paper. If you paint on the top sheet, the bottom sheet does not change. If you clean the top sheet, you can see the bottom sheet again.

The engine has two of these layers, on white paper.

## A layer is an array

A layer has one pixel for each position, row by row. Thus it has `width * height` pixels.

Each pixel has four bytes: red, green, blue, and alpha. Alpha is the coverage of the pixel. 0 is clear plastic, and 255 is solid paint.

```zig
/// `extern` fixes the field order in memory. A row of these values has the
/// R, G, B, A bytes in the order that a browser canvas expects. Thus the
/// display needs no conversion.
pub const Rgba = extern struct {
    r: u8,
    g: u8,
    b: u8,
    a: u8,

    pub const transparent: Rgba = .{ .r = 0, .g = 0, .b = 0, .a = 0 };
    pub const white: Rgba = .{ .r = 255, .g = 255, .b = 255, .a = 255 };

    pub fn opaqueRgb(c: [3]u8) Rgba {
        return .{ .r = c[0], .g = c[1], .b = c[2], .a = 255 };
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Rgba` from `examples/paint/src/engine/pixel.zig`.*

`extern` fixes the order of the fields in memory: R, G, B, A, one byte each. A browser canvas expects that order. Thus the code can copy the screen buffer to a canvas with no conversion. With a plain Zig `struct`, the compiler can change the order of the fields.

Two layers at 640 by 400 hold 2 × 640 × 400 × 4 = 2,048,000 bytes. The program does not store the white paper. The white paper is the start value of the drawing.

## Draw the stack

To get the colour of one screen pixel, start with white paper. Then put each visible layer on it, from the bottom up:

```zig
    /// One screen pixel: white paper, then each visible layer from the
    /// bottom up.
    fn composite(d: *const Document, x: u32, y: u32) Rgba {
        const i = @as(usize, y) * d.width + x;
        var out: Rgba = .white;
        for (d.layers, d.visible, 0..) |layer, visible, li| {
            if (!visible) continue;
            var p = layer[i];
            if (d.stroke) |active| {
                if (active.layer == li) p = applyStroke(active, p, d.mask.coverage[i], d.mask.color[i]);
            }
            out = pixel.over(p, out);
        }
        return out;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `composite` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

The order is important. A solid pixel on the top layer hides the bottom layer. If you change the order of the layers, the result is the opposite.

The engine does this only for the rectangle that changed. A dab touches some hundreds of pixels. Thus the engine composites only those pixels again.

## Premultiplied alpha

There are two ways to store a red pixel with half coverage:

- **Straight** alpha stores the colour and the coverage separately: (255, 0, 0, 128). This is full red with half coverage.
- **Premultiplied** alpha stores the colour after a multiplication by the coverage: (128, 0, 0, 128).

The layers in this program are premultiplied, because of the eraser.

## The eraser

On white paper, white paint and the eraser look the same.

Over another layer, they are different. White paint covers the layer below it. The eraser removes paint from its own layer, thus you can see the layer below.

To erase means "keep less of this pixel". With premultiplied values, that is the same multiplication on all four channels:

```zig
/// Remove `amount` (0 to 65535) of `dst`. White paint and the eraser look
/// the same on white paper. Over another layer, white covers it and the
/// eraser reveals it.
pub fn erase(dst: Rgba, amount: u32) Rgba {
    const keep = full - amount;
    return .{
        .r = @intCast(scale(dst.r, keep)),
        .g = @intCast(scale(dst.g, keep)),
        .b = @intCast(scale(dst.b, keep)),
        .a = @intCast(scale(dst.a, keep)),
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `erase` from `examples/paint/src/engine/pixel.zig`.*

If you erase a pixel fully, each channel becomes 0. No colour remains.

With straight alpha, a red pixel after a full erase is (255, 0, 0, 0). You cannot see it, but it is still red. That hidden red is a known cause of bugs. If you scale or blur the layer, the code averages the hidden red with the pixels near it. Then the red is visible again as a red edge along each erased area.

## Paint and combine

To paint, the code puts a colour over a pixel with a given coverage:

```zig
/// Lay `color` over `dst` with coverage `amount` (0 to 65535).
pub fn paint(dst: Rgba, color: [3]u8, amount: u32) Rgba {
    const keep = full - amount;
    return .{
        .r = @intCast(scale(color[0], amount) + scale(dst.r, keep)),
        .g = @intCast(scale(color[1], amount) + scale(dst.g, keep)),
        .b = @intCast(scale(color[2], amount) + scale(dst.b, keep)),
        .a = @intCast(scale(255, amount) + scale(dst.a, keep)),
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `paint` from `examples/paint/src/engine/pixel.zig`.*

To combine two layers, the code uses the "over" operator from the [Alpha Blending](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/blending/) chapter, without its first multiplication. The colour in `top` is already multiplied by its alpha:

```zig
/// `top` over `below`, both premultiplied. This is the operator from the
/// Alpha Blending chapter, without its multiply: the colour in `top` is
/// already scaled by its alpha.
pub fn over(top: Rgba, below: Rgba) Rgba {
    const keep = (255 - @as(u32, top.a)) * 257; // 255 * 257 = 65535
    return .{
        .r = @intCast(top.r + scale(below.r, keep)),
        .g = @intCast(top.g + scale(below.g, keep)),
        .b = @intCast(top.b + scale(below.b, keep)),
        .a = @intCast(top.a + scale(below.a, keep)),
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `over` from `examples/paint/src/engine/pixel.zig`.*

All of this is integer arithmetic, with rounding to the nearest whole number. Two roundings in one sum can cause a problem: if two halves both round up, the total is one too large. In a `u8`, that total is 256, which does not fit. Then `@intCast` stops a safe build.

That cannot occur here, but the reason is not obvious. Thus a test examines each of the 65,536 coverage values:

```zig
test "paint never overflows a byte, at any coverage" {
    // The sum of the two rounded parts is 255 or less. The sum of their
    // exact values is 255. Both parts can round up only if both end in
    // exactly .5, and `amount / 257` never does. This test examines the
    // claim. It does not trust it.
    var amount: u32 = 0;
    while (amount <= full) : (amount += 1) {
        const out = paint(.white, .{ 255, 255, 255 }, amount);
        try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 255), out.a);
        try std.testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 255), out.r);
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `paint never overflows a byte, at any coverage` from `examples/paint/src/engine/pixel.zig`.*

## Blend in bytes, not in light

The [Linear Light](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/linear-light/) chapter shows that a mix of stored bytes is not the same as a mix of light.

This engine mixes bytes. A browser canvas does the same, and so do most 8-bit paint programs.

That is a decision. Each layer stays at 4 bytes for each pixel, and the colours do what users of other paint programs expect. A program that mixes in linear light needs 8 bytes for each pixel to keep the dark tones. That doubles each number in this chapter.

## Checks

This test makes sure that a red pixel with half coverage is premultiplied:

```zig

    const p = paint(.transparent, .{ 255, 0, 0 }, full / 2 + 1);
    try std.testing.expectEqual(Rgba{ .r = 128, .g = 0, .b = 0, .a = 128 }, p);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `half red on an empty layer is stored premultiplied` from `examples/paint/src/engine/pixel.zig`.*

This test uses the eraser and white paint on the top layer, over a red bottom layer:

```zig
test "the eraser reveals the layer below, white paint covers it" {
    var d = try newDoc();
    defer d.deinit();
    const red: [3]u8 = .{ 220, 0, 0 };
    // Bottom layer: solid red everywhere.
    _ = try d.fillAt(0, 0, red);
    // Top layer: solid blue everywhere.
    _ = d.setActiveLayer(1);
    _ = try d.fillAt(0, 0, .{ 0, 0, 220 });

    const hard: Brush = .{ .radius = 5, .hardness = 1, .flow = 1, .color = .{ 255, 255, 255 } };
    d.beginStroke(hard, .eraser, .{ .x = 16, .y = 24 });
    d.endStroke();
    d.beginStroke(hard, .brush, .{ .x = 48, .y = 24 });
    d.endStroke();
    _ = d.render();

    try testing.expectEqual(Rgba.opaqueRgb(red), d.display[24 * 64 + 16]); // erased: red shows
    try testing.expectEqual(Rgba.white, d.display[24 * 64 + 48]); // white paint
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `the eraser reveals the layer below, white paint covers it` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

## Explain before you read the answer

The top layer has a solid blue pixel, (0, 0, 220, 255). You erase it at 50%.

What does the pixel store? What does the screen show over a red bottom layer?

The pixel stores (0, 0, 110, 127). Each channel is half of the channel in (0, 0, 220, 255), after rounding.

On the screen, the result is half of the blue over the red: (128, 0, 110), a purple.

Red paint at 50% over the blue shows the same purple. The difference occurs later. If you change the bottom layer to green, the erased pixel shows blue over green. The painted pixel still shows the red that you painted.

---

## Undo

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/undo/*

People expect one Undo to remove one action. One action is one stroke or one fill. It is not one dab, and it is not one pointer sample.

Thus the history saves data one time for each action, immediately before the action changes a layer. The question is which data to save.

## A copy of the full picture is expensive

The simplest answer is a copy of each layer.

At 640 by 400 with two layers, one copy is 2 × 640 × 400 × 4 = 2,048,000 bytes. Eight undo steps need 16,384,000 bytes, about 15.6 MiB.

That is much memory for a short line in one corner. Most of each copy is pixels that the action did not touch.

## Save only the changes

Each action in this program knows the rectangle that it touches:

- A stroke gets the rectangle from the `dirty` rectangle of the stroke buffer.
- A fill knows the bounds of the area that it found.

Thus the history copies that rectangle, from that one layer, immediately before the action changes it.

A stroke 100 pixels wide and 60 pixels high saves 100 × 60 × 4 = 24,000 bytes. That is about 1% of a full copy.

```zig
pub const Entry = struct {
    layer: u32,
    rect: Rect,
    /// `rect.area()` pixels, row by row.
    pixels: []Rgba,

    fn bytes(e: Entry) usize {
        return e.pixels.len * @sizeOf(Rgba);
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Entry` from `examples/paint/src/engine/history.zig`.*

## Undo and redo are one swap

To undo, put the saved pixels back into the layer.

But redo needs the pixels that the action made. If undo puts the old pixels back with a copy, the new pixels are lost.

Thus undo does not copy. It **swaps**: the saved pixels go into the layer, and the current pixels of the layer go into the entry. Now the entry holds the newer pixels. Redo is the same swap again.

```zig
    fn swap(e: Entry, layer: []Rgba, width: u32) void {
        var i: usize = 0;
        var y = e.rect.y0;
        while (y < e.rect.y1) : (y += 1) {
            const row = @as(usize, y) * width;
            for (layer[row + e.rect.x0 .. row + e.rect.x1], e.pixels[i..][0..e.rect.width()]) |*a, *b| {
                std.mem.swap(Rgba, a, b);
            }
            i += e.rect.width();
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `swap` from `examples/paint/src/engine/history.zig`.*

One function does the two jobs. Thus undo and redo cannot become different.

## Two stacks in one array

The usual design has two stacks:

- Undo removes an entry from the **past** stack and adds it to the **future** stack.
- Redo does the opposite.

In this program, the two stacks are one array and an index, `cursor`. You can undo the entries before the cursor. You can redo the entries from the cursor to the end.

```
entries   [ A ][ B ][ C ][ D ]
                         ^
                       cursor
```

In this example, you can undo A, B and C, and you can redo D.

```zig
pub const History = struct {
    entries: std.ArrayList(Entry) = .empty,
    cursor: usize = 0,
    budget: usize,
    used: usize = 0,

    // ...
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `History` (fields only) from `examples/paint/src/engine/history.zig`.*

Undo moves the cursor back one position and swaps. Redo swaps and moves the cursor forward:

```zig
    /// Undo the newest action. Returns the entry so the caller knows which
    /// layer and rectangle to redraw, or null when there is nothing to undo.
    pub fn undo(h: *History, layers: []const []Rgba, width: u32) ?Entry {
        if (!h.canUndo()) return null;
        h.cursor -= 1;
        const e = h.entries.items[h.cursor];
        swap(e, layers[e.layer], width);
        return e;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `undo` from `examples/paint/src/engine/history.zig`.*

To move an entry from one stack to the other, the code needs space in the other stack. An allocation for that space can fail. A change to an index cannot fail. Thus undo and redo never allocate, and they never fail.

## A new action removes the future

Draw A, then draw B. Undo B. Then draw C.

Can Redo put B back now?

It must not. You drew B on top of A, before C existed. If Redo puts B over C, the result is a picture that never existed.

Thus, before `record` saves a new action, it deletes all entries from the cursor to the end. That is the first step of `record`.

## A memory budget

The history has a limit in bytes. If a new entry goes over the limit, the history removes the oldest entries until the new entry fits.

When the history removes the oldest entry, you cannot undo the earliest actions. That is the cost of a limit.

One entry can also be larger than the full budget. An example is a fill of the full page with a small budget. Then the history removes all of its entries.

If the history kept the older entries, the result would be worse. Undo would skip the action that the history could not save. Then the older entries would put back pixels from before that action, in some areas and not in others. The result would be a picture that never existed.

## When the memory is not sufficient

This is the full `record` function:

```zig
    /// Copy `rect` of `layer` before an action changes it. Returns false when
    /// the history cannot keep the copy. The copy alone can be larger than the
    /// budget, or the memory can be full. In both cases, do the action.
    pub fn record(
        h: *History,
        gpa: std.mem.Allocator,
        layer: u32,
        pixels: []const Rgba,
        width: u32,
        rect: Rect,
    ) bool {
        if (rect.isEmpty()) return true;

        // A new action starts a new branch. The entries for redo do not agree
        // with the picture now. Thus the code removes them.
        h.dropFrom(gpa, h.cursor);

        const need = rect.area() * @sizeOf(Rgba);
        if (need > h.budget) {
            // An empty history also cannot hold this entry. If the code kept the
            // old entries, undo would skip this action and restore a picture that
            // never existed. Thus the code also removes the old entries.
            h.dropFrom(gpa, 0);
            return false;
        }
        while (h.used + need > h.budget) h.dropOldest(gpa);

        // Make space in the list first. Then a failure after the copy cannot
        // leave a copy that nothing owns.
        while (true) {
            if (h.entries.ensureUnusedCapacity(gpa, 1)) |_| break else |_| {}
            if (h.entries.items.len == 0) return false;
            h.dropOldest(gpa);
        }
        const copy = while (true) {
            if (gpa.alloc(Rgba, rect.area())) |buf| break buf else |_| {}
            if (h.entries.items.len == 0) return false;
            h.dropOldest(gpa);
        };

        var i: usize = 0;
        var y = rect.y0;
        while (y < rect.y1) : (y += 1) {
            const row = @as(usize, y) * width;
            @memcpy(copy[i..][0..rect.width()], pixels[row + rect.x0 .. row + rect.x1]);
            i += rect.width();
        }
        h.entries.appendAssumeCapacity(.{ .layer = layer, .rect = rect, .pixels = copy });
        h.cursor = h.entries.items.len;
        h.used += need;
        return true;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `record` from `examples/paint/src/engine/history.zig`.*

`record` returns `bool`, not an error.

In Zig, a failed allocation is an ordinary error value, `error.OutOfMemory`. The program decides what to do with it.

In this program, the stroke is more important than its undo step. If the code cannot make the copy, the stroke still goes onto the layer. Only the undo step is lost, and `record` returns `false`. Then the studio shows a line below the canvas: you cannot undo the last action.

Before `record` stops, it removes the oldest entries one at a time and tries again. Old undo steps are less important than the new undo step.

The order of the two allocations is also important. The code first makes space in the list, and then makes the copy. If the code made the copy first and then the list could not grow, the copy would have no owner. Then the memory of the copy would leak.

## Checks

This test does undo, redo, and then the two again:

```zig
test "undo restores, redo repeats, and both can go back and forth" {
    const gpa = testing.allocator;
    var layer: [8 * 8]Rgba = @splat(.transparent);
    const layers = [_][]Rgba{&layer};
    var h: History = .init(1 << 20);
    defer h.deinit(gpa);

    const rect: Rect = .{ .x0 = 2, .y0 = 2, .x1 = 5, .y1 = 4 };
    try testing.expect(h.record(gpa, 0, &layer, 8, rect));
    fillRect(&layer, 8, rect, 9);
    const drawn = layer;

    _ = h.undo(&layers, 8).?;
    const empty: [8 * 8]Rgba = @splat(.transparent);
    try testing.expectEqual(empty, layer);
    _ = h.redo(&layers, 8).?;
    try testing.expectEqual(drawn, layer);
    _ = h.undo(&layers, 8).?;
    _ = h.redo(&layers, 8).?;
    try testing.expectEqual(drawn, layer);

    try testing.expect(h.redo(&layers, 8) == null);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `undo restores, redo repeats, and both can go back and forth` from `examples/paint/src/engine/history.zig`.*

This test is the A, B, C example:

```zig
test "drawing after an undo drops the redo branch" {
    const gpa = testing.allocator;
```

This test examines the budget, with space for exactly three entries and five actions:

```zig
test "the budget drops the oldest entries" {
    const gpa = testing.allocator;
    var layer: [8 * 8]Rgba = @splat(.transparent);
    const layers = [_][]Rgba{&layer};
    // Room for exactly three 2x2 copies.
    var h: History = .init(3 * 4 * @sizeOf(Rgba));
    defer h.deinit(gpa);

    for (0..5) |i| {
        const x: u32 = @intCast(i);
        const r: Rect = .{ .x0 = x, .y0 = 0, .x1 = x + 2, .y1 = 2 };
        try testing.expect(h.record(gpa, 0, &layer, 8, r));
        fillRect(&layer, 8, r, @intCast(i + 1));
        try testing.expect(h.used <= h.budget);
    }
    try testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), h.entries.items.len);
    var undone: usize = 0;
    while (h.undo(&layers, 8) != null) undone += 1;
    try testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 3), undone);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `the budget drops the oldest entries` from `examples/paint/src/engine/history.zig`.*

This test examines memory failures. The testing allocator of Zig can fail on purpose. The test runs the same four actions many times. Each time, a different allocation fails, until each allocation failed one time:

```zig
test "running out of memory loses undo steps, never pixels, and leaks nothing" {
    // Run the same four actions one time for each allocation that they make.
    // In each run, that one allocation fails.
    // `std.testing.checkAllAllocationFailures` cannot do this job. It expects
    // an error as the result of the failure, and here the failure must not
    // give an error.
    var fail_index: usize = 0;
    while (true) : (fail_index += 1) {
        var failing: std.testing.FailingAllocator = .init(testing.allocator, .{ .fail_index = fail_index });
        const gpa = failing.allocator();

        var layer: [8 * 8]Rgba = @splat(.transparent);
        const layers = [_][]Rgba{&layer};
        var h: History = .init(1 << 20);
        var kept: usize = 0;
        for (0..4) |i| {
            const x: u32 = @intCast(i * 2);
            const r: Rect = .{ .x0 = x, .y0 = 0, .x1 = x + 2, .y1 = 2 };
            if (h.record(gpa, 0, &layer, 8, r)) kept += 1;
            fillRect(&layer, 8, r, 200); // the action happens either way
        }
        // Every undo the history still holds must restore real pixels.
        while (h.undo(&layers, 8)) |e| {
            for (e.rect.y0..e.rect.y1) |y| for (e.rect.x0..e.rect.x1) |x| {
                try testing.expectEqual(Rgba.transparent, layer[y * 8 + x]);
            };
        }
        h.deinit(gpa);
        try testing.expectEqual(failing.allocated_bytes, failing.freed_bytes);
        if (!failing.has_induced_failure) {
            try testing.expectEqual(@as(usize, 4), kept);
            break; // every allocation has now been made to fail once
        }
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `running out of memory loses undo steps, never pixels, and leaks nothing` from `examples/paint/src/engine/history.zig`.*

Each run examines three things:

- Each action changed the layer.
- Each undo step that the history kept puts back the correct pixels.
- The test freed each byte that it allocated.

## Explain before you read the answer

The budget is 16 MiB. You fill the full 640 by 400 top layer. Then you draw 20 small strokes.

How many undo steps are there?

There are 21 undo steps. The fill saved one full layer, 1,024,000 bytes, and the strokes saved only their rectangles. The total is much less than 16 MiB. Thus the history removed nothing.
