## Fill

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/fill/*

The Fill tool paints a full area in one action.

You click one pixel. Each pixel that has the same colour and connects to that pixel changes to the new colour. The fill stops at all other colours.

That set of pixels is the **region**. The work is to find the region.

## The fill finds the region a small number of pixels at a time

The fill cannot know the shape of the region before it starts. It knows only the first pixel.

The neighbours of the first pixel that have the same colour are also in the region. Their neighbours with the same colour are in the region too, and so on.

Thus each pixel that the fill accepts can give more pixels to examine.

## Recursion is short, but it is the wrong answer

The shortest code is a function that fills one pixel and then calls itself on the four neighbours of that pixel. The code is short, but it is incorrect for a paint program.

Each call waits for the calls that it makes, thus the calls nest. A fill of an empty 640 by 400 layer nests 256,000 calls deep. Each call needs some stack space. The stack of a thread is usually 8 MiB or less, and in a browser it is much less. The program stops before the fill is complete.

## A queue and a visited map

Instead, the code keeps a list of the pixels that it must examine. This list is a **queue**, and the code takes pixels from the front:

1. Put the clicked pixel in the queue.
2. Take the next pixel from the queue.
3. Examine each of the four neighbours of that pixel. If a neighbour has the target colour and it has no mark, put a mark on it and add it to the queue.
4. Do step 2 again until the queue is empty.

The marks are in a **bit set**, with one bit for each pixel of the image. A 640 by 400 image needs 256,000 bits, which is 32,000 bytes.

```zig
/// Find the region of `pixels` connected to (`x`, `y`) that has exactly the
/// colour at (`x`, `y`).
pub fn find(
    gpa: std.mem.Allocator,
    pixels: []const Rgba,
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    x: u32,
    y: u32,
) !Region {
    const total = @as(usize, width) * height;
    var inside: std.bit_set.Dynamic = try .initEmpty(gpa, total);
    errdefer inside.deinit(gpa);

    // Each pixel goes into the queue one time at most, because the code marks
    // it when it goes in, not when it comes out. Thus the queue never needs
    // more space than the number of pixels in the image. A plain array with a
    // read position is sufficient, because the code never moves an entry.
    const queue = try gpa.alloc(u32, total);
    defer gpa.free(queue);
    var head: usize = 0;
    var tail: usize = 0;

    const target = pixels[@as(usize, y) * width + x];
    const start: u32 = y * width + x;
    inside.set(start);
    queue[tail] = start;
    tail += 1;

    var bounds: Rect = .{ .x0 = x, .y0 = y, .x1 = x + 1, .y1 = y + 1 };
    while (head < tail) {
        const i = queue[head];
        head += 1;
        const px = i % width;
        const py = i / width;
        bounds = bounds.join(.{ .x0 = px, .y0 = py, .x1 = px + 1, .y1 = py + 1 });

        // The four neighbours. Skip each neighbour that is outside an edge.
        const neighbours = [4]?u32{
            if (px > 0) i - 1 else null,
            if (px + 1 < width) i + 1 else null,
            if (py > 0) i - width else null,
            if (py + 1 < height) i + width else null,
        };
        for (neighbours) |maybe| {
            const n = maybe orelse continue;
            if (inside.isSet(n)) continue;
            if (!std.meta.eql(pixels[n], target)) continue;
            inside.set(n);
            queue[tail] = n;
            tail += 1;
        }
    }
    return .{ .inside = inside, .bounds = bounds, .count = tail };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `find` from `examples/paint/src/engine/fill.zig`.*

## Why the queue never needs to grow

The code puts a mark on a pixel when the pixel goes into the queue, not when it comes out.

Because of this small decision, no pixel can go into the queue two times. Thus the queue never holds more entries than the number of pixels in the image. The code can allocate exactly that size at the start.

The code never removes entries from the front, thus it never moves entries. The code reads at `head` and writes at `tail`. Both indexes move only forward.

For 640 by 400, the queue is 256,000 `u32` values, which is 1,024,000 bytes. The code frees the queue when `find` returns.

## Four neighbours, and the soft edge

The fill examines four neighbours: left, right, up and down. Thus two pixels that touch only at a corner are not connected. A fill stops at a diagonal gap.

The match is also exact. A pixel is in the region only if all four of its bytes are equal to the bytes of the start pixel.

The soft edge of a brush stroke has pixels with partial coverage, thus none of them is an exact match. A fill inside a soft circle stops before the edge. It leaves a thin ring of the old colour. For this reason, paint programs have a **tolerance** setting. This engine does not have tolerance, because the region rule stays simple without it.

## Fill and undo

The `fillAt` function of the document finds the region and saves its bounding rectangle for undo. Then it changes each pixel in the region:

```zig
    /// Fill the area around (`x`, `y`) on the active layer with an opaque
    /// colour. Returns false if there was nothing to change.
    pub fn fillAt(d: *Document, x: u32, y: u32, color: [3]u8) !bool {
        if (d.stroke != null or x >= d.width or y >= d.height) return false;
        const layer = d.layers[d.active_layer];
        const new: Rgba = .opaqueRgb(color);
        // If the region already has the fill colour, the fill finds the full
        // region and changes nothing.
        if (std.meta.eql(layer[@as(usize, y) * d.width + x], new)) return false;

        var region = try fill.find(d.gpa, layer, d.width, d.height, x, y);
        defer region.deinit(d.gpa);

        d.history_ok = d.history.record(d.gpa, d.active_layer, layer, d.width, region.bounds);
        var it = region.inside.iterator(.{});
        while (it.next()) |i| layer[i] = new;
        d.stale = d.stale.join(region.bounds);
        return true;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `fillAt` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

`fillAt` also examines the colour first. If a region already has the fill colour, the fill searches the full region and changes nothing. Then it leaves an undo step that does nothing.

The `errdefer` in `find` is important here. If the allocation of the queue fails, the code frees the bit set that it allocated before. Then the error returns to the caller. A test examines this: it causes each allocation to fail, one after the other.

## Explain before you read the answer

A queue gives its entries from the front. A **stack** gives its entries from the back.

If `find` took the newest pixel instead of the oldest pixel, would it find the same region?

Yes, it would. It would examine the pixels in a different order. It would go far in one direction before it returns. But it still examines each pixel that it can get to, exactly one time. The region is the same. Only the order of the visits changes.

## Save a PNG

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/saving/*

Save PNG in the studio writes the picture that you see: each visible layer over white paper.

The [Write a PNG](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/png/) chapter makes a PNG writer by hand: the signature, the chunks, a CRC on each chunk, and zlib compression. Read that chapter first. This chapter shows the changes for a real document.

There are two changes. The writer takes an allocator, and it selects a filter for each row.

## Flatten the layers

A PNG can store the transparency of the layers. But people expect to save the picture on the screen, with the white paper behind it.

The screen buffer already holds exactly that picture. Thus the save starts from the screen buffer:

```zig
    /// The picture as a PNG, flattened onto white paper.
    pub fn writePng(d: *Document, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
        d.stale = .{ .x0 = 0, .y0 = 0, .x1 = d.width, .y1 = d.height };
        _ = d.render();
        try png.write(d.gpa, out, d.display, d.width, d.height);
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `writePng` from `examples/paint/src/engine/document.zig`.*

`writePng` marks the full screen as stale and renders it first. Usually the engine draws again only the areas that changed. A saved file must not depend on the last areas that the engine drew.

## An allocator, not global variables

The writer in the PNG chapter kept its buffers in global variables. That works for one fixed size of picture.

A document can be of any size. Thus this writer takes an allocator and gets the memory that it needs:

- The state of the compressor, about 224 KB. This is too large for a small stack.
- The 64 KB window that the compressor needs.
- Two rows of pixels, and five filtered copies of a row.
- The compressed output, which grows while the writer writes it.

Each allocation has a `defer` immediately below it. Thus the code frees each allocation on each path out of the function, and this is also true on the error paths.

## A filter for each row

The PNG chapter tried two filters on the full picture and kept the smaller file. With Sub, a gradient became smaller, from 3801 bytes to 133. The flat test scene became larger.

A real picture has both types of area. The sky in a painting is smooth, and the edge of a stroke is not smooth. Thus the best filter changes from row to row.

There are five filters. Each filter predicts a byte from bytes that the writer wrote before, and stores the difference:

- **None** predicts 0. Thus it stores the byte without a change.
- **Sub** predicts the byte to the left.
- **Up** predicts the byte above.
- **Average** predicts the average of the left byte and the byte above.
- **Paeth** predicts the one of left, above and above-left that is nearest to `left + above − above-left`.

```zig
/// The one of left, above and above-left that is nearest to `left + up - up_left`.
/// Ties go to left, then above, as the specification says.
fn paeth(left: u8, up: u8, up_left: u8) u8 {
    const p = @as(i16, left) + up - up_left;
    const pa = @abs(p - left);
    const pb = @abs(p - up);
    const pc = @abs(p - up_left);
    if (pa <= pb and pa <= pc) return left;
    if (pb <= pc) return up;
    return up_left;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `paeth` from `examples/paint/src/engine/png.zig`.*

## Select a filter

The writer tries all five filters on each row and keeps one of them.

To compress each row in five ways costs too much time. Thus the writer uses an estimate. A good prediction gives differences near zero. The writer adds the differences, and reads each byte as a signed number from −128 to 127. Then it keeps the filter with the smallest total.

```zig
/// Write `pixels` as an 8-bit RGB PNG. The function ignores alpha. Give it
/// pixels that are already flattened onto the paper.
pub fn write(
    gpa: std.mem.Allocator,
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    pixels: []const Rgba,
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
) !void {
    const stride = @as(usize, width) * 3;

    // The compressor is about 224 KB. A small stack cannot hold that size.
    // Thus the compressor goes on the heap with its 64 KB window.
    const compressor = try gpa.create(flate.Compress);
    defer gpa.destroy(compressor);
    const window = try gpa.alloc(u8, flate.max_window_len);
    defer gpa.free(window);

    // Two rows of plain RGB, this one and the one above, and one filtered
    // candidate per filter.
    const rows = try gpa.alloc(u8, stride * 2 + (stride + 1) * 5);
    defer gpa.free(rows);
    var above = rows[0..stride];
    var current = rows[stride .. stride * 2];
    @memset(above, 0); // the row above the first row counts as zeros

    var idat: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = try .initCapacity(gpa, 4096);
    defer idat.deinit();
    compressor.* = try .init(&idat.writer, window, .zlib, .default);

    for (0..height) |y| {
        for (0..width) |x| {
            const p = pixels[y * width + x];
            current[x * 3 ..][0..3].* = .{ p.r, p.g, p.b };
        }

        // Try all five filters. Keep the filter whose bytes are smallest when
        // the code reads them as signed numbers. Small numbers mean values near
        // their prediction, and those values compress well. The rule is an
        // estimate, but libpng uses the same estimate, and it costs little.
        var best: []const u8 = undefined;
        var best_score: u64 = std.math.maxInt(u64);
        inline for (all_filters, 0..) |filter, k| {
            const candidate = rows[stride * 2 + k * (stride + 1) ..][0 .. stride + 1];
            candidate[0] = @backingInt(filter);
            var score: u64 = 0;
            for (0..stride) |i| {
                const left: u8 = if (i >= 3) current[i - 3] else 0;
                const up = above[i];
                const up_left: u8 = if (i >= 3) above[i - 3] else 0;
                const predict: u8 = switch (filter) {
                    .none => 0,
                    .sub => left,
                    .up => up,
                    .average => @intCast((@as(u16, left) + up) / 2),
                    .paeth => paeth(left, up, up_left),
                };
                const v = current[i] -% predict;
                candidate[1 + i] = v;
                score += @abs(@as(i8, @bitCast(v)));
            }
            if (score < best_score) {
                best_score = score;
                best = candidate;
            }
        }
        try compressor.writer.writeAll(best);
        std.mem.swap([]u8, &above, &current);
    }
    try compressor.finish();

    try out.writeAll(signature);
    var ihdr: [13]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, ihdr[0..4], width, .big);
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, ihdr[4..8], height, .big);
    ihdr[8..13].* = .{ 8, 2, 0, 0, 0 }; // 8-bit, RGB, zlib, standard filters, no interlace
    try writeChunk(out, "IHDR", &ihdr);
    try writeChunk(out, "IDAT", idat.written());
    try writeChunk(out, "IEND", "");
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `write` from `examples/paint/src/engine/png.zig`.*

The PNG specification recommends this estimate, and libpng uses it. The estimate costs little: one pass over the row for each filter.

`inline for` runs the loop body one time for each of the five filters, at compile time. Thus the compiler decides the `switch` on the filter inside the body. Each copy of the body does one type of prediction, with no branch in the inner loop.

## Give the file to the browser

The engine writes the PNG into its own memory. The studio copies the bytes out and puts them in a `Blob`. Then it starts a download:

```ts
const length = e.paint_export_png();
const bytes = new Uint8Array(e.memory.buffer, e.paint_png(), length).slice();
const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([bytes], { type: "image/png" }));
```

The `.slice()` copies the bytes. Without it, the `Blob` points into the memory of the engine. The next export frees that memory and uses it again.

## Checks

This test uses a picture with flat rows, smooth rows and noise. After the round trip, the pixels must be exactly the same. The writer must also select more than one filter for the picture:

```zig
test "pixels survive the round trip, whatever filters were chosen" {
    const gpa = testing.allocator;
    const w = 37;
    const h = 23;
    var pixels: [w * h]Rgba = undefined;
    // Smooth areas, flat areas and noise, so that more than one filter wins.
    var r = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(3);
    for (0..h) |y| for (0..w) |x| {
        const noise = r.random().int(u8);
        pixels[y * w + x] = .{
            .r = @intCast((x * 7) % 256),
            .g = if (y < 10) 40 else noise,
            .b = @intCast((x * y) % 256),
            .a = 255,
        };
    };

    var png: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
    defer png.deinit();
    try write(gpa, &png.writer, &pixels, w, h);

    const decoded = try decodeForTest(gpa, png.written(), w, h);
    defer gpa.free(decoded.rgb);
    for (pixels, 0..) |p, i| {
        try testing.expectEqualSlices(u8, &.{ p.r, p.g, p.b }, decoded.rgb[i * 3 ..][0..3]);
    }

    // The picture mixes flat rows, smooth rows and noise. Thus the choice
    // for each row must not use one filter for all rows.
    var kinds: usize = 0;
    for (decoded.used) |u| kinds += @intFromBool(u);
    try testing.expect(kinds >= 2);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `pixels survive the round trip, whatever filters were chosen` from `examples/paint/src/engine/png.zig`.*

This test examines the rule for ties in Paeth, which the specification fixes. A decoder with a different rule for ties decodes a different picture:

```zig
test "paeth breaks ties in the order the specification gives" {
    try testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 10), paeth(10, 10, 10));
    try testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 20), paeth(10, 20, 10)); // p = 20, closest is up
    try testing.expectEqual(@as(u8, 10), paeth(10, 20, 30)); // p = 0, closest is left
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `paeth breaks ties in the order the specification gives` from `examples/paint/src/engine/png.zig`.*

If the reader of the engine agrees with the writer of the engine, that does not prove much. The two can have the same mistake. Thus the browser test of the site pushes Save PNG and decodes the file with a separate decoder. That decoder uses zlib from Node, and the site tests use their own code from the PNG specification. Its pixels must be the same as the pixels of the canvas.

## Explain before you read the answer

A row is 640 pixels of one flat colour. The row immediately above it has a different flat colour.

Which filter gives the smallest total?

Sub or Paeth. After the first pixel, both filters store zeros. Sub predicts the byte to the left. Paeth also selects the left byte, because the row above is flat.

The two filters are different only on the first pixel. The first pixel has nothing to its left. Thus Sub stores its colour without a change, and Paeth predicts the pixel above and stores the difference. The filter whose three bytes are nearer to zero gives the smaller total.

Up gives a larger total. It stores the difference between the two colours in each of the 1,920 bytes.

---

## Projects and Presets

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/projects-and-presets/*

A PNG is for a completed picture that you share. It is a bad format for a picture that you will change again.

A PNG is flat. When the program saves a PNG, it merges the layers into one image. When you open the PNG again, nothing tells which paint was on which layer. Thus the eraser cannot show the bottom layer again. Two layers and the size of the page can make the picture again. One merged PNG cannot.

Thus the studio has two more types of file:

- **Save project** keeps each layer, and records which layers are visible.
- **Save brush** keeps the settings of a brush as a **preset**. A preset is a name and the numbers that control the brush. A preset holds no pixels.

## The project format

Before the code, the top of the file that implements the format describes it, field by field:

```
header, 16 bytes
  0  magic      4 bytes  "ZPNT"
  4  version    u16      1
  6  width      u32
 10  height     u32
 14  layers     u8       1 to 8
 15  active     u8       less than layers

each layer
  0  visible    u8       0 or 1
  1  size       u32      bytes of compressed pixels that follow
  5  pixels     size bytes, zlib: width * height premultiplied RGBA
```

The [Binary Files](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/files/binary-files/) chapter makes a format in the same way. The **magic** bytes tell the type of the file. The **version** tells which edition of the format the file uses. Thus a later program can change the format and still identify an old file.

The program compresses the pixels of each layer with zlib, the same compressor that the [PNG writer](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/graphics/png/) uses. An empty layer of 640 by 400 is 1,024,000 bytes of zeros. After compression, it is about one kilobyte.

```zig
pub fn save(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, doc: *const Document, out: *std.Io.Writer) !void {
    try out.writeAll(magic);
    try out.writeInt(u16, version, .little);
    try out.writeInt(u32, doc.width, .little);
    try out.writeInt(u32, doc.height, .little);
    try out.writeInt(u8, @intCast(doc.layers.len), .little);
    try out.writeInt(u8, @intCast(doc.active_layer), .little);

    const window = try gpa.alloc(u8, flate.max_window_len);
    defer gpa.free(window);
    const compressor = try gpa.create(flate.Compress);
    defer gpa.destroy(compressor);

    for (doc.layers, doc.visible) |layer, visible| {
        var packed_layer: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = try .initCapacity(gpa, 4096);
        defer packed_layer.deinit();
        compressor.* = try .init(&packed_layer.writer, window, .zlib, .default);
        try compressor.writer.writeAll(std.mem.sliceAsBytes(layer));
        try compressor.finish();

        try out.writeInt(u8, @intFromBool(visible), .little);
        try out.writeInt(u32, @intCast(packed_layer.written().len), .little);
        try out.writeAll(packed_layer.written());
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `save` from `examples/paint/src/engine/project.zig`.*

## To open a file is to read bytes from an unknown source

To save is easy. The program wrote the data, and it trusts the data.

To open is different. The file can be from an older version. A failed download can cut it short, or a disk can damage it, or the file can be a different type. The program reads input from outside, thus it examines each field before it uses the field.

```zig
pub const OpenError = error{
    /// The first four bytes are not "ZPNT".
    NotAProject,
    /// A later version of this program wrote the file.
    NewerVersion,
    /// Width or height is 0 or larger than `max_side`.
    BadSize,
    /// No layers, too many, or an active layer that does not exist.
    BadLayers,
    /// The file ends before all of the data that it promised.
    Truncated,
    /// The compressed pixels do not decompress to exactly one layer.
    BadPixels,
    /// The colour of a pixel is larger than its alpha. A premultiplied pixel
    /// can never have such a value.
    NotPremultiplied,
    /// Bytes after the last layer.
    TrailingBytes,
    OutOfMemory,
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `OpenError` from `examples/paint/src/engine/project.zig`.*

Each type of problem in a file has its own error. The studio changes each error into a sentence that tells the person what to do. The picture on the screen does not change.

## Build the new document first

If an open fails, the work on the screen must not change.

Thus `open` makes a complete new document, separate from the open document. The studio swaps in the new document only if each layer decodes and each check passes. If something fails, `errdefer` frees the partial document. The open picture does not change.

```zig
/// Build a new document from a project file. If an error occurs, the
/// function returns no document and changes nothing.
pub fn open(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, bytes: []const u8, history_budget: usize) OpenError!Document {
    var in: Cursor = .{ .bytes = bytes };

    if (!std.mem.eql(u8, try in.take(4), magic)) return error.NotAProject;
    const file_version = try in.int(u16);
    if (file_version > version) return error.NewerVersion;
    if (file_version != version) return error.NotAProject;

    const width = try in.int(u32);
    const height = try in.int(u32);
    if (width == 0 or height == 0 or width > max_side or height > max_side) return error.BadSize;
    const layer_count = try in.int(u8);
    const active = try in.int(u8);
    if (layer_count == 0 or layer_count > max_layers or active >= layer_count) return error.BadLayers;

    // Read the layer table one time before any allocation. Eight layers of
    // 4096 by 4096 is 512 MB, and a 16-byte header can ask for that size. If
    // some layers are not in the file, or bytes follow the layers, the file
    // fails here at a low cost, before the large allocation.
    {
        var scan = in;
        for (0..layer_count) |_| {
            _ = try scan.int(u8);
            _ = try scan.take(try scan.int(u32));
        }
        if (scan.at != bytes.len) return error.TrailingBytes;
    }

    var doc: Document = try .init(gpa, width, height, layer_count, history_budget);
    errdefer doc.deinit();
    doc.active_layer = active;

    const window = try gpa.alloc(u8, flate.max_window_len);
    defer gpa.free(window);

    for (doc.layers, doc.visible) |layer, *visible| {
        const flag = try in.int(u8);
        if (flag > 1) return error.BadLayers;
        visible.* = flag == 1;

        const size = try in.int(u32);
        const compressed = try in.take(size);

        // Decompress into the layer, then ask for one more byte. If a layer is
        // too short, the first read fails. If a layer is too long, a byte
        // remains for the second read.
        var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(compressed);
        var inflate: flate.Decompress = .init(&reader, .zlib, window);
        inflate.reader.readSliceAll(std.mem.sliceAsBytes(layer)) catch return error.BadPixels;
        var extra: [1]u8 = undefined;
        if (inflate.reader.readSliceShort(&extra)) |n| {
            if (n != 0) return error.BadPixels;
        } else |_| return error.BadPixels;

        for (layer) |p| {
            if (p.r > p.a or p.g > p.a or p.b > p.a) return error.NotPremultiplied;
        }
    }

    doc.stale = .{ .x0 = 0, .y0 = 0, .x1 = width, .y1 = height };
    return doc;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `open` from `examples/paint/src/engine/project.zig`.*

## A small file can ask for much memory

The header gives the size of the picture, and the program allocates the document from that size.

Eight layers of 4096 by 4096 pixels is 512 MB. A file that is only 16 bytes long can ask for that quantity, with no data after its header.

Thus, before it allocates anything, `open` reads the layer table one time:

- It reads the size of each layer and makes sure that the bytes are in the file.
- It makes sure that nothing follows the last layer.

If a file gives incorrect data about its contents, the file fails here, before the large allocation.

A test proves this with an allocator that refuses each request. If `open` asked for memory before the checks, the test would get `OutOfMemory` instead of `Truncated`.

## Checks inside the pixels

Two more checks examine the compressed pixels.

A layer must decompress to exactly `width × height × 4` bytes. `open` reads that number of bytes, and then asks for one more byte. If a layer is too short, the first read fails. If a layer is too long, a byte remains for the second read.

Each pixel must also be **premultiplied**, as the [Layers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/layers-and-the-eraser/) chapter explains. No colour channel can be larger than the alpha. The engine never writes a pixel that breaks this rule. Thus such a pixel means that the file is damaged, or that a different program wrote it.

## Brush presets

A preset is small, and a person can want to read or edit it. Thus presets are JSON:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "name": "Fine sketch",
  "brush": {
    "radius": 4,
    "flow": 0.7,
    "color": "#26334d"
  }
}
```

If the file does not have a field, the field gets the value of the default brush. The program skips fields that it does not know. Thus a preset from a later version still opens if its known fields are valid.

## 0.2, not 0.20000000298023224

The first preset from this code had `"aspect": 0.20000000298023224`.

The brush stores its settings as `f32`. `std.json` first changes an `f32` to an `f64`, and then writes it. The `f32` that is nearest to 0.2 is not exactly 0.2. After the change to `f64`, the difference is visible.

The file was correct, and it gave the same brush when the program read it. But a preset is for people to read and edit, and no person typed that number.

Thus `write` changes each setting into the shortest decimal that gives the same `f32` when the program reads it again. Zig's `{d}` format prints that decimal. `write` stores the decimal as an `f64`, and JSON then prints `0.2`:

```zig
/// The shortest decimal that gives `x` when a program reads it again, as
/// an `f64`. For the `f32` nearest to 0.2, the result is 0.2. A plain
/// change to `f64` gives 0.20000000298023224.
fn decimal(x: f32) f64 {
    var buf: [64]u8 = undefined;
    const text = std.mem.print(&buf, "{d}", .{x}) catch unreachable;
    return std.fmt.parseFloat(f64, text) catch unreachable;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `decimal` from `examples/paint/src/engine/preset.zig`.*

When the program reads the file, it changes `0.2` back to an `f32` and gets the same bits that the brush had. The round-trip test examines this.

## Refuse, do not repair

The brush already has a function that moves each setting into its range: `sanitized`, in `brush.zig`. Each stroke sends its brush through this function. Thus a slider can never give the engine a value that it cannot draw with.

A preset file must not use `sanitized` to repair its values. A file with a radius of −3 is a damaged file. If the program silently changes −3 into 0.5, it hides the damage, and the person gets a brush that they did not make.

But `sanitized` is still useful here, as the definition of a valid brush. A brush is valid only when `sanitized` changes nothing:

```zig
/// Read a preset. The name in the result points into `name_buf`.
pub fn parse(gpa: std.mem.Allocator, json: []const u8, name_buf: *[max_name]u8) ParseError!Preset {
    const parsed = std.json.parseFromSlice(File, gpa, json, .{ .ignore_unknown_fields = true }) catch |err| switch (err) {
        error.OutOfMemory => return error.OutOfMemory,
        else => return error.NotAPreset,
    };
    defer parsed.deinit();
    const file = parsed.value;

    if (file.version > version) return error.NewerVersion;
    if (file.version != version) return error.NotAPreset;

    if (file.name.len == 0 or file.name.len > max_name) return error.BadName;
    for (file.name) |c| if (c < 0x20 or c == 0x7f) return error.BadName;

    const s = file.brush;
    const brush: Brush = .{
        .radius = @floatCast(s.radius),
        .hardness = @floatCast(s.hardness),
        .flow = @floatCast(s.flow),
        .opacity = @floatCast(s.opacity),
        .spacing = @floatCast(s.spacing),
        .follow = @floatCast(s.follow),
        .pressure = @floatCast(s.pressure),
        .jitter = @floatCast(s.jitter),
        .scatter = @floatCast(s.scatter),
        .aspect = @floatCast(s.aspect),
        .angle = @floatCast(s.angle),
        .follow_direction = s.follow_direction,
        .contact = @floatCast(s.contact),
        .bristles = s.bristles,
        .pickup = @floatCast(s.pickup),
        .drain = @floatCast(s.drain),
        .color = try parseColor(s.color),
    };
    // Valid means that the engine can draw with the brush without a change.
    // If `sanitized` must move a value, the value is out of range. NaN is
    // never equal to itself, thus a NaN also fails here.
    if (!std.meta.eql(brush.sanitized(), brush)) return error.OutOfRange;

    @memcpy(name_buf[0..file.name.len], file.name);
    return .{ .name = name_buf[0..file.name.len], .brush = brush };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `parse` from `examples/paint/src/engine/preset.zig`.*

NaN is never equal to itself, thus a NaN setting fails the same comparison. The code does not repeat a list of ranges. Thus the preset check and the sliders cannot disagree.

## The cost of JSON

The browser build was 49 KB before the file features. After them, it is 146 KB.

To find where the 97 KB went, remove one function at a time and build again:

| part | adds |
|---|---|
| read a preset with `std.json` | 67 KB |
| open a project (zlib decompression) | 15 KB |
| write presets and projects, and the remainder | 15 KB |

`std.json` is general. It can parse any JSON into any Zig type. That is why `parseFromSlice(File, ...)` is one line. Most of the cost comes from that general design. A parser written by hand for only this one shape would be smaller. But it would be a second part of the code that must stay correct.

The page loads the engine only when you push Start. Thus only people who use the studio pay the cost, one time. For a program that loads on each page, it would be better to write the small parser.

## Checks

This test makes sure that a saved project opens with the same layers, visibility and active layer:

```zig
test "a saved project opens with the same layers, visibility and active layer" {
    const gpa = testing.allocator;
    var doc: Document = try .init(gpa, 48, 32, 2, 1 << 20);
    defer doc.deinit();
    doc.beginStroke(.{ .radius = 6, .color = .{ 200, 40, 40 } }, .brush, .{ .x = 4, .y = 4 });
    doc.moveStroke(.{ .x = 44, .y = 28 });
    doc.endStroke();
    _ = doc.setActiveLayer(1);
    _ = try doc.fillAt(40, 2, .{ 30, 90, 200 });
    doc.setVisible(0, false);

    var out: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(gpa);
    defer out.deinit();
    try save(gpa, &doc, &out.writer);

    var back = try open(gpa, out.written(), 1 << 20);
    defer back.deinit();
    try testing.expectEqual(doc.width, back.width);
    try testing.expectEqual(@as(u32, 1), back.active_layer);
    try testing.expectEqualSlices(bool, doc.visible, back.visible);
    for (doc.layers, back.layers) |a, b| try testing.expectEqualSlices(Rgba, a, b);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `a saved project opens with the same layers, visibility and active layer` from `examples/paint/src/engine/project.zig`.*

This test makes sure that each type of damage gives its own error:

```zig
test "each kind of damage is rejected with its own error" {
    const gpa = testing.allocator;
    const good = try sample(gpa);
    defer gpa.free(good);
    const bad = try gpa.dupe(u8, good);
    defer gpa.free(bad);

    const Case = struct { offset: usize, value: u8, want: OpenError };
    const cases = [_]Case{
        .{ .offset = 0, .value = 'X', .want = error.NotAProject },
        .{ .offset = 4, .value = 2, .want = error.NewerVersion },
        .{ .offset = 6, .value = 0, .want = error.BadSize }, // width 48 -> 0
        .{ .offset = 14, .value = 9, .want = error.BadLayers }, // 9 layers
        .{ .offset = 15, .value = 2, .want = error.BadLayers }, // active 2 of 2
        .{ .offset = 16, .value = 7, .want = error.BadLayers }, // visible = 7
    };
    for (cases) |c| {
        @memcpy(bad, good);
        bad[c.offset] = c.value;
        try testing.expectError(c.want, open(gpa, bad, 1 << 20));
    }
    try testing.expectError(error.Truncated, open(gpa, good[0 .. good.len - 1], 1 << 20));

    const longer = try std.mem.concat(gpa, u8, &.{ good, "!" });
    defer gpa.free(longer);
    try testing.expectError(error.TrailingBytes, open(gpa, longer, 1 << 20));
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `each kind of damage is rejected with its own error` from `examples/paint/src/engine/project.zig`.*

This test cuts the file at each possible length, and changes each byte, one after the other:

- A cut file must never open.
- A file with a changed byte can still open, if the decompressed pixels are valid. But nothing can crash.
- If something leaks, the testing allocator makes the test fail.

```zig
test "every truncation and every flipped byte is rejected or opens cleanly, and nothing leaks" {
    const gpa = testing.allocator;
    const good = try sample(gpa);
    defer gpa.free(good);

    // Cut the file at each length.
    for (0..good.len) |n| {
        if (open(gpa, good[0..n], 1 << 20)) |doc| {
            var d = doc;
            d.deinit();
            return error.TestUnexpectedResult; // a cut file must never open
        } else |_| {}
    }

    // Flip each byte, one after the other. Some flips change compressed data
    // that still decodes to valid premultiplied pixels. Thus a file with a
    // flip can open. It must never crash, and the testing allocator makes
    // sure that it never leaks.
    const bad = try gpa.dupe(u8, good);
    defer gpa.free(bad);
    for (0..good.len) |i| {
        @memcpy(bad, good);
        bad[i] ^= 0xff;
        if (open(gpa, bad, 1 << 20)) |doc| {
            var d = doc;
            d.deinit();
        } else |_| {}
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `every truncation and every flipped byte is rejected or opens cleanly, and nothing leaks` from `examples/paint/src/engine/project.zig`.*

This test uses the 512 MB header:

```zig
test "a header asking for 512 MB with no data behind it allocates nothing" {
    var header: [16]u8 = undefined;
    @memcpy(header[0..4], magic);
    std.mem.writeInt(u16, header[4..6], version, .little);
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, header[6..10], max_side, .little);
    std.mem.writeInt(u32, header[10..14], max_side, .little);
    header[14] = max_layers;
    header[15] = 0;
    // An allocator that refuses each request. If `open` tried an allocation
    // before its checks, this test would get OutOfMemory instead.
    var none: std.testing.FailingAllocator = .init(testing.allocator, .{ .fail_index = 0 });
    try testing.expectError(error.Truncated, open(none.allocator(), &header, 0));
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `a header asking for 512 MB with no data behind it allocates nothing` from `examples/paint/src/engine/project.zig`.*

There is also a **fuzz test**. `zig build test --fuzz` runs it with inputs that the fuzzer makes and changes. The fuzzer searches for a byte sequence that crashes `open`. An ordinary test run gives the fuzz test only the valid file that it starts from.

This test makes sure that presets contain the numbers that a person types:

```zig
test "settings are written as typed: 0.2, not 0.20000000298023224" {
    var out: std.Io.Writer.Allocating = .init(testing.allocator);
    defer out.deinit();
    try write(&out.writer, "Nib", .{ .aspect = 0.2, .hardness = 0.95 });
    try testing.expect(std.mem.find(u8, out.written(), "\"aspect\": 0.2,") != null);
    try testing.expect(std.mem.find(u8, out.written(), "\"hardness\": 0.95,") != null);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `settings are written as typed: 0.2, not 0.20000000298023224` from `examples/paint/src/engine/preset.zig`.*

This test refuses presets for each reason:

```zig
test "a bad preset is refused with a reason, never repaired" {
    const Case = struct { json: []const u8, want: ParseError };
    const cases = [_]Case{
        .{ .json = "not json", .want = error.NotAPreset },
        .{ .json = "{\"version\":2,\"name\":\"x\",\"brush\":{}}", .want = error.NewerVersion },
        .{ .json = "{\"version\":1,\"name\":\"\",\"brush\":{}}", .want = error.BadName },
        .{ .json = "{\"version\":1,\"name\":\"x\",\"brush\":{\"color\":\"red\"}}", .want = error.BadColor },
        .{ .json = "{\"version\":1,\"name\":\"x\",\"brush\":{\"radius\":-3}}", .want = error.OutOfRange },
        .{ .json = "{\"version\":1,\"name\":\"x\",\"brush\":{\"flow\":7}}", .want = error.OutOfRange },
        .{ .json = "{\"version\":1,\"name\":\"x\",\"brush\":{\"bristles\":99}}", .want = error.OutOfRange },
    };
    var name: [max_name]u8 = undefined;
    for (cases) |c| try testing.expectError(c.want, parse(testing.allocator, c.json, &name));
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `a bad preset is refused with a reason, never repaired` from `examples/paint/src/engine/preset.zig`.*

## Explain before you read the answer

You get a project file from version 2 of this program. Version 2 added a field to the header.

Must version 1 try to open the file, and skip the field that it does not know?

No, it must not. Version 1 cannot know the position or the length of the new field. Thus it cannot know where the layers start. It refuses the file with `NewerVersion`, which tells the person exactly what to do: update the program. A preset is different. JSON gives a name to each field, thus the program can safely skip an unknown field.

## Watercolour

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/watercolour/*

Wet paint on wet paper does not stay where the brush put it.

The water spreads into the paper around it, and the water carries the colour. Then the paper dries, and the colour stays where the water left it.

The brushes in the previous chapters cannot do this. A brush decides each pixel one time, when the dab occurs. Watercolour continues to change after the brush moves away.

Thus this is a separate experiment with its own state, and the experiment runs over time:

*Interactive: the watercolour simulation, compiled to WebAssembly. Click to drop water and pigment. Drag for a trail. Each step is 1/30 of a second. It runs on the web page of this chapter.*

## A grid of paper

The program divides the paper into cells, 80 across and 50 down. On the 640 by 400 page, each cell is 8 by 8 pixels.

Each cell keeps three numbers:

- **water**: how wet the paper is, from 0 (dry) to 1 (fully wet).
- **mobile**: pigment that is still in the water. This pigment can move.
- **deposited**: pigment that is now in the paper. This pigment cannot move.

```zig
pub const Watercolor = struct {
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    water: []f32,
    mobile: []f32,
    deposited: []f32,
    /// How quickly pigment settles in each cell, from 0.6 to 1.4 times the
    /// base rate. The code makes it one time, thus the grain of the paper
    /// does not move.
    grain: []f32,
    /// The second buffer for the spread. A step reads one buffer and writes
    /// the other, then swaps them.
    next: []f32,

    /// How fast water and pigment spread. At most 0.25: see `spread`.
    spread_rate: f32 = 0.18,
    /// How much of its wetness the paper keeps after one second.
    retention: f32 = 0.8,
    /// How fast mobile pigment settles, per second.
    settle_rate: f32 = 0.8,
    /// The pigment's colour.
    color: [3]u8 = .{ 40, 90, 160 },

    // ...
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Watercolor` (fields only) from `examples/paint/src/engine/watercolor.zig`.*

The program stores a grid as one long array, row by row. Cell (x, y) is at `y * width + x`. On a grid 80 wide, cell (3, 2) is number 2 × 80 + 3 = 163.

80 × 50 is 4,000 cells. One `f32` field is 16,000 bytes, and all five fields are 80,000 bytes. The grid is coarse on purpose. The full simulation fits in a small cache, and it runs 30 times each second on a slow laptop.

The picture on the page is these 4,000 cells, scaled up smoothly. The blur from the scaling gives the soft edge that watercolour must have.

## Neighbours

Water spreads to the cells next to it: left, right, above and below.

At the edge of the paper, some of those cells do not exist. The code examines the coordinates before it makes an index:

```zig
    /// Left, right, above and below, or null where that neighbour is
    /// outside the paper. The code examines the coordinate first. Thus a
    /// cell on the left edge cannot get to the right edge of the row above.
    pub fn neighbours(w: Watercolor, x: u32, y: u32) [4]?usize {
        return .{
            if (x > 0) w.index(x - 1, y) else null,
            if (x + 1 < w.width) w.index(x + 1, y) else null,
            if (y > 0) w.index(x, y - 1) else null,
            if (y + 1 < w.height) w.index(x, y + 1) else null,
        };
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `neighbours` from `examples/paint/src/engine/watercolor.zig`.*

If the code examined the index instead, that would be a bug. The cell to the left of (0, 5) would be index 5 × 80 − 1 = 399. That index is the last cell of row 4, on the opposite side of the paper.

A middle cell has four neighbours, and a corner has two. Water at an edge can only move back in. Thus the paper keeps all of its water.

## Spread

In each step, each cell moves a small distance towards each of its neighbours:

```
next = current + rate × (sum of (neighbour − current))
```

With `rate` 0.18, a fully wet centre with four dry neighbours keeps 1 + 0.18 × (−4) = 0.28. Each neighbour gets 0.18. The total is still 1.

```zig
    /// Spread `field` between neighbour cells. Read the old values, and
    /// write the new values to a second buffer.
    ///
    /// Each cell moves towards its neighbours by `spread_rate` multiplied by
    /// each difference. A cell with four neighbours keeps `1 - 4 * rate` of
    /// its own value. Thus `rate` must be 0.25 or less. If not, that weight
    /// is negative, and values can go too far, change sign and grow without
    /// limit.
    ///
    /// `order` exists only to show that the order has no effect. No cell
    /// reads a value from the same step. Thus a backwards scan gives the
    /// same result.
    pub fn spread(w: *Watercolor, field: []f32, wet: ?[]const f32, order: Order) void {
        const n = field.len;
        for (0..n) |k| {
            const i = if (order == .forward) k else n - 1 - k;
            const x: u32 = @intCast(i % w.width);
            const y: u32 = @intCast(i / w.width);
            var change: f32 = 0;
            for (w.neighbours(x, y)) |maybe| {
                const j = maybe orelse continue;
                var amount = w.spread_rate;
                if (wet) |water| amount *= @min(@min(water[i], water[j]), 1);
                change += amount * (field[j] - field[i]);
            }
            w.next[i] = field[i] + change;
        }
        @memcpy(field, w.next);
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `spread` from `examples/paint/src/engine/watercolor.zig`.*

## Read the old grid, write a new grid

`spread` reads from `field` and writes to `next`. Then it copies `next` back.

This is important. If `spread` wrote into `field` during the scan, the cell after a changed cell would read the new value, not the old value. Then the result would depend on the order of the scan, and water would move in the direction of the scan.

With two buffers, each cell reads the state from before the step. The `order` parameter exists only for a test. That test scans backwards and gets the same answer.

## A limit on the rate

A cell with four neighbours keeps `1 − 4 × rate` of its own value.

At 0.25, the cell keeps 0. Above 0.25, the value is negative. A cell gives away more water than it has, and its value goes below zero. Then the next step moves the value in the opposite direction, farther each time.

Thus, for this rule, the rate must be 0.25 or less. A test sets the rate to 0.4. In one step, the centre becomes negative.

If the code clamped the values to 0 after the step, it would hide the problem. It would also silently make or remove water. When the rate stays in its range, the model stays correct.

## Pigment moves with water

Pigment in the water spreads with the same rule, but only as fast as the wetness of the paper allows. Between two cells, the quantity that moves is in proportion to the wetness of the drier cell:

```zig
if (wet) |water| amount *= @min(@min(water[i], water[j]), 1);
```

Between two dry cells, nothing moves. That is why a dry stroke keeps its shape.

The quantity that moves from one cell to another is the same in the two directions. Thus the spread never makes or loses pigment.

## Dry the paper, with units

The paper must not dry two times as fast when the computer runs two times as many steps.

Thus the rate at which the paper dries is a rate for each second. `retention` is the part of its water that a cell keeps after one second. One step is `dt` seconds. Thus one step keeps `retention` to the power `dt`.

```zig
    /// One step of 1/30 of a second.
    pub fn step(w: *Watercolor) void {
        // Water spreads to drier neighbours. Pigment also spreads, but only
        // where the paper is wet. Between two cells, the pigment moves in
        // proportion to the wetness of the drier cell.
        w.spread(w.water, null, .forward);
        w.spread(w.mobile, w.water, .forward);

        // The paper dries. `retention` is what remains after one full second.
        // Thus one step of `dt` seconds keeps `retention` to the power `dt`.
        // Thirty steps then keep exactly `retention`, at any step size.
        const keep = std.math.pow(f32, w.retention, dt);
        for (w.water) |*v| v.* *= keep;

        // The pigment settles. A part of the mobile pigment moves into the
        // paper. The step moves it and does not remove it: the total pigment
        // does not change.
        for (w.mobile, w.deposited, w.grain) |*m, *d, g| {
            const share = 1.0 - @exp(-w.settle_rate * g * dt);
            const moved = m.* * share;
            m.* -= moved;
            d.* += moved;
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `step` from `examples/paint/src/engine/watercolor.zig`.*

With `retention` 0.8, thirty steps of 1/30 of a second keep 0.8, and sixty steps keep 0.64. Two half seconds give the same answer as one second, because powers multiply: 0.8^0.5 × 0.8^0.5 = 0.8.

## The pigment settles

If the picture showed only water, the picture would disappear when the paper dried. Thus pigment has its own state.

In each step, a part of the mobile pigment goes into the paper. That part comes from a rate for each second, in the same way as the rate for water. The part that stays mobile after `dt` seconds is `exp(−rate × dt)`. Thus the part that settles is one minus that value.

At rate 0.8, one step settles 1 − e^(−0.8/30), about 2.63%. From 0.6 of mobile pigment, about 0.0158 settles.

The step moves the pigment, but it does not remove it. `mobile` decreases by exactly the quantity that `deposited` increases. The total never changes.

Each cell multiplies the rate by its own **grain**, from 0.6 to 1.4. The code makes the grain one time from a seed, as it makes the paper in [Bristles and Paper](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/bristles-and-paper/). Pigment settles faster in some cells than in others. This gives the spotted look of real watercolour, which has the name granulation.

## The page controls the clock

`step` takes no time argument. It always moves the simulation forward exactly 1/30 of a second.

The page keeps the clock. In each frame, the page adds the time since the last frame to an **accumulator**. Then it runs full steps while the accumulator holds at least 1/30 of a second:

```ts
while (accumulator >= DT && steps < MAX_STEPS_PER_FRAME) {
  e.wc_step();
  accumulator -= DT;
  steps++;
}
if (steps === MAX_STEPS_PER_FRAME) accumulator = 0;
```

If the accumulator holds 0.05 seconds, one step runs, and about 0.0167 seconds stay for the next frame.

The limit of four steps is important on a slow computer. Without the limit, a frame that took too long would need more steps. Then the next frame would take longer again. With the limit, the experiment becomes slower, and the page continues to respond.

The engine never sees a clock. Thus a test can run 600 steps without a wait, and examine exactly how much the paper dries in 20 seconds.

## The same run in all builds

The simulation uses `pow` and `exp` on `f32` values. Two builds of the same program can start to disagree at these functions.

Thus, as with the brush demo, the engine contains a fixed run: three drops and three seconds, with a fixed hash of its picture. The native tests and the self-test of the browser build both compare with that hash. If the results are different, the site does not publish.

## Checks

This test examines the cell numbers, and the neighbours at a corner and at an edge:

test "spreading keeps the total and never goes negative" {
    var w = try lab(30, 20);

This test makes sure that no pigment is lost when it settles:

```zig
test "settling moves pigment into the paper and loses none" {
    var w = try lab(30, 20);
    defer w.deinit(testing.allocator);
    w.drop(15, 10, 5, 1, 0.6);
    const pigment = Watercolor.total(w.mobile);
    for (0..600) |_| w.step();
    const now = Watercolor.total(w.mobile) + Watercolor.total(w.deposited);
    try testing.expectApproxEqRel(pigment, now, 1e-4);

}
```

## Explain before you read the answer

Does `rate` 0.18 mean that real paper spreads water at a measured speed?

No, it does not. The number makes this grid act like wet paper, within the limit that keeps the rule stable. A finer grid would need a different number for the same look, because each step would move water a shorter distance. Only the units for the water that dries and the pigment that settles are real here. They are rates for each second.

## A Native Window

*A Paint Program. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/a-native-window/*

The studio on the first page is the engine in a browser.

The same engine also runs in a desktop window. **raylib** draws the window. raylib is a small C library for windows, graphics and input.

The front end is one file, `native.zig`. It does the same work as the browser front end. It reads input, calls the engine, and copies the changed rectangle to the screen.

```
cd examples/paint
./fetch-raylib.sh      # once: download raylib's C at a pinned commit
zig build run          # open the window
```

## raylib as C, not as a package

The program uses raylib as a folder of C files, and its own `build.zig` compiles them.

`fetch-raylib.sh` downloads the files at a fixed commit. The [Lane Dodger](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/lane-dodger/the-build/) game uses the same commit. That chapter tells why the program vendors the C and does not use a Zig package. The build script of a package must stay current with Zig master, and the build script of raylib often is not current.

This is the full raylib build:

```zig
fn raylibModule(b: *std.Build, target: std.Build.ResolvedTarget, optimize: std.lang.Optimize) *std.Build.Module {
    const mod = b.createModule(.{
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
        .link_libc = true,
        // This C does not come from this project. The UBSan runtime would only
        // report problems in a fixed upstream release.
        .sanitize_c = .off,
    });
    const lib = b.addLibrary(.{ .name = "raylib", .linkage = .static, .root_module = mod });

    inline for (.{
        .{ "_GNU_SOURCE", "" },
        .{ "GL_SILENCE_DEPRECATION", "199309L" },
        .{ "PLATFORM_DESKTOP_GLFW", "" },
        .{ "GRAPHICS_API_OPENGL_33", "" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RSHAPES", "1" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RTEXTURES", "1" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RTEXT", "1" },
        // A paint program makes no sound and loads no 3D models.
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RAUDIO", "0" },
        .{ "SUPPORT_MODULE_RMODELS", "0" },
    }) |macro| mod.addCMacro(macro[0], macro[1]);

    const windows = target.result.os.tag == .windows;
    mod.addCMacro(if (windows) "_GLFW_WIN32" else "_GLFW_X11", "");
    mod.addIncludePath(b.path(raylib_root ++ "/platforms"));
    mod.addIncludePath(b.path(raylib_root ++ "/external/glfw/include"));
    mod.addCSourceFiles(.{
        .root = b.path(raylib_root),
        .files = &.{ "rcore.c", "rshapes.c", "rtextures.c", "rtext.c", "rglfw.c" },
        .flags = &.{"-std=gnu99"},
    });
    const libs: []const []const u8 = if (windows)
        &.{ "opengl32", "gdi32", "winmm", "user32", "shell32" }
    else
        &.{ "GL", "X11", "Xrandr", "Xinerama", "Xi", "Xcursor" };
    for (libs) |name| mod.linkSystemLibrary(name, .{});

    const translated = b.addTranslateC(.{
        .root_source_file = b.path(raylib_root ++ "/raylib.h"),
        .target = target,
        .optimize = optimize,
        .link_libc = true,
    });
    const rl = translated.createModule();
    rl.linkLibrary(lib);
    return rl;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `raylibModule` from `examples/paint/build.zig`.*

`addTranslateC` reads `raylib.h` and changes it into a Zig module. Then the front end calls `rl.InitWindow`, `rl.DrawTexture` and the other functions as Zig functions.

A paint program makes no sound and loads no 3D models. Thus two macros turn off the audio and model modules. Five C files remain.

## The front end

The window shows a texture with the size of the document. In each frame, the loop does these steps:

1. It reads the mouse.
2. It calls the engine.
3. It uploads only the rectangle that `render` returns as changed.

```zig
pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const gpa = init.gpa;
    var doc: engine.Document = try .init(gpa, width, height, engine.default_layers, engine.default_history_budget);
    defer doc.deinit();

    const headless = build_options.frames != null;
    if (headless) {
        rl.SetTraceLogLevel(rl.LOG_WARNING);
        // A smoke run draws the demo picture of the engine. Thus CI makes sure
        // that a window can show the picture that the tests drew.
        try engine.demo.draw(&doc);
    }

    rl.InitWindow(width, height + bar, "Paint");
    defer rl.CloseWindow();
    rl.SetTargetFPS(60);

    // The texture has the size of the document. At the start, it is a copy
    // of the display. After that, the loop uploads only changed rectangles.
    _ = doc.render();
    const texture = rl.LoadTextureFromImage(.{
        .data = doc.display.ptr,
        .width = width,
        .height = height,
        .mipmaps = 1,
        .format = rl.PIXELFORMAT_UNCOMPRESSED_R8G8B8A8,
    });
    defer rl.UnloadTexture(texture);

    // Space for a copy of one changed rectangle, row by row. A texture update
    // needs the pixels of the rectangle next to each other.
    const scratch = try gpa.alloc(engine.Rgba, width * height);
    defer gpa.free(scratch);

    var preset: usize = 0;
    var color: usize = 0;
    var size: f32 = 8;
    var tool: Tool = .paint;
    var seed: u32 = 1;
    var drawing = false;
    var frame: usize = 0;
    var message: [:0]const u8 = "";

    while (!rl.WindowShouldClose()) : (frame += 1) {
        if (build_options.frames) |n| if (frame >= n) break;

        // ---- keyboard --------------------------------------------------------
        const ctrl = rl.IsKeyDown(rl.KEY_LEFT_CONTROL) or rl.IsKeyDown(rl.KEY_RIGHT_CONTROL);
        if (!drawing) {
            if (ctrl and rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_Z)) _ = doc.undo();
            if (ctrl and rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_Y)) _ = doc.redo();
            if (ctrl and rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_S)) {
                message = if (save(init.io, &doc)) "Saved painting.png" else |_| "Saving failed";
            }
            if (!ctrl) {
                for (0..presets.len) |i| {
                    if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_ONE + @as(c_int, @intCast(i)))) preset = i;
                }
                if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_P)) tool = .paint;
                if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_E)) tool = .erase;
                if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_F)) tool = .fill;
                if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_C)) color = (color + 1) % colors.len;
                if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_LEFT_BRACKET)) size = @max(1, size - 2);
                if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_RIGHT_BRACKET)) size = @min(80, size + 2);
                if (rl.IsKeyPressed(rl.KEY_L)) _ = doc.setActiveLayer(1 - doc.active_layer);
            }
        }

        // ---- mouse -------------------------------------------------------------
        // A mouse has no pressure, and the browser sends 0.5 for a mouse. The
        // native build does the same, thus the two builds draw the same stroke.
        const m = rl.GetMousePosition();
        const p: engine.Point = .{ .x = m.x, .y = m.y, .pressure = 0.5 };
        if (rl.IsMouseButtonPressed(rl.MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) and m.y < height) {
            switch (tool) {
                .fill => _ = doc.fillAt(@intFromFloat(@max(m.x, 0)), @intFromFloat(@max(m.y, 0)), colors[color]) catch false,
                .paint, .erase => {
                    var brush = presets[preset].brush;
                    brush.radius = size;
                    brush.color = colors[color];
                    brush.seed = seed;
                    doc.beginStroke(brush, if (tool == .erase) .eraser else .brush, p);
                    drawing = true;
                },
            }
        } else if (drawing and rl.IsMouseButtonDown(rl.MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT)) {
            doc.moveStroke(p);
        } else if (drawing) {
            doc.endStroke();
            drawing = false;
            seed += 1;
        }
        if (drawing and !rl.IsWindowFocused()) {
            // The window lost focus during a stroke. Drop the stroke. The browser
            // does the same.
            doc.cancelStroke();
            drawing = false;
        }

        // ---- picture -----------------------------------------------------------
        const r = doc.render();
        if (!r.isEmpty()) {
            var i: usize = 0;
            var y = r.y0;
            while (y < r.y1) : (y += 1) {
                const row = @as(usize, y) * width;
                @memcpy(scratch[i..][0..r.width()], doc.display[row + r.x0 .. row + r.x1]);
                i += r.width();
            }
            rl.UpdateTextureRec(texture, .{
                .x = @floatFromInt(r.x0),
                .y = @floatFromInt(r.y0),
                .width = @floatFromInt(r.width()),
                .height = @floatFromInt(r.height()),
            }, scratch.ptr);
        }

        rl.BeginDrawing();
        rl.ClearBackground(.{ .r = 40, .g = 42, .b = 54, .a = 255 });
        rl.DrawTexture(texture, 0, 0, rl.WHITE);
        var status_buf: [160]u8 = undefined;
        const status = std.mem.printSentinel(&status_buf, "{s}  {s}  size {d}  {s} layer   1-9 brush  P/E/F  [ ]  C colour  L layer  Ctrl+Z/Y  Ctrl+S   {s}", .{
            presets[preset].name,
            @tagName(tool),
            @as(u32, @intFromFloat(size)),
            if (doc.active_layer == 0) "bottom" else "top",
            message,
        }, 0) catch "";
        const c = colors[color];
        rl.DrawRectangle(6, height + 6, 16, 16, .{ .r = c[0], .g = c[1], .b = c[2], .a = 255 });
        rl.DrawText(status.ptr, 28, height + 8, 12, .{ .r = 220, .g = 222, .b = 230, .a = 255 });
        rl.EndDrawing();
    }

    if (build_options.screenshot) |path| {
        // raylib wants a C string, ending in a zero byte.
        var path_buf: [std.Io.Dir.max_path_bytes]u8 = undefined;
        rl.TakeScreenshot((try std.mem.printSentinel(&path_buf, "{s}", .{path}, 0)).ptr);
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `main` from `examples/paint/src/native.zig`.*

The texture update of raylib needs the pixels of the rectangle next to each other in memory. In `display`, the pixels are not next to each other: each row of the rectangle is one row of a 640-pixel image. Thus the code first copies the rows into `scratch`.

A mouse has no pressure. Thus each point gets 0.5, which is the value that browsers send for a mouse. The window and the studio draw the same stroke for the same movement.

## Cross-compile

Zig compiles for other operating systems with one flag:

```
zig build native -Dtarget=x86_64-windows
```

On Linux, this command builds a `paint.exe` of about 1.3 MB that works. You do not have to install anything first.

The cross-compile works because of the libraries that raylib needs from Windows: `opengl32`, `gdi32`, `winmm`, `user32` and `shell32`. The compiler contains the import libraries for these, from the MinGW project. The `build.zig` above only selects `_GLFW_WIN32` instead of `_GLFW_X11` and gives the names of those libraries.

One more line is important on Windows:

```zig
if (target.result.os.tag == .windows) exe.subsystem = .windows;
```

A Windows program is a console program or a window program. When you double-click a console program, it opens a terminal window behind the paint window. `.windows` selects a window program.

CI builds the Windows `.exe` on each run, from a Linux computer. If a change in Zig or raylib breaks the Windows build, the nightly build fails. CI does not run the `.exe`, because it has no Windows computer.

## The limits of cross-compilation

For other Linux systems, a build is more difficult. For macOS, a build from Linux is not possible.

- **Linux on a different CPU**, such as a 64-bit ARM board, needs the X11 header files for that system. Zig does not contain them, thus they must come from that system. They are only headers, thus the build is possible. But it is not one flag.
- **macOS** needs the Apple SDK: the headers and libraries for Cocoa, IOKit and OpenGL that raylib uses on a Mac. Zig does not contain them, and the Apple licence does not let other people ship them. The compiler can do the job, but nobody can legally copy the files that it needs.

Thus you must build the macOS version on a Mac, where the SDK is already installed. GitHub gives Mac computers for CI. Thus a macOS build costs more, but it is possible.

## A smoke test without a screen

CI has no screen. CI runs the window inside **Xvfb**, a virtual display that draws into memory.

`-Dframes=30` makes the program draw the demo picture of the engine, show it for 30 frames, and stop. `-Dshot` saves the last frame:

```
zig build native -Dframes=30 -Dshot=demo-native.png
xvfb-run ./zig-out/bin/paint
```

The compile proves that the raylib calls still agree with the headers. The run proves that the window opens and that raylib draws the texture.

## Explain before you read the answer

For the same movement, the browser studio and the native window send the same points to the engine.

Do they draw exactly the same pixels?

The engine does. With the same calls, it calculates the same picture on all computers. The demo check in the first chapter proves this for the browser and native builds.

The calls can be different. A browser can send more than one sample in each frame. The studio gives all of the samples to the engine. raylib reads the mouse one time in each frame. Thus a fast stroke gets more points in the browser. The spacing from the [Strokes](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/paint/strokes/) chapter keeps the dabs at equal distances in both cases. But where the path bends between samples, the two paths are slightly different.

---

## What You Will Build

*A Chat Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/what-we-are-building/*

This project builds a chat room. A client connects over WebSocket and picks
a nickname. Then each message that a member sends goes to each member of the
room. When a member joins or leaves, the others see a notice.

The server uses only the Zig standard library. It uses the parts from the
four WebSocket chapters of Networking:

- [The WebSocket Handshake](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-handshake/): the
  server answers the upgrade with `std.http.Server`.
- [WebSocket Frames](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-frames/): the header, the
  length forms and the mask.
- [A WebSocket Client](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-client/): the client in
  the last chapter of this project is that client, imported from its file.
- [A WebSocket Server on a Socket](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-server/): the
  gaps in std that this project must fill.

Read those four first if WebSocket is new to you.

## The parts

The server has four parts. Each part is one file, and each file is a snippet
that CI compiles and runs:

| File | What it does | Runs where |
|---|---|---|
| `chat-protocol.zig` | Parses commands from clients and formats events for clients | browser |
| `chat-hub.zig` | Keeps the members and copies each line into their outboxes | browser |
| `chat-frames.zig` | Reads frames from a client, with fragments and close codes | browser |
| `chat-server.zig` | Puts the parts on real sockets, with three clients | native |

The first three files take bytes and return bytes. They never see a socket,
thus their chapters run in your browser. The last file imports the other
three and adds the sockets and the tasks.

## Four decisions

A chat server looks simple: read a message, and send it to everybody. Four
questions make it difficult, and each chapter answers one of them.

1. **What does a message mean?** WebSocket frames the bytes. It does not
   say what the bytes mean. [The Protocol](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/protocol/)
   defines a small text protocol.
2. **Who writes to a socket?** Each member receives lines from many other
   members, and each sender runs in a different task. If two tasks write to
   one socket at the same time, the frames can mix.
   [The Hub](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/hub/) gives each connection one writer.
3. **What if a client does not read?** A broadcast that waits for one slow
   member stops the room. [Slow Clients](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/slow-clients/)
   drops that member instead.
4. **What does std not read?** std refuses a message in fragments and does
   not return the close code.
   [Read the Frames Yourself](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/frames/) writes the reader
   that the server needs.

[The Server](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/the-server/) puts the four answers on real
sockets.

## What it does not do

The room is one room, with up to eight members. It keeps no history, so a
new member sees only the messages that arrive after the member joins. It has no
accounts, no TLS and no persistence. Each of those is a separate decision,
and none of them changes the four parts above.

---

## The Protocol

*A Chat Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/protocol/*

WebSocket delivers messages with clear edges. One message is one frame, or
one set of fragments, and the receiver gets the whole message. Thus this
protocol needs no delimiter and no length prefix, unlike the protocols in
[Three Ways to Frame](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/framing/). The protocol only says
what the bytes in one message mean.

The protocol has two directions:

- A client sends **commands**: `nick tejas` to pick a name, and
  `say hello` to talk.
- The server sends **events**: `welcome`, `joined`, `left`, `msg` and
  `error`.

Text is easy to read in a trace and easy to type into a test client. A
binary protocol would be smaller, and a chat line is small already.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// WebSocket already frames each message, thus a command is one message
/// and needs no delimiter. The protocol only has to say what the bytes in
/// a message mean.
pub const max_nick = 16;
pub const max_text = 120;

/// What a client can send.
pub const Command = union(enum) {
    nick: []const u8,
    say: []const u8,
};

pub const ParseError = error{
    UnknownCommand,
    MissingArgument,
    BadNick,
    TextTooLong,
};

/// Parse one message from a client. The slices in the result point into
/// `message`.
pub fn parseCommand(message: []const u8) ParseError!Command {
    const space = std.mem.findScalar(u8, message, ' ');
    const verb = message[0 .. space orelse message.len];
    const arg = if (space) |i| message[i + 1 ..] else "";

    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "nick")) {
        if (arg.len == 0) return error.MissingArgument;
        if (arg.len > max_nick) return error.BadNick;
        for (arg) |c| {
            if (!std.ascii.isLower(c) and !std.ascii.isDigit(c) and c != '_') return error.BadNick;
        }
        return .{ .nick = arg };
    }
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "say")) {
        if (arg.len == 0) return error.MissingArgument;
        if (arg.len > max_text) return error.TextTooLong;
        return .{ .say = arg };
    }
    return error.UnknownCommand;
}

/// Why the server refused a command. The parse errors, and the errors of
/// the hub in the next chapter.
pub const Refusal = ParseError || error{ NickTaken, RoomFull, NoNickYet, AlreadyJoined };

/// What the server sends.
pub const Event = union(enum) {
    welcome: struct { nick: []const u8, online: u8 },
    joined: []const u8,
    left: struct { nick: []const u8, reason: Reason },
    msg: struct { nick: []const u8, text: []const u8 },
    err: Refusal,

    pub const Reason = enum { quit, too_slow };
};

/// One event, formatted, in a fixed buffer. The hub copies a Line into
/// the outbox of each member, thus a Line must not point anywhere else.
pub const Line = struct {
    pub const capacity = 160;
    buf: [capacity]u8 = undefined,
    len: u8 = 0,

    pub fn bytes(line: *const Line) []const u8 {
        return line.buf[0..line.len];
    }
};

// The longest event is a `msg` with the longest nick and text. The
// compiler checks that it fits, thus `format` cannot fail at run time.
comptime {
    const longest = "msg ".len + max_nick + ": ".len + max_text;
    if (longest > Line.capacity) @compileError("Line.capacity is too small for a msg event");
}

pub fn format(event: Event) Line {
    var line: Line = .{};
    var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&line.buf);
    (switch (event) {
        .welcome => |e| w.print("welcome {s} ({d} online)", .{ e.nick, e.online }),
        .joined => |nick| w.print("joined {s}", .{nick}),
        .left => |e| w.print("left {s} ({t})", .{ e.nick, e.reason }),
        .msg => |e| w.print("msg {s}: {s}", .{ e.nick, e.text }),
        .err => |e| w.print("error {t}", .{e}),
    }) catch unreachable;
    line.len = @intCast(w.buffered().len);
    return line;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    try out.print("commands from a client:\n", .{});
    const long_nick: [max_nick + 1]u8 = @splat('a');
    const long_text = "say " ++ @as([max_text + 1]u8, @splat('x'));
    const inputs = [_][]const u8{
        "nick tejas",
        "say hello, room",
        "say  two spaces",
        "nick Tejas",
        "nick " ++ long_nick,
        "say",
        long_text,
        "shout hello",
        "",
    };
    for (inputs) |input| {
        const shown = if (input.len > 24) "(long input)" else input;
        try out.print("  {s:<24} -> ", .{shown});
        if (parseCommand(input)) |command| switch (command) {
            .nick => |n| try out.print("nick \"{s}\"\n", .{n}),
            .say => |t| try out.print("say \"{s}\"\n", .{t}),
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("error.{t}\n", .{err});
        }
    }

    try out.print("\nevents from the server:\n", .{});
    const events = [_]Event{
        .{ .welcome = .{ .nick = "tejas", .online = 3 } },
        .{ .joined = "vishaka" },
        .{ .msg = .{ .nick = "vishaka", .text = "hello, room" } },
        .{ .left = .{ .nick = "shivam", .reason = .quit } },
        .{ .left = .{ .nick = "shivam", .reason = .too_slow } },
        .{ .err = error.NickTaken },
    };
    for (events) |event| {
        const line = format(event);
        try out.print("  {s}\n", .{line.bytes()});
    }

    const nick: [max_nick]u8 = @splat('a');
    const text: [max_text]u8 = @splat('x');
    const longest = format(.{ .msg = .{ .nick = &nick, .text = &text } });
    try out.print("\nthe longest event: {d} of {d} bytes\n", .{ longest.len, Line.capacity });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.chat-protocol`)*

## Commands: parse into a tagged union

```zig
/// Parse one message from a client. The slices in the result point into
/// `message`.
pub fn parseCommand(message: []const u8) ParseError!Command {
    const space = std.mem.findScalar(u8, message, ' ');
    const verb = message[0 .. space orelse message.len];
    const arg = if (space) |i| message[i + 1 ..] else "";

    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "nick")) {
        if (arg.len == 0) return error.MissingArgument;
        if (arg.len > max_nick) return error.BadNick;
        for (arg) |c| {
            if (!std.ascii.isLower(c) and !std.ascii.isDigit(c) and c != '_') return error.BadNick;
        }
        return .{ .nick = arg };
    }
    if (std.mem.eql(u8, verb, "say")) {
        if (arg.len == 0) return error.MissingArgument;
        if (arg.len > max_text) return error.TextTooLong;
        return .{ .say = arg };
    }
    return error.UnknownCommand;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `parseCommand` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-protocol.zig`.*

The result is a `Command`, a tagged union with one field for each verb. The
code after the parser uses a `switch`, and the compiler requires a case for
each verb. If you add a verb, each `switch` that forgets it fails to
compile.

```
commands from a client:
  nick tejas               -> nick "tejas"
  say hello, room          -> say "hello, room"
  say  two spaces          -> say " two spaces"
  nick Tejas               -> error.BadNick
  nick aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa   -> error.BadNick
  say                      -> error.MissingArgument
  (long input)             -> error.TextTooLong
  shout hello              -> error.UnknownCommand
                           -> error.UnknownCommand
```

Three rules in the parser are deliberate:

- **The text of `say` is exact.** The parser splits at the first space only.
  `say  two spaces` keeps the second space as the first byte of the text.
- **A nickname is lowercase letters, digits and `_`, 16 bytes or fewer.**
  Each event prints the nickname, thus a nickname with a space or a colon
  could make a `msg` event look like a different event.
- **Text has a limit of 120 bytes.** The next section shows why the limit is
  necessary.

The slices in a `Command` point into the message. The parser copies
nothing. The message must stay valid while you use the command. In the server,
the frame reader keeps the message in its buffer until the next call.

## Events: format into a fixed line

```zig
/// One event, formatted, in a fixed buffer. The hub copies a Line into
/// the outbox of each member, thus a Line must not point anywhere else.
pub const Line = struct {
    pub const capacity = 160;
    buf: [capacity]u8 = undefined,
    len: u8 = 0,

    pub fn bytes(line: *const Line) []const u8 {
        return line.buf[0..line.len];
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Line` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-protocol.zig`.*

The hub copies each event into the outbox of each member. A slice would
point into memory that one task owns, and the other tasks read it later. A
`Line` is a fixed array with a length, thus each copy owns its bytes, and
the hub needs no allocator.

A fixed buffer needs a maximum. The longest event is a `msg` with the
longest nickname and the longest text. A `comptime` block in the file adds
the four lengths: `"msg ".len`, `max_nick`, `": ".len` and `max_text`. If
the sum is larger than `Line.capacity`, the block calls `@compileError`.

The check runs in the compiler. If you raise `max_text` to 150, the program
does not compile. Because of that check, `format` uses `catch unreachable`:
the buffer can hold each event.

```zig
pub fn format(event: Event) Line {
    var line: Line = .{};
    var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&line.buf);
    (switch (event) {
        .welcome => |e| w.print("welcome {s} ({d} online)", .{ e.nick, e.online }),
        .joined => |nick| w.print("joined {s}", .{nick}),
        .left => |e| w.print("left {s} ({t})", .{ e.nick, e.reason }),
        .msg => |e| w.print("msg {s}: {s}", .{ e.nick, e.text }),
        .err => |e| w.print("error {t}", .{e}),
    }) catch unreachable;
    line.len = @intCast(w.buffered().len);
    return line;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `format` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-protocol.zig`.*

```
events from the server:
  welcome tejas (3 online)
  joined vishaka
  msg vishaka: hello, room
  left shivam (quit)
  left shivam (too_slow)
  error NickTaken
```

The `{t}` format prints the name of an enum tag or of an error. Thus the
reason of a `left` event and the name of a refusal need no table of
strings. The program also formats the longest possible event, and CI
compares the result:

```
the longest event: 142 of 160 bytes
```
