## The refusals

`Refusal` is the set of errors that the server can send back as an `error`
event:

```zig
/// Why the server refused a command. The parse errors, and the errors of
/// the hub in the next chapter.
pub const Refusal = ParseError || error{ NickTaken, RoomFull, NoNickYet, AlreadyJoined };
```

*Quoted from the source: `Refusal` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-protocol.zig`.*

It joins the errors of the parser with the errors of the hub (the next
chapter) with `||`. Thus one `error` event covers both, and the `err` field
of `Event` cannot hold an error that a client must never see, for example
`error.ReadFailed`.

---

## The Hub

*A Chat Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/hub/*

Each connection in the server has its own task, which reads from its
socket. When tejas says something, the task of tejas must send a line to
vishaka and to shivam. The simple design is to write to their sockets
directly. That design has a race.

A WebSocket frame is a header and a payload, and a large frame can need
more than one write. Two tasks can write to the socket of shivam at the same
time, for example the tasks of tejas and vishaka. Then the bytes of the two
frames can mix.
Then shivam gets a frame that is not valid, and closes the connection.

A lock for each socket would prevent the mix. But a task that holds that
lock waits for the network of shivam, and a slow network then stops each
member who talks.

## One writer for each socket

The hub uses a different design:

1. Each connection has an **outbox**, a bounded queue of lines.
2. Each connection has one **writer task**. Only the writer task writes to
   the socket. It takes a line from the outbox and sends it.
3. The hub puts lines into outboxes. It never touches a socket.

Thus no two tasks write to one socket. A task that talks only puts lines into
queues, and a queue operation is short.

```zig
/// One connection, as the hub sees it. The hub never writes to a socket.
/// It puts lines into the outbox, and one writer task for the connection
/// takes them out and sends them. Thus only one task writes to a socket.
pub const Peer = struct {
    outbox: Outbox,
    /// The code of the close frame that the writer sends after somebody
    /// closes the outbox. The hub sets it before `close`, and the writer
    /// reads it after `error.Closed`. The lock in the queue orders the two.
    close_code: u16 = 1000,
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `Peer` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-hub.zig`.*

The outbox is `std.Io.Queue`, the bounded channel from
[Queues](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/queues/). Its capacity comes from the buffer
that you give to `init`. A `Peer` belongs to the connection, and the hub
keeps a pointer to it.

The program below plays three members in memory. After each action, it
takes the lines out of each outbox, as a writer task would, and prints
them.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const protocol = @import("chat-protocol.zig");
const Line = protocol.Line;
const Event = protocol.Event;

/// One frame for the writer task. Chat lines are text frames. The pong
/// for a ping goes through the outbox too, because only the writer task
/// may write to the socket.
pub const Outgoing = struct {
    opcode: std.http.Server.WebSocket.Opcode = .text,
    line: Line,
};

pub const Outbox = std.Io.Queue(Outgoing);

/// One connection, as the hub sees it. The hub never writes to a socket.
/// It puts lines into the outbox, and one writer task for the connection
/// takes them out and sends them. Thus only one task writes to a socket.
pub const Peer = struct {
    outbox: Outbox,
    /// The code of the close frame that the writer sends after somebody
    /// closes the outbox. The hub sets it before `close`, and the writer
    /// reads it after `error.Closed`. The lock in the queue orders the two.
    close_code: u16 = 1000,
};

pub const max_members = 8;

const Member = struct {
    peer: *Peer,
    nick_buf: [protocol.max_nick]u8,
    nick_len: u8,

    fn nick(m: *const Member) []const u8 {
        return m.nick_buf[0..m.nick_len];
    }
};

pub const Hub = struct {
    mutex: std.Io.Mutex = .init,
    members: [max_members]?Member = @splat(null),

    /// Find a member by its peer, never by its slot. The hub can drop a
    /// member and give the slot to a new member. A slot number that the old
    /// connection kept would then point at the new member.
    fn find(hub: *Hub, peer: *const Peer) ?usize {
        for (hub.members, 0..) |slot, i| {
            if (slot) |m| if (m.peer == peer) return i;
        }
        return null;
    }

    /// Add a member, send the welcome to that member, and tell the others.
    pub fn join(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io, peer: *Peer, nick: []const u8) (protocol.Refusal || std.Io.Cancelable)!void {
        try hub.mutex.lock(io);
        defer hub.mutex.unlock(io);

        if (hub.find(peer) != null) return error.AlreadyJoined;
        var free: ?usize = null;
        var online: u8 = 1;
        for (&hub.members, 0..) |*slot, i| {
            if (slot.*) |*m| {
                if (std.mem.eql(u8, m.nick(), nick)) return error.NickTaken;
                online += 1;
            } else if (free == null) {
                free = i;
            }
        }
        const id = free orelse return error.RoomFull;
        var m: Member = .{ .peer = peer, .nick_buf = undefined, .nick_len = @intCast(nick.len) };
        @memcpy(m.nick_buf[0..nick.len], nick);
        hub.members[id] = m;

        hub.deliver(io, id, protocol.format(.{ .welcome = .{ .nick = nick, .online = online } }));
        hub.broadcast(io, protocol.format(.{ .joined = nick }), id);
        hub.dropSlow(io);
    }

    /// A message from a member goes to each member, the sender too. The
    /// sender sees its own line in the same order as everybody else.
    pub fn say(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io, peer: *const Peer, text: []const u8) (protocol.Refusal || std.Io.Cancelable)!void {
        try hub.mutex.lock(io);
        defer hub.mutex.unlock(io);
        const m = &hub.members[hub.find(peer) orelse return error.NoNickYet].?;
        hub.broadcast(io, protocol.format(.{ .msg = .{ .nick = m.nick(), .text = text } }), null);
        hub.dropSlow(io);
    }

    /// The member closed the connection. Close its outbox, so that the
    /// writer task sends what is left and ends.
    /// If the hub already dropped the member, `leave` only closes the outbox.
    pub fn leave(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io, peer: *Peer) std.Io.Cancelable!void {
        try hub.mutex.lock(io);
        defer hub.mutex.unlock(io);
        const id = hub.find(peer) orelse return peer.outbox.close(io);
        const m = hub.members[id].?;
        hub.members[id] = null;
        m.peer.outbox.close(io);
        hub.broadcast(io, protocol.format(.{ .left = .{ .nick = m.nick(), .reason = .quit } }), null);
        hub.dropSlow(io);
    }

    pub fn isMember(hub: *Hub, peer: *const Peer) bool {
        return hub.find(peer) != null;
    }

    fn broadcast(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io, line: Line, except: ?usize) void {
        for (hub.members, 0..) |slot, i| {
            if (slot == null or (except != null and i == except.?)) continue;
            hub.deliver(io, i, line);
        }
    }

    /// Put one line into one outbox, and never wait. With `min` 0, `put`
    /// adds what fits now and returns. A return of 0 means that the outbox
    /// is full: the member reads slower than the room talks.
    fn deliver(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io, id: usize, line: Line) void {
        const m = &(hub.members[id] orelse return);
        const added = m.peer.outbox.put(io, &.{.{ .line = line }}, 0) catch 0;
        if (added == 0) m.peer.close_code = 1008;
    }

    /// Remove each member that `deliver` marked, and tell the others. The
    /// notice can fill another outbox, thus repeat until no member has the
    /// mark. Each pass removes a member, thus the loop ends.
    fn dropSlow(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io) void {
        while (true) {
            const id = for (hub.members, 0..) |slot, i| {
                if (slot) |m| if (m.peer.close_code == 1008) break i;
            } else return;
            const m = hub.members[id].?;
            hub.members[id] = null;
            m.peer.outbox.close(io);
            hub.broadcast(io, protocol.format(.{ .left = .{ .nick = m.nick(), .reason = .too_slow } }), null);
        }
    }
};

/// Take each line that is in an outbox now. Do not wait for more.
pub fn drain(io: std.Io, outbox: *Outbox, lines: []Outgoing) []Outgoing {
    const n = outbox.get(io, lines, 0) catch 0;
    return lines[0..n];
}

// The demonstration: three members, and the lines that each outbox holds
// after each action. A writer task would send those lines.

const names = [_][]const u8{ "tejas", "vishaka", "shivam" };

fn report(out: *std.Io.Writer, io: std.Io, action: []const u8, peers: []Peer) !void {
    try out.print("{s}\n", .{action});
    var lines: [8]Outgoing = undefined;
    for (peers, names) |*peer, name| {
        for (drain(io, &peer.outbox, &lines)) |*item| {
            try out.print("  {s:<8} <- {s}\n", .{ name, item.line.bytes() });
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var storage: [3][8]Outgoing = undefined;
    var peers: [3]Peer = undefined;
    for (&peers, &storage) |*peer, *s| peer.* = .{ .outbox = .init(s) };

    var hub: Hub = .{};
    try hub.join(io, &peers[0], "tejas");
    try report(out, io, "tejas joins", &peers);
    try hub.join(io, &peers[1], "vishaka");
    try report(out, io, "vishaka joins", &peers);
    try hub.join(io, &peers[2], "shivam");
    try report(out, io, "shivam joins", &peers);

    var extra_storage: [8]Outgoing = undefined;
    var extra: Peer = .{ .outbox = .init(&extra_storage) };
    if (hub.join(io, &extra, "tejas")) |_| {} else |err| {
        try out.print("a second tejas joins\n  refused: error.{t}\n", .{err});
    }

    try hub.say(io, &peers[1], "hello, room");
    try report(out, io, "vishaka says \"hello, room\"", &peers);
    try hub.leave(io, &peers[0]);
    try report(out, io, "tejas leaves", &peers);

    // `leave` closed the outbox of tejas. Its writer task reads
    // the rest of the lines, then gets error.Closed and ends.
    var lines: [1]Outgoing = undefined;
    const closed = peers[0].outbox.get(io, &lines, 1);
    try out.print("\nthe outbox of tejas after leave: {s}\n", .{if (closed) |_| "a line" else |err| @errorName(err)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.chat-hub`)*

*Figure: Three outboxes, for tejas, vishaka and shivam, and the lines that the hub puts into each one for each action. The actions and deliveries from the program above, one step for each action.*

## Join

```zig
    /// Add a member, send the welcome to that member, and tell the others.
    pub fn join(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io, peer: *Peer, nick: []const u8) (protocol.Refusal || std.Io.Cancelable)!void {
        try hub.mutex.lock(io);
        defer hub.mutex.unlock(io);

        if (hub.find(peer) != null) return error.AlreadyJoined;
        var free: ?usize = null;
        var online: u8 = 1;
        for (&hub.members, 0..) |*slot, i| {
            if (slot.*) |*m| {
                if (std.mem.eql(u8, m.nick(), nick)) return error.NickTaken;
                online += 1;
            } else if (free == null) {
                free = i;
            }
        }
        const id = free orelse return error.RoomFull;
        var m: Member = .{ .peer = peer, .nick_buf = undefined, .nick_len = @intCast(nick.len) };
        @memcpy(m.nick_buf[0..nick.len], nick);
        hub.members[id] = m;

        hub.deliver(io, id, protocol.format(.{ .welcome = .{ .nick = nick, .online = online } }));
        hub.broadcast(io, protocol.format(.{ .joined = nick }), id);
        hub.dropSlow(io);
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `join` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-hub.zig`.*

`join` holds the `std.Io.Mutex` of the hub from the check to the last
delivery. Two clients can ask for the same nickname at the same
time. Only one gets it: the second client waits for the lock, and then the
hub finds the first.

The order inside `join` is important. The new member gets the welcome
first, then the others get `joined`. Each member sees the room in one
order, and the order is the same for each member.

```
shivam joins
  tejas    <- joined shivam
  vishaka  <- joined shivam
  shivam   <- welcome shivam (3 online)
a second tejas joins
  refused: error.NickTaken
```

The refusal returns an error to the caller. The hub does not send it. The
connection that asked puts the `error` event into its own outbox, as the
last chapter shows.

## Say: the sender gets the line too

```zig
    /// A message from a member goes to each member, the sender too. The
    /// sender sees its own line in the same order as everybody else.
    pub fn say(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io, peer: *const Peer, text: []const u8) (protocol.Refusal || std.Io.Cancelable)!void {
        try hub.mutex.lock(io);
        defer hub.mutex.unlock(io);
        const m = &hub.members[hub.find(peer) orelse return error.NoNickYet].?;
        hub.broadcast(io, protocol.format(.{ .msg = .{ .nick = m.nick(), .text = text } }), null);
        hub.dropSlow(io);
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `say` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-hub.zig`.*

The broadcast has no `except`, thus the sender gets its own line back:

```
vishaka says "hello, room"
  tejas    <- msg vishaka: hello, room
  vishaka  <- msg vishaka: hello, room
  shivam   <- msg vishaka: hello, room
```

The echo has a purpose. The hub holds its lock for the whole broadcast,
thus messages enter all outboxes in one order. When the line returns to vishaka, vishaka knows its position among the other messages. A client
that shows its own message at once, before the echo, can show the messages
in a different order from everybody else.

## A slot number is not a name

`say` and `leave` take the `*Peer` of the connection, not the number of a
slot in `members`:

```zig
    /// Find a member by its peer, never by its slot. The hub can drop a
    /// member and give the slot to a new member. A slot number that the old
    /// connection kept would then point at the new member.
    fn find(hub: *Hub, peer: *const Peer) ?usize {
        for (hub.members, 0..) |slot, i| {
            if (slot) |m| if (m.peer == peer) return i;
        }
        return null;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `find` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-hub.zig`.*

The first version of the hub returned the slot number from `join`, and the
connection kept it. That fails in a case that the next chapter adds. The
hub can drop a member, and the next member to join gets the free slot. The
task of the dropped member still runs and still has the old number. Its next
`say` then speaks as the new member.

The `Peer` lives as long as the connection, and no other connection has the
same pointer. Thus the hub searches the members for the pointer. With eight
slots, the search is eight comparisons.

## Leave

```zig
    /// The member closed the connection. Close its outbox, so that the
    /// writer task sends what is left and ends.
    /// If the hub already dropped the member, `leave` only closes the outbox.
    pub fn leave(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io, peer: *Peer) std.Io.Cancelable!void {
        try hub.mutex.lock(io);
        defer hub.mutex.unlock(io);
        const id = hub.find(peer) orelse return peer.outbox.close(io);
        const m = hub.members[id].?;
        hub.members[id] = null;
        m.peer.outbox.close(io);
        hub.broadcast(io, protocol.format(.{ .left = .{ .nick = m.nick(), .reason = .quit } }), null);
        hub.dropSlow(io);
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `leave` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-hub.zig`.*

`leave` closes the outbox. A closed `std.Io.Queue` still gives the lines
that it holds. After the last line, `get` returns `error.Closed`. Thus the
writer task sends each line that is still in the outbox, then sees
`error.Closed`, sends the close frame and ends. The close of the queue tells
the writer to stop, and no flag or extra message is necessary.

```
the outbox of tejas after leave: Closed
```

---

## Slow Clients

*A Chat Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/slow-clients/*

A client can stop. It reads nothing more. Its network can be slow, its laptop can sleep,
or its process can stop in a debugger. The server still has lines for that
client, and the lines wait in its outbox. The outbox has a fixed capacity,
thus it fills.

When the outbox is full, the hub has three choices:

1. **Wait** until the writer takes a line out.
2. **Discard the line**, and keep the member.
3. **Drop the member.**

The first choice is the dangerous one. The hub holds its lock during a
broadcast. If the broadcast waits for one member, each other member that
talks waits for the lock. One laptop in sleep mode then stops the room.

The second choice keeps the room alive, but a member who misses lines has a
wrong view of the conversation, and nothing tells that member. This hub
uses the third choice.

## Put, and never wait

```zig
    /// Put one line into one outbox, and never wait. With `min` 0, `put`
    /// adds what fits now and returns. A return of 0 means that the outbox
    /// is full: the member reads slower than the room talks.
    fn deliver(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io, id: usize, line: Line) void {
        const m = &(hub.members[id] orelse return);
        const added = m.peer.outbox.put(io, &.{.{ .line = line }}, 0) catch 0;
        if (added == 0) m.peer.close_code = 1008;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `deliver` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-hub.zig`.*

The last argument of `put` is `min`, the number of elements that `put` must
add before it returns. With `min` set to 1, `put` waits for space. With
`min` set to 0, `put` adds what fits now and returns at once. A return of 0
means that the outbox is full.

`deliver` does not remove the member. It only marks the peer with close
code 1008. `deliver` runs inside the loop of `broadcast`, and that loop
reads `members`. A change to `members` inside the loop would skip a member
or visit one twice.

```zig
    /// Remove each member that `deliver` marked, and tell the others. The
    /// notice can fill another outbox, thus repeat until no member has the
    /// mark. Each pass removes a member, thus the loop ends.
    fn dropSlow(hub: *Hub, io: std.Io) void {
        while (true) {
            const id = for (hub.members, 0..) |slot, i| {
                if (slot) |m| if (m.peer.close_code == 1008) break i;
            } else return;
            const m = hub.members[id].?;
            hub.members[id] = null;
            m.peer.outbox.close(io);
            hub.broadcast(io, protocol.format(.{ .left = .{ .nick = m.nick(), .reason = .too_slow } }), null);
        }
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `dropSlow` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-hub.zig`.*

`dropSlow` runs after the broadcast. It removes each member that `deliver` marked, closes
its outbox, and tells the others. The notice is a broadcast too, and it can
fill another outbox. Thus `dropSlow` repeats until no member has the mark.
Each pass removes one member, so the loop ends.

## A member that reads nothing

The program uses outboxes of 4 lines. tejas and vishaka read each line at
once. shivam reads nothing.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const protocol = @import("chat-protocol.zig");
const chat = @import("chat-hub.zig");

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    // Small outboxes, to make the problem visible in a few steps. A real
    // server selects the capacity from the memory that it can give to a
    // member that is behind.
    const capacity = 4;
    var storage: [3][capacity]chat.Outgoing = undefined;
    var peers: [3]chat.Peer = undefined;
    for (&peers, &storage) |*peer, *s| peer.* = .{ .outbox = .init(s) };
    const names = [_][]const u8{ "tejas", "vishaka", "shivam" };
    try out.print("outbox capacity: {d} lines of {d} bytes\n", .{ capacity, @sizeOf(chat.Outgoing) });

    var hub: chat.Hub = .{};
    for (&peers, names) |*peer, name| try hub.join(io, peer, name);

    // tejas and vishaka read each line at once. shivam reads nothing: the
    // network of shivam is slow, or a debugger stopped its process.
    var lines: [capacity]chat.Outgoing = undefined;
    _ = chat.drain(io, &peers[0].outbox, &lines);
    _ = chat.drain(io, &peers[1].outbox, &lines);
    try out.print("after the joins, shivam has 1 line waiting: its welcome\n\n", .{});

    const said = [_]struct { who: usize, text: []const u8 }{
        .{ .who = 0, .text = "hi" },
        .{ .who = 1, .text = "hello" },
        .{ .who = 0, .text = "shivam?" },
        .{ .who = 1, .text = "still there?" },
    };
    for (said) |s| {
        try hub.say(io, &peers[s.who], s.text);
        try out.print("{s} says \"{s}\"\n", .{ names[s.who], s.text });
        for (peers[0..2], names[0..2]) |*peer, name| {
            for (chat.drain(io, &peer.outbox, &lines)) |*item| {
                try out.print("  {s:<8} <- {s}\n", .{ name, item.line.bytes() });
            }
        }
        try out.print("  shivam is a member: {}\n", .{hub.isMember(&peers[2])});
    }

    // The slot of shivam is free again, and urvashi gets it. If the hub
    // used slot numbers as names, the reader task of shivam (still on the
    // old connection) could now speak as urvashi.
    var urvashi_storage: [capacity]chat.Outgoing = undefined;
    var urvashi: chat.Peer = .{ .outbox = .init(&urvashi_storage) };
    try hub.join(io, &urvashi, "urvashi");
    try out.print("\nurvashi joins, in the free slot\n", .{});
    if (hub.say(io, &peers[2], "i am back")) |_| {
        try out.print("  the old connection of shivam says \"i am back\": sent\n", .{});
    } else |err| {
        try out.print("  the old connection of shivam says \"i am back\": error.{t}\n", .{err});
    }

    // The writer task of shivam still gets the lines that are in the
    // outbox, then error.Closed. Then it sends the close code.
    try out.print("\nthe writer of shivam reads its outbox:\n", .{});
    while (true) {
        var one: [1]chat.Outgoing = undefined;
        if (peers[2].outbox.get(io, &one, 1)) |_| {
            try out.print("  {s}\n", .{one[0].line.bytes()});
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("  error.{t}: send close {d}\n", .{ err, peers[2].close_code });
            break;
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.chat-slow-client`)*

*Figure: Three outboxes of 4 lines. Two empty after each message. The outbox of shivam fills, and on the next message the hub drops shivam. The messages from the program above. The figure stops when the outbox of shivam is full and asks what the hub should do.*

The welcome of shivam and three messages fill its outbox. The fourth
message does not fit:

```
vishaka says "still there?"
  tejas    <- msg vishaka: still there?
  tejas    <- left shivam (too_slow)
  vishaka  <- msg vishaka: still there?
  vishaka  <- left shivam (too_slow)
  shivam is a member: false
```

tejas and vishaka get the message without delay, and then the notice. The
writer of shivam still has the four lines from before the drop. It sends
them, then gets `error.Closed`, and then it sends close code 1008:

```
the writer of shivam reads its outbox:
  welcome shivam (3 online)
  msg tejas: hi
  msg vishaka: hello
  msg tejas: shivam?
  error.Closed: send close 1008
```

Code 1008 is "policy violation" in RFC 6455. No code means "too slow"
exactly. 1008 is the general code for "the server ended the connection
because of a rule", and the rule here is the size of the outbox.

## The free slot

After the drop, the slot of shivam is free. urvashi joins and gets it. The
task of shivam on the old connection can still run, so the program makes it
talk:

```
urvashi joins, in the free slot
  the old connection of shivam says "i am back": error.NoNickYet
```

The hub finds members by their `*Peer`, as the
[last chapter](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/hub/) explains. The old peer is not in
the room, thus the hub refuses. With slot numbers, the hub would send the line to the room as a message
from urvashi.

## How large is the outbox?

The capacity is the number of lines that a member can be behind before the
hub drops the member. Four lines makes the problem visible in a short trace. The
server in the last chapter uses 16. The program prints the size of one item:

```
outbox capacity: 4 lines of 162 bytes
```

Thus 16 items cost about 2.6 KB for each member: the 160-byte line, its
length and the opcode.

The outbox is not the only buffer. The kernel has a send buffer for each
TCP socket, and the writer task fills it before it waits. On Linux, the
kernel grows that buffer up to the maximum in `net.ipv4.tcp_wmem`, which
is 4 MB by default. A slow member first fills the
kernel buffer, then the outbox. The outbox decides what happens after the
kernel buffer is full.

A real server also needs a time limit on each write. A writer that waits
for a client that never reads would wait for ever, and the drop only closes
the outbox. The writer must still finish its write before it sees
`error.Closed`.

---

## Read the Frames Yourself

*A Chat Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/frames/*

[WebSocket Frames](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-frames/) listed what
`readSmallMessage` in std refuses or leaves out. Two of those gaps matter
for this server:

- **Fragments.** A browser can split a message into frames. std returns
  `error.MessageOversize` for the first fragment.
- **The close frame.** std stops after the first two bytes. The server does
  not get the close code, and the rest of the frame stays unread in the
  stream.

The second gap has a cost that is easy to miss. If the server closes its
socket with unread bytes, the kernel sends a reset in place of a normal
close. Thus the server in
[A WebSocket Server on a Socket](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-server/) had to
wait for the client to close first. RFC 6455 asks for the opposite order.

The client in [A WebSocket Client](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-client/)
already reads frames itself. This reader is the server half of that code,
with three differences:

1. Each frame from a client **must** have the mask, and the reader removes
   it.
2. The reserved bits must be 0, because the server agreed to no extension.
3. The reader reads a close frame to its end, and returns the code and the
   reason.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const WebSocket = std.http.Server.WebSocket;
const Opcode = WebSocket.Opcode;

/// Reads frames from a client. It does the work that `readSmallMessage`
/// leaves to you. It joins fragments and answers nothing by itself. It reads
/// each frame to its end, thus it never stops in the middle of a frame.
pub const FrameReader = struct {
    in: *std.Io.Reader,
    /// The message so far. Its length is the largest message accepted.
    buffer: []u8,
    fragment: ?Opcode = null,
    fragment_len: usize = 0,

    pub const Event = union(enum) {
        text: []const u8,
        binary: []const u8,
        ping: []const u8,
        pong: []const u8,
        /// 1005 if the frame had no code.
        close: struct { code: u16, reason: []const u8 },
    };

    pub const Error = error{
        UnmaskedFrame,
        ReservedBits,
        ProtocolError,
        MessageTooBig,
        InvalidUtf8,
    } || std.Io.Reader.Error;

    pub fn next(r: *FrameReader) Error!Event {
        while (true) {
            const header = try r.in.takeArray(2);
            const h0: WebSocket.Header0 = @bitCast(header[0]);
            const h1: WebSocket.Header1 = @bitCast(header[1]);
            // No extension is in use, thus each reserved bit must be 0.
            if (h0.rsv1 != 0 or h0.rsv2 != 0 or h0.rsv3 != 0) return error.ReservedBits;
            if (!h1.mask) return error.UnmaskedFrame;
            const len: u64 = switch (h1.payload_len) {
                .len16 => try r.in.takeInt(u16, .big),
                .len64 => try r.in.takeInt(u64, .big),
                else => @backingInt(h1.payload_len),
            };
            const control = switch (h0.opcode) {
                .ping, .pong, .connection_close => true,
                .text, .binary, .continuation => false,
                _ => return error.ProtocolError,
            };

            // Control frames are short and complete, and they can arrive
            // between two fragments. They use their own small buffer, so
            // the message in `buffer` stays as it is.
            if (control) {
                if (len > 125 or !h0.fin) return error.ProtocolError;
                const mask = (try r.in.takeArray(4)).*;
                const payload = try r.in.take(@intCast(len));
                unmask(payload, mask);
                switch (h0.opcode) {
                    .ping => return .{ .ping = payload },
                    .pong => return .{ .pong = payload },
                    else => return closeEvent(payload),
                }
            }

            switch (h0.opcode) {
                .continuation => if (r.fragment == null) return error.ProtocolError,
                else => {
                    if (r.fragment != null) return error.ProtocolError;
                    r.fragment = h0.opcode;
                    r.fragment_len = 0;
                },
            }
            // Refuse a frame that is too big before you read its payload.
            // The length is 8 bytes from the client, and it can be anything.
            if (len > r.buffer.len - r.fragment_len) return error.MessageTooBig;
            const mask = (try r.in.takeArray(4)).*;
            const part = r.buffer[r.fragment_len..][0..@intCast(len)];
            try r.in.readSliceAll(part);
            unmask(part, mask);
            r.fragment_len += part.len;
            if (!h0.fin) continue;

            const data = r.buffer[0..r.fragment_len];
            const opcode = r.fragment.?;
            r.fragment = null;
            if (opcode == .binary) return .{ .binary = data };
            if (!std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(data)) return error.InvalidUtf8;
            return .{ .text = data };
        }
    }

    fn unmask(bytes: []u8, mask: [4]u8) void {
        for (bytes, 0..) |*b, i| b.* ^= mask[i % 4];
    }

    fn closeEvent(payload: []const u8) Error!Event {
        if (payload.len == 0) return .{ .close = .{ .code = 1005, .reason = "" } };
        // A close payload is a 2-byte code, then a UTF-8 reason.
        if (payload.len == 1) return error.ProtocolError;
        const reason = payload[2..];
        if (!std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(reason)) return error.InvalidUtf8;
        return .{ .close = .{ .code = std.mem.readInt(u16, payload[0..2], .big), .reason = reason } };
    }
};

/// The close code to send when `next` fails. RFC 6455, section 7.4.1.
pub fn closeCodeFor(err: FrameReader.Error) u16 {
    return switch (err) {
        error.UnmaskedFrame, error.ReservedBits, error.ProtocolError => 1002,
        error.InvalidUtf8 => 1007,
        error.MessageTooBig => 1009,
        error.ReadFailed, error.EndOfStream => 1006,
    };
}

// The demonstration. `frame` builds a client frame by hand.

fn frame(w: *std.Io.Writer, opcode: Opcode, fin: bool, payload: []const u8) !void {
    const mask = [4]u8{ 0x11, 0x22, 0x33, 0x44 };
    try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header0{ .opcode = opcode, .fin = fin }));
    if (payload.len <= 125) {
        try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header1{ .payload_len = @fromBackingInt(@intCast(payload.len)), .mask = true }));
    } else {
        try w.writeByte(@bitCast(WebSocket.Header1{ .payload_len = .len16, .mask = true }));
        try w.writeInt(u16, @intCast(payload.len), .big);
    }
    try w.writeAll(&mask);
    for (payload, 0..) |b, i| try w.writeByte(b ^ mask[i % 4]);
}

fn printEvent(out: *std.Io.Writer, event: FrameReader.Event) !void {
    switch (event) {
        .text => |t| try out.print("text \"{s}\"\n", .{t}),
        .binary => |b| try out.print("binary, {d} bytes\n", .{b.len}),
        .ping => |p| try out.print("ping \"{s}\"\n", .{p}),
        .pong => |p| try out.print("pong \"{s}\"\n", .{p}),
        .close => |c| try out.print("close {d} \"{s}\"\n", .{ c.code, c.reason }),
    }
}

/// Give one stream to a new reader with a 64-byte limit. Print each event,
/// or the error and the close code that the server sends for it.
fn readAll(out: *std.Io.Writer, name: []const u8, bytes: []const u8) !void {
    var in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(bytes);
    var message: [64]u8 = undefined;
    var r: FrameReader = .{ .in = &in, .buffer = &message };
    try out.print("{s}:\n", .{name});
    while (true) {
        const event = r.next() catch |err| {
            if (err == error.EndOfStream) break;
            try out.print("  error.{t} -> send close {d}\n", .{ err, closeCodeFor(err) });
            break;
        };
        try out.print("  ", .{});
        try printEvent(out, event);
        if (event == .close) {
            try out.print("  unread bytes after the close frame: {d}\n", .{in.bufferedLen()});
            break;
        }
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [2048]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var wire: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&wire);

    try frame(&w, .text, false, "Hel");
    try frame(&w, .ping, true, "beat");
    try frame(&w, .continuation, false, "lo, ");
    try frame(&w, .continuation, true, "room");
    try frame(&w, .binary, true, &.{ 1, 2, 3 });
    try frame(&w, .connection_close, true, "\x03\xe9going home");
    try readAll(out, "a message in three fragments, a ping between", w.buffered());

    try out.print("\nframes that the server must refuse, limit 64 bytes:\n", .{});
    const cases = [_]struct { name: []const u8, opcode: Opcode, fin: bool, payload: []const u8, raw: ?[]const u8 = null }{
        .{ .name = "unmasked text", .opcode = .text, .fin = true, .payload = "", .raw = "\x81\x02hi" },
        .{ .name = "a reserved bit set", .opcode = .text, .fin = true, .payload = "", .raw = "\xc1\x80\x00\x00\x00\x00" },
        .{ .name = "opcode 3", .opcode = @fromBackingInt(@intCast(3)), .fin = true, .payload = "?" },
        .{ .name = "ping in fragments", .opcode = .ping, .fin = false, .payload = "beat" },
        .{ .name = "continuation first", .opcode = .continuation, .fin = true, .payload = "lo" },
        .{ .name = "200 bytes", .opcode = .binary, .fin = true, .payload = &@as([200]u8, @splat(0)) },
        .{ .name = "text that is not UTF-8", .opcode = .text, .fin = true, .payload = "\xc3\x28" },
        .{ .name = "close with 1 byte", .opcode = .connection_close, .fin = true, .payload = "\x03" },
    };
    for (cases) |case| {
        var case_w: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&wire);
        if (case.raw) |raw| try case_w.writeAll(raw) else try frame(&case_w, case.opcode, case.fin, case.payload);
        var in: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(case_w.buffered());
        var message: [64]u8 = undefined;
        var r: FrameReader = .{ .in = &in, .buffer = &message };
        try out.print("  {s:<24} -> ", .{case.name});
        if (r.next()) |event| {
            try printEvent(out, event);
        } else |err| {
            try out.print("error.{t}, close {d}\n", .{ err, closeCodeFor(err) });
        }
    }

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`11-networking.chat-frames`)*

## The reader

```zig
/// Reads frames from a client. It does the work that `readSmallMessage`
/// leaves to you. It joins fragments and answers nothing by itself. It reads
/// each frame to its end, thus it never stops in the middle of a frame.
pub const FrameReader = struct {
    in: *std.Io.Reader,
    /// The message so far. Its length is the largest message accepted.
    buffer: []u8,
    fragment: ?Opcode = null,
    fragment_len: usize = 0,

    pub const Event = union(enum) {
        text: []const u8,
        binary: []const u8,
        ping: []const u8,
        pong: []const u8,
        /// 1005 if the frame had no code.
        close: struct { code: u16, reason: []const u8 },
    };

    pub const Error = error{
        UnmaskedFrame,
        ReservedBits,
        ProtocolError,
        MessageTooBig,
        InvalidUtf8,
    } || std.Io.Reader.Error;

    pub fn next(r: *FrameReader) Error!Event {
        while (true) {
            const header = try r.in.takeArray(2);
            const h0: WebSocket.Header0 = @bitCast(header[0]);
            const h1: WebSocket.Header1 = @bitCast(header[1]);
            // No extension is in use, thus each reserved bit must be 0.
            if (h0.rsv1 != 0 or h0.rsv2 != 0 or h0.rsv3 != 0) return error.ReservedBits;
            if (!h1.mask) return error.UnmaskedFrame;
            const len: u64 = switch (h1.payload_len) {
                .len16 => try r.in.takeInt(u16, .big),
                .len64 => try r.in.takeInt(u64, .big),
                else => @backingInt(h1.payload_len),
            };
            const control = switch (h0.opcode) {
                .ping, .pong, .connection_close => true,
                .text, .binary, .continuation => false,
                _ => return error.ProtocolError,
            };

            // Control frames are short and complete, and they can arrive
            // between two fragments. They use their own small buffer, so
            // the message in `buffer` stays as it is.
            if (control) {
                if (len > 125 or !h0.fin) return error.ProtocolError;
                const mask = (try r.in.takeArray(4)).*;
                const payload = try r.in.take(@intCast(len));
                unmask(payload, mask);
                switch (h0.opcode) {
                    .ping => return .{ .ping = payload },
                    .pong => return .{ .pong = payload },
                    else => return closeEvent(payload),
                }
            }

            switch (h0.opcode) {
                .continuation => if (r.fragment == null) return error.ProtocolError,
                else => {
                    if (r.fragment != null) return error.ProtocolError;
                    r.fragment = h0.opcode;
                    r.fragment_len = 0;
                },
            }
            // Refuse a frame that is too big before you read its payload.
            // The length is 8 bytes from the client, and it can be anything.
            if (len > r.buffer.len - r.fragment_len) return error.MessageTooBig;
            const mask = (try r.in.takeArray(4)).*;
            const part = r.buffer[r.fragment_len..][0..@intCast(len)];
            try r.in.readSliceAll(part);
            unmask(part, mask);
            r.fragment_len += part.len;
            if (!h0.fin) continue;

            const data = r.buffer[0..r.fragment_len];
            const opcode = r.fragment.?;
            r.fragment = null;
            if (opcode == .binary) return .{ .binary = data };
            if (!std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(data)) return error.InvalidUtf8;
            return .{ .text = data };
        }
    }

    fn unmask(bytes: []u8, mask: [4]u8) void {
        for (bytes, 0..) |*b, i| b.* ^= mask[i % 4];
    }

    fn closeEvent(payload: []const u8) Error!Event {
        if (payload.len == 0) return .{ .close = .{ .code = 1005, .reason = "" } };
        // A close payload is a 2-byte code, then a UTF-8 reason.
        if (payload.len == 1) return error.ProtocolError;
        const reason = payload[2..];
        if (!std.unicode.utf8ValidateSlice(reason)) return error.InvalidUtf8;
        return .{ .close = .{ .code = std.mem.readInt(u16, payload[0..2], .big), .reason = reason } };
    }
};
```

*Quoted from the source: `FrameReader` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-frames.zig`.*

The structure is the same as the client: control frames first, then data
frames, with the state of a message in fragments in two fields.

**The size check comes before the payload.** The length field of a frame
can say 2<sup>63</sup> bytes. The reader compares the length with the space
left in `buffer` and refuses the frame before it reads one byte of payload.
The reader allocates nothing, thus a large length cannot make the server
use memory.

**Control frames use the buffer of the reader, not `buffer`.** A ping can
arrive between two fragments. If the ping used `buffer`, it would
overwrite the part of the message that is already there. `take` returns the
ping payload as a slice of the buffer in the `std.Io.Reader`, and `buffer`
stays as it is.

```
a message in three fragments, a ping between:
  ping "beat"
  text "Hello, room"
  binary, 3 bytes
  close 1001 "going home"
  unread bytes after the close frame: 0
```

The last line is the reason for this chapter. After the close frame,
nothing is unread. The server can send its close frame and then close the
TCP connection first, with a normal FIN and no reset.

## A close code for each failure

RFC 6455 gives a close code for each type of failure. One function maps
the errors of the reader to the codes:

```zig
/// The close code to send when `next` fails. RFC 6455, section 7.4.1.
pub fn closeCodeFor(err: FrameReader.Error) u16 {
    return switch (err) {
        error.UnmaskedFrame, error.ReservedBits, error.ProtocolError => 1002,
        error.InvalidUtf8 => 1007,
        error.MessageTooBig => 1009,
        error.ReadFailed, error.EndOfStream => 1006,
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `closeCodeFor` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-frames.zig`.*

```
frames that the server must refuse, limit 64 bytes:
  unmasked text            -> error.UnmaskedFrame, close 1002
  a reserved bit set       -> error.ReservedBits, close 1002
  opcode 3                 -> error.ProtocolError, close 1002
  ping in fragments        -> error.ProtocolError, close 1002
  continuation first       -> error.ProtocolError, close 1002
  200 bytes                -> error.MessageTooBig, close 1009
  text that is not UTF-8   -> error.InvalidUtf8, close 1007
  close with 1 byte        -> error.ProtocolError, close 1002
```

The switch in `closeCodeFor` has no `else`. If a new error joins `FrameReader.Error`, the compiler requires a case for
it. Thus no failure can reach a client with a code that nobody selected.

Code 1006 is special. It means "the connection closed with no close frame",
and RFC 6455 forbids a close frame with that code. `closeCodeFor` returns
it for `ReadFailed` and `EndOfStream` so that the server can log one code
for each end of a connection. The writer in the last chapter checks for
1006 and sends no close frame.

After a protocol error, the stream is not trustworthy. The reader can stop
in the middle of a frame, for example after the header of a frame that is
too big. Thus after an error, the server sends its close frame and closes
the connection. It does not try to read more frames.

---

## The Server

*A Chat Server. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/the-server/*

This chapter puts the parts on real sockets. The file imports four other
snippets:

- `chat-protocol.zig` for commands and events
- `chat-hub.zig` for the room and the outboxes
- `chat-frames.zig` for the frame reader
- `websocket-client.zig` for the clients that talk to the server

The server code is about 100 lines. The rest of the file is the three
clients and the order of their actions.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const Io = std.Io;
const WebSocket = std.http.Server.WebSocket;
const protocol = @import("chat-protocol.zig");
const chat = @import("chat-hub.zig");
const FrameReader = @import("chat-frames.zig").FrameReader;
const closeCodeFor = @import("chat-frames.zig").closeCodeFor;
const Client = @import("websocket-client.zig").Client;

// ------------------------------------------------------------------ server

/// The only code that writes to the socket of a connection. It sends each
/// frame from the outbox. When the hub or the reader closes the outbox, the
/// writer sends the close frame with the code that the closer set, and
/// ends. Code 1006 means that the connection is gone, and a close frame
/// must never carry it.
fn writeLoop(io: Io, peer: *chat.Peer, ws: *WebSocket) void {
    while (true) {
        const item = peer.outbox.getOne(io) catch break;
        ws.writeMessage(item.line.bytes(), item.opcode) catch return;
    }
    if (peer.close_code == 1006) return;
    var payload: [2]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(u16, &payload, peer.close_code, .big);
    ws.writeMessage(&payload, .connection_close) catch {};
}

/// Put a reply to this client into its own outbox. Only this connection
/// waits if the outbox is full, thus a blocking put is correct here.
fn reply(io: Io, peer: *chat.Peer, opcode: WebSocket.Opcode, bytes: []const u8) void {
    var item: chat.Outgoing = .{ .opcode = opcode, .line = .{} };
    @memcpy(item.line.buf[0..bytes.len], bytes);
    item.line.len = @intCast(bytes.len);
    peer.outbox.putOne(io, item) catch {};
}

fn refuse(io: Io, peer: *chat.Peer, err: protocol.Refusal) void {
    reply(io, peer, .text, protocol.format(.{ .err = err }).bytes());
}

/// Read frames until the client closes or breaks the protocol. On return,
/// `leave` closes the outbox, and the writer sends the close frame.
fn readLoop(io: Io, in: *Io.Reader, peer: *chat.Peer, hub: *chat.Hub) void {
    defer hub.leave(io, peer) catch {};
    // "say " and the longest text fit. A larger message gets close 1009.
    var message: [4 + protocol.max_text]u8 = undefined;
    var frames: FrameReader = .{ .in = in, .buffer = &message };
    while (true) {
        const event = frames.next() catch |err| {
            peer.close_code = closeCodeFor(err);
            return;
        };
        switch (event) {
            .ping => |p| reply(io, peer, .pong, p),
            .pong => {},
            .binary => refuse(io, peer, error.UnknownCommand),
            .close => |c| {
                // Answer with the code of the client. 1005 means "no code",
                // and a close frame must not carry it.
                peer.close_code = if (c.code == 1005) 1000 else c.code;
                return;
            },
            .text => |t| {
                const command = protocol.parseCommand(t) catch |err| {
                    refuse(io, peer, err);
                    continue;
                };
                const result = switch (command) {
                    .nick => |nick| hub.join(io, peer, nick),
                    .say => |text| hub.say(io, peer, text),
                };
                result catch |err| switch (err) {
                    error.Canceled => return,
                    else => |refusal| refuse(io, peer, refusal),
                };
            },
        }
    }
}

/// One connection, as a task. The handshake is std. The frames are the
/// frame reader. The connection closes the TCP stream when both of its
/// tasks are complete. The frame reader reads each close frame to its
/// end, thus nothing is unread, and the server can close first.
fn connection(io: Io, stream: Io.net.Stream, hub: *chat.Hub) void {
    defer stream.close(io);
    var read_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var write_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = stream.reader(io, &read_buf);
    var writer = stream.writer(io, &write_buf);
    var http = std.http.Server.init(&reader.interface, &writer.interface);

    var request = http.receiveHead() catch return;
    const key = switch (request.upgradeRequested()) {
        .websocket => |k| k orelse return request.respond("", .{ .status = .bad_request }) catch {},
        .none, .other => return request.respond("a WebSocket chat\n", .{}) catch {},
    };
    var ws = request.respondWebSocket(.{ .key = key }) catch return;
    ws.flush() catch return;

    var storage: [16]chat.Outgoing = undefined;
    var peer: chat.Peer = .{ .outbox = .init(&storage) };
    // `concurrent`, not `async`: the writer blocks on the outbox until the
    // reader closes it. If `async` ran the writer on this thread, the
    // reader would never start.
    var writer_task = io.concurrent(writeLoop, .{ io, &peer, &ws }) catch return;
    readLoop(io, &reader.interface, &peer, hub);
    writer_task.await(io);
}

fn acceptLoop(io: Io, listener: *Io.net.Server, hub: *chat.Hub, group: *Io.Group) void {
    while (true) {
        const stream = listener.accept(io) catch return;
        group.concurrent(io, connection, .{ io, stream, hub }) catch stream.close(io);
    }
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------- clients

/// One person: a connection, the client from the WebSocket chapter, and
/// a record of each line that the person sent and received.
const Person = struct {
    name: []const u8,
    stream: Io.net.Stream,
    read_buf: [1024]u8,
    write_buf: [1024]u8,
    reader: Io.net.Stream.Reader,
    writer: Io.net.Stream.Writer,
    client: Client,
    log_buf: [1024]u8,
    log: Io.Writer,
    message_buf: [256]u8,

    fn connect(p: *Person, io: Io, name: []const u8, addr: Io.net.IpAddress, random: std.Random) !void {
        p.name = name;
        p.stream = try addr.connect(io, .{ .mode = .stream });
        p.reader = p.stream.reader(io, &p.read_buf);
        p.writer = p.stream.writer(io, &p.write_buf);
        p.client = .{ .in = &p.reader.interface, .out = &p.writer.interface, .random = random };
        p.log = .fixed(&p.log_buf);
        try p.client.sendHandshake("127.0.0.1", "/chat");
        try p.client.finishHandshake();
    }

    fn send(p: *Person, text: []const u8) !void {
        try p.log.print("  -> {s}\n", .{text});
        try p.client.send(.text, text);
    }

    /// Read events until one prints as `expected`. Log each event.
    fn until(p: *Person, expected: []const u8) !void {
        while (true) {
            var line_buf: [192]u8 = undefined;
            const line = switch (try p.client.receive(&p.message_buf)) {
                .text => |t| t,
                .binary => "(binary)",
                .ping => |d| try std.mem.print(&line_buf, "ping {s}", .{d}),
                .pong => |d| try std.mem.print(&line_buf, "pong {s}", .{d}),
                .close => |code| try std.mem.print(&line_buf, "close {d}", .{code}),
            };
            try p.log.print("  <- {s}\n", .{line});
            if (std.mem.eql(u8, line, expected)) return;
        }
    }
};

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    const io = init.io;
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var hub: chat.Hub = .{};
    const any_port = try Io.net.IpAddress.parse("127.0.0.1", 0);
    var listener = try any_port.listen(io, .{});
    defer listener.deinit(io);
    const addr = listener.socket.address;

    var connections: Io.Group = .init;
    var acceptor = try io.concurrent(acceptLoop, .{ io, &listener, &hub, &connections });

    var seed: [8]u8 = undefined;
    io.random(&seed);
    var prng = std.Random.DefaultPrng.init(std.mem.readInt(u64, &seed, .little));

    // Each action waits until each person who must see the result sees
    // it. The threads of the server then cannot change the order of lines
    // that a person receives, and CI can compare the output.
    var people: [3]Person = undefined;
    const tejas = &people[0];
    const vishaka = &people[1];
    const shivam = &people[2];

    try tejas.connect(io, "tejas", addr, prng.random());
    try tejas.send("nick tejas");
    try tejas.until("welcome tejas (1 online)");

    try vishaka.connect(io, "vishaka", addr, prng.random());
    try vishaka.send("say hi");
    try vishaka.until("error NoNickYet");
    try vishaka.send("nick vishaka");
    try vishaka.until("welcome vishaka (2 online)");
    try tejas.until("joined vishaka");

    try shivam.connect(io, "shivam", addr, prng.random());
    try shivam.send("nick tejas");
    try shivam.until("error NickTaken");
    try shivam.send("nick shivam");
    try shivam.until("welcome shivam (3 online)");
    try tejas.until("joined shivam");
    try vishaka.until("joined shivam");

    try tejas.send("say hello, room");
    for (&people) |*p| try p.until("msg tejas: hello, room");

    try vishaka.log.print("  -> ping beat\n", .{});
    try vishaka.client.send(.ping, "beat");
    try vishaka.until("pong beat");

    try shivam.send("shout hi");
    try shivam.until("error UnknownCommand");

    try shivam.log.print("  -> close 1000\n", .{});
    try shivam.client.close(1000);
    try shivam.until("close 1000");
    try tejas.until("left shivam (quit)");
    try vishaka.until("left shivam (quit)");

    try tejas.send("say bye");
    try tejas.until("msg tejas: bye");
    try vishaka.until("msg tejas: bye");

    try vishaka.log.print("  -> close 1000\n", .{});
    try vishaka.client.close(1000);
    try vishaka.until("close 1000");
    try tejas.until("left vishaka (quit)");

    try tejas.log.print("  -> close 1000\n", .{});
    try tejas.client.close(1000);
    try tejas.until("close 1000");

    for (&people) |*p| p.stream.close(io);
    acceptor.cancel(io);
    connections.cancel(io);

    for (&people) |*p| try out.print("{s}:\n{s}", .{ p.name, p.log.buffered() });
    try out.flush();
}
```

*CI builds and runs this snippet natively: three clients talk to the server over real loopback sockets. Browser wasm has no sockets. (`11-networking.chat-server`)*

## Two tasks for each connection

```zig
/// One connection, as a task. The handshake is std. The frames are the
/// frame reader. The connection closes the TCP stream when both of its
/// tasks are complete. The frame reader reads each close frame to its
/// end, thus nothing is unread, and the server can close first.
fn connection(io: Io, stream: Io.net.Stream, hub: *chat.Hub) void {
    defer stream.close(io);
    var read_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var write_buf: [512]u8 = undefined;
    var reader = stream.reader(io, &read_buf);
    var writer = stream.writer(io, &write_buf);
    var http = std.http.Server.init(&reader.interface, &writer.interface);

    var request = http.receiveHead() catch return;
    const key = switch (request.upgradeRequested()) {
        .websocket => |k| k orelse return request.respond("", .{ .status = .bad_request }) catch {},
        .none, .other => return request.respond("a WebSocket chat\n", .{}) catch {},
    };
    var ws = request.respondWebSocket(.{ .key = key }) catch return;
    ws.flush() catch return;

    var storage: [16]chat.Outgoing = undefined;
    var peer: chat.Peer = .{ .outbox = .init(&storage) };
    // `concurrent`, not `async`: the writer blocks on the outbox until the
    // reader closes it. If `async` ran the writer on this thread, the
    // reader would never start.
    var writer_task = io.concurrent(writeLoop, .{ io, &peer, &ws }) catch return;
    readLoop(io, &reader.interface, &peer, hub);
    writer_task.await(io);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `connection` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-server.zig`.*

The connection task does the handshake with `std.http.Server`, as in
[The WebSocket Handshake](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/networking/websocket-handshake/). Then it
makes the `Peer` and starts the writer task. The connection task itself
becomes the reader.

The writer task starts with `io.concurrent`, not `io.async`. The writer
waits on the outbox until the reader closes it. `io.async` can run a task
on the thread that calls it, and then the writer would wait for ever, and
the reader would never start. `concurrent` promises a separate task, or it
fails with `error.ConcurrencyUnavailable`.
[Cancellation](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/concurrency/cancellation/) shows the same trap with
`Group.async`.

The `Peer` and its outbox live on the stack of the connection task. That
is correct because the connection task waits for the writer with
`writer_task.await(io)` before it returns. The outbox cannot go away while
the writer uses it.

## The writer

```zig
/// The only code that writes to the socket of a connection. It sends each
/// frame from the outbox. When the hub or the reader closes the outbox, the
/// writer sends the close frame with the code that the closer set, and
/// ends. Code 1006 means that the connection is gone, and a close frame
/// must never carry it.
fn writeLoop(io: Io, peer: *chat.Peer, ws: *WebSocket) void {
    while (true) {
        const item = peer.outbox.getOne(io) catch break;
        ws.writeMessage(item.line.bytes(), item.opcode) catch return;
    }
    if (peer.close_code == 1006) return;
    var payload: [2]u8 = undefined;
    std.mem.writeInt(u16, &payload, peer.close_code, .big);
    ws.writeMessage(&payload, .connection_close) catch {};
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writeLoop` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-server.zig`.*

The writer uses the `WebSocket` value that `respondWebSocket` returned.
`writeMessage` from std writes a server frame to any writer, so the server
needs no frame writer of its own. Only the reader side needed new code.

## The reader

```zig
/// Read frames until the client closes or breaks the protocol. On return,
/// `leave` closes the outbox, and the writer sends the close frame.
fn readLoop(io: Io, in: *Io.Reader, peer: *chat.Peer, hub: *chat.Hub) void {
    defer hub.leave(io, peer) catch {};
    // "say " and the longest text fit. A larger message gets close 1009.
    var message: [4 + protocol.max_text]u8 = undefined;
    var frames: FrameReader = .{ .in = in, .buffer = &message };
    while (true) {
        const event = frames.next() catch |err| {
            peer.close_code = closeCodeFor(err);
            return;
        };
        switch (event) {
            .ping => |p| reply(io, peer, .pong, p),
            .pong => {},
            .binary => refuse(io, peer, error.UnknownCommand),
            .close => |c| {
                // Answer with the code of the client. 1005 means "no code",
                // and a close frame must not carry it.
                peer.close_code = if (c.code == 1005) 1000 else c.code;
                return;
            },
            .text => |t| {
                const command = protocol.parseCommand(t) catch |err| {
                    refuse(io, peer, err);
                    continue;
                };
                const result = switch (command) {
                    .nick => |nick| hub.join(io, peer, nick),
                    .say => |text| hub.say(io, peer, text),
                };
                result catch |err| switch (err) {
                    error.Canceled => return,
                    else => |refusal| refuse(io, peer, refusal),
                };
            },
        }
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `readLoop` from `snippets/11-networking/chat-server.zig`.*

The `defer` on the first line runs on each path out of the function. The
three paths are a close from the client, a protocol error, and a lost
connection. `leave`
closes the outbox in each case, also when the hub dropped the member
already. Thus the writer always ends.

The reader puts its own replies into the outbox: the `error` events and
the pong for a ping. It never writes to the socket. A reply waits with
`putOne` if the outbox is full. That wait is correct here, because only
this connection waits. The hub never waits, as
[Slow Clients](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/slow-clients/) requires.

A `say` before a `nick` gives `error.NoNickYet` from the hub, because the
hub does not find the peer. The reader needs no state of its own for that
case.

## The order of a close

When a client sends close:

1. The frame reader reads the whole close frame and returns `.close`.
2. The reader sets `close_code` to the code of the client and returns.
3. The `defer` calls `leave`. The hub removes the member, closes the
   outbox and tells the others.
4. The writer sends each line that is still in the outbox, then gets
   `error.Closed` and sends the close frame.
5. The connection task returns, and its `defer` closes the TCP stream.

The server closes the TCP connection first, as RFC 6455 asks. That is
possible because of step 1: no byte of the close frame is left unread.

## Three clients, in a fixed order

The clients in `main` use the client from the WebSocket chapter over real
sockets. The server has a task for each connection, thus lines can arrive
at different clients in a different order on each run. CI compares the output, so the program must fix the order.

The program fixes the order with one rule. After each action, it waits
until each client that must see the result receives it. Then it starts
the next action. For example, after tejas sends `say hello, room`, `main`
calls `until("msg tejas: hello, room")` on all three clients.

A wait on the sender alone is not enough: the broadcast can still be in progress for vishaka when tejas
already has the line. Each client records what it sent and received, and
`main` prints the records at the end:

```
vishaka:
  -> say hi
  <- error NoNickYet
  -> nick vishaka
  <- welcome vishaka (2 online)
  <- joined shivam
  <- msg tejas: hello, room
  -> ping beat
  <- pong beat
  <- left shivam (quit)
  <- msg tejas: bye
  -> close 1000
  <- close 1000
```

The record of vishaka shows each part of the server:

- the refusal before a nickname
- the welcome, and the notices for other members
- a broadcast from tejas
- a ping that the writer of vishaka answered
- the close handshake

The output was the same in 50 runs. The runs were 30 on all cores, 10 on
one core and 10 on two cores.

## A slow client on a real socket

The program has no slow client. A slow client on loopback is hard to make in a test. The kernel buffers of
the socket hold megabytes before the outbox starts to fill. [Slow Clients](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/chat-server/slow-clients/)
shows the drop with the same hub code and no sockets, where the result is
the same on each run.

## The next steps

- **Many rooms.** Give the hub a map from a room name to a set of members.
  The outboxes and the writers do not change.
- **History.** Keep the last 50 lines in a ring buffer in the hub, and put
  them into the outbox of a new member before the welcome.
- **A time limit on writes.** A writer that waits for a client that never
  reads keeps its task for ever. Cancel the writer when a write takes too
  long, and close the connection.
- **TLS.** Wrap the stream before the handshake. The reader and the writer
  take any `std.Io.Reader` and `std.Io.Writer`, so nothing else changes.
