# Track: Practice

The algorithms that a contest problem expects you to know. Each program prints the steps that it took.

## Binary Search

*Competitive Programming. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/binary-search/*

Binary search is a small loop, but some details must be correct. One common mistake gives the wrong index. A different mistake makes the loop run forever.

Both versions compile. Thus you must know exactly what each variable means.

The program below prints each step of the search. Each line shows `lo`, `hi`, `mid`, the value at `mid`, and the part of the array that the search did not remove.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The problem, as text.
///
/// A snippet here runs under WASI in a browser tab. The tab has no stdin to
/// read. A contest problem gives you a line of sorted values and a line of
/// queries. This constant holds the same two lines. The parser below reads
/// the constant in the same way that it reads a real file.
const input =
    \\1 3 3 4 7 7 7 9 11 11 15 20
    \\7 5 20 0 21
;

/// Read one line of whitespace-separated integers into `out`.
///
/// The function takes a `*std.Io.Reader` instead of the string. The
/// networking chapters use the same method for protocols. The function changes
/// bytes into values. Thus the same code works with a file, a socket, or a
/// string literal that CI can check.
fn readRow(reader: *std.Io.Reader, out: []i32) ![]i32 {
    const line = (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) orelse return error.MissingRow;
    var count: usize = 0;
    var fields = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    while (fields.next()) |field| {
        if (count == out.len) return error.RowTooLong;
        out[count] = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, field, 10);
        count += 1;
    }
    return out[0..count];
}

/// The first index with a value that is not less than `key`.
///
/// The window is half-open: each index that can be the answer is in
/// `items[lo..hi]`. `lo` moves only past values that are too small. `hi`
/// moves down only to values that are sufficiently large. Thus the answer
/// always stays in the window. When `lo` gets to `hi`, the window is empty
/// and `lo` is the answer. For this reason, the function has no separate case
/// for a value that it cannot find.
///
/// Use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`, not `(lo + hi) / 2`. The second form adds two
/// indices. Each index is valid, but on a large array the sum can be too
/// large.
fn lowerBound(items: []const i32, key: i32) usize {
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (items[mid] < key) lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}

/// The first index with a value that is greater than `key`.
///
/// The only difference from `lowerBound` is one character. With `<=`, the
/// loop moves past each value that is equal to the key. It does not stop at
/// the first equal value.
fn upperBound(items: []const i32, key: i32) usize {
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (items[mid] <= key) lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}

/// Right-align a value in a cell of `width` characters.
///
/// `{d:>4}` is shorter, but it prints a `+` before a non-negative signed
/// integer when you give a width. This function formats the digits first and
/// then adds the padding. Thus the table is easy to read.
fn writeCell(out: *std.Io.Writer, value: i32, width: usize) !void {
    var digits: [12]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&digits, "{d}", .{value});
    try out.splatByteAll(' ', width - text.len);
    try out.writeAll(text);
}

/// One line of the trace: the counters, then the array. The line shows the
/// current window, and the middle value is in brackets.
///
/// A value outside `items[lo..hi]` prints as a dot. Thus you can see the window
/// become half as large. You do not have to calculate it from three numbers.
fn writeStep(
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    items: []const i32,
    step: usize,
    lo: usize,
    mid: usize,
    hi: usize,
) !void {
    try out.print("  step {d}  lo={d:>2} mid={d:>2} hi={d:>2} ", .{ step, lo, mid, hi });
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        if (i < lo or i >= hi) {
            try out.writeAll("   .");
        } else if (i == mid) {
            try out.writeByte('[');
            try writeCell(out, value, 2);
            try out.writeByte(']');
        } else {
            try writeCell(out, value, 4);
        }
    }
    try out.writeByte('\n');
}

/// The same search as `lowerBound`, but it prints the window at each step.
///
/// This function is separate, thus `lowerBound` keeps the shape that you can
/// copy into a solution. The run below checks that the two functions return
/// the same index. It does not assume that they do.
fn traceLowerBound(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, key: i32) !usize {
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len;
    var step: usize = 0;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        step += 1;
        try writeStep(out, items, step, lo, mid, hi);
        if (items[mid] < key) lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid;
    }
    try out.print("  window empty after {d} steps: lo = hi = {d}\n", .{ step, lo });
    return lo;
}

/// The off-by-one bug, as a program that you can run.
///
/// `lo = mid` looks safe next to `lo = mid + 1`. `mid` was too small, thus
/// it looks like `mid` in the window costs only one more comparison. But
/// `lo = mid` stops the loop. When `hi - lo` is 1, `mid` is `lo`. Then
/// `lo = mid` does not change the window, and the next step is the same as
/// this step.
///
/// The step limit lets the program print the problem. Without the limit, the
/// loop does not stop.
fn stalledLowerBound(
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    items: []const i32,
    key: i32,
    budget: usize,
) !?usize {
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len;
    var step: usize = 0;
    while (lo < hi) {
        if (step == budget) {
            try out.print("  no progress: gave up at step {d} with lo={d} hi={d}\n", .{ step, lo, hi });
            return null;
        }
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        step += 1;
        try writeStep(out, items, step, lo, mid, hi);
        if (items[mid] < key) lo = mid else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}

/// The comparator that `std.sort` needs: the key first, the element second.
///
/// Compare the order of the arguments with the source of `std.sort`. A
/// comparator with the arguments in the opposite order compiles. Then it
/// returns an index that looks correct but is wrong.
fn orderKeyFirst(key: i32, item: i32) std.math.Order {
    return std.math.order(key, item);
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(input);
    var value_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    var query_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    const values = try readRow(&reader, &value_storage);
    const queries = try readRow(&reader, &query_storage);

    try out.print("{d} sorted values parsed from the input\n", .{values.len});
    try out.writeAll("  idx ");
    for (0..values.len) |i| try out.print("{d:>4}", .{i});
    try out.writeAll("\n  val ");
    for (values) |v| try writeCell(out, v, 4);
    try out.writeAll("\n\n");

    // The search with a trace, and the search without a trace. The two must
    // give the same answer.
    try out.writeAll("lower bound of 7, the first index whose value is not less than 7\n");
    const traced = try traceLowerBound(out, values, 7);
    try out.print(
        "  traced {d}, plain lowerBound {d}, same answer -> {}\n\n",
        .{ traced, lowerBound(values, 7), traced == lowerBound(values, 7) },
    );

    // Two bounds change a search into a range. A contest problem usually
    // asks for this: how many, not where.
    const first = lowerBound(values, 7);
    const past = upperBound(values, 7);
    try out.print("upper bound of 7 is {d}\n", .{past});
    try out.print("7 occupies items[{d}..{d}], which is {d} copies\n\n", .{ first, past, past - first });

    try out.writeAll("every query, answered with the same two calls\n");
    try out.writeAll("  key  lower  upper  count  present\n");
    for (queries) |key| {
        const lo = lowerBound(values, key);
        const hi = upperBound(values, key);
        try writeCell(out, key, 5);
        try out.print(
            "  {d:>5}  {d:>5}  {d:>5}  {s}\n",
            .{ lo, hi, hi - lo, if (hi > lo) "yes" else "no" },
        );
    }
    try out.writeAll("\n");

    // The window must become smaller at each step. This search shows the
    // result when the window stops at one size.
    try out.writeAll("the same search with lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1\n");
    const stalled = try stalledLowerBound(out, values, 7, 6);
    try out.print("  answer -> {?d}\n\n", .{stalled});

    // The standard library has the two bounds. Thus a solution does not need
    // the code above. This file has the code because the index from a bound
    // is useful only when you know which bound you used.
    try out.writeAll("std.sort, on the same array\n");
    try out.print(
        "  std.sort.lowerBound(7) = {d}, ours = {d}\n",
        .{ std.sort.lowerBound(i32, values, @as(i32, 7), orderKeyFirst), lowerBound(values, 7) },
    );
    try out.print(
        "  std.sort.upperBound(7) = {d}, ours = {d}\n",
        .{ std.sort.upperBound(i32, values, @as(i32, 7), orderKeyFirst), upperBound(values, 7) },
    );
    try out.print(
        "  std.sort.equalRange(7) = {any}\n",
        .{std.sort.equalRange(i32, values, @as(i32, 7), orderKeyFirst)},
    );
    try out.print(
        "  std.sort.binarySearch(5) = {?d}, lowerBound(5) = {d}\n",
        .{ std.sort.binarySearch(i32, values, @as(i32, 5), orderKeyFirst), lowerBound(values, 5) },
    );

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`23-competitive.binary-search`)*

## The search window

```zig
/// The first index with a value that is not less than `key`.
///
/// The window is half-open: each index that can be the answer is in
/// `items[lo..hi]`. `lo` moves only past values that are too small. `hi`
/// moves down only to values that are sufficiently large. Thus the answer
/// always stays in the window. When `lo` gets to `hi`, the window is empty
/// and `lo` is the answer. For this reason, the function has no separate case
/// for a value that it cannot find.
///
/// Use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`, not `(lo + hi) / 2`. The second form adds two
/// indices. Each index is valid, but on a large array the sum can be too
/// large.
fn lowerBound(items: []const i32, key: i32) usize {
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (items[mid] < key) lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `lowerBound` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search.zig`.*

`lo` and `hi` give the part of the array that the search did not remove. This part is the search window.

The range is half-open, `items[lo..hi]`. The window includes `lo`, but it does not include `hi`.

At each step, the loop keeps one rule: each index that can be the answer stays inside the search window.

The loop has two branches:

- If `items[mid] < key`, then `mid` cannot be the answer. The values are in ascending order, thus each value before `mid` is also too small. The loop sets `lo = mid + 1`. This removes `mid` and all of the values before `mid`.
- If not, `items[mid]` is greater than or equal to the key. Then `mid` can be the answer. The loop keeps `mid` inside the search window with `hi = mid`.

Thus one branch moves past `mid`, and the other branch keeps `mid` in the window.

When `lo == hi`, the search window is empty and the search is complete. Then `lo` is the lower-bound position. The function does not have a separate case for a value that it cannot find.

```
  step 1  lo= 0 mid= 6 hi=12    1   3   3   4   7   7[ 7]   9  11  11  15  20
  step 2  lo= 0 mid= 3 hi= 6    1   3   3[ 4]   7   7   .   .   .   .   .   .
  step 3  lo= 4 mid= 5 hi= 6    .   .   .   .   7[ 7]   .   .   .   .   .   .
  step 4  lo= 4 mid= 4 hi= 5    .   .   .   .[ 7]   .   .   .   .   .   .   .
  window empty after 4 steps: lo = hi = 4
```

The array has twelve values, and the search stops after four steps. A dot shows an index that the search removed. Each step removes approximately half of the range that is still in the window.

The figure below plays the same four rows. Use **Next step** to move one state at a time. The highlighted line is the line of `lowerBound` that runs. At step 2, the figure stops and asks you to predict the branch.

*Figure: Binary search for the lower bound of 7 in twelve sorted values, with lo, mid and hi pointers and the lowerBound source. The trace of lowerBound(7) from the program above. Each step shows mid, the branch, and the window that is left.*

The program calculates the midpoint as `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`. You can also see `(lo + hi) / 2` in other code. The second form is shorter, but `lo + hi` can overflow if the two values are sufficiently large. The first form does not have this problem.

The overflow is more probable with small integer types and very large arrays. `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` is the safer form, and the cost is only one subtraction.

## The off-by-one bug

```zig
/// The off-by-one bug, as a program that you can run.
///
/// `lo = mid` looks safe next to `lo = mid + 1`. `mid` was too small, thus
/// it looks like `mid` in the window costs only one more comparison. But
/// `lo = mid` stops the loop. When `hi - lo` is 1, `mid` is `lo`. Then
/// `lo = mid` does not change the window, and the next step is the same as
/// this step.
///
/// The step limit lets the program print the problem. Without the limit, the
/// loop does not stop.
fn stalledLowerBound(
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    items: []const i32,
    key: i32,
    budget: usize,
) !?usize {
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len;
    var step: usize = 0;
    while (lo < hi) {
        if (step == budget) {
            try out.print("  no progress: gave up at step {d} with lo={d} hi={d}\n", .{ step, lo, hi });
            return null;
        }
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        step += 1;
        try writeStep(out, items, step, lo, mid, hi);
        if (items[mid] < key) lo = mid else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `stalledLowerBound` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search.zig`.*

A common mistake is to write `lo = mid` instead of `lo = mid + 1`.

At first, `lo = mid` can look correct. If `mid` is too small, the answer is not before `mid`. But `mid` also cannot be the answer. Thus the loop must remove `mid` from the search window.

If the loop keeps `mid`, the loop can stop progress. When `hi - lo` becomes 1, integer division gives `mid == lo`. Then `lo = mid` does not change a value. The next iteration gets the same values again.

```
  step 3  lo= 3 mid= 4 hi= 6    .   .   .   4[ 7]   7   .   .   .   .   .   .
  step 4  lo= 3 mid= 3 hi= 4    .   .   .[ 4]   .   .   .   .   .   .   .   .
  step 5  lo= 3 mid= 3 hi= 4    .   .   .[ 4]   .   .   .   .   .   .   .   .
  step 6  lo= 3 mid= 3 hi= 4    .   .   .[ 4]   .   .   .   .   .   .   .   .
  no progress: gave up at step 6 with lo=3 hi=4
```

Steps four, five and six are the same. The example has a step limit, thus the program can find the problem and stop. Without the limit, the loop does not stop. On a competitive programming judge, the result is usually a time-limit error.

The next figure runs both versions on the same array. Select a branch, and step through the search. The steps have the same names in the two versions, thus you can change the branch at any step. Up to step 2, the two windows are the same. At step 3, `lo = mid` keeps index 3, and the window stops at two values.

*Figure: The same binary search twice: with lo = mid + 1 it ends after four steps, and with lo = mid it repeats one window. Select a branch. The steps have the same names in both, thus you can switch at any step and compare the two windows.*

A simple rule helps you find this bug: the search window must become smaller after each iteration. In this implementation, each branch makes the window smaller by one index or more.

## lowerBound and upperBound

```zig
/// The first index with a value that is greater than `key`.
///
/// The only difference from `lowerBound` is one character. With `<=`, the
/// loop moves past each value that is equal to the key. It does not stop at
/// the first equal value.
fn upperBound(items: []const i32, key: i32) usize {
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (items[mid] <= key) lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `upperBound` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search.zig`.*

`lowerBound` and `upperBound` are almost the same search. The only difference is the comparison.

`lowerBound` uses `<`. It finds the first position with a value that is greater than or equal to the key:

```
first value >= key
```

`upperBound` uses `<=`. It finds the first position with a value that is greater than the key:

```
first value > key
```

If the key occurs more than one time, `lowerBound` points to the first copy. `upperBound` points to the position immediately after the last copy.

The two bounds make a half-open range:

```
[lowerBound, upperBound)
```

Thus the count of duplicates is easy to calculate:

```
count = upperBound - lowerBound
```

The results for the example array are:

```
  key  lower  upper  count  present
    7      4      7      3  yes
    5      4      4      0  no
   20     11     12      1  yes
    0      0      0      0  no
   21     12     12      0  no
```

For key `7`, the range is:

```
[4, 7)
```

Thus the array has three copies of `7`.

For key `5`, the two bounds are 4. Thus the array does not contain `5`. Position 4 is also the position where an insert of `5` keeps the array sorted.

For key `21`, the two bounds are 12, which is the end of the array. Thus an insert of `21` goes after all of the values.

`lowerBound` is also useful when the array does not contain the value:

- It gives the first position where you can insert the value.
- It gives the count of values that are smaller than a given limit.

## Use the Zig standard library

`std.sort` already has these operations: `lowerBound`, `upperBound`, `equalRange` and `binarySearch`. In usual code, you do not have to write the binary-search loop.

You must supply a comparator. Be careful with one detail: the comparator gets the key first and the array element second.

```zig
/// The comparator that `std.sort` needs: the key first, the element second.
///
/// Compare the order of the arguments with the source of `std.sort`. A
/// comparator with the arguments in the opposite order compiles. Then it
/// returns an index that looks correct but is wrong.
fn orderKeyFirst(key: i32, item: i32) std.math.Order {
    return std.math.order(key, item);
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `orderKeyFirst` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search.zig`.*

The order of the arguments is important. If the two arguments have the same type, the wrong order can still compile. But then the comparison has a different meaning, and the result can be wrong.

The results for the array in this example are:

```
  std.sort.lowerBound(7) = 4, ours = 4
  std.sort.upperBound(7) = 7, ours = 7
  std.sort.equalRange(7) = .{ 4, 7 }
  std.sort.binarySearch(5) = null, lowerBound(5) = 4
```

`std.sort.binarySearch` returns `?usize`:

- If the value is in the array, the function returns an index of the value.
- If the value is not in the array, the function returns null.

When the array has duplicates, `binarySearch` does not guarantee the first index of the value. Use `lowerBound` when you need the first position of the value.

The last line shows the difference between `binarySearch` and `lowerBound`. For key `5`, `binarySearch` returns null, because the array does not contain `5`:

```
binarySearch(5) = null
```

But `lowerBound` returns 4, which is the position where an insert of `5` goes:

```
lowerBound(5) = 4
```

All of these functions expect sorted input. `std.sort` does not check the order for you.

[Sorting](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/sorting/) tells about `std.mem.sort`, the stable and unstable variants, and the context argument that these comparators also use.

## Read the example input

```zig
/// Read one line of whitespace-separated integers into `out`.
///
/// The function takes a `*std.Io.Reader` instead of the string. The
/// networking chapters use the same method for protocols. The function changes
/// bytes into values. Thus the same code works with a file, a socket, or a
/// string literal that CI can check.
fn readRow(reader: *std.Io.Reader, out: []i32) ![]i32 {
    const line = (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) orelse return error.MissingRow;
    var count: usize = 0;
    var fields = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    while (fields.next()) |field| {
        if (count == out.len) return error.RowTooLong;
        out[count] = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, field, 10);
        count += 1;
    }
    return out[0..count];
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `readRow` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search.zig`.*

The examples on this site run under WASI in the browser. A program in the browser does not have standard input in the same way as a usual command-line program. Thus the source file keeps the example input as a string.

`readRow` does not use the string directly. It accepts a `*std.Io.Reader`. Thus the same function can parse input from different sources: a string, a file, a socket or standard input. On a competitive programming judge, you can give the same function a reader on stdin.

[Readers and Writers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/readers-and-writers/) tells about the interface and the buffer that it reads through.

---

## Two Pointers

*Competitive Programming. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/two-pointers/*

The input is a sorted array and a target sum. The task is to find two values with a sum that is equal to the target.

One method is to try each possible pair. That method takes O(n²) time. For an array with 100,000 values, the number of comparisons is much too large.

The values are in ascending order. Thus a better method is possible:

1. Put one index at the start and a second index at the end.
2. Add the two values.
3. Use the result to move one of the indices toward the center.

Each step removes one value from the search.

The trace below shows each step. Marks show the two active indices. A dot shows a position that the search removed.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The problem, as text.
///
/// A browser tab under WASI has no stdin. Thus the file holds the four lines
/// that a judge gives to the program. The lines are the sorted values, the
/// target sums, some words for the palindrome test, and a row of heights for
/// the last section.
const input =
    \\2 3 5 8 11 17 20 24
    \\25 5 44 31 100 4
    \\racecar level abcba noon zig
    \\1 8 6 2 5 4 8 3 7
;

/// One line, or an error if the input has no more lines.
fn readLine(reader: *std.Io.Reader) ![]const u8 {
    return (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) orelse error.MissingRow;
}

/// Read one line of whitespace-separated integers into `out`.
///
/// The parameter is a `*std.Io.Reader`, not a string. Thus the same function
/// reads a file on a judge and a literal here. Only the reader changes.
fn readRow(reader: *std.Io.Reader, out: []i32) ![]i32 {
    const line = try readLine(reader);
    var count: usize = 0;
    var fields = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    while (fields.next()) |field| {
        if (count == out.len) return error.RowTooLong;
        out[count] = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, field, 10);
        count += 1;
    }
    return out[0..count];
}

/// The indices of two values with the sum `target`, or null.
///
/// `items` must be sorted. Because of the sort, only one move is correct.
///
/// The value at `hi` is the largest partner for `lo` in the range. Thus a sum
/// below the target shows that `lo` is in no pair, and `lo` moves up. The
/// value at `lo` is the smallest partner for `hi` in the range. Thus a sum
/// above the target shows the same about `hi`, and `hi` moves down.
///
/// Each step removes one index permanently. Thus the search is a single pass.
fn twoSum(items: []const i32, target: i32) ?[2]usize {
    if (items.len < 2) return null;
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const sum = items[lo] + items[hi];
        if (sum == target) return .{ lo, hi };
        if (sum < target) lo += 1 else hi -= 1;
    }
    return null;
}

/// Right-align a value in a cell of `width` characters.
///
/// A width on a signed integer also prints a sign. Thus `{d:>4}` shows 7 as
/// `  +7`. This function writes the digits first and adds the padding by hand.
/// Thus the columns do not show plus signs.
fn writeCell(out: *std.Io.Writer, value: i32, width: usize) !void {
    var digits: [12]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&digits, "{d}", .{value});
    try out.splatByteAll(' ', width - text.len);
    try out.writeAll(text);
}

/// The array with the current range: `>` at `lo`, `<` at `hi`, and a dot for
/// each index that the search removed.
fn writeWindow(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, lo: usize, hi: usize) !void {
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        if (i < lo or i > hi) {
            try out.writeAll("   .");
        } else if (i == lo) {
            try out.writeByte('>');
            try writeCell(out, value, 3);
        } else if (i == hi) {
            try writeCell(out, value, 3);
            try out.writeByte('<');
        } else {
            try writeCell(out, value, 4);
        }
    }
    try out.writeByte('\n');
}

const Search = struct { pair: ?[2]usize, steps: usize };

/// The same search as `twoSum`, but it prints the pair and the result at each
/// step.
///
/// The print calls are here. Thus `twoSum` keeps the shape that you can copy
/// into a solution. The function also returns the number of steps, because
/// that number is the claim to check: it never gets to the length of the
/// array.
fn traceTwoSum(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, target: i32) !Search {
    if (items.len < 2) return .{ .pair = null, .steps = 0 };
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len - 1;
    var steps: usize = 0;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const sum = items[lo] + items[hi];
        steps += 1;
        try out.print("  step {d}  ", .{steps});
        try writeCell(out, items[lo], 2);
        try out.writeAll(" + ");
        try writeCell(out, items[hi], 2);
        try out.writeAll(" = ");
        try writeCell(out, sum, 3);
        const verdict = if (sum == target) "match" else if (sum < target) "too small" else "too big";
        try out.print("  {s}", .{verdict});
        try out.splatByteAll(' ', 11 - verdict.len);
        try writeWindow(out, items, lo, hi);
        if (sum == target) return .{ .pair = .{ lo, hi }, .steps = steps };
        if (sum < target) lo += 1 else hi -= 1;
    }
    return .{ .pair = null, .steps = steps };
}

/// True when `text` is the same in the two directions.
///
/// The movement is the same as above, with a different comparison. When the
/// bytes at the two ends are equal, the two positions are complete. Thus the
/// two indices move, and the middle part becomes two bytes smaller. When two
/// bytes are not equal, the search stops, because that pair is a pair in each
/// direction of the string.
fn isPalindrome(text: []const u8) bool {
    if (text.len == 0) return true;
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = text.len - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
        if (text[lo] != text[hi]) return false;
        lo += 1;
        hi -= 1;
    }
    return true;
}

/// `isPalindrome`, but each checked byte prints as a dot.
fn tracePalindrome(out: *std.Io.Writer, text: []const u8) !bool {
    if (text.len == 0) return true;
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = text.len - 1;
    var steps: usize = 0;
    while (lo < hi) {
        steps += 1;
        const matched = text[lo] == text[hi];
        try out.print("  step {d}  {c} {s} {c}  ", .{
            steps,
            text[lo],
            if (matched) "=" else "!",
            text[hi],
        });
        var row_buf: [256]u8 = undefined;
        var row: std.Io.Writer = .fixed(&row_buf);
        for (text, 0..) |byte, i| {
            if (i < lo or i > hi) {
                try row.writeAll(" . ");
            } else if (i == lo) {
                try row.print(">{c} ", .{byte});
            } else if (i == hi) {
                try row.print(" {c}<", .{byte});
            } else {
                try row.print(" {c} ", .{byte});
            }
        }
        try out.writeAll(std.mem.trimEnd(u8, row.buffered(), " "));
        try out.writeByte('\n');
        if (!matched) return false;
        lo += 1;
        hi -= 1;
    }
    try out.print("  {d} steps, nothing left to pair\n", .{steps});
    return true;
}

const Area = struct { best: i32, lo: usize, hi: usize };

/// The largest rectangle between two of `heights`: the water between two
/// walls on a flat floor.
///
/// The area is the shorter wall times the distance. Thus the shorter wall
/// limits the area. Each other pair with that wall is narrower than the pair
/// that the function measured, and it is not taller. Thus no such pair has a
/// larger area, and the function can remove the wall. The trace prints the
/// side that moved.
fn maxArea(out: *std.Io.Writer, heights: []const i32) !Area {
    if (heights.len < 2) return .{ .best = 0, .lo = 0, .hi = 0 };
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = heights.len - 1;
    var found: Area = .{ .best = 0, .lo = 0, .hi = 0 };
    var steps: usize = 0;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const height = @min(heights[lo], heights[hi]);
        const width: i32 = @intCast(hi - lo);
        const area = height * width;
        if (area > found.best) found = .{ .best = area, .lo = lo, .hi = hi };
        steps += 1;
        const shorter_is_left = heights[lo] < heights[hi];
        try out.print("  {d:>4}  {d:>3}  {d:>3}", .{ steps, lo, hi });
        try writeCell(out, heights[lo], 6);
        try writeCell(out, heights[hi], 6);
        try writeCell(out, width, 7);
        try writeCell(out, area, 6);
        try writeCell(out, found.best, 6);
        try out.print("  {s}\n", .{if (shorter_is_left) "lo" else "hi"});
        if (shorter_is_left) lo += 1 else hi -= 1;
    }
    return found;
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(input);
    var value_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    var target_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    var height_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    const values = try readRow(&reader, &value_storage);
    const targets = try readRow(&reader, &target_storage);
    const words = try readLine(&reader);
    const heights = try readRow(&reader, &height_storage);

    try out.print("{d} sorted values parsed from the input\n", .{values.len});
    try out.writeAll("  idx ");
    for (0..values.len) |i| try out.print("{d:>4}", .{i});
    try out.writeAll("\n  val ");
    for (values) |v| try writeCell(out, v, 4);
    try out.writeAll("\n\n");

    // The search with a trace, and the search without a trace. The two
    // results must agree.
    try out.writeAll("two values that add up to 25\n");
    const traced = try traceTwoSum(out, values, 25);
    const pair = traced.pair.?;
    try out.print(
        "  items[{d}] + items[{d}] = {d} + {d} = 25 in {d} steps\n",
        .{ pair[0], pair[1], values[pair[0]], values[pair[1]], traced.steps },
    );
    try out.print(
        "  plain twoSum agrees -> {}\n\n",
        .{std.meta.eql(twoSum(values, 25), traced.pair)},
    );

    // Each step removes one index. Thus the length of the array limits the
    // number of steps, for all values.
    try out.writeAll("every target, with the steps it cost\n");
    try out.writeAll("  target    pair    values  steps\n");
    var sink: std.Io.Writer.Discarding = .init(&.{});
    var worst: usize = 0;
    for (targets) |target| {
        const found = try traceTwoSum(&sink.writer, values, target);
        worst = @max(worst, found.steps);
        try writeCell(out, target, 8);
        if (found.pair) |p| {
            try out.print("  {d:>2},{d:>2}   ", .{ p[0], p[1] });
            try writeCell(out, values[p[0]], 2);
            try out.writeAll(" +");
            try writeCell(out, values[p[1]], 3);
        } else {
            try out.writeAll("     -          -");
        }
        try out.print("  {d:>5}\n", .{found.steps});
    }
    try out.print("  one index retires per step, so {d} values allow {d} steps at most\n", .{
        values.len,
        values.len - 1,
    });
    try out.print("  the worst row above took {d}\n\n", .{worst});

    // The same movement on bytes.
    try out.writeAll("racecar, checked from both ends\n");
    const symmetric = try tracePalindrome(out, "racecar");
    try out.print("  palindrome -> {}\n\n", .{symmetric});

    try out.writeAll("zig, where the first pair already answers it\n");
    const asymmetric = try tracePalindrome(out, "zig");
    try out.print("  palindrome -> {}\n\n", .{asymmetric});

    try out.writeAll("every word on the third input line\n");
    var word_fields = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, words, ' ');
    while (word_fields.next()) |word| {
        try out.print("  {s:<9}{}\n", .{ word, isPalindrome(word) });
    }
    try out.writeAll("\n");

    // To remove a candidate, the search needs a reason. Here the reason
    // shows that the search can remove the shorter wall.
    try out.writeAll("most water between two walls\n");
    try out.writeAll("  step   lo   hi  h[lo]  h[hi]  width  area  best  moved\n");
    const water = try maxArea(out, heights);
    try out.print("  best {d} between index {d} and index {d}\n", .{
        water.best,
        water.lo,
        water.hi,
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`23-competitive.two-pointers`)*

## Decide which pointer moves

```zig
/// The indices of two values with the sum `target`, or null.
///
/// `items` must be sorted. Because of the sort, only one move is correct.
///
/// The value at `hi` is the largest partner for `lo` in the range. Thus a sum
/// below the target shows that `lo` is in no pair, and `lo` moves up. The
/// value at `lo` is the smallest partner for `hi` in the range. Thus a sum
/// above the target shows the same about `hi`, and `hi` moves down.
///
/// Each step removes one index permanently. Thus the search is a single pass.
fn twoSum(items: []const i32, target: i32) ?[2]usize {
    if (items.len < 2) return null;
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const sum = items[lo] + items[hi];
        if (sum == target) return .{ lo, hi };
        if (sum < target) lo += 1 else hi -= 1;
    }
    return null;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `twoSum` from `snippets/23-competitive/two-pointers.zig`.*

`lo` and `hi` mark the part of the array that the search did not remove. The current range is `items[lo..hi + 1]`. The search removed each value outside this range.

At each step, the loop calculates `items[lo] + items[hi]`. There are three possible cases:

- If the sum is equal to the target, the loop has the answer.
- If the sum is smaller than the target, `lo` must move.
- If the sum is larger than the target, `hi` must move.

When the sum is too small, look at `items[hi]`. It is the largest value in the range that can be a pair with `items[lo]`. If that pair is too small, no other value in the range can make a sufficiently large sum with `items[lo]`. Thus `items[lo]` cannot be part of the answer. The loop removes it with `lo += 1`.

When the sum is too large, look at `items[lo]`. It is the smallest value in the range that can be a pair with `items[hi]`. If that pair is already too large, each other possible partner for `items[hi]` gives an equal or larger sum. Thus `items[hi]` cannot be part of the answer. The loop removes it with `hi -= 1`.

Each step removes exactly one index from the search. The two pointers never move backward. Thus the distance between `lo` and `hi` becomes smaller on each iteration, and the loop runs O(n) times or fewer.

This argument is correct only when the values are in ascending order. If they are not in order, a move of `lo` or `hi` tells you nothing about the values in the range. The function does not check the order of the values. Thus sort the input first.

[Sorting](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/sorting/) explains `std.mem.sort` and its comparator.

In this example, the two pointers start at opposite ends and move toward each other. A different common pattern has two pointers that move in the same direction, with a contiguous range between them. [Sliding Window](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/sliding-window/) explains that pattern.

## Follow the search

```zig
/// The same search as `twoSum`, but it prints the pair and the result at each
/// step.
///
/// The print calls are here. Thus `twoSum` keeps the shape that you can copy
/// into a solution. The function also returns the number of steps, because
/// that number is the claim to check: it never gets to the length of the
/// array.
fn traceTwoSum(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, target: i32) !Search {
    if (items.len < 2) return .{ .pair = null, .steps = 0 };
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = items.len - 1;
    var steps: usize = 0;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const sum = items[lo] + items[hi];
        steps += 1;
        try out.print("  step {d}  ", .{steps});
        try writeCell(out, items[lo], 2);
        try out.writeAll(" + ");
        try writeCell(out, items[hi], 2);
        try out.writeAll(" = ");
        try writeCell(out, sum, 3);
        const verdict = if (sum == target) "match" else if (sum < target) "too small" else "too big";
        try out.print("  {s}", .{verdict});
        try out.splatByteAll(' ', 11 - verdict.len);
        try writeWindow(out, items, lo, hi);
        if (sum == target) return .{ .pair = .{ lo, hi }, .steps = steps };
        if (sum < target) lo += 1 else hi -= 1;
    }
    return .{ .pair = null, .steps = steps };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `traceTwoSum` from `snippets/23-competitive/two-pointers.zig`.*

`>` marks `lo`, and `<` marks `hi`. A dot shows a position that the search removed:

```
  step 1   2 + 24 =  26  too big    >  2   3   5   8  11  17  20 24<
  step 2   2 + 20 =  22  too small  >  2   3   5   8  11  17 20<   .
  step 3   3 + 20 =  23  too small     .>  3   5   8  11  17 20<   .
  step 4   5 + 20 =  25  match         .   .>  5   8  11  17 20<   .
```

The trace has four steps:

1. The sum is too large. Thus the search moves `hi` and removes 24.
2. The sum is too small. Thus the search moves `lo` and removes 2.
3. The sum is too small again. Thus the search removes 3.
4. `5 + 20` is equal to the target.

The two ends do not have to move at the same rate. The current sum alone decides which pointer moves.

The same search for each target on the second input line gives these results:

```
  target    pair    values  steps
      25   2, 6    5 + 20      4
       5   0, 1    2 +  3      7
      44   6, 7   20 + 24      7
      31   4, 6   11 + 20      6
     100     -          -      7
       4     -          -      7
```

The array has eight values. No search takes more than seven steps. This is also true when no pair has the target sum.

For target 100, each possible sum is too small. For target 4, each possible sum is too large. The pointers move until they meet. If they meet and the search did not find the target, no pair has the target sum.

## Use the same method for a palindrome

```zig
/// True when `text` is the same in the two directions.
///
/// The movement is the same as above, with a different comparison. When the
/// bytes at the two ends are equal, the two positions are complete. Thus the
/// two indices move, and the middle part becomes two bytes smaller. When two
/// bytes are not equal, the search stops, because that pair is a pair in each
/// direction of the string.
fn isPalindrome(text: []const u8) bool {
    if (text.len == 0) return true;
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = text.len - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
        if (text[lo] != text[hi]) return false;
        lo += 1;
        hi -= 1;
    }
    return true;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `isPalindrome` from `snippets/23-competitive/two-pointers.zig`.*

You can use the same two-pointer structure with strings. Do not add the values at the two ends. Compare them.

One pointer starts at the first byte. The other pointer starts at the last byte. If the two bytes are equal, move the two pointers toward the center.

For `racecar`, the search has these steps:

```
  step 1  r = r  >r  a  c  e  c  a  r<
  step 2  a = a   . >a  c  e  c  a< .
  step 3  c = c   .  . >c  e  c< .  .
  3 steps, nothing left to pair
```

The string has seven bytes, but the function needs only three comparisons. The function does not compare the middle `e` with a different byte. The condition `while (lo < hi)` stops before the middle value.

If the two sides are not equal, the function can return `false` immediately:

```
  step 1  z ! g  >z  i  g<
```

The function does not have to check the other bytes. In a palindrome, each pair from the outside to the center must be equal. Thus one pair that is not equal proves that the string is not a palindrome.

This implementation compares bytes. For ASCII text, one character is one byte. Thus the function gives the correct result.

For Unicode text, a character can use more than one byte. For example, the characters of `été` are the same in the two directions. But the UTF-8 bytes of `été` are not all single-byte characters. For general Unicode text, decode the string into code points before you use the same two-pointer method.

## Container with most water

```zig
/// The largest rectangle between two of `heights`: the water between two
/// walls on a flat floor.
///
/// The area is the shorter wall times the distance. Thus the shorter wall
/// limits the area. Each other pair with that wall is narrower than the pair
/// that the function measured, and it is not taller. Thus no such pair has a
/// larger area, and the function can remove the wall. The trace prints the
/// side that moved.
fn maxArea(out: *std.Io.Writer, heights: []const i32) !Area {
    if (heights.len < 2) return .{ .best = 0, .lo = 0, .hi = 0 };
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var hi: usize = heights.len - 1;
    var found: Area = .{ .best = 0, .lo = 0, .hi = 0 };
    var steps: usize = 0;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const height = @min(heights[lo], heights[hi]);
        const width: i32 = @intCast(hi - lo);
        const area = height * width;
        if (area > found.best) found = .{ .best = area, .lo = lo, .hi = hi };
        steps += 1;
        const shorter_is_left = heights[lo] < heights[hi];
        try out.print("  {d:>4}  {d:>3}  {d:>3}", .{ steps, lo, hi });
        try writeCell(out, heights[lo], 6);
        try writeCell(out, heights[hi], 6);
        try writeCell(out, width, 7);
        try writeCell(out, area, 6);
        try writeCell(out, found.best, 6);
        try out.print("  {s}\n", .{if (shorter_is_left) "lo" else "hi"});
        if (shorter_is_left) lo += 1 else hi -= 1;
    }
    return found;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `maxArea` from `snippets/23-competitive/two-pointers.zig`.*

The same pattern solves the container-with-most-water problem. Each number is the height of a vertical wall. For two walls at positions `lo` and `hi`, the shorter wall limits the quantity of water between them.

The area has these parts:

- The width is `hi - lo`.
- The height is `@min(heights[lo], heights[hi])`.
- Thus the area is `@min(heights[lo], heights[hi]) * (hi - lo)`.

The search starts with the widest possible pair: the first wall and the last wall. After that, each move makes the width smaller. Thus a move is useful only if it can find a taller wall. This rule decides which pointer moves.

For example, `heights[lo]` is the shorter wall. Each new pair that keeps `lo` has a smaller width. Its height can never be greater than `heights[lo]`, because the height of a pair is never more than the height of either wall. Thus no pair that keeps this wall can have a larger area than the pair that the search already measured.

Thus the search can safely remove `lo`. The same argument applies to `hi` when the right wall is shorter.

The program prints the first four steps:

```
  step   lo   hi  h[lo]  h[hi]  width  area  best  moved
     1    0    8     1     7      8     8     8  lo
     2    1    8     8     7      7    49    49  hi
     3    1    7     8     3      6    18    49  hi
     4    1    6     8     8      5    40    49  hi
```

At step one, the left wall is shorter. Thus `lo` moves. At step two, the right wall is shorter. Thus `hi` moves, and the best area becomes 49.

At step four, the two walls have the same height. In this case, either pointer can move. The code moves `hi` because of the form of the comparison, but a move of `lo` is also correct.

Always move the shorter wall. A move of the taller wall can work for some inputs. But it can remove a pair that has the maximum area.

The figure plays all eight steps. The shaded area is the water between `lo` and `hi`. After step 2, a dashed outline keeps the best area on the drawing.

*Figure: Nine walls of heights 1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7. The water between lo and hi is drawn at each step, and a dashed outline marks the best area. The trace from the program above. At each step, the shaded area is the water between the two walls, and the lower wall moves.*

## Sliding Window

*Competitive Programming. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/sliding-window/*

The example uses ten numbers and two questions about them:

1. What is the largest sum of four consecutive values?
2. What is the shortest consecutive range with a sum of 19 or more?

The two problems use a contiguous part of the array. A sliding window solves them with two indices that move from left to right.

The trace below shows the window at each step. Each line also shows the value that entered, the value that left, and the current sum.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The problem, as text.
///
/// A snippet here runs under WASI in a browser tab. The tab has no stdin to
/// read. The first line has the values. The second line has the window width
/// and the target for the second half of the program.
const input =
    \\2 7 1 9 4 3 8 5 6 2
    \\4 19
;

/// A second array, for the case that the window with a variable size gets
/// wrong.
///
/// One negative value is sufficient. `2 + 3` gets to 5 with two values. The
/// window never examines that pair, because it shrinks only a window that it
/// already made larger than that pair.
const with_a_negative = [_]i32{ 2, -1, 2, 3 };

/// Read one line of whitespace-separated integers into `out`.
///
/// The function takes a `*std.Io.Reader` instead of the string. The
/// networking chapters use the same method for protocols. On a judge, give
/// the function a reader on stdin. The function does not change.
fn readRow(reader: *std.Io.Reader, out: []i32) ![]i32 {
    const line = (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) orelse return error.MissingRow;
    var count: usize = 0;
    var fields = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    while (fields.next()) |field| {
        if (count == out.len) return error.RowTooLong;
        out[count] = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, field, 10);
        count += 1;
    }
    return out[0..count];
}

/// Half-open: `items[span.lo..span.hi]` is the window, and `span.hi` is one
/// position after the last value. The binary search chapter uses the same
/// convention.
const Span = struct {
    lo: usize,
    hi: usize,

    fn len(self: Span) usize {
        return self.hi - self.lo;
    }
};

/// The largest sum of `k` consecutive values, from the full sum of each window.
///
/// `adds` counts the additions, because this function shows the cost. Each
/// of the `n - k + 1` windows costs `k` additions. Thus the work increases
/// with the product. A wide window on a long array does much repeated work.
fn resumMaxWindow(items: []const i32, k: usize, adds: *usize) ?i64 {
    if (k == 0 or k > items.len) return null;
    var best: i64 = std.math.minInt(i64);
    for (0..items.len - k + 1) |lo| {
        var sum: i64 = 0;
        for (items[lo..][0..k]) |value| {
            sum += value;
            adds.* += 1;
        }
        best = @max(best, sum);
    }
    return best;
}

/// The same answer, from one addition and one subtraction for each step.
///
/// Two windows one step apart are different by two values: the value that
/// entered on the right and the value that left on the left. All the values
/// between them are in the two sums. Thus a second addition of these values
/// repeats work. Add the first window, then keep the total and change it.
///
/// Use `i64`, not `i32`. Ten small values fit in the two types. A contest
/// array of a hundred thousand values near the limit of `i32` does not fit.
fn slidingMaxWindow(items: []const i32, k: usize, adds: *usize) ?i64 {
    if (k == 0 or k > items.len) return null;
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    for (items[0..k]) |value| {
        sum += value;
        adds.* += 1;
    }
    var best = sum;
    for (k..items.len) |hi| {
        sum += items[hi]; // enters on the right
        sum -= items[hi - k]; // leaves on the left
        adds.* += 2;
        best = @max(best, sum);
    }
    return best;
}

/// The shortest run of values with a sum of `target` or more.
///
/// The right edge grows by one value on each pass. The left edge moves only
/// while the window satisfies the condition. Each window on the path of the
/// left edge is a candidate. `lo` never moves backwards. Thus each index
/// enters one time and leaves a maximum of one time. The inner loop cannot
/// run more than `items.len` times in the full call.
///
/// The shrink rule needs non-negative values. The removal of a value from the
/// left must not make the sum larger. If it can, a window that failed the
/// condition at one step can satisfy the condition again later.
fn shortestAtLeast(items: []const i32, target: i64, moves: *usize) ?Span {
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    var best: ?Span = null;
    for (items, 0..) |value, hi| {
        sum += value;
        moves.* += 1;
        while (sum >= target) {
            const span: Span = .{ .lo = lo, .hi = hi + 1 };
            if (best == null or span.len() < best.?.len()) best = span;
            sum -= items[lo];
            lo += 1;
            moves.* += 1;
        }
    }
    return best;
}

/// The same answer, from each start index in sequence.
///
/// This function is quadratic. The outer loop sets a start. The inner loop
/// makes the range longer until the sum gets to the target. The next start
/// uses nothing from the previous start. `sums` counts the additions. Thus
/// you can compare the two numbers, and you do not have to assume them.
fn everyStartAtLeast(items: []const i32, target: i64, sums: *usize) ?Span {
    var best: ?Span = null;
    for (0..items.len) |lo| {
        var sum: i64 = 0;
        for (lo..items.len) |hi| {
            sum += items[hi];
            sums.* += 1;
            if (sum >= target) {
                const span: Span = .{ .lo = lo, .hi = hi + 1 };
                if (best == null or span.len() < best.?.len()) best = span;
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    return best;
}

/// Right-align a value in a cell of `width` characters.
///
/// `{d:>4}` is shorter, but it prints a `+` before a non-negative signed
/// integer when you give a width. This function formats the digits first and
/// then adds the padding. Thus the columns are easy to read.
fn writeCell(out: *std.Io.Writer, value: i64, width: usize) !void {
    var digits: [24]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&digits, "{d}", .{value});
    try out.splatByteAll(' ', width - text.len);
    try out.writeAll(text);
}

/// The array, with the current window shown in it.
///
/// Four characters for each value: a bracket or a space, the value in two
/// characters, a bracket or a space. All rows align. Thus you can see the
/// window move. You do not have to calculate it from two indices.
fn writeWindow(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, span: Span) !void {
    const inside = span.lo < span.hi;
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        try out.writeByte(if (inside and i == span.lo) '[' else ' ');
        try writeCell(out, value, 2);
        const closing: u8 = if (inside and i + 1 == span.hi) ']' else ' ';
        // No space at the end of a row. CI compares the output with the expected
        // output byte for byte, and a space that you cannot see is easy to get
        // wrong.
        if (closing == ' ' and i + 1 == items.len) break;
        try out.writeByte(closing);
    }
}

/// One trace row: a label, three counters, then the window.
///
/// A counter of `null` prints a dot. The first row of the fixed trace needs
/// the dot. The trace of the shortest run also needs it before it has an
/// answer.
fn writeRow(
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    label: []const u8,
    a: ?i64,
    b: ?i64,
    c: ?i64,
    items: []const i32,
    span: Span,
) !void {
    try out.print("  {s: <8}", .{label});
    for ([_]?i64{ a, b, c }) |maybe| {
        if (maybe) |value| try writeCell(out, value, 6) else try out.writeAll("     .");
    }
    try out.writeAll("  ");
    try writeWindow(out, items, span);
    try out.writeByte('\n');
}

/// `slidingMaxWindow`, but it prints the window at each step.
///
/// This function is separate, thus the function above keeps the shape that you
/// can copy into a solution. The run below checks that the two functions give
/// the same result. It does not assume that they do.
fn traceSlidingMaxWindow(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, k: usize) !i64 {
    try out.writeAll("  move     enter leave   sum  window\n");
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    for (items[0..k]) |value| sum += value;
    var best = sum;
    try writeRow(out, "first", null, null, sum, items, .{ .lo = 0, .hi = k });
    for (k..items.len) |hi| {
        const entering = items[hi];
        const leaving = items[hi - k];
        sum += entering;
        sum -= leaving;
        best = @max(best, sum);
        try writeRow(out, "slide", entering, leaving, sum, items, .{ .lo = hi - k + 1, .hi = hi + 1 });
    }
    return best;
}

/// `shortestAtLeast`, but it prints a row for each move.
///
/// A `grow` row shows the value that entered and the window after it. A
/// `shrink` row shows the window that satisfied the condition and the value
/// that leaves next. Thus the page shows the candidate that the loop recorded.
fn traceShortestAtLeast(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, target: i64) !?Span {
    try out.writeAll("  move     value   sum   len  window\n");
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    var best: ?Span = null;
    for (items, 0..) |value, hi| {
        sum += value;
        try writeRow(out, "grow", value, sum, @intCast(hi + 1 - lo), items, .{ .lo = lo, .hi = hi + 1 });
        while (sum >= target) {
            const span: Span = .{ .lo = lo, .hi = hi + 1 };
            if (best == null or span.len() < best.?.len()) best = span;
            try writeRow(out, "shrink", items[lo], sum, @intCast(span.len()), items, span);
            sum -= items[lo];
            lo += 1;
        }
    }
    return best;
}

/// Print a span as the values in it, or tell that there is no answer.
fn writeSpan(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, maybe: ?Span) !void {
    const span = maybe orelse {
        try out.writeAll("no run reaches the target\n");
        return;
    };
    try out.print("items[{d}..{d}], {d} values summing to ", .{ span.lo, span.hi, span.len() });
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    for (items[span.lo..span.hi]) |value| sum += value;
    try out.print("{d}\n", .{sum});
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(input);
    var value_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    var param_storage: [2]i32 = undefined;
    const values = try readRow(&reader, &value_storage);
    const params = try readRow(&reader, &param_storage);
    const k: usize = @intCast(params[0]);
    const target: i64 = params[1];

    try out.print("{d} values parsed from the input\n", .{values.len});
    try out.writeAll("  idx ");
    for (0..values.len) |i| try out.print("{d:>4}", .{i});
    try out.writeAll("\n  val ");
    for (values) |v| try writeCell(out, v, 4);
    try out.writeAll("\n\n");

    // A fixed window. The loop changes the sum. It does not calculate the sum
    // again.
    try out.print("largest sum of {d} consecutive values\n", .{k});
    const traced = try traceSlidingMaxWindow(out, values, k);
    var sliding_adds: usize = 0;
    var resum_adds: usize = 0;
    const rolled = slidingMaxWindow(values, k, &sliding_adds).?;
    const resummed = resumMaxWindow(values, k, &resum_adds).?;
    try out.print("  best {d}, traced {d}, re-summed {d}\n", .{ rolled, traced, resummed });
    try out.print(
        "  {d} additions sliding, {d} re-summing every window\n\n",
        .{ sliding_adds, resum_adds },
    );

    // A window that changes size. The right edge grows, and the left edge
    // shrinks.
    try out.print("shortest run of values summing to {d} or more\n", .{target});
    const shortest = try traceShortestAtLeast(out, values, target);
    try out.writeAll("  answer: ");
    try writeSpan(out, values, shortest);

    var moves: usize = 0;
    var starts: usize = 0;
    const windowed = shortestAtLeast(values, target, &moves);
    const brute = everyStartAtLeast(values, target, &starts);
    try out.print(
        "  window and every-start agree -> {}\n",
        .{windowed.?.len() == brute.?.len()},
    );

    // The amortised argument, checked with two numbers. Each index enters the
    // window one time and leaves a maximum of one time. Thus the moves cannot
    // be more than 2n, for all possible runs of the inner loop.
    try out.print(
        "  {d} moves over {d} values, ceiling 2n = {d}\n",
        .{ moves, values.len, 2 * values.len },
    );
    try out.print("  {d} additions to try every starting index instead\n\n", .{starts});

    // The shrink rule needs a sum that does not increase when a value leaves on
    // the left.
    try out.writeAll("the same window on an array with a negative value\n");
    try out.writeAll("  val ");
    for (&with_a_negative) |v| try writeCell(out, v, 4);
    try out.writeAll("\n");
    var ignored: usize = 0;
    var also_ignored: usize = 0;
    try out.writeAll("  window says      ");
    try writeSpan(out, &with_a_negative, shortestAtLeast(&with_a_negative, 5, &ignored));
    try out.writeAll("  every start says ");
    try writeSpan(out, &with_a_negative, everyStartAtLeast(&with_a_negative, 5, &also_ignored));

    // The negative value has no effect on the fixed window. The fixed window
    // never selects which values to keep.
    var negative_adds: usize = 0;
    try out.print(
        "  largest sum of 2 consecutive values is still {d}\n",
        .{slidingMaxWindow(&with_a_negative, 2, &negative_adds).?},
    );

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`23-competitive.sliding-window`)*

## Calculate each window again

```zig
/// The largest sum of `k` consecutive values, from the full sum of each window.
///
/// `adds` counts the additions, because this function shows the cost. Each
/// of the `n - k + 1` windows costs `k` additions. Thus the work increases
/// with the product. A wide window on a long array does much repeated work.
fn resumMaxWindow(items: []const i32, k: usize, adds: *usize) ?i64 {
    if (k == 0 or k > items.len) return null;
    var best: i64 = std.math.minInt(i64);
    for (0..items.len - k + 1) |lo| {
        var sum: i64 = 0;
        for (items[lo..][0..k]) |value| {
            sum += value;
            adds.* += 1;
        }
        best = @max(best, sum);
    }
    return best;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `resumMaxWindow` from `snippets/23-competitive/sliding-window.zig`.*

A simple solution calculates the sum of each possible window from the start. This solution gives the correct answer.

For a window size of four, there are seven possible windows in an array of ten values. Each window needs four additions.

The problem is the quantity of repeated work. There are `n - k + 1` windows, and each window needs `k` additions. Thus the time complexity is `O(n * k)`.

For 200,000 values with a window size of 1,000, the result is approximately 200 million additions. Most of these additions are not necessary.

Two adjacent windows share `k - 1` values. Do not add these values again. Keep the previous sum, and change the sum only for the two values that are different.

## Use one addition and one subtraction

```zig
/// The same answer, from one addition and one subtraction for each step.
///
/// Two windows one step apart are different by two values: the value that
/// entered on the right and the value that left on the left. All the values
/// between them are in the two sums. Thus a second addition of these values
/// repeats work. Add the first window, then keep the total and change it.
///
/// Use `i64`, not `i32`. Ten small values fit in the two types. A contest
/// array of a hundred thousand values near the limit of `i32` does not fit.
fn slidingMaxWindow(items: []const i32, k: usize, adds: *usize) ?i64 {
    if (k == 0 or k > items.len) return null;
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    for (items[0..k]) |value| {
        sum += value;
        adds.* += 1;
    }
    var best = sum;
    for (k..items.len) |hi| {
        sum += items[hi]; // enters on the right
        sum -= items[hi - k]; // leaves on the left
        adds.* += 2;
        best = @max(best, sum);
    }
    return best;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `slidingMaxWindow` from `snippets/23-competitive/sliding-window.zig`.*

First, calculate the sum of the first window in the usual way. After that, each new window is different from the previous window by only two values:

- One value enters from the right.
- One value leaves from the left.

Thus you do not calculate the full sum again. Change the current sum in two steps:

1. Add the new value.
2. Subtract the old value.

The first four windows are:

```
  move     enter leave   sum  window
  first        .     .    19  [ 2   7   1   9]  4   3   8   5   6   2
  slide        4     2    21    2 [ 7   1   9   4]  3   8   5   6   2
  slide        3     7    17    2   7 [ 1   9   4   3]  8   5   6   2
  slide        8     1    24    2   7   1 [ 9   4   3   8]  5   6   2
```

In the third row, 3 enters the window and 7 leaves the window. The sum changes from 21 to 17. The program does not add the values in the middle again.

The program also counts the additions in the two methods:

```
  16 additions sliding, 28 re-summing every window
```

For ten values, the difference is small. The difference becomes larger when the array becomes larger.

The sliding version does approximately `2n - k` additions and subtractions. The version that calculates each sum again does `k(n - k + 1)` additions. Thus the sliding version is O(n), and the calculation of each window from the start is O(nk).

The total uses `i64`, but each value is `i32`. The sum of many `i32` values can be too large for an `i32`. A wider type for the total prevents this overflow.

## Use a window that changes size

```zig
/// The shortest run of values with a sum of `target` or more.
///
/// The right edge grows by one value on each pass. The left edge moves only
/// while the window satisfies the condition. Each window on the path of the
/// left edge is a candidate. `lo` never moves backwards. Thus each index
/// enters one time and leaves a maximum of one time. The inner loop cannot
/// run more than `items.len` times in the full call.
///
/// The shrink rule needs non-negative values. The removal of a value from the
/// left must not make the sum larger. If it can, a window that failed the
/// condition at one step can satisfy the condition again later.
fn shortestAtLeast(items: []const i32, target: i64, moves: *usize) ?Span {
    var lo: usize = 0;
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    var best: ?Span = null;
    for (items, 0..) |value, hi| {
        sum += value;
        moves.* += 1;
        while (sum >= target) {
            const span: Span = .{ .lo = lo, .hi = hi + 1 };
            if (best == null or span.len() < best.?.len()) best = span;
            sum -= items[lo];
            lo += 1;
            moves.* += 1;
        }
    }
    return best;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `shortestAtLeast` from `snippets/23-competitive/sliding-window.zig`.*

The second problem is different. The answer is the shortest consecutive range with a sum that is equal to or more than the target. The window size is not fixed. Thus the window must grow and shrink.

The window changes in two ways:

- The right edge moves forward and adds values to the sum.
- When the sum gets to the target, the left edge moves forward to make the window smaller. The left edge continues to move while the window satisfies the condition.

A `shrink` row in the trace shows a valid window and the value that the next step removes:

```
  grow         6    22     4    2   7   1   9   4 [ 3   8   5   6]  2
  shrink       3    22     4    2   7   1   9   4 [ 3   8   5   6]  2
  shrink       8    19     3    2   7   1   9   4   3 [ 8   5   6]  2
  grow         2    13     3    2   7   1   9   4   3   8 [ 5   6   2]
```

The addition of 6 makes the sum 22. This sum is equal to or more than the target, thus the current window is valid. The length of the window is four.

Then the loop removes 3 from the left. The values 8, 5 and 6 stay in the window, and their sum is 19. This sum also gets to the target. Thus the loop has a shorter valid window, with a length of three.

Next, the loop removes 8. The sum becomes less than the target, thus the left edge stops. The right edge starts to move again.

The final answer is:

```
  answer: items[6..9], 3 values summing to 19
```

The loop records the current window before it removes the left value. If the loop removes the value first and checks the window after the removal, the loop can miss a valid candidate.

The figure plays the 17 rows of the trace. The outline is the window. It grows to the right until the sum gets to 19, then it shrinks from the left. At the end, a dashed outline marks the answer.

*Figure: Ten values, 2, 7, 1, 9, 4, 3, 8, 5, 6, 2, with an outline for the window. The outline grows to the right and shrinks from the left. The trace from the program above, one row for each step. The outline is the window, and the dashed outline at the end is the answer.*

## Why the inner loop is still O(n)

```zig
/// The same answer, from each start index in sequence.
///
/// This function is quadratic. The outer loop sets a start. The inner loop
/// makes the range longer until the sum gets to the target. The next start
/// uses nothing from the previous start. `sums` counts the additions. Thus
/// you can compare the two numbers, and you do not have to assume them.
fn everyStartAtLeast(items: []const i32, target: i64, sums: *usize) ?Span {
    var best: ?Span = null;
    for (0..items.len) |lo| {
        var sum: i64 = 0;
        for (lo..items.len) |hi| {
            sum += items[hi];
            sums.* += 1;
            if (sum >= target) {
                const span: Span = .{ .lo = lo, .hi = hi + 1 };
                if (best == null or span.len() < best.?.len()) best = span;
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    return best;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `everyStartAtLeast` from `snippets/23-competitive/sliding-window.zig`.*

The `while` loop inside the `for` loop is still O(n). [The Monotonic Stack](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/monotonic-stack/) gives the reason.

Each value enters the window one time and leaves the window a maximum of one time. Here, `lo` never moves backwards. Thus the two edges together move a maximum of approximately `2n` times.

The counts for this example are:

```
  17 moves over 10 values, ceiling 2n = 20
  34 additions to try every starting index instead
```

The window grows ten times and shrinks seven times. The total is 17 moves.

The other version starts a new sum at each possible start position. It repeats the work that the earlier start positions did. Thus that version is quadratic.

The sliding-window version uses the current state again and never resets `lo`.

## When the shrink rule fails

```zig
/// A second array, for the case that the window with a variable size gets
/// wrong.
///
/// One negative value is sufficient. `2 + 3` gets to 5 with two values. The
/// window never examines that pair, because it shrinks only a window that it
/// already made larger than that pair.
const with_a_negative = [_]i32{ 2, -1, 2, 3 };
```

*Quoted from the source: `with_a_negative` from `snippets/23-competitive/sliding-window.zig`.*

The window with a variable size above needs one property. When the loop removes a value from the left, the sum must stay the same or become smaller.

- If all values are non-negative, this property is true.
- If the input can have negative values, this property is not true.

Look at this input:

```
  val    2  -1   2   3
  window says      items[0..4], 4 values summing to 6
  every start says items[2..4], 2 values summing to 5
```

The sum of the full array is 6, thus the window gets to the target. Then the algorithm removes the first value, 2. The sum becomes 4. The sum is now less than the target, thus the left edge stops.

But the window still contains `-1`. If the loop also removes that negative value, the last two values `2` and `3` give a shorter valid window with a sum of 5. The usual shrink rule never gets to that window. Thus the sliding-window solution with a variable size is not correct for arbitrary negative values.

The brute-force version checks each start position and finds the correct answer, but it needs O(n²) time.

The fixed-size sliding window does not have this problem. The fixed window does not make decisions from an increase or a decrease of the sum. It only adds the value that enters and removes the value that leaves. Thus the fixed window is also correct with negative values:

```
  largest sum of 2 consecutive values is still 5
```

A problem with a contiguous answer does not always mean that a sliding window will work. For a sliding window with a variable size, the condition must usually change in a predictable way when the window grows or shrinks.

For example, with non-negative numbers:

- An added value cannot make the sum smaller.
- A removed value cannot make the sum larger.

These two facts give a safe rule for when to grow and when to shrink. Other examples are a limit on the number of different characters in a window, or on the number of forbidden values in a window.

If the condition does not have this property, a different technique can be necessary, for example prefix sums, a deque, or a heap.

Two indices that start at the two ends of a sorted array and move towards each other use a different pattern. [Two Pointers](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/two-pointers/) tells about that method.

---

## Prefix Sums and Difference Arrays

*Competitive Programming. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/prefix-sums/*

A range-sum query asks for the total of one part of an array. This problem has many of these queries.

For one query, a loop can add the values in the range. This method is satisfactory when there are only a small number of queries. But with 100,000 values and 100,000 queries, a loop over each range can need billions of additions.

A prefix sum prepares the array one time. After that, one subtraction gives the sum of a range.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The problem, as text.
///
/// A snippet here runs under WASI in a browser tab. The tab has no stdin to
/// read. The first line has the values. The second line has five half-open
/// ranges as `lo hi` pairs. The third line has three range updates as
/// `lo hi delta`.
const input =
    \\3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6
    \\0 3 2 5 1 8 4 4 0 8
    \\0 3 5 2 6 -1 4 8 10
;

/// Read one line of whitespace-separated integers into `out`.
///
/// The function takes a `*std.Io.Reader` instead of the string. The
/// networking chapters use the same method for protocols. On a judge, give
/// the function a reader on stdin. The function does not change.
fn readRow(reader: *std.Io.Reader, out: []i32) ![]i32 {
    const line = (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) orelse return error.MissingRow;
    var count: usize = 0;
    var fields = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    while (fields.next()) |field| {
        if (count == out.len) return error.RowTooLong;
        out[count] = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, field, 10);
        count += 1;
    }
    return out[0..count];
}

/// Half-open: `items[span.lo..span.hi]` is the range, and `span.hi` is one
/// position after the last value. The binary search chapter uses the same
/// convention.
const Span = struct {
    lo: usize,
    hi: usize,

    fn len(self: Span) usize {
        return self.hi - self.lo;
    }
};

/// `out[i]` becomes the sum of the first `i` values. Thus `out` is one cell
/// longer than `items`. The extra cell lets the code read a range that starts
/// at index 0 in the same way as all other ranges.
///
/// Use `i64`, not `i32`. Eight small values fit in the two types. A hundred
/// thousand values near the top of `i32` do not fit. Thus the totals use the
/// wider type. `adds` counts the additions, because the build cost helps you
/// decide if a prefix array is cheaper than a loop.
fn buildPrefix(items: []const i32, out: []i64, adds: *usize) []i64 {
    out[0] = 0;
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        out[i + 1] = out[i] + value;
        adds.* += 1;
    }
    return out[0 .. items.len + 1];
}

/// The sum of `items[lo..hi]`, from two reads and a subtraction.
///
/// `pre[hi]` counts all values below `hi`, and `pre[lo]` counts all values
/// below `lo`. Thus the difference is exactly the part between them.
/// `lo == hi` gives zero without a branch. `lo == 0` reads `pre[0]`, and the
/// extra cell already set `pre[0]` to zero.
fn rangeSum(pre: []const i64, span: Span) i64 {
    return pre[span.hi] - pre[span.lo];
}

/// The same sum, from the addition of each value.
///
/// This function lets you compare the two results. You do not have to assume
/// that they agree. It also lets you compare its count of additions with the
/// count from `buildPrefix`.
fn rangeSumByLoop(items: []const i32, span: Span, adds: *usize) i64 {
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    for (items[span.lo..span.hi]) |value| {
        sum += value;
        adds.* += 1;
    }
    return sum;
}

/// Record "add `delta` to every value in `items[lo..hi]`" in two writes.
///
/// `diff` is one cell longer than the array that it describes. The reason is
/// the same as for the prefix array. An update that goes to the last index
/// writes its end mark at `items.len`, and that cell must exist.
///
/// The cost does not change with the width of the range. A range on the full
/// array is two writes, and a range on one value is also two writes.
fn applyRange(diff: []i64, span: Span, delta: i64) void {
    diff[span.lo] += delta;
    diff[span.hi] -= delta;
}

/// The cumulative sum of `diff`. This sum gives the values that `diff`
/// recorded.
///
/// The last cell of `diff` never adds a value to the output. The last cell
/// cancels the deltas that started. Thus after the pass, the total is zero
/// again.
fn accumulate(diff: []const i64, out: []i32) []i32 {
    var running: i64 = 0;
    for (diff[0 .. diff.len - 1], 0..) |value, i| {
        running += value;
        out[i] = @intCast(running);
    }
    return out[0 .. diff.len - 1];
}

/// The difference between each value and the value before it.
///
/// The inverse of `accumulate`. Use this function on an array, then use
/// `accumulate` on the result. The output is the original array.
/// `out[items.len]` closes the array, because it subtracts the last value.
fn difference(items: []const i32, out: []i64) []i64 {
    var previous: i64 = 0;
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        out[i] = value - previous;
        previous = value;
    }
    out[items.len] = -previous;
    return out[0 .. items.len + 1];
}

/// Apply each update in the slow way: write each cell of each range.
///
/// The difference array must agree with this reference. The cost of this
/// function is the sum of the range widths. The two writes for each update
/// replace this cost.
fn applyRangesDirectly(out: []i32, spans: []const Span, deltas: []const i64) []i32 {
    @memset(out, 0);
    for (spans, deltas) |span, delta| {
        for (out[span.lo..span.hi]) |*cell| cell.* += @intCast(delta);
    }
    return out;
}

/// Right-align a value in a cell of `width` characters.
///
/// `{d:>4}` is shorter, but it prints a `+` before a non-negative signed
/// integer when you give a width. This function formats the digits first and
/// then adds the padding. Thus the columns are easy to read.
fn writeCell(out: *std.Io.Writer, value: i64, width: usize) !void {
    var digits: [24]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&digits, "{d}", .{value});
    try out.splatByteAll(' ', width - text.len);
    try out.writeAll(text);
}

/// The array, with one range shown in it.
///
/// Four characters for each value: a bracket or a space, the value in two
/// characters, a bracket or a space. An empty range shows no brackets. The
/// row for `[4,4)` on the page shows this result.
fn writeRange(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, span: Span) !void {
    const inside = span.lo < span.hi;
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        try out.writeByte(if (inside and i == span.lo) '[' else ' ');
        try writeCell(out, value, 2);
        const closing: u8 = if (inside and i + 1 == span.hi) ']' else ' ';
        // No space at the end of a row. CI compares the output with the expected
        // output byte for byte, and a space that you cannot see is easy to get
        // wrong.
        if (closing == ' ' and i + 1 == items.len) break;
        try out.writeByte(closing);
    }
}

/// A row of `i64` cells with a label. Each cell is four characters.
///
/// The label field is 13 characters wide. Thus the update trace aligns under
/// a header of column numbers. Only this alignment shows which two cells a
/// range update changed.
```
