```zig
fn writeWideRow(out: *std.Io.Writer, label: []const u8, cells: []const i64) !void {
    try out.print("  {s: <13}", .{label});
    for (cells) |value| try writeCell(out, value, 4);
    try out.writeByte('\n');
}

/// A row of `i32` cells with a label. Each cell is four characters.
fn writeNarrowRow(out: *std.Io.Writer, label: []const u8, cells: []const i32) !void {
    try out.print("  {s: <4}", .{label});
    for (cells) |value| try writeCell(out, value, 4);
    try out.writeByte('\n');
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(input);
    var value_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    var query_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    var update_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    const values = try readRow(&reader, &value_storage);
    const query_fields = try readRow(&reader, &query_storage);
    const update_fields = try readRow(&reader, &update_storage);

    var query_buf: [16]Span = undefined;
    var query_count: usize = 0;
    var q: usize = 0;
    while (q + 1 < query_fields.len) : (q += 2) {
        query_buf[query_count] = .{
            .lo = @intCast(query_fields[q]),
            .hi = @intCast(query_fields[q + 1]),
        };
        query_count += 1;
    }
    const queries = query_buf[0..query_count];

    var update_span_buf: [16]Span = undefined;
    var update_delta_buf: [16]i64 = undefined;
    var update_count: usize = 0;
    var u: usize = 0;
    while (u + 2 < update_fields.len) : (u += 3) {
        update_span_buf[update_count] = .{
            .lo = @intCast(update_fields[u]),
            .hi = @intCast(update_fields[u + 1]),
        };
        update_delta_buf[update_count] = update_fields[u + 2];
        update_count += 1;
    }
    const update_spans = update_span_buf[0..update_count];
    const update_deltas = update_delta_buf[0..update_count];

    try out.print("{d} values parsed from the input\n", .{values.len});
    try out.writeAll("  idx ");
    for (0..values.len) |i| try out.print("{d:>4}", .{i});
    try out.writeByte('\n');
    try writeNarrowRow(out, "val", values);
    try out.writeByte('\n');

    // The build. One pass, one addition for each value, and one cell more than
    // the array that it summarises.
    var build_adds: usize = 0;
    var prefix_storage: [65]i64 = undefined;
    const pre = buildPrefix(values, &prefix_storage, &build_adds);
    try out.print("the prefix array holds {d} cells for {d} values\n", .{ pre.len, values.len });
    try out.writeAll("  idx ");
    for (0..pre.len) |i| try out.print("{d:>4}", .{i});
    try out.writeByte('\n');
    try out.writeAll("  pre ");
    for (pre) |v| try writeCell(out, v, 4);
    try out.writeAll("\n\n");

    // Each query is two reads and a subtraction, for all sizes of range.
    try out.print("{d} range sums, each one a subtraction\n", .{queries.len});
    try out.writeAll("  range   pre[hi] pre[lo]   sum  values\n");
    var loop_adds: usize = 0;
    var all_agree = true;
    for (queries) |span| {
        var label: [16]u8 = undefined;
        const text = try std.mem.print(&label, "[{d},{d})", .{ span.lo, span.hi });
        const fast = rangeSum(pre, span);
        const slow = rangeSumByLoop(values, span, &loop_adds);
        if (fast != slow) all_agree = false;
        try out.print("  {s: <7}", .{text});
        try writeCell(out, pre[span.hi], 8);
        try writeCell(out, pre[span.lo], 8);
        try writeCell(out, fast, 6);
        try out.writeAll("  ");
        try writeRange(out, values, span);
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }
    try out.print("  every sum matches a loop over the same values -> {}\n\n", .{all_agree});

    // The program pays for the build one time. An array that changes between
    // queries needs a new build each time, and then the loop is cheaper.
    try out.writeAll("what the build costs, against what it saves\n");
    var plan: [40]u8 = undefined;
    const built_once = try std.mem.print(&plan, "build once, then {d} lookups", .{queries.len});
    try out.print("  {s: <28}{d:>4} adds\n", .{ built_once, build_adds });
    try out.print("  {s: <28}{d:>4} adds\n", .{ "rebuild before each lookup", build_adds * queries.len });
    try out.print("  {s: <28}{d:>4} adds\n\n", .{ "no prefix array at all", loop_adds });

    // The opposite direction. Two writes record a change on a full range.
    try out.print("{d} range updates on a difference array\n", .{update_spans.len});
    var diff_storage: [65]i64 = undefined;
    const diff = diff_storage[0 .. values.len + 1];
    @memset(diff, 0);
    try out.print("  {s: <13}", .{"update"});
    for (0..diff.len) |i| try out.print("{d:>4}", .{i});
    try out.writeByte('\n');
    try writeWideRow(out, "start", diff);
    for (update_spans, update_deltas) |span, delta| {
        applyRange(diff, span, delta);
        var label: [24]u8 = undefined;
        const sign: []const u8 = if (delta < 0) "" else "+";
        const text = try std.mem.print(&label, "{s}{d} on [{d},{d})", .{ sign, delta, span.lo, span.hi });
        try writeWideRow(out, text, diff);
    }
    try out.writeByte('\n');

    // One pass reads the totals.
    try out.writeAll("one running sum turns those marks into values\n");
    var totals_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    const totals = accumulate(diff, &totals_storage);
    try out.writeAll("  idx ");
    for (0..totals.len) |i| try out.print("{d:>4}", .{i});
    try out.writeByte('\n');
    try writeNarrowRow(out, "tot", totals);
    var direct_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    const direct = applyRangesDirectly(direct_storage[0..values.len], update_spans, update_deltas);
    try out.print(
        "  writing every cell of every range agrees -> {}\n",
        .{std.mem.eql(i32, totals, direct)},
    );
    var covered: usize = 0;
    for (update_spans) |span| covered += span.len();
    try out.print(
        "  {d} writes for {d} updates, against {d} cells the slow way\n\n",
        .{ 2 * update_spans.len, update_spans.len, covered },
    );

    // Each operation cancels the other. Thus the round trip checks the two
    // operations.
    try out.writeAll("a running sum undoes a difference\n");
    var gaps_storage: [65]i64 = undefined;
    const gaps = difference(values, &gaps_storage);
    var back_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    const back = accumulate(gaps, &back_storage);
    try writeNarrowRow(out, "val", values);
    try out.writeAll("  diff");
    for (gaps) |v| try writeCell(out, v, 4);
    try out.writeByte('\n');
    try writeNarrowRow(out, "back", back);
    try out.print("  back equals val -> {}\n", .{std.mem.eql(i32, values, back)});

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`23-competitive.prefix-sums`)*

## Build the prefix array

```zig
/// `out[i]` becomes the sum of the first `i` values. Thus `out` is one cell
/// longer than `items`. The extra cell lets the code read a range that starts
/// at index 0 in the same way as all other ranges.
///
/// Use `i64`, not `i32`. Eight small values fit in the two types. A hundred
/// thousand values near the top of `i32` do not fit. Thus the totals use the
/// wider type. `adds` counts the additions, because the build cost helps you
/// decide if a prefix array is cheaper than a loop.
fn buildPrefix(items: []const i32, out: []i64, adds: *usize) []i64 {
    out[0] = 0;
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        out[i + 1] = out[i] + value;
        adds.* += 1;
    }
    return out[0 .. items.len + 1];
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `buildPrefix` from `snippets/23-competitive/prefix-sums.zig`.*

The prefix array keeps cumulative sums. `pre[i]` is the sum of the first `i` values. Because of this definition, the prefix array has one more cell than the original array.

- `pre[0]` is the sum of zero values. Thus `pre[0]` is 0.
- `pre[1]` contains the first value.
- `pre[2]` contains the sum of the first two values.
- The other cells continue in the same way.

The prefix array for the example input is:

```
  idx    0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
  val    3   1   4   1   5   9   2   6

the prefix array holds 9 cells for 8 values
  idx    0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
  pre    0   3   4   8   9  14  23  25  31
```

The prefix indices are easier to understand as boundaries. `pre[3]` is 8, because `pre[3]` holds the three values before index 3: `3 + 1 + 4`. `pre[0]` is the boundary before the first value. `pre[8]` is the boundary after the last value.

Without the extra cell at index 0, a range that starts at index 0 needs a special case. For example, code that uses `pre[lo - 1]` fails when `lo` is 0. The extra zero at the start lets the same formula work for all ranges.

## Calculate a range sum with one subtraction

```zig
/// The sum of `items[lo..hi]`, from two reads and a subtraction.
///
/// `pre[hi]` counts all values below `hi`, and `pre[lo]` counts all values
/// below `lo`. Thus the difference is exactly the part between them.
/// `lo == hi` gives zero without a branch. `lo == 0` reads `pre[0]`, and the
/// extra cell already set `pre[0]` to zero.
fn rangeSum(pre: []const i64, span: Span) i64 {
    return pre[span.hi] - pre[span.lo];
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `rangeSum` from `snippets/23-competitive/prefix-sums.zig`.*

Use the half-open range `[lo, hi)`:

- `pre[hi]` contains the sum of all values before `hi`.
- `pre[lo]` contains the sum of all values before `lo`.

Thus the range sum is `pre[hi] - pre[lo]`. The values before `lo` are in the two prefix values, and the subtraction removes them.

The program calculates five ranges:

```
  range   pre[hi] pre[lo]   sum  values
  [0,3)         8       0     8  [ 3   1   4]  1   5   9   2   6
  [2,5)        14       4    10    3   1 [ 4   1   5]  9   2   6
  [1,8)        31       3    28    3 [ 1   4   1   5   9   2   6]
  [4,4)         9       9     0    3   1   4   1   5   9   2   6
  [0,8)        31       0    31  [ 3   1   4   1   5   9   2   6]
```

The cost does not change with the width of the range. The range `[0,3)` contains three values, and the range `[1,8)` contains seven values. The two queries use the same two reads from the prefix array and one subtraction.

The empty range `[4,4)` also works: `pre[4] - pre[4] = 0`. A special case is not necessary. The full array is `pre[8] - pre[0]`, which gives 31.

Half-open ranges also agree with usual Zig slices. If you use an inclusive range, the formula becomes `pre[hi + 1] - pre[lo]`. The method is the same.

## When to use prefix sums

```zig
/// The same sum, from the addition of each value.
///
/// This function lets you compare the two results. You do not have to assume
/// that they agree. It also lets you compare its count of additions with the
/// count from `buildPrefix`.
fn rangeSumByLoop(items: []const i32, span: Span, adds: *usize) i64 {
    var sum: i64 = 0;
    for (items[span.lo..span.hi]) |value| {
        sum += value;
        adds.* += 1;
    }
    return sum;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `rangeSumByLoop` from `snippets/23-competitive/prefix-sums.zig`.*

The build of the prefix array takes O(n). After the build, each range query takes O(1). Thus prefix sums are useful when the array does not change and the program must answer many queries.

The costs for this small example are:

```
  build once, then 5 lookups     8 adds
  rebuild before each lookup    40 adds
  no prefix array at all        21 adds
```

One build of the prefix array needs eight additions. After that, the five queries use only subtraction. For an array this small, a loop over each range needs only 21 additions. Thus the difference is not large. The advantage becomes larger with many values and many queries.

Prefix sums also have a limit. If the original array changes, the prefix array is out of date. For example, if the value at index 3 changes, each prefix value after that position can be wrong. A new build of the prefix array costs O(n).

Thus prefix sums are not a good choice when a problem has many updates between its queries. For that type of problem, a Fenwick tree or a segment tree can do both updates and queries in O(log n).

Prefix sums and sliding windows solve different problems:

- A prefix sum can answer arbitrary range queries in any order.
- A sliding window is usually useful when the program examines the ranges in sequence, and each range is almost the same as the next range.

[Sliding Window](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/sliding-window/) tells about that pattern.

## Use a difference array

```zig
/// Record "add `delta` to every value in `items[lo..hi]`" in two writes.
///
/// `diff` is one cell longer than the array that it describes. The reason is
/// the same as for the prefix array. An update that goes to the last index
/// writes its end mark at `items.len`, and that cell must exist.
///
/// The cost does not change with the width of the range. A range on the full
/// array is two writes, and a range on one value is also two writes.
fn applyRange(diff: []i64, span: Span, delta: i64) void {
    diff[span.lo] += delta;
    diff[span.hi] -= delta;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `applyRange` from `snippets/23-competitive/prefix-sums.zig`.*

Some problems have many range updates instead of many range queries. For example:

- add 5 to every value in `[0,3)`
- subtract 1 from every value in `[2,6)`
- add 10 to every value in `[4,8)`

The direct method changes each value in each range. That method costs O(width) for each update.

A difference array records each range update with only two writes. The values do not change immediately. Instead, the difference array records where the change starts and where it stops.

The three updates above give this result:

```
  update          0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
  start           0   0   0   0   0   0   0   0   0
  +5 on [0,3)     5   0   0  -5   0   0   0   0   0
  -1 on [2,6)     5   0  -1  -5   0   0   1   0   0
  +10 on [4,8)    5   0  -1  -5  10   0   1   0 -10
```

To add 5 to `[0,3)`, write `+5` at index 0 and `-5` at index 3. Thus the change starts at 0 and stops at 3. Indices 1 and 2 do not need a write.

For the update on `[4,8)`, write `+10` at index 4 and `-10` at index 8. Index 8 is one position after the last array value. The extra position lets an update that goes to the end of the array close correctly.

The difference array does not directly contain the final values. It contains changes, and a later step must add them together.

## Change the differences back to values

```zig
/// The cumulative sum of `diff`. This sum gives the values that `diff`
/// recorded.
///
/// The last cell of `diff` never adds a value to the output. The last cell
/// cancels the deltas that started. Thus after the pass, the total is zero
/// again.
fn accumulate(diff: []const i64, out: []i32) []i32 {
    var running: i64 = 0;
    for (diff[0 .. diff.len - 1], 0..) |value, i| {
        running += value;
        out[i] = @intCast(running);
    }
    return out[0 .. diff.len - 1];
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `accumulate` from `snippets/23-competitive/prefix-sums.zig`.*

To get the final values, calculate a cumulative sum over the difference array. Each difference value changes the cumulative sum from that position to the end.

The result for the three updates above is:

```
  idx    0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
  tot    5   5   4  -1   9   9  10  10
  writing every cell of every range agrees -> true
  6 writes for 3 updates, against 11 cells the slow way
```

The `+5` at index 0 makes the cumulative sum 5. Indices 1 and 2 have no change, thus the cumulative sum stays at 5. At index 3, the `-5` removes that update. The other range changes work in the same way.

There are three updates, and each update needs two writes. Thus the difference-array version needs six writes. The direct version changes eleven array cells in total, because eleven is the sum of the widths of the three update ranges. For wider ranges, the difference between the two methods becomes larger.

The final `-10` at index 8 is not in the output array, because index 8 is outside the original eight values. The `-10` closes the update after the last value. If the cumulative sum continues through index 8, the cumulative sum becomes zero again. This result is a useful check that the differences are consistent.

The figure plays the three updates, then the running sum, one index at a time. Before the sum, it stops and asks you to predict one value.

*Figure: A difference array of 9 marks. 3 range updates each write two marks, and a running sum turns the marks into 8 values. The updates and the running sum from the program above. The figure stops before the sum and asks you to predict one value.*

## A running sum undoes a difference array

A difference array keeps the change between adjacent values. The difference array for the input array is:

```
  val    3   1   4   1   5   9   2   6
  diff   3  -2   3  -3   4   4  -7   4  -6
  back   3   1   4   1   5   9   2   6
```

The first difference is 3, because the first value changes from an initial 0 to 3. The next difference is `1 - 3 = -2`. The difference after that is `4 - 1 = 3`, and the other differences continue in the same way.

A prefix sum of these differences gives the original values again. Thus the two methods are closely related:

- A prefix array costs O(n) to build. Then each range-sum query costs O(1).
- A difference array records each range update in O(1). The change back to final values costs O(n).

Select the method for the problem:

- If you have many queries and a small number of updates, use prefix sums.
- If you have many range updates and need only the final array after them, use a difference array.

---

## The Monotonic Stack

*Competitive Programming. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/monotonic-stack/*

The problem: for each value in an array, find the first larger value to its right. Some values find a larger value immediately. Some values must look much farther. Some values do not have a larger value to their right.

A simple solution starts at each index and scans to the right until it finds a larger value. That solution works, but in the worst case it checks almost each pair of values.

A monotonic stack solves the same problem in one pass. The question changes. The question is not "What is the answer for this index?". The question is "Which earlier indices can the current value answer?". The stack keeps the indices that still wait for a larger value.

```zig
const std = @import("std");
const Allocator = std.mem.Allocator;

/// The problem, as text.
///
/// A snippet here runs under WASI in a browser tab. The tab has no stdin to
/// read. The problem needs only one line of values. The parser below reads
/// the line in the same way that it reads a real file.
const input =
    \\3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 5 3 7
;

/// The worst array for a scan and the easiest array for the stack.
///
/// No value has a greater value to its right. Thus the scan goes to the end
/// from each index, and the stack never pops.
const decreasing = [_]i32{ 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 };

/// The opposite of `decreasing`. The scan stops at its first comparison each
/// time. The stack pops the index that it pushed on the step before.
const increasing = [_]i32{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 };

/// Read one line of whitespace-separated integers into `out`.
///
/// The function takes a `*std.Io.Reader` instead of the string. The
/// networking chapters use the same method for protocols. On a judge, give
/// the function a reader on stdin. The function does not change.
fn readRow(reader: *std.Io.Reader, out: []i32) ![]i32 {
    const line = (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) orelse return error.MissingRow;
    var count: usize = 0;
    var fields = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    while (fields.next()) |field| {
        if (count == out.len) return error.RowTooLong;
        out[count] = try std.fmt.parseInt(i32, field, 10);
        count += 1;
    }
    return out[0..count];
}

/// The two counters that the amortised argument uses.
///
/// The count costs two lines. It answers a question that is easy to get wrong
/// if you only think about the nested loop.
const Work = struct {
    pushes: usize = 0,
    pops: usize = 0,
};

/// For each index, the index of the first greater value to its right.
///
/// The direct solution. Select an index, then move right to a greater value,
/// or stop at the end of the array. `comparisons` counts the values that the
/// scan examines. This number increases with the square of the input size.
fn scanRight(items: []const i32, out: []?usize, comparisons: *usize) void {
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        out[i] = null;
        for (items[i + 1 ..], i + 1..) |other, j| {
            comparisons.* += 1;
            if (other > value) {
                out[i] = j;
                break;
            }
        }
    }
}

/// The same answers from one pass over the array.
///
/// The stack holds the indices that do not have an answer yet. The values of
/// these indices become smaller from bottom to top. When `value` comes, each
/// index on the stack with a smaller value has its answer. Because of the
/// order, these indices are together at the top. Pop them, record `i`, and
/// push `i`.
///
/// The loop itself keeps the order. Each index that stays after the pops has
/// a value that is equal to or larger than `value`. Thus with `i` on top, the
/// values on the stack still become smaller from bottom to top.
///
/// Use `>=`, not `>`. An equal value is not greater. Thus a second 7 does not
/// answer an index that waits for a value greater than 7.
///
/// The loop never writes the indices that are still on the stack at the end
/// of the array. Before the loop, `@memset` set each item in `out` to null.
/// Thus an index without an answer does not need a separate case.
fn nextGreater(gpa: Allocator, items: []const i32, out: []?usize, work: *Work) !void {
    var stack: std.ArrayList(usize) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);
    @memset(out, null);

    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        while (stack.last()) |top| {
            if (items[top] >= value) break;
            out[top] = i;
            _ = stack.pop();
            work.pops += 1;
        }
        try stack.append(gpa, i);
        work.pushes += 1;
    }
}

/// The first smaller value to the left, from the same method.
///
/// There are two changes. First, the comparison is the opposite. Thus the
/// values on the stack become larger from bottom to top. Second, the answer
/// comes from the index that stays on the stack, not from the popped indices.
/// After the pops, the index on top is the nearest index to the left with a
/// smaller value.
fn previousSmaller(gpa: Allocator, items: []const i32, out: []?usize, work: *Work) !void {
    var stack: std.ArrayList(usize) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);
    @memset(out, null);

    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        while (stack.last()) |top| {
            if (items[top] < value) break;
            _ = stack.pop();
            work.pops += 1;
        }
        out[i] = stack.last();
        try stack.append(gpa, i);
        work.pushes += 1;
    }
}

/// Right-align a value in a cell of `width` characters.
///
/// `{d:>4}` is shorter, but it prints a `+` before a non-negative signed
/// integer when you give a width. This function formats the digits first and
/// then adds the padding. Thus the columns are easy to read.
fn writeCell(out: *std.Io.Writer, value: i32, width: usize) !void {
    var digits: [12]u8 = undefined;
    const text = try std.mem.print(&digits, "{d}", .{value});
    try out.splatByteAll(' ', width - text.len);
    try out.writeAll(text);
}

/// A value that can be absent, right-aligned. A dot means no answer.
fn writeMaybe(out: *std.Io.Writer, value: ?i32, width: usize) !void {
    if (value) |v| return writeCell(out, v, width);
    try out.splatByteAll(' ', width - 1);
    try out.writeByte('.');
}

/// The stack, bottom to top, as `index:value` pairs.
///
/// The values next to the indices show the order. A column of only indices
/// hides the property that the method needs.
fn writeStack(out: *std.Io.Writer, items: []const i32, indices: []const usize) !void {
    for (indices, 0..) |idx, k| {
        if (k > 0) try out.writeByte(' ');
        try out.print("{d}:{d}", .{ idx, items[idx] });
    }
}

/// The indices that this step resolved, each with its answer.
///
/// All these indices get the same answer, because the same new value popped
/// them. The row shows the answer for each index. Thus the row is easy to
/// compare with the answers table below.
fn writeResolved(out: *std.Io.Writer, popped: []const usize, answer: i32, width: usize) !void {
    var used: usize = 0;
    if (popped.len == 0) {
        try out.writeByte('.');
        used = 1;
    }
    for (popped, 0..) |idx, k| {
        if (k > 0) {
            try out.writeAll(", ");
            used += 2;
        }
        var digits: [24]u8 = undefined;
        const text = try std.mem.print(&digits, "{d} -> {d}", .{ idx, answer });
        try out.writeAll(text);
        used += text.len;
    }
    try out.splatByteAll(' ', width - used);
}

/// `nextGreater`, but it prints a row for each new value.
///
/// This function is separate, thus `nextGreater` keeps the shape that you can
/// copy into a solution. The run below checks that the two functions agree. It
/// does not assume that they do. The last row also shows the result at the
/// end: each index on the stack at that time never found a greater value.
fn traceNextGreater(out: *std.Io.Writer, gpa: Allocator, items: []const i32) !void {
    var stack: std.ArrayList(usize) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);

    try out.writeAll("   i  val  resolved (index -> answer)   stack after (bottom to top)\n");
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        var popped: [16]usize = undefined;
        var count: usize = 0;
        while (stack.last()) |top| {
            if (items[top] >= value) break;
            popped[count] = top;
            count += 1;
            _ = stack.pop();
        }
        try stack.append(gpa, i);

        try writeCell(out, @intCast(i), 4);
        try writeCell(out, value, 5);
        try out.writeAll("  ");
        try writeResolved(out, popped[0..count], value, 28);
        try writeStack(out, items, stack.items);
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }

    try out.print("  {d} indices never popped: ", .{stack.items.len});
    try writeStack(out, items, stack.items);
    try out.writeByte('\n');
}

/// One row of the cost table: the cost of the scan and the cost of the stack.
///
/// The two methods use the same array. Thus you can compare the two numbers,
/// because they do not come from different runs. The count for the scan is
/// comparisons, and the count for the stack is moves. No array can make the
/// stack moves more than `2n`.
fn writeCostRow(out: *std.Io.Writer, gpa: Allocator, name: []const u8, items: []const i32) !void {
    var storage: [64]?usize = undefined;
    const answers = storage[0..items.len];

    var comparisons: usize = 0;
    scanRight(items, answers, &comparisons);

    var work: Work = .{};
    try nextGreater(gpa, items, answers, &work);

    try out.print("  {s: <12}", .{name});
    try out.print("{d:>3}{d:>7}{d:>8}{d:>6}\n", .{
        items.len,
        comparisons,
        work.pushes,
        work.pops,
    });
}

/// An answers table: the value at each index and the position of its answer.
fn writeAnswers(
    out: *std.Io.Writer,
    items: []const i32,
    answers: []const ?usize,
    heading: []const u8,
) !void {
    try out.print("  idx  val  {s}   at\n", .{heading});
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        try writeCell(out, @intCast(i), 5);
        try writeCell(out, value, 5);
        const at = answers[i];
        try writeMaybe(out, if (at) |a| items[a] else null, 14);
        try writeMaybe(out, if (at) |a| @as(i32, @intCast(a)) else null, 5);
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;
    const gpa = init.gpa;

    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(input);
    var value_storage: [64]i32 = undefined;
    const values = try readRow(&reader, &value_storage);

    try out.print("{d} values parsed from the input\n", .{values.len});
    try out.writeAll("  idx ");
    for (0..values.len) |i| try out.print("{d:>4}", .{i});
    try out.writeAll("\n  val ");
    for (values) |v| try writeCell(out, v, 4);
    try out.writeAll("\n\n");

    // The pass, with a trace. Each pop resolves an index. On each row, the
    // values on the stack become smaller from bottom to top.
    try out.writeAll("next greater to the right, one pass with a stack\n");
    try traceNextGreater(out, gpa, values);

    var stack_answers: [64]?usize = undefined;
    var scan_answers: [64]?usize = undefined;
    var work: Work = .{};
    try nextGreater(gpa, values, stack_answers[0..values.len], &work);
    try out.print(
        "  {d} pushes, {d} pops over {d} values, ceiling 2n = {d}\n\n",
        .{ work.pushes, work.pops, values.len, 2 * values.len },
    );

    // The answers, and the scan that they must agree with.
    var comparisons: usize = 0;
    scanRight(values, scan_answers[0..values.len], &comparisons);
    try out.writeAll("the answers, and the scan they have to agree with\n");
    try writeAnswers(out, values, stack_answers[0..values.len], "next greater");
    try out.print(
        "  stack and scan agree -> {}\n\n",
        .{std.mem.eql(?usize, stack_answers[0..values.len], scan_answers[0..values.len])},
    );

    // The rates, not the totals. Eleven values are not sufficient to show the
    // cost of the scan. Thus the program also uses the two arrays at the two
    // limits.
    try out.writeAll("what each array costs\n");
    try out.writeAll("  array         n  scans  pushes  pops\n");
    try writeCostRow(out, gpa, "the input", values);
    try writeCostRow(out, gpa, "decreasing", &decreasing);
    try writeCostRow(out, gpa, "increasing", &increasing);
    try out.writeAll("\n");

    // The same stack with the opposite comparison. The answer comes from the
    // index that stays on the stack, not from the popped indices.
    try out.writeAll("previous smaller to the left, from the same stack\n");
    var left_answers: [64]?usize = undefined;
    var left_work: Work = .{};
    try previousSmaller(gpa, values, left_answers[0..values.len], &left_work);
    try writeAnswers(out, values, left_answers[0..values.len], "prev smaller");
    try out.print(
        "  {d} pushes, {d} pops, same ceiling\n",
        .{ left_work.pushes, left_work.pops },
    );

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`23-competitive.monotonic-stack`)*

## Scan right from each index

```zig
/// For each index, the index of the first greater value to its right.
///
/// The direct solution. Select an index, then move right to a greater value,
/// or stop at the end of the array. `comparisons` counts the values that the
/// scan examines. This number increases with the square of the input size.
fn scanRight(items: []const i32, out: []?usize, comparisons: *usize) void {
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        out[i] = null;
        for (items[i + 1 ..], i + 1..) |other, j| {
            comparisons.* += 1;
            if (other > value) {
                out[i] = j;
                break;
            }
        }
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `scanRight` from `snippets/23-competitive/monotonic-stack.zig`.*

The direct solution is easy to understand. For each index, scan to the right until you find a larger value:

- If you find a larger value, store it.
- If you get to the end of the array, that index has no answer.

This solution is correct. The problem is the number of comparisons, and the number changes with the input.

For an array in ascending order such as `1 2 3 4 5`, each value except the last value finds its answer immediately. Thus each of these indices needs only one comparison.

For an array in descending order such as `9 8 7 6 5`, no value finds a larger value to its right. The first index checks four values, the second index checks three, then two, then one. The total is `n(n - 1) / 2` comparisons. Thus the worst-case time complexity is O(n²).

## The stack keeps the indices that wait for an answer

```zig
/// The same answers from one pass over the array.
///
/// The stack holds the indices that do not have an answer yet. The values of
/// these indices become smaller from bottom to top. When `value` comes, each
/// index on the stack with a smaller value has its answer. Because of the
/// order, these indices are together at the top. Pop them, record `i`, and
/// push `i`.
///
/// The loop itself keeps the order. Each index that stays after the pops has
/// a value that is equal to or larger than `value`. Thus with `i` on top, the
/// values on the stack still become smaller from bottom to top.
///
/// Use `>=`, not `>`. An equal value is not greater. Thus a second 7 does not
/// answer an index that waits for a value greater than 7.
///
/// The loop never writes the indices that are still on the stack at the end
/// of the array. Before the loop, `@memset` set each item in `out` to null.
/// Thus an index without an answer does not need a separate case.
fn nextGreater(gpa: Allocator, items: []const i32, out: []?usize, work: *Work) !void {
    var stack: std.ArrayList(usize) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);
    @memset(out, null);

    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        while (stack.last()) |top| {
            if (items[top] >= value) break;
            out[top] = i;
            _ = stack.pop();
            work.pops += 1;
        }
        try stack.append(gpa, i);
        work.pushes += 1;
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `nextGreater` from `snippets/23-competitive/monotonic-stack.zig`.*

The monotonic-stack solution examines the problem from the other direction. At index `i`, the solution does not immediately try to find the answer for `i`. Instead, the current value can answer some earlier indices. The stack contains the indices that do not have their next greater value yet.

The current value is `items[i]`. For each value, do these steps:

1. Look at the index on the top of the stack.
2. If `items[i] > items[stack_top]`, the current value is the next greater value for that index. Pop that index and record the answer.
3. Do steps 1 and 2 again. Stop when the stack is empty or the top value is greater than or equal to the current value.
4. Push `i`.

The values of the indices on the stack become smaller from the bottom to the top. For example, if the stack contains the values `9 7 5 3`, a new value of 6 can answer 3 and 5. The value 6 cannot answer 7. Thus the pops stop at 7.

The stack keeps this order without more work. Before the push of a new value, the loop already removed each smaller value at the top. Then the loop pushes the new value above values that are greater than or equal to it.

The comparison must be correct for equal values. An equal value is not a greater value. If an index waits for a value greater than 5, a second 5 does not answer that index.

At the start, all the values in `out` are null. The loop writes an answer only when it pops an index from the stack. If an index is still on the stack at the end of the loop, there was no larger value to its right. Thus the output for that index stays null.

The stack is a `std.ArrayList(usize)`, and the code uses only one end of it. [Stacks](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/standard-library/stacks/) tells about `append`, `pop` and `last`. [Growable Array](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/data-structures/growable-array/) tells how the storage below the list grows.

If you know the maximum size, the same algorithm can use a fixed array and a length counter instead.

## Follow the stack

```zig
/// `nextGreater`, but it prints a row for each new value.
///
/// This function is separate, thus `nextGreater` keeps the shape that you can
/// copy into a solution. The run below checks that the two functions agree. It
/// does not assume that they do. The last row also shows the result at the
/// end: each index on the stack at that time never found a greater value.
fn traceNextGreater(out: *std.Io.Writer, gpa: Allocator, items: []const i32) !void {
    var stack: std.ArrayList(usize) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);

    try out.writeAll("   i  val  resolved (index -> answer)   stack after (bottom to top)\n");
    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        var popped: [16]usize = undefined;
        var count: usize = 0;
        while (stack.last()) |top| {
            if (items[top] >= value) break;
            popped[count] = top;
            count += 1;
            _ = stack.pop();
        }
        try stack.append(gpa, i);

        try writeCell(out, @intCast(i), 4);
        try writeCell(out, value, 5);
        try out.writeAll("  ");
        try writeResolved(out, popped[0..count], value, 28);
        try writeStack(out, items, stack.items);
        try out.writeByte('\n');
    }

    try out.print("  {d} indices never popped: ", .{stack.items.len});
    try writeStack(out, items, stack.items);
    try out.writeByte('\n');
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `traceNextGreater` from `snippets/23-competitive/monotonic-stack.zig`.*

Each row shows one new value:

- The `resolved` column shows the earlier indices that got an answer.
- The last column shows the stack after the step for the current value.
- Each stack entry has the form `index:value`, from the bottom to the top.

```
   i  val  resolved (index -> answer)   stack after (bottom to top)
   0    3  .                           0:3
   1    1  .                           0:3 1:1
   2    4  1 -> 4, 0 -> 4              2:4
   3    1  .                           2:4 3:1
   4    5  3 -> 5, 2 -> 5              4:5
   5    9  4 -> 9                      5:9
   6    2  .                           5:9 6:2
   7    6  6 -> 6                      5:9 7:6
   8    5  .                           5:9 7:6 8:5
   9    3  .                           5:9 7:6 8:5 9:3
  10    7  9 -> 7, 8 -> 7, 7 -> 7      5:9 10:7
  2 indices never popped: 5:9 10:7
```

At index 0, the value is 3. No index waits, thus the loop pushes index 0.

At index 1, the value is 1. The value 1 is not larger than 3, thus no index gets an answer. The loop pushes index 1 above index 0.

At index 2, the value is 4. The value 4 is larger than 1, thus the loop pops index 1, and its answer becomes 4. The value 4 is also larger than 3, thus the loop pops index 0, and its answer also becomes 4. The stack is now empty. The loop pushes index 2.

Later, at index 10, the value is 7. The value 7 answers indices 9, 8 and 7. Then the loop gets to index 5, which has the value 9. The value 7 is not larger than 9, thus the pops stop.

At the end, two indices stay on the stack: `5:9` and `10:7`. These two indices do not have a larger value to their right. Thus their answers stay null.

The figure plays the same trace. Each step moves `i` to the next value, pops the entries that the value answers, and pushes the new index. At index 2 and at index 10, the figure stops. Predict the pops, then press **Reveal**.

*Figure: Eleven input values scanned left to right. Each value pops the smaller values from a stack and writes their next greater value. The trace from the program above, one index for each step. Two steps stop and ask you to predict the pops.*

The program compares the stack solution with the direct scan:

```
  stack and scan agree -> true
```

## Why the nested loop is still O(n)

```zig
/// One row of the cost table: the cost of the scan and the cost of the stack.
///
/// The two methods use the same array. Thus you can compare the two numbers,
/// because they do not come from different runs. The count for the scan is
/// comparisons, and the count for the stack is moves. No array can make the
/// stack moves more than `2n`.
fn writeCostRow(out: *std.Io.Writer, gpa: Allocator, name: []const u8, items: []const i32) !void {
    var storage: [64]?usize = undefined;
    const answers = storage[0..items.len];

    var comparisons: usize = 0;
    scanRight(items, answers, &comparisons);

    var work: Work = .{};
    try nextGreater(gpa, items, answers, &work);

    try out.print("  {s: <12}", .{name});
    try out.print("{d:>3}{d:>7}{d:>8}{d:>6}\n", .{
        items.len,
        comparisons,
        work.pushes,
        work.pops,
    });
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writeCostRow` from `snippets/23-competitive/monotonic-stack.zig`.*

The algorithm has a `while` loop inside a `for` loop. At first, this can look like O(n²), but it is O(n). To see why, count how many times an index can go onto the stack and come off the stack.

- The loop pushes each index exactly one time. Thus there are exactly `n` pushes.
- The loop can pop an index a maximum of one time. After the pop, the loop never adds that index again. Thus there can be a maximum of `n` pops.

Thus the full function has a maximum of approximately `2n` stack operations. The counts for this example are:

```
  11 pushes, 9 pops over 11 values, ceiling 2n = 22
```

The inner loop can run many times in one iteration of the outer loop. But these pops cannot occur again later. Thus the total work for the full array stays linear.

The example compares the two methods on different inputs:

```
  array         n  scans  pushes  pops
  the input    11     19      11     9
  decreasing    9     36       9     0
  increasing    9      8       9     8
```

For the `decreasing` array, the direct scan does 36 comparisons. The monotonic stack does nine pushes and no pops.

For the `increasing` array, the direct scan does only eight comparisons. The stack does nine pushes and eight pops.

Thus the stack is not always faster on each input. Its advantage is the worst-case bound. The direct scan can increase to O(n²). The monotonic stack stays O(n) for all inputs.

A nested loop does not always mean quadratic time. Count how many times each item can go into the inner loop in the full algorithm. If that count has a constant limit, the total work can still be linear.

## Previous smaller element

```zig
/// The first smaller value to the left, from the same method.
///
/// There are two changes. First, the comparison is the opposite. Thus the
/// values on the stack become larger from bottom to top. Second, the answer
/// comes from the index that stays on the stack, not from the popped indices.
/// After the pops, the index on top is the nearest index to the left with a
/// smaller value.
fn previousSmaller(gpa: Allocator, items: []const i32, out: []?usize, work: *Work) !void {
    var stack: std.ArrayList(usize) = .empty;
    defer stack.deinit(gpa);
    @memset(out, null);

    for (items, 0..) |value, i| {
        while (stack.last()) |top| {
            if (items[top] < value) break;
            _ = stack.pop();
            work.pops += 1;
        }
        out[i] = stack.last();
        try stack.append(gpa, i);
        work.pushes += 1;
    }
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `previousSmaller` from `snippets/23-competitive/monotonic-stack.zig`.*

The same method solves a different common problem: for each value, find the nearest smaller value to its left. The structure is almost the same, with two changes:

- The comparison is different.
- The answer comes from the index that stays on the stack after the loop removes the larger or equal values.

The program prints:

```
  idx  val  prev smaller   at
    0    3             .    .
    1    1             .    .
    2    4             1    1
    3    1             .    .
    4    5             1    3
    5    9             5    4
    6    2             1    3
```

Look at index 6, which has the value 2. At that step, the stack contains the values 5 and 9 above an earlier 1. The values 5 and 9 are too large to be the previous smaller value for 2. Thus the loop pops them. The next value is 1 at index 3. That value is smaller than 2, thus index 3 is the answer.

The popped indices are not useful for future values. The current 2 is nearer to future positions, and it is smaller than both of the popped values. Thus a future value that can use 5 or 9 as a previous smaller value can use 2 instead.

Rows 1 and 3 have no previous smaller value. These two rows contain 1, which is the smallest value up to those positions. The stack becomes empty before the loop reads their answer.

The number of stack operations is still linear:

```
  11 pushes, 7 pops, same ceiling
```

The method gives a common family of monotonic-stack problems:

- next greater element
- next smaller element
- previous greater element
- previous smaller element

The same basic structure works for all four. These items change:

- the direction of the scan: from left to right, or from right to left
- the order of the stack: values that become larger or smaller from the bottom to the top
- the condition for a pop: on greater values, or on smaller values
- the source of the answer: the current value, or the stack after the pops

---

## Binary Search on the Answer

*Competitive Programming. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/binary-search-answer/*

A company ships packages by boat, and it has a list of packages. The company must load the packages onto a boat in the same order that they arrive. The goal is to ship all of the packages in four days or fewer.

The task is to find the minimum capacity of the boat. The input does not contain this value directly. Thus there is no sorted array to search.

But for each capacity, you can ask a simple question:

Can a boat with this capacity ship all of the packages in four days or fewer?

For example, a capacity of 9 tonnes is not sufficient. A capacity of 61 tonnes is sufficient. Also, if a capacity works, each larger capacity also works.

Thus the results have this shape:

```
no no no no ... yes yes yes yes ...
```

The answer changes from `no` to `yes` at one point. Binary search can find that point.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The problem: package weights in the order of arrival, then the number of days.
const input =
    \\5 3 8 2 9 4 7 6 1 8 3 5
    \\4
;

/// Read one line of whitespace-separated values into `out`.
fn readRow(reader: *std.Io.Reader, out: []u32) ![]u32 {
    const line = (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) orelse return error.MissingRow;
    var count: usize = 0;
    var fields = std.mem.tokenizeScalar(u8, line, ' ');
    while (fields.next()) |field| {
        if (count == out.len) return error.RowTooLong;
        out[count] = try std.fmt.parseInt(u32, field, 10);
        count += 1;
    }
    return out[0..count];
}

/// The ship, the deadline, and a count of the calls to the predicate.
///
/// The ship loads the packages in the order of arrival. Thus a capacity sets
/// the full plan. Fill the current day until the next package does not fit,
/// then start the next day. `calls` counts each call to the predicate. Thus
/// you can compare the cost of the two searches below.
const Ship = struct {
    weights: []const u32,
    limit: u32,
    calls: usize = 0,

    /// The days necessary at this capacity, or null when a package does not fit.
    fn daysNeeded(self: *Ship, cap: u32) ?u32 {
        self.calls += 1;
        var days: u32 = 1;
        var load: u32 = 0;
        for (self.weights) |w| {
            if (w > cap) return null;
            if (load + w > cap) {
                days += 1;
                load = 0;
            }
            load += w;
        }
        return days;
    }

    /// True when this capacity completes the work in the time limit.
    ///
    /// The result is false below the boundary and true at or above it. It
    /// changes one time. No other code in this file can assume this property.
    /// The run below checks it.
    fn feasible(self: *Ship, cap: u32) bool {
        const days = self.daysNeeded(cap) orelse return false;
        return days <= self.limit;
    }

    /// The same question with a second condition: on each day, half of the
    /// hold or more must be full.
    ///
    /// This plan looks better, but the predicate is not monotonic. A big ship
    /// completes the work early and is half empty on the last day. Thus a
    /// capacity that works can fail when you add one tonne to it.
    fn feasibleAndFull(self: *Ship, cap: u32) bool {
        const days = self.daysNeeded(cap) orelse return false;
        if (days > self.limit) return false;
        var lightest: u32 = std.math.maxInt(u32);
        var load: u32 = 0;
        for (self.weights) |w| {
            if (load + w > cap) {
                lightest = @min(lightest, load);
                load = 0;
            }
            load += w;
        }
        lightest = @min(lightest, load);
        return lightest * 2 >= cap;
    }
};

const Predicate = *const fn (*Ship, u32) bool;

/// The first capacity in `[low, high]` that the predicate accepts.
///
/// The loop is the loop from the binary search chapter, without the array.
/// `items[mid] < key` becomes `!pred(mid)`: mid is too small to be the answer.
/// Thus `lo = mid + 1` removes mid. In the other branch, mid can be the
/// answer, and the loop keeps it. When the window is empty, `lo` is the
/// boundary.
fn firstFeasible(ship: *Ship, low: u32, high: u32, pred: Predicate) u32 {
    var lo = low;
    var hi = high;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (pred(ship, mid)) hi = mid else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}

/// The same search, but it prints one row for each step.
///
/// This function is separate. Thus the function above keeps the shape that you
/// can copy into a solution. The run checks that the two functions return the
/// same capacity.
fn traceFirstFeasible(out: *std.Io.Writer, ship: *Ship, low: u32, high: u32) !u32 {
    var lo = low;
    var hi = high;
    var step: u32 = 0;
    try out.writeAll("  step   lo   hi  mid  days  ok   window after\n");
    while (lo < hi) {
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        step += 1;
        const days = ship.daysNeeded(mid);
        const ok = days != null and days.? <= ship.limit;
        try out.print("  {d:>4} {d:>4} {d:>4} {d:>4}  {d:>4}  {s:<4} ", .{ step, lo, hi, mid, days orelse 0, if (ok) "yes" else "no" });
        if (ok) hi = mid else lo = mid + 1;
        try out.print("[{d:>3},{d:>3}]  {d} left\n", .{ lo, hi, hi - lo + 1 });
    }
    try out.print("  window closed after {d} steps on capacity {d}\n", .{ step, lo });
    return lo;
}

/// One day of the plan: the packages on the boat, then the total weight.
fn writeDay(out: *std.Io.Writer, day: u32, items: []const u32, load: u32) !void {
    try out.print("  day {d}:", .{day});
    var used: usize = 0;
    for (items) |w| {
        try out.print(" {d:>2}", .{w});
        used += 3;
    }
    if (used < 38) try out.splatByteAll(' ', 38 - used);
    try out.print("load {d:>2}\n", .{load});
}

/// Run the greedy pack at one capacity and print the plan that it makes.
fn writePacking(out: *std.Io.Writer, ship: *Ship, cap: u32) !void {
    try out.print("capacity {d}, packed in arrival order\n", .{cap});
    var start: usize = 0;
    var load: u32 = 0;
    var day: u32 = 1;
    for (ship.weights, 0..) |w, i| {
        if (w > cap) {
            try out.print("  package of {d} does not fit at all\n", .{w});
            return;
        }
        if (load + w > cap) {
            try writeDay(out, day, ship.weights[start..i], load);
            day += 1;
            start = i;
            load = 0;
        }
        load += w;
    }
    try writeDay(out, day, ship.weights[start..], load);
    try out.print("  {d} days against a limit of {d} -> {s}\n\n", .{
        day,
        ship.limit,
        if (day <= ship.limit) "feasible" else "too slow",
    });
}

/// The result of a full scan of the range.
const Scan = struct {
    first_true: ?u32,
    flips: usize,
    calls: usize,
};

/// Ask the predicate about each capacity in the range and print the answers.
///
/// The function prints one character for each capacity. Thus you can see the
/// shape of the predicate, and you do not have to assume it. A monotonic
/// predicate changes one time. Binary search cannot answer a different shape.
fn writeScan(out: *std.Io.Writer, ship: *Ship, low: u32, high: u32, pred: Predicate) !Scan {
    const before = ship.calls;
    var first_true: ?u32 = null;
    var flips: usize = 0;
    var previous = false;
    try out.print("  {d:>3} ", .{low});
    var cap = low;
    while (cap <= high) : (cap += 1) {
        const ok = pred(ship, cap);
        try out.writeByte(if (ok) '#' else '.');
        if (ok and first_true == null) first_true = cap;
        if (cap > low and ok != previous) flips += 1;
        previous = ok;
    }
    try out.print(" {d}\n", .{high});
    return .{
        .first_true = first_true,
        .flips = flips,
        .calls = ship.calls - before,
    };
}

pub fn main(init: std.process.Init) !void {
    var buf: [4096]u8 = undefined;
    var file_writer = std.Io.File.stdout().writerStreaming(init.io, &buf);
    const out = &file_writer.interface;

    var reader: std.Io.Reader = .fixed(input);
    var weight_storage: [64]u32 = undefined;
    var day_storage: [1]u32 = undefined;
    const weights = try readRow(&reader, &weight_storage);
    const days = try readRow(&reader, &day_storage);

    var heaviest: u32 = 0;
    var total: u32 = 0;
    for (weights) |w| {
        heaviest = @max(heaviest, w);
        total += w;
    }

    var ship: Ship = .{ .weights = weights, .limit = days[0] };
    try out.print("{d} packages, {d} days\n  ", .{ weights.len, ship.limit });
    for (weights) |w| try out.print("{d:>3}", .{w});
    try out.print("\n  heaviest {d}, total {d}\n\n", .{ heaviest, total });

    // The bounds. A capacity below the heaviest package cannot hold that
    // package. One day at the total always works. Thus the boundary is between
    // the two bounds.
    try out.print("search range: [{d}, {d}], {d} candidates\n\n", .{
        heaviest,
        total,
        total - heaviest + 1,
    });

    // The work of one call to the predicate.
    try writePacking(out, &ship, heaviest + (total - heaviest) / 2);

    ship.calls = 0;
    try out.writeAll("binary search over the capacities\n");
    const answer = try traceFirstFeasible(out, &ship, heaviest, total);
    const search_calls = ship.calls;
    try out.print("  plain firstFeasible agrees -> {}\n\n", .{
        answer == firstFeasible(&ship, heaviest, total, Ship.feasible),
    });

    // The two plans on the two sides of the boundary prove the answer.
    try out.writeAll("either side of the boundary\n");
    try writePacking(out, &ship, answer - 1);
    try writePacking(out, &ship, answer);

    ship.calls = 0;
    try out.print("every capacity from {d} to {d}, '#' means feasible\n", .{ heaviest, total });
    const scan = try writeScan(out, &ship, heaviest, total, Ship.feasible);
    try out.print("  first '#' at {?d}, binary search said {d}, agree -> {}\n", .{
        scan.first_true,
        answer,
        scan.first_true == answer,
    });
    try out.print("  the predicate flips {d} time, so it is monotonic\n", .{scan.flips});
    try out.print("  predicate calls: {d} scanning, {d} searching\n\n", .{ scan.calls, search_calls });

    // Move a bound, and the search still returns a number.
    const average = total / ship.limit;
    const bad = firstFeasible(&ship, heaviest, average, Ship.feasible);
    try out.print("with the high bound set to total / days = {d}\n", .{average});
    try out.print("  the search returns {d} and feasible({d}) = {s}\n", .{
        bad,
        bad,
        if (ship.feasible(bad)) "yes" else "no",
    });
    try out.print("  {d} days needed there, limit {d}\n\n", .{ ship.daysNeeded(bad).?, ship.limit });

    // A predicate that changes more than one time. The loop stops and returns
    // a capacity. That capacity is not the smallest one that the predicate
    // accepts.
    ship.calls = 0;
    try out.writeAll("now require every day to fill at least half the hold\n");
    const flicker = try writeScan(out, &ship, heaviest, total, Ship.feasibleAndFull);
    const found = firstFeasible(&ship, heaviest, total, Ship.feasibleAndFull);
    try out.print("  the predicate flips {d} times, so there is no boundary\n", .{flicker.flips});
    try out.print("  binary search returns {d}, first '#' is at {?d}\n", .{ found, flicker.first_true });
    var accepted_below: u32 = 0;
    var cap = heaviest;
    while (cap < found) : (cap += 1) {
        if (ship.feasibleAndFull(cap)) accepted_below += 1;
    }
    try out.print("  feasibleAndFull({d}) = {}, and {d} smaller capacities pass too\n", .{
        found,
        ship.feasibleAndFull(found),
        accepted_below,
    });

    try out.flush();
}
```

*Runnable: compiled to WebAssembly and executed by CI against Zig master. (`23-competitive.binary-search-answer`)*

## The predicate

```zig
    /// True when this capacity completes the work in the time limit.
    ///
    /// The result is false below the boundary and true at or above it. It
    /// changes one time. No other code in this file can assume this property.
    /// The run below checks it.
    fn feasible(self: *Ship, cap: u32) bool {
        const days = self.daysNeeded(cap) orelse return false;
        return days <= self.limit;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `feasible` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search-answer.zig`.*

The packages must go onto the boat in the order of arrival. For a given capacity, the function adds packages to the load of the current day. If the next package does not fit, the function starts a new day.

The function has no other choices to make. Thus the same capacity always gives the same number of days for the same list of packages.

`daysNeeded` returns null when one package is heavier than the given capacity. That capacity can never work, because the boat cannot load the package. Thus `feasible` uses `false` for null.

```zig
    /// The days necessary at this capacity, or null when a package does not fit.
    fn daysNeeded(self: *Ship, cap: u32) ?u32 {
        self.calls += 1;
        var days: u32 = 1;
        var load: u32 = 0;
        for (self.weights) |w| {
            if (w > cap) return null;
            if (load + w > cap) {
                days += 1;
                load = 0;
            }
            load += w;
        }
        return days;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `daysNeeded` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search-answer.zig`.*

For example:

```
capacity 35, packed in arrival order
  day 1:  5  3  8  2  9  4                    load 31
  day 2:  7  6  1  8  3  5                    load 30
  2 days against a limit of 4 -> feasible
```

A capacity of 35 completes the work in two days. Thus the capacity is feasible.

The binary search does not have to know that the work took exactly two days. The binary search needs only the result:

```
true
```

Each call to `feasible` reads the list of packages one time. This is the `n` part of the final time complexity.

## Choose the lower and upper bounds

The lower bound is the weight of the heaviest package. The heaviest package weighs 9 tonnes. Thus the capacity of the boat must be 9 or more. Do not test a value below 9.

The upper bound is the total weight of all of the packages. The total is 61 tonnes. With a capacity of 61, the boat can load all of the packages in one day.

Thus the answer is between 9 and 61. These bounds come directly from the input. Thus they stay correct when the weights of the packages change.

A bound that you guess can make the binary search return the wrong answer. For example, the average load for each day is an incorrect upper bound:

```
with the high bound set to total / days = 15
  the search returns 15 and feasible(15) = no
  6 days needed there, limit 4
```

The binary search returns 15, because 15 is the highest value in the search range. The loop did not make a mistake. The search range was wrong, and the range did not contain a feasible value.

Thus it is useful to check the result after the search:

- The returned answer must be feasible.
- The value immediately below the answer must not be feasible.

## Use a predicate in the binary search

```zig
/// The first capacity in `[low, high]` that the predicate accepts.
///
/// The loop is the loop from the binary search chapter, without the array.
/// `items[mid] < key` becomes `!pred(mid)`: mid is too small to be the answer.
/// Thus `lo = mid + 1` removes mid. In the other branch, mid can be the
/// answer, and the loop keeps it. When the window is empty, `lo` is the
/// boundary.
fn firstFeasible(ship: *Ship, low: u32, high: u32, pred: Predicate) u32 {
    var lo = low;
    var hi = high;
    while (lo < hi) {
        const mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (pred(ship, mid)) hi = mid else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `firstFeasible` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search-answer.zig`.*

[Binary Search](https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/binary-search/) explains the half-open search window and the invariant of this loop. The main difference here is the comparison.

A usual lower-bound search can use a comparison such as:

`items[mid] < key`

If the comparison is true, `mid` is too small. Thus the search moves the lower bound to:

`mid + 1`

This search uses:

`!pred(ship, mid)`

If the predicate returns false, that capacity is too small. Thus the search again moves to:

`mid + 1`

If the predicate returns true, `mid` can be the answer. Thus the search keeps `mid` inside the search range.

The structure of the binary search does not change. The search does not read a value from an array. It calls a function that tells if the current value works.

For this example:

```
binary search over the capacities
  step   lo   hi  mid  days  ok   window after
     1    9   61   35     2  yes  [  9, 35]  27 left
     2    9   35   22     4  yes  [  9, 22]  14 left
     3    9   22   15     6  no   [ 16, 22]  7 left
     4   16   22   19     4  yes  [ 16, 19]  4 left
     5   16   19   17     4  yes  [ 16, 17]  2 left
     6   16   17   16     4  yes  [ 16, 16]  1 left
  window closed after 6 steps on capacity 16
```

There are 53 possible capacities from 9 to 61. Binary search finds the answer with six calls to the predicate.

At step three, capacity 15 fails because it needs six days. Thus the search removes 15 and each smaller capacity.

## Check the boundary

Capacity 15 does not work:

```
capacity 15, packed in arrival order
  day 1:  5  3                                load  8
  day 2:  8  2                                load 10
  day 3:  9  4                                load 13
  day 4:  7  6  1                             load 14
  day 5:  8  3                                load 11
  day 6:  5                                   load  5
  6 days against a limit of 4 -> too slow
```

Capacity 15 needs six days. Thus it does not meet the limit of four days.

Capacity 16 works:

```
capacity 16, packed in arrival order
  day 1:  5  3  8                             load 16
  day 2:  2  9  4                             load 15
  day 3:  7  6  1                             load 14
  day 4:  8  3  5                             load 16
  4 days against a limit of 4 -> feasible
```

Thus 16 is the minimum feasible capacity.

When the capacity increases from 15 to 16, the boundaries of several days change. The algorithm packs the packages again from the start. It does not change the plan for capacity 15.

## Verify the result with a full scan

```zig
/// Ask the predicate about each capacity in the range and print the answers.
///
/// The function prints one character for each capacity. Thus you can see the
/// shape of the predicate, and you do not have to assume it. A monotonic
/// predicate changes one time. Binary search cannot answer a different shape.
fn writeScan(out: *std.Io.Writer, ship: *Ship, low: u32, high: u32, pred: Predicate) !Scan {
    const before = ship.calls;
    var first_true: ?u32 = null;
    var flips: usize = 0;
    var previous = false;
    try out.print("  {d:>3} ", .{low});
    var cap = low;
    while (cap <= high) : (cap += 1) {
        const ok = pred(ship, cap);
        try out.writeByte(if (ok) '#' else '.');
        if (ok and first_true == null) first_true = cap;
        if (cap > low and ok != previous) flips += 1;
        previous = ok;
    }
    try out.print(" {d}\n", .{high});
    return .{
        .first_true = first_true,
        .flips = flips,
        .calls = ship.calls - before,
    };
}
```

*Quoted from the source: `writeScan` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search-answer.zig`.*

This example has only 53 possible capacities. Thus the program can also test each capacity. The program prints one character for each value:

```
every capacity from 9 to 61, '#' means feasible
    9 .......############################################## 61
  first '#' at 16, binary search said 16, agree -> true
  the predicate flips 1 time, so it is monotonic
  predicate calls: 53 scanning, 6 searching
```

A dot shows a capacity that does not work. A `#` character shows a capacity that works.

The output changes exactly one time:

```
false -> true
```

Binary search on the answer must have this property. For a small test case, a scan of the full range is a useful method to verify that the predicate is monotonic.

Here, binary search uses six calls to the predicate instead of 53. The difference is much more important when the range is large.

For example, the range of possible capacities can contain one billion values:

- A full scan can need one billion calls to the predicate.
- Binary search needs only approximately 30 calls, because each step removes approximately half of the search range. `2^30` is a little more than one billion.

Each call to the predicate reads the `n` packages one time. Thus the binary-search solution takes:

```
O(n log range)
```

A full scan takes:

```
O(n * range)
```

For a large range, a scan of each possible answer is usually too slow.

## The predicate must be monotonic

```zig
    /// The same question with a second condition: on each day, half of the
    /// hold or more must be full.
    ///
    /// This plan looks better, but the predicate is not monotonic. A big ship
    /// completes the work early and is half empty on the last day. Thus a
    /// capacity that works can fail when you add one tonne to it.
    fn feasibleAndFull(self: *Ship, cap: u32) bool {
        const days = self.daysNeeded(cap) orelse return false;
        if (days > self.limit) return false;
        var lightest: u32 = std.math.maxInt(u32);
        var load: u32 = 0;
        for (self.weights) |w| {
            if (load + w > cap) {
                lightest = @min(lightest, load);
                load = 0;
            }
            load += w;
        }
        lightest = @min(lightest, load);
        return lightest * 2 >= cap;
    }
```

*Quoted from the source: `feasibleAndFull` from `snippets/23-competitive/binary-search-answer.zig`.*

Now add a different rule: each day must also use half of the capacity of the boat or more.

This change looks small, but it removes the property that binary search needs. Now a larger capacity can make a plan fail that worked before.

For example:

```
now require every day to fill at least half the hold
    9 .......####...####....#############.................# 61
  the predicate flips 7 times, so there is no boundary
  binary search returns 31, first '#' is at 16
  feasibleAndFull(31) = true, and 8 smaller capacities pass too
```

The predicate changes between true and false many times. There is no single boundary of this form:

```
false false false ... true true true ...
```

Binary search continues to run and returns 31. Capacity 31 satisfies the predicate, but 31 is not the smallest value that satisfies it. Capacity 16 also works, and so do some other smaller values.

The binary search cannot find this problem. At each step, the search assumes that one result of the predicate lets it remove half of the range. That assumption is correct only when the predicate is monotonic.

For the original problem, the monotonic property is clear. If a capacity can ship all of the packages in the necessary number of days, a larger capacity cannot need more days. Thus when the predicate becomes true, it stays true for each larger capacity.

The half-full rule does not have this property. Before you use binary search on the answer, make sure that you can explain why the predicate is monotonic. For small test cases, you can also scan the full range and count the changes of the predicate.

---

## Breadth-First Search on a Grid

*Competitive Programming. https://www.ziglang.in/learn/competitive-programming/grid-bfs/*

Breadth-first search, or BFS, is useful to find the shortest path on a grid when each move has the same cost.

The queue does not know about shortest paths. The shortest paths come from the order in which BFS visits cells:

- BFS processes the cells one move away before the cells two moves away.
- BFS processes the cells two moves away before the cells three moves away.

Because of this order, the first route that BFS finds to a cell is the shortest route to that cell.

The example uses a grid with 9 rows and 13 columns. The grid has walls, one cell that BFS cannot get to, a start position `S`, and a target `T`.

The program finds the shortest route from `S` to `T` and prints the distance field. It also shows a common mistake with the mark on a cell.

```zig
const std = @import("std");

/// The grid, as text.
///
/// A snippet here runs under WASI in a browser tab. The tab has no stdin to
/// read. `#` is a wall, `.` is open, `S` is the start and `T` is the target.
/// The parser below reads the grid in the same way that it reads a real file.
const input =
    \\S.....#......
    \\......#...#..
    \\......#..#.#.
    \\......#...#..
    \\..###.#......
    \\..#...#......
    \\..#.#####....
    \\..#..........
    \\..#.........T
;

/// The position of a cell. Rows and columns are `usize` because they are
/// indices.
const Pos = struct { r: usize, c: usize };

/// One of the four moves, as a pair of signed offsets.
///
/// Use `i8`, not `usize`. A move up from row 0 must give a value that is
/// clearly off the grid. A subtraction of one from an unsigned row of zero
/// does not give such a value. The subtraction overflows. In a safety build,
/// the overflow causes a panic, and in the release build that this page ships,
/// it is undefined behaviour. The offsets stay signed until the bounds check
/// is complete.
const Step = struct { dr: i8, dc: i8, name: []const u8 };

/// Up, down, left, right. The order does not change the distances. But the
/// order decides which path a depth-first search finds.
const moves = [4]Step{
    .{ .dr = -1, .dc = 0, .name = "up" },
    .{ .dr = 1, .dc = 0, .name = "down" },
    .{ .dr = 0, .dc = -1, .name = "left" },
    .{ .dr = 0, .dc = 1, .name = "right" },
};

/// A rectangle of characters, addressed by row and column.
const Grid = struct {
    cells: []const u8,
    rows: usize,
    cols: usize,

    fn count(g: Grid) usize {
        return g.rows * g.cols;
    }

    fn index(g: Grid, p: Pos) usize {
        return p.r * g.cols + p.c;
    }

    fn at(g: Grid, i: usize) Pos {
        return .{ .r = i / g.cols, .c = i % g.cols };
    }

    fn char(g: Grid, i: usize) u8 {
        return g.cells[i];
    }

    fn isOpen(g: Grid, i: usize) bool {
        return g.cells[i] != '#';
    }

    /// The cell one move from `p`, or null when that move leaves the grid.
    ///
    /// The arithmetic uses `isize`, where -1 is a normal value. The function
    /// checks the two bounds before it changes the result back to `usize`.
    /// Thus no code in the file subtracts one from an index with the value zero.
    fn step(g: Grid, p: Pos, m: Step) ?Pos {
        const r = @as(isize, @intCast(p.r)) + m.dr;
        const c = @as(isize, @intCast(p.c)) + m.dc;
        if (r < 0 or c < 0) return null;
        if (r >= @as(isize, @intCast(g.rows)) or c >= @as(isize, @intCast(g.cols))) return null;
        return .{ .r = @intCast(r), .c = @intCast(c) };
    }

    fn find(g: Grid, wanted: u8) !usize {
        return std.mem.findScalar(u8, g.cells, wanted) orelse error.MissingCell;
    }
};

/// Read the grid out of a reader, one line per row.
///
/// The function takes a `*std.Io.Reader` instead of the string. The
/// networking chapters use the same method for protocols. On a judge, give the
/// function a reader for a file. The function does not change. The function
/// rejects rows of different lengths here. Thus the error does not occur later,
/// at the first index that goes past the end of a row.
fn readGrid(reader: *std.Io.Reader, out: []u8) !Grid {
    var rows: usize = 0;
    var cols: usize = 0;
    var used: usize = 0;
    while (try reader.takeDelimiter('\n')) |line| {
        if (rows == 0) cols = line.len;
        if (line.len != cols) return error.RaggedGrid;
        if (used + line.len > out.len) return error.GridTooBig;
        @memcpy(out[used..][0..line.len], line);
        used += line.len;
        rows += 1;
    }
    if (rows == 0) return error.EmptyGrid;
    return .{ .cells = out[0..used], .rows = rows, .cols = cols };
}

/// One cell in the queue: its position, and its distance from the start.
///
/// The queue holds the distance, and the searches do not read it from the
/// distance array. Thus the two searches below are comparable. The only
/// difference between them is the point where a cell gets its mark.
const Entry = struct { cell: usize, dist: u32 };

/// A queue that is an array, a read index and a write index.
///
/// `pop` moves `head` forward and never uses the slot behind it again. Thus
/// the queue needs one slot for each push in the full search. The largest
/// number of entries at one time is not the limit. The two searches below give
/// different numbers of pushes.
const Queue = struct {
    slots: []Entry,
    head: usize = 0,
    tail: usize = 0,

    fn push(q: *Queue, e: Entry) !void {
        if (q.tail == q.slots.len) return error.QueueFull;
        q.slots[q.tail] = e;
        q.tail += 1;
    }

    fn pop(q: *Queue) ?Entry {
        if (q.head == q.tail) return null;
        defer q.head += 1;
        return q.slots[q.head];
    }

    fn waiting(q: Queue) usize {
        return q.tail - q.head;
    }
};

/// The cost of a search.
const Cost = struct {
    pushes: usize = 0,
    pops: usize = 0,
    repeats: usize = 0,
    longest: usize = 0,
};

/// The fewest moves from `start` to each cell that the search can get to.
///
/// The search marks a cell at the time of its push. Thus each push takes a
/// cell that no earlier push took. The number of cells is the limit for the
/// pushes, and you can choose the size of the queue one time, at the start.
///
/// The distances are correct because the queue gives back cells in the order
/// that they went in. The search pushes all the cells at distance `d` before a
/// cell at `d + 1`. Thus the cells at distance `d` also leave first. When the
/// search first gets to a cell, the route is as short as each other route.
fn bfsMarkOnPush(
    g: Grid,
    start: usize,
    dist: []?u32,
    from: []?usize,
    seen: []bool,
    slots: []Entry,
    cost: *Cost,
) !void {
    @memset(dist, null);
    @memset(from, null);
    @memset(seen, false);

    var q: Queue = .{ .slots = slots };
    seen[start] = true;
    dist[start] = 0;
    try q.push(.{ .cell = start, .dist = 0 });
    cost.pushes += 1;

    while (q.pop()) |e| {
        cost.pops += 1;
        cost.longest = @max(cost.longest, q.waiting());
        for (moves) |m| {
            const next = g.step(g.at(e.cell), m) orelse continue;
            const j = g.index(next);
            if (!g.isOpen(j) or seen[j]) continue;
            seen[j] = true;
            dist[j] = e.dist + 1;
            from[j] = e.cell;
            try q.push(.{ .cell = j, .dist = e.dist + 1 });
            cost.pushes += 1;
        }
    }
}

/// The same search, but it marks a cell when the cell leaves the queue.
///
/// The mark moves from the push to the pop, and the answers do not change. Now a cell
/// enters the queue one time for each neighbour that expands before the first
/// pop of the cell. Thus the limit for the pushes is the number of moves
/// between cells, not the number of cells. The skip at the pop keeps the
/// result correct. The skip is the only reason that the extra copies are safe.
fn bfsMarkOnPop(
    g: Grid,
    start: usize,
    dist: []?u32,
    seen: []bool,
    slots: []Entry,
    cost: *Cost,
) !void {
    @memset(dist, null);
    @memset(seen, false);

    var q: Queue = .{ .slots = slots };
    try q.push(.{ .cell = start, .dist = 0 });
    cost.pushes += 1;

    while (q.pop()) |e| {
        cost.pops += 1;
        cost.longest = @max(cost.longest, q.waiting());
        if (seen[e.cell]) {
            cost.repeats += 1;
            continue;
        }
        seen[e.cell] = true;
        dist[e.cell] = e.dist;
        for (moves) |m| {
            const next = g.step(g.at(e.cell), m) orelse continue;
            const j = g.index(next);
            if (!g.isOpen(j) or seen[j]) continue;
            try q.push(.{ .cell = j, .dist = e.dist + 1 });
            cost.pushes += 1;
        }
    }
}

/// The distances again, from repeated relaxation instead of a queue.
///
/// Sweep the full grid, and make the distance smaller for each cell that a
/// neighbour can improve. Do the sweep again until a sweep changes nothing.
/// This function shares no code with the searches above. Thus its agreement is
/// an independent check. It also costs one sweep for each level, because it
/// does not know the correct order of the cells.
fn relaxDistances(g: Grid, start: usize, dist: []?u32, sweeps: *usize, looks: *usize) void {
    @memset(dist, null);
    dist[start] = 0;
    var changed = true;
    while (changed) {
        changed = false;
        sweeps.* += 1;
        for (0..g.count()) |i| {
            if (!g.isOpen(i)) continue;
            for (moves) |m| {
                looks.* += 1;
                const next = g.step(g.at(i), m) orelse continue;
                const j = g.index(next);
                if (!g.isOpen(j)) continue;
                const near = dist[j] orelse continue;
                if (dist[i] == null or dist[i].? > near + 1) {
                    dist[i] = near + 1;
                    changed = true;
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

/// The first path that a depth-first search finds, with the order of moves
/// above.
///
/// The search marks a cell as seen when it enters the cell, and it never
/// removes the mark. Thus it visits each cell one time, and it returns a path,
/// not the shortest path. `path` holds the cells that are still on the stack.
/// These cells are the route back to the start.
fn dfsFirstPath(
    g: Grid,
    at: usize,
    target: usize,
    seen: []bool,
    path: []usize,
    len: *usize,
) bool {
    seen[at] = true;
    path[len.*] = at;
    len.* += 1;
    if (at == target) return true;
    for (moves) |m| {
        const next = g.step(g.at(at), m) orelse continue;
        const j = g.index(next);
        if (!g.isOpen(j) or seen[j]) continue;
```
